Specifically, a Mersenne- Twister general-purpose PRNG provides a source of (deterministic) randomness for generating uniformly distributed numbers. However, especially for smaller samples, random numbers generated using this method can be distributed very unevenly (Halton, 1960). Instead, Low-Discrepancy Sequences provide sequences of pseudo-randomly generated points that more evenly cover the domain (Cl´ement et al., 2023). In ES, quasi-random point sets have been used as an alternative sampling strategy Auger et al. (2005); Teytaud and Gelly (2007); de Nobel et al. (2024b), replacing the source of randomness of uj. In ModCMA, both Halton (Halton, 1960) and Sobol (Sobol’, 1967) sequences can be used instead of the standard PRNG. 3.2 Sample Transformation Instead of transforming uj to a normally distributed random sampling using the Gaussian PPF, we can transform uj to another continuous multivariate distribution. In general, the CMA-ES generates λ offspring every generation, and uses the µ best individuals to perform weighted intermediate recombination (see line 11 in Algorithm 1). 4.1 Elitism The elitism module determines whether CMA-ES uses (µ + λ) selection instead of the default (µ, λ) scheme. In (µ + λ) selection, both the µ parent individuals, i.e., the µ selected individuals from the previous generation, and the newly generated λ offspring are considered during selection (Igel et al., 2007). However, in real-valued evolution strategies, non-elitist selection is generally preferred because it exhibits stronger exploratory behavior (Schwefel, 1987; Beyer, 2001). This is done by estimating a positive-definite covariance matrix C, which determines the orientation and scaling of the iso-density contours of the mutation distribution to form an arbitrarily rotated and scaled hyper-ellipsoid. In the canonical CMA-ES, covariance matrix adaptation is tightly coupled with step-size adaptation via the cumulative step-size adaptation (CSA) mechanism. Specifically, the update of the step-size evolution path (line 13 in Algorithm 1) requires applying the inverse square root of the 10

Although efficient solvers exist for symmetric positive-definite matrices, this operation has a computational complexity of O(d3), which becomes prohibitive as the dimensionality d increases. To mitigate this cost, the eigenvalue decomposition is typically performed only intermittently, once every �10d(c1 + cµ) −1 generations in the standard implementation. Additionally, in ModCMA, when CSA is not used as the step-size adaptation mechanism and C−1/2 is therefore not required, A is computed via a Cholesky decomposition AA⊤= C. While this decomposition still scales cubically with d, it has a significantly smaller constant factor and is therefore computationally more efficient in practice. The second approach, Restart, resets the CMA-ES using the same parameters as in the initial run (Auger et al., 2004). The initial position x0 can be reused or resampled uniformly from [lb, ub]d. This flexibility is also present in the next two strategies: 1. Increasing Population (IPOP) (Auger and Hansen, 2005): In order to achieve fast convergence on simple problems, the CMA-ES has a relatively small population size compared to traditional ES (Beyer, 2001; Hansen and Ostermeier, 2001). However, on multimodal functions, a larger population size λ is required to solve them effectively (Hansen and Kern, 2004; Lunacek et al., 2008). The IPOP strategy first attempts to optimize with the default small λ, then increases λ by a factor of 2 at each restart. The population size is limited to a maximum of 29λ0, where λ0 denotes the original population size specified by the user. This maintains competitive performance on simple functions that do not require restarts, while improving performance on complex multimodal landscapes in subsequent restarts. 2. Bi-Population (BIPOP) (Hansen, 2009a): BIPOP extends the IPOP concept by alternating between two regimes: one with an increasing population size (as in IPOP), and one with a smaller, randomly parameterized population size. Each regime tracks its own evaluation budget independently. On each restart, the regime with fewer total evaluations is selected. Initially, the CMA-ES is started with standard parameters, and the increasing regime is used for the first restart. The population size for the small regime is sampled on each restart as: λ = $ λ0 1 2 · λl λ0 U(0,1)2% (12) where λl is the current population size of the large regime, and U(0, 1) is a uniform random variable. Additionally, the step size in the small regime is randomized as σ = σ0 × 10−2·U(0,1). The balance between the exploratory, increasing, and exploitative smaller regimes yields a highly effective strategy. The BIPOP CMA-ES is currently one of the top-performing algorithms on BBOB (Hansen et al., 2022). 6.2 Repelling Native restart strategies can be effective for multimodal landscapes but typically ignore information gained from previous runs. Several module choices are necessarily fixed or disabled in this regime. Expected Running Time (ERT) We report the expected running time (ERT). Let ∆f = f(x) −f⋆denote the precision to the optimum. For a given target precision ∆ftarget, ERT measures the expected number of function evaluations required to reach ∆f ≤∆ftarget. Specifically, we have R independent runs, and let s denote the number of runs that successfully reach the target. Then, let Ti be the number of function evaluations required to reach the target if successful, and let B denote the evaluation budget for unsuccessful runs. The ERT is then defined as ERT = PR i=1 Ti + PR−s i=1 B s , (13) Lower ERT values indicate better performance, and, if s = 0, ERT = ∞. text: Configuration Objective. During the SMAC runs, configurations are evaluated using a nor- malized log-precision measure derived from the best-so-far function values. For each run, precision values are clipped to the interval [10−8, 102], transformed to a logarithmic scale, and averaged over the evaluation budget. This yields a scalar performance metric that reflects the convergence speed of a configuration: the area over the convergence curve, equivalent to the area under the empirical cumulative distribution L´opez-Ib´a˜nez et al. (2024). This objective is to be minimized, such that lower values correspond to faster convergence. Selection and Validation. After optimization, we take only the configurations that have been evaluated for 25 repetitions by the intensification procedure. The configurations are ranked by their average SMAC objective value, and the five best configurations per function are retained. Each of these candidates is then evaluated on 50 independent BBOB instances that were not used during tuning. For each function, the reported tuned configuration is the candidate with the lowest ERT on this validation set. 9.2 Benchmark Results For the performance comparison, we again use ERT (see Section 8.2), with a predefined target precision of 10−8 following the standard COCO/BBOB Hansen et al. To enable feature attribution, we train a regression model that predicts a con- figuration’s performance from its parameter settings. We use a CatBoost regressor Prokhorenkova et al. Given the trained surrogate model (CatBoost), we compute feature attributions using the TreeSHAP method Lundberg and Lee (2017). For each evaluated configuration, SHAP assigns a contribution value to every parameter, indicating how much that parameter influences the performance. Note that a negative contribution value indicates a positive impact on performance, as the cost is minimized. text: We presented ModCMA, a modular framework for constructing and studying CMA-ES variants from interchangeable algorithmic components. By exposing modules for sampling, selection, step-size adaptation, matrix adaptation, and restarting within a unified implementation, ModCMA enables the systematic combination, benchmarking, and configuration of a large space of CMA-ES variants. Through a focused analysis of matrix adaptation, we showed that different adaptation mechanisms exhibit clear trade-offs between computational cost and optimization performance. In particular, alternatives such as Cholesky- and Matrix-based adaptation can substantially reduce runtime while retaining competitive performance on many benchmark problems. We further demonstrated the usefulness of the framework for automated configuration with SMAC Lindauer et al. (2022), where per-function tuning on BBOB produced specialized variants that substantially improved over the default configuration and outperformed the established bbob2009 reference set Hansen et al. (2010) on half of all the functions. Finally, the SHAP-based analysis demonstrated that the resulting tuning data can be used to interpret the roles of individual modules and options, revealing both global trends and problem-specific effects. Overall, these results show that ModCMA is not only a practical implementation of many CMA-ES variants, but also a tool for studying algorithmic design choices and their interactions. Evolve on the Host, Predict on the Edge: Deploying Online Neuroevolutionary Architecture Search for Cross-sectional Stock Return Prediction Jonathan Chang1, Zimeng Lyu2 1 Union County Magnet High School 2Department of Computer Science and Technology, Kean University jonathanbokeunchang@gmail.com, zimeng.lyu@kean.edu
title: Evolve on the Host, Predict on the Edge: Deploying Online Neuroevolutionary

text: Accurate forecasting models are usually large, expensive to update online, and fixed in architecture once trained. We apply ONE-NAS, an online neuroevolutionary architecture search that evolves a population of small recurrent networks as each window of data arrives, to daily cross-sectional stock return prediction, and pilot it on a host and endpoint pipeline: the host runs the search and ships each generation’s champion genomes over TCP/IP to a Raspberry Pi 4B, which predicts online. On the Pi a single champion predicts a 50-stock window in 24.6 ms and the ensemble of 40 island champions in 556 ms, far inside the daily decision cycle. On four panels of US mid- cap equities over 2022–2024, reading the population as a rank- mean ensemble of island champions returns +27.5% net of realised transaction costs, against +11.3 to +14.8% for online LSTM, online GRU and monthly-retrained LSTM baselines and +4.5% for the single best genome used in prior ONE- NAS work. 1
title: Evolve on the Host, Predict on the Edge: Deploying Online Neuroevolutionary

text: Real-world time series forecasting tasks usually face data drift: a model fitted once on historical data degrades as the generating process drifts from its training sample. Online forecasting updates the model as new observations arrive (Pham et al. 2022; Wen et al. 2023; Zhao and Shen 2025), but accurate forecasting models are usually large (Das et al. 2023; Ansari et al. 2024; Woo et al. 2024): expensive to update at the cadence of the stream, expensive to serve where the data are produced, and fixed in architecture once trained, so only their weights can adapt. The problem is acute in stock forecasting, where daily returns have a low signal-to-noise ratio and the feature-to- return relationship shifts with market regimes, so a model fitted to one period often fails in the next (Zhao, Kong, and Shen 2023). Deep stock models (Li et al. 2024) are refitted on a schedule, and incremental learning (Zhao, Kong, and Shen 2023) updates their weights between refits, but in both cases the architecture is fixed in advance. We address adaptation with online neural architecture search. text: (Lyu, Ororbia, and Desell 2023) extends evolutionary architecture search (Liu et al. 2021) to the on- line setting: a population of recurrent neural networks, or- Copyright © 2027, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved. ganised in islands, evolves as each window of data arrives, with offspring trained briefly from inherited parent weights and survivors selected on the most recent data. Architectures and weights both adapt, so there is no offline training phase to go stale. We apply ONE-NAS to daily cross-sectional stock return forecasting on CRSP (Center for Research in Security Prices) data, and show that the result depends on how the population is read: the single best genome of prior ONE- NAS work trails every neural baseline, while a rank-mean ensemble of the island champions outperforms them all. An online neuroevolutionary NAS algorithm deploys as two workloads: the parallel and expensive search runs on a cloud service or a workstation, and the forecasting, cheap because the evolved networks are small, runs on an edge endpoint device (Figure 1). Each generation the host sends the champion genomes over TCP/IP to a Raspberry Pi, which forecasts as each day’s features arrive and keeps forecasting from the last received genomes if the host is unavailable. The Pi is a constrained target: inference that meets the daily cadence

The Pi is a constrained target: inference that meets the daily cadence there does so on any hardware a practitioner owns. The contributions of this paper are: • A deployment workflow for stock forecasting and for trad- ing on the forecasts, with ONE-NAS running the online neuroevolutionary NAS on a host and a Raspberry Pi endpoint running the online inference (Section 3.4). • Measurements on the Pi showing that online inference with the single champion and with the ensemble of 40 island champions runs in real time, far inside the daily decision cycle, at low compute and energy cost (Sec- tion 5.1). • Evidence that forecasting with a rank-mean ensemble of the island champions earns a much higher net return than forecasting with the single champion used in prior ONE- NAS work (Section 5.3). 2

text: Machine learning for cross-sectional stock return prediction is established (Gu, Kelly, and Xiu 2020), and deep models such as MASTER (Li et al. 2024) and StockMixer (Fan and Shen 2024) set the current benchmarks for daily stock ranking (Olorunnimbe and Viktor 2023). They are trained on a fixed span and refitted on a schedule, so they degrade between refits as the market drifts. Incremental learning updates a fixed arXiv:2610.10038v1 [cs.CE] 7 Oct 2026

Online time series forecasting addresses the same concept drift problem (Lu et al. 2018) for general streams: FSNet (Pham et al. 2022) adds fast and slow adaptation paths to a fixed backbone, OneNet (Wen et al. 2023) learns online combination weights over fixed backbones, and Proceed (Zhao and Shen 2025) adapts parameters before drifted data arrive. In all of these the architecture is fixed before the stream starts and only weights or mixture weights adapt. Evolutionary NAS searches architectures with a popula- tion under selection (Stanley et al. 2019; Liu et al. 2021). EXAMM (Ororbia, ElSaid, and Desell 2019) evolves RNN topologies and cell types from a minimal seed genome with parent-to-offspring weight inheritance, so each candidate needs only brief training; it has been applied to power plant forecasting (Lyu et al. 2021) and, offline, to stock return prediction, where it matched or outperformed transformer and recurrent baselines with far fewer parameters and no GPU (Lyu et al. 2025). ONE-NAS (Lyu and Desell 2022; Lyu, Ororbia, and Desell 2023) moves this search online and outperformed online linear, LSTM, GRU and ARIMA baselines on wind turbine and stock index data, reading the population through its single best genome. text: Ororbia, and Desell 2023) moves this search online and outperformed online linear, LSTM, GRU and ARIMA baselines on wind turbine and stock index data, reading the population through its single best genome. Other NAS for financial forecasting searches fixed chain-structured spaces offline (Levchenko et al. 2025). Reading an evolved popula- tion as an ensemble dates to early neuroevolution (Yao and Liu 1998), and neural ensemble search (Zaidi et al. 2021) showed that architecturally diverse ensembles are more ro- bust under dataset shift; neither idea has been combined with online architecture search. Deployment on constrained hardware is usually handled on the model side. Hardware-aware NAS (Wang 2021; Lin et al. 2020) searches for networks that meet a latency or memory budget, and once-for-all training (Cai et al. 2019) extracts a subnetwork per device from one supernet; in both the search finishes before deployment. On-device learning (Ren, Anicic, and Runkler 2021) updates the weights of a fixed network on the device. End-edge-cloud collaborative computing (Wang et al. 2024) instead trains on a resourced host and infers on the device that receives the data, shipping the model between them. Our pipeline follows this pattern, except that the host runs a continuous architecture search and ships a new set of small networks each generation rather than new weights for one. An individual, a genome, is a directed graph encoding both an architecture and its weights, with hidden nodes drawn from a library of recurrent cell types and edges that are either feedforward

text: than sam- pling from a fixed architecture space. An individual, a genome, is a directed graph encoding both an architecture and its weights, with hidden nodes drawn from a library of recurrent cell types and edges that are either feedforward or recurrent, a recurrent edge carrying a value forward in time. The search starts from a minimal seed genome holding only input-to-output connections, so depth, recurrent connectivity and cell composition are outcomes of the search. Offspring are produced by mutation (node and edge in- sertion or deletion, recurrent edge insertion, and cell type change) and by crossover between two parents. Weights are inherited for every retained component and randomly ini- tialised only for new ones, so each offspring starts from a partially trained network and needs only a few backpropaga- tion epochs, which keeps the search within the data cadence. The search runs on N islands, sub-populations that evolve in parallel, each seeded independently with a minimal genome and growing as its offspring accumulate. Islands exchange genetic material only through inter-island crossover at a low rate, so they become increasingly distinct over time, and a sufficient number of islands is kept to preserve diversity in the evolutionary search. A main process holds the islands, generates offspring, and dispatches each one to the next available worker, which trains and evaluates it

text: distinct over time, and a sufficient number of islands is kept to preserve diversity in the evolutionary search. A main process holds the islands, generates offspring, and dispatches each one to the next available worker, which trains and evaluates it and returns it with its fitness; the main then places it back into its island and issues the next genome to that worker. Workers are not synchronised with one another, so a generation’s wall-clock cost depends on the number of workers rather than the population size. At the end of each generation, every island ranks the genomes it holds and retains the best performing of them as parents for the next generation. The best genome on an island is its champion, and the champion of highest fitness across all islands is the global best genome. Champions are re-selected every generation, so the networks that forecast the next window are the current best of the search rather than

text: a model fixed in advance (Section 3.3). 3.2 Online Protocol The input stream is partitioned into consecutive windows of W trading days, with one generation per window (values in Section 4). At the start of generation t, the revealed history Ht is split into a validation block (its V most recent win- dows) and a training pool (all earlier windows). Each island generates offspring from its elites and trains them on sub- sequences of length L drawn from the training pool alone; all genomes are then scored by mean squared error on the validation block, each island keeps its top-ranked genomes as elites, and the genomes designated by the prediction rule (Section 3.3) predict window t+1 day by day as its features arrive. When window t+1 closes, its realised returns are ap- pended to form Ht+1, the validation block slides forward one window, and generation t+1 begins. Training draws on the full history while fitness is measured on the most recent data, so the population tracks the current regime without discarding earlier ones. Leakage is prevented by construction: a window is pre- dicted before its labels are revealed, enters the validation block only afterwards, and enters the training pool only after leaving it, so no genome is trained on data it is scored on or selected on data it later

A master process generates genomes and workers train them asynchronously, so a gen- eration’s wall-clock cost depends on the number of workers rather than the population size. 3.3 Prediction Rules Which genomes predict window t+1 is a scoring-time deci- sion that does not affect the search, so the two rules below are compared on the same runs and any difference between them is attributable to how the population is used rather than how it was built. Under the single champion rule, used in all prior ONE-NAS work, the global best genome alone predicts. Under the island-champion ensemble rule, the best elite of each island predicts, each predicted cross-section is converted to ranks, and the ranks are averaged across the N members. Ranks rather than raw outputs are averaged be- cause the members have non-comparable output scales and every trading rule used here reads only the ordering. 3.4 Deployment Architecture Search and inference run on separate machines because pop- ulation training is parallel and expensive whereas evaluating the resulting networks is not (Figure 1). text: rule used here reads only the ordering. 3.4 Deployment Architecture Search and inference run on separate machines because pop- ulation training is parallel and expensive whereas evaluating the resulting networks is not (Figure 1). The search host is a cloud instance or workstation with enough cores to train a generation’s offspring in parallel; it stores the price history, advances the window clock, and performs all evolutionary operations. The endpoint is a Raspberry Pi; it performs no training and stores only the last received genomes and the current day’s features. The Pi is a deliberately constrained target: meeting the data cadence there bounds the hardware required at the point of use. After selection in generation t, the host serialises the genomes designated to predict window t+1 (the global best genome or the N island champions) into a binary encoding of graph structure, cell types and weights, and transmits it to the endpoint over TCP/IP. The endpoint deserialises the networks and predicts each day of window t+1 as its fea- tures arrive, applying rank aggregation when an ensemble is received, while the host trains generation t+1. Prediction and search thus overlap in time but are decoupled across hardware. Inference cost scales only with N and the number of secu- rities, so a larger island count leaves the endpoint’s hardware requirement unchanged. The

The endpoint is also stateless with respect to the search: if the host is unavailable it keeps pre- dicting with the last received genomes and resumes at the next hand-off. 4 Dataset and Experimental Setup The ONE-NAS implementation, the trading simulation, and the scripts that build the panels from CRSP are open source,1 and Appendix A gives the full experimental detail. 4.1 Dataset The Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) database is the standard source of U.S. stock prices, returns and vol- umes in academic finance, because it is survivorship-bias free and adjusts returns for splits, dividends and delistings. From it we build four disjoint portfolios, V 1 to V 4, of 50 S&P 500 stocks each, drawn at random from the 203 con- stituents with market capitalisation between 2 and 50 billion USD and at least 20 years of history; each portfolio runs from early 2004 to the end of 2024. Each model receives seven daily per-stock inputs, all stan- dard predictors computed from information available at or before the prediction day: the daily return and its cross- sectional

Each model receives seven daily per-stock inputs, all stan- dard predictors computed from information available at or before the prediction day: the daily return and its cross- sectional rank, bid–ask spread, illiquidity, 20-day prior re- turn, turnover acceleration and 21-day volatility. The output is the next day’s return, rank-normalised across that day’s stocks. A rank is predicted rather than a raw return because raw returns are noisy and their scale drifts over two decades, whereas the trading rules act only on which stocks are ex- pected to do better than which. Feature definitions and the normalisation are given in Appendix A.1. 4.2 ONE-NAS Setup ONE-NAS runs on a weekly clock: each window is W = 5 trading days, one generation is executed per window, fitness is MSE on the validation block, the V = 5 most recent windows, and offspring train for 10 backpropagation epochs on subsequences of L = 40 days. Architectures and training settings are in Appendix A.3. 4.4 Trading Rules and Metrics Predictions are turned into positions by three trading rules, each reading only the ordering of the day’s predicted cross- section: Overlapping, which each day buys the 10 top-ranked stocks, sells short the 10 bottom-ranked, and holds the po- sition for 10 days (Efficiency 1993); Banded, which enters a stock when it reaches the top 10 and holds it until it falls past rank 35, so that small rank changes do not trigger trades (Novy-Marx and Velikov 2016); and Conditional long–short, the daily rebalancing rule of our prior study (Lyu et al. 2025). text: This work proposed a host and endpoint pipeline that deploys online neuroevolutionary NAS for stock forecasting and for trading on the forecasts: ONE-NAS evolves the population on a search host and ships each generation’s champions to a Raspberry Pi, which forecasts online. Results on the Pi show that the deployment can be used in practice: the single champion predicts a 50-stock window in 24.6 ms and the ensemble of 40 island champions in 556 ms, far inside the daily cadence and at low energy. This work also explored two ways of using the evolved population for prediction, the single champion of prior ONE- NAS work and the island-champion ensemble. Results show that the ensemble is far better: on four panels of US mid- cap equities over 2022–2024 it returns +27.5% net of costs against +4.5% for the single champion, a paired gain of +23.0 points (t = 18.2) at no search-time cost, positive in every configuration we trained, and it outperforms online LSTM, online GRU and monthly-retrained LSTM baselines, which return +11.3 to +14.8% under the same rule and costs (t > 6.5). Future work includes the full deployment: adding an execution layer and live measurement of realised costs, and having users in the industry run the pipeline and give feedback.

A.1 Dataset Construction The universe is the set of S&P 500 constituents in the CRSP daily panel with current market capitalisation 2 ≤Mi < 50 billion USD and at least 20 years of continuous trading his- tory. Mid-cap stocks receive less analyst and institutional scrutiny than large-caps and are therefore less efficiently priced. The restriction leaves 203 names, from which 200 were drawn at random, shuffled, and split evenly into V 1– V 4, so no stock appears in more than one portfolio. Each portfolio is stored as one series per ticker with a panel-level date

A.4 Trading Rules Every rule reads only the ordering of each day’s predicted cross-section, so all reported metrics are invariant to any strictly monotone transform of a model’s output. Overlap- ping is the rule used throughout Section 5; Banded and Conditional long–short are run on the same predictions in Section 5.4 (Table 12). Overlapping. Following the overlapping-portfolio con- struction of Efficiency (1993), each day a new portfolio is formed that goes long the k = 10 highest-ranked names and short the 10 lowest-ranked, with equal notional per name, and is held for H = 10 trading days; the portfolio formed H days earlier is closed. Ten portfolios are therefore open at any time, each

text: = 10 highest-ranked names and short the 10 lowest-ranked, with equal notional per name, and is held for H = 10 trading days; the portfolio formed H days earlier is closed. Ten portfolios are therefore open at any time, each funded with 1/H of the capital. Positions are netted across portfolios before trading, so a name that appears in several consecutive portfolios is held rather than repeatedly bought and sold, and transaction costs are charged only on the change in aggregate notional per name. Banded. Following the buy/hold spread of Novy-Marx and Velikov (2016), a name is entered when its predicted rank reaches the top 10 and is held until its rank falls past 35. Names between the two thresholds are neither bought nor sold, which removes the churn caused by small day-to-day changes in rank near the boundary. Conditional long–short. text: Evolutionary Architecture Search for Chlorophyll-𝑎 Prediction in Lakes using Sentinel-2 Kürşat Kömürcü1, 2, 3 Linas Petkevičius1 1Vilnius University, Institute of Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence Methods Lab 2IRISA, Universite Bretagne Sud 3European Commission Joint Research Center Abstract Small tabular datasets with expert-designed spectral features are the norm in operational Earth observation, and the networks applied to them are typically hand-designed. We revisit one such published model – a Sentinel-2 algal bloom classifier – and ask what architecture search adds, holding the task, the features and the lake-level train/test split of the original study fixed. Searching an extended multilayer-perceptron space with regularized evolution, and selecting on inner-cross-validation AUC only, we find networks that improve held- out AUC from 0.790 to 0.820 and accuracy from 0.733 to 0.748 while using 409 trainable parameters, 26 times fewer than the strongest hand-designed reference. The search converges on a consistent recipe – a single narrow layer, RMS normalisation, tanh activation, step- decayed RMSprop and weight averaging – that a practitioner would be unlikely to reach by default. At 1.6 kB the resulting model is small enough to serve as an onboard screening trigger, which is the setting that motivates the work. Code: https://github.com/VU-AIML/ automl4eo-bloom-nas.
title: Evolutionary Architecture Search for Chlorophyll-𝑎

text: Operational Earth observation tasks are frequently small and tabular: in-situ labels are expensive, so datasets run to a few thousand rows of expert-designed spectral features rather than to millions of images. The networks applied to them are correspondingly hand-designed, as remains common for tabular problems generally (Gorishniy et al., 2021; Grinsztajn et al., 2022). Neural architecture search is a mature toolbox (Elsken et al., 2019), but is applied overwhelmingly to large-scale vision; its behaviour in this regime is much less characterised, and it is not obvious that a search should help at all when the task offers so little signal to search against. We study it on one such task. Grendait˙e and Petkevičius (2024) assembled a dataset of Baltic lakes matching in-situ observations to Sentinel-2 overpasses and trained a family of hand-designed networks – plain stacks, residual stacks, and stacks with parallel dense heads – on per-lake spectral features, reporting 71.6 % accuracy for bloom classification. Holding their task, features and lake- level split fixed, we ask what architecture search adds. The question matters beyond accuracy. Downlink bandwidth rather than sensing is the binding constraint for many Earth observation products, and onboard inference has been demonstrated in orbit as a way to transmit only informative data (Giuffrida et al., 2020, 2022; Marin et al., 2021). How small a competitive model

How small a competitive model can be is therefore an operational question, not only an efficiency one. We search an extended multilayer-perceptron (MLP) space with regularized evolution, selecting on inner-cross-validation AUC alone. Our contributions are: • Searched architectures that outperform all three hand-designed reference networks on held-out AUC, accuracy and 𝐹1, with all ten highest-ranked configurations beating every baseline on AUC. text: • A 409-parameter model – 26 to 47 times smaller than the references – that achieves this, making onboard screening plausible at 1.6 kB. • A characterisation of the design region the search converges on, and an account of why selection must be driven by AUC at this sample size. 2 Task, data and protocol Data. The dataset released with Grendait˙e and Petkevičius (2024) contains 1151 observations from 429 monitoring sites in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, collected between 2017 and 2021.1 Each row holds Sentinel-2 surface reflectances together with derived radiometric indices of the kind established for chlorophyll retrieval in turbid inland waters (Mishra and Mishra, 2012), for one lake on one date, with a binary bloom label. Classes are close to balanced (624 non-bloom, 527 bloom), so accuracy is interpretable against a 52.9 % majority-class floor. We use the same 14 features as the reference study. Split. We reproduce the reference split exactly, including its random seed: 70 % of the unique site codes are drawn for training and every measurement from a selected lake follows, giving 801 training and 350 test rows over 129 held-out lakes. Grouping by lake rather than by row is essential here, since a single lake contributes up to 17 observations and row-level splitting would allow a model to memorise individual water bodies. Nested

text: and 350 test rows over 129 held-out lakes. Grouping by lake rather than by row is essential here, since a single lake contributes up to 17 observations and row-level splitting would allow a model to memorise individual water bodies. Nested evaluation. All search signal comes from a lake-grouped 5-fold cross-validation inside the 801-row training split; the 350-row test split is opened once, after the search has terminated. This nesting is not a formality at this scale: selecting the best of thousands of candidates on the same data used to report performance yields the maximum of a noisy statistic rather than a generalisation estimate, and the resulting optimism can rival the differences between the methods compared (Varma and Simon, 2006; Cawley and Talbot, 2010). Selection metric. We select on AUC rather than accuracy, for two reasons. Operationally, an onboard trigger ranks candidate scenes against a transmission budget, so the decision threshold is a deployment parameter rather than a property of the model. Empirically, accuracy on a 160- row validation fold is dominated by how a handful of near-threshold observations happen to fall, whereas AUC uses the full ordering: the seed-to-seed standard deviation of held-out accuracy reaches 0.019 in our runs while that of AUC stays at or below 0.008. Since the variance of the selection criterion, not only its bias, governs

Since the variance of the selection criterion, not only its bias, governs how badly model selection overfits (Cawley and Talbot, 2010), this choice does more work than the metric definition alone suggests. 3 Search space and method Space. The space (Table 1) stays within the MLP family, so that the comparison against the hand- designed networks is like-for-like, but widens the axes those networks left implicit; it contains all three reference architectures as individual points. Five block types are available: plain dense blocks, residual blocks, the parallel-dense “multi-head” block used in the reference implementation, gated linear units, and gated residual blocks, the last two following components that have proved useful in tabular deep learning (Gorishniy et al., 2021). Width is specified by a base width together with a profile, since the reference networks use tapering stacks that a single global width cannot express. Optimiser, schedule, warmup, label smoothing, class weighting, gradient clipping and weight averaging (Izmailov et al., 2018) are searched alongside the topology. Candidates above 200k trainable parameters are rejected: with 801 training rows, larger networks cannot be constrained by the data, and the onboard setting rules them out regardless. 1The

Random search is a strong default in spaces of this kind (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Li and Talwalkar, 2019) and we used it in preliminary work, but the space above is roughly a trillion configurations and rewards local exploitation. We therefore use regularized evolution (Real et al., 2019): an initial random population of 64, then rounds in which 20 children are bred by tournament selection (size 10) and one to three random dimension edits, with the oldest individuals retired regardless of score. Age-based rather than score-based retirement is the important detail at this scale: a single cross-validation estimate carries one to three points of standard deviation, so a configuration can enter the population through luck, and score-based retirement would let it persist indefinitely while its mutations took over. Retirement by age forces a lineage to re-earn its score at every generation. Each candidate is scored by 5 folds × 3 weight seeds, averaged. The run evaluated 2720 candidates (1827 distinct architectures after collapsing configurations that differ only in inactive dimensions) in approximately five hours on 20 CPU cores. The run evaluated 2720 candidates (1827 distinct architectures after collapsing configurations that differ only in inactive dimensions) in approximately five hours on 20 CPU cores. The networks are small enough that CPU evaluation parallelised across trials is faster than GPU execution. 4 Results Table 2 reports the comparison. To ensure that any gain is attributable to the searched configuration rather than to an incidentally better training loop, the reference architectures are expressed in the same space and trained by the same code, using the optimiser and schedule settings of the original implementation. The searched models improve held-out AUC by 3.0 points over the best baseline and accuracy by 1.5 points, using 409 parameters against 10 625 for the strongest reference network – a 26-fold 3

text: reduction, or 47-fold against the multi-head variant. All ten highest-ranked configurations beat every baseline on AUC, so the result does not rest on a single fortunate candidate. The searched models are also markedly more stable, with a seed-to-seed standard deviation of 0.001 in AUC against 0.006–0.010 for the baselines, which we attribute to the weight averaging the search selected (Izmailov et al., 2018). The optimism of the cross-validation estimate – the gap between inner-CV and held-out AUC – is only 0.006 for the selected models, indicating that selection on AUC at this budget is not materially inflated by the selection bias Cawley and Talbot (2010) describe. What the search converged on. Among the 100 highest-ranked configurations, several choices are unanimous: plain dense blocks, RMSprop, step decay, RMS normalisation, tanh activation, weight EMA with decay 0.999, and class weighting. The median configuration uses a single layer of width 24 trained for 300 epochs. Three of these sit away from what a practitioner would pick by default. The tanh activation has largely been displaced by ReLU-family functions, yet it is bounded, which limits how confidently a small network can commit on the 801 training rows available. Weight averaging plays a similar role and is the main source of the stability noted above. Most strikingly, the search settles on a single hidden layer:

Most strikingly, the search settles on a single hidden layer: the depth of the reference networks is not merely unnecessary but actively unhelpful at this sample size. We did not anticipate this combination, which is the argument for searching rather than designing. 5 Discussion: onboard feasibility At 409 parameters the selected model occupies 1.6 kB in float32 and requires on the order of 400 multiply-accumulates per lake. On the class of processor flown in onboard-AI demonstrations (Giuffrida et al., 2022) this cost is negligible, and the model could screen candidate observations in orbit so that only lakes flagged as blooming consume downlink capacity – the same argument that motivated onboard cloud rejection (Giuffrida et al., 2020). We should be precise about what this does and does not establish. The features used here derive from atmospherically corrected Level-2A products computed on the ground, together with water masking; porting that chain to the satellite is a separate and harder problem (Marin et al., 2021). What our result establishes is that the decision layer of such a pipeline is essentially free, and that the capacity a hand-designed model spends on it can be

text: the satellite is a separate and harder problem (Marin et al., 2021). What our result establishes is that the decision layer of such a pipeline is essentially free, and that the capacity a hand-designed model spends on it can be reduced by more than an order of magnitude at no cost – indeed with a gain. 6 Limitations and future work The evaluation rests on one dataset and one train/test split. We preserved the reference split deliberately, for comparability, but a single 350-row test split carries roughly 2.4 points of standard error on accuracy, and we have not measured how the ranking behaves across resampled lake splits. The public data release also appears to predate the revision used for the published numbers, so our baselines are a reimplementation rather than an exact reproduction. The search itself converged narrowly: the ten highest-ranked configurations are minor variations of one architecture, and duplicate suppression with periodic random re-injection would characterise the space more broadly. Three extensions follow naturally: the same protocol applied to the chlorophyll-𝑎regression task released with the reference study; feature selection as a search dimension, which is operationally relevant since reading fewer bands means less onboard processing; and quantisation-aware search, which would turn the onboard claim from a parameter count into a measured latency and energy figure on representative hardware.

text: Learning to Orchestrate Evolutionary Search: Progression-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic DE-CMA-ES Coordination in Optimization and Structural Model Updating Lechen Lia,b,1, Rongye Shic, Wanhuan Zhoua aState Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City, University of Macau, Macau 519000, China bCollege of Water Conservancy and Hydropower Engineering, Hohai University, Nanjing 210098, China cSchool of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University, Beijing 100191, China Abstract: Solving high-dimensional structural model updating problems requires an algorithm capable of navigating complex, non-convex landscapes with correlated parameters. Existing hybrid evolutionary algorithms typically rely on static architectures or fixed switching rules, resulting in disjointed search phases. To address this, this study proposes a Deep Reinforcement Learning-governed dynamic DE-CMA- ES Orchestration (DRL-DCO) algorithm, in which a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG)-based actor-critic agent continuously governs the evolutionary process as a single, unified system rather than a mechanical concatenation of algorithms. Guided by a progression-aware state representation and a diversity-informed reward, the agent fluidly reallocates computational resources between the difference- vector-based exploration of Differential Evolution (DE) and the covariance-guided exploitation of CMA-ES, while jointly regulating population size, elite preservation, and a restart mechanism to escape local optima. This allows DRL-DCO to autonomously transition between exploration-dominant, exploitation-dominant, and mixed-strategy regimes across generations. This allows DRL-DCO to autonomously transition between exploration-dominant, exploitation-dominant, and mixed-strategy regimes across generations. Beyond the training phase, the trained actor can operate in a supervision-free inference mode, where the internalized policy autonomously orchestrates DE and CMA- ES control from observed search states through forward inference alone, without critic evaluation or weight updates, enabling faster deployment while retaining full effectiveness. Validated on high-dimensional single-objective optimization benchmarks and the IASC-ASCE structural health monitoring benchmark, DRL-DCO achieves superior convergence accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art adaptive and hybrid evolutionary algorithms, as well as single-operator DRL-governed baselines. Keywords: Evolutionary reinforcement learning; deep deterministic policy gradient; DE-CMA-ES orchestration; supervision-free policy inference; finite element model updating

text: 1.1 Background and existing studies Structural model updating, as an essential back-analysis strategy within Structural Health Monitoring (SHM), has been studied for decades for its effectiveness in assessing a structural system's condition through tracking key physical parameters. In recent years, the field has continued to evolve in response to the growing population of aging structures requiring condition assessment, and, more importantly, in response to continually and explosively advancing data-driven and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven techniques [1, 2]. One of the earliest and most influential stages in the evolution of structural model updating methods centers on optimization, since most model updating and related back-analysis tasks are fundamentally minimization problems over the discrepancy between a model’s predicted response and the observed response of the target structure [3]. This framework is typically built upon a physical model, e.g., a Finite Element Model (FEM), whose structural parameters are optimized until the simulated output matches the observations, giving rise to the well-known Finite Element Model Updating (FEMU) framework [4, 5]. Accordingly, a wide range of optimization algorithms has been extensively studied. Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) were among the earliest and most thoroughly investigated optimizer classes [6], with representative examples including Genetic Algorithms (GA) [7], Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) [8], Differential Evolution (DE) [9], Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) [10], and their many subsequent variants and hybrids

text: and intuitive search logic within the FEMU framework, but they also present practical challenges: model evaluations can be computationally expensive, and hyperparameter calibration typically demands considerable empirical experience, since properly balancing exploration and exploitation to locate the global optimum while avoiding local minima remains inherently difficult [12]. Beyond EA-based model updating, which optimizes structural parameters directly and deterministically, Bayesian model updating offers a probabilistic and more information-rich alternative that fully incorporates observation data: a prior distribution over the unknown model parameters (informed by expert judgment) is updated to a posterior distribution once the observations are taken into account [13]. Classical approaches to estimating these posteriors are dominated by Monte Carlo methods, including Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) [14], Transitional MCMC (TMCMC) [15], and particle filter-based approaches (also known as Sequential Monte Carlo) [16]. Recent studies cover some relatively more advanced approaches such as those based on variational Bayesian inference [17, 18], which are generally based on approximating the target posterior density with a variational density searched from a rich family of parameterized densities by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the true posterior density and the variational one. With the rapid growth of AI, AI-driven methods have become increasingly prominent across engineering fields, and data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as another major thrust in structural model updating research [19]. With the rapid growth of AI, AI-driven methods have become increasingly prominent across engineering fields, and data-driven surrogate modeling has emerged as another major thrust in structural model updating research [19]. Surrogate models have strong potential to reduce reliance on high-level FEM expertise and to lower the computational cost of repeated FEM evaluations, thereby facilitating practical FEMU implementation [20]. Neural network-based surrogates in particular, enable efficient inverse analysis and rapid, adaptive parameter identification [20]. Sabamehr et al. [21] combined neural networks with GAs to relate natural frequency shifts to sectional property changes in bridges, outperforming traditional matrix-based FEMU methods. Yin et al. [22] developed a Bayesian neural network for FEMU of a pedestrian bridge that achieved greater accuracy and efficiency than finite-difference approaches. Zhang et al. [23] introduced a physics-guided neural network integrating data-driven learning with FEM principles to improve damage detection in both simulated and experimental settings. Despite these advances, existing data-driven surrogates still fall short of fully integrating physical principles with measured response data, and cannot yet reliably substitute for FEMU or other physics-based models in capturing the full complexity of structural dynamic behavior [17]. This gap has also been observed in many advanced Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), which, despite explicitly embedding physical constraints into the learning process, continue to struggle under ambiguous boundary conditions or noisy measurements [24]. These limitations, however, also mark out a broad and promising direction for further development of data-driven surrogate modeling. This AI-driven mindset in model updating has so far concentrated mainly on data-driven surrogates, with comparatively less attention paid to the optimization side of the problem. One representative optimization strategy that does incorporate AI is Bayesian Optimization (BO), which uses an acquisition function to decide where to sample next, generally in conjunction with a data-driven surrogate such as Gaussian Process models [25, 26]. Notably, many of these BO methods accelerate convergence and reduce the number of required FEM evaluations, but remain fundamentally a data-driven (probabilistic) surrogate-based model updating framework rather than a direct or efficient advance in optimization strategies. More recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL), emerging from optimal control theory and increasingly driven by AI, has been extensively developed and applied across engineering fields, including SHM [27]. text: EA and RL mechanisms into a new direction termed Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) [33], which has shown notable performance gains. Two primary sub-directions stand out: EA-assisted optimization of RL [33] , where the EA’s population-based evolutionary mechanism generates a more diverse set of experiences to improve DRL training, and RL-assisted optimization of EAs [34] , where RL dynamically guides the EA's search and refinement process. The RL-assisted EA direction still faces notable challenges. First, generalization remains largely unresolved, since many methods are developed for specific target problems, constrained by EA operators suited only to a single problem type. Second, many existing methods offer only limited control over key hyperparameters, typically restricted to mutation and crossover rates [35], because designing RL-assisted dynamic hyperparameter outputs from the actor model requires a deep understanding of both the EA’s internal mechanisms and the target problem’s properties [34]. Moreover, many ERL or DRL-based methods remain focused on purely mathematical or control benchmarks with limited real-world engineering application, and are further hindered by heavy reliance on supervised-style feedback, large EA populations, and long per-episode training. These limitations can leave them without efficient, generalizable inference once training ends, often making them poorly suited to real-world model updating tasks that already carry the added cost of neural network training and/or physical simulation on top of the optimization itself.

The DRL-DCO algorithm employs an actor-critic orchestration agent, built upon the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) method [36], to dynamically coordinate the DE and CMA-ES search mechanisms through a multi- dimensional continuous action space governing key hyperparameters and orchestration decisions, guided by a progression-aware state representation and a diversity-informed reward function. Whereas many existing RL-assisted EA approaches confine the RL component to intermittent intervention on a single evolutionary strategy and/or limited landscape or progression awareness, DRL-DCO’s actor-critic agent maintains continuous, progression-aware oversight of two parallel evolutionary processes throughout the search. This persistent, multi-dimensional governance represents a more thorough realization of the RL-assisted EA paradigm. The DRL-DCO algorithm is evaluated across high-dimensional single-objective optimization benchmarks and a practical FEMU task, spanning both synthetic optimization landscapes and practical structural engineering generalization. The key contributions are summarized as follows. 1) Rather than hard-switching between algorithms, the DRL-DCO algorithm performs continuous orchestration of

text: across high-dimensional single-objective optimization benchmarks and a practical FEMU task, spanning both synthetic optimization landscapes and practical structural engineering generalization. The key contributions are summarized as follows. 1) Rather than hard-switching between algorithms, the DRL-DCO algorithm performs continuous orchestration of DE and CMA-ES through a compositional control mechanism governed by a continuously learnable balancing parameter. This parameter allocates search effort between the two operators on the non-elite subset of each generation, preserving the global distributional structure tracked by CMA-ES through its covariance model while retaining the aggressive, direction-agnostic local search of DE. By adaptively regulating this balance, the agent reduces over-aggressive search steps and mitigates premature convergence. 2) The DRL-DCO algorithm is equipped with an enhanced landscape-informed state representation that augments the candidate solution vector with additional progression-aware descriptors, including population diversity, distributional shape statistics, and convergence-rate indicators. This enriched state gives the actor a comprehensive, temporally coherent view of the search dynamics and geometry, enabling more informed and timely adjustment of DE and CMA-ES hyperparameters across generations. 3) To further enhance adaptability, the DRL-DCO algorithm incorporates a learnable population-scaling factor together with an elite-preservation mechanism, jointly adjusting the effective population size and the proportion of elite solutions carried forward across generations based on the current search state. This allows the agent to deploy smaller, computationally efficient populations during exploitation-dominant

This restart policy is complemented by two auxiliary, independently learnable CMA-ES control actions, a step-size parameter and a covariance-scaling action, which continuously regulate the search radius and distribution shape across generations to support the agent's broader 3

This design enables the learned search strategy to be reused across different optimization runs without online policy adaptation, providing a practical route toward efficient and automated DRL-assisted evolutionary optimization.

text: The DRL-DCO algorithm reformulates evolutionary optimization as a controlled stochastic process, in which the DE and CMA-ES operators are adaptively regulated by a learned control policy rather than a static architecture or predefined switching rule. Here, the DRL-DCO algorithm refers to the overall optimization framework developed for both FEMU and general single-objective optimization problems, integrating dynamic DE–CMA-ES orchestration, population evolution, and RL-based adaptive search. Embedded within this framework, the DRL agent (specifically, the DDPG-based actor–critic agent introduced in Section 1.2) serves as the decision-making component, learning a control policy that regulates the evolutionary process through state observation, action generation, and reward feedback. From this perspective, the optimization process is a sequence of population transformations driven by a learnable control policy, of which classical EAs represent a special case with a static or heuristic-based policy. In the DRL-DCO algorithm, this policy instead observes population-level statistics, fitness- progression signals, and convergence indicators to jointly orchestrate DE’s difference-vector-driven search and CMA-ES's covariance-based search within a single, unified process. The remainder of this section develops this formulation of the DRL-DCO algorithm in detail: Section 2.1 first presents the mathematical formulation of the FEMU problem, followed by the controlled evolutionary process view (Section 2.2), the DRL core mechanism (Section 2.3), the resulting dynamic DE–CMA-ES orchestration mechanism (Section 2.4), and the algorithm implementation details (Section 2.5).

Let θ ∈RNd denote the vector of updating parameters, where Nd is the problem dimensionality; these may represent stiffness modifiers, material properties, mass scaling factors, or other physically meaningful quantities within a finite element or reduced-order model. In this study, the updating parameters are chosen as stiffness-related coefficients since stiffness degradation is generally the dominant contributor to structural damage. The goal is to determine θ∗that minimizes the objective function f (θ). The resulting optimization problem is high dimensional and exhibits strong parameter coupling induced by structural dynamics, such that multiple, physically distinct parameter combinations may yield similar modal responses. This non-uniqueness, combined with modeling uncertainty, gives rise to a nonconvex, multimodal objective landscape. Consequently, even where gradient information can be derived, gradient- based methods can remain prone to convergence toward local optima and is highly sensitive to the initial parameter guess. These motivate the use of gradient-free, population-based optimization strategies 4

This study addresses the FEMU problem within a two-stage, modal-property-based updating framework: rather than directly matching time or frequency domain structural responses, the updating process minimizes discrepancies in modal properties obtained through eigenvalue analysis, substantially reducing the computational burden of repeated finite element evaluations while retaining the dynamic information essential for reliable parameter identification. The present study focuses on this second-stage optimization problem and the proposed DRL-DCO solver, without addressing the preceding system identification procedure. 2.2 Evolutionary Optimization as a Controlled Stochastic Process Let χ(t) = {x(t) 1 , x(t) 2 , . . . , x(t) Ns} denote a population of Ns candidate solutions at generation t, where each solution x(t) k ∈RNd is an Nd-dimensional vector (k = 1, . . . , Ns). In a general evolutionary optimization framework, the population evolves according to a transformation: χ(t+1) = Te  χ(t); θ  where the operator Te(·) represents the evolutionary operations and effects, including mutation, re- combination, selection, and adaptation mechanisms, and θ denotes the hyperparameters governing them. In conventional EAs, Te(·) and θ are fully specified before the optimization begins. As a result, the search dynamics are largely decoupled from the actual landscape encountered during optimization. In this study, the DRL-DCO algorithm instead reformulates this evolutionary process as a controlled stochastic system: χ(t+1) = Ts  χ(t) a(t) , a(t) = π  s(t) where a(t) denotes an action (control) vector applied at generation t, and s(t) is the state observed by the agent, constructed from χ(t). Under this formulation, the operator Ts(·) plays the role of the stochastic system dynamics; the population χ(t) represents the underlying system state; and the action vector a(t) regulates exploration intensity, exploitation strength, and structural adaptation of the search. This formulation provides a mathematically principled mechanism for learning an optimal control policy that governs the evolution operator based on the observed search state. The MDP is defined by a state space, an action space, transition dynamics (inherited from the population evolution operator Ts(·) in Section 2.2), and a reward function, each specified for the DRL-DCO algorithm in the following subsections. The optimization proceeds over successive generations t, with the FEMU (or general optimization objective function) f (θ) providing the basis for evaluating population fitness and constructing the reward signal at each generation. 2.3.1 State Space The state at generation t, denoted s(t), is constructed to characterize both the current search quality and the evolutionary dynamics of the population. Formally, this can be expressed as finding a policy π that maximizes the expected discounted return: J(π) = E "T −1 X t=0 γtr(t+1) # where γ ∈(0, 1) is a discount factor balancing immediate and future rewards, and T is the number of generations in an episode. This policy is learned through a DDPG-based actor–critic scheme, constructed from two parametric neural networks: an actor and a critic. The proposed dynamic DE–CMA-ES orchestration differs fundamentally from conventional hybrid EAs, which typically combine operators through predefined rules, staged execution, or hard switching, imposing rigid interactions that often require problem-specific manual tuning. By contrast, the DRL-DCO algorithm formulates operator coordination as a continuous control problem, where the embedded DRL agent adaptively regulates population size, offspring allocation, and internal evolutionary update rates according to the observed optimization state, allowing the search process to transition smoothly among exploration-dominant, exploitation-dominant, and mixed regimes. Accordingly, for the high-dimensional FEMU and related optimization problems, this adaptive orchestra- tion offers two practical benefits: it preserves the global exploration capability of the DE while utilizing the covariance-learning mechanism of the CMA-ES for efficient local refinement, and it avoids rigid hybridization rules, allowing the framework to automatically adjust search behavior across optimization stages while reducing the need for manual algorithm configuration. 2.5 Implementation details and algorithm workflow The DRL-DCO algorithm can operate in either of two distinct phases, each capable of independently solving the optimization task, that together govern its interaction between evolutionary optimization and DRL-based policy learning. In the agent-training phase, the embedded DDPG-based actor–critic agent operates simultaneously with population evolution, as the evolutionary operators search for improved solutions, the actor and critic networks are concurrently updated through deterministic

In the agent-training phase, the embedded DDPG-based actor–critic agent operates simultaneously with population evolution, as the evolutionary operators search for improved solutions, the actor and critic networks are concurrently updated through deterministic policy gradients and temporal-difference learning, respectively (Section 2.3.4). Alternatively, in the agent-inference phase, a previously trained actor network instead generates generation-wise control actions independently, without further parameter updates, critic evaluation, or reward feedback, offering a more efficient deployment mode once training has been completed. To achieve stable adaptive regulation of the evolutionary process, appropriate constraints are imposed on the action space. text: the Ackley, Griewank, Rastrigin, Rosenbrock, and Schwefel functions [41]. These functions are standard test cases in the optimization literature because they collectively span a diverse and complementary range of challenging landscape properties, including multimodality, non-convexity, inter-variable coupling, ill-conditioning, and deceptive optima, enabling a rigorous assessment of global search capability, local refinement precision, and robustness against premature convergence. Briefly, the Ackley function combines a flat outer region with a sharply structured, multi-optima central basin; the Griewank function exhibits widespread low-amplitude oscillations with strong inter-variable coupling that intensifies with dimensionality; the Rastrigin function presents a highly multimodal landscape with densely and regularly distributed local minima; the Rosenbrock function forms a narrow, ill-conditioned curved valley that is comparatively easy to locate but difficult to traverse toward its unique global optimum; and the Schwefel function is strongly deceptive, with its global optimum located far from the majority of local optima. Together, these properties test complementary aspects of exploration, exploitation, and convergence robustness, consistent with the practical implications of the No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem [42], which states that no single algorithm can universally dominate across all problem classes. In this mode, the trained agent autonomously governs all key algorithmic configurations, including the DE and CMA-ES operator parameters, effective population size, resource allocation between the two operators, and restart behavior, relying entirely on its internalized policy to navigate the search landscape. As this agent-inference capability tests generalization of the orchestration policy specifically, and the non-DRL baselines possess no such learned policy, while DRL-DE and DRL-CMA-ES fix β(t) and thus retain no such orchestration mechanism, only DRL-DCO is evaluated here. The agent-inference phase represents a qualitatively distinct mode of operation from both the adaptive EA baselines and the agent-training phase itself. The inference phase relies solely on the actor network's forward pass to determine each control action, eliminating the critic evaluation and temporal-difference weight updates required during training. This yields a notably lower per-generation computational cost while retaining the full adaptive intelligence encoded in the trained policy, allowing the inference-phase DRL-DCO to independently locate the global optimum across problem instances without requiring online supervision or feedback-driven adjustment. The benchmark structure, shown in Figure 6(a), is a four-story, 2-bay by 2-bay steel frame with a 2.5 m by 2.5 m plan and a uniform story height of 3.5 m. This configuration yields a 12-DOF system, with each floor possessing three degrees of freedom, translational motion in the x and y directions and torsional rotation about the z-axis. Among the various loading and configuration conditions defined in the original benchmark study, this work focuses on Case 4, in which structural asymmetry is introduced by placing an additional 150 kg slab mass eccentrically on the top floor. This eccentricity couples the lateral and torsional responses across all four floors, engaging all 12 DOFs simultaneously and making the modal identification problem considerably more demanding than the symmetric baseline cases, providing an appropriately challenging testbed for evaluating the robustness and accuracy of DRL-DCO in a practical FEMU context. Further details of the benchmark structure and experimental setup are available in Johnson et al. [48]. Conclusions This study introduces a novel Deep Reinforcement Learning-governed dynamic DE–CMA-ES Orchestration (DRL-DCO) algorithm, built upon a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG)-based actor–critic agent that adaptively harmonizes Differential Evolution (DE) and Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) through a continuous multi-dimensional action space, a progression-aware state representation, and a diversity-informed reward function. To better address the limitations in many existing RL-assisted EA approaches, which confine the RL component to intermittent intervention on a single evolutionary strategy or leave it with limited landscape or progression awareness, and to enable supervision-free search with full automation, DRL-DCO’s actor–critic agent sustains continuous, progression-aware oversight of two evolutionary processes operating in parallel, offering a more complete realization of the RL-assisted EA paradigm. Through a critic-supervised agent-training phase and a supervision-free agent-inference phase operating via forward inference alone, the algorithm achieves robust and accurate performance across challenging high-dimensional benchmark optimization problems and demonstrates strong engineering generalization on the IASC-ASCE benchmark FEMU task. The key conclusions are as follows. 1) The proposed continuous DE–CMA-ES orchestration constitutes a fundamental departure from conventional hard-switching hybridization. During the agent-training phase, the actor–critic agent learns the orchestration policy through online interaction with the optimization environment and critic-mediated reward feedback. After training, the agent-inference phase uses the trained actor alone to generate generation-wise control actions through forward inference, without further policy updates or online adaptation. The stable control trajectories observed during inference indicate that the trained policy has captured effective search behavior rather than relying on continued learning during optimization. Notably, a single training run of 20–30 episodes produces a policy that generalizes reliably to independently initialized instances across all tested problem classes, demonstrating the practical reusability and self-contained intelligence of the proposed method. Although DRL-DCO and related RL-assisted evolutionary approaches demonstrate strong adaptability, they inevitably inherit the stochastic uncertainty of neural network training, coupling the optimization of the target problem with the stochastic training of the policy itself. Future work will therefore investigate more physically informed, model-based reinforcement learning strategies, incorporating explicit mathematical mappings between structural parameters and target modal characteristics. Replacing or augmenting the data-driven critic with mechanistically transparent physics-based models and gradient- informed feedback may further reduce training uncertainty, enhance interpretability, and improve the reliability of RL-assisted optimization for structural model updating and other engineering inverse problems. text: Black-box optimization (BBO) arises in many scientific and engineering prob- lems where objective evaluations are expensive and limited. Recent large lan- guage model (LLM) agents offer a new way to approach BBO by combining task semantics, computation, optimization tools, and feedback-driven decision mak- ing, showing great potential due to the integration with mathmatically rigorours tools. However, existing agentic BBO studies use different task domains and sys- tem configurations, making their results difficult to compare and the effects of individual design choices hard to isolate. We therefore introduce AgenticBBO- Bench, a cross-domain benchmark for agentic BBO spanning synthetic functions, hyperparameter optimization, database tuning, chip design, and molecular design under a unified finite-budget evaluation protocol. In our experiments, agentic BBO achieves higher family-averaged scores than direct LLM-based methods in all five domains and outperforms the best numerical optimizers in four. We further study three factors shaping agent performance: optimization tools, task information and prior knowledge, and the role of the LLM during search. Our results show that additional numerical tools do not consistently improve performance, task seman- tics are broadly useful while more specific priors are less reliable, and numerical optimizers can effectively absorb gains from search trajectories established by the agent. Finally, we introduce a five-task frontier challenge within AgenticBBO- Bench and evaluate seven LLMs under Codex agent harness, where GPT-6

text: Black-box optimization (BBO) considers optimization problems where the objective function can be evaluated, but its analytical form and gradients are unavailable (Shahriari et al., 2016; Frazier, 2018). It has been widely used in applications including chemical design (Hase et al., 2018), materi- als optimization (Frazier & Wang, 2016), and complex system configuration (Golovin et al., 2017), where each objective evaluation can be expensive. Classical BBO methods, such as Bayesian op- timization (Garnett, 2023) and evolutionary algorithms (Eiben & Smith, 2015; Zhou et al., 2019), mainly operate on numerical observations. Their search behavior is determined by predefined heuris- tics like surrogate models, acquisition functions, or search operators (Jones et al., 1998; Srinivas et al., 2010; Hansen, 2016). However, real optimization problems often come with additional infor- mation beyond numerical observations, such as task descriptions, variable semantics, and domain knowledge. LLMs provide a natural way to exploit such information alongside the numerical search history (Song et al., 2024). This has motivated a growing line of LLM-based BBO methods that use language models to propose candidate solutions, model the objective, or support specific stages of the optimization process (Yang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Ran et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). ∗Corresponding to Ke Xue and Chao Qian: {xuek,qianc}@lamda.nju.edu.cn. 1 arXiv:2610.12183v1 [cs.LG] 8 Oct 2026

Although LLMs have been incorporated into different stages of BBO, they are typically used as fixed components of the optimization procedure. At each round, the surrounding algorithm invokes the LLM to perform a predefined operation, such as generating the next candidate, while the rest of the optimization loop is specified in advance (Schwanke et al., 2026; Meindl et al., 2025). Recent work has begun to move toward a more agentic formulation (Maus et al., 2026; Brunzema et al., 2026; Suwandi, 2026), in which the LLM interacts with an optimization environment rather than serving as a single fixed operator. Before submitting a candidate, the LLM can inspect the search state, execute code, invoke some domain-specific tools, observe their outputs, and decide what action to take next. Before submitting a candidate, the LLM can inspect the search state, execute code, invoke some domain-specific tools, observe their outputs, and decide what action to take next. Crucially, the sequence of these intermediate actions is determined online by the LLM rather than prescribed by the optimization algorithm. We refer to this setting as Agentic BBO. Placing the LLM in this agentic role also makes comparisons between methods less direct. The re- sulting search behavior depends not only on the optimization problem, but also on what information the agent observes, which tools it can access, and how the surrounding harness manages its interac- tion with the environment. Similar sensitivity to the agent harness has also been observed in general LLM-agent evaluation (Kapoor et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Existing Agentic BBO studies make different choices along these dimensions and are typically evaluated within individual domains, making their results difficult to compare. Recent benchmarks have begun to standardize evaluation within specific settings, such as sequential hyperparameter optimization (Huai et al., 2026), but a systematic comparison across heterogeneous BBO problems is still missing. As a result, it remains unclear which findings reflect general properties of Agentic BBO and which depend on a particular task or system design. text: standardized leaderboard for comparing future general-purpose optimization agents. 2 BLACK-BOX OPTIMIZATION Black-box optimization (BBO) seeks an optimal candidate x⋆∈arg max x∈X f(x), where X denotes the search space and f(x) ∈R is an objective whose analytical form and gradi- ents are unavailable. The search space may contain continuous, integer, categorical, or mixed vari- ables (Daxberger et al., 2020), and may also consist of more structured objects such as molecules, biological sequences, or executable programs (G´omez-Bombarelli et al., 2018; Angermueller et al., 2020; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024). In many applications, evaluating f requires costly physical or computational procedures, making efficient use of a limited evaluation budget essential (Trabucco et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2025). In this work, we consider finite-budget sequential optimization. After t −1 evaluations, the optimizer has observed: Ht−1 = {(xi, yi)}t−1 i=1 , yi = f(xi). At round t, it selects a candidate xt based on the available information, submits it to the black-box evaluator, and observes yt = f(xt). The observation is then appended to the history, and the process continues until the evaluation budget B is exhausted. The outer optimization loop can therefore be summarized as Ht−1 −→xt −→yt = f(xt) −→Ht. The loop above specifies how the optimizer interacts with the black-box objective, while the proce- dure for selecting xt from the observed history

text: is exhausted. The outer optimization loop can therefore be summarized as Ht−1 −→xt −→yt = f(xt) −→Ht. The loop above specifies how the optimizer interacts with the black-box objective, while the proce- dure for selecting xt from the observed history depends on the optimization method. Different BBO methods implement this decision in different ways. Classical methods largely specify the search procedure in advance: random search samples from a predefined distribution, evolution- ary algorithms apply predefined selection and variation operators, and Bayesian optimization selects candidates using a surrogate model and acquisition rule (Bergstra et al., 2011; Snoek et al., 2012; Bull, 2011). Learning-to-optimize methods instead learn part or all of this decision rule from previ- ously solved, related, or synthetic optimization tasks (Volpp et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025). Large language models further broaden the information that can influence the search by al- lowing optimizers to condition on task descriptions, variable semantics, documentation, constraints, and other forms of prior knowledge that are difficult to encode in a fixed numerical representa- tion (Brahmachary et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Rankovi´c et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026).
