Traditional BO follows a fixed optimizer-driven procedure, whereas Agentic BBO lets an LLM agent organize the intermediate decision process before each expensive evaluation. The actions shown in the agent loop are representative examples rather than a fixed or exhaustive workflow: the agent may dynamically choose, skip, repeat, combine, or introduce other actions before proposing a candidate. 3 AGENTIC BLACK-BOX OPTIMIZATION We use Agentic BBO to describe a setting in which a LLM agent controls the decision process that precedes each expensive black-box evaluation. Rather than mapping the current history directly to the next query through a fixed procedure, an optimization round may contain a variable sequence of intermediate actions: (Ht−1, I) −→at,1 −→· · · −→at,Kt −→xt −→yt = f(xt), where I denotes task-level information and at,k denotes an internal operation chosen by the agent before committing xt. Such actions may include reading task information and prior knowledge, ana- lyzing the historical evaluations, using external tools such as optimizers or simulators, and planning the next candidate before submission. Rather than following a fixed sequence, the agent decides which

text: Such actions may include reading task information and prior knowledge, ana- lyzing the historical evaluations, using external tools such as optimizers or simulators, and planning the next candidate before submission. Rather than following a fixed sequence, the agent decides which actions to execute and how to combine their outputs before submitting xt for evaluation. As illustrated in Figure 2, this replaces a fixed optimization procedure with a decision process whose intermediate computation is organized by the agent. This differs from common LLM-based optimization methods, where the language model is assigned a predefined role, such as generating candidates, predicting objective values, or initializing a down- stream optimizer (Yang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2026). In Agentic BBO, the intermediate procedure itself is instead determined online by the agent. Under this view, a classical BBO optimizer is only one possible tool available to the agent. The agent may query it for suggestions or predictions, modify or ignore its outputs, and combine them with other information before selecting the next candidate. Recent agentic BO systems similarly expose numerical optimizers as tools while leaving the final candidate choice to the agent (Brunzema et al., 2026). More importantly, the agent is also not limited to tools provided in advance: it can write code and build its own task-specific analyses or

More importantly, the agent is also not limited to tools provided in advance: it can write code and build its own task-specific analyses or optimization tools during the search. This added flexibility means that evaluating Agentic BBO requires considering the full agent system, not just the underlying LLM. 4

text: Preprint. 3.1 EVALUATING AGENTIC BBO SYSTEMS In practice, an Agentic BBO system is determined not only by the underlying LLM, but also by the task information provided to it, the agent harness that manages its interaction and state, and the tools and numerical backends it can access. Together, these choices determine what the agent can observe and what actions it can take before each evaluation. Evaluating Agentic BBO therefore requires considering the entire agent system rather than the lan- guage model alone. Even with the same underlying model, changing the harness, task information, or available tools can lead to different optimization behaviors. Similar effects have been observed for general LLM agents, where performance can vary substantially across model–harness configu- rations (Kapoor et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Existing Agentic BBO methods also differ in the tasks and evaluation settings they use, making their reported results difficult to compare directly. End-to-end performance alone therefore does not reveal whether a difference comes from the agent design, the task being optimized, or the evaluation setup. These issues motivate two goals for our benchmark: enabling fair comparison across diverse BBO tasks and supporting controlled analysis of the components that shape agent behavior. We therefore use a unified black-box interaction and evaluation protocol across tasks, while varying task infor- mation, optimization tools, and the

Drawing on the tool interfaces in Sara’s framework (Brunzema et al., 2026), we adapt GP-based optimization tools to our benchmark and consider two augmentations of the base Agentic configuration. + GP Suggest adds a GP candidate-proposal interface, while + GP Tools additionally exposes surrogate prediction, acquisition scoring, diagnostics, and controls over the search region and acquisition policy. The agent remains free to accept, modify, or reject GP suggestions. All three configurations otherwise share the same agent environment and evaluation protocol. The base Agentic configu- ration achieves the highest mean score of 0.589, compared with 0.574 for + GP Suggest and 0.538 for + GP Tools. Looking beyond the mean scores, the effect of the GP interfaces varies across tasks, improving performance on some tasks while hurting it on others. To understand why, we examine how agents use Python and GP-based tools during optimization. Figure 3a shows that custom Python remains common even after GP tools are introduced: with + GP Tools, 35.4% of rounds use only Python and another 17.4% use both Python and GP tools. This suggests that agents do not simply hand the search over to the provided optimizer. Figure 3b gives a concrete example on the chip placement task Bigblue1: the agent fits a linear proxy from observed layouts, uses the learned pattern to construct a new placement, and continues refining it in later rounds, improving the best-so-far score from 0.551 after the first new evaluation to 0.664 after four evaluations and 0.676 eventually. This case suggests that custom Python allows the agent to build task-specific analyses from the observed trajectory, rather than relying on the fixed inductive bias of a fixed GP backend. This may explain why a fixed GP interface does not always benefit Agentic BBO, as the agent can already discover useful task-specific patterns from the search trajectory. text: We introduce AgenticBBO-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in black- box optimization under a unified protocol. Across five optimization domains, Agentic configuration consistently improves over direct LLM optimization and is competitive with established numerical 9
title: Preprint.

text: Preprint. optimizers. Our controlled studies further show that additional optimization tools do not always improve performance, task semantics are broadly useful while more specific priors are less reliable, and numerical optimizers can sometimes continue effectively from search trajectories established by the agent. We also establish a compact five-task frontier challenge for comparing future models and agent systems under the same setting. Together, these results provide a benchmark and empirical basis for studying how general-purpose agents can be used for black-box optimization. We discuss several directions for future Agentic BBO systems in Appendix C. A BENCHMARK DETAILS A.1 BENCHMARK TASKS We construct the benchmark from five established task families covering synthetic numerical opti- mization, hyperparameter optimization, database tuning, chip design, and molecular design. Below we describe the source benchmark and evaluation setup for each family. BBOB. We use the noiseless BBOB suite from COCO (Hansen et al., 2021). BBOB is a standard benchmark for continuous black-box optimization and has been widely used to evaluate Bayesian optimization and other derivative-free optimization methods (Santoni et al., 2024). Its functions cover a range of landscape properties, including separability, conditioning, variable interactions, and multimodality. The objective is evaluated directly using the corresponding analytic benchmark function. Hyperparameter optimization. We construct hyperparameter optimization tasks from Bayesmark (Turner et al., 2021). Each task specifies a machine-learning model, dataset, and mixed-type hyperparameter search space. A candidate corresponds to a complete hyperparameter configuration, and its objective value is determined by the predictive performance of the resulting model on the fixed task. HPO has also become a common setting for evaluating LLM-based optimization methods (Huai et al., 2026). Database tuning. For database configuration tuning, we use the surrogate-based benchmark in- troduced by Zhang et al. (2022). The search space consists of mixed-type database configuration knobs whose interactions can have substantial effects on system performance. To make repeated evaluation efficient and reproducible, the benchmark
title: Preprint.

text: tuning, we use the surrogate-based benchmark in- troduced by Zhang et al. (2022). The search space consists of mixed-type database configuration knobs whose interactions can have substantial effects on system performance. To make repeated evaluation efficient and reproducible, the benchmark evaluates configurations using fixed learned surrogate models constructed from measurements of the underlying database system. Macro placement. We use macro-placement tasks derived from BBOPlace-Bench (Xue et al., 2026). A candidate specifies the positions of movable macros and is decoded into a physical place- ment before evaluation. The placement must satisfy task-specific physical constraints, and valid layouts are evaluated using the corresponding placement objective. Our experiments use the com- pact 32-macro setting, which provides a tractable but structurally constrained EDA optimization problem. Molecular optimization. We use goal-directed molecular optimization tasks from Gua- caMol (Brown et al., 2019). Candidates are represented as SMILES strings and evaluated using task-specific molecular scoring functions. Unlike the vector-valued search spaces above, this setting requires optimization over structured discrete objects while maintaining chemical validity. Gua- caMol has also been used in recent work on language-agent-based black-box optimization (Maus et al., 2026). text: (Maus et al., 2026). A.2 BENCHMARK INTERACTION PROTOCOL All agentic methods interact with the benchmark through the same containerized workspace inter- face. Each run is executed in an isolated Docker container, where the agent can inspect benchmark- provided files, use native Bash and Python for analysis, and access benchmark operations through a shared workspace interface. The objective evaluator and other hidden task state remain host- managed and are not directly accessible from the container. Workspace and observable information. At the beginning of each run, the workspace contains a compact task card (task.md) and shared optimization instructions (instructions.md). The task card specifies the optimization objective, evaluation budget, candidate representation, and the task information exposed to the agent. Large search spaces and optimization histories are not inserted directly into the task prompt. Instead, they remain available on demand through workspace files and benchmark interfaces. This avoids repeatedly placing large task state in the language-model context while preserving access to the same information throughout the run. 15

The base protocol provides the following common interfaces: • get task context: retrieve task descriptions, scoring information, mechanisms, or domain knowledge exposed under the current experimental condition; • get search space: inspect parameter names, types, bounds, and available semantic definitions; • get trial history: retrieve previous objective observations and, when requested, their candidate configurations; • get incumbent: retrieve the best observed objective value and, when requested, its configuration; • write candidate: optionally validate and save a candidate draft without evaluating it; • submit candidate: validate and submit a candidate for host evaluation. The interface itself is shared across experimental conditions, while the information exposed through it may vary according to the corresponding ablation. Additional optimizer interfaces used in the controlled tool studies are described separately in Appendix B.5. Optimization loop. Optimization proceeds in a persistent agent session. At each round, the agent receives the current evaluation state, may inspect any benchmark-visible information or perform local analysis, and then attempts to submit one legal candidate. A submitted candidate is first validated by the host. If validation fails, the candidate is rejected without consuming objective budget, and the agent may revise and resubmit within the same round. Once a valid candidate is accepted, the round ends and the host evaluates the candidate. The resulting objective value is returned to the same

B.2 TASKS AND EVALUATION BUDGETS The broad benchmark contains 77 tasks from five families: 24 BBOB functions, 25 HPO tasks, six database-tuning tasks, 12 BBOPlace macro-placement tasks, and ten GuacaMol molecular-design objectives. Table 4 summarizes the objective-evaluation budgets used in the broad benchmark and controlled studies. Within each matched comparison, all methods receive the same evaluated initialization and the same number of subsequent objective evaluations. Only benchmark evaluations of submitted candidates consume objective budget. Intermediate LLM reasoning, Bash/Python execution, and calls to opti- mization tools do not consume this budget. The broad benchmark uses two independent runs per task. The controlled diagnostic studies use four runs per task and condition unless stated otherwise. The five-task frontier challenge is intended as a compact cross-model snapshot and uses one run per task and model configuration. For example, the tool, task-information, and LLM-role studies reuse selected BBOB, HPO, DBTune, and BBOPlace instances in order to perform matched comparisons under controlled interventions. text: generate multiple internal candidates, but true objective evaluations are returned through the same host evaluation interface and truncated at the common budget. GP-BO. GP-BO follows the surrogate and acquisition design of the GP backend used in Agentic BO (Brunzema et al., 2026). It uses a BoTorch SingleTaskGP with a Mat´ern-5/2 kernel, normal- ized inputs, standardized outputs, and a logarithmic expected-improvement acquisition. Kernel and likelihood parameters are fitted from the accumulated observations throughout optimization. For acquisition optimization, we use a dimension-dependent candidate budget M(d) = min{5000, max{2048, 200d}}, where d is the encoded search dimension. TuRBO. We use TuRBO-1 (Eriksson et al., 2019) with a single trust region and Thompson sam- pling, following its reference implementation. The trust-region update policy follows the original TuRBO design, and candidate generation uses the same dimension-dependent pool M(d) as GP-BO. When a trust region is restarted, the new Sobol initialization evaluations count against the common objective budget. CMA-ES. We use the pycma implementation of CMA-ES. Search is performed in the trans- formed unit cube and starts from the best configuration in the shared initialization. We use the standard dimension-dependent population size λ = 4 + ⌊3 log d⌋ and set the initial step size to σ0 = 0.18. Population members are evaluated sequentially under the common objective budget. C FUTURE DIRECTIONS Our experiments expose several open problems that go beyond the particular agents and optimizers evaluated in this benchmark. Rather than treating the current results as a final recipe for Agentic BBO, we highlight several directions for developing more general and effective optimization agents. From fixed tools to task-adaptive tool selection. Our results suggest that the value of an op- timization tool depends more on whether it matches the task than on how powerful the tool is in isolation. Recent agentic optimization systems have begun to expose numerical backends as tools that the agent can selectively query and control (Brunzema et al., 2026). A natural next step is to provide a portfolio of complementary optimizers and let the agent select or combine them
title: Preprint.

text: Preprint. From given priors to useful prior discovery. Task information can substantially affect optimiza- tion, but richer prior knowledge is useful only when it can guide concrete search decisions. Recent LLM-based optimizers have shown that natural-language priors and retrieved domain knowledge can be incorporated directly into optimization (Brunzema et al., 2026; Maus et al., 2026). Future agents could go further by actively identifying and acquiring useful priors, such as important vari- ables, interactions, or promising search regions. From always-on LLMs to cost-aware routing. Our handoff experiments show that continued LLM control is not always necessary once a useful search trajectory has been established. Related hybrid approaches have similarly combined LLM-guided exploration with statistical optimization later in the search (Chang et al., 2025). This motivates cost-aware routing that decides when addi- tional LLM reasoning is worth its computational cost. From task-specific search to generalizable algorithm discovery. Using LLMs to develop op- timizers shifts the challenge from online search to cross-task generalization, a central problem in Meta-BBO and automated algorithm discovery (Ma et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). Future work should study how to construct representative development sets and encourage reusable optimization strategies rather than heuristics that overfit a small set of tasks. text: study how to construct representative development sets and encourage reusable optimization strategies rather than heuristics that overfit a small set of tasks. From fixed harnesses to evolving agent systems. Our results show that tools, task information, and control interfaces can substantially change optimization behavior even with the same backbone model, consistent with recent studies of harness effects (Yao et al., 2026). Recent work has fur- ther begun to optimize the harness itself together with the model (Chen et al., 2026), suggesting that future Agentic BBO systems could jointly adapt their tools, optimizer interfaces, and control strategies. From isolated optimization to reusable experience. A general-purpose optimization agent should not need to start from scratch on every new problem. Recent work has explored using previ- ous optimization trajectories or agent executions as reusable experience (Ran et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026). An important direction is therefore to build an optimization experience library and retrieve relevant strategies, tools, and priors for new tasks while avoiding negative transfer. title: Universal Construction and Exact Self-Reproduction

text: A fixed network of McCulloch–Pitts threshold units with weights in {−1, 0, 1} can hold other threshold networks in its state and run them: the state is a ring of banks of records, each record a unit of a stored network, and each step evaluates one record. We use such a network to carry out von Neumann’s universal construction and self-reproduction exactly. As a cellular automaton keeps its rule, the fixed network keeps its weights, and what reproduces is a stored network. A constructor of 143 records reads the description of a network from its tape, builds that network in the next bank, copies the description onto the next tape and hands control to what it built; started on its own description, it rebuilds itself, weights included, in every generation. The scheme scales to a universal computer. A SUBLEQ computer of 17,598 ternary units, stored as 36,080 records and running a program of 27 instructions, builds any network that fits a bank and reproduces itself in the same way, at every word width from eight bits on; run directly, it emits the serialization of its own weights, memory and tape. Integer pre-activations give every orbit a margin of 1/2, and replicating each unit r times multiplies it by r. That suffices against noise of any size on the pre-activations, but

text: McCulloch and Pitts introduced networks of binary threshold units as a logical calculus of neural activity [1], and von Neumann used their notation for the logical design of the stored-program computer [2]. He later asked how a machine can build a copy of itself, and answered with a universal constructor: given the description of a machine, it builds that machine, and, supplied with its own description and a mechanism that copies descriptions, it builds a copy of itself together with a copy of the description [3]. The self-reproducing automata that followed [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], surveyed in [9], reproduce configurations of a cellular space under a fixed transition rule. This paper asks the same question of threshold networks: whether the weights of a threshold network can be reproduced exactly by the dynamics of a threshold network. The networks have weights in {−1, 0, 1} and integer thresholds and are iterated as a fixed composition of layers, so that each is a map F : {0, 1}n →{0, 1}n whose behaviour is the orbit of an initial state. Exactness comes from the integers. A trained network that outputs an approximation of its weights loses information in every generation, while an orbit of integer pre-activations carries a weight set bit for bit and survives every perturbation of a pre-activation below one

text: from the integers. A trained network that outputs an approximation of its weights loses information in every generation, while an orbit of integer pre-activations carries a weight set bit for bit and survives every perturbation of a pre-activation below one half. We answer it with a fixed ternary network that holds other networks as data. Its state is a ring of banks of records with a tape for each bank. A record is a two-input unit of a stored network, and each step evaluates one record of the active bank. The fixed network plays the part of von Neumann’s transition rule and the stored networks the part of his configurations. As in a cellular automaton, the transition rule keeps its weights, and what reproduces is the stored network, its weights and biases included. 1 arXiv:2610.12251v1 [cs.LO] 8 Oct 2026

text: These objects exist by classical results. By Kleene’s recursion theorem a universal computer has programs that print their own text [10]; universal circuits and fixed-weight networks run any circuit or network whose code they are given [11, 12]; and von Neumann’s design separates construction from copying [3]. This paper builds them as ternary threshold networks and proves what they do. It gives exact sizes and depths for every parameter, shows where ternary weights and threshold units cost a level of depth, reproduces a stored network bit for bit, weights and biases included, and bounds the effect of noise. 1.1 Contributions (1) A network that runs stored networks. The ring machine holds K banks of S records and K tapes of L cells, with heads at absolute positions, and a fixed ternary netlist of depth 19 computes its step from every state, for every window, ring, bank and tape (Theorem 3.2). One pass over a bank evaluates the netlist stored in it, and every ternary unit compiles into records (Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4). (2) A self-reproducing constructor. An organism of 143 records with a description code of its own builds every network whose description fits a tape into the next bank, copies the description onto the next tape and hands control to what it built. Started on its own description it

Started on its own description it reproduces: the copies accumulate until every bank holds one, and from then on the state repeats every K generations (Theorems 4.5 and 4.6). (3) A universal computer. A family HA of ternary networks executes SUBLEQ, a computer with a single instruction [13], on 2A words of A bits. Its step has depth 13 at every word width, and the member with eight-bit words has 17,598 units (Proposition 5.9); a read and the branch each need two levels of ternary units (Lemma 5.7, Remark 5.5). A program of 21 instructions builds every byte string from a run-length description of it, and one of 27, which separates construction from copying as von Neumann did, makes the host emit the serialization of itself, its memory and its tape (Theorems 6.9 and 6.12). This is the quine scheme on a universal machine: a map outside the network turns the emitted bytes back into a running network. (4) A universal computer that reproduces by the dynamics. Stored in the ring machine, the host of every word width from 8 on runs the second program, builds every network that fits a bank and reproduces in every ring as the organism does, with no map outside the network; with eight-bit words it is 36,080 records (Theorems 7.4 to 7.6). (5) Reproduction under noise. Every orbit survives perturbations below 1/2 of each pre-activation. Replicating every unit r times, Pierce’s interwoven redundancy [14] with threshold units, mul- tiplies that margin by r. This suffices against Gaussian noise of any size on the pre-activations. Against von Neumann’s output flips with probability ε it suffices only for ε < 1/(2ek∗), k∗ the largest fan-in, and above 1/(2k∗) a disjunction of fan-in k∗fails with a probability that tends to one (Theorem 8.8, Proposition 8.10). A bound computed from the orbit is the exact probability that some unit of a step fails, as measured, and exceeds the rate at which the host leaves its orbit by the 5 to 6% of failures that the state does not show; a second-order bound certifies the complete run of the threefold host where the first-order bound exceeds one (Propositions 8.5 and 8.14). The Heaviside function is H: R →{0, 1}, with H(z) = 1 if z ≥0 and H(z) = 0 otherwise, applied coordinatewise to vectors. 2.1 Units and layered maps Definition 2.1 (Ternary threshold unit). Let k ≥0. A ternary threshold unit with k inputs is a map u: {0, 1}k →{0, 1} of the form u(x) = H(⟨w, x⟩+ θ), w ∈{−1, 0, 1}k, θ ∈Z. The integer ⟨w, x⟩+ θ is the pre-activation. The effective fan-in of u is |{j : wj̸ = 0}|. Example 2.2. AND(x, y) = H(x + y −2), OR(x, y) = H(x + y −1), NAND(x, y) = H(1 −x −y), NOT(x) = H(−x), and the identity x = H(x−1) on {0, 1}. More generally H(P i∈P xi −P i∈N xi − |P|) is the conjunction of the literals xi (i ∈P) and ¬xi (i ∈N), and H(P i∈P xi−P i∈N xi+|N|−1) is their disjunction, so a negated literal costs no unit. Ternary threshold units therefore form a functionally complete basis. A function that is not linearly separable, such as parity, needs depth at least two [16]; the exclusive or is XOR(x, y) = AND(OR(x, y), NAND(x, y)), of depth two. text: machine This section gives a fixed network whose state holds threshold networks as data. The state is a window of cells, in which a stored network keeps its state, and a ring of banks and tapes; a bank lists the units of a stored network as records. Each step evaluates the record under the slot head of the active bank on the window and moves that head on by one slot. Three more heads read one tape and write the next bank and the next tape, and this is how one stored network builds another (Figure 1). Every head moves by absolute positions, so a bank or a tape need not have the size of what it holds. Definition 3.1 (The ring machine). Let α ≥4, K ≥2 and S, L ≥1, and put β = 8+3α. An image is the sequence of the bits of a list of records, and a bank holds an image ready when it holds it from slot 0, followed by empty slots, with its slot head at slot 0. For A = 8 it has 17,086 units and 120,508 edges, against 17,598 and 51,132 for Nhost. 6 Programs for the host This section programs the host. Section 6.1 says what it means for the host, with a memory image and a tape, to reproduce itself. A program P of 21 instructions decodes a run-length recipe into the byte string it describes, which makes the host a universal constructor of byte strings (Section 6.2). A program P ∗of 27 instructions also copies the recipe, so that the host emits a serialization of itself from which it is rebuilt (Section 6.3). Both programs are stated for Nhost = H8 and run on HA at every word width from 8 on (Remark 6.14). 6.1 Instances and reproduction An instance pairs a network with an initial memory and a tape, and it reproduces itself when its output rebuilds it. The serialization σ(N) of a clocked netlist N is a byte string from which N, the order of its units included, is recovered; Appendix A specifies it. Section 7 removes this map: held as records in the ring machine, the host carries out the same step by the dynamics, as the organism does. 6.2 Universal construction A universal constructor emits any prescribed object from a description of it. Here the objects are byte strings and the descriptions are run-length recipes. Every string has a recipe barely longer than itself, the encoder used later attains that bound, and the program P turns any recipe into the string it describes. For a byte x we write ν(x) = (−x) mod 256. Definition 6.4 (Recipe language). The set R ⊆Σ∗of recipes is generated by the grammar R ::= T ∗END, T ::= LIT | REP, END = 0x00, where a literal token LIT is a byte n with 1 ≤n ≤127 followed by n bytes, and a repeat token REP is a byte t with 129 ≤t ≤255 followed by one byte. text: 6.3 Self-reproduction Von Neumann’s self-reproducing automaton uses its description twice: once as instructions for building, and once as data to be copied. The program P ∗does the same on the host. Phase (A) decodes a recipe into the string it describes, phase (R) rewinds the tape, and phase (B) copies the recipe itself. Run on a recipe for the host’s own serialization and memory image, it emits everything from which the instance is rebuilt. Construction 6.11. The program P ∗consists of three phases. (A) Construction. The twenty instructions of the decoding loop of P, unchanged, except that on reading the end token control passes to phase (R) instead of halting. (R) Rewind. It has 27 instructions, occupying 0x00 to 0x50 (Table 3). Appendix B gives GA, wA and the bounds in closed form. 8 Reproduction under noise The reproductions of Sections 4 to 7 are exact because every pre-activation is an integer: a run rebuilds the weights bit for bit while no perturbation of a pre-activation reaches one half. This section asks how much noise a reproducing run tolerates. It proves this margin of one half, bounds the probability of leaving the orbit under random perturbations from the pre-activations the orbit visits, and compares the bounds with the host under noise (Section 8.1). It shows that replicating every unit multiplies the margin, which keeps a run exact under three models of noise, below a threshold in one of them (Section 8.2), and it gives the noise under which a generation of the stored host, which rebuilds the host’s weights in the next bank, runs exactly (Section 8.3). 22

A ternary row cannot hold the weight r, and reading r copies of an input with weight 1 is how it realizes one. Remark 8.11 (Thresholds and restoring organs). In von Neumann’s multiplexing [23] every compo- nent fails with a fixed probability p whatever its inputs, and a restoring organ of majority elements follows every level; reliable computation then needs redundancy logarithmic in the size of the cir- cuit [26, 27] and is possible only below a threshold on p [24, 25]. The amplification F (r) is Pierce’s interwoven redundant logic [28, 14] with threshold units. The restoring organ is absorbed into every unit, which sums the r copies of each input with one weight, and the identity rows of Lev become majority units. text: Threshold computers. Von Neumann’s EDVAC report describes the stored-program computer with McCulloch–Pitts elements [2]. Goto’s parametron computes the majority of three inputs, an in- put inverted by reversing the polarity of its coupling [29], so parametron circuits are networks of ternary threshold units; MUSASINO-1 [30] and PC-1, of about 4,200 parametrons [31], were stored-program machines built from them, and DONUT a general-purpose computer of about 500 threshold gates [32]; see also [16]. Weighted threshold circuits of depth d are simulated by majority circuits of depth d + 1 [33, 34, 35], and Remark 5.5 is the smallest instance of that exchange. Networks as programmable computers. Recurrent networks of saturated-linear units with ra- tional weights are Turing-universal [36, 37], and programs have been compiled into neural net- works [38, 39]. A looped transformer with fixed weights executes SUBLEQ programs placed in its input [40], as does a looped ReLU perceptron [41]; a fixed transformer simulates any transformer of a class from a description in its input [42], and Loom executes compiled C programs in a looped transformer whose state holds the program [43]. A programmable neural network, a fixed-weight network with auxiliary inputs, behaves as any network of a class when those inputs carry a code of its weight matrix [12]. These use real-valued weights. Von Neumann’s universal constructor uses a description once as instruc- tions for construction and once as data to be copied [3, 47]. Moore and Myhill gave abstract formulations [49, 50], Lee and Thatcher constructed Turing machines that print their own descrip- tion [21, 22], cellular constructions were given by Arbib, Codd, Langton, Pesavento, and Perrier, Sipper and Zahnd, the last with an attached program and a growing data tape [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], and Ib´a˜nez et al. reproduce by self-inspection [51]. Self-replicating field-programmable arrays copy configurations between cells [52], and Cell Matrix cells read and write the truth tables of their neighbours [53]. Program replicators include Tierra [54] and those that emerge in [55]. Cotler, Hongler and Hudcov´a give an informal condition for self-replication in cellular automata and place the automata that meet it strictly between the globally and the locally universal ones, so that Tur- ing universality does not imply self-replication; they require the encoder and the decoder between symbolic computation and the dynamics to be computationally simpler than the computation at- tributed to the system [56]. In those terms the host running P ∗(Section 6.3) is a replicator relative to an instantiation map. The organism and the stored host need no such map: each is a configu- ration of a fixed threshold network, the only map between the computation and the dynamics is the encoding of a state of the ring machine in the bits of that network (Theorem 3.2), and what is reproduced includes the weights of the network that computes. Networks that produce their own parameters. Neural networks have been trained to output their own weights [57, 58], to reproduce over generations [59, 60] and to emit the program text that trains them [61]; hypernetworks and self-referential weight matrices generate or modify weights [62, 63, 64]. In each case the relation between a network and its parameters is learned and approximate. Machine-checked universal machines. A universal Turing machine has been programmed and verified in Coq, with polynomial time and constant-factor space overhead [65], and the Game of Life has been simulated in the Game of Life by circuits verified in HOL4 [66]. Here one Rocq development covers the interpreter, the universal computer, construction, reproduction and noise. 10

text: A fixed network of ternary threshold units holds threshold networks as records and runs them, and a stored network can build any network that fits a bank, copy its description and hand control to what it built. The organism and the stored SUBLEQ host rebuild themselves in this way, weights and biases included, in every ring, and integer pre-activations keep every generation exact while no perturbation of a pre-activation reaches one half. The fixed network itself is not reproduced. Its netlist is ternary and compiles into records by Lemma 3.4, but its state, which contains the window, the banks and the tapes, cannot fit in its own window, so a network that also rebuilds the network that runs it needs another construction. Other questions are open: whether a ternary step of SUBLEQ can have depth below 11, since Lemma 5.7 and Remark 5.5 bound only a read and the branch; how few records a self-reproducing stored network needs; and how much noise a reproducing run tolerates when the perturbations are correlated or drift, which the independence assumed in Section 8 excludes. The serialization σ(N) is the safetensors encoding of four integer vectors: (i) the bias of each unit, in the order of N; (ii) the number of predecessors of each unit, in the same order; (iii) one signed entry per edge, its magnitude the index of the predecessor plus one and its sign the weight, the edges of a unit consecutive and in the order the unit lists them; (iv) for each state bit, the index of the signal computing its next value. The file is an eight-byte little-endian header length, a JSON header object, and the concatenated tensor data in little-endian order. The biases are stored as eight-bit integers, and the fan-ins, the edges and the next-state indices as sixteen-bit integers when their values fit and as thirty-two- bit integers otherwise. Seven thirty-two-bit scalars record the address width, the data width, the number of memory words, the width of the program counter, the number of state bits, the number of units and the version of the format. Four choices that a general-purpose serializer leaves open are fixed. The header object begins with the key metadata , whose value lists the machine name, the quantization tag, the state layout and the device addresses of Table 1, in that order. The remaining entries are the tensors, ordered by element type and

Proof of Proposition 8.14. Call a copy wrong when its output differs from the replicated orbit. Every copy of a row v reads the same copies, and a wrong copy of an input u moves the pre- activation of a copy of v by w(1 −2yu) = ±1, toward the comparator exactly when u ∈U(v). Let Sv be the set of wrong copies of the rows of U(v). By Proposition 8.7(ii) a copy of v is wrong only if its perturbation, on the far side of the comparator, has magnitude at least Dv −|Sv|; given the perturbations of the earlier layers the three copies of v therefore fail independently, each with probability at most q|Sv|(v). Call a layer a stop when it holds a wrong copy of a row v with |Sv| ≥2, or when it is the last layer of a step and one of its rows has two wrong copies. The state read by majority is wrong

text: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies Stuart Farmer Casa Dilauro Independent Research (casadilauro.com) stuart@casadilauro.com github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable Abstract—EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable’s relative performance and the contributions of its components.
title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search

text: This work was motivated by the broader study of recursive self-improvement and LLM-guided program search: how these algorithms are structured, which tasks they address, how well their solutions generalize, and which mechanisms support improvement. The study examines one part of that motivation: whether a program-search algorithm inspired by prior work can also show improvement through repeated eval- uation and revision. In program search, one part of the improvement loop proposes a solution, often source code or an executable policy. Another part, the evaluator, provides a score or feedback on how that solution performs on the task. Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) illustrates this feedback pattern: a language model receives a task de- scription and previously evaluated solutions, then uses that feedback to propose further solutions [1]. FunSearch makes this feedback loop concrete for ex- ecutable programs. It uses an island-based database of solutions, maintaining multiple populations to support diversity. Its applications include cap-set constructions and online bin-packing heuristics [2]. AlphaEvolve extends evolutionary code modification to scientific and computational problems, using evalu- ator feedback to guide revisions [3]. In these systems, evaluation gives program search an external measure of whether a proposed change is useful. These algorithms differ in what they retain and how they generate candidates. ShinkaEvolve combines par- ent sampling, code-novelty rejection, and bandit-based selection among language models [4]. Evolution

text: gives program search an external measure of whether a proposed change is useful. These algorithms differ in what they retain and how they generate candidates. ShinkaEvolve combines par- ent sampling, code-novelty rejection, and bandit-based selection among language models [4]. Evolution of Heuristics evolves descriptions of heuristic ideas together with their executable implementations, giving the language model both conceptual and code- level information about the solutions it explores [5]. EliteTable draws on these approaches through a fixed- capacity table of high-scoring programs. New candidates compete with retained solutions after each generation, while three operators generate fresh proposals, edits, and remixes. The design aims to provide a simple feedback loop for repeated program improvement. Keeping incumbents eligible guarantees that the best recorded search score cannot decrease, but does not guar- antee that newly generated solutions improve. A search may retain elites based on similar heuristics and become confined to a local optimum [2]. Selected solutions may also fail to generalize to new episodes, so held-out evalu- ation is necessary [10]. The study asks two questions. First, do in-sample winner scores and candidate-score distributions improve across generations? Second, do selected-winner gains transfer to held-out episodes? I examine these questions across six Gymnasium control tasks [7]. Records were kept for every candidate across the sixty searches. Between generations one and ten, pooled candidate-score medians

text: The retained table supplies context for sub- sequent proposals and preserves previously discovered high-scoring programs. 2.1 Generation and repair EliteTable uses three operators: new, edit, and remix. Generation one contains only fresh proposals; the top K evaluated solutions enter the elite table. Subsequent generations use the allocation in Table 2. Fresh proposals receive elite descriptions and scores, edits receive one parent’s source, and remixes combine information from up to three parents. Parents are sampled uniformly from the table frozen at the start of the generation. Before evaluation, proposed solutions are checked for schema compliance, valid source edits, and parseable Python syntax using the abstract syntax tree (AST). Solutions must satisfy the required policy interface and pass duplicate checks. Duplicate detection compares AST structures rather than source text. Solutions are then passed to the evaluator. If the revised solution still fails, it returns to the repair loop, up to five repairs per candidate slot. Candidate timeouts are treated as failures, not zero- reward episodes or successful truncations. Infrastruc- ture failures interrupt execution rather than enter the candidate-repair loop. 2.2 Elite selection As briefly mentioned, EliteTable retains the highest- scoring programs across completed generations. For elite capacity K, the update rule is Et = TopK (Et−1 ∪Ct) . (1) Here Et is the retained elite set after generation t, Ct contains valid new candidates from that generation, and TopK selects up to K programs. Candidates are ranked by descending mean search reward. For equal scores, edits take priority over remixes, fol- lowed by incumbent elites and then fresh proposals. Any remaining ties

text: new candidates from that generation, and TopK selects up to K programs. Candidates are ranked by descending mean search reward. For equal scores, edits take priority over remixes, fol- lowed by incumbent elites and then fresh proposals. Any remaining ties are resolved by ascending organism identi- fier. This persistent elitist mechanism ensures that the high- est recorded search-panel reward cannot decrease between completed generations, assuming previously recorded eval- uations remain unchanged. Each began at generation zero with no existing solutions. Evaluation ran on an AMD64 host using eight worker processes, with up to 25 concurrent model operations for generation and repair. The config- ured deadlines were 45 seconds per episode, ten seconds per policy action, and 120 seconds per model-operation attempt. The episode and action deadlines exclude Docker startup, queueing, and final cleanup. Generated poli- cies ran in Docker containers with networking disabled, a read-only root filesystem, and resource limits. The completion rate describes the combined pro- cedure and does not isolate the repair loop’s contribution. 5 Discussion and Conclusion The rising candidate-score medians show progress beyond retaining a single strong initial solution. Newly generated populations also shift toward higher returns. In four tasks, every final selected winner improved over its first- generation counterpart on the fixed held-out episode panel. These endpoint gains do not by themselves rule out overfitting to the selection panel. Acrobot-v1 exposes a limitation: search scores rose while the median paired held-out change was negative. Further examination is needed to identify the cause. Held- out evaluation covers each generation’s selected winner, not every retained elite, so it does not describe the full elite population. Search used ten episode seeds, compared with 100 held-out seeds. Future studies could test whether broader selection panels reduce specialization; the current design does not isolate that effect. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved with- out reaching their reporting targets. The tested budget does not establish whether additional generations would eventually solve these tasks. Their gains should therefore be distinguished from task attainment. 5.1 Program search and neural-policy training EliteTable revises policy source code rather than up- dating neural-policy

text: targets. The tested budget does not establish whether additional generations would eventually solve these tasks. Their gains should therefore be distinguished from task attainment. 5.1 Program search and neural-policy training EliteTable revises policy source code rather than up- dating neural-policy weights through policy gradients. Source edits can change numerical constants as well as program structure. Policy-gradient methods instead up- date parameterized policies, often neural networks, using estimates of the gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters [8]. The selected tasks are drawn from Gymnasium’s stan- dard reinforcement-learning environments [7]. Matched comparisons are needed to assess the relative strengths of program search and neural-policy training on these tasks. Source revisions can alter control structures, numeri- cal constants, state, and execution flow. Programmatic reinforcement learning can also combine program search with guidance from a trained neural policy [9]. These are different update mechanisms; the present study provides no matched comparison of their learning efficiency. 6

text: 5.2 Limitations and next steps Understanding EliteTable’s components requires abla- tions and comparisons with other systems. The observed improvements cannot yet be attributed specifically to reuse, editing, remixing, retention, or repair. Ten searches per environment quantify variation under fixed episode panels, but do not establish robustness across episode distributions, language models, prompts, or search con- figurations. The tasks are well known, so the model may have encountered descriptions or potential solutions during training. Time-based deadlines can produce different outcomes on different hardware. Hosted-provider variation can also change model outputs and search trajectories, even when the same model route is requested. The final solutions are Python programs available for inspection, but source availability alone does not establish human interpretability. I would prioritize budget-matched comparisons with other program-search algorithms, including a history- independent generation baseline, followed by complete- search ablations and comparisons across language models. Longer budgets, new episode panels, and other task fami- lies would test the limits of the observations. The present results provide development evidence for those designs rather than confirmatory evidence of comparative superi- ority.
title: 5.2 Limitations and next steps

text: EliteTable contributes to the study of self-improving LLM-assisted program search. Across sixty searches, candidate populations improved on selection episodes, while held-out evaluation distinguished transferable gains, saturation, and regression. This work supports further investigation of repeated program improvement as part of the broader agenda toward recursive self-improvement. It does not test a system that modifies its own optimizer or language model.

text: The value of information and the emergence of communication in evolved e-puck robots Fernando Montes-Gonzalez Instituto de Investigaciones en Inteligencia Artificial, Universidad Veracruzana, Mexico ORCID: 0000-0002-8024-3023 Correspondence: fmontes@uv.mx
title: The value of information and the emergence of communication in

text: We study when communication emerges between autonomous agents and what role an innate action selection architecture plays. Two e-puck robots, reconstructed in PyBullet from their Webots model and validated against it, must find a feeding zone that can only be detected when a robot passes over it. Each robot can emit a one-bit signal whose direction is detected by the receiver. Control is provided by a GRU recurrent network with a residual path, either operating alone or as a channel within an Embedded Action Selection Architecture (EASA). Fitness measures only the time the robots spend over the food. When the robots receive a compass pointing to the food, use of the signal disappears completely. Without a compass, in a small arena, three independent runs achieved similar performance using different strategies: a referential signal, a permanent beacon, or no use of the signal. As the arena expands, the strategy based on a referential signal generalizes best. In contrast, evolving directly in the large arena does not increase the frequency of communication, but it does separate the strategies, and the referential signal clearly outperforms solitary searching. Within EASA, innate reflexes constrain the network and reduce performance. As its priorities evolve, evolution consistently weakens those reflexes. The results suggest that communication emerges in proportion to the value of the information it transmits, and

text: clearly outperforms solitary searching. Within EASA, innate reflexes constrain the network and reduce performance. As its priorities evolve, evolution consistently weakens those reflexes. The results suggest that communication emerges in proportion to the value of the information it transmits, and that an innate scaffolding designed for isolated agents can be an impediment in a social task. text: Communication allows one organism to modify the behavior of another at low cost. Understanding how a signaling system arises is difficult in animals because its origin can almost

text: never be observed. Evolutionary robotics offers an alternative. In it, the controllers of the robots are selected based on their performance in a task, and behavior emerges from the interaction between the agent, its body, and the environment [1]. This approach has shown that simulated and physical robots can develop useful signals for foraging [2] and for group navigation [3]. This work has transformed robots into a laboratory for studying biological questions about the evolution of social behavior [4]. A central question in this line of inquiry is under what conditions communication emerges. The genetic relationship between individuals and the level at which selection operates influence the reliability of signals [2], [5]. History also plays a role. Populations that start from the same conditions can arrive at different signaling strategies due to historical contingency [6]. A more basic condition has received less attention. A signal is useful when it conveys information that the receiver cannot obtain independently. Otherwise, the signal becomes redundant, reducing the selective pressure for its maintenance. This condition is easy to overlook when designing an experiment. When the controller receives inputs such as the direction or distance to the target, in addition to its sensors, evolution is facilitated, but communication can become unnecessary. In that case, communication signals may appear only if bonuses are added to the

In that case, communication signals may appear only if bonuses are added to the fitness function or rules are used to force their emission, and it becomes difficult to distinguish a signal that evolved from one that was imposed. Added to this is the gap between simulation and reality [7]. A poorly validated robot model can produce behaviors that depend on simulator artifacts rather than the task itself. In previous work, we transferred a communication protocol co-evolved in 2D directly to a 3D physical simulation without retraining, and the transfer was partial and asymmetric [8]. Here we take the opposite route. We evolve directly in a validated 3D model and ask under which conditions communication emerges at all. A second question refers to the controller architecture. Vertebrates solve the problem of choosing what to do using the basal ganglia, a set of nuclei that arbitrates between competing motor programs [9]. Computational models of these circuits have been incorporated into robots and have produced coherent behavioral sequences in foraging tasks [10], [11]. However, it is not obvious that an innate repertoire is helpful when the task is social. A reflex designed for an isolated agent could interfere with behaviors that depend on the partner. In this work, we address both questions with a system built from scratch to avoid the aforementioned problems. Two e-puck robots [14], reconstructed from their official model in Webots [15] and reproduced in the PyBullet physics simulator [16], must find a food zone that they only detect by passing over it with their floor sensors. Neither robot receives information about the food's position. The only communication channel is a one-bit signal, the direction and intensity of which are perceived by the receiver. Each robot is controlled by a recurrent network with GRU units [17] and a residual connection, which acts alone or as an additional channel within the EASA basal ganglia architecture. Fitness is implicit. It only rewards the time the robots spend over the food, without rewarding transmission or approach [1]. Based on this, we manipulated two factors. text: 2.1 Evolution of communication in robots Early models of artificial life gave agents a dedicated signaling channel from the outset. Quinn [18] challenged this practice. A predefined channel presupposes precisely what it aims to explain, and his model showed that coordination behaviors without a dedicated channel can become communicative. Marocco and Nolfi [3] evolved simulated robots that solved a collective navigation task and developed a non-trivial signaling system. In their work, communicative and non-communicative behavior adapted to one another, such that they could not be understood separately. Another line of research explored the conditions that favor the emergence of reliable signals. Floreano et al. [2] evolved foraging robot colonies in an environment containing both food and poison, and found that communication emerged rapidly when individuals were related or when selection operated at the colony level. When the robots' interests conflicted, selection favored the suppression of information [5], and the degree of relatedness influenced the reliability of the signals [19]. Wischmann et al. [6] further demonstrated that populations initiated under identical conditions can develop different signaling strategies due to historical contingency. The theory of the evolution of communication adds a caveat. Sending a signal is pointless if no one responds, and responding is pointless if no one sends a signal. As a result, a population that does not communicate tends to

text: The theory of the evolution of communication adds a caveat. Sending a signal is pointless if no one responds, and responding is pointless if no one sends a signal. As a result, a population that does not communicate tends to remain that way. Scott-Phillips et al. [20] showed that this state of non-interaction is evolutionarily stable, so communication may not emerge even if it benefits both parties. In this study, we adopted the conditions that the literature identifies as favorable, a homogeneous team with team-level selection, to isolate a distinct factor: the informational value of the signal.

text: 2.2 Action selection and basal ganglia in robots A robot with multiple behaviors needs a mechanism to decide which one to execute at any given time. Layered architectures solved this problem with fixed priorities, in which higher layers suppress lower ones [21]. Redgrave et al. [9] proposed that the basal ganglia fulfill this function in vertebrates, acting as a central selector between systems competing for motor control. Gurney et al. [22] formalized this idea in a model where each action has a salience and selection occurs through disinhibition, with a selection pathway, a control pathway, and dopaminergic modulation. This model was incorporated into a Khepera robot, where it produced coherent behavioral sequences under a wide range of sensory and motivational conditions [10]. Subsequent work with the same architecture studied the effect of reducing or increasing simulated dopamine on the robot's behavior [11]. EASA is an open reimplementation of this model that operates under realistic contact physics [12]. These studies share a fundamental idea: that robot and vertebrate control architectures organize behavior in layers with a common selection mechanism [13]. In all these cases, the basal ganglia select among hand-designed behaviors. Less attention has been given to what happens when one of the channels is a network whose behavior is acquired through evolution, and even less when the task requires coordination

Less attention has been given to what happens when one of the channels is a network whose behavior is acquired through evolution, and even less when the task requires coordination with another agent. This is the second question we address. 2.3 Simulation and design of the fitness function Evolutionary robotics relies on simulation because evaluating thousands of controllers on physical robots is impractical. The risk is that evolution will exploit simulator flaws that do not exist in the real world. Jakobi et al. [7] showed that carefully validated simulations with adequate noise treatment reduce this gap. Simulators such as Webots offer detailed models of commercial robots [15], including the e-puck, a robot widely used in collaborative and educational robotics [14]. In this work, we reconstructed the e-puck from its Webots model within PyBullet [16] and verified each component before using it. The design of the fitness function is the other critical decision. Nolfi and Floreano [1] distinguish between explicit functions, which reward specific aspects of behavior, and implicit functions, which only measure the outcome of the task. The former guide the search but can impose the designer's solution. In the context of basal ganglia-inspired controllers, Montes-Gonzalez et al. Methods 3.1 Robot model and environment We reconstructed the e-puck in its version 1 based on the official Webots model [15]. All measurements were copied from the model file. The body is a cylinder with a 37 mm radius and 45 mm height, with a mass of 0.15 kg, and the center of mass and inertia matrix are those of the original model. The wheels have a 20 mm radius and are 5 mm wide, and are spaced 52 mm apart by an axle. The maximum wheel angular velocity is 6.28 rad/s, resulting in a linear speed of 0.126 m/s. Two changes were necessary to adapt the model to PyBullet [16]. Webots makes the robot slide on a small box under its body, but in PyBullet, that box drags. We replaced it with two low- friction spheres at the front and rear, half a millimeter above the floor. Additionally, the collision engine adds a margin of about 1 mm to the cylinders,

Additionally, the collision engine adds a margin of about 1 mm to the cylinders, causing the robot to move 5% faster than it should. Therefore, the collision radius of the wheels is 19 mm, with an effective rolling radius of 20 mm. We validated the model against Webots' kinematics before using it. In a straight line, the robot reaches 0.1255 m/s compared to the expected 0.1256 m/s, and when turning on its axis, it reaches 4.62 rad/s compared to the expected 4.83 rad/s, a difference attributable to wheel slippage. These kinematic checks can be reproduced with the validation script included in the repository (test_step1_kinematics.py; see Data and code availability). The robot has eight infrared proximity sensors and three floor sensors.

text: 3.2 Signal The signal was modeled after the emitter and receiver of the Webots e-puck. It is a single bit with no content. At each control step, the robot decides whether or not to emit. The receiver knows whether its partner emitted, from which direction the packet arrives in its own frame of reference, and with what strength, which decays with the square of the distance. As in Webots, a packet sent in one step arrives in the next, and the range is unlimited. This signal does not indicate the location of the food. A receiving robot only knows that its partner emitted the signal and from where. Whether the signal becomes associated with food or anything else depends entirely on evolution. 3.3 Control Architecture 3.3.1 Recurrent network with residual path (Res-GRU) Each robot is controlled by a recurrent network with 16 GRU units [17] and a residual input- to-output connection (Figure 2). The network receives 17 inputs. The eight proximity readings are log-transformed and scaled between 0 and 1, and the three ground readings are scaled so that 0 corresponds to the floor and 1 to the food. The signal itself carries a single bit, but the receiver perceives how it arrives. Four inputs encode this percept: a reception indicator, the sine and cosine of the bearing from which

text: corresponds to the floor and 1 to the food. The signal itself carries a single bit, but the receiver perceives how it arrives. Four inputs encode this percept: a reception indicator, the sine and cosine of the bearing from which the signal arrives, and its normalized strength. The sine and cosine represent the bearing without the discontinuity of an angle at ±180°. All four inputs are zero when no signal is received. The two remaining inputs are the motivations of fear and hunger. The GRU layer follows the standard equations. The reset gate r controls how much of the previous state enters the computation of a candidate state h̃(t), and the update gate z controls how much of the state is replaced by that candidate, so that h(t) = (1 - z) h(t - 1) + z h̃(t). In Cho et al. [17] the roles of z and 1 - z are swapped, which is equivalent to renaming the gate. The output layer sums the contribution of memory and the residual pathway, which directly connects the inputs to the outputs. This pathway allows for reactive responses that do not depend on memory. This homogeneous team design, with selection at the team level, favors the evolution of communication [2] and leaves the informational value of the signal as the variable of interest. We use a genetic algorithm with a population of 48 individuals over 150 generations. The 10 best individuals are passed on unchanged to the next generation. The rest are obtained by uniform crossover of two parents chosen at random from the 25 best individuals, and each offspring receives Gaussian noise with a probability of 0.2 and a standard deviation of 0.12 in all its genes. text: The best individual of each generation was selected on the basis of only six episodes, so its fitness estimate is biased upward, since it may have been partly lucky. For each run, we choose a champion from the best of the last ten generations, evaluating them in 12 validation episodes that were not used during evolution. The one with the highest average fitness is the champion. Each champion is tested in 100 new episodes with three versions of the signal. In the normal version, the signal functions as in evolution. In the disabled version, no packets arrive. In the random version, packets arrive as expected, but with a randomly chosen direction, preserving the information that the partner emitted a signal while destroying information about its location. Since all three versions use the same episodes, we compare them using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Comparisons between conditions with three runs use Welch's t-test on the average of each run. The disabled version must be interpreted with caution. If a network transmits almost continuously, its peer may rely on that input as if it were constant, and removing it could disrupt the network for reasons unrelated to the information itself. Therefore, we interpret the disabled version in conjunction with the random version and signal specificity.

Three changes appeared in all three runs. The weight of obstacle detection on avoidance decreased from 0.9 to between 0.53 and 0.79, weakening the reflex. Other changes were not replicated. The coupling between net bidding and avoidance was positive in two runs and negative in the third, and dopamine shifted substantially in only one run. Overall, evolution reduced the weight of innate factors in all three runs. Discussion 5.1 Communication follows the value of information The most direct result is that of the compass. When the robots were given the direction of the food, the signal disappeared completely, even though everything else was identical. Without a compass, however, a signal used by the other robots appeared in two out of three runs. Communication does not arise simply from having an available channel, but because it transmits something the receiver cannot know on its own. This has a practical consequence for experimental
title: Fig. 7 Champion fitness in the nominal condition and in three conditions not observed during evolution: a 1.5 m arena

text: design. If the controllers receive privileged information about the target, communication can become redundant, and the only way to obtain communication is to enforce it with bonuses or rules, making it difficult to determine whether it emerged through evolution. In our earlier transfer study, the controllers received the relative bearing to the food and a distance-based term as inputs [8]. This may explain why communication there had to be supported by additional mechanisms. However, the value of the information does not guarantee that communication will emerge. One in three runs, in both the small and large arenas, solved the task without a signal. This is consistent with the argument of Scott-Phillips et al. [20]. Sending a signal is pointless if no one responds, and responding is pointless if no one sends a signal, so a population without communication tends to remain that way. The runs that did communicate also evolved different forms, such as a referential signal or a beacon, which is reminiscent of the historical contingency described by Wischmann et al. [6]. 5.2 When the task is more difficult, what the signal says matters We expected a larger arena to make communication more frequent. This was not the case. What changed was the relative value of the strategies. In the small arena, the referential signal, the beacon, and the

text: what the signal says matters We expected a larger arena to make communication more frequent. This was not the case. What changed was the relative value of the strategies. In the small arena, the referential signal, the beacon, and the solitary search showed similar performance. In the large arena, the referential signal clearly outperformed the solitary search, and the beacon performed even worse than not communicating at all. The robustness test showed the same order with champions that had evolved in the small arena. A signal indicating the location of food retains its value when the search becomes difficult, whereas a beacon that only indicates the location of the partner can lead the receiver astray. The difficulty of the task did not create communication, but it did separate useful communication from unhelpful communication. This complements our earlier transfer study, which suggested that a communication protocol transfers well only if the ecological and navigational conditions under which it evolved are preserved [8]. Here, the referential signal evolved in the small arena kept its value in a larger one, whereas solitary search did not. 5.3 Innate scaffolding in a social task The expectation that innate reflexes would facilitate evolution was not met. All three EASA variants performed worse than GRU and were also less robust in the large arena. The diagnosis points

text: search for and approach the partner. In this task, a repertoire designed for an isolated agent proved ill-suited when success depended on another agent. Evolution's response was consistent. When allowed to adjust priorities, it weakened the avoidance reflex, protected the network from obstacle inhibition, and reduced the drive to explore, always in the direction of yielding control to what has been learned. This supports the idea of reducing designer intervention in basal ganglia-inspired controllers [23] and qualifies the idea of layered architectures with fixed priorities [13], [21]. The persistence provided by the basal ganglia was confirmed in the isolated test, but it was not enough to compensate for the interference. One possibility we did not explore is that the basal ganglia select among several learned proposals rather than among fixed reflexes, which would be closer to the vertebrate organization, in which the cortex proposes and the basal ganglia select [9]. 5.4 Limitations Each main condition has three runs. This is sufficient to show large and consistent differences, but not to accurately estimate the frequency of each communication strategy. Conclusions about behavior are based on the champion of each run, not the entire population. All results are from simulations, although with a model validated against Webots. Simulation physics are not identical across computers, so all runs were performed on the same

text: behavior are based on the champion of each run, not the entire population. All results are from simulations, although with a model validated against Webots. Simulation physics are not identical across computers, so all runs were performed on the same machine. Finally, we used a single task, a single network form, and a single evolutionary algorithm, and the EASA variant explores only one way of combining innate reflexes with a learned network. 6. Conclusions We built an open, validated system of two e-puck robots to study the emergence of a one-bit signal. With it, we showed three things. First, communication disappears when the information it provides is available through another channel. When it is not, communication appears in most runs, though not in all of them. Second, a more difficult task does not make communication more frequent, but it does distinguish the referential signal, which retains its value, from less informative strategies. Third, in a social task, the innate reflexes of a basal ganglia architecture constrain the learned network, and evolution consistently responds by shifting control to the learned network. A natural next step is to test an architecture in which the basal ganglia select among learned proposals, and to verify these results with physical robots.

text: REMBGO for Evaluation-Limited Optimization: CEC2022 Benchmarking and EAF–STATCOM Generalization Vikram Chekuri, Narapareddy Ramarao, Prashanth N A Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, BMS Institute of Technology and Management, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India Affiliated to Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, Karnataka, India Corresponding author: vikramchekuri@bmsit.in
title: REMBGO for Evaluation-Limited Optimization:

text: Metaheuristic comparisons are often reported at evaluation budgets far larger than an expensive engineering simu- lation can afford. This paper presents REMBGO, an evaluation-budget-aware refinement of EMBGO. Its contribution is not any single operator: it is the integration of population preservation, scale-normalized exploration and recovery mechanisms whose parent-relative benefit is concentrated under restricted function-evaluation budgets. REMBGO is evaluated on CEC2022 at a primary, application-aligned budget of 1040 function evaluations, with a surrounding bud- get ladder reported descriptively to characterise budget dependence rather than as a family of controlled hypotheses. A component-removal study finds no individual mechanism whose removal survives multiplicity correction, consis- tent with an integrated rather than a single-operator contribution. The algorithm is then applied to EAF–STATCOM controller tuning, and the resulting frozen gain vectors are transferred without retuning to twenty pre-specified unseen stochastic arc realizations (210 fixed-gain simulations, all feasible). The selected gain-vector main effect accounts for only 3.6–5.8% of the crossed validation variation, against approximately 61.4% for interaction plus residual, and the matched REMBGO–EMBGO paired differences are controller-dependent in sign and not statistically significant. REMBGO is therefore presented as a resource-aware refinement whose benefit must be stated together with the eval- uation budget, not as a universally superior optimizer. Keywords: evaluation-limited optimization; REMBGO; CEC2022 benchmarking; metaheuristic optimization; STAT- COM; electric arc furnace. 1
title: REMBGO for Evaluation-Limited Optimization:

text: Controller tuning by simulation can be computationally expensive because every candidate gain vector requires a MATLAB/Simulink electromagnetic-transient (EMT) simulation. In the EAF–STATCOM application considered here, the adopted tuning protocol uses exactly 1040 objective evaluations. This is much smaller than the largest CEC2022 [1] budgets, so optimizer rankings obtained only at competition budgets should not automatically be assumed to represent behaviour around 103 evaluations. Benchmark reports commonly emphasize final-quality performance at comparatively large evaluation budgets, whereas the intended application here operates near 103 objective evaluations, and the ranking observed at a com- petition budget need not preserve the same ordering when the methods are reconfigured to spend far less. Schedules that anneal a search radius, a mutation scale, or a step length over the run behave differently when the run is short, so a method configured for a large budget and halted early is a different configuration from the same method configured for a small budget. For an application that can afford only about 103 evaluations, the useful question is how the methods compare at that budget when each budget is run as an independently configured experiment rather than read from an early point of a long run. The optimizer studied here belongs to the multiplayer battle-game family. The Multiplayer Battle Game Optimizer (MBGO) [6] models candidates as players that improve

text: run as an independently configured experiment rather than read from an early point of a long run. The optimizer studied here belongs to the multiplayer battle-game family. The Multiplayer Battle Game Optimizer (MBGO) [6] models candidates as players that improve through pairwise contests; the Efficient Multiplayer Battle Game Optimizer (EMBGO) [7] streamlines that scheme for numerical optimization. REMBGO augments the EMBGO search structure with elitism, a fitness-weighted centroid, normalized neighbourhood control, additional perturbation operators, stagnation handling and partial restart, with the aim of improving search when evaluations are limited, while retaining the battle-game core. The study therefore addresses two linked questions: whether the REMBGO refinements improve on EMBGO when objective evaluations are scarce, and whether optimizer-selected controller gains retain their performance when exposed to unseen stochastic EAF trajectories. Budget-dependent benchmarking evaluates an optimizer at several function-evaluation budgets rather than judging it only by its final result at one large budget. Restricted function-evaluation budgets are a defin- ing constraint of expensive optimization [10], and methods aimed at that setting, such as emulation-based adaptive differential evolution [11], target the small-evaluation regime directly. On the application side, metaheuristic STAT- COM tuning has been reported with hybrid ACO–PSO and differential-evolution/harmony-search approaches [12, 13], broader VSC-based FACTS control is reviewed in [14], and for electric-arc-furnace service, STATCOM flicker mitiga- tion has been addressed through conventional and energy-storage STATCOMs [15], nonlinear control [16], and more recently multi-objective evolutionary tuning [17]. The cited STATCOM and EAF studies report performance at a fixed experimental setting and do not address the budget-resolved and transfer questions examined here. The methodological gap addressed here is the combined evaluation of a refined optimizer across matched FE budgets, against its parent, at the exact application budget, and on unseen stochastic application trajectories.
