A five-optimizer, thirty-run CEC2022 study over a common set of independently configured evaluation budgets at D=10 and D=20, including the exact 1040-evaluation budget used in the application (Sections 4–5). 2. A parent-relative analysis of REMBGO against EMBGO, together with a 1040-evaluation component-removal analysis and an associated supplementary sensitivity study. 3. [18], with Holm correction [19] applied within each planned func- tion family. 2 Application Context and Objective Function This section gives the application detail needed to read the fixed-gain transfer study of Section 5; the paper is otherwise self-contained. A STATCOM compensates a point of common coupling (PCC) that feeds an electric arc furnace (EAF) whose time-varying nonlinear arc dynamics produce rapidly varying reactive power and PCC-voltage modulation. The application uses an 11 kV, 50 Hz EAF–STATCOM EMT plant with 5 MVA grid short-circuit capacity and X/R = 7; a 500 kVA two-level VSC-STATCOM is connected in shunt at the PCC through its coupling transformer and LCL filter. Two controllers are considered. The DQ-PI controller uses decoupled current PI control with filtered dc-link regulation, split-frequency reactive-power control, bounded slow integral action, current limiting and anti-windup. The Lyapunov controller is a nonlinear design with full reactive-power PI regulation, voltage droop, dc-link regulation and nonlinear inner current feedback with the associated limiting. (4) 3.2 Inherited EMBGO structure and its limitations EMBGO [7] advances each player through one of three search behaviours. A player inside a safe region around the current best moves by a current-to-best-and-mean differential update (sinusoidally weighted differential vectors toward the best and the population mean); a player outside that region performs Lévy-flight exploration; and in a separate opponent battle a random opponent sets the direction, the player recombining with a stronger opponent by dimension- wise crossover and otherwise taking a single cosine-modulated step. Three features limit this scheme for a simulation- expensive, penalty-constrained objective: the arithmetic-mean attractor is pulled toward poor or penalised candidates; the neighbourhood radius is measured in raw coordinate units and is dominated by the widest-ranging variable; and although greedy replacement protects a parent from a worse trial, EMBGO keeps no explicit elite set and no stagnation or diversity recovery, so search effort is spent perturbing even the current best and a prematurely converged population is never re-diversified. 3.3 REMBGO search cycle REMBGO retains the battle-game core and addresses these three features. text: search effort is spent perturbing even the current best and a prematurely converged population is never re-diversified. 3.3 REMBGO search cycle REMBGO retains the battle-game core and addresses these three features. Before the equations, the search cycle is read as a fixed sequence. Each generation (i) ranks the current population and identifies the best and worst players; (ii) preserves a few elite players unchanged; (iii) measures population diversity and forms a fitness-weighted centroid, an adaptive neighbourhood radius, a decaying step scale and an adaptive patience; (iv) generates one trial for every non-elite player by selecting a single operator from a fixed portfolio; (v) applies a stagnation-dependent jitter and repairs any boundary violation; (vi) evaluates the trials while respecting the remaining evaluation budget and keeps, for each player, the better of parent and trial; and (vii) detects stagnation or low diversity and partially restarts the weakest players. The cycle repeats until the function-evaluation budget is spent. Each generation copies the Ke=3 elites into the trial population and generates only N −Ke = 37 new trials, yet the implementation evaluates all N = 40 trials and restores the stored elite fitnesses before selection, so one generation spends 40 evaluations for 37 new candidates and a run of T generations costs N(T + 1) evaluations including initialization. When B is not an integer multiple of N beyond initialization the final generation is evaluated only partially (Algorithm 1), so the requested budget is met exactly. Every algorithm receives the same budget with objective calls counted identically, so the comparison is matched in objective-call budget rather than in newly generated candidates: REMBGO spends three of every forty generation-level calls re-evaluating copied elite rows (3/40 = 7.5%), which the other four methods do not, amounting at the 1040-evaluation budget to 25 × 3 = 75 of 1040 calls (7.21%); this overhead is retained without compensation. FP-SHADE is a fixed-population implementation of success-history adaptive differential evolution using current-to-pbest/1 mutation, an external archive and success-history adaptation of F and CR (H = 6, p = 0.1, archive rate 1.0); linear population- size reduction is not used [25]. Results for FP-SHADE are therefore not evidence about population-reducing SHADE variants. All five implementations share a strict evaluation-budget controller and per-evaluation best-so-far recording. 4.2 Benchmark and evaluation budgets The CEC2022 suite [1] provides twelve functions on [−100,100]D: F1 unimodal, F2–F5 basic multimodal, F6–F8 hy- brid, F9–F12 composition, with known optima F∗. The five optimizers are compared at D ∈{10,20} with population N = 40, thirty official runs per function, the official CEC2022 Rand_Seeds list with the prescribed Mersenne-Twister generator, and the identical uniform-random initial population X0 supplied to every optimizer for each matched (func- tion, dimension, run). No warm-start row is inserted. 6

text: Each evaluation budget is run as a separate, independently configured experiment rather than read as a checkpoint from a single long run. Because the safe radius, mutation scale and step schedules are driven by the consumed fraction τ of the iteration budget, a run configured for a large budget and halted early is a different configuration from a method configured for the smaller budget. For a requested budget B the iteration count is TB = lB−N N m , (17) and strict function-evaluation accounting is enforced. The common ladder spans fourteen budgets per dimension: D=10: 200, 316, 502, 796, 840, 1040, 1261, 2000, 3169, 5023, 7962, 12619, 20000, 200000 FEs; D=20: 125, 227, 414, 754, 840, 1040, 1373, 2500, 4551, 8286, 15085, 27464, 50000, 1000000 FEs, for a total of 5 ×12×30×28 = 50,400 optimizer runs. The largest budget in each dimension matches the CEC2022 technical-report budget. The 1040-evaluation rung is one ordinary rung of this common ladder and is the exact budget used in the EAF–STATCOM tuning application (N = 40, 25 updates, 40 × (25 + 1) = 1040); it is referred to as the exact application-aligned budget. Each benchmark function is one statistical block. For every (dimension, budget) condition the per-function summary is the median terminal error over the thirty runs; the algorithms are ranked once per function, giving a rank matrix that drives the Friedman test and the mean ranks. Because the algorithms share seeds and identical initial populations, the primary pairwise test is the two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the thirty matched pairs per function, with the direction taken from the signed-rank statistic and Holm correction applied across the twelve functions separately for each planned comparison [19]. Win/ tie/loss (W/T/L) counts report REMBGO better / no significant difference / EMBGO better after this correction. For each of the five optimizers and each of the two controllers the gain vector with the lowest recorded Jtot is selected (ten fixed vectors), mapped to controller parameters by the same transformation used during tuning. Be- fore the corrected campaign, a separate provenance qualification replay reproduced the ten archived training scores to a maximum absolute difference of 2.03×10−8, confirming the frozen gains and the objective implementation; that provenance check is not part of the corrected transfer set. The corrected campaign then evaluates each of the ten vectors on twenty pre-specified unseen arc realizations plus one corrected base-42 reference realization, giving 210 one-second EMT simulations in total: 200 unseen and 10 reference. Two stochastic conditions are distinguished here: STO-SR, the fixed-seed stochastic-mode realization that defined the original application tuning condition, and STO-ENS, the independent multi-realization stochastic ensemble used for frozen-gain transfer. STO-ENS is a methodological role and its realization count is paper-specific; here it is the twenty pre-specified unseen arc realizations, and the corrected base-42 realization is a separate reference case that is excluded from all STO-ENS statistics. Archived identifiers containing STO are retained in the source files for traceability. A post-campaign audit established that the sampler used during the original campaign produced a periodic rather than broadband trajectory. The twenty unseen bases were therefore re-drawn under an exact integer implementation and pre-specified before any corrected result was computed; one candidate base was excluded by the pre-specified screen because one of its phase seeds fell on the degenerate short orbit. This constant is inher- ited from an earlier application-oriented implementation; it does not delimit the admissible region of the engineering objective used here, whose nominal hard-penalty levels are of order 104 and 105 and whose observed campaign values lie well below 107. On raw CEC2022 functions the objective is the benchmark value itself and its magnitude is function dependent, so the same constant can become operationally active. A side-effect-free audit at the primary budget repro- duced all 720 archived terminal values exactly and found activation confined to F1, F6 and F8. A matched sensitivity run that removed only the finite cutoff left every originally inactive run bit-identical and produced no Holm-significant terminal-performance difference in any affected function–dimension cell. The threshold is therefore operationally ac- tive and objective-scale dependent on a subset of CEC2022 functions, but this analysis provides no evidence of a material terminal-performance change from removing the finite cutoff at the tested 1040-evaluation condition, so the reported benchmark conclusions do not rest on it. Recent analysis of the CEC2022 winner shows that added mechanisms and hidden parameters should not auto- matically be read as useful complexity, and that a simplified variant of that algorithm can outperform the original [4]. Component value should therefore be established empirically rather than asserted, which is why REMBGO is assessed here through a matched parent comparison, a component-removal study and a budget-dependent characterization rather than through terminal-rank claims. The component-removal result, in which no single removal survives multiplicity correction, is reported in that spirit: it indicates that the behaviour arises from interacting components and cannot be attributed confidently to any one mechanism. In the transfer test the selected-vector main effect accounts for only 3.6% (DQ-PI) and 5.8% (Lyapunov) of the descriptive crossed validation variation, against 35.0% and 32.8% for arc realization and approximately 61.4% for interaction plus residual, so robustness across stochastic trajectories matters more than the small differences among nominal tuning winners; this does not conflict with the benchmark parent result, as the two experiments answer different questions. 7 Limitations The benchmark study covers the CEC2022 suite only, at D=10 and D=20 with thirty runs per condition, and Holm correction is applied within each budget without cross-budget multiplicity control, so the win/tie/loss counts describe breadth and direction rather than

text: Limitations The benchmark study covers the CEC2022 suite only, at D=10 and D=20 with thirty runs per condition, and Holm correction is applied within each budget without cross-budget multiplicity control, so the win/tie/loss counts describe breadth and direction rather than magnitude. The application study uses one EAF–STATCOM plant family, two con- trollers, a single tuning trajectory and twenty unseen stochastic arcs, evaluated by simulation replay rather than on hard- ware. Finally, two implementation details—range-normalization of the neighbourhood radius and the midpoint-based restart subgroup—have limited identifiability on the symmetric isotropic CEC2022 box, though matched diagnostics found no detectable change in the reported conclusions. Benchmark breadth is a further limitation. CEC2022 contains twelve functions per dimension, which is small by the standards of recent benchmarking methodology [2]: although the present design compensates partly through thirty repetitions, two dimensions, several evaluation budgets, a matched parent comparison, a component-removal study and an independent engineering transfer test, cross-suite validation remains necessary before broader optimizer-ranking claims are made. text: Optimizer ordering depends materially on the evaluation budget, so optimizer selection for simulation-expensive con- troller tuning should use a budget representative of the intended application. REMBGO is not universally best: at 1040 evaluations it holds the lowest observed mean rank at D=10 and GWO at D=20, while FP-SHADE leads at large budgets. Selecting a nominal winner on one stochastic trajectory does not by itself establish robust generalization. In the corrected transfer study all ten frozen champions remained feasible across twenty pre-specified unseen stochastic arcs. The average shift from the STO-SR training objective to the unseen-arc mean was +0.0198, with smaller mean degradation for the DQ-PI vectors (+0.0059) than for the Lyapunov vectors (+0.0338), and the arc realization and its interaction with the selected vector accounted for far more of the validation variation than the choice of vector itself. The matched REMBGO−EMBGO paired differences were controller-dependent in sign and not statistically significant for either architecture, so the EAF experiment supports fixed-gain transfer robustness rather than an application-side REMBGO superiority claim. Future work should examine multi-trajectory or risk-aware controller tuning under the same restricted evaluation-budget setting. Data availability. The numerical results and methodological details supporting the reported findings are provided in the article and supplementary material.

text: S3 Additional REMBGO component diagnostics Restart-reference behaviour on symmetric bounds. The partial restart (R11) regenerates part of its group as mul- tiplicative neighbours of a reference point xref. On the symmetric CEC2022 bounds xref defaults to the box midpoint, which is the origin, so the multiplicative rule xref ⊙(1+0.3U [−1,1]D) returns the origin unchanged and that subgroup injects identical zero vectors. A matched diagnostic replaced the reference subgroup with an alternative non-degenerate reference and re-ran REMBGO under identical seeds; the alternative reference produced no detectable change on the isotropic benchmark. Failure to detect a difference is not evidence of equality; the reported benchmark results are stated as conditional on the implemented behaviour, and this diagnostic does not alter the parent-relative records or the application study, which never uses the symmetric-box reference. Coordinate-normalization cancellation. The normalized decaying neighbourhood radius (R3) combines range nor- malization with the temporal decay ρ(τ) = 1.5 −0.7τ. For the idealized rule with εR = 0, if every coordinate has the same range s then R0 = ∥xb −xw∥2 δ ρ(τ)/s and the membership condition ∥xi −xb∥2/s ≤R0 reduces exactly to ∥xi−xb∥2 ≤∥xb−xw∥2 δ ρ(τ), so the scale cancels. The implemented form keeps the regularizer εR = 10−12 inside the norm; nevertheless, on the isotropic CEC2022 box the runs with and without range normalization were bit-identical for

The implemented form keeps the regularizer εR = 10−12 inside the norm; nevertheless, on the isotropic CEC2022 box the runs with and without range normalization were bit-identical for every tested seed, function and budget. Thus, only the temporal-decay contribution is active in these isotropic CEC2022 tests, and range normalization neither helps nor harms; it is retained because it becomes active on anisotropic domains outside the CEC2022 specification. For each (dimension, function, run) the initial population is drawn uniform-randomly over [l,u] from the official CEC2022 Rand_Seeds list with the prescribed Mersenne-Twister gen- erator, and the identical population is supplied to every optimizer, so all comparisons are matched. text: objective call is counted identically across optimizers. A complete T-generation run with population N costs N(T + 1) evaluations including initialization. For a requested budget B, TB = ⌈(B−N)/N⌉sets the maximum generation count, and the final generation is truncated when necessary so that exactly B objective calls are consumed. In a truncated final generation the trial rows are evaluated in implementation order, and REMBGO does not reshuffle the copied elite rows before truncation. Per-function differences are formed per seed as d = fEMBGO −fREMBGO; exact zero differences are dropped following Wilcoxon’s rule and the effective sample size reduced accordingly; tied absolute differences receive average ranks; the test is the two-sided exact signed-rank test; the direction is taken from the signed-rank statistic; and Holm correction is applied across the twelve functions, one family per budget. Seeds are never pooled across functions. Component-removal statistical conventions. The component-removal study reported in the main paper is run at the exact 1040-evaluation budget on the same matched CEC2022 records, separately for D=10 and D=20. Eleven configurations are compared: the full REMBGO configuration and its ten implementation-level mechanism-removal variants. Each of the twelve CEC2022 functions is a statistical block; within a block the per-configuration observation is the median terminal error over the thirty matched runs. The mean rank reported for a removal is obtained by ranking

text: implementation-level mechanism-removal variants. Each of the twelve CEC2022 functions is a statistical block; within a block the per-configuration observation is the median terminal error over the thirty matched runs. The mean rank reported for a removal is obtained by ranking the eleven configurations on each function by this median error and averaging the rank across the twelve functions, so the full REMBGO configuration also carries a rank and a removal that improves on it scores a lower rank. The displayed median ∆log10 is the median over the twelve functions of log10(removal median error)−log10(full-REMBGO median error), so a positive value means the removal degrades performance. Two Wilcoxon signed-rank families are distinguished. An exploratory per-function family applies the two-sided exact signed-rank test to the thirty matched pairs of each function, with Holm correction across the twelve functions for each removal. The suite-level family— the “Holm p” reported in Table 3 and the basis for the statement that no removal is significant after the suite-level Holm correction—applies the exact signed-rank test across the twelve per-function log10 medians for each full-versus- removal contrast and then Holm-corrects across the ten planned removal contrasts, separately for each dimension. Because REMBGO uses sequential branch selection under a fixed objective-call budget, disabling one branch redistributes search exposure among the remaining branches, and removing elitism also changes the number of newly generated candidates per generation. The contrasts therefore quantify the effect of removing each component from the integrated implementation, rather than an isolated causal contribution obtained with all other operator exposures held fixed; this reinforces the reading of REMBGO as an interacting search design. text: Highlights A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models Ivan Moloshnikov, Dmitry Kunitsyn, Alexander Sboev, Maksim Skorokhodov, Roman Rybka, Yuanchao Liu • A multi-agent large language model framework tunes functional blocks of specialized neural networks. • The same framework transfers across five spiking classification and physics-informed neural network tasks. • MNIST accuracy rises +13 pp; selected GNLSE errors drop up to 2500x and 325x. • Detailed prompts substantially improve performance of less capable large language models. arXiv:2610.13663v1 [cs.AI] 9 Oct 2026
title: Highlights

text: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models Ivan Moloshnikova,∗, Dmitry Kunitsyna, Alexander Sboeva,b,∗∗, Maksim Skorokhodova, Roman Rybkaa,c and Yuanchao Liud aNational Research Centre “Kurchatov Institute”, 1 Akademika Kurchatova Square, Moscow, 123182, Moscow, Russia bNational Research Nuclear University MEPhI, 31 Kashirskoye Shosse, Moscow, 115409, Moscow, Russia cMoscow Institute of Physics and Technology, 9 Institutskiy Lane, Dolgoprudny, 141701, Moscow, Russia dHarbin Institute of Technology, No. 92 West Dazhi Street, Nangang District, Harbin, 150001, Heilongjiang, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Large language models Multi-agent systems Automated machine learning Physics-informed neural networks Spiking neural networks A B S T R A C T Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles— analyst, coder, and recorder —with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged.
title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized

text: Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks—spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (KS) equations—the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant- preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

text: Large language models (LLMs) have become the foundation of a new class of tools —agent systems that can not only respond to queries but also plan actions, use tools, execute code, and accumulate experience from previous steps Xi, Chen, Guo et al. (2023); Yao, Zhao, Yu et al. (2023b). Such agents are already used in programming, ML engineering, and individual scientific disciplines Jimenez, Yang, Wettig et al. (2024); Chan, Chowdhury, Jaffe et al. (2024); Lu, Lu, Lange et al. (2024); Schmidgall, Su, Wang et al. (2025); however, their use as a meta-optimizer for specialized neural network models remains understudied. A detailed review of related work is given in Section 2. The quality of specialized neural network models depends strongly on the task: the representation of inputs and outputs, the method for decoding internal activity, the balance of loss-function terms, and other components must be selected anew for each problem, and no universal selection rule exists. In practice, this selection is performed manually, which makes the process labor-intensive and poorly reproducible. At the same time, models of different types can be decomposed into similar modules: input encoding and preprocessing, a trainable feature transformation, a decoding or output transformation, and a loss function. The tuning task is therefore reduced not to redesigning the entire network for every new problem but to modifying

text: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning Studies in which LLM agents are used as a general tool for automatic tuning of individual functional blocks of a model with a fixed architecture and training procedure are almost absent from the open literature (see Section 2). Existing systems focus either on programming tasks and the general ML cycle or on constructing a network from a textual task description. In contrast, the proposed framework does not build a network but modifies its predefined blocks using a single agent interaction pattern that does not depend on the particular application task. The main contributions are as follows. 1. We propose a multi-agent LLM framework for the automatic tuning of individual functional blocks of a neural network model (Section 3). 2. We show that the same framework transfers across five tasks with different types of information representation without changes to its internal structure (Section 5, Table 1). 3. We show that a detailed prompt improves the performance of less capable LLMs, bringing it closer to that of more advanced models (Section 5.2, Table 2). 4. Unlike NAS, the proposed approach uses an LLM, exploits domain knowledge and knowledge of model properties, locally modifies a selected module of an existing network without searching a fixed space of variants, and stores the history of hypotheses in natural language, so that each subsequent iteration can use a substantive analysis of previous iterations rather than only their numerical results. To the authors’ knowledge, the open literature contains no work in which LLM agents are used as a general tool for automatically tuning individual functional blocks of neural network models without redesigning the network itself. MLE-STAR Nam et al. (2026) is the closest agent system; the similarity is limited to two components: logged experiment memory and a sandboxed execution environment. MLE-STAR applies iterative code modifications with an update only when the metric improves on the outer loop, processes the entire ML script, selects the target block with a separate agent, assigns web search to a separate retriever agent, and involves more than ten agents. 3. text: optimizes a selected functional block while keeping the rest of the task pipeline fixed. Before a run, the Human Researcher specifies the task, the block that the agents may modify, the evaluation metric, the software contract for the generated code, and a baseline. These settings allow the same framework to be applied to different problems without changing its architecture or execution loop. The framework is built on top of an OpenAI-compatible API and separates hypothesis generation, software implementation, and experiment documentation into three LLM roles. A sandboxed execution environment and an external experiment log close the iterative loop (Fig. 1). The framework consists of five main components: • LLM Analyst receives the task prompt and the current experiment log. It proposes one hypothesis for the agent-modifiable block and expresses the idea as a technical specification with a fixed structure. If the Human Researcher provides a taxonomy of method classes, the Analyst also assigns the hypothesis to one of these classes. • LLM Coder translates the technical specification into Python code. In addition to implementing the proposed method, the code must satisfy a task-specific software contract that defines the allowed dependencies, class names, call signatures, input and output shapes, and trainable parameters. • Sandboxed execution environment (Docker) inserts the generated module into the fixed task pipeline, first performs a short functional

text: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning Standard and detailed Analyst prompts. The framework supports two modes of hypothesis generation. The standard prompt contains the Analyst role, problem statement, target metric, implementation constraints, required format of the technical specification, and complete experiment log. The detailed prompt retains these elements and adds a structured Chain-of-Thought procedure and a list of method classes specified by the Human Researcher for systematic exploration. Each hypothesis is assigned to one principal class, which is also stored in its experiment-log record, and the log is converted into a dynamically updated coverage map. For every class, the map reports the number of evaluated hypotheses, the best metric value, and a coverage status such as “not explored,” “limited data,” or “explored.” The map is included in the next Analyst prompt, which prioritizes suitable classes with little or no coverage and revisits an explored class only when a substantially different hypothesis is proposed. This mechanism structures an open natural-language search without reducing it to a finite list of implementations. The task-specific prompt configurations are described in Section 4; the detailed-mode prompt materials are provided in Supplementary Materials. 3.1. At each iteration, one hypothesis is tested in six steps: 1. The Analyst receives the task prompt and the current experiment log. At the first iteration, the log contains only the baseline record. The code undergoes an automatic functional test on a small sample in the sandboxed environment. If the test fails, the error message, generated code, and original specification are returned to the Coder. The Coder analyzes the reported error and rewrites the code while preserving the proposed method and software contract; the revised version is then tested again. Task-specific prompt configurations The two universal Analyst modes defined in Section 3 are instantiated differently across the experiments. The PINN tasks use only the standard mode, with prompts that specify the differential equation, the modifiable transformations, the software contract, and the physical target metric; they do not use a method-family catalog, Chain-of-Thought procedure, or coverage map. The SNN classification experiments compare the standard mode, denoted the simple prompt in the result tables, with the detailed mode. The simple prompt specifies the Analyst role, classification problem, target accuracy, data-use and implementation constraints, examples of admissible decoder types, required technical-specification format, and complete experiment log. The detailed prompt adds a researcher-defined taxonomy of 12 decoder-method classes, a structured Chain-of-Thought procedure for coverage and failure analysis, an explicit class field in the technical specification, and the dynamically updated coverage map. Search baselines and budget: SNN decoder on MNIST The quality reached by the framework depends both on the search performed by the LLM Analyst and on the constraints that the Human Researcher writes into the prompt. To separate these two contributions, we compare the framework with baselines that search the same space of decoders without an Analyst. All comparisons in this subsection are performed on MNIST, where the argmax baseline gives 79.88 %. Shared search space. The decoder catalog is a fixed discrete space of estimators with grids of their hyperparameters, together with the operators that build ensembles and multistage pipelines. It is specified once as a TPOT config_dict that is listed in Supplementary Section E.2 and its classes follow the decoder taxonomy of the detailed Analyst prompt (Section 4.3, Supplementary Materials). The Analyst prompt permits exactly the decoders contained in the catalog. The restriction reaches the systems in different ways: the agent receives it as text and can in principle depart from it, whereas the baselines receive it as a constraint on the sampler. We inspected the Experiment logs of all agent runs and found no record outside the catalog. Three baseline configurations are compared with the framework, each with a budget of 250 evaluated decoders per run. • Random Choice is an LLM-based sampler that draws decoder configurations from the same catalog through independent calls to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 deployed on a rented GPU, without a Chain-of-Thought stage and without a debugging cycle. A call that yields a configuration outside the catalog, a configuration that fails the functional test, or a repetition of a configuration already recorded is discarded and does not enter the Experiment log. Its 𝐹𝐼supplies a normalized traveling-wave coordinate, normalized time, and a local nonlinearity-density feature; 𝐹𝑂uses the analytical traveling-wave amplitude and phase and interprets the MLP outputs as bounded amplitude and phase corrections. The best Claude Opus 4.6 configuration, PCDS-LCC-EXP-NLOG-MIXCROSS, uses seven analytical features, including normalized and logarithmic envelopes and two amplitude–time cross-features, while 𝐹𝑂applies time-gated exponential amplitude and additive phase corrections with separate envelope weights. The best Qwen configuration, LogPhaseHybridNorm, normalizes the analytical soliton coordinate at the input and reconstructs the field from the analytical amplitude and carrier phase multiplied by learned complex corrections. Thus, all three best configurations exploit the known soliton structure in both the representation and the reconstruction. A detailed analysis of the hypotheses is provided in Appendix C. 5.5. Discussion The experiments show that prompt detail can partially compensate for the limitations of the analyst model, although the degree of compensation depends on the LLM used. Claude Opus 4.6 achieves accuracy above 90 % with both prompt variants. With the simple prompt, Perplexity Sonar remains at the baseline level in all ten complete runs, but with the detailed prompt it consistently exceeds 90 % and reaches the level of Claude Opus 4.6. For Qwen3-30B-A3B- Instruct-2507, the detailed prompt also produces a substantial gain: the best result increases from 79.88 % to 89.16 %. At the same time, the higher variability of the maxima (85.88 ± 2.42 %) and the absence of any run with a maximum accuracy above 90 % show that the instruction structure does not fully compensate for the limitations of this model. Limitations Despite the results reported above, the present study has several limitations that should be taken into account when interpreting the findings and when comparing our system with alternative approaches. • Restricted search space. The agent modifies a fixed catalogue of editable blocks (encoders, neuron models, connectivity schemes for SNNs; loss weights, activation functions and sampling strategies for PINNs). Structural transformations that fall outside this catalogue – for example, adding auxiliary networks or replacing the entire training paradigm – cannot be discovered by the current agent and would require an extended action space. • Flat experiment log without a hypothesis graph. text: To date, automatic tuning of neural networks has been carried out mainly within the framework of an allocated single metric of the given competition: agent-based systems optimize the entire ML script, NAS approaches search over architectures according to accuracy, and PINN frameworks train networks to minimize the relative error. For tasks whose quality is defined by a multidimensional signal—by the conservation of a set of physical invariants or by additional structural requirements—frameworks of a different class are required. The results reported in this paper demonstrate the robustness and generalization ability of the proposed multi-agent framework, which consists of an analyst, a programmer, and a recorder, together with a sandboxed execution environment and an experiment log serving as external memory, on tasks of different nature without changes to its internal structure. The same unchanged framework was applied to five tasks with different types of information representation: accuracy increased from 79.88 % to 92.83 % on MNIST and from 90.83 % to 96.67 % on digits; in the single-soliton PINN problem, the relative amplitude error decreased by a factor of approximately 2491; in the more complex problem with a Gaussian perturbation and no known analytical solution, the conservation error of the integrals of motion decreased by a factor of approximately 325 in the selected run and by factors of 116 and 103,
title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning

text: in the more complex problem with a Gaussian perturbation and no known analytical solution, the conservation error of the integrals of motion decreased by a factor of approximately 325 in the selected run and by factors of 116 and 103, respectively, based on the mean errors over ten additional trainings of the residual-selected and invariant-selected configurations (Table 11); and in the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky problem, the boundary-value-problem residual decreased by a factor of 9.3 and mass drift by a factor of 14 (Tables 1 and 7). A separate result concerns the interaction between the analyst model and prompt structure. On MNIST, the detailed prompt enabled Perplexity Sonar to exceed 90 % accuracy in all ten complete runs and to reach a maximum of 92.70 %, close to the result of Claude Opus 4.6. For Qwen3-30B-A3B- Instruct-2507, maximum accuracy increased from the baseline level of 79.88 % to 89.16 %, but the target threshold was not reached. Prompt design can therefore substantially improve the performance of a less capable LLM, but only partially compensates for differences between models. Future work includes increasing the complexity of the PINN problem (the interaction of two solitons and other regimes without analytical solutions), jointly tuning several blocks (the decoder and plasticity rules for the SNN), and constructing models that account for the constraints of neuromorphic systems. The approach is applied to two datasets: MNIST (28 × 28, 𝑁= 784 spike generators) and the scikit-learn digits Pedregosa et al. (2011) (8 × 8, 𝑁= 64). text: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness Daniel Szelogowski Department of Computer Science University of Wisconsin–Whitewater szelogowdj19@uww.edu
title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling

text: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between ob- jective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysi- cal computational framework coupling Borbély’s two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper’s hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop cir- cuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33–0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology. 1
title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling

text: Sleep disorders affect an estimated 10%–30% of the global adult population, contributing substantially to cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, affective disorders, and cognitive decline [3, 30]. Clinical polysomnography (PSG) serves as the diagnostic benchmark for evaluating sleep pathology, categorizing sleep into discrete 30-second epochs comprising wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) stages N1, N2, and N3 slow-wave sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep [3]. Despite the widespread clinical adoption of macroscale PSG metrics such as total sleep time (TST) and sleep efficiency (SE), these indices frequently fail to correlate with patients’ perceived daytime impairment or neurocognitive recovery [14, 20]. This divergence is evident in paradoxical insomnia, clinically designated as sleep state misperception. Patients suffering from paradoxical insomnia report profound subjective insomnia and daytime exhaustion, despite objective overnight PSG recording normal sleep duration, normal sleep onset latency (SOL), and preserved macro- architecture [14, 20]. Conversely, patients diagnosed with narcolepsy type 1 frequently accumulate equal or greater TST than healthy individuals over a 24-hour cycle, yet suffer from severe daytime somnolence (excessive daytime sleepiness and the inability to maintain consolidated wakefulness) Project source code available at https://github.com/danielathome19/DyssomniaNN. These symptoms arise from the selective loss of hypothalamic neurons producing hypocretin and orexin, which destabilizes transitions between wakefulness, NREM, and REM sleep [26, 11, 34]. Addressing these clinical discrepancies requires computational models capable of bridging micro- scopic synaptic and neuromodulatory mechanisms with macroscopic sleep architecture. Traditional computational models of sleep have largely existed in isolation: phenomenological differential equations modeling macroscopic circadian and homeostatic sleep propensity [5, 10, 1], lumped-rate models of hypothalamic switching [32, 33, 27], or biophysical spiking neural networks (SNNs) composed of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons focused on local cortical oscillations during brief sleep spindles or slow waves [12, 17]. Prior modeling efforts have not united these biophysical scales into a continuous, multi-day simulation capable of reproducing distinct human dyssomnias within an identical environmental photoperiod (the structured daily cycle of ambient light and dark exposure, here configured as a 16-hour light/8-hour dark schedule). text: Computational modeling of sleep regulation originates from the classic Two-Process Model formu- lated by Borbély and colleagues [5, 10]. The model posits that sleep timing and duration emerge from the nonlinear interaction between a homeostatic sleep pressure process (S), which accumulates during wakefulness and discharges during sleep, and an oscillatory circadian process (C) driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) [5, 10]. While the two-process model provides a robust mathe- matical formulation of sleep debt and circadian gating, it operates strictly at the phenomenological level and lacks direct representation of the subcortical nuclei that execute state transitions. Subsequent neurobiological investigations by Saper and colleagues identified the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) and lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) as the anatomical core of a mutual inhibitory flip-flop circuit governing sleep-wake transitions [32, 33, 16]. Inhibitory GABAergic and galaninergic projections (axonal pathways that transmit signals to distant brain regions) from the VLPO inhibit ascending monoaminergic and peptidergic arousal centers, including the locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe, tuberomammillary nucleus, and orexinergic neurons in the LHA [32, 33]. In contrast, excitatory glutamatergic and monoaminergic projections stimulate cortical activation and arousal pathways. Reciprocally, monoamines from the arousal systems inhibit the VLPO [32, 8]. Mathematical rate models of this reciprocal inhibition demonstrate that mutual inhibition generates bistability (a dynamical regime/operating state possessing two distinct stable equilibria — consolidated wake and

text: and arousal pathways. Reciprocally, monoamines from the arousal systems inhibit the VLPO [32, 8]. Mathematical rate models of this reciprocal inhibition demonstrate that mutual inhibition generates bistability (a dynamical regime/operating state possessing two distinct stable equilibria — consolidated wake and consolidated sleep — separated by an unstable boundary) and hysteresis, preventing intermediate, erratic state transitions in healthy physiology [39, 33, 27]. When orexinergic stabilization is lost, as observed in narcoleptic canine and human brains lacking prepro-orexin peptides [26, 9, 11, 37], the bistable switch undergoes rapid, involuntary transitions. At the cellular and network scale, computational neuroscience has explored the ionic and synaptic mechanisms underlying sleep rhythms using conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley and LIF models 2

Thalamocortical loops produce low-frequency delta oscillations (0.5–4.0 Hz) through hyperpolarization-activated cation currents (inward ionic currents carried by positively charged ions such as Na+ and Ca2+, specifically hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated currents Ih and low-threshold T-type calcium channels IT ) during deep N3 sleep [12, 36]. These currents interact to generate sleep spindles (transient 12.0–16.0 Hz waxing-and-waning oscillatory bursts lasting 0.5–2.0 s generated by reciprocal interactions between thalamic reticular interneurons and thalamocortical relay cells) during stage N2 sleep [12, 36]. In primary insomnia, quantitative EEG analyses demonstrate an elevated presence of high-frequency beta (15.0–30.0 Hz) and gamma activity during NREM sleep [25, 20], supporting the neurobiological hyperarousal model formulated by Riemann et al. [30]. However, existing SNN models typically simulate isolated windows of several seconds or minutes, lacking coupling to continuous multi-day homeostatic and circadian drivers. DyssomniaNN bridges this division by driving recurrent corticothalamic LIF networks via continuous hypothalamic and homeostatic inputs over multi-day trajectories. 3 Biophysical Framework The architecture of DyssomniaNN comprises three interconnected hierarchical layers depicted in Figure 1: homeostatic-circadian regulation, hypothalamic bistable switching, and a recurrent corticothalamic SNN. text: 3.1 Two-Process Homeostatic and Circadian Model Homeostatic sleep pressure S(t) ∈[0, 1] represents the neurochemical accumulation and clearance of endogenous somnogens (naturally occurring biochemical compounds synthesized within the central nervous system that promote sleepiness — primarily extracellular adenosine, inflammatory cytokines, and prostaglandin D2). Neurochemical assays (in vivo microdialysis and electrochemical biosensor measurements of interstitial brain fluid) demonstrate that extracellular adenosine accumulates in the basal forebrain and cerebral cortex during wakefulness as a consequence of sustained metabolic consumption of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) by active neurons and astrocytes (star-shaped non-neuronal glial cells that regulate synaptic transmission, clear neurotransmitters, and release adenosine via gliotransmission) [29, 2]. During sleep, astrocytic reuptake and enzymatic breakdown by adenosine deaminase rapidly reduce extracellular adenosine concentrations [29]. This configuration places the hypothalamic switch firmly within the bistable regime, establishing two distinct stable attractors: a consolidated wake state (A ≈1, V ≈0) and a consolidated sleep state (V ≈1, A ≈0), separated by an unstable threshold manifold. This non-equilibrium bistability generates wide hysteresis (the dependence of the state of the system on its prior history, meaning greater excitatory drive is needed to switch states than to maintain an existing state), ensuring that behavioral transitions are decisive and resistant to baseline fluctuations [32, 33]. Fast action potentials produce an inward sodium current flanked symmetrically by outward potassium currents, creating an opposing quadrupolar current configuration. The electric fields of these quadrupoles decay rapidly with distance as 1/r3, resulting in extensive spatial cancellation and negligible contributions to macroscopic recordings. In contrast, synchronized postsynaptic currents flowing into the aligned apical dendrites of layer V pyramidal neurons (large excitatory projection neurons whose elongated dendrites span multiple cortical layers perpendicular to the brain surface) create an open sink-source current configuration that acts as a current dipole. The electric fields of current dipoles decay more slowly as 1/r2 and sum coherently across large cortical assemblies, dominating both the local field potential (LFP) recorded within tissue and scalp EEG signals [23, 6, 21]. Accordingly, the synthetic LFP is modeled by convolving the network’s aggregate spiking events with an alpha-function postsynaptic dendritic response kernel h(t): LFP(t) = 1 N N X i=1 Z ∞ 0 h(τ)si(t −τ) dτ, h(t) = t τdend e−t/τdend, (13) where τdend = 4.0 ms encapsulates dendritic cable low-pass filtering and the extracellular resistive- capacitive impedance of cortical tissue [6, 21]. text: Chronic [Psychophysiological] Insomnia. Models conditioned cognitive and auto- nomic hyperarousal [30]. Chronic insomnia patients exhibit elevated sympathetic nervous activity, increased nocturnal cortisol secretion, and higher whole-body metabolic rates [30]. In DyssomniaNN, this allostatic load (the cumulative physiological wear and tear resulting from sustained neuroen- docrine and autonomic hyperactivation) is parameterized by a chronic depolarizing arousal bias (Iarousal = +0.60 pA). Concurrently, subcortical sleep-inducing strength is compromised by reducing VLPO inhibitory efficacy to wav = 0.95 [33, 30]. Because wav · wva = 0.95 × 2.0 = 1.9, the flip-flop switch remains above the critical bifurcation point (0.8) but operates close to the boundary, making the sleep attractor (the stable equilibrium state corresponding to consolidated sleep in phase space) shallow and vulnerable to spontaneous awakenings. Cohort 3: Paradoxical Insomnia (Sleep State Misperception). Characterized by a dissociation between subcortical sleep staging and cortical spectral activity [14, 20]. Subcortical hypothalamic parameters remain identical to the healthy control cohort (∆ϕ = 0.0 h, Ωtone = 1.0, wav = 2.1). However, proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) studies in insomnia patients docu- ment substantial (20%–30%) reductions in cortical GABA concentrations [28]. In our model, this is formalized by scaling cortical interneuron synaptic gain down to γinh = 0.25. This selective cortical disinhibition prevents the suppression of fast recurrent synaptic currents during slow-wave sleep, generating pathological high-frequency

text: Cohort 4: Narcolepsy Type 1. Models the selective autoimmune destruction of approximately 70,000 hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons in the posterolateral hypothalamus (in which autoreac- tive cytotoxic T-lymphocytes target and destroy hypocretin-synthesizing cells in genetically suscepti- ble individuals carrying the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele) [26, 37, 11, 34]. In clinical practice, definitive diagnosis requires CSF orexin-A concentrations ≤110 pg/mL (over 90% reduction relative to nor- mal) [11, 34]. This deficit is formalized by setting Ωtone = 0.05. In addition, the lack of orexinergic stabilization on REM-off monoaminergic nuclei disinhibits brainstem REM-generating structures such as the sublaterodorsal nucleus [9, 24]. This is parameterized by lowering the REM entry latency threshold from θrem = 70.0 min down to θrem = 5.0 min, reproducing diagnostic sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) observed on the Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) [11, 3]. text: Inference 1: Dissociation Between TST and Restorative Alertness The simulation data provides a quantitative demonstration of the divergence between objective sleep quantity and sleep quality. As detailed in Table 2 and illustrated in Figure 4, the Paradoxical Insomnia cohort achieved an objective TST (21.15 h, 7.05 h/night), SOL (29 min), nocturnal WASO (172 min), and cycle count (13 cycles) identical to the healthy normal control. However, its Well-Rested Index collapsed from 86.4% (Optimal) to 37.6% (Non-Restorative) — the lowest in the entire study. Because subcortical hypothalamic switching operates normally while cortical interneuron inhibition is impaired (γinh = 0.25), the LIF network sustains waking-level high-frequency beta activity (Pβ ≈0.70) throughout stage N3 sleep [25, 20]. Consequently, as shown in Figure 4C, the model’s internal subjective wakefulness meter remains elevated at 85%–95% during objective slow-wave sleep. Macro-architectural PSG alone fails to detect state misperception unless paired with spectral decomposition of high-frequency cortical hyperarousal. 10

(B) Concurrent PSG hypnograms scored via AASM criteria (W=Wake, N1–N3=NREM stages, R=REM), displaying physiological 90-minute ultradian cycling in normal sleep, prolonged nocturnal awakenings in chronic insomnia, and daytime sleep attacks in narcolepsy. 6.2 Inference 2: Circadian Desynchrony and the Phase-Shifted Clearance Deficit In the CRSWD cohort, a +4.0 h phase shift in the endogenous pacemaker delayed the circadian nadir until 10:00 (see Figure 2A). Although the model accumulated 16.63 h of sleep, its Well-Rested Index was restricted to 47.9%. The delay forced sleep episodes past the 06:30 dawn threshold into ambient sunlight (10,000 lux). The photic stimulation provoked premature LHA activation, causing elevated nocturnal latency (SOL = 99 min), fragmented sleep continuity (WASO = 454 min), and incomplete homeostatic clearance (Snadir ≈0.38 versus 0.18 in controls) [31, 38]. 11

The normal control displays sharp, bistable transitions with pronounced hysteresis. In contrast, narcolepsy type 1 exhibits crippled LHA tone (Ωtone = 0.05), inducing state instability, nocturnal sleep fragmentation, and involuntary daytime transitions. 6.3 Inference 3: Loss of Bistable Boundary Hysteresis in Hypocretin Deficiency In the Narcolepsy Type 1 cohort, hypocretinergic tone was reduced to Ωtone = 0.05. The model accumulated the largest aggregate sleep duration of all groups (26.18 h, 36.4% of observation time), yet achieved only a 48.2% restorative score. Inspection of subcortical trajectories in Figure 3 reveals that without orexinergic stabilization, the flip-flop switch loses hysteresis. The LHA cannot maintain sustained firing against VLPO inhibition, causing nocturnal sleep to shatter into recurrent awakenings (WASO = 781 min). During daylight hours, the lack of wake stabilization produces involuntary sleep attacks. Furthermore, the relaxation of REM threshold kinetics generated 35 diagnostic SOREMPs [11, 3]. (C) Subjective wakefulness meter, showing that persistent cortical hyperarousal induces a perceived wakefulness state of 85%–100% despite objective electrophysiological sleep. 7 Discussion and In Silico Pharmacology The multi-scale architecture of DyssomniaNN provides a versatile computational platform for in silico pharmacological investigation (i.e., investigations performed via computer simulation, in contrast to in vivo biological testing and in vitro laboratory preparations): • Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists (DORAs): Compounds such as suvorexant and lem- borexant promote sleep by blocking OX1 and OX2 receptors [34]. In DyssomniaNN, this mechanism corresponds to attenuating Ωtone and reducing Iarousal. In DyssomniaNN, elevating Ωtone from 0.05 toward 0.80 restores flip-flop bistability, suppressing daytime SOREMPs and consolidating nocturnal sleep. • Positive Allosteric GABA-A Modulators: In paradoxical insomnia, pharmacologically augmenting the cortical inhibition scale

Future extensions will incorporate multi-area spatial connectivity (frontal, central, occipital) to capture traveling slow waves and topographic spindle gradients. Furthermore, while the Saper flip- flop captures the primary wake-sleep switch, modeling REM sleep via extended sublaterodorsal (SLD) and ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) networks will refine micro-architectural REM transitions [24]. 7.2

text: A strong potential avenue for future development is the integration of formal pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) modeling into the simulation pipeline. Current simulated drug effects are parameterized as static shifts in model variables (such as altering Ωtone or γinh). Incorporating compartmental pharmacokinetic models will allow explicit simulation of drug absorption, distribution volumes, metabolic clearance rates, and biological half-lives. This capability would enable virtual clinical trials that compare compound release kinetics (such as immediate-release versus extended- release hypnotic formulations) and predict nocturnal efficacy alongside morning residual sedation. Furthermore, DyssomniaNN provides a foundation for personalized computational medicine in sleep disorders. By fitting individual patients’ physiological parameters (∆ϕ, τr, τd, γinh, Iarousal) to ambulatory data from consumer wearables, actigraphy, and longitudinal home EEG headbands, the framework can be customized to generate patient-specific digital twins. Clinicians could test virtual therapeutic interventions in silico, optimizing chronotherapeutic schedules (such as light therapy timing and melatonin dosing) and identifying targeted pharmacotherapies tailored to an individual’s specific neurochemical phenotype before initiating clinical regimens. 14

text: DyssomniaNN establishes an end-to-end multi-scale biophysical framework that bridges molecular, subcortical, and cortical mechanisms of human sleep regulation. By uniting Borbély’s two-process homeostatic and circadian drivers with Saper’s hypothalamic mutual inhibitory flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic LIF network, the model reproduces the multi-day electrophysiological and architectural signatures of diverse human sleep pathologies across a standardized 72-hour photoperiod. Synthetic LFPs generated by the spiking network exhibit close convergence against empirical human PSG spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical EEG frequency bands, confirming that the simulated macroscale dynamics emerge directly from biophysically parameterized neuronal interactions. The multi-cohort simulations resolve the long-standing discordance between objective sleep duration and subjective sleep quality. In paradoxical insomnia, normal macroscale PSG architecture and sleep duration (21.15 h) coexist with severe restorative impairment (R = 37.6%), driven by cortical disinhibition and unsuppressed high-frequency beta intrusions during slow-wave sleep. In narcolepsy type 1, the destruction of orexinergic stabilization collapses subcortical flip-flop hysteresis, producing severe sleep-state fragmentation, nocturnal wakefulness (WASO = 781 min), and daytime SOREMPs despite elevated aggregate sleep volume (26.18 h). Total sleep time represents an incomplete proxy for restorative sleep in the presence of cortical hyperarousal or subcortical boundary instability. DyssomniaNN provides a rigorous computational testbed for evaluating targeted neuropharmaco- logical interventions. By formalizing targeted neurochemical perturbations, including hypocretin loss, preoptic disinhibition, and cortical GABAergic hypofunction, the framework enables predictive evaluation of targeted pharmacological interventions such as dual orexin receptor antagonists and orexin agonists prior to clinical implementation. text: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? Two Reasons for Shrinking Importance Estimates in Continual Learning SAURAV K. ARYAL, Howard University, USA Regularization-based continual learning protects each parameter in proportion to an estimate of its importance, yet these estimates come from finite samples and heuristics and are used as if they were exact. We report four studies that start from a biologically inspired mechanism and end with a statistical explanation of it. Motivated by dendritic nanotubes, we let transient lateral links diffuse importance tags between hidden units. Links between co-active units gave no significant gain, but random links with lifetimes of 25 or 200 steps raised final accuracy on 20-task Permuted MNIST by 1.5 to 2.6 points. We show that random diffusion implements linear shrinkage of importance toward the layer mean in expectation. A simulation of the link process alone predicts shrinkage weights of 0.23 and 0.52 for these lifetimes, and graph-free shrinkage at 0.25 and 0.5 reproduces both the accuracy and the dispersion of the consolidated importance, while every activity-dependent rule did worse than random links. A five-seed screen across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task-incremental Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on
title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes?

text: across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task-incremental Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on Permuted MNIST. For EWC, the gain fell by about ten points per tenfold increase in samples, from 19.6 points with 10 samples to −0.4 with 1000, a variance effect. For MAS, a gain of about one point persisted at 1000 samples, consistent with a bias in the importance measure rather than noise. Shrinkage had no detectable effect for MAS on a domain-incremental CIFAR-100 benchmark. Finally, we show that a standard heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule shrinks the largest Fisher-type estimates most, which may explain its poor results, and point to a log-scale alternative. text: Neural networks trained on a sequence of tasks tend to overwrite what they learned before, a failure known as catastrophic forgetting [13, 29]. Regularization-based methods address it by anchoring each parameter near its value after earlier tasks, with a strength proportional to an estimate of that parameter’s importance. Elastic weight consolidation (EWC) uses the diagonal of the Fisher information [20], synaptic intelligence (SI) accumulates each parameter’s contribution to the decrease of the loss along the training path [43], and memory aware synapses (MAS) measure how strongly the network output depends on each parameter [3]. In all three, the importance vector is the method’s entire account of what should be preserved. These vectors are estimates, and noisy ones. EWC is usually computed from a modest number of single-example gradients, SI from correlated steps of one optimization trajectory, and MAS from output gradients on a sample of inputs. How the Fisher information is computed changes the performance of EWC substantially [40], and the empirical Fisher differs systematically from the true one [22, 28]. Yet the methods treat the estimates as exact. Statistics has a standard response to estimating many quantities at once. When three or more normal means are estimated together, shrinking the individual estimates by a suitable amount toward a common value lowers the expected total squared error [16, 39], and

When three or more normal means are estimated together, shrinking the individual estimates by a suitable amount toward a common value lowers the expected total squared error [16, 39], and empirical Bayes methods choose the amount of shrinkage from the data [11]. text: 2 S. K. Aryal The simplest shrinkage operator is familiar under another name. Pulling every importance value toward its group mean by a fixed fraction adds to the method’s own penalty an L2 penalty toward the anchor that is uniform within each group, and L2 penalties of this kind are a standard baseline [20]. To our knowledge, however, nobody has studied systematically when and why shrinking importance estimates helps in regularization-based continual learning. We did not start from statistics. This work began with a biological observation. Chang et al. [7] identified dendritic nanotubes, thin tubes that connect the dendrites of neighboring neurons, in mammalian cortex. In dissociated neurons these actin-rich tubes propagated calcium over long distances, and they actively transported small molecules and amyloid-𝛽. Calcium signals gate synaptic plasticity [27], and synaptic tagging and capture describes how a local tag decides which synaptic changes become permanent [12, 34]. A channel that moves plasticity signals between neurons is therefore a natural candidate for a cross-cellular consolidation mechanism. We implemented the idea as transient lateral links that diffuse importance tags between the hidden units of a layer and tested it on Permuted MNIST. Several methods assign importance to units rather than to single weights [1, 17], which is the granularity of our Studies 1 and 2. Bayesian approaches make the uncertainty of each parameter explicit, through structured Laplace approximations [36], variational inference [10, 30], or metaplasticity that scales learning by synaptic uncertainty [6]. Benzing [5] showed that the importance measures of SI and MAS are closely related to the square root of the Fisher information, a relation we return to in Section 6. 2.2 Estimating importance Each importance measure is an estimate, and the estimators differ in how much noise and bias they carry. The diagonal Fisher can be computed with labels sampled from the model, which gives the true Fisher, or with the observed labels, which gives the empirical Fisher, and the two can differ sharply [22, 28]. van de Ven [40] showed that how EWC computes the Fisher, including the number of samples, has a large effect on its performance. Importance estimates also become less reliable when data are noisy or shift between tasks. In EEG-based emotion recognition, Peire et al. [33] found that importance heuristics degraded under noise and covariate shift and that importance accumulated over tasks over-constrained the model.

None of these works shrinks the estimates. 2.3 Shrinkage and empirical Bayes When three or more independent normal means with a common known variance are estimated together, the vector of sample means is inadmissible under total squared error. Shrinking it by a suitable amount toward a fixed point lowers the expected total error for every value of the means [16, 39], and the same holds for shrinkage toward the average of the estimates when there are four or more. Empirical Bayes reads such estimators as posterior means under a prior whose spread is estimated from the data, which sets the shrinkage weight automatically [11]. Shrinkage of the same kind regularizes large covariance matrices [25]. In our setting the means are the importance values of individual parameters or units, and the common value is their mean within a layer or a parameter tensor. Importance estimates are neither normal nor equally noisy, so these results motivate shrinkage rather than guarantee that it helps. 2.4 Biological motivation Synaptic tagging and capture proposes that a transient local tag marks the synapses whose changes may

text: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? 7 4 Experimental Design 4.1 Benchmarks and models Permuted MNIST (P-MNIST). Twenty tasks built from MNIST [24], the first with the original pixel order and each of the others with a fixed random permutation of the pixels [13]. All tasks share one 10-way output layer, so the protocol is domain-incremental [41]. The network is a multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers of 256 ReLU units. Studies 1 and 2 train on all 60,000 training images and report test accuracy over a grid of 𝜆. Studies 3 and 4 hold out 10% of the training images for validation and select 𝜆on validation accuracy only. Split CIFAR-100 (Study 3). Ten tasks of ten CIFAR-100 classes each in a fixed class order [21], with a separate 10-way head per task, a task-incremental protocol. The heads are not regularized. CIFAR-100 superclass (Study 4). Five tasks. Task 𝑘contains the 𝑘-th fine class of each of the 20 superclasses, and the label is the superclass, predicted by one shared 20-way head. Unlike the multi-head split, this domain-incremental protocol leaves substantial room for forgetting. All parameters are regularized. Both CIFAR benchmarks use a convolutional network with four 3 × 3 convolutional layers of 32, 32, 64, and 64 channels with padding 1 and ReLU activations, 2 × 2 max pooling
title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes?

text: substantial room for forgetting. All parameters are regularized. Both CIFAR benchmarks use a convolutional network with four 3 × 3 convolutional layers of 32, 32, 64, and 64 channels with padding 1 and ReLU activations, 2 × 2 max pooling after the second and fourth, and a fully connected layer of 256 ReLU units, without batch normalization. Inputs are standardized per channel with training-set statistics, and we use no data augmentation. The CIFAR networks train for five epochs per task with batches of 64, and the P-MNIST networks for three epochs per task with batches of 128. Unless stated otherwise we use Adam with learning rate 10−3 [19], reset at the start of each task, and add the gradient of the penalty to the task gradient. After 20 tasks, pruning had removed all but 1.1% of the lateral weights, and the network matched the plain MLP (ACC 32.3% against 32.6%), while the parameter-matched wider MLP did slightly better (35.1%). The surviving density depends on the L1 penalty, the pruning threshold, and the length of training, since a 3-task pilot kept 37%, so it says nothing about how many connections biology uses. Without consolidation all three networks forgot almost everything, with BWT between −65 and −68 points. Consolidation dominated everything else, lifting ACC from about 33% to between 73% and 80%. When importance comes from few samples, as with EWC at 𝑛= 10 or 50, the estimates are noisy and heavy-tailed, the penalty concentrates on the parameters that happened to receive large values, and shrinkage spreads protection back out. Its benefit then disappears as samples accumulate, and too much shrinkage hurts. When the importance measure is precise but miscalibrated for retention, as MAS appears to be on P-MNIST, a small fixed weight helps
title: S. K. Aryal

text: and shrinkage spreads protection back out. Its benefit then disappears as samples accumulate, and too much shrinkage hurts. When the importance measure is precise but miscalibrated for retention, as MAS appears to be on P-MNIST, a small fixed weight helps at every sample size. Fixed shrinkage mixes the importance- weighted penalty with a uniform one within each group, 𝜆Í 𝑖[(1−𝛽)Ω𝑖+ 𝛽¯Ω𝐺(𝑖)](𝜃𝑖−𝜃∗ 𝑖)2, where ¯Ω𝐺(𝑖) is the mean importance of the group that contains parameter 𝑖. It therefore adds an L2 floor that limits the cumulative drift of parameters that every task rates as unimportant. That reading fits the finding that MAS approximates the square root of the Fisher information [5], a profile that is already flattened relative to EWC, but the floor is a hypothesis we did not test directly.

text: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? 15 The distinction suggests a practical check. Compare the unshrunk method at two sample sizes. If it improves with more samples, the problem is variance, and the remedy is more samples or shrinkage that adapts to 𝑛. If it does not, a fixed shrinkage weight chosen on validation data is worth trying as a second hyperparameter beside 𝜆. 6.2 Why the empirical Bayes rule did not deliver EB moved in the right direction for the variance effect, shrinking hard when 𝑛was small and little when it was large, yet it lost to a fixed weight at small 𝑛and to no shrinkage at large 𝑛. Proposition 3.2 suggests one reason. For Fisher-type estimates the sampling noise is multiplicative, so the heteroscedastic rule assigns its largest weights to the largest estimates. It pulls the most important parameters toward the mean and leaves the rest almost untouched, which removes protection from the parameters with the largest estimated importance. A log-scale rule would shrink every estimate by the same factor in log space, a power transform of the importance whose exponent approaches one as 𝑛grows. We expect such a rule to keep the adaptivity of EB to 𝑛without concentrating shrinkage on the largest estimates, and testing it is the obvious next experiment. For MAS, where much of

text: the importance whose exponent approaches one as 𝑛grows. We expect such a rule to keep the adaptivity of EB to 𝑛without concentrating shrinkage on the largest estimates, and testing it is the obvious next experiment. For MAS, where much of the benefit at large 𝑛does not come from noise, a variance-driven rule cannot recover it, and the EB weights of Study 4 were indeed near zero for 𝑛≥50. At 𝑛= 10, where EB shrank as much on average as the fixed weight and still lost accuracy, the allocation again appears to be the problem. 6.3 Shrinkage trades plasticity for stability Because every task has a fixed protection budget, shrinkage moves protection from high-importance to low-importance parameters, and the latter are the ones new tasks would otherwise use freely. Shrinkage lowered learning accuracy in most cells of Studies 3 and 4, a form of the intransigence that consolidation penalties are known to cause [8]. It therefore pays when forgetting is the bottleneck, as on P-MNIST with a shared head, where BWT without shrinkage ranged from −8 to −13 points in Study 3, and it costs accuracy when forgetting is not, as on the multi-head Split CIFAR-100, where BWT ranged from −0.9 to −1.6 points. The CIFAR-100 superclass benchmark has plenty of forgetting but showed no detectable effect for MAS, possibly because
title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes?

text: 3, and it costs accuracy when forgetting is not, as on the multi-head Split CIFAR-100, where BWT ranged from −0.9 to −1.6 points. The CIFAR-100 superclass benchmark has plenty of forgetting but showed no detectable effect for MAS, possibly because the selected penalty was weak there. 6.4 What remains of the nanotube idea Our results give no support to the hypothesis that activity-dependent exchange of plasticity signals improves consolidation. The biologically motivated rules never beat random links, and random links appear to help because, in expectation, they implement a statistical correction that needs no graph at all. The results do establish a weaker fact that may still be useful. Any mass-conserving exchange of plasticity signals between randomly paired units acts as shrinkage of noisy importance, with a strength set by how many links are alive and how long they last. Whether biological nanotubes form at random with respect to plasticity signals is an empirical question that these experiments cannot answer. The same logic matters for applied continual learning with noisy, subject-specific data. In EEG- based emotion recognition, importance heuristics degrade under noise and covariate shift [33], and fixed or log-scale shrinkage of importance is a cheap intervention to test in that setting. 6.5 Limitations • The networks and benchmarks are small, a two-layer MLP and a four-layer CNN on MNIST

text: The question in our title has a short answer. Links that follow activity, the feature we borrowed from dendritic nanotubes, did not help our networks, while random links did, because in expectation they shrink noisy importance estimates. A biologically inspired mechanism for sharing plasticity signals between neurons thus turned out, in its only working form, to be a shrinkage estimator in disguise. Taking that seriously led to a simple intervention for regularization-based continual learning, shrinking importance estimates toward their mean, and to a test that separates two reasons it helps. On Permuted MNIST, for EWC with few samples it reduces variance, and its benefit vanishes as samples grow. For MAS it also corrects something that more samples do not remove, which we read as bias. The heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule we tried shrinks the largest Fisher-type estimates most, and a log-scale rule is the natural next step. Importance estimates are estimates, and treating them as such adds almost no computation.

text: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to re- alise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential — but obtaining the gradient that de- scent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model’s FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR- 10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropaga- tion: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation’s parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge

To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilib- rium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architec- ture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation. 1
