text: Modern generative models are expensive to train (Strubell et al., 2019) and expensive to sam- ple (Luccioni et al., 2024): diffusion, flow matching and related methods typically produce one image by integrating a velocity field over hundreds of sequential steps, each a full pass through a large network. Sequential work of this kind suits a GPU poorly and a physical system well. A substrate that relaxes to the minimum of an energy performs in one continuous settling what a GPU performs as hundreds of discrete evaluations, and analog neuromorphic devices promise large gains in speed and energy on that basis. Two things stand in the way: finding a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and removing the backpropagation that training relies on. Energy Matching (Balcerak et al., 2025) is one such algorithm. It generates by gradient descent on a potential Vθ(x), the scalar output of a feedforward network, whose minima are where the data lies. The potential does not change with time, so every step descends the same fixed landscape, which is what a physical system does when it relaxes. But the velocity it follows is −∇xVθ, and in its original formulation obtaining that gradient is a backward pass — once per integration step during sampling, on top of the usual ∇θL backward pass per training step. A backpropagation-free algorithm is of little use if the architecture it trains is itself hard to realise in analog, and two components of the one we inherit from Energy Matching are: group normalisation, which couples every channel through a shared statistic, and attention, whose pairwise products are not a fixed weighted sum. We find that removing both costs nothing measurable at this scale — a network of only convolutions, pointwise nonlinearities and UNet skips, every operation of the kind an analog crossbar performs natively, reaches a CIFAR-10 FID of 3.51 (Section 5.1). 2

text: 2.1 ENERGY MATCHING Energy Matching (Balcerak et al., 2025) generates images by relaxation on a learned scalar potential. A feedforward network with a scalar output defines Vθ(x) = α Fθ(x), (1) where Fθ(x) is the network output and α a fixed output scale set by the architecture, and samples are produced by integrating ˙x = −∇xVθ(x) from noise. Unlike diffusion or flow matching, the velocity field is the gradient of a time-independent potential: the same landscape is descended at every step, and the model’s minima are where the data lies. Training has two phases. The first is flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) on exact optimal-transport couplings (Tong et al., 2024): for a noise sample x0 paired with a data sample x1, an interpolant xt = (1 −t)x0 + tx1 with t ∼U[0, 1), and a target velocity u = x1 −x0, the loss is L(θ) = 1 2 −∇xVθ(xt) −u 2. (2) The coupling is needed because the field −∇xVθ is time-independent and curl-free by construction, while the marginal velocity it is asked to match need be neither; pairing each x0 with its transport- optimal x1 reduces the overlap between conditional trajectories, so that the marginal they define is 2

The second phase adds a contrastive term, ∇θV (x+) − ∇θV (x−) between data samples and model samples produced by a short Langevin chain. We refer to these throughout as phases 1 and 2. Sampling integrates dx = −∇xVθ(x) dτ + p ϵ(τ) dW (3) to a stopping time τs, with the noise ϵ switched off below τ = 1 and held at a fixed level beyond it: up to τ = 1 it is a noiseless ODE transporting noise to data, and beyond that a Langevin chain at fixed temperature. Because the landscape does not change with time, integrating past τ = 1 is further equilibration rather than extrapolation into an untrained regime, as it would be for a time- conditioned flow-matching model, so τs is a free parameter, chosen per model over a ladder of values (App. J). 2.2 PREDICTIVE CODING NETWORKS A predictive coding network (Rao & Ballard, 1999; Whittington & Bogacz, 2017) assigns a dynam- ical variable hk to each node of a feedforward architecture and an energy to the mismatch between each node and the prediction made of it by its predecessor: E = N X k=1 1 2 fk(hk−1) −hk 2, ek = fk(hk−1) −hk. (4) Inference is not a forward pass but a relaxation: with the input h0 = x clamped, the states descend E to a stationary point, and outputs are read from the settled state. Two properties of that stationary state are what Section 3.1 builds on. First, with only error terms present the minimum is e = 0, which by induction from h0 = x is exactly the forward pass: left to itself the relaxation reproduces the feedforward network it was built from. Second, stationarity ∂E/∂hk = 0 at an interior node gives ek = J⊤ k+1ek+1 with Jk+1 = ∂fk+1/∂hk, so any error introduced at the top propagates downwards through transposed Jacobians. Each term of equation 4 involves only a node and its predecessor, so both the relaxation and the parameter gradients ∂E/∂θk = e⊤ k ∂fk/∂θk are local: every quantity a weight needs is present at its two ends. This is what makes predictive coding a candidate for analog implementation, where the relaxation is performed by the physics rather than simulated. 2.3 EQUILIBRIUM PROPAGATION Equilibrium Propagation (Scellier & Bengio, 2017; Laborieux et al., 2020) is an alternative learning algorithm to

text: is what makes predictive coding a candidate for analog implementation, where the relaxation is performed by the physics rather than simulated. 2.3 EQUILIBRIUM PROPAGATION Equilibrium Propagation (Scellier & Bengio, 2017; Laborieux et al., 2020) is an alternative learning algorithm to backpropagation for systems whose dynamics settle to stationary points, from which their outputs are read. It uses only local measurements at equilibrium, making it a natural candidate for neuromorphic hardware. Consider a system with state s, parameters θ and energy E(s; θ), relaxing to an equilibrium s∗ whose position we want to train so that the outputs reduce a cost C(s). Adding βC(s) to the energy displaces that equilibrium towards lower cost, and the parameter gradient can be read from where and how far it moves. Each training sample therefore takes three phases: a free phase relaxing to s∗, then two nudged phases relaxing E ±βC to s∗±β, at lower and higher cost respectively. text: PCN needs no nudge at all. 3.2.1 THE LINEARISED NUDGE GradEP’s cost is the loss as a function of the visible state, C(x) = 1 2∥v(x) −u∥2, and being quadratic in x, its nudge acts as a second spring (of strength β) against the tether (of strength λ). Balancing the two forces gives a nudged equilibrium x∗β −x∗= −βγg/λ(λ + β), with g = v∗−u (App. C), which is nonlinear in β. The ±β displacements are therefore asymmetric about the free equilibrium, and the centred difference equation 11 acquires an O((β/λ)2) bias. This is standard EP’s weak-nudge requirement, with the tether’s λ in place of an ordinary network’s O(1) curvature. At λ = 1 it caps β near one, which is restrictive since the displacement the parameter update is read from scales with βγ and must stay resolvable in finite-precision arithmetic, while γ must stay small for the correspondence. We therefore instead nudge with the loss’s linearisation at the free equilibrium, as in Dual Prop- agation (Høier et al., 2023): freezing g after the free phase and taking Clin(x) = g⊤v(x), which targets the same parameter gradient but adds no curvature in x. Two components we inherit from Energy Matching are not easily realised on an analog substrate: group normalisation, which couples every channel at a layer through a shared statistic, and attention, whose pairwise products are not a fixed weighted sum. We therefore ask how much generation quality is lost when both are removed. Replacing them with weight standardisation, which normalises each filter’s weights rather than its activations, residual scaling by 1/√depth, and a flat linear head in place of the ViT (App. I) leaves an architecture with no operation beyond fixed weighted sums and pointwise nonlinearities — both native to

text: Predictive coding. Generative predictive coding typically places the image at the bottom of a hierarchy of predictions: Monte Carlo predictive coding samples it by adding Langevin noise to inference, at MNIST scale (Oliviers et al., 2024), and Langevin predictive coding samples a latent code the same way and decodes it, reaching CIFAR-10 at FID 113 (Zahid et al., 2023). In both, the image is the predicted layer of a prediction-error likelihood. In ours it is the input of a network whose scalar output is an explicit potential, and the force on it is that potential’s gradient. 9

text: Preprint. Under review. Generation by energy descent. Energy Matching (Balcerak et al., 2025), which we build on, generates by descent on an explicit scalar potential. Equilibrium Matching (Wang & Du, 2025) learns a time-invariant gradient field, in its best-performing form without an explicit energy, and Rodriguez et al. (2026) train it on an Energy Transformer, whose blocks relax latent tokens on a Hopfield-type energy, reaching class-conditional FID 28.56 on CIFAR-10. There the image-space update is a learned function of the relaxed tokens rather than the gradient of any energy in x; in ours it is the gradient of γ−1EPCN = Vθ + O(γ). Each of these works trains by backpropagation. Physical and neuromorphic generation. A parallel line generates with physical substrates. Sim- ulated Kuramoto oscillators (Unconventional AI, 2026) and continuous spins descending a learned quadratic energy (Sun et al., 2026) evolve a latent state from a random start and render it through a small convolutional decoder, reaching class-conditional CIFAR-10 FID 8.76 and clean-FID 9.71 respectively, the former also at ImageNet 64 × 64. Optical systems have implemented a diffusion model’s denoiser (Oguz et al., 2024) and a single-pass generator (Chen et al., 2025), demonstrated in hardware at MNIST scale, and spiking diffusion models target event-driven neuromorphic chips (Cao et al., 2024). All of these are trained by backpropagation. B¨osch et

Ours relaxes in image space with no decoder, and uses Equilibrium Propagation to obtain local updates for an energy with hidden layers. 7 DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS Simulation cost. On a GPU, an EP training step costs about sixteen times a backpropagation step, and an implicit-solve step about five, with the relaxation budgets dominating. A substrate that settles physically would not pay that cost, but its speed, energy and settling accuracy remain unmeasured: everything here is simulated. Locality and hardware realisation. The relaxation is local in the sense EP requires: every quan- tity a weight update needs is present at its two ends. The nodes of our training runs are, however, architecture blocks rather than single weight matrices, chosen to reduce simulation cost, so a literal implementation would need circuitry to carry the error through each block’s internal layers. One node per weight matrix removes this, and left the training gradient unchanged in the one checkpoint we measured (App. D).

Analog EP also obtains the backward drive J⊤e from a feedback pathway programmed to match the forward one; any drift between the two leaves dynamics that descend no energy at all (Kendall et al., 2020). Scope of the evidence. App. K collects the scope of each claim. Each arm is a single run, so train- ing variance is unknown, and the small FID differences do not establish a ranking. We demonstrate EP training on CIFAR-10 only; at ImageNet-32 we verify the inference correspondence on the au- thors’ released checkpoints, but did not train. The hardware-plausible architecture was trained and sampled only as a feedforward network, so it has not been demonstrated together with EP. The equi- libria were computed by noise-free digital relaxation in error coordinates; the local state dynamics share their fixed points (App. E) but were not run to equilibrium at this scale. Analog noise, finite bit depth and forward–backward pathway mismatch remain untested. 10

Five quantities appear in the training construction besides γ. The spring stiffness λ is not tuned: with the visible state updated as x ←x −dtx ∇xEfree, the spring extension contracts by (1−dtx λ) per sweep, up to the O(γ) curvature of EPCN in x (App. C), so λ dtx = 1 settles it in a single step, exactly as the error parameterisation settles h in one sweep; larger λ dtx overshoots. Phase 1 uses λ = 1, dtx = 1 and phase 2 uses λ = 2, dtx = 0.5 (App. J). The nudge strength β is the one parameter that must be chosen: it sets the displacement between the two nudged equi- libria, which must be large enough to resolve in finite-precision arithmetic and small enough for equation 11 to hold, a window Section 3.2.1 derives and Section 4.2 measures. D PREDICTIVE CODING ON A DAG D.1 FROM CHAINS TO DAGS Predictive coding networks are usually written on a chain, with node k predicted from node k −1 alone: Echain = N X k=1 1 2 fk(hk−1) −hk 2, (34) with h0 the clamped input. The UNet we adopt is not a chain: its decoder blocks consume a concatenation of their predecessor and a topologically distant encoder state, so a node may have several parents, and an encoder node several children. Predictive coding has been formulated on arbitrary computation graphs (Millidge et al., 2022), and we use that construction unchanged: nodes h1, . . . , hN are taken in topological order, each with a parent list pa(k), and E = N X k=1 1 2 fk �hpa(k)  −hk 2 + γα o, (35) with o = hN the scalar output node and γα the injection of Section 3.1. The prediction functions are the unmodified architecture blocks; where a node has several parents they are concatenated

D.2 RELAXATION DYNAMICS Writing ek = fk(hpa(k)) −hk and Jc,j = ∂fc/∂hj, each state evolves under ∂E ∂hj = −ej + X c ∈ch(j) J⊤ c,j ec + γα δjN, (36) the node’s own error term, the error term of every child that consumes it, and the output injection. In a chain ch(j) = {j + 1}; in the DAG a node with fan-out is driven by all its children at once, and stationarity is the multivariable chain rule (App. A). Every term lives on an edge of the graph, so locality is preserved. D.3 NODE GRANULARITY How a network is partitioned into nodes is a free choice. A node can be an architecture block — one residual block, one attention block, or the ViT head etc — in which case only the block’s output relaxes and its internal activations are computed feedforward inside fk; or it can be a single weight matrix and its activation, in which case every hidden activation relaxes.

(2026) and relax the prediction errors ek = fk(hpa(k))−hk, recovering states by the topological scan hk = fk(hpa(k))− ek. This is an invertible change of variables on the same energy, so the two parameterisations share their stationary points. Their curvature, however, is very different, and at the step sizes of a practical simulation only one of them converges in a usable number of sweeps. The error parameterisation is a simulation device rather than dynamics a substrate would run: ∂E/∂e is a reverse-mode derivative through the scan, and a single sweep from e = 0 at dt = 1 is one backward pass (Goemaere et al., 2026, Thm. Measured curvature. On the CIFAR-10 replication checkpoint at the operating γ = 10−4, power iteration on Hessian–vector products gives a largest Hessian eigenvalue µmax of 1.0001 in error coordinates and at least 8 × 104 in state coordinates. Gradient descent at step dt is stable only for dt < 2/µmax: below 2 in error coordinates, which admits the deadbeat step dt = 1, and below 2.4 × 10−5 in state coordinates. The state parameterisation is impractically slow. At dt = 1 the state relaxation diverges within a few sweeps, in float64 as in float32, so the failure is a dynamical instability rather than a precision floor. Below the stability bound it does converge, monotonically and to the same fixed point as the error relaxation, as a shared stationary point requires. But it converges at a measured rate implying a condition number of about 2×107: at dt = 2×10−5, reaching equilibrium takes of the order of 108 sweeps, against one in error coordinates. This cost is a property of the explicit discretisation rather than of the dynamics: a continuous system settles at the rate

text: 2×107: at dt = 2×10−5, reaching equilibrium takes of the order of 108 sweeps, against one in error coordinates. This cost is a property of the explicit discretisation rather than of the dynamics: a continuous system settles at the rate of its slowest mode, not its fastest, and Goemaere et al. (2026, App. B.5) make the same point, that the decay which makes discrete state updates slow is an artefact of time discretisation. Consequences. The error parameterisation is therefore not just a convenience but what makes the relaxation of this network practical. Three further properties follow from its near-identity Hessian, each measured elsewhere in the paper. The relaxation reaches equilibrium in a single deadbeat sweep from feedforward initialisation (App. F). The implicit-gradient solve of Section 3.2 inverts a matrix already close to the identity, so one conjugate-gradient step is as accurate as fifty (App. H). Finally, float32 suffices: at the operating γ the velocity’s deviation from autograd’s sits below the arithmetic’s own floor (Section 4.1). Part of the reason is that the error parameterisation never forms an error as the difference of two nearly equal states, which in state coordinates costs significant digits of precision in every error. The PCN relaxation velocities vPCN and the FFN autograd velocities vFFN are both evaluated in the stated arithmetic, and each saturates at its own floor. I THE HARDWARE-PLAUSIBLE ARCHITECTURE This appendix specifies the norm- and attention-free architecture of Section 5.1 in enough detail to reimplement, together with the training recipe it needed. It shows only that competitive generation is possible on an architecture an analog substrate could run, not that this particular architecture is the optimal one. We give our reasons for the individual choices where we have them, but which of them are necessary, and at what cost, we leave to future work. What was removed and what replaced it. The architecture is built from the Energy Match- ing UNet but with three changes. Firstly, all 51 group-normalisation layers are replaced by the identity. Secondly, all 6 attention blocks are replaced by the identity, which must be done on the built module tree rather than by configuration: the UNet’s middle block hardcodes ResBlock– Attention–ResBlock, so setting the attention resolutions alone cannot produce an attention-free net- work. Thirdly, the ViT head is replaced by a flat one, which flattens the UNet’s 3 × 32 × 32 output and applies Linear(3072, 512), SiLU, Linear(512, 1). We re-initialise the UNet’s final convolution from N(0, 0.02) rather than leaving it at the flow-matching codebase’s zero initialisation, after an earlier variant of the head failed to train from zero. We did not test whether the flat
title: Preprint. Under review.

text: Linear(512, 1). We re-initialise the UNet’s final convolution from N(0, 0.02) rather than leaving it at the flow-matching codebase’s zero initialisation, after an earlier variant of the head failed to train from zero. We did not test whether the flat head trains without this. Two further changes are made to the remaining convolutions and residual blocks. Firstly, weight standardisation (Qiao et al., 2020) replaces each convolution’s weights by ˆwi = gi wi σi √ fan-in + ϵ , σi = std(wi), (41) per output filter i, with gi a learned per-filter gain initialised to σi √ fan-in so that the reparameteri- sation is exactly the identity at initialisation. No mean subtraction is applied. It is applied to every convolution except the zero-initialised ones — therefore 42 convolutions are standardised and 23 are left plain on the built model. Those 23 are each ResBlock’s second convolution, zero-initialised by the flow-matching codebase so that every block starts as the identity; standardising an all-zero filter would leave both its weight and gain gradients at zero, so it could never leave that initialisa- tion. Secondly, residual scaling replaces each ResBlock’s output by skip + ρ (f(x) −skip) with ρ = 1/ √ 22 = 0.213, one over the square root of the number of ResBlocks (De & Smith, 2020). text: Secondly, residual scaling replaces each ResBlock’s output by skip + ρ (f(x) −skip) with ρ = 1/ √ 22 = 0.213, one over the square root of the number of ResBlocks (De & Smith, 2020). Nei- ther requires computation at inference: ˆw depends only on the weights, so a crossbar is programmed with it once and never recomputes a normalisation at runtime, and ρ is a wiring gain. The resolution-changing path needed no modification: downsampling is a stride-2 convolution rather than pooling, upsampling is nearest-neighbour interpolation followed by a stride-1 convolution, and both are weighted sums like any other convolution. Module census. The built model contains 42 standardised convolutions, 23 plain convolutions, 22 ResBlocks, 26 linear layers, 69 SiLU activations, and zero group-normalisation, attention or layer- normalisation modules, against 51, 14 and 16 of those respectively in the architecture it replaces. It carries 78.4M parameters against 50.0M, from the flat head’s 3072 × 512 first linear layer and a base channel width of 192 against 128, which widens every stage through the same multipliers. How we arrived at this configuration. We reached it by trial rather than by systematic search. Attention and the ViT head could each be removed without much cost, but removing normalisation made training diverge, and weight standardisation was what made the fully stripped network train- able.

A PCN training step evaluates the network many times: Tfree sweeps during the free phase and Tnudge in each nudged phase, each with Kh inner sweeps, where a feedforward step evaluates it once. C.9). That is a choice of simulation method: the claim of Sec- tion 3.1 is a property of the equilibrium, not of the route to it. The local state dynamics equation 36 share that equilibrium exactly and converge towards it (App. E), but too slowly under explicit dis- cretisation to run at this scale. What the paper establishes is that a state whose local errors carry −∇xV exists, that the parameter updates EP reads from it match backpropagation’s, and that train- ing on those updates works at CIFAR-10 scale. text: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem Vladimir Kirill Bickov Delft University of Technology, The Netherlands me@nevolodia.com Neil Yorke-Smith Delft University of Technology, The Netherlands n.yorke-smith@tudelft.nl
title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the

text: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent re- cursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recur- rently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy de- coding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing. 1
title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the

text: Solving a combinatorial optimization problem in a single, end-to-end pass of a neural network is inherently difficult. A learned model must navigate a constrained and exponentially large solution space with limited computation. Increasing network depth provides more computation, but also raises training and inference costs [1]. Neural-based routing methods commonly construct routes autoregressively or iteratively refine complete solutions [2–4]. Both approaches simplify the task by breaking the solution process into a series of simpler decisions. However, this simplicity comes at the cost of an information bottleneck. If only the updated solution is carried between iterations, information that exists only in the latent state, such as intermediate reasoning, is lost. This creates a form of representational ‘amnesia’ that makes it difficult to accumulate a richer understanding of the problem. Latent recursion avoids this bottleneck by carrying the internal state, rather than the candidate solution, between iterations. A solution can be decoded at any stage but is not fed back into the model: each subsequent stage continues directly from the preceding latent state. Every depth therefore produces both an intermediate computation and a valid solution point. Recent latent-recursive models perform strongly on Sudoku, maze solving, and ARC-AGI [5]. However, whether latent recursion transfers from supervised reasoning to reinforcement learning for graph combinatorial optimization remains unclear. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems

text: Figure 1: Overview of RELAGRAM. A CVRP instance is encoded as edge-token input x; the answer state y and workspace z start from fixed vectors. The shared transformer first updates z from x+y+z (red), then updates y from y +z (blue). Both states (y, z) are carried forward (magenta) in a recursive loop. A linear head maps yt to edge logits, which are decoded into a solution. We introduce RELAGRAM, a novel application of the latent recursion idea to graph combinatorial optimization, and demonstrate it on CVRP. After brief training, a 0.53M model reaches a 13.4% greedy gap on CVRP-100, reducing it to 8.3% under a 256-candidate search. On CVRP-1000, RELAGRAM achieves gaps of 29.9% and 21.7% under greedy and 256-candidate decoding, respectively. Notably, it continues to improve beyond its trained depth: on CVRP-1000 it achieves its best greedy gap of 28.45% at depth ten — six stages deeper than seen during training. 2

text: Latent recursion. Latent recursion applies the same network repeatedly to an internal state. The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) keeps two states: a solution state y and a latent reasoning state z. One cycle refines z over repeated passes conditioned on the input and on y, then updates y from the refined z; a supervision step chains several such cycles, all but the last without gradients. Deep supervision gives every step its own loss, and the states are detached between steps, so the model learns successive corrections without backpropagating across them. TRM achieves strong results on Sudoku, maze solving, and ARC-AGI benchmarks [5]. Edge heatmaps. An edge heatmap records the model’s confidence that each transition belongs to a high-quality solution. DIFUSCO produces such heatmaps for the travelling salesman problem by iteratively denoising edge variables [6]. However, DIFUSCO’s learned edge representation is separate from the procedure that converts it into a discrete solution. Feasible decoding. A heatmap is not itself a route. For CVRP, each decision must account for the visited customers and remaining vehicle capacity. The Attention Model, a neural routing model, constructs a route autoregressively, selecting one node at a time while masking infeasible actions [2]. DeepACO instead learns a heuristic measure for an ant colony optimization system: a population of simulated ants builds routes in parallel, each choosing only

text: model, constructs a route autoregressively, selecting one node at a time while masking infeasible actions [2]. DeepACO instead learns a heuristic measure for an ant colony optimization system: a population of simulated ants builds routes in parallel, each choosing only feasible transitions [7]. Learning from sampled routes. REINFORCE allows a routing policy to learn without optimal labels: complete routes are sampled, scored by their cost, and used to improve the policy [2, 8]. The signal is sparse, however, because one route-level reward must guide every edge decision made during construction. Self-imitation adds denser feedback: the lowest-cost sampled route serves as a temporary teacher, and a cross-entropy loss trains the heatmap to favour its transitions [9]. 3 RELAGRAM RELAGRAM brings latent recursion to routing. Between depths it passes its internal state rather than the route itself, so intermediate reasoning is never discarded (Figure 1). 2

text: Directed edge representation. RELAGRAM encodes a CVRP instance as sparse directed edge tokens. Each customer i connects to the depot and its k −1 nearest customers, while the depot connects to every customer; opposite directions are encoded independently. For each edge e = (i, j), the encoder collects nine features: the coordinates, demands, and depot indicators of i and j, and their Euclidean distance. A bias-free linear layer projects them to xe ∈Rd and scales by √ d. Recursion over edge tokens. RELAGRAM maintains answer and workspace states yt, zt, initial- ized as fixed random vectors y0, z0 ∈Rd. The network Fθ is a two-block transformer, each block applying self-attention and SwiGLU [10] sublayers with post-norm residuals and RMSNorm [11] without learned scale, as in TRM. At each depth, it updates z then y: zt = Fθ(zt−1 + yt−1 + x), yt = Fθ(yt−1 + zt). (1) A bias-free linear head maps yt,e to Ht,ij, the score of moving from i to j. Edges absent from the sparse encoding receive a logit of −10, providing a fallback when every encoded move is masked. Route decoding. Starting at the depot, the decoder constructs a route vertex by vertex. The row of Ht scores each move after masking visited and capacity-infeasible customers. Stochastic decoding samples the remaining logits; greedy takes the largest.

Self-imitation pulls the unmasked heatmap toward the shortest sampled route τ elite t using cross-entropy loss. We set λSI = 0.3; Θ represents trainable parameters. The model has 0.53M parameters and is trained at four depths. Runs use a batch size of 16 with 16 sampled routes per instance, which across the four recursion depths yields 1,024 routes per batch. We evaluate RELAGRAM under two training budgets: 40,000 optimizer updates with a training time of 2.98 hours to compare RELAGRAM with DeepACO; and 160,000 optimizer updates with a training time of 11.94 hours to assess performance and its scaling under a larger training budget. Training uses a 10 GB A100 GPU slice. DeepACO is chosen as our baseline because it is a competitive neural combinatorial optimizer with a similar design: a learned edge heatmap guides a separate solution search. DeepACO iterates through pheromone updates, whereas RELAGRAM updates latent states. We train it as a 0.52M-parameter model with the same k = 20 neighbour mask and optimizer updates matched to RELAGRAM’s 40,000. The models use similar numbers of training trajectories (9.60M for DeepACO and 10.24M for RELAGRAM), but the comparison is not compute-matched: DeepACO sees twice as many base graphs and takes 1.87 times longer to train. Solution quality across graph sizes. We evaluate RELAGRAM trained for 160,000 updates on CVRP-100. The model reaches an 8.30% gap on CVRP-100 under 256-candidate decoding (Table 1). Without retraining, the model achieves gaps of 15.64% and 21.65% on CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000 under 256-candidate decoding. On CVRP-1000, expanding one greedy decode to 256 candidates improves the gap from 29.91% to 21.65%. The decoder therefore offers test-time scaling that strengthens with instance size, worth 5.10 points on CVRP-100 and 8.26 on CVRP-1000. 3

RELAGRAM does not yet achieve solution quality competitive with DeepACO. Under 256 candidates, the two converge as instances grow: ants sample every step, so DeepACO’s candidate scaling weakens with size while RELAGRAM’s does not. In the matched ablation, the single-pass model achieves slightly lower greedy gaps than RELAGRAM at 10k and 20k updates (18.47/17.60% versus 18.89/17.86%; Appendix A). Neither difference is statistically significant: the comparison provides no evidence of an advantage from recursion. Recursion as refinement and search. RELAGRAM improves from its first stage to the trained fourth stage at every size (Table 2). Progress is non-monotonic: a later stage may worsen before producing a better route, so the deepest output is not always the strongest. Applying the loop further yields gains that are negligible at the trained size but grow with instance size: the best observed gap beyond depth four improves on the depth-four gap by 0.05, 0.74, and 1.45 points on CVRP-100, CVRP-500, and CVRP-1000 at depths six, eleven, and ten, respectively. 5 Discussion and Conclusion RELAGRAM shows that a small latent-recursive model successfully learns to route. It transfers without retraining to graphs up to ten times larger and can improve beyond its trained depth, suggesting promising inference-time depth scaling.

text: ten, respectively. 5 Discussion and Conclusion RELAGRAM shows that a small latent-recursive model successfully learns to route. It transfers without retraining to graphs up to ten times larger and can improve beyond its trained depth, suggesting promising inference-time depth scaling. The model does not reach state-of-the-art results, and the matched greedy comparison finds no significant advantage from recursion. We therefore see RELAGRAM as a proof of concept for applying latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. We hypothesize that an important limitation is the sparse RL signal, which needs further engineering for latent recursion. Importantly, y and z receive only indirect RL signal, making learning harder. Lastly, RELAGRAM’s recursive nature may be very useful for dynamic problems. The loop already runs zero-shot past the conditions it was trained under; if it handles an updated instance as well as extra depth, a single model with a decoder could solve such problems end-to-end, by recurrently processing the last latent state and the updated problem. 4

text: A Further Model Evaluation The main experiments compare RELAGRAM and DeepACO on solution quality. Here, we look more closely at how the models work and provide a matched comparison with a single-pass control. Both models learn edge scores, but iteration happens in different places. RELAGRAM repeatedly refines a latent state using the same network before decoding the final heatmap. DeepACO instead uses an anisotropic GNN to produce a heuristic for Ant Colony Optimization, where completed solutions update the pheromone state and guide subsequent search. DeepACO performs better overall, although RELAGRAM is competitive in two Combined256 settings: 17.11% versus 17.38% on CVRP-500 and 24.32% versus 23.31% on CVRP-1000. We compare RELAGRAM with a direct model that maps the input straight to one heatmap. Both use the same 0.526M-parameter transformer and are matched in optimizer updates, unique training instances, and sampled routes. p-values are from two-sided paired t-tests over 256 shared evaluation instances (α = 0.05). The recursive/direct greedy gaps are 18.886/18.467% at 10k updates (p = 0.226) and 17.857/17.596% at 20k (p = 0.406). Neither difference is statistically significant, so we find no evidence that RELAGRAM outperforms this control under greedy decoding at these checkpoints. RELAGRAM nevertheless provides an additional test-time scaling axis: greater depth can improve solution quality without retraining, particularly after transfer to larger instances. text: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language Models Dan Saunders Luma AI danjsaund@gmail.com Benjamin Ren X School ultraman1234502@gmail.com Catherine He X School catherinezhanghe@gmail.com
title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language

text: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency–accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models [Zhu et al., 2023] (RWKV backbone [Peng et al., 2023]) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from 3 × 1017 to 1 × 1019 FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is Nopt ∝C0.56, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. [2022] report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity. 1
title: Compute-Optimal Scaling Laws for Spiking Language

text: Scaling laws address a basic allocation question: given a fixed compute budget C, how should it be split between model size N and data D to minimize loss? Kaplan et al. [2020] established power-law scaling for Transformers, and Hoffmann et al. [2022] (Chinchilla) introduced the IsoFLOP methodology and revised the optimal allocation toward roughly equal scaling of N and D. How these laws transfer to spiking neural networks is unknown. SpikeGPT [Zhu et al., 2023] binarizes activations into spikes on an RWKV backbone [Peng et al., 2023] for energy-efficient neuromorphic inference, but was trained far below the regime where compute-optimal behavior is characterized, leaving open both how a spiking model should be scaled and what accuracy its sparsity costs. We conduct a Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP study across a grid of compute budgets, fitting parabo- las to recover compute-optimal (Nopt, Dopt) at each budget. Our contributions are: (1) the first compute-optimal IsoFLOP scaling law for a spiking language model, Nopt ∝C0.56, close to dense Transformers; (2) non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines at every budget, which separate a constant backbone cost (∼0.16 nats) from a spiking cost that falls to about 0.23 nats and then levels off; and (3) evidence that the apparent departure from the Chinchilla exponent is largely a parameter-counting artifact. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). text: Scaling Laws. Kaplan et al. [2020] established power-law scaling of transformer loss with model size, data, and compute; Hoffmann et al. [2022] (Chinchilla) revised the compute-optimal allo- cation toward scaling N and D in roughly equal proportion, using three estimators including the IsoFLOP profiles (their Approach 2) we adopt. Pearce and Song [2024] show that much of the Kaplan–Chinchilla exponent discrepancy is a parameter-counting artifact (non-embedding versus total parameters), a point central to our analysis (Section 4.3). Shen et al. [2024] extend IsoFLOP fitting to linear-complexity, non-softmax sequence models from 70M to 7B parameters, finding scaling broadly similar to transformers; we apply the same methodology to spiking RWKV models. Spiking Language Models. RWKV [Peng et al., 2023] replaces quadratic self-attention with a linear-time recurrence, removing the sequence-length term that complicates transformer FLOP accounting. Zhu et al. [2023] build SpikeGPT on this backbone, binarizing activations into discrete spikes for energy-efficient, event-driven inference on neuromorphic hardware. A separate line spikes large pretrained LLMs post hoc [Xing et al., 2024]. To our knowledge, no prior work characterizes compute-optimal scaling for spiking language models trained from scratch, which we address here. 3 Methods 3.1 Experimental Settings All models are trained with the AdamW optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) using a batch size of 16 and a context length of 1024 tokens. text: trained from scratch, which we address here. 3 Methods 3.1 Experimental Settings All models are trained with the AdamW optimizer (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999) using a batch size of 16 and a context length of 1024 tokens. Text is tokenized using the EleutherAI/gpt-neox-20b tokenizer [Black et al., 2022], and training data is drawn from the FineWeb-EDU sample-100BT split [Penedo et al., 2024]. Spiking neuron dynamics follow the standard leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) model [Gerstner and Kistler, 2002, Maass, 1997], with the arctangent (arctan) surrogate gradient [Neftci et al., 2019] used to enable backpropagation through the non-differentiable spiking threshold. The peak learning rate at each width comes from a power law LRopt(d) = k d−p fit to a pilot sweep (Appendix D), with cosine decay to one-tenth, so loss differences across the grid reflect the N/D allocation rather than learning-rate tuning. We estimate training compute as C ≈6ND [Kaplan et al., 2020]; RWKV has no attention term, so matrix multiplies dominate. 3.2 Parameter Counting With a 50,257-token vocabulary the embedding is 11–50% of all parameters, so how N is counted matters. We distinguish the strict non-embedding count (13ld2, Kaplan), the FLOP-matmul count entering C = 6ND (N\E = 13ld2 + vd, retaining the output projection), and the total count (NT = 13ld2 + 2vd), with v the vocabulary size. This has two consequences. First, small-scale IsoFLOP exponents should not be compared across studies without matching the counting convention. text: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies Yifeng Mao1, Yuze Feng1, Yutong Shen1, Liyang Gao1, and Zhixiang He1* Beijing University of Technology, Beijing, China maoyifeng@emails.bjut.edu.cn, zxhe@bjut.edu.cn *Corresponding author Abstract. Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero- cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usu- ally captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unsta- ble rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architec- tures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complemen- tary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and syn- ergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% la- beled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall’s Tau (τ) of 0.70, outperform- ing representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test ac- curacy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the

In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test ac- curacy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architec- tures under limited evaluation budgets. text: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) [9] has become an important technique for au- tomatically designing deep neural network architectures. It has achieved strong results in computer vision and natural language processing and provides a scal- able way to adapt architectures to different tasks, datasets, and deployment constraints. However, conventional NAS methods usually require training or par- tially training a large number of candidate architectures, which leads to substan- tial computational overhead. Therefore, accurate performance estimation under extremely limited evaluation budgets has become a central challenge for efficient NAS [30]. arXiv:2610.15307v1 [cs.LG] 11 Oct 2026

The overall framework of FENAS. The pipeline consists of three decoupled stages: (1) Feature Extraction: raw zero-cost proxy scores are extracted from com- plementary physical dimensions. (2) CAST Feature Engineering: heterogeneous proxy scores are aligned and transformed into a compact feature manifold. (3) Meta- predictor: a lightweight meta-learner uses extremely few-shot labels to output accu- rate performance rankings. Zero-Cost Proxies (ZCPs) offer a promising solution by estimating architec- ture quality at initialization from a single forward or backward pass. They can quickly screen weak candidates before expensive training and thus greatly re- duce search cost. However, individual proxies are often unstable because each one captures only a limited physical property of an architecture, such as ex- pressivity, trainability, or connectivity. As a result, their rank correlations vary significantly across datasets, tasks, and search spaces [23,31], making raw ZCPs difficult to use as universal and reliable performance indicators. Few-shot predictors based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) or other topol- ogy encoders [24,32,4] provide another way to reduce evaluation cost. By ex- plicitly modeling architecture graphs

text: [23,31], making raw ZCPs difficult to use as universal and reliable performance indicators. Few-shot predictors based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) or other topol- ogy encoders [24,32,4] provide another way to reduce evaluation cost. By ex- plicitly modeling architecture graphs and learning topology-aware representa- tions, these methods can improve prediction quality under limited supervision. Nevertheless, they introduce additional overhead from graph construction, mes- sage passing, and structured inference. More importantly, in extreme few-shot regimes, e.g., less than 1% labeled samples, learning high-dimensional topology representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient and prone to overfitting. Our experiments show that on topology-stable benchmarks such as NAS-Bench- 201, a lightweight topology-agnostic predictor can already outperform heavy topology-based methods; with only 78 labeled architectures, FENAS achieves a τ of 0.695 on CIFAR-10, surpassing DCL-ENAS [36] (0.610) and CAP [11] (0.600). To address the tension between the instability of individual ZCPs and the complexity of topology-based predictors, we propose FENAS (Few-shot meta- Ensembling Neural Architecture Search), an efficient and topology-agnostic per- formance prediction framework. Our key insight is that, instead of spending model capacity on explicit topology learning, it is more effective to directly model the intrinsic priors of architectures and learn how to combine them with minimal supervision. Specifically, we extract features from four complementary physical dimensions: expressivity, trainability, connectivity, and parameter ca- pacity. To

text: 2.1 Neural Architecture Search (NAS) Neural Architecture Search (NAS) aims to automate the design of high-performing neural networks, but its practical use is often limited by the high cost of evalu- ating candidate architectures in large search spaces. Early NAS methods based on reinforcement learning and evolutionary algorithms [37,26] typically require training or partially training many architectures, leading to substantial com- putational overhead. To improve efficiency, differentiable and low-cost search strategies [15] have been proposed to reduce the reliance on exhaustive evalua- tion. In parallel, benchmark suites such as NAS-Bench-201 [7] provide standard- ized search spaces with ground-truth performance records, enabling controlled analysis of efficient NAS algorithms.

text: 4 Y. Mao et al. 2.2 Zero-Cost Proxies (ZCPs) Zero-Cost Proxies (ZCPs) estimate architecture quality at initialization using statistics from a single forward or backward pass [1]. Existing proxies characterize architectures from different physical perspectives. Gradient and pruning-based methods, such as SynFlow [27], measure parameter sensitivity or information flow, while activation-based methods such as NASWOT [21] capture expressivity through feature-map statistics or activation patterns. Although these proxies provide useful training-free priors, each individual proxy usually reflects only one local property of an architecture, making its ranking reliability highly dependent on the dataset and search space. 2.3 Few-Shot Prediction and Proxy Fusion Few-shot NAS predictors aim to reduce the number of labeled architectures re- quired for accurate performance estimation. Recent methods usually rely on graph topology encoding, self-supervised learning, or supernet-based mecha- nisms [33,29,17,16]. While topology-aware predictors can improve prediction quality, they introduce additional overhead from graph construction, message passing, and structured inference. Under extremely limited labels, learning high- dimensional architecture embeddings from scratch may also suffer from cold-start difficulty and overfitting. Another related direction studies the fusion of multiple ZCPs, for example through adaptive weighting [14]. However, purely zero-cost fusion often relies on manually designed aggregation rules or search heuristics, and thus cannot di- rectly learn task-dependent relationships between proxy signals and final accu- racy. FENAS bridges few-shot prediction and

FENAS bridges few-shot prediction and ZCP fusion by representing each architecture with complementary topology-agnostic physical priors and using minimal ground-truth supervision for data-driven integration. With CAST, het- erogeneous proxy scores are aligned and transformed into a compact feature space, allowing lightweight meta-learners to adaptively combine expressivity, trainability, connectivity, and capacity cues for robust architecture ranking. 3

text: We now detail the main components of FENAS. The overall idea is to con- vert each architecture into a compact feature manifold using multi-dimensional zero-cost proxy signals, and then train a lightweight meta-predictor for few-shot performance estimation. 3.1 Overview To address the ranking instability of existing Zero-Cost Proxies (ZCPs) across search spaces [23,31] and the high evaluation cost of traditional NAS, we propose FENAS (Few-shot meta-Ensembling Neural Architecture Search). As

text: FENAS 5 illustrated in Figure 1, FENAS does not rely on high-dimensional graph topology embeddings [29]. Instead, it extracts low-dimensional physical dynamics features from each architecture and learns a model-agnostic predictor with only a small number of labeled architectures. The pipeline is decoupled into two stages. First, for an architecture α, FENAS extracts raw proxy scores from four complementary physical dimensions and reshapes them through CAST: Φ(α) = CAST(zE ⊕zT ⊕zC ⊕zP ) (1) where α denotes a candidate architecture; zE, zT , zC, and zP denote the proxy scores for expressivity, trainability, connectivity, and parameter capacity, respectively; ⊕denotes feature concatenation; CAST(·) denotes the proposed Copula Alignment and Synergy Transformation operator; and Φ(α) is the re- sulting feature manifold used for prediction. Second, the constructed feature manifold is fed into a meta-predictor: ˆy = fθ(Φ(α)) (2) where fθ denotes a parameterized meta-predictor with learnable parame- ters θ, and ˆy denotes the predicted performance of architecture α. Since CAST concentrates heterogeneous proxy information into a compact feature space, fθ can be instantiated as either a nonlinear tree ensemble [2,3] or a simple linear regression model. 3.2 Pre-Training Feature Engineering The goal of pre-training feature engineering is to map a discrete architecture α into a continuous, low-dimensional, and informative vector Φ(α). The trainability score is: zT = X w∈α ∥gw∥2 (4) where w denotes a trainable weight in architecture α, Ltrain is the training loss, gw is the corresponding gradient, and ∥· ∥denotes the Euclidean norm. Connectivity (zC). We adopt SynFlow [27] to evaluate global connectiv- ity using a data-free path integral. Given a structure-preserving metric R, the connectivity score is: zC = X w∈α |w| ⊙ ∂R ∂w (5) where w is a trainable weight, |w| is its absolute magnitude, R denotes the structure-preserving SynFlow objective, ∂R ∂w is the derivative of R with respect to w, and ⊙denotes the Hadamard product. This score reflects whether information can flow through the architecture without structural bottlenecks. Capacity (zP ). Parameter count provides a basic physical constraint on model capacity. We define it as: zP = L X l=1 |wl| (6) where L is the total number of layers, wl denotes the set of trainable parame- ters in the l-th layer, and |wl| denotes the number of trainable parameters in that layer. The four scores form the raw feature vector v(α) = [zE, zT , zC, zP ]T ∈R4. 2) Copula Alignment and Synergy Transformation (CAST) The

The four scores form the raw feature vector v(α) = [zE, zT , zC, zP ]T ∈R4. 2) Copula Alignment and Synergy Transformation (CAST) The raw proxy vector v(α) contains heterogeneous features with different scales and distributions. To make them comparable and learnable, CAST applies Cop- ula Alignment [22] followed by Synergy Transformation. We first use the Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function (ECDF) [28] to map each raw feature into a percentile rank. For the k-th feature, the aligned value is: uk = ˆFk(vk) = 1 |Aref| X α′∈Aref I(vk(α′) ≤vk(α)) (7) where vk(α) is the raw value of the k-th proxy feature for architecture α, ˆFk(·) is the empirical cumulative distribution function of the k-th feature, Aref is the reference architecture set, |Aref| is its size, α′ denotes an architecture sampled from Aref, and I(·) is an indicator function that equals 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise. The resulting uk ∈[0, 1] represents the percentile rank of vk(α) among the reference architectures. Applying this to all four dimensions yields the normalized vector u = [uE, uT , uC, uP ]T .

text: FENAS 7 Next, we construct two high-order synergy features. The first feature mea- sures expressivity per unit capacity: pE = uE log(1 + uP ) (8) where uE is the aligned expressivity score, uP is the aligned capacity score, and pE denotes the efficiency feature. The second feature models the joint effect of trainability and connectivity: pS = uT × uC (9) where uT is the aligned trainability score, uC is the aligned connectivity score, and pS denotes the synergy feature. Finally, we concatenate the aligned base features and the two synergy features: Φ(α) = CAST(v(α)) = u ⊕[pE, pS]T ∈R6 (10) where v(α) is the raw 4-dimensional proxy vector, u is the aligned 4-dimensional vector, [pE, pS]T is the 2-dimensional synergy vector, ⊕denotes concatenation, and Φ(α) ∈R6 is the final characteristic manifold. 3.3 Meta-Predictor Instantiation After CAST, FENAS becomes a model-agnostic prediction framework. The experiments cover NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, and the DARTS search space, and are designed to verify whether the proposed CAST-based proxy fusion is more robust than individual ZCPs and more efficient than topology-heavy predictors. 4.1 Experimental Settings Benchmarks and protocols. NAS-Bench-101 [34] contains 423,624 CIFAR-10 [13] architectures with diverse graph topologies, while NAS-Bench-201 [7] contains 15,625 operation-on-edge architectures with complete records of CIFAR-10, CIFAR- 100 [13], and ImageNet16-120 [5]. We also evaluate practical search in the large- scale DARTS space [15], an open-domain search space that contains approxi- mately 1018 candidate architectures. FENAS uses a lightweight Random Forest meta-learner over four CAST-processed ZCPs: Fisher, NASWOT, SynFlow, and #Params. We compare it with SOTA few-shot predictors such as CAP [11] and PINAT [16], as well as pure ZCP baselines. Ranking is measured by Kendall’s τ and Spearman’s ρ; search quality is measured by top-1 test accuracy and search cost. To ensure statistical robustness, all results are averaged over 10 indepen- dent runs with fixed random seeds, and we report both mean and standard deviation. 4.2 Ranking Performance 1) Comparison with Few-shot Methods on NAS-Bench-201. We further evaluate FENAS in the large-scale DARTS search space [15], which contains approximately 1018 candidate architectures. Since unconstrained prior- based search may favor degenerate architectures with excessive “none” opera- tors [35,6], we apply a lightweight structural validity constraint during evolution- ary search [26]. In practice, FENAS is fine-tuned using 100 randomly sampled architectures trained for 50 epochs, then used to rank 100,000 valid candidates. The top-3 predicted architectures are retrained from scratch for 600 epochs. As shown in Table 4, FENAS remains highly efficient, requiring only 0.3 GPU days while achieving 97.25% ± 0.09% test accuracy after retraining. Although FENAS does not outperform PINAT comparing the accuracies, its topology- agnostic design avoids costly graph processing and additional pretraining, en- abling direct ranking through lightweight meta-ensembling of initialization-based priors. These results show that FENAS is a practical open-domain NAS method under strict computational budgets. 4.4 Discussion and Ablation 1) Synergy among ZCPs. text: In this paper, we presented FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot NAS predictor that integrates multi-dimensional zero-cost proxies with the CAST feature trans- formation pipeline. By aligning heterogeneous proxy distributions and modeling their complementary interactions, FENAS achieves accurate and stable architec- ture ranking under extremely limited supervision. Experiments on NAS-Bench- 101, NAS-Bench-201, and the DARTS search space show that FENAS provides competitive ranking and search performance with low computational cost. These results suggest that physically grounded proxy fusion is an efficient alternative to topology-heavy predictors, especially when only a small number of evaluated architectures are available.

text: Preprint CoFlu-Brain: An fMRI Connectivity Foun- dation Model with Cofluctuation-Based Pretraining Ziteng Sui1, Junfeng Xia1, Wenhao Ye1,3, Mo Wang1,2,*, Quanying Liu1,* 1Department of Biomedical Engineering, Southern University of Science and Technology, China 2Department of Computer Science, University of Warwick, UK 3School of Biomedical Engineering, Shenzhen University, China *Corresponding authors: 12250099@mail.sustech.edu.cn, liuqy@sustech.edu.cn
title: Preprint

text: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) commonly characterizes large-scale brain organization through functional connectivity (FC). How- ever, an observed FC matrix is not a fixed brain graph but a statistical estimate determined by the finite BOLD frames used to compute it. Con- ventional FC-based approaches typically represent each scan with a single Pearson-correlation matrix, leaving frame-resolved variations in regional interactions unexploited. To address this limitation, we introduce CoFlu- Brain, which organizes framewise cofluctuation observations into multiple retained and dropped views, each summarized as an FC matrix. The model learns connectivity structure reproducible across retained views and pre- dicts the representations of the corresponding dropped views, while adopt- ing SIGReg from LeJEPA to prevent representation collapse. We pretrained CoFlu-Brain on 13,444 subjects from eight dataset groups and evaluated its representations via frozen-encoder linear probing on seven classification and two age-prediction tasks across seven datasets. CoFlu-Brain showed strong transfer across demographic, developmental, and clinical prediction tasks, outperforming the evaluated released models on most tasks. Ran- dom frame partitioning improved aggregate transfer, while the complete objective achieved the strongest overall performance. Code is available. 1

text: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides a non-invasive view of large-scale functional brain organization and its relationships with cognition, behavior, and disease. As large multi-site fMRI collections continue to grow, self-supervised pretraining offers a path toward transferable brain representations without requiring downstream task labels during pretraining (Ortega Caro et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2024; Gijsen et al., 2026). A common route from fMRI measurements to brain-network representations is to parcellate the brain into regions of interest (ROIs), extract a regional BOLD time series from each ROI, and estimate the statistical dependence between regional signals. Pearson correlation organizes these pairwise dependencies into a compact and interpretable functional connectivity (FC) matrix. By explicitly representing interregional functional coupling, FC has become a widely used input for brain-network modeling and connectome-based pretraining (Kan et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2026a). An observed Pearson-FC matrix, however, is not a sampling-independent brain graph but a scan-level statistical estimate formed from a finite BOLD sequence. Its value can vary with the frames included in the estimation, such that different frame compositions produce non-identical but statistically related FC estimates. 1 arXiv:2610.15450v1 [cs.NE] 11 Oct 2026

text: Preprint Figure 1: From a single FC estimate to cofluctuation based multi-view learning. Conventional FC aggregates all frames into a single connectivity estimate, whereas CoFlu-Brain uses different compositions of framewise cofluctuation observations to construct multiple FC views. Existing FC representation models typically operate on a single Pearson-FC matrix or graph for each scan (Kan et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2026a), leaving frame-resolved variation unused during representation learning. Framewise cofluctuation provides a finer-grained description of regional interactions by characterizing the joint standardized activity of regional pairs at individual frames (Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2020; Faskowitz et al., 2020). This perspec- tive makes it possible to construct multiple training views from different compositions of framewise observations. This gap raises a central question: can different compositions of framewise cofluctuation observations provide self-supervision for learning stable and transferable connectivity rep- resentations? We hypothesize that retained frame sets sampled from the same segment provide different views of subject-specific cofluctuation structure. Although the resulting FC views may differ numerically, their shared connectivity structure should remain repro- ducibly inferable. Moreover, a retained view should contain suﬀicient information to predict the representation of the corresponding non-overlapping dropped view. The former encour- ages consistency across retained views, whereas the latter captures predictive relationships between retained and dropped observations. Motivated by this gap, we propose CoFlu-Brain, a cofluctuation-based approach

text: information to predict the representation of the corresponding non-overlapping dropped view. The former encour- ages consistency across retained views, whereas the latter captures predictive relationships between retained and dropped observations. Motivated by this gap, we propose CoFlu-Brain, a cofluctuation-based approach to self- supervised FC pretraining. For each fMRI segment, CoFlu-Brain repeatedly partitions the frames into retained and dropped sets, organizes their framewise cofluctuation observations into separate FC views, and uses the dropped-view representations as prediction targets. Its joint-embedding objective promotes consistent representations across retained views while requiring each retained representation to predict its corresponding dropped-view represen- tation in latent space. We evaluate the resulting representations through multi-dataset pretraining, frozen transfer, and systematic ablations. Our contributions are: 1. We propose a cofluctuation-based FC pretraining approach that constructs retained and dropped views from framewise observations and couples consistency across retained views with retained-to-dropped latent prediction. 2. We develop CoFlu-Brain, an FC foundation model pretrained on multi-cohort fMRI data, and demonstrate strong frozen-transfer performance across demographic, developmental, and clinical downstream tasks. 3. We conduct a systematic empirical analysis across nine downstream tasks, ex- amining the contributions of the learning objectives and the effects of data coverage, branch count, and temporal sampling, while assessing seed robustness for the pri- mary and temporal-sampling comparisons. 2

text: fMRI representation models differ first in what they model. Time-series methods recon- struct masked BOLD signals, predict masked latent targets, or align representations across temporal views (Ortega Caro et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2024; Gijsen et al., 2026). They preserve temporal dynamics, but interregional connectivity remains an implicit property of the learned activity representation. Voxel-level models instead operate directly on 4D fMRI volumes (Wang et al., 2026b; 2025; Xia et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a). They retain fine-grained spatial information without relying on a predefined atlas, but require high-dimensional inputs and do not use connectivity as the primary modeling unit. FC models represent each scan as a connectivity matrix or graph, directly encoding interre- gional coupling (Kawahara et al., 2017; Li et al., 2021; Kan et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2026a;b). Most treat the resulting Pearson-FC matrix as the object to encode, reconstruct, augment, or align. This overlooks that FC is a finite-sample estimate whose values depend on its supporting frames (Noble et al., 2019; Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2020; Faskowitz et al., 2020). Dynamic-FC methods instead model temporal variation across win- dows or graph sequences (Hutchison et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2021), but address evolving connectivity states rather than reproducibility across alternative estimates. Dynamic-FC methods instead model temporal variation across win- dows or graph sequences (Hutchison et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2021), but address evolving connectivity states rather than reproducibility across alternative estimates. CoFlu-Brain retains the interpretability of FC modeling while extending its learning unit from one scan-level estimate to multiple related estimates. These views arise from comple- mentary frame observations and preserve a direct relationship to FC estimation, promoting representations stable across frame compositions and predictive of held-out observations. Self-supervised methods also differ in how they define their learning signal. Masked au- toencoding reconstructs omitted input content, whereas JEPA predicts masked targets in latent space (He et al., 2022; Ortega Caro et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2026a; Dong et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2023). Joint-embedding methods such as BYOL and DINO instead align representations across views, while VICReg and SIGReg regularize the fea- ture distribution against collapse (Grill et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2022; Balestriero & LeCun, 2025). Other directions include metadata-conditioned diffusion pretraining across brain states (Xia et al., 2026a), organizing pretraining domains and downstream transfer through measured learning relations (Xia et al., 2026c), and jointly examining data size, model size, and training duration (Ye et al., 2026). These studies complement the design of FC-specific training views explored

text: al., 2026a), organizing pretraining domains and downstream transfer through measured learning relations (Xia et al., 2026c), and jointly examining data size, model size, and training duration (Ye et al., 2026). These studies complement the design of FC-specific training views explored here. CoFlu-Brain integrates these principles through FC-specific view relations. Consistency across retained estimates promotes stability under frame resampling; prediction from re- tained to complementary dropped estimates captures information predictive of held-out observations; and SIGReg maintains representation diversity. Together, these components use the finite-sample structure of FC to define which views should agree and which comple- mentary evidence should be predicted. 3 Method 3.1 Overview CoFlu-Brain constructs multiple retained–dropped FC pairs from each fMRI segment. As illustrated in Figure 2, a shared encoder maps each estimate to a scan-level representa- tion. Training combines consistency across retained-frame representations, prediction of the paired dropped-frame representation, and distributional regularization. After pretraining, the projector and predictor are discarded, and the shared FC encoder provides representa- tions for downstream tasks. 3

text: Preprint Non-collapse regularization. Consistency and prediction specify relationships among paired FC estimates. We additionally apply SIGReg to the collection of retained and dropped projections following LeJEPA (Balestriero & LeCun, 2025), regularizing their dis- tribution against representational collapse. The complete objective is ℒ= ℒpred + 𝜆con𝛾(𝑒)ℒcon + 𝜆regℒSIGReg, where 𝛾(𝑒) controls the contribution of consistency through an initial full-weight phase followed by linear decay: 𝛾(𝑒) = ⎧ { ⎨ { ⎩ 1, 𝑒≤𝐸𝑤, max(1 −𝑒−𝐸𝑤 𝐸𝑑 , 0) , 𝑒> 𝐸𝑤. Here, 𝑒is the training epoch, 𝐸𝑤is the duration of the initial full-weight phase, and 𝐸𝑑 is the subsequent decay duration. In the main configuration, 𝐸𝑤= 1 and 𝐸𝑑= 24, so the consistency weight reaches zero at epoch 25. The schedule emphasizes alignment early in training and shifts the later objective toward dropped-frame prediction. The three loss terms respectively promote latent prediction, reproducibility across finite FC estimates, and a non-degenerate representation distribution. 4 Results 4.1 Experimental setup CoFlu-Brain was pretrained on 13,444 subjects from eight dataset groups: CHCP, HCP, ABCD, ABCC, HBN, PNC, MDD, and AOMIC PIOP1/2 (Ge et al., 2023; Van Essen et al., 2013; Casey et al., 2018; Feczko et al., 2021; Alexander et al., 2017; Satterthwaite et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2019; Snoek et al., 2021). All inputs were represented as Schaefer-400 cortical time series (Schaefer et al., 2018), and 200-frame segments were used for pretraining. Downstream evaluation comprised two in-cohort tasks from HCP and ABCD, whose unlabeled scans contributed to pretraining, and seven out-of-cohort tasks from SALD, PPMI, ADNI, ABIDE, and ADHD200, which were excluded from pretraining (Van Essen et al., 2013; Casey et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2018; Marek et al., 2011; Weiner et al., 2010; Di Martino et al., 2014; ADHD-200 Consortium, 2012). No downstream labels were used during pretraining. Frozen representations were evaluated with logistic regression for classification and ridge regression for age prediction. For age prediction, nMAE was computed after standardizing the target using the training-fold mean and population standard deviation. Cross-dataset ranks used weighted F1 for classification and nMAE for age prediction. Endpoint ranks were averaged within each cohort, and the dispersion of method mean ranks was evaluated using two million method-label permutations within cohort blocks. text: Preprint 5 Discussion CoFlu-Brain shows that relationships among FC estimates supported by different frame com- positions provide useful self-supervision. Its representations transferred across demographic, developmental, and clinical tasks, while random partitioning improved aggregate transfer. The complete objective combines retained-view consistency, dropped-view prediction, and distributional regularization as complementary signals. Limitations and future directions. CoFlu-Brain uses the framewise cofluctuation de- composition of Pearson connectivity to construct multiple FC estimates with explicitly con- trolled frame support. Because each view aggregates the selected framewise products into a subset-specific FC matrix, the current model does not preserve the timing, order, or am- plitude of individual cofluctuation events. Its scope is instead to learn from structured relationships among finite-sample FC estimates: reproducibility across retained-frame com- positions and prediction of complementary held-out estimates. Future work could com- bine this estimate-level objective with order-aware or edge-time-series encoders to capture transient dynamics. Biological validation, causal analysis, and integration with voxel-level features remain important directions beyond the predictive evaluations considered here. text: Preprint A Experimental Details A.1 Datasets and downstream tasks Pretraining datasets. The pretraining corpus contained 13,444 usable subjects from eight dataset groups. Only fMRI inputs, without downstream labels, were used during pretraining. Preprocessing. We started from cohort-specific preprocessed derivatives: the HCP min- imal preprocessing pipeline for HCP and CHCP, ABCD-HCP derivatives for ABCD and ABCC, fMRIPrep derivatives for AOMIC PIOP1/2, and available MNI-space preprocessed derivatives for HBN, PNC, and the multisite MDD data. Thus, low-level operations, in- cluding motion correction and any nuisance-signal handling, were inherited from the corre- sponding source pipeline rather than re-estimated with a single cross-cohort pipeline. We then applied a common input harmonization procedure: all fMRI volumes were represented at 2-mm isotropic resolution, and only datasets with a source TR different from 0.72 s were temporally interpolated to 0.72 s using cubic B-spline interpolation. Regional signals were extracted using the Schaefer-400 atlas, and each regional time series was Z-standardized along the temporal dimension. Files with exactly 200 frames were used directly; during pre- training, contiguous 200-frame windows were sampled from longer series, whereas sequences shorter than 200 frames were excluded without zero-padding. BrainGFM pretrains a shared graph encoder across multiple parcellations us- ing graph contrastive learning and masked graph autoencoding (Wei et al., 2026a). We used the authors’ released pretrained checkpoint with Schaefer-100 inputs (Schaefer et al., 2018). Raw Pearson-FC rows served as node features, and FC values above 0.3 defined the graph adjacency. BrainMASS constructs augmented FC views by dropping BOLD observa- tions and learns with masked-ROI modeling and latent representation alignment (Yang et al., 2024). text: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming A Black-Box Security Testing Framework for LLM-Based Software Systems ABRAR ALOTAIBI, King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Saudi Arabia and Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Saudi Arabia MOATAZ AHMED, King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Saudi Arabia and SDAIA-KFUPM Joint Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Saudi Arabia Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass their safety training. Existing automated red-teaming methods either require privileged access unavailable in production, rely on manually engineered per-model templates, or optimize a single objective without population-level diversity. We present REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box framework that discovers adversarial prompts through evolutionary optimization driven entirely by a compressed open- weight 7B reflective model on a single consumer GPU. REPRO introduces two mechanisms absent from prior work, both isolated in a component ablation: semantic crossover, an LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator, and Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling informed by structured failure analysis. We catalog REPRO’s behavior on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, including GPT-5-nano, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Grok-4.1. Under our protocol REPRO reaches 100% attack success rate (ASR) on every evaluated target in a single turn, at a median of 24 target queries per behavior.

Two properties of the protocol qualify that figure. The judge scoring candidates during optimization also produces the reported ASR, and search halts when it accepts, so ASR reports whether search succeeded within the iteration budget rather than success at a fixed budget. All baseline figures are transcribed from their original papers, which use different judges, budgets, and model versions. We therefore present this as a catalog of model coverage under one protocol rather than a head-to-head ranking, and develop both qualifications in the paper. text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now core components of production software systems, powering applications from customer-service automation to healthcare diagnostics, code generation, and educational platforms [7, 30]. Despite extensive alignment through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [31] and constitutional AI [6], contemporary LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that bypass safety guardrails and elicit harmful content. As these models are integrated into safety- and privacy-sensitive software pipelines, software engineers face an urgent practical question: how can the security of an LLM-based system be evaluated rigorously, automatically, and reproducibly before deployment? Manual red-teaming does not scale with the rapidly evolving threat landscape [13, 32], and existing automated approaches either rely on brittle template matching that fails against context-aware defenses [39], require white-box access to model Authors’ Contact Information: Abrar Alotaibi, amotaibi@iau.edu.sa, King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Information and Computer Science Department, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia and Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, College of Computer Science and Information Technology, Dammam, Saudi Arabia; Moataz Ahmed, moataz@kfupm.edu.sa, King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Information and Computer Science Department, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia and SDAIA-KFUPM Joint Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. arXiv:2610.15513v1 [cs.CL] 11 Oct 2026
