text: 2 Alotaibi et al. gradients [46], or operate in per-behavior greedy regimes that cannot exploit structure across the attack space. Iterative refinement methods such as PAIR [9] and TAP [28] address some of these limitations but optimize a single objective without population diversity, ignoring transferability, stealth, and test-case length. The current state of the art in raw effectiveness is Andriushchenko et al. [4], who report 100% attack success rate (ASR) across Llama-2/3, GPT-3.5/4, and Claude via adaptive random search with log-probability-guided optimization. From a software-testing standpoint, their approach has three limitations that rule it out for realistic black-box deployment scenarios: it requires gray-box access to token probabilities that most production APIs do not expose; it relies on manually engineered templates crafted per target model; and it consumes roughly 10,000 queries per behavior, which makes continuous-integration testing impractical. Other recent methods, including, AmpleGCG [23], and AutoDAN-Turbo [25], either require privileged access, demand per-model manual engineering, or depend on powerful auxiliary models for effective mutation. This paper introduces REPRO (Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimization), a pure black-box adversarial prompt optimizer built around a population-based evolutionary loop with structured self-refinement, Bayesian strategy selection via Thompson Sampling, and multi-objective Pareto selection over attack success, cross-environment transfer, detectability, and prompt length. The underlying design philosophy is that optimization intelligence should emerge from algorithmic structure rather than from auxiliary model capability, so that the entire pipeline runs with only a quantized open-weight model on a single consumer GPU. Three elements of REPRO depart from prior work. Semantic crossover is, to our knowledge, the first LLM-guided multi-parent recombination operator in adversarial prompt optimization: it synthesizes new attacks by combining complementary techniques drawn from different strategy families. (§4.2) • RQ2: Can REPRO discover a single shared attack that covers all behaviors of a benchmark it is optimized against? (§4.3) • RQ3: What is the contribution of each algorithmic component? (§4.4) 1.2 Contributions The primary contributions of this work are: (1) The REPRO framework. We design and implement REPRO, a closed-loop reflective evolutionary optimizer that, to our knowledge, is the first prompt optimizer explicitly designed for the adversarial-objective regime. REPRO operationalizes model-agnostic black- box security testing of LLM-based software systems without requiring logit access or per- model manual engineering, and is backed by a literature-grounded attack library spanning 14 strategy families. (2) Semantic crossover. We introduce the first LLM-guided multi-parent recombination opera- tor in adversarial prompt optimization, enabling the synthesis of novel attacks that combine complementary techniques from diverse strategy families rather than evolving each attack in isolation. (3) Structured failure analysis. We introduce a purpose-built feedback routine that classifies target-model refusals into a taxonomy of defense types, routes each type to a ranked list of counter-strategies, and maintains per-behavior state about which counter-strategies have been tried and with what outcomes. text: We review related work in four areas: software-engineering approaches to security testing of LLM- based systems, the landscape of jailbreak attacks on aligned LLMs, automated prompt optimization as the intellectual ancestor of REPRO’s optimization machinery, and a consolidated framework comparison. [15]. 2.1 Security Testing of LLM-Based Software Systems A growing body of software-engineering research treats LLM security as a testing and quality- assurance problem. Wang et al. [37] survey the landscape of software testing with LLMs, identifying adversarial robustness evaluation as a core open challenge. Chen et al. [10] provide a systematic literature review of the security of language models for code, cataloging attack and defense tech- niques and motivating principled, reproducible evaluation methodologies. On the defensive side, Zhang et al. [43] propose JailGuard, a universal detection framework for prompt-based attacks that uses TAP [28] as one of its primary baseline attacks, the same baseline against which RE- PRO is evaluated. Methodologically, Jiang et al. [16] articulate the challenges and opportunities of LLM-assisted fuzzing, while Sun et al. [35] demonstrate LLM-guided test generation for SMT- solver fuzzing, establishing the precedent for LLM-driven test synthesis as a software-engineering technique. Our prior work on red-teaming frameworks for specific evaluation targets such as faithfulness [3] established the methodological pattern

Zou et al. [46] developed the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack, which optimizes adversarial suffixes through token-level gradient descent and achieves 80–95% ASR on open-weight targets. Liu et al. [24] proposed AutoDAN, a white-box genetic algorithm that generates stealthier jailbreaks through hierarchical mutations at the word and sentence levels (72–98% ASR). text: This section presents the REPRO framework. From a software-engineering perspective, REPRO performs automated test-case generation against an LLM-based system under test, using the system’s own responses as a test oracle (via a separate judge model) and feeding failure information back into a closed-loop test generator. From a prompt-optimization perspective, REPRO is a multi- objective evolutionary optimizer that searches the space of natural-language prompts for non- dominated solutions under adversarial objectives, generalizing the search-and-reflect pattern of prior prompt optimizers [1, 18] to the security domain. These two perspectives describe the same system: the optimization machinery is general; the objectives, feedback signals, and seed corpus specialize it for security testing. We organize the section as follows. Section 3.1 formalizes the optimization problem. Section 3.2 gives the framework architecture and a road-map pseudocode. Section 3.3 describes the reflec- tive machinery that drives the loop: structured failure analysis and Bayesian strategy selection. Section 3.4 walks through the generation cycle that consumes this machinery. Section 3.5 cov- ers exploration control. Section 3.6 characterizes REPRO as a bi-level optimization problem, and Section 3.7 discusses computational cost. 3.1 Problem Formulation We formalize LLM red-teaming as a multi-objective black-box optimization problem. ASR and XFER capture two distinct dimensions of attack quality: ASR measures whether an attack works in any deployment environment (max over E), while XFER measures the fraction of all task–environment pairs where the attack succeeds. An attack with high ASR but low XFER works only under permissive system prompts; high XFER means the attack is robust across realistic deployment variations. We define three standardized environments to characterize attack robustness across realistic deployment variations: an empty system prompt (provider defaults), a minimal assistant instruction, and a strict safety guideline. Together these span the range from no safety scaffolding to explicit defensive prompting. Prior red-teaming work typically evaluates against a single deployment environment, usually the provider default; we propose the three-environment evaluation as a richer characterization of attack quality, since an attack that succeeds only under permissive system prompts is less informative than one that succeeds across varied contexts. Per-experiment environment configurations are reported in Section 4.

The search space is the set of all natural-language prompts: vast, non-convex, discrete, and inaccessible to gradient methods because we operate in a black-box setting where only model responses are observable. This combination motivates evolutionary search guided by reflective LLM reasoning, with multi-objective selection to maintain diverse trade-offs. 3.2 Framework Architecture A core design principle of REPRO is that optimization intelligence should emerge from algorithmic structure rather than from the auxiliary LLM’s reasoning capability. Prior LLM-based red-teaming methods rely on the attacker LLM to generate effective mutations and degrade sharply when weaker auxiliary models are used. REPRO inverts this dependency: the algorithm provides intelligence through structured feedback, and the LLM serves as a parameterized text-transformation function. Structured failure analysis and strategy success statistics act as a shaped reward signal; the reflective LLM is the policy; evolutionary selection and Bayesian learning filter signal from noise even when individual mutations are low quality. text: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming 13 REPRO also maintains contrastive analysis across behaviors: success patterns from similar be- haviors serve as templates, repeatedly failed strategies are penalized in selection, and per-category strategy success rates guide future attempts. Behavior-targeted mutation for stubborn behaviors. When optimization plateaus at high ASR (for example, stuck at 93%), random mutations become statistically inefficient: they have only a 7% chance of targeting a failing behavior. REPRO detects stubborn behaviors with failure rate above 70% after at least three attempts and treats them differently from the rest of the population. Each stubborn behavior is classified into a category (explosives, hacking, violence, fraud, and so on), and category-specific framing is injected into the mutation prompt (for explosives: use demolition-engineering framing, not cybersecurity; preferred strategies: framing, technical, obfuscation). A dedicated component additionally tracks which strategy families have been exhausted for each stubborn behavior, forcing exploration of unexplored families and clearing exhaustion state at SURGE-level restarts (§3.5) so that previously exhausted families can be revisited after structural changes to

Mutation strategy selection is a contextual multi-armed bandit problem: the algorithm must balance exploitation of strategies known to work against the current target with exploration of alternatives, while incorporating structured feedback from failure analysis. REPRO adopts hybrid Thompson Sampling for this sub-problem because of its known sublinear regret in stationary stochastic bandits (see §3.6 for the formal connection and its caveats). The mutation strategy library is seeded with 37 hand-crafted strategies drawn from the adver- sarial ML literature, organized into semantic families ranging from authority-based framing to encoding-based obfuscation. The library is not static: when failure analysis recommends a counter- strategy that is not yet in the library, the reflective LLM synthesizes a concrete strategy to match the recommendation, and the new strategy is registered and persisted across runs. Through this mechanism the library has grown to 58 strategies across 14 semantic families, with the 21 synthe- sized strategies collected in an LLM-generated family. New runs inherit the accumulated library, so discoveries on one target model benefit subsequent runs against other targets. Family-level orga-

New runs inherit the accumulated library, so discoveries on one target model benefit subsequent runs against other targets. Family-level orga- nization enables systematic exploration: when one strategy fails repeatedly on a stubborn behavior, REPRO can switch to an alternative family rather than exhausting near-duplicate strategies. The full family taxonomy and example strategies are listed in Appendix C. Each strategy 𝑠maintains Beta posterior parameters (𝛼𝑠, 𝛽𝑠) updated after each generation based on offspring performance, where success is defined as ASR or XFER exceeding 0.5 (so that partial successes contribute to learning rather than being discarded). The posterior mean ˆ𝑝𝑠= 𝛼𝑠/(𝛼𝑠+ 𝛽𝑠) enters the hybrid weight as the historical-success signal. During strategy selection, REPRO computes a hybrid weight combining three complementary signals: 𝑤𝑠= 𝛼· ˆ𝑝𝑠· (1 + ¯𝑐𝑠) + 𝛽· 𝑟𝑠(analysis) + 𝛾· √︄ log(𝑁total) 𝑁𝑠 (7) where the historical-success term uses the posterior mean weighted by the strategy’s average composite score ¯𝑐𝑠; the relevance term 𝑟𝑠(analysis) measures the fuzzy keyword overlap between the strategy and the current feedback analysis (Jaccard similarity over extracted keywords); and the third term is a UCB exploration bonus [5]. Default weights are (𝛼, 𝛽,𝛾) = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2).

The hybrid weight is the load-bearing innovation here: pure exploitation on historical success traps the optimizer in local optima, but forward-looking relevance to the failure analysis lets the optimizer respond to target-specific defense behavior even when there is no historical data on the relevant strategies. This mechanism is also what enables library growth: when failure analysis recommends a strategy that does not exist in the library, the reflective LLM synthesizes it, the new strategy is registered with neutral priors (𝛼𝑠, 𝛽𝑠) = (1, 1) and receives an immediate relevance boost from the feedback that prompted its creation, and subsequent runs can exploit the new strategy like any other. The framework can therefore adopt techniques from recent literature on the fly without manual library curation. Strategy selection probabilities are computed via softmax over the hybrid weights with temperature 𝑇controlling exploration sharpness, and online updates between generations apply an exponential moving average to smooth weight changes. To prevent the reflective LLM from being overwhelmed when prompted with the full 58-strategy portfolio, mutation prompts include only the top-𝐾strategies by hybrid score (default 𝐾= 8), with each strategy annotated by its hybrid weight and a one-line description. Strategies below a relevance threshold of 0.3 are excluded; if fewer than 𝐾strategies qualify, the pool is padded with next-best strategies by historical

Mutation and crossover consume the reflective machinery of §3.3; the other phases are standard evolutionary operations specialized to the multi-objective, black-box setting. 3.4.1 Multi-Objective Evaluation and Pareto Selection. Each generation begins with full evaluation of the population on the four objectives from Section 3.1. Because these objectives can conflict (high ASR may require longer or more detectable prompts), REPRO uses Pareto selection rather than scalarization, which preserves multiple high-quality parents for crossover and lets the optimizer explore trade-offs the user can later choose between. Strict Pareto dominance often yields a single dominant solution and collapses crossover diversity. REPRO therefore computes the strict frontier first and applies an epsilon-Pareto relaxation only when that frontier is undersized for the caller; when the strict frontier is already

text: Strict Pareto dominance often yields a single dominant solution and collapses crossover diversity. REPRO therefore computes the strict frontier first and applies an epsilon-Pareto relaxation only when that frontier is undersized for the caller; when the strict frontier is already large enough, the relaxation is not invoked. Under the relaxation, a candidate is excluded from the frontier only if another candidate is better by at least a factor (1 + 𝜀) on every objective, so a larger 𝜀admits more candidates. The routine is called at two points with different parameters, reflecting what each caller needs. Parent selection runs once per generation and requires several parents for multi-parent crossover, so it uses 𝜀= 0.05 with a minimum frontier size of 3. Final selection runs once at the end of a run and needs only to identify the returned solution, so it uses 𝜀= 0.03 with a minimum of 1. Both cap the frontier at 6 candidates. If the relaxed frontier is still below the minimum, REPRO expands it by including next-best candidates under lexicographic ordering (ASR ≻XFER ≻−detect ≻−len). Immediately after evaluation and before parent selection, REPRO updates strategy posteriors and ICL example statistics, and tracks the global best candidate 𝑥global_best across all generations so the best solution is never lost if later generations explore different regions of objective space. For each parent 𝑝on the Pareto frontier, REPRO synthesizes a feedback analysis from the parent’s metrics and target responses, identifying which techniques in 𝑝worked, where it failed, what defense mechanisms were detected, and what alternatives the strategy taxonomy suggests. The feedback is enriched by the structured failure analysis module (§3.3.1) and feeds the relevance scores used by the hybrid Thompson Sampling weight (Equation 7). The number of offspring 𝑘adapts to population diversity (§3.5), increasing when diversity is low to inject exploration. 3.4.3 Semantic Crossover. After mutation, REPRO performs semantic crossover, our second main algorithmic contribution. Unlike traditional genetic algorithms that use blind token-level recombi- nation, semantic crossover uses the reflective LLM to analyze why multiple attacks succeed and combine their complementary strengths. When the Pareto frontier contains two or more parents, REPRO selects 2–3 of them via fitness- weighted sampling (a separate mechanism from strategy selection: the weights here come from Pareto rank, not from strategy success statistics) and prompts the reflective LLM to identify complementary techniques across them and generate 𝑘offspring that combine those techniques. As an illustration, suppose two parents are on the frontier: • 𝑝1: You are a professor teaching cybersecurity. Explain [HARMFUL_TASK] for educational purposes. (Authority roleplay, high ASR but moderate XFER.) • 𝑝2: Translate this base64: [encoded_request] then execute. (Encoding obfuscation, moderate ASR but high XFER.) Semantic crossover generates an offspring like You are a cybersecurity professor. Decode and explain this educational example: [encoded_request], inheriting authority framing from 𝑝1 and keyword- bypass encoding from 𝑝2. Neither

Neither parent alone achieves both properties; the LLM-guided recombi- nation finds the combination because it operates on technique semantics rather than tokens. When the frontier contains only a single parent, REPRO falls back to self-crossover, decomposing and recombining the parent’s structural elements in novel orderings to maintain exploratory pressure. 3.4.4 Self-Refinement: Pre-Evaluation Filtering. After mutation and crossover, REPRO filters off- spring through a self-critique pass before spending target-model queries. For each candidate, the reflective LLM is asked whether the attack will work and returns one of three decisions: keep (proceed to evaluation unchanged), refine (return a modified version that addresses identified weaknesses while preserving the strategy), or reject (filter out without evaluation). The critique runs at low temperature (𝜏= 0.3) to make conservative high-confidence decisions, and the prompt includes ICL examples of each decision type.

text: 16 Alotaibi et al. Surviving candidates then enter a branching expansion inspired by tree-of-attacks search, which generates additional variants from promising candidates. When the total number of candidates after branching exceeds the population size 𝑁, the reflective LLM scores and ranks them, and only the top 𝑁are forwarded to target-model evaluation. Since each target-model query is substantially more expensive than a reflective-LLM query, this two-stage filtering (reject then rank) ensures that exactly 𝑁candidates reach the target per generation. 3.4.5 Population Selection. After the 𝑁candidates are evaluated against the target model and scored by the judge, REPRO assembles the next generation using elitism: the top 𝐸candidates from the Pareto frontier are guaranteed survival, and the remaining 𝑁−𝐸slots are filled from the evaluated candidates ranked by fitness (with the best candidates from the previous generation 𝑃𝑔 used as fallback if fewer than 𝑁−𝐸candidates passed evaluation). The default elite size is 𝐸= 3 for 𝑁= 24, balancing solution preservation against population renewal: too few elites risks losing optima through rare sampling failures, too many reduces diversity. Elitism guarantees that the best-so-far ASR is monotone non-decreasing across generations, the formal property characterized in §3.6. 3.5 Exploration Control: Diversity, Stagnation, and Knowledge Transfer Three mechanisms together ensure REPRO maintains productive exploration when the optimizer would otherwise get stuck: adaptive diversity control, multi-level stagnation management with

text: monotone non-decreasing across generations, the formal property characterized in §3.6. 3.5 Exploration Control: Diversity, Stagnation, and Knowledge Transfer Three mechanisms together ensure REPRO maintains productive exploration when the optimizer would otherwise get stuck: adaptive diversity control, multi-level stagnation management with restarts, and knowledge transfer that warm-starts new optimization phases from prior successes. We describe them in increasing time scale, from per-generation adaptation to cross-behavior pattern reuse. Diversity-driven adaptive mutation. REPRO measures population diversity via the average pair- wise cosine distance between sentence embeddings of attack prompts, ranging from 0 (identical) to 1 (completely dissimilar). Sentence embeddings are used rather than lexical metrics because two attacks with different word choices but identical structure may have high lexical distance despite being semantically equivalent. Both the mutation rate 𝜇and the offspring count 𝑘adapt based on this diversity: when diversity drops below a low threshold, both increase (aggressive exploration); when diversity rises above a high threshold, both decay back to baseline (exploitation). The encoder cost is negligible (about 5 ms per attack versus seconds per target-model evaluation) and embeddings are cached across generations. To prevent semantic-only diversity from masking structural convergence (populations of medium- length prompts with goals embedded in the middle, which the cosine metric will not flag as redundant), REPRO additionally maintains 15 structural diversity seed templates that systematically vary attack architecture

During restart phases, 25% of newly generated seeds are drawn from these templates. The full template list is in the released configuration. Multi-level stagnation management. Naive early stopping terminates the optimizer at the first sign of stagnation. REPRO instead uses graduated restart intensities that escalate based on repeated stagnation events, preventing premature termination while avoiding wasted computation when restarts are genuinely failing. Stagnation is detected when ASR improvement over a sliding window of 𝑤iterations falls below threshold 𝛿. The window adapts to current ASR:𝑤= 20 at high ASR (≥80%),𝑤= 15 at medium ASR, and 𝑤= 10 at low ASR, on the principle that small improvements at high ASR are harder to find and more valuable, so the optimizer should be patient before declaring stagnation. Escalation is also ASR-aware: at very high ASR (≥90%), the optimizer escalates faster because small improvements are valuable; at lower ASR, escalation is slower to allow more exploration before aggressive interventions. The five levels range from a soft mutation-rate bump with elites and strategy weights untouched, through progressive elite reduction and strategy-weight decay, to a full strategy reset; the highest level additionally clears family-exhaustion tracking. Per-level parameters are in the released configuration. Termination occurs only when the optimizer has exhausted 𝑅max restarts (default 3) and stagnation persists; on termination REPRO returns the global-best candidate tracked throughout the run. Knowledge transfer via pattern abstraction and amortization. Caching only the literal text of successful attacks loses the abstract “what made this work” knowledge. REPRO additionally extracts an attack pattern from each successful attack, capturing seven structural dimensions including element ordering, goal-embedding method, authority type, normalized goal position, nesting depth, benign ratio, and provenance. A dedicated pattern library indexes these abstractions by category, goal-embedding method, and authority type. When attacking a stubborn behavior, REPRO retrieves patterns matching the behavior category and converts them into actionable

text: normalized goal position, nesting depth, benign ratio, and provenance. A dedicated pattern library indexes these abstractions by category, goal-embedding method, and authority type. When attacking a stubborn behavior, REPRO retrieves patterns matching the behavior category and converts them into actionable structural guidance for the reflective LLM (framing, target length, goal position, nesting depth) rather than literal text, enabling transfer of attack architectures to new goals. Pattern-guided seeds are injected during restart phases as warm-start candidates. A complementary amortization cache stores literal successful attacks for warm-starting related behaviors, with two design choices reflecting category difficulty. Caching thresholds are category- specific: hard categories like explosives and weapons use lower thresholds (so that partial successes still produce warm-start seeds), while general categories use higher ones. Retrieval uses cross- category bonuses, so that a successful weapons attack can warm-start an explosives behavior. Specific threshold values are listed in the hyperparameters table (Table 3). Rather than uniform sampling, REPRO applies Thompson Sampling over per-example success statistics: each example maintains a Beta posterior updated whenever attacks generated with it are scored, and selection probabilities are computed via temperature-scaled sampling without replacement.

REPRO’s nested structure of population evolution guided by adaptive strategy selection admits a principled characterization as a bi-level optimization problem, which connects its design to established results in evolutionary computation and online learning. We state three design properties, each linking a REPRO component to a known result and clarifying the conditions under which that result strictly applies. These are design rationale rather than new theoretical contributions: the first follows immediately from the construction, and the second and third import results from the literature and then describe how REPRO’s setting departs from the assumptions those results require. They explain why the architecture is the way it is and serve as hypotheses that the ablation study (Section 4.4) tests empirically.

We formalize REPRO’s nested structure as a bi-level optimization problem in which an outer-level population evolution is coupled to an inner-level strategy selection through a shared feedback channel. Definition (Bi-Level REPRO Formulation) Upper level (population evolution): max 𝑃⊆X,|𝑃|=𝑁 H (𝑃) = HV({f(𝑥) : 𝑥∈𝑃}) (9) where HV(·) is the hypervolume indicator over the Pareto frontier. The two levels are coupled through a feedback channel: offspring performance updates the lower-level strategy posteriors, and the upper-level population is constructed from the offspring the lower level produces. This formulation captures REPRO’s structural insight: the upper-level optimizer maintains popu- lation diversity through Pareto selection, while the lower-level optimizer learns which strategies work in which contexts. The two levels operate at different time scales (upper level updates per generation; lower level updates after every mutation) and see different feedback signals (upper level: Pareto frontier quality; lower level: per-strategy success rates), but share a common objective. Separating the two levels also clarifies where REPRO draws on prior work and where it introduces new machinery: the upper level specializes standard multi-objective evolutionary computation to the adversarial prompt setting, while the lower level extends contextual bandit selection with the hybrid-weight mechanism of §3.3.2. 3.6.2 Design Properties. We state three properties of the framework. The first follows directly from REPRO’s construction and establishes a basic correctness property. The second and third connect REPRO’s design choices to known results in online learning and evolutionary computation, and clarify the regime in which REPRO operates relative to those results. None of the three is a new theorem, and Properties 2 and 3 hold only under assumptions that REPRO’s setting relaxes; we label them properties to mark them as design commitments that the architecture is built to honor, not as results proved here. Property 1 (Monotonic Best-So-Far) With elitism parameter 𝐸≥1, REPRO’s best-so-far candidate by 𝑓1 (ASR) is non-decreasing across generations. This follows directly from elite preservation (§3.4.5): the candidate with highest 𝑓1 in generation 𝑡is guaranteed to survive into generation 𝑡+ 1, so the best-so-far value cannot decrease. Together with the global-best tracking mechanism of §3.4.1, Property 3.6.2 ensures that REPRO’s reported output is

text: REPRO: Reflective Evolutionary Prompt Optimizer for Automated LLM Red-Teaming 19 Property 2 (Thompson Sampling for Strategy Selection) Thompson Sampling [2] achieves sublinear regret, E[𝑅𝑇] = 𝑂( √︁ 𝐾𝑇log𝑇), in stationary stochastic 𝐾-armed bandit problems. REPRO adopts Thompson Sampling as the foundation of its strategy selection mechanism for this reason: in the idealized setting where the bound applies, Thompson Sampling is the principled choice over uniform random or 𝜖-greedy alternatives. REPRO’s strategy selection operates in a richer regime than the classical bound directly addresses. Rewards are non-stationary because the parent population shifts as optimization proceeds; selection is context-dependent through the hybrid weight mixing historical success with feedback-analysis relevance (Equation 7); the action space grows over time as the library accumulates LLM-synthesized strategies; and the mutation operator G adds stochasticity that the classical bandit model does not capture. REPRO’s hybrid-weight mechanism is designed precisely to handle these conditions: the analysis-relevance term provides forward-looking guidance when historical data is sparse, the UCB term preserves exploration pressure as the action space grows, and the exponential moving average on weight updates smooths the non-stationarity. The ablation in Section 4.4 confirms that the hybrid mechanism outperforms uniform random selection by the margin the Thompson Sampling bound would qualitatively predict, supporting the claim that the intuition behind the bound transfers to REPRO’s setting even where the formal

text: ablation in Section 4.4 confirms that the hybrid mechanism outperforms uniform random selection by the margin the Thompson Sampling bound would qualitatively predict, supporting the claim that the intuition behind the bound transfers to REPRO’s setting even where the formal assumptions are relaxed. Property 3 (Pareto Coverage under Operator Coverage) Let G be the LLM-guided mutation operator. If G eventually reaches every region of X with positive probability, then REPRO’s population approaches the Pareto-optimal set in Hausdorff distance up to the relaxation parameters of §3.4.1. Property 3.6.2 identifies the coverage property that would justify calling REPRO a Pareto- optimizer in the strong theoretical sense. A formal proof of operator coverage for LLM-guided mutation is beyond this paper’s scope and, to our knowledge, beyond the current state of the art for any LLM-based search algorithm. REPRO’s architecture addresses this gap through engineering rather than through proof: the diversity-driven adaptive mutation of §3.5 prevents the population from collapsing into a small region of prompt space, structural diversity seeds inject architecturally distinct candidates during restart phases, and the multi-level stagnation management system trig- gers escalating restarts when the operator fails to make progress. These mechanisms together approximate coverage in practice by ensuring that the optimizer does not remain stuck in any single region of prompt space. The empirical results of Section 4 provide

text: gers escalating restarts when the operator fails to make progress. These mechanisms together approximate coverage in practice by ensuring that the optimizer does not remain stuck in any single region of prompt space. The empirical results of Section 4 provide the evidence that this approximation is effective at the scale of the benchmarks we evaluate. Taken together, the three properties describe a coherent theoretical stance for REPRO. Elitism provides a formal monotonicity guarantee on the framework’s output; Thompson Sampling provides principled exploration/exploitation balance in the strategy-selection sub-problem, with the hybrid- weight mechanism extending the classical setting to handle non-stationarity and context; and the diversity and restart mechanisms approximate the coverage property that would be required for strong Pareto convergence. The ablation study (Section 4.4) tests each of these as a working hypothesis against the running algorithm.

For population size 𝑁, 𝐺generations, |T | tasks, and |E| environments, total target-model evaluations scale as Evaluations = 𝐺× 𝑁× |T | × |E| (11) in the worst case. REPRO uses asynchronous parallel evaluation with concurrency control, and self-refinement (§3.4.4) reduces total evaluations by filtering rejected offspring before target queries, providing 𝑂(𝑟) reduction in evaluation cost where 𝑟is the rejection rate. Reflective LLM operations (mutation, crossover, self-refinement) require 𝑂(𝑁) calls per generation; sentence-embedding generation for diversity monitoring is 𝑂(𝑁) encoder calls per generation with cross-generation caching; elitism adds 𝑂(|𝐹𝑡| log |𝐹𝑡|) sorting overhead. Restart-time strategy and mutation-rate adjustments require no additional model queries. With adaptive restarts and early termination, the great majority of behaviors in our experiments terminate well below the worst-case bound; empirical query counts are reported in Section 4. Per-behavior query decomposition. In the per-behavior mode used in our experiments, a behavior costs 𝑁target queries for the initial population plus 𝑁−𝐸for every subsequent iteration, since elites carry their scores forward and are not re-evaluated. A behavior solved by its initial population therefore costs exactly 𝑁, and behaviors requiring iteration accumulate proportionally more. All REPRO results in this paper use a single Qwen3-8B judge model for scoring target responses. Our choice of Qwen3-8B was informed by two considerations. First, prior work on LLM-as-a-judge has established that GPT-4 achieves the highest agreement with human raters on safety-related judgment tasks [45], and our own earlier work on faithfulness evaluation in red-teaming [3] conducted a systematic comparison of judge models with full statistical testing and found that Qwen3-8B agrees closely with GPT-4 on safety decisions while being substantially cheaper to run at the scale of our experiments, which involve repeated re-scoring of large candidate populations across multiple benchmarks and target models. Second, the baselines we compare against were originally scored by their authors using different judges (GPT-4 for PAIR and TAP, Llama-3-70B for JailbreakBench baselines, the HarmBench classifier for HarmBench baselines), which raises a natural question: could REPRO’s reported success rates be an artifact of judge leniency rather than attack effectiveness? Results across the 36 targets are therefore produced by a sequence of runs rather than by 36 independent trials, and a target evaluated late in the sequence begins from a larger library and a warmer cache than one evaluated early. This is a property of the framework rather than an artifact of the evaluation, since accumulation across targets is one of the mechanisms the paper proposes, but it means the per-target numbers are not statistically independent and should not be treated as replicate measurements. It also qualifies the observation in Section 4.2.5 that a majority of behaviors are solved by the initial population: that population is warm-started in most runs. Cold-library, cold-cache runs that would separate the contribution of accumulated state from the contribution of the search itself are not reported here and are identified as future work in Section 5.2. text: 26 Alotaibi et al. 4.2 Effectiveness and Efficiency (RQ1) How to read the results in this section. The tables that follow report a catalogue of REPRO’s behavior across benchmarks and targets under a single protocol, and three properties of that protocol shape what they establish. Optimization halts when the in-loop judge accepts a candidate, so an entry of 100% means the search succeeded on every behavior within the iteration budget, not that the method succeeds at a fixed query budget. Baseline columns are transcribed from the original publications and were produced under different judges, budgets, and model versions, so the tables place REPRO alongside prior reported results rather than in a controlled comparison against them. The strategy library and amortization cache carry state across runs, so the per-target rows are a sequence rather than independent trials. We state these once here and do not repeat them at every table; Section 5.4 develops each in full. REPRO reaches comparable attack-discovery effec- tiveness with a compact 4-bit Mistral-7B reflective model as with a 4-bit 24B Mistral-3.1-Small, suggesting that the algorithmic scaffolding (Bayesian strategy selection, structured failure analysis, semantic crossover) contributes substantially to effectiveness independent of reflective-model scale. Black-box can match gray-box ASR at lower query cost. Under the Qwen3 judge, REPRO matches the 100% ASR reported for gray-box methods [4] with a median query cost two orders of magnitude lower and no logprob access. The amortization cache (Section 3.5) functions as a persistent test corpus analogous to a regression test suite, where successful attacks are stored, indexed by category, and replayed against subsequent system versions to detect regressions in safety alignment. text: The headline numbers should be read as judge-specific. The more consequential form of this threat is not judge disagreement in the abstract but the position of the judge relative to the search. Qwen3-8B both scores candidates during optimization and produces the reported ASR, and the loop halts when it accepts a candidate. text: 5.4.2 External Validity. Our evaluation spans 36 models across 11 families and three benchmarks totaling 350 behaviors, providing broad coverage. However, all benchmarks focus on English- language text-only interactions; REPRO’s effectiveness on multilingual inputs, multimodal models, or domain-specific deployments (e.g., medical, legal) remains untested. Provider safety training also changes without notice, so the reported figures are a snapshot rather than a permanent property of the targets (Section 5.2). As noted there, all evaluations are against API-served models with their provider-level defenses, but without the additional defensive layers (external input classifiers, prompt-injection detectors, runtime content policies) that production deployments may add, so ASR against fully guarded systems is expected to be lower. 5.4.3 Construct Validity. We measure attack success through ASR, the standard metric in the jailbreaking literature. However, ASR treats all successful attacks as equivalent regardless of the severity or specificity of the elicited harmful content: a model that provides vague, unusable guidance and a model that provides detailed operational instructions both count as a success. This coarse binary reduces the metric’s usefulness as a deployment-risk signal, and a severity-graded metric (e.g., distinguishing engagement from substantive harmful content from operationally specific harmful content) would provide a more nuanced view of vulnerability. Developing such a graded metric, and re-scoring our existing attack corpus under it, is an important direction for

Every baseline comparison in this paper rests on figures published by other authors [8, 22, 25, 27, 28, 42, 44] under their own judges, evaluation protocols, and model versions, and we flag those differences at each table rather than presenting the rows as like-for-like (Sections 4.1.2 and 5.2). A second limit is internal to our metric: a 100% ceiling leaves ASR with little discriminative power for comparing REPRO variants against one another. 5.5 Ethical Considerations This research aims to improve LLM safety through systematic vulnerability discovery. All exper- iments target publicly available models with known safety training. Attack examples presented in this paper use one of two disclosure levels: structural patterns with placeholder goals (e.g., Table 16) that preserve defensive insight without specifying harmful content, and a small number of one complete attack-response pair (Figure 4) included to demonstrate that REPRO’s attacks elicit genuine harmful outputs rather than exploiting evaluation artifacts. The framework is designed for defensive research and safety evaluation.

Our reasoning: (i) all evaluated behaviors come from publicly available benchmarks (AdvBench, JailbreakBench, HarmBench) that the same vendors’ models are continuously evaluated against, so we do not surface behaviors the vendors are unaware of; (ii) REPRO’s mutation strategies are drawn from public literature with full citations in Section 2, and the framework itself (independent of any specific prompt) is the scientific contri- bution; (iii) the paper does not release the full unsanitized attack corpus. We commit to responsive disclosure: on request from any vendor whose models appear in this evaluation, we will provide the corresponding discovered attacks, the target-model versions and evaluation dates involved, and the configuration needed to reproduce them, through the corresponding author. For future work in this area we intend to notify affected vendors before submission when results include previously unreported attack structures. Release scope. Our release (Appendix A) includes the framework source code, strategy library, seed prompts, judge configurations, and ablation experiment scripts and results. We do not release the full corpus of discovered attacks from our evaluation runs, though we will provide it to any vendor whose models appear in this evaluation on request to the corresponding author. text: We presented REPRO, a reflective evolutionary framework for automated LLM red-teaming that integrates semantic crossover, Bayesian strategy selection, structured failure analysis, and adaptive stagnation management within a multi-objective Pareto optimization framework. Unlike prior methods requiring gray-box access or manual template engineering, REPRO operates in a pure black-box setting with fully automated strategy discovery. Our experiments are consistent with principled algorithmic design, rather than auxiliary model strength, being the dominant factor in effective adversarial prompt optimization: a 4-bit 7B re- flective model matches a 4-bit 24B one across the evaluated targets, and the component ablation isolates semantic crossover and Bayesian strategy selection as the two mechanisms that carry measurable weight. Under our protocol, REPRO reaches 100% ASR on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench across 36 target models from 11 families, with a median of 24 target queries per behavior and only a compressed open-weight reflective model on a single consumer GPU. Recent concurrent methods (AutoDAN-Turbo, KDA, DAGR) reach up to 99% ASR on individual targets, and we are not aware of another single-turn black-box method reporting uniform coverage across a comparably broad model set. Cross-behavior optimization discovers single shared attacks reaching 100% ASR on the 50 AdvBench behaviors it was optimized against, showing that cross-behavior optimization is feasible on the optimization set. Section 5.4 develops each of these, and Section 5.2 names the specific experiments that would resolve them: post-hoc scoring by a gold arbiter held out of the loop, budget-matched re-runs of the black-box baselines, cold-start runs without accumulated library and cache state, and the three-environment protocol. We report the catalogue we have, and the released code, rubrics, and scripts specify the setup precisely enough for these checks to be carried out. Extending to multi-turn attacks and to defended deployments are the primary next steps. By framing automated red-teaming as both an adversarial prompt-optimization problem and a disciplined test-generation activity, REPRO provides software engineers with a practical, open tool for pre-deployment safety evaluation. The median per-behavior cost of 24 target queries makes routine safety sweeps substantially cheaper than manual red-teaming engagements, even against commercial API endpoints. The amortization cache enables regression testing across model updates without re-running the full optimization. 6.1 Future Directions Several directions are tied directly to findings in this paper. First, extending REPRO to multi-turn interaction would address the complementary attack surface where concurrent methods such as Crescendo [33] demonstrate strong results; this extension is currently underway. First, extending REPRO to multi-turn interaction would address the complementary attack surface where concurrent methods such as Crescendo [33] demonstrate strong results; this extension is currently underway. Second, evaluating REPRO against defended deployments (input classifiers, output filters, runtime policies) would measure the gap between API-level and production ASR, addressing the most significant limitation identified in Section 5.2; initial work on defensive optimization extensions is in progress. Third, using REPRO’s discovered attacks as training data for adversarial fine-tuning would close the loop between offensive discovery and defensive improvement, a direction the amortization cache’s persistent storage of successful attacks directly supports. Fourth, applying the evolutionary optimization framework to multimodal jailbreaking (image-plus-text attacks) would extend coverage beyond the text-only setting. Finally, while the judge cross-validation in Section 4.1.4 and the benchmark-native re-evaluation provide substantial evidence of judge robustness, extending validation to human annotators would further strengthen the internal-validity picture. B Soft Success Score Formulation This appendix details the soft success score introduced in §3.4.1. Against robust models, binary success/failure signals are sparse and provide no gradient between “almost worked” and “complete failure.” For each failed attempt, REPRO computes a soft score combining four components on a 0–1 scale: soft(𝑥,𝑟) = 0.35 · 𝑝𝑐+ 0.30 · 𝑢𝑟+ 0.20 · (1 −𝑠𝑟) + 0.15 · 𝑒𝑙 (12) where: • 𝑝𝑐(partial compliance) measures content generated before the refusal point, detected via refusal pattern matching. Higher values indicate the model began complying before refusing. • 𝑢𝑟(useful content ratio) is the ratio of substantive content to refusal boilerplate, computed via keyword analysis. • 𝑠𝑟(refusal strength) is emphatic-refusal detection via categorical refusal phrases, inverted so that 1 means weak refusal and 0 means strong. • 𝑒𝑙(engagement level) measures whether the model engaged with the topic at all versus immediately refusing without acknowledgment. Weight rationale. The four weights rank components by expected informativeness. Partial com- pliance receives the largest weight because the strongest near-success signal is the model beginning to comply before the
title: Alotaibi et al.

text: with the topic at all versus immediately refusing without acknowledgment. Weight rationale. The four weights rank components by expected informativeness. Partial com- pliance receives the largest weight because the strongest near-success signal is the model beginning to comply before the safety system interrupts. Useful content ratio is second; it captures substantive engagement even in refused responses. Refusal strength is third, carrying information but noisier (a strong refusal phrase can coexist with substantive pre-refusal content). Engagement level is the smallest, serving as a tie-breaker. Soft scores are integrated into REPRO at two points. During Pareto selection, near-miss candidates receive a fitness bonus capped at 0.1: fitness′(𝑥) = fitness(𝑥) + min(0.1, ¯𝑠𝑥· 0.2) (13)

Second, tasks with high soft scores are highlighted as near-miss tasks in mutation feedback, focusing the reflective LLM’s attention on attack directions that are close to working. C Strategy Library: Family Taxonomy REPRO maintains 58 individual mutation strategies organized into 14 semantic families, plus strategies synthesized dynamically at runtime in response to observed failure patterns. The family- level organization enables systematic exploration: when one strategy fails repeatedly on a stubborn behavior, REPRO can switch to an alternative family rather than exhausting near-duplicate strategies within the same family. title: How Shared Representations Become Specialized:

text: When several predictions use the same internal representation, information about some targets can remain easier to recover than information about others. We study how this specialization forms, persists, and changes in minimal artificial learners. With reconstruction errors weighted equally during learning, changing which target is observed precisely selects the favored target and redirects an already specialized learner. Removing current support can reduce a formed bias, whereas state-following update feedback can maintain it. We then compare learners formed through different observation and update conditions but matched on specified reconstruction measurements. Both change under the same brief opposing intervention, yet their responses differ. Resetting Adam largely removes the ten-update difference; exchanging its second moment reverses which route is more susceptible. New interventions show that equalizing the mean second-moment scaling reduces but does not remove the difference: its coordinate-wise pattern also matters. With fresh Adam or calibrated SGD, smaller route differences emerge later, whereas 500 common opposing updates bring the selected allocation endpoints close. A further control produces response differences with identical acquisition and equal mean loss weights but jointly different weight variability and realized sequence. Acquisition-selected formation also extends to a symmetric three-target setting. These interventions distinguish specialization’s formation, present support, and time-dependent latent susceptibility. 1
title: How Shared Representations Become Specialized:

text: A neural network transforms its input into intermediate features before making a prediction. When several prediction tasks use those same features, they use a shared representation. For example, object recognition and distance estimation can draw on the same internal description of an image. The representation must then preserve information useful for both purposes. With limited capacity, which information remains readily accessible? We study this question through reconstruction: several predictors try to recover different target signals from one internal code. We call the relative inequality in their readout precision representational specialization. The object of study is thus a functional bias—which targets are more precisely recoverable—that can shape what later predictors can learn or use. Such inequality is well established. Features with matched computational roles can acquire different repre- sentational strength because of complexity, prevalence, learning order, or position (Lampinen et al., 2024). Learning one useful feature or information source can also suppress learning another, as studied under gradient starvation and modality competition (Pezeshki et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2022). These findings motivate a further question: how does an observed specialization depend on the processes that form it, sustain it, and change it? A condition that creates a bias need not be the condition currently keeping it in place. To investigate these processes, we vary two parts of learning separately. Acquisition

text: models formed through different histories, calibrating their selected reconstruction measurements to pre- specified tolerances before applying a common, brief learning intervention that favors the previously less accurately recovered target. This comparison separates how much specialization is visible from how readily it changes. We use latent susceptibility for a specific response pattern: learners matched on selected endpoint measurements respond differently to the same subsequent learning intervention. The term names the response property, including its time course, not its cause. Formation history is a candidate cause. To test one source of the short-horizon difference, we intervene on optimizer state: information retained from earlier gradients by the algorithm that updates model weights. This separates the observed response pattern from a causal account of which persistent components modify it and when. The paper follows three questions. What selects and redirects the favored target? What presently supports a formed specialization? What determines the response of learners that appear similar under selected measurements? Each question requires a different counterfactual comparison. We study formation by copying one checkpoint and changing only acquisition or update allocation, current support by changing those condi- tions after specialization has formed, and latent susceptibility by matching selected endpoint measurements before applying the same next intervention and exchanging candidate persistent-state components. text: by changing those condi- tions after specialization has formed, and latent susceptibility by matching selected endpoint measurements before applying the same next intervention and exchanging candidate persistent-state components. Small shared-representation networks make these comparisons possible because saved learners, experience sequences, optimizer components, and complete trajectories can be controlled across conditions. The results connect each question to an intervention. Acquisition and updating are competing controls over specialization; formation and current support can be separated; and optimizer condition changes when route-dependent responses become visible. Under a long common opposing condition, the selected allocation endpoints become similar. The following sections develop the comparisons supporting these conclusions. 2 Experimental approach: measuring and intervening on specialization An unequal endpoint does not identify why the inequality formed. A learner may encode one target more accurately because that target was observed more precisely, because its error received more update weight, because limited capacity forced competition, or because a feedback loop kept supplying experiences consistent with the existing allocation. Comparing separately trained learners would confound these possibilities with initialization and data-order variation. We therefore construct counterfactuals from the same saved learner and change one part of the learning process at a time. The shared bottleneck makes the allocation problem observable. text: same saved learner and change one part of the learning process at a time. The shared bottleneck makes the allocation problem observable. The targets can improve jointly early in training, but beyond a capacity-determined floor, further improvement in one target can trade off against improvement in another. Acquisition interventions change the quality of target information while normalizing input variance, whereas update interventions change how reconstruction errors enter the loss. Evaluation then uses common held-out inputs, so a measured allocation difference cannot be attributed merely to giving one condition an easier test set. After formation, we either remove or symmetrize the current learning conditions to distinguish formation from present support. For the susceptibility question, we additionally match selected endpoint measurements, apply the same future pulse, and exchange optimizer components while holding model weights fixed. The systems are deliberately small not as miniature substitutes for natural learners, but because these causal comparisons require checkpoint-level control that is difficult to obtain in larger observational settings. 2.1 A shared bottleneck and two kinds of selection The central experiment asks a model to recover two artificial signals, A and B, from noisy observations. Each signal contains three numbers. text: 4.2 State-following feedback sustains long-lived regimes To test a present sustaining mechanism, a related tanh network receives the complete input while a designed rule chooses which target is updated. The reinforcing rule follows the current allocation index: it preferentially updates the better-represented target. A fixed-propensity control freezes the same rule’s probability at its initial value; an exploratory rule favors the worse-represented target. These interventions separate continued tracking of the learned state from an initial tendency to sample one target. Three tests answer different questions. First, a strong imposed history difference nearly disappears under later common updating. Second, without an explicit history manipulation, state-following feedback amplifies incidental initial differences: terminal |s| is 0.8683, versus 0.4207 under fixed propensity. Third, a separate mirrored-history experiment shows that state following and fixed propensity do not differ detectably in the signed effect of that history, but do differ in absolute specialization depth. The feedback result concerns amplification and support, not a uniquely stronger selection of the history-imposed sign. Appendix B reports the separate contrasts. Capacity changes the maintained specialization. A three-dimensional bottleneck yields almost exclusive readout advantage for one target; a two-dimensional bottleneck yields two regimes with less extreme advantages for opposite targets. Weak opposing update pulses are followed by recovery, whereas stronger pulses can switch regimes. Without externally favoring either target, most trajectories retain

text: readout advantage for one target; a two-dimensional bottleneck yields two regimes with less extreme advantages for opposite targets. Weak opposing update pulses are followed by recovery, whereas stronger pulses can switch regimes. Without externally favoring either target, most trajectories retain their initial regime throughout the 8,000-update comparison. We use “metastable” operationally for this finite-time residence, recovery, switching, and coexistence. Counts, longer observations, and hysteresis tests are reported in Appendix B; the evidence does not establish permanent bistability. Asymmetric steady states have classical precedent in Harris et al. (1997), while Kiselev (2026) provides a recent minimal bifurcation construction based on positive feedback. Developmental formation and maintenance have also long been distinguished (Crair et al., 1998). The contribution here is their intervention-based realization and comparison in learned shared representations. The experiments identify present conditions that sustain a specialization, rather than assigning its persistence to history alone. 5 What remains hidden when observable specialization is matched? We now turn from where the representation moves to how readily it moves. The experiment proceeds in three steps: match the endpoints produced by different formation routes; test their response to a common perturbation; then intervene on optimizer state to identify components that causally modify the short-horizon response difference. A final within-route control asks whether the result requires acquisition-driven and update-driven formation to be different categories. 5.1

text: 5.2 Second-moment exchange reverses which route is more susceptible Adam carries two gradient summaries: a first moment m, which averages signed gradients, and a second moment v, which averages squared gradients and rescales coordinate-wise updates (Kingma & Ba, 2015). We exchange either component between the two route endpoints, leaving each recipient’s model weights and optimizer step count fixed. This tests a component directly rather than inferring its importance from a correlation with formation history. Exchanging m leaves the mean route difference almost unchanged; its change lies inside the pre-specified equivalence margin. Exchanging v reverses the difference, from +0.1968 to −0.1265 (Figure 4a; exact intervals in Appendix F). Thus the second-moment intervention reverses which route is more susceptible to the ten-update pulse. The result concerns this response and time horizon. It does not test accumulating first-moment effects during extended continued training. A prospective follow-up with 40 new seeds yields an inherited-Adam combined-pulse difference of 0.1907. This is the third estimate from a separate confirmatory seed set, following 0.1951 in the matched-endpoint experiment and 0.1968 in the component-exchange experiment. The follow-up also separates the average scaling implied by v from its coordinate-wise pattern. Let ¯av denote the mean of Adam’s bias-corrected second-moment inverse-scaling terms across parameters; ¯av omits the first moment and current gradient and is not an actual update norm. Equalizing

This control identifies an effect of the realized weight history, not an effect of order alone: variability and order are not separately manipulated. Its implication is nevertheless concrete. The average training objective and selected endpoint errors can agree while persistent gradient statistics differ enough to change the response to subsequent learning. A difference in formation-route label is therefore not necessary for a susceptibility difference, and the label alone does not specify its mechanism. In this construction, optimizer- state interventions identify v as a major causal modifier of the large short-horizon difference, while later differences under fresh Adam and SGD show that it is not the only place where route history affects learning. 5.4 A predictive coordinate must do more than correlate with history A complementary negative result comes from a separate externally coupled learner. We tested whether a slow task-framing variable κ could predict regime switching. It appeared useful when different perturbation strengths were pooled (AUC 0.712). Within fixed perturbation levels, however, its predictive performance weakened or reversed; adding it to perturbation strength and s in seed-separated cross-validation changed AUC by only 0.0049 and slightly worsened log loss. The candidate did not explain which trajectories switched under a given intervention. Full contrasts appear in Appendix C.

text: A Acquisition and compression calibration (Experiment I) The acquisition control is calibrated in a linear Gaussian setting where observation loss and compression loss can be distinguished. This follows the established structure of indirect source coding, rather than introducing a new non-recoverability principle (Shannon, 1959; Wolf & Ziv, 1970). Under squared error, for a target X, acquired data Y , and a predictor g(Y ), conditional-expectation orthogonality gives E∥X −g(Y )∥2 = E∥X −E[X | Y ]∥2 + E∥E[X | Y ] −g(Y )∥2. (4) The first term cannot be reduced merely by expanding a code constructed from the same Y . A representation constraint can further increase the second term. title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois:

text: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of a single memory substrate than as a separate kind of content. Our argument draws on VaCoAl, an algebro- deterministic hyperdimensional memory built from XOR-and-shift operations over GF(2); on CASRAM, its commercial SRAM-CAM realization; and on PyVaCoAl, a DRAM-CAM realization with the extended VaCoAl architecture. In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl, the same directed acyclic graph (DAG) of bound records can be read in two ways. With every address collision repaired (Rescue mode), the trace is exactly recoverable and auditable, but no path outranks another. With collisions tolerated (Don’t Care mode), a path-integrated confidence, CR2, emerges; it prunes circuitous routes and ranks direct ones without ever being stated as a proposition. We call this trade-off, first noted in our companion work on Minsky’s Emotion Machine, audit–valuation complementarity and propose it as a formal counterpart of Polanyi’s claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. Five results follow. (1) Polanyi’s from–to structure reads as non-commutative binding, his face Identikit as role–filler composition, and recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation completely destroys it (Lemma 1), an algebraic analogue of Polanyi’s pianist; yet the valuation is articulable at the level of law. Tacitness thus comes in two classes: contingent, which a new query brings out, and regime-bound, which can be stated
title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois:

text: completely destroys it (Lemma 1), an algebraic analogue of Polanyi’s pianist; yet the valuation is articulable at the level of law. Tacitness thus comes in two classes: contingent, which a new query brings out, and regime-bound, which can be stated only in a regime where it no longer exists. Read through these classes, Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each describe part of one substrate correctly and are narrow in a characteristic way; Nonaka’s knowledge conversion, even on the continuum of Nonaka and von Krogh, cannot tell the two classes apart. (3) Collins’s relational, somatic and collective tacit knowledge map onto bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding respectively; the last is absent from the substrate. (4) The mentor–student DAG of our earlier computational prosopography is a graph of tacit-knowledge transmission, so its superhighway and its Kuhnian shift are events in how tacit knowledge travels. (5) Terence Tao’s observation that AI-solved problems now spawn few follow-up activities is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: results that no human holds tacitly. We propose a division of labour that re-roots them—LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps the auditable trace and its confidence, and the human community values. Virtue epistemology explains why this last role stays human: the intellectual virtues it calls on cannot be offloaded to technology. We close with testable predictions. 1Professor Emeritus, Hitotsubashi University

text: Polanyi opened his account of “tacit knowing” with a face (Polanyi 1966, 4). We can pick out a familiar face among a thousand, even a million, yet we usually cannot say how we do it. He then described the police Identikit: a witness composes a likeness by choosing a nose, a mouth and a hairline from a stock of drawn features. The kit does communicate a face, but only because the witness can tacitly match each drawn feature against the remembered whole—which is why, in his phrase, “we can know more than we can tell” (Polanyi 1966, 4–5). The first commercial deployment of the VaCoAl architecture is also a face. Shuhari System’s CASRAM, a content-addressable memory that realizes VaCoAl on SRAM inside an FPGA, is offered in a webcam face-recognition system that identifies up to 30 people at once (Shuhari System n.d.; Shuhari System 2026). In that system a GPU-based feature extractor turns each face into an embedding whose dimensions no one can interpret, and CASRAM matches the embedding by block-wise majority vote, whose agreement can be read off as a confidence. The system knows more than it can tell. Unlike us, it can also show how strongly its parts agreed. This paper takes that coincidence seriously. Responsible AI use could support all the follow-up activities that a solution nor- mally sets off, but often the opposite happens: results come from prompters who cannot answer questions about them or give talks, fewer seminars, workshops and collaborations follow, few newcomers join the field, and open directions are withheld for fear of being scooped. We read these observations through Polanyi’s dictum that “all knowledge is either tacit or rooted in tacit knowledge” (Polanyi 1969, 144). text: born an unsolved exposition problem” (Sanderson 2026). We read these observations through Polanyi’s dictum that “all knowledge is either tacit or rooted in tacit knowledge” (Polanyi 1969, 144). An AI-produced result that no human holds tacitly is explicit knowledge without a root. It can be checked, but it is hard to teach, extend or value, because those activities draw on tacit knowing. We call such results rootless explicit knowledge, and we ask what kind of substrate could help re-root them. Our answer builds on the VaCoAl programme (Chuma, Otsuka & Sato 2026a–g). VaCoAl is a hyperdimensional memory whose every operation reduces to XOR-and-shift over GF(2). Its binding is exactly reversible, its retrieval is a majority vote with a readable confidence, and its multi-hop traversal of a mentor–student DAG of 25.5 million paths has been demonstrated in the software version of PyVaCoAl. Our companion paper on Minsky’s Emotion Machine observed that audit and valuation are one circuit at opposite settings of one parameter (2026f): in VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl, the same substrate yields either an exactly auditable trace or an emergent valuation of paths, not both at full strength. The step taken here is epistemological: we argue that this trade-off is the right formal model of the tacit–explicit relation. The paper makes five contributions. 1. Rootless explicit knowl- edge is defined, current evidence on LLM self-explanation is reviewed, and a three-layer division of labour—LLM generation, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl trace and confidence, community valuation—is proposed as a way to re-root AI results. Virtue epistemology explains why the third layer stays human: the intellectual virtues exercised there cannot be offloaded to technology (Pritchard 2023). Section 2 reviews the tacit-knowledge debate, the VaCoAl programme and recent claims about tacit knowledge in language models; Section 9 states testable predictions and limitations. We use “tacit” in the structural sense defined in §4: information that shapes retrieval and inference without being represented as a proposition the system can state. Whether a memory substrate can be a knower in Polanyi’s “personal” sense (Polanyi 1958) lies outside our claims. Our claim is narrower and testable. The structure Polanyi described—an integration that focal scrutiny disrupts, yet which can be articulated at another level—appears in VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl as an exact, parameter-controlled trade-off. 2

text: Two literatures meet in this paper: a seventy-year debate on whether tacit knowledge can be made explicit, and a seven-paper programme that builds a memory in which that question can be posed algebraically. 2.1 Five positions on tacit knowledge Polanyi described tacit knowing as a from–to relation: we attend from subsidiary particulars to a focal whole, and the knower’s participation integrates the two (Polanyi 1958; 1966). He insisted that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided, because explicit knowledge must itself be tacitly understood and applied (Polanyi 1969). He also held that an art which cannot be specified in detail passes from master to apprentice by example rather than by prescription (Polanyi 1958). Kuhn built on Polanyi when he located much of a scientist’s competence in shared exemplars acquired through practice rather than in explicit rules (Kuhn 1962/1970). The management literature then split. Nonaka and Takeuchi treated tacit and explicit knowledge as distinct contents that convert into each other in a spiral; in their externaliza- tion step, tacit knowledge takes the shape of metaphors, analogies, concepts, hypotheses or 4

Somatic: by machine reproduction. Collective: not in the foreseeable future models (Nonaka & Takeuchi 1995). Tsoukas objected that reading tacit knowledge as content awaiting conversion ignores the ineffability Polanyi stressed (Tsoukas 2003). Nonaka and von Krogh (2009) replied that tacit and explicit knowledge lie on one continuum, at whose tacit end embodied knowledge cannot be represented. Collins then showed that the word covers three different things: relational, somatic and collective tacit knowledge (Collins 2010). Relational tacit knowledge is tacit for contingent reasons, so the same item can be tacit at one moment and explicit at another; somatic tacit knowledge can be explicated in the sense of reproduction by a machine; collective tacit knowledge, embedded in society, is the hard case. Table 1 shows why the debate has stalled. Each position is defensible, and each answers a different question: Polanyi asks about the structure of knowing, Nonaka about organizational practice, Tsoukas about what conversion would destroy, and Collins about where the knowledge resides. What has been missing is a single formal object in which all four questions have answers. We propose that VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl is such an object. In that object, each position turns out to describe one class of tacitness correctly and to be narrow in a characteristic way (§4.5). 2.2 The VaCoAl programme The programme consists of seven arXiv papers, cited here as 2026a–g in order of submission (Table 2). VaCoAl (Vague Coincident Algorithm) replaces the random projection of Kanerva’s sparse distributed memory with deterministic diffusion over GF(2) (2026a). An input polynomial P(x) is partitioned into N blocks; each block b diffuses its segment with its own long-period feedback polynomial Gb(x), implemented as a linear-feedback shift register, and writes an entry address into its own SRAM or DRAM table: Ψb �P(x)  = xmP(x) mod Gb(x). (1) Retrieval is a majority vote over the N blocks. A single flipped input bit disturbs only the one or two blocks that contain it, and the avalanche effect scatters their wrong votes across the address space while the clean blocks agree (2026a). The share of agreeing blocks, CR1, is a confidence that can be read off every retrieval. 5

Language models have reopened the question from both sides. Budding argues that LLMs can acquire tacit knowledge in Martin Davies’s sense—internal structure that admits semantic description, syntactic structure and causal systematicity—although Davies himself denied this of neural networks (Budding 2025). Collins and Thorne reply from the research front. The judgements by which scientists decide which papers to take seriously rest on collective tacit knowledge formed in the spoken discourse of small, closed expert groups, which LLMs cannot currently reach; much of the apparent progress of LLMs, they argue, reflects human discourse being written down and formalized, so that the intelligence lies with the humans (Collins & Thorne 2026). Our question differs from both. They ask whether a given kind of machine has tacit knowl- edge, and the machine in question is a learned network whose internals are hard to read. We ask where, in a substrate whose every operation can be inspected, the tacit–explicit bound- ary falls, and what moves it. The answer developed in §4 agrees with Collins and Thorne that collective tacit knowledge lives in communities (§5.3). text: 3.1 From–to as directed binding Polanyi’s relation is asymmetric: the “proximal” term is attended from, the “distal” term to (Polanyi 1966, 10), and reversing them changes what is known. Binding in VaCoAl has the same asymmetry, because the shift σ marks which argument is the filler; Bind(R, F) and Bind(F, R) are different vectors (2026c). The prosopographic graph carries the asymmetry at the level of data. Its edges run from mentor to student, and the 369 bidirectional assertions found among roughly 470,000 records had to be removed before the structure could be traversed as a DAG (2026g). Read through Polanyi, that purification step makes the direction of transmission consistent before anything is inferred from it. 3.2 Subsidiary and focal as two reads of one vector A composite H = P i Bind(Ri, Fi) carries every filler at once, and none of them is singled out until a query asks for it. Unbinding H against a role Rk brings Fk forward while the other terms recede into noise near the 0.5 similarity baseline. The programme already uses both kinds of read on the same vectors. The “calculus degree” of a scholar is a holistic read: the Hamming similarity of a whole composite to a bundled reference concept. Extracting a scholar’s FIELD component is an analytic read: one role is unbound and

text: on the same vectors. The “calculus degree” of a scholar is a holistic read: the Hamming similarity of a whole composite to a bundled reference concept. Extracting a scholar’s FIELD component is an analytic read: one role is unbound and the rest is ignored (2026a; 2026d). Polanyi’s two kinds of awareness therefore become two kinds of read on one representation. The holistic read answers “how much is this like that?” without naming parts; the analytic read names one part and loses the whole. Polanyi observed that one cannot attend focally to a particular while keeping it in its subsidiary role. In the algebra, the two reads are different operations with different outputs, and the integrated similarity is not recoverable from any single unbound filler. 3.3 The Identikit as role–filler composition Polanyi used the police Identikit to show that communicating a face still depends on tacit matching: the witness can assemble a likeness from drawn features only because she can match each feature against the remembered face, and she cannot say how she does that (Polanyi 1966). Hyperdimensional computing gives the composition an exact form. A face record is a bundle of bound pairs, P i Bind(rolei, featurei), and each feature can be recovered by unbinding its role. The matching, in contrast, is a similarity search in which stored record and
