text: composition an exact form. A face record is a bundle of bound pairs, P i Bind(rolei, featurei), and each feature can be recovered by unbinding its role. The matching, in contrast, is a similarity search in which stored record and probe vote block by block. CASRAM’s face-recognition system divides the work between two machines (Shuhari System 2026). An edge PC with a GPU extracts a feature embedding from each face; an FPGA module carrying CASRAM, connected to it over PCIe, performs the 1:N match; and the interface overlays each identified face with an ID and a confidence. We do not claim that this product binds faces as role–filler pairs. What the product shows is that the tacit–explicit boundary can be moved. For Polanyi’s witness, the composition could be told and the matching could not. In this system it is the other way round. The matching is done by a memory whose decisions are majority votes with a readable confidence (2026a), while the encoding that produced the embedding is the part no one can state. The boundary has not disappeared; it has moved, and it now runs along a physical link between two pieces of hardware. That is the thesis of §4 in miniature: where the boundary falls depends on the substrate and its operations, not on the knowledge itself. 3.4

Such a system cannot state a rule for why the winner won. It can, however, state how much its blocks agreed, 8

text: which blocks dissented, and how the agreement decayed along a path. Retrieval confidence is the vote share CR1, and multi-hop confidence is CR2 (2026a). This is a third condition between Polanyi’s poles. The system is articulate about agreement and inarticulate about reasons. People are usually inarticulate about both; we feel more or less sure but cannot count our votes. The partial telling matters for §8, because confidence and trace are exactly what a human needs in order to re-root a result. 3.5 Indwelling and the fixed scaffold Polanyi described tools and probes as things we come to “dwell in” (Polanyi 1966, 17–18): the blind man feels the end of his stick, not its pressure on his palm. On this reading indwelling is not a mystery added to cognition. It is the ordinary condition of any substrate whose orthogonalizer is hardwired and therefore invisible to its own queries. 4 Audit–valuation complementarity: tacit

text: Structurally tacit. Information can be at work in a memory without ever being stated by it. We can tell that it is there because the answers come out differently with it than they would without it, yet none of the questions we can ask gets it back as an answer. The knowledge that lets us recognize a face is like this (§1): it decides the answer, “that is my friend”, but it is not part of the answer, and we cannot say what it is. We call such information structurally tacit because its tacitness is a fact about the memory, the way it is run and the questions it can answer, not about the information itself. Take AlphaGo, and suppose the only question we can put to it is “what is your move?” Everything that led it to Move 37, its famous move against Lee Sedol in 2016, is then structurally tacit. The futures it weighed, and the hunches it weighed them with, made it choose that move rather than another, yet the answer itself is a single stone. Contingently tacit. Some structurally tacit information is unstated only because no one has yet asked the right question. Add a new kind of question, change nothing else about how the memory is run, and the information comes out as an answer.

Because CR2(n) = CR2(n−1)·CR1(n− 1), with CR2 starting at 1, a regime that repairs every collision, so that CR1 = 1 at every step, assigns CR2 = 1 to every path, and CR2 cannot rank candidates. Why does the regime produce a valuation at all? Because the search is bounded. On a DAG whose paths grow multiplicatively with depth, an absolute exact match over all paths cannot exist, so VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl builds in a cognitive bound, the frontier size, and ranks the candidates inside it by CR2 (2026d, Appendix C). Without the bound every path could be kept and none would need to be preferred. This places tacit valuation where Simon placed satisficing: it is what a bounded searcher uses to decide what to keep when it cannot keep everything (Simon 1955). Polanyi’s name for what guides a discoverer among too many possibilities was “intellectual passion” (Polanyi 1958, ch. 6); in the substrate, the corresponding guide is a closed-form decay that favours direct routes. 12

A continuum of this kind cannot say why something stays unstated. It may be that no query has yet reached it, which is contingent tacitness, or that every regime that could state it is one in which it no longer exists, which is regime-bound tacitness. Only in the second case does explication cost what it explicates. Tsoukas is right about regime-bound tacitness and narrow in the opposite direction. He denies conversion for all tacit knowledge, yet contingently tacit structure does become explicit when a new operation is added (§4.6). Collins’s account divides the classes most finely, because his three kinds fall into different classes. Relational knowledge is contingently tacit, somatic knowledge is regime-bound yet articulable at the level of law (§4.4), and collective knowledge lies outside the substrate (§5). What it does not show is the dial that trades the somatic stratum against exact audit. Polanyi’s dictum covers every class at once. What it leaves open is what sets the boundary in a given substrate and what moves it, and that is what the dial of §4.2 supplies. 13

The “calculus degree” and the Giant Score are new compositions of binding, bundling, unbinding and Hamming similarity (2026a; 2026d). Regime A, the entorhinal–CA3 route, is a scaffolded vector-index substrate in which similarity and attractor completion dominate. Regime B, the trisynaptic route from entorhinal cortex through the dentate gyrus and mossy fibres to CA3, supports sparse, directed relational writes—edge-list or ontology-like commitments—gated by neuromodulation and extended by adult neurogenesis. The brain does not partition cleanly: both regimes contribute to both kinds of query, with task-dependent gain set by acetylcholine and dopamine, and the silicon rescue flag is only a readout-statistics analogue of the biological distinction (2026b). Both pathways have been conserved for more than 520 million years (2026b). Read through the present paper, the hippocampus keeps both readouts and mixes them by neuromodulatory gain: a similarity-completion regime suited to holistic, hard-to-tell recognition, 15

Collins’s study of laser builders found the same at the bench: groups that had spent time with a working laser’s builders could build one, while groups working only from published accounts could not (Collins 1974). An apprenticeship edge is therefore a socialization channel in Nonaka’s sense, and the topology of the graph records the routes by which tacit knowledge travelled. The nodes carry something else. Field, language, employer, society membership and dates are explicit attributes, bound into each hub’s composite vector (2026d, Appendix C). A DAG memory of this kind thus holds both channels at once: tacit transmission in its edges, codified content in its node vectors. We read this as Mokyr’s Republic of Letters, as 2026d does, and add one gloss. Academies, correspondence and lineages are institutions for multiplying socialization. They are, nearly item for item, the follow-up activities Tao lists—talks, meetings with experts, workshops, newcomers joining a field. 6.3 Newton, Thurston, and the follow-up gap Newton and Leibniz have nearly equal calculus-content scores in the graph, but only four of the 64 lineages pass through Newton, against 47 through Leibniz; Newton, for all his genius, worked largely in isolation and trained few successors (2026d). Newton’s influence travelled abundantly through texts, and nothing here measures it. But the apprenticeship channel is exactly the channel of tacit knowledge, so the finding is about the right thing. Alongside classical cases like Newton, Thurston recorded a similar human precedent (Thurston 1994). After his classification theorem for foliations, the field began to empty within a couple of years. His papers explained little of the background they presupposed and set down only the key points, so the barrier to entry was high: many graduate students and mathematicians struggled to learn and understand the proofs of key theorems and left the field. He concluded that “more than the knowledge, people want personal understanding.” The follow-up gap is therefore not new; what is new is the rate at which answers can now be produced without anyone acquiring the understanding that used to come with them. The AI-solved results Tao describes are the limiting case: possession without any human possessor, and therefore without the apprenticeship edges along which understanding normally flows (Tao 2026a). Before them, education was organized in monastic and cathedral schools as a communal affair, and such channels produced no structured mentor–student records; the Wall marks where personal academic mentorship first became record-generating in Europe (2026d; 2026g). In Collins’s terms the Wall is a shift in the medium of tacit transmission, from a communal medium close to collective tacit knowledge to a dyadic medium of apprenticeship. It is not an absence of transmission. It is the point at which transmission changed form and began to leave the kind of trace our instrument can read. 6.5 Is a second wall forming? Results would be attached to nodes that have few or no human apprentice edges, because what was learned in producing them was learned by no person. We call this hypothetical boundary an AI wall. The derivation exists, but it is not a walkable trace. A transformer’s forward pass is itself a directed acyclic computation, and interpretability tools can recover parts of it as a computational graph. A credit system that rewards possession pushes a field toward Newton’s thin thread; one that rewards transmission pushes it toward Leibniz’s hourglass. text: Tacit knowing, on this account, is an operating regime of a memory rather than a kind of content stored in it. VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl makes the claim concrete because one substrate, under one dial, yields either an exactly auditable trace or an emergent valuation of paths, and not both at full strength. Read with a relational definition of tacitness, that single trade-off gives each classical position its place: Polanyi’s non-separation, the pianist who falters under focal scrutiny, Tsoukas’s ineffability at the object level, Nonaka’s externalization by new operations, and Collins’s three kinds as three strata, the last of which lives in the community rather than in the substrate. The same reading changes what our earlier results are about. The mentor–student DAG is a record of tacit transmission, the Leibnizian hourglass is institutionalized socialization, and the Monastery Wall is a change in the medium through which tacit knowledge travelled. Newton’s thin thread, Thurston’s emptied field and Tao’s AI-solved problems without seminars share one structure: possession without transmission. AI-generated results are rootless by default. They can be verified, but nobody yet holds them tacitly, and their derivations leave no walkable trace. We have proposed that VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl can supply the missing middle layer between generation and valuation—an exact trace with its confidence—and stated predictions by which that proposal can fail. text: Conflict-graph search can stagnate despite effective operators when interventions fail to address the conflicts blocking progress. A dis- ruptive intervention may also require further search before its value emerges. We propose CIPHEUR, a large language model (LLM)- guided framework that connects conflict evidence to coordinated intervention and recovery through Structured Intervention Units (SIUs). The shared control interface supports offline synthesis of executable policies and online contextual decisions. Asynchronous online control sustains native search during inference, while all policies preserve the original objective and feasibility constraints. Across eight satellite–ground scheduling conflict views with five runs per view and a 900-second evaluation cap, CIPHEUR-online achieves the highest mean objective among 11 configurations and increases mean scheduled contact duration by 14.84% over the greedy baseline GWMIN. It exceeds the strongest external per-view mean in seven of eight views and outperforms CHILS in all 40 paired runs. Within the same runs, its normalized objective im- provement from 360 to 900 seconds is 1.50–1.86 times that of the two programmatic controllers. A separately frozen, one-shot LLM- generated controller also improves the mean objective over CHILS without runtime model calls. Together, these results demonstrate how structural search control translates LLM design knowledge and contextual reasoning into improved solution quality and sustained search progress. text: Effective combinatorial optimization depends on matching search actions to the opportunities available in the current state. Learning- assisted optimization and selection hyper-heuristics have made such decisions an explicit target of algorithm design [3, 10, 12]. Learning to schedule existing primal heuristics, for example, im- proves the allocation of search effort within a solver [8]. In conflict- graph optimization, this allocation also has a structural dimension: the value of an operation depends on the activities it displaces and the combinations it makes accessible. Exploiting this relationship calls for control decisions that connect observed conflicts to the subsequent course of search. We study maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) optimiza- tion on resource-labelled conflict graphs. Weighted vertices repre- sent candidate activities, and edges encode pairwise incompatibil- ity. In satellite–ground scheduling, resource and temporal labels describe the conflicts among communication opportunities. A reconstruction can also reduce a trajectory’s immediate value while creating opportunities for later improvement or exchange. These dependencies motivate the joint choice of how to intervene, where to act, and how search should continue. The resulting control problem links structural targeting with the delayed effects of intervention (Figure 1). Large language models (LLMs) offer complementary capabilities for addressing this problem. They can construct executable heuris- tics from problem descriptions and evaluative feedback [22, 26, 38], and make state-dependent heuristic choices during optimiza- tion [35, 40]. Bringing these capabilities to conflict-graph search requires an actionable connection between contextual judgment and structural change. A useful decision must identify its target, organize the intervention and its continuation, and remain mean- ingful as the solver progresses. This motivates a common control abstraction through which both generated policies and runtime reasoning can direct a continuing search. To express these decisions, we introduce the Structured Intervention Unit (SIU), which jointly specifies a structural target, an intervention, and its continuation. Candidate SIUs are grounded in the conflicts affecting current search trajectories. The solution-quality changes observed across executed intervention–recovery periods inform subsequent choices, closing the loop between structural evidence and search behavior. Two working modes realize control over this common SIU space. In the offline mode, an LLM translates problem semantics and the control specification into customized executable policies. These policies select SIUs from evolving observations and may update their internal estimates from accumulated execution feedback. In the online mode, an LLM makes the same type of SIU choice di- rectly from current structural evidence and search history. Offline synthesis provides reusable control logic, while online reasoning retains contextual judgment during a solve. Both modes act through a shared execution interface that preserves the original objective and feasibility constraints; asynchronous online decisions allow native search to progress throughout model inference. The contributions are threefold. First, we propose CIPHEUR, an LLM-guided structural search-control framework for conflict-graph optimization that turns conflict evidence and search experience into adaptive control of ongoing search. Second, we design SIUs that couple structural targets with intervention and recovery, using feed- back from executed intervention–recovery periods to guide subse- quent choices.

text: 2.1 Independent-Set Search and Structural Guidance MWIS heuristics exploit solution structure to combine intensifi- cation with exploration. METAMIS uses efficient local moves and path relinking within a GRASP framework [9], while CHILS com- bines iterated local search with cooperation based on differences among solutions [13]. Learning-based graph optimization [5, 19] offers another form of structural guidance: Li et al. [20] use graph- convolutional predictions to guide tree search for independent sets. These approaches share the goal of using graph and solution infor- mation to expose promising combinations [2]. CIPHEUR studies this relationship at the level of search inter- ventions. Resource-specific blocking evidence connects candidate activities to the trajectories that exclude them, providing a basis for choosing where to redirect search. A coordinated continuation then explores the opportunities created by the intervention. The emphasis is on converting structural evidence into decisions about the course of a population search, complementing work on local moves, solution exchange, and vertex-level guidance. 2.2 Adaptive and Temporally Extended Search Control Selection hyper-heuristics adapt the use of low-level heuristics to search state and history [10]; dynamic algorithm configuration learns policies for changing algorithm settings during execution [1]. Learned heuristic scheduling similarly allocates effort among ex- isting solver components [8]. Adaptive large neighborhood search coordinates competing removal and insertion heuristics through performance feedback [27], and learned neighborhood selection chooses variables for solver-based reoptimization [15, 34, 39]. To- gether, these studies establish policy adaptation, effort allocation, and intervention targeting as complementary dimensions of search control [32, 37]. Temporal abstraction provides a further dimension by treating an extended course of action as a decision unit, as formalized by the options framework [30]. SIUs combine structural targeting with an explicit intervention–recovery sequence. A conflict anchor guides reconstruction priorities across the candidate activities, and the accompanying continuation specifies how the altered trajectory contributes to further search. Feedback summarizes quality changes over the executed sequence. This coupling makes the structural scope and observed effects of an intervention jointly available to the controller. 2.3 LLM-Based Algorithm Design and Search Decisions LLM-based algorithm design couples program generation with em- pirical evaluation [6, 31]. HeurAgenix combines heuristic evolution with model-guided filtering and Monte Carlo continuation estimates for selection, and also trains a lightweight selector [35]. CIPHEUR makes the joint choice of target, intervention, and recovery the common task for generated policies and online LLMs. The design focus is a control policy over structurally grounded interventions: directed SIUs specify which trajectory to redirect, which conflict relationships to emphasize, and how search should proceed afterward. Offline synthesis turns this decision task into a reusable controller, while online inference resolves it from the current search context. Both modes therefore operate over the same structural and temporal decision space. Feedback relates policy decisions to changes in solution quality across their intervention–recovery periods. In online mode, asyn- chronous inference lets the optimizer continue searching while the model chooses its next intervention. The resulting design princi- ple is to make structurally targeted search behavior the adaptable object, while retaining objective evaluation and feasibility enforce- ment in the native solver. 3 CIPHEUR CIPHEUR uses LLM capabilities to construct search controllers offline or choose interventions online. text: CIPHEUR treats conflict-graph search control as a joint decision over structural targets, interventions and their continuation. SIUs give generated programs and online LLMs a common executable task, while native search preserves the original optimization se- mantics. The completed experiments show broad terminal competi- tiveness, stronger late-search progress for the online configuration, and a reconstruction–recovery pattern that motivates interval-level feedback. A frozen one-shot controller further demonstrates de- ployment without runtime model calls. Together, these findings identify structural search control as a practical way to use LLM design knowledge and contextual reasoning in combinatorial opti- mization.

text: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering with nature-inspired optimisation Bahrul Ilmi Nasutiona, Rezzy Eko Carakab,c, Robert Kurniawand aDepartment of Social Statistics The University of Manchester, Manchester, M13 9PL, Manchester, UK bResearch Center for Data and Information Sciences, Research Organisation for Electronics and Informatics National Research and Innovation Agency Bandung, 40135, West Java, Indonesia cSchool of Economics and Business Telkom University Bandung, 40257, West Java, Indonesia dDepartment of Statistical Computation Polytechnics Statistics STIS Jakarta, 13330, West Java, Indonesia
title: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering

text: We present an overview of R package called naspaclust, a tool for spa- tial fuzzy clustering improvement by hybridising the Fuzzy Geographically Weighted Clustering (FGWC) with nature-inspired optimisation algorithms. There are seven optimisation algorithms in general, namely Artificial Bee Colony, Flower Pollination Algorithm, Gravitational Search Algorithm, Harris- Hawk Optimisation, Intelligent Firefly Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimi- sation, and Teaching-Learning Based optimisation. The optimisation algo- rithms available do not only use the basic algorithms, but also the modified version of several parts such as randomisation terms and updating rules. Furthermore, we also provide additional options by providing more distance metrics options based on the rdist package. This study showed the imple- mentation of the naspaclust package in various cases, as well as comparing the performance of the algorithms in the scope of basic algorithms. The naspaclust package allows to improve the performance of fuzzy clustering, mainly in spatial context. Keywords: fuzzy geographically weighted clustering, geo-demographic analysis, nature-inspired optimisation, R package, spatial Preprint October 14, 2026 arXiv:2610.16356v1 [cs.NE] 12 Oct 2026

text: Clustering is a method used to divide a dataset into meaningful groups called clusters (Caraka et al., 2020). Objects within the same cluster ex- hibit homogeneity while differing significantly from objects in other clusters. Clustering methods are frequently used for automatic classification in di- verse fields, including medical sciences, engineering, and socio-economic anal- ysis (Han et al., 2011). One notable socio-economic application of clustering is geo-demographic Analysis (GDA), a specialised area within Geographic Information Systems (GIS) that utilises spatial analysis techniques to iden- tify and categorise demographic characteristics of specific regions (Paez et al., 2011). Such an analysis provides essential support for the development of tar- geted socio-economic policies (Wijayanto and Purwarianti, 2014a; Wijayanto et al., 2016). The application of clustering techniques within GDA is particu- larly critical for policy making, as it allows efficient and precise assessments of regional characteristics, thus helping decision-makers who otherwise would spend considerable effort evaluating each region individually (Spiezia and Weiler, 2007). A widely used clustering method in GDA is fuzzy clustering, notably the Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) algorithm (Kwon, 1998). FCM is valued for its sim- plicity and improved performance over traditional hard clustering methods such as K-Means and Hard C-Means (Singh et al., 2013). Based on FCM, Mason and Jacobson (2007) introduced fuzzy geographic weighted clustering (FGWC), a spatially aware variant of FCM

text: its sim- plicity and improved performance over traditional hard clustering methods such as K-Means and Hard C-Means (Singh et al., 2013). Based on FCM, Mason and Jacobson (2007) introduced fuzzy geographic weighted clustering (FGWC), a spatially aware variant of FCM that incorporates geographi- cal information into the clustering process, enabling geographically coherent clusters (Wijayanto et al., 2016). However, despite its advantages, both FCM and FGWC are sensitive to the initial selection of cluster centroids, leading to suboptimal or unstable so- lutions (Izakian and Abraham, 2011; Wijayanto et al., 2016). This drawback requires enhancements to achieve globally optimal clustering results that bet- ter represent the underlying spatial-demographic structure of the data (Wi- jayanto et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2008; Nayak et al., 2014). Metaheuristic opti- misation algorithms have emerged as promising solutions to overcome these initialisation issues by combining local and random search capabilities. To date, optimisation algorithms such as Ant Colony Optimisation (ACO) (Wi- jayanto et al., 2017; Nurmala and Purwarianti, 2015), Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA) (Pamungkas and Pramana, 2019), Particle Swarm Opti- misation (PSO) (Wijayanto and Purwarianti, 2014b), and Firefly Algorithm 2

Moreover, previous studies indicate that modifying the distance met- ric used to calculate the membership of data points can significantly im- prove clustering outcomes (Bezdek et al., 1984). FCM and FGWC tradi- tionally use Euclidean distance; however, evidence suggests that the use of alternative distance metrics could improve clustering performance (Srivas- tava et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2013; Gueorguieva et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2012). Currently, the only publicly available package that specifically ad- dresses FGWC is spatialClust, which provides limited options, primarily the classical FGWC and a version optimised with GSA (Pamungkas and Pra- mana, 2019)—and uses solely Euclidean distance. On the other hand, the ppclust package offers a variety of alternative distance metrics, but lacks integration with spatial clustering methods or optimisation algorithms. To address these gaps, this article aims to introduce our new R package called naspaclust, which comes from the abbreviation of nature-inspired spatial clustering. The main contribution of this study lies in the adaptation of several previous works on fuzzy clustering, particularly in the spatial con- text (Rao and Patel, 2012; Rao et al., 2012; Bhadoria et al., 2016; Wijayanto, 2015; Wijayanto and Purwarianti, 2014a; Wijayanto et al., 2016; Pamungkas and Pramana, 2019; Wijayanto and Purwarianti, 2014b; Nasution and Kurni-

text: clustering, particularly in the spatial con- text (Rao and Patel, 2012; Rao et al., 2012; Bhadoria et al., 2016; Wijayanto, 2015; Wijayanto and Purwarianti, 2014a; Wijayanto et al., 2016; Pamungkas and Pramana, 2019; Wijayanto and Purwarianti, 2014b; Nasution and Kurni- awan, 2018; Nasution et al., 2020; Caraka et al., 2020; Nasution and Siregar, 2022; Nasution et al., 2022; Sumargo et al., 2024). Moreover, this package can behave simultaneously like its predecessors such as spatialClust regarding the optimisation in FGWC and ppclust regarding the distance adjustments. To address these gaps, this study introduces a novel package named naspaclust (nature-inspired spatial clustering), which significantly extends existing packages by incorporating multiple nature-inspired optimisation al- gorithms and diverse distance metrics into fuzzy spatial clustering methods. Specifically, naspaclust implements seven metaheuristic algorithms: Ar- tificial Bee Colony (ABC), Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA), Flower Pollination Algorithm (FPA), Firefly Algorithm (FA), Harris-Hawk Optimi- sation (HHO), Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO), and Teaching-Learning- Based Optimisation (TLBO). In particular, recent advances such as intel- ligent search in FA (Fateen and Bonilla-Petriciolet, 2013; Nasution et al., 2020), rapid progressive dives in HHO (Bairathi and Gopalani, 2019), and elitism strategies in TLBO (Rao and Patel, 2012; Rao et al., 2012; Bhadoria et al., 2016; Nasution and Siregar, 2022) are integrated to enhance algorith- 3

Furthermore, various ran- domisation strategies for algorithms like FPA and FA (Fister et al., 2013a; Nasution et al., 2022) and numerous distance metrics from the rdist pack- age (Blaser, 2020), including Minkowski and Canberra distances, have been implemented, improving cluster flexibility and quality based on specific data characteristics. Section 2 describes the background information to provide an initial un- derstanding of fuzzy clustering, FGWC, and the metaheuristic algorithms used in naspaclust, together with the research workflow. Section 3 explains the experimental setting used to compare different optimised FGWC algo- rithms on different data. Further, Section 4 describes the simple description and usage of the naspaclust package, as well as the experimental results FGWC using standard optimisation algorithms. We provided an in-depth discussions of the package and the results in Section 5. Last but not least, this study summarises everything in Section 6 and provides limitations and future directions of the implementation of naspaclust.

text: 2.1. Fuzzy Clustering In 1965, Lotfi Zadeh introduced a fuzzy logic concept that states that a certain subject has a true value between zero and one Zadeh (1965). In a clustering context, fuzzy logic works by defining that a subject can be- long to more than one cluster with a specific calculated degree of member- ship (Bezdek, 1981; Han et al., 2011). The most common fuzzy clustering method in GDA is Fuzzy C-means (FCM) which was introduced by Dunn (1973) and developed by Bezdek (1981). FCM is a fuzzy clustering method that uses the degree of membership of an object with the object’s distance to the center of the group (Mason and Jacobson, 2007). An object will be a member of a cluster if the object has the highest degree of membership in the cluster (Nasution and Kurniawan, 2018). The objective of FCM is to min- imise the weighted average of errors as a consequence of substituting data x into the center of the cluster (centroid) v using Equations (1) and (2) (Bezdek et al., 1984): Jm(U, v) = n X i=1 c X j=1 µm ijd2 ij (1) 4

Cluster Validation Measurement Evaluating clustering results is essential to compare different models, se- lect the optimal number of clusters, and ensure that the formed cluster re- flects the underlying data structure(Bezdek et al., 1984). In conventional clustering, indices such as the silhouette, Dunn, and Davies–Bouldin indices measure how compact and well separated the clusters are. However, these indices assume that each data point is assigned to one cluster and only one. These measurements is relevant when one wants to compare the fuzzy to non-fuzzy clustering methods. Due to the fuzzy nature, previous studies developed evaluation measure- ments that measure separation by involving the membership in each cluster. These measurements are relevant when selecting the appropriate fuzzy clus- tering methods in their case. This package provides seven well-known cluster validation measurements, namely: Partition coefficient (PC), Classification 6

Nature-inspired optimisation features in naspaclust There are many approaches to obtain the optimal parameter that pro- duce an optimal objective function. The traditional approach uses numerical 9

text: methods such as the Lagrange multiplier and Newton-Raphson (Yang, 2014). However, as the function becomes more complex, it is difficult to find the op- timal solution using the traditional approach. Thus, an approach was devel- oped by implementing the search algorithm based on the natural phenomenon in the world, known as nature-inspired optimisation algorithms (Fister et al., 2013b). This approach employs exploitation and exploration as the basic components to find the optimum solution (Blum and Roli, 2003). In the context of FGWC, we attempt to optimise the centroid to overcome the lack in FGWC. Thus, the position of k -th swarms (e.g., particles, fireflies, flow- ers, etc.) in each algorithm represents the centroid with notation v. The hybridisation of FGWC and the nature-inspired optimisation algorithm can be seen in Algorithm 2. The following Subsubsections explain briefly about the optimisation algorithms that are implemented in naspaclust. 2.4.1. Artificial Bee Colony ABC algorithm is inspired from the bee colony behavior. Flower Pollination Algorithm FPA has two pollination processes in motion: cross-pollination and self- pollination (Yang, 2012). Cross pollination is defined as a global pollination performed by pollinators who can fly to the k-th flower in long distances represented by Levi flights (Caraka et al., 2021). Mathematically speaking, this motion is calculated in Equation (17). vt+1 k = vt k + γL(λ)(gbest −vt k) (17) With γ being the insect movement scaling factor and L (λ) is a Levy distributed random number with scalar factor λ (Nasution et al., 2022). On the other hand, local or self-pollination is the pollination of a certain flower that occurred when there is no pollinators (Yang, 2014). The local pollination is represented in Equation (18) vt+1 k

The local pollination is represented in Equation (18) vt+1 k = vt k + ϵ �vt h −vt k  , h̸ = k (18) ϵ is the random pollination factor that is basically uniform [0,1]. We add the flexibility of the random pollination factor in naspaclust by adding more distribution options inspired by randomised FA. Those distributions become uniform, normal, Levy flights, and two types of chaotic maps (logis- tic and kent) (see Fister et al. (2013a) for full details). Moreover, chaotic randomisation has also been implemented in FPA, particularly in a clus- tering context (Arora and Anand, 2017; Kaur et al., 2020; Nasution et al., 2022). To determine whether a flower receives global or local pollination, a random number between 0 and 1 is compared to the probability of switch p. If the random number is less than p, the flower receives global pollination. Otherwise, the flower does local pollination (Dhal et al., 2019). 12

Limitations and Future Directions In addition to the introductions of this package, this study still has some limitations. First, the experiment in this study is only limited to the default features of the optimisation algorithms because the goal is to introduce the naspaclust package in R. Furthermore, we also only use benchmark data that have been used in previous studies using FGWC as the algorithms. Thus, the limitations open many possibilities to continue the optimisa- tion algorithms in FGWC studies. Firstly, one may apply these algorithms to solve real-world problems that require the clustering algorithm at the re- gional level using different optimised FGWC. Using spatial information may give more insight into the clustering results. Conclusions and Future Studies This study aims to introduce the naspaclust package which utilises the nature-inspired optimisation algorithms to improve fuzzy clustering perfor- mance, particularly FGWC. We have briefly described the implementation of the package in R software as well as providing the performance evaluation of some optimisation algorithms. This study found that the optimisation al- gorithms is proven to improve the performance of FGWC in any type of data and produce spatial patterns of the clustering results. Moreover, TLBO has the most potential to optimise FGWC in all cases. However, the available algorithms still have potential disadvantages in finding unexpected cluster formation which is not consistent with the initialised number of clusters in certain simulations. Therefore, we hope that this paper could become founda- tion for everyone wants to do GDA which needs spatial clustering techniques to improve the cluster quality. text: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning∗ Yuxiang Zeng1, Kun Xie1†, Yang Wang1, Jigang Wen2, Xiaocan Li1, Guangxing Zhang3, Gaogang Xie3, Jiannong Cao4 1Hunan University 2Hunan University of Science and Technology 3Chinese Academy of Sciences 4The Hong Kong Polytechnic University {zengyuxiang@hnu.edu.cn, xiekun@hnu.edu.cn}
title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph

text: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. The key difficulty is that neural architectures are operation-labeled DAGs: edge direction defines computational flow, but existing predictors often treat direction as a local structural cue. We propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer based on encoder-wide directional consistency, which preserves directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encod- ing, pairwise interaction, and feature update. DTA-GT realizes this principle with direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spec- tral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation- sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation. Code: https://github.com/ZengYuXiang7/DTA-GT 1

text: Deep learning has been widely applied across various fields [1–6]. Neural architecture design is central to task performance and deployment efficiency, and Neural Architecture Search (NAS) automates this process by searching a candidate architecture space for models that meet performance and deployment constraints [7–12]. However, evaluating candidates during search is expensive: accuracy typically requires full network training, while latency requires hardware measurement or profiling. A practical way to reduce this cost is to train predictors under a limited evaluation budget, where only a small subset of candidate architectures is evaluated and the remaining unseen candidates are estimated by the predictor [13–16]. ∗This is a preprint of a paper accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Global direction prior refers to an explicit graph-level direction-aware structural or spectral prior, not merely local edge-direction cues. Learning-based predictors therefore rely on continuous representations of candidate architectures. This representation problem is nontrivial be- cause a neural architecture is an operation-labeled directed acyclic graph (DAG), rather than a mere undirected connectivity pattern. A directed edge u →v indicates that the output of operation u feeds into operation v, so the representation should preserve directed information flow. For accu- racy and latency prediction, this requires capturing operator composition along directed paths, branch splitting and merging, and reachability- related dependencies. Their undirected skeletons match. Table 1 provides a design-oriented comparison of representative predictor families with respect to explicit topology and direction modeling. Despite the need to preserve directed computational semantics, existing predictors cover these aspects only partially. Sequence-based methods [8, 17, 18] linearize architectures and can obscure explicit DAG topology and edge-direction semantics. GNN- based predictors [13, 19–22] explicitly model architecture graphs and local edge directions, but higher- order topology and long-range directed dependencies rely on repeated local message passing, where global structural and directional patterns can be weakened. Transformer and hybrid methods [14– 16, 23–25] use self-attention to capture long-range interactions and inject topology-aware cues through operation/topology tokenization, graph-aided attention, relation masks, or bidirectional aggregation. However, these designs still treat direction as scattered structural cues rather than a coordinated modeling principle.

However, these designs still treat direction as scattered structural cues rather than a coordinated modeling principle. They provide partial directional signals, but usually leave them local or stage-specific rather than combining topology encoding, local direction cues, a global direction prior, and direction-aware updates in one encoder. Thus, the main gap is not whether graph structure is used, but whether directional semantics are modeled consistently across the encoder. The challenge is therefore to preserve the asymmetry induced by directed computation while still capturing DAG topology, motivating the following question: How can a neural architecture encoder explicitly model directed computational semantics while capturing DAG topology? Our key insight is that directionality in architecture DAGs should be preserved throughout represen- tation learning, rather than injected once as a structural cue. We define encoder-wide directional consistency as the requirement that directed computational semantics be preserved across node-role encoding, global direction-aware spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature update. Without such consistency, direction-aware cues introduced at one stage may be diluted by later direction- agnostic transformations. This motivates preserving direction across the main encoder stages rather than relying on an isolated structural signal. We propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer

Together, these modules prevent directional information from being reduced to an isolated structural cue. We evaluate DTA-GT on four prediction settings spanning accuracy and latency prediction over NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench- 201. Across multiple limited-budget settings and evaluation metrics, DTA-GT consistently improves over representative predictors. Stage-wise ablations assess the contribution of the coordinated direction-aware stages, Magnetic spectral controls isolate the effect of the edge-orientation-sensitive spectral prior, and mechanistic diagnostics examine whether the internal behaviors align with the intended directed computational semantics. text: Existing architecture predictors mainly follow three representation paradigms: sequence-based encodings, GNN-based graph modeling, and Transformer/hybrid architectures. These paradigms differ in how they encode topology and direction, and we focus on whether they preserve directed computational semantics beyond local structural cues. Sequence-based Methods. Peephole [17], NAO [18], and PNAS [8] encode architectures as flattened vectors or operation sequences. This paradigm prioritizes compact architecture descriptions and efficient predictor training under limited evaluation budgets. However, because the DAG is linearized, these methods do not explicitly model topology or preserve edge-direction semantics. As a result, directed computational dependencies among operations are difficult to capture. GNN-based Methods. BRP-NAS [13], Neural Predictor [19], NPENAS [22], GATES [20], Semi- NAS [28], DNNPerf [29], and NNLP [21] represent architectures as DAGs or graph-structured objects. Compared with sequence encodings, GNNs explicitly use graph topology and can exploit edge directions within local neighborhoods. However, in message-passing backbones, higher-order topology and long-range dependencies are mainly captured through repeated local propagation, where information can be mixed, over-smoothed, or over-squashed. Meanwhile, directional bias remains mostly local, and an explicit global direction-aware prior is usually absent. Transformer-based and Hybrid Methods. Transformer-based and hybrid predictors, including TNASP [24], NAR-Former [14], PINAT [25], FlowerFormer [23], NAR-Former V2 [15], and NN- Former [16], use self-attention to model global interactions among architecture tokens. Each ar- chitecture a ∈A is represented as an operation-labeled directed acyclic graph (DAG) G = (V, E, τ), where nodes represent computational operations, directed edges encode data-flow dependencies, and τ : V →O assigns an operation type to each node. We adopt the adjacency convention that Au,v = 1 indicates a directed edge u →v. Each architecture has a scalar target attribute y ∈R, such as accuracy or latency. Given a measured subset D = {(ai, yi)}N i=1 sampled from A, we learn a predictor fϑ : A →R to estimate attributes for remaining unmeasured candidates in the same architecture space, without fully training or profiling each candidate. We decompose fϑ into an encoder hϕ and a prediction head pψ: zG = hϕ(G) and ˆy = pψ(zG), with ϑ = {ϕ, ψ}. The challenge is to preserve operation semantics, graph topology, and directed computational semantics across the encoder, rather than allowing directional information to be lost after a single encoding stage. 3.2 Overall Architecture Fig. 2 illustrates DTA-GT, which maps an architecture DAG G to a graph-level representation zG = hϕ(G) under the encoder-wide directional consistency principle. Specifically, the encoder first initializes node states as H(0) = NodeEmbed(G) + DirSpecEnc(G), combining operation/local directed-role features with a global edge-orientation-sensitive spectral prior. It then applies L residual layers [30] alternating direction-dual structural attention and direction-sensitive MoE-FFN updates, using RG and A for relation-aware interaction and predecessor/successor-aware updates. Finally, attention-based readout produces zG = AttnReadout(H(L)), which is passed to pψ for prediction without altering the original architecture DAG. 4 Method 4.1 Direction- and Topology-Aware Node Initialization Before global spectral encoding and attention-based interaction, each node should carry a basic description of its computation and its directed role in the architecture DAG. Role-aware attributes. Each node vi is described by five discrete features: operation label τ(vi), indegree deg−(vi), outdegree deg+(vi), forward depth ℓfwd(vi), and reverse depth ℓrev(vi). The forward depth is the maximum length of a directed path from an input node to vi, and the reverse depth is the maximum length of a directed path from vi to an output node. The operation label captures computational semantics, indegree and outdegree characterize local merging and branching roles, and (ℓfwd, ℓrev) locates the node along the directed input-to-output flow. This depth pair distinguishes nodes with the same forward depth but different remaining distances to the output side. These features make local in/out roles and input-to-output positions available before attention-based interaction. text: Spectral Encoding The node initialization X provides operation semantics and local directed roles, but not a global direction-aware spectral prior over the architecture DAG. Existing predictors usually lack an explicit global direction-aware spectral prior [13–16, 19–21, 23–25], while standard Laplacian encodings capture symmetric connectivity but not the asymmetry between u →v and v →u. We therefore derive P from the Magnetic Laplacian [31, 32], whose complex phase records edge orientation. This supplies the global spectral stage of encoder-wide directional consistency. (3) 4.3 Direction-Dual Structural Attention Standard self-attention [14, 33] evaluates pairwise interactions from node representations. The Magnetic spectral encoding in Sec. 4.2 supplies a node-level global direction-aware spectral prior. Direction-dual structural attention complements this representation with explicit pairwise relation sup- ports, providing encoder-wide directional consistency. It organizes pairwise interactions through six directional relation channels. Each channel specifies a distinct structural context for query–key interac- tions, covering local dependencies, directed reachability, or shared-successor and shared-predecessor structures. Within each channel, content-based attention adaptively weights the admissible keys according to their node representations. 5

For each direction-sensitive relation family, we construct paired channels over ordered or role-specific node-pair patterns, allowing attention to distinguish forward from backward dependencies and downstream-shared from upstream-shared branch structures. We instantiate three paired relation types, yielding six directional relation channels: (1) local adjacency, where A and A⊤indicate direct forward and backward dependencies; (2) directed reachability, where Rfwd(u, v) = 1 if v is reachable from u, and Rbwd = R⊤ fwd captures the reverse relation; and (3) shared successors/predecessors, where AA⊤captures common successors and A⊤A captures common predecessors. We keep the predictor head deliberately simple, so most modeling capacity remains in the direction-aware graph encoder rather than in a task-specific regressor. Architecture attribute prediction requires both calibrated value estimates and reliable attribute ranking, so we train with point-wise regression, pairwise ranking, and the routing regularizer introduced in Sec. 4.4. Training Objective. For a mini-batch of size B, the mean squared error (MSE) loss calibrates attribute values as Lmse = 1 B PB i=1(ˆyi −yi)2. To preserve the relative order of candidate architectures under the target attribute, we use a pairwise ranking loss over sampled non-tied architecture pairs P: Lrank = 1 |P| P (i,j)∈P log �1 + exp(−sgn(yi −yj)(ˆyi −ˆyj))  . This term encourages the predicted attribute order to match the measured order and aligns training with rank-based metrics such as Kendall’s τ. The final objective is Ltotal = λmseLmse +λrankLrank +λauxLaux, with Laux denoting the negative-entropy routing regularizer for the Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN; the λ terms control the relative weights of the three objectives. The MSE and ranking terms therefore serve different purposes: the former preserves target-scale calibration, while the latter directly constrains the ordering that predictor-based NAS relies on when selecting candidate architectures. 5 Experiments 5.1 Experimental

The “w/o Directed Node Fea- tures” variant retains operation embeddings but omits in-degree, out-degree, forward-depth, and reverse-depth features from node initialization. Direction-aware DTA-GT outperforms its undirected counterpart across the reported metrics, supporting the importance of directional information in architecture representations. Removing direction-aware components at individual encoder stages also degrades performance, supporting our central principle that directionality should be preserved throughout the encoder. These results support maintaining directional information from node ini- tialization and global spectral encoding through pairwise interaction and feature update. Removing directed node features or Magnetic spectral encoding reduces performance, supporting the use of both local directed-role information and a global orientation-sensitive spectral prior. Removing structural attention or MoE-FFN also weakens performance, supporting the contribution of directional relations during node interaction and predecessor/successor contexts during feature updates. CLS readout performs worse than attention pooling, which aggregates existing nodes without introducing virtual graph connections that would alter directional structural relations and Magnetic Laplacian encoding. The MSE-only control also underperforms the proposed training objective. Combining regression with ranking supervision is appropriate for predictor-based NAS: MSE fits numerical attribute values, while the ranking term explicitly constrains their relative order for candidate selection. 5.3 Main Results Table 3 compares all methods across the

Our architecture-prediction evaluation focuses on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201. Transfer to other search spaces requires aligned operation vocabularies and dependency semantics, since graph nodes may represent computations at different granularities. Dense directed-relation masks and pairwise attention also incur quadratic storage and attention costs as graph size grows. The effect of improved predictor ranking on end-to-end NAS remains to be evaluated. Future work. We will investigate a shared operation-level representation for cross-space pretraining and adaptation, and explore sparse or hierarchical attention with compact reachability representations to support larger computational graphs. We also plan to integrate DTA-GT into NAS pipelines and evaluate the selected architectures and total search cost under a fixed end-to-end evaluation budget. Appendix G elaborates on these directions. 7

text: We presented DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for neural architecture attribute prediction. DTA-GT is built on encoder-wide directional consistency, which preserves directed computational semantics across node initialization, global direction-aware spectral en- coding, pairwise interaction, and feature update. By combining direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN, DTA-GT strengthens topology-aware architecture representations while explicitly modeling edge-direction semantics. Experiments on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS- Bench-201 demonstrate consistent gains on accuracy and latency prediction across limited-budget settings. Ablations, Magnetic spectral controls, and mechanistic diagnostics further support the contribution and intended behavior of the proposed direction-aware stages. text: A Additional Experimental Details A.1 Implementation Platform The NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 attribute-prediction experiments are implemented in PyTorch 2.4.0 and conducted on a workstation running Ubuntu 22.04 with an Intel Core i9-13900K CPU, 64 GB RAM, and a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with 24 GB memory. The large-DAG scalability experiments are conducted separately on an NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB GPU, with the corresponding hardware configuration and timing protocol reported in Appendix F. A.2 Datasets, Splits, and Training Budgets NAS-Bench-101 [34] contains 423,624 unique cell-based architectures with at most 7 nodes and 9 edges per cell. NAS-Bench-201 [35] contains 15,625 candidate cells with 4 nodes and 6 edges per cell. For NAS-Bench-201, we represent edge operations as nodes in the predictor input graph, whose encoding topology is fixed across operation assignments. The NAS-Bench-201 authors trained candidate architectures on CIFAR-10 for 200 epochs and recorded their validation accuracies, alongside latency measurements collected with a batch size of 256. These measurements serve as labels for our accuracy and latency prediction tasks, with accuracy averaged over the available benchmark runs for each architecture. NAS-Bench-101 provides accuracy labels but not latency labels; therefore, we measure NAS-Bench-101 latency on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU using batch size 1 to complete the four-task evaluation. Because latency labels are benchmark- and device-specific, latency magnitudes are compared only within the same

text: labels but not latency labels; therefore, we measure NAS-Bench-101 latency on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU using batch size 1 to complete the four-task evaluation. Because latency labels are benchmark- and device-specific, latency magnitudes are compared only within the same benchmark setting. For each task and training budget, each method is evaluated over five runs using a shared set of five random seeds. For each seed, architectures are randomly shuffled to form the training and validation partitions. The partitions vary across seeds, and all methods share the same partitions for a given seed. The @ notation in the result tables denotes the number of architectures used for predictor fitting, and the validation set contains 1,024 architectures. Because the predictor serves the candidate screening stage of NAS, its objective is to score and rank the complete architecture pool and identify promising candidates for costly downstream evaluation. We therefore compute Kendall’s τ and MAPE over the full benchmark architecture set, including the training and validation architectures and all remaining candidates. A.3 Fair Comparison and Reproducibility Within each seed, all methods use the same training and validation partitions, full-set evaluation target, training budgets, and metrics. When reproducing baselines, we use the official implementations when available and preserve their original model configurations; otherwise, hyperparameters are selected by grid search within the ranges reported by

When reproducing baselines, we use the official implementations when available and preserve their original model configurations; otherwise, hyperparameters are selected by grid search within the ranges reported by the corresponding papers. DTA-GT uses one fixed default configuration across tasks and budgets. The main comparison and ablation tables report means over five runs; Appendix H also reports the corresponding standard deviations. C.3 Design Choices for Practical Scalability The analysis above identifies two scale-dependent costs: graph-dependent construction at first use and dense pairwise storage and computation during encoder evaluation. DTA-GT addresses these costs through three complementary execution choices that preserve the same direction-aware representation. Sparse retained-mode spectral computation. The large-graph spectral path represents the Mag- netic Laplacian sparsely and uses thick-restart Lanczos to compute only the retained eigenpairs through sparse matrix-vector products in a compact Krylov subspace. It therefore constructs the spectral modes consumed by the encoder without forming a complete spectral basis, with runtime determined by graph sparsity, solver tolerance, and the iterations required for convergence. 19
title: Conv. Branch

text: Reusable graph-dependent preprocessing. The retained eigenpairs and directional relation masks depend only on the architecture graph, so they are constructed once and reused across encoder layers, training epochs, and repeated predictions of the same architecture. This design separates graph-input construction from model evaluation and amortizes structural and spectral construction whenever an architecture is revisited. Topology- and support-aware relation handling. Deployment-oriented architecture design bal- ances predictive quality against computational cost, making sparse-to-moderately-dense connectivity a practically important regime for support-aware execution. The practical motivation for support- aware relation handling is that computational graphs exhibit structured, architecture-dependent connectivity rather than a single density regime. ResNet-style architectures introduce selected shortcut edges, whereas DenseNet-style blocks create a denser support pattern by connecting each layer to all preceding layers within a block. Deriving relation supports from the observed topology preserves this variation and provides the structural basis for sparse execution whenever the graph admits it. The six directional relations expose their supported node pairs explicitly, allowing relation construc- tion to exploit known graph structure. Let S denote the total number of supported pairs across the six relations. A support-indexed attention implementation evaluates only stored supported pairs, yielding an O(Sd) attention term, while sparse predecessor and successor aggregation costs O(md). The explicit relation supports therefore provide the execution interface for support-proportional computation as graph scale increases. Appendix

The number of experts follows this decomposition of directed computational context. A node-dependent router learns adaptive mixing weights over the three contexts from the current node representation. This allows each node to combine its local state with upstream and downstream information according to the prediction task. The four directional stages provide complementary information throughout the encoder. Node initial- ization represents local directed roles, and Magnetic spectral encoding supplies a global orientation- sensitive prior.

F Evaluation on Larger DAGs F.1 Predictive Accuracy on MalNet-Derived DAGs We further evaluate the direction-aware encoder on larger DAGs derived from the five-class MalNet- Tiny graph-classification dataset [37]. The derived graphs contain 5–4,993 nodes, with a mean of 1,407 nodes. This experiment examines the effectiveness of the directional design on larger graphs under limited training supervision. We contract each strongly connected component into a node to obtain a condensation DAG. Each node receives a shared operation token, so the compared predictors must derive their graph representations from the structure of the resulting DAG. All compared methods use the same derived graphs and data partitions. We use a stratified 5%/5%/90% training/validation/test split and fit each model on the 5% training partition. All classification metrics are computed on the held-out 90% test partition. The five classes contain equal numbers of graphs, and stratification preserves their proportions in each partition. We compare DTA-GT with BRP-NAS, Graphormer, and NN-Former and report accuracy, macro-F1, macro-precision, and macro-recall. Table 14 reports the mean over five runs. 23

text: The MalNet classification results and A800 profiles jointly characterize representation quality and computational cost on larger DAGs. DTA-GT provides the strongest classification results among the evaluated MalNet predictors, while BRP-NAS has lower latency in the large-graph profiles. The staged A800 measurements support the intended roles of retained-mode spectral computa- tion, reusable graph-dependent preprocessing, and topology-aware relation construction within the evaluated range. The reported scaling evidence covers graphs with up to 32,768 nodes; sparse or hierarchical attention and compact reachability representations remain important directions for substantially larger computational graphs. G Extended Discussion Cross-space representation and adaptation. A node in a cell-based CNN space may denote a primitive convolution or pooling operation, whereas a node in another space may denote an entire Transformer layer or Mamba block. These different computational granularities motivate a canonical operation-level representation for cross-space adaptation. Composite blocks could be decomposed into shared semantic units or mapped to a common operation vocabulary with aligned edge definitions and target protocols. For spaces with compatible operation definitions and dependency semantics, future work can investigate reusing DTA-GT’s directional encoder and graph preprocessing, with new vocabulary entries and embeddings for additional operation types. This would enable studies of cross-space pretraining followed by adaptation on a small evaluated subset from the target space. Task adaptation and NAS evaluation. For a new DAG-level task with

text: with new vocabulary entries and embeddings for additional operation types. This would enable studies of cross-space pretraining followed by adaptation on a small evaluated subset from the target space. Task adaptation and NAS evaluation. For a new DAG-level task with compatible atomic units and directed-dependency semantics, adapting the prediction head and fine-tuning the encoder on a small labeled subset provides a natural extension. This would allow the same direction-aware representation principle to be studied under different graph-level targets. A complementary direction is to integrate the predictor into a NAS search loop and evaluate how candidate ranking affects architecture selection under a fixed end-to-end evaluation budget. Relation-channel design and extension. The three paired relation families in Section 4.3 are heuristic choices motivated by DAG semantics, providing a concrete instantiation of direction-dual structural attention. They capture local dependencies, multi-hop reachability, and shared predeces- sor/successor structure. Additional directional information, such as hop-specific dependencies or directed motif patterns, can be represented by further ordered or role-specific relation supports, with a corresponding extension of the relation-to-head assignment. The relation set can therefore be tailored to the directional semantics available in a target graph domain. Our experiments evaluate the six-channel instantiation; the predictive value and computational cost of expanded relation sets remain to be studied. Computational scaling. Directed reachability can grow quadratically even when the original
title: The MalNet classification results and A800 profiles jointly characterize representation quality and

text: the directional semantics available in a target graph domain. Our experiments evaluate the six-channel instantiation; the predictive value and computational cost of expanded relation sets remain to be studied. Computational scaling. Directed reachability can grow quadratically even when the original adjacency is sparse. For example, a directed chain has n −1 edges but n(n −1)/2 reachable ordered pairs. Dense relation masks therefore require quadratic storage, and dense masked attention incurs quadratic pairwise computation for a fixed hidden dimension. The A800 profiles in Appendix F.2 demonstrate execution on generated DAGs with up to 32,768 nodes. Extending Graph Transformer predictors to substantially larger computational graphs calls for sparse or hierarchical attention together with compact representations of directed reachability. Combining these mechanisms with reusable spectral preprocessing could extend the encoder to larger computational graphs while retaining its direction-aware representation. Future evaluations should measure prediction quality, first-use graph-input construction, model-forward latency, and GPU memory under matched graph and hardware settings. text: PREPRINT 1 Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning Huan Luo, Na Lu, Xiaopeng Wang, and Ziyang Shang Abstract— Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) usually processes continuous EEG signal with fixed-length sliding windows, which is inflexible, human intervened, and misaligned with neural events. Time window optimization has shown promising improvement as a substitute solution. However, the existing optimiza- tion methods typically evaluate windows isolatedly and fail to model temporal dependencies across consecutive windows, which may produce fragmented and physiologi- cally implausible sequences. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforce- ment Learning (TSE-RL) framework. This framework em- beds prior temporal-structure knowledge of MI events into a stable RL formulation, reformulating window optimization as a constrained Markov Decision Process with ordinal re- lation enforcement of neural event. First, the evaluation and action selection upon each window has been changed from simply “retain/discard” to semantic alignment between win- dow and neural events as Discard/Onset/sustain/Offset. Second, action masking is imposed by a finite-state ma- chine (FSM) which enforces physiologically plausible de- cision orders with constraint of neural activity progress in term of planning/execution/recovery, enhancing both rationality, interpretability and classification performance. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder is designed to capture long-range inter-window dependencies in parallel, improving training stability and efficiency compared with existing
title: PREPRINT

text: orders with constraint of neural activity progress in term of planning/execution/recovery, enhancing both rationality, interpretability and classification performance. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder is designed to capture long-range inter-window dependencies in parallel, improving training stability and efficiency compared with existing recurrent architectures. Besides, TSE-RL adopts a plug-and-play design that can be integrated with diverse MI classifiers. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that TSE-RL consistently improves decoding performance in both cross-session and cross- subject settings. Visualization analyses further suggest that the learned policy of window optimization aligns with neurophysiological principles. B RAIN computer interface (BCI) technology establishes a direct communication and control pathway between the brain and external devices by decoding neural activ- ity [1]. It has broad potential in diverse fields such as neurorehabilitation, entertainment [2], and human-machine interaction [3]. Among non-invasive acquisition modalities, electroencephalography (EEG) is widely adopted due to its high temporal resolution and relatively low cost [4]. In motor imagery (MI) BCIs, users voluntarily imag- ine limb movements to elicit event-related desynchroniza- tion/synchronization (ERD/ERS) patterns [5], [6], thereby enabling device control without external stimuli. Recent years have witnessed significant advances in MI- EEG signal decoding techniques, most of which analyze a predefined post-cue segment (typically 0–4 s) for feature ex- traction and classification [7]. Representative approaches range from Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) [8], which learns spatial filters by maximizing inter-class variance, to diverse deep learning methods. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) like EEGNet [9] and M-ShallowConvNet [10]

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) like EEGNet [9] and M-ShallowConvNet [10] efficiently cap- ture spatio-temporal patterns with depthwise separable convo- lutions or shallow designs. FBCNet [11] performs frequency- band fusion via multi-view convolutions, while ATCNet [12] integrates attention mechanisms with temporal convolutional networks. More recently, Transformer-based models have been explored in EEGConformer [13] and TSLANet [14]. And CSPNet [15] embeds CSP principles within a neural net- work framework. Riemannian geometry-based methods such as manifold attention network (mAtt) [16] characterize EEG patterns on the Riemannian manifold of symmetric positive- definite (SPD) matrices. Although these methods perform well in offline evaluations, their performance in online scenarios are constrained by using a single, shared temporal segment to represent MI activity across trials. Some windows may cover only a fraction of an MI event, some may contain excessive pre-event baseline activity, and some may be contaminated by burst artifacts, the majority of which are misaligned with actual neural events. Correlation-based Time Window Selection (CTWS) [17] adjusts the onset of window by correlating sliding windows with reference signals. Approaches based on Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) [18] and Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA) [19] employ meta-learning and heuristic searches to identify optimal configurations in time-frequency parameter space. However, these techniques typically evaluate and select candidate windows independently, treating each as an isolated “good/bad” decision based on the quality of the window , with configurations searched offline and applied uniformly across trials [20], [21]. This limitation can result in fragmented or physiologically implausible window sequences that fail to capture the coherent evolution of MI events. In contrast, our method optimizes the time window sequence, conditioning each decision on cross-window history and on the constraint of MI phases. Such an evolution suggests distinct MI phases from onset to sustained imagery and finally to offset. Our work instead optimizes the window itself, taking each incoming window as the decision unit, assigning it an explicit semantic role, and constraining the action space by the structure of MI events. Therefore, we propose a Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (TSE-RL) framework for adaptive time window optimization in MI-EEG decoding. The core innovation of this framework is to embed prior temporal- structure knowledge of MI events into a stable RL framework, transforming window optimization from isolated “good/bad” judgments to semantic alignment of complete neural events. Specifically, TSE-RL incorporates three mechanisms to make this idea practical and reliable. The first mechanism transforms the action selection upon each time window from simply “retain/discard” to semantic alignment between window and neural events as Discard/Onset/sustain/Offset. This seman- tic alignment mechanism imposes physiological patterns on window optimization of EEG signal. The second mechanism adopts Finite State Machine (FSM) for constrained action masking which enables safe reinforcement learning in re- stricted action space. METHODS We formulate time-window optimization for online MI- EEG decoding as an constrained sequential decision-making problem. In contrast to fixed-length window decoding and traditional window optimization, TSE-RL learns to assign each candidate window a semantic role (Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset). As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), TSE-RL encodes the MI event’s temporal structure as a Finite State Machine (FSM) that governs the valid action space of an RL agent via action masking. This mechanism ensures the learned policy adheres to physiological plausibility, elevating window optimization from isolated “good/bad” judgments to semantic alignment of complete neural events. Moreover, TSE-RL employs a Transformer-based history encoder to stably integrate histori- cal information in parallel, preventing the training instability and sequential overhead commonly observed in recurrent RL. This section presents the problem formulation, the temporal- structure embedding mechanism, the overall framework, and the learning procedure.

At each time step, this policy dynamically decides whether the current window should be discarded or retained. And if retained, the policy must decide whether the window should be marked as the Onset, Sustain, or Offset phase of the MI event. The objective is to retain and mark an sequence of most informative windows such that the final classification accuracy based on this sequence is maximized. We formulate this problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple (S, A, T , R, γ). Action set A: The agent executes one of the four discrete actions an ∈{0, 1, 2, 3}. Specifically, action an = 0 indicates that the current window is considered to be highly noisy and is discarded. To incorpo- rate the prior knowledge that an MI event follows an On- set→Sustain→Offset temporal structure, we introduce a dis- crete phase indicator ϕn ∈{Planning, Execution, Recovery}. Importantly, ϕn is an internal phase of sensorimotor cortex rather than an additional MDP state. It is only used to constrain the legal actions given the current phase via a finite-state machine (FSM). • Planning phase. At the beginning of each trial, the agent is in the Planning phase. It has been demonstrated that subtle rhythmic changes often precede the actual onset of MI performing, representing a preparation or planning phase [22]. In this phase, the agent searches for the onset of the event, and the legal actions are APlanning = {0 (discard), 1 (Onset)}. Choosing an = 1 marks the current window as Onset and switches the phase to Execution. • Execution phase. After the first Onset has been detected, the agent enters the Execution phase, which covers the duration of the active MI. During this phase, the sen- sorimotor cortex typically exhibits a significant power reduction in the µ (8–13 Hz) and β (13–30 Hz) rhythms, a phenomenon known as ERD [22]. This reduction persists as long as the subject actively performs the imagery task.

First, the agent must respect safety constraints so that selected window sequences remain physiologically meaningful. Sec- ond, the agent has to learn from long sequences of noisy EEG observations in a stable and data-efficient way. text: remain physiologically meaningful. Sec- ond, the agent has to learn from long sequences of noisy EEG observations in a stable and data-efficient way. The proposed TSE-RL framework addresses these issues through a temporal structure embedding mechanism that combines an FSM-constrained action mask with a Transformer-based history encoder. This design enforces the decision of window optimization alignment with MI neural patterns, while provid- ing a stable architecture for learning. MI events exhibit contralateral desynchronization of the µ (8–13 Hz) and β (13–30 Hz) rhythms during MI execution, and exhibit a rebound of synchronization of the β-rhythm after the event ends [22]. Conventional isolated window optimization methods ignore this temporal pattern, leading to discontin- uous or semantically incomplete window sequences. This consequently reduces classification accuracy and diminishes interpretability. Reward shaping can, in principle, discourage such sequences by penalizing non-contiguous or incomplete window selections. However, this soft constraint can only indirectly influence the policy through policy gradients. During the early stages of training, the policy that is not aligned with physiological patterns can still be explored. Even during inference, a converged policy employing stochastic sampling cannot entirely prevent the occurrence of invalid action se- quences. To ensure that the selected time window consistently consti- tutes a valid MI event, we embed the temporal structure of MI events into the decision process using FSM-constrained
