text: stochastic sampling cannot entirely prevent the occurrence of invalid action se- quences. To ensure that the selected time window consistently consti- tutes a valid MI event, we embed the temporal structure of MI events into the decision process using FSM-constrained action masking. We employ FSM to model the legal phase transitions of events, restricting valid actions Aϕn based on the current phase ϕn. The probability of all invalid actions is set to zero before the action sampling. This hard constraint reduces the policy search space, forcing the agent to follow physiologically plausible trajectories. Huang et al. [27] showed that invalid- action masking yields more effective gradient updates, with benefits increasing as the number of invalid actions grows. Masking scales well when invalid actions are numerous, while penalty-based methods struggle to explore the task. Further- more, Stolz et al. [28] found that focusing exploration on state- specific valid actions significantly improves learning efficiency and the predictability of the agent in safety-critical tasks. Therefore, in EEG decoding, we propose FSM-constrained action masking combined with the reward function described in Section II-A to guide the agent to generate continuous and complete MI windows.

text: LUO et al.: TSE-RL 5 The second challenge is to integrate information over the histories of extended observation when the agent determines actions. Traditional RL methods employ RNNs, but they suffer from instability, particularly in MI-EEG tasks with trials spanning dozens of windows over several seconds [26]. Each additional window in the sequence elongates the gradient path, causing gradient to decay or explode exponentially. Beyond in- stability, RNNs require careful management of variable-length sequences and hidden states during training, complicating the implementation of batching strategies. These challenges can hinder the deployment of recurrent RL approaches in MI-EEG scenarios. We thereby adopts a non-recurrent Transformer-based his- tory encoder. Instead of propagating hidden states, it processes the recent history Hn (as feature vectors {fn−k, . . . , fn−1}) in parallel using self-attention mechanisms. This generates a fixed-dimensional context vector hn that captures temporal dependencies across history observations. When concatenated with the current window feature fn and trial progress ρn, this forms the full input for the policy network. By eliminating recursive propagation of hidden state, the design circumvents gradient instability while leveraging parallel computation for efficiency. The Transformer’s multi-head attention effectively captures long-range temporal dependencies. This architecture has demonstrated superior performance in partial-observation RL tasks [29]. C. Learning framework To address the low sample efficiency and training instability of end-to-end RL from random initialization, the TSE-RL framework is trained in three stages that progressively shift from supervised learning to policy optimization. Stage 1: Supervised pretraining. In the first stage, we train the feature extractor F and discriminator D as a standard classifier on full time windows. From each training trial, we extract time windows Xn using the window length L and stride ∆, and assign each window the corresponding trial label ytrue. The backbone then produces pn = D �F(Xn)  for each window, and we minimize the cross-entropy loss LCE = − X n log pn(ytrue), (11) temporally aggregated over all windows in a mini-batch. At the end of this stage, F has learned discriminative spatio-temporal representations of EEG windows, and D has learned the class distribution whose probabilities pn will be reused in the reward design. Stage 2: Policy learning. After the convergence of super- vised pretraining, the parameters of F and D are frozen. Then we train the history encoder G and the FSM-constrained policy network Π by reinforcement learning. We adopt Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [30] algorithm. In each trial, the agent interacts with the environment as described in Section II- A: the frozen extractor F converts the current and historical windows into features, the frozen discriminator D provides window-level probabilities pn for computing rdisc and rterm, the history encoder G produces the context vector hn, and the policy network Π maps zn = [fn; hn; ρn] to an action distribution that is masked by the current phase ϕn. During this stage, PPO gradients update only the parameters of G and Π. Consequently, the mapping from raw windows to features and probabilities does not change while the agent is learning decision policy. The FSM-based action mask is active throughout, restricting the exploration to phys- iologically plausible action. Stage 3: Joint fine-tuning. Once the policy has reached stable performance, we perform a final joint fine-tuning. We unfreeze the last few layers of the feature extractor F while keeping the discriminator D fixed, and continue PPO training with a smaller learning rate. Policy gradients are now allowed to slightly adjust the high-level feature representations, which allows mild adaptation of the feature representation to the learned policy while preserving the stability gained in Stage 2. text: FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT Kaixiang He1, Yujie Wu1∗ 1Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University kaixiang.he@connect.polyu.hk, yu-jie.wu@polyu.edu.hk
title: FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT

text: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their training inherently sequential and in- efficient for long sequences. Existing methods achieve full- sequence parallelism in SNNs through two main strategies: redesigning or approximating spiking dynamics to avoid reset- coupled temporal dependencies, or relying on iterative re- laxed fixed-point solvers that suffer from excessive memory costs and iteration-dependent backward overhead. To address these limitations, we present FidLIF, a novel framework that reconciles the incremental update and hard-reset behavior of standard spiking LIF neurons with parallel forward propa- gation and BPTT-equivalent backward propagation. FidLIF iteratively recovers the full-sequence membrane-potential tra- jectory in parallel. By exploitingthe lowerbidiagonal structure induced by the local recurrence of LIF neurons, FidLIF formu- lates each forward trajectory correction and backward adjoint propagation as associative scans with an O(log T) temporal depth. This formulation also supports input-dependent neu- ronal parameters and allows the same neuron to perform full- sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step infer- ence at deployment. In our numerical convergence evaluation, FidLIF achieves a mean absolute error below 10−7 relative to the matched serial relaxed LIF dynamics, while yielding gradients numerically equivalent to exact BPTT. Our Tri- ton implementation further delivers favorable long-sequence latency and memory scaling, while achieving competitive performance on four

text: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) integrate stateful neuronal dynamics with sparse, event-driven communication (Maass 1997; Roy, Jaiswal, and Panda 2019), enabling highly energy- efficient computation on neuromorphic hardware. With re- cent advances in surrogate-gradient learning, backpropaga- tion through time (BPTT) (Werbos 1990) can be effectively applied to SNN training. This has allowed SNNs to achieve competitive performance across a growing range of static or ∗Corresponding author. short-sequence tasks, such as image classification and object tracking (Neftci, Mostafa, and Zenke 2019; Wu et al. 2018). Despite the great potential, training SNNs for long- sequence tasks remains an open challenge due to linearly increasing computational and memory costs. Take the stan- dard leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) spiking neurons as an ex- ample. Although the subthreshold dynamics of LIF neurons are linear and theoretically parallelizable, threshold-based spike generation introduces resets and alters the subsequent evolution. Since we cannot obtain the spikes and resets in ad- vance, forward propagation has to proceed sequentially over time, resulting in training costs that grow with the number of time steps. To improve SNN capabilities for long-sequence learning, several parallel training approaches have been explored in recent years. For instance, some methods, such as Parallel Spiking Neurons (PSN) (Fang et al. 2023), achieve paral- lelization by completely removing the reset mechanism to decoupletemporal dependencies.Alternatively,ForwardPar- allel Training (FPT) (Feng et al.

For instance, some methods, such as Parallel Spiking Neurons (PSN) (Fang et al. 2023), achieve paral- lelization by completely removing the reset mechanism to decoupletemporal dependencies.Alternatively,ForwardPar- allel Training (FPT) (Feng et al. 2025) treats the soft-reset LIF neuron as a trajectory-solving problem, evaluating all time steps in parallel via iterations. However, these previous works face significant trade-offs: modifying the core spiking dynamics sacrifices the temporal expressivity and hard-reset nature of standard SNNs, while existing iterative solvers re- quire backpropagating through all solver iterations, incurring excessive memory overhead. Moreover, most of these meth- ods sacrifice incremental step-by-step inference capabilities while achieving parallelization, which is disadvantageous for deployment. Therefore, achieving efficient parallel training without compromising the fidelity of recurrent LIF dynamics or deployment inference remains largely unsolved. To address these limitations, we propose FidLIF, a frame- work for reconciling parallel forward trajectory recovery and temporal credit assignment with high-fidelity recurrent hard-reset LIF neurons. In forward propagation, FidLIF ap- plies Newton iterations to a differentiable trajectory equation, where the Heaviside function is relaxed by a sigmoid during the iterative solve. At each iteration, linearizing the causal LIF dynamics yields associative temporal updates, allowing all time steps to be updated in parallel with a scan. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce FidLIF, a novel framework that retains high-fidelity hard-reset dynamics of LIF neurons while enabling full-sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step inference within the same neuron. text: Parallel Methods for Spiking Neurons There are several parallel methods for spiking neurons. Some studies primarily focus on parallelizing subthreshold evo- lution by exploiting refractory periods or chunks between spikes (Taylor, King, and Harper 2023; Morrill, Pehle, and Zador 2026). To parallelize the full sequence, another line of work redesigns or approximates spiking dynamics to avoid reset-related temporal dependencies. SPSN (Yarga and Wood 2023) introduces stochastic spiking, separating the nonlinear spiking function and thus enabling parallel computing. PSN (Fang et al. 2023) removes the reset of the spiking neuron and leverages a temporal matrix to capture temporal dependency. Its variants, Masked-PSN and sliding PSN, only maintain a window of a limited number of steps and thus capture only recent steps. PSU (Li et al. 2024) points out the importance of the reset mechanism and estimates the reset via a paral- lelizable reset estimation component. Building upon PSN, MF-PSN (Xue et al. 2026) also removes the reset and further designs channel-wise temporal convolutions, using bit shift- ing to replace multiplication operations. The Dynamic Decay Spiking Neuron (Huang et al. 2026) analyzes the function of reset and, based on this, redesigns the neuronal dynamics to achieve parallelization. PMSN (Chen et al. 2026) uses state space models (SSMs) to model multi-compartment spiking neurons and achieves parallelization via temporal-decoupled reset. SpikingSSMs (Shen et al.

text: the function of reset and, based on this, redesigns the neuronal dynamics to achieve parallelization. PMSN (Chen et al. 2026) uses state space models (SSMs) to model multi-compartment spiking neurons and achieves parallelization via temporal-decoupled reset. SpikingSSMs (Shen et al. 2025) uses a surrogate dy- namic network to estimate the LIF dynamics for acceleration. Although these methods are effective, most of them achieve parallelization by modifying or approximating the neuronal dynamics to eliminate temporal dependencies, which may compromise fidelity to standard LIF dynamics. Fixed-Point Iteration and Associative Scan Fixed-point iteration has been widely used in deep learning. These methods solve for the equilibrium states (fixed points) of the network and use implicit differentiation for training (Bai, Kolter, and Koltun 2019; El Ghaoui et al. 2021). This idea is then adopted in SNNs with feedback, where the av- erage firing rate serves as the equilibrium state (Xiao et al. 2021, 2023; Cao et al. 2024). Another approach treats the
title: Figure 1: Overall workflow of FidLIF. (a) In forward propagation, FidLIF uses Newton’s method to recover the membrane

text: entire state trajectory of the recurrent neural network (RNN) as a fixed-point problem, thus enabling parallel evaluation over the sequence (Lim et al. 2024; Danieli et al. 2023; Gon- zalez et al. 2024). In SNNs, FPT (Feng et al. 2025) is the first to apply this approach to spiking neuron parallelization. Un- like methods that take average firing rate as the equilibrium state, FPT frames the membrane potential trajectory across all time steps as the fixed-point and solves it through iteration, achieving parallelization of the soft-reset LIF dynamics. However, FPT mainly considers soft-reset LIF. The for- ward propagation iteration is merely repeated substitution, and its backpropagation goes through the iterative process in the forward pass. Therefore, its forward iteration may con- verge slowly, and the memory consumption increases with the number of iterations, limiting its use in long sequences. Associative scan is an algorithm that computes sequences of associative operations in logarithmic depth (Blelloch 1990). It has been widely used to accelerate the linear RNN and SSMs (Lim et al. 2024; Smith, Warrington, and Linder- man 2023; Gu and Dao 2024; Yau et al. 2026). It has also been shown to be applicable for computing BPTT in RNNs (Wang, Bai, and Pekhimenko 2020). In SNNs, it has been used for parallel computation of the subthreshold dynam- ics of continuous SNNs

In SNNs, it has been used for parallel computation of the subthreshold dynam- ics of continuous SNNs (Morrill, Pehle, and Zador 2026). However, these studies do not use scans to solve discrete hard-reset LIF dynamics or their backpropagation. Input-Dependent Neuron Parameters To enhance the expressive capacity of the neuron, we make the time constant τi and resistance Ri adaptive to the recent input context, which is inspired by recent studies in sequence models (Gu and Dao 2024; Peng et al. 2023). Let Ci = (ci−n+1, . . . , ci) denote a causal window containing the most recent n inputs. A small causal parameter generator gψ gives (∆τi, ∆Ri) = gψ(Ci). (21) To constrain the range of parameters and improve training stability, we define the final dynamics parameters as follows: τi = τmin + (τmax −τmin)σ(τbase + ∆τi), Ri = Rmin + (Rmax −Rmin)σ(Rbase + ∆Ri). (22) The bounds τmin, τmax, Rmin, Rmax and the base values τbase, Rbase are tunable hyperparameters; we always con- strain τi > 0 so that ρi = exp(−∆t/τi) < 1, preserving the membrane potential decay characteristic of the LIF model. All {τi, Ri}T i=1 are generated from causal input contexts before the iterative solve, so no future inputs are required and step-by-step inference is preserved. (23) Equation (23) explains why Newton’s method can converge faster than the repeated substitution used in FPT. FPT com- putes every state in the (m + 1)-th iteration solely from the previous iteration v(m). Therefore, a newly updated state cannot affect time steps after it until the next iteration. Newton’s method instead estimates the latest changes in the current iteration using first-order derivatives. In Equation (23), the first term computes the dynamics using the previous iteration, while the second term estimates the change caused by the latest update v(m+1) i−1 −v(m) i−1. If this estimation is

The following theorem further guarantees exact recovery of the trajectory within at most T iterations. Theorem 1 (Finite-step convergence). In exact arith- metic, Eq. (23) recovers the membrane potential trajectory within at most T iterations for any initialization, provided that all coefficients remain finite. Fidelity to LIF Dynamics We evaluate the fidelity of FidLIF on a single layer using Gaussian input currents c ∼N(0, 1). Except for the repre- sentative trajectory, results are averaged over five trials with shaded regions denoting one standard deviation. Fig. 2 compares FidLIF directly with the Heaviside-gated hard-reset LIF dynamics. As the number of iterations in- creases, both the membrane potential error and the spike mismatch rate decrease. The residual error arises from two sources: the finite-iteration error in recovering the sigmoid- relaxed trajectory, and the discrepancy between the sigmoid- relaxed and original Heaviside-gated dynamics. These results confirm that FidLIF faithfully recovers the dynamics of the Heaviside-gated hard-reset LIF within very few iterations. Finally, we compare the gradient calculated after each itera- tion with the reference gradient. text: We proposed FidLIF, a framework that enables parallel train- ing while preserving high-fidelity hard-reset LIF dynamics and step-by-step inference. FidLIF applies Newton’s method to recover the membrane-potential trajectory iteratively in parallel. In the backward pass, FidLIF’s reverse adjoint scan achieves BPTT-equivalent gradients without passing through the forward iterations, making memory cost almost inde- pendent of the number of iterations. FidLIF also supports input-dependent neuronal parameters, improving the repre- sentational ability. Experiments show that our Triton imple- mentation achieves significant speedup and memory savings, particularly on long sequences. In real sequential bench- marks, FidLIF achieves competitive accuracy within 3 itera- tions, and the trained model supports step-by-step inference without extra conversion. FidLIF thus combines high-fidelity hard-reset LIF dynamics with sequence parallelism, allowing SNNs to take advantage of modern accelerators during train- ing while executing step-by-step during deployment. These features help SNNs strike a better balance between biological plausibility, efficiency, and edge deployment.

text: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm’s superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RUSTKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on k and on the dataset—single-tree search is fastest at k=1 on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at k≥5 on the three largest—and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a 7.5× fac- tor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is 1.6× slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at d=32, 1.31× at d=54, and 1.49× at d=784); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. text: Nearest neighbor algorithms, and data structures to accelerate/improve them, exist in many forms. There are algorithms for pruning the search space like the KD-tree [1], sketches for calculating approximations of distance functions faster [2], and more. This line of research has been highly impactful in real-world systems, from information retrieval to clustering/visualization and even in Large Language Models via retrieval-augmented generation and vector databases. While approxi- mate methods have dramatically gained popularity in recent years, exact metric-space k-NN remains necessary when the distance itself is the object of interest or approximate recall is unacceptable— for example, in cases like anomaly detection over raw features, protein-structure comparison under graph kernels, or retrieval under Wasserstein distance. However, when we survey papers (see Ap- pendix K) in this broad area, we find that few consider basic details, such as distinguishing between a hold-out set’s query performance and the original training data (26%). Fewer still report both distance-comparison counts and runtime (15%), even though the two are not always correlated, document micro-optimization details (11%)—the low-level implementation choices we isolate in Section 4.2—or batch vs. single-instance queries (10%). 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). We support that argument by developing RUSTKNN as an example, re-evaluating the methods behind the seminal cover tree data structure—a structure with multiple proposed vari- ants and one of the few with both empirical success and theoretical grounding for reducing nearest neighbor queries. We re-implement a cache-efficient cover tree with three query settings (single, batch, and dual-tree). Working in a compiled language allows both effective runtime evaluation and easy isolation of six micro-optimizations used in the literature (five of which we ablate), along with poorly documented nuances of the cover tree “base” parameter, which to our knowledge has never been independently tested. text: Nearest neighbor data structures. Spatial indexing methods for nearest neighbor search can be organized along two axes: exact versus approximate, and coordinate-based versus general metric space. Among exact methods for coordinate spaces, KD-trees [3] achieve O(log n) query time in low dimensions but degrade to O(n) as dimensionality grows, and their axis-aligned splits tie them to a coordinate representation; ball trees [4] improve on KD-trees through hierarchical ball decompo- sition, extending efficient search to moderate dimensions; because they partition by distance to cen- ters rather than along axes, they apply to any proper metric. For general metric spaces, vantage-point trees [5] use binary partitions around single pivot points but offer only O(n) worst-case query time. Navigating nets [6] introduced the theoretical framework of the doubling dimension c (also called the “expansion constant”), which cover trees [7] made practical with an O(c6 log n) query algorithm, later improved by Izbicki and Shelton [8] with simplified and nearest ancestor variants(though a history of nuanced theoretical runtime errors and fixes [9–12] is beyond this study), tree merging for parallel construction, and cache-optimized packing. On the approximate side, locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) [13] provides sublinear search but requires metric-specific hash families, while hier- archical navigable small world graphs (HNSW) [14] achieve state-of-the-art recall–speed tradeoffs for approximate search but offer no exactness guarantees. Cover trees are a practical structure com- bining exact search, arbitrary metric spaces, and query complexity parametrized by intrinsic rather than ambient dimensionality. They are not alone in that combination—navigating nets, cited above, share it—but they are the variant with the broadest empirical track record, which is why we take them as our case study. 2

text: Implementations and libraries. The original cover tree C++ reference implementation [7], last updated in 2014, is single-threaded with distance-level optimizations (batched computation, aligned memory) but no tree-level cache packing. mlpack [15] provides the most actively maintained cover tree implementation, including dual-tree traversal and extensive test coverage. FLANN [16] of- fers randomized KD-trees and is widely used in robotics and computer vision, though it targets coordinate spaces only. Among approximate and GPU-accelerated systems, FAISS [17] scales to billions of vectors with quantization-based search on GPUs; Annoy [18] uses random projection trees with memory-mapped files for production use; and ScaNN [19] employs learned anisotropic vector quantization. Existing cover tree implementations span C++, Haskell, and Java [20, 21] (e.g., JSAT & WEKA) -but no two of them implement the same set of variants, query modes, and micro- optimizations, and none is Rust-native. Critically, cross-language and cross-codebase comparisons confound algorithmic effects (e.g., nearest ancestor vs. simplified) with implementation effects (e.g., compiler optimizations, memory layout, distance computation strategy), making it difficult to at- tribute performance differences to their true cause. Our work focuses on cover trees specifically, but we believe the insight of delineating implementation details applies to other search structures and can reveal new research directions; Section 5.5 gives direct evidence for a second structure. text: 3.1 Metric Spaces and the Doubling Dimension A metric space (X, d) is a set X equipped with a distance function d : X × X →R≥0 satisfying non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles (d(x, y) = 0 ⇐⇒x = y), symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Given a finite dataset S ⊂X, the doubling constant c is the minimum value such that every ball of radius r centered on a point in S can be covered by at most c balls of radius r/2 [6, 37]. The doubling dimension is dimD = log2 c. Crucially, c is a property of the dataset, not of the ambient space: data lying on a low-dimensional manifold embedded in RD can have small c even when D is large. Cover tree query complexity is O(c6 log n), parametrized by c rather than D— this is what makes cover trees effective in high dimensions, unlike KD-trees whose performance degrades exponentially with D. 3.2 Cover Tree Invariants A cover tree is a leveled tree in which each node stores a single data point. Intuitively, each level represents a different resolution: the root sees the dataset at coarse scale, and deeper nodes refine the picture. Three structural invariants govern parent-child relationships (Definition 1 of Beygelzimer et al. [7]): 1. Leveling invariant. Every node p has an integer level(p), and

text: different resolution: the root sees the dataset at coarse scale, and deeper nodes refine the picture. Three structural invariants govern parent-child relationships (Definition 1 of Beygelzimer et al. [7]): 1. Leveling invariant. Every node p has an integer level(p), and every child q satisfies level(q) = level(p) −1. Each level down is a finer resolution. 2. Covering invariant. Define the covering distance covdist(p) = blevel(p). For each child q of p, d(p, q) ≤covdist(p). No child lies beyond its parent’s covering radius. 3. Separating invariant. Define the separation distance sepdist(p) = blevel(p)−1. For dis- tinct children q1, q2 of p, d(q1, q2) > sepdist(p). No two siblings are too close together. 3

text: The base parameter b controls the ratio between covering and separating distances. The original formulation uses b = 2, but Beygelzimer et al. [7] found empirically that b = 1.3 reduces distance computations by 10–71% on benchmark datasets. Our experiments default to b = 1.3. Each node also caches maxdist(p) = maxq∈descendants(p) d(p, q), the greatest distance from p to any of its descendants, which is upper bounded by covdist(p) · b/(b−1) (a geometric series over descendant levels; this equals 2 · covdist(p) when b=2 and ≈4.3 · covdist(p) at the default b=1.3). This value enables the key pruning rule during queries: a subtree rooted at q can be skipped entirely when d(query, q) −maxdist(q) > dbest, because even the closest descendant of q must be farther than the current best candidate. From Beygelzimer et al. [7], the maximum number of children per node is O(c4) and the maximum tree depth is O(c2 log n). 3.3 Algorithmic Variants The original cover tree [7] was defined as an implicit infinite structure in which every internal node also appears as its own child—the nesting invariant. The explicit representation stores O(n) nodes. Izbicki and Shelton [8] observed that the nesting invariant is unnecessary for the runtime analysis and introduced two improved variants that eliminate self-children, reducing the node count to exactly n. text: child—the nesting invariant. The explicit representation stores O(n) nodes. Izbicki and Shelton [8] observed that the nesting invariant is unnecessary for the runtime analysis and introduced two improved variants that eliminate self-children, reducing the node count to exactly n. Simplified cover tree construction. The simplified insertion of Izbicki and Shelton [8] builds a tree via depth-first search: starting from the root, the algorithm finds the first child whose covering distance accommodates the new point and recurses; if no child qualifies, the point becomes a new child at level −1. If the new point lies beyond the root’s covering distance, the root level is raised. The tree contains exactly n nodes, one per data point, eliminating the self-children of the original formulation. Construction runs in O(c6n log n) time. Nearest ancestor cover tree construction. This variant adds a fourth invariant: for every point p with ancestor q1 and sibling q2 of q1, we require d(p, q1) ≤d(p, q2)—every point’s ancestor at each level is the closest possible. Insertion sorts children by distance to the new point and invokes a rebalance procedure that extracts descendants violating the invariant and reinserts them under the new point. Construction is costlier, but the resulting tree has tighter maxdist values, leading to more aggressive pruning; the trees are also deeper, so querying is not always quicker than the simplified variant. Parallel cover tree construction. Two cover trees are merged by matching children between them at each level, enabling parallel construction: partition the dataset across processors, build indepen- dent trees, then merge via binary reduction in O(log p) rounds. Roughly 1% of distance computa- tions occur during the merge; the bottleneck is cache performance in the parallel construction phase. We implement this but do not time it in our experiments; Table 9 reports its distance counts. Single-tree query. Nearest-neighbor search traverses the tree depth-first from the root, visiting children in order of increasing distance to the query. A child q is pruned when d(query, q) − maxdist(q) > dbest, yielding O(c6 log n) runtime. Batch single-tree query. This algorithm, derived from the code of Beygelzimer et al. [7] but not described in detail in their paper, organizes the query set into its own cover tree and maintains cover sets—lists of candidate reference nodes, indexed by scale level—that are passed top-down through the query tree hierarchy. At each scale level, three cases arise (Figure 20 in the appendix):

text: the query set into its own cover tree and maintains cover sets—lists of candidate reference nodes, indexed by scale level—that are passed top-down through the query tree hierarchy. At each scale level, three cases arise (Figure 20 in the appendix): (i) ref- erence descent—expand each candidate reference node by replacing it with its children, computing distances and pruning; (ii) query split—when a query node has children at the current scale, each query child receives a filtered copy of the parent’s cover sets with distances recomputed and entries pruned against the child’s bound; the parent point continues as a “virtual self-child,” inheriting the cover sets directly; (iii) base case—at the leaf scale, score remaining candidates. The key mecha- nism is cover-set inheritance: once a reference candidate is pruned from a query node’s cover set, no descendant query point will ever see it. A mutable upper bound threaded through the recursion means any improvement from scoring one query point immediately tightens the threshold for sib- lings and descendants. The amortization scales with query tree depth: in all-NN mode (query = ref- erence) the query tree has full depth O(c2 log n) with many split points, maximizing amortization, 4

Dual-tree traversal [38, 39] simultaneously descends query and reference trees, pruning entire (query-subtree, reference-subtree) pairs via the triangle inequality—a joint pruning that can discard more work per distance computation than batch single-tree’s per-query bounds, at the cost of more bookkeeping per node pair. We summarize this algorithm in Figure 21 in the Appendix. Why interactions matter. These three query modes, combined with the base parameter b and micro-optimizations, create a multi-dimensional performance landscape. As we show in Section 5, the optimal configuration depends on k, dataset geometry, and evaluation protocol in ways that are not apparent from any single comparison. 4 Implementation and Optimization Ablation 4.1 Implementation Overview RUSTKNN comprises approximately 13,000 lines of Rust organized around a generic Distance<T> trait that enables arbitrary metric spaces. After cover tree construction, pointer-based trees are con- verted to a contiguous PackedCoverTree in depth-first order (a simpler alternative to the van Emde Boas layout of Izbicki and Shelton [8]) for cache locality: each packed node occupies ∼40 bytes, fitting within a single 64-byte cache line. The dual-tree traversal adapts the framework of Curtin et al. [39] to cover trees without self-children, using a three-phase expansion with triangle inequal- ity pre-filters (details in Appendix C).

Early-exit distance: Euclidean distance computation with four independent accumulators and periodic bound checks; exits early when the partial sum exceeds the pruning bound, avoiding the full O(d) computation. 2. Halfsort: Partial sort of children, O(n) versus O(n log n) full sort. 3. SmallVec: Stack-allocated child arrays for the typical 3–5 children per node at base 1.3. 4. k=1 fast path: Dedicated single-comparison path in the k-NN state machine. 5. Triangle pre-filters: Each reference child caches its parent distance dparent(rc) at con- struction time. Before computing d(q, rc), the triangle inequality gives a free lower bound |d(q, rp) −dparent(rc)| using the already-known parent score d(q, rp). If this lower bound minus the child’s maxdist exceeds the current kth-best distance, the entire subtree is skipped without a metric evaluation. Single-tree search runs one independent descent per query, pruning against that query’s current kth-best distance. At k=1 that radius is the nearest-neighbor distance, which is small, and the dedicated k=1 path keeps the per-candidate bookkeeping to a single comparison: on mnist the single-tree all-NN issues 6× fewer distance computations than the dual-tree traversal (312M vs. 1.87B, Table 9). As k grows, the pruning radius widens to the kth- nearest distance and every one of the n independent descents pays for it separately: from k=1 to k=5, single-tree time on mnist grows 6.5× while dual-tree time grows 1.2× (Table 4). text: base sensitivity curves appear in Appendix A.4. 5.4 All-NN vs. Held-Out Divergence The all-nearest-neighbor benchmark, in which query and reference sets coincide, is the standard evaluation in KNN literature [7, 8]. This setting can enable some memory and algorithmic opti- mizations since the query and reference sets can use the same cover tree. However, most practical workloads involve held-out queries against a pre-built index. Table 5 (Appendix A.2) shows held-out performance diverges from all-NN rankings. Ranking divergence. The clearest case is mlpack’s two query modes. In the all-NN benchmark they are within about 2× of each other on every dataset, and dual-tree is the faster of the two on five of them (Table 3); held out, mlpack-Dual is 7.8× slower than mlpack-Single on pendigits and 250× slower on covtype at nq=512 (Table 5). An evaluation that used only the all-NN benchmark would never see a gap of that size. The best RUSTKNN mode changes in the same way: on mnist, single-tree search wins the all-NN benchmark at k=1, but held out at nq=512 dual-tree search is 1.8× faster than single-tree (8.4 vs. 15.1 s; Appendix A.2). And on covtype, the C++ reference ties RUSTKNN’s best mode in all-NN at k=1 (13.0K vs. 13.6K ms, intervals overlapping) but is 1.5× faster held out at nq=512 (53.0 vs. 81.1 ms, intervals disjoint).

And on covtype, the C++ reference ties RUSTKNN’s best mode in all-NN at k=1 (13.0K vs. 13.6K ms, intervals overlapping) but is 1.5× faster held out at nq=512 (53.0 vs. 81.1 ms, intervals disjoint). This divergence is systematic: in all-NN mode the query tree is the reference tree, so dual-tree and batch methods amortize their tree-building and expansion costs over all n points; held out, the query tree is shallow and that amortization is small. Where our implementation loses. Table 5 also contains a result worth stating plainly rather than glossing: on covtype held-out—arguably the most practically relevant cell in the paper, being the one dataset with both large n and moderate d—the C++ reference is fastest at every nq, and RUSTKNN’s best mode (dual-tree) is 1.2–1.5× slower. RUSTKNN-Single is also slower than mlpack-Single at nq ≥128 (176 vs. 142 ms at nq=512). But single-tree is the wrong RUSTKNN mode here: RUSTKNN-Dual is 2.2× faster than RUSTKNN-Single at nq=512 and 1.75× faster than mlpack- Single. Both facts are the same lesson from opposite directions—an implementation evaluated in only one query mode gets misranked, whichever way the misranking happens to fall. 9

text: Implications for evaluation. We recommend reporting both all-NN and held-out results: the for- mer stresses scalability, the latter approximates serving latency. Full held-out scaling curves appear in Appendices A.2–A.3. 5.5 Beyond Cover Trees: A KD-Tree Under the Same Harness The factors we isolate above are cover-tree-specific in their details, which raises the question of whether the methodological finding—that implementation choices can dominate algorithmic ones— holds for other index structures. To test this without rewriting the study, we added a median-split KD-tree inside RUSTKNN, reusing the identical kernel, candidate structure, distance counter, and timing code, so it runs the same five feature-flag ablations. We also benchmarked kiddo, an in- dependent Rust KD-tree crate, under the same 20-allocation protocol, separating the effect of the codebase from that of the index. Full tables are in Appendix H. The better index reverses with dimension. On all-NN at k=1, the KD-tree is 13× faster than single-tree cover trees on corel (254 vs. 3,248 ms; same-allocation values from Table 11) and 23× faster on covtype (4,465 vs. 100,590 ms), because axis-aligned box pruning is highly effective at moderate d. At d=784 that pruning collapses—the KD-tree issues 594M distance computations— and it becomes 12× slower than the single-tree cover tree (4.09M vs. 334,487 ms): a textbook curse-of-dimensionality crossover, measured with no cross-codebase confounders. The same algorithm in a different codebase differs by up to 9×. Our KD-tree and kiddo im- plement the same algorithm, yet kiddo is 9× faster on pendigits (7.8 vs. 72 ms) while being 2.9× slower on covtype and 2.0× slower on mnist (8.31M vs. 4.09M ms): each wins on different data. A practitioner comparing “KD-tree vs. cover tree” would reach the same verdict with either library here, but not the same magnitude: on covtype the KD-tree beats the best cover-tree mode by 3.1× with ours but by only 7% with kiddo—precisely the confounding this paper argues against, now shown outside cover trees. The five-flag KD-tree ablation (Table 12) shows the same structure: only early exit helps beyond noise, and only at d=784 (1.11×). 6
title: Implications for evaluation.

text: Using RUSTKNN as a controlled experimental platform, we have shown that cover tree perfor- mance depends on interactions between query strategy, k, base parameter, and micro-optimizations in ways not apparent from cross-codebase comparisons. The best query mode depends on k and on the dataset—single-tree search at k=1 on most of our larger datasets, dual-tree search at k≥5 on the largest—and choosing the wrong mode costs up to 7.5×; base 1.3 is not a safe default for dual-tree search (2.0 or more is optimal in 22 of 24 dataset–k cases); early-exit distance is the one micro- optimization that matters, and its benefit grows with dimension (1.31× at d=54, 1.49× at d=784) while leaving the traversal unchanged; and all-NN and held-out benchmarks produce different im- plementation rankings, so both should be reported. Reporting the main results over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap intervals is what separated these effects from measurement noise. Our conclusions are scoped to exact nearest neighbor search under Euclidean distance, single- threaded, on datasets up to n≈581K. We do not study approximate methods; whether these effects transfer to HNSW/IVF-style indexes is open, as are non-Euclidean metrics, parallel scaling, and n > 106. Timings on the smallest datasets are noise-limited (Section 4.2); cross-codebase tim- ings carry an instruction-set disparity (AVX-512 vs. SSE2; Appendix B), though within-RUSTKNN comparisons are unaffected. text: B Experiment Details Hardware. All experiments run on a multi-node SLURM cluster. Each compute node contains two Intel Xeon Platinum 8490H processors (Sapphire Rapids, 60 cores per socket, two hardware threads per core, 112.5 MiB of L3 per socket, maximum clock 1.90 GHz, i.e., no turbo boost) with 2 TB of RAM, running Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Linux 5.15). Every benchmark job is allocated one physical core (--cpus-per-task=1 under core-granularity scheduling) and its own memory, so jobs never share a core; they do share each socket’s L3 cache and memory bandwidth with the other jobs on the node. Node load. That sharing matters on the large datasets. On an otherwise idle node, N pinned copies of the mnist all-NN, split evenly across the two sockets, slow down by 1.48× (N=15), 1.61× (N=30), and 1.99× (N=60) for the C++ reference, and by 1.43× (N=15) and 2.07× (N=60) for RUSTKNN single-tree search (each copy pinned to its own physical core): the two degrade at the same rate, so ratios between implementations measured under the same load are stable even though absolute times are not. Because the clock is fixed, the slowdown is cache and memory- bandwidth contention rather than frequency scaling. We therefore ran every campaign with the nodes held at a similar, high load (about 110 memory-heavy benchmark jobs per 120-core node),

We therefore ran every campaign with the nodes held at a similar, high load (about 110 memory-heavy benchmark jobs per 120-core node), using filler jobs that run the same mnist workloads while a campaign’s last allocations finished, so that no configuration was measured on an emptying node. One of the three nodes ran large-dataset allocations 1.1–1.5× slower than the other two at the same job count; allocations were spread across nodes, so this mainly widens the upper confidence bounds on covtype and mnist rather than moving the medians. On pima and pendigits, per-allocation timings are bimodal for reasons we have not isolated (Section 4.2). Software. [7] is compiled with g++ 11.4.0 (-O3 -ffast-math -funroll-loops). ml- pack 4.7.1 [15] is compiled with g++ 11.4.0 (-std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG). All implementations use a cover-tree base parameter of 1.3 unless otherwise noted (sensitivity analysis in Appendix A.4). Note that the Rust binaries are built on the cluster’s login node (Xeon Platinum 8358, Ice Lake) with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native", i.e., AVX-512 code that also runs on the Sapphire Rapids compute nodes,

text: C Implementation Details This appendix provides full implementation details for RUSTKNN, supplementing the overview in Section 4. C.1 Architecture and Trait-Based Generics The core abstraction enabling arbitrary metric spaces is the Distance<T> trait: pub trait Distance <T> { fn distance (&self , p: &T, q: &T) -> f64; fn distance_with_bound (&self , p: &T, q: &T, upper_bound: f64) -> f64 { self.distance(p, q) } } Users implement a single method; the library provides optimized built-in implementations for Eu- clidean and Manhattan metrics. The optional distance with bound method enables early-exit distance computation: the built-in Euclidean implementation uses four independent accumulators with 8-element unrolled loops for instruction-level parallelism, checking partial squared sums every 16–64 dimensions. If the partial sum exceeds upper bound2, the function returns a sentinel value without computing the final square root. The generic node structure Node<T: Clone> stores the data point, level, cached maxdist, cached parent distance d parent, children as Vec<Box<Node<T>>>>, and an is duplicate flag for merge-created duplicates. Fields are ordered for cache locality: hot query fields (point, maxdist, d parent) appear first. The library is organized into three variant modules (simplified/, nearest ancestor/, packed/) sharing common algorithms in a core/ directory. A zero-cost CoverTree enum wrapper delegates via pattern matching. C.2 Packed Trees and Cache Optimization After construction, the pointer-based tree is converted to a
title: Implementation Details

text: organized into three variant modules (simplified/, nearest ancestor/, packed/) sharing common algorithms in a core/ directory. A zero-cost CoverTree enum wrapper delegates via pattern matching. C.2 Packed Trees and Cache Optimization After construction, the pointer-based tree is converted to a PackedCoverTree via a single depth- first traversal. All nodes are stored in a contiguous Vec<PackedNode<T>>, with child relationships in a separate shared Vec<usize> array. Each PackedNode carries u32 fields (child index start, child index count) as indices into the shared array. This yields compact nodes: PackedNode<f64> occupies approximately 40 bytes, with hot query fields spanning ≤32 bytes—fitting within a single 64-byte cache line. Using u32 saves 8 bytes per node versus usize. Approximately 1,000 nodes fit in a 32 KB L1 cache. During packing, children are sorted by d parent (ascending) so closer children appear first in mem- ory, tightening the pruning bound sooner. C.3 Dual-Tree Traversal The dual-tree traversal requires several adaptations for cover trees without self-children. When expanding one side’s children while holding the other constant, the held-constant node’s point must still score against the expanded children. Two helper routines (point vs subtree, subtree vs point) simulate the missing self-child. When both nodes have children, the traversal proceeds in three phases: (1) query point × ref- erence children, (2) query children × reference point, and (3) child–child pairs
title: Implementation Details

text: helper routines (point vs subtree, subtree vs point) simulate the missing self-child. When both nodes have children, the traversal proceeds in three phases: (1) query point × ref- erence children, (2) query children × reference point, and (3) child–child pairs using trian- gle inequality lower bounds from phases 1 and 2 as free pre-filters: lb = max(|d(qp, rcj) − dparent(qci)|, |d(qci, rp) −dparent(rcj)|). Pairs whose lower bound minus combined maxdist exceeds the pruning threshold are skipped without additional distance computation. Per-query-point bounds are cached in a flat Vec indexed by node index. Two bound modes are supported: full recursive B1/B2 bounds with epoch-based cache invalidation (the default), and a Beygelzimer-style bound. A cheaper per-point kth-distance bound was removed: it drops the per- subtree margin and can prune true neighbors. 38
title: Implementation Details

text: C.4 Parallel Construction Parallel construction follows the partition-build-merge strategy of Izbicki and Shelton [8]. The dataset is partitioned into equal chunks, each thread builds an independent cover tree, and trees are merged via binary reduction in O(log p) rounds. The merge algorithm aligns tree levels, parti- tions children into covered and uncovered sets, recursively merges covered children, and reinserts uncovered points. Exact maxdist recomputation after merge restores optimal pruning bounds. 39

text: I Naive Search with Partial Distance Computation A reasonable question about any index is whether it earns its complexity. We added a naive variant—a linear scan—to the same harness, using the same early-exit (“partial distance”) Eu- clidean kernel and the same distance counter as every other implementation. Building it with no-early-exit yields the full-distance twin. Both perform identical n2 distance calls, so any runtime difference is purely the per-call dimension work that early exit skips—this isolates the partial-distance effect on the simplest possible baseline. Corel is the instructive case: early exit is worth 2.5× in the linear scan but nothing in the cover tree (Table 1), consistent with the tree having already pruned most of the far candidates whose distance computations early exit would otherwise cut short. The benefit of a kernel-level optimization thus depends on the structure that calls the kernel, not only on the data. The absolute numbers also answer the “is an index worth it?” question directly. Naive all-NN on mnist requires 3.6×109 distance calls (43–70 minutes) and on covtype 3.4×1011 (6–10 hours), against milliseconds to minutes for the trees. At the same time, on the smallest datasets the naive scan is competitive in absolute terms—another reason the tiny-dataset results in this paper should not drive implementation decisions. 46

text: J Synthetic Manifolds with Known Intrinsic Dimension The cover tree’s O(c6 log n) query bound is stated in terms of the doubling dimension, not the ambi- ent dimension, but on real datasets the intrinsic dimension is unknown, so the distinction cannot be tested directly. We therefore generated synthetic data where it is known by construction: n=20,000 points sampled on a d-dimensional latent manifold, then linearly embedded in ambient dimension D ≥d: latent coordinates are uniform on [0, 1]d, the embedding is a fixed random D × d matrix with N(0, 1) entries, and isotropic Gaussian noise (σ=0.01) puts points near rather than exactly on the manifold, with a fixed seed per configuration. This is direct empirical support for the claim that cover-tree query cost is governed by intrinsic rather than ambient dimen- sionality, which the theory asserts but which, to our knowledge, has not previously been isolated experimentally. Wall-clock behaves differently from distance count in Sweep B, and the difference is informative: cover-tree time still rises with D (501→1,203 ms) even though the number of distance computations does not, because each computation is D-dimensional. This is the distance-count-versus-runtime decoupling discussed in Section 4.2, and it is why we report both throughout: a paper reporting only distance counts here would conclude, incorrectly, that ambient dimension is free. 47

text: K Literature Survey: Evaluation Practices in Metric Space Search To contextualize our experimental contributions, we surveyed 61 papers from the metric space near- est neighbor search literature and classified each on four evaluation-practice dimensions that our work addresses: 1. text: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search Systems in WeChat Jiajun Han∗, Guoxin Ma∗, Felix∗†, Liangsheng Xu#, Ruiqi Yu#, Yingdi Guo, Zongbing Wang, Xinhua Ye, Chenyan Hua, Xin Xie, Pengcheng Yang, Haijun Wu
title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search

text: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, its effectiveness is limited by two key chal- lenges. First, existing Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to incor- porate collaborative signals while maintaining effective codebook utilization, limiting their ability to distinguish items and achieve high-quality retrieval. Second, existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods suffer from severe reward sparsity under exact SID match- ing, leaving many sampled trajectories without effective learning signals and hindering preference optimization. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified generative retrieval frame- work consisting of two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) incor- porates query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals while mitigating codebook collapse through codebook refresh and com- plementary regularization, enabling more informative and balanced SID representations. Building upon these SIDs, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands both reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons, reducing learning difficulty while leveraging behavioral reward signals at different levels of the SID hierarchy, without relying on auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate the effective- ness of WeGR in improving retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search demonstrates relative improvements of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, while reducing online CPU and GPU usage
title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search

text: WeGR in improving retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search demonstrates relative improvements of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, while reducing online CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%, respec- tively. The system has been successfully deployed across multiple search scenarios in WeChat, serving billions of users, generating tens of millions of PVs daily. text: As illustrated in Figure 1, modern industrial search systems typically organize candidate generation, pre-ranking, and ranking as a multi- stage cascade. Such systems maintain multiple retrieval channels and pass their merged candidate set through downstream ranking stages, increasing both serving complexity and computational cost. Generative retrieval (GR) offers an alternative paradigm by rep- resenting each item as a sequence of discrete tokens, commonly referred to as a Semantic ID (SID), and directly generating candi- date SIDs conditioned on the query and user context [1, 25, 29, 33]. text: scale industrial search system, however, depends on learning be- haviorally informative SIDs and aligning the policy model with observed user feedback in a robust and transferable manner. The first challenge lies in constructing SIDs that preserve collab- orative semantics while maintaining effective codebook utilization. Existing quantization methods mainly follow two paradigms. RQ- VAE-based methods support end-to-end learning and allow task- specific supervision to directly shape SID construction, but discrete assignment and successive residual decomposition can produce imbalanced codeword usage and codebook collapse [25, 31]. RQ- Kmeans-based methods provide more explicit control over cluster assignments and can incorporate balancing strategies or alterna- tive quantizers [2, 9]; however, collaborative and business-specific signals are usually encoded only in upstream item representations and may be attenuated or distorted during multi-level residual quantization. Consequently, existing paradigms offer complemen- tary strengths but do not fully reconcile collaborative-information preservation with stable codebook utilization, limiting the repre- sentational capacity of the resulting SID space. The second challenge lies in aligning the generative policy with user preferences. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) maximizes the like- lihood of observed positive SIDs but does not explicitly distinguish the relative value of generated candidates. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) facilitates preference optimization by leveraging re- ward signals from user interactions [12, 37]. Larger rollout bud- gets incur substantial computation, while beam search introduces a mismatch between selected trajectories and the policy’s sampling distribution. On the other hand, auxiliary rankers—trained strictly on candidates from upstream retrieval stages—provide unreliable scores for medium- and long-tail items explored by the genera- tive policy. Furthermore, practical ranking scores often rely on hand-crafted heuristics tailored to specific scenarios, limiting cross- scenario generalizability and requiring costly adaptation. Thus, denser rewards do not necessarily yield better preference align- ment and may instead inject misleading supervision. To address these challenges, we present WeGR, a unified gen- erative retrieval framework for industrial search systems. First, the Col- laborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) incorpo- rates query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative supervision into continuous representation learning. It further combines first-layer codebook refresh with residual-fidelity and collision regularization, mitigating persistent codeword underutilization while preserving semantic structure across quantization layers. Second, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) leverages the hierarchical structure of SIDs for coarse-to-fine GRPO optimization. Second, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) leverages the hierarchical structure of SIDs for coarse-to-fine GRPO optimization. By pro- gressively expanding the horizons for both reward evaluation and policy optimization, DHPO allows sampled trajectories to receive behavioral rewards through prefix matching during early training, before gradually transitioning to exact item-level preference opti- mization. This enables more effective use of click- and order-based outcome rewards without auxiliary reward models. We further introduce Multi-Positive Supervised Fine-Tuning (MSFT) to learn from multiple positive items and provide stable learning signals when group-relative rewards become uninformative. We evaluate WeGR in large-scale production search. In controlled online A/B tests, the V1.2 deployment removes 80% of candidates from conventional retrieval channels while achieving relative im- provements of 2.539%, 1.508%, and 1.381% in orders, CTR, and CVR, respectively. This reduces the number of candidates entering pre- ranking by 38.10%, yielding CPU and GPU savings of 25.5% and 26.1%. WeGR also reduces average serving latency by 21.7 ms in WeChat Channels Search and 15.4 ms in WeChat Search. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We introduce CoCo-VAE, a behavior-aware residual quanti- zation framework that integrates collaborative supervision with codebook refresh, residual-fidelity preservation, and collision regularization to mitigate codebook underutiliza- tion without sacrificing SID semantics. • We propose DHPO, a reward-model-free GRPO variant that progressively expands the horizons of reward evaluation and policy optimization along the SID hierarchy, alleviating outcome reward sparsity while maintaining generalizability across diverse search scenarios. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of WeGR via production ex- periments and fine-grained analyses, showing improvements in business metrics with reduction in candidate volume, serv- ing resources, and latency. For item retrieval, each item is repre- sented as a Semantic ID (SID), a sequence of discrete tokens encod- ing its semantic information. Such SIDs are constructed through two paradigms: RQ-VAE-based learnable quantization [17, 25] and RQ-Kmeans-based residual clustering [2, 9]. RQ-Kmeans-based methods. [20] construct SIDs by successively clustering item embeddings and residuals, with explicit assignment control. OneRec [9] uses balanced clustering, while OneSearch [2] combines selective cluster balancing with optimized product quanti- zation of the remaining residual [13]. These designs separate quanti- zation from behavior-aware representation learning. In OneSearch, collaborative signals enter upstream contrastive embeddings, but subsequent clustering does not directly optimize behavioral objec- tives. Preserving these signals in SIDs thus relies on quantization fidelity, not direct behavioral supervision of code assignment. RQ-VAE-based methods. learn representations and codebooks via reconstruction and quantization, allowing task supervision. LC-Rec [38] combines learned indices with collaborative-semantic alignment tasks, while LETTER [32] directly regularizes the tok- enizer via collaborative contrastive alignment and code-assignment diversity. ETEGRec [19] couples tokenization and recommendation via sequence–item and preference–semantic alignment. These ap- proaches differ in whether alignment targets the recommender, the tokenizer, or their joint training, rather

Given predicted semantic-code values, GPR’s Value-Guided Trie-based Beam Search [34] allocates beam widths under trie con- straints without updating the generative policy. Training-based approaches [18] incorporate utility into super- vised or preference objectives. text: In this section, we present WeGR, a unified generative retrieval framework for e-commerce search. WeGR consists of two comple- mentary components. First, CoCo-VAE (§ 3.1) incorporates query- to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals into SID construction while mitigating codebook collapse through complementary reg- ularization. Building on these SIDs, DHPO (§ 3.2.1) progressively expands reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons, en- abling coarse-to-fine preference learning under sparse outcome rewards without relying on auxiliary reward models. The overall framework is illustrated in Figure 2. 3.1 Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer To preserve collaborative information while maintaining effective codebook utilization, we propose CoCo-VAE, a collaborative-aware residual quantization framework. Specifically, CoCo-VAE incor- porates query-to-item (Q2I) and item-to-item (I2I) collaborative signals to guide representation learning, while combining Code- book Refresh with Fidelity Anti-collapse Regularization (FAR) to mitigate codebook collapse during hierarchical quantization. 3.1.1 Q2I And I2I Collaborative Regularization. We introduce Q2I and I2I collaborative signals to address the lack of co-occurrence in- formation in multimodal embeddings [40]. Specifically, an auxiliary contrastive loss is employed to capture collaborative relationships and guide SID construction. Unlike existing methods that impose constraints directly within the discrete codebook space, which can cause codebook collapse by forcing semantically dissimilar embed- dings to share the same SID, we apply such constraints exclusively to the continuous representations of the encoder with a detached projection head.

Although Codebook Refresh mitigates codebook collapse in the first quantization layer 𝐿1, codewords in deeper layers may remain underutilized. To ad- dress this issue, we introduce Fidelity Anti-collapse Regularization (FAR) from two complementary perspectives. At the sample level, we enable each sample to update multiple semantically relevant codewords instead of only its nearest one, expanding gradient cov- erage. At the codeword level, we regularize codeword assignments across samples by penalizing excessive collisions, preventing a large number of samples from concentrating on a few codewords.

We extract high-quality user interactions from WeChat e-commerce search logs collected between June and July 2026 for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). The dataset spans 31 days, with the first 30 for training and the last for testing. All offline evaluations and ablation studies use this dataset. The Click and Order test sets each contain 20,000 search interactions with observed positive items. Evaluation Metrics. Following existing generative retrieval stud- ies [2, 3, 9, 31], we evaluate recall and ranking performance using Hit Rate (HR) and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). We report results at 𝐾∈{6, 50, 200}, averaged over all evaluation samples. Baseline Methods. We compare WeGR with SID construction and preference optimization baselines. SID construction baselines include RQ-Kmeans-based methods, namely RQ-Kmeans [9], RQ- Kmeans with balancing, and RQ-OPQ [2], as well as RQ-VAE-based methods such as RQ-VAE [16, 25, 32] and R3-VAE [31]. For pref- erence optimization, we compare DPO [24], S-DPO [2, 5], and LDPO [12, 28] as off-policy RL baselines, and vanilla GRPO [27], TPMA-GRPO [3], and HCGRec [35] as

For pref- erence optimization, we compare DPO [24], S-DPO [2, 5], and LDPO [12, 28] as off-policy RL baselines, and vanilla GRPO [27], TPMA-GRPO [3], and HCGRec [35] as on-policy RL baselines. Implementation Details. We adopt GPT-2 Small [23] as the back- bone for both offline evaluation and online deployment due to its computational efficiency and low inference latency. For CoCo-VAE, we use three codebook layers with sizes of (16384, 128, 128). The loss weights 𝜆fid, 𝜆collision, 𝜆FAR, 𝜆Q2I, 𝜆I2I, and 𝜆Rec are set to 0.9, 1.0, 0.4, 0.2, 0.05 and 1.0, respectively. For RL, we assign rewards of 𝑟𝑜= 2 and 𝑟𝑐= 1 to orders and clicks, respectively, and set the MSFT weight to 𝜆= 0.5. We use a GRPO group size of 𝐺= 8 and 𝜂= 300 optimization steps per DHPO stage, with 𝜂adjustable to control stage duration. We update the model daily, performing SFT followed by RL. 4.2 Offline Performance Table 1 summarizes the performance of SID construction and pref- erence optimization methods on the Click and Order datasets. As shown in Table 1, existing methods often struggle to improve preference ranking while maintaining retrieval capability. DPO-based methods underperform the SFT baseline, mainly because shared SID prefixes between chosen and rejected items lead to conflicting gradients and weaken learning signals. Moreover, DPO may suffer from reward hacking, increasing preference margins by lowering rejected-item probabilities rather than increasing those of chosen items. Beyond the improvements in business metrics, WeGR substantially reduces online serving costs. The key reason is that WeGR replaces, rather than simply supplements, a large fraction of candidates produced by conventional retrieval channels. In V1.2, cutting off 80% of the candidates from the other retrievers reduces the number of items entering pre-ranking to 61.90% of the baseline, i.e., 38.10% fewer items need to be scored. Since pre-ranking performs item-wise feature processing and model inference over the merged candidate set, this reduction directly decreases its CPU and GPU workloads. As shown in Figure 3, the normalized CPU and GPU usages decrease from 100% to 74.5% and 73.9%, corresponding to resource savings of 25.5% and 26.1%, respectively. The resource reduction is smaller than the reduction in scored items because the online pipeline still incurs fixed overhead from retrieval, request processing, and other serving components. These results demonstrate that WeGR improves online effectiveness while alleviating computation cost of the downstream cascade. Online latency reduction. title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search Systems in WeChat

text: In this work, we presented WeGR, a unified generative retrieval framework for industrial search systems in WeChat. By combining collaborative-aware SID construction with progressive preference optimization, WeGR effectively improves retrieval and ranking performance while addressing codebook collapse and reward spar- sity. Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate its effectiveness in improving business outcomes and reducing serving costs, highlighting the potential of generative retrieval to simplify industrial search systems. Furthermore, evalu- ations in an independent live-stream search scenario demonstrate the applicability of DHPO across different industrial search settings.

text: Tracing Money Flows in the Multi-Token Cryptocurrency Network Natkamon Tovanich1[0000−0001−9680−9282] and C´elestin Coquid´e2[0000−0001−8546−6587] 1 TU Wien, Vienna, Austria natkamon.tovanich@tuwien.ac.at 2 UTINAM Institute, UMR 6213 CNRS, Universit´e Marie et Louis Pasteur, Besan¸con, France coquide31@gmail.com Abstract. Tracing money flows in cryptocurrency transaction networks is challenging because funds can move across accounts, transactions, and token layers. We propose a transaction-aware graph in which nodes represent account–asset states within transactions, while edges encode observed transfers, inferred asset transformations, and temporal inter- transaction sequences. Applied to Aave borrow–repay flows, we com- pare graph construction and edge-pruning strategies and extract shortest paths using a heuristic weighting. Our results reveal a trade-off between reachability and interpretability and uncover frequent token sequences underlying how borrowed assets are transformed before repayment. This work lays a foundation for general, interpretable multi-token flow tracing. Keywords: cryptocurrency flow tracing, transaction networks, decen- tralized finance, blockchain analytics 1
title: Tracing Money Flows in the Multi-Token

text: Tracing money flows in cryptocurrency transaction networks is increasingly chal- lenging, as smart contract blockchains such as Ethereum enable developers to create new tokens and decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, creating on-chain ecosystems for trading, lending, and liquidity provision. As these activities grow more complex, strategies involving flash loans, maximal extractable value (MEV), and arbitrage combine multiple protocols and assets, making it difficult to de- termine how value moves across accounts, transactions, and token layers. Understanding these flows is important for analyzing how DeFi protocols are used and how participants execute on-chain financial strategies. However, conventional transaction graphs represent accounts as nodes and transfers as edges, making them less suitable for tracking value across multiple tokens and related transaction sequences. To address this gap, we introduce a transaction- aware network representation and compare path finding strategies for tracing multi-token money flows. Our contributions are threefold: 1. We model each node as an account–asset state within a transaction and connect these states using observed transfers, inferred asset transformations (e.g., swaps), and temporal inter-transaction relationships. arXiv:2610.16981v1 [cs.SI] 12 Oct 2026

text: 2 Natkamon Tovanich and C´elestin Coquid´e 2. We compare graph construction and edge pruning strategies and introduce a heuristic weighting scheme that distinguishes directly observed, inferred, and lower-confidence connections. 3. Using Aave borrow–repay flows as a case study, we characterize how these modeling choices affect path reachability, length, composition, and similarity, and analyze frequent token transformation patterns. Our results reveal trade-offs among multi-token flow-tracing strategies and illustrate how borrowed assets move across transactions and token layers. These findings lay the groundwork toward a general, interpretable framework for trac- ing cryptocurrency flows and analyzing on-chain financial activity. 2

text: Although cryptocurrency flow tracing is central to blockchain forensics, multi- token representations and tracing strategies remain underexplored. Early work has focused on Bitcoin, applying taint-allocation rules such as Poison, Haircut, FIFO, and LIFO [12], or representing taint flows as dynamic graphs [13]. For account-based blockchains, TRacer formulates tracing as a graph search over directed, weighted, temporal, and multi-relational networks [19]. Cryptocurrency flow is widely used to detect fraudulent and illicit activ- ity. On Bitcoin, MFScope traces funds linked to Dark Web addresses [8], while graph learning methods classify illicit Bitcoin transactions [16]. On Ethereum, DenseFlow identifies Ethereum laundering groups and pathways [9], and Wu et al. trace heist assets through token swaps and service providers [18]. Recent works incorporate transaction semantics for EVM and cross-chain tracing [4, 6, 17]. These methods rely on black-box machine learning models to flag suspi- cious activity from known illicit accounts, whereas our interpretable approach reconstructs multi-token paths, with forensic use as a possible extension. Ethereum token transfers have also been studied as account-level networks [2, 10, 15]. Within DeFi, prior network work has examined protocol compositions [7] and used token transfer motifs to identify transaction methods [14]. Studies of decentralized lending investigate motivations behind using Aave [3], liquidation risks [11], and time to repayments [5]. We complement this literature by con- necting transaction-specific account–asset

We complement this literature by con- necting transaction-specific account–asset states to trace how borrowed assets are used and transformed between Aave borrowing and repayment events. 3 Material and Methods 3.1 Data Acquisition and Preprocessing For each ego account and tracing instance, we retrieve the relevant history of native-currency, ERC-20 (fungible), ERC-721 (non-fungible, NFTs), and ERC- 1155 (multi-token) transfers from the Alchemy Transfer API [1]. Each transfer event records the block number, transaction hash, sender, recipient, token con- tract, asset symbol, transfer category, and the amount transferred.

text: Tracing Money Flows in the Multi-Token Cryptocurrency Network 3 Before constructing the network, we remove self-loops because they do not represent movement between distinct accounts. Native ETH transfers are rela- beled as WETH to represent native and wrapped Ether in a common asset layer, while technical wrapping and unwrapping transfers involving the WETH con- tract are removed. Missing ERC-721 and ERC-1155 quantities are set to one. For mint and burn events, the zero-address endpoint is replaced with the cor- responding token contract address, attributing token creation or destruction to the issuing contract rather than to a shared zero-address node. Finally, transfers with the same block number, transaction hash, sender, recipient, asset, and token-contract address are aggregated by summing their amounts. This produces a single weighted transfer for repeated movements of the same asset between the same accounts within a transaction. 3.2 Transaction-Aware Multi-Token Network We represent the multi-token flow network as a directed graph G = (V, E), where each node v = (h, a, τ) denotes a transaction hash h, account address a, and asset τ. Unlike an account-level graph, this separates the same account across transactions and assets, preserving temporal and asset-specific information. The network combines within-transaction and inter-transaction edges. Within-Transaction Edges connect token transfers and asset exchanges that occur within the same transaction. The weighting scheme is defined as follows. Within-transaction weighting. Within a transaction, we favor paths that follow asset transfers or exchanges, while using teleportation only as a fallback when no direct path exists. – Transfer edges are assigned a low cost of 0.1, as directly observed token movements. – Swap edges receive an even lower cost of 0.01 to encourage inferred conver- sions between received and spent assets. – Teleportation edges are assigned a substantially higher cost of 100 as they represent connections without an explicit transfer or an identifiable swap. Furthermore, an inter-transaction edge directly connecting the borrowing node to the ego-account state in a repayment transaction is assigned a cost

Furthermore, an inter-transaction edge directly connecting the borrowing node to the ego-account state in a repayment transaction is assigned a cost of 100 to prevent the path from bypassing the intermediate fund movements under investigation.

text: 6 Natkamon Tovanich and C´elestin Coquid´e Inter-transaction weighting. We prefer temporally closer expenditures within the LIFO-cutoff and discourage shortcuts that bypass intermediate transactions. An edge within the cutoff costs 1, whereas an edge beyond it costs 10. This penalty steers the path toward the earliest plausible subsequent expenditure rather than a distant one. Edges involving alter accounts incur an additional cost of 50 (51 within the cutoff, 60 beyond), prioritizing ego-account continuity, since alter accounts’ his- tories are only partially observed and could otherwise create artificial shortcuts (e.g., a deposit followed by a later withdrawal). These weights are heuristic traversal costs rather than probabilities or empiri- cally calibrated confidence scores. They were set manually to encode an ordinal preference with roughly order-of-magnitude gaps, so rank order matters more than exact values. The weighted path should be read as the one that best satis- fies our preference hierarchy, rather than as definitive evidence that the traced funds followed that exact route. 4 Results We analyze 1,505 borrower accounts on Aave v3 on the Ethereum mainnet, each with a cumulative borrowed amount of at least 1 million USD between the protocol’s launch on January 27, 2023, and April 9, 2026. The dataset com- prises 175,601 borrow events and 288,764 borrow–repay matches identified using recency-based matching, which we refer to as the LIFO-cutoff.
