text: 12 Natkamon Tovanich and C´elestin Coquid´e 5 Discussion and Future Work We introduced a transaction-aware representation for tracing multi-token flows and compared shortest path configurations on Aave borrow–repay flows. The results reveal a trade-off between reachability and interpretability: teleporta- tion edges recover more paths but may introduce implausible shortcuts, whereas restricting inter-transaction edges reduces coverage. Reachability should thus not imply reconstruction accuracy. Heuristic weighting balances these effects by retaining uncertain edges as fallbacks while favoring transfers, swaps, and tem- porally proximate links. Frequent token patterns reveal round-trip swaps and supply–withdraw cycles, but also artifacts from debt-token shortcuts and miss- ing asset transformations. Our approach has some limitations. A shortest path cannot capture flows that split, merge, or form cycles, and it may bypass intermediate transactions by linking borrowing directly to repayment. Since no ground truth exists (only the borrow and repay events are observed, while the route between them is inferred), we assess structural properties and pattern interpretability, treating the paths as hypotheses rather than verified trajectories. Future work could apply k-shortest paths, flow decomposition, and cycle detection to recover more complete strategies, and use sensitivity analysis over the weights and alternative allocation rules (e.g., FIFO, Haircut) to quantify the uncertainty from inferred edges and heuristic weights. As a partial sanity check, individual conversion steps could be validated against event
title: Natkamon Tovanich and C´elestin Coquid´e

text: more complete strategies, and use sensitivity analysis over the weights and alternative allocation rules (e.g., FIFO, Haircut) to quantify the uncertainty from inferred edges and heuristic weights. As a partial sanity check, individual conversion steps could be validated against event logs (e.g., supply, withdrawal, and swap events). Beyond event logs, synthetic DeFi transaction data with known ground truth could be generated to evaluate the accuracy of the entire set of inferred paths. To better characterize borrowers’ trading strategies, we plan to enrich the network model by representing each transaction as a hypergraph and incorpo- rating account and protocol labels, transaction semantics, and inter-transaction timing. More broadly, we aim to extend the approach beyond Aave by adding cycle-aware tracing and path uncertainty analysis to study evolving DeFi use cases such as on-chain trading, liquidity management, and arbitrage. text: From Conceptual EneMonIE to an Executable Backend: A Modular Architecture for Energy Information Extraction and Grounded Question Answering Janik Lesage, Khadim Lô, and Jean-Sébastien Dessureault Département de mathématiques et d’informatique, Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières, Canada
title: From Conceptual EneMonIE to an Executable Backend:

text: The original EneMonIE proposal describes a Web-based semantic system for continuously monitoring energy trends through targeted information extraction from het- erogeneous online media. This article presents EneMonIE- Backend, an implementation-derived redesign that con- verts that conceptual pipeline into a modular, executable, and application-independent backend. The architecture separates five concerns: data sources, acquisition and nor- malization, semantic processing, knowledge organization, and persistent storage. It operationalizes configurable connectors for RSS feeds, URL collections, arXiv, social- media JSON files, and open-data CSV files; it also intro- duces question-driven Web search and scraping. Relevant documents pass through energy categorization, named- entity recognition, temporal and event extraction, source- sensitive sentiment analysis, and extractive summariza- tion. The resulting semantic representations support entity co-occurrence graphs, cross-document interlinking, cluster-level information fusion, and relational persistence in SQLite. Three grounded question-answering paths are exposed at the backend level: live Web evidence, the stored corpus, and selected configured resources. Answer generation uses a language model when configured and otherwise falls back to deterministic extractive output. Unlike the original proposal, the presented architecture deliberately excludes the user-interface and server-side application layers, allowing the semantic core to be em- bedded in different applications. A deterministic smoke validation confirms relevance filtering, persistence, clus- tering, evidence retrieval, and document deletion. The work provides a reproducible architectural basis for future evaluation on larger multilingual energy corpora.

text: Energy systems generate a continuous stream of heteroge- neous information: news articles, research papers, public datasets, policy announcements, organizational reports, and social-media posts. The value of these materials lies not only in their individual content but also in their relationships. A power-grid investment reported by a util- ity, discussed by the public, and evaluated in a research preprint may represent a single underlying development. Manually monitoring such evidence is costly, slow, and difficult to reproduce. The conceptual EneMonIE architecture was originally proposed by Dilek Küçük [Küçük, 2022]. The present work implements, restructures, and extends that proposal as an application-independent backend. The original conceptual design combines text categorization, named-entity recog- nition (NER), temporal-expression and event extraction, sentiment analysis, social-network construction, media interlinking, information fusion, summarization, a central database, and Web-based retrieval and visualization. It also emphasizes modularity, bilingual processing, and the reuse of domain ontologies and lexical resources. The original proposal is deliberately broad. It speci- fies the semantic functions that the system should pro- vide, but it does not prescribe an executable control flow, concrete storage schema, connector contract, question- answering strategy, or graceful degradation mechanism. These implementation decisions become essential when the architecture is turned into software. They determine how duplicate documents are handled, how relevance is en- forced before expensive analysis, how semantic objects are represented, and how

They determine how duplicate documents are handled, how relevance is en- forced before expensive analysis, how semantic objects are represented, and how evidence is exposed to downstream consumers. This article presents EneMonIE-Backend, a backend architecture derived from a working Python implemen- tation of the EneMonIEKüçük [2022] concept. The central design decision is to isolate the semantic and data-management core from any particular application. FastAPI endpoints, a desktop client, an HTML dashboard, and Web visualization are therefore outside the boundary of the architecture described here. The backend can in- stead be invoked by a command-line process, a scheduler, a test harness, or a future service layer. The main contributions are as follows: 1) an exe- cutable five-layer decomposition of the original EneMonIE concept. 2) normalized ingestion through configurable source adapters and stable document identifiers. 3) an ex- plicit semantic-processing sequence with an early energy- relevance gate. 4) operational definitions for entity graphs, media similarity, clustering, and fusion. 5) a normalized SQLite schema connecting documents, semantic anno- tations, entity edges, and clusters. 6) three evidence- 1 arXiv:2610.17243v1 [cs.CL] 12 Oct 2026

Never-Ending Language Learning (NELL) emphasized persistent learning from Web content [Carlson et al., 2010]; DeepDive demon- strated large-scale knowledge-base construction using sta- tistical learning and inference [Niu et al., 2012]; and Knowledge Vault combined Web extraction with proba- bilistic knowledge fusion [Dong et al., 2014]. EneMonIE narrows this general objective to the energy domain, where entities, events, dates, technologies, organizations, and public opinions must be related across sources. Several components of the original design are well- established NLP tasks. NER over informal text is challeng- ing because social media frequently departs from conven- tional spelling and syntax [Ritter et al., 2011]. Temporal normalization links textual expressions to comparable dates [Strötgen and Gertz, 2010], while event extraction structures occurrences that may have policy, operational, environmental, or technological consequences [Ritter et al., 2012]. Sentiment analysis provides a coarse represen- tation of expressed opinion [Pang and Lee, 2008], and multi-document or social-media summarization reduces repeated evidence to concise statements [Chakrabarti and Punera, 2011]. Energy ontologies further provide domain vocabulary and conceptual

text: et al., 2012]. Sentiment analysis provides a coarse represen- tation of expressed opinion [Pang and Lee, 2008], and multi-document or social-media summarization reduces repeated evidence to concise statements [Chakrabarti and Punera, 2011]. Energy ontologies further provide domain vocabulary and conceptual structure [Küçük, 2015]. An executable architecture must coordinate these tasks and define their data contracts. In particular, down- stream clustering should not operate on raw text alone when normalized entities, event types, and dates are avail- able. Similarly, question answering should not bypass the semantic pipeline when live Web pages are collected. EneMonIE-Backend addresses these concerns by using one normalized document model and one processing function for both scheduled ingestion and question-driven evidence collection. 2.2 Design requirements The redesign follows six requirements: 1) Modularity. Source-specific acquisition and semantic analyzers must be replaceable behind stable interfaces. 2) Early filtering. Non-energy documents must be rejected before semantic extraction and persistence. 3) Traceability. Every de- rived object must remain connected to its source document and, where available, its original URL. 4) Determinism by default. Core extraction, storage, ranking, and fall- back answering must operate without a remote language model. 5) Evidence grounding. Generated answers must be based on a bounded evidence set rather than unconstrained model knowledge, following the grounding motivation of retrieval-augmented generation [Lewis et al., 2020]. 6) Application independence. Transport and presentation layers must not own the semantic pipeline or the database model. 3 Proposed Architecture Figure 1 presents the complete backend architecture. The main pipeline consists of five layers, while a separate lower section illustrates question-driven execution paths that reuse the same processing and persistence services. More specifically, the upper pipeline is responsible for acquiring, normalizing, analyzing, organizing, and stor- ing energy-related documents, whereas the lower sec- tion presents three backend question-answering workflows. User-interface, web-server, and visualization components are intentionally excluded from the architectural design. 3.1 Layer 1: heterogeneous data sources The first layer represents both configured and on-demand inputs. Configured sources include RSS news or video feeds, lists of Web pages, arXiv queries, social-media records stored as JSON Lines, and open energy data represented as CSV. These inputs cover the principal media types identified in the original EneMonIE proposal while making each acquisition mechanism explicit. Question-driven Web retrieval is modeled separately because its lifecycle differs from scheduled polling. In- stead of collecting all items from a predeclared source, it transforms a question into an energy-oriented query, obtains candidate results,

text: while making each acquisition mechanism explicit. Question-driven Web retrieval is modeled separately because its lifecycle differs from scheduled polling. In- stead of collecting all items from a predeclared source, it transforms a question into an energy-oriented query, obtains candidate results, downloads a bounded number of pages, and submits those pages to the standard seman- tic pipeline. This design prevents the question-answering path from becoming an unfiltered shortcut around En- eMonIE processing. 3.2 Layer 2: acquisition and normaliza- tion All configured connectors implement a common fetch operation and return a normalized Document. A document contains a stable identifier, source type, source name, title, text, URL, language, publication time, and arbitrary metadata. Source adapters hide format-specific details such as RSS XML, arXiv Atom records, HTML cleaning, JSONL decoding, and CSV row serialization. Normalization is followed by identifier-based dedupli- cation. Within a collection run, documents are indexed by doc_id; repeated identifiers overwrite earlier occur- rences before semantic processing. At storage time, the same identifier becomes the relational primary key and en- ables idempotent upserts. This two-stage strategy reduces duplicate processing while supporting updated represen- tations of a previously observed source. The orchestrator exposes three operational modes. A 2

En- tities are assigned labels such as energy organization, location, technology, company, feeder, power plant, or miscellaneous proper name. Canonical lowercase forms support comparison across documents. 2) Temporal ex- traction detects supported date formats and weekdays, then normalizes parseable values to ISO timestamps. 3) Event extraction uses domain trigger lexicons for out- ages, plant commissioning, policy changes, investments, accidents, and research breakthroughs. Confidence is in- creased when a sentence includes reporting cues, a normal- ized time, or sufficient context. 4) Sentiment analysis is applied only to social-media documents. English and French lexicons produce a positive, negative, or neutral label from the difference between positive and negative token counts. 3

This separation enables vocabulary updates without changing orchestra- tion code. 3.4 Layer 4: knowledge organization The knowledge-organization layer operates across pro- cessed documents. First, the social-graph builder creates one undirected edge for each pair of unique canonical entities that co-occurs in a document. Edge weight is the number of documents containing the pair. The result is a compact association graph that can be analyzed or visualized by downstream software. Second, the media interlinker estimates whether two documents discuss the same development. Each returns a structured object containing the question, answer, evi- dence, model identifier, and scope. 4.1 Question-driven Web QA The Web path augments a question with energy terms when necessary, then attempts multiple search providers. Candidate URLs are scraped into normalized documents. Each page must pass the same energy categorization and semantic extraction used during scheduled ingestion. Ac- cepted pages become bounded evidence items containing a title, source, URL, category, score, summary, entities, events, and excerpt. Evidence may optionally be per- sisted, thereby allowing a question-driven discovery to enrich the monitored corpus. 4.2 Database QA The database path retrieves either the full stored corpus or an explicit list of document identifiers. text: 4.3 Selected-resource QA The selected-resource path accepts indexes of configured sources, fetches only those sources, processes and stores relevant documents, and delegates answering to database QA constrained to the newly stored identifiers. It there- fore combines controlled acquisition with the consistent retrieval semantics of the central corpus. 4.4 Answer synthesis and graceful degra- dation When a language-model API key is configured, evidence blocks are sent to the selected model with an instruction to answer only from the supplied evidence and to cite bracketed source numbers. When no model is available, or when synthesis fails, the backend returns an extractive evi- dence summary. The fallback is important architecturally: collection, semantic analysis, persistence, retrieval, and inspectable evidence remain available without external model access. The language model is intentionally placed after re- trieval rather than inside the semantic extractors. This limits its authority to presentation and synthesis, pre- serves deterministic structured annotations, and supports independent evaluation of retrieval quality and answer faithfulness. 5 Relationship to the Original EneMonIE Design The original EneMonIE proposal [Küçük, 2022] defines the conceptual foundation, while the present architecture in- troduces the concrete implementation choices summarized in Table 2. The EneMonIEPipeline class composes these packages and owns the central database. Lightweight data classes define documents, enti- ties, temporal expressions, events, sentiment results, pro- cessed documents, and clusters. Configuration is loaded from YAML, making sources and thresholds deployment- specific. 6.2 Preliminary Evaluation: Methodol- ogy and Results An offline evaluation assessed relevance filtering, informa- tion extraction, evidence retrieval, and local processing latency. First, it establishes a single semantic path for scheduled monitor- ing and question-driven discovery. As a result, evidence collected for a question is filtered and represented consis- tently with the rest of the corpus. Second, it separates deterministic semantic state from optional generative syn- thesis. Database rows, event confidence, entity canonical- ization, and cluster membership can be inspected inde- pendently of a model-generated answer. Third, it gives downstream applications a stable relational and object- level contract instead of coupling them to source formats. The architecture is also suitable for incremental mod- ernization. Rule-based NER can be replaced by a trans- former model; lexical ranking can be replaced by hybrid sparse-dense retrieval; SQLite can be migrated to a server database; and connected-component clustering can be replaced by a time-aware or learned method. Because each responsibility is localized, these changes need not alter all consumers simultaneously. 6

text: 7.2 Limitations The current system remains a research prototype and therefore presents several limitations. First, it relies heav- ily on lexical methods. Weighted keywords, gazetteers, and trigger lists are interpretable, but they provide limited recall for paraphrases, spelling variations, and emerging terminology. Additionally, the temporal component sup- ports only a bounded set of explicit date patterns and does not resolve complex relative expressions or event-specific temporal scopes. Another limitation concerns sentiment analysis. Lexicon-based counts do not adequately capture nega- tion, sarcasm, opinion targets, or aspect-specific senti- ment. The system also relies on transitive clustering, which may cause connected components to group chains of documents even when the first and last documents are only weakly related. Moreover, confidence assigned to singleton clusters should not be interpreted as evidence of corroboration. 7.3 Evaluation agenda Future work should evaluate each stage separately and end to end. Relevance filtering can be measured with precision, recall, and F1 on a stratified energy/non-energy corpus. Entity, temporal, and event extraction require span- and type-level annotations. Interlinking should be evaluated using document-pair and cluster metrics, with attention to time-separated events sharing the same entities. Retrieval can be measured with recall@k, mean reciprocal rank, or normalized discounted cumulative gain. Grounded answer quality should include factual consistency, citation correctness, evidence sufficiency, and abstention when the corpus is incomplete. Scalability experiments

Scalability experiments should report ingestion through- put, per-document processing time, database growth, pair- wise clustering cost, and the effect of source failures. Finally, multilingual expansion should move beyond isolated English and French lexicons. Language identi- fication, multilingual entity normalization, cross-lingual clustering, and evaluation on comparable reports are nec- essary to fulfill the original multilingual ambition of En- eMonIE. 8
title: Limitations

text: This article introduced EneMonIE-Backend, an exe- cutable backend reinterpretation of the EneMonIE energy- monitoring architecture. The design retains the original semantic objectives while making acquisition, normaliza- tion, relevance filtering, extraction, interlinking, fusion, persistence, and question answering operational. Its five- layer decomposition is complemented by three evidence- grounded QA paths that reuse the same semantic pipeline. The deliberate exclusion of user-interface and server-side application components creates a reusable core that can support multiple future applications. The implementation demonstrates architectural feasibil- ity and passes a deterministic integration smoke test. It does not yet establish large-scale extraction or question- answering performance. The next scientific step is there- fore a component-wise and end-to-end evaluation on la- beled, multilingual energy corpora, followed by targeted replacement of rule-based modules where measured limi- tations justify greater model complexity. Reproducibility Statement The accompanying Overleaf project contains this manuscript, the architecture figure, and the BibTeX database. The described validation is deterministic and does not require an external language model. Live Web acquisition remains dependent on third-party source avail- ability and should be evaluated with recorded URLs and retrieval timestamps.

text: Generative recommendation models have shown promising re- sults by representing items as semantic IDs and generating these IDs autoregressively. We introduce an approach showing that ex- plicitly incorporating hierarchical and attribute-level supervision into generative recommendation can simultaneously improve train- ing efficiency and long-tail recommendation performance. Exist- ing approaches typically optimize semantic ID prediction with a standard causal cross-entropy objective, which does not explic- itly exploit the hierarchical structure of semantic IDs and can re- quire substantial training to learn effective item representations. Moreover, data-sparse tail items often suffer from poor represen- tations due to limited supervision, resulting in weaker long-tail recommendation performance. We address these challenges with HASTE (Hierarchical and Attribute-aware Supervision for gen- eraTive rEcommendation), a unified training framework that in- troduces hierarchical and attribute-specific supervision. HASTE’s Hierarchical Loss explicitly exploits the multi-level structure of semantic IDs, providing supervision at each level of the item hi- erarchy and substantially accelerating training convergence. Its Attribute-Specific Losses encourage the model to preserve fine- grained item attributes, leveraging the language model’s inherent semantic knowledge to improve representations and recommenda- tions for tail items. We extensively evaluate HASTE on a fashion recommendation benchmark and across multiple domains of the Amazon dataset. HASTE improves recommendation performance across datasets and item-frequency regimes. Notably, the Hierar- chical Loss achieves approximately 2× faster convergence than the standard

text: Large language models (LLMs) have triggered a paradigm shift across modalities, replacing task-specific pipelines with a single model that is pre-trained once and then adapted through instruc- tions or lightweight fine-tuning [3, 33]. Recommender systems are undergoing an analogous shift. Industrial recommenders are con- ventionally built as cascades, commonly described as matching, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking [23, 27], whose stages are developed and trained as separate models with their own objec- tives: YouTube’s two-stage system, for instance, trains candidate generation as an extreme multiclass classification problem and ranking under a watch-time-weighted logistic objective [5], while pre-ranking [37] and re-ranking [25] each introduce objectives of their own. Generative recommendation instead casts the entire retrieval problem as a single sequence-to-sequence task: given a user’s interaction history, the model generates the identifier of the next item directly. [10] TIGER [26] established the form this now takes, replacing arbitrary item IDs with residual-quantized seman- tic IDs. Subsequent work has shown that ranking and retrieval can be unified in a single generative backbone [7, 40], whose quality scales as a power law of training compute [40]. A parallel line of work marries generative recommendation with LLM backbones in order to exploit the world knowledge and seman- tic priors that recommendation data alone cannot supply [11, 41]. Semantically similar items share prefixes, so the identifier space itself carries item semantics, and the model can generalise to items with little or no interac- tion history [26]. Semantic IDs are typically produced by residual quantization—either RQ-VAE [17, 26] or the training-free residual 𝑘-means of Quantitative Alignment Multi-Modal Recommenda- tion [21]—and are therefore hierarchical by construction. Crucially, this makes the levels asymmetric: because every later code quan- tizes the residual left by the earlier ones, an error at a coarse level redefines the target of every level below it, whereas an error at the finest level perturbs only a local refinement. Despite this structure, essentially all existing generative recom- menders supervise semantic-ID generation with a flat causal cross- entropy (CE) loss over the extended vocabulary. The consequence is not merely that the model must rediscover the coarse-to-fine or- ganisation residual quantization already encoded—it is that flat CE loss actively erodes it. We show in Section 4 that fine-tuning under flat CE cuts the cosine coupling between adjacent SID levels by 35% relative to initialization (from 0.55 to 0.36), while a level-aware objective retains it

A second, orthogonal limitation is that the supervision an item receives is proportional to how often it appears as a training target. Head items accumulate enough gradient to acquire useful represen- tations; data-sparse tail items do not. This matters because semantic IDs are quantized from holistic item embeddings, so they organ- ise the catalogue by overall similarity rather than by any single attribute: a property a user actually asks for (color, material, fit, pattern) is smeared across levels rather than localised. Yet the LLM backbone already knows what a “ribbed burgundy wool cardi- gan” is: the interaction log is the bottleneck, not the backbone’s semantic knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose HASTE (Hierarchical and Attribute-aware Supervision for generaTive rEcommendation), a fine-tuning framework that introduce two complementary objec- tives. The Hierarchical Loss replaces flat causal CE with level- aware supervision: coarser levels carry larger base weights, and each level’s weight is gated by the model’s detached confidence in the upstream codes it is conditioned on, so fine-grained su- pervision is amplified only once the coarse decisions it depends on are actually resolved. Because confidence estimates are unre- liable early in training, the objective anneals from purely static hierarchical weighting to fully confidence-gated weighting. Sched- uled sampling [1] further perturbs the upstream prefix, exposing the model to the upstream errors it is likely to encounter dur- ing decoding rather than only to clean, teacher-forced trajectories. The Attribute-Specific Losses attach lightweight MLP regression heads to the hidden state already used to predict the fine-grained SID code, and supervise them against catalogue-derived attribute targets. Sequential rec- ommenders predict the next item from an ordered interaction his- tory. GRU4Rec [12] models sessions with recurrence, while SAS- Rec [15] and BERT4Rec [29] use unidirectional and bidirectional self-attention respectively. All three represent an item as an atomic embedding in a table that grows with the catalogue, so a rare item’s representation is learned almost entirely from its few occur- rences, and retrieval needs a nearest-neighbour index maintained separately from the model. Generative retrieval removes the in- dex: the model decodes the target’s identifier token by token [31]. GENRE [6] first cast retrieval this way, generating entity names autoregressively; DSI [32] replaced names with structured semantic identifiers obtained by hierarchical clustering; and NCI [35] added a prefix-aware decoder. Recommenders built on language-model backbones tune on recommendation data instead: P5 [10] unifies several tasks as text-to-text but with arbi- trary numeric item IDs, LC-Rec [41] aligns semantic-ID tokens with language through auxiliary alignment tasks, and IDGenRec [30] generates textual identifiers instead of quantized codes. This work follows the semantic-ID line and investigates the training objec- tive itself, given a fixed architecture. Whereas LC-Rec introduces additional alignment tasks, HASTE reshapes the loss on the recom- mendation task and derives attribute targets from the catalogue, requiring no additional task data or prompt engineering. Se- mantic IDs (SIDs) generated by residual quantization encode items through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy, where earlier codes capture broad semantics and later codes progressively refine the represen- tation. However, standard causal cross-entropy treats SID tokens as independent vocabulary predictions and does not explicitly model dependencies across hierarchy levels. text: We propose HASTE, a unified fine-tuning framework that improves semantic-ID-based generative recommendation through two com- plementary forms of supervision. Given a user interaction context, the model autoregressively generates an item’s semantic ID as a sequence of discrete codes obtained through residual quantiza- tion. While standard causal cross-entropy provides supervision for predicting these codes, it treats the semantic-ID sequence uni- formly and does not explicitly account for its hierarchical structure. Moreover, item-level attributes provide complementary semantic information that can be particularly valuable for learning represen- tations of data-sparse tail items. Figure 1 provides an overview of the proposed training framework. HASTE introduces two auxiliary objectives to address these lim- itations. The first is a Hierarchical Loss, which explicitly exploits the multi-level structure of semantic IDs and provides level-aware supervision during semantic-ID generation. By aligning the train- ing objective with the hierarchical organization of the semantic-ID space, the model can learn coarse-to-fine item semantics more

text: We presented HASTE, a unified framework for generative recom- mendation with hierarchical and attribute-aware supervision. By exploiting the multi-level structure of semantic IDs and incorporat- ing confidence-aware gating, level weighting, and scheduled sam- pling, HASTE improves hierarchical prediction. Experiments across multiple Amazon domains and a large-scale fashion dataset show consistent improve- ments over strong baselines, with ablations confirming the comple- mentary benefits of the proposed components.

We additionally use scheduled sampling to reduce the exposure gap between teacher-forced training and autoregressive inference. A first forward pass, performed without gradient computation, samples the predicted code at the coarsest SID level from the model’s categorical distribution. With probability ss_prob, this prediction replaces the corresponding ground-truth code in the input sequence. A second forward pass then computes the hierarchical loss on the resulting sequence. The scheduled- sampling probability is linearly increased from 0 to 0.3 over 200,000 optimizer steps. Multinomial sampling is used rather than greedy decoding to expose the model to the stochasticity of autoregressive generation. Category-specific configurations. First, only the newly introduced SID embeddings are optimized for 50,000 steps using flat cross-entropy with a learning rate of 1 × 10−3. The resulting checkpoint initializes the second stage, in which all model parameters are jointly fine-tuned using the hierarchical loss and the configuration in Table 10. During evaluation, autoregressive generation is constrained to catalog-valid SID sequences using a prefix-tree logits processor constructed from up to 100K training sequences. If a generated prefix is not present in the tree, decoding falls back to a per-position vocabulary mask over the 256 valid SID codes at the corresponding level. 9.2.2 Attribute-Specific Losses. Shared architecture and attachment. We use the same auxiliary- head architecture for both color and material composition predic- tion. The head is attached to the last-layer hidden state at the L2 semantic-ID prediction position, ℎ𝐿2, after the model has consumed the preceding L0 and L1 codes. Each head is a two-layer MLP, MLP(ℎ) = Linear(4096, 64) →GELU →Linear(64,𝑑out), where𝑑out = 3 for color and𝑑out = 15 for material composition. The heads are trained

The auxiliary heads are saved separately from the Hugging Face model checkpoint. 9.2.3 Hyperparameter Settings for the Hierarchical-Loss Component Ablation. Table 12 reports the hyperparameter settings used for the hierarchical-loss component ablation. Each variant is derived from the full configuration by disabling the other mechanisms, allow- ing the contribution of static weighting (SW), confidence gating (CG), and scheduled sampling (SS) to be isolated. The CE base- line disables all three mechanisms and applies uniform weighting to all SID tokens. HL w/ SW uses static level weights while dis- abling confidence gating and scheduled sampling. HL w/ CG uses confidence-based gating with uniform base weights, while disabling scheduled sampling. HL w/ SS uses scheduled sampling with uni- form base weights and no confidence gating. HL w/ SW, CG, SS corresponds to the full hierarchical-loss configuration. All variants use the same optimizer and training configuration: learning rate 2×10−5, effective batch size 16, 20 training epochs, and a cosine learning-rate schedule. Scheduled sampling, when enabled, uses an annealing period of 200,000 steps. The static level weights are (3.0, 2.0, 1.0) from the coarsest to the finest level. title: Computed, not Memorized: Bit-Factorized Identifiers for Efficient

text: Generative retrieval is known for its efficient end-to-end indexing and retrieval. In partic- ular, numeric Document Identifiers (DocIDs) are generally more efficient because they are shorter and generally fixed-length sequences over a small vocabulary, requiring fewer de- coding steps during beam search. However, they tend to generalize poorly to unseen doc- uments and must be learned during indexing- stage training. In this paper, we propose a nu- meric DocID design for generative retrieval that enables better adaptation to unseen docu- ments without retraining. Our DocID design inherits the language model’s knowledge: each DocID is a sequence of tokens factorized into bits, and each token is scored as the sum of its bits. Unlike existing numeric DocIDs, whose tokens carry meaning only through embeddings memorized during indexing training, each bit here derives its meaning from the model’s rep- resentation. Therefore, the DocIDs of unseen documents remain scorable without retrain- ing. Experiments on three benchmarks show that our DocID design substantially improves unseen-document retrieval while maintaining comparable performance on seen documents. It achieves over 20 percentage points higher Hit@10 on unseen documents and up to 7× lower inference latency than existing numeric DocID designs on NQ320K and TriviaQA, while performing only 3 percentage points be- low weight-update methods on MS MARCO without additional training. These results show that an appropriate DocID design

text: Generative Retrieval is a retrieval paradigm in which an input query text is directly matched to a document identifier (DocID) using a lan- guage model, typically a sequence-to-sequence model. This design can offer in- ference and memory efficiency advantages (Kim et al., 2024). Two different DocID designs exist for genera- tive retrieval systems: numeric DocIDs and textual DocIDs. Both have their own strengths: Numeric DocIDs offer computational advantages, as they reduce the complexity of beam-search decoding (Wang et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). In contrast, textual DocIDs can exploit the semantic priors encoded in pretrained language models and are able to give more interpretable doc- ument identifiers (Bevilacqua et

text: beam-search decoding (Wang et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). In contrast, textual DocIDs can exploit the semantic priors encoded in pretrained language models and are able to give more interpretable doc- ument identifiers (Bevilacqua et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022; Askari et al., 2026). One of the major challenges in current genera- tive retrieval research is adapting to the retrieval of previously unseen documents. Generative re- trieval models typically require an indexing stage during training, where the model learns to associate documents with their corresponding DocIDs. text: result, the model tends to be biased toward DocIDs seen during training. This lack of generalization is especially pronounced for numeric DocIDs (Zhang et al., 2025), but also textual DocIDs lead to sub- stantially lower effectiveness on unseen than on seen documents (Zhang et al., 2025). While incremental training methods adapt nu- meric DocIDs to new documents (Mehta et al., 2023; Kishore et al., 2023), updating model pa- rameters remains computationally expensive. Re- cent model-editing approaches update only a small subset of parameters while achieving performance comparable to full retraining (Zhang et al., 2026b). However, editing the model for newly added docu- ments still requires computation with each update, making frequent updates costly. To address the poor adaptation of numeric Do- cIDs and the cost of updating model weights, we propose Computed Bit-Factorized Identifiers for Generative Retrieval (CoBIGR). CoBIGR repre- sents each document with a sign-projection binary code of its document vector and factorizes the re- trieval score over its identifier bits, which inherit the model’s knowledge of the document rather than a memorized embedding learned from indexing training. Additionally, the proposed bit-factorized IDs are flat and their score is permutation-invariant. This property enables multi-tree beam search dur- ing inference, which substantially improves effec- tiveness on unseen documents, while scoring with one forward pass keeps decoding efficient (see Fig- ure

Our contributions are: (1) We propose a bit- factorized numeric DocID: its bits derive mean- ing from the language model, so unseen DocIDs can still be retrievable. (2) We study direct DocID adaptation to dynamic corpora without weight up- dates, addressing an underexplored gap in costly generative retrieval training. (3) Our experiments show that our approach achieves comparable perfor- mance on seen documents to prior DocID designs while substantially improving performance on un- seen documents, with 40–60 percentage points higher Hit@1 and Hit@100 than other numeric DocIDs. It also remains within 3 percentage points of methods that update model weights. Our source code is available at https://anonymous.4open. science/r/bit_factorized_token-2C13/ 2

text: DocID in Generative Retrieval Generative re- trieval maps a query directly to a DocID. During training, the DocID serves as the output target for both document-to-DocID (indexing) and query-to- DocID (retrieval) training. For text-based iden- tifiers, titles (De Cao et al., 2020), URLs (Zhou et al., 2022), document substrings (Bevilacqua et al., 2022), and term sets (Zhang et al., 2024) are commonly used as identifiers. In contrast, numeric identifiers are often derived through using cluster- ing methods such as k-means (Wang et al., 2022) or through representation-based quantization meth- ods such as Product Quantization (PQ), Residual Quantization (RQ) and RQ-VAE (Zhou et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Rajput et al., 2023). These IDs are semantically structured. Although the numeric identifiers produce compact beam trees and enable more efficient decoding, they often suffer from lim- ited generalization. Hashing in Retrieval Hashing has been widely used for efficient retrieval by providing compact representations and approximate similarity mea- sures based on Hamming distance (Yamada et al., 2021; He et al., 2025). Recently, FLASH (Zhang et al., 2026a) uses hash codes as the first step of retrieval: the generated code seeds a Hamming- radius search and is reconstructed into a continu- ous embedding for reranking. Our method follows generative retrieval paradigm: it directly gener- ates valid DocIDs, decoded token by token un- der

Our method follows generative retrieval paradigm: it directly gener- ates valid DocIDs, decoded token by token un- der a prefix-tree constraint and ranked by log- probability. Dynamic Corpus Adaptation for Numeric Iden- tifiers Existing work primarily focuses on retrain- ing the retrieval model when new documents are arrived: DSI++ (Mehta et al., 2023) reduces catas- trophic forgetting by optimizing for flatter loss landscapes and incorporating pseudo-queries in continual training. IncDSI (Kishore et al., 2023) perform a constraint optimization to adapt to dy- namic corpus, this avoids the full re-training of the decoder. However, the method is restricted to atomic document identifiers. DOME (Zhang et al., 2026b) further generalizes document insertion by optimizing edit vectors with soft-label guidance, enabling effective adaptation under structured doc- ument identifier schemes. Each document d is associ- ated with a DocID cd = (c1, . . . , cT ), a length-T sequence of tokens from a predefined vocabulary. Given a query q, a generative retrieval model pθ returns a ranked list of DocIDs by directly generat- ing them. Typically, pθ is a sequence-to-sequence model that factorizes the DocID probability autore- gressively, pθ(cd | q) = L Y t=1 pθ(ct | c<t, q) , (1) The most relevant DocIDs are obtained by con- strained beam search over the prefix tree of valid identifiers, so that only DocIDs of documents in D can be produced. Training combines two ob- jectives: an indexing step that learns to bind each document d to its DocID cd, and a retrieval step that learns to map a query to the DocIDs of its relevant documents. Dynamic Corpus In practice, the document col- lection D changes over time. We therefore consider newly arrived documents after the model is trained. The model is trained on an initial seen document set D0, using queries whose relevant documents all be- long to D0. After training, a set of

text: m = 12 bits each, giving k = 120 total bits. Multi-trees beam search. Beam search scores DocIDs token by token on the partial sum P t′≤t log pt′(ct′ | q) and prunes prefixes as it goes. One potential problem is that pruning may discard a relevant DocID early, even if its remaining bits match the query well. Because our tokens are inde- pendently scored through bit factorization, any bit permutation, followed by regrouping into tokens, generates a valid prefix tree. We therefore build h trees using different bit permutations, run beam search on each tree, and rank the union of their candidates by log-probability. Since different bit orders prune based on different bits, using multi- ple trees can recover documents that a single tree would miss. We set h = 8 in our main experiments and analyze the effect of different values. 4 Experimental Settings 4.1 Datasets We follow prior work (Tay et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025, 2026b) to use Natural Questions (NQ320K) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), MS MARCO (Nguyen et al., 2016), and TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) in our experimetns. text: We follow prior work (Tay et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023) to report Hit@N, which is defined as the proportion of queries for which the relevant document appears in the top-N retrieved results. Because distinct documents can share one DocID, we solve such ties by expectation (McSh- erry and Najork, 2008): All documents sharing a retrieved identifier are returned, and each metric is its expected value over all orderings of the tied documents. 4.4 Baselines All baselines are generative retrievers, the paradigm we follow. Our core research question is whether an alternative numeric DocID design improves gen- eralization to newly added documents, so we focus on numeric DocID baselines. Following recent studies of generative retrieval over dynamic corpora (Zhang et al., 2025, 2026b), we cover four numeric DocID designs: hierarchi- cal k-means, used by DSI (Tay et al., 2022) and NCI (Wang et al., 2022); PQ, used by ULTRON- PQ (Zhou et al., 2022); RQ, used by MEVI (Zhang et al., 2023); RQ-VAE, used by TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023). Efficiency Our method provides efficient re- trieval: token scores for all positions come from one encoder forward pass, so decoding needs no autoregressive decoder calls. We measure single- query latency (batch size 1) on a single A100 GPU on the NQ320K dataset, and find that our method takes 24 ms per query and is at least 7× faster than NCI, DSI, and MEVI, 28× faster than ULTRON, and 397× faster than SEAL. We find that existing numeric DocID designs perform well on seen doc- uments but degrade substantially on unseen docu- ments, while our approach maintains comparable performance on seen documents and improves on unseen documents by a large margin over previous methods, and remains close to methods

This suggests that our DocID design for incorporating new documents without retraining is promising, especially given the high computational cost of retraining generative retriev- ers. Limitations Flat identifiers make early pruning harder. In our token design, no prefix is more informative than another, so early decoding prunes on limited infor- mation. Multi-tree beam search reduces this effect, but Hit@100 on seen documents remains slightly below some baselines. In future work, we plan to combine bit factorization with residual quantiza- tion such as RQ-VAE, whose coarse-to-fine codes may make early levels more informative and reduce pruning errors. Language. Like most of the prior work, we only focus on English datasets. This is common because most of benchmark datasets are in English. Our method is completely data-driven and not dependent on labeled data and it is therefore applicable to other languages than English.

title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo

text: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence. Keywords: collective intelligence; efficiency; interaction dynamics; multi-agent models; perceptual decision-making; recurrent neural networks; reservoir computing 1

text: Understanding how groups can exceed individuals on cognitive tasks is a central question of collective intelligence. One way that groups may be collectively intelligent is by exhibiting greater cognitive capacities than their individual members. For example, murmurations of starlings attain an extended sensory range compared to individual birds, allowing flocks to better respond to threats in their environment (Cavagna et al., 2010). However, the cost of interaction between agents may exceed the relative performance gain of adding members. This interaction cost may be offset, however, if interacting groups can perform tasks more efficiently than the aggregation of individual efforts. For example, cetaceans may reduce the energetic cost 1 arXiv:2610.17506v1 [physics.soc-ph] 13 Oct 2026

text: of swimming when traveling in groups by exploiting hydrodynamics effects of nearby swimmers (Spina et al., 2024). Interaction in human group problem-solving has been shown to yield both performance gains and efficiencies. Interacting dyads can achieve greater outcomes than either of their best individual performances (Bahrami et al., 2010; Berger et al., 2026), and groups can also speed up decision-making by minimizing independent cognitive exploration (Almaatouq et al., 2021; Dreyer et al., 2025; Szary & Dale, 2013, 2014). At the same time, interaction may also suppress the benefits associated with independent exploration (Janis, 2008; Rotter & Portugal, 1969). Classic findings in group performance show that interaction can impair collective outcomes relative to equivalent non-interacting groups, such as by reducing the number of unique ideas generated during category recall (Szary et al., 2015; Weldon & Bellinger, 1997). Yet other approaches suggest that independent aggregation, without interaction at all, may yield the best statistical outcome (Surowiecki, 2005). There are open questions about the underlying mechanisms driving these mixed observations. One approach to this puzzle is to investigate the underlying dynamics that interaction introduces to these collective decisions and the conditions under which such dynamics may facilitate performance. When humans interact they can exhibit interpersonal synchronization across multiple biome- chanical and behavioral dimensions, including gait, posture, physiology, gaze, head movement, and speech (Abney et al., 2014; Branigan, 2007; Brennan, 1996; Felsberg & Rhea, 2021; Hamil- ton & Konvalinka, 2026; Pardo, 2006; Richardson & Dale, 2005; Shockley et al., 2003; Trujillo et al., 2023; Yi & Palmer, 2026). Although the functional role of synchrony is debated, it has been argued to support joint action, prosociality, mutual understanding, and the formation of linguistic conventions (Dale et al., 2013; daSilva & Wood, 2025; Hawkins et al., 2023; Hove & Risen, 2009; Louwerse et al., 2012; Stolk et al., 2016). Consistent with this view, interpersonal synchrony has been linked to successful group problem-solving across multiple tasks (Abney et al., 2021; Dideriksen et al., 2023). By contrast, aggregating independent guesses has been shown to produce a collective response that is more accurate than any individual guess, what is sometimes called the "wisdom of crowds" (Surowiecki, 2005). This effect leverages a general benefit of statistical facilitation in certain problem spaces and was first demonstrated by pooling guesses of the weight of an ox (Galton, 1907). Empirical illustrations of this statistical effect in general knowledge domains show that just a few pooled guesses from independent individuals can improve precision (Ariely et al., 2000). These effects of statistical independence are sufficiently robust that some research has shown they can hold across multiple guesses from a single person (Vul & Pashler, 2008). Nevertheless, the potential for bias within underlying distributions of individuals can raise concerns about how to achieve optimal outcomes (Becker et al., 2017) and the effect is still subject to factors such as relative level of knowledge across a population (Bang & Frith, 2017). Although the general advantage of the wisdom of crowds is well-known, and cited as a canonical example of collective intelligence, it does not shed light on the cognitive role of human interaction. In the present study, we investigate the benefits of interaction in collec- tive intelligence on both overall performance and on computational efficiency by developing a novel computational model of interaction dynamics in collective intelligence. text: 1.1 Performance Gains in Interacting Dyads Bahrami et al. (2010) provide us with a paradigm and experimental results to test our model of collective performance gains. They showed pairs of participants sets of Gabor patches (si- nusoidal grating patterns with a Gaussian blur) in two consecutive intervals. Participants were tasked with identifying which interval, the first or the second, contained a contrast oddball. Individual responses were collected on each trial. When responses differed, participants con- ferred with each other to reach a joint decision. Individual and joint decisions across a range of contrast differences were fit with psychometric curves representing the perceptual sensitivity of each member and the dyad. The study showed that some dyads’ discriminability exceeded the perceptual sensitivity of their best member. Furthermore, the authors showed that this dyadic advantage was modu- lated by differences in individual member discriminability: Dyads composed of members with approximately similar perceptual sensitivities exhibited the greatest dyadic gain, and this gain diminished as the disparity between individual ability increased. The authors argued that this inverse linear relationship is consistent with the hypothesis that dyads communicated their level of confidence in their guesses to produce joint decisions (Bang et al., 2014; Fusaroli et al., 2012). There is an open question about the process by which dyads shared their confidences during joint decision-making. On the
title: Performance Gains in Interacting Dyads

text: dyads communicated their level of confidence in their guesses to produce joint decisions (Bang et al., 2014; Fusaroli et al., 2012). There is an open question about the process by which dyads shared their confidences during joint decision-making. On the one hand, communication may only serve to integrate guesses after individual decision-making has terminated. In this case, the dyadic advantage would reflect the same baseline statistical facilitation also leveraged by wisdom of crowds. On the other hand, individual decision-making may continue during communication, and interaction between the decision processes themselves may produce an emergent benefit beyond what is attained by statistical facilitation. These two theoretical alternatives are illustrated in Figure 1b. In the present study, we investigate these alternatives by modeling dyads performing a classification task and testing if interaction or aggregation better accounts for the Bahrami et al. results. The question is whether or not interaction may benefit collective intelligence by enabling group performance gains above those that are explainable by statistical facilitation. 1.2 Computational Efficiency in Interacting Collectives In addition to performance gains, interaction may also benefit collective intelligence by enabling groups to accomplish a task more efficiently. For example, recent findings showed that the force output of weaver ants increased superlinearly with group size such that force per ant nearly doubled when they coordinated as groups to

text: intelligence by enabling groups to accomplish a task more efficiently. For example, recent findings showed that the force output of weaver ants increased superlinearly with group size such that force per ant nearly doubled when they coordinated as groups to pull and fold leaves into nests (Stewardson et al., 2025). Alternatively, in humans, "social loafing," where effort per individual decreases with increasing group size, may grant collective efficiency if group performance is maintained or even increases despite the drop in individual effort. This is exactly what was found in a simulated real-world crisis mapping scenario: As group size increased, collective performance increased, effort per individual decreased, and collaboration across members increased, suggesting that interaction can distribute effort across human teams (Mao et al., 2016). At the same time, while some studies show that the cost of interaction, as measured by response time, can outweigh benefits to accuracy (Almaatouq et al., 2024; Straub et al., 2023), other studies show that interaction can help groups respond more quickly and more accurately. For instance, one study found that group interaction led to more accurate decisions in monetary policymaking compared to individual decisions without an increase in response time (Blinder & Morgan, 2005). Speed advantages without loss in accuracy have also been reported in groups 3

text: in mathematical reasoning tasks, "20-questions" -style games, general trivia, and crossword puzzles (Laughlin et al., 2006; Szary & Dale, 2013, 2014; Taylor & Faust, 1952). More recently, Hsieh et al. (2020) examined if dyads more efficiently process information in a contrast oddball task similar to Bahrami et al. (2010). They replicated the dyadic advantage and further showed that correct dyad responses were actually faster and more frequent than would be expected by independent decision-makers. These findings suggest that dyadic interaction can result in a gain in both processing speed and perceptual sensitivity. We use the modeling framework developed herein to test for collective efficiency gains by measuring if performance improves with group size while controlling for the total amount of computational resources expended. Specifically, we test whether or not collective interaction among larger groups of computationally "cheaper" individuals leads to better performance than smaller groups of more "expensive" individuals, where computational resources are equal between comparison groups. 1.3 Modeling Collective Dynamics using Ensemble Reservoir Computing Our approach to testing different hypotheses about collective performance is to model the ensemble dynamics of recurrent neural networks trained to perform a benchmark classification task. Recurrent connections are notoriously difficult to train and analyze, so we chose echo state networks (ESNs), a kind of reservoir computer that has three key benefits for our purposes.

text: of recurrent neural networks trained to perform a benchmark classification task. Recurrent connections are notoriously difficult to train and analyze, so we chose echo state networks (ESNs), a kind of reservoir computer that has three key benefits for our purposes. First, recurrent connections in ESNs are fixed and a read-out layer is configured to map their dynamics onto targets, which avoids complications with training recurrent weights, learning rates, and other associated hyperparameters. Second, ESNs are computationally inexpensive which facilitates the analysis of model interactions over time in groups of agents that vary in size. Lastly, ESNs can be easily coupled in different ways to test how interaction versus aggregation affects the collective dynamics of decision-making. In our simulations, we reproduce the dyadic advantage observed in Bahrami et al. (2010) using coupled ESNs, and we show that larger populations of interacting agents can achieve greater performance even when matched on overall computational cost. We first present a novel dyadic ESN architecture, which may be tested either as an aggregate of individual processes (qua wisdom of crowds) or as a coupled information-processing system (qua dyadic interaction). We test this model on a benchmark classification task to evaluate collective performance with and without interaction. We show that interaction via pooled-feedback over the course of processing produces a dyadic advantage similar to the original

We show that interaction via pooled-feedback over the course of processing produces a dyadic advantage similar to the original study. This effect is diminished with independent (self-) feedback, showing that interaction yielded a benefit beyond statistical facilitation. We analyze the network decision trajectories and show that pooled-feedback stabilizes network dynamics over time in unstable agents, allowing coupled networks to exhibit a collective benefit when they process the task as an interacting dyad. We then expand this model architecture to simulate performance in larger interacting col- lectives. We control the quantity of nodes and edges in the network to produce a range of fixed computational resources available for information processing. We compare performance on the same signal classification task across group size and computational budget. We show a performance advantage in distributed, multi-agent architectures compared to individual net- works matched on computational resources. The relative advantage increases with budget size and group size, suggesting an avenue for scaling reservoir computers by leveraging collective dynamics in distributed, coupled systems. 4

text: 2 Reservoir Computing and Echo State Networks Reservoir computing is an approach to neural network modeling that leverages the dynamics of a fixed, recurrent network of artificial neurons to perform general-purpose computations. When the dynamical memory of the reservoir balances signal retention with signal separation over time, the projection of inputs onto the nonlinear reservoir may be used to learn a linear "read-out" function, analogous to how biological intelligences may flexibly exploit naturally- occurring intrinsic dynamics for cognition without requiring task-specific wiring (Maass et al., 2002). Because the read-out function is linear, it can be solved directly using a least mean squares algorithm instead of a learning algorithm like backpropagation that requires gradual weight updates over repeated input presentations. As a result, reservoir networks offer simple, dynamical models of processing that have been applied to modeling the brain (Enel et al., 2016), chaotic time series forecasting (Jaeger & Haas, 2004; Pathak et al., 2018), speech recognition (Verstraeten et al., 2006), and many other classification and prediction tasks. We employ ESNs as a dynamical model of decision-making that can be readily extended to collective processing among two or more networks. 2.1 Modeling Methods We trained pairs of ESNs to classify speech signals from the Japanese Vowels dataset (Kudo et al., 1999) that consists of 640 recordings of nine native, male Japanese

text: extended to collective processing among two or more networks. 2.1 Modeling Methods We trained pairs of ESNs to classify speech signals from the Japanese Vowels dataset (Kudo et al., 1999) that consists of 640 recordings of nine native, male Japanese speakers pronouncing the vowel cluster /ae/ repeatedly. We randomly sample 28 recordings for each of the nine speakers for training data, which were cepstrum-coded to produce 12 linear prediction coefficients (LPCs) that encode the auditory signal on each time step, 25.6 msecs per step, with frames shifted by 6.4 msecs. Twenty-four additional recordings per speaker were sampled for the testing set. The first 10 LPC time steps of each recording were 𝑧-score transformed (recordings less than 10 time steps in length were excluded) and used as sequential inputs to the reservoir. The speaker identification task was coded by nine read-out units, where each unit represented one of the nine speakers and target vectors were one-hot coded. Each ESN was composed of three layers: An input layer, a recurrent reservoir network, and a read-out (output) layer. The 12 LPCs were represented as 12-dimensional input vectors per time step, 𝑢(𝑡), and connections from input units into the reservoir were defined by an input weight matrix 𝑊𝑖𝑛. Input nodes were randomly connected to reservoir nodes with a probability of 𝑝𝑖𝑛𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑘, and input weights were randomly set to 1 or -1 with equal probability. Symmetric weights serve two primary functions. First, zero-mean input weights (paired with zero-mean inputs) prevent a systematic directional bias in how external inputs perturb the reservoir. Second, high variance input weights increase the effective rank of the reservoir state matrix. This reduces correlations among reservoir nodes and maintains diversity in the reservoir state trajectories, which improves the linear separability of the resulting reservoir features. text: 3.3.2 Interaction Stabilizes Network Dynamics Next we compared the dynamics in the read-out layer over the time course of signal processing with self- and pooled-feedback to investigate how interaction alters the decision process of networks in the dyadic model. Figure 3a shows time series for each of the nine decisions averaged over signals. Time series were compiled such that the first trajectory (plotted with o’s) corresponds to the correct response and the following trajectories (plotted with x’s) indicate competing decisions ordered by rank. With self-feedback, networks failed to retain the correct classification decisions until the end of a signal, demonstrated by trajectories that increasingly diverge from their target activation as signals persist. However, with pooled-feedback this divergence was mitigated. Networks maintained more stable decision trajectories over time, shown by a delay in how quickly, and to what extent, each trajectory diverges in the coupled networks. The first-order temporal difference (Equation 3) averaged over test signals was used to measure the dispersion of the trajectories over time in each condition (Figure 3b). A linear mixed-effects regression model with condition as a predictor of dispersion and random effects of node, signal, and time step confirmed that trajectories with pooled-feedback dispersed significantly less over time compared to self-feedback (𝛽= −0.13, p < 0.0001). (2010) can be reproduced by coupled ESNs. When individual networks are prone to instability interaction can stabilize their dynamics, yielding distributed improvements and a superadditive benefit in collective performance. Networks were trained on stimuli and targets with an average expected value of zero, allowing read-outs to represent confidence over classification targets (with the most confident target class taken as a response). Pooling read-outs to generate coupled feedback therefore provides a simple mechanistic implementation of confidence sharing, hypothesized to underlie the original effect (Bahrami et al., 2010; Bang et al., 2014). Importantly, the model shows how confidence sharing shapes joint dynamics and identifies the conditions under which it produces a collective advantage. Nevertheless, the dyadic advantage requires two individuals to solve a shared problem, doubling the computational resources involved. One may ask if the performance gain persists when dyads are matched to individuals in total computational cost. This question is difficult to address in biological collectives, where adding members necessarily increases computational resources; however, our modeling framework allows computational cost to be controlled directly. Performance was measured as percent correct on test signals. 4.2.1 Dyadic Advantage Extends to Larger Ensembles First, we looked at the overall effect of group size on performance. Figure 4 shows a monotonic increase in performance with more ESNs interacting, averaged over all tested reservoir sizes. Compared to an individual ESN, ensembles of 16 ESNs exhibited an improvement of almost 20 percentage points. Performance appears to begin to asymptote at 16 ESNs, although it is unclear how many ESNs can be added while performance gains continue to accrue. Figure 4 also shows that the rate of increase in performance differs for ensembles composed of different reservoir sizes. Ensembles composed of 10-unit reservoirs exhibit the strongest effect of group size. Single 10-unit reservoirs show some of the lowest performance, but ensembles of 16 show equivalent performance as larger networks. This result suggests that larger ensembles of small reservoirs can compete with the performance of larger networks for less total computational cost. 4.2.2 Larger Ensembles of Smaller Networks Are More Efficient Figure 5a

In summary, group performance scaled up with ensemble size more than ESN size; the best average performance we observed was for 16 ESNs with reservoirs of only 20 units each. While this scaling effect may be attributed to ESNs and how read-outs were pooled, our model nonetheless demonstrates how ensemble dynamics can scale up with ensemble size to support collective performance. 4.3 Summary Our model allows systematic investigation into the collective benefit of interaction in larger groups by controlling underlying factors such as the computational budget of individuals. Our findings with groups are consistent with the benefits of pooled-feedback observed in dyadic networks in the first experiment. We also show that the relative gains from interaction depend on the group size and capacity of the networks. We observe that smaller, less capable networks in larger groups generally benefit more from pooling information compared to smaller groups of larger networks. These findings suggest that distributing computation among relatively simple agents can be advantageous not only in terms of collective outcomes but in terms of collective 14

The ability to systematically vary group size and computational capacity also offers a framework that can be readily extended to test factors in optimal team composition. Prior work on team composition suggests a number of factors impact group outcomes, including relative performance of individuals, group size, and group structure (Lamberson & Page, 2012). These factors can be translated into testable predictions within our model and used to investigate potential underlying mechanisms systematically (McClelland, 2009). ESNs implement well defined and parameterized processes that can be precisely tuned for computational budget and individual training as well as leveraged across many tasks. This framework could thus contribute new mechanistic links between cognitive processes and collective outcomes (Scott-Phillips & Nettle, 2022; Smaldino et al., 2023). 5 General Discussion In this paper, we ask what dynamics enable dyads and groups to perform better when deliberating together versus independently and how interaction can be leveraged for efficient collective decision-making. We offer a novel model of joint decision-making using coupled ESNs that shows how dyads can outperform their best individual member. They can do so somewhat through statistical facilitation, but interaction through step-by-step pooling of read-outs yielded even better performance and also better accounted for the data. This

They can do so somewhat through statistical facilitation, but interaction through step-by-step pooling of read-outs yielded even better performance and also better accounted for the data. This benefit of coupling ESNs via interactions grew further still with larger ensemble sizes, in terms of absolute performance as well as computational efficiency. Our model shows how interactions among reservoir networks can shape their individual dynamics in the service of collective decision-making. Reservoir computing is general-purpose and our model could be used to investigate the role of dynamics in many different kinds of collective tasks and performances. 5.1 Interaction and Crowd Wisdom In our model, pooling feedback offers a simple mechanism to fulfill the function of weighted confidence-sharing proposed by Bahrami et al. (2010). On each time step, read-out vectors encoded both a decision (most active node) and a degree of confidence in whether the vowel token came from each of the nine speakers–specifically, unit magnitudes encoded confidence because their expected values were zero when the reservoir provided no reduction in the uncertainty of speaker identification. As identification information becomes available in the reservoir, units move away from their zero baselines towards identification of one or more speakers over others. As identification information becomes available in the reservoir, units move away from their zero baselines towards identification of one or more speakers over others. Therefore, a more confident ESN contributed larger read-out magnitudes compared with a less confident ESN, and larger magnitudes exerted more influence on collective decisions. Weighted confidence-sharing does not specify how interaction alters decision-processing over time. Individual guesses could be combined after independent decision-making has terminated, which would predict that integrating decisions across independent networks would show the same dyadic advantage as coupled networks, or better. Instead, we found that pooling feedback step-by-step as inputs came in over time provided a better account of the data, which we take as evidence that the collective benefit in perceptual decision-making and similar tasks can emerge from interactions that shape both individual and collective processing dynamics. Our model also shows how structured interaction can enhance the benefit of crowd wisdom. For example, Navajas and colleagues (2018) found that small-group consensus can outperform 15

Likewise, we observe that while aggregating independent network decisions yields a modest collective benefit, this benefit increases in both magnitude and scope when pooled- feedback is introduced. There is also evidence that variability among individual judgments is important for crowd wisdom (Barrera-Lemarchand et al., 2024). Likewise, it was important that we randomized and trained our ESNs individually so their dynamics would be distinct during testing, allowing them to make distinct contributions to interactions and their collective effects via pooled-feedback. Finally, network structure and response weighting can amplify or suppress crowd wisdom (Baten & Mahjabin, 2025; Becker et al., 2017). Such effects could be simulated and tested with our model, and simulations of larger social networks under various coupling rules may help us understand the functional connections between individual and social dynamics. The generality of our framework aside, we focused on a classic nine-choice speaker classifi- cation benchmark so we could investigate and analyze the model in depth. Bahrami et al. It would also be useful to simulate other tasks and results that both do and do not confer a benefit to collective interaction. 5.2 Collective Stabilization of Positive Feedback We found that the benefit of interaction over statistical facilitation only held for relatively unstable reservoirs that needed pooling to guide their runaway dynamics. Runaway dynamics came from positive feedback between each reservoir and its read-out units, and such dangers of positive feedback are common and well-known in neural and behavioral dynamics. In the case of decision-making, positive feedback can manifest as "overthinking," such as when a student revises a correct multiple-choice answer because deliberation continues after sufficient evidence has been reached. One can imagine that interaction with a peer might help the student avoid overthinking and stick with their original answer. Positive feedback can also enable exploration and adaptation but unchecked it runs the risk of causing instability (Brandman & Meyer, 2008; May, 1972). For example, attempts to maintain a constant vocal volume often lead to unintentional amplification (Zollinger & Brumm, 2011), while excessive positive feedback in brain circuits can produce seizures (Huguenard & McCormick, 2007; Jirsa et al., 2014). Negative feedback stabilizes neural

text: For example, attempts to maintain a constant vocal volume often lead to unintentional amplification (Zollinger & Brumm, 2011), while excessive positive feedback in brain circuits can produce seizures (Huguenard & McCormick, 2007; Jirsa et al., 2014). Negative feedback stabilizes neural dynamics, supporting homeostasis, and disruptions in the balance of positive and negative feedback contribute to psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia (Molina et al., 2020). Neural computation is thought to emerge near this balance at the "edge of chaos" (Hengen & Shew, 2025; Kello, 2013), a regime also exploited by reservoir computing to maximize both stability and flexibility (Bertschinger & Natschläger, 2004). Our work demonstrates that balancing positive and negative feedback can emerge from the interplay of individual and collective dynamics. Agents like reservoir networks that are individually susceptible to positive feedback can achieve stable performance by leveraging negative feedback loops introduced through dyadic and group interaction. This finding extends the idea that nonlinear interactions across scales can transform the dynamical properties of individual components and overall behavior to collective systems (Kelty-Stephen et al., 2023). In particular, collective near-critical dynamics can emerge from interactions among agents whose individual dynamics are not themselves optimally tuned (Bessone & Plantec, 2026). Thus our model highlights a functional mechanism available to groups with collective tasks and 16
