text: Evaluation of ten off-the-shelf sparse and dense retrieval models, without fine-tuning, shows that aggregate ranking performance alone can mask important weaknesses. Dense encoders achieve substantially higher ranking quality than BM25 [36] (nDCG@10 = 0.87 vs. 0.77), yet the best model achieves only 0.51 accuracy on four-way hierarchical relevance classification. Model scale is also not consistently predictive: the 4B Qwen3 [42] encoder slightly outperforms its 8B counterpart on sibling discrimination. Attribute-level evaluation further localizes these differences: models per- form strongly on product type and gender (> 0.93) but sub- stantially worse on material (≈0.52) and style (≈0.43). Finally, a human study comparing benchmark queries with real user queries shows comparable perceived naturalness and strong intent clarity, supporting Fashion-RQBENCH as a proxy for real-world fashion search. Our contributions are: • We repurpose RQ-VAE semantic identifiers as an auto- matic annotation mechanism and introduce an attribute exclusivity loss that encourages quantization levels to encode coherent attributes. Prefixes define relevance sets, prefix length controls granularity, and shared-prefix length defines graded relevance. • We introduce a cluster-conditioned query generation pro- cedure that captures each cluster’s attribute distribution and its relational differences from parent and sibling clusters, enabling automatic generation of shopper-style queries. • We introduce FASHION-RQBENCH, comprising 588 clusters, 5,380 attribute-enriched queries, and 44,446 products, with deterministic graded relevance and four complementary evaluation tasks. •

Related Works Fashion Retrieval Datasets and Benchmarks. Fash- ion retrieval involves fine-grained attributes such as product type, color, pattern, material, occasion, season, and price. Existing resources address different aspects of this prob- lem. DeepFashion [22] and DeepFashion2 [11] provide large-scale benchmarks for fashion recognition, detection, segmentation, and retrieval; Fashion200K [12] and Shop- ping100k [3] support attribute-based search; FACAD [53] focuses on fashion captioning; and Fashion Product Im- ages [2] provides the catalog schema used in our work. Language-conditioned retrieval is studied primarily through composed image retrieval, including FashionIQ [51], and more general benchmarks such as CIRR [23], CIRCO [4], and LaSCo [20], with fashion-oriented encoders includ- ing FashionCLIP [6], Marqo-FashionSigLIP [16], and GCL [57]. Most existing fashion benchmarks use single-target rele- vance, whereas open-ended product queries can correspond to a set of valid items; CIRCO [4] is a notable exception, but at modest scale. Graded set-valued relevance is avail- able in product search: ESCI [33], for example, provides exact, substitute, complement, and irrelevant

text: open-ended product queries can correspond to a set of valid items; CIRCO [4] is a notable exception, but at modest scale. Graded set-valued relevance is avail- able in product search: ESCI [33], for example, provides exact, substitute, complement, and irrelevant labels, but re- quires 2.6M manual judgments for 130K queries. Manual construction also fixes the query distribution and catalog snapshot, making large-scale regeneration costly. Outside fashion, QUEST [25] automatically constructs set-valued queries from Wikipedia categories, but relies on an exist- ing taxonomy. In contrast, FASHION-RQ derives both rel- evance sets and queries from the catalog’s learned semantic structure, avoiding manual relevance annotation and prede- fined taxonomies. Generative Retrieval and Semantic Identifiers. Genera- tive retrieval directly decodes item identifiers from queries. DSI [40] and NCI [49] established this paradigm, with hier- archical identifier construction shown to be effective. Sub- sequent approaches learn identifiers through discrete auto- encoding [39] or residual quantization for relevance-aware, prefix-scorable representations [55]. In recommendation, TIGER [32] represents items using SIDs produced by an RQ-VAE [19, 45]; its coarse-to-fine codebooks induce a prefix hierarchy, while Singh et al. [38] demonstrate bene- fits for cold-start and long-tail recommendation. Recent work explicitly shapes this hierarchy. HiD- VAE [9] supervises quantization levels with hierarchical item tags and introduces a uniqueness objective to reduce code collisions. These approaches, however, use seman- tic

HiD- VAE [9] supervises quantization levels with hierarchical item tags and introduces a uniqueness objective to reduce code collisions. These approaches, however, use seman- tic identifiers primarily as representations for downstream retrieval or recommendation. FASHION-RQ instead repur- poses the hierarchy as an annotation structure: prefixes de- fine product groups at different granularities and shared- prefix length provides graded relevance. We further intro- duce level-wise attribute supervision with an attribute ex- clusivity loss to encourage semantically coherent clusters, using the resulting tree to construct the benchmark rather than the retrieval identifiers themselves. Automated Query and Relevance Construction. Syn- thetic query generation reduces the cost of manual anno- tation. Doc2Query [30] generates queries for documents, while InPars [5] and Promptagator [8] use LLM-generated query–document pairs for retrieval training. These ap- proaches are primarily document-conditioned: a query is generated from an individual document and typically inher- its a single positive target. Rahmani et al. [31] extend synthetic generation to evaluation, using LLM-generated queries and judgments to reproduce retrieval rankings, but the resulting relevance labels remain pairwise LLM assess- ments. BEIR [43], in contrast, aggregates existing man- ually annotated datasets, while ExcluIR [56] focuses on phenomenon-specific retrieval with manually constructed
title: Evaluation of ten off-the-shelf sparse and dense retrieval

text: queries. FASHION-RQ uses cluster-conditioned generation: queries are generated from a purified cluster’s attribute dis- tribution together with its relational differences from par- ent and sibling clusters. The cluster itself therefore de- fines a multi-item relevance set, while the relational con- text encourages queries that distinguish the target group from nearby alternatives. The LLM only verbalizes catalog- derived evidence; it does not assign relevance, keeping the resulting labels independent of the generator. Evaluating Retrieval Beyond Binary Relevance. Graded metrics such as nDCG [15] require relevance judgments, motivating LLM-based assessors such as UMBRELA [44]. Such assessors produce holistic query–item scores and therefore do not reveal which attributes are satisfied or vio- lated. Attribute-level evaluation has been explored through attribute-specific retrieval metrics [24], conditional simi- larity [47], compositionality benchmarks [13, 54], and constraint-satisfaction measures [1]. However, these set- tings either evaluate individual attributes, use curated dis- tractors, or operate over restricted constraint types rather than decomposing relevance over a ranked product catalog. FASHION-RQ combines set-valued graded relevance with joint attribute-level evaluation. Our weighted query- relevance score and per-attribute metrics are computed from the structured query representation ϕ(q), separating overall intent satisfaction from fine-grained attribute satisfaction. Because relevance is inherited deterministically from the semantic-ID hierarchy and attribute scores use a fixed cata- log schema, the evaluation is reproducible and inspectable without per-pair human or

FASHION-RQ: Automated Benchmark Generation We introduce FASHION-RQ, an automated framework for constructing retrieval benchmarks from product catalogs without manual query or relevance annotation. It exploits the hierarchical structure induced by residual quantization: SID prefixes define relevance sets at multiple granularities, while catalog statistics generate natural-language queries that represent the target cluster and discriminate it from nearby alternatives. Given a catalog I = {i1, . . . , iN}, each item i is rep- resented by a dense embedding ei ∈R1024 and catalog metadata including product type, category, color, gender, usage, price, and textual information. A hierarchical to- kenizer maps each item to a SID si = (s(1) i , s(2) i , s(3) i ), with L = 3 quantization levels and K = 64 codes per level. Our benchmark construction consists of four stages: (1) hierarchical semantic representation, which induces a coarse-to-fine catalog hierarchy; (2) cluster purification, which removes unreliable clusters; (3) relational context construction, which identifies attributes distinguishing each cluster from its parent and siblings; and (4) automatic query generation, which produces queries satisfying coverage and discriminability requirements. Fashion retrieval should be eval- uated across multiple levels of semantic granularity, as queries may target broad product groups or fine-grained subsets. We use an RQ-VAE to induce this hierarchy, as residual quantization captures entangled attribute interactions and organizes products into semantically coherent clusters at multiple granularities. This structure provides a catalog- grounded basis for realistic query generation and repro- ducible evaluation of fashion retrieval systems. text: 4. Benchmark Definition & Tasks. Source Dataset. We propose FASHION-RQBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating fine-grained fashion retrieval and ranking. It is constructed from the public Myntra Fashion Product Images [2] catalog, comprising 44,446 products with structured metadata, free-text descriptions, and prod- uct images. Each item is represented by a 1024-dimensional embedding generated using Marqo-FashionSigLIP [16], and assigned a 3-level SID using the RQ-VAE model de- scribed in Section 3. Attribute values exhibit substantial lexical diversity, supporting evaluation beyond a fixed vocabulary. Benchmark Tasks. We define four complementary tasks over the same SID hierarchy, with candidate construction and relevance labels derived deterministically, eliminating the need for an independently authored product taxonomy. For a level-3 anchor cluster, candidates receive four graded relevance levels: Exact (same level-3 prefix), Sibling (same level-2 prefix), Related (same level-1 prefix), and Irrele- vant (different level-1 prefix), with scores 3, 2, 1, and 0, respectively. Thus, a single representation defines semantic neighborhoods, evaluation instances, and graded relevance, yielding a consistent and reproducible protocol. • Query–Product Ranking. Given a natural-language query and a fixed candidate pool containing Exact, Sib- ling, Related, and Irrelevant items, rank the candidates according to relevance. We report nDCG@10 and Recall@10, both overall and for explicitly constrained at- tributes. • Hierarchical Relevance Classification. Given a query– product pair, predict one of the four relevance classes. We report accuracy and macro-F1. • Sibling Discrimination. Given one target item and closely

text: and Recall@10, both overall and for explicitly constrained at- tributes. • Hierarchical Relevance Classification. Given a query– product pair, predict one of the four relevance classes. We report accuracy and macro-F1. • Sibling Discrimination. Given one target item and closely related sibling distractors, identify the target leaf cluster. The task emphasizes fine-grained distinc- tions between semantically similar products. We report nDCG@3 and Recall@3 for ranked predictions, or binary accuracy when a single item is selected. • Query Paraphrase Robustness. We use the query groups generated by our method in Section 3 as para- phrases: since all queries from a cluster describe the same target intent by construction, we evaluate them against a shared candidate pool. This isolates sensitivity to query wording from candidate-pool variation. We measure ro- bustness using Consistency@K, the mean pairwise Jac- card overlap of top-K retrieved item sets. 5. Evaluation Framework FASHION-RQ evaluates retrieval quality at three com- plementary levels: (i) task-level performance using the hierarchy-derived relevance labels, (ii) overall query rel- evance based on attribute satisfaction, and (iii) attribute- level diagnostics that identify specific strengths and fail- ure modes. All metrics are computed from the automati- cally constructed queries, query metadata, and SID hierar- chy, without requiring additional human annotation. For Query–Product Ranking (T1), we report nDCG@5/10 and Recall@5/10, both overall and for ex- plicitly constrained attributes. For Hierarchical Relevance Classification (T2), we report accuracy and macro-F1, with per-class precision, recall, and F1 for additional analysis. For Sibling Discrimination (T3), we report nDCG@1/3 and Recall@1/3 to measure fine-grained target-cluster identification. For Query Paraphrase Robustness (T4), we measure retrieval stability using Consistency@5/10, defined as the mean pairwise Jaccard overlap between the top-K result sets across paraphrases, and report the mean nDCG@10 across paraphrases. The attribute weights in R(q, p) are distilled from a cross- encoder trained on real product-search data, including the ESCI [34] filtered to fashion relevant queries and inter- nal production-scale proprietary data. Since its proprietary training data precludes direct use as an evaluation model, we use the cross-encoder as a knowledge source and esti- mate attribute importance through matched twin-pair abla- tion and regression-based analysis. We normalize the re- sulting estimates to obtain non-negative weights wa that sum to one, which are used to aggregate per-attribute match scores into the model-agnostic query-relevance score. The resulting weights are shown in Table 3; full estimation pro- cedures, per-attribute confidence diagnostics, and sample sizes are provided in supplementary. Baselines. We evaluate FASHION-RQ using ten off-the- shelf retrieval baselines spanning sparse lexical and dense semantic retrieval. The sparse family includes BM25 [36] on settings. The dense family comprises nine pretrained encoders covering 355M–8B parameter scales, different pooling strategies, and both non-instruction-tuned and instruction-tuned query encoders. These include general- purpose sentence encoders as well as recent large embed- ding models. All baselines are evaluated without train- ing or fine-tuning on FASHION-RQ; queries and catalog products are encoded using their native published config- urations, and candidates are ranked by lexical matching or embedding similarity, respectively.

text: RQBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating fashion retrieval models through complementary retrieval tasks, weighted query-relevance evaluation, and attribute-level metrics. To- gether, FASHION-RQ and FASHION-RQBENCH provide a scalable and semantically grounded alternative to manu- ally curated fashion retrieval benchmarks. FASHION-RQ depends on catalog quality, the underlying multimodal rep- resentation, and LLM-generated queries, which may intro- duce coverage and linguistic biases. The automatically de- rived relevance structure also approximates rather than re- places human judgments. Future work will explore human validation, broader domains and attributes, richer semantic relations, and adaptive benchmark generation. 8. Appendix 8.0.1. Codebook Size Ablation Study. We study the effect of RQ-VAE [19] codebook size on the semantic-ID hierarchy by comparing codebook sizes of 64, 128, and 256 with three quantization levels, while keeping all other settings fixed. The results characterize the trade-off between cluster purity and cluster fragmentation. As the codebook size increases, the available semantic-ID space grows from 643 = 262,144 to 2563 = 16,777,216, substan- tially exceeding the 44,446 catalog items. Consequently, larger codebooks produce increasingly fragmented clusters, reducing the number of items sharing the same semantic-ID prefixes. Table 5. Query Generation Methodology. Signature construction. For each semantic-ID prefix, we derive attribute signatures using combinations of masterCategory, subCategory, articleType, brandName, baseColor, gender, usage, price, and productDisplayName. We construct two comple- mentary signature sets. Discriminating signatures identify highly specific cluster characteristics, requiring at least 10% cluster coverage and 90% precision against the full cata- log; the top eight are retained based on exclusivity, pre- cision, and coverage. These signatures guide query gen- eration toward attributes that distinguish the target cluster from its siblings. Coverage signatures require at least 5% coverage and 50% precision, with the top 20 retained, and are used to ensure that queries collectively cover the ma- jor product types within the cluster. The primary product- type axis is selected as the most specific attribute whose dominant value provides the highest cluster purity, with masterCategory as the fallback. Query generation. For each qualified prefix, the Gemini prompt combines fixed generation instructions with cluster- specific evidence. The instructions require natural and complete-sentence queries, coverage of all product types accounting for at least 5% of the cluster plus a catch-all for minority types, and discrimination from sibling clusters. Queries are grounded in productDisplayName and de- scription language while avoiding queries based solely on an attribute value unless that value is shared by all clus- ter items. The prompt further provides the major product types and their frequencies, sibling-level attribute contrasts, and a structured DATA CONTEXT containing the prefix metadata, attribute signatures, attribute distributions, parent statistics, and sibling differences. For a given query, only the subset of at- tributes A(q) actually expressed in that query’s structured representation contribute to its relevance score; the cor- responding cross-encoder weights wa are renormalized to sum to 1 over A(q) before the weighted sum is taken. Cross-Encoder-Based Attribute Importance Esti- mation We estimate attribute-level importance using a cross- encoder trained on real fashion search interactions. The cross-encoder serves as an independent relevance oracle, al- lowing us to derive attribute weights without relying on the retrieval systems or evaluation metrics being compared in Fashion-RQBENCH. We use two complementary estima- tion procedures: a controlled matched-pair ablation and an independent regression-based cross-check. Cross-encoder oracle. We train a cross-encoder using the ModernBERT-large [50] architecture on a combination of proprietary internal relevance dataset (prop-rel) and a fashion-filtered subset of ESCI [34]. The model predicts binary query–product relevance, and we use its raw out- put logit as the relevance score. As ESCI’s US-locale subset spans fashion and non-fashion domains, we filter it to (query, product) pairs whose title or description con- tains fashion-specific keywords, treating products labeled exact for a given query as relevant and those labeled sub- stitute, complement, or irrelevant as irrelevant; a query may be paired with multiple products, yielding multiple query- product pairs. Combining this ESCI-filtered subset with prop-rel gives 539,849 training samples over 44,670 unique queries and 58,792 validation samples over 4,985 unique queries. text: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation Bum Jun Kim∗ Makoto Kawano Yusuke Iwasawa Yutaka Matsuo The University of Tokyo
title: Neural Dimensional Analysis:

text: Modern Transformers rely on many scale- control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale con- sistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neu- ral units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as phys- ical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimen- sionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diag- nosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experi- ments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperform- ing Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT’s normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quan- tization increases GCT’s validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics- informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA’s benefits beyond language mod- eling. These results establish dimensional con- sistency as a neural network design principle. ∗Corresponding author: bumjun.kim@weblab.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp 1
title: Neural Dimensional Analysis:

text: Deep learning employs a broad family of mechanisms for controlling internal scale. Batch normalization, layer normalization (LayerNorm), and root-mean-square nor- malization (RMSNorm) normalize activations (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015; Ba et al., 2016; Zhang and Sennrich, 2019). DeepNet, ReZero, LayerScale, and Fixup con- trol the scale of residual additions (Wang et al., 2024; Bachlechner et al., 2021; Touvron et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2019). Attention scaling and query–key normal- ization (QK-Norm) regulate softmax inputs (Vaswani et al., 2017; Henry et al., 2020; Dehghani et al., 2023; Team, 2024). Loss-balancing methods and adaptive optimizers manage scale imbalances in objectives and parameter updates (Kendall et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Kingma and Ba, 2015; You et al., 2020). These scale-control mechanisms play a critical role in improving training stability and perfor- mance (Xiong et al., 2020; Zhai et al., 2023; Wortsman et al., 2024). All of these mechanisms manage how quantities of different scales interact within a neural network (Figure 1). We interpret these scale-control mechanisms through dimensional consistency. In physics, terms added to- gether must have compatible units, and the arguments of exp and log must be dimensionless. A physical unit, such as a centimeter or a meter, provides a reference scale for expressing a measured quantity. Inspired by physical units and dimensions, we define a

Inspired by physical units and dimensions, we define a neural unit as the rule governing how an internal tensor scales when the computation graph is rescaled. Neural units describe internal scaling behavior even when the data have no physical units. In terms of neural units, each scale-control mechanism in deep learning becomes a unit operation. Normalization removes units, residual branches restore stream units, attention temperatures convert logits to dimensionless quantities, loss weights convert loss units, and optimizers map gradient units back to parameter units. For example, units-equivariant learning handles the physical units of input and output data (Villar et al., 2023), maximal-update parameterization (µP) prescribes parameterization and update scales for hy- perparameter transfer (Yang and Hu, 2021; Yang et al., 2021), unit scaling chooses scales for low-precision train- ing (Blake et al., 2023), and the normalized Transformer (nGPT) constrains activations and weights to the unit hypersphere (Loshchilov et al., 2025). In contrast, our NDA framework offers a unified view of scale control over the whole computation graph, covering activations, objectives, gradients, and optimizers, and additionally provides diagnostics and local corrections. App. C.6 develops these connections. Contributions. We make three contributions: 1. A graph-level unit calculus covering activations, objectives, gradients, and updates, together with a theoretical analysis. This calculus links forward computation and backpropagation through a single set of unit rules (Prop. 1). To guide unit-consistent network design and training, we prove theorems on loss weighting, optimizer updates, canonical factorization, and quantization error (App. E). 2. Diagnostics and designs derived from the calcu- lus. To make the unit rules testable in trained networks, we introduce dimensionless UVI and a weight-space audit with per-block rescaling predic- tions (Prop. 6). Vision and physics-informed neural network (PINN) studies validate the same principles beyond language modeling (App. I). 2 NEURAL UNIT CONSISTENCY This section formulates local rules for managing scale on a neural network’s computation graph. The rules specify which quantities can be added and which inputs must be dimensionless. The rules also determine how loss weights must compensate for changes in loss units and how gradients must rescale when activations or parameters are rescaled. text: Neural Dimensional Analysis Activations and gates. Standard non-homogeneous activations, including sigmoid, tanh, the Gaussian error linear unit (GELU), and the sigmoid linear unit (SiLU), require dimensionless arguments. In gated MLPs z := v ⊙g, units multiply. To retain the value-branch unit u(v) at the output, the gate must be dimensionless, u(g) = 1. The raw gate aσ(a) of a Swish-gated linear unit (SwiGLU) silently assumes that a is dimensionless, whereas the normalized gate ˜g := (a/sa)σ(a/sa) is typed. App. F.7 gives the homogeneity and transition- scale examples. Loss aggregation. text: Our NDA framework establishes a typing principle for scale management across the computation graph. The NDA rules unify the scale-control mechanisms used in Transformers, including normalization, resid- ual scaling, attention temperature, loss weighting, and parameter updates. UVI diagnostics and the weight- space audit make these rules testable and actionable by locating scale mismatches and checking the rescaling behavior predicted by NDA. GCT implements these scale-control rules in a Transformer architecture, and the typed multi-loss objective makes each loss dimen- sionless before combining the terms. Experiments span- ning 51M to 1B parameters show that GCT achieves learning-rate and depth transfer, internal-rescaling in- variance, and improved residual-stream quantization robustness while retaining competitive clean validation performance. Vision and PINN studies support the use of NDA beyond language modeling. These results demonstrate the benefits of explicit scale management grounded in NDA for neural network design.

text: C.1 Normalization, residual scaling, and attention temperature Batch normalization established the practice of restandardizing internal activations (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015), and LayerNorm and RMSNorm carry that practice into the Transformer (Ba et al., 2016; Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), where Pre-LN placement stabilizes depth (Xiong et al., 2020) and NormFormer adds post-attention and mid-MLP normalization with head scaling (Shleifer et al., 2021). Residual connections make depth trainable in the first place (He et al., 2016), and DeepNet, ReZero, SkipInit, LayerScale, and Fixup control residual-branch magnitude to sustain that trainability (Wang et al., 2024; Bachlechner et al., 2021; De and Smith, 2020; Touvron et al., 2021b; Zhang et al., 2019). A complementary line removes the normalizer instead of tuning the normalizer’s placement, through a learnable elementwise squashing (Zhu et al., 2025) or through analytically scaled residual blocks with adaptive gradient clipping (Brock et al., 2021). The same accounting governs the attention interface. Depth-wise µP scales residual-branch contributions as 1/ √ L to enable the same transfer across depth (Yang et al., 2024). A parallel line makes the metric on weight space explicit. The modular norm equips a network with a norm under which well-scaled updates transfer across width and depth (Large et al., 2024), and modular duality with the efficient Muon realization casts the optimizer as a duality map that sends dual gradient vectors to primal update directions (Bernstein and Newhouse, 2025; Jordan et al., 2024). text: Neural Dimensional Analysis C.3 Rescaling symmetries and normalized architectures A classical line studies weight rescalings that leave a network’s function invariant. For positive-homogeneous activations, paired rescalings of incoming and outgoing weights form a symmetry group. Path-norm methods and path-normalized variants of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimize in the induced quotient (Neyshabur et al., 2015), and the same reparameterizations show that sharpness measures are not invariant (Dinh et al., 2017), imprint conservation laws on gradient flow (Kunin et al., 2021), and define the orbits used by teleportation methods (Zhao et al., 2022). Weight normalization exploits the same freedom constructively by splitting each weight vector into a direction and an explicit magnitude (Salimans and Kingma, 2016), which is the radial coordinate that becomes irrelevant under the downstream-nondimensionalization hypothesis of Prop. 6. A normalizer creates this freedom by making the upstream weight block scale-invariant. The scale-invariant weight block’s norm then acts only through an effective learning rate (van Laarhoven, 2017; Hoffer et al., 2018; Arora et al., 2019), which App. E.3 recovers as the p ≡1 case of Prop. 3, and weight decay on such a block is equivalent to a learning-rate schedule (Li and Arora, 2020). C.4 Quantization and activation-scale management Quantization research documents substantial variation in the scale of internal language-model activations. Integer inference represents tensors as scales times integer grids (Jacob et al., 2018; Nagel et al., 2021), connecting integer inference to the factorization in Sec. 4. Relevant phenomena include outlier features (Dettmers et al., 2022), massive activations (Sun et al., 2024), and attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2024). These observations motivate examining both cross-token scale variation and within-vector concentration. Methods for low-bit inference include mixed-precision decomposition (Dettmers et al., 2022), error-compensated weight rounding (Frantar et al., 2023), activation-scale migration (Xiao et al., 2023), activation-aware weight quantization (Lin et al., 2024), and rotations that reduce coordinate outliers (Ashkboos et al., 2024). Logit soft-capping provides a complementary architectural control at attention and output interfaces (Team, 2024). These methods address different aspects of the scale and precision problem. text: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo C.5 Typed objectives and units of physical data Uncertainty weighting (Kendall et al., 2018), gradient normalization (Chen et al., 2018), and gradient-statistics annealing for PINNs (Wang et al., 2021) adapt loss weights during training, and practitioner guides for PINNs also recommend nondimensionalizing the problem before training (Wang et al., 2023). NDA instead types the objective. A weight λi factorizes into a dimensionless preference αi and an inverse-unit converter 1/Si with u(Si) = u(Li). Thm. 2 shows that every invariant linear rule whose weights depend on the characteristic scales carries this inverse-unit factor, with the remaining scale dependence confined to dimensionless π groups, and Cor. 1 shows that the preferences are constant within this class when the loss units vary independently. Deriving Si from observable characteristic scales makes the objective invariant to the data’s unit system without adaptive weighting. Adaptive methods can then adjust dimensionless preferences among the normalized terms. This typing connects to the broader use of units in scientific machine learning, where dimensional analysis constrains learned models of physical systems (Villar et al., 2023), Buckingham–π style reductions are classical (Buckingham, 1914), and recent work learns the dimensionless groups from data (Bakarji et al., 2022). Outside machine learning, units-of-measure type systems check the dimensional consistency of a program at compile time
title: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

text: (Villar et al., 2023), Buckingham–π style reductions are classical (Buckingham, 1914), and recent work learns the dimensionless groups from data (Bakarji et al., 2022). Outside machine learning, units-of-measure type systems check the dimensional consistency of a program at compile time and infer unit-polymorphic types (Kennedy, 2009). All of these lines attach externally declared physical units to inputs, outputs, and program variables. NDA instead assigns units to internal tensors as transformation laws under internal rescalings, a gauge structure of the computation graph that applies when no physical unit exists. The gauge terminology follows geometric deep learning, where equivariance is stated relative to a choice of local frame rather than to a single global symmetry (Cohen et al., 2019). C.6 Positioning summary The related methods address complementary parts of scale management. Parameterization methods such as µP and unit scaling prescribe initialization, multipliers, and update scales (Yang and Hu, 2021; Yang et al., 2024; Blake et al., 2023). Normalized architectures control activation magnitude (Loshchilov et al., 2025; Karras et al., 2024). Weight-space symmetry analyses describe function-preserving reparameterizations (Neyshabur et al., 2015; Dinh et al., 2017; Kunin et al., 2021). Modular norms and duality maps organize optimizer updates (Large et al., 2024; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2025). Loss-balancing and quantization methods address scale in objectives and finite-precision computation, respectively (Kendall et al., 2018; Chen et
title: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

text: al., 2017; Kunin et al., 2021). Modular norms and duality maps organize optimizer updates (Large et al., 2024; Bernstein and Newhouse, 2025). Loss-balancing and quantization methods address scale in objectives and finite-precision computation, respectively (Kendall et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018; Dettmers et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2023). Units-of-measure type systems and units-equivariant learning provide the closest conceptual parallels for externally declared units (Kennedy, 2009; Villar et al., 2023). Our NDA framework unifies these perspectives in one graph-level description. Units are transformation laws under declared internal rescalings. This definition lets NDA apply to tensors without physical units. Forward consistency determines reverse-mode units (Prop. 1), while UVI diagnostics and the parameter-gauge audit make the declarations testable on trained networks. Through NDA, we also connect training-time scale control to PTQ. Our contribution is this unified treatment and the resulting diagnostics and constructions. Assume that the canonicalization floors are zero and every vector being normalized is nonzero. This invariance holds at every block-input boundary, including h0, and at the final block-output boundary because the stated head also canonicalizes the final block output. Derivation. A GCT block including entry canonicalization has the same output on h and ch wherever the block’s canonicalizations are defined. H EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS H.1 Language-model training and controlled comparisons Under matched controls, we test how unit consistency affects training robustness, functional rescaling invariance, deployment quantization, and unit-system-invariant multi-loss optimization. All runs use a single NVIDIA GH200-96GB GPU. Within each controlled comparison, architectures share data order, budget, and recipe. Only the declared intervention changes, which in the main comparisons is the block structure. Main language models. The main language models are decoder-only Transformers with d = 768, L = 12, 12 heads, and context length 1024. These models have approximately 124M parameters, with all variants matched to within 0.3%. We train the models from scratch on
title: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

text: The main language models are decoder-only Transformers with d = 768, L = 12, 12 heads, and context length 1024. These models have approximately 124M parameters, with all variants matched to within 0.3%. We train the models from scratch on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) with the Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 (GPT-2) byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizer (Radford et al., 2019) for 2.75B tokens. This budget is approximately Chinchilla-optimal for the model size (Hoffmann et al., 2022). A disjoint shard supplies a held-out 43M-token validation split. Training recipe. The training recipe follows standard practice at this scale (Karpathy, 2022; Touvron et al., 2023). We use Adam with decoupled weight decay (AdamW), setting β = (0.9, 0.95) and weight decay 0.1 on matrices only (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). The peak learning rate is 6 × 10−4, the warmup occupies 2.7% of training and lasts 151 steps at 124M, and cosine decay ends at 10% of the peak rate. The global batch contains 491,520 tokens, the gradient clip is 1.0, and training uses bf16 autocast and weight tying. Every variant uses rotary positional encoding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), which strengthens the Pre-LN baseline relative to learned positions. All eight architectures are replicated with three seeds at 124M. Unless a table explicitly reports a multi-seed aggregate, perturbation and quantization analyses evaluate one model
title: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo

text: encoding (RoPE) (Su et al., 2024), which strengthens the Pre-LN baseline relative to learned positions. All eight architectures are replicated with three seeds at 124M. Unless a table explicitly reports a multi-seed aggregate, perturbation and quantization analyses evaluate one model per architecture trained with the primary seed. The remaining seeds quantify training variability. App. H.4 states the seed protocol for every scale. Architectures compared. The comparison includes Pre-LN with LayerNorm and GELU in the GPT-2 style (Radford et al., 2019; Xiong et al., 2020). LLaMA-style blocks use RMSNorm and SwiGLU (Touvron et al., 2023). QK-Norm adds per-head RMS normalization of Q and K (Henry et al., 2020; Dehghani et al., 2023). We also include NormFormer (Shleifer et al., 2021) and LayerScale initialized at 0.1 (Touvron et al., 2021b). Three further variants control scale through normalized or explicitly corrected representations. nGPT is the closest normalized-representation prior to GCT and uses a sphere-normalized state, per-dimension eigen-learning- rate linear-interpolation updates, unit-norm weights, and QK-Norm (Loshchilov et al., 2025). UCT uses the local-correction modules of App. H.4, and GCT is the canonical design derived in Sec. 4.

text: Neural Dimensional Analysis Learning-rate robustness and seeds at 51M. The robustness study uses d = 512, L = 8 models with parameter counts from 50.9M to 51.5M, referred to as 51M models. Small-scale learning-rate sweeps are used to study training instabilities that also arise at larger scales (Wortsman et al., 2024). Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, QK-Norm, nGPT, and GCT train for 600M tokens with learning rates in {3, 6, 12, 24, 48} × 10−4, spanning a factor of 16. The protocol includes the strong QK-Norm baseline in every stress test. Each architecture also has three seeds at the default learning rate. UVI-based early stopping. At the additional learning rate 9.6 × 10−3, we apply the same preset stopping rule to Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, nGPT, and GCT. Pre-LN and LLaMA-style cross this threshold at step 100 of 1220, while nGPT and GCT complete training under the same rule. These early stops record threshold crossings, not observed numerical divergence. Depth probes and ablations. We apply PTQ to the same trained models to evaluate sensitivity to finite-precision storage and computation. The protocols include symmetric per-channel weight quantization at 8 and 4 bits and int8 activation quantization at every linear input, using both dynamic and calibration-based static scales in the standard integer-inference format (Jacob et al., 2018). The per-tensor, per-channel, and per-token granularities compared in Sec. 5.5 are the standard PTQ options (Nagel et al., 2021). Weight quantization uses round-to-nearest rather than error-compensated rounding (Frantar et al., 2023), because the comparison isolates activation- and stream-scale management rather than weight-rounding quality. text: Neural Dimensional Analysis The weight-space shadow. A bias-free matrix product x := Wu is 1-homogeneous in W. When this product is the block’s only dependence on W, with no tied use or additive W-dependent path, the ray W 7→etW realizes the activation rescaling x 7→etx. If the downstream graph nondimensionalizes that activation, the same ray becomes an exact symmetry of the loss. Proposition 6 (Weight-space shadow of activation typing). Let W be a parameter block whose only effect on the loss is through x := Wu, where u is independent of W. Suppose the graph nondimensionalizes x such that the downstream computation is invariant to x 7→cx for c > 0 when all other quantities are fixed. Then L(etW) = L(W) for all t ∈R, and the radial Euler pairing vanishes exactly wherever the derivative is defined: ⟨W, ∇W L⟩F = 0. The proof is given in App. G.10, and the architecture-specific predictions and measurement protocol are given in App. H.6. If instead the graph fails to nondimensionalize x, the weight-space radial pairing equals the corresponding activation-space pairing ⟨x, ∇xL⟩and is generally nonzero. App. G.10 gives the derivation. text: A common practice in instance retrieval is to grow the gallery size to improve a benchmark’s discrimination capability. One prominent example is ILIAS, which adds up to 100 million distractor images. The prevailing assumption is that faith- ful evaluation demands web scale, and that indexing all 100M images through the backbone is the unavoidable price of a comparable number. That price is steep: hundreds of GPU-hours and ∼200 GB of descriptors per model, paid again for every method or ablation. We show the web-scale indexing price is largely avoid- able: evaluation itself obeys a scaling law. The number of distractors that outrank a positive is Binomial in the gallery size. We define the per-query retrieval hard- ness, a gallery-scale agnostic quantity that yields a retrieval metric at any scale, and demonstrate it can be derived from a small random sample. The underlying sampled-rank machinery is long established in recommender-system and biomet- ric evaluation, but to our knowledge has never been adapted to visual retrieval. We make the law per-query and estimable, and validate it at true 100M scale on ILIAS and INSTRE, and on the full 759k-distractor Google Landmarks v2 pool. Concretely, within a 5% sample (a flat 20× less indexing), every backbone’s tail- aware (EVT) estimate has converged onto the large-scale mAP, to within ∼0.01 (mean absolute error 0.005),

text: Progress in instance-level image retrieval is measured by growing the gallery. To separate strong em- beddings from weak ones, benchmarks add large sets of distractor images: revisited Oxford/Paris add a million (R1M) (Radenovi´c et al., 2018), Google Landmarks indexes millions (Weyand et al., 2020), and ILIAS (Kordopatis-Zilos et al., 2025) adds one hundred million. This works: perfor- mance keeps dropping as the gallery grows, which is exactly what makes these benchmarks discrim- inative. The price, however, is paid in indexing. Encoding 100M images through a ViT-L backbone costs on the order of 556 GPU-hours and produces ∼200 GB of descriptors for one model. The field treats this as the unavoidable cost of a meaningful comparison. That cost is paid again for every method, ablation, resolution, or backbone. Most of that cost is unnecessary. A natural shortcut is to evaluate against a small random subset of the distractors. This shortcut is distrusted because the resulting number is optimistic and, taken at face value, can mis-rank methods. So practitioners either pay the full price or retreat to smaller galleries. These are either ad-hoc random subsets, which are optimistic and not comparable across papers, or hand-built proxies such as mini-ILIAS (Kordopatis-Zilos et al., 2025), which report their own number rather than the web-scale one. The probability the positive holds rank one is (1 −x)N, where the single per-query hardness x is the fraction of the distractor similarity distribution above the positive. This x is size-independent. It is a property of the model and the distractor source, and it does not depend on how many distractors one draws. From it, the metric at any scale follows in closed form. The corollary that matters in practice: a small random sample suffices to estimate x, and the large-scale number can be predicted rather than measured. Why has retrieval not been doing this? The sampled-rank machinery is mature, but it has lived elsewhere: classical IR (Madigan et al., 2003; Hawking & Robertson, 2003), recommender sys- tems (Krichene & Rendle, 2020; Jin et al., 2021), and biometrics (NIST, 2022; Scheirer et al., 2011; Grother & Phillips, 2004; Slavutsky & Benjamini, 2021; Rocher et al., 2025). That machin- ery has been used with a single assumed score distribution and no sample-based estimation (e.g. Madigan et al. (2003) analyze one shared relevant/irrelevant score pair); what has been missing for visual retrieval is estimating, per query and from a small sample, these extremely rare exceedance probabilities and validating the resulting metric against

(2003) analyze one shared relevant/irrelevant score pair); what has been missing for visual retrieval is estimating, per query and from a small sample, these extremely rare exceedance probabilities and validating the resulting metric against a real system at web scale. We turn that machinery into a practical, validated evaluation framework for web-scale instance retrieval: per-query hardness estimated from a small sample with a tail-aware estimator, validated at genuine 100M scale, and turned into a low-cost protocol. Contributions. 1. We bring the distractor-scaling law to instance retrieval and derive its retrieval form. The positive’s rank is 1 + Binomial(N, xq) with per-query hardness xq = 1 −Fq(s⋆), so the reported metric mAP@k(N) follows in closed form. This is an exact identity in the 2

A small sample turns it into a predictor through the population hardness, with error we quantify for the smooth term and evaluate empirically at the top-k boundary (App. C). The mechanism is broad, multi-decade (approximately power-law) hardness ⇒ near-logarithmic, non-saturating decay (log-uniform is the idealized limit). 2. A low-cost web-scale evaluation. From an affordable 1/20 distractor subset a tail-aware (EVT) estimate predicts the web-scale metric. The estimate recovers the large-scale metric to mean absolute error 0.005 on ILIAS and ≤0.008 on INSTRE and GLDv2, beating curve- fit and recommender-systems baselines. 3. Validation at true 100M scale. On ILIAS and INSTRE the estimator reproduces the offi- cial mAP over all 100M YFCC distractors; on Google Landmarks v2 (a different domain with a separate 759k pool) it recovers the official mAP@100. It holds across all five tested backbones and every benchmark. 4. A public release. We release code and per-query hardness so results on these benchmarks can be compared at any gallery size without re-indexing. 2

text: We organize prior work by which axis of cost it addresses. Training-side scaling laws predict error from training data/compute. Evaluation-side work either subsamples the query axis or estimates metrics from sampled judgments. We occupy a different cell: predicting the metric along the dis- tractor/gallery axis. Distractor-scaling benchmarks (the cost we remove). Revisited Oxford/Paris add the R1M hard-distractor set (Radenovi´c et al., 2018), Google Landmarks indexes millions (Weyand et al., 2020), and ILIAS scales to 100M distractors (Kordopatis-Zilos et al., 2025). These works measure how accuracy falls as the gallery grows and report a few fixed operating points. None make the metric-versus-scale curve estimable from a sample or use it to cut evaluation cost. We do. The ILIAS authors do release mini-ILIAS, a VLM-mined 5M-distractor proxy that retains the hardest distractors as a cheaper stand-in for the full pool (Kordopatis-Zilos et al., 2025). It reports a number on a deliberately harder subset, whereas we predict the true 100M number from a uniform random sample. A hard-mined subset is non-uniform by design, so it does not yield the size-independent hardness our estimator needs. Collection-size analysis in classical IR (closest in spirit). The relationship between collection size and retrieval effectiveness was modeled analytically two decades ago. Madigan et al. (2003) derive the distribution of irrelevant documents outscoring the relevant ones (“contamination at K”).

Madigan et al. (2003) derive the distribution of irrelevant documents outscoring the relevant ones (“contamination at K”). This is a Binomial/Poisson sampled-rank model whose K=1 case is our Theorem 1. Theirs as- sumes a single score distribution shared by all queries, with no sample-based estimation (which they pose as future work). The same authors later applied extreme-value theory to the growing-collection asymptotics of retrieval effectiveness (Madigan et al., 2006), still for a single shared score distribu- tion and without sample-based estimation or 100M-scale validation. Hawking & Robertson (2003) empirically observe that mAP rankings are largely preserved between a sample and the full collec- tion. We supply what this line lacked: the heterogeneous per-query law, a sample-based tail-aware estimator, and validation at 100M. Sampled / low-cost retrieval evaluation (judgment axis). A long IR tradition estimates met- rics from incomplete or sampled relevance judgments: bpref (Buckley & Voorhees, 2004), statAP/infAP (Yilmaz et al., 2008; Yilmaz & Aslam, 2006), and minimal test collections (Carterette et al., 2006). In recommendation, Krichene and Rendle (Krichene & Rendle, 2020) show sampled top-k metrics are biased and collapse toward AUC, and propose corrected estimators (an unbiased rank estimator and a bias–variance variant); a subsequent line learns the global rank distribution by maximum likelihood (Jin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). These estimate an aggregate rank distri- bution (Recall/NDCG@k over a catalogue) and cure the sampling “blind spot” by sampling more items, not by extrapolating the unobserved tail. Our count baseline (Sec. 5) is the Krichene–Rendle unbiased estimator specialized to the top rank; because mAP depends on the per-positive hard tail (invisible below 1/S) it fails to recover the large-N value, and enlarging the sample to resolve that tail is exactly the web-scale indexing we avoid—which is why we instead extrapolate it. 3

(3), so numbers obtained with different distractor budgets become directly comparable. Estimating hardness from a size-S sample. Draw S random distractors and, per query, record s⋆and the sample similarities. The difficulty is that the queries which dominate large-N accuracy have hardness xq ≲1/S and are invisible in the sample. We consider: (i) Count ˆxq = 1 S #{Si > s⋆} – unbiased but quantized at 1/S; it returns 0 for the invisible tail and so predicts those queries survive forever. This is exactly the Krichene–Rendle unbiased rank estimator specialized to the top rank, and it is over-optimistic. text: queries survive forever. This is exactly the Krichene–Rendle unbiased rank estimator specialized to the top rank, and it is over-optimistic. (ii) Tail extrapolation via extreme-value theory (EVT) (Scheirer et al., 2011; Bahri et al., 2023) – for these queries no sampled distractor reaches s⋆, so count- ing is blind to them. Extreme-value theory states that above a high threshold the far tail of es- sentially any continuous score distribution converges to a universal two-parameter shape, a gen- eralized Pareto. We fit that shape to the highest-scoring distractors we do observe and extend it out to s⋆, recovering a small nonzero hardness. The move is the same one used to esti- mate a never-observed “100-year flood” from the tail of recorded flood heights (full procedure in App. B). (3) with the empirical count/tail diagnostic and a query-bootstrap confidence interval. Requirement: the sample must be i.i.d. The law assumes the S distractors are drawn uniformly at random from the pool. This is the one assumption a practitioner can silently violate. A conve- nience sample, such as the first S files of a pool ordered by crawl date, cluster, or upload, is not uniform: correlated images concentrate the score tail and bias the hardness estimate. Hash-based or shuffled sampling is the actual guarantee that the drawn sample represents the omitted pool. The per-shard check—split the sample into feature shards and confirm per-shard accuracy is constant (Sec. 5)—is a diagnostic that catches drift within the drawn sample (visible as shard-to-shard varia- tion), not a proof of representativeness. 6

text: Preprint The law holds (Fig. 2). For DINOv3-L the per-query prediction tracks measured mAP across eight decades to 0.266 at 100M (the value computed on the full official feature release). By contrast, a homogeneous single-x model collapses to zero. Recovering the official number end-to-end validates the pipeline and the law at ground truth. Hardness follows an approximate power law x−α (α ≈1.2; 1.16–1.32 across the five backbones and three benchmarks): a large fraction of queries stay near- immune even at 100M, and the resolved rest bleed accuracy at a near-constant rate per decade—log- uniform (α=1) is the idealized limit of Cor. 1 and gives exactly that. This never-saturating decay is also why reading the metric off a 50k subset is optimistic by +0.34 at 100M (Fig. 2). The independence assumption is benign in practice (Fig. 3). The exact (1 −x)N form assumes independent distractors. Empirically the residual between the independent prediction and the mea- sured incremental curve is at most a few percent at 100M across all 5 backbones, and the prediction is stable to 0.004 across three disjoint 5M sub-pools (App. B). Analytically, near-duplicate clusters of size c leave the expected rank unchanged (1 + Nxq, clustering-invariant by linearity) and inflate only its variance by ∼c; on the real crawl ordering the measured curve sits at c ≈1, so

The reported interval is a query confidence interval; the remaining noise sources are quan- tified in App. C. We compare against the baselines a practitioner would reach for, all from the same 5% sample. text: Web-scale retrieval evaluation is largely predictable: a per-query tail-aware estimator recovers 100M-scale accuracy from a small random distractor sample to 0.005 mean error, covering the truth for every backbone we test on ILIAS, INSTRE, and GLDv2. Validated across five back- bones, three benchmarks, and two distractor pools, it turns web-scale evaluation from an indexing problem into a prediction problem—for method comparisons whose margins exceed the extrapola- tion error. text: Preprint B THE TAIL-AWARE (EVT) ESTIMATOR For a query whose best positive has similarity s⋆, the hardness xq = Pr[sim(q, d) > s⋆] is the probability that a random distractor outscores the answer. When xq is small—the regime that domi- nates large-N accuracy—no distractor in a size-S sample reaches s⋆, so the empirical count returns xq = 0 and we must estimate the probability of an event that did not occur in the sample. Extreme-value theory makes this possible without knowing the full score distribution. The Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem states that, for any distribution in an extreme-value domain of attraction (essentially all continuous distributions), the excesses over a high threshold u (the amounts sim −u by which scores exceed u) converge to a generalized-Pareto distribution (GPD) as u grows. In words: the far tail has a universal two-parameter shape, independent of the bulk, so we can fit it from the part of the tail we observe and extend it. Per query we (1) retain the top T=4000 distractor similarities—all that bear on the upper tail, the rest falling far below s⋆—and set the threshold u to their 95th percentile, i.e. the top ≈200 scores; because T is fixed, this is a fixed exceedance count independent of S (the same ≈200 at S=50k or 5M); (2) fit the GPD shape ξ

We use the empirical count when at least c=5 sampled distractors exceed s⋆(Alg. 1); with fewer, the count is too noisy (and c=0 would force xq=0), so we read the hardness off the fitted tail instead. text: a never-observed “100-year flood” by fitting the tail of recorded flood heights and extrapolating. The tail shape must exclude power-law growth. The GPD shape ξ sets how heavy the tail is: ξ > 0 is an infinite, power-law tail, whereas cosine similarities cannot exceed 1, so the distractor-score distribution has bounded support. By extreme-value theory a distribution with bounded support lies in the Weibull/Gumbel domain, ξ ≤0; a positive ξ would model a physically impossible power-law tail. We therefore cap ξ ≤0 (refitting the scale at the boundary when the unconstrained maximum- likelihood fit returns ξ > 0). This excludes the over-stated hard mass that otherwise inflates hardness on exactly the near-immune queries that dominate large-N accuracy. Everything else stays fully adaptive: the threshold u, scale σ, and exceedance rate ζu are fit per query from its own scores. Robustness to the threshold. The estimator’s most consequential knob is the peaks-over- threshold quantile q (we use the 95th percentile; T and ξ ≤0 are fixed once, below). text: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks Francesco Panetta1, Federico Di Valerio1 (�), and Michela Proietti2 1 Sapienza University of Rome, Italy panetta.1950468@studenti.uniroma1.it, divalerio@diag.uniroma1.it 2 Goethe University Frankfurt, Germany m.proietti@em.uni-frankfurt.de Abstract. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy- efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the in- tegration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time- stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which pro- vide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explana- tions are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy–memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substan- tially less storage. The code is available at this link. Keywords: Spiking Neural Networks · Continual Learning · Explain- able AI · Experience Replay. 1

text: Artificial intelligence systems deployed in real-world environments must adapt to evolving data while meeting strict computational and energy constraints. Yet standard neural networks still suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where learning new tasks disrupts previously acquired representations [13]. Continual learning (CL) addresses this by preserving prior knowledge while integrating new infor- mation over time. Among CL strategies, replay-based methods are particularly effective, storing representative samples from past tasks and mixing them with current data during training [3,21]. However, their performance depends on mem- ory capacity: larger buffers improve retention but are impractical for resource- constrained systems. To reduce this cost, Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) stores saliency-guided image patches rather than full samples, substantially re- ducing memory requirements while maintaining competitive CL performance [23]. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for energy-efficient machine intelligence, using sparse spike events rather than arXiv:2610.17998v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2026
title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in

text: 2 F. Panetta et al. continuous-valued activations [12]. Surrogate-gradient learning has enabled deep SNNs to achieve competitive performance on vision benchmarks [16,28], while Batch Normalization Through Time (BNTT) improves training stability and reduces inference latency [8]. However, continual learning in SNNs remains un- derexplored [14]. Replay-based approaches have only recently been adapted to SNNs, first through standard experience replay to mitigate catastrophic forget- ting [18], and more recently through compact latent replay to reduce storage and computation costs in neuromorphic systems [4]. To the best of our knowl- edge, no prior work has used explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to guide SNN learning and mitigate catastrophic forgetting, despite its effectiveness in artificial neural networks (ANNs) [19]. In this work, we investigate whether temporally grounded saliency signals in SNNs can guide memory-efficient replay. Specifically, we adapt EPR [23] to deep SNNs by replacing conventional ANN saliency mechanisms with Spike Activation Maps (SAM) [9], which produce forward-only explanations from inter-spike in- terval dynamics. Using BNTT-trained VGG9 SNNs [8] operating at low latency (25 timesteps) on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 CL benchmarks, we show that saliency-guided replay can be effectively transferred to the spiking domain, improving performance under equal memory budgets and reducing forgetting in low-memory regimes. 2

text: SNNs provide a sparse, event-driven alternative to conventional ANNs, making them particularly attractive for neuromorphic and energy-efficient learning sys- tems. Modern SNNs can be trained either through ANN-to-SNN conversion or di- rectly with surrogate-gradient methods, enabling competitive performance across a range of vision and learning tasks [6,16,25,28]. Continual learning in SNNs has recently attracted increasing attention, motivated by the need for adaptive neuromorphic systems that can learn over time under memory and energy con- straints [15]. Existing approaches mostly focus on regularization-based mecha- nisms to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, including adaptive synaptic plasticity, Bayesian learning, and sparse selective activation [17,26,27]. In contrast, replay- based continual learning for SNNs remains under-explored [18]. Recent work on compressed latent replay for SNNs further confirms the relevance of rehearsal- based strategies in spiking models, while highlighting the need for memory- efficient replay mechanisms tailored to temporal spiking representations [4]. In parallel, recent continual learning methods for conventional ANNs have begun to exploit XAI to identify and preserve task-relevant information from previ- ous experiences [1,5,7,22,23]. Among these, EPR [23] is particularly relevant to our work: it uses saliency maps to select discriminative image patches and stores only those patches in the replay buffer. This reduces memory require- ments while maintaining competitive continual learning performance. However, most saliency-guided replay methods rely on explanation mechanisms originally designed for

text: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep SNNs 3 overlooks the distinctive properties of spiking computation, including sparse event-driven activity and temporal dynamics. This motivates spike-compatible explanation strategies that can exploit temporal spiking activity [2,9]. Our work addresses this gap by adapting the principle of saliency-guided replay to SNNs. Instead of using Grad-CAM-based image patches as in EPR, we use SAM-based spatio-temporal saliency [9] to select compact replay information. In this way, ex- planation becomes a functional component of continual learning in SNNs, rather than only a diagnostic tool. 3 Methods This section introduces a continual learning framework for SNNs that combines Spike Activation Maps (SAM) [9] with a replay strategy inspired by Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) [23]. The key idea is to use temporally grounded saliency to store only the most informative regions of past samples, enabling memory-efficient replay in neuromorphic continual learning. 3.1 Spike Activation Maps Standard gradient-based explanation methods, such as Grad-CAM [24], are dif- ficult to apply to SNNs because of their discrete and non-differentiable spike dy- namics. We therefore adopt SAM, a forward-only explanation mechanism that extracts saliency directly from spike-train activity. Given a spike tensor S ∈{0, 1}T ×C×H×W , where T is the number of timesteps, C the number of channels, and H × W the spatial resolution, SAM is computed using

Given a spike tensor S ∈{0, 1}T ×C×H×W , where T is the number of timesteps, C the number of channels, and H × W the spatial resolution, SAM is computed using a causal temporal kernel: K(τ) = ( exp(−γτ), τ > 0, 0, τ = 0, (1) where γ controls the decay rate. This kernel assigns larger weights to recent spikes while ensuring that only past activity contributes to the current timestep. Next, a neuronal contribution score is computed: NCSc,h,w(t) = t−1 X τ=1 K(τ) Sc,h,w(t −τ). (3) The resulting tensor H ∈RT ×H×W captures the spatio-temporal importance of neural activations during the forward pass. For replay selection, we reduce the

Each buffer exemplar contains the extracted patch, its original coordinates (top, left), the class label, the aggregated SAM heatmap used for selection and optionally a SAM history for offline explanation-drift analysis. We then scan the image with a sliding window of size P × P, with P = 24 by default, and compute the saliency score of each candidate patch: s(top,left) = top+P X h=top left+P X w=left Hfull(h, w). text: validation set used for early stopping. The used architec- ture is taken from [8] and consists of a VGG-9-inspired SNN. Convolutional layers are made of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons [11] with a fixed threshold of 1.0 and soft-reset dynamics, and are paired with per-timestep batch normal- ization [8]. Input images are encoded as Poisson spike trains over T=25 discrete timesteps. A two-layer classification head outputs task-specific logits via indepen- dent task-specific linear layers, each mapping the shared feature representation to the classes of its corresponding task. We consider both task- (TIL) and class- incremental (CIL) learning scenarios, where task identities are available during both training and testing and just during training, respectively. In the CIL sce- nario, all task heads are concatenated at inference time and the class with the highest logit across all seen tasks is selected. Since the heads from previous tasks are frozen while training on the current task, we add a separate replay phase after each training epoch, in which the heads are unfrozen and samples from previous tasks are replayed. Limitations include dependence on SAM quality, the use of a fixed patch size, and evaluation on small-scale image classification benchmarks. Future work could explore pre- trained backbones to improve early explanation quality, enabling better patch selection and memory initialization. title: Same Function, Different Trajectory: No Standard Optimizer

text: We show that two Transformers represent- ing the same function can follow different training trajectories. For example, doubling a query matrix and halving its key matrix preserves the model’s function but changes the gradient scales seen by the optimizer. Our theoretical analysis establishes that standard block-local first-order optimizers fail to scale updates with parameters under a shared learn- ing rate. For AdamW, transforming the first- and second-moment estimates alone does not correct the mismatch between parameter and update scales. To make runs restarted from equivalent checkpoints follow the same tra- jectory, we balance matrix pairs and trans- form their moment estimates together, bring- ing distinct but equivalent training states to the same starting point. To correct scale imbalance between paired Transformer ma- trices without changing predictions, we pro- pose Symmetry-Aware Gradient Geometry Stabilization (SAGGS), which periodically equalizes the Frobenius norms of exact sym- metry pairs, and its damped variant, Soft SAGGS. SAGGS reduces perplexity (PPL) by 0.374 ± 0.026 at 101M parameters on WikiText-103, and Soft SAGGS reduces PPL by 0.780±0.040 in a 31M modern-architecture replication, both under scale imbalance. In a 123.8M checkpoint-resume experiment, recip- rocally rescaling matrix pairs barely changes validation loss at restart but increases final PPL by 3.78±0.42; hard and soft rebalancing recover to within 0.02 PPL of the control. ∗Corresponding author 1

text: Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) serve as the stan- dard architecture for large language models (Radford et al., 2019; Touvron et al., 2023). Each Transformer layer consists of a multi-head self-attention block and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The attention block is built from query, key, value, and output projections, and the MLP is based on rectified linear units (ReLU) or Swish-gated linear units (SwiGLU) (Shazeer, 2020). Several of these weight matrices form pairs whose scales can be traded against each other without changing the output. For example, attention compares queries and keys through the product (W Q)⊤W K of the query and key matrices, so replacing (W Q, W K) with (cW Q, c−1W K) for any c > 0 leaves every attention score, and hence every prediction, unchanged. We call a pair of matrices (A, B) an exact symmetry pair when replacing the pair with (cA, c−1B) preserves the model’s function for every c > 0. Rescaling the exact symmetry pairs of a model in this way yields a whole set of parameterizations that all compute the same function, which we call a symmetry orbit. These parameterizations represent the same function but lead to different training trajectories. The reason is that the gradients scale inversely to the weights: Multiplying A by c multiplies its gradient by c−1, and multiplying

Standard optimizers already include mechanisms such as adaptive gradient normalization, but these mecha- nisms still do not remove this dependence on the param- eterization. Adam normalizes gradients using moving averages of gradients and squared gradients (Kingma and Ba, 2015), which cancels constant-factor scaling of the gradients: Both models receive the same numerical update (Figure 1(2)). To keep the two models equiva- lent, however, the update of the enlarged matrix would have to be c times larger and the update of its shrunken partner c times smaller. The same update is too small for the enlarged matrix and too large for its shrunken partner. Transforming Adam’s moment estimates along with the weights does not fix this mismatch, because both models still use the same learning rate (Sec. 3). Appendix A discusses in detail how this work relates to and differs from prior studies of rescaling-aware op- timization, weight balancing, and symmetry-induced learning dynamics (Neyshabur et al., 2015; Stock et al., 2019; Kunin et al., 2021). To avoid disrupting optimizer state that has adapted to imbalanced scales, Soft SAGGS applies only a fraction of this correction at each rebalancing step. Both operations leave the current function un- changed and only rebalance the weights from which training continues. SAGGS also gives an exact restart procedure: Applied together with a matching trans- formation of the moment estimates, SAGGS moves any two checkpoints on the same symmetry orbit to the same balanced state, from which training follows the same trajectory (Corollary 4). Proofs for this section are in Appendix C. 4 SAGGS REBALANCING No standard optimizer keeps two equivalent models equivalent under a shared learning rate (Theorem 5); thus, the position of a model on its orbit affects training. SAGGS leaves the optimizer unchanged and instead periodically moves the model along its orbit to the balanced point, where the two matrices of each exact pair have equal Frobenius norms (Proposition 1). The current function stays the same, and training continues from balanced pairs. Hard SAGGS makes this move at once (Sec. 4.1); its damped variant, Soft SAGGS, makes only part of the move at each rebalance so as not to disrupt optimizer state that has adapted to the imbalance (Sec. 4.2). 4.1 Hard SAGGS Hard SAGGS applies the balancing map of Proposi- tion 1 to every exact pair once every Tbal optimization steps (Algorithm 1). Each application shrinks the larger matrix of a pair and enlarges the smaller one by the same factor, so that both norms become the geometric mean of the two; in Figure 1(4), the rectangle becomes a square of the same area. The case studies also test canonical restart on GPT-2 774M, fine-tuned from the released check- point and from an exact Q–K edit of this checkpoint: Canonicalizing both checkpoints at restart makes the two runs identical, whereas without canonicalization the edited run predicts a different top-1 token than the canonicalized runs at 7.3% of held-out positions after 200 updates. Appendix D gives the training configurations, hardware, and seed protocol, and Appendix E defines the paired statistics, states their test assumptions, and separates primary from supporting comparisons. Appendix F gives the full protocols, tables, and paired contrasts for Secs. 5.2 and 5.3, together with optimizer-state diagnos- tics for reset and stale moments.

text: Even two Transformers that represent the same func- tion can train differently. Our analysis characterizes exact AdamW equivariance, identifies the obstruction for standard block-local updates, and establishes exact restart equivalence through canonicalization of weights and moments. SAGGS and Soft SAGGS provide simple function-preserving corrections for pair-scale imbalance. The normalization layers of a Transformer, weight de- cay, and gradient clipping do not restore pair balance (Appendix H). A rebalance rescales each pair only as much as the pair is imbalanced, so rebalancing can be kept on throughout training. Across paired language- model experiments and checkpoint-resume workflows, these corrections recover the performance lost to this imbalance, in particular after an exact orbit edit. These findings show that the pair-scale imbalance introduced by a parameterization strongly affects training, whether training starts from initialization or resumes from a checkpoint.

text: Parameterization and initialization. Variance-preserving initialization (Glorot and Bengio, 2010; He et al., 2015) fixes a single scale at the start of training. The Maximal Update Parametrization (µP) of Yang et al. (2021) provides a principled framework for hyperparameter transfer across widths. T-Fixup (Huang et al., 2020) instead rescales residual branches so that deep Transformers can be trained more stably at a fixed width. Our work is complementary: µP governs how to scale across widths, and T-Fixup chooses a particular residual scale, while reparameterization symmetry reveals a continuous family of forward-equivalent configurations at fixed width and depth. Weight normalization and reparameterization. Weight normalization (WeightNorm) (Salimans and Kingma, 2016) decouples the direction and magnitude of weight vectors, implicitly addressing some scale ambiguities. Dinh et al. (2017) explicitly derive the inverse gradient-coordinate law under function-preserving reciprocal rescaling. We use that law as background for the full-state optimizer analysis. Neyshabur et al. (2015) introduced path-regularization to account for rescaling invariances in ReLU networks. Transformer-NFN (Tran et al., 2025) characterizes more general matrix symmetries of multi-head attention; the scalar Q–K and V–O rescalings used here are special cases. Our focus is the response of first-order optimizer states and resumed trajectories to these edits. SAGGS instead selects the Frobenius-balanced representative of an exact scalar pair orbit. SAGGS is a coordinate change on the symmetry orbit, whereas practical optimizers also maintain state variables. To separate the effect of the orbit move from the possible perturbation of optimizer state, we also evaluate a state-covariant variant. If a rebalance applies A′ := A/c and B′ := cB, then the data-gradient coordinates transform as ∇A′L = c∇AL and ∇B′L = c−1∇BL. Accordingly, for an Adam-family first-moment buffer or a Lion momentum buffer (mA, mB) we map m′ A := cmA and m′ B := c−1mB, and for Adam-family second-moment estimates (vA, vB) we map v′ A := c2vA and v′ B := c−2vB. By default, both hard and Soft SAGGS leave the optimizer buffers unchanged, so neither method needs access to the internal state of the optimizer. We use the state-covariant variant only as a diagnostic: In the Lion state ablation (Appendix F.5), this variant measures how leaving Lion’s momentum buffer in the old coordinates affects the cost of hard rebalancing. At interval Tbal, this rebalancing adds amortized work of O((nA +nB)/Tbal) per pair per optimization step. With full-layer Q–K, V–O, and MLP pairs there are 3L pairs; independent headwise Q–K and V–O pairs give (2H + 1)L for standard H-head attention. Interaction with weight decay. A common decoupled decay factor multiplies both matrices equally and leaves their norm ratio unchanged (Zhang et al., 2019). The one-step balance-defect recursion in Eq. 22 records the contribution of this decay factor; we discuss the measured drift in Appendix H.3. Numerical skip guard. The implementation skips a pair when either norm is below δskip := 10−12, whereas Algorithm 1 states the ideal positive-norm map. For a scheduled soft event k with positive norms, let rk := log(∥A∥F / ∥B∥F) before the event and let zk be the log-ratio afterward. The implemented correction obeys, in exact arithmetic, αeff k := α1{min{∥A∥F , ∥B∥F} ≥δskip}, zk = (1 −αeff k )rk. (25) A skipped positive-norm pair has zk = rk, so the hard canonicalizer and fixed-α contraction identities apply to executed corrections.
