text: Motivation. The 123.8M scale replication in Appendix G.15 measures sensitivity to orbit imbalance at initialization. We now test a checkpoint-resume setting in which weights are edited and training continues with a fresh optimizer. For each seed, one shared phase-1 checkpoint is cloned into four continuation branches, isolating the effect of the edit and subsequent rebalancing. Design. For each of the seven paired seeds, we train the same RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, and GQA T5 SentencePiece model used in the 123.8M scale replication for 10K normal WikiText-103 AdamW steps. We then reset the optimizer and branch into four 5K-step resumes: control, surgery without SAGGS, surgery with hard SAGGS, and surgery with Soft SAGGS. The non-control branches receive an exact all-pairs λ = 0.2 orbit surgery at the handoff; the SAGGS branches then rebalance Q–K, V–O, and SwiGLU value–output pairs every 50 steps. Hard SAGGS applies an initial exact rebalance at the handoff; Soft SAGGS applies α = 0.5 at the handoff and during the resume. The optimizer state is deliberately not carried across the handoff. Each phase uses a fresh cosine schedule with 10% warmup: 1K steps in phase 1 and 500 steps in phase 2. The base learning rate, weight decay, batch size, context length, and precision match the 123.8M scale replication. The handoff uses an exact symmetry edit: Across all

H FURTHER DISCUSSION The results distinguish invariance of the current function from equivariance of an optimizer trajectory. Standard adaptive and sign-based rules can cancel gradient scales while retaining a dependence on parameter scales. Transforming moments alone does not correct the update-scaling mismatch under shared hyperparameters. Full-state canonicalization addresses this dependence at restart by bringing orbit-related checkpoints to the same numerical state. Periodic rebalancing serves a different practical role: controlling pair-scale imbalance as training proceeds. Its strongest measured benefits occur after deliberately imposed rescaling, including the checkpoint-resume workflows. Imbalance also arises naturally, in both trained-from-scratch and public models, and rebalancing can be kept on throughout training to control this imbalance: A rebalance rescales each pair only as much as the pair is imbalanced, correcting a large imbalance and leaving pairs that are already close to balance almost untouched. Soft SAGGS brings the same control to Lion, whose update depends on a momentum buffer of past gradients: Soft SAGGS leaves the optimizer state unchanged
title: Same Function, Different Trajectory

text: correcting a large imbalance and leaving pairs that are already close to balance almost untouched. Soft SAGGS brings the same control to Lion, whose update depends on a momentum buffer of past gradients: Soft SAGGS leaves the optimizer state unchanged and applies the correction in several smaller steps, so the update changes gradually, and training recovers from the degradation caused by an edit. The normalization layers of a Transformer, either layer normalization or RMSNorm, do not remove the pair symmetries, because these layers act on the residual stream rather than on the paired matrices. Global gradient clipping rescales all gradients by one common factor, set by their total norm, so the gradients enlarged by an orbit edit can shrink the gradients of all other blocks. The following subsections expand on this discussion, covering adaptive and sign-based optimizers, natural drift and weight decay, initialization, and training stability. H.1 Adaptive Normalization and Trajectory Equivariance Adam and AdamW normalize gradients using per-parameter moment estimates. With covariantly transformed moments and ϵ = 0, their normalized directions are unchanged by reciprocal rescaling. Equivariance requires the parameter displacements to scale with the parameters, which a shared learning rate does not provide (Theorem 2). Theorem 5 extends this obstruction to the standard block-local rules considered here. For ideal degree-zero rules on corresponding histories, Corollary 6 shows that the distortion in the log-ratio of relative data updates is half the distortion of gradient descent. This factor concerns the data-update term under the stated assumptions; full increments can also reflect weight decay, a fixed positive ϵ, and differences in clipping. Theorem 2 supplies a mechanism for a residual surgery gap even with correctly transformed moments. The depth and λ sweeps measure the training response, while the state-preserved, stale-state, and partial-state experiments (Appendices F.8, F.9, and F.10) examine the additional role of moment history. Adaptive-optimizer qualifications. Reset or stale moments and time-varying orbit moves can break the correspondence between current gradients and past statistics. A fixed positive ϵ must also be transformed according to Theorem 2 to preserve trajectory equivariance. Global gradient clipping generally changes its common clipping multiplier under a nonuniform diagonal rescaling of the gradient. text: Bum Jun Kim I.5 Summary Case studies on public checkpoints complement the paired training comparisons. The case studies show that pair imbalance also arises in ordinary training, to a degree that varies across models and pairs. In Pythia 410M, for example, the query and key matrices start with nearly equal norms, but during pre-training their norms drift apart by a factor of up to about 6 in deep layers, which corresponds to a log-norm ratio of 1.86. The case studies also test canonical restart on a released model. We fine-tune GPT-2 774M with fresh AdamW moments, starting from the released checkpoint and from an exact Q–K edit of this checkpoint that maps WQ 7→WQ/8 and WK 7→8WK. Canonicalizing both checkpoints at restart makes the two runs identical, with the same predictions and token NLLs at every evaluation. Without canonicalization, the edited run predicts a different top-1 token than the canonicalized runs at 7.3% of held-out positions after 200 updates. Periodic Soft SAGGS reduces this fraction to 1.1% but not to zero. Canonical restart also works when the moments are kept rather than reset: In a GPT-2 124M case whose edit transforms the moments along with the weights, canonicalizing both weights and moments fully restores the trajectory of the unedited run. text: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM Decisions Already Made Ayoub Merimi and Souhail Bakkali and Abdeljalil Sakat
title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM

text: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the mo- ment it is made; the action it commits to is la- tent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of deci- sion validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a fresh- ness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remain- ing risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to af- fected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision’s times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch con- ditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to fron- tier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on de- cisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger’s index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remain- ing errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out. 1
title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM

text: At 13:05, a user asks an assistant for a walk-in din- ner at 20:30. The assistant chooses Lovage Corner, the best-rated restaurant within walking distance, in the Bellhaven district. At 18:40, the grid op- erator announces emergency works at the Gorran substation from 19:50, leaving every area it sup- plies without power; the Gorran substation supplies the Bellhaven district (Figure 1). The choice was right at 13:05 and is wrong at 20:30. Grey dots are other notices in the window. behind its district. This decision comes from our test streams (Appendix B.1). The example separates two properties of a de- cision. Evidence freshness describes what was known when the choice was made. Action valid- ity describes whether the choice is right when it is carried out. Research on time in language models secures the first: benchmarks track how models age (Lazaridou et al., 2021; Dhingra et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024), test answers against evolving news (Liška et al., 2022; Kasai et al., 2023), and refresh models with search (Vu et al., 2024). This framing fits question answering, where an answer is used the moment it is produced. LLM agents produce de- cisions that are carried out later, such as itineraries (Xie et al., 2024b) and service actions (Yao et al., 2025), and these are judged by the second. This paper develops a theory of action validity and answers the title question: freshness is nec- essary and insufficient. Six timestamps define a decision, from when its evidence is written to when its outcome is judged. A freshness ceiling shows 1 arXiv:2610.18126v1 [cs.AI] 13 Oct 2026

text: that, under a constant rate of change, the probabil- ity that evidence still holds when the user acts is bounded by the execution gap between deciding and acting, whatever the freshness at decision time. The remaining risk lies in information published inside that gap. Decision accuracy then factorises into routing, whether that information reaches the decision before its revision deadline, and judgment, whether the model reads it correctly for the time of action (Section 3). The theory comes with a model of the system that realises it. A decision ledger is persistent state (Bakkali and Merimi, 2026) that stores each deci- sion with its times, its evidence and its background knowledge, and a router delivers each new item to the open decisions it matches (Section 4). A query retrieves what the user asks about today; a ledger retrieves what yesterday’s decisions still need. The ledger also makes the theory testable: what a router can reach follows from what the ledger indexes, and what the model does with a delivered item follows from its judgment. We derive four predictions and test them in con- trolled decision streams, in which every label fol- lows from timestamps and stated facts, under three conditions that vary how news refers to a deci- sion and how hard its negatives are: decisive news that names the

The tests confirm all four predictions across five LLMs, from Ministral 8B to GPT-6.1 Sol. • P1, the freshness ceiling holds. With perfect evidence at decision time and nothing after- wards, accuracy equals the share of decisions that should stand. • P2, delivery is sufficient for change. Once decisive news arrives, models switch in 91– 100% of cases under every router, so the ac- curacy of changing decisions tracks routing recall, and recall follows the ledger’s index: the decision text reaches 37.5% of news that uses another name for a dependency, and back- ground knowledge in the ledger reaches all of it. • P3, misleading deliveries cost correct de- cisions. Every misleading item delivered is a chance to abandon a decision that should stand. Watch conditions written at decision time reach 92.2% of decisive news with 20 misleading deliveries against 89 for the whole background, and broadcasting helps only mod- els that judge well. •

This is a theory paper with controlled empiri- cal tests. It contributes a temporal theory of LLM decisions with a freshness ceiling and a routing– judgment factorisation (Section 3), the decision ledger as a model of the system that realises it, including watch conditions (Section 4), and con- trolled tests that confirm the theory’s predictions across five models (Sections 5–7). 2

text: Freshness and temporal knowledge. Language models degrade on text written after their training data (Lazaridou et al., 2021) and can be probed and refreshed for time-dependent facts (Dhingra et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024). Benchmarks over evolving news and time-sensitive questions test whether answers are current (Chen et al., 2021; Liška et al., 2022; Kasai et al., 2023), search aug- mentation keeps them current (Lewis et al., 2020; Vu et al., 2024), and evaluation sets themselves go stale as facts change (Jiang et al., 2026). Temporal reasoning benchmarks test ordering and arithmetic over time (Fatemi et al., 2025). These works judge the model when it answers; we judge a decision when it is carried out. Updates, conflicts and revision. Knowledge editing changes stored facts (Meng et al., 2022), and multi-hop and ripple-effect evaluations require an update to reach every fact that depends on it (Zhong et al., 2023; Cohen et al., 2024). Models re- solve conflicts between parametric and contextual knowledge unevenly (Xie et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2024), including conflicts that arise while agents act (Lyu et al., 2026), and revise conclusions under new premises with mixed success (Kassner et al., 2021; Wilie et al., 2024). Post-decision routing carries the ripple-effect requirement to decisions: a new fact must reach every open decision that 2

Agent benchmarks evaluate plans and actions executed after reasoning (Yao et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024b; Yao et al., 2025). Time-aware simulations score how agents sched- ule work (Zhang et al., 2024), and agents misjudge when elapsed time calls for fresh tool calls (Cheng et al., 2026). Proactive agents decide when to in- tervene (Lu et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Xiaohongshu Dots Studio and Evolvent AI, 2026), maintain long-term intents through trigger conditions (Shi et al., 2026), and accept user correc- tions during execution (Zhai et al., 2026). We study many concurrent decisions with revision deadlines, a shared stream of world news, and the cost of deciding which news reaches which decision. Memory and retrieval. Agent memories store and retrieve past interactions (Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), invalidate outdated facts in temporal graphs (Rasmussen et al., 2025), index memories by time and topic (Tian et al., 2026), and are evaluated on long-term recall (Wu et al., 2025; Du, 2026). Evidence is written at tw and last verified at tv. The model decides at td with evidence verified at tv ≤td. The decision can be revised until the revision deadline tr, is carried out at ta, and its outcome is observed at te, with td < tr ≤ta ≤te. text: The freshness ceiling. Let s(t) be the state of the world and U(a, s) the utility of action a in state s. The model chooses ˆa at td, and the outcome is U(ˆa, s(ta)), so the target is the best action at ta. The age of the evidence at action time decomposes as ta −tv = (td −tv) | {z } ∆fresh + (ta −td) | {z } ∆act . (1) Retrieval and knowledge updates shrink the fresh- ness gap ∆fresh; the execution gap ∆act is set by the task. If a fact f changes at a constant hazard rate λf, it still holds τ time units after verification with probability e−λfτ, so Pr[f holds at ta] = e−λf∆fresh e−λf∆act. (2) Proposition 1 (Freshness ceiling). For any fact f and execution gap ∆act, the probability that f holds at action time is at most e−λf∆act, for every degree of freshness. Appendix A proves the proposition and extends it to decisions with several dependencies. Fresh- ness is a property of the evidence; validity at action time is a property of the whole pipeline. Post-decision routing. A ledger holds open de- cisions. Decision i has a chosen option ai, alter- natives, evidence Ei, times ti d < ti r ≤ti a and an activity [ti a, ti a + hi]. A stream delivers items xj, each written and published at tj w. Item j is deci- sive for decision i if it is published in the revision window, ti d < tj w < ti r, concerns ai or an entity ai depends on, and blocks ai over an interval Ij that overlaps the activity, so that ai stops being the best option. An item about ai or its dependencies that is not decisive is related: a change outside the activity, or news that leaves ai usable. Routing uses no model calls; the model is called again only for decisions that receive news. What the entry indexes sets what the router can reach. Routing sets ρ and the items each decision sees; judgment sets S, L and K (Appendix A derives Eq. 3 and the trade-off between routers it implies). A routing failure leaves a decision stale; a judg- ment failure ignores decisive news or abandons a decision that should stand. A decisive item reaches the chosen option in one of four ways: it names the option (Lovage Corner), the dependency stated in the evidence (the Bellhaven district), another name for that dependency (Chime Green, as the district is known locally), or an entity upstream of it (the Gorran substation, which supplies the dis- trict). The theory makes four predictions. P1: without post-decision routing (ρ = 0, L = 0, K = 1), accuracy equals 1 −π, the share of de- cisions that should stand, for every model. P2: delivery is sufficient for change (S ≈1), so the accuracy of changing decisions tracks ρ, and ρ is set by whether the router’s index contains the entity a decisive item names. P3: each misleading item delivered lowers K at a rate set by the model’s judg- ment, so routers trade recall against exposure, and broadcasting, which maximises both, helps only models that judge well. P4: with oracle routing (ρ = 1, every related item and nothing else), the residual error concentrates on temporal judgment: deciding whether Ij overlaps the activity. 4 The Decision Ledger Each ledger entry is persistent state that outlives the session in which the decision was made (Bakkali and Merimi, 2026). When the model decides at td, it writes the entry: the chosen option and its alter- natives, the action time ta, the revision deadline tr, the evidence about the chosen option, and a dossier of background facts, such as other names of the en- tities the

In deployment, the dossier holds what the assistant looked up while deciding, in- cluding much that is irrelevant to the user’s activity. When an item xj is published, a router scores the open entries and sends the item to the K highest- scoring ones. At the revision deadline, the model reads the entry and the routed items in order of publication and keeps or switches. Decisions that receive no items keep their choice without a model call. Routers differ in what they index, which by P2 sets what they can reach. Decision text. The decision text is expanded with every dossier fact, reaching news about other names and upstream entities together with news about everything else the dossier mentions. Watch conditions. text: with every dossier fact, reaching news about other names and upstream entities together with news about everything else the dossier mentions. Watch conditions. At td, the model reads the entry and writes three to eight conditions wi1, . . . , wik describing events that would stop the user’s activity. The conditions name every entity the activity depends on, including other names and upstream entities, and leave out what the user does not need (Appendix C). The router in- dexes the decision text with the conditions (BM25) or scores each decision by its best condition, maxk cos(e(xj), e(wik)), with a sentence encoder e. Watch conditions are document expansion (Nogueira et al., 2019) performed once, at write time, by the component that knows why the option was chosen; by P3 they should match the dossier’s reach with less exposure. Time filter. A rule drops an item for a decision when the item states a start time after the deci- sion’s activity ends, performing by rule the tempo- ral check of P4. 5 Controlled Decision Streams Testing the predictions requires exact control over which items are decisive, how they refer to the option, and when changes take effect. Real logs offer none of this, and real entities let models an- swer from memory. We therefore generate fictional 4

text: decisions and news streams in which every label follows from timestamps and stated facts; the gen- erator and data are released with the paper. Decisions and labels. Each decision has two options. Option 1 is better at td (higher rating, lower price, faster journey, better views) and is the model’s initial choice; option 2 is acceptable but worse. Option 1 depends on an entity named in its evidence: a district, a rail operator, a sales or permit platform, a mountain range or a shopping centre. Lags between deciding and acting range from three hours to three days, and revision deadlines precede the action by 0.5 to 2 hours. A decision’s gold answer is option 2 if some item published in its re- vision window targets option 1, its dependency or an entity upstream of it and blocks option 1 during the activity, and option 1 otherwise. The genera- tor excludes decisions invalidated before they were made and asserts every label (Appendix B). Three conditions. Each condition stresses a dif- ferent part of the theory. DIRECT measures every term of Eq. 3 with an open model; STRESS adds hard negatives that name the option, testing expo- sure (P3) and temporal judgment (P4); INDIRECT moves the reference from the decision text into background knowledge, testing whether the index sets recall (P2). DIRECT spans five domains with independent random news per decision: a decisive item (p=0.5) that names the option or its stated de- pendency, a late item (p=0.3) that blocks the option only after the activity, a harmless item (p=0.5), and two unrelated items. STRESS adds, for every deci- sion, a same-name decoy, a blocking notice about a different entity whose name extends the option’s (“Clove Fork Annex”), and, each with probability 0.85, a late and a harmless notice naming the op- tion itself; eleven rules paraphrase event wording. INDIRECT spans four domains and fixes every pro- portion. Half of the decisions should switch, and their decisive notice uses each of the four ways of reference for 16 decisions; only the first two match the decision text. The other half should stand and receive one of four hard negatives, each for 16 de- cisions: a change that starts after the activity, a change that is over before it starts, harmless news, and a disruption to a facility the user does not need (a tram line for a user who walks). The controlled tests confirm each prediction: freshness alone leaves changing decisions stale, delivery is sufficient for change and recall follows what the ledger indexes, misleading deliveries cost correct decisions in proportion to weak judgment, and the residual error is mostly temporal. The theory yields three design princi- ples for LLM agents: record each decision with its times and what it depends on; route news to it until its revision deadline, through an index written when the decision is made; and revalidate it by checking when each change is in effect. Limitations Controlled streams. The decision streams are synthetic by design: exact control over timing, ref- erence and labels is what lets each prediction be tested in isolation. Real news is longer and nois- ier, dependencies can be implicit, and relevance can be uncertain, so the magnitudes we report be- long to these streams while the predictions concern mechanisms. Testing the theory on logged agent decisions, and in languages beyond English, is the next step. Scope of the theory. The theory models a deci- sion as a choice among options with one revision deadline and a binary outcome, and the freshness ceiling assumes a constant hazard rate. Real com- mitments are staged, partly reversible and graded in utility, and facts change in bursts. The factori- sation of Eq. 3 carries over, because information must reach a decision before it can change it, but its terms then depend on time and on the cost of revising. Reach of the ledger. Routing recall is bounded by the dependencies the ledger records at decision time, and the ledger treats routed news as trustwor- thy. Discovering dependencies after the decision and weighing the credibility of sources extend the ledger beyond this paper. Ethics Statement The decision streams use fictional entities and con- tain no personal data, and hosted models were queried on this synthetic data only. Systems that revise decisions on a user’s behalf can act on false or adversarial news; routing should be paired with source verification and, for consequential decisions, with user confirmation.

System Two uses GPT to plan searches and integrate findings into answers or rankings. System One uses Jev to guide parallel evidence inspection and return source passages; the dashed loop indicates adaptive reading.
title: JevGPT: Thinking Fast and Slow in Autonomous Research

text: Autonomous research agents must acquire and reason over evidence within a limited budget. Yet relevant sources can remain uninspected or unused, leaving a gap between retrieval cov- erage and the evidence that informs research. The challenge is to align fast local judgments with changing evidence needs and feed their findings back into research decisions. We intro- duce JevGPT, a dual-system architecture for autonomous research that couples fast evidence processing with deliberative research planning. System Two sets evidence objectives and in- tegrates findings, while System One locates support, assesses relevance, and guides further inspection. Independent source judgments run in parallel; selected original passages inform the next research step. Experiments on fixed- corpus question answering and document rank- ing show that JevGPT achieves leading task performance, with faster completion and lower cost than comparably effective research agents. Evidence analysis shows broader source inspec- tion and greater coverage of supporting docu- ments in the research loop, highlighting effi- cient evidence processing as a route to more capable autonomous research. 1
title: JevGPT: Thinking Fast and Slow in Autonomous Research

text: Language models equipped with retrieval and tool use have enabled autonomous agents to investi- gate questions using external evidence (Lewis et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2023). In autonomous research, an agent searches for sources, follows emerging leads, and synthesizes findings into an answer or a document ranking. Interleaving retrieval and rea- soning allows intermediate findings to shape subse- quent searches (Trivedi et al., 2023), requiring the agent to coordinate research planning with repeated source inspection. The capability of such an agent depends on how it allocates a limited research budget. Each search exposes candidate sources that must be inspected before their contents can inform further decisions. Time spent assessing these sources affects how many leads the agent can pursue and how much support it can gather. Efficient evidence process- ing therefore offers an opportunity to expand the evidence available for reasoning and support more capable research. Yet retrieval coverage does not ensure evidence use. Recent work on agentic search finds that in- 1 arXiv:2610.18272v1 [cs.CL] 13 Oct 2026

Relevant sources can thus be available with- out contributing to subsequent research decisions. Fast judgment models offer a way to make re- peated source assessments more efficient (Almeida, 2026). Prior systems separate document processing from research reasoning (Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). The challenge here is to make fast local judgments guide evidence acquisition throughout an evolving investigation. This requires inspect- ing many sources within budget while adapting to changing evidence needs; a partial finding may redirect search or reading. Our key observation is that research planning and local evidence judgments require different scopes of information. Planning uses the accumu- lated investigation, whereas a source judgment can be bounded by an explicit evidence objective. Inde- pendent judgments under that objective can run in parallel, while their findings return

text: local evidence judgments require different scopes of information. Planning uses the accumu- lated investigation, whereas a source judgment can be bounded by an explicit evidence objective. Inde- pendent judgments under that objective can run in parallel, while their findings return to the research process to inform the next objective. We introduce JevGPT, a dual-system architec- ture for autonomous research illustrated in Figure 1. System Two sets evidence objectives and integrates findings. Jev (Almeida, 2026) serves as System One, guiding source selection, passage localiza- tion, and continued reading; proactive discovery inspects additional candidates. Selected original passages return to System Two, connecting these local decisions to the next research action and the final answer or ranking. Experiments on BrowseComp-Plus and Neu- CLIRBench (Chen et al., 2026; Lawrie et al., 2025) cover fixed-corpus question answering and document ranking. Figure 2 shows that JevGPT achieves leading task performance at lower cost than comparably effective research agents. JevGPT also completes research faster. Evidence analysis and an ablation study examine how the architecture turns retrieved sources into useful evidence and how its components affect task performance. 2

text: Agentic Search and Autonomous Research. Autonomous research combines search, source in- spection, and evidence integration. Schmidhu- ber (2015) proposed a reinforcement learning con- troller that queries a recurrent world model for reasoning and planning. ReAct and IRCoT in- terleave reasoning with external information ac- cess (Yao et al., 2023; Trivedi et al., 2023), while Search-R1 learns to search through reinforcement learning (Jin et al., 2025). WriteHERE interleaves recursive planning and execution across retrieval, reasoning, and composition (Xiong et al., 2025). In fixed-corpus research, BCP/ReAct provides a tool loop (Chen et al., 2026); Pi-Serini separates retrieval, browsing, and document reading (Hsu et al., 2026). RISE exposes a bounded document workspace (Zhuang et al., 2026), while AtlasNav provides persistent corpus navigation (Guo et al., 2026). JevGPT connects local source judgments to subsequent research decisions. Dual-System Reasoning and Collaboration. Dual-process accounts distinguish fast, intu- itive judgments from slower, deliberative reason- ing (Kahneman, 2011). History compression con- solidates recurrent predictors (Schmidhuber, 1992); One Big Net extends this principle to control and prediction skills (Schmidhuber, 2018). Model cascades and routers allocate computation across models to balance quality and cost (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025). AVI-Talking uses LLM- generated instructions to guide a specialized facial synthesis model (Sun et al., 2024), while SciDia- gramEdit coordinates editor, judge, and coach roles to evolve diagram

BM25 and RM3 supply lexical retrieval and relevance feed- back (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009; Lavrenko and Croft, 2001), while Reason-ColBERT uses late interaction (Chaffin and Sourty, 2025). RankGPT and Qwen3-Reranker rerank candidates (Sun et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). Self-RAG adapts re- trieval and generation through reflection (Asai et al., 2024), while CRAG uses a lightweight evaluator to trigger corrective retrieval (Yan et al., 2024). JevGPT uses explicit evidence requests to guide passage selection, further candidate inspection, and surrounding-context reading. 3 Method Given a question or topic, an autonomous research agent gathers evidence from a fixed corpus to pro- duce an answer or document ranking. In the re- search loop of Figure 3, System Two plans searches, requests evidence, and integrates findings. System One assesses sources against these requests and guides further reading. Readers return selected original passages to inform subsequent research actions and the final output. 3.1 Problem Formulation An item is a question or topic q over a fixed cor- pus D. text: full topic; the region contains original text blocks and their source coordinates. We use Jev’s three output types (Almeida, 2026). A Noul judgment returns the probability that re- gion r satisfies a stated property, such as contain- ing relevant evidence. A Choice judgment returns a distribution over a finite set of options, such as source blocks or reading actions. A Score judgment returns a distribution over ordinal levels. The spec- ified objective and output type bound each source judgment. 3.2 System Two: Research Loop System Two turns an unresolved aspect of the task into a search query or evidence request. Retrieval supplies ranked candidates; an evidence request selects sources and asks System One to assess them against the requested objective. Evidence requests spec- ify Ct and ut; after a search, discovery uses the original task and eligible top-K candidates, return- ing findings asynchronously. Selected leads carry original excerpts and en- ter the research history asynchronously, informing subsequent source inspection or query refinement. 4 Experiments We examine whether coupling fast local evidence judgments with research planning improves the quality and efficiency of autonomous research. We first compare final task performance and resource use, then examine the evidence available during research, component contributions, and model choices. 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate factual question answer- ing on all 830 BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2026) questions and document ranking on all 105 NeuCLIRBench (Lawrie et al., 2025) topics. These tasks require locating answer evidence and assess- ing document relevance, respectively. NeuCLIR- Bench uses English queries and English document translations. Baselines. On BrowseComp-Plus, we compare with six agent configurations: BCP/ReAct (Chen et al., 2026), Reason-ColBERT (Chaffin and Sourty, 2025), Pi-Serini (Hsu et al., 2026), Agen- tica (Symbolica, 2025), AtlasNav (Guo et al., 2026), and RISE (Zhuang et al., 2026). NeuCLIR- Bench comparisons cover retrieval, reranking, and research agents adapted for document ranking.

text: The main GPT-based comparisons use GPT-5.5 at medium reasoning effort. JevGPT pairs it as System Two with Jev as System One under a 300-second research budget, following Pi- Serini’s time-budget protocol (Hsu et al., 2026). We report answer accuracy for BrowseComp-Plus and nDCG@20 and F1@20 for NeuCLIRBench. Efficiency is measured by elapsed time, System Two token usage, search counts, and total API cost across both systems.1 4.2 Quantitative Results BrowseComp-Plus. JevGPT achieves the high- est observed accuracy in Table 1, while completing research faster and making fewer searches than the compared agents. Its API cost is also lower than that of comparably accurate methods such as Reason-ColBERT, RISE, and AtlasNav. Pi-Serini remains cheaper but produces less accurate an- swers. NeuCLIRBench. JevGPT also achieves the high- est observed ranking quality on both metrics in Ta- ble 2. Relative to Pi-Serini, the strongest research baseline on this task, it uses substantially fewer System Two tokens and finishes sooner. Local judgments contribute little to API spending, and total cost remains the lowest among the GPT-based methods. These results extend the benefits of lo- cal evidence judgments from answer generation to document ranking. 4.3 Evidence Analysis Evidence Acquisition. text: Limitations This work studies the coordination of fast and slow thinking at the level of agent architecture. JevGPT assigns local evidence judgments and research plan- ning to separate components. A natural next step is to integrate these capabilities within a unified model that learns when to make rapid local judg- ments and when to engage in extended reasoning. Joint training could allow the model to adapt this balance to the evolving needs of an investigation and allocate computation accordingly. Our evaluation focuses on question answering and document ranking over fixed corpora. Extend- ing this approach to open-web research and long- form synthesis would help explore how fast and slow thinking can support a broader range of re- search tasks. Ethical Considerations Data and Intended Use. We use the publicly released BrowseComp-Plus and NeuCLIRBench benchmarks and their fixed corpora for research evaluation. We collect no additional source data, involve no human participants or annotators, and do not redistribute either corpus. Research agents may reproduce errors and biases in retrieved sources. JevGPT returns original passages with source loca- tions to support evidence inspection. Source relia- bility still requires independent assessment. Use of AI Assistants. text: Appendix A Experimental Details A.1 Implementation The main configuration uses GPT-5.5 with medium reasoning effort as System Two and Jev-1.13.0 as System One. Each task has a 300-second research budget and a submission reminder at 210 seconds. Evidence memory is maintained separately for each question or topic. Candidate Retrieval. On both benchmarks, pas- sages contain a title and up to 250 body words, and min-max normalization maps constant score lists to zero. On BrowseComp-Plus, document and passage BM25 each return 1,000 hits, using (k1, b) = (25, 1) and (0.9, 0.4), respectively. Fu- sion ranks the union of their parent documents, with a missing score component set to zero. The ranked documents then form retrieval units: doc- uments of at most 8,000 UTF-16 code units re- main whole, while longer documents contribute up to two ranked passages. On NeuCLIRBench, passage scores refine the top 500 document can- didates, with both document and passage BM25 using (k1, b) = (0.9, 0.4). Passage scoring uses document-level inverse document frequency and a mean passage length of 144.7 analyzed tokens. Each document remains one retrieval unit. Evidence Processing. When scanning a candi- date ranking, the reader inspects retrieval units in batches of ten, up to 60 units per request. Ex- plicitly named QA sources form the initial batch. Local judgments run in parallel across

text: retrieval unit. Evidence Processing. When scanning a candi- date ranking, the reader inspects retrieval units in batches of ten, up to 60 units per request. Ex- plicitly named QA sources form the initial batch. Local judgments run in parallel across source re- gions for QA and across documents for ranking; regions within a ranking document are read sequen- tially. QA uses up to 16 overlapping regions per retrieval unit, each covering at most 60,000 UTF-8 bytes of source text. For ranking, source pages are text excerpts of at most 4,000 UTF-16 code units; consecutive pages form regions containing at most 48,000 UTF-8 bytes of source text. Each response includes at most 100,000 UTF-16 code units of source text and preserves original source coordinates. For QA, evidence localization uses up to six lo- cal evidence questions supplied by System Two. For each question, the reader estimates whether a source region contains information addressing it. A region qualifies for evidence selection when this probability reaches τloc = 0.5 in Equation 6. Within a qualifying region, the reader selects the original block with the highest Choice probability. If that probability is below 0.8, it also selects the second most probable block, provided that the sec- ond block’s probability is at least 0.15. Adaptive reading can add up to two pages of surrounding context

text: the highest Choice probability. If that probability is below 0.8, it also selects the second most probable block, provided that the sec- ond block’s probability is at least 0.15. Adaptive reading can add up to two pages of surrounding context before reassessing whether the requested questions are supported. For ranking, relevance assessment first reuses completed document judgments. When scanning a candidate ranking, continuation judgments begin after twenty candidates requiring fresh assessment and are repeated after each later batch. This judg- ment estimates whether further inspection will find additional relevant documents; the reader contin- ues if that probability is at least 0.5. Fully assessed documents are retained when their probability of being relevant or highly relevant reaches θ = 0.25 in Equation 7. Incompletely assessed candidates remain eligible. Within retained documents, a page is selected when its probability of being useful for assessing relevance is at least 0.5. Pages without a completed usefulness judgment also remain eligi- ble. If no page is selected, a document meeting the relevance cutoff supplies its best available page. Evidence Discovery. Evidence discovery uses Sys- tem One to assess additional retrieved candidates against the original question or topic while System Two continues its research. We set the candidate inspection depth to K = 60. After each search, the first K retrieval units in its ranking are

text: One to assess additional retrieved candidates against the original question or topic while System Two continues its research. We set the candidate inspection depth to K = 60. After each search, the first K retrieval units in its ranking are eligible for discovery. Units that have already been assessed or scheduled are excluded, without replacement from lower ranks, so the number of newly inspected units can be smaller than K. A new discovery batch starts only when at least 45 seconds remain before the submission reminder. For QA, the branch splits the original question at sentence and clause boundaries into up to six clue statements. Evidence localization identifies pas- sages addressing them. Only sources with at least one located clue are eligible to be returned. Their priority score follows Equation 8: each located clue contributes 1/nj, where nj counts the documents containing that clue in the assessed batch. Sum- ming these contributions combines clue coverage with specificity, giving more weight to clues found in fewer documents. We set τlead = 0.5 and m = 3 in Equation 9, returning at most three sources in descending priority. If no source reaches the cutoff 11

Selected leads are returned with original excerpts through subsequent search, paging, or assessment responses. This asynchronous delivery adds the excerpts to the research history, where System Two can use them to inspect promising sources or refine subsequent queries. A.2

text: The main comparisons use all 830 BrowseComp- Plus questions over 100,195 documents and all 105 NeuCLIRBench topics. The BrowseComp- Plus ablation and System Two model comparisons share 415 questions, selected by taking every sec- ond question ID from the numerically sorted of- ficial set. On NeuCLIRBench, queries combine the English topic title and description and search English machine translations of Persian, Russian, and Chinese documents. The topics comprise 54 from 2023 and 51 from 2024. Gold answers and relevance judgments are used only for evaluation. Answer quality on BrowseComp-Plus is mea- sured by accuracy, using the official grading tem- plate with GPT-5.5 at medium effort. Ranking qual- ity on NeuCLIRBench is measured by nDCG@20 and F1@20. nDCG@20 uses the official relevance gains g ∈{0, 1, 3}, while F1@20 treats documents with g > 0 as relevant and uses 20 as the precision denominator. Unjudged documents receive zero gain. Ranking metrics are computed per topic and then averaged across topics. Failed tasks receive a score of zero. Research budgets are fixed within each study. text: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based Profile Enrichment for Conversational Recommender Systems Erfan Shahabi*1, Amirhossein Roshandel*1, Mohammad Sadegh Sadeghi1, and Azadeh Shakery1,2 1School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, College of Engineering, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran 2Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM), Tehran, Iran {erfanshahabi, roshandel.amir, mhmssadeghi74, shakery}@ut.ac.ir
title: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based

text: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) require reliable user simulators for cost- effective evaluation. LLM-based simulators have made realistic simulation possible but typ- ically condition on profiles derived from ex- plicit ratings, demographics, and static sources capturing surface preferences while omitting implicit behavioral characteristics such as decision-making style, aspect-level preferences, and domain expertise. We propose SimInter, a pipeline that elicits these attributes via syn- thetic interviews between two LLM agents, grounded in the user’s statistical profile and his- torical conversational evidence. Before profile enrichment, an audit agent explicitly flags po- tential fabrication and stereotyping at the turn level. We instantiate and evaluate SimInter on movie recommendation. We simulate 300 Re- Dial users and, on a matched subset of 100 users, compare SimInter with a statistics-only baseline: SimInter significantly increases the diversity of expressed preference aspects (fil- tered aspect entropy: 1.619 vs. 0.859; paired d = 0.96, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). This gain persists when the simulator converses with two trained recommenders, KBRD and Uni- CRS, under two independent evaluation judges (+0.28 to +0.56 nats; all p < 0.001). Human evaluation finds 94.3% of enriched-attribute claims supported or partially supported, while human judgments agree with 95.2% of the au- ditor’s binary filtering decisions on a stratified sample. 1
title: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based

text: Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) have become a primary interface for content dis- covery (Fu et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2012), but their evaluation remains difficult: studies with real users are expensive, slow, and rarely reproducible, with outcomes depending on the specific sample *Equal contribution, ordered randomly. recruited (Zhu et al., 2024a). User simulation has emerged as a complementary methodology in which artificial users interact with a CRS in place of humans, enabling controlled, repeatable exper- imentation at scale (Balog and Zhai, 2025; Zhu et al., 2024b). Early simulators were rule-based or agenda- based (Ruß et al., 2012; Afzali et al., 2023), of- fering controllability at the cost of behavioral real- ism. Large language models (LLMs) have changed this picture, but LLM-based simulators still exhibit characteristic failure modes: repetitive responses, narrow choice ranges, binary reactions, and drift to- ward generic “average user” behavior (Yoon et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024a). We argue that an impor- tant source of these limitations is the user profile that conditions the simulator. The profile bottleneck. Most LLM-based simu- lators condition generation on profiles built from observable signals: ratings, interaction histories, and demographic attributes. Such profiles capture what a user has consumed but leave largely unspec- ified how the user makes choices: whether they satisfice or maximize, whether their choices are driven by mood
title: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based

text: built from observable signals: ratings, interaction histories, and demographic attributes. Such profiles capture what a user has consumed but leave largely unspec- ified how the user makes choices: whether they satisfice or maximize, whether their choices are driven by mood or social context, and how will- ing they are to accept unfamiliar recommendations. These behavioral dispositions strongly shape con- versational behavior yet are precisely what ratings- based profiles omit (Tigunova et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2024). A natural alternative—prompting an LLM to infer behavioral attributes from a static profile—has a known failure mode: LLMs tend to produce stereotyped inferences, inflating apparent profile richness while reducing individual fidelity. The same risk applies to self-play dialogue, where two agents can amplify rather than reveal latent attributes, fabricating plausible-sounding traits not grounded in actual behavior. Our approach. We propose SimInter, which de- rives behavioral attributes from synthetic dialogue 1 arXiv:2610.18308v1 [cs.CL] 13 Oct 2026
title: SimInter: Evidence-Grounded User Simulation with Interview-Based

text: while explicitly defending against fabrication via four design choices. (i) Statistical grounding: we first compute behavioral statistics (acceptance rate, reference style, genre distribution, exploration ra- tio) from the user’s interaction history; the syn- thetic dialogue is then conditioned on these statis- tics and the user’s historical conversational evi- dence. (ii) Interview rather than peer dialogue: generation is cast as an asymmetric interview, with the interviewee anchored to the user’s profile and the interviewer as a neutral elicitor probing specific dimensions (Tigunova et al., 2019), preventing mu- tual reinforcement of speculative content. (iii) Turn- level auditing: an Audit Agent flags fabrication, his- tory contradictions, and caricature (generic persona templates and invented rationalizations). Depend- ing on severity, flagged turns are excluded from pro- file enrichment, while structurally compromised di- alogues trigger regeneration. (iv) Evidence-linked enrichment: an LLM agent enriches the user’s sta- tistical profile with attributes extracted from the audited interview, with each categorical or scored attribute paired with a supporting evidence quote; human annotators verify that 94% of these enriched claims are supported by the interview. Contributions. (1) We identify the profile bot- tleneck in LLM-based user simulation. (2) We propose SimInter, combining statistical grounding, asymmetric interview dialogue, turn-level audit- ing, and evidence-linked profile enrichment; the audit uses a flag taxonomy that distinguishes un- supported claims from invented rationalizations. text: User simulation provides a scalable alternative to human evaluation of conversational recommender systems (CRSs) (Balog and Zhai, 2025; Zhu et al., 2024b; Zhang and Balog, 2020; Bernard and Balog, 2025). Earlier approaches relied on agenda-based control, later extended with neural generation in frameworks such as GenTUS (Afzali et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2022). LLM-based frameworks, includ- ing iEvaLM, enable more flexible interactions but raise concerns about behavioral realism, data leak- age, and controllability (Wang et al., 2023; Yoon et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024a). Recent approaches incorporate richer user mod- els. RecUserSim combines bounded-rationality principles with memory tracking (Chen et al., 2025a); PerCRS uses assigned personality traits (Zhao et al., 2025), while PUB infers Big-Five traits from behavioral logs (Ma et al., 2025). PEARL derives persona knowledge from user re- views (Kim et al., 2024), and CSHI offers control- lable, target-conditioned simulation (Zhu et al., 2024b). Other work investigates LLM-based and user-centric CRS evaluation and parameterized be- havioral traits (Chen et al., 2025b; Jin et al., 2024; Sekuli´c et al., 2024). SimInter differs by eliciting implicit behavioral attributes through synthetic interviews grounded in historical conversational evidence. Unlike pre- defined trait configurations or review-derived per- sonas, SimInter uses user-specific dialogue and au- dits potentially fabricated or stereotyped content before profile enrichment. Table 1 compares these frameworks in terms of datasets, profile sources, available ground truth, target conditioning, reliability mechanisms, evalu- ation objectives, and data requirements. Notably, while CSHI addresses target-item leakage and Per- CRS uses knowledge-graph grounding, SimInter audits interview-derived claims against historical user evidence before profile enrichment. 3 Method Figure 1 illustrates the SimInter pipeline. The method consists of six stages: (1) constructing ba- sic user profiles from historical interactions, (2) ex- tracting behavioral statistics from these profiles, (3) generating synthetic interviews between two LLM-based agents, (4) auditing the generated con- versations with an audit agent, (5) extracting im- plicit user attributes and enriching the profiles, and (6) simulating users interacting with a CRS using their enriched profiles. We instantiate the LLM- based components with Gemini 2.5 Flash (Co- manici et al., 2025) for interview generation and user simulation, Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025) for auditing, Tencent Hy3 (Tencent Hy Team, 2026) for enrichment, and GPT-4o-mini (Achiam et al., 2023) as the CRS the simulated user interacts with. text: Basic User Profiles and Behavioral Statistics Stage 1 (Basic User Profiles). We construct basic user profiles from ReDial (Li et al., 2018), treating each crowdworker as a user across both seeker and recommender roles. Of the 1,112 workers in the 11,348 ReDial dialogues, we retain the 618 with at least two conversations. Each profile contains observed movie preferences (liked, disliked, and implicitly disliked movies, derived from ReDial’s post-conversation questionnaires) and the user’s historical conversations. Stage 2 (Behavioral Statistic Extraction). We augment these profiles with rule-based behavioral statistics derived from historical interactions: ac- ceptance and rejection rates, reference style (genre, mood, actor, director, year), genre and decade dis- tributions, exploration ratio, and popularity score. Together these form a behavioral fingerprint that grounds the synthetic interview. Figure 2 shows an example. Of the 618 profiles, 543 meet our eli- gibility criteria, requiring at least one seeker-role conversation and a nonzero acceptance or implicit- rejection signal. We randomly sample 300 users from this eligible set for the full SimInter pipeline, and randomly select a subset of 100 of these users for matched ablation experiments and comparison with CSHI (§4.1). 3.2 Synthetic Interview Generation Stage 3 (Synthetic Interview Generation). Conversations often contain implicit information that provides deeper insights into users (Tigunova et al., 2019; Torbati et al., 2021). We exploit LLMs’ role-playing capabilities (Wang

Conversations often contain implicit information that provides deeper insights into users (Tigunova et al., 2019; Torbati et al., 2021). We exploit LLMs’ role-playing capabilities (Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024) to simulate interviews between two agents: an interviewee anchored to the user’s pro- file and an interviewer that elicits it. For each of the 300 sampled users, the interviewee agent receives the user’s statistical profile and one historical Re- Dial conversation in which the user acts as a seeker. The interviewer, in contrast, has no access to the profile or the ReDial history; it sees only the ongo- 3

It opens with one of four predefined open-ended questions, chosen at random (e.g., “Walk me through the last movie you really enjoyed — what was it and what stuck with you?”; all four are listed in Appendix J.1), and dynamically adapts its follow-up questions to the interviewee’s responses. Each interview comprises an initial six-turn elicitation phase followed by four clarification turns, for a total of 10 turns. Figure 3 shows an example; full system prompts are in Ap- pendix J. 3.3 Conversation Auditing Stage 4 (Conversation Auditing). An Audit Agent checks each interviewee turn against the user’s own evidence, namely the statis- tical profile and the historical ReDial conversation, for three types of issues. Fabrication covers spe- cific claims that are neither stated in nor plausibly inferable from this evidence, such as invented view- ing experiences or personal anecdotes. Caricature covers stereotyped persona performances and in- vented rationalizations: plausible-sounding justi- fications for preferences that the profile does not attest, or recognizable persona archetypes it does not support. History contradiction covers state- ments that conflict with the user’s liked and disliked

text: covers stereotyped persona performances and in- vented rationalizations: plausible-sounding justi- fications for preferences that the profile does not attest, or recognizable persona archetypes it does not support. History contradiction covers state- ments that conflict with the user’s liked and disliked movies or with their earlier ReDial conversation. In addition, deterministic structural checks verify the number of turns, the alternation of speaker roles, and the absence of empty turns. The auditor assigns each flag a severity (low, medium, or high), and a deterministic rule derives the dialogue-level decision. Any structural error or ≥3 high-severity flags trigger REGENERATE (up to two retries, with a corrective nudge appended to the interviewee prompt). At least one high-severity or ≥3 medium-severity flags trigger PARTIAL: the interview is retained, but its high- and medium- severity turns are excluded from enrichment. All other interviews are accepted (ACCEPT). For ex- ample, in one interview, the interviewee claimed to have enjoyed Blue Streak, although the user’s Re- Dial conversation indicated that they had not seen it. In another, the interviewee dismissed the action in Justice League as hard to care about, although the film is on the user’s liked list. The auditor flagged both turns, so they could be excluded before profile enrichment. Full auditor prompts, flag definitions, and representative examples are in Appendix B. 3.4 Profile Enrichment Stage 5 (Profile Enrichment). From audited interviews, we extract six implicit user attributes grounded in prior user-modeling lit- erature: aspect-level preferences (Radlinski et al., 2019), pickiness (Yoon et al., 2024), decision- making style (Scott and Bruce, 1995; Hayati et al., 2020), viewing motivation (Oliver and Raney, 2011), novelty preference (Tang and Liao, 2022), and domain expertise (Kostric et al., 2025). Each attribute reveals behavior not observable in the static profile: aspect preferences organize prefer- ences along Movie/Genre/Person/Other anchors; pickiness captures selectivity; decision-making style ranges across rational, intuitive, dependent, 4
title: Figure 2: Example ReDial user profile after Stage 2,

text: avoidant, and spontaneous; viewing motivation combines a hedonic-eudaimonic score (1–5) with a primary category (escapism, hedonic, eudai- monic, social, catharsis, arousal); novelty prefer- ence scores openness to unfamiliar content (1–5); and domain expertise classifies users as novice, in- termediate, or cinephile. Full attribute schemas, evidence-extraction prompts, and an example en- riched profile are in Appendix H. The inferred attributes and derived pickiness are combined with the Stage 2 statistical profile to form the enriched profile that conditions user simulation in Stage 6. 3.5 User Simulation Stage 6 (User Simulation). The enriched profile of each user conditions Gemini 2.5 Flash (Comanici et al., 2025) to sim- ulate that user’s behavior in conversation with a CRS powered by GPT-4o-mini (Achiam et al., 2023). Each user is simulated in four conversations varying the opening strategy across aspect, movie, mood, and expertise prompts. After each CRS turn, starting from the fourth, an LLM termination judge classifies the last exchange as true acceptance (the user explicitly commits to a specific recommenda- tion), resigned acceptance, explicit give-up, other, or continue; any label other than continue ends the conversation, which is otherwise capped at eight CRS turns. 4

text: We evaluate SimInter on ReDial using 300 users in the full pipeline and a matched subset of 100 users for comparisons against two baselines: STA- TISTICALONLY and CSHI. We ask four questions: do enriched users (T1) mention a more diverse set of items? (T2) express preferences correlated with population-level movie ratings? (T3) discuss movies along richer behavioral aspects? (T4) differ in surface linguistic variety? We additionally con- duct a targeted human evaluation (§4.6) and report a separate cross-CRS robustness experiment with two trained ReDial recommenders, KBRD (Chen et al., 2019) and UniCRS (Wang et al., 2022) (Appendix E). Our evaluation focuses on profile- conditioned simulated user behavior, rather than the recommendation accuracy of the underlying CRS models. 4.1 Experimental Setup FULL represents the complete SimInter pipeline, combining behavioral statistics, audited inter- views, and enriched user attributes. STATIS- TICALONLY uses only the behavioral statistics, without interview-based profile enrichment. We additionally compare against CSHI, an existing user-simulation baseline that follows a target- conditioned dialogue protocol. We run FULL on 300 ReDial users, generating four conversations per user (1,200 conversations). For matched comparisons, we select a subset of 100 users and evaluate STATISTICALONLY and CSHI on the same users, generating 400 conversations per baseline. All comparisons use the corresponding 100-user subset of FULL. We report descriptive metrics for the full 300- user cohort

For each compari- son, we compute user-level mean differences with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (20,000 paired resamples), two-sided paired sign-flip tests (50,000 randomizations), and paired Cohen’s dz (Cohen, 2013). text: After filtering generic placeholders (e.g., movie, film, story), we compute per-user Shannon entropy over remaining aspects and over the sentiment dis- tribution. Higher aspect entropy indicates the sim- ulator articulates preferences along a wider range of behavioral dimensions rather than collapsing to a single template. T4 — Linguistic surface variety. Per-user met- rics over user turns: corpus-level type-token ratio (TTR), n-gram monotony (mean Jaccard overlap of bigrams/trigrams between turn pairs), and SBERT semantic diversity (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). TTR and n-gram monotony measure lexical variety, SBERT diversity measures the semantic spread of requests, and T3 captures semantic-content variety; these can move oppositely. 4.3 Results Table 2 summarizes the matched 100-user com- parisons. Thus, T3 and T4 capture comple- mentary properties: enrichment can increase aspect richness and semantic diversity while narrowing lexical expression. These distinctions matter when diagnosing CRS breakdowns (Bernard and Balog, 2024), particularly when varied user phrasing is important. Comparison with CSHI. Under its target- conditioned protocol with the same GPT-4o-mini CRS, CSHI produces markedly less diverse simu- lated behavior than FULL: aspect entropy is 0.194 vs. 1.619 (dz = 1.85), item entropy 1.454 vs. 2.034 (dz = 1.13), and SBERT diversity 0.345 vs. 0.532 (dz = 1.30; all padj < 0.001), while JSD from ReDial does not differ. CSHI requests are also lexically repetitive (n-gram monotony 0.300 vs. 0.028), and its population correlation is weak (r = 0.074, 88 movies). Because CSHI steers each conversation toward a predefined target item, these differences reflect both profile content and protocol, not profile enrichment alone. 4.4 Auditor Behavior The Audit Agent processed 300 interviews: AC- CEPT (209, 70%), PARTIAL (91, 30%), REGENER- ATE (0). All other corrective action was therefore turn-level exclusion under PARTIAL, removing 196 interviewee turns from enrichment. The auditor raised 676 flags (372 caricature, 173 history con- tradiction, 131 fabrication); the full taxonomy and example dialogues are in Appendix B. Three observations follow. First, the dominant is- sue is not fabrication but caricature (372/676 flags, 55%), mostly invented rationalizations. For ex- ample, one interviewee explained a dislike of The Hangover and Superbad, both on the user’s dis- liked list, by calling them “loud and obnoxious,” although the user likes comparably broad come- dies; the dislike is attested, but the reason is not. Second, the human evaluation shows a matching pattern (§4.6): decision-making style, which has no quantitative anchor in the profile, is the least supported attribute (21.4% Unsupported; 28.6% Evidence-grounded), whereas pickiness, derived from the rejection rate, is among the best supported (97.0%); this correspondence offers limited, indi- rect evidence of audit calibration. Third, the ab- sence of final REGENERATE decisions indicates that gross structural failure is rare with capable LLMs at our interview scale; the dominant failure mode is local, which makes turn-level exclusion an appropriate response. 4.5 Human Evaluation of Audit Decisions We evaluated Stage 4 auditing on

Three co-author annotators indepen- dently examined each synthetic response along- side evidence from the corresponding user’s orig- inal ReDial conversations, without seeing the au- 7

text: ditor’s decisions, flags, or rationales. They as- signed one of three labels: EXCLUDED (a seri- ous, evidence-supported issue warrants removing the turn), FLAGGED–RETAINED (a meaningful is- sue exists but does not warrant removal), or UN- FLAGGED (no meaningful issue is identified). The annotators agreed unanimously on 70/105 turns (66.7%; Fleiss’ κ = 0.664). Using majority human judgments as the refer- ence, the auditor achieved 86.7% three-class accu- racy (91/105), with agreement on 31/35 excluded, 31/35 flagged-but-retained, and 29/35 unflagged turns. Collapsing both retained classes yielded 95.2% binary filtering accuracy (100/105): four auditor-excluded turns were judged retainable and one auditor-retained turn was judged excludable. These results suggest that Stage 4 can distinguish concerns that warrant removal from those that need not discard an otherwise usable response. The fig- ures are human-referenced accuracies on this bal- anced sample, not prevalence-adjusted estimates over all audited turns; annotation protocol, dis- agreements, and limitations are detailed in Ap- pendix G. 4.6 Human Evaluation of Enriched Attributes Three annotators independently evaluated enriched- attribute claims from FULL profiles. text: We presented SimInter, a pipeline for LLM-based user simulation that elicits qualitative behavioral attributes through structured synthetic interviews and guards against fabrication via explicit turn- level auditing. On 300 ReDial users, simulators conditioned on enriched profiles discuss movies along substantially richer behavioral aspects than a statistics-only baseline (dz = 0.96, padj < 0.001; zero-aspect users drop from 41% to 5%); pooled popularity alignment with MovieLens-25M reaches r = 0.347; and 94% of enriched-attribute claims are human-supported. Enrichment also con- centrates item mentions and reduces lexical variety, consistent with profile-conditioned generation nar- rowing expression toward profile vocabulary. User- simulation quality in CRS is thus multidimensional: the goal is not to maximize every diversity metric, but to gain more on dimensions that matter for CRS evaluation than is lost on those that do not. 8

text: Limitations Evidence grounding and audit reliability. Sim- Inter grounds enriched attributes in historical user evidence, while independent validation against real user behavior remains an important direction for future work. Human evaluation assesses evidence support rather than direct behavioral fidelity. More- over, audit decisions involve uncertainty, particu- larly when distinguishing unsupported rationaliza- tions from legitimate preference elaboration. Auto- matically retrieved evidence and differences in an- notator judgments further limit conclusions about audit reliability. Evaluation scope and generalizability. Our ablations do not include direct LLM-based at- tribute inference without interviewing, leaving the interview’s independent contribution unresolved. Sparse and imbalanced preference evidence limits individual-level alignment evaluation. Enrichment also involves trade-offs between aspect richness, item diversity, and lexical variety. Although cross- CRS experiments support the robustness of aspect- level findings, they rely on automated evaluation and do not establish agreement with real-user as- sessments of recommenders. Generalization be- yond English movie recommendation remains to be investigated. This appendix documents why per-user and persona-anchored variants are not reportable. A.1 Per-User Popularity Correlation For each user, the per-user popularity Pearson r is the correlation between the simulator’s rating and the MovieLens-25M mean rating across the movies that user mentioned. This requires a minimum sample of ∼30 (user, movie) pairs per user for a reliable estimate. Only 6/300 FULL users reach this threshold (me- dian 7 pairs per user, maximum 47); on the matched subset, only 2 users in each of FULL and STATIS- TICALONLY reach this threshold. A paired test across users is therefore not feasible. The pooled estimate in Table 2 aggregates all (user, movie) pairs across the cohort, treating each pair as an in- dependent observation, a weaker statistical claim than per-user testing would provide, but the only one available at our sample size. A.2 Persona-Anchored T2 (Liked vs. Disliked) A second variant of T2 correlates the simula- tor’s in-conversation rating with the user’s ReDial liked/disliked label (binary ground truth). Table 4 reports the diagnostics. In every condition, 94– 97% of high-confidence ground-truth labels are liked, giving varianceredial < 0.1, a near-constant variable. Pearson r against a near-constant variable is driven by a handful of disliked pairs and is not a reliable discriminative metric, so the apparent ordering across conditions is not interpreted. A.3 Balanced Accuracy as an Alternative A natural alternative is balanced accuracy on liked/disliked classification. Computing this re- quires users with both classes in ground truth. As shown above, only 2 users per condition satisfy this, too few to estimate a meaningful per-user bal- anced accuracy distribution. Pooled simple accu- racy (94–96%) equals the majority-class rate and is uninformative. Recommendation for future work. Invented rationalization is the dominant pattern (372/676 flags are caricature, 69% of them medium severity): the simulator frequently produces reasons for preferences that sound plausi- ble but are not attested in the profile. 2. Flags grounded in the user’s own evidence are the most reliable. Contradictions with the liked and disliked lists or with the ReDial con- versation can be checked directly (Examples 2–4). Fabrication flags about film facts rely on the audi- tor’s parametric knowledge and are less reliable: in several cases the auditor flagged accurate scene descriptions as fabricated. Such errors are conser- vative: they can remove grounded content from the enrichment input, but they do not introduce unsupported claims into the profile. 3. REGENERATE is rare. The auditor reserves REGENERATE for structural failure or ≥3 high- severity flags. This occurred in one of 300 inter- views, and the regenerated interview received PAR- TIAL, indicating that gross structural failure is rare with capable LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash) at our in- terview scale. text: Auditor explanation: “The user claims Justice League’s CGI battles don’t earn stakes and are hard to care about, but Justice League is in their liked movies list with no negative commentary in the pro- file.” This illustrates an invented rationalization: a plausible reason for a dislike that the user’s history does not support. Auditor explanation: “This response performs a snobby cinephile persona dismissing comedies as ‘loud and obnoxious,’ but the profile shows the user actually likes comedies like Super Troopers, Beerfest, and Tommy Boy.” Both films are on the user’s disliked list, so the dislike itself is attested; the stated reason is not. F Human Evaluation Protocol F.1 Annotation Task Each annotation task presented an annotator with a single claim (one of the six attribute values from a FULL-enriched user profile), the user’s behavioral profile (Stage 1–2 statistics), and the user’s in- terview transcript (Stage 3 output, including any turns the auditor had flagged). Annotators were asked to judge whether the claim was supported by the interview evidence. F.2 Rating Scales Support (4-class): • Supported: the claim is directly justified by specific content in the interview. • Partially supported: the interview contains relevant content but does not fully justify the specific claim (e.g., the claim is more specific or stronger than the evidence). • Unsupported: the interview does not contain evidence relevant to the claim, even

text: • Contradicted: the interview contains evidence inconsistent with the claim. Grounding (3-class): • Evidence-grounded: the claim is anchored to a specific quotation or behavioral pattern in the interview. • Generic: the claim is consistent with the in- terview but could apply to many users; the evidence is weak or non-specific. • Cliche/stereotype: the claim performs a rec- ognizable persona archetype not specifically attested in the user’s data. Numeric ratings (1–5): • Consistency: how consistent the claim is with the user’s behavioral profile (1 = inconsistent, 5 = highly consistent). • Usefulness: how useful the claim would be for conditioning a simulator (1 = not useful, 5 = highly useful). • Overreach: how much the claim overshoots the available evidence (1 = no overreach, 5 = severe overreach). • Confidence: the annotator’s confidence in their judgment (1 = uncertain, 5 = highly con- fident). Mean ratings across all 315 annotations are 3.77 (consistency), 3.61 (usefulness), 1.70 (overreach), and 3.00 (confidence). These examples illustrate turn-level judgments, not independent validation of individual audit flags. Scope and limitations. The equal 35/35/35 al- location, together with at most one sampled turn per historical ReDial user, means that the reported sample accuracies are not unbiased estimates of ac- curacy over all Stage 4 turns. Consecutive presenta- tion blocks may confound audit stratum with order, learning, or fatigue effects. The ReDial excerpts were retrieved automatically; although matched to historical users, their relevance and completeness were not exhaustively adjudicated, and missing con- text may affect individual decisions. In addition, the annotators were co-authors and majority vote is an operational human reference rather than an independently established ground truth. The eval- uation therefore characterizes human agreement with Stage 4 turn-level outcomes, not the validity of each issue flag or population-level recall. The 14 three-class disagreements, particularly the five affecting the remove-versus-keep action, remain priorities for further evidence-based adjudication. text: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions Arastun Mammadli University of Exeter United Kingdom am2169@exeter.ac.uk Herbert Woisetschläger IBM Research Switzerland h.woisetschlaeger@ibm.com Jawad Fayaz University of Exeter United Kingdom j.fayaz@exeter.ac.uk Shiqiang Wang University of Exeter United Kingdom s.wang9@exeter.ac.uk
title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions

text: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality- cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs N compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model’s strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed

text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings as part of a larger compound system. However, a growing share of deployers treat the inter-agent dynamics, competitive and cooperative alike, as a black box. This makes it hard to build systems that remain capable, efficient, and reliable. Existing work addresses pieces of this problem in isolation. The strategic decision-making literature focuses on a fixed model’s play under a specified game setting [7, 28, 37]. In parallel, LLM routing addresses model selection under performance-cost trade-off [5, 26, 31], but with a static task distribution and no notion of a strategic structure or opponent. Neither accounts for the fact that contemporary LLM portfolios differ not only in scale and cost, but also in the type and quality of strategic behaviour they exhibit. Our work reframes model selection itself as a strategic decision. Concretely, we extend the game- theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the opponent-conditioned meta game layered on top of the base game. Here the base game is played between the fielded LLMs, while the meta game is played between two strategic selectors that field a model of their choice each round. In repeated settings, the dynamic and adaptive nature of this problem (as opposed to traditional routers operating on a fixed distribution of tasks) means our selection should
title: Introduction

text: between two strategic selectors that field a model of their choice each round. In repeated settings, the dynamic and adaptive nature of this problem (as opposed to traditional routers operating on a fixed distribution of tasks) means our selection should be strategic. Beyond balancing the performance-cost trade-offs, such a selection layer can help steer the deployer’s general play, adding control over the reliability and safety of the interaction (Figure 1). We ask the question: Given LLM strategic capabilities vary across different games and models, can a selector exploit this by learning which model to field against an unknown and possibly adaptive opponent? Why This Matters. Traditional routers operate under the assumption of a fixed task distribution, learning a static mapping from queries to optimal models. In contrast, operating against an adaptive opponent transforms this into a non-stationary learning problem, where the optimal strategy can continuously shift over time. A further challenge arises from the partial observability of the meta game’s payoff matrix. In practice, a selector cannot observe the opponent’s net gain, since the opponent’s model choice is unknown, nor can it observe the counterfactual payoffs of fielding an alternative model in the current game state.
