In strategic selection, we introduce an additional layer of environmental noise through the dynamic responses of the opponent. Therefore, benchmarking and result reporting call for a careful statistical treatment. Our contributions are threefold: • Strategic Model Selection. We formalise strategic selection as a repeated general-sum meta game between two players. Beyond capability and cost, this lets us treat the interaction itself as a first-class design consideration for model selection. • Quantifying Noise in Strategic Play. We characterise the signal and noise levels across games, and suggest adapting methods from traditional hypothesis testing to decide on the number of seeds per a game-portfolio pair. • Empirical Investigation. To set up our empirical investigation, we select 10 models from different families, and adapt a range of existing routing methods (Table 1). We first show that LLM strategic capabilities are scenario-dependent and exploitable by a selector. We then investigate the performance of adapted methods against both fixed models and selector opponents. 2

text: 2.1 Strategic LLM Decision-Making A growing literature explores LLMs in strategic settings (e.g. how LLMs play games against each other). Game-theoretic benchmarks [7, 10, 28, 36] and frameworks [11, 33, 34, 37] test LLMs in normal-form games and find that performance is uneven and structure-dependent. Others [3, 24, 32, 35] evaluate capability on a higher level (e.g. planning, collaboration, theory of mind) and consistently find spiky, uneven profiles across models. Similarly, Mei et al. [13] and Horton et al. [9] run behavioural Turing tests and show that different models exhibit different strategic dispositions (i.e. behavioural profiles). Motivated by such findings, Raman et al. [19] outlines the need for an element-level (model, prompt, domain) selection approach, but leaves it to future work. We note that despite extensive coverage, the existing literature always fixes the model per player. 2

These works represent queries as vector embeddings to semantically capture their scope and difficulty. However, we argue that discriminative signal in strategic selection largely comes from evolving game history (actions and outcomes), and two consecutive rounds with near identical embeddings can call for opposite model choices. In the absence of routing methods that explicitly model this structure, we also consider bandit-style per-round feedback [2, 29] as a paradigm suited to a non-stationary interactive signal. 3 Strategic LLM Selection 3.1 What is Strategic Selection? In multi-agent systems, a setting is non-strategic if the objective concerns only the overall performance of the system or its performance-cost trade-off. A setting is strategic if it also accounts for the interaction between agents, including how they communicate, coordinate, and negotiate. Modelling this interaction can produce systems that are more reliable and efficient. In a cooperative setting, it improves the coordination between agents [12]. In a competitive setting, it gives the deployer more control over the interaction with an opponent and helps steer the interaction toward the deployer’s preferences. For example, for a given business, the reward of the negotiation, the cost of using AI, and the consistency (i.e. associated risk) of the results can all matter at varying levels. 3.2 Problem Formulation We formalise strategic LLM selection as a repeated, contextual, general-sum game with two layers: a base game that fielded models play, and a selection meta game that the deployers play. Strategic selection focuses on the meta layer, a two-player game with i indexing the player (deployer) and −i its opponent. Repeated games are played over rounds t = 1, . . . , T, where each round t is associated with context xi,t ∈X (e.g. game setup, instructions, past history). Deployer i’s set of pure strategies (meta game actions) Si is defined as the set of models {1, . . . , Mi} in its portfolio. In each round, i selects a model si,t ∼σi(· | xi,t), where σi ∈∆(Si) is a mixed strategy (i.e. selection policy). Per-round context xi,t is then passed down to the fielded model to produce the base game action si,t(xi,t) →ai,t. The base game (i.e. of fielded models si,t against s−i,t) produces a utility vi,t at

The base game (i.e. of fielded models si,t against s−i,t) produces a utility vi,t at an inference cost ci,t (tokens spent), as well as a net gain of gi,t that captures their trade-off. Together, player i’s game outcome is denoted as ξi,t = (si,t, ai,t, gi,t). Drawing from the online learning literature, each selector maintains an adaptive parameter vector θi,t that updates after each round based on observed context xi,t and game outcome ξi,t: si,t ∼σi(· | xi,t; θi,t), θi,t+1 = UPDATE(θi,t, xi,t, ξi,t). Such options can include classical multi-armed bandit samplers [29], neural network-based classifiers [5, 26], or at the frontier, an LLM prompted with game history. Consequently, θi,t’s definition depends on the backbone, such as the network weights for a classifier, or the per-arm posterior for a Thompson sampler. We note that the game outcome is also incorporated into the next round’s context xi,t+1 = f(xi,t, ξi,t) to be used in base game decision-making. Related work addresses LLM evaluations by adapting cross-disciplinary methods such as signal processing [8], experiment-design theory [14], and psy- chometrics [15]. They find that in tradi- tional evaluations (e.g. question-answering benchmarks), even a modest amount of replication (e.g. N ≈5) substantially sta- bilises the estimates. We argue that due to its interactive opponent-conditioned struc- ture, strategic LLM evaluation is inherently noisier and requires a higher number of replications. To quantify the noise in strate- gic play, we define a method to measure the levels of signal and noise across games by adapting Heineman et al. [8]’s work. Building on this, we develop approaches to choose N for a given game-portfolio pair [14]. See Appendix B for further details. 3.4 Evaluation Metrics To measure

The game utility vi is min-max normalised (ˆvi ∈[0, 1]) based on its game-specific bounds (e.g. the economic profit in Cournot Duopoly, or the number of winning battlefields in Colonel Blotto game). The associated inference cost ci is represented by the per-model token usage cost (in dollars $) using the OpenRouter1 listings as market proxies. This cost is min-max normalised (ˆci ∈[0, 1]) based on the portfolio-bounds (minimum and maximum per-token price observed across the model portfolio). Following these findings, a suite of selectors is run against fixed but unknown models (i.e. opponent is a fixed LLM) to evaluate their potential as strategic selectors. Finally, these selectors are deployed against adaptive opponents to simulate the non-stationary dynamics of real-world settings. Models and Games. The model portfolio draws on 10 open-weight LLMs across four families (Granite, Mistral, Llama, and Qwen) ranging from 3B to 70B to capture varying capability levels, usage costs, and dispositions. The game inventory captures 5 classical game-theoretic scenarios (Colonel Blotto, Cournot Duopoly, Stag Hunt, Vickrey Auction, Chicken Game) spanning zero-sum to cooperative dilemmas. Experiments are run through OutplayArena2, which owns the base game rules, turn sequencing, and scoring. Selectors. A suite of selectors spanning traditional and adversarial bandit samplers [2, 29], con- temporary LLM routers [5, 26], and an LLM self-reflection framework [21] is then incorporated to draw on this portfolio. Table 2 reveals that strategic competence is uneven and game dependent. For example, the Llama models are top performers in Cournot Duopoly but fail to make the podium in Chicken Game. In addition, the substantial performance variance among models within individual games highlights an opportunity to adopt a selector. Figure 2a underscores that model scale does not reliably translate into strategic capability. Across our evaluations, we find only a weak positive correlation between model scale and utility (Pearson’s r = 0.37), and a moderate negative relationship when accounting for the usage costs (r = −0.54). Upon a closer look, we also see that smaller models have game-specific usability. For example in Vickrey Auction, due to its high rationality (i.e. always bidding the true value), the Granite4.1 3B outperforms other much bigger models that range from 24B to 70B parameters. Upon closer inspection, we find that it also falls behind nearly every fixed model across most games (Appendix D.3). The Causal LLM Router and RouterDC show relative improvement but are still beaten by several fixed models in multiple games. We attribute this to the fact that strategic settings require special treatment of the game context and the learning signal. Methods that rely on query embeddings for semantic similarity matching (Causal LLM Router, RouterDC), or on LLM reflection (LLM Selector), fail to surface implicit strategic signals. A simple bandit algorithm using Thompson sampling achieves the highest net gain among all selectors in every game, despite relying on nothing more than per-round outcome feedback. However, even in Cournot Duopoly, where the Thompson sampler proves most dominant, it fails to beat the best fixed model (Llama3.1 8B), indicating significant room for improvement. We believe a better selector algorithm should learn to directly infer the latent, hidden per-game strategic signal, rather than relying solely on observed game outcomes. It should build an understanding of the performance of its own portfolio models, and the opponent under the current scenario. 5.2 Games as Strategic Testbeds We saw that best-performing models vary noticeably across the 5 evaluated games, each setup capturing a particular strategic scenario (a model-to-model interplay) (Table 2). Moreover, an observation can be made that games vary in difficulty (i.e. complexity). For example, one can say that identifying the equilibrium strategy would require higher model reasoning capabilities in a game like Cournot Duopoly (an economic profit game) than in Colonel Blotto, which relies on a simple per-battlefield resolution rule (the larger number wins). Empirically, this idea is reflected in the correlation between model scale and performance, which is the highest in Cournot Duopoly (Pearson’s r = 0.66), and much lower in games like Stag Hunt (r = 0.12) and Colonel Blotto (r = 0.24) (Figure D.3). Mathematically, there are an infinite number of normal- and extensive-form games that range in complexity and the strategic interplay captured. Future work should therefore establish well-defined methods to classify a game’s difficulty and strategic value. Such methods are 7

Inputs are noisy, and the agents involved often hold different, sometimes conflicting objectives. Our results show that a model’s competence is shaped by the opponent it faces, and how both sides adapt as the interaction unfolds. Traditional benchmarks fail to capture this, as they test one model at a time against a fixed correct answer. This makes game inventories a natural fit for evaluating models in decision-pressured, interactive settings that they are actually deployed to in practice. Moreover, because game states are generated dynamically through interaction, games are more resistant to the training-data contamination that increasingly undermines static benchmarks [23]. That said, games are not immune to saturation. Even without contamination, the discriminative signal can erode as models approach equilibrium play (strategy profiles from which no player can gain by unilaterally deviating). More specifically, under standard no-regret learning, adaptive play converges to the set of coarse correlated equilibria (CCE), a superset of Nash equilibria [20]. In two-player zero-sum games such as Colonel Blotto, every equilibrium yields the same expected payoff, so once models play near-equilibrium strategies, none can outperform another and their results become indistinguishable. In contrast, in general-sum games the set of CCE is typically large and contains outcomes with very different payoffs. This suggests favouring general-sum games when building inventories meant to remain discriminative. 6 Conclusion and Future Work We extend game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as a repeated opponent- conditioned meta game layered on top of the base game. Initial evaluations across 5 games and 10 models show that LLM strategic capability varies substantially across games and models, leaving considerable room for a selector to exploit. By adapting a range of selection methods, we report that the existing methods do not transfer equally well even against a simple fixed-model opponent, and that a plain bandit algorithm can surpass structurally heavier pre-trained encoders and LLM reflection methods. Subsequent runs against a selector opponent reveal that simple adaptations like discounted and adversarial bandit algorithms are not able to capture the non-stationary dynamics of opponent-conditioned strategic selection, and fail to outclass the plain sampler. Overall, the results highlight the challenges of strategic model selection, and motivate a selector

Overall, the results highlight the challenges of strategic model selection, and motivate a selector design that can extract and learn from signals across 3 different dimensions: model capability, usage cost, and strategic disposition, in noise-heavy interactive settings. Our investigation was scoped to the analysis of 5 games. However, to better understand agent-to-agent interplay and the underlying safety and risk factors, it is important to consider games from a range of fields, including economics, social sciences, and operations research. We believe this choice should reflect both the measurable effect of the game and the underlying practical application of the selector. We also relied on explicit parsed game actions as a communication method between the models, which underestimates both the strategic capabilities (e.g. persuasion), and the associated risk factors in deployment. A more realistic setting should capture agent-to-agent natural language interactions [27]. We leave such free-form interactions to future work. Finally, high-stakes repeated interactions (e.g. negotiations, auctions) involve a risk factor not captured by expected gain. This can include catastrophic losses, regulatory penalties, or reputational damage. Capturing the variance in realised gain to account for involved risk is another future direction. text: Ratio Following Heineman et al. [8], we first define a descriptive method that characterises signal and noise levels across games. Fix a game G and let S denote its set of models under evaluation, with j, k ∈S ranging over the pair of models compared in G. For a model s ∈S, let τ = 1, . . . , N index its seeds, where a seed is a single independent evaluation run. Let vG,s,τ be the bounds-normalised score on seed τ of G played by model s. Let vG,s denote the mean of vG,s,τ over all N seeds, and let vG denote the mean of vG,s over all models s ∈S. Noise, signal, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) are then noise(G, s) = Stdτ(vG,s,τ) vG,s , signal(G) = maxj,k∈S |vG,j −vG,k| vG , SNR(G) = signal(G) noise(G) . (3) Here Stdτ(·) denotes the standard deviation taken over the seed index τ, and noise(G) denotes noise(G, s) averaged over every model s ∈S. Noise is a coefficient of variation, a model’s own seed-to-seed spread relative to its mean. Signal is the largest gap between any two models’ means, relative to the game’s overall mean. SNR is high when models are well separated relative to how much a single model’s score jitters across seeds, and low when the two quantities are comparable.

text: • Cournot Duopoly is a simultaneous quantity-setting game where two firms choose outputs that jointly fix market price and profit. It isolates a single continuous best-response signal that separates models by how closely each converges toward the equilibrium quantity. • Stag Hunt is a coordination game with a risk-dominant and a payoff-dominant equilibrium. It measures whether a model favors the safer but lower-payoff option over the cooperative one when the opponent’s action is uncertain. • Vickrey Auction is a second-price sealed-bid auction where each bidder submits a value- based bid. It measures how closely a model’s bid tracks its private valuation under the auction’s truthful-bidding equilibrium. • Chicken Game is an anti-coordination game built around brinkmanship, where mutual insistence is worst for both players. It measures a model’s willingness to escalate or concede as the risk of mutual loss grows. Table C.2: The five base games G used across experiments, all played between 2 players. Fixed Model. One fixed model across all seeds N that keeps context and past outcomes across rounds t = 1, . . . , T unless otherwise stated. Per-Opponent Full-Information. Given the identity of the fixed opponent, it looks up the round-robin table (our prior) once at construction and commits to whichever candidate scores highest against that opponent, fielding it every round with no further adaptation. LLM Selector. Uses llama3.3:70b as the selecting model and relies on the Reflexion framework [21] to pick the model to field. Namely, each round it is queried once with a description of the game, an entry per portfolio model (tier and per-token price), and a log of past rounds covering its own fielded model, action, and outcome signal. It parses a JSON response giving the picked model, a confidence, and a reasoning. Prior information enters only as in-context history, a rolling log of past rounds inside the prompt, with default sampling temperature = 1.0. RouterDC. Adapted from Chen et al. [5]. Each round a frozen sentence encoder embeds the current query, built from player’s own model, action, and signal history, and the pick is whichever candidate’s trained embedding has highest cosine similarity to that query embedding. The

text: Chen et al. [5]. Each round a frozen sentence encoder embeds the current query, built from player’s own model, action, and signal history, and the pick is whichever candidate’s trained embedding has highest cosine similarity to that query embedding. The embeddings come from a checkpoint fit offline, once per game. All prior information is folded into this pre-trained checkpoint at training time. Causal LLM Router. We follow the doubly robust regret-minimising rule of Tsiourvas et al. [26]. Each round it draws a candidate from a softmax over its current per-(candidate, opponent) belief, with a floor that keeps every candidate at nonzero pick probability. It then folds in a doubly robust correction of the observed signal, using the pick probability it assigned as its own propensity instead of fitting a separate propensity model. We use the defaults surrogate = softmax, tau = 1.0, and propensity_floor = 0.05. Thompson Sampler. It keeps a per-model Gaussian belief over the chosen signal that is refined as a running mean after every round. Each round it draws one sample per model from its current belief and fields the model with the highest draw. Additionally, we implement two non-stationary variants that change the belief update. title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified

text: Dense vector retrieval can miss evidence connected through intermediate entities, while direct graph retrieval requires access to the graph at query time. We compare five offline graph- based embedding transformations and strategies for using the resulting graph-modified embed- dings alongside the originals, without query-time graph access. On a synthetic professional- network benchmark with complete supporting-evidence sets, direct replacement of the original embeddings reduces evidence recovery. Multi-stage strategies improve recovery by using graph-modified embeddings to guide the search while retaining the originals for semantic relevance. On questions requiring linked facts or comparisons among candidates, the strongest configuration improves recovery by up to 25.9 % relative to plain vector retrieval. It also matches baseline recovery with 40 % fewer returned nodes. Controls confirm that graph infor- mation contributes beyond multi-stage retrieval alone. Across the tested methods, retrieval performance depends more on how graph-modified embeddings are used than on how they are produced. 1
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified

text: Retrieval is a central component of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where external evidence is retrieved to support large language model (LLM) outputs [1]. It also supports LLM agents and long-term memory systems by identifying relevant documents, passages, or stored facts. Dense retrieval embeds queries and passages in a shared vector space and ranks candidates by vector similarity [2]. This approach is effective when supporting evidence is semantically close to the query, but may miss relevant passages connected through intermediate entities or multi-step relations. Knowledge graphs represent these connections explicitly, but using them for retrieval introduces two challenges. Traversing or reranking the graph for every query increases query-time complexity, while modifying embeddings according to graph structure may distort the semantic relationships captured by the original embeddings. This leads to the central question of this work: can graph structure be incorporated offline into graph-modified embeddings that improve retrieval without requiring graph access at query time or replacing the original embeddings? Prior work has either incorporated relational knowledge into embeddings [3, 4, 5], used graphs directly at query time [6, 7], or refined retrieval through textual feedback alone [8, 9, 10]. Our work connects these directions by examining both how graph-modified embeddings should be constructed and how they should be used in multi-stage retrieval. We construct graph-modified embeddings offline using several transformations, including local
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified

text: through textual feedback alone [8, 9, 10]. Our work connects these directions by examining both how graph-modified embeddings should be constructed and how they should be used in multi-stage retrieval. We construct graph-modified embeddings offline using several transformations, including local neighbourhood aggregation, random-walk endpoints, community centroids [11], and convex neighbour pull. We then compare retrieval strategies ranging from replacing the original embeddings with graph-modified embeddings to multi-stage strategies that combine both. text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint query time, every strategy uses only cosine-similarity searches over stored embeddings; the graph is neither traversed nor queried. Our central hypothesis is that graph-modified embeddings are more useful for guiding the expansion of retrieval than for measuring relevance to the original query. The best-performing strategies therefore assign distinct roles to the two sets of embeddings. An initial search over the original embeddings retrieves semantically relevant results (seeds). Their graph-modified embeddings are then aggregated to guide the selection of candidates that are both relevant to the query and related to the seeds through the graph. Finally, the original embeddings of the selected candidates are used to reformulate the query for another search over the original embeddings [8, 9, 10]. We refer to this use of graph-modified embeddings to guide retrieval as graph conditioning. To evaluate these strategies, we introduce a synthetic professional-network benchmark in which the corpus, graph, questions, answers, and supporting evidence are generated from the same underlying facts. The benchmark includes single-fact, relational and collection, and extremisation questions, together with exact gold answers and complete gold-evidence sets containing the intermediate and competing records required to establish each answer [12]. We select configurations on a development corpus and report results on separately generated validation data (Section 3.1). All methods use the same original embeddings,

text: and complete gold-evidence sets containing the intermediate and competing records required to establish each answer [12]. We select configurations on a development corpus and report results on separately generated validation data (Section 3.1). All methods use the same original embeddings, cosine similarity, and the same 40-node retrieval limit. Multi-stage controls without graph conditioning allow us to distinguish improvements produced by graph-modified embeddings from those produced by multi-stage retrieval alone. None of the graph-modified representations improves direct retrieval over the original embed- dings in our experiments. The original embeddings recover 73.1 % of the gold evidence, whereas the five transformations recover between 52 % and 72.9 %. In contrast, multi-stage retrieval improves performance across all five transformations, and the choice of retrieval strategy has a greater effect than the transformation used to construct the graph-modified embeddings. The strongest configuration improves gold-evidence recovery relative to plain vector retrieval by 25.9 % on extremisation questions and by 10.0 % on relational and collection questions (19.2 % across the two groups). It also matches the gold-evidence recovery achieved by plain vector retrieval with 40 nodes after returning only 24, corresponding to 40 % fewer returned nodes. text: Our work connects research on graph-modified embeddings, feedback-based and multi-hop retrieval, and graph-based retrieval. We also draw on evidence-level evaluation to assess whether these approaches recover the passages needed to answer a question. Encoding graph structure into embeddings. Retrofitting adapts pretrained embeddings using external relational knowledge. Faruqui et al. [3] introduced an objective that balances fidelity to the original embeddings with attraction between connected concepts. Counter-fitting adds attraction and repulsion constraints [4], while Functional Retrofitting introduces relation- specific transformations for heterogeneous knowledge graphs [5]. Retrofitting has also been applied beyond word embeddings, including multilingual sentence representations aligned through Abstract Meaning Representation [13] and sense representations specialised using WordNet relations [14]. Related approaches use entity descriptions and language models to construct representations for knowledge-graph completion, incorporating structural information through different training objectives or architectures [15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Another line of work derives node representations from graph connectivity. DeepWalk learns embeddings from contexts generated by truncated random walks [20], while node2vec uses biased walks to capture different network neighbourhoods [21]. These methods are conceptually related to our random-walk transformation, which instead averages existing textual embeddings at walk endpoints without learning new representations from walk sequences. Simple Graph Convolution separates graph-based feature propagation from a learned classifier [22], providing a related perspective on our neighbourhood-based aggregation of existing embeddings. We draw
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings

text: instead averages existing textual embeddings at walk endpoints without learning new representations from walk sequences. Simple Graph Convolution separates graph-based feature propagation from a learned classifier [22], providing a related perspective on our neighbourhood-based aggregation of existing embeddings. We draw on these ideas to study graph-modified embeddings for evidence retrieval, rather than intrinsic similarity, node classification, or knowledge-graph completion. In particular, we compare their use as direct search representations with their use as intermediate signals in a multi-stage retriever. Feedback-based and multi-hop dense retrieval. Pseudo-relevance feedback refines a query using the results of an initial retrieval stage and then performs a second search. NPRF (neural pseudo-relevance feedback) brought the idea into learned ranking, feeding the top-ranked documents of a first pass into a neural ranking model [8]. More recent approaches apply the same principle to dense retrieval, where the query is a vector rather than a set of terms, and differ in what that vector is allowed to be. ColBERT-PRF keeps a multi-vector query and extends it, extracting representative embeddings from the pseudo-relevant documents and adding them to the query representation before re-retrieval [9]. ANCE-PRF keeps a single query vector but learns an encoder that consumes the initially retrieved passages, leaving the document index unchanged [10]. Multi-hop retrieval extends this sequential approach to questions whose supporting evidence cannot be identified
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings

text: representation before re-retrieval [9]. ANCE-PRF keeps a single query vector but learns an encoder that consumes the initially retrieved passages, leaving the document index unchanged [10]. Multi-hop retrieval extends this sequential approach to questions whose supporting evidence cannot be identified from the original query alone. Multi-Hop Dense Retrieval conditions successive searches on previously retrieved passages to recover chains of supporting evidence [23]. Other approaches use generated text to guide subsequent retrieval. IRCoT interleaves retrieval with intermediate chain-of-thought reasoning steps [24], while Iter- RetGen alternates retrieval and generation, using each generated output to inform the next retrieval iteration [25]. Our method uses offline graph-modified embeddings to guide intermediate retrieval, followed by a Rocchio-style update that blends the query with the mean embedding of retrieved nodes in the original space [26], without query-time graph access or LLM generation. Controls without graph conditioning (Section 4.5.2) isolate the contribution of graph conditioning. 3

text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint Graph-based retrieval. Graph-based systems use explicit relations to find evidence that semantic similarity may miss, such as education records linked to a company through its employees. GRAFT-Net reasons over question-specific subgraphs of facts and text [6]; PullNet expands them through iterative retrieval [7]; and HippoRAG propagates relevance through entity connections using Personalized PageRank [29]. These systems use the graph during query processing, whereas we encode its relations into embeddings offline and retrieve evidence through stored vectors alone. GraphRAG uses community summaries to answer global questions about a corpus [30]. Although related to our use of graph communities, it produces text for corpus-level synthesis, whereas we produce node-level vectors for retrieving question-specific evidence under a fixed budget. Evidence-level evaluation. Multi-hop question-answering benchmarks support evaluation beyond final-answer accuracy by identifying the evidence needed for reasoning. HotpotQA provides sentence-level supporting facts alongside questions and answers, including both bridge and comparison questions [27]. MuSiQue constructs multi-hop questions by composing single-hop questions whose reasoning steps depend on one another, explicitly addressing shortcuts that allow apparently multi-hop questions to be answered without combining the required evidence [28]. Ground-truth-subgraph benchmarks such as SynthKGQA and GTSQA further support the evaluation of graph retrieval independently of answer generation [12]. We adopt this evidence- centred perspective: our synthetic corpus and questions are generated from

Ground-truth-subgraph benchmarks such as SynthKGQA and GTSQA further support the evaluation of graph retrieval independently of answer generation [12]. We adopt this evidence- centred perspective: our synthetic corpus and questions are generated from the same structured facts, enabling us to specify question-specific gold-evidence sets and measure their recovery directly. The benchmark includes relational and collection questions and extremisation questions, allowing us to examine retrieval of both indirectly connected evidence and the competing records required to establish an extremum. 3 Experimental Setup We evaluate how graph-based embedding transformations and retrieval strategies affect evidence recovery on a synthetic professional-network benchmark. 3.1 Dataset and Knowledge Graph We use separate development and validation corpora, generated by the same pipeline and containing synthetic resumes and organisational personnel rosters. Each corpus is represented as a tripartite graph with three node types: documents, chunks (textual evidence from those documents), and entities (people and organisations). Three relation types connect them: part_of links chunks to documents, about links documents to their primary entities, and mentions links chunks to entities referenced in their text. The schema admits only these three edge patterns. Each corpus contains approximately 1,200 chunks, 370 entities, 230 documents, and 3,700 edges. text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint 3.2 Questions and Gold Evidence We generate questions and ground-truth (gold) answers from the structured facts underlying the dataset. Gold evidence includes every chunk required to establish an answer. The benchmark contains 11 question families, detailed in Appendix A. We group them into three categories: Single-fact questions: These ask for attributes directly associated with entities mentioned in the query and generally require a single evidence chunk or an immediate relation. For example, “What skills did a person use at a given employer?” can be answered using a job chunk that mentions the person, employer, and skills. Relational and collection questions: These ask for attributes or entities connected to a named entity through intermediate entities. For example, “Which universities were attended by the employees of an organisation?” requires evidence linking the organisation to its employees and those employees to their universities. The target chunks may lie two or three relations from the named entity and share little surface content with the query. Extremisation questions: These compare candidates to identify a maximum and may then request another attribute of the selected candidate. Establishing the maximum requires the relevant records of all competing candidates. For example, “What certifications does the most experienced worker at a given company hold?” requires experience records for the comparison and the winner’s

text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint Original embeddings encode chunk text or, for document and entity nodes, their names. We embed nodes and queries with OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small, using 1,536 dimensions. Each transformation produces one modified vector per node. We denote the original and modified embeddings of node i by xi and zi, respectively. Appendix B lists all evaluated transformations and hyperparameter configurations. One-hop neighbour blend (hop-1). For each node i, we consider its one-hop neighbours. We define Si as the 20 % of these nodes with the lowest cosine similarity to the original embedding xi, selecting at least two whenever available. The modified embedding zi combines the original vector with the mean of the original embeddings of the selected neighbours: zi = αxi + (1 −α) 1 |Si| X j∈Si xj, (1) where α = 0.2. Selecting the least semantically similar one-hop neighbours is intended to introduce graph-related information that is not already encoded in the source representation. Two-hop neighbour blend (hop-2). This method uses the same selection and blending procedure, applied to nodes at graph distance exactly 2. Convex neighbour pull. Let Z collect the modified node embeddings and E denote the graph’s edge set. We minimise the classical retrofitting objective [3] with uniform anchor and edge weights: J(Z) = X i ∥zi −xi∥2 2 + X (i,j)∈E ∥zi

text: neighbour pull. Let Z collect the modified node embeddings and E denote the graph’s edge set. We minimise the classical retrofitting objective [3] with uniform anchor and edge weights: J(Z) = X i ∥zi −xi∥2 2 + X (i,j)∈E ∥zi −zj∥2 2. (2) The first term anchors each node to its original embedding, while the second pulls adjacent nodes closer together in the modified space. The anchoring term makes the objective strictly convex, ensuring a unique global minimiser to which the iterative optimisation procedure converges. Random-walk endpoint blend (walk). This transformation launches 100 random walks of exactly two steps from each node. The modified embedding is computed as the frequency-weighted mean of the endpoints’ original embeddings. Louvain cluster blend. This transformation partitions the unweighted, undirected graph using Louvain community detection at resolution 0.5; we refer to Blondel et al. [11] for details of the community-construction algorithm. Each node i is then moved towards the centroid µc(i) of its community c(i): zi = αxi + (1 −α)µc(i). (3) Each centroid is the mean of its community’s original embeddings and remains fixed. The selected configuration uses α = 0.5, assigning equal weight to the node’s original embedding and its community centroid. 3.4 Retrieval Strategies We compare retrieval strategies that use the original and graph-modified embeddings separately or together. text: We first test graph-modified embeddings in direct retrieval, then compare strategies that combine original and modified representations. text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint At the full budget, the controls recover 54.7 % and 55.5 % of the gold evidence, compared with 51.0 % for plain retrieval (Figure 9). Graph condi- tioning thus contributes slightly more than half of its 9.8-point gain over plain retrieval. The advantage emerges during the fused stage and persists through later searches. After twelve returned nodes, recovery is 39.6 %, against 31.4 % and 32.8 % for the controls. The full method also matches plain retrieval’s 40-node recovery after returning only 24 nodes, or 40 % fewer returned nodes. 5

text: Our results show that graph structure can improve evidence retrieval without graph access at query time. Graph-modified embeddings guide the search for additional evidence, while the original embeddings maintain semantic relevance to the query. This supports developing graph-modified embeddings specifically for multi-stage retrieval and evaluating their contribution to the complete retrieval process. Retrieval should adapt as evidence accumulates. The question and earlier results should guide when to use graph information, how to allocate the remaining search budget, and when enough evidence has been found to support an answer. Future evaluation should test the approach on natural corpora, additional embedding models, and graphs with missing or incorrect relations. It should also establish whether smaller retrieved contexts offset the cost of additional searches. The broader goal is to design retrieval with the final answer in mind, using semantic similarity and graph structure together to provide the evidence needed within practical computational limits. text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint Appendix Overview Appendix A — Graph and dataset. How the corpus was built: the generation procedure, the graph schema, the rendering of structured facts as text, the determinism guarantees, and the construction of the questions, answers, and gold-evidence sets. Appendix B — Retrofitting strategies. The formulation of each embedding transforma- tion, its parameter grid, and the implementation choices the main text states only in outline. Appendix C — Retrieval strategies. The same for the retrievers: the stage schedules, their quotas, and the parameters that distinguish them. Appendix D — Per-family results. Results for the six harder question families separately, whereas Section 4 reports them pooled into groups. A Graph Construction and Evaluation Dataset A.1 Graph Construction The corpus is a fully synthetic professional network of fictional candidates, organisations, resumes, employer rosters, and textual evidence. Generation is deterministic under a fixed seed and does not involve a language model: every fact is sampled from predefined source pools and then rendered into text by fixed templates. Because the graph is built before any question exists, no answer information can enter its construction. Candidate identity. A candidate’s name is a first–last pair drawn from two flat pools of 512 and 458 entries. A used_names set rejects any repeat and the draw is retried, so every person in
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings

text: answer information can enter its construction. Candidate identity. A candidate’s name is a first–last pair drawn from two flat pools of 512 and 458 entries. A used_names set rejects any repeat and the draw is retried, so every person in the dataset has a distinct full name before the identity-collision checks performed at ingest. With roughly 2.3 × 105 available combinations and a few hundred candidates per graph, rejection is rare. Uniqueness is what allows the human-readable entity:person:<Name> identifier to serve as the canonical key: two candidates sharing a name would otherwise collapse into a single node and silently merge their evidence. What is generated. Each candidate is assigned a primary sector sampled uniformly from eleven, which governs certifications and supplies the default source for employer and role attributes. A candidate receives one or two education records, between one and four jobs, zero to two projects per job, zero to three certifications, and zero to two endorsements. Education degrees are sampled with weights 50 % Bachelor’s, 35 % Master’s, and 15 % PhD, and universities come from a global pool that is not sector-scoped. Project descriptions reuse a subset of the skills attached to their job, so project evidence is correlated with the job rather than sampled independently. Controlled cross-sector bridges. With probability 0.2 a job’s role attributes—title, skills, responsibilities,
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings

text: that is not sector-scoped. Project descriptions reuse a subset of the skills attached to their job, so project evidence is correlated with the job rather than sampled independently. Controlled cross-sector bridges. With probability 0.2 a job’s role attributes—title, skills, responsibilities, tenure, salary band, team size, and project name—are drawn from a different sector, selected through a fixed affinity map, while the employer remains tied to the candidate’s primary sector. This prevents the graph from collapsing into isolated sector-specific clusters and produces known bridges between otherwise sector-oriented regions, such as technology roles inside healthcare organisations. Dual-perspective evidence. Employment information is represented from two document perspectives. Resume-side chunks describe one person’s education, jobs, projects, endorsements, 16

text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint and certifications. After all candidate histories are generated, a second pass groups jobs by employer: any employer with at least two employees receives a roster document and a roster chunk listing every employee and title, which mentions the organisation and each employee individually. The same employment fact therefore appears both in a person’s job chunk and in an employer’s roster chunk, so information about one entity is distributed across documents connected only through shared entities. This is what makes the corpus suitable for graph-retrieval experiments rather than reducible to independent flat documents. Schema. The graph is a plain JSON dictionary with three node types and three edge types. Every node exposes an embed_field naming the field embedded at ingest: name for entities and documents, text for chunks. The graph itself is therefore not embedded during generation. Category Type Semantics Node entity Person or organisation Node document Resume or roster Node chunk Textual evidence Edge part_of Chunk →document Edge about Document →entity Edge mentions Chunk →entity For each person the generator creates an entity:person:<Name> node and a document:resume:<Name> node joined by about. Every education, job, project, endorsement, and certification record becomes a chunk, linked to the resume by part_of and to the person by mentions. Educa- tion chunks also mention a university entity and job
title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings

text: and a document:resume:<Name> node joined by about. Every education, job, project, endorsement, and certification record becomes a chunk, linked to the resume by part_of and to the person by mentions. Educa- tion chunks also mention a university entity and job and project chunks an employer entity; organisation nodes are created on first use and reused thereafter. Identifiers are deliberately human-readable—entity:person:<Name>, chunk:job:<Name>:<i>—and these are the canoni- cal evaluation identifiers, preserved downstream in the vector store and in the result artefacts. The schema admits exactly three edge patterns and no others, so the graph is tripartite. One hop from a chunk reaches the entities it mentions and the document it belongs to; two hops return to other chunks through a shared entity. Figure 10 draws the schema and one instance from the validation corpus; the recurring chunk–entity–chunk route it shows is what the two-hop neighbour blend exploits. 17

Shape marks the node type: a circle is a chunk, a rounded square a document, a square an entity. Counts on the schema edges are those of the validation graph. In the instance, a resume document is about a person, its chunks are part_of it, and each chunk mentions the entities named in its text. Because mentions always runs from a chunk to an entity, two hops lead from one chunk to another through an entity they share — here two employees of the same organisation. Structured facts and gold supervision. Every generated fact is retained in two synchronised forms. Filtering keeps only nodes whose type is in GOLDEN_NODE_TYPES = ("chunk",). Entities named in the question are query inputs, not retrieval targets: the re- triever already has them. What it must recover is the text that carries the evidence. Rewarding a system for returning an entity the question itself names would measure nothing. Filtering happens at record-writing time only, and changes neither the question text, nor the computed answer, nor the sampling or reasoning depth. Question families. Eleven families span basic, compositional, and multi-hop reasoning. Basic families retrieve or aggregate local attributes, compare candidates, or select extrema; compositional families chain two basic operations and union their evidence; multi-hop families traverse explicit person–organisation–university relations over one, two, or three hops, alternating between two predefined chains at each level. B.3 Convex Neighbour Pull This anchored neighbour-attraction formulation is related to retrofitting [3], applied here to corpus-node embeddings. convex_neighbor_pull jointly adjusts node embeddings by balancing fidelity to their original textual representations against agreement between graph neighbours. A useful physical interpretation is a system of springs: each node is attached to its original position and to every adjacent node. The modified embeddings are the equilibrium of this coupled system. Objective and uniqueness. Let xi be the original embedding and zi the unknown modified embedding. Let E contain unordered edge pairs, each counted once, and let N(i) be the corresponding neighbour set. The objective is J(Z) = a X i ∥zi −xi∥2 2 + b

The objective is J(Z) = a X i ∥zi −xi∥2 2 + b X (i,j)∈E ∥zi −zj∥2 2. (7) Here a = anchor_weight > 0 and b = edge_weight ≥0. We use a rather than α to distinguish this penalty weight from the blending coefficient used by other transformations. Squared Euclidean distances yield a differentiable quadratic objective with linear stationarity equations. The positive anchor term makes the objective strictly convex, so its minimiser is unique. The implementation rejects nonpositive anchor weights. With a = 0 and b > 0, any embedding configuration constant within each connected component has zero energy; the minimiser is no longer unique. (9) The original vector has weight a, while each neighbour has weight b. Thus, total graph influence grows with degree: the denominator is a + 3b for three neighbours and a + 60b for sixty. text: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings Preprint Gauss–Seidel solver. The solver initialises Z with the original embeddings and visits nodes in sorted identifier order. Each update is written immediately, so later nodes in the same sweep use the newest available neighbour vectors. This is Gauss–Seidel iteration, rather than a synchronous Jacobi update based entirely on the previous sweep. It requires no learning rate or gradient clipping, although the objective weights and stopping controls remain configuration choices. For this anchored quadratic, convergence is to the same unique minimiser; finite-sweep results and convergence speed can depend on update order. Sorted identifiers ensure a reproducible order. Stopping rule. During sweep t, the solver records the largest Euclidean displacement over all node updates, δt = max i ∥zafter update i −zbefore update i ∥2. (10) The displacement is measured before overwriting each vector. Convergence is declared when δt < 10−6; the criterion uses the maximum rather than the mean, so every node must satisfy the tolerance. On the reported development graph of 1,811 nodes, convergence took approximately forty sweeps, with a final maximum displacement of 9× 10−7. A safety cap of 200 sweeps returns the current configuration even if convergence has not been reached; the manifest records the sweep count and final displacement so that incomplete convergence remains visible. text: Retrieval Disagreement as a Signal: Diagnosing and Steering Multilingual Dense Embedders Faeze Ghorbanpour Shaghayegh Kolli Jana Diesner Alexander Fraser School of Computation, Information and Technology, TU Munich Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) {faeze.ghorbanpour, shaghayegh.kolli}@tum.de
title: Retrieval Disagreement as a Signal: Diagnosing and Steering

text: Multilingual dense retrievers place all lan- guages in one shared space so that a question finds relevant documents, regardless of which language they are written in. We show that the same question, asked in different languages, re- trieves substantially different documents, and this disagreement is not because of weak lan- guage understanding. Each language retrieves well on its own and ranks candidates consis- tently with the other languages; divergence ap- pears only when languages share an index. We trace the mechanism: each language keeps its own ranking, but in the shared index, its correct answers are pushed far down, buried under non- relevant documents that are either in the query’s own language or in English, depending on the model. Because this disagreement is structured, it can also serve as a correction signal. We in- troduce disagreement-guided steering: for each language, we contrast the documents that other languages agree on for a question against those that language retrieves idiosyncratically, and take the difference of their representations as a language-specific direction, added to that lan- guage’s queries at inference. Against baselines of language-mean removal, subspace removal, and per-language rotation, it most strongly re- duces same-language crowding while remain- ing competitive on recall, trading off against mean removal, which better preserves ranking quality. 1
title: Retrieval Disagreement as a Signal: Diagnosing and Steering

text: Multilingual dense retrievers map queries and doc- uments from many languages into one vector space, so that relevance rather than language decides what is retrieved (Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). The intent is met unevenly. The same model re- trieves well for some query languages and fails badly for others, as documents in the query’s own language, or in English, fill the top ranks and push relevant foreign-language documents out (Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Amiraz et al., 2025). What separates the languages that fail from those that succeed is not visible in their scores. Scoring a language against gold labels shows how often it retrieves the right documents, but not why it misses them. To see why, we ask the same question in several languages and compare what each retrieves. The retrieved sets diverge, and how they diverge is diagnostic. We call this cross-lingual disagreement and make it our object of study. It requires no relevance labels and char- acterizes failed language by its departure from suc- cessful languages rather than by a single number. Disagreement is diagnostic because it separates two explanations that a single score cannot. A language may fail because the model represents it poorly, or because the languages interfere only once they share an index. The two call for
title: Retrieval Disagreement as a Signal: Diagnosing and Steering

text: single number. Disagreement is diagnostic because it separates two explanations that a single score cannot. A language may fail because the model represents it poorly, or because the languages interfere only once they share an index. The two call for dif- ferent fixes, better training in the first case, a ge- ometric correction in the second, but from gold scores alone, they look identical. Prior work does not separate them: monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval are typically measured on different col- lections, confounding the effect of mixing with a change of items, while audits quantify how unequal the mixed ranking is (Wang et al., 2026), and mit- igations act on the output space, transforming the index (Jang et al., 2026), removing language iden- tity post hoc (Kim et al., 2026), projecting out a language subspace (Xie et al., 2022), or correct- ing hubness (Lample et al., 2018; Sakhawat et al., 2026). Each presupposes which explanation holds rather than testing it. Disagreement can be read at three points, each answering a different question. Among languages retrieving only within their own documents, it asks whether they behave alike in isolation. They do: every language retrieves competently and orders concepts much as the others do, so representational quality is not the binding constraint. text: rather than order: each language keeps its internal ranking, while its documents drop far down the combined list, displaced by same-language non- relevant material rather than by globally popular hub documents (Lample et al., 2018; Sakhawat et al., 2026). Among languages competing in- side the mixed index, it asks whether they con- verge. They do not, and the divergence follows two regimes: some models crowd a query with its own language, while others pull the ranking toward En- glish. The pattern is directional: a language’s doc- uments stay reachable by other languages’ queries, while its own queries retrieve almost exclusively within that same language (Lim et al., 2025). Disagreement is also actionable. Knowing which documents other languages retrieve and which they miss gives not only the size of the gap but also a direction across it. We introduce disagreement-guided steering: contrast the doc- uments other languages agree on for a question against those a language retrieves idiosyncratically, and add the difference of their representations to that language’s queries at inference. This requires no neuron attribution, no training, and no relevance labels; its directions are estimated on a separate corpus, never on the evaluation data. We compare it against per-language mean removal (Libovický et al., 2020), language-subspace removal (Xie et al., 2022), and rotation toward a cross-lingual consen- sus (Liu et

text: labels; its directions are estimated on a separate corpus, never on the evaluation data. We compare it against per-language mean removal (Libovický et al., 2020), language-subspace removal (Xie et al., 2022), and rotation toward a cross-lingual consen- sus (Liu et al., 2019). The corrections are separated by what they repair: mean removal gives the best ranking quality and rank agreement, while steer- ing gives the largest reduction in same-language crowding and remains competitive on recall, and holds up on non-parallel corpora, where documents are not translations of one another. Our contributions are: (1) Cross-lingual dis- agreement as a label-free diagnostic, read within languages, across the monolingual-to-mixed transi- tion, and among languages sharing an index. (2) An anatomy of cross-lingual retrieval failure: demo- tion rather than loss of correct answers, displace- ment by same-language non-relevant documents rather than hubs, two model-dependent crowding regimes, and a directional asymmetry between doc- uments and queries. (3) Disagreement-guided steer- ing, an inference-time correction derived from re- trieval disagreement, requiring no training and no access to the evaluation corpus. 1 1Code, scripts, and the estimation pools will be released publicly upon acceptance. 2

text: Geometry of Multilingual Embedding Spaces A long line of work characterizes multilingual em- bedding spaces through their geometry and corrects them accordingly. Lample et al. (2018) showed that a few hub vectors become nearest neigh- bors of almost everything in high-dimensional spaces and proposed CSLS as a correction, which later work extended with normalization steps that strip language-specific structure before alignment (Ruder et al., 2019; Aboagye et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2025). A second strand targets language identity di- rectly: Roy et al. (2020) and Reimers and Gurevych (2020) showed that embeddings clustering by lan- guage causes retrievers to prefer irrelevant same- language documents over relevant foreign ones, Libovický et al. (2020) and Yang et al. (2021) re- moved this bias by subtracting per-language means, and Xie et al. (2022) showed that language identity occupies a low-rank subspace that can be projected away. Orthogonal Procrustes alignment provides a third correction, long used to relate separately trained embedding spaces (Liu et al., 2019; Lample et al., 2018). We evaluate all three under identi- cal conditions and against a correction that, rather than assuming a fixed geometric form, derives its direction from retrieval behavior. Language Bias in Multilingual Retrieval Lan- guage bias in retrieval has been documented and mitigated at the level of the final ranking. Yang et al. (2025) showed

text: rather than assuming a fixed geometric form, derives its direction from retrieval behavior. Language Bias in Multilingual Retrieval Lan- guage bias in retrieval has been documented and mitigated at the level of the final ranking. Yang et al. (2025) showed that multilingual retrievers treat query languages unequally and proposed a training objective to reduce the gap. Wang et al. (2026) found that multilingual RAG pipelines sys- tematically promote English and query-language documents. Mitigations transform the document index (Jang et al., 2026) or edit language identity out of the output embeddings (Kim et al., 2026). All of these measure a language against gold labels: they establish that some languages retrieve worse than others, but not why, since a per-language score never compares one language’s retrievals against another’s. We measure languages against one an- other instead, which requires no relevance judg- ments and distinguishes retrieving different mate- rial from retrieving the same material in a worse position. Steering and Model Interventions Modifying model weights at inference has become a standard alternative to fine-tuning, both for controlling gen-

(2025) identifies expert neurons and mod- ulates them to increase cross-lingual alignment in multilingual language models, reporting gains on cross-lingual retrieval, while Guo et al. (2024) steers activations in a generative reader within a CLIR pipeline, and Pokharel et al. (2026) se- lectively modulates neuron activations for multi- lingual classification and generation. These ap- proaches locate the intervention through attribution, by identifying which units encode a property, and require an anchor language or a target behavior to steer toward. Our construction differs in the source of the direction: we obtain it from the retrieval behavior of the languages themselves. 3

text: Multilingual retrievers are trained so that a query in any language reaches the relevant documents in every other language. Whether they do is nor- mally judged one language at a time, by scoring each ranking against relevance labels. Such a score establishes that some languages are served worse than others, but it does not reveal the character of the loss: a language may retrieve unrelated mate- rial, or the right material only in its own language, or the right material demoted beneath documents no other language would have chosen. These are distinct failures with distinct remedies, and a single number cannot separate them. We therefore evaluate the rankings against each other rather than against labels alone. On parallel collections, one information need exists in every language, and each passage exists as translations that we treat as one item, so the rankings produced by different languages become directly comparable. Their pairwise relation, which we call cross-lingual agreement, is measured at three points that isolate successive stages of retrieval: within languages restricted to their own documents, where competi- tion is absent; between a language’s restricted and shared-index rankings, where the only change is the presence of other languages; and among lan- guages inside the shared index, where they compete directly. Disagreement also shows how to fix a failing lan- guage. For a

text: a language’s restricted and shared-index rankings, where the only change is the presence of other languages; and among lan- guages inside the shared index, where they compete directly. Disagreement also shows how to fix a failing lan- guage. For a question, the other languages find doc- uments that this language misses, and it retrieves documents they avoid. Subtracting the average of the second group from the average of the first, in embedding space, gives a direction that points from where this language’s queries land toward where the others’ do. We average this over ques- tions to get one direction per language, weighting questions by how much the language disagrees on them, and add it to its queries at retrieval time. We steer queries only, leaving document embeddings untouched. text: 5.1 Diagnosis We read cross-lingual disagreement at the three points defined in Section 3.2, moving from each language in isolation to the languages competing in a shared index. Table 1 reports the first reading, Table 2 the second and third. Languages are strong in isolation. When each language is retrieved only from its own documents, every model performs well, with only minor varia- tion across languages. On both collections, mono- lingual nDCG@20 ranges from 88 to 97 and re- call from 96 to 100 across every language, for all models but the compact Gemma-300M; cross- language rank agreement is moderate and roughly uniform (50–66). Gemma-300M is the lone ex- ception (nDCG 70/76, recall 87/92, agreement 0.35/0.46): as the smallest model and a general- purpose rather than retrieval-specialized embedder, it produces weaker and less consistent rankings even before competition. The difference that later separates a failing language from a succeeding one is therefore not a difference in how well the model represents it in isolation, where every language is retrieved well, but something that emerges under competition. Mixing demotes rather than disorders. Placing all languages in one index changes retrieval sharply, but not by scrambling them. text: We studied multilingual dense retrieval through cross-lingual disagreement: how the rankings dif- ferent languages produce for the same need diverge in isolation and under competition in a shared in- dex. This view separates failures that look iden- tical under relevance metrics. A language may retrieve well alone, preserve its internal ranking under mixing, and still fail in the shared index be- cause its relevant foreign-language documents are demoted beneath the same-language or English ma- terial. The failure is thus one of interference, not absent representation: correct cross-lingual docu- ments are pushed down rather than lost, replaced mostly by non-relevant material whose language follows model-dependent regimes. The same signal also corrects. Among training- free interventions estimated from an external cor- pus, mean removal, subspace removal, rotation, and disagreement-guided steering repair different aspects of the failure: mean removal gives stronger ranking quality, while steering improves recall and reduces own-language crowding. Relevance, agree- ment, and language composition move separately, so multilingual retrieval should be judged not only by how many relevant documents are found but by how languages disagree about what to retrieve. Cross-lingual disagreement offers both a label-free diagnostic of this interference and a practical signal for inference-time correction.

text: Limitations Our analysis treats retrieval disagreement as a di- agnostic signal, not as an objective that should al- ways be minimized. Different languages may legit- imately retrieve different documents when corpora are not fully parallel, when relevance judgments are incomplete, or when the translated queries em- phasize different aspects of the same information need. This is especially important for Multi-EuP, whose documents are not translation-equivalent and whose relevance judgments are graded rather than one-to-one. We therefore interpret disagree- ment on Multi-EuP as evidence of behavior under realistic multilingual competition, not as a direct se- mantic mismatch in the same sense as on Belebele and XQuAD. The interventions require language identifiers and an external multilingual estimation corpus. We use FLORES to avoid fitting directions on the evaluation index, but this assumes that the language offsets and disagreement directions esti- mated from FLORES transfer to the target domain. Domain mismatch, noisy language identification, code-switching, and languages absent from the esti- mation corpus may reduce reliability. The steering method is training-free, but it still requires esti- mating one direction per language and choosing a scale; these choices may not be optimal for all models, domains, or retrieval depths. We evaluate single-vector dense retrieval at the fi- nal embedding layer. We do not study sparse-dense hybrid retrieval, rerankers, late-interaction models, or full retrieval-augmented generation
title: Limitations

text: a scale; these choices may not be optimal for all models, domains, or retrieval depths. We evaluate single-vector dense retrieval at the fi- nal embedding layer. We do not study sparse-dense hybrid retrieval, rerankers, late-interaction models, or full retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, where later components may compensate for or amplify the disagreements observed here. We also focus on top-20 retrieval, which is appropriate for common retrieval and RAG settings but does not fully characterize deeper ranking behavior. Finally, our interventions are diagnostic rather than definitive fixes. Mean removal, subspace re- moval, rotation, and disagreement-guided steer- ing reveal different aspects of the geometry, but none removes multilingual retrieval bias uniformly. In particular, improving recall, improving nDCG, reducing own-language crowding, and increasing cross-language agreement are not the same objec- tive. This trade-off is part of our finding, but it also limits how directly any single correction can be deployed as a universal solution. Ethics Statement This work mitigates a fairness-relevant failure, the unequal treatment of query languages in multilin- gual retrieval, and its gains fall most on the lowest- served languages. Two caveats: our steering cor- rection can raise the English share of results on non-parallel data, which a language-sensitive de- ployment should weigh; and it assumes the query language is known, so noisy language identifica- tion could redistribute rather than remove bias.

A Datasets: Languages, Access, and Licensing We accessed all datasets from their public Hugging Face repositories and used them solely for research evaluation, consistent with each dataset’s intended use. Belebele (Bandarkar et al., 2024) is a parallel reading comprehension benchmark with 900 ques- tions per language. We use ten languages spanning high- and mid-resource levels and five scripts: En- glish, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, Rus- sian, Arabic, Hindi, Chinese, and Japanese. It is released under CC-BY-SA-4.0, which permits re- search use with attribution. XQuAD (Artetxe et al., 2019) is a parallel ques- tion answering benchmark of 240 passages and 1,190 question–answer pairs per language, trans- lated from SQuAD v1.1. We use six languages, again spanning high- and mid-resource levels: En- glish, Spanish, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, and Chi- nese. It is released under CC-BY-SA-4.0, permit- ting research use with attribution. Multi-EuP (Yang et al., 2023) is a non-parallel collection from European Parliament debates cov- ering all 24 official EU languages, which range

text: from high-resource (English, German, French) to lower-resource official languages (Maltese, Esto- nian, Latvian, Lithuanian). Its imbalanced pools and binary relevance make it our realistic stress test. Derived from public parliamentary proceed- ings, it is released for non-commercial research, under which our use falls. FLORES-200 (Team et al., 2022) is a parallel corpus covering 200 languages. We use it to esti- mate the language statistics for XQuAD and Multi- EuP, taking 500 sentences per language from the development split for the languages present in each set. It is released under ODC-By, which permits research use with attribution. TED2020 (Qi et al., 2018) is a corpus of TED and TED-X talk subtitles, crowd-translated into over 100 languages and sentence-aligned across them; this broad, many-way parallel coverage is what lets it serve as an estimation corpus. It is dis- tributed under the TED Talks Usage Policy, under which the talks are licensed CC BY–NC–ND 4.0, permitting the non-commercial research use. Belebele comprises 9,000 queries over a 4,880- document index (10 languages), XQuAD 7,140 queries over 1,440 documents (6 languages), and Multi-EuP 22,504 queries over 25,883 documents (24 languages). For the parallel collections, each query has a single cross-lingual gold per language; on Multi-EuP, the number of relevant documents varies (median: 23, range: 1–188). We evaluate seven publicly available em- bedding models, all accessed through their Hug- ging Face repositories and run in inference only, without fine-tuning. Table 5 summarizes their provenance, size, architecture, multilingual status, and license. All are explicitly multilingual and in- tended for multilingual retrieval, with the exception of e5-mistral, which is trained primarily on English data but is widely used for multilingual retrieval and included here to test whether our findings ex- tend to a decoder not optimized for cross-lingual use. We read out each model in the pooling and prompt configuration, its documentation specifies: mean pooling with the official query:/passage: prefixes for the mE5 models, CLS pooling for bge- m3, last-token pooling for the Qwen and e5-mistral decoders, and mean pooling with the projection heads applied for embedding-gemma. For the layer-wise analysis, we extract a representation at every layer by applying each model’s deployed pooling to that layer’s hid- den states and run retrieval on the pooled vectors. The pooling is identical across layers, so differ- ences between layers reflect the representations, not the readout. Hyperparameters. All retrieval uses cosine simi- larity over the final-layer embedding with a cutoff of K = 20. All correction hyperparameters are se- lected on the estimation corpora, and each is set to the value that performs best there: the steering scale α, the subspace rank r for subspace removal, and the shrinkage weight for mean removal. The sub- space rank peaks at r = 10 for both a representative encoder and decoder, so no setting advantages our method over the baselines. The steering scale α is tuned per model rather than shared across models, since the architectures tolerate different amounts of steering. Disagreement-guided steering (α) is in the range 0.1–0.3, norm-scaled by each query’s magnitude, with the consensus for each language formed by reciprocal-rank fusion (rank constant 60) over the other languages. text: each language formed by reciprocal-rank fusion (rank constant 60) over the other languages. Compute and training. Our method trains nothing. Every correction, including disagreement-guided steering, is estimated in closed form from precom- puted embeddings: it introduces no learnable pa- rameters, runs no gradient updates, and adds only a per-language vector or matrix applied to queries at inference. The only forward passes through the models are to extract embeddings for documents, queries, and the FLORES estimation corpus, done once per model and cached. All experiments run on a single GPU (NVIDIA A100 40GB); embedding extraction takes minutes to a few hours per model, depending on size, dominated by the 8B decoders, and every intervention on the cached embeddings, including the full alpha sweep and the multi-seed runs, completes in minutes. The per-language steer- ing directions are the same dimension as the em- bedding (up to 4096) and add negligible cost at retrieval time. text: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve Yuyang Bai1, Yu Wang2, Yu Zhang1 1Texas A&M University, 2University of Georgia {ybai, yuzhang}@tamu.edu
title: Knowledge Graphs as Files:

text: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual ev- idence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or pro- cess retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execu- tion feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evi- dence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled abla- tions show the benefits of multi-turn program- ming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents re- vising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI. 1

Fig- ure 1(a) illustrates this on a request for “papers on data quality enhancement algorithms affiliated with the University of the Balearic Islands”. A neighbors call returns only some of the institu- tion’s affiliated researchers. The agent must choose which researchers’ papers to examine and make calls to check whether those papers satisfy the topic constraint. In the illustrated run, it never encoun- ters the gold paper. Writing code to batch these calls can simplify this process, but each call still inherits the API’s limits on the evidence it returns. To bridge this gap, we propose direct knowl- edge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which agents write and revise their own code to access text-rich KGs. Inspired by the idea of direct corpus interaction over text corpora (Li et al., 2026), we expose both textual node records and typed graph relations as files, together with the graph schema. Unlike Setting ②in Table 1, where code uses graph query languages or APIs, or operates on
title: (a) Predefined graph tools

text: over text corpora (Li et al., 2026), we expose both textual node records and typed graph relations as files, together with the graph schema. Unlike Setting ②in Table 1, where code uses graph query languages or APIs, or operates on retrieved subgraphs, DKGI lets the agent implement graph access directly over the complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow rela- tions, combine sets of nodes, and inspect textual attributes. It freely interleaves code execution with shell search and record inspection, refining its code as new evidence becomes available. We provide the graph files, their format description, and an exe- cution environment. The agent constructs the graph access tools that each request needs (Setting ③in Table 1). On the same request, DKGI writes and revises graph access code (tool creation) and executes it to gather evidence (tool use). Execution feedback guides which access operations to create or refine. The resulting code, in turn, changes how the agent explores the graph and what evidence it obtains. Tool creation and tool use thus co-evolve: the agent develops its tools as it searches, and its evolving tools guide the subsequent search (Figure 1(b)). We evaluate DKGI as a training-free method on the three KGs (Amazon, MAG, and Prime) from the STaRK benchmark (Wu et al., 2024b), using both the
