text: tools as it searches, and its evolving tools guide the subsequent search (Figure 1(b)). We evaluate DKGI as a training-free method on the three KGs (Amazon, MAG, and Prime) from the STaRK benchmark (Wu et al., 2024b), using both the minimal Pi harness (Zechner and Pi Con- tributors, 2026) and the more feature-rich Codex CLI (OpenAI, 2026a). Even in Pi, our best DKGI configuration exceeds the strongest published base- line (Tao et al., 2026) by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every dataset. Controlled ablations examine the role of agent-written graph access code. With the backbone, harness, and budgets held fixed, shell- only access trails predefined graph tools, whereas allowing the agent to write and execute Python code improves overall Hit@1 by 6.9 points and re- verses this comparison. A single Python execution recovers little of this gain, supporting the value of multi-turn interaction. Analysis of trajectories fur- ther shows that agents use execution feedback to create and refine graph access code, which in turn guides further search. Tool creation and tool use thus co-evolve during graph search. To summarize, our contributions are: • We introduce DKGI, a harness in which agents create and refine graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. 2

text: • We show that training-free DKGI achieves state- of-the-art performance on the STaRK benchmark using a minimal agent harness. • Controlled ablations and trajectory analyses show the benefits of interleaving tool creation and tool use and characterize how the two co-evolve dur- ing agent–KG interactions. 2 Direct Knowledge Graph Interaction 2.1 Overview and Notation DKGI places complete graph files in an agent har- ness. The harness provides an execution environ- ment and returns observations, while the agent de- termines how to acquire and combine the evidence needed for each request (Figure 1). Formally, a text-rich KG is a graph G = (V, E) with typed nodes and relations, in which each node v carries attributes xv, including text (Wu et al., 2024b). Given a query q that may combine re- lational and textual constraints, the agent returns candidate nodes ranked by their relevance to q. We adopt a ReAct-style interaction loop (Yao et al., 2023), in which reasoning over the query and pre- vious observations guides subsequent actions. At step t, the LLM agent π selects an action at and receives an observation ot, at ∼π(· | q, a<t, o<t), ot = view(run(at)), where run(·) executes the action in an environment containing the graph files and the task’s scratch files, and view(·) determines what the agent ob- serves. The agent

text: receives an observation ot, at ∼π(· | q, a<t, o<t), ot = view(run(at)), where run(·) executes the action in an environment containing the graph files and the task’s scratch files, and view(·) determines what the agent ob- serves. The agent uses shell tools for file inspection (e.g., cat, head, sed) and text search (e.g., grep, rg) (Li et al., 2026). More importantly, it writes and executes Python code to implement graph ac- cess directly over the node and edge files, follow- ing relations, intersecting node sets, and filtering textual attributes. Writing or revising this access code constitutes tool creation, while executing it constitutes tool use. We next describe the graph representation (§2.2), agent-written graph opera- tions (§2.3), output handling (§2.4), and how tool creation and tool use co-evolve (§2.5). 2.2 Knowledge Graphs as Files Before answering queries, DKGI exports a KG into text files Φ(G) = (N, {Er}r∈R, S), where R is the set of relation types. The node data N are stored as one JSON line per node v, containing its ID, type, and attributes xv. Each relation type r has a tab-separated edge list Er ⊆V × V whose columns identify the source and target nodes. The schema S describes the node and relation types. This representation preserves all nodes, attributes, and edges, so each query has access

This representation preserves all nodes, attributes, and edges, so each query has access to the same complete graph. The file layout supports both text search and code execution. Text search locates nodes by matching their attributes, while Python can extract the fields needed for further reasoning. A format description specifies the file locations and how to lo- cate nodes by ID. Edge endpoints let code follow a relation in either direction, with the schema guiding interpretation of entity roles. The agent is directed to inspect the format description and schema at the start of a task, then decides which nodes, relations, and attributes to inspect. Appendix A documents the concrete export layout used in our experiments. 2.3 Graph Operations Written by the Agent The agent writes Python code that reads Φ(G) di- rectly and implements the access procedure needed for the current request. Section 3.3 compares this design with using pre- defined graph tools directly or through Python code under controlled conditions. 2.4 Large Outputs as Files Broad searches and graph traversals can produce outputs that exceed the model’s context budget. Output handling therefore affects both the current observation and the evidence available for later ac- tions (Sen et al., 2026). Following the use of output files in Pi (Zechner and Pi Contributors, 2026) and DR-DCI (Lu et al., 2026), our Pi implementation saves the complete output yt = run(at) of every shell command as a file ℓt in the task’s scratch directory. It presents the model with view(yt) = ( yt, |yt| ≤B, head(yt)∥nt∥tail(yt), |yt| > B, where B is the display threshold, head(·) and tail(·) return the beginning and end of yt, and the notice nt gives its full size and the path ℓt. This head-and-tail truncation bounds what enters the model’s context while retaining the complete ex- ecution result. Later code can search or filter ℓt, recover IDs omitted from the displayed excerpt, or combine its contents with other evidence. Ac- cess code can also return compact candidate lists or selected text fields,

text: retaining the complete ex- ecution result. Later code can search or filter ℓt, recover IDs omitted from the displayed excerpt, or combine its contents with other evidence. Ac- cess code can also return compact candidate lists or selected text fields, giving the agent control over the evidence presented in subsequent observations. Thus an output of tool use can become an input to subsequent tool creation. Appendix C specifies the thresholds and notice, while §2.6 describes the differences between harnesses. 2.5 Co-Evolving Toolbox Execution provides candidate IDs, intermediate sets, empty matches, and error messages. The agent can use these observations in later turns to choose another traversal, narrow a filter, inspect a file’s structure, or revise earlier code. The revised code determines which nodes and relations subsequent executions examine. Tool creation and tool use therefore co-evolve: evidence guides the construc- tion of access procedures, and those procedures guide further evidence gathering. In our Pi implementation, the toolbox Tt consists of access code retained in the interaction history for reuse and revision, while Lt denotes the saved shell-output files. When an action executes code pt and saves an output ℓt, these sets become Tt+1 = Tt ∪{pt}, Lt+1 = Lt ∪{ℓt}. For actions that contribute no access code or no saved output, the corresponding set is unchanged. Subsequent code can reuse snippets

This process develops the access code within a task, without model training or a tool library learned across tasks. Section 3.4 examines these behaviors, with the measurement rules in Appendix G. 2.6 Implementation We instantiate DKGI in two general-purpose har- nesses: the minimal Pi (Zechner and Pi Con- tributors, 2026) and the more feature-rich Codex CLI (OpenAI, 2026a). Pi provides a simple setting for controlled ablations of graph access and agent- written code, with the model, harness, and budgets held fixed (§3.3). Codex tests the same design with richer runtime support. Both provide read- only graph files, a format description, a schema, and a writable scratch directory. Following Li et al. text: Direct tool use. Retrieve-then-reason meth- ods (Jiang et al., 2023b; Luo et al., 2024b; Kim et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Mavromatis and Karypis, 2025; Li et al., 2025b) retrieve reason- ing paths or subgraphs from the KG and reason over them. In KG agents such as ToG (Sun et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025), the LLM steers a prede- fined beam search over entities and relations, and StructGPT (Jiang et al., 2023a), Graph-CoT (Jin et al., 2024), GoG (Xu et al., 2024) and Plan-on- Graph (Chen et al., 2024a) give it other sets of predefined graph functions. GRA (Dragic et al., 2026) explores hybrid KGs through seven prede- fined Unix-style tools such as ls, cat and grep. Code over a graph interface. Outside KGs, CodeAct agents (Wang et al., 2024a) act through executable Python, and other methods cre- ate tools as code (Cai et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Wölflein et al., 2025). Graph-as-Code (Finkelshtein et al., 2026) itera- tively writes and executes code over a table of node features, neighbor lists and labels for node classification. For entity search over typed, multi- relational KGs, DKGI is to our knowledge the first harness that lets agents implement graph operations over complete node and edge files.

text: We presented DKGI, a harness where LLM agents write and execute their own graph access code over the complete node and edge files. With GPT-6- Astra, the training-free DKGI achieves the high- est H@1 and MRR on every STaRK dataset. In controlled ablations with GPT-6-Luna, the agent achieves higher overall H@1 than predefined graph tools, whether called directly or composed in code, and it gains most when it writes and revises pro- grams over several turns. Its trajectories show how tool creation and tool use co-evolve within a task. 8

text: Limitations Scope. Our evaluation covers the three text-rich KGs of STaRK, which have at most 10 entity types, 18 relation types, 1.9M entities and 39.8M edges (Wu et al., 2024b). Other KG benchmarks such as WebQSP, CWQ or GrailQA (Yih et al., 2016; Talmor and Berant, 2018; Gu et al., 2021), graphs with Freebase- or Wikidata-scale schemas, aggregation questions and the scaling of DKGI with graph size are left to future work. Where a KG is too large to scan or a question needs exact ag- gregation, purpose-built indexes, graph databases and query languages may be more suitable, and an agent could write its graph operations on top of them. A comparison with an agent in the same harness that queries a graph database through a query language such as Cypher or SPARQL (Feng et al., 2025) is also left to future work. GraphRAFT, which fine-tunes a text-to-Cypher model, enters the comparison through its published numbers. Models, baselines and data. Our main results use the proprietary models GPT-6-Luna and GPT- 6-Astra, which we accessed through an API in September and October 2026. Exact reproduction depends on the continued availability of these mod- els. Open-weight models remain to be tested. We release the code under the MIT License and the exported graphs, prompts and all trajectories under CC BY 4.0. Baseline

text: A Knowledge Graph Export We export each of the three STaRK knowl- edge graphs once from the graph data re- leased with the benchmark (Hugging Face dataset snap-stanford/stark, revision 88269e2), using a script that makes no model calls. For Ama- zon, we use the default graph, which includes brand, category and color nodes. STaRK built these graphs from Amazon product reviews and metadata (He and McAuley, 2016; McAuley et al., 2015) together with Amazon question-answer data (McAuley and Yang, 2016), from the Mi- crosoft Academic Graph (Sinha et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020) through the OGB datasets ogbn-mag and ogbn-papers100M (Hu et al., 2020), and from PrimeKG (Chandak et al., 2023). Each exported graph consists of four parts. Node files. Each node is stored as one JSON line with four fields: node_id (the benchmark ID, which is also the answer ID), node_type, is_candidate and attributes. The attributes field contains all source attributes of the node unchanged, except that non-finite numbers are written as null. Nodes are stored in ID order in shards of 10,000 nodes each (nodes/NNNN.jsonl). Edge files. The edges of each relation type are stored in one tab-separated file, edges/RR.tsv, where RR is the relation-type ID. Each file has a header row (source_id, target_id) and one row for every edge stored in the benchmark’s edge in- dex.

The agent’s final message must be a JSON object with the single key node_ids and a list of at most 100 entries, and any other output counts as a failed attempt. Entries are scored in order, and an entry that is a non-integer, a non- candidate ID or a repeat keeps its position and counts as a miss. H@1 is 1 if the first entry is a gold answer. R@20 is the number of gold answers among the first 20 entries divided by the number of gold answers. MRR is the reciprocal rank of the first gold answer among the first 100 entries, and a list whose entries are all incorrect counts as a miss. Five runs on the test sets returned 21 IDs, one more than the 20 requested, and each of them has an incorrect answer at rank 21, so every reported MRR equals MRR over the first 20 entries. A Llama 3.2-3B planner, fine-tuned on 1,000 sampled training queries with LLM- generated planning graphs, outlines the entities that a query involves and the relations between them. A layer-wise traversal follows this plan and at each layer merges the neighbors of the planned node type with textual matches, which come from BM25 on Amazon and MAG and from a fine-tuned Con- triever on Prime. GPT-4o-mini identifies the entities in the query, and a name without an exact match is resolved to its most similar nodes through a vector index over ada-002 node embed- dings. A text-to-Cypher model then generates Cypher queries whose decoding is restricted to the schema-valid multi-hop queries around the iden- tified entities, and the most probable queries are executed until the retrieved subgraph reaches a size limit. A Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct model then reads the textualized subgraph and selects and orders the answers. The text-to-Cypher model starts from Neo4j’s Gemma 2-9B text2cypher checkpoint, and both models are fine-tuned with LoRA on MAG and Prime. We report the full system from Table 1 of the paper, which covers these two datasets. GRASP (Tao et al., 2026) is a three-stage retrieval pipeline. A prompted Qwen3-27B-Instruct plan- ner writes a JSON plan of anchors, hops and a target, which is compiled into one Cypher query on Neo4j. The resulting candidates are rescored with Qwen3-Embedding-4B on Amazon and MAG and with SapBERT on Prime. Their ranking is then fused with that of a trained mFAR retriever under a weight that can depend on the plan. BM25 scores a doc- ument by the frequency of the query terms in it, adjusted for term rarity and document length, and ColBERTv2 matches token-level embeddings of the query against those of each document. A global search ranks node texts with BM25, and a one-hop neighbor- hood search can filter the neighbors of a node by node and edge type and rank them by a subquery. Three agents run in parallel for at most 20 steps each, and the nodes they select are fused by vote count. We report its GPT-5.2 results from Table 5 in the appendix of the paper.

ToG (Sun et al., 2024) runs an LLM-guided beam search on the KG that alternates relation and entity exploration and stops once the LLM judges the retained reasoning paths sufficient or the search reaches a maximum depth. RoG (Luo et al., 2024b) generates relation paths grounded in the KG as plans, retrieves the reason- ing paths that follow these plans and lets the LLM reason over them. In its original form, RoG’s plan- ner is Llama 2-Chat-7B instruction-tuned on We- bQSP and CWQ (Yih et al., 2016; Talmor and Be- rant, 2018). GoG (Xu et al., 2024) is a training-free KG agent that interleaves thinking, searching and generation steps, in which the LLM proposes new triples from its own knowledge and verifies them. F Closed-Book Probes The closed-book probes measure how many queries the model answers from its parametric knowledge alone (§3.3). Design. Both probes run GPT-6-Luna in Pi with reasoning effort high, and the model answers in a single closed-book turn (prompts in Appendix B). The ID probe asks for up to 20 STaRK node IDs, ranked by confidence, and is run on the full test sets of all three datasets (7,108 queries). Since node IDs are arbitrary integers, a correct ID could indi- cate that the model has memorized benchmark files. The name probe asks for up to 20 answer names (exact paper titles for MAG and exact PrimeKG entity names for Prime), which we map to node IDs offline. Because Amazon product titles are long and rarely match exactly, it is run on the full MAG and Prime test sets (5,466 queries). text: Structural Segmentation for Brazilian Legal Document Retrieval Leandro Carísio Fernandes 1, João Alberto de Oliveira Lima 2, Hudson de Martim 2, Eduardo Seiti de Oliveira 3, Roberto Lotufo 3, Jayr Pereira 3,4 1Câmara dos Deputados, Brasília, Brazil. 2Senado Federal, Brasília, Brazil. 3Faculdade de Engenharia Elétrica e da Computação, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP), Campinas, São Paulo, Brazil. 4Centro de Ciências e Tecnologia, Universidade Federal do Cariri (UFCA), Juazeiro do Norte, Ceará, Brazil. title: Structural Segmentation for Brazilian Legal Document

text: Long legal documents are often represented as single retrieval units, which can dilute rele- vant content and limit retrieval effectiveness. This study investigates structural segmentation as a document representation strategy to improve Brazilian legal document retrieval. Using the hierarchical structure of legal acts, we represent each document as a collection of chunks. We evaluate four representation strategies: a multi-layered hierarchy representation and three simplified versions based on core chunks (articles and non-normative document components), with varying contextual details. We test these strategies on two publicly available Brazilian legal datasets containing normative acts and legislative proposals, using both lexical and dense retrieval models. Results show that structural segmentation improves dense retrieval com- pared with whole-document indexing, despite substantially increasing the number of indexed units. However, it does not consistently benefit lexical retrieval. Finally, we find that full hier- archicy representation is not necessary: core chunks enriched with document metadata yield comparable or better results. Keywords: legal information retrieval, document segmentation, dense retrieval, Brazilian legal acts

text: Recent advances in information retrieval (IR) have increasingly used dense vector representations. Unlike traditional lexical approaches, dense retrieval represents queries and documents as vectors, allowing semantic matching beyond exact word matches. However, long documents remain chal- lenging to represent [1, 2]. A single vector may provide a broad and imprecise representation of a document containing multiple topics, making relevant content harder to distinguish from unre- lated information. One approach to this problem is to represent documents using smaller retrieval units, allowing the retriever to identify specific portions of a document that are relevant to a query. This problem is relevant in legal information retrieval (legal IR), which applies IR techniques to legal documents. Legal documents differ from general-purpose text in several ways. They are often 1 arXiv:2610.18622v1 [cs.IR] 13 Oct 2026
title: Structural Segmentation for Brazilian Legal Document

text: long, contain domain-specific terminology, and are highly structured, with relationships between their content and their organizational structure [3]. Relevant information in a legal document may be concentrated in a single provision or section, while the remainder of the document may address different topics. Treating the whole document as a single retrieval unit can therefore result in an overly broad representation in which relevant information is diluted by unrelated content [4]. The structure of legal documents provides an opportunity to address this problem. Structural components can be indexed separately, allowing retrieval models to match queries against more focused portions of the document. At the same time, smaller units may lose information needed to interpret their content. The choice of retrieval unit therefore involves a trade-off between repre- senting localized information and preserving the context in which that information occurs. Legal documents are suitable for studying this trade-off because their structural organization is explicitly defined [5]. Brazilian legal documents provide a useful setting for this investigation. Legislative propos- als, laws, and other normative acts follow formal drafting rules that organize their content into explicit structural units [6, 7]. These units include articles and their subdivisions, as well as higher- level components such as sections and chapters. They provide natural boundaries for document segmentation, enabling retrieval representations based on the structure of legal

They provide natural boundaries for document segmentation, enabling retrieval representations based on the structure of legal acts. The Brazilian legal retrieval context also presents challenges for current retrieval approaches. A recent benchmark of five Brazilian legal datasets showed that lexical retrieval models remained competitive with and, in some cases, outperformed dense retrieval models [8]. The largest gaps occurred on NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus, two collections of highly structured legal documents [9, 10]. In this paper, we investigate structural segmentation of Brazilian legal acts for document retrieval. We represent each document as a set of structural chunks and evaluate different repre- sentation strategies. During retrieval, the model matches queries with individual chunks, and the resulting scores are mapped back to the original documents for document-level ranking. We evalu- ate these strategies on NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus using both lexical and dense retrieval models. 1.1 Research Questions We address two research questions: RQ1. text: Passage-based retrieval addresses the limitations of whole-document representations by splitting documents into smaller textual units and scoring them independently. The passage scores can then be aggregated to produce a document-level ranking. A document can thus receive a high score when one or more of its passages are considered relevant to the query. Early studies showed that passage-level retrieval can outperform document-level retrieval [1]. Later work has extended this approach through language models, probabilistic passage scoring, and alternative strategies for aggregating passage scores into document-level rankings [11–13]. 2

text: In Legal IR, passage-based retrieval has also been explored. Rosso et al. applied it to treaties, patents, and contracts in their experiments to find relevant sections rather than full documents [14]. Aumiller et al. study the trade-off between document-level and smaller representations using a collection of English Terms of Service documents [4]. They argued that document-level repre- sentations may be too broad, whereas sentence- or paragraph-level representations may omit the contextual information needed to understand a topic. They proposed structural text segmentation based on topical coherence, identifying coherent sections that may span multiple paragraphs. Sim- ilarly, Malik et al. investigated semantic segmentation of legal documents using rhetorical roles [15]. Their corpus consists of English-language documents from the Indian legal system, and their method identifies semantically coherent units corresponding to functions such as facts, arguments, issues, precedents, and rulings. Nguyen et al. investigated the retrieval of sets of legal articles related to a query or its negation in Japanese statute law, using individual legal articles as retrieval units rather than entire legal documents [16]. Another approach uses structural information that is already present in legal documents. Structure-aware retrieval methods consider organizational or functional information to represent legal documents and their components. SAILER, for example, incorporates the structure of legal case documents into a pre-trained language model for legal case retrieval [17].

text: already present in legal documents. Structure-aware retrieval methods consider organizational or functional information to represent legal documents and their components. SAILER, for example, incorporates the structure of legal case documents into a pre-trained language model for legal case retrieval [17]. The authors argued that legal cases contain logical structures and key legal elements that are important for deter- mining relevance, and they designed the model to exploit relationships between these structural components. Yang et al. also incorporated structured information into legal case retrieval, com- bining textual representations with structured factual representations based on event chains and participant roles [18]. These studies show that document structure can provide information about how different parts of a legal document should be represented. The importance of document structure is especially clear in legal acts that follow formal drafting conventions. In such documents, structure is part of how information is organized. Brazilian legal acts provide an example. Complementary Law No. 95/1998 establishes drafting rules for Brazilian laws, including rules concerning their organization and hierarchical structure [6]. Other normative documents, including regulations, resolutions, ordinances, and legislative proposals, are organized according to similar principles (e.g. [7, 19]). This formal organization provides explicit boundaries that may be used for document segmentation and retrieval. Legal IR has developed around a range of specialized tasks and benchmarks, with much of

Legal IR has developed around a range of specialized tasks and benchmarks, with much of the established literature focusing on judicial case retrieval and legal datasets from a limited number of jurisdictions. More recently, interest in Legal IR for Brazilian Portuguese has grown, with the development of publicly available datasets, retrieval pipelines, and benchmarking initiatives [8–10, 20–22]. These resources have enabled systematic comparisons of retrieval methods across different collections. However, relatively little work has considered the internal organization of Brazilian legal documents for retrieval [23, 24]. In the Brazilian context, Lima proposed a multi-layered representation for Brazilian legal acts [23]. Originally developed for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, it exploits their hierarchical organization to represent each document at different structural levels. In this work, we investigate its use for Legal IR, where the goal is to retrieve the source document rather than individual chunks. We also conduct ablation studies to evaluate simplified represen- tations derived from Lima’s approach by varying which chunks are indexed and which contextual information is included with them.

text: The methodology is organized into five subsections. First, we describe the datasets used in the experiments. Second, we segment the documents according to their structural organization, repre- senting each document as a collection of chunks. Third, we consider four document representation strategies based on these chunk collections, varying which chunks are indexed and what contextual information is included with them. Fourth, we index the chunks according to each representation strategy and retrieve them using lexical and dense retrieval models, mapping chunk scores to doc- ument scores. Finally, we evaluate the resulting document rankings using nDCG@10 and MRR against whole-document baselines. Figure 1 shows an overview of the methodology. 3

text: Fig. 1 Overview of the proposed methodology. 3.1 Test collections We conduct the experiments on two public Brazilian legal test collections: NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus [9, 10]. NormasTCU contains 14,469 normative acts from the Brazilian Federal Court of Accounts. Its 46 queries are based on real user searches and mostly consist of short keywords. Query–document pairs were assessed by a panel of four domain experts using three relevance levels: irrelevant, partially relevant, or relevant Ulysses-RFCorpus contains 105,669 legislative proposals from the Brazilian Chamber of Deputies. Each proposal also contains a justification section in which the deputy explains the moti- vation for the proposal, which is not present in the documents in NormasTCU. Its 693 queries correspond to requests made by deputies for legislative proposals. The relevance judgments were provided by 54 domain experts, with each query and its associated documents assessed by a single expert using three relevance levels: irrelevant, partially relevant, or relevant. Both collections consist of raw text that generally follows the official legal drafting standards discussed in Section 2 [6, 7]. 3.2 Strucutural segmentation Brazilian legal acts follow drafting rules that organize their content into explicit structural units. In these documents, articles (artigos) are the main units of the normative text. Each article consists of a lead paragraph (caput) and optional paragraphs (parágrafos) that complement it. Each lead

text: drafting rules that organize their content into explicit structural units. In these documents, articles (artigos) are the main units of the normative text. Each article consists of a lead paragraph (caput) and optional paragraphs (parágrafos) that complement it. Each lead paragraph or paragraph may contain one or more levels of enumeration (inciso, alínea, and item) [23]. Articles can be organized into higher-level structural units, such as subsections (subseção), sections (seção), chapters (capítulo), titles (título), books (livro), and parts (parte). Together, these elements organize the main body of the normative document [23]. Documents also have a title identifying their type, number, date of enactment, and a summary (ementa). They may also contain other structural elements, such as tables, annexes, or a justification of the proposal (justificação). In this work, we adopt the segmentation proposed by Lima [23], which represents each document as a multi-layered collection of chunks at the following levels: • Document level: the whole text; • Document component level: the main normative text and non-normative components, such as tables, annexes, and the justification of legislative proposals; • Basic unit hierarchy level: each higher-level grouping of articles (e.g., subsection, section, chapter, title, book, or part); 4
title: Fig. 1 Overview of the proposed methodology.

text: • Basic unit level: each article, including all of its subdivisions; • Basic unit component level: each lead paragraph (caput) and each paragraph within an article; and • Enumeration level: each individual enumerated item within a lead paragraph or paragraph. Each chunk can be enriched with contextual information, including the document title, summary, and titles of all enclosing structural units (e.g., chapter, section, or subsection). To evaluate structural segmentation, we focus on segmentation levels from the document com- ponent level to the enumeration level. Document-level retrieval has already been evaluated in a public benchmark and is used as a baseline for comparison [8]. text: We evaluate each representation strategy on the document-level rankings for NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus. Both collections provide graded relevance judgments on a three-level scale. text: Hierarchical Chunks boosts nDCG@10 for the three dense retrievers on both collections. On NormasTCU, the largest relative gains occur for retrievers with the weakest baselines: 36% for text-embedding-3-small (from 0.263 to 0.358), 16% for jua-4B-mixed (0.305 to 0.355), and 8% for Qwen3-Embedding-4B (0.307 to 0.333). On Ulysses-RFCorpus, the relative gains are more uniform, ranging from 9% to 14% across the three dense retrievers. For BM25, nDCG@10 decreases on NormasTCU (from 0.364 to 0.342) and remains almost unchanged on Ulysses-RFCorpus (from 0.531 to 0.532), i.e., lexical retrieval does not benefit from segmentation in the same way as dense retrieval. The simplified core-based representations with context achieve results comparable to or bet- ter than Hierarchical Chunks while indexing fewer units. With Core Chunks + Full Context, nDCG@10 is close to that of Hierarchical Chunks on Ulysses-RFCorpus (absolute differences of at most 0.006). On NormasTCU, it outperforms Hierarchical Chunks with two of the three dense retrievers, yielding gains of +0.028 for jua-4B-mixed and +0.018 for Qwen3-Embedding-4B, while underperforming by −0.016 with text-embedding-3-small. Core Chunks + Metadata shows a similar pattern, with differences of at most 0.008 on Ulysses-RFCorpus. On NormasTCU, this strategy achieves the highest nDCG@10 among all evaluated dense retrievers, reaching 0.392 with jua-4B-mixed. text: 5 Discussion of the Results and Practical Implications 5.1 Discussion of the Results Overall, the gains from segmentation are larger on NormasTCU than on Ulysses-RFCorpus. The characteristics of Ulysses-RFCorpus may help explain this difference. Its whole-document baselines are already strong, leaving less room for improvement through segmentation. This may be related to both the documents and the queries. On the document side, each legislative proposal includes a justification in which the deputy describes the problem to be solved and the proposed solution. This section semantically enriches the document and mitigates the vocabulary mismatch problem of lexical retrieval. On the query side, deputies use natural-language descriptions of the intended legislative proposal. In contrast, NormasTCU has no justification sections and usually has short keyword queries whose terms may not appear in the normative text. The gains on Ulysses-RFCorpus are also limited by the documents that do not follow the expected hierarchical structure. Approximately one-third of the collection cannot be segmented and is therefore represented as a single indexed unit. For these documents, the segmented indexes behave like whole-document indexing, reducing the potential gains from segmentation on this collection. The results allow us to answer the proposed research questions: RQ1. Does structural segmentation improve Brazilian legal document retrieval compared with whole-document indexing? text: Answer: For dense retrievers, representations based on core chunks with contextual enrichment use substantially fewer indexed units than Hierarchical Chunks while achieving comparable or better retrieval results in most cases. We found no clear evidence that full hierarchical context outperforms core chunks enriched with document metadata (title and summary). We therefore recommend the simpler Core Chunks + Metadata representation. 5.2 Practical Implications The results suggest that legal retrieval systems can use the structure of legal acts without index- ing all levels of their hierarchy. The Core Chunks + Metadata representation achieved results comparable to or better than Hierarchical Chunks while indexing substantially fewer units. They also show that contextual information is important, as removing document metadata consistently reduced retrieval effectiveness. Thus, practical implementations can focus on core structural units, such as articles, enriched with concise document-level metadata. 6 Limitations of the study This study has four main limitations. First, we evaluated only two Brazilian legal test collections, NormasTCU and Ulysses-RFCorpus. They are the only available datasets that match the charac- teristics required by this study and cover different types of legal documents and query formulations, but they do not represent the full diversity of Brazilian legal documents. Moreover, about one-third of the Ulysses-RFCorpus documents do not follow the expected structure and therefore cannot be represented using the proposed hierarchical segmentation.

Second, we evaluated BM25 and three dense embedding models using max-score aggregation only. Our findings may not generalize to other retrieval models or chunk aggregation methods. Third, we tested four representation strategies based on Lima [23]. Although our experi- ment show the effects of core chunks and contextual enrichment, we dit not test every possible combination of structural components and contextual information. Finally, our evaluation focuses on retrieval effectiveness measured by nDCG@10 and MRR. These metrics capture different aspects of ranking quality, but do not measure other practical dimensions of a retrieval system, such as storage or computational costs. 7 Conclusions We investigated whether structural segmentation improves the retrieval of Brazilian legal doc- uments. We tested four document representations based on their multi-layered structure: one hierarchical representation and three simplified representations based on core chunks with different levels of context. The results show that context-enriched representations improve dense retrieval over whole- document indexing. text: The results show that context-enriched representations improve dense retrieval over whole- document indexing. On the evaluated test collections, Hierarchical Chunks increased nDCG@10 for all three dense retrievers relative to whole-document indexing, despite substantially increasing the number of indexed units. The same pattern was generally observed for MRR. For BM25, however, structural segmentation did not improve nDCG@10, although it improved MRR in some configurations. Ablation studies show that the complete hierarchical representation is not necessary to achieve these gains. The Core Chunks + Full Context and Core Chunks + Metadata representations achieved results close to – and in some cases better than – Hierarchical Chunks, while indexing substantially fewer indexed units. In contrast, removing context consistently reduced retrieval effectiveness. Overall, structural segmentation effectively boosts Brazilian legal information retrieval. How- ever, the complete structure of a legal act is not necessary to achieve these gains, and a simplified representation based on core chunks enriched with document metadata offers a favorable trade- off between representation complexity and retrieval effectiveness. Future work should evaluate additional structural representations, retrieval models, and aggregation methods, including seg- mentation strategies for legal documents that do not follow the structure considered in this article. 11

text: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report OneRec Team Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer. As KV memory, they can be further compressed without coarsening the representation passed between layers: Compressed KSA (C-KSA) pools groups of Summary KV into layer-local Meta entries, raising a larger chunk distant history compression. As sparse index, the summary token could conduct exact-access layers where to look: Sparse

text: Serving long contexts incurs substantial storage and computation costs. With full attention, the key– value (KV) cache grows linearly with context length, prefill attention is quadratic, and each decoding query reads the full history. Per-token KV compression (Ainslie et al., 2023; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024) reduces storage per position but retains an entry for every token. Sparse attention (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025) reduces each query’s read set while retaining token-level KV. Sliding-window and recurrent linear attention (Jiang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025) reduce both storage and computation, but do not preserve direct access to distant tokens. Hybrid architectures balance these trade-offs by interleaving compact-memory layers with full-attention layers that retain direct access to the original text. Summary-token hybrids are a strong instance of this design. Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) (Chu et al., 2026) appends a learned Summary token after every 𝑘𝑠text tokens; in KSA layers, text queries read nearby chunks at full resolution and distant chunks through their Summaries. Hybrid KSA interleaves three such layers with one full-attention layer (Figure 2) and retrieves long-range information better than a same-size full-attention model. In these hybrids, however, the Summaries are underused. They are computed and refined at every layer, yet serve only as low-resolution memory for KSA layers, leaving an inefficiency on

text: 2) and retrieves long-range information better than a same-size full-attention model. In these hybrids, however, the Summaries are underused. They are computed and refined at every layer, yet serve only as low-resolution memory for KSA layers, leaving an inefficiency on each side. On the efficient side, compression is tied to chunk size: a KSA layer stores one entry per distant chunk, so compressing further requires larger chunks, which also coarsen the Summaries that every later layer reads and refines. The KSA report’s 4B ablation shows that coarser Summary chunks can degrade retrieval performance. On the exact side, full-attention layers read every token, although most barely matter. At 128K, oracle block selection restricts the main-attention read set to about 4% of text positions, yet retains about 82% of decode attention mass and near-dense retrieval performance in a frozen Hybrid KSA (Figure 12; Table 10). What is missing is a cheap way to know where to look, and the Summaries, which describe every chunk, are never consulted. We argue that a single summary hierarchy can play both roles. As memory, Summaries can be compressed a second time when stored, without coarsening the representation that is propagated; as an index, they can direct exact-access layers to the few original-text blocks worth reading. text: be compressed a second time when stored, without coarsening the representation that is propagated; as an index, they can direct exact-access layers to the few original-text blocks worth reading. Efficient layers store coarse, exact layers read fine, and the Summaries connect the two. We instantiate this idea with two drop-in layer types, which together form KSA V2. Compressed KSA (C-KSA) pools every 𝑘𝑚consecutive Summary KV entries into one layer-local Meta entry, using learned dimension-wise weights as in DeepSeek-V4 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026). Meta entries are never fed forward, so the Summary sequence keeps its granularity while distant-history storage shrinks by a factor of 𝑘𝑠𝑘𝑚(1024× with 𝑘𝑠= 8 and 𝑘𝑚= 128). Sparse KSA (S-KSA) replaces full attention: each Summary pools the tokens of each 𝑏-token block in its chunk into a routing key, a Lightning Indexer (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) selects the top blocks, and the main attention reads their original KV with attention sinks and a local window. Routing needs 𝑏× fewer candidates than token-level indexing in DSA, and unlike CSA (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), the main attention never reads compressed text. Because both layer types reuse existing Summaries, neither adds tokens nor changes the Summary layout, so both can be retrofitted into a pretrained hybrid. Cache Structure and Updates To support efficient decoding, we design a compact KV cache structure for C-KSA (Figure 5). This structure allows each text query to read all visible KV entries through a single contiguous slice, avoiding per-step concatenation of cache segments. Each C-KSA layer maintains two components: an Attention KV Cache and a Summary Ring Buffer. The illustration uses 𝑘𝑠= 2, 𝑊= 4, and 𝑘𝑚= 4, with 𝑇𝑖, 𝑆𝑐, and 𝑀𝑔denoting text, Summary, and Meta KV entries, respectively. Cache layout. The Attention KV Cache stores keys and values in separate tensors with the same layout: the current chunk, a local text ring, and remote history, followed by free slots (Figure 5a). At a chunk boundary, the Summary query attends only to the completed chunk’s text KV and its own KV. In the example, 𝑇23 completes chunk 11 (Figure 5b), and 𝑆11 attends to 𝑇22, 𝑇23, and itself (Figure 5c). Updating the text and Summary rings. Once text and Summary attention finish, the completed chunk’s text KV is copied into the local text ring, and its Summary KV and auxiliary compression state are stored in the Summary Ring Buffer. If the rings are not yet full, the new entries occupy unused slots. Otherwise, they replace the oldest local chunk and its Summary record; the old Summary KV moves into remote history, with its auxiliary state retained for compression. The shared pointer advances to the next chunk slot. In Figure 5d, chunk 11 replaces chunk 7: 𝑆7 enters remote history, 𝑆11 takes its Summary ring slot, and the pointer advances to the slot holding 𝑆8. Compressing remote Summaries. When 𝑘𝑚uncompressed Summaries accumulate in remote history, they are compressed into a single Meta KV entry. The ranges and masks are computed within the kernel, with no dense attention mask or block-index table stored in memory. Prefill integration. The text-query kernel carries each query’s online-softmax state across the text, Summary, and Meta segments, applying the log 𝑘𝑚correction only to Meta logits. A separate local kernel computes each Summary query over its own text chunk and self-KV. Both kernels write outputs directly to their interleaved positions. Decoding. The KV cache in Section 2.3.1 stores the visible KV entries in a contiguous region, allowing attention to be computed directly with scaled dot-product attention (SDPA). 2.4.2. S-KSA S-KSA uses fused block scoring and a sparse KV-tile schedule to support query-dependent access to original text. The scoring optimization also applies during decoding. Fused block scoring. Using separate kernels for dot products and head aggregation requires storing intermediate scores in GPU memory. To reduce this memory traffic, we compute block scores with a fused kernel that performs dot products and combines weighted head scores on chip. A separate selection step then chooses remote blocks independently for each query under a 𝐾-token budget (up to 𝐾/𝑏blocks); each row of the blue IDs matrix on the right lists the block indices selected for one query. KV-tile scheduling. For each query group, we map its selected remote blocks and local windows to KV tiles and construct a conservative schedule of tiles to visit. The schedule skips inactive KV tiles, while per-query masks enforce block selection, local visibility, and causality within the scheduled tiles. We supply this schedule and the masks to the FlashAttention forward kernel for tiled prefill execution. Decoding. Gathering selected KV entries into temporary buffers incurs extra memory reads and writes before attention computation. To avoid this overhead during decoding, we use a custom sparse kernel that reads directly from the KV cache using the selected block indices. 3. text: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report 3.1. Experimental Setup Pretrained model and variants. We start from the 128K checkpoints of the 1.9B and 4B Hybrid KSA models in the KSA report (Chu et al., 2026). The 1.9B backbone has 24 multi-head attention (MHA) layers; the 4B backbone has 36 grouped-query attention (GQA) layers with 32 query heads and eight KV heads. Both interleave three KSA layers with one Full layer and insert one Summary after every 𝑘𝑠= 8 text tokens. We evaluate two successive variants: C-KSA+Full compresses remote Summary KV in KSA layers; C-KSA+S-KSA further replaces the Full layers with S-KSA. Although C-KSA supports layer-specific compression, each evaluated configuration uses a common 𝑘𝑚across its C-KSA layers. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments use the backbone and module configurations in Table 2. Baselines and training data. We reuse the KSA report’s from-scratch results at 1.9B and continual- pretraining results at 4B. The baselines include Full, Hybrid SWA, Hybrid SCA, Pure KSA, and Hybrid KSA at both scales, plus Hybrid GDN at 1.9B and Hybrid Linear at 4B. Hybrid KSA serves as the parent-model reference for capability retention, while Full provides a dense-attention reference. We report module-only and full-parameter training budgets separately. A continuation study found no consistent RULER improvement for 1.9B Hybrid KSA under the tested recipe and budgets (Table 11), supporting

text: Multi-head attention (MHA) is a fundamental component of Transformer language models, with separate query, key, and value projections for each head (Vaswani et al., 2017). Full attention provides direct access to preceding tokens, but its computation during training and prefill grows quadratically with sequence length, while its KV cache grows linearly during autoregressive decoding. FlashAttention reduces memory traffic for exact attention (Dao et al., 2022), while PagedAttention improves KV-cache allocation and sharing (Kwon et al., 2023). These system-level optimizations complement research on memory compression, sparse attention, and hybrid architectures. 4.1. Memory Compression One line of memory compression reduces storage at each token position. Multi-query attention (MQA) shares a single KV head across all query heads (Shazeer, 2019), while grouped-query attention (GQA) 23
title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report

text: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report shares KV heads within groups of query heads (Ainslie et al., 2023). Multi-head latent attention (MLA) stores compact per-token latent states (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024), and quantization methods such as KIVI reduce the precision of cached entries (Liu et al., 2024). These approaches reduce storage per position without removing historical positions. Other methods retain only a subset of token-level KV entries: H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) and SnapKV (Li et al., 2024b) use attention statistics to identify important positions, while StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2024) retains initial attention sinks together with a recent window. Another direction compresses historical context into fixed-size recurrent states rather than retain- ing token-level KV entries. Linear Transformers (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) achieve this through kernel feature maps and recurrent accumulation of key–value statistics. Subsequent designs introduce decay in RetNet (Sun et al., 2023), data-dependent gating in GLA (Yang et al., 2024), and gated delta-rule updates in Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025). Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Kimi Team et al., 2025) further extends Gated DeltaNet with finer-grained gating for recurrent memory updates. Related approaches include RWKV (Peng et al., 2024), with matrix-valued recurrent states, and selective state-space models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024) and Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024). In their recurrent forms, these models maintain a
title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report

text: recurrent memory updates. Related approaches include RWKV (Peng et al., 2024), with matrix-valued recurrent states, and selective state-space models such as Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2024) and Mamba-2 (Dao and Gu, 2024). In their recurrent forms, these models maintain a state size independent of context length, but access historical information through aggregated states rather than separately retained memory entries. Sequence-level aggregation represents multiple context positions with fewer memory entries that remain accessible to attention. Compressive Transformer (Rae et al., 2020) compresses older hidden-state memories, while Dynamic Memory Compression (Nawrot et al., 2024) learns adaptive KV-cache compression. Learned summary and memory representations are explored in Gist (Mu et al., 2023), ICAE (Ge et al., 2024), and UniGist (Deng et al., 2025a). AutoCompressors (Chevalier et al., 2023) uses summary vectors as soft prompts, whereas Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2025b) retains compressed KV activations at each layer. GMSA (Tang et al., 2026) combines group merging and layer semantic alignment in an encoder–decoder context-compression framework. Cartridges (Eyuboglu et al., 2026) instead optimizes corpus-specific KV representations offline for reuse across subsequent queries. KSA (Chu et al., 2026) interleaves Summary tokens with fixed-size text chunks. In KSA layers, text queries directly access nearby text and retrieve distant context through Summary KV, while the Summary hidden states continue to be updated across layers. A systematic study

In KSA layers, text queries directly access nearby text and retrieve distant context through Summary KV, while the Summary hidden states continue to be updated across layers. A systematic study of gist-based compression identifies task-dependent limitations, particularly in synthetic recall (Deng et al., 2025b). These findings underscore the importance of evaluating retained capabilities rather than compression ratio alone. Other designs organize compressed memory at multiple resolutions. MELODI (Chen et al., 2025) combines recurrent short-term memory with further-compressed long-term memory constructed at an intermediate layer. AdmTree (Li et al., 2025) organizes gist representations into adaptive semantic trees for hierarchical context compression. H-SSA (Mao et al., 2026) inserts meta-gist tokens to summarize groups of gist tokens and support coarse-to-fine retrieval. DeepSeek-V4 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) applies learned dimension-wise aggregation to text-token KV, using different compression granularities in Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA). C- KSA instead applies dimension-wise aggregation to Summary KV, forming Meta entries used only within the layer that constructs them, rather than introducing additional tokens into the hidden-state sequence. This further reduces distant-history storage without coarsening the Summary sequence passed between layers, and permits each layer to choose its own KV compression ratio. 24

text: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report 4.2. Sparse Attention Sparse attention reduces computation by restricting the positions read by each query. Sparse Trans- former (Child et al., 2019) uses structured sparse factorizations, Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020) combines local windows with global attention, and BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020) additionally incorpo- rates random connections. Sliding-window attention, used in Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023), restricts each layer’s direct access to nearby tokens. Another line exploits attention sparsity in pretrained models without additional training. QUEST (Tang et al., 2024) estimates the relevance of KV-cache pages to each query and reads only the selected pages. MInference (Jiang et al., 2024) combines head-specific pattern templates with input-dependent sparse indices to accelerate prefill, while SpargeAttention (Zhang et al., 2025a) and XAttention (Xu et al., 2025) estimate attention importance to skip low-contribution computations. These methods sparsify attention through prescribed patterns or inference-time selection, without training an auxiliary routing module. Content-dependent sparse architectures integrate routing into the attention mechanism. SeerAt- tention (Gao et al., 2025) learns block-level gates by self-distilling dense attention, while DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) uses a Lightning Indexer to select individual tokens. At block granularity, MoBA (Lu et al., 2025) scores mean-pooled token keys, whereas Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) (Qiu et al., 2026) mean-pools auxiliary index keys within micro-blocks; both
title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report

text: (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) uses a Lightning Indexer to select individual tokens. At block granularity, MoBA (Lu et al., 2025) scores mean-pooled token keys, whereas Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) (Qiu et al., 2026) mean-pools auxiliary index keys within micro-blocks; both attend to the selected blocks’ original-token KV. Native Sparse Attention (NSA) (Yuan et al., 2025) uses learned block compression to guide fine-grained selection and combines compressed, selected, and local attention branches. In contrast, DeepSeek-V4’s CSA (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) selects compressed KV entries for its remote attention. S-KSA also reduces routing to block granularity, but reuses existing KSA Summaries as aggregation queries to construct routing representations and retains original-token KV for the main attention. Learned memory tokens can also provide an interface for block retrieval. Landmark Attention (Mo- htashami and Jaggi, 2023) represents each context block with a landmark token and learns to retrieve blocks through attention to these landmarks. Simplified Sparse Attention (SSA) (Mao et al., 2026) scores gist keys and unfolds selected chunks to recover their original tokens. HiLS-Attention (Hu et al., 2026) uses landmark queries to pool token keys, then combines within-chunk attention outputs using entropy-corrected chunk weights. This allows the language-modeling loss to train routing; SAS (Li et al., 2026) similarly learns context ranking through differentiable gates inside attention normalization. In S-KSA, Summaries guide auxiliary aggregation
title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report

text: token keys, then combines within-chunk attention outputs using entropy-corrected chunk weights. This allows the language-modeling loss to train routing; SAS (Li et al., 2026) similarly learns context ranking through differentiable gates inside attention normalization. In S-KSA, Summaries guide auxiliary aggregation rather than serving directly as routing keys. We train the aggregation modules and Indexer by attention distillation and use the resulting scores only for block selection. The main attention applies a single softmax over selected original tokens and local context, without using routing scores as additional attention weights. 4.3. Hybrid Architectures Hybrid architectures seek to retain the fine-grained retrieval of attention while reducing the cost of processing long contexts. A common strategy interleaves several efficient layers with a smaller number of full-attention layers. Hybrid H3 (Fu et al., 2023), Mamba-2-Hybrid (Waleffe et al., 2024), and Jamba (Lenz et al., 2025) combine state-space layers with attention, while Kimi Linear (Kimi Team et al., 2025) combines KDA with MLA. Local attention provides another complementary component: RecurrentGemma (Botev et al., 2024) and Samba (Ren et al., 2025) pair it with recurrent or state- space layers, whereas Gemma 3 (Gemma Team et al., 2025) and MiMo-V2-Flash (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026) interleave it with global attention. Beyond layer-wise interleaving, other designs exploit sharing or finer-grained mixing. Zamba (Glo- rioso et al., 2024) reuses

text: space layers, whereas Gemma 3 (Gemma Team et al., 2025) and MiMo-V2-Flash (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team et al., 2026) interleave it with global attention. Beyond layer-wise interleaving, other designs exploit sharing or finer-grained mixing. Zamba (Glo- rioso et al., 2024) reuses a shared attention module at multiple depths of a Mamba backbone. 25

text: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report YOCO (Sun et al., 2024) stacks a cross-decoder on an efficient self-decoder and shares a global KV cache across cross-decoder layers. HySparse (Gao et al., 2026) reuses token selections and global KV from full-attention layers in subsequent sparse layers, while DeepSeek-V4.1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) introduces cross-layer KV and index reuse within compressed sparse attention. At a finer granularity, Hymba (Dong et al., 2025) runs attention and state-space heads in parallel within the same layer. Hybrid KSA (Chu et al., 2026) combines Summary-based KSA layers with full-attention layers in a 3:1 layout. KSA V2 retains this layer-wise structure while improving both components: C-KSA further compresses the Summary KV used for distant-history access, and S-KSA replaces dense attention over original text with Summary-guided block-sparse attention. 5. Conclusion and Future Work We showed that the Summaries of a summary-token hybrid can serve both as compressible memory and as a routing index. C-KSA compresses Summary KV within each layer without coarsening the Summaries passed between layers, and S-KSA replaces full attention with Summary-guided block- sparse attention over original text. Retrofitted into a pretrained 1.9B Hybrid KSA model, KSA V2 retains its retrieval performance and largely preserves general capabilities, while reducing cache size and improving inference throughput. Additional experiments on a 4B GQA backbone retain near-parent RULER performance, supporting transfer

text: Retrofitted into a pretrained 1.9B Hybrid KSA model, KSA V2 retains its retrieval performance and largely preserves general capabilities, while reducing cache size and improving inference throughput. Additional experiments on a 4B GQA backbone retain near-parent RULER performance, supporting transfer to a larger model with shared KV heads. The remaining cost lies mainly in the original-text KV stored by the sparse layers, a natural target for
title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report

text: Our evaluation covers 1.9B MHA and 4B GQA backbones with contexts up to 128K. General- capability evaluations and efficiency measurements are limited to 1.9B; the 4B validation covers RULER retrieval. Future work will explore longer contexts and larger models, including whether additional compression levels can provide further savings while preserving useful information. We will also explore how to allocate compression factors across layers. Evaluating long-document understanding and multi-step reasoning will also help establish how well the observed retrieval performance transfers to broader long-context tasks. 26

text: Revisiting Generative vs. Dense Retrieval: A Static Value Prior Reverses the Gap Renbo Tu1,2∗ Yang Liu1 Shuying Sun1† 1 Shopify 2 University of Toronto
title: Revisiting Generative vs. Dense Retrieval:

text: Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a strong candidate gen- erator for sequential recommendation as language models and semantic-item identifiers have improved. However, GR is not a uniformly stronger replacement of dense retrieval (DR) in online retail candidate generation. We examine their differences on two Amazon Toys datasets under different metrics. GR leads on best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. With deep analysis, we find that popularity contributes the most to GR’s measured value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this lead and keeps recall above GR. Finally, on an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, we show that a 14B SID-LLM still under- performs a 47× smaller dense encoder. Our code and artifacts are open-sourced at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/gr-dr-release- BCE4. Keywords generative retrieval, dense retrieval, sequential recommendation, semantic IDs, popularity bias, recommendation evaluation ACM Reference Format: Renbo Tu, Yang Liu, and Shuying Sun. 2026. text: Dense retrieval (DR) has long been a standard candidate-generation approach for recommendation. It encodes a user’s interaction his- tory and catalog items in a shared embedding space, then retrieves nearby items [3, 36]. Advances in language models and semantic IDs have made generative retrieval (GR) an increasingly viable al- ternative. GR represents items with semantic IDs and generates the next item’s ID one token at a time [6, 21, 25, 31, 32]. The apparent winner depends on how retrieval is evaluated. This metric choice is particularly crucial in e-commerce candidate generation, where retrieved products differ not only in relevance to the user but also its commercial value. To understand why, we need to know whether GR’s value lead comes from the user’s history or from generally valuable items. Recall and target NDCG show whether the held out item is retrieved and where it ranks. They do not account for other relevant items, their ranks, or their value. To understand the disagreement, in this paper, we measure both the best relevant item and relevant value across the full list. We ap- ply these metrics in controlled GR and DR comparisons on Amazon Toys 2014 and 2023 [11, 14, 23, 25, 35]. The metric disagreement persists on both public e-commerce datasets. Our main contributions are: • We define complementary metrics for sequential recommen- dation in e-commerce scenario and show that they favor different methods in the GR and DR comparison. • We decompose GR’s measured value lead and find that pop- ularity is its largest component on both public datasets. • We propose a training-free value prior, applied to DR as a single rerank of its retrieval results. text: The Generative Turn for Retrieval Systems. Prior to decoder-only approaches, sequential recommendation models for retrieval have been prevalent in production [3, 36]. The canonical dense retrieval (DR) is therefore defined as bidirectional sequential models for next- item prediction [13, 18, 30]. Generative retrieval (GR) enters the foreground as a constrained autoregressive decoding mechanism to generative identifier tokens, semantic IDs (SIDs), mappable to an underlying item, whose codebook construction follows RQ-VAE [6, 21, 31, 32]. SID generative retrieval benefits from the rise of LLMs and demonstrates generalization, establishing itself for indus- try applications [25, 26, 41–43]. Note that GR umbrellas non-SID approaches such as P5 and HSTU [9, 22, 38]. Our controlled DR-GR comparison is grounded on LIGER, while research on GR’s scaling difficulties and DR’s capacity limits bounds our conclusions without determining them [24, 33, 35]. Difficulty of Retrieval Evaluation. Offline recommendation evalu- ation suffers from sensitivity to missing feedback, candidate sam- pling and temporal splitting decisions [2, 4, 5, 17, 20, 27]. Audits on these decisions reveal that they can change recommendation rankings, while recent studies identify GR artifacts from SID colli- sion and benchmark shortcuts[8, 10, 12, 29, 40]. Our contribution identifies substitute non-identifiability under exact-target metrics and show how it worsens with catalog scale. Popularity Bias is a Static Prior. Our contribution identifies substitute non-identifiability under exact-target metrics and show how it worsens with catalog scale. Popularity Bias is a Static Prior. In recommendation, popularity of certain products are deeply associated with benchmark accu- racy [15, 28]. However, popularity also presents itself as a bias that degrades exposure and fairness for non-popular items [1, 19]. Pop- ularity bias in GR becomes prominent due to inherent bias within LLMs [7, 37, 39]. While these works mitigate popularity bias, our result show that under a same model GR-DR comparison, the ad- vantage from popularity is replaceable by a user-independent prior that can be transferred to DR without decoding. 3 Controlled Comparison Setup Problem Definition. text: 𝑗. Models. We compare GR and DR using the TIGER and LIGER framework [25, 35]. Both arms use the same interaction data, item catalog, and jointly trained T5 encoder decoder. GR decodes valid semantic IDs through prefix constrained beam search, while DR ranks items by cosine similarity using the encoder representation of the same history. Thus, the arms differ mainly in their retrieval readout. Datasets. Our public evaluation uses the 2014 and 2023 releases of Amazon Toys. The 2014 dataset contains 11,924 items and 19,412 user histories under a leave last out split. Among their held out targets, 19,116 were seen during training and 296 were absent from training. Our results reproduce the LIGER Recall@10 values, while our GR recall exceeds the published TIGER result. The 2023 catalog is 13.6× larger, which tests whether the observed pattern and the proposed intervention survive a substantial increase in catalog scale [14]. text: Exact Match: Substitute Blindness Exact target evaluation cannot distinguish a substitute from an irrelevant item because both receive zero credit. We refer to this limitation as substitute blindness. text: In this paper, we revisited the GR and DR in a controlled e-commerce comparison and we find two distinct parts to GR’s measured advan- tage. First, metric choice changes the apparent winner. GR leads on the value of the best relevant item, while DR leads on exact target recall and relevant value across the ranked list on both pub- lic datasets. Second, popularity makes the largest contribution to GR’s value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this gap while preserving DR’s recall lead. Cold target and substitute credit checks do not reveal a broader GR advantage. Graded judgments on an industrial dataset place DR above a larger GR model and DR with the prior above both. These results make DR with a static value prior a useful baseline for future GR systems. 4

text: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures Mingfei Zhang, Amit Surana, Ziauddin Majid, Chenxi Wang, Michael Xu Apple Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then- Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an al- ternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on Tool- Bench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross- category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single- tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt- oss-120b). text: Tool-augmented LLM agents operate over registries of thousands of APIs under tight context constraints (Qin et al., 2024b; Patil et al., 2024). The dominant approach directly embeds the user query and retrieves the top-k most similar APIs before passing them to the planner (Patil et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2024b; Yuan et al., 2024), assuming the semantic gap between user intent and API documentation is small enough to bridge by embedding alone. Recent work shows this assumption often fails (Shi et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024), motivating an alternative direction where the LLM generates query reformulations or plans before retrieval to better express functional intent (Fang and Glass, 2026). However, such works propose training-dependent systems aimed at improving retrieval quality, rather than characterizing when and why each approach is preferable. The underlying paradigm comparison remains unexplored. Prior work has studied retrieval-side improvements: Tool Retrieval Bridge (Chen et al., 2026) rewrites queries into retriever-friendly forms; Re-Invoke (Chen et al., 2024) enriches tool descriptions with synthetic queries; TaskBench (Shen et al., 2024) benchmarks the decompose-then-select pipeline; and Tool-MVR (Ma et al., 2025) treats stub hallucination as a bug to fix (we show it is a feature on complex queries). ToolFlood (Jawad and Brunel, 2026) and a recent survey (Qin et al., 2024a) provide broader context on retrieval robustness and tool

Left (RtP): the user query is embedded directly and matched against the tool registry via vector search; the top-k results are passed to the LLM planner. Right (PtR): the LLM first generates a draft plan with imaginary tool stubs, whose embeddings are used to query the registry; the matched real tools are returned to the planner for final execution planning. and LATM (Cai et al., 2024) has LLMs create tools from scratch. The closest prior work to the paradigm we study is TOOLQP (Fang and Glass, 2026), which generates multi- round query reformulations to improve API retrieval, trained with reinforcement learning. Our approach differs in three ways: stubs are generated in a single zero-shot prompt call with no training, we generate hypothetical function signatures rather than query reformulations, and we study PtR as a controlled paradigm rather than proposing a new system. Despite this active area, no prior work has directly compared these two retrieval paradigms in a controlled setting at large registry scale, characterized how the trade-off changes with query complexity, or analyzed how retrieval differences cascade into planner behavior. We term the dominant paradigm Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP) and the alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR), and present the first systematic apples-to-apples comparison at industrial scale (50k APIs). We term the dominant paradigm Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP) and the alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR), and present the first systematic apples-to-apples comparison at industrial scale (50k APIs). A key analytical lens we introduce is Intent-Registry Coupling: the semantic gap between how users describe tasks and how APIs are documented. Our PtR instantiation generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures) as retrieval queries in a single zero-shot prompt call with no training. Our contributions: (1) a complexity- dependent crossover (RtP wins on simple queries, PtR wins on multi-tool queries) robust to retrieval budget, registry size, and model family; (2) a characterization of stub hallucination as a dual mechanism: it degrades retrieval when queries have high Intent-Registry Coupling, and improves it when they do not; (3) an analysis of token overhead showing that directing single-tool queries to RtP and multi-tool queries to PtR reduces discovery-call overhead by ∼36% with no retrieval quality loss, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction consistent with prior work on complexity-aware retrieval (Jeong et al., 2024). 2 Method 2.1 Architectures Figure 1 illustrates both pipelines. Since we do not execute API calls, all measurements reflect the planner’s intended behavior. Trajectory divergence measures whether the two architectures lead to the same intended tool calls (via Jaccard similarity). Trajectory fidelity measures whether the planner stays within the retrieved set (100% = planner always names an API it was given). Trajectory fidelity is at least 96% across all subsets: the planner almost always selects from the retrieved set, confirming retrieval is the binding constraint on what the agent can do. On G1, coupling is high: the raw query often contains the API’s name or brand directly, giving RtP a direct embedding match while a planning step only abstracts away this signal. On G2/G3, coupling is low: a single embedding cannot capture multi- faceted intent. G2 queries require a mean of 6.5 Ground-Truth APIs vs. 5.2 on G1; PtR generates 2.4–2.5 stubs per query, each anchoring to a different functional sub-need and retrieving independently. The G1 finding is unaffected: even at k=10, RtP G1 recall (0.453) far exceeds PtR at k=5 (0.279). As a result, architecture choice at retrieval time fully determines downstream behavior: PtR’s planner generates more ambitious plans on G3 (4.1 intended steps, 1.4 APIs named vs. 3.6 steps, 1.1 APIs) and uses a higher fraction of retrieved APIs (27–29% vs. 21–27%), reflecting the broader, more coherent candidate sets produced by stub-guided retrieval. PtR’s discovery call adds ∼75–104% token overhead (Appendix E, Table 8); on G1 this hurts (−0.072 recall) while on G2 it pays off (+0.042 recall). Beyond token cost, this discovery call sits on the critical path: because discovery and retrieval are sequential, PtR adds one full LLM round-trip of latency before retrieval and planning begin, so the overhead is both a token cost and a wall-clock latency penalty. text: We present a systematic head-to-head comparison of Retrieve-then-Plan and Plan-then-Retrieve at industrial scale (50k APIs). Three findings stand out. First, there is a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP wins on single-tool queries; PtR wins significantly on intra-category multi-tool queries (G2: recall +0.045, p<0.001, n=200) and directionally on cross-category queries (G3: recall +0.012, n=100, not significant individually; pass rate difference is significant). This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1–20), every registry size (1k–47k APIs), and replicates on gpt-oss-120b, confirming the result is architectural rather than model- specific. Second, stub hallucination is a double-edged sword: it destroys high-coupling signals on simple queries but productively decomposes multi-faceted intent on complex ones. Third, the retrieval step is the binding constraint on agent behavior: planners faithfully execute whatever tools they are given (at least 96% fidelity), so architecture choice at retrieval time largely determines the downstream trajectory. These findings motivate complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction: directing single-tool queries to RtP and multi-tool queries to PtR reduces discovery-call overhead by ∼36% with no retrieval quality loss. A cross-model replication on gpt-oss-120b (Appendix J) confirms the crossover directions are consistent across model families. Limitations This work is scoped as a controlled architectural comparison: we isolate the retrieval paradigm as the single varying factor, holding the planner, embedding model, and benchmark fixed (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GTE-base, ToolBench).
