text: The main findings replicate. On G1, RtP outperforms PtR on precision (+0.088), recall (+0.113), and pass rate (+0.069). On G2, PtR outperforms RtP on precision (+0.039) and recall (+0.051); pass rate is a statistical tie (0.826±0.029 vs. 0.820±0.029). On G3, RtP has higher precision (0.135 vs. 0.123±0.008, n.s.) and recall (0.160 vs. 0.146±0.008, p=0.035) while PtR leads on pass rate (0.805±0.013 vs. 0.790±0.008, n.s.); unlike Gemini, the small G3 recall gap reverses toward RtP here, underscoring that G3 (the smallest set) is the least stable across model families. RtP retrieval metrics are identical to the Gemini results, confirming they depend only on the query embedding and registry. The slightly lower PtR precision and recall for gpt- oss-120b vs. Gemini on G1 suggests stub quality varies across model families, though the crossover direction is preserved. text: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine Thomas Hannagan thomas.hannagan@stellantis.com Stellantis
title: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival

text: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Each thinking step is an attracting but strongly non-normal map exhibiting balanced am- plification (Murphy & Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initial- ization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach’s theorem, the neural state has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve’s motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7% of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

text: The Continuous Thought Machine (Darlow et al., 2025) evolves a neural state for a fixed number of internal ticks against frozen image features, choosing at each tick where to attend and reading a prediction from the synchronization between neurons — a decayed second moment of their co-activations. It has been applied to classification, mazes, parity, sorting and reinforcement learning, and displays emergent behaviour, including low-frequency trav- eling waves across its neurons, that has not been explained. We take the official ImageNet checkpoint, without further training, and ask what kind of object the internal trajectory is. The CTM’s neural synchronization latent acts like a memory: when it is held fixed, a tick is an ordinary map whose local behaviour is read from one Jacobian; that map is contractive in spectrum but strongly non-normal, so it has a locally unique attracting fixed point that the state never quite reaches. Because the memory changes each tick, the target moves, and inference is a curve of moving fixed points followed one step behind (§3). Most of the curve’s motion is shared across images, and attention follows a schedule that is shared as well (§4). The model does not store Zt: it keeps St as a running accumulator, with an exponential decay rij = exp(−δij) learned per neuron pair — one scalar each, fixed after training and identical for every input and every tick. The out-side latent representation St out is read out by a linear map Wout to that tick’s logits yt and certainty Ct, and the action-side St action is projected through a linear layer to form the next query: yt = Wout St out, Ct = 1 −H(yt), qt+1 = Win St action. This matters later: because every trajectory starts from the same point, where a trajectory ends and the direction it travelled in are two descriptions of the same thing. Training objective. T is the thought budget: fixed in advance, identical at training and inference, with no halting mechanism and no early exit. The loss is a dual-tick cross- entropy, averaging the cross-entropy at whichever tick had the lowest loss and at whichever had the highest certainty, both chosen per input. Nothing weights later ticks, requires an answer before T, or rewards the synchronization statistic directly. Throughout, each sample’s decision tick is its tick of highest certainty, tdec = arg maxt Ct, as in Darlow et al. (2025), and every decision-dependent quantity is computed over [1, tdec]. Sample sizes differ between analyses because some (materialized Jacobians, Schur forms) are expensive; the sample size is stated with each result. 3

text: Hannagan Design choices specific to ImageNet. Under the official ImageNet checkpoint the synchronization memory uses random pairing: rather than forming the full D × D matrix, a fixed set of neuron pairs (i, j) is drawn once at initialization and only those entries are tracked, so the action and output slices are long vectors rather than a dense matrix. The checkpoint tracks 8196 pairs for the output slice and 2048 for the action slice, against D = 4096 neurons. The sampling is broad rather than selective: a neuron takes part in 4.0 output pairs on average and 98% of neurons appear in at least one, so the readout draws on the population as a whole rather than on a privileged subset. None of this affects any state-space quantity used here. What is known about how the CTM forms decisions. The original CTM paper reports several findings on ImageNet-1K (Darlow et al., 2025) at a budget of 50 ticks. Most images pass a 0.8 certainty threshold within ten ticks with a long tail out to fifty, so the budget could in principle be halted early, as in adaptive-computation-time recurrent net- works (Graves, 2016); the logits are unusually well calibrated without post-hoc adjustment; and reading the prediction at the most certain tick beats reading the current one beyond roughly fifteen ticks, while

text: principle be halted early, as in adaptive-computation-time recurrent net- works (Graves, 2016); the logits are unusually well calibrated without post-hoc adjustment; and reading the prediction at the most certain tick beats reading the current one beyond roughly fifteen ticks, while averaging logits does worst—so the model passes through low- certainty, sometimes incorrect states before settling. That certainty rises—equivalently, that output entropy falls—along the thought in most cases is therefore already known, and is in fact built into the CTM’s objective. The attention trajectory over image features also emerges through training, and visual inspection shows diverse, multiscale dynamics with low-frequency traveling waves across a learned feature map arising with no driving signal—a phenomenon with a long history in cortex (Muller et al., 2018). One further property of the released ImageNet checkpoint bears on what follows: its learned decay rates are negligible over the 50-tick budget, so Sout is in effect a running average of the state’s co-activations, a deterministic quadratic functional of z1, . . . , zt. text: its fixed points live. 3. An attracting, non-normal fixed-point curve What governs the state’s motion? One way to study recurrent network dynamics is to locate the fixed points of the recurrence and linearize there (Sussillo and Barak, 2013)—we hold the memory context At fixed, which turns the tick into an ordinary map zt+1 = f(zt; At) on state space. We reconstruct that map exactly (a single reconstructed step reproduces the model’s next state to < 10−6) and iterate it: it converges at 3055 of 3072 image–tick pairs from 256 images (residual < 10−6; App. A), and at every one of these fixed points z⋆the Jacobian J, read by autograd power iteration, has spectral radius well below one (ρ(J) = 0.15 median, 95% interval 0.14–0.16, max 0.95). By Banach’s theorem, applied in an adapted norm (App. A), the fixed point is locally unique and attracting: the state has one well-defined target at each tick. Beyond the neighbourhood the theorem covers, 3456 restarts from random states and from other images’ states all converged to the same fixed point, and we found no second basin (App. A). The map is nevertheless strongly non-normal: although every eigenvalue decays, the largest singular value exceeds one (σmax(J) = 3.2 median, up to 74), so it briefly stretches a few directions even while contracting overall (Fig. 2a).

The non-normality is balanced amplification. Schur-triangularizing J = UTU∗, almost the whole operator lives in the strictly upper-triangular, feed-forward part: that fraction — which equals Henrici’s departure from normality — is 0.99, against 0.71 for a Ginibre matrix and 0.93 for the random core (equivalently, the eigenvalues carry 2.0% of ∥J∥2 F , against 14% for the random core), while the antisymmetric part sits at the random- matrix level. With ρ(J) < 1, this triad of near-maximal feed-forward non-normality, stable eigenvalues and chance-level rotation is the structure Murphy and Miller (2009) identified as balanced amplification: a hidden feed-forward chain that amplifies activity in transit while every mode decays (App. B). 4. The fixed point curve is a traveling wave The curve (§3) accounts for a phenomenon the CTM authors report: low-frequency traveling waves across a UMAP of activation profiles, arising with no driving signal. They are the moving fixed point made visible. Ordering the D neurons by the phase of the fixed-point trajectory z⋆(At) or by their own phase recovers the same traveling wave (Fig. 5, left vs middle). This ordering recovers the authors’ activation-phase ordering (peak-tick Spearman 0.82, circular phase correlation 0.88; medians over 128 images) — as expected, since the state tracks z⋆within about one step, so activation phase is essentially fixed-point phase. The neurons’ peak activation times are spread across essentially the whole window — standard deviation 15.0 of 50 ticks for both the fixed points and the activations, against ≈14.4 for a uniform spread — so neurons traverse the shared motion in staggered phase rather than together, which is what makes the front travel rather than stand. Because ρ(J) < 1 the fixed point moves smoothly and the resulting pattern is a transient propagating pulse rather than a sustained standing wave, matching the low-frequency, driverless character of the reported phenomenon. text: A fixed-point curve in the CTM The cascade account, and why it fails. The balanced-amplification structure of §3 suggests a compelling alternative account of the waves. If the tick map is an almost-pure feed-forward cascade that also organizes the observed dynamics, then the traveling waves should appear when neurons are ordered by their position in that cascade. They do not. Ordering neurons by their position in J’s feed-forward chain — each neuron’s mean index in the Schur basis J = UTU∗, weighted by its participation P k U2 ik, using J at the mid- trajectory tick — peak activation time does not advance: the rank correlation between cascade position and peak tick is −0.08 over all D neurons, and between cascade position and activation phase +0.01 (medians over 16 images). The reason is structural: J — and with it its Schur ordering — is redefined at every tick, so no single instantaneous cascade can organize a trajectory that runs over all ticks; and because the state sits on the moving fixed point, the bulk of the activation is carried by where that fixed point is, while the balanced-amplification transient governs only the one-step residual. Smaller models Two D=128 models, one on MNIST and one on CIFAR-10, separate what is intrinsic to CTM inference from what ImageNet elicits. Both have a dense synchronization matrix: unlike the ImageNet checkpoint’s random pairing, every tracked entry is a pair among the first 16 neurons, giving action and output slices of 136 entries each. The CIFAR model uses a ResNet-9 backbone, which lifts its accuracy to 0.84 from 0.64 with the original backbone and lets us treat it as a competent classifier rather than a toy. The curve is universal, the transient amplification is not. Measured the same way as the ImageNet model, both have a spectral radius near a tenth at the fixed point (ρ(J) = 0.10 on MNIST, 0.068 on CIFAR), but a largest singular value below one throughout on MNIST (σmax(J) = 0.49, max 0.77) and in the median on CIFAR (0.36, max 3.06; about one CIFAR fixed point in ten does stretch)—these maps are Euclidean contractions, in contrast to the ImageNet map’s several-fold stretch (Table 2). Discussion CTM inference on ImageNet tracks a curve of fixed points, largely shared across images, while attention follows a schedule that is shared as well. The attracting, non-normal maps we uncover suggest how the CTM transiently amplifies activity while staying stable. Non- normal recurrence as a substrate for transient amplification and memory has been studied in neural circuits (Ganguli et al., 2008; Murphy
title: Hannagan

text: as well. The attracting, non-normal maps we uncover suggest how the CTM transiently amplifies activity while staying stable. Non- normal recurrence as a substrate for transient amplification and memory has been studied in neural circuits (Ganguli et al., 2008; Murphy and Miller, 2009; Goldman, 2009; Hennequin et al., 2014; Bondanelli and Ostojic, 2020) and built into trained recurrent networks (Kerg et al., 2019); locating and linearizing around the fixed points of a trained network follows Sussillo and Barak (2013); Golub and Sussillo (2018); Maheswaranathan et al. (2019). What differs here is that the map, and with it the fixed point, is redefined at every tick. On ImageNet, where the CTM attends next can be predicted one step ahead, and the model might gain freedom from image-dependent decay rates, a variant of fast-weight memories (Ba et al., 2016; Schlag et al., 2021). text: A fixed-point curve in the CTM Appendix A. Method and robustness Computing the Jacobian of one thought cycle. To study the CTM’s neural dynamics we freeze the memory at a chosen tick. With the image tokens, the memory accumulators, and the short pre-activation history held fixed, one tick becomes an ordinary map from states to states, zt+1 = f(zt; At), where At bundles everything held constant. We reconstruct this map from the model’s own components and verify that a single reconstructed step reproduces the true next state to within numerical error. Iterating the map gives its fixed point; the Jacobian at the fixed point, obtained by automatic differentiation, gives its local behavior. From that Jacobian we read two numbers by power iteration: the spectral radius, which governs whether the map settles, and the largest singular value, which measures how much it can stretch a direction in a single step. Objects. Fix a tick and its context A. The frozen map f(·; A) : RD →RD of §2 is C1. A fixed point z⋆= z⋆(A) solves z⋆= f(z⋆; A); the Jacobian there is J = ∂f/∂z z⋆, with spectral radius ρ(J) = maxi |λi(J)| and operator norm σmax(J) = p λmax(J⊤J). The map is non-normal when J⊤J̸ = JJ⊤, which permits σmax(J) > 1 ≥ρ(J): transient stretching of some directions despite

The map is non-normal when J⊤J̸ = JJ⊤, which permits σmax(J) > 1 ≥ρ(J): transient stretching of some directions despite every eigenvalue decaying. Banach’s fixed-point theorem. If (X, ∥·∥) is complete and g : X →X is a contraction — ∥g(u) −g(v)∥≤L∥u −v∥for some L < 1 and all u, v — then g has a unique fixed point x⋆, and the iteration uk+1 = g(uk) converges to it geometrically, ∥uk −x⋆∥≤Lk∥u0 −x⋆∥. How we apply it. We do not have a global Euclidean contraction: σmax(J) > 1, so f can push nearby points apart in Euclidean norm, and Banach does not apply in ∥· ∥2. Local uniqueness and attraction follow instead from the spectral radius, through a standard fact (Householder): for any matrix J and any ε > 0 there is a vector norm whose induced operator norm satisfies ∥J∥⋆≤ρ(J) + ε. Since we measure ρ(J) = 0.15 < 1, choosing ε with ρ(J)+ε < 1 yields a norm ∥·∥⋆in which J is a contraction; because f is C1, it is then a contraction in ∥· ∥⋆on a neighborhood of z⋆, and Banach applies there. The fixed point is therefore locally unique and the iteration converges geometrically in ∥·

The fixed point is therefore locally unique and the iteration converges geometrically in ∥· ∥⋆— matching the observation that iterating from the current state reaches residual < 10−6 at 99.4% of image–tick pairs (see Estimation below). The non-normality (σmax(J) ≫ρ(J)) is exactly why convergence need not be monotone in the Euclidean norm, and why the state lags the moving fixed point by about one step even while it is strongly attracted in ∥· ∥⋆. Establishing non-normality. A stability check based on random directions is there- fore misleading: it averages f’s action over directions, reporting something close to the typical stretch — about 0.07 here, comfortably below one — and never samples the few directions stretched most. We confirm the stretching is genuine, not an artifact of differen- tiation, by perturbing z⋆along the single most-stretched direction and measuring the effect by finite differences (over 32 fixed points, the finite-difference stretch and the autograd op- erator norm agree to a median ratio of 1.000; median stretch 2.7). Appendix B. Balanced amplification: the Schur form of the tick map Pseudospectra and a random-matrix null. The object behind the transient stretching is the ε-pseudospectrum of J (Trefethen and Embree, 2005): because J is non-normal, its pseudospectrum reaches well outside the unit disk even though its spectrum sits at radius ρ(J) ≈0.15, which is what allows the one-step Euclidean growth and the lag. Repeated multiplication by a fixed random matrix is on its own enough to organize structured neural codes (Hannagan et al., 2018), so a random matrix is the natural yardstick for an operator applied repeatedly. To ask what produces this non-normality, we compare the measured σmax(J)/ρ(J) (of order 30) against two same-size nulls. A Ginibre matrix (i.i.d. Gaussian entries) gives σmax(J)/ρ(J)≈2 by the circular law, so a generic light-tailed random matrix is far more normal than J. What produces the non-normality. An entry-shuffle of J—which preserves J’s heavy- tailed entry distribution but destroys its learned arrangement—gives a median σmax(J)/ρ(J) of about 13 over 60 image–tick pairs, already six times the Gaussian value; the measured ≈30 adds a further factor of about 2.3 on top. Both ingredients therefore matter: the heavy- tailed entry distribution accounts for most of the gap from a Gaussian matrix, while the specific learned arrangement still contributes a substantial additional amount. Either way J is sharply distinguished from a Gaussian matrix of the same size. Part of the non-normality is architectural—an untrained CTM gives σmax(J)/ρ(J) ≈7—and training multiplies it; training increases it on the small models too, but less (§8). Against the same Ginibre and entry-shuffle nulls, and against the random core (the trained backbone with the recurrence at initialization), J is near-maximally feed-forward (0.99 vs 0.71/0.81/0.93) with a chance-level rotational part (0.71)—the balanced-amplification signature of Murphy and Miller (2009); reading a recurrent operator’s hidden feed-forward organization off its Schur form follows Goldman (2009). The attention schedule in detail The attention map comes apart into a shared schedule, which depends only on the tick, and the image’s features, which decide where that schedule lands. Discarding each image’s own query and substituting the population-average query at the matching tick still recovers the image’s true attention map at cosine similarity 0.936 (400 held-out images; Figs. 4 and 8). text: RCER: Reconstructing Cross-Evidence Relations for Iterative Retrieval-Augmented Generation Linyao Zheng1,∗ Xuhang Shi2 Zhifang Mao2 Xiuquan Hou1 Sai Zhou1 1Xi’an Jiaotong University 2Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications ∗Corresponding author: zhengly@stu.xjtu.edu.cn
title: RCER: Reconstructing Cross-Evidence Relations

text: Iterative retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) accumulates knowledge from retrieved evi- dence to answer complex questions, but ex- isting methods struggle to reconstruct entity correspondences and inferential dependencies across retrieved passages as new information emerges. We propose RCER, an iterative RAG method that reconstructs these cross-evidence relations directly from accumulated source pas- sages. Inter-round relational evidence ac- quisition identifies entity correspondences and relational dependencies to drive dynamic prob- lem decomposition and iterative retrieval. Rea- soning context reconstruction independently constructs a coherent reasoning context through joint selection of complementary passages and derivation of cross-evidence inferences. Cross- evidence compositional reasoning leverages these inferences to establish entity correspon- dences and compose relations across selected passages for answer derivation. Experiments show that RCER outperforms the best base- lines by 2.83 EM and 3.06 F1 points on aver- age across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and achieves superior performance on narrative and implicit reasoning tasks. 1
title: RCER: Reconstructing Cross-Evidence Relations

text: Iterative retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) builds on standard RAG (Lewis et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2024) by interleaving retrieval and reason- ing to answer complex questions (Trivedi et al., 2023). Intermediate findings identify new infor- mation needs and guide subsequent searches. Re- cent methods organize acquired knowledge into evolving representations. KAIR maintains an in- dex of salient keywords and their relations (Wu et al., 2026), MGranRAG combines evidence mem- ory with graph-calibrated passage rankings (Hu et al., 2026), and CIRAG integrates candidate triples using retrieval history (Wei et al., 2026). This knowledge-state updating preserves and prior- itizes acquired information for subsequent retrieval and answer generation. Knowledge-state updating represents facts and relations from retrieved evidence to guide retrieval and generation. As retrieval progresses, newly acquired evidence can establish entity correspon- dences and relational dependencies that change how earlier facts support compositional reason- ing. However, accumulating relevant facts does not ensure that these emerging relations inform sub- sequent retrieval decisions and answer derivation. Figure 1 illustrates this issue with an example from MuSiQue. This raises an open question. How can iterative RAG turn progressively acquired knowl- edge into reliable cross-round reasoning? We propose RCER, an iterative RAG method that complements knowledge-state updating with cross-evidence relational reconstruction to estab- lish how accumulated facts jointly support reason- ing for the current question. text: turn progressively acquired knowl- edge into reliable cross-round reasoning? We propose RCER, an iterative RAG method that complements knowledge-state updating with cross-evidence relational reconstruction to estab- lish how accumulated facts jointly support reason- ing for the current question. Inter-Round Rela- tional Evidence Acquisition jointly analyzes earlier and newly acquired passages to establish entity correspondences and relations. These judgments specify or revise the next information need, guiding dynamic problem decomposition and subsequent retrieval. After acquisition, Reasoning Context Re- construction independently analyzes the final can- didate pool to select complementary passages and derive cross-document inferences. Cross-Evidence Compositional Reasoning uses these inferences alongside the selected sources to bind entities and compose relations under the question’s conditions. The main contributions are as follows. • We propose Inter-Round Relational Evidence Acquisition, which jointly analyzes accu- mulated source passages to update earlier facts’ inferential roles with new evidence. Relational judgments specify information needs through dynamic problem decomposi- tion and guide retrieval queries. Retrieved 1 arXiv:2610.19398v1 [cs.IR] 14 Oct 2026

text: 2.1 RAG RAG grounds generation in retrieved passages (Lewis et al., 2020). BM25 and dense passage retrieval identify relevant passages through lexical matching and learned representations, respectively (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009; Karpukhin et al., 2020). Structure-augmented approaches organize knowledge for retrieval and reasoning. HippoRAG and HippoRAG 2 exploit graph-based associations (Gutiérrez et al., 2024, 2025), while GraphRAG and RAPTOR use graph-community and hier- archical summaries (Edge et al., 2024; Sarthi et al., 2024). EvLink retrieves bridge passages through source-grounded evidence links (Anony- mous, 2026a). OriginRAG preserves demand– passage provenance during graph retrieval and grounds supported demands in verbatim source spans (Anonymous, 2026b). SG-RAG aligns sub- graphs with query constraints (Xie et al., 2026), and LogicRAG constructs query-dependent reasoning structures (Chen et al., 2026a). SetR addresses pas- sage selection through set-level reasoning, identi- fying information requirements and selecting com- plementary passages (Lee et al., 2025b). 2.2 Iterative RAG Reasoning-driven iteration uses intermediate findings to guide subsequent searches. IRCoT in- terleaves chain-of-thought reasoning with retrieval (Trivedi et al., 2023), while self-ask generates inter- mediate questions (Press et al., 2023). S2G-RAG assesses evidence sufficiency and identifies infor- mation gaps to guide further retrieval (Li et al., 2026). text: recon- structing relations across accumulated passages. For a question q, initial retrieval from corpus Dq produces A0. At iteration t, the controller input xt contains q together with the accumulated passages At and query history Ht. The latest batch ∆t is identified within At, whose passages retain acqui- sition order. An LLM-based retrieval controller jointly analyzes the passages to determine how new evidence connects with earlier facts and what requires further investigation. It generates (ft, It, Mt, qt+1) = Cθ(xt). (1) Here ft specifies the relation under investigation, with It identifying the passages considered jointly. The relational analysis Mt expresses their current interpretation through mt entries Mt = [(rtj, utj, Btj)]j∈[mt]. (2) Each entry pairs a relation rtj with its current interpretation utj, including unresolved aspects. The passage identifiers Btj connect this interpre- tation to the retrieved text. Newly established entity correspondences can make an earlier fact a premise for the current investigation. Dynamic problem decomposition translates these judgments into the next subquestion, specifying the entity and relation that require further evidence. The controller expresses this information need as the retrieval query qt+1. Let Ut contain the corpus passages not yet retrieved. Dense retrieval returns the bt+1 passages 3

text: 4.1 Experimental Setup Dataset Questions Passages HotpotQA 1,000 9,811 2WikiQA 1,000 6,119 MuSiQue 1,000 11,656 NarrativeQA 1,000 74,742 StrategyQA 1,000 9,254 Table 1: Dataset statistics. Passages are indexed retrieval units. NarrativeQA uses story-local retrieval. Datasets. Five datasets covering three categories of complex question answering are used for evaluation. For multi-hop QA, HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), 2WikiQA (Ho et al., 2020), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022) assess retrieving complementary evidence across passages and composing factual relations to answer multi-step questions. HotpotQA includes bridge and comparison questions, 2WikiQA emphasizes explicit relation composition, and MuSiQue connects two to four reasoning steps. For narrative QA, NarrativeQA (Koˇciský et al., 2018) assesses locating and integrating evidence about characters and events distributed across full-length novels and screenplays. For implicit reasoning QA, StrategyQA (Geva et al., 2021) assesses identifying and combining unstated factual premises for yes/no reasoning. Table 1 summarizes dataset sizes. See Appendix A for details. Metrics. Normalized exact match (EM) and token F1 (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) are reported for multi-hop and narrative QA. EM measures exact agreement with a reference answer. F1 is the harmonic mean of token-level precision and recall. With multiple references, each prediction receives its highest score across the reference answers. StrategyQA uses accuracy, the proportion of correctly answered yes/no questions. Baselines. The baselines are grouped into three categories.

text: NV-Embed-v2. StrategyQA accuracy improves by 11.60 percentage points over NV-Embed-v2. Qwen relies on parametric knowledge, making access to task-specific evidence valuable. Original-query retrieval can still miss facts whose retrieval requires an intermediate entity or premise. RCER identifies these through evidence-informed decomposition and retrieves complementary support. Compared with structure-enhanced RAG. RCER gains 8.44 average multi-hop F1 points over OriginRAG. It improves NarrativeQA F1 over LogicRAG by 1.38 points and StrategyQA accuracy over RankCoT by 2.90 percentage points. HippoRAGv2 identifies graph-associated passages, but relevance does not establish how their facts jointly answer a question. OriginRAG jointly selects sources and grounds evidence demands in source spans. However, its demands are derived before retrieval and remain unchanged when retrieved evidence reveals intermediate entities. LogicRAG’s rolling summaries can omit details needed later. RankCoT refines an existing passage set without retrieving additional support. RCER uses reconstructed relations to refine subsequent information needs, then selects complementary sources and retains cross-document inferences for answering. Compared with iterative RAG. Against RetroRAG, RCER gains 4.72 F1 points on 2WikiQA and 3.77 on MuSiQue. Its MuSiQue F1 is also 7.89 points higher than MGranRAG. On NarrativeQA, it improves F1 over RetroRAG by 1.73 points. StrategyQA accuracy reaches 87.40%, compared with 84.70% for IRCoT. Iterative retrieval can acquire the necessary facts while retaining an incorrect relational interpretation. 5

text: Limitations Further work is needed to balance reasoning quality and computational cost. Different questions may require different allocations of computation across retrieval rounds. Learned policies could adapt these allocations to each question’s information needs. Ethical Considerations We use existing QA datasets and their associated text collections. Any release of narrative source texts must follow the original copyright and redis- tribution conditions. Retrieved content and gener- ated answers can contain factual errors, requiring validation in downstream applications. We report inference-token consumption to document compu- tational resource use. Generative AI was used to assist with English language polishing.

title: AdCoEvo: A Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Advertising

text: Digital advertising is an important means for platforms to reach potential users and drive business growth. Advertising delivery is the core link between marketing objectives and actual returns. Existing methods have achieved partial automation in individual tasks such as bidding and budget allocation, but they still rely on human operators for overall coordination, making it difficult to support large-scale operations. They also often fail to achieve optimal performance, and individual experience remains difficult to turn into reusable operational capabilities. In addition, as advertising markets change, advertising delivery systems need timely strategy updates to remain effective in dynamic markets. To automate the entire advertising operations process and improve adaptability to market changes, we propose AdCoEvo, a co-evolving multi-agent advertising delivery system. Specifically, the system connects delivery decisions across different timescales and operational granularities through role specialization. Diagnostic results guide account planning and strategy adjustment in the next period. The multi-agent system updates its model parameters based on actual delivery outcomes and continually improves delivery strategies through mutual feedback among planning, adjustment, and diagnosis, thereby achieving co-evolution. Experiments show that, relative to the rule-based operational baseline (Rule), AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 14.02% while reducing cost per acquisition by 7.07%. Compared with a multi-agent system with fixed parameters, AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 3.96% and reduces cost per acquisition by 1.24%, indicating

Training policies for the entire delivery process requires linking business feedback to specific decisions. Budget planning and ad-unit adjustments continue to affect subsequent delivery, and their effects need to be evaluated through cumulative returns; post-delivery diagnosis takes effect through planning and adjustment in the next period. Organizing multi-agent collaboration by operational responsibility therefore also requires constructing training signals according to each decision’s scope of influence and feedback timing, and scheduling role updates after feedback settlement, enabling models to co-evolve during continuous delivery. Meanwhile, the advertising delivery market is not static: a continually changing auction environment may create a mismatch between historical strategies and current conditions, requiring timely updates to delivery strategies [3, 7]. Beyond autonomous execution, we therefore need to study how multi-agent systems use continuous business feedback to adjust strategies and jointly adapt to market changes through collaboration. To automate the entire advertising delivery process and improve adaptability to market changes, we propose AdCoEvo, a co-evolving multi-agent advertising delivery system. text: 2.1 Advertising Delivery Research on advertising delivery has largely focused on automating individual tasks. Automated bidding has progressed from optimizing bid functions under budget constraints [1] to using reinforcement learning [10, 11] or generative modeling [12] for sequential decision-making. RTBAgent incorporates expert knowledge and reflection on past experience into bidding decisions [13]. AdComB jointly optimizes budget allocation and bidding [5], while HiBid uses a hierarchical mechanism to connect cross-channel budgets with within-channel bidding [4]. AuctionNet evaluates automated bidding through traffic generation and auction interactions [14]. AdPilot supports end-to-end autonomous advertising delivery through a Reflector–Actor workflow informed by current states and historical memory. Post-training further improves its delivery decisions [2]. AdCoEvo organizes operational responsibilities into roles with separate policies. Period-end diagnosis guides account planning and strategy adjustment in the next period, while settled feedback supports role-policy updates during continuous delivery. 2.2 Multi-Agent Collaboration The core advantage of multi-agent systems is decomposing complex processes into roles with clear responsi- bilities. Roles address distinct objectives and contexts, then make collective decisions through interaction. Studies have applied complementary roles and task decomposition to complex problem solving and workflow automation, supporting multi-step tasks that are difficult for a single agent to complete independently [15–19]. Current research on multi-agent systems organizes role collaboration through standardized workflows, dynamic task allocation, and runtime supervision [17, 20–23]. It also

text: problem solving and workflow automation, supporting multi-step tasks that are difficult for a single agent to complete independently [15–19]. Current research on multi-agent systems organizes role collaboration through standardized workflows, dynamic task allocation, and runtime supervision [17, 20–23]. It also trains models using joint execution trajectories, role evaluations, or interaction rewards to improve collaborative decision-making capabilities [24, 25]. Our work focuses on the collaboration and continual evolution of multi-agent systems in advertising delivery tasks. 2.3 Agentic RL Agentic RL uses feedback from environmental interactions to optimize multi-step decision-making and tool-use policies [26–28]. For example, ReTool uses tool-call outcomes to improve when and how tools are called [29], while AgentFlow uses multi-turn trajectories to improve planning policies [30]. MARTI uses multi-agent interaction trajectories for distributed training updates [31]. We continually update role policies through alternating reinforcement learning, focusing on mutual adaptation among roles during continuous delivery. Training signals reflect each role’s scope of influence and feedback timing. Cross-period diagnosis and subsequent joint execution allow each role’s policy updates to shape feedback for other roles’ subsequent decisions and learning. 3 Problem Formulation We formulate continuous advertising delivery as sequential decision-making, with objectives for value generation and conversion costs under budget and adjustment-count constraints. 3

text: 5.1 Experimental Setup Experimental environment: Experiments use the AuctionNet simulator [14] with its official period length and traffic volume. The environment contains 48 ad units that can purchase traffic. We control 12 units organized into 3 accounts, each containing 4 units, all using Abid as the fixed underlying bidder. We use two environments, AuctionNet (Sparse) and AuctionNet (General). The former uses the public simulation environment, where each controlled account’s initial budget is 1/12 of the total budget of all units. For AuctionNet (General), we calibrate the pValue generation scale, ad-unit budgets, and CPA constraints using the public General dataset, while keeping the other auction mechanisms unchanged. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix D. Evaluation metrics: Delivery performance is measured using ADV, CPA, and a composite score. For ADV, which uses tCPA-weighted predicted conversion values [8], we report the per-period average of total ADV across all controlled accounts within the evaluation scope. CPA is total spend divided by total conversions over the same evaluation scope [9]. The invalid output rate IR is the fraction of responses that violate the required format or action specifications, such as parsing failures, incorrect ad-unit decision counts, or tCPA multipliers outside the allowed set. Relaxing the limit to 12 lowers ADV and raises CPA, so more adjustment opportunities do not necessarily improve performance. 6 Discussion and Conclusion We present AdCoEvo, a multi-agent system for advertising delivery that organizes delivery decisions through role specialization across different timescales and operational granularities, and improves delivery policies through offline development of operational capabilities and co-evolution. Experiments show that operational- level decisions, role collaboration, and post-training all help improve delivery performance, while co-evolution provides further gains beyond offline reinforcement learning. However, gains vary across environments, and the effectiveness of co-evolution still needs evaluation in specific delivery scenarios. How operational roles’ decision frequencies and scopes of influence affect co-evolution, and how advantage estimation and update mechanisms can be improved accordingly, warrant further study to help multi-agent systems use actual delivery feedback more effectively.

text: A Role Reward Computation We detail aggregation scopes and parameters for offline and co-evolution rewards (Section 4.2). A.1 Rewards for Planner and Optimizer Equations (6)–(7) combine separate returns for the current account and all controlled accounts. Planner uses results from observation end to period end; Optimizer uses current-step increments. Each term aggregates ADV, spend, and conversions F, C, N in its scope to compute the scaled proxy return. The CPA target averages initial tCPA across all units, weighted by conversions. For settlement window W, let du be unit u’s initial tCPA and Nu,W its conversions. The target cost allowance MW = P u duNu,W and total conversions NW = P u Nu,W give ρ = MW/NW; when NW = 0, we set ρ = 0. Both Sparse and General use this computation. Training sets η = 1, s = 10000, and ω = 0.2 to control the cost-deviation weight, reward scaling, and overall reward weight, respectively. Planner’s reward settles at period end; Optimizer’s current-step reward is used in the advantage recursion in Appendix C.1. text: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity Nima Dehghani 1)McGovern Institute for Brain Research, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA 2)The NSF AI Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Fundamental Interactions (IAIFI), Cambridge, Massachusetts, USAa) Mandlebrot’s coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest. b Keywords: neural

text: The question How long is the coast of Britain? did more than introduce a memorable fractal1. It exposed a dependence that ordinary measurement language tends to hide: the answer belongs jointly to an object and to a ruler. A coarse ruler crosses bays and omits bound- aries that a fine ruler must follow. The resulting lengths disagree without either measurement being erroneous. The point neuron is neuroscience’s coarse ruler. From early threshold-unit models onward, a large branch of theoretical neuroscience has represented a cell by a small number of state variables and an input–output rule2–6. This abstraction underlies theories of recurrent dynam- ics, chaos, balanced excitation and inhibition, and popu- lation computation, and has proved extraordinarily pro- ductive despite suppressing the spatial structure of the cell. A related statistical tradition asks how much of pop- ulation activity can be captured by low-order dependen- cies alone. In small groups of cells, pairwise maximum- entropy models reproduce surprisingly rich collective ac- tivity from first- and second-order statistics7. That ade- quacy is conditional: it is expected in small, sparsely ac- tive populations whatever the underlying interactions8, it gives way to explicit higher-order terms in larger pop- ulations under natural stimulation9, and it changes with which cells the model retains10. Against this background, a recent maximum-entropy analysis reports striking support for the coarse descrip-
title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron?

text: the underlying interactions8, it gives way to explicit higher-order terms in larger pop- ulations under natural stimulation9, and it changes with which cells the model retains10. Against this background, a recent maximum-entropy analysis reports striking support for the coarse descrip- a)Electronic mail: nima.dehghani@mit.edu b)For Context & overview see: https://neurovium.science/posts/pblog-CoastOfNeuron tion at the level of the single cell: direct, equal-time de- pendencies on relatively few recorded neurons explain more than 90% of output entropy in mouse record- ings and 62% in C. elegans11. The analysis is careful about what is measured. Its inferred weights are func- tional dependencies among recorded cells, not necessar- ily synapses, and unexplained variability can combine higher-order dependence, temporal dependence, unob- served inputs, and stochasticity. We propose a scale-theoretic fromalism. The success of a direct model at the resolution of a population record- ing characterizes an effective relation among the variables that survive measurement and projection. It does not imply that the cellular computation realizing that rela- tion is itself direct, additive, or single-stage. This dis- tinction matters because a neuron is not, at finer resolu- tion, a single computational degree of freedom. Dendrites contain spatially distributed nonlinear subunits12–14, and the input–output transformation of a detailed neuron can require a multilayer artificial network for accurate func- tional emulation15,16. Thus, the population-level and dendritic descriptions are not competing
title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron?

text: a single computational degree of freedom. Dendrites contain spatially distributed nonlinear subunits12–14, and the input–output transformation of a detailed neuron can require a multilayer artificial network for accurate func- tional emulation15,16. Thus, the population-level and dendritic descriptions are not competing accounts of the same object; they are descriptions at different obser- vational scales, connected by a many-to-one projection. The question is therefore not whether the reduced model is useful, but whether predictive adequacy at one scale warrants identifying its effective dependencies with the computation that produces them at another. The coastline analogy is deliberately epistemic. We do not claim that every dendrite possesses an exact frac- tal dimension over an unlimited range. Neuronal ar- bors do exhibit scale-dependent geometric organization and constrained branching17–19, but geometry is not the premise of the argument. What matters is that obser- vation can collapse many underlying degrees of freedom arXiv:2610.19487v1 [q-bio.NC] 14 Oct 2026

We instead ask how much of a neuron’s computa- tion is resolved at a given observational scale, which distinctions are erased by projection, and which reap- pear as the ruler is refined. We approach this prob- lem through an information-theoretic lens together with constructive counterexamples in which the efficiency of neural-network architectures depends on the representa- tion available at each scale. These examples show that the same coarse input–output relation can be compati- ble with markedly different internal computations, even when the reduced description is highly predictive. The coastline problem for a neuron is therefore not whether computation is visible or hidden, but how its apparent structure changes with the scale at which it is observed. II. METHODS & RESULTS A. The data- processing inequality gives I(Y ; Z) ≤I(Y ; Xε). (12) Thus coarse-graining cannot increase the total predictive information available about Y . In the notation of the previous section, Iavail can only decrease or remain un- changed as information is discarded by the projection. It is important, however, to separate this absolute in- formation loss from changes in the structure of the surviv- ing dependence. Equation (12) does not, by itself, order either the higher-order residual Ihigher or the normalized direct fraction F. The reason is that the optimal direct model is defined relative to the observable coordinates themselves, and that admissible family changes when Xε is replaced by Z. A blanket claim that higher-order infor- mation must decrease under every coarse-graining would therefore be false. A stronger statement becomes possible under an addi- tional closure condition. Form the joint direct surrogate Q⋆ ε(y, x) = Pε(x)Q⋆ ε(y | x), (13) which preserves the true distribution of the observed in- puts while replacing the conditional response by its op- timal direct approximation. text: The ruler can change the apparent order of the computation. D. The Branch-To-Soma Cascade Having established that interaction order can change under mathematical projection, we now translate the same logic into a neuron-like architecture. The purpose is not to construct a compartmental model of a particu- lar dendrite. It is to show, with an exactly enumerable example, how familiar biophysical operations—local co- incidence detection, saturating integration, and somatic mixing—can act as successive coarse-graining maps. We therefore follow the same signal through three observa- tional rulers. Individual synaptic contacts, two dendritic branches, and a single somatic variable. The underlying input–output law is fixed throughout. What changes is the set of distinctions available to the observer, and un- der coarse-graining a neuron with genuinely synergistic substructure can masquerade as an additive unit. 1. The fine-scale ground truth: NMDA coincidence detection We begin at the finest resolution of the construction. Six independent binary inputs, x ∈{0, 1}6, are divided evenly between two three-input subunits. Think of a neu- ron receiving six independent binary inputs, distributed evenly across two dendritic branches. In this construct, the output probability is governed strictly by third-order interactions of the two input branches: P(Y = 1 | x) = 0.06 + 0.40(x1x2x3 + x4x5x6). (18) Thus the baseline firing probability is 0.06, one active triplet raises it to 0.46,

text: the output probability is governed strictly by third-order interactions of the two input branches: P(Y = 1 | x) = 0.06 + 0.40(x1x2x3 + x4x5x6). (18) Thus the baseline firing probability is 0.06, one active triplet raises it to 0.46, and simultaneous activation of both triplets gives the maximum probability 0.86. All 26 = 64 input configurations can therefore be enumerated exactly. The two products in Eq. (18) are deliberately sharp abstractions of local dendritic coincidence detection. NMDA-dependent dendritic events provide the biological motivation: because NMDA conductance is strongly volt- age dependent through extracellular Mg2+ block, suffi- ciently coordinated local excitation can recruit a regener- ative response that isolated inputs do not produce12,13,22. The number three is not intended as a literal universal threshold for an NMDA event. Its role is mathemati- cal: x1x2x3 is nonzero only when all three members of the local group are active, providing the simplest exact representation of a third-order coincidence. At this contact-level ruler, the generative law is there- fore explicitly organized around third-order products. This does not mean that individual contacts carry no predictive information. Marginalizing over the other in- puts produces direct one-coordinate effects that an ad- ditive model can capture. What it cannot reconstruct is the full dependence on the joint configuration. Suppose that individual contacts are no longer resolved and that the observer instead has access to one effective variable from each dendritic branch. We define those branch observables by the saturated sums B1 = min(x1 + x2 + x3, 2), B2 = min(x4 + x5 + x6, 2), (20) so that each branch can now occupy only the states 0, 1, or 2. The hard ceiling in Eq. (20) is a stylized represen- tation of saturating or sublinear local integration, not a quantitative membrane equation. Real dendritic re- sponses can become sublinear through several conduc- tance and driving-force mechanisms12. As a local den- dritic membrane depolarizes toward the reversal poten- tial of its excitatory ion channels, the electrochemical driving force decreases, and voltage summation plateaus. However, active dendrites can also exhibit strongly supra- linear regimes13,14. What matters for the present con- struction is the many-to-one character of the map. Ex- plicitly, distinct microscopic input configurations become indistinguishable once only B1 and B2 are retained. The state collapse can be seen directly. To test the dependence on the projection itself, we replace the symmetric mixture by Z = 0.6B1 + 0.4B2. Unequal weighting is biologically natural as an effective description because dendritic sig- nals undergo location- and state-dependent electrotonic transfer before reaching the soma12. A branch physically closer to the soma will experience less electrotonic at- tenuation than a distal branch. The particular 0.6/0.4 values are not intended as a fit to a specific morphology; they provide a controlled perturbation of the projection geometry. E. From One Weight To A Field Of Contacts The branch-to-soma cascade showed how spatial ag- gregation can make a neuron appear increasingly direct even when its fine-scale input–output law contains ex- plicit higher-order interactions. We now apply the same argument to a more elementary object in network mod- els: the synaptic weight. The question is what a single edge wij represents when the biological connection that it summarizes is resolved at progressively finer spatial scales. At point-neuron resolution, one connection is naturally represented by one effective coefficient. At contact res- olution, however, the same anatomical relation can con- tain multiple spatially embedded synaptic events whose influence depends on where they arrive and on the local state into which they arrive. The purpose of this section is therefore not to deny the usefulness of a scalar weight. It is to identify what has already been integrated out when a spatially distributed, state-dependent biological connection is represented by one number. 1. The scalar-weight abstraction In a standard point-neuron description, the influence from

The scalar-weight abstraction In a standard point-neuron description, the influence from presynaptic cell j to postsynaptic cell i is repre- sented by a scalar coefficient wij. Depending on the model, that coefficient may multiply an instantaneous activity variable, a filtered spike train, or another effec- tive presynaptic signal. In each case, however, the spatial structure of the connection inside neuron i has been re- moved from the representation. The model retains one edge between two neuronal nodes rather than the indi- vidual sites at which that edge is physically realized. At a finer microscopic ruler ε, the appropriate object need not be a single scalar. text: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? 8 2. Context-dependent influence and higher-order structure Consider one resolved contact k from neuron j onto a dendritic branch of neuron i. Its contribution cannot in general be specified from presynaptic activity alone. If the local branch is relatively hyperpolarized and away from a conductance or voltage-saturation regime, acti- vation of the contact can produce one incremental re- sponse. If coincident activity elsewhere has already al- tered the local voltage, recruited active conductances, or changed the balance of excitation and inhibition, acti- vation of the same contact can produce a substantially different response12–14 (e.g. the same spike from cell j at synapse k may generate zero additional depolarization). The relevant point is therefore not simply that synap- tic strength varies. It is that the effect assigned to one contact can depend on the state created by other con- tacts. Let Nε denote this fine-scale context: local mem- brane voltage, active conductance state, nearby synaptic activity, and other unresolved variables relevant at ruler ε. The contribution associated with w(k) ij is then con- ditional on Nε rather than being an independent term whose effect is fixed across states. This dependence can be stated directly in the language of the direct-family model introduced in Eq. (1). Let xk denote the state of contact k

This distinction gives a precise information-theoretic meaning to local dendritic context. A contact whose ef- fective contribution is invariant across the surrounding state can remain informationally direct even if its abso- lute magnitude differs across cells or locations. A contact whose contribution changes according to the configura- tion of other resolved variables instead participates in a joint dependence. The latter is the fine-scale structure that disappears when the local context is removed from the observer’s coordinate system. This is the microscopic version of the branch example in Section V. At the fine ruler, that influence can be distributed across contacts whose effects depend jointly on their dendritic location and on the activity surrounding them. The anatomical connection remains monosynaptic; the informational de- composition need not remain additive. 3. The point neuron as a coarse-graining map A point-neuron model does not observe r, the individ- ual elements of Wij,ε, or the local state Nε. The operator Πε stands for everything involved in passing from the resolved contact description to the effective somatic one: dendritic integration, electrotonic propagation, marginal- ization over unresolved local states, measurement, and finally the effective parameterization used by the coarse model. This makes clear what the scalar weight does and does not mean. The quantity wsoma ij need not correspond to any individual member of the contact field in Eq. (22). Anatomical vs. informational directness The distinction exposes a conceptual trap that recurs throughout computational neuroscience and connection- ist network models: anatomical directness and informa- tional directness answer different questions. Anatomical directness asks whether cell j forms a direct connection onto cell i. Informational directness asks whether the dependence of the output on the variables resolved by the observer can be represented without irreducible joint terms. The distinction can be stated formally. Let Aij = 1 de- note the existence of an anatomical connection from neu- ron j to neuron i, so that at contact resolution Aij = 1 whenever nij(ε) > 0. Informational directness at ruler ε, by contrast, is the condition that the resolved conditional

Effective descriptions need a scale The adequacy of a low-order statistical model in ex- plaining observed neural activity is a joint property of the underlying generative mechanism and the ruler through which it is observed. Pairwise maximum-entropy models can explain collective activity in small, sparsely active population of neurons7, but this measure permits accu- rate fits even when the underlying interactions are not pairwise8. Common input can be a source of higher- order correlations24, and larger neural
title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron?

text: models can explain collective activity in small, sparsely active population of neurons7, but this measure permits accu- rate fits even when the underlying interactions are not pairwise8. Common input can be a source of higher- order correlations24, and larger neural populations can have explicit higher-order terms9. The finding that di- rect, pairwise dependencies explain much of the output entropy of recorded neurons11 therefore establishes an ef- fective description at an observation scale rather identify- ing the underlying fine-scale computational mechanism. It does not provide a window to the computation im- plemented by intracellular voltages, channel states and contact locations absent from that description. Our prior work illustrate why both the observable and the measure scale matter. In human cortex, pair- wise models that exclude inhibitory neurons substan- tially overestimate excitatory synchrony10. In multielec- trode recordings from cats, monkeys and humans, neu- ral avalanche statistics differ between spikes and field- potential, cautioning against interpreting apparent scal- ing as a unique criticality signature of the underlying generative mechanism25. Spike avalanches show no clear power-law scaling, and the apparent scaling of local-field- potential negative peaks is shared by positive peaks un- related to firing. Temporal coarse-graining of excita- tory and inhibitory ensemble activity reveals coordina- tion that persists across scales, while surrogates that ran- domize the precise timing of spikes disrupt that struc-

In other words, the somatic drive can adequately predict the measured spiking output. Cable theory provides the bound when the hypothesis is justified. If the dendritic tree were pas- sive, linearity and superposition would translate to each synaptic contribution being routed through a fixed trans- fer impedance. In that case, the somatic drive would be exactly equivalent to a weighted-sum of presynaptic currents, and the sufficiency condition would hold. Ac- tive dendritic conductances or nonlinear synaptic inter- actions violate superposition. This departure from pas- sivity can invalidate the weighted-sum sufficiency even if a low-order fit appears to provide adequate statistical predictivity. Neuronal biophysics determines how spatially dis- tributed inputs invoke local dendritic responses and turn into somatic signals. Con- tacts share the local voltage (Vloc) over a neighbourhood set by the electrotonic length constant (ℓ= p dRm/4Ra, where d is dendritic diameter, and Rm and Ra: the membrane and axial resistivities), and by the impedance mismatch at branch points. Together with branch- point impedance and active conductances, electrotonic coupling defines the functional domains represented by Si(ε). Thin branches, having high input impedance and weak coupling to their neighbours, behave as nonlin- ear compartments13,29. However, their effective inde- pendence depends on state: several-fold fall in effective membrane resistance can shorten electrotonic reach in

These domains support distal– proximal coupling32, temporal sequence discrimination33 and branch-specific calcium spikes gate plasticity34. The appropriate spatial ruler (the number of effectively inde- pendent subunits and the weights of the somatic mixture) therefore depends on the network state as well as the ge- ometry of the excitable units. Read in the other direction, the same physics ex- plains why neuronal geometry and spatial organiza- tion of contacts is computationally load-bearing. Scat- tering a multi-contact connection across electrically semi-independent compartments need not be anatomical redundancy; it can enlarge the set of nonlinear features available to the cell. Synaptic convergence onto a nonlin- ear compartment invokes local coincident activity13,14,16. In contrast, scattered input across compartments pre- serves distinct response and limits shared saturation12. Therefore, how the inputs share compartments determine what nonlinear combination of the inputs can be eco- nomically computed by the neuron15. Multicontact seg- regation therefore enables the retention of higher-order cross-terms as distinct features that a single summa- tion node would otherwise erase. Those transformations are determined by morphology, conductances and contact placement rather than by con- tact count alone. Compressing each neuron’s compu- tation to a node and each connection to a scalar edge removes contact-to-subunit assignments unless they are compensated through additional state or effective param- eters. Cell-level connectivity therefore constrains the cir- cuit but does not fully determine the computation per- formed at its nodes. D. In our compari- son, three aligned subunits can reach the accuracy that forty fixed sigmoid random features (Fig. 3). Shuffling the contacts degrades the network performance despite preserving contact count and subunit count. The gain therefore depends on which inputs share a nonlinear op- eration. One options is to harness useful interactions by by adding variables inside each unit so those compu- tations remain local. Alternatively, one can keep units simple and rely on a larger network to reconstruct the same interactions. A biological neuron and an artificial unit need not occupy the same computational scale. Connectome-constrained models reproduce fly visual tuning35 and sensorimotor responses36. Their suc- cess supports the tested cell-level descriptions, but it does not recover the within-cell organization lost via projec- tion. Functional connectomics can provide a practical route from biological measurements to network design if the ex- tracted priors reflect scale-dependent measurements. Us- ing MICrONS (Machine Intelligence from Cortical Net- works) data37, we have shown how activity-derived rela- tionships and cortical geometry can guide recurrent net- works that outperform randomly initialized baselines38. We used functional relationships to initialize recurrent weights, neuronal positions to define spatial costs, and anatomical connectivity to constrain network communi- cability. These constraints improve task performance. Functional initialization provides the largest performance gain, while measured geometry adds a further bene- fit without increasing model size38. Our scale-indexed decomposition framework extends this design question to dendritic structure, where contact-to-subunit assign- ments determine which nonlinear features become acces- sible. The biophysical models provide concrete implemen- tations of the interactions our theory highlights. The voltage-dependent NMDA factor in Eq. (44) couples each contact to local depolarization, enabling context- dependent integration. In detailed model of pyramidal neurons, optimizing synaptic strengths and locations can enable reasonable XOR and ten-bit parity performance39. Removing NMDA conductances or dendritic structure impairs that capability. These are in-silico model demon- strations, not evidence of in-vivo computation. How- ever, they illustrate that computational power depends on internal organization suppressed by single-node de- scriptions. A bilinear reduction captures part of that or- ganization through location- and timing-dependent pair- wise coefficients40. Seen through the lens of our frame- work, such approach enlarges the effective family within

text: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? 18 its tested subthreshold regime. For neuro-inspired design, the question is therefore ex- plicit: which contact groups, nonlinear features and state dependencies should each model unit retain? The same question applies when reducing circuit motifs for compo- sition. We have shown that coupled models of canonical circuit motifs (divisive competition and winner-take-all normalization) can generate joint computational oper- ations absent from the uncoupled motifs41. A reduc- tion adequate for an isolated motif must therefore be reassessed when that motif interacts with others, an- swering does the composition preserve the state dependen- cies through which the coupling acts? Our scale-indexed decomposition and computational results provide con- trolled comparisons that answer the question of what to retain, beyond merely matching cell counts or copying cell-level connectivity. E. How long is, then, the coast of a neuron? In analogy with Mandelbrot’s coastline paradox 1, the question is well posed only after specifying i) the ruler, ii) the target observable, iii) the class of perturbations, and iv) the domain of conditions. Our scale-dependent con- struction makes mechanistic non-identifiability explicit and shows why the amount of information lost at a given scale in a biological regime must be determined empiri- cally. One should hold the output fixed and then ask how much extra predictive information finer-grained variables
title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron?

text: mechanistic non-identifiability explicit and shows why the amount of information lost at a given scale in a biological regime must be determined empiri- cally. One should hold the output fixed and then ask how much extra predictive information finer-grained variables contribute. That comparison is a direct test of observa- tional sufficiency (Eq. (43)). Doing so isolates the con- tribution of higher-order interactions and finer variables from the residual that any fitted model family leaves un- explained. One can then apply perturbations (such as branch-targeted inhibition, shifts in spatial input cluster- ing, or changes to the temporal input regime) to probe whether an observational description that was adequate continues to be so under new conditions. The continued success across such tests supports the validity of reduc- tion and corase-graining within the tested domain. Such empirical support, however, does not uniquely identify the microscopic implementation. A coarse variable can be simple to record, easy to fit, and straightforward to simulate. It may even ac- count for most of the in-distribution output entropy. Yet that convenience can be misleading. The same somatic or point description that suffices to forecast spikes in a fixed population regime may fail to capture phenomena that depend on subcellular detail. Branch voltages, for example, may be essential to explain coincidence detec- tion or distal–proximal coupling. Likewise, contact- or
title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron?

text: point description that suffices to forecast spikes in a fixed population regime may fail to capture phenomena that depend on subcellular detail. Branch voltages, for example, may be essential to explain coincidence detec- tion or distal–proximal coupling. Likewise, contact- or spine-resolved variables are often required for questions about plasticity. Conversely, resolving more microscopic detail can in- crease estimation error without improving the prediction of interest23. Interaction order, directness, sparsity, and capacity are joint properties of the neuron and the cho- sen scale of description. Integrating out hidden degrees of freedom renormalizes apparent interaction strengths and can change which orders of interaction appear dominant. The appropriate scale is therefore question-dependent. Neither tractability nor goodness of fit alone establishes that a coarse-graining preserves the quantities an infer- ence about computation requires. The point-neuron is then a ruler. It is a useful, predictive abstraction. How- ever, it becomes misleading when its readings are re- ported as properties of the coast. text: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation Shijun Li1*, Yang Liu2, Najmeh Sadoughi2, Dongmei Wang2, Xinjie Li2, Zhu Liu2, Rohith Mysore Vijaya Kumar2, Yuzong Liu2 1The University of Texas at Austin, 2Amazon shijunli@utexas.edu
title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement

text: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by pro- viding supplementary information such as id- iom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine trans- lation systems typically apply predefined re- trieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial- evidence regime: LLM’s parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evi- dence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired trans- lation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to trans- late directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimiz- ing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett–Luce optimiza- tion and translation-quality contrastive train- ing for retriever-training. Experiments on id- iom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating re- trieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing. 1

text: Large language models (LLMs) have become strong general-purpose machine translation (MT) systems, particularly after multilingual instruction tuning and translation-specific adaptation (Jiao et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024). In particular, re- cent LLMs demonstrate strong ability to inter- *Work was done while Shijun was interning at Amazon. These capabilities have motivated retrieval- augmented MT systems that provide bilingual ex- amples, idiom definitions, terminology, or support- ing documents to further support and improve trans- lation quality (Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). However, recent studies (Sun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023) have shown that retrieval is not uni- formly beneficial for translation. Existing retrieval- augmented MT pipelines typically apply a prede- fined retrieval strategy: retrieve for every input with a heuristic, similarity-based matching rule. This overlooks a fundamental gap in LLM-based translation: for some inputs, the model’s paramet- ric knowledge is already sufficient, while for oth- ers, external evidence such as idiom interpretations, canonical entities, technical terms, or background knowledge can be crucial. Moreover, heuristic, similarity-based retrieval can provide no help and even introduce noisy or misleading context that distracts the model and degrades an otherwise cor- rect translation (Sun et al., 2026). text: retrieval settings, in which a relevant document often directly contains the evidence needed to pro- duce the final response. We refer to this setting as the partial-evidence regime, which captures two properties of retrieval in MT. First, external evidence is beneficial for only a subset of inputs where the model’s para- metric knowledge doesn’t suffices. Second, when evidence is needed, retrieval based solely on seman- tic similarity may fail to surface the most useful evidence. This raises two learning problems. The first is retrieval adaptivity: the model must deter- mine when additional evidence is useful instead of retrieving by default. The second is retrieval qual- ity alignment: once retrieval is invoked, the system must determine what evidence actually improves the final translation quality. To address them, we propose Selective Retrieval- Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement-learning framework that treats rea- soning, retrieval, and translation as actions in a unified policy. Given a source input, the model’s action space at each step includes reasoning about the translation, generating a retrieval query and in- corporating the returned evidence, or terminating with the final translation. Rather than supervis- ing which examples should retrieve, we optimize complete trajectories using final translation qual- ity. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) allows trajectories with differ- ent retrieval decisions and queries to compete for
title: retrieval settings, in which a relevant document

text: final translation. Rather than supervis- ing which examples should retrieve, we optimize complete trajectories using final translation qual- ity. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) allows trajectories with differ- ent retrieval decisions and queries to compete for the same input, thereby learning when retrieval is worthwhile and what to retrieve to improve final translation quality. Moreover, we develop two approaches for fur- ther aligning the retriever with downstream trans- lation quality rather than simple semantic similar- ity. First, a natural and principled approach is to jointly optimize the LLM translator and retriever end-to-end. To achieve it, we replace determinis- tic top-k selection during training with a Plackett– Luce ranking policy (Plackett, 1975), whose selec- tion log-probability allows trajectory-level transla- tion reward to update the retriever through a score- function gradient. However, this joint signal can be noisy: a trajectory contains many LLM policy decisions but only a few retrieval actions, mak- ing credit assignment to the retriever inherently high-variance. To address this, we further intro- duce translation-quality contrastive training, which fixes the translator, evaluates candidate retrieval evidence by their measured effect on translation quality, and converts these into direct contrastive supervision. This isolates the effect of retrieval from other policy decisions, providing the retriever with substantially more targeted training signals. We evaluate SRAT across three translation settings:

This isolates the effect of retrieval from other policy decisions, providing the retriever with substantially more targeted training signals. We evaluate SRAT across three translation settings: idiom translation, knowledge-intensive translation, and document-level translation. The first two use offline retrieval corpora, while the document-level setting additionally evaluates SRAT with online retrieval. Across these settings, SRAT consistently outperforms never-retrieve and always-retrieve baselines, demonstrating the bene- fit of learning when to retrieve and what evidence to seek. Ablations show that quality-aligned re- triever training provides further significant gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. We also find that the retrieval policy can be optimized with a frontier black-box translator, outperforming its direct translation and indicating that the adap- tive retrieval decision training can be decoupled from the translator and optimized as a modular component for external generation models. Our main contributions are threefold: • Selective retrieval as a translation decision. We characterize LLM-based RAG translation as a partial-evidence regime in which external knowl- edge is useful only conditionally. We formulate machine translation by LLM as a sequential pol- icy over reasoning, retrieval, and final translation, enabling the model to learn when and what to retrieve from translation outcomes rather than fixed routing rules. • Quality-aligned evidence retrieval.
