A chat request that changes criteria or the schema is saved as a draft, and confir- mation is a canvas action (Appendices A.7 and H). Project memory stores the conversation history, cur- rent configurations, confirmed configuration snap- shots, and each stage’s status and PRISMA counts. In conversation, the Lead Agent receives its task instructions, the current request, the saved project state, and the conversation history. Its instructions give saved state precedence over superseded re- quests and distinguish drafts from confirmed con- figurations. Researchers reuse a previous project’s configuration by importing it as a draft that again re- quires confirmation. The system does not retrieve memories across projects automatically or learn preferences from corrections. To override a screening decision, researchers se- lect a confirmed criterion or guidance rule and give a reason. They also give reasons when correcting extracted values. Original decisions and values re- main in review history. A change to a confirmed configuration or reviewed record marks affected downstream outputs as outdated until rerun. 4 Experiments & Results We evaluate screening and structured information extraction separately against the expert annota- tions in PERG, a dataset released with AgentSLR (Padarha et al., 2026). Researchers con- firm criteria and schemas, a Prompt Agent writes review-specific guidance and coding rules for ap- plying them, and a project memory retains con- figurations and corrections. Across three LLMs, ReviewPilot achieves higher screening macro F1, pooled extraction F1, and verified-correct rates on PERG than a single-prompt LLM and AgentSLR. Limitations Broad validation across reviews, evidence types, and review teams remains incomplete. ReviewPi- lot’s screening procedure and prompt-design skill are refined using scores from the same PERG pools used for evaluation, so the reported gains do not establish performance on unseen reviews. Expert decisions and reference values are excluded from the Prompt Agent’s inputs. Quantitative extraction covers five fields from epidemiological transmis- sion models. The case-study screening audits use small, non-random pools labeled by our research team, and the selected extraction inspections pro- vide qualitative error analysis. Full-text eligibility decisions are not independently audited. We re- port one run per method and model without confi- dence intervals. These estimates do not character- ize variation across repeated runs. Macro-averaged screening metrics do not isolate include-class sen- sitivity, which matters for avoiding missed studies (Cohen et al., 2006; O’Mara-Eves et al., 2015). AgentSLR’s original high reasoning setting is re- placed with medium reasoning or provider defaults. Excerpt verification establishes textual presence, but does not assess semantic support or whether excerpts cover every value in a multi-value field (Gao et al., 2023). Search coverage is limited to PubMed, arXiv, and OpenAlex and constrained by the query and per-source result limits. Full-text

Researchers can add PDFs manually, but the reported work- flows do not separately quantify retrieval outcomes by publication access status. The contribution of subscription barriers to unretrieved reports there- fore remains unquantified in the reported results. Access constraints may affect which studies enter extraction and categorization. Assessments based on abstracts or web sources are not separately vali- dated. Future evaluations should use reviews held out from method development, cover further evidence types and extraction schemas, and independently audit full-text eligibility and semantic support for extracted values. Before reporting a stage as complete, the Lead Agent checks that the stage’s expected arti- facts exist and contain their required fields. A.3 Screening Preprocessing The Screening Agent first filters records by publica- tion date. Records with missing dates, or with date intervals that overlap the search range, are retained. It then removes exact and near duplicates. Exact matching normalizes title case, punctuation, and whitespace. Near-duplicate detection compares title and author signatures with term frequency– inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) cosine simi- larity, computed with scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), at a default threshold of 0.70. Records with distinct nonempty DOIs or PubMed identifiers are kept separate. Each removal is recorded with the relevant reason. A.4 Full-Text Retrieval The PDF Download Tool selects sources from each record’s identifiers and metadata. Routes in- clude direct links, publisher pages, DOI resolution, PubMed Central, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, arXiv, 12

text: bioRxiv, and medRxiv, with request throttling, re- tries, and a browser fallback that can be disabled. The identity check compares the text of the PDF’s opening page with the expected title. A.5 Extraction In the schema S, fj, τj, and δj denote a field’s name, JSON-compatible type, and description. Fields may also have value constraints. The Ex- traction Agent reads the PDF text with pypdf and inserts a page marker before the text of each page. The schema checks cover field presence, declared types, and value constraints. Proposed excerpts are matched against normalized PDF text, and a located excerpt is recorded with the page on which it is found. A.6 Categorization For a selected field fj with nonempty extracted values Vj, the Lead Agent proposes the cate- gory plan Kj = fLLM(fj, sample(Vj), m), where sample(Vj) takes the first 150 distinct values in record order, each shortened to 300 characters, and m selects single-label or multiple-label assignment. It has at most five categories, fewer when the field has few distinct values, and includes an Other cat- egory within that limit when some values fit none. Returned labels are normalized when they match approved names. Multiple-label responses contain- ing other labels are rejected. Papers with no value for the field are marked as unavailable. AgentSLR’s screening tem- plate states the PERG criteria, and all three meth- ods use these 11 rules: AgentSLR runs its pub- lished template unchanged, and ReviewPilot and the single-prompt baseline receive the same rules as an inclusion list and an exclusion list. There are five inclusion criteria: (1) the target pathogen; (2) En- glish; (3) peer-reviewed original research, with systematic reviews and meta-analyses given spe- cial consideration; (4) human subjects, or animal studies that report transmission or vector parame- ters; and (5) at least one of ten content types (out- break details, a transmission model, transmission, timing, severity or genetic parameters, overdisper- sion, seroprevalence, risk factors, or vector param- eters). There are six exclusion criteria: (1) an- other pathogen; (2) non-English; (3) conference abstracts, posters, or correspondence; (4) in-vitro work only; (5) animal-only studies without trans- mission parameters; and (6) laboratory outbreaks. A requested database is a setting even when ReviewPilot cannot search it (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore); the app tells the user which requested databases it cannot search. 4. Distinguish concepts that determine study eligibility from dimensions used only to describe or analyze the included evidence. Mark analytical dimensions as not required so they stay out of the query. 5. Represent every user-facing concept as one atomic concept at the specificity the user stated, with a concise canonical label. Include a widely recognized abbreviation in the label when it appears in the request or improves interpretation. 6. Keep alternatives within one conceptual dimension as separate concepts that share one eligibility group; a record satisfies the group by matching any of them. Concepts in one group share a role. 7. Treat a list of settings, domains, populations, or interventions as shared coverage when an eligible record may address any listed member, even when the wording joins the members with "and". 8. Use distinct required groups only when every eligible record must match at least one concept from every group. Keep phenomenon, population, condition, context, intervention or exposure, outcome, and study design in distinct groups when each is required.

Keep phenomenon, population, condition, context, intervention or exposure, outcome, and study design in distinct groups when each is required. 9. Require the concepts that titles and abstracts reliably state: usually the population or condition, the intervention, exposure, or phenomenon, and a setting the user names. Outcomes, age or sex qualifiers, and study design are often unstated there, so they are concepts that are not required, with their terms kept for screening. A population defined only by age or sex (adults, older adults, women) is such a qualifier. In an effect question ("how does X affect Y"), Y is the outcome of interest. Naming one of them in the research question describes the review's interest; it becomes required only when the user asks for the search itself to use it ("search on mortality", "restrict the search to randomized trials"). For "exercise for fatigue in adults with multiple sclerosis", multiple sclerosis and exercise are required, while fatigue and adults are not; for "how does telemedicine affect HbA1c in adults with type 2 diabetes", telemedicine and type 2 diabetes are required, while HbA1c and adults are not. 10. text: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent Discovery in LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Systems Giancarlo Maldonado Cárdenas, Carlos A. Astudillo, and Nelson L. S. da Fonseca Institute of Computing – State University of Campinas, Brazil E-mails: giancarlo@lrc.ic.unicamp.br, castudillo@unicamp.br, and nfonseca@ic.unicamp.br Abstract—Large-scale multi-agent ecosystems require mech- anisms for discovering suitable agents without exposing entire registries to a large language model (LLM) orchestrator. The challenge is not only to retrieve relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also to maintain a compact candidate context, since each additional candidate increases prompt size, inference cost, latency, and the risk of exceeding the model context window. We formulate this problem as candidate-context scalability and propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), our deterministic and training-free retrieval method designed for Agent Card discovery. SSR derives structural lexical signals from capability-bearing Agent Card fields, weights them using inverse document frequency (IDF), and uses an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) for selective candidate scoring. We evaluate SSR using a synthetic agent benchmark, a public MS MARCO adaptation, and end-to-end LLM orchestration. At 1,000 agents, SSR reduces LLM input by 98.8% and orchestration latency by 70.9% relative to full-catalog orchestration. On MS MARCO, IDF improves retrieval effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves retrieval effectiveness and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%. End-to-end experiments show that candidate pre-selection maintains a
title: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent

On MS MARCO, IDF improves retrieval effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves retrieval effectiveness and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%. End-to-end experiments show that candidate pre-selection maintains a compact candidate context as registry size grows and avoids the operational failures observed with full-catalog orchestration. text: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), in- teroperable agent protocols, and machine-readable capability descriptions are enabling multi-agent ecosystems in which autonomous agents can be dynamically discovered and orches- trated [1], [2]. Protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) expose structured descriptions of tools and agents [3], [4]. In particular, A2A defines an Agent Card as a machine-readable description of an agent’s identity, capabilities, skills, interfaces, and related metadata [4]. We use Agent Card throughout this paper to denote such structured capability descriptions. A straightforward orchestration strategy is to present every available Agent Card to an LLM and ask it to select the most suitable agent. However, this full-catalog approach directly couples registry size to the amount of information presented to the LLM orchestrator. As the registry grows, more Agent Cards must be incorporated into the prompt, increasing context consumption, inference cost, and latency, while eventually reaching practical model or API limits. Related context-scaling concerns have motivated retrieval and candidate filtering in large tool collections [5]–[7]. Candidate pre-selection itself is therefore not new. Existing work has explored large-scale tool retrieval, context-aware filtering, learned routing, and relational tool–agent retrieval [5], [7]–[10]. Our focus is complementary: scalable agent discovery must account not only for retrieving relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also for controlling the amount
title: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent

text: explored large-scale tool retrieval, context-aware filtering, learned routing, and relational tool–agent retrieval [5], [7]–[10]. Our focus is complementary: scalable agent discovery must account not only for retrieving relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also for controlling the amount of candidate information ultimately presented to the LLM orchestrator. We formulate this systems problem as candidate-context scalability: registry-scale retrieval should remain operationally independent of the compact candidate context subsequently presented to the LLM. Under this formu- lation, retrieval may operate over the complete registry, while a maximum candidate budget K controls the number of top- ranked Agent Cards forwarded to the LLM orchestrator. This separation makes retrieval coverage, retrieval computation, and orchestration context distinct and independently measurable components of the discovery pipeline. To address this problem, we propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), our deterministic and training-free retrieval method designed specifically for Agent Card discovery. SSR constructs an explicit retrieval representation directly from capability-bearing fields already present in Agent Cards. It deterministically derives structural lexical signals from these fields, weights matched signals using inverse document fre- quency (IDF), and uses an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) to restrict scoring to Agent Cards that share structural evidence with the user query. The resulting candidates are ranked and a compact pool of up to K top-ranked Agent Cards is presented to the LLM

text: an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) to restrict scoring to Agent Cards that share structural evidence with the user query. The resulting candidates are ranked and a compact pool of up to K top-ranked Agent Cards is presented to the LLM orchestrator for final agent selection. This design decouples the growth of the agent registry from the amount of candidate information processed by the LLM while preserving a direct correspondence between each retrieval score and the explicit Agent Card signals that produced it. The methodological contribution of SSR does not lie in IDF weighting, inverted indexing, or candidate pre-selection individually. Rather, SSR integrates these established retrieval mechanisms into a dedicated pre-orchestration retrieval layer for Agent Card discovery in LLM-based multi-agent infras- arXiv:2610.21113v1 [cs.MA] 15 Oct 2026

Within this layer, capability-bearing Agent Card fields provide explicit structural signals for candidate genera- tion and ranking, while a maximum candidate budget controls the compact candidate context subsequently presented to the LLM orchestrator. To distinguish improvements arising from candidate pre- selection in general from properties specific to SSR, the end-to-end evaluation also instantiates the same candidate- selection architecture using the Best Matching 25 (BM25) ranking function [11]. SSR and BM25 operate under the same maximum candidate budget and the same LLM arbitration procedure. This controlled comparison allows the effects of maintaining a compact candidate context to be separated from differences attributable to the retrieval mechanism itself. The evaluation addresses three research questions: • RQ1: How does full-catalog LLM orchestration scale with registry size, and to what extent can SSR-based candidate pre-selection reduce its operational overhead? • RQ2: How effective and efficient is the SSR retrieval mechanism on naturally occurring text, and what are the contributions of IDF weighting and the ISI? • RQ3: How does retrieval-based candidate pre-selection affect end-to-end agent selection, candidate context, cost, latency, and operational reliability as registry size grows, and how does SSR compare with BM25 under the same maximum candidate budget? text: A. Agent Discovery and Routing Large-scale agent ecosystems require mechanisms for dis- covering suitable capabilities from machine-readable descrip- tions [1], [2]. Recent work increasingly frames this problem as retrieval or routing. One approach [12] combines capa- bility announcement with task-driven discovery and scalable indexing. Tool-to-Agent Retrieval [8] embeds tools and parent agents in a shared vector space, while Agent-as-a-Graph [9] combines vector retrieval with explicit graph structure. MoMA [13] and ACE-Router [10] instead study learned routing over heterogeneous models, tools, or agents. These works establish candidate pre-selection as an im- portant scalability mechanism. Our focus is complementary: we formulate candidate-context scalability for Agent Card discovery and propose SSR as a deterministic, training-free, field-derived retrieval mechanism that separates registry-scale retrieval from the compact candidate context presented to the LLM orchestrator. B. Tool and Skill Retrieval under Context Constraints Tool retrieval provides the closest neighboring litera- ture. ToolRet [5] formulates large-scale tool retrieval as an information-retrieval problem, PORTS [6] aligns retrieval with downstream tool selection, ToolDreamer [14] addresses lexical–semantic mismatch, and ToolScope [7] combines tool consolidation with context-aware filtering. Other methods make retrieval adaptive. Dynamic Tool De- pendency Retrieval (DTDR) [15] updates retrieval as the tool- calling plan evolves, ToolQP [16] decomposes requests into iterative retrieval queries, and SkillRet [17] extends retrieval to large libraries of reusable agent skills. Recent work on

text: retrieval adaptive. Dynamic Tool De- pendency Retrieval (DTDR) [15] updates retrieval as the tool- calling plan evolves, ToolQP [16] decomposes requests into iterative retrieval queries, and SkillRet [17] extends retrieval to large libraries of reusable agent skills. Recent work on adaptive shortlist depth [18] further treats candidate count as a decision variable governing the trade-off between retrieval coverage and LLM selection. This literature shows that candidate pre-selection and retrieval-first orchestration are established ideas. Our contri- bution is therefore not the retrieve-then-shortlist pattern itself, but its explicit formulation and systems-level characterization for Agent Card discovery. C. Retrieval Foundations SSR builds on established information-retrieval principles. Sparse methods such as BM25 use lexical matching and term- weighted inverted indexes [11], whereas dense approaches such as DPR [19] and ColBERT [20] learn semantic represen- tations that reduce dependence on exact lexical overlap. RAG [21] illustrates the broader retrieval-first principle of selecting external evidence before language-model generation. SSR does not claim novelty for IDF weighting, sparse retrieval, or inverted indexing. LLM Agent Systems and Interoperability Protocols LLM-based agent systems study reasoning, coordination, workflow execution, learning, and tool use [22]–[24]. Repre- sentative systems span multi-agent coordination [25]–[27] and reasoning, tool-use, embodied, or learning settings [28]–[31]. The present work focuses on the preceding systems question of which candidate capabilities should enter the LLM context before final arbitration. Interoperability protocols provide the machine-readable ob- jects over which such discovery can operate. MCP exposes structured tool descriptions [3], while A2A represents agents through Agent Cards containing identity, capabilities, skills, interfaces, and related metadata [4]. These protocols define capability representation and interaction but do not prescribe a large-registry relevance-ranking mechanism. SSR comple- ments them by operating directly over field-derived Agent Card information before LLM arbitration. III. STRUCTURAL SIGNAL RETRIEVER The Structural Signal Retriever (SSR) is the retrieval method proposed in this work for Agent Card discovery. It is deterministic and training-free, operates directly over machine- readable Agent Cards, and produces a compact pool of top- ranked candidates for LLM arbitration. SSR uses explicit lex- ical signals derived from capability-bearing Agent Card fields, inverse document frequency (IDF) weighting, and an Inverted Signal Index (ISI), without requiring dense representations or supervised retrieval training. B. Signal Extraction and Scoring The first component of SSR defines an explicit and traceable representation for Agent Cards and queries. A structural signal is a lexical unit extracted deterministically from capability- bearing fields such as an Agent Card’s name, description, declared skills, capability tags, examples, or tool descriptions. Here, structural refers to signal provenance from explicit fields of the agent representation, not to syntactic or latent semantic structure. Because retained signals remain individually identi- fiable, each retrieval score can be traced to the matched signals that contributed to it. Agent Cards and queries use the same deterministic nor- malization procedure. Text is lowercased, alphanumeric units are extracted with [a-z0-9]+, tokens shorter than two characters and fixed stopwords are removed, and the retained sequence generates unigram and consecutive-bigram signals. Duplicate signals are removed, so scoring uses binary signal presence rather than term frequency. Each representation contains at most 64 signals. VI. DISCUSSION The results support treating scalable agent discovery as a joint retrieval–orchestration problem. Full-catalog orchestra- tion couples registry size directly to the amount of informa- tion presented to the LLM, whereas candidate pre-selection separates registry-scale retrieval from the compact candidate context used for final arbitration. RQ3 shows that this systems effect is not specific to SSR: both SSR and BM25 maintain small candidate pools under the same maximum candidate budget, while full-catalog context grows rapidly with registry size. This distinction is central to the interpretation of SSR. RQ2 shows that BM25 achieves higher raw retrieval effectiveness on the MS MARCO adaptation, so SSR should not be viewed as a general replacement for established lexical retrieval. Instead, SSR provides a deterministic, training-free, field- derived retrieval mechanism for Agent Cards. Within this mechanism, IDF weighting improves ranking effectiveness, the Inverted Signal Index (ISI) reduces explicit structural scoring, and the maximum candidate budget K controls the amount of candidate information presented to the LLM orchestrator. Adaptive shortlist depth further treats candidate count itself as a decision variable [18]. The contribution of this work is therefore not candidate pre-selection, IDF weighting, or inverted indexing in isola- tion. Rather, we formulate candidate-context scalability for Agent Card discovery, propose SSR as an Agent-Card-native retrieval mechanism, and characterize how retrieval coverage, retrieval computation, candidate context, cost, latency, relia- bility, and LLM arbitration evolve under controlled registry growth. BM25 candidate pre-selection provides an important control because it separates the general effect of maintaining a compact candidate context from properties specific to SSR. Table VI summarizes this conceptual positioning relative to representative retrieval and routing approaches. SSR also provides score-level traceability: matched struc- tural signals and their IDF contributions remain identifiable for each retrieved Agent Card. This property applies to the retrieval stage and should not be interpreted as making subse- quent LLM arbitration explainable. C. Limitations Several limitations qualify the conclusions. First, RQ2 and RQ3 use a document-derived Agent Card abstraction. MS MARCO provides natural text and large-scale relevance judg- ments, but not native Agent Cards, structured skills, interfaces,

text: subse- quent LLM arbitration explainable. C. Limitations Several limitations qualify the conclusions. First, RQ2 and RQ3 use a document-derived Agent Card abstraction. MS MARCO provides natural text and large-scale relevance judg- ments, but not native Agent Cards, structured skills, interfaces, authentication requirements, or operational metadata. The results therefore characterize retrieval and candidate-context behavior under this abstraction rather than in a production agent registry. Second, SSR-AgentBench is synthetic and uses one des- ignated target per query. Its controlled construction supports reproducible registry scaling but does not capture the full heterogeneity, documentation quality, capability evolution, ac- cess constraints, or multiple valid agents found in operational ecosystems. Third, SSR deliberately relies on explicit lexical unigrams and bigrams. Vocabulary mismatch can reduce recall, and the MS MARCO results show that this representation does not outperform BM25. More expressive field-derived, semantic, or hybrid retrieval may improve coverage. Fourth, although independent validation supports K = 20, the original sensitivity analysis and end-to-end evaluation reuse the same 200 RQ3 queries. A cleaner prospective design would select and freeze K on validation data and evaluate it once on a disjoint end-to-end test set. Finally, RQ3 uses 200 queries and one LLM/API configu- ration, and the BM25 run was executed separately from the SSR/full-catalog run. Absolute latency, token usage, cost, and the observed full-catalog failure point should therefore not

Absolute latency, token usage, cost, and the observed full-catalog failure point should therefore not be generalized across models, providers, prompts, or context limits. Reported online latency also excludes offline index construction, so preprocessing, storage, and maintenance costs remain outside the present evaluation. D. Future Directions Future work should first investigate query-adaptive can- didate depth, using score concentration, margins, or other confidence signals to choose K(q) while preserving a hard maximum candidate budget [18]. Second, SSR could pro- vide inexpensive candidate generation followed by semantic retrieval or reranking when lexical evidence is weak; Tool- Dreamer illustrates one semantic reformulation strategy [14]. Third, retrieval could become execution-aware, recomputing queries or candidate pools as a plan evolves, as suggested by DTDR and ToolQP [15], [16]. Evaluation should also move toward native public Agent Card and skill collections, multi-relevance judgments, prospec- tive validation/test splits, and dynamic registry updates. Large distributed deployments further motivate incremental, authorization-aware, and federated indexing.

text: This work studied candidate-context scalability in LLM- based agent discovery: the separation between registry-scale retrieval and the compact candidate context presented to the LLM orchestrator. We propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), a deterministic, training-free method for Agent Card discovery based on field-derived lexical signals, inverse doc- ument frequency (IDF), and an Inverted Signal Index (ISI). The three experiments provide complementary evidence. On SSR-AgentBench, SSR reduces mean LLM input by 98.8% and mean successful orchestration latency by 70.9% at N = 1000 relative to full-catalog orchestration. On the MS MARCO adaptation, IDF improves ranking effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves the positive-scoring Structural+IDF ranking and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%, yielding a 74.2× mean retrieval- latency speedup over exhaustive scoring. BM25 achieves higher raw retrieval effectiveness, so SSR is not presented as a universally superior lexical retriever. In end-to-end evaluation, SSR and BM25 candidate pre-selection show comparable observed effectiveness under the same maximum candidate budget K = 20; no statistically detectable difference in end-to-end correctness is observed after Holm correction. At N = 5000, both candidate-pre-selection pipelines remain operational, whereas none of the 200 full-catalog LLM re- quests completes successfully under the evaluated model/API configuration. These results show that the main candidate-context reduc- tion arises from effective candidate pre-selection rather than from SSR scoring alone. The

These results show that the main candidate-context reduc- tion arises from effective candidate pre-selection rather than from SSR scoring alone. The contribution of this work is the formulation and systems-level characterization of candidate- context scalability for Agent Card discovery, together with SSR as an Agent-Card-native, deterministic, training-free, field-derived, and score-traceable retrieval mechanism. The conclusions remain limited by the synthetic nature of SSR- AgentBench, the document-derived Agent Card abstraction used with MS MARCO, retrospective validation of the fixed candidate budget, a single LLM/API configuration, and the exclusion of offline index construction from online latency. Future work should evaluate native Agent Card collections, prospective budget selection, query-adaptive and hybrid re- trieval, and dynamic or distributed registries.

title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach

text: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system re- quirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output- level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alterna- tive by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender sys- tems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parame- ter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learn- able preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional gen- erative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness con- straints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demon- strate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and ef- fective controllability while delivers 165–228× faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

text: Modern recommender systems optimize multiple, often conflicting objectives beyond a single metric [13, 15, 21, 29, 46, 48]. While exist- ing multi-objective recommender systems address these trade-offs during training, they typically enforce fixed preferences at infer- ence time [16, 24]. In practice, however, the preference weights on objectives are often dynamic, shifting across users’ or systems’ requirements. This motivates Controllable Multi-Objective Recom- mendation (CMOR), which enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining [32]. Research on CMOR can be categorized into two paradigms based on the stage of intervention: post-processing and in-processing ap- proaches. Post-processing approaches, such as rule-based reranking like MMR [3] intervene by adjusting the initially generated recom- mendation lists. While being model-agnostic, their performance is constrained by the fixed candidate set, often leading to a narrow scope of trade-off solutions. In-processing focuses on parameter- level modulation, primarily through parameter generation. These parameter generation approaches learn the mapping from user preferences over multiple objectives to the parameter space of rec- ommendation model by employing generative architectures, such as hypernetworks [4, 11, 24] or diffusion models [34]. Despite deliv- ering superior performance, these in-processing approaches inflate the training cost with a massive number of additional parameters from the generative modules and incur non-negligible inference latency, while often suffering from optimization instability. This raises a critical open

Despite deliv- ering superior performance, these in-processing approaches inflate the training cost with a massive number of additional parameters from the generative modules and incur non-negligible inference latency, while often suffering from optimization instability. This raises a critical open question: why not reuse existing rec- ommendation models to efficiently achieve controllable trade-offs, rather than constructing new parameters from scratch? Recent ad- vances in large language models offer a promising answer: model merging, which adjusts model behavior through weighted merging of existing model parameters according to multi-objective prefer- ences, eliminating the need for retraining or additional parameter- generating modules [14, 25, 26, 37, 41]. This paradigm is particularly well-suited for recommender systems, where multiple indepen- dently trained, objective-specialized sub-models (e.g., for accuracy or diversity) commonly coexist in industrial training pipelines [2, 7]. Rather than discarding these costly pre-trained checkpoints, model merging offers an efficient mechanism for reusing and combining their expertise. text: 3.2, recommendation task vectors substantially deviate from the linear regime hypothesis that under- pins most task-vector merging approaches. The absence of a shared low-dimensional linear subspace renders naive linear interpolation ineffective and prone to cross-objective interference, motivating the need for a merging strategy tailored to the complex parameter geometry of recommendation models. To address these challenges, we propose RecSoup, a two-stage framework for controllable multi-objective recommendation. In the first stage, RecSoup employs a fine-grained pruning strategy to resolve parameter interference. Unlike magnitude-based ap- proaches, we jointly consider objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance, which establishes a harmonious param- eter foundation for merging. In the second stage, RecSoup moves beyond linear interpolation. We integrate a learnable mechanism that captures the mapping from user preference vectors to merg- ing coefficients, allowing the model to dynamically navigate the parameter space. The synergy between pruning-driven conflict mitigation and adaptive merging enables RecSoup to generate high- quality Pareto solutions with superior controllability, bypassing the optimization instability and architectural overhead of generative approaches. text: Model Merging integrates task-specific specialists into a unified model without joint retraining, and has been widely studied in LLMs [14, 23, 37, 41]. Existing methods mainly address interfer- ence among task-specific updates, or task vectors, through conflict mitigation [6, 8, 12, 20, 22, 35, 40, 42, 45] or coefficient determina- tion [6, 43]. The former reduces conflicts by pruning redundant or conflicting parameters, such as TIES-merging [40], DARE [45], CABS [44], and LwPTV [47], or by projecting task vectors into orthogonal subspaces, such as TATR [35]. These methods motivate our pruning design, but their criteria are not tailored to recommen- dation objectives and overlook objective-specific contribution and cross-objective relevance. The latter determines how to combine task vectors. AdaMerging [43] adaptively learns merging weights, while PCB-merging [6] considers both intra-task and inter-task bal- ancing, which inspires our pruning design. However, these methods typically yield a single fixed merged model, resulting in a “one-size- fits-all” solution [1] that is unsuitable for CMOR, where different preference vectors require different trade-offs among accuracy, di- versity, and fairness. Recent Pareto merging methods learn multiple solutions via low-rank structures [5], surrogate evaluation [19], or MoE-based coefficient generation [36]. Following Tang et al. [36], we adopt a preference-conditioned coefficient generator as deter- miner and tailor it with our pruning criterion to CMOR. Parameter Generation enables controllability by

Parameter Generation enables controllability by dynamically gen- erating model weights to meet specific task demands. This approach was pioneered in controllable multi-task learning [24, 27], which demonstrated that hypernetworks could map preference vectors to task-specific parameters. Subsequent advances such as PHN [24] and PHN-HVI [11] have shown that a single hypernetwork can effectively approximate the entire Pareto front. In recommendation, CMR [4] adapts hypernetwork by generating sensitive re-ranking parameters for instant preference adjustment, while Hyperban- dit and its variant further extend this idea to time-varying user preferences in streaming recommendation [31, 33]. Beyond hy- pernetworks, Paragon [34] employs diffusion models to synthe- size objective-conditioned adapters, matching the performance of retraining at lower cost. Despite their effectiveness in achieving Pareto optimality, parameter generation paradigms face significant challenges regarding architectural complexity and training stability. 3 Problem Formulation and Analyses This section formulates the problem of controllable multi-objective recommendation via model merging and analyzes the limitations of naive task-vector merging in sequential recommendation models. 3.1 Problem Formulation Let U and I denote the sets of users and items, respectively. Task arithmetic (e.g., linear merging of task vectors) has proven effective in models such as CLIP, where its success is grounded in the linear regime hypothesis [14, 37, 38]. This hypothesis assumes that fine-tuning operates within a lin- ear regime, where task-specific parameter updates (task vectors as defined in Eq. (1)) are confined to a shared, composable linear subspace consistent with the neural tangent kernel (NTK) approxi- mation. This implies that all task-specific parameter updates are restricted within the linear subspace defined by the NTK tangent space. Different tasks’ 𝜏𝑖can therefore be interpreted as distinct vector combinations within this shared subspace. Empirical Violation of the Linear Regime. To assess whether this assumption extends to sequential recommendation models, we employ Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to characterize the geometric structure of task vectors. As formalized in Ortiz et al. [25] (Property 2), the linear regime inherently requires that task-specific parameter updates reside within a shared linear subspace (the NTK tangent space). In this scenario, the model’s output change after fine-tuning can be approximated by a first-order Taylor expansion (𝑓(𝑥;𝜃∗) −𝑓(𝑥;𝜃0) ≈𝜏⊤∇𝜃𝑓(𝑥;𝜃0)), which manifests in PCA as a distinctive structural signature: task vectors should exhibit tight clustering along a small number of principal components (PCs), with the majority of parameter variation concentrated in these dominant dimensions. However, our PCA results (Figure 2) reveals that sequential rec- ommendation models lack this signature of a shared linear subspace. Task vectors optimized for accuracy and diversity are dispersed across disjoint regions of the PCA space, with no evidence of cluster- ing along dominant components: PC1 explains only 25.66%–26.23% of the total variance, and the top two components collectively capture less than 45% of the variance. This motivates the need for adaptive merging to learn preference-conditional coefficients that navigate this manifold. At the same time, sequential recommendation models exhibit heterogeneous parameter importance: although approxi- mately 30% of parameters can be removed without severe degra- dation (Figure 3), pruning affects objectives differently. Accuracy- oriented updates are highly sensitive, while diversity-oriented ones are robust. This asymmetry suggests that naively merging dense vectors risks suppressing critical parameters and retaining interfer- ing updates, making preference-based merging unstable and less controllable. Together, these observations motivate a two-stage design: first, conflict mitigation via pruning reduces interfer- ence and preserves task-critical parameters, and second, adaptive merging explores the complex manifold to achieve controllable multi-objective trade-offs. 4 RecSoup: The Proposed Approach In this section, we present RecSoup, a novel controllable multi- objective recommendation framework that decouples the merging process into two stages: determining which parameters to combine and defining how to weight them. This stage sparsifies task vectors by filtering parameters based on importance and relevance, thereby mitigating interference. (2) Adaptive Model Merging. This stage dynamically optimizes coefficients within a learned Pareto manifold to balance competing metrics (e.g., accuracy and diversity). By distinguishing parameter selection from coefficient determination, RecSoup ensures robust control. At inference, a gating network generates coefficients for any preference vector in a single forward pass, enabling efficient control without retraining. Overall, these results demonstrate the scalability of RecSoup in multi-objective recommendation settings. 7 Conclusions This work shows that task-vector merging, despite its success in large language models, cannot be directly applied to multi-objective sequential recommendation due to the absence of a shared linear regime. Motivated by this observation, we propose RecSoup, which mitigates parameter interference through pruning and enables con- trollable trade-offs via a lightweight gating network. Empirical results further indicate that model-merging approaches offer a more efficient and effective paradigm than parameter-generation approaches for controllable multi-objective recommendation. The coefficient learner is im- plemented as a lightweight routing module conditioned on the preference vector. In all experiments, we use a single-layer linear router. The routing weights are initialized using a Gaussian distri- bution with standard deviation 0.01. During training, the backbone model and expert task vectors are frozen, and only the routing parameters are updated. The coefficient learner is optimized using Adam with learning rate 0.001, batch size 512. text: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents Tanish Kher* Sarvesh DK Abedelkadir Asi Sparsha Chennarayapatna Sundaresh Dezhi Hong Microsoft
title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents

text: Modern agents select tools from registries, but exposing entire registries incurs high token costs and can impair selection as they grow. We present TRACER, a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. On a mixed retail-and-telecom τ 2 environment, TRACER improves GPT-5.4’s tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while reducing input tokens per step by 80%, exposing just 5 of 128 tools. In au- tonomous full-turn execution, it matches GPT- 5.4’s full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step. Across six environ- ments and four models, TRACER improves tool- selection accuracy over full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with aver- age gains of 6 to 10 points; the three exceptions trail by at most 2.2. We analyze failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work. 1
title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents

text: Modern language-model agents use tool calling to resolve user requests (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023), often executing multi-turn sequences of function calls over registries of internal services and external APIs (Barres et al., 2025). Systems such as Claude Cowork (Anthropic, 2026), Copilot Cowork (Microsoft, 2026), and Codex (OpenAI, 2025) illustrate the growing use of tool-mediated interaction in agentic workflows (Xu et al., 2026). A central challenge is selecting and invoking the right tool from a potentially large registry. Expos- ing many tool schemas simultaneously increases context and token costs, while long, detailed inputs can make relevant information harder to use reli- ably (Sakizli, 2026; Liu et al., 2024a). text: using tool descriptions to identify candidates. However, description-based retrieval can confuse semantically similar tools, and retrieval errors can propagate to downstream execution. As registries grow, tool selection and schema management there- fore remain important sources of inefficiency and unreliability despite progress in tool retrieval and tool-use training (Liu et al., 2026; Gillespie and Perry, 2026; Qin et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2024; Gan and Sun, 2025). The core gap is that each step is treated as in- dependent search, when tool retrieval is really se- quential prediction: which call comes next, given those already made. Within a single turn, a τ 2 re- tail request is resolved in a logical order: identify the customer, pull their account, open the order in question, then act on it. The calls already made therefore constrain the next one. Built on this intuition, we propose TRACER (Trie Retrieval Across Contextual Edges, Reweighted), a state-conditioned front-end that offers a small, ac- curate candidate set at every step and still leaves the final choice to the model (Figure 6, Appendix A.8). It rests on three ideas. Full-prefix conditioning: execution history is a trie over observed tool-call sequences, the agent’s prefix within a turn is a node, and the tools seen after it are its candidates, so ear- 1 arXiv:2610.21267v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026
title: TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents

text: lier calls separate next steps that the last call alone leaves equally plausible. Transition-specific us- age memory: each edge stores the conversations that transition was taken in, telling apart candi- dates whose descriptions do not. State-dependent weighting: history and semantics are not equally informative, so a learned per-step blend sets how much each should count at any step. Where a reg- istry’s calls concentrate in generic utility tools that no single state predicts, TRACER+G unions a small global set into every candidate set. On a mixed τ 2 environment spanning retail and telecom domains, TRACER paired with GPT-5.4 outperforms the standalone frontier GPT-5.4 model by 4.7 points in tool-selection accuracy, 57.2% to 61.9%, all while cutting prompt tokens per step by 80% (Figure 1). Running a full turn on its own selections, TRACER matches full-registry task suc- cess, 58.3% against 58.2%, despite presenting only 23% of the tools at any time and cutting per-step tokens by 61%. Similar results largely hold across five other environments, four models, and budgets k from 3 to 30 (§5). Contributions. • A comprehensive state-conditioned retrieval front-end. We combine full-prefix condition- ing, transition-specific usage memory and a learned per-state blend in a single index. • A benchmark environment built for retrieval. text: Matching requests to fixed tool representations. Retrievers over large registries rank tools by sim- ilarity to the request (Qin et al., 2024; Patil et al., 2024; Gan and Sun, 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Repan- tis et al., 2026). Description matchers differ only in how that match is trained (Zheng et al., 2024; Molfetta et al., 2025; Sengupta et al., 2026); Tool2Vec (Moon et al., 2024) matches past requests rather than documentation; and MCP-Zero (Fei et al., 2025) has the model write its own query, better aligned to tool descriptions than the user’s words. Each improves the query; all still score it against a representation fixed in advance. Fixed once, it cannot separate several plausible candi- dates, and it cannot register that one tool serves different purposes at different points. Past usage at that point does both. Relating tools to one another. TGR (Gao et al., 2025) smooths each tool’s embedding toward the tools it depends on, so prerequisites are retrieved alongside what needs them; ProTIP (Anantha et al., 2023) retrieves progressively, subtracting the em- beddings of tools already chosen so the query car- ries what remains. While these take real steps, they ignore what makes tool-calling dynamic: ev- ery choice must be read against the calls and turns that came before it. TGR pools dependency over all prefixes, fixing

text: so the query car- ries what remains. While these take real steps, they ignore what makes tool-calling dynamic: ev- ery choice must be read against the calls and turns that came before it. TGR pools dependency over all prefixes, fixing once a relationship that holds only sometimes, and ProTIP’s subtraction keeps no record of the order the previous calls came in. Conditioning on execution. ToolNet (Liu et al., 2024b) offers the successors of the last call, weighted by bigram counts; AutoTool (Jia and Li, 2026) widens that to two and blends the count with SimCSE similarity at a constant α=0.5, using the result to bypass the model. Neither asks how the current conversation resembles the ones that pre- viously took each transition: ToolNet has no such signal, and AutoTool’s compares against a tool’s description (21 points worse on API-Bank in our ablation). Both also fix the blend once. TRACER improves this by learning the balance of factors per state instead, worth 0.9 to 7.6 points (Table 6; Table 1 compares all methods). 3 Method 3.1 Problem definition and notation An agent answers a request q by emitting an or- dered sequence of tool calls; at step i it has emitted 2

text: can we use histori- cal successful trajectories to select k ≪|R| tools that contain the gold tool the agent should call next, cutting per-step token cost while improving selection accuracy? 3.2 Overview We model this with a trie built from a dataset D of training trajectories (Figure 6, Appendix A.8). At each step the front-end reads the conversation context ctx(q, Si) and the current prefix Si, locates Si in the trie (§3.3), and scores that node’s children on two signals: an empirical prior over the transi- tions observed out of Si (§3.4), and a contextual prior measuring how closely the current conversa- tion resembles the ones in which each transition was historically taken (§3.5). A learned per-step blend (§3.6) combines them into one score, and the top k form the candidate set K ⊂R from which the model makes its choice. Every system we com- pare changes which tools reach the prompt, but the model always chooses. 3.3 Trie construction We build the execution trie by inserting every prefix of every trajectory in D as a node. Figure 2 shows a hypothetical example. For any prefix node Si, its children C(Si) are the tools observed immediately after Si in training. Each edge from Si to a child node t carries two kinds of information: the conditional probability of a training

Each edge from Si to a child node t carries two kinds of information: the conditional probability of a training turn traversing Si →t, the empirical prior (§3.4); and the mean-pooled embedding of the training contexts in which turns traversed Si → t, an edge memory m(Si →t) from which the contextual prior is computed (§3.5). The two are scoped differently by design. The trie is turn-local, resetting to the root at each turn boundary, which keeps prefixes estimable instead of fragmenting the state space across a whole con- versation; we train on turns drawn from throughout a conversation so the model sees resets at varied positions. The edge memory is not turn-local: it embeds the full conversation, so cross-turn infor- mation reaches the retriever without entering the trie as structure. 3.4 The empirical prior P(t) Formally, the empirical prior is the normalized tran- sition frequency out of that node, and at inference we write P(t) = log �Ptrie(t | Si) + ϵ  for the resulting log-signal, adding a small smoothing con- stant ϵ so that candidates carrying no observed tran- sition from this state have a finite value. text: fallback The retriever falls back to global vector search in two cases: an unseen state (C(Si) = ∅) and a flat score distribution (κ < τ). Fallback ranks the full registry by the cosine similarity of the embedded step context e(ctx(q, Si)) to each tool’s description and returns the top k, replacing the trie candidates entirely. We set τ = 0.20. This gate gives the trie-based methods well-defined behavior on states absent from training, behavior the full-registry and stateless baselines do not model. 4 Data and Experimental Setup 4.1 Benchmarks We evaluate on four benchmarks, sweeping the pri- mary one at three registry sizes (Small, Medium, Large) for six environments in total (Table 7). Our primary benchmark, Mixed Tau2 R&T, is a mixed retail + telecom environment built combining real graded trajectories from τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025) with vetted synthetic ones. Tau3 Banking is the banking domain of τ 3-Knowledge (Shi et al., 2026), mixing more sophisticated banking tools with compliance requirements and search over roughly 700 interconnected documents. BFCL v3 (Patil et al., 2025) is smaller but spans many weakly-related API families (file-system, vehicle, trading, travel), stressing cross-domain retrieval. Trajectory provenance is in Appendix A.2; the curation gates are in Appendix A.3. 4.3 Synthetic generation and validation for Mixed Tau2 R&T Real trajectories alone under-populate the registry, leaving too few plausible alternatives and mak- ing retrieval look artificially easy. We expand each domain’s registry with synthetic APIs and trajectories drawn from a co-occurrence graph, so that each is a realistic in-context path. Every one clears blocking gates for ground-truth validity, non- substitutability against real tools, API disjointness, and non-cloning (99.8% of retail and 99.9% of tele- com clear the last), with accept-sets seeded where a different real tool may legitimately substitute for the gold call (Table 10, Appendix A.3). The diagnostic C3 judge compared real τ 2 tra- jectories against our synthetic ones and picked ours as the human-authored one in 57.0% of re- tail and 68.9% of telecom pairs. A blind human study agreed: told that exactly one of each pair was human-authored, three reviewers picked ours in 40 of 59 decided pairs, 67.8% of the time (Figure 5, Appendix A.5). Our τ 2-style policy prompts are validated the same way, so that no clause contradicts any gold trajectory (C6, Appendix A.4). 4.4 Execution regimes We evaluate in two execution regimes, differing only in what is appended to the context between steps. Teacher-forcing records each selection but feeds the benchmark’s gold call forward in its place, so a wrong selection at step i cannot corrupt step i+1. This is our primary regime because it measures the front-end in isolation, which is what this paper contributes. Under free-running, the agent’s own emitted call and its reasoning are appended and carried forward, so errors compound: a wrong selection changes the prefix the retriever conditions on. An inference episode ends when our grader confirms the task is complete, or after a cap of 20 steps. Our grader scores a turn by the database hash its gold actions produce, plus the read operations a read-only turn must contain (Appendix A.15). 4.5 Algorithms We test TRACER against two baselines that ig- nore execution history and two variants of our own. LLM-ONLY places the entire registry in context at every step, as a post-disclosure domain list, upper-bounding candidate coverage at maxi- mal cost. VECTOR

text: We test TRACER against two baselines that ig- nore execution history and two variants of our own. LLM-ONLY places the entire registry in context at every step, as a post-disclosure domain list, upper-bounding candidate coverage at maxi- mal cost. VECTOR ranks the full registry by the cosine similarity of the embedded step context to each tool’s description and returns the top k, the same mechanism the confidence gate falls back to (§3.7). TRACER-fixed is an ablation: it fixes the blend instead of predicting it, scoring s(t) = L(t)+P(t), and is identical to TRACER in every other respect, so the gap between them isolates the value of the learned blend. TRACER+G is a configuration for registries whose calls concentrate in context- independent utility tools that no state prior sur- faces; it unions a small, fixed, per-fold global set G into every candidate set after ranking, K = TOPK(s, k) ∪G. G holds the |G| = 3 tools with the highest prefix entropy H(S | t), the entropy over the states from which t is the gold next call, so it collects the tools whose calls spread most widely across the trie (§A.8). 4.6 Models, metrics, and protocol Models and metrics. This filtering matters when the competitor is not merely confusing but dangerous. For in- stance, when a customer asked for a prepaid re- turn label, LLM-ONLY incorrectly tried to initi- ate a return (return_delivered_order_items), while TRACER ranked that tool 9th on the contextual prior at that prefix, dropping the destructive tool from even being given to the model, so it cor- rectly chose the precision tool get_return_label (Appendix A.12). 7

Many deploy- ments gate a consequential action behind a prereq- uisite call, and the ordering is itself the require- ment. In banking, a sensitive tool must be un- locked by unlock:X before it can be called, and under the full registry LLM-ONLY skips that step when asked to open an account. The trie withholds the raw write: no successful trajectory reaches open_bank_account from Si without passing through unlock:open_bank_account. The edge memory sup- plies the other half, matching the conversation to the unlock (Figure 4). 5.5 When the global set is needed Adding a global set to TRACER (TRACER+G) helps when some tools not bound to any prefix take a large share of tool calls. This explains TRACER’s low performance on Tau3 Banking, whose registry mostly uses generic tools that cover many subtasks under one umbrella (KB_search for any knowledge- base lookup, grep for any text match), so they ap- pear throughout the trie. (C) Trie key depth. We truncated the trie’s keys to just the last two calls and ran TRACER on this last-2 trie, which raised selection accuracy by 1.5 to 2.9 points on Grok-4-20-reasoning and Mixed Tau2 R&T (Large) compared to the full current- turn prefix (Appendix A.11). While this is within one SD (3.7 to 4.3), it points to key depth as a parameter worth testing in future work. The shorter key leaves 9.6% of steps out of trie against 12.4% for the full prefix, and the two are indistinguishable on the steps that do fall out. text: embeddings that no bigram front-end has (§2). 6 Conclusion and Future Work TRACER is the first tool-retrieval front-end to make selection history-aware and dynamic at every pre- fix: it keys on the full execution prefix, ranks candi- dates against the conversations each transition was taken in, and learns how best to weight the two sig- nals for the situation. It beats full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs while cutting per-step tokens by 80% on our primary testbed, at a cost that tracks the budget rather than the registry. The budget k already moves with domain and model (Table 3), and the global set recovers most of the Tau3 Banking gap; both are fixed here and should adapt. TRACER gained 15.2 points for GPT- 5.4-mini and matched GPT-5.4’s full-registry task success at 23% of the registry, but did not carry gains at most of GPT-5.4’s budgets, largely be- cause running on its own prefix roughly triples the share of steps that fall outside the trie. Limitations Cold start. TRACER indexes a dataset D of graded trajectories (§3.3), so a registry with no usage history has no trie to consult and every step falls to the vector fallback, where accuracy is far below the rest of the run: presenting the full reg- istry on those steps instead would raise it by 38 points on average (Table 16). The method there- fore assumes a deployment that has already logged successful runs. How quickly a trie becomes useful as trajectories accumulate is the obvious next mea- surement, and one our fixed-size corpora cannot answer. Trie key depth. We key the trie on the full current-turn prefix (§3.3) and did not tune that choice. A shorter key is not obviously worse (§5.6), so the depth we use may not be the best one. Free-running episodes are terminated by the grader. An episode ends when the grader con- firms completion or at a cap of 20 steps (§4.4); the agent never judges for itself that it is done. Task success therefore measures whether the front-end supplies the tools needed to

text: grader. An episode ends when the grader con- firms completion or at a cap of 20 steps (§4.4); the agent never judges for itself that it is done. Task success therefore measures whether the front-end supplies the tools needed to reach the goal, not whether an agent built on it would know when to stop. Selection accuracy discards ordering freedom. Several tools can often be called in different orders and still complete a task, but accuracy is scored against one recorded ordering, so a valid alterna- tive counts as wrong. Accept-sets (§4.6) and free- running task success, which asks only whether the goal was reached, bound the distortion.

text: Blind real-vs-synthetic judge prompt (C3). # C3 -- Real vs. synthetic (paired indistinguishability) ## SYSTEM PROMPT ---Role--- You are shown two conversations between a person and an assistant. One was written by a human; one was written by a model. Decide which is the model-written (synthetic) one, or that you cannot reliably tell. Judge ONLY the human-language wording. DO: - Judge only the dialogue's language: word choice, tone, rhythm, and how naturally the person and the assistant phrase things. - Weigh natural human signals: hedging, self-corrections, brevity, small talk, the way real people under- or over-explain. - If both read as equally natural language, answer "cannot_tell". DON'T: - Don't judge the scenario or topic. The two conversations may be about different things and need not line up in topic, order, or structure; any task is in scope. - Don't judge by the number of requests, or whether they relate to each other. - Don't use the masked tool labels (tool_a, tool_b, ...), their count, or the hidden call arguments/outputs -- the same redaction is applied to both sides and is not a clue. - Don't judge by conversation length or number of turns. - Don't reward messiness or penalize clean writing on its own, and don't try to recall or match specific datasets or examples. Reason first, then output only

[...] ## Generic action rules You do not need to look up or re-verify an order's status before choosing a tool; select the operation that matches the user's request, even when the order is at an intermediate status or no status has been retrieved yet. When exchanging or modifying items, be sure that all items to be changed are collected into a list before making the tool call. A given exchange or item-modification action is generally applied once per order. ## Cancel pending order The cancel-pending-order action is the tool for cancelling an order that is still pending (before it ships). Cancelling a delivered order, or cancelling an individual item, are separate operations with their own dedicated tools and are not limited to pending orders. The user needs to confirm the order id and the reason for cancellation (commonly 'no longer needed' or 'ordered by mistake'). After user confirmation, the order status will be changed to 'cancelled', and the total will be refunded via the original payment method

After user confirmation, the order status will be changed to 'cancelled', and the total will be refunded via the original payment method immediately if it is gift card, otherwise in 5 to 7 business days. ## Modify pending order The modify-pending-order actions are the tools for changing an order that is still open -- typically a pending order, including one already altered by an earlier change (for example a status such as 'pending (item modified)', 'address_updated', or 'items_modified'). For a pending order, the modify-pending-order actions cover its shipping address, payment method, or product item options. In particular, remember to remind the customer to confirm they have provided all the items they want to modify. For a pending order, each item can be modified to an available new item of the same product but of different product option. There cannot be any change of product types, e.g. modify shirt to shoe. The user must provide a payment method to pay or receive refund of the price difference. If the user provides a gift card, it must have enough balance to cover the 13

A.13 Compute, software, and artifacts Model size and compute. The only trained com- ponent is the blend head of §3.6: two linear heads over the five standardized features of §A.9, so θ = (a, bw, c, bT ) holds 12 parameters. It fits on CPU on one workstation VM; no GPU was used at any point, so we report no GPU hours. All infer- ence ran on hosted endpoints through an internal service that does not expose per-call cost, so we report no dollar figure. The embedder and the four evaluated models are proprietary, with undisclosed parameter counts. Inference spans four models and five algorithms over five folds in six environments at each swept budget (§4.6). Software and settings. We use NumPy, scikit- learn (GROUPKFOLD for the task-grouped folds), PyTorch for the blend head, tiktoken for token counts, and the provider’s Python client for hosted inference. Decoding uses temperature 1, other pa- rameters at provider defaults. The hyperparameters in §A.8 and §A.9 were

TRACER narrows the tools an agent sees, so a retrieval failure can hide a needed tool; the con- fidence gate and out-of-trie fallback (§3.7) bound that, and Table 16 quantifies where it still fails. Built from observed trajectories, the trie inherits their biases and will under-serve rare but legitimate tool sequences. We see no societal risk beyond those already present in tool-using agents. text: To show that a medical device complies with regulation, experts judge whether documents and records meet each requirement and record the judgment for others to verify. For each assessment item that experts define, large language models could prepare a preliminary assessment: a label such as Satisfied or Not satisfied, a reason and quoted evidence. We sent fourteen commercial deployments of such models (seven models from three providers, through six routes) the same request repeatedly, with the deterministic sampling settings each accepted; every deployment returned differing assessments for at least one request, and in twelve the label changed. Reducing reasoning where the interface allows it did not reduce the variation, and prompts of retrieved passages removed it only for the smallest models. The same open-weight model was reproducible or not depending only on how it was served. A pipeline we built to be deterministic at every stage—text extraction and optical character recognition (OCR), chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval and inference— returned byte-identical output at each stage across reruns, interruptions, edits, machines of one graphics processing unit (GPU) model and days, for blood glucose meter and infusion pump documents. OCR, embedding and approximate retrieval varied when their own serving was not made invariant, and outputs changed with the GPU model and with the inference engine’s scheduling settings, which therefore belong in the recorded

OCR, embedding and approximate retrieval varied when their own serving was not made invariant, and outputs changed with the GPU model and with the inference engine’s scheduling settings, which therefore belong in the recorded configuration. End-to-end determinism is achievable and gives a testable basis for audit and change control. text: Demonstrating that a medical device complies with regulation is expert work that must leave a record. Experts interpret the applicable requirements, judge whether the documents and records—technical files, test reports and data held in electronic quality man- agement systems—meet them, and record each judg- ment with its evidence. The work recurs with every submission, design change and audit, on the manu- facturer’s side and on the side of notified bodies and regulators, and the records are kept for at least ten years [1]; a notified body must document its confor- mity assessment so that its conclusions “can represent objective evidence of such compliance to persons that are not themselves involved in the assessment” [1], and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reviews the substance of a 510(k) (premarket notifica- tion) submission only after a completeness screening [2, 3]. Large language models (LLMs) could help with this work [4–6]. We take a limited view of their role. Deciding which regulations, standards and guidance apply, and stating what must be shown as assess- ment items, remains the experts’ work. For each item that experts define, an LLM can prepare a prelim- inary assessment—a label such as Satisfied or Not satisfied, a short reason and the passages it relies on, quoted verbatim—for a qualified expert to check against the source; the judgment,

Regulators’ guidance recommends exactly this form of evidence, quoted sentences that can be checked [6], and warns against the documented tendency of even expert users to over-rely on an automated suggestion [8–10]. Software used in a quality management system must be vali- dated for its intended use, including when it changes (ISO 13485:2016, subclause 4.1.6, incorporated by 21 CFR 820.10(a); 11–14), and electronic-record systems for “accuracy, reliability, consistent intended perfor- mance, and the ability to discern invalid or altered records” [15, §11.10(a)]; with a system whose output varies from run to run, a single difference observed after a change—to a document, an item, a model or the hardware—cannot be told from ordinary variation without repeated runs, and the individual assess- ments the change affects cannot be identified. An LLM pipeline does not give the same output for the same input by construction: floating-point reductions depend on how requests are batched [16], embeddings and retrieval drift with precision and with insertions [17], a commercial deployment runs on hardware and software the user cannot see [18], and in a recent preprint covering five API providers, repeated out- puts at temperature zero were character-identical 22% of the time on average for the two models evalu- ated on every task [19]. text: 22% of the time on average for the two models evalu- ated on every task [19]. Reproducibility is a separate axis from accuracy, and this paper concerns only reproducibility. Deterministic inference is now available: batch- invariant kernels and, more recently, verified and scheduling-based engines make a model’s output inde- pendent of how requests are batched [16, 20–23]. What has not been tested is whether a complete assessment pipeline, in which inference is one stage among several, can be made reproducible, and what a user of a commercial deployment actually observes in the fields of an assessment record. We asked whether preliminary assessments of public FDA documents can be produced again, byte for byte, and found three things. Commercial LLM deployments did not repro- duce their assessments at the deterministic sampling settings they accepted: the quoted evidence changed more often than the label, one model varied differ- ently through different routes, another changed labels only between days, and reducing reasoning did not help. For the open-weight models we served, repro- ducibility was a property of how the model was served. A pipeline deterministic from text extrac- tion to inference reproduced every intermediate result and output across repetition, reordering, concurrency, interruption, corpus edits, machines and days for two device types, provided the GPU model and the inference engine’s configuration are held fixed

text: pipeline deterministic from text extrac- tion to inference reproduced every intermediate result and output across repetition, reordering, concurrency, interruption, corpus edits, machines and days for two device types, provided the GPU model and the inference engine’s configuration are held fixed and recorded; left to their defaults, OCR, embedding and approximate retrieval were themselves sources of vari- ation. We argue that, where judgments recorded in a quality system rest on LLM-prepared preliminary assessments, byte-level reproducibility of the entire pipeline is a strong and testable engineering con- dition for auditing those judgments and controlling change. It is not a regulatory requirement, and it is not sufficient for validation. Results Each preliminary assessment has four outputs (Table 1): a label (here Satisfied, Not satisfied or Can- not determine), a comment giving the reason, the passages quoted as evidence, and the files they come from. We compared repeated runs of the same prompt on six fields in two layers. The substance layer is what an expert relies on: the label, the cited files and the cited passages, where two runs cite the same passage when their quotations overlap at the same place in the same document. The text layer is what the assess- ment record stores: the exact quotation strings, the comment and the full output, compared character for character. Table 1 compares two

Reproducibility depended on how the model was served The same open-weight model was reproducible or not depending only on how it was served. As a posi- tive control, we sent the 70 prompts, on the same schedule, to the judgment stage of the determinis- tic pipeline described below (“Ours” in Table 2): Gemma 4 31B (FP8) served by vLLM with batch- invariant inference [16, 20] on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU; all 700 outputs over two days were byte- identical, including prompts of about 130,000 tokens. A dedicated server sent one request at a time might be stable without any special measure, so we also sent the prompts from eight concurrent senders with batch invariance enabled and disabled, all else equal. This changes one thing on one server, and is a direct form of the attribution that Rover et al. reached indirectly: variation comes from how the serving infrastructure executes a request, not from cloud hosting as such [19]. The budget by itself changes nothing; when several prompts share a budget too small for them, how the scheduler divides their prefills across engine steps depends on which requests are present, and the batch- invariant kernels do not make the result independent of that division. The list of what changed and at which stage is the change-impact analysis a validation team needs when hardware or engine settings change, and both the GPU model and the engine’s scheduling settings are therefore part of Θ. Discussion We propose that, where LLMs prepare assessments for regulated work such as that of the medical device industry, byte-level reproducibility of the whole pipeline be a testable engineering condition: the same documents, assessment items and configura- tion should yield the same assessment, at every stage. The fourteen commercial deployments we measured did not provide this at the deterministic sampling set- tings they accepted, with reasoning at its default or at its minimum,

text: assessment items and configura- tion should yield the same assessment, at every stage. The fourteen commercial deployments we measured did not provide this at the deterministic sampling set- tings they accepted, with reasoning at its default or at its minimum, and where the label held, the evidence behind it often changed; the open-weight models we served were reproducible or not depending on how they were served; and a pipeline built to be deter- ministic at every stage reproduced every intermediate result and output for two device types, on one hard- ware class and engine configuration. We measured the commercial deployments from the outside, as any cus- tomer would, so we do not attribute their variation to causes, and our results do not rank the models. They do show that a deployment’s reproducibility cannot be established once and then assumed: it dif- fered between models, for one model between routes, and for another between days, so that a test confined to one session would have missed it. End-to-end determinism makes three things pos- sible that agreement between runs alone does not. A stored assessment can be regenerated as well as kept: producing it again from the stored documents, items and configuration and obtaining the same bytes shows that the record is what the recorded config- uration still produces for these inputs,
