text: A stored assessment can be regenerated as well as kept: producing it again from the stored documents, items and configuration and obtaining the same bytes shows that the record is what the recorded config- uration still produces for these inputs, and lets an auditor see the passages and prompt behind a judg- ment exactly as the expert saw them. The effect of a change can be listed: when a document, an item, a prompt template, a model or the hardware is changed and the assessments are run again, every difference is caused by that change, and the per-stage hashes show which assessments changed and at which stage, as the H100 run did, so that the judgments that relied on them can be looked at again—although a listed dif- ference is not thereby a meaningful one (a change of GPU model alone moved 30 of 650 labels on identi- cal prompts), nor is an unchanged assessment thereby unaffected. And when documents change, only the assessments whose retrieved evidence changed need the model again, since an unchanged input to the model has an unchanged output; retrieval is cheap and inference is not (Supplementary Table S3). What determinism does not give is correctness: a system that reproduces a wrong assessment exactly has reproduced a wrong assessment, and we have not measured how often

text: an unchanged output; retrieval is cheap and inference is not (Supplementary Table S3). What determinism does not give is correctness: a system that reproduces a wrong assessment exactly has reproduced a wrong assessment, and we have not measured how often the assessments are right. Two alternatives are weaker. Storing every output with an audit trail preserves what was produced, and is what remains once a hardware class is retired, but cannot show that the validated system still produces it, nor which later changes would alter it. Statistical consis- tency suffices for population-level questions [4, 30], and disagreement between runs is itself used as a signal of uncertainty [31–34]; a recorded judgment, however, is an individual decision made on an indi- vidual assessment, and a deterministic pipeline can still estimate uncertainty by varying the configura- tion deliberately, as the H100 and chunk-budget runs did. For manufacturers choosing such tools today, the results suggest testing reproducibility directly, across days and on the quoted evidence, and record- ing the route, the engine settings and the hardware class, because the same model name covered differ- ent behaviour; without determinism, a vendor’s silent change can be detected only statistically [35–37], and served behaviour has changed under unchanged 7

text: model identifiers [38–40]. For auditors, whether the preliminary assessment behind a recorded judgment can be produced again is a concrete question, to be scaled to risk as Computer Software Assurance recommends [14]. Determinism holds within a hardware class, so records outlive the hardware that produced them only as stored outputs. Technical documentation must be kept for at least 10 years, and 15 for implantable devices [1, 41], longer than a GPU model may be available and far longer than a hosted model ver- sion, which providers retire on months’ notice [42–44]. Container images, model weights and drivers should therefore be archived with the records, and reference outputs re-established on new hardware by listing the changed assessments. This favours models an organ- isation serves itself, which today means open-weight models whose architecture the serving software sup- ports deterministically; batch invariance cost 18% in wall time in our test, and newer engines narrow the gap in some regimes [21, 22]. Regulations and regulators’ guidance do not require byte-level reproducibility, but they repeat- edly ask that a recorded result can be checked, and industry guidance frames validation by risk [45, 46]. Part 11 requires audit trails and reliable, consistent performance of electronic-record systems, applies to records that predicate rules require, here the expert’s recorded judgment, and has been enforced with dis- cretion since

Part 11 requires audit trails and reliable, consistent performance of electronic-record systems, applies to records that predicate rules require, here the expert’s recorded judgment, and has been enforced with dis- cretion since 2003 [15, 47]; the EU device regulations require the technical documentation to locate the evi- dence of conformity [1, 41]; the FDA–EMA principles for AI in drug development ask for “detailed, trace- able, and verifiable” documentation [48, Principle 6]; EU GMP Annex 11 requires life-cycle validation [49]; and the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems, from 2028 for devices under notified-body assessment, to log events and to perform “consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle” [50, 51], which we cite by analogy. Only a consultation draft of EU GMP Annex 22 names identical outputs, limiting its scope to “models with a deterministic output” and excluding LLMs from critical use [52], and its drafting group has since discussed admitting generative mod- els under a risk-based strategy [53, 54]. FDA’s 2019 discussion paper defines a “locked” algorithm as one that gives the same result for the same input [55], and FDA’s and PMDA’s 2026 papers on generative- AI devices list reproducibility across repeated runs among the properties to evaluate [56, 57]. Previous work has made individual stages deter- ministic or measured variation,

text: same result for the same input [55], and FDA’s and PMDA’s 2026 papers on generative- AI devices list reproducibility across repeated runs among the properties to evaluate [56, 57]. Previous work has made individual stages deter- ministic or measured variation, but not tested a complete assessment pipeline. Batch-invariant and tree-based kernels, verified replay and fixed execution shapes make inference independent of batching [16, 20–23, 58]; ReproRAG finds embeddings and FAISS retrieval reproducible run to run under fixed seeds but displaced by insertions [17], and deterministic-first retrieval, retrieval-aware ingestion and a finance- oriented harness address other stages without extrac- tion or OCR [59–62]. Variation of hosted LLMs at temperature 0 has been measured in research set- tings [19, 63, 64], the same model has been found to differ between routes [36, 40, 65], and providers describe seeds as “best effort” and temperature 0 as not “fully deterministic” [66, 67]. LLMs have been validated for extraction from FDA device documents without repeated runs [4] and proposed for source- linked safety analysis [7]. To our knowledge, no prior work tests byte-level reproducibility of a complete assessment pipeline from text extraction to quoted evidence, relates it to medical-device quality work, or measures, field by field on an assessment record, how commercial deployments vary across repeated requests, routes and days. The study has limitations. It concerns repro- ducibility only; the assessment items are guidance sentences chosen by rule, and public 510(k) docu- ments for two device types stand in for manufactur- ers’ records. The pipeline used one judgment model family on a single GPU, relies on the batch-invariant mode of one inference engine, and its six proper- ties were sufficient under the operations tried, which is an empirical finding, not a proof; no one outside the author’s company has yet reproduced it. The commercial measurements cover two days per deploy- ment, one client region and pay-as-you-go tiers, with eight deployments sampled at provider defaults; the prompts were whole documents, and the 70 prompts come from 49 device–item pairs resampled as inde- pendent units; the positive control, the concurrency test, the between-day count and the two addenda were added during the study (Supplementary Note 2). Usefulness is a property of assessments in the hands of experts, and this study establishes reproducibility, not usefulness: how often the assessments are cor- rect, whether the quoted evidence is what an expert would cite, and whether review helps or biases

text: is a property of assessments in the hands of experts, and this study establishes reproducibility, not usefulness: how often the assessments are cor- rect, whether the quoted evidence is what an expert would cite, and whether review helps or biases the expert [9, 68] are questions we cannot answer alone, and we publish this preprint in part to find the reg- ulatory and quality-management experts with whom to answer them. With a deterministic pipeline, what the experts evaluate is fixed, and any later difference can be attributed to a change. Methods Definitions. An assessment item is a requirement to be assessed, defined by the assessment’s administrator, who also defines the label set. A preliminary assessment is, for one item and a set of documents, a label from the label set, a comment giving the reason, and quoted evidence—passages copied verbatim from the docu- ments, each with its cited file; the model’s internal reasoning is not part of it. The assessment record is 8

text: the stored preliminary assessment with the hashes that identify its inputs and configuration; the qual- ity record is the expert’s recorded judgment, which is what quality-system requirements and Part 11 concern, and we assume that an assessment record is retained with the judgment that relied on it. A route is the way a model is reached (a provider’s API, a cloud platform or a self-hosted server) and a deployment is a model reached through a partic- ular route. The configuration Θ is everything other than the inputs that can change an output: the extraction, chunking and embedding components, the retrieval parameters, the prompt template and label set, the model weights, the inference engine’s ver- sion and settings, including its prefill chunk budget and concurrency limit, and the hardware class (GPU model with its driver and CUDA versions); the inputs are the document bytes and the assessment items, and a manifest is the recorded listing of Θ. Byte- level reproducibility means that, for a fixed Θ, every intermediate result and output is identical byte for byte across runs that differ only by operations that should not matter: repeating, restarting, interrupt- ing and resuming, reordering, changing concurrency, and adding and deleting a document. We use repro- ducibility in the computational sense; in the terms of FDA’s draft guidance on AI-enabled device software

Documents and assessment items. The main corpus is the public FDA documents for over-the-counter blood glucose test systems (prod- uct code NBW; in vitro diagnostic devices for self- testing in the EU) with a decision date from 2015 to 2025 in openFDA and a published 510(k) summary: 133 510(k) summaries, 132 decision summaries and 72 predicate summaries, 337 PDFs. The assessment items are the 11 sentences of FDA’s 2020 guidance for these systems that state a numeric minimum of a counted item (“at least” or “a minimum of” followed by a numeral and a count of meters, strips, vials, lots, days, measurements or concentrations). An item is paired with a device when the device’s decision sum- mary has a section whose heading matches the item’s topic, so that every pair has a section in which to look for evidence; 83 devices had such a section, giv- ing 776 pairs, of which the reference run labelled 356

text: Experiment 2: pipeline. Six properties fix what each stage does. Con- tent addressing: every document version, extraction, chunk set, embedding set, retrieval result, prompt and raw output is identified by the SHA-256 hash of its content and of the producing component’s manifest, which lists that component’s models, libraries and parameters, not the pipeline’s source code. Determin- istic extraction: the same file yields the same text, including pages read by OCR with a self-hosted model under batch-invariant inference and greedy decoding. Deterministic embedding: for a fixed configuration the same text yields the same chunks and the same vec- tors bit for bit whenever they are computed; within one database, vectors are stored under their content hash and reused. Exact, scoped retrieval: the result depends only on the query and the documents in scope. Serving-invariant judgment: for a fixed engine configuration, the model’s output depends only on the prompt, not on which other requests are served with it, their order, or whether cached prefixes are reused; implemented with batch-invariant inference, greedy decoding and grammar-constrained output. Deterministic records: quotations are verified against the source by rule, unverifiable ones removed and the label downgraded by rule, and every run is written to a hash-chained ledger. The implementation tested is AskDona Assessment, a product of the author’s com- pany (Competing interests). Pages whose text layer

text: First Mathematical Runtime Analyses of Evolutionary Multitask Multi-Objective Optimization Danyang Zhang∗ Weijie Zheng*†‡ October 16, 2026
title: First Mathematical Runtime Analyses of

text: To facilitate the solving of complex problems, evolutionary mul- titask optimization is regarded as a promising technique due to its capacity for cross-task knowledge transfer. In contrast to empirical evidences, no mathematical runtime support exists for this technique within the domain of multi-objective optimization. In this work, we aim to fill this important gap. We analyze how the representative mul- tiobjective multifactorial evolutionary algorithm (MO-MFEA) covers the Pareto fronts of two bi-objective problems simultaneously. For the two-task problem of maximizing the classic bi-objective OMM and the multimodal OJZJ benchmarks, the MO-MFEA requires only an expected runtime of O(n2 log n)—the same as optimizing the simple OMM alone—yet achieves a speedup by a factor of Θ(nk−1/ log n) compared to optimizing OJZJ alone (with gap size k). Similarly, for the task pair comprising the classic LOTZ and the multimodal DLTB benchmarks, a speedup of Θ(n) is attained over optimizing DLTB alone, while the runtime matches that of optimizing LOTZ alone. 1

text: Evolutionary computation is a versatile and widely applied optimization tech- nique. However, improving its efficiency for complex problems remains a ∗School of Computer Science and Technology, State Key Laboratory of Smart Farm Technologies and Systems, International Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen, China †Pengcheng Laboratory, Shenzhen, China ‡Corresponding author. 1 arXiv:2610.21311v1 [cs.NE] 15 Oct 2026

text: significant challenge. To address this, evolutionary multitask optimization (EMTO) was first proposed by Gupta, Ong, and Feng [GOF16]. The core idea is to enhance overall performance by transferring knowledge gained from solving one (often simpler) task to assist in solving another, structurally sim- ilar but more complex task. Their seminal work demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed Multifactorial Evolutionary Algorithm (MFEA) on a set of combinatorial optimization problems (two quadratic assignment problems and one capacitated vehicle routing problem), showing faster convergence and a lower makespan (total time to complete all tasks) compared to sequen- tial single-task optimization. For the general more complex multi-objective scenarios, incorporating the total order defined by the non-dominated sort- ing and the crowding distance from the NSGA-II (the most intensively used multi-objective evolutionary algorithm) [DPAM02], Gupta et al. [GOFT17] further extended this MFEA framework to a multi-objective version, called MO-MFEA. Similar empirical evidences of the advantage of the multitask optimization were also shown for the composite manufacturing processes (resin transfer molding and injection/compression liquid composite mold- ing). Since then, the evolutionary multitask optimization attracts more and more attention for the complex problem solving, like the point cloud regis- tration [WSD+24], the jop shop scheduling [CLW+25], etc. One could refer to [WWZ+22] for more evolutionary multitask optimization algorithms and applications. Despite empirical success, a rigorous theoretical understanding of EMTO, particularly its runtime behavior, has lagged far behind. The first theoretical runtime analyses were conducted by Lian et al. LeadingOnes and OneMax task pair and TrailingZeros and OneMax task pair were further analyzed in [HCZ20]. The reason is that the two tasks in the latter pair are with less similarity. Crucially, all (only two) existing theoretical results are for the domain of single-objective optimization. Under this general population setting, the distri- bution of individuals corresponding to different tasks and the dynamic and complex nature of cross-task knowledge transfer have not been studied in ex- isting theories. How to establish the mathematical runtime analysis for the evolutionary multitask multi-objective optimization remains an important open problem. Our contributions. This work takes the first step. text: This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the multitask multi-objective optimization problem and the general framework of the MO-MFEA. Section 3 presents four general results applicable to the MO-MFEA, which serve as theoretical foundations for the subsequent runtime analyses. Sec- tions 4 and 5 provide complete runtime analyses for two-task (OMM, OJZJ) and (LOTZ, DLTB) problems, respectively. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. Following common practice in runtime analysis research [HZLL21, ZD24b, ODNS24, LZZD25], and supported by ample empirical evidence in the literature [GOF16, GOFT17], this work focuses on establishing theoret- ical foundations; additional experiments are therefore not conducted. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Multitask Multi-Objective Optimization Problem Multitask multi-objective optimization problem consists of multiple tasks each of which is a multi-objective optimization problem. Following the the- ory community of evolutionary multi-objective optimization, in this paper, we consider the maximization of multiple objectives defined on binary space {0, 1}n for each task. For an ℓ-task (A1, ..., Aℓ) problem, we denote the objec- tive function in the i-th task Ai by f i = (f i 1, . . . , f i mi) : {0, 1}n →Rmi, where n ∈N is the problem size of Ai and mi ∈N is the number of objectives. For any task Ai, i ∈[1..ℓ], we call X weakly dominates Y , denoted by X ⪰Y , w.r.t. f i, if f i j(X) ≥f i j(Y ) for all j ∈[1..mi]. If further at least one inequality is strict, then we say that X dominates Y , denoted by X ≻Y . A solution X ∈{0, 1}n is called Pareto optimal w.r.t. f i if there exists no solution Y ∈{0, 1}n such that Y ≻X. The set of all Pareto optimal solutions is called the Pareto set. We call the set of f i values of the Pareto set the Pareto front, and each element of the Pareto front is called a Pareto front point. When the context is unambiguous, we do not differentiate the Pareto front of f i from that of task Ai. For some i ∈[1..ℓ], let W i be a subset of {0, 1}n, and M i be the Pareto front w.r.t. f i. [GOFT17], is the multi-objective variant of the representative evolutionary multitask algorithm. It employs a population of size N to solve a multitask multi-objective (A1, ..., Aℓ) problem. Each individual is responsible for a specific task, reflected by its skill factor τ (that is, if its τ value equals to i ∈[1..ℓ] then it is used to solve task Ai and only its f i value will be evaluated). The population P0 = {X1, . . . , XN} is randomly initialized in {0, 1}n, and Xr, r ∈[1..N], is assigned with its skill factor of ⌈rℓ/N⌉to ensure that each task has a similar number of associ- ated individuals. text: The scalar fitness of an individual is derived from the total order estab- lished by NSGA-II [DPAM02]. Specifically, for all individuals sharing the same skill factor (i.e., assigned to a same specific task Ai, where i ∈[1..ℓ]), the algorithm first performs a ranking based on non-dominated sorting and crowding distance. Non-dominated sorting partitions this group into suc- cessive fronts F1, F2, . . . . Here, Fj is defined as the set of non-dominated solutions within Si \ ∪j−1 r=1Fr, where Si denotes the entire set of individuals for task Ai. For each front Fj, the crowding distance (cDis) is computed for every solution. These individuals are then sorted into a total order: an individual X precedes Y if X belongs to a front with a smaller index, or if both are in the same front but cDis(X) > cDis(Y ) (ties are broken ran- domly). Each individual is subsequently assigned a factorial rank equal to its position in this sorted list. Finally, its scalar fitness is set to the reciprocal of this factorial rank. The detailed procedure is outlined in Algorithm 2. text: 5 Runtime for the (LOTZ, DLTB) Problem This section focuses on another pair of structurally similar tasks that are ex- pected to yield positive knowledge transfer. We investigate a two-task opti- mization problem consisting of DLTB [ZLDD24], a complex and multimodal bi-objective benchmark, and LOTZ [LTZ04], a relatively simple yet similar bi-objective benchmark. Our analysis will show that jointly optimizing these tasks allows the runtime for DLTB to be reduced to the same order as that for LOTZ alone. 5.1 Two-Task (LOTZ, DLTB) Problem Here we formally define the two-task (LOTZ,DLTB) problem (Definition 13). The LOTZ is the bi-objective extension of the single-objective Leading- Ones problem. The first objective counts the number of leading ones, and the second objective counts the number of trailing zeros. The DLTB bench- mark is the bi-objective counterpart of the multimodal Deceptive Leading Blocks (DLB) problem [LN19]. Its two objectives are symmetric: the first is the original DLB function (a deceptive variant of LeadingOnes), while the second is its mirror image defined over the count of zeros. Definition 13. text: This work presents the first mathematical runtime analysis of evolutionary multitask optimization in the multi-objective domain, thereby bridging a critical gap between its empirical success and theoretical foundations. By analyzing the representative MO-MFEA on pairs of bi-objective benchmarks, we demonstrate that when a complex, multimodal problem (e.g., OJZJ or DLTB) is paired with a structurally similar yet simpler one (e.g., OMM or LOTZ), the algorithm can solve both tasks simultaneously in asymptotically the same time required to solve the simpler task alone. Specifically, we proved an expected runtime of O(n2 log n) for the multi- task problem (OMM, OJZJ), which translates to a speedup of Θ(nk−1/ log n) over optimizing OJZJ in isolation. Similarly, for the pair (LOTZ, DLTB), the algorithm achieves a runtime of O(n3)–matching that of optimizing LOTZ alone–while attaining a Θ(n) speedup compared to optimizing DLTB alone. Beyond these specific findings, the theoretical framework and properties established for MO-MFEA in this work will facilitate future runtime anal- yses for a broader class of multitask multi-objective optimization problems. Extending this analysis to other popular evolutionary multitask algorithms, as well as to problems with more than two objectives or tasks, constitutes a compelling direction for future research. title: VoteGEO-Bench: Measuring the Impact of Generative Engine

text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to obtain election information, and the web sources they use can shape the responses presented to voters. Existing work on LLMs in political settings mainly studies political bias in model outputs and AI-driven political persuasion, while much less is known about how external web content affects the political information presented by LLMs. Generative engine optimization (GEO) focuses on rewriting web content to improve its visibility in generated responses. Existing GEO research typically takes a fixed webpage pool as input and stud- ies how rewriting changes page visibility in generated responses, providing a natural framework for studying this question. To inves- tigate the potential risks of GEO in voting scenarios (VoteGEO), we introduce VoteGEO-Bench, a benchmark built on the 2024 U.S. presidential election and the 2026 Japanese House of Repre- sentatives election, combining election-related queries, historical webpages, and voter personas. We first analyze the sources cited by generative engines, find- ing that many citations come from lower-cost owned and open- platform sources and that some webpages often remain visible across days. We then benchmark 11 rewriting strategies across 4 categories and study whether specifying a target candidate or party in the rewrite matters, which strategies work across gener- ative engines and elections, and how voter personas affect expo- sure. Notably, strategies that improve page organization or strengthen a posi- tion through argumentation show stronger gains than those that add supporting evidence or mainly change wording. text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to obtain election-related information, including candidate comparisons and voting advice [2, 18]. Unlike traditional search engines that rank and present webpages, generative engines such as ChatGPT and Gemini retrieve web sources and use their content to generate responses. Existing work on LLMs in political settings mainly follows two lines. One studies political bias and alignment in LLM responses across models and political contexts [5–7, 9, 15]. The other studies whether LLM-generated political messages can influence voters and which factors drive political persuasion [11, 16]. These studies focus on LLM outputs and their effects on users. Much less is known about how external web content shapes political information in generative engine responses. Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content to improve its visibility in generative engine responses [1, 25]. Ex- isting GEO research typically takes a fixed webpage pool as in- put and studies how rewriting changes page visibility in gener- ated responses [1, 8, 24, 25, 29, 30], providing a natural frame- work for studying this question. To investigate the potential risks of GEO in voting scenarios, which we call VoteGEO, it remains two sets of questions. text: GEO in voting scenarios, which we call VoteGEO, it remains two sets of questions. First, which source channels do generative engines use, how accessible are they to content publishers, and how long do the same webpages remain visible? Second, how does webpage rewriting affect candidate or party exposure in gener- ated responses? Specifically, does specifying a target candidate or party in the rewrite matter, which strategies work across gen- erative engines and elections, and how do voter personas affect baseline exposure and rewriting gains? To answer these questions, we introduce VoteGEO-Bench, a benchmark built on the 2024 U.S. presidential election [7] and the 2026 Japanese House of Rep- resentatives election [19]. After preprocessing, VoteGEO-Bench contains 28,200 election-related query cells across days and engines and 17,251 webpages. We further incorporate 3 categories of voter personas, including demographic identities, partisan identities, and questionnaire-derived profiles constructed from pre-treatment re- sponses of 2,306 U.S. participants [16]. We first analyze which sources generative engines use and how long the same webpages remain visible. We find that many cited sources come from lower-cost channels, including candidate or party websites and open platforms such as Reddit. Together, these findings highlight potential risks through lower- cost source channels, with longer exposure windows for stable queries and faster source turnover for current events. We then benchmark 11 rewriting strategies across 4 categories. Structure strategies improve page organization or reformat webpages into more LLM-friendly layouts. Evidence strategies add quotations, sta- tistics, or source attributions to support existing claims. Style strate- gies modify wording without adding substantive content. These three categories follow existing GEO work [1, 25]. Motivated by political persuasion research [11, 16], we further introduce 2 Argu- mentation strategies, which strengthen a position by emphasizing its distinctions from plausible alternatives or explicitly addressing opposing arguments. Our results reveal three main patterns. First, target-unspecified rewriting rarely increases target exposure, whereas target-specified rewriting more often does so. This distinction is important because election webpages often discuss multiple parties. In the U.S. setting, 92% of retrieved webpages mention both major parties, so rewriting without an explicit target does not indicate which party’s exposure should increase. Second, Structure and Argumentation strategies show stronger gains than Evidence and Style strategies across gen- erative engines and elections. Consistent with this pattern, one strategy from each of these two categories shows the strongest

Consistent with this pattern, one strategy from each of these two categories shows the strongest overall gains across settings and exposure metrics. Third, for these two strongest strategies, rewriting gains remain broadly positive across the 15 evaluated U.S. personas, while persona conditioning shows no consistent tendency to increase or decrease these gains. In contrast, explicit partisan identities can create baseline exposure gaps of up to 11.6 percentage points, larger than the gain from rewriting a single webpage. Generative engine optimization (GEO) aims to improve the visibility of web content in such re- sponses through content rewriting [1, 25]. text: Political bias in LLMs. Existing work studies political bias in LLM outputs across models and political contexts. Studies report a left- progressive lean in U.S. political content but more mixed patterns in South Korea [15], stronger alignment of GPT-4o with left-leaning German parties [6], and overrepresentation of radical-right actors in European election queries [9]. Other work finds that such patterns do not always persist for concrete voting decisions, such as Swiss referenda [5]. These studies examine political bias in model outputs, whereas we study how modifying external web content changes candidate or party exposure in generated responses. Voter persuasion with LLMs. Prior work identifies several fac- tors relevant to political persuasion with LLMs, including factual and evidence-rich information, personalization, and refutational counterargumentation. Factual and evidence-rich information re- peatedly emerges as an important driver of persuasion [3, 11, 16], while the additional benefit of personalization is mixed across stud- ies [11, 16, 17, 27]. Refutational messages can also improve persua- sion or reduce issue polarization [13, 21]. These studies focus on how LLM responses influence voters. In contrast, we study how external content influences the information produced by LLMs. Generative engine optimization. Existing GEO studies develop strategies for improving source visibility or item ranking in gener- ative engine responses. Adversarial approaches use model-directed instructions or optimized content to manipulate preferences and

Unlike prior GEO work that mainly optimizes source visibility or item ranking, we study target exposure within webpages that may discuss multiple candidates or parties. 3 Data Collection and Preprocessing We construct three datasets, us-election-24, ai-persuasion, and jp- election-26, from two electoral settings, the 2024 U.S. presidential election between the Democratic and Republican parties and the proportional-representation component of the 2026 Japanese House of Representatives election involving 11 parties. us-election-24 and jp-election-26 contain election-related query cells and their corre- sponding webpage pools, while ai-persuasion provides question- naire information for constructing richer voter personas in the U.S. setting. Structure strategies modify page organization and pre- sentation without changing the underlying factual content. Both strategies follow C-SEO [25]. Content Improvement improves the organization and presentation of the page through clearer sections, more logical ordering, stronger emphasis on key information, and reduced redundancy, while preserving factual information, exist- ing citations, and overall length. LLMs.txt reformats the page into an LLM-oriented layout. It adds an LLM Guidance block with the topic, key facts, and citation priority, reorganizes the body using Markdown headings, key points, summaries, lists, and bold text, and adds a final citation section explaining why the page should be cited and what information it uniquely provides. Evidence. Evidence strategies strengthen support for existing claims by adding quotations, quantitative evidence, or source attri- butions. All three follow GEO [1]. Quotes inserts direct quotations attributed to credible figures while preserving the remaining con- tent and formatting. Statistics inserts persuasive numerical evidence, such as percentages, growth rates, and counts, at relevant positions while modifying only the sentences receiving the numbers. Au- thoritative adds five to six relevant attributions to credible sources while preserving the core content, length, and local structure. Style. Style strategies rewrite the same information at the lexical
title: VoteGEO-Bench: Measuring the Impact of Generative Engine Optimization on Electoral Visibility

text: relevant positions while modifying only the sentences receiving the numbers. Au- thoritative adds five to six relevant attributions to credible sources while preserving the core content, length, and local structure. Style. Style strategies rewrite the same information at the lexical and sentence levels without adding new substantive content. All four follow GEO [1]. Fluency improves sentence flow, clarity, and readability. Simple Language paraphrases sentences using simpler and clearer language while keeping the information and length unchanged. Technical Terms rephrases individual sentences using more technical terminology without adding or removing content. Unique Words introduces more distinctive vocabulary while pre- serving the original meaning and core information. 5.2 Argumentation Strategies Existing GEO strategies primarily modify page structure, support- ing evidence, or linguistic style. Voting webpages may additionally contain competing political claims or recommendations. Motivated by political persuasion research on argument framing and counter- argument [11, 16], we introduce two argumentation strategies. Comparative Distinction. This strategy strengthens a compar- ative case by emphasizing what makes one option distinctively strong relative to plausible alternatives. It foregrounds concrete distinctions in policy positions, commitments, timelines, mecha- nisms, or other actionable details that can make the option stand out rather than appear merely acceptable. The rewriting prompt instructs the model to preserve the original factual information and maintain a similar overall length. This design is motivated by

text: nisms, or other actionable details that can make the option stand out rather than appear merely acceptable. The rewriting prompt instructs the model to preserve the original factual information and maintain a similar overall length. This design is motivated by prior work on contrast advertising in political campaigns, which compares candidates or positions to differentiate the favored option from alternatives [23]. Refutational. This strategy strengthens a position through refu- tational two-sided argumentation [11, 21]. It introduces plausible opposing arguments and explicitly rebuts them with reasoning or supporting information. Each opposing argument must be substan- tive and directly addressed rather than weakened into a straw man. The original core content and overall position are preserved. 6 VoteGEO-Bench This section evaluates VoteGEO through three research questions: • RQ1: Does Target Specification Matter? Table 3 reports the mean exposure improvement across strategy categories and generative engines, together with the placebo as the no-rewriting reference. Target specification is important for effective rewriting. Target- unspecified rewriting rarely increases target exposure, whereas target-specified rewriting does so in most evaluated settings. Among the 36 category, engine, and metric settings, target-unspecified rewriting produces only one significant positive gain, while four show significant negative changes and the remaining 31 are not significant. text: 6.3 RQ2: Which Rewriting Strategies Work? We next compare rewriting effectiveness across generative engines and elections, and then examine individual strategies. Structure and Argumentation show stronger gains than Ev- idence and Style across engines. Table 3 shows that Structure produces significant gains in all 9 engine and metric settings and Argumentation in 7, compared with 6 for Evidence and only 2 for Style. Notably, Structure consistently improves all three exposure metrics across engines, while Argumentation also shows positive gains in most settings. The magnitude of improvement varies across engines, with smaller gains on gpt-5-mini. This coincides with its higher refusal rate on evaluative queries such as “which candidate is most X”, leaving fewer responses for rewriting to affect. Structure and Argumentation remain strongest across elec- tions, with larger relative gains for lower-exposure parties. Table 4 shows that Structure and Argumentation show stronger gains than Evidence and Style in both the U.S. and Japan. Across elections and target tiers, rewriting produces similar absolute gains, but these gains correspond to larger relative improvements for par- ties with lower baseline exposure. For example, under Structure in Japan, the Top and Low tiers gain 4.28 and 4.12 percentage points in Mention Coverage, corresponding to relative improvements of 5.9% and 14.4%. text: In this work, we introduce VoteGEO-Bench to investigate the po- tential risks of GEO in voting scenarios. We find that generative engines frequently cite lower-cost source channels and that some webpages remain visible across days, motivating our subsequent evaluation of how webpage rewriting affects electoral exposure. Our experiments show that explicitly specifying the target is im- portant for effective rewriting, while Structure and Argumentation strategies show stronger gains across engines and elections. We fur- ther find that rewriting gains remain broadly positive across voter personas, while partisan information can strongly shift baseline exposure. Future work may explore ethically controlled end-to-end evaluation and further investigate contextual sentiment, factual quality, semantic fidelity, and human persuasion. 8 Limitations and Ethics Statement Offline evaluation. Our rewriting experiments use fixed historical webpage pools with web retrieval disabled, leaving the effects of rewriting on live retrieval and citation selection unexamined. A live end-to-end evaluation would typically require publishing rewritten political content for crawling and indexing by search and generative engines. Even after removal, such content could persist in caches or archived snapshots and potentially reach real voters. To avoid these risks, we conduct all rewriting experiments offline without publishing rewritten political content to live websites. Exposure and factuality. Our evaluation measures changes in candidate or party exposure without distinguishing favorable from unfavorable mentions or assessing factual
title: Conference’17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA

text: voters. To avoid these risks, we conduct all rewriting experiments offline without publishing rewritten political content to live websites. Exposure and factuality. Our evaluation measures changes in candidate or party exposure without distinguishing favorable from unfavorable mentions or assessing factual accuracy and voter per- suasion. Moreover, we do not systematically verify the factual cor- rectness or semantic fidelity of rewritten webpages. Some estab- lished GEO Evidence strategies may introduce supporting material not present in the original webpage, while our Structure and Argu- mentation prompts instruct the rewriter to preserve the original fac- tual information or core position. We therefore interpret observed gains only as changes in exposure, rather than improvements in information quality or evidence of voter persuasion. Privacy and dual-use risks. The persona analysis uses previously collected datasets and reports aggregate results without target- ing individual voters. Nevertheless, releasing rewriting strategies and their effectiveness comparisons carries dual-use risks, as these findings could be used to influence political exposure in deployed systems. We hope these findings help researchers understand the effectiveness and risks of GEO and inform safeguards against ma- nipulation through retrieved web content. A.2 Party attribution The response prompt asks engines to wrap candidate and party men- tions in <ENT> tags without revealing the closed entity set or target. Tagged spans are normalized and mapped to party entities using a curated longest-match alias dictionary. U.S. aliases for Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, and the Democratic Party map to Democratic, while aliases for Donald Trump and the Republican Party map to Republican. Running mates and third-party candidates are not mapped. In Japan, the dictionary contains the 11 party names and unambiguous abbreviations, with ambiguous short forms excluded and predecessor aliases mapped to their corresponding successor party. In Japan, the dictionary contains the 11 party names and unambiguous abbreviations, with ambiguous short forms excluded and predecessor aliases mapped to their corresponding successor party. Japanese candidate names are not mapped. This leaves 0.8% of tagged spans in baseline Japanese responses and 7.5% in U.S. responses unmapped, with the latter mostly consisting of third- party candidates. A sentence-level alias scan additionally recovers untagged party mentions using word-boundary matching for ASCII aliases and substring matching for CJK aliases. The same mapping procedure is used for target selection and exposure measurement. Complete alias dictionaries are released with the artifact. text: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy with Weight Perturbation on MNIST Patrick Inoue∗
title: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy

text: Weight perturbation (WP) estimates learning directions from random parameter perturbations and a scalar change in loss, without backpropagating derivatives. We examine how batch size, training duration, and estimator stabilization affect its attainable accuracy in fully connected MNIST networks. In the shallow configuration, large-batch training reaches approximately 97% test accuracy, compared with an early backpropagation (BP) reference near 97.5–98%. The same comparison exposes a substantial efficiency gap: under a ten-epoch budget, shallow WP reaches 90.2%, whereas the reported BP reference reaches 97.4%. Epoch-indexed curves show diminishing returns from increasing batch size beyond 4,000. Learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbation-based updates also stabilize deeper networks, although their recorded results do not establish BP-level accuracy. We distinguish these empirical findings from a finite-horizon approximation argument: under stated regularity conditions, population WP can approximate a fixed gradient-descent trajectory arbitrarily closely at any fixed finite depth. Positive classification margins then suffice to preserve the reference predictions on a finite test set with arbitrarily high probability. Together, the results identify near-BP accuracy as a configuration- and budget-dependent possibility, rather than evidence of equal efficiency or an unconditional accuracy guarantee across depth. Keywords: weight perturbation; node perturbation; backpropagation; MNIST; gradient estimation.

text: Learning from global performance feedback without transmitting error derivatives through neural circuitry is a central challenge in biologically plausible credit assignment. Backpropagation (BP) solves this problem computationally, but its conventional implementation relies on coordinated forward and backward computations, precise layer-specific error signals, and corresponding feedback pathways whose biological realization remains debated [1, 27]. Biological synapses, in contrast, exhibit spontaneous fluctuations and remodeling, while synaptic plasticity can be regulated by neuromodulatory signals associated with reward and behavioral outcomes [28–31]. These properties motivate learning mechanisms that exploit local stochastic exploration and globally available evaluative signals to guide synaptic adaptation. Weight perturbation (WP) offers a particularly direct approach to this problem. Synaptic weights are transiently perturbed, and the resulting change in task performance determines the direction of subsequent plasticity [2, 3]. Each synapse requires only information about its own perturbation and a shared scalar feedback signal. The learning rule operates without an explicit differentiable model of the network, backward error propagation, or symmetric feedback weights. WP therefore provides a model-free candidate for biologically motivated learning, connecting stochastic synaptic plasticity with gradient-based optimization [8, 12, 28]. Perturbation-based learning has also been combined with competitive Hebbian plasticity in sparse excitatory neural networks [25], illustrating its compatibility with additional biologically motivated learning mechanisms. The principal obstacle is the statistical efficiency of high-dimensional credit assignment. WP infers

This gap raises a fundamental question: does stochastic synaptic credit assignment impose a limit on attainable classification accuracy, or can improved estimator stability and extended training overcome it? Here, we show that extended large-batch training brings WP to approximately 97% test accuracy on MNIST, approaching the early BP reference of 97.5–98% in a fully connected network with one hidden layer. The remaining accuracy gap is approximately 0.5–1 percentage point. Training efficiency remains substantially different: under a ten-epoch budget, WP achieves 90.2%, compared with 97.4% for the reported BP reference. We further show that learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbation estimates can stabilize WP training in networks with five hidden layers. Finally, a finite- horizon analysis establishes conditions under which population WP can approximate a gradient-descent trajectory arbitrarily closely. These findings demonstrate that high classification accuracy is attainable through model-free, perturbation-based synaptic learning, while identifying the training conditions and computational costs that govern its practical performance [4]. 1.1 Perturbation learning: foundations and recent developments Scalar-feedback learning has a substantial history in model-free learning, stochastic error descent, and statistical gradient-following algorithms [2, 3, 5]. text: Weight perturbation on MNIST Patrick Inoue 3.3 Stabilization of deeper networks The five-hidden-layer comparison exposes a stronger stability constraint. At B = 4,000, Scen1 initially improves but subsequently collapses below the plotted range. At B = 10,000, its solid curve reaches approximately 93% before the dashed extension begins. Larger batches can improve trainability without establishing deep-network parity. The thesis further reports that decreasing the learning rate stabilizes narrow deep networks. Population averaging provides a complementary intervention: ten perturbations in Scen1 yield accuracy comparable to a reduced-learning-rate reference, while four perturbations stabilize the wide five-hidden-layer configuration where preceding single-perturbation settings failed [4, Sec. 3.4.3]. Indeed, the thesis’s final comparison states that the deeper reference had not achieved BP-comparable accuracy within the considered budgets [4, Sec. 3.6]. 4 Discussion WP can attain near-BP accuracy on MNIST in a fully connected network trained through scalar loss feedback. Extended large-batch training reaches approximately 97% test accuracy, within about 0.5–1 percentage point of the early BP reference (Fig. 2). This result demonstrates that the lower accuracies observed in the small-batch runs are not an intrinsic ceiling of the WP learning rule. A substantial part of the accuracy deficit can be recovered through stabilization and additional training. The experiments therefore separate two properties that are easily conflated when evaluating biologically motivated learning: attainable accuracy and learning efficiency. The high-accuracy regime extends the earlier MNIST comparison of Züge et al. [12]. Their network with one hidden layer reached 92.3% with WP and 97.7% with SGD after 50,000 updates at a batch size of 1,000. Our extended experiments show that WP can move substantially closer to the BP reference when larger batches and longer training are available. The contribution is this empirical demonstration of near-BP accuracy in the hidden-layer setting. It complements the established interpretation of WP as a stochastic gradient estimator [2, 3, 11] by showing how much performance can be recovered in a nonlinear classification network. Computational efficiency remains the principal practical limitation. In the ten-epoch comparison, WP reaches 90.2%, whereas the reported BP reference reaches 97.4% (Table 1). Approaching the latter accuracy with WP requires substantially more training. This behavior is consistent with the variance introduced when a high-dimensional update is estimated from a scalar loss difference [11, 12]. Smaller learning rates limit destabilizing parameter changes, while averaging independent perturbation estimates reduces update variability [10]. These mechanisms support continued learning, but they incur costs through

Smaller learning rates limit destabilizing parameter changes, while averaging independent perturbation estimates reduces update variability [10]. These mechanisms support continued learning, but they incur costs through additional updates or additional forward evaluations. The batch-size comparison further shows why more averaging is not automatically more efficient. Larger batches expose each perturbation to a greater fraction of the task, while population averaging combines independent perturbation realizations. In the update-indexed curves, batches from 4,000 to 10,000 approach similar accuracies. When performance is indexed by epochs, the largest batch loses its advantage (Fig. 3). The useful operating regime therefore balances update stability against the amount of computation devoted to each step. Maximizing batch size or population size alone can yield diminishing returns; the objective is sustained learning with an affordable amount of averaging. Network depth makes this balance more demanding. In the tested deeper architectures, settings that support shallow learning can produce unstable updates, and recovering useful learning requires smaller learning rates or stronger averaging. These interventions improve trainability, although the deeper configurations remain below the BP comparison within the investigated budgets. A larger representation hierarchy increases the demands on the learning process, so architectural capacity and effective training progress must be considered together. Improving the information extracted from each perturbation is consequently an important direction for extending WP to deeper networks. Hybrid learning provides a complementary direction. Stricker et al. [25] combine competitive Hebbian feature learning with a joint Hebbian–WP classification-layer update in sparse excitatory networks. Inoue et al. [26] extend this framework to deeper nonnegative architectures using a PCA-related competitive 7

text: Weight perturbation on MNIST Patrick Inoue update and inter-layer normalization. In these systems, hidden representations develop through local activity-dependent learning, while perturbation-based supervision acts at the readout. The present study addresses WP across all weight matrices. Together, these approaches motivate examining how the allocation of learning between local representation mechanisms and scalar-feedback updates affects accuracy, stability, and computational cost. The empirical scope of the present results is fully connected MNIST classification. Extending the comparison to more complex tasks will determine how the required training budget changes with problem difficulty and network size. Relating the large exposure budgets to biologically feasible learning times is also an important question. The immediate methodological priority is to reduce the cost of reaching the high-accuracy regime demonstrated here, through more informative perturbation estimates and a better balance between learning rate, batch size, and population averaging. 4.1
title: Weight perturbation on MNIST

text: Model-free weight perturbation reaches approximately 97% accuracy on MNIST and approaches the performance of backpropagation. This demonstrates that a biologically motivated learning rule can support high classification accuracy despite substantially slower learning. Larger batches, longer training, and stable updates are decisive in recovering that performance. The accompanying finite-horizon analysis establishes conditions for arbitrarily close approximation of a fixed gradient-descent trajectory. For the configurations examined here, the main practical challenge is the efficiency with which WP reaches high accuracy, especially as network depth increases. text: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail to Use Available Evidence Owen Walters* Lihu Chen Francesca Toni Department of Computing, Imperial College London, UK {lihu.chen, ft}@imperial.ac.uk
title: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs

text: Web search allows LLMs to access up-to- date information, but it remains unclear why they sometimes produce outdated answers even when relevant evidence is available. To study this problem, we construct temporal facts whose values changed after the mod- els’ training cutoffs. We evaluate one propri- etary model under deployed web search and six open-weight model configurations under controlled retrieval. We find that models of- ten answer from search snippets without open- ing the source pages, which is associated with higher rates of outdated answers and unfaith- ful citations. Our controlled experiments and layer-wise analysis reveal a gap between the availability of evidence and its effective use. Even when retrieved evidence influences inter- nal predictions, models may still favour out- dated information in their final answers. We hope these findings will help advance research on the reliable use of retrieved evidence in search-augmented LLMs. 1
title: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs

text: Deployed LLM assistants such as ChatGPT (Ope- nAI, 2024) often use web search to access up-to- date information. However, retrieving relevant search results does not guarantee that models use the information correctly. Even when updated evi- dence is available, search-augmented LLMs may still produce outdated answers or cite sources that contradict their responses (Figure 1). This mat- ters because citations lend answers provenance. This raises an important question: Why do search- augmented LLMs fail to use available evidence? Prior work has studied temporal knowl- edge (Mousavi et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025), cita- tion faithfulness (Wallat et al., 2025b) and failures in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Chen *Work done while at Imperial College London. However, how search- augmented LLMs use web search results has re- ceived less attention, and it is unclear why these models fail even when relevant evidence is avail- able. To this end, we construct a dataset of post-cutoff temporal facts, whose values changed after the de- ployed model’s training cutoff. We build a deter- ministic and regenerable pipeline that generates these facts from primary sources, and draw 225 facts from its output, across six domains including sports, finance and medicine.1 Each fact has an outdated value and a current value. This lets us identify outdated answers, test whether models use updated evidence correctly and check whether the cited pages support the models’ claims. We first study a proprietary LLM under its na- tive web search to identify failures in a deployed setting. We then test whether these failures recur under controlled retrieval, giving the same propri- etary LLM and six open-weight model configura- tions an identical menu of frozen search results. text: Temporal knowledge and web search. Prior benchmarks measure whether LLMs answer time- sensitive questions correctly (Mousavi et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Wallat et al., 2025a; Cheng and Dou, 2025), but not whether the answers come from the retrieved evidence. Kale (2026) finds that four models from two families invoke native search on 87.5–93.9% of questions that need it, without checking whether the cited pages support the answers. Premature stopping and top-result re- liance also surface in evaluations of search agents and LLM-based search engines (Gupta et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). We extend these studies by examining snippet reliance in both proprietary and open-weight LLMs. Citation faithfulness. Citation quality is usually scored as whether a cited passage supports a claim (Gao et al., 2023). Wallat et al. (2025b) separate this correctness from faithfulness, that is, whether the source actually produced the answer. On a single open model in a controlled pipeline with adversarially modified documents, they report up to 57% post-rationalisation. Other studies examine how LLMs handle conflicts between parametric knowledge and external evidence, from external behaviour (Xie et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024) to internal representations (Ortu et al., 2024; Halawi et al., 2024). We use post-cutoff facts to study citation faithfulness under both live and controlled web search. 3 Setup Post-cutoff temporal facts. To

As a common thresh- old, we use 16 February 2026, the latest reported training cutoff among the evaluated models (Ope- nAI, 2026a). We exclude a change if it took effect on or before this date or was announced before 1 February 2026, and we exclude FDA claims that can be answered from standard medical knowledge. We draw 225 treatment facts across six domains (FDA 62, finance 52, sports 47, people 43, SEC 13, chemical 8), plus control facts that did not change across the cutoff. On 50 sports claims, gemma-4- 31b and gpt-oss-20b endorse the stale claim 14/50 and 11/47 times when they have to find the page in the search menu, but only 0/50 and 1/50 times when the same Wikipedia page is in the prompt. In all 14 of its failures, gemma-4-31b opens no page; qwen3-8b benefits less (from 16/49 to 8/49; Appendix H). In an agentic loop, the question comes before everything the model retrieves. We therefore test whether restating the full prompt after each opened page helps, keeping the menu, pages and sampling settings unchanged. text: Each club is scored at the answer slot. 5 Mechanistic Analysis of Evidence Use Providing evidence directly reduces failures but does not eliminate them. We investigate why mod- els may still give outdated answers when the correct evidence is available. We use player transfer facts from the sports do- main and three open-weight models: gpt-oss-20b, gemma-4-31b and qwen3-8b. For each fact, we construct two prompts that assert an outdated club and ask for the player’s current club. One prompt also includes the player’s current Wikipedia page (Figure 3). Comparing the two prompts shows how models choose between the outdated and cur- rent answers. We use the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) and the Jacobian lens (J-lens; Gurnee et al., 2026) to probe how the model represents the two candidate answers across layers. Both methods project intermediate hidden states at the answer position onto token-level logits. Each club’s score is the highest logit among selected first tokens of its name, so a higher score indicates stronger sup- port for that club. We track the ranks of both clubs across layers and compare their scores with and without the page (Table 12 in Appendix J). Figure 2 shows how the two candidate answers compete across layers in qwen3-8b. In success- ful cases, the retrieved club gains an advantage in the upper layers and

text: their scores with and without the page (Table 12 in Appendix J). Figure 2 shows how the two candidate answers compete across layers in qwen3-8b. In success- ful cases, the retrieved club gains an advantage in the upper layers and keeps it until the final lay- ers. In failed cases, the retrieved club ranks above the outdated club early in the upper layers, but the outdated club overtakes it in the final layers. This suggests that retrieved evidence can influence in- ternal predictions even when the model fails. The same crossover appears in gpt-oss-20b, while in gemma-4-31b the outdated club rises first and stays ahead (Appendix J). Averaged over the upper third of layers, the page still promotes the retrieved club in failures, though less than in updates (∆new > 0, p ≤0.04), but suppresses the outdated club far less, and in gemma-4-31b not at all (Table 13). 6

text: We study why search-augmented LLMs fail to use available evidence correctly. We find that models often retrieve relevant evidence but answer from search snippets without opening the source pages. Such answers are more likely to be stale and to carry unfaithful citations. Providing relevant evi- dence directly reduces failures but does not elim- inate them. To understand the remaining failures, we analyse how models process retrieved evidence across layers. The retrieved answer can gain an early advantage in the upper layers but lose it to the outdated answer in the final layers. Future work can explore strategies that help models make more effective use of source pages when needed. Causal interventions and latent debate (Chen et al., 2026) can be used to better understand how retrieved evi- dence competes with outdated knowledge and how to improve it. These findings may help guide the 4
title: qwen3-8b

text: development of search-augmented LLMs that use retrieved evidence better and give more reliable responses. Limitations We study only one proprietary model, the lightest of the three GPT-5.6 tiers, chosen for cost. A natural extension is to run the experiments on additional frontier models, which may demonstrate different behaviour. Z.ai’s GLM-5.3-Flash discloses no training cut- off, so we check for contamination through its be- haviour instead. We find its control-fact perfor- mance and closed-book accuracy match those of the models with stated cutoffs (Appendix B). We include it because it is one of the most capable open-weight models available. Most prompts require a fixed answer line, so that answers can be graded mechanically rather than by an LLM. This ‘contract’ can result in dif- ferent model behaviour compared to exclusively free prose. In the study’s pre-registered answer- line check, it lowered Luna’s false endorsement by 17.5 points (Appendix C). Luna’s deployed failures, which anchor the carry-over analysis, are therefore likely to be lower bounds. We keep the answer line because it gives standardised, reliable grading across the more than 30,000 replies in the deployed and frozen runs. Unfaithful citations are rare for some models under frozen retrieval (1.0% of Luna’s graded an- swers and 1.8% of GLM-5.3-Flash’s), so a few grading errors could shift these rates substantially, in both absolute and

Unfaithful citations are rare for some models under frozen retrieval (1.0% of Luna’s graded an- swers and 1.8% of GLM-5.3-Flash’s), so a few grading errors could shift these rates substantially, in both absolute and relative terms. We therefore took particular care with grading. An LLM marker (DeepSeek-V4-Flash; DeepSeek-AI, 2026) helps grade that the deterministic grader cannot decide, but it can only pass a reply, never assign an adverse label. Every unfaithful citation, and every other adverse label that needs judgement, is assigned or confirmed by a human (Appendix D). Failures also vary substantially across domains: sports drives the severe rates, while SEC (13 facts) and chemical (8) are underpowered because few usable post-cutoff facts exist for them. We include them because they add variety to the study. That sports drives so many failures is a finding in its own right, since the answer usually sits in the first line of the player’s Wikipedia page, whereas FDA questions require reading long label sections and reasoning about often complex medical knowledge. The layer-wise analysis with the logit lens and J- lens uses sports transfers only, because the answer, a club name, is only a few tokens long. It charac- terises the failure but does not test a mechanism causally, for example by activation patching. Ethical Considerations

Ethical Considerations Our finding that search-augmented LLMs often answer from snippets alone could help malicious actors spread misinformation, since misleading text that appears in a snippet may be repeated without the model opening the page. To limit this risk, we report only aggregate failure rates and release no tools for manipulating search snippets. All facts in the study are public. Most come from moderated sources (Wikipedia and Wikidata) or from govern- ment records (FDA drug labels and SEC filings); every finance value we use is the figure reported in an SEC filing, and we re-derive all 52 from SEC EDGAR. The people domain names individuals whose deaths are recorded on Wikipedia. These facts cannot be anonymised, because each concerns a named person, but they are already public, and the outdated claims about them are used only as test items. Outdated drug-label information carries clinical risk, which is one of the main reasons we include FDA label changes. text: A Models Table 3 lists the seven configurations. All frozen- retrieval runs go through OpenRouter, with the serving provider pinned because providers serve different quantisations. Temperature is 0 where the provider exposes it, and Luna runs at the provider default. The layer-wise readouts in Section 5 use the open weights of gpt-oss-20b, gemma-4-31b and qwen3-8b. Frozen retrieval. The open models have no provider-native search tool, so our tool loop sup- plies one, and Luna uses the same loop under frozen retrieval. It offers three functions in standard function-calling format, search, open page and find in page, which each model’s own chat template renders; in the closed-book condition no tools are offered. Every search call returns the fact’s frozen menu, so the query is recorded but has no effect. A menu always has exactly ten entries, each with a title, URL and snippet. Where the ground-truth page is not in the organic top ten, it is inserted at a seeded position and the tenth entry is dropped (62 of the 223 menus), and the tool result gives no sign of this. Opening a page returns its frozen text in windows of 40,000 characters, and pages not on the menu are refused. Each episode allows at most five searches, five page opens and eight assistant turns. First, a deterministic en- gine decides everything mechanical. It matches the value the reply asserts against terms derived from the fact, requires a quote to be an exact substring of the archived page, and checks each citation against the value the reply asserts rather than against the ground truth. Second, what the engine cannot de- cide goes to an LLM marker, DeepSeek-V4-Flash served through OpenRouter. The marker is not among the evaluated models and shares no model family with them. It matches paraphrases rather than judging: it reads the archived page without seeing the reply, must back every finding with a verbatim quote that code verifies against the page, and may assign only passing outcomes. Adverse findings, splits and unverified quotes go to a human. A route can use the marker only once it agrees with human

text: Community question-answering (cQA) platforms are important ecosystems for knowledge sharing, yet research on what makes an answer “best” or a question engaging has often focused on either individual lexical features or broad topics. This exploratory study examines both levels in Yahoo! Chiebukuro, asking which nouns and semantic noun clusters are associated with best-answer selection and question engagement. We analyze a large corpus of questions and answer-tier posts collected under the keyword “logistics,” using an offline machine-translation pipeline with manually validated noun-level fidelity. Best-answer selection is modeled with conditional logistic regression within question threads, controlling for answer length, order, and question-answer noun overlap. Engagement is modeled in two stages: whether a question receives any response and, conditional on receiving one, how many responses it attracts. Operational logistics nouns such as “distribution,” “warehouse,” and “center” are associated with best-answer selection, whereas broader civic and infrastructure nouns such as “car,” “tax,” and “shinkansen” are associated with higher engagement. At the cluster level, most semantic noun clusters are associated with best-answer selection, while the clusters associated with response likelihood and response volume are largely distinct. These findings reveal differentiated content-outcome profiles across answer and question levels and provide a domain- wide descriptive map of engagement and answer selection in logistics-related cQA discourse. Keywords Community question answering, Best-answer selection, User engagement, Keyness analysis, Semantic noun

Keywords Community question answering, Best-answer selection, User engagement, Keyness analysis, Semantic noun clustering, Logistics discourse ​ 1 Introduction On a community question-answering (cQA) platform, two structural outcomes indicate whether a post is seen as valuable: whether an answer is selected as “best,” and whether a question generates sustained back-and-forth. Both outcomes are, in principle, related to content — an answer is chosen partly because of what it says, a question attracts replies partly because of what it asks — yet studies of platform discourse often examine con­ tent either at the level of broad topics (what the community talks about) or at the level
title: Discover Networks

text: Page 2 of 20 Naganawa Discover Networks (2026) 2:41 of individual lexical features, rather than connecting the two, and rarely ask whether a content-outcome association survives once an obvious confound like post length is taken into account. This paper is an exploratory empirical study that works across both levels, using Yahoo! Chiebukuro discourse on logistics as a case. Because the analysis is restricted to nouns extracted from a machine translation, it characterizes the topi­ cal lexical content of posts — which referential nouns and semantic clusters they con­ tain — rather than wording in the broader linguistic sense (style, politeness, hedging, sentiment). Logistics is a useful case for this kind of content-outcome analysis. It is a professional, operational domain where questions range from narrow transactional queries (tracking a specific parcel, comparing shipping services) to broad, debatable civic and infrastruc­ ture topics (road congestion, transportation policy, retail supply chains), giving the cor­ pus real variation in both the concreteness of its content and the structural fate of its posts. We ask three questions. First, which nouns are associated with an answer being selected as “best” rather than passed over on the same question? Second, which nouns are associated with a question attracting many answers and replies rather than few or none? Third, do these word-level patterns aggregate into coherent semantic clusters,

text: being selected as “best” rather than passed over on the same question? Second, which nouns are associated with a question attracting many answers and replies rather than few or none? Third, do these word-level patterns aggregate into coherent semantic clusters, and are those clusters still associated with the two outcomes once the length of the post — and, for the question-level models, its posting year — is statistically controlled? Throughout, the study is observational: it reports conditional associations between con­ tent and outcomes, not causal effects, and the answer-level and question-level analyses are associations measured on different units of text. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on platform affordances, online knowledge sharing, answer selection, and social media discourse in logistics contexts. Section 3 describes the data collection, translation, and preprocessing pipeline, and the keyness and cluster-regression methods used to ana­ lyze it. Section 4 presents the results: the noun vocabulary associated with best-selected answers and high-engagement questions, the semantic cluster structure recovered from the corpus, and which clusters are associated with each outcome. Section 5 discusses these results together with the study’s limitations and avenues for future research, and Sect. 6 concludes.

text: 2.1 Platform affordances and structural constraints Platform architecture shapes how users interact and produce content [5]. The concept of “affordances” — coined by Gibson [5, 17] and adapted to technology by Norman [24] and Treem and Leonardi [33] — refers to the actionable properties between an actor and an object; on social platforms these affordances bound the space of possible interaction modes [4, 33]. Community question-answering platforms such as Yahoo! Chiebukuro, Quora, and Stack Exchange are explicitly built around asynchronous, reciprocal infor­ mation-seeking [1, 29]; thread loops, best-answer selection, and reputation or incentive systems shape the quality and structure of the resulting exchange [7, 31].

text: Page 3 of 20 Naganawa Discover Networks (2026) 2:41 2.2 Online knowledge sharing and interaction modes Online knowledge sharing depends on participants’ willingness to externalize tacit knowledge into explicit digital form [23, 34]. In cQA environments this exchange is largely goal-oriented and problem-driven [2, 10]: participants are motivated to contrib­ ute operational narratives and practical knowledge by reputation, reciprocity, and self- efficacy [6, 15]. Studies of Yahoo! Chiebukuro specifically document it as a venue where users request and disseminate everyday, often highly personal, domain-specific concerns and knowledge [30]. What this literature has not examined is whether the specific lexical content associated with an answer’s “best” status, or with a question’s sustained atten­ tion, can be characterized systematically across a large corpus, at a level of detail finer than topic. A substantial body of work examines answer selection and quality directly, using lexical, semantic, user, and interaction features to predict which answers are cho­ sen or rated helpful [3, 14]. More recent studies emphasize the relationship between an answer and its question: perceived helpfulness rises when an answer’s language attri­ butes, including concreteness, are congruent with the question’s [26], and thematic consistency between answer and question is positively related to helpfulness while senti­ ment consistency is not [16]. On the question side, how a question is crafted — including strategies affecting
title: Page 3 of 20

text: including concreteness, are congruent with the question’s [26], and thematic consistency between answer and question is positively related to helpfulness while senti­ ment consistency is not [16]. On the question side, how a question is crafted — including strategies affecting its concreteness — is correlated with both audience engagement and answer quality [8]. It is important to note that an asker-selected “best answer” reflects the asker’s subjective judgment rather than objectively verified correctness [12, 29]. Accordingly, this study treats best-answer selection as an indicator of perceived value within the platform, rather than as a measure of answer correctness. Relative to this predictive and experimental literature, the present study takes a descriptive approach. Rather than seeking to maximize predictive performance, we examine a domain-specific corpus to identify which individual nouns and semantic clusters are associated with each outcome. 2.3 Social media in logistics and supply chain discourse Social media research has extensively covered consumer behavior, political discourse, and entertainment, but its application to professional discourse in logistics and supply chain management remains comparatively underdeveloped [11, 13]. Logistics knowledge communication has traditionally been studied through formal organizational channels and B2B networks [19, 27]; recent supply-chain disruptions have driven practitioners toward informal digital spaces for real-time insight and peer validation [28], and recent reviews explicitly call for more social-media-based analysis in supply-chain and

A related recent strand applies NLP and large-language-model meth­ ods to logistics-relevant social media text from a different platform, YouTube: one study extracts logistics challenges from video subtitles and comments and characterizes them into recurring concern areas — time management, driver welfare, technological invest­ ment, policy transparency [22] — and a companion study uses the same YouTube corpus to generate policy proposals via graph-based retrieval-augmented generation [21]. Both target aggregate discourse characterization or policy generation rather than the fine- grained, word- and cluster-level question this paper addresses on a different platform: which specific content is associated with a post’s structural fate.
