text: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression Ability across Large Language Models Weiting Liu1,*,‡, Zhiyu Pan2,3,*, Shuhong Wang1,*, Zhenquan Yao4,*, Jungang Li5, Li Zhao3, Jian Jiang6, Jianfeng Feng1, Ai Han3,†, Wenlian Lu1,† 1Fudan University, 2Huazhong University of Science and Technology, 3JD.com, 4Harbin Institute of Technology, 5The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou), 6Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences *Equal contribution. ‡Project leader. †Corresponding authors. hanai5@jd.com, wenlian@fudan.edu.cn
title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression

text: Context compression in long-running applica- tions of large language models (LLMs) must preserve goal-relevant information, often be- fore specific downstream questions are known. We introduce GACC-Bench, a benchmark for Goal-Adaptive Context Compression that evaluates how reliably LLMs adapt informa- tion retention to specified high-level goals. For each source context, we derive one or more high-level goals by grouping source- grounded questions according to shared down- stream objectives. The benchmark contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 docu- ment and agent-trace contexts from seven col- lections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. The compressor receives a source context, a goal, and a context-length budget, with the associ- ated evaluation questions withheld. A fixed reader answers these questions individually using the same compressed context. Our evaluation of ten LLM compressors reveals substantial gaps to full-context performance even for the best-performing model, partic- ularly in supporting correct answers to ev- ery question associated with a goal. Com- pared with goal-agnostic compression, target- goal conditioning consistently improves accu- racy, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. GACC-Bench is available at https: //github.com/weiting24/GACC-Bench. 1
title: GACC-Bench: Benchmarking Goal-Adaptive Context Compression

text: Large language models (LLMs) (Singh et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026) are increasingly deployed for long-horizon tasks (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024), where accumulated instructions and intermediate findings can exceed the available context budget. Coding assistants such as Codex CLI and Claude Code already use context com- paction in long sessions. Claude Code also allows users to specify the focus of compaction. At com- pression time, users may know their next objective even when the specific questions needed to pur- sue it are unknown. We define a goal as a high- level description of the intended future use of a source context. Goal-adaptive compression aims to preserve information for multiple subsequent questions associated with that goal. Prior work has studied query-aware (Jiang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024), query-agnostic (Pan et al., 2024), and task-aware (Corallo et al., 2026) com- pression. However, it remains unclear how reliably a compressed context supports multiple withheld questions for a context-specific goal, and whether gains depend on which goal guides compression. In a motivating experiment, we use DeepSeek- V4-Pro (Xu et al., 2026) to compress each con- text separately for each associated goal and eval- uate each compressed context on questions asso- ciated with all goals for that context. Figure 1 reports changes in question-level

Our contributions are threefold. First, we intro- duce GACC-Bench, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for goal-adaptive context com- pression. It contains 500 goals and 2,571 questions over 281 document and agent-trace contexts from seven collections spanning diverse domains, with all instances reviewed by human experts. Second, we design a compressor–reader–judge framework to evaluate goal-adaptive compression under dif- ferent retention budgets, with the reader and judge held fixed. Third, we evaluate ten LLM compres- sors and conduct goal ablations across six models. Our experiments show that target-goal condition- ing improves accuracy over goal-agnostic compres- sion, yet even the best-performing compressor falls substantially short of full-context performance in supporting correct answers to every question asso- ciated with a goal. 2 Related Works Context Compression with Downstream Guid- ance. text: We construct GACC-Bench by generating source- grounded questions, grouping them by shared in- formation needs, and synthesizing a high-level goal for each group. Quality control checks question re- dundancy, within-group coherence, goal–question alignment, and cross-goal distinctiveness. Figure 3 summarizes the three stages: instance construction, quality control, and compression evaluation. 3.1 Instance Construction Given a source context c drawn from natural- language documents, code repositories, or inter- action histories, we generate questions grounded in the source. A future goal may depend on a stated fact, a relation among facts, or a condition that changes how those facts should be used. To test whether compression preserves these forms of in- formation, we use seven strategies for generating questions. Information retrieval asks for a fact explicitly stated in the source, such as a reported value or decision. Multi-step derivation requires combin- ing facts stated in the source through successive logical or numerical steps rather than recalling an 3

Whole decomposition reconstructs a source- defined whole from its components and, where supported, derives a share or residual. Rule appli- cation applies a stated rule, threshold, or exception to a specified case, including a hypothetical change to an explicit input. Bounded trend extrapolation uses a stated rate, recurrence, or sufficiently speci- fied series to derive a limited next value or range. Conflict resolution identifies competing or revised claims, retains their provenance and scope, and de- termines which claim governs only when the source establishes an authority or temporal ordering. Each question has a reference answer and supporting evidence. A strategy is used only when it is sup- ported by the source. The generation prompts are provided in the appendix B.1.1. Before question generation, candidate facts and their locations in c are identified. Each question is generated with a reference answer and a record link- ing its requested answer components to the relevant facts and source passages. During quality control, these recorded links are used to assess source sup- port and whether the selected evidence is sufficient to answer the question. Using the source context and generated questions, an LLM groups questions that serve a shared future task and synthesizes a goal g for each group. Questions in a group may require different information but should jointly sup- port that task. The goal describes what the retained information should enable, without listing ques- tions or revealing answers. The resulting instance is z = (c, g, Qg), where Qg = {q1, . . . , qng} con- tains the associated evaluation questions. 3.2 Quality Control We screen instances for source validity, context dependence, question coherence, and goal align- ment before compression evaluation. Checks re- move invalid questions or goal groups; unrelated compound questions are separated only when their answer requirements can be assigned to coherent new questions. Source-Grounded Audits. A question is retained only if it is unambiguous, its factual premises are supported by the source, and the essential claims in its generated reference answer are correct. The recorded facts and source passages are used to check whether each requested answer component has sufficient support. To assess completeness in- dependently of the generated answer, an LLM iden- tifies all requested items from the question and source, including alternative correct

text: facts and source passages are used to check whether each requested answer component has sufficient support. To assess completeness in- dependently of the generated answer, an LLM iden- tifies all requested items from the question and source, including alternative correct answers when the question permits them. These requirements are audited before the final reference answer is con- structed. We also reject questions whose requested relations or conditions lack source support or do not follow their assigned generation strategy. Ques- tions about incidental details that do not serve a substantive downstream task, such as command counts or line numbers in SWE-agent histories, are removed. Goal Validity and Alignment. Each synthesized goal must describe a coherent future task grounded in the source and supported by its assigned ques- tions. Topic labels, restatements of questions, and goals that reveal answers are rejected. Within each group, questions must fit the goal, and their an- swer requirements must concern information worth retaining for that task. Three models assess each requirement; any valid negative judgment removes the question. When a context has multiple goals, an LLM must select the assigned goal for each ques- tion and an assigned question for each goal from alternatives in the same context. A failed selection removes the tested question or goal, respectively. A goal is also removed if it covers information re- quested by a question from another group, judged from that question and its reference answer without the source. Groups with fewer than four remaining questions are discarded. Context Dependence. Context dependence is checked in both directions: the full source must enable a correct answer, while the question alone should not. Answers must be correct across re- peated attempts with the full context. For ques- tions combining source facts, the selected source passages must also suffice to answer the question; within this selection, at least two passages must contribute necessary information. To test answer- ability without the source, four models each receive only the question, without the goal or reference an- swer. Their responses are judged against the full source; any correct response removes the question. Questions that disclose their own answers are re- moved as well. Information-Level Deduplication. Question pairs within each goal group are compared at two levels. First, if all information requested by one question is covered by another, the more informative ques- tion is retained. If any request is duplicated across two questions, one en- tire question is removed, even if its other requests differ. Expert Human Review. A team of five human experts reviewed all benchmark instances follow- ing the automated quality checks. Each instance was reviewed by two experts to recheck all crite- ria covered by the automated checks, including whether questions were grounded in their source contexts, reference answers were supported by the source, and goals were aligned with their associated questions. The two reviewers initially disagreed on approximately 5% of the reviewed goal groups. Disagreements between the two reviewers were dis- cussed with a third expert. Instances with identified quality issues were removed. 3.3 Compression Evaluation GACC-Bench evaluates goal-adaptive compression using a two-stage Compressor–Reader framework, in which the compressor condenses the source con- text and the reader answers questions based on the resulting compressed context. text: Compressor–Reader framework, in which the compressor condenses the source con- text and the reader answers questions based on the resulting compressed context. Goal-conditioned context compression. Token counts are measured using cl100k_base as a com- mon reference tokenizer. For a given retention ratio, the absolute token budget is calculated by multiplying the source-context length by the reten- tion ratio and taking the floor, with a minimum budget of one token. The compressor receives the source context, the goal, and the resulting absolute token budget, and produces a compressed context that preserves goal-relevant information and rela- tions. A single compressed context is generated for each context–goal–ratio tuple and reused for all questions associated with the same goal. Af- ter generation, the output is tokenized using the same reference tokenizer. If the generated output exceeds the budget, we retain its first L tokens as the compressed memory. If the output is shorter than L tokens, it is retained without padding. No length-based regeneration or rewriting is applied. We record both the raw generated length and the final retained length. Compressed-context question answering. For each question associated with a goal, the fixed reader receives the corresponding compressed con- text and the question, and produces a candidate answer. text: 4 Experiments In this section, we evaluate goal-adaptive con- text compression on GACC-Bench, a multi-source benchmark spanning seven heterogeneous collec- tions. The complete release contains 500 goals, 281 unique source contexts, and 2,571 source-grounded questions. The complete benchmark data and eval- uation scripts are publicly available in the accom- panying anonymous repository. Detailed source-, goal-, and question-level distributions are provided in Appendix A.1 and Appendix A.2. We evalu- ate compression extrinsically through downstream source-grounded answerability. For each goal, its associated questions probe complementary infor- mation required to fulfill that goal. This proto- col measures whether compression preserves goal- relevant evidence under a fixed token budget rather than evaluating standalone summary quality. 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmark. GACC-Bench is constructed from seven established long-context and domain-specific benchmarks: LongBench-v2 (LBv2) (Bai et al., 2025), HELMET (Yen et al., 2025), L-Eval (An et al., 2024), Loong (Wang et al., 2024), Meet- ingBank (MB) (Hu et al., 2023), LongCodeBench (LCB) (Rando et al., 2025), and SWE-Bench Ver- ified (SWE) (Jimenez et al., 2024). For the SWE- Bench source, we use agent trajectories collected from SWE-Bench Verified tasks with the Open- Hands harness (Wang et al., 2025). We use these abbreviations consistently throughout the paper. Models and comparison conditions. All exper- iments use a fixed DeepSeek-V4-Pro reader and judge. text: Verified tasks with the Open- Hands harness (Wang et al., 2025). We use these abbreviations consistently throughout the paper. Models and comparison conditions. All exper- iments use a fixed DeepSeek-V4-Pro reader and judge. The reader answers each question from the provided context, while the judge evaluates the an- swer against the original source context, the ques- tion, and the reference answer. Keeping the reader and judge fixed provides a common evaluation set- ting for comparing compressors. Evaluation settings and metrics. We measure the token length of each source context using the cl100k_base tokenizer. Given a budget ratio r, the target budget is set to L = ⌊rN⌋, where N is the original context length, and L is provided explic- itly in the compression prompt. We report Micro accuracy, defined as the fraction of all questions answered correctly, and Macro accuracy, defined as the fraction of goals for which all associated questions are answered correctly. 4.2 Main Results Table 3 reports the performance of the fixed DeepSeek-V4-Pro reader under no-context and full- context conditions. Near-ceiling full-context ac- curacy, contrasted with low no-context accuracy, indicates that answering the benchmark questions generally requires source information. Table 2 re- ports compression results using a fixed DeepSeek- V4-Pro reader and judge. Larger retention budgets generally improve accuracy, but compressed con- texts remain substantially below the full-context reference, particularly in Macro accuracy. The tested compressors therefore recover answers to individual questions more reliably than they sup- port correct answers to every question associated with a goal. This persistent gap highlights the chal- lenge of retaining information across the different aspects of a shared goal, even when more tokens are available. Compression difficulty also varies across sources. LongBench-v2 and SWE-agent generally retain stronger answerability, whereas MeetingBank and L-Eval are more challenging un- der tight budgets. Model rankings can also differ between Micro and Macro accuracy, showing that strong aggregate question-level performance does not necessarily imply reliable goal-level coverage. 4.3 Goal Ablation Studies To isolate the effect of goal information during compression, we conduct a controlled ablation on GACC-Bench-testmini, which contains 124 goals, 62 source contexts, and 651 source-grounded ques- tions. Each context is associated with exactly two goals. In the Own goal condition, the compressor receives the target goal. In No goal, it receives no goal information. In Cross goal, it receives the alternative goal from the same context, while the reader is evaluated on the target-goal

In Cross goal, it receives the alternative goal from the same context, while the reader is evaluated on the target-goal questions in all conditions. Table 4 reports overall Micro accu- racy under 5% and 10% retention budgets. Own goal consistently outperforms No goal and Cross goal across all models and budgets, with larger gains at the higher budget. Cross goal performs worst throughout, indicating that an unrelated goal can misdirect evidence selection rather than serve as a useful substitute. These results show that goal conditioning directs compression toward task- relevant evidence, although it does not by itself guarantee complete goal-level retention. 6

The ad- vantage is especially clear for goal-level Macro accuracy: at a 20% budget, the goal-conditioned setting achieves 61.44% Micro and 19.35% Macro accuracy, compared with 42.55% and 6.45% with- out a goal. The Micro curve improves steadily as more tokens become available, whereas Macro accuracy remains much lower at tight budgets be- cause it requires all questions associated with a goal to be answered correctly. The token statistics further show that, under the same token-budget in- struction, compression without a goal uses more to- kens on average, yet achieves lower accuracy. This highlights the importance of goal instructions for directing information retention: goal-conditioned compression uses the budget more effectively by prioritizing goal-relevant evidence rather than sim- ply producing

This highlights the importance of goal instructions for directing information retention: goal-conditioned compression uses the budget more effectively by prioritizing goal-relevant evidence rather than sim- ply producing longer compressed memories. 4.5 Comparison of Compression Mechanisms We compare GACC Prompt with LLMLingua, LLMLingua-2, and LongLLMLingua on GACC- Bench-testmini under a nominal 5% retention bud- get. All methods use the same fixed DeepSeek- V4-Pro reader and judge. GACC Prompt receives the target goal and performs prompt-based com- pression followed by prefix truncation, whereas the baselines use task-agnostic or query-conditioned token pruning. As shown in Table 5, GACC Prompt achieves the highest Micro and Macro ac- curacy, reaching 27.04% and 4.84%, respectively. LLMLingua-2 is the strongest external baseline in Micro accuracy at 11.52%, while all external baselines obtain zero Macro accuracy. This Micro– Macro contrast suggests that token-pruning meth- ods may preserve evidence for individual ques- tions but fail to retain the complementary evi- dence required for complete goal coverage. text: We introduce GACC-Bench to evaluate goal- adaptive context compression in LLMs, using with- held, goal-relevant questions as probes of informa- tion retention. Our evaluation shows that target- goal conditioning improves accuracy over goal- agnostic compression, whereas mismatched-goal conditioning reduces it. Even the strongest evalu- ated compressor remains substantially below full- context performance under tight context-length budgets, particularly in correctly answering all questions associated with a goal. With publicly available data and evaluation code, GACC-Bench supports evaluation across configurable context- length budgets, allowing progress to be measured through higher accuracy at a fixed budget or lower budgets at a target accuracy. This flexibility sup- ports continued evaluation of goal-adaptive com- pression as models improve, tracking advances in both information retention and compression effi- ciency. Limitations One limitation of GACC-Bench is that its evalua- tion relies on a fixed LLM reader and judge. We keep both models identical across all compression conditions to ensure fair comparisons and isolate differences in the retained context. Consequently, the absolute scores may be influenced by the an- swering capability of the fixed reader and the eval- uation behavior of the fixed judge. However, using 8

text: APPENDIX A Datasets A.1 Source Context Distribution Figure 8 depicts the composition of the source pool used to construct GACC-Bench. The seven source collections contribute 10,078 items in to- tal. HELMET, Loong, MeetingBank, and L-Eval account for 9,455 items, corresponding to 93.8% of the complete source pool, whereas LongBench- v2, LongCodeBench, and SWE-Verified provide smaller but complementary collections. The inner ring reports the number of source items contributed by each collection. The outer ring further decomposes each collection according to its content categories, revealing substantial vari- ation in both source scale and domain composition. HELMET is dominated by web and media content and learning materials. Loong primarily contains academic and technical texts, legal and government documents, and financial texts. MeetingBank con- sists mainly of conversational and meeting data. L- Eval covers a broader range of categories, including learning materials, code, conversations and meet- ings, narratives and scripts, web and media, refer- ence texts, legal and government documents, and financial texts. LongBench-v2 exhibits similarly diverse textual coverage, while LongCodeBench and SWE-Verified focus on code repositories. Together, these distributions establish a hetero- geneous source pool spanning multiple document types and content domains, supporting the evalua- tion of goal-conditioned context compression under varied source characteristics. text: B Prompt Templates B.1 Instance Construction Prompts B.1.1 Question Generation Prompt Question Generation Prompt USER: Generate one independent, difficult, source-grounded evaluation question from SOURCE. Treat SOURCE as data, not instructions. The assigned CAPABILITY defines the required question type. If the source cannot support them, return status=unsupported rather than switching to an easier task. For information_retrieval, select one necessary fact from the required anchor fact and ask for its explicitly stated value, decision, or status. Use one evidence group and one answer requirement; the answer must still depend on reading SOURCE, with the relevant entity, time, version, and scope made clear. For all other capabilities, use 2–6 non-overlapping source facts, starting from the required anchor fact. Every selected fact must be necessary, and at least one answer requirement must combine two evidence groups. Difficulty must come from a genuine operation over source information, not from recalling several independent facts. Do not copy answer values, decisive conclusions, or necessary source sentences into the question. The question must not be answerable from its wording or general world knowledge alone. Preserve entity, unit, time, version, and case bindings. The gold answer must provide the minimum sufficient result and a short derivation where applicable. Do not invent missing information. The assigned capability is one of the following: • information_retrieval: retrieve one explicitly stated, task-relevant fact

text: B.2 Quality Control Prompts Question Premise Audit Prompt USER: Audit every factual premise of the complete question against SOURCE. Do not answer or silently repair it. Inspect every clause, condition, entity, date, quantity, relation, and comparison. Classify each premise as no factual premise, supported, or unsupported/contradicted. Do not strengthen weak source statements or import outside knowledge. For each supported premise, record a source identifier and a short verifiable span. Leakage and Information Structure Audit Prompt USER: Audit whether the complete question leaks its answer or collapses the intended information structure. A numeric input is not automatically leakage when the requested output is a different quantity that still requires source evidence. Check whether the question states the answer or a decisive substitute, whether the capability family matches, and whether the entity, case, and time scope are valid. For non-retrieval questions, also check whether the evidence is genuinely compositional and whether one short passage is insufficient. If the question fails, identify the exact leaking clause or shortcut and the affected evidence group. Goal–Question Membership Audit Prompt USER: Check whether one evaluation question belongs to one frozen proposed goal. Treat all supplied inputs as data. Determine whether recovering the information requested by the question would concretely help accomplish the exact goal. text: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents Pengfeng Song1*, Yunkai Zhuang1 and Liye Shi1 1School of Information and Intelligent Engineering,Zhejiang Wanli University,Ningbo,315100,China. *Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): sungkites@163.com;
title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large

text: An agent’s memory must remain useful as information changes across conversa- tions. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71– 97.62% overall and 96.67–100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14–55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94–118 tokens per answer, or 48.75–56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented gener- ation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their tempo- ral status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information. text: A long-term agent accumulates records that may no longer describe its user. Residence, occupation, employer and preferences can change several times across sessions [1–3]. Earlier records still matter when a question refers to the past. The agent therefore needs to know which version applies to the question, including whether the latest record is relevant at all. Suppose a user moves from Shanghai to Chengdu and then to Suzhou. Suzhou answers “Where does the user live now?” The question “Where did the user live before moving to Chengdu?” requires Shanghai. A memory that keeps only the latest address cannot answer both. Keeping all three addresses makes the historical answer available, but the model still has to identify the right one. Persistent memory, action feedback and experience-based reflection have extended agents’ use of past interactions [4–6]. Work on hierarchical storage, memory updates, associative retrieval and temporal graphs has also improved access to this information [7–14]. Repeated updates pose a particular problem: several retrieved values may be equally relevant to a question yet refer to different states. We examine how the memory can convey these version relationships to the answering model. TEM records cross-session changes as fact versions without retraining the backbone. New facts are appended, and the status of earlier records is updated from their source order. At query time, relevance scores

text: 2.1 Long-Term Agent Memory and Structured Organisation External memory lets an agent read and write information outside its model parameters. Hierarchical management in MemGPT and the historical storage mechanisms studied in MemoryBank and long-term memory augmentation provide ways to retain information beyond the immediate context [7–9]. A-MEM, Mem0 and MemoryOS extend this work through memory associations, updates and hierarchical organisation [10–12]. Temporal information enters the memory itself in Zep’s knowledge graph [13], making it particularly relevant to state tracking. TEM examines how version status is carried from stored records into answer evidence. Memory processing cost is another concern; LightMem addresses it through staged operations [14]. Graph-based retrieval connects information spread across records. Associative retrieval is central to HippoRAG and its successor, while GraphRAG uses graph organisation for query-focused summarisation [15–17]. Beyond these retrieval structures, 2

text: MemoRAG uses global memory to guide evidence access, and MemOS considers knowledge access across the memory lifecycle [18, 19]. KG-RAG combines knowledge-graph retrieval and question decomposition for multi- hop question answering without additional training [20]. CTRN addresses complex time constraints through implicit temporal and relational representations [21]. MGIT models temporal dependencies at multiple granularities [22]. These graph-based question- answering methods are relevant to TEM’s use of structured evidence. Our focus is the management of fact versions as conversations update a state, including how the resulting status information reaches the generator. 2.2 Long-Term Memory Evaluation and Retrieval Augmentation LongMemEval and LoCoMo evaluate cross-session information use, fact updates and temporal reasoning [23, 24]. LongBench covers a broader set of long-context tasks [25]. Lost in the Middle shows that the position of relevant information can affect model performance [26]. For state tracking, finding a relevant passage does not settle which version answers the question. We study this choice in controlled update tasks and evaluate hybrid retrieval on public multi-session questions. RAG and dense retrieval provide the basis for accessing external evidence [27, 28]. Self-RAG evaluates evidence, RAPTOR organises it hierarchically, and interleaved retrieval supports chain-of-thought reasoning [29–31]. Source order determines the status of each version. Retrieval then selects the facts to include in the answer evidence. text: and 4.6). 4 Experiments and Results 4.1 Experimental Setup The state-update benchmark contains 60 personas, 600 sessions and 420 questions involving residence, occupation and drinks. There are 180 current-state questions, 180 other historical questions and 60 questions about residence immediately before the latest move. For a historical question, the reference answer is the most recent applicable fact before the target update. Running six memory configurations with four backbones produced 10,080 answers. We compared TEM with naive RAG, session-aware RAG and full context. Session- aware RAG keeps retrieved source turns in session order. The fact-memory comparison uses three configurations. Overwrite keeps only the latest version. Unmarked keeps all versions in source order, and TEM-Status adds historical labels to the same content without changing that order. Experiments used an A100 40 GB GPU. Extraction and answering within a con- figuration used the same frozen backbone. We retrieved at most 15 candidates with all-mpnet-base-v2 and set temperature to zero and the random seed to 42. Llama and Qwen ran in BF16 with a 512-token answer limit; Qwen thinking was disabled. A dash indicates an unreported or inapplicable value. 5 Discussion The state-update results separate two requirements of historical question answering. A memory must first keep earlier values accessible. Once those values are available, the generator still needs to identify which one applies. In the ablation, historical labels improved hit rates without changing the facts or their source order. Retrieval therefore did not account for the difference between the two configurations. The result supports treating version status as part of the evidence presented to the generator, even when it can in

text: without changing the facts or their source order. Retrieval therefore did not account for the difference between the two configurations. The result supports treating version status as part of the evidence presented to the generator, even when it can in principle be inferred from the ordered records. On LoCoMo, marked and unmarked hybrid memory obtained similar scores, and both exceeded session-aware RAG under the same evidence budget. The contrast with the state-update task helps define the role of the labels. They directly indicate whether a retained value has been superseded, but do not supply missing event details or cross-session associations. These are also needed for public dialogue questions. The hybrid-memory gain on LoCoMo is therefore better understood at the level of evidence organisation, without attributing it to historical labels alone. TEM uses source-session order to assign state, assuming explicit single-valued updates. This is sufficient for the controlled update setting considered here. A delayed report may place an earlier event in a later session, and contradictory values can occur within one session. Preferences may also remain valid simultaneously. Handling these cases requires event-validity times or explicit treatment of conflicting relations beyond the present ordering rule.

text: TEM couples history-preserving fact storage with evidence that makes version status explicit. The update rule operates on complete version groups, and retrieval passes source order and historical labels to the generator. Across four backbones, retaining 12

text: and labelling versions improved historical information use in state-update tasks with compact fact evidence. Hybrid memory also exceeded session-aware RAG on public multi-session questions at the same evidence budget. Together, the results support managing fact versions throughout storage and answering when information changes across conversations. text: Learning Speech Attribute Representations via Multi-Teacher Distillation Maryem Bouziane LIA Avignon Universit´e Avignon, France 0009-0002-6483-7881 Salima Mdhaffar LIA Avignon Universit´e Avignon, France 0000-0002-8472-6890 Yannick Est`eve LIA Avignon Universit´e Avignon, France 0000-0002-3656-8883 Abstract—Recent post-training approaches have shown that self- supervised speech encoders can be adapted to learn a single utterance- level speech attribute through knowledge distillation. In this work, we investigate whether a single speech encoder can simultaneously preserve multiple complementary utterance-level speech representations. We pro- pose a multi-attribute multi-teacher distillation framework that learns semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations from four frozen teacher models using a shared SSL backbone and attribute-specific branches. Experiments on multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verifi- cation, language identification, and speech emotion recognition show that the proposed model achieves performance close to dedicated single-task students while requiring only a single shared encoder. Furthermore, the learned layer aggregation strategies reveal that different speech attributes naturally emerge at different depths of the SSL encoder, providing new insights into the organization of speech representations.
title: Learning Speech Attribute Representations

text: Speech conveys multiple complementary types of information beyond its linguistic content. In addition to the lexical message, an utterance carries information about the speaker identity, the spoken language, emotional state, speaking style, and other paralinguistic characteristics. These complementary attributes are essential for a broad range of applications including multilingual speech retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, conversational agents, speech analytics, and affective computing. Nevertheless, they are generally modeled independently, leading to multiple task-specific encoders that duplicate computation and fail to exploit the common structure underlying speech. Recent advances in self-supervised learning (SSL) have profoundly changed speech representation learning. Foundation models such as wav2vec 2.0 [1], HuBERT [2], WavLM [3], and w2v-BERT [4] are trained on thousands of hours of unlabeled speech and produce generic contextual representations that achieve remarkable perfor- mance across many downstream tasks. While these models natu- rally produce frame-level representations, many applications require utterance-level embeddings that summarize global properties of an entire speech segment. Rather than redesigning SSL pre-training ob- jectives, several recent works have demonstrated that these foundation models can be effectively adapted through post-training, transferring knowledge from pretrained expert models into a shared speech encoder. A particularly successful direction consists in learning seman- tic speech embeddings through teacher-student knowledge distilla- tion. Frameworks such as SAMU-XLSR [5], SONAR [6], [7], and SENSE [8] align speech representations with
title: Learning Speech Attribute Representations

text: from pretrained expert models into a shared speech encoder. A particularly successful direction consists in learning seman- tic speech embeddings through teacher-student knowledge distilla- tion. Frameworks such as SAMU-XLSR [5], SONAR [6], [7], and SENSE [8] align speech representations with multilingual sentence embedding spaces, enabling multilingual and multimodal retrieval. More recently, multi-teacher post-training has been proposed to jointly learn semantic and speaker representations within a single SSL speech encoder [9]. These results demonstrate that multiple utterance-level attributes can coexist in a unified representation while preserving competitive performance on both semantic retrieval and speaker verification. However, extending this paradigm beyond two attributes remains an open challenge. Semantic content, speaker identity, language identity, and emotion emerge at different abstraction levels within SSL speech encoders and rely on heterogeneous supervision signals originating from different datasets and teacher models. Simply adding new objectives may lead to conflicting optimization dynamics and representation interference. Whether a single post-trained SSL en- coder can simultaneously preserve these complementary dimensions of speech therefore remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing a holistic multi-teacher post-training framework that learns four complementary utterance-level representations from a single shared SSL speech encoder. The proposed framework distills semantic, speaker, lan- guage, and emotion representations from four specialized frozen teachers while introducing two key mechanisms to facilitate joint optimization. text: framework that learns four complementary utterance-level representations from a single shared SSL speech encoder. The proposed framework distills semantic, speaker, lan- guage, and emotion representations from four specialized frozen teachers while introducing two key mechanisms to facilitate joint optimization. First, each attribute learns its own layer aggregation strategy, allowing different branches to exploit the encoder layers that are most informative for their target representation. Second, we propose a gain-based loss weighting strategy derived from mono- task learning dynamics to balance heterogeneous teachers exhibiting different convergence behaviors. We evaluate the proposed framework on four downstream tasks covering all distilled attributes: multilingual semantic retrieval, speaker verification, language identification, and speech emotion recognition. The contributions of this work are fourfold: • We significantly extend recent multi-teacher post-training ap- proaches by jointly learning four complementary utterance-level speech attributes instead of two. • We propose a holistic post-training framework for SSL speech encoders combining attribute-specific layer aggregation with a gain-based loss weighting strategy. • We demonstrate that a single shared encoder preserves seman- tic, speaker, language, and emotion representations across four independent downstream evaluation tasks. • We provide an analysis of layer utilization showing how different speech attributes emerge at different depths of a shared SSL speech encoder.

text: A. Post-training of speech foundation models Recent work has increasingly viewed post-training as a distinct stage in the lifecycle of speech foundation models, complementing large-scale self-supervised pre-training. Rather than modifying the expensive pre-training process, post-training adapts a generic speech arXiv:2610.21941v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

text: encoder to downstream objectives through techniques including do- main adaptation, instruction tuning, continual learning, and knowl- edge distillation [10], [11]. Existing post-training approaches can be broadly categorized into four directions: adaptation, alignment, reasoning, and efficiency [12]. Such post-training approaches have also explored efficiency through model compression and knowledge distillation [13]. In this work, rather than compressing a single expert, we consolidate the knowledge of multiple specialized teacher models into a single shared speech encoder, reducing the number of deployed encoders while preserving multiple speech attributes. The resulting model replaces multiple task-specific encoders with a single backbone capable of producing semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations. B. Learning utterance-level speech representations While self-supervised speech encoders naturally produce con- textual frame-level representations, many downstream applications require compact utterance-level embeddings that summarize an entire speech segment. Early efforts mainly focused on learning a single attribute. Semantic speech representations have received particular attention through teacher-student distillation, where speech utter- ances are aligned with multilingual sentence embedding spaces. Representative examples include SAMU-XLSR [5], SONAR [6], [7], and SENSE [8], which produce language-agnostic utterance embeddings suitable for multilingual speech-speech and speech-text retrieval. These approaches demonstrate that semantic information can be effectively transferred from powerful text encoders to speech foundation models while preserving cross-lingual generalization. Beyond semantics, several studies have investigated utterance- level representations dedicated to specific

These approaches demonstrate that semantic information can be effectively transferred from powerful text encoders to speech foundation models while preserving cross-lingual generalization. Beyond semantics, several studies have investigated utterance- level representations dedicated to specific paralinguistic attributes. Speaker verification systems typically rely on speaker embeddings extracted from models such as ECAPA-TDNN [14], while language identification has similarly benefited from utterance-level embeddings trained on multilingual corpora such as VoxLingua107 [15]. More recently, speech emotion representation learning has attracted increas- ing attention, with models such as emotion2vec [16] demonstrating that large-scale self-supervised pre-training can produce transferable emotion embeddings across a wide range of downstream emotion recognition tasks. Although these representations target different speech properties, they share a common characteristic: each embedding space is op- timized independently for a single attribute. As a consequence, practical systems typically require several specialized encoders op- erating in parallel, increasing memory usage, computational cost, and deployment complexity. Only recently have a few studies begun to investigate whether multiple utterance-level representations can be jointly learned from a shared speech encoder through multi- teacher distillation [9]. These first results suggest that multiple speech attributes can coexist within a common SSL encoder, opening new perspectives for unified utterance-level representation learning. III. METHOD Figure 1 illustrates the proposed framework. A shared SSL speech encoder processes the input utterance and produces contextual hidden representations at all encoder layers. Four attribute-specific branches, corresponding to semantic content, speaker identity, language identity and emotion, independently aggregate these hidden representations through learnable layer interpolation, followed by attention pooling and a projection layer. Each branch is supervised by a frozen teacher model through cosine embedding distillation. The entire architecture is trained end-to-end while sharing a single speech encoder across all attributes. We propose a holistic multi-teacher distillation framework for learning several utterance-level speech representations with a single shared speech encoder. Let A denote the set of target attributes: A = {sem, spk, lang, emo}, corresponding respectively to semantic content, speaker identity, language identity, and emotion. Each attribute a ∈A is associated with a frozen teacher model Ta, which defines a target embedding space for that attribute. The student model consists of a shared speech foundation encoder followed by attribute-specific branches. Each branch produces one utterance-level embedding and is trained to match the corresponding teacher representation. Multi-teacher distillation objective For each attribute a, the student branch is trained to maximize the cosine similarity with the corresponding teacher representation. The attribute-specific loss is defined as: La i = 1 −cos(zi,a, ya i ). A central difficulty in holistic multi-teacher distillation is that the different teachers have heterogeneous embedding dimensions, training dynamics, and levels of difficulty. Uniform loss weighting may therefore over-emphasize attributes that are easier to optimize or whose losses have larger magnitudes. Mono-task learning provides an estimate of how much useful information can be transferred from each teacher into the student architecture. Attributes exhibiting larger learning gains tend to cor- respond to teachers that are easier for the student to approximate. Assigning them larger weights encourages the Multi-Attribute optimization to focus on supervision signals that are better aligned with the student capacity, while avoiding over-emphasizing attributes that are intrinsically difficult or noisy. We introduce a gain-based weighting strategy derived from mono- task learning dynamics. For each attribute a, we first train a mono- task student using the same architecture but retaining only branch a. Let Lmono a (e) denote the normalized validation loss of this mono- task model

text: derived from mono- task learning dynamics. For each attribute a, we first train a mono- task student using the same architecture but retaining only branch a. Let Lmono a (e) denote the normalized validation loss of this mono- task model at epoch e. The learning gain for attribute a is defined as: ga = Lmono a (1) −min e Lmono a (e). The final Multi-Attribute weight is obtained by normalizing the gains across attributes: λa = ga P b∈A gb . This strategy assigns larger weights to attributes for which the student shows stronger learning progress in the corresponding mono- task setting, while reducing the contribution of attributes that rapidly saturate or provide weaker training gains. Unlike dynamic weighting strategies such as uncertainty weighting or GradNorm [18], the pro- posed weights are estimated once from mono-task learning dynamics and remain fixed during multi-teacher training, avoiding additional optimization variables and training instability. IV. EXPERIMENTS In order to evaluate the relevance of our proposition, we benchmark it on different tasks related to the targeted sentence-level attributes. A. Teacher supervision We target four utterance-level attributes in our multi-teacher stu- dent learning framework: semantics, speaker, language, and emotion continuous representations. For each attribute, we used a specialized teacher: the BGE-M3 text encoder (when transcription is avail- able) or the SENSE speech encoder for semantics (BGE-M3 and SENSE share the same semantic continuous space), an ECAPA- TDNN speaker embeddings trained on VoxCeleb for speaker attribute, an ECAPA-TDNN language embedding model trained on VoxLin- gua107, and emotion2vec-base [16] as a teacher for emotion attribute. All teacher models remain frozen throughout training.

Implementation and training details The shared speech encoder is initialized from w2v-BERT 2.0. We implement the multi-teacher model in SpeechBrain, based on the open-source SENSE implementation. All teacher embeddings are pre- computed before training in order to reduce the training cost. We fine- tune the shared w2v-BERT 2.0 encoder with Adam using a learning rate of 10−5. The task-specific modules are optimized separately with Adadelta using an initial learning rate of 1.5. Training is performed with a batch size of 14 for both training and validation. The model is trained for 17,613 iterations using 32 H100 GPUs. E. Tasks To evaluate the quality of the semantic representation learned by our approach, we assess the model on multilingual speech retrieval. We evaluate the learned speaker representations on a speaker ver- ification benchmark, and the language branch through a language identification experiment based on a classifier trained on the extracted embeddings. Last, we evaluate the emotion branch on speech emotion recognition datasets using dataset-specific classifiers. For each attribute, we compare three types of representations: the corresponding frozen teacher model, a single-task student model trained only for the considered attribute, and the proposed multi- teacher student model. This comparison allows us to quantify the impact of joint training and to evaluate whether a unified encoder can preserve attribute-specific information while sharing most of its parameters across tasks. 1) Multilingual speech retrieval: We assess the semantic branch on multilingual speech retrieval. For each experiment, we define a query set and a search set. The query set contains speech utterances, while the search set contains the corresponding translated items in another language. The objective is to retrieve the correct translation of each query from all candidates in the search set. Each query utterance is encoded into an utterance-level embedding using the semantic branch of the evaluated model. When the search set contains speech, candidate utterances are encoded with the same speech encoder. When the search set contains text, target sentences are encoded with BGE-M3. Embeddings are normalized before retrieval, and candidates are ranked according to cosine similarity. Performance is reported with Recall@1. text: We presented a holistic multi-teacher post-training framework that enables a single self-supervised speech encoder to learn multiple complementary utterance-level speech representations through knowl- edge distillation. By jointly distilling semantic, speaker, language, and emotion representations from four specialized teacher models, the proposed approach replaces several task-specific encoders with a single shared backbone while preserving competitive performance across four independent downstream evaluation tasks. Despite the heterogeneous nature of the supervision signals and datasets, the proposed model consistently approaches the performance of dedicated single-task students, while even improving semantic retrieval and showing that semantic and language representations can provide complementary information for language identification. Be- yond the downstream results, the learned layer interpolation weights reveal that different speech attributes naturally emerge at different

More broadly, this work suggests that post-training can transform generic SSL speech encoders into holistic representation models capable of supporting multiple speech understanding tasks without requiring dedicated backbones. We believe that this direction opens a promising path toward universal speech foundation models producing rich, reusable utterance-level representations for a wide range of downstream applications. text: P2TPO: Structure-Aligned Page-to-Token Credit Assignment for Full-Page Document Parsing Yong Zu§‡1,2, Ninghua Yang§1, Zezhong Tan1, Xinhong Ma1, Ziqiang Dong∗1 and Yang Yang†1 1Qwen Business Unit, Alibaba, 2Xidian University §Core contributors. ∗Project lead. †Team lead. ‡Work done during an internship at Alibaba. End-to-end full-page document parsing must preserve the content and structure of heterogeneous elements, yet otherwise accurate outputs can contain local errors and omissions. A single page-level advantage does not explicitly identify which elements differ in quality across sampled outputs or where their errors occur. We introduce Page-to-Token Policy Optimization (P2TPO), a structure-aligned credit-assignment framework that operates on full-page policy trajectories. Reference-element alignment first associates block-level quality contrasts with generated spans. Unified Anchor Pricing (UAP) incorporates matched and missing element outcomes and provides feedback relative to a fixed quality ceiling when sampled outputs receive identical but imperfect scores for a reference element. Within matched blocks, Span Credit Redistribution (SCR) redistributes existing block credit according to aligned correct and erroneous spans, using boundary proxies for within-block omissions while preserving the total block-derived advantage across its tokens. Under a fixed-weight additive page utility, we show that element-indexed contrasts retain local quality differences that page-level aggregation can cancel out. In the main experimental comparison, P2TPO outperforms all evaluated policy optimization baselines in seed-averaged scores on each of the six document parsing benchmarks. Additional

text: End-to-end document parsers transcribe images of digital documents, scans, and photographs into a single structured sequence in reading order (Blecher et al., 2024; Taghadouini et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2025; Du et al., 2025). We study full-page Markdown transcription, with faithful text, LATEX formulas, and HTML tables. Dense heterogeneous content, skew, warping, and uneven illumination challenge accuracy and com- pleteness (Ouyang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). Errors are often local: an otherwise accurate output may corrupt a formula, omit words, or miss an entire element. Supervised next-token learning serves as the foundation for these parsers, while reinforcement learning (RL) is used for post-training optimization of reference-based measures for fully generated documents. These measures evaluate content accuracy, structural fidelity, and completeness. Recent parsers highlight the ef- fectiveness of reinforcement learning in post-training through layout-aware rewards and verifiable unit tests (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Poznanski et al., 2025). A key question for full-page transcription is how to convert these measurements into feedback that corrects missing or corrupted content while preserving correctly transcribed sections. With page-level outcome rewards, GRPO assigns one response advantage to all generated tokens (Shao et al., 2024). Yet two outputs of the same page can receive similar overall scores while making opposite local errors: one transcribes a formula correctly but omits a
title: P2TPO: Structure-Aligned Page-to-Token Credit

text: outcome rewards, GRPO assigns one response advantage to all generated tokens (Shao et al., 2024). Yet two outputs of the same page can receive similar overall scores while making opposite local errors: one transcribes a formula correctly but omits a table, whereas the other recovers the table and corrupts the formula (Figure 1(a)). A shared response coefficient does not preserve these element-specific contrasts. GDPO normalizes reward dimensions separately before combining them into a shared response coefficient (Liu et al., 2026b); CSPO routes table-wide functional-attribute advantages to corresponding tokens (Yang et al., 2026). Our focus is the remaining reference-instance question: how to compare corresponding individual elements across full-page outputs, include missing outcomes, and allocate their signed credit to generated positions. arXiv:2610.21979v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026

text: P2TPO: Structure-Aligned Page-to-Token Credit Assignment for Full-Page Document Parsing We analyze this phenomenon at three levels. First, reference identity maintains contrasts between individual elements, including instances of the same type. Second, element-wise comparisons must account for missing outcomes and retain feedback when all outcomes are equally imperfect: an omitted element lacks a generated span, and centering tied scores diminishes its relative signal. Third, feedback must differentiate erroneous positions from correct content within a matched block, rather than assigning uniform credit across the block. Together, the four failure modes illustrated in Figure 1(b) highlight three key requirements: preserve element identity, complete the comparison outcomes, and control where credit is assigned. We introduce Page-to-Token Policy Optimization (P2TPO), which assigns local credit while retaining full- page generation and page-level feedback (Figure 1(c)). It first aligns each output to reference elements so that corresponding instances can be compared across rollouts. Unified Anchor Pricing (UAP) completes these comparisons with missing outcomes and uses a quality ceiling to retain feedback at imperfect consensus. Matched coefficients act on generated blocks; whole-element omissions act through existing boundary tokens. text: Matched coefficients act on generated blocks; whole-element omissions act through existing boundary tokens. Span Credit Redistribution (SCR) then reallocates an eligible matched block’s coefficient toward aligned errors when negative and correct positions when positive, preserving its sign and total credit mass. The final update combines this local feedback with the shared page term. Our contributions are fourfold: • Reference-element credit assignment. We retain individual element identities across full-page rollouts and characterize the local quality contrasts that aggregation can erase under a fixed-weight additive page utility. • Complete outcome feedback. We propose the UAP, which outlines a unified set of rules for handling matches, managing missing values, and addressing uniformly imperfect outcomes. This includes a feedback mechanism for instances where an entire element is absent. • Budget-preserving intra-block redistribution. We developed the SCR mechanism, which reallocates block credits while preserving both the sign and the total amount of matched block credits. We proved the conservation of credits and specified the conditions under which informative masks can increase the allocation to the target position. • Empirical effectiveness and generality. Using a shared supervised checkpoint, matched update budgets, and a five-seed run, P2TPO outperforms four response-level baselines on all 13 primary splits across six benchmarks that include digital documents, scanned pages, and real-world photographs. text: Document parsing and reinforcement post-training. End-to-end parsers such as Donut and Nougat generate structured documents directly from images (Kim et al., 2022; Blecher et al., 2024). Recent systems extend this setting to diverse layouts and capture conditions (Cai et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Reinforcement post-training introduces rewards for transcription, layout, reading order, output validity, and structural fidelity (Wang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Poznanski et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Hunyuan Vision Team et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Table- and element-specific approaches further tailor the prediction unit and reward to local content (Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026c). These systems motivate heterogeneous quality measures, while P2TPO studies how feedback for individual reference elements reaches tokens within a full-page rollout. Appendix A.1 compares reward units and optimization supports. Group-relative optimization and reward normalization. GRPO and RLOO construct response advantages from sampled groups without a learned critic (Shao et al., 2024; Ahmadian et al., 2024). GSPO uses sequence- level importance weighting and clipping, while DAPO and Dr. GRPO revise sampling, clipping, reduction, or normalization (Zheng et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025). GDPO, RDPO, and GD2PO address the normalization and interaction of multiple reward dimensions (Liu et al., 2026b; Bai et

text: and Dr. GRPO revise sampling, clipping, reduction, or normalization (Zheng et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025). GDPO, RDPO, and GD2PO address the normalization and interaction of multiple reward dimensions (Liu et al., 2026b; Bai et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a). NGRPO combines virtual-maximum calibration with asymmetric clipping to learn from homogeneous failures (Nan et al., 2025). UAP shares ceiling-informed feedback, while unifying missing outcomes and imperfect reward consensus within reference-element comparisons and routing their feedback to generated tokens. Appendix C.1.4 details the evaluated baselines; Appendix A.1 compares reward interfaces. Structured and local credit assignment. Process supervision evaluates reasoning steps (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024); GiGPO compares repeated environment states while retaining trajectory feedback (Feng et al., 2025). CSPO extends GRPO with table-wide functional-attribute rewards whose normalized advantages are routed to corresponding tokens alongside global feedback (Yang et al., 2026). P2TPO performs local comparisons for individual reference-block instances in full-page rollouts, preserving quality differences between elements of the same type and supporting omission feedback and intra-block redistribution. Functional-attribute assessment and reference-instance comparison are complementary; Appendix A.2 discusses possible adaptations. 4. Retaining reference-block identity preserves distinctions that these aggregations can erase before normalization. Appendix D.1 proves this result (Proposi- tion D.1) and quantifies the coefficient-reconstruction error imposed by coarser routing (Lemma D.2). Discussion and Limitations P2TPO constructs element-level feedback from ground-truth references, so its alignment and quality scores depend on annotation accuracy and serialization conventions. Annotation noise, repeated text, and alternative valid serializations can introduce ambiguity into element matching and token labels. text: We introduced P2TPO for structure-aligned RL post-training of full-page document parsers. It preserves reference-element identity, completes feedback for missing outcomes and imperfect consensus through UAP, and localizes matched-block credit through budget-preserving SCR. Our analysis characterizes local quality contrasts that fixed additive aggregation can erase. From a shared supervised checkpoint, P2TPO exceeds four response-level baselines in five-seed mean score on all 13 primary splits across six benchmarks, including a 0.74-point gain over the strongest baseline on OmniDocBench v1.6. Additional settings and ablations support its applicability and the complementarity of outcome feedback and alignment-informed token allocation. text: P2TPO: Structure-Aligned Page-to-Token Credit Assignment for Full-Page Document Parsing A.3. Scope of reported parsing recipes Recipe scope and auxiliary tasks. HunyuanOCR’s row describes its document-parsing RL recipe, not every task supported by the model. LightOnOCR’s row covers its OCR recipe; its separate bounding-box recipe uses IoU-based localization rewards and is not element transcription. PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 uses layout detection followed by task-prompted region recognition; its RL tasks include text, formulas, and tables as well as charts, seals, and spotting. DocPO’s row covers mixed text/formula/table patch recognition. Its step-aware sharpening follows the training step and still yields one response coefficient. Document question answering. DocR1 (Xiong et al., 2025) and DocThinker (Yu et al., 2025b) optimize answers and reasoning rather than page transcriptions, so they are outside the table’s parsing targets. DocR1’s EviGRPO sums format, answer ANLS, and evidence-page F1 rewards. DocThinker combines format, answer accuracy, RoI IoU, and question-rephrasing rewards before GRPO. Both use a Sum →Scalar interface. B. text: with pieces from the aligned reference using SequenceMatcher with autojunk=False. Comparison keys strip leading and trailing whitespace from each piece. Equal pieces receive label +1, and inserted or replaced predicted pieces receive −1. A reference deletion assigns −1 to the next predicted token, or the final token at the block boundary, overriding any earlier match label. For nonempty reference-piece sequences, whitespace-only pieces and standalone display-math delimiter pieces are then assigned 0. Error labels seed the error mask. We merge error runs separated by at most 𝑔non-error tokens, including the intervening tokens in the merged mask. Positive labels outside this mask form the correct mask. SCR selects the error mask for a negative block coefficient and the correct mask for a positive coefficient. Redistribution requires the raw block reward to be at least its type-specific quality threshold. Algorithm 2 converts the selected mask into nonnegative weights with unit mean over the block. Token mapping. Predicted pieces use response-text token offsets; reference pieces use tokenizer offsets without special tokens, with per-token decoding as a fallback. Reference formula delimiters are removed before piece construction. Packed token endpoints determine each block’s span. 16

text: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi- agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning- critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL- based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph–reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time- indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout- return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Exper- iments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4%. text: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting ego trajectories that are safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi- agent interactions [2, 6, 8, 11, 13]. Despite rapid progress in learning- based planning, robust closed-loop decision making in dense ur- ban scenes remains challenging [2, 6, 13]. A core challenge is that planning performance depends not only on average-case trajec- tory realism but on learning from a small set of planning-critical trajectories—those arising in highly interactive, safety-sensitive, and rule-constrained scenarios such as merging, yielding, and in- tersection conflicts [2, 6, 13]. In practice, however, most training trajectories are semantically flat, weakly constrained, and low- conflict, contributing limited signals to the decision boundaries that matter most for planning [6]. This long-tail structure makes pure imitation learning insufficient, since abundant easy trajectories dominate supervision, while naive reinforcement learning is also inadequate because generic rewards are difficult to design stably for complex multi-agent interactions. These challenges motivate graph-structured relational modeling to prioritize planning-critical trajectories and support planning-oriented policy improvement. Existing methods improve planning from different angles, but the core issue remains unresolved. Interaction-centric methods, such as Game- Former [10], improve multi-agent relation modeling, but mainly at the representation level, without explicitly using relational struc- ture to determine trajectory value or optimization priority. Diffusion- based planners, such as Diffusion Planner [31], provide flexible multi-modal trajectory generation, while reward-guided variants such as Diffusion-ES [28] demonstrate the promise of reward-driven optimization. However, existing approaches still rely either on be- havior cloning objectives, which suffer from compounding errors and exposure bias in closed-loop inference, or on generic reward- driven optimization, which does not explicitly encode planning- oriented relational semantics. This leaves open how relational se- mantics should shape both the training distribution and the opti- mization objective, rather than serving only as scene representa- tions or sampling-time guidance. To address this gap, we propose GRID-Planner, a Graph-Reward Integrated Diffusion planner that uses graph-structured scene se- mantics to directly shape the optimization signal of generative planning. Rather than treating graph structure as just an input representation, we use it to define both trajectory importance and planning-oriented return. text: the optimization signal of generative planning. Rather than treating graph structure as just an input representation, we use it to define both trajectory importance and planning-oriented return. Our framework answers three questions left open by prior planners: which trajectories should matter more during training, how their quality should be evaluated for plan- ning, and how relational signals should reshape diffusion-based policy learning. Specifically, our framework contains three tightly coupled components: ❶Graph-Aware Importance Weighting, which upweights trajectories from complex, high-risk scenes us- ing scene-interaction centrality and collision-risk cues; ❷Rela- tional Reward Surrogate (RRS), which evaluates candidate roll- outs through time-indexed ego-centric scene graphs, producing a dense trajectory-level signal with smooth bounded penalties over safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort; and ❸Graph-Reward Integrated Diffusion Objective, which incorporates structured returns into a low-variance advantage-weighted diffusion objec- tive, coupled with an advantage-gated on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mechanism. The resulting advantage reweights diffusion denoising and gates OPSD teacher selection and updates, forming a rollout–return–advantage–update loop in which graph-reward signals directly drive policy improvement. text: Imitation-Based and Interaction-Centric Planning. A major line of work learns autonomous driving policies from expert demon- strations [2, 6, 8, 11, 12, 20, 27]. UrbanDriver [21], PlanTF [5], and PLUTO [4] achieve strong closed-loop performance through care- fully designed imitation objectives, while UniAD [8], VAD [14], VADv2 [3], SparseDrive [23], DTPP [9], GameFormer [10], Inter- Fuser [22], and Causal-Planner [29] improve scene representation and interaction modeling. However, these approaches mainly op- timize expert imitation or relational representations, without ex- plicitly using scene relations to determine trajectory importance or planner-oriented value. GRID-Planner instead uses graph structure to prioritize planning-critical trajectories and construct relational returns over safety, lane/route consistency, and comfort. Generative Planning with Diffusion. Generative planners model future trajectories as samples from expressive distributions, sup- porting multi-modal driving behaviors [15, 25]. GenAD [30], Dif- fusion Planner [31], and Diffusion-ES [28] explore latent gener- ation, diffusion-based closed-loop planning, and reward-guided sampling, respectively. Flow Planner [24], DiffusionDrive [16], and BridgeDrive [17] further improve interactive modeling and diffusion- policy design. These methods primarily focus on trajectory genera- tion or sampling-time guidance, whereas GRID-Planner incorpo- rates structured relational signals into training through trajectory prioritization, relational evaluation, and diffusion-policy refine- ment. RL-Based Policy Improvement for Generative Planning. Re- inforcement learning has been combined with diffusion policies for reward-driven optimization. DDPO [1], advantage-weighted regression methods [18, 19], and diffusion policies [26] adapt policy- improvement principles to expressive generative models. However, they generally rely on generic scalar rewards rather than planning- oriented relational semantics. GRID-Planner couples graph-weighted relational returns with advantage-weighted denoising and advantage- gated on-policy self-distillation, allowing relational signals to di- rectly shape policy updates. 3

We evaluate GRID-Planner in closed-loop simulation on two established autonomous driving benchmarks. Following the standard protocol [5, 31], we report nuPlan [2] results on Val14, Test14-random, and Test14-hard, covering general performance and long-tail robustness. We further evaluate on interPlan [7], which emphasizes interaction-intensive scenarios such as nudging around parked vehicles, unprotected overtaking, and jaywalker encounters. Evaluation Metrics. For nuPlan, we report the official Closed- Loop Score (CLS) under Non-Reactive (NR) and Reactive (R) simu- lation [2]. CLS aggregates route progress, comfort, and rule compli- ance while penalizing safety failures such as at-fault collisions. For interPlan, we report the Overall Score and representative scores on Nudge Around, High Traffic Density, and Jaywalk. Diagnostic Metrics. Beyond the official scores, we report Colli- sion Rate, corresponding to 𝑅safety; Lane Deviation, a lane/route- consistency proxy corresponding to 𝑅rule; Jerk, a smoothness indi- cator corresponding to 𝑅comfort; and Latency, the average planner- side inference time. These metrics are diagnostic only. Red-light violations are not evaluated separately due to limited traffic-signal state extraction. 4.2 Implementation Details GRID-Planner uses 2 seconds of history to predict an 8-second trajectory at 10 Hz, with 21 historical timestamps including the
title: MM ’26, November 10–14, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

text: These metrics are diagnostic only. Red-light violations are not evaluated separately due to limited traffic-signal state extraction. 4.2 Implementation Details GRID-Planner uses 2 seconds of history to predict an 8-second trajectory at 10 Hz, with 21 historical timestamps including the current frame and 80 future steps. Each waypoint is represented as (𝑥,𝑦, cos𝜃, sin𝜃) in the ego-centric frame. The scene encoder retains up to 32 neighboring agents, 70 lane polylines, 25 route-lane polylines, and 5 static control elements. Training has three stages: (1) base diffusion training for 400 epochs with AdamW (batch size 2048, learning rate 10−4, weight decay 0.01, and EMA decay 0.999), CFG, and 0.3 neighbor dropout; (2) graph-aware reward fine-tuning with GAIW and RRS for 10 epochs at 5 × 10−5; and (3) online self- distillation for 2 epochs, sampling four candidates per scene and ranking their graph-weighted returns to select the teacher and supervise the student. At inference, the distilled planner uses four update steps with a CFG scale of 1.8. Latency is the mean planner- side compute_trajectory runtime at batch size 1 on the same hardware, excluding simulator overhead, and is reported only as a relative runtime diagnostic. 4.3 Main Results nuPlan benchmark. text: GRID-Planner achieves the best overall score of 57.25, outperforming both Diffusion Planner and Flow Planner (52.90 and 54.83, respectively). The improvement is especially evident in spatially constrained and highly uncertain scenarios, including High Traffic Density (65.37 vs. 56.41 against Flow Planner) and Jaywalk (43.20 vs. 41.64 against Flow Planner, and 26.20 against Diffusion Planner). Since success in these cat- egories depends on resolving ambiguous right-of-way conflicts rather than nominal path tracking, these results support the role of the proposed relational learning mechanism in shaping safer and more interaction-aware behavior. The gains are not uniform across all categories: in Nudge Around, GRID-Planner slightly ex- ceeds Flow Planner (58.77 vs. 58.02) but remains below Diffusion Planner (60.48), suggesting that our method is most advantageous in scenarios where relational reasoning and safety–progress trade- offs under dynamic uncertainty dominate the planning difficulty. Qualitative rollouts in Fig. 5 further support this observation: in sev- eral challenging intersection scenarios, the baseline collides while GRID-Planner remains safe on the same scenes, showing improved closed-loop handling of interactive conflicts. 4.4 Ablation Studies Main ablation. text: We presented GRID-Planner, a graph–reward integrated diffusion planner that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals for autonomous driving. By combining Graph-Aware Im- portance Weighting (GAIW), a Relational Reward Surrogate (RRS), and a unified on-policy diffusion objective with actor–critic and self-distillation, our framework improves trajectory prioritiza- tion, rollout evaluation, and policy refinement in a coherent man- ner. Limitations and Future Work. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that GRID-Planner consistently improves closed- loop performance, especially in reactive and interaction-intensive scenarios, while our current design still relies on hand-crafted graph weighting and a limited set of relational reward signals; future work will explore richer relational cues, more adaptive graph-based weighting, and more efficient on-policy optimization for large-scale real-world autonomous driving deployment.
