text: Semantic segmentation is critical for the reliable navigation and scene understanding of autonomous systems, yet its performance degrades severely in low-light environments due to noise, artifacts, colour distortion, and the loss of structural details. To address this challenge, this work introduces VesperMUSE, a unified multi-modal framework designed to achieve robust image semantic segmen- tation across diverse illumination conditions. The architecture addresses the light deficiency prob- lem on multiple levels: proposing a novel physics-informed synthetic low-light adaptation algorithm, approaching Low-Light Image Enhancement (LLIE) through a thermal-guided paradigm, and finally aiming to recover the intrinsic scene details for semantic segmentation through a multi-modal fusion approach. Following enhancement, the framework dynamically integrates the primary RGB features with auxiliary thermal representations and surface normal maps highlighting geometric discontinu- ities and material boundaries. At the core of this integration is a highly scalable, modality-agnostic self-attention mechanism that extracts both global context and fine local features from an arbitrary number of auxiliary inputs. By combining and projecting these hierarchical multi-modal represen- tations into a unified component, the attention module allows the network to selectively attend to relevant cross-modal cues without requiring any architectural modifications when different sensor configurations are used. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VesperMUSE successfully recovers missing visual cues, providing a flexible, state-of-the-art (SOTA) solution for machine perception in extreme and unstructured real-world environments. 11
title: Abstract

text: Semantic Segmentation. The performance and goal-achievement capability of autonomous or Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) systems, which have become a preferred choice for navigating dangerous environments in recent years, rely strongly on scene understanding. High-level Computer Vision (CV) tasks such as pixel-level semantic segmentation [1, 2] or instance-level object detection [3] have emerged as powerful tools for mapping sensor observations into information and cues that guide decision-making. The main challenge remains robust perception under varying conditions [4, 5]. Semantic segmentation achieves scene understanding by assigning each pixel in an image to a specific class, with classes defined during training. In this way, the entire scene is parsed, and objects can be more easily identified by their shape or distinct attributes. Due to its highly reliable approach, the applications of semantic segmentation extend beyond outdoor scene parsing to do- mains such as medicine [6], indoor environments [7], and even more challenging missions such as survivor localisation [8] in hazy or poorly lit conditions. Usually, high-level CV tasks perform best under near-ideal conditions: consistent illumination that ensures accurate colour balance, without haze, smoke, noise, or other degradations. However, real- world environments rarely provide such conditions, therefore, robust systems must be capable of handling non-ideal sensor inputs [9, 10]. Low-Light Conditions. Light-deficient environments occur as frequently as daylight scenes, mak- ing them not merely an edge case of CV systems but a domain that requires rigorous treatment [12]. What makes low-light images particularly challenging is that limited illumination introduces additional issues beyond the obvious reduced exposure, such as global and local structure loss, noise, artifacts, and prominent colour distortions [13, 14]. There are multiple approaches to im- proving semantic segmentation performance under such conditions, with the main categories being: enhancement-based methods [15] (where a network is applied prior to segmentation to enhance the images), knowledge distillation [16] (where a student network trained on low-light images is con- strained to match the internal representations of a teacher network trained on well-lit data), single- network approaches (where the feature space is analyzed using frequency-domain techniques [17] with a greater emphasis being placed on edge information), and multi-modal fusion approaches [18, 19], in which the limited information in low-light images is compensated by

However, this modality presents several limitations, including poor separation of objects or surfaces with similar tempera- tures [22], background interference when ambient temperatures approximate those of objects [23], and the absence of colour information, which remains an essential cue for accurate scene parsing and object identification [24]. Despite these constraints, the practical acquisition of thermal data has become increasingly accessible. The commercial miniaturization of Long-Wave Infrared micro- bolometers has rendered these sensors both cost-effective and easy to integrate into real-world au- tonomous systems. In the scope of this study, the thermal modality is technically leveraged to en- hance low-light RGB data by providing a high Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) in environments where visible-spectrum sensors succumb to photon scarcity. Specifically for semantic segmentation, ther- mal data provides an invariant heat-signature prior very helpful for class-specific identification (e.g., distinguishing biological entities from inanimate structures). text: inanimate structures). Improving Segmentation Performance Through Enhancement. VesperMUSE adopts a pre- segmentation thermal-guided enhancement approach, where low-light images are first enhanced using a model trained separately from the semantic segmentation network. This design provides greater modularity, allowing the framework to be extended to other degradations, like haze or blur, by simply replacing the enhancement module. Another advantage is that the training data can be de- coupled, removing the need for low-light, well-lit, and semantic segmentation annotations to coexist within the same dataset. Since the enhancement network is trained independently, its predictions achieve a high degree of visual quality, as the module is optimized to approximate normal lighting conditions. In contrast, jointly trained (one-stage) networks may produce intermediate-enhanced outputs represented in latent space which is not suitable for direct human evaluation. This aspect is particularly important for the present work, as the low-light enhanced RGB map is further used as input for additional representations. Challenge Understanding Through Data. By routing the degraded inputs through the independently trained enhancement module, the network successfully recovers critical scene context, elevating the segmentation performance to 0.7010 and 0.5711 on the two datasets. While this enhancement bridges a significant gap, it does not fully restore the optimal original well-lit RGB performance (0.7855 and 0.7275). Further improvements. In the context of VesperMUSE, to aid the semantic parsing process, LLIE is conducted on the low-light images with thermal being brought as an extra representation. The in- frared imagery is later employed [9] for the segmentation training as well, since it provides relevant cues for both tasks. To make the current approach more robust, several questions need answers in order to move forward: How to integrate more structural information if thermal maps do not provide all that is needed? How will the information be fused in such a way that if specific scenarios might require more modalities, such as Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) [29], or event cameras, the network will structurally support that without architecture modifications? The answer to the first question lies in the use of surface normal maps derived from monocular depth estimation. Specifically, DepthAnything V2 [30] is employed to extract monocular depth 15

text: maps from the RGB input (which may be the original RGB or synthetic low-light adapted and en- hanced depending on the configuration and objective). These monocular depth maps provide addi- tional structural information which might be missing from the RGB and thermal maps by leverag- ing the pre-trained representations. Surface normals are then obtained by normalising these maps through gradient extraction. The main innovation introduced by the core component of the VesperMUSE, its semantic segmenta- tion module, lies in the attention mechanism employed during the encoding stage. The underlying concept is that each modality is analyzed both globally and at the level of fine local features, thereby providing a comprehensive representation. To capture the contribution of each modality, hierarchical feature maps are fused and treated as inputs to the main attention components. Given that the atten- tion mechanism is conceptually designed for one primary modality and k ∈N auxiliary modalities, it can be readily configured to support an arbitrary number of modalities with varying channel con- figurations (e.g., RGB with three channels or single-channel thermal maps). This flexibility makes the model highly adaptable to diverse scenarios and imaging conditions where the availability of different modalities is different than the current analysed scenario, thereby addressing the second question proposed before. While multi-modal semantic segmentation datasets pro- vide a high degree of reliability, and a wide range of datasets serve as effective benchmarks for LLIE, no available dataset integrates well-lit and low-light counterparts RGB, thermal imagery, structural information, and annotated semantic maps simultaneously. text: 2.1 Synthetic Low-Light Image Adaptation The development of LLIE models has been historically hampered by the limited dataset availability and the quality of light-deficient representations. Early efforts such as the SID dataset [31] focused on capturing short-exposure raw images along with long-exposure counterparts. This was a good representation of how a LLIE dataset should look like, however it was limited in terms of the format it used: RAW. The consumer and surveillance hardware operate much more easily using conven- tional formats such as PNG or JPG, which also provide more efficient computational processing. Moreover, the conversion of RAW images into other encodings fails to replicate the natural noise and illumination patterns captured in the low-light conditions, the quality of the resulting data hin- dering the supervised learning process of LLIE models. More recently, the problem with data limitation was fixed with the appearance of paired real-world datasets such as LOL [32], LOL-v2 real [33], SDSD-in/out [34], and LOL-Blur [35]. Another field of concern, however, lies in the reliance of synthetic low-light adaptation methods. Widely-used current approaches, such as the work of Yang et al. through their LOL-v2 synthetic dataset [33] have provided a very solid foundation for how synthetic low-light images should be constructed: follow- ing a real-world dataset illumination distribution extracted from multiple datasets and delivering the result into
title: 2.1 Synthetic Low-Light Image Adaptation

text: of Yang et al. through their LOL-v2 synthetic dataset [33] have provided a very solid foundation for how synthetic low-light images should be constructed: follow- ing a real-world dataset illumination distribution extracted from multiple datasets and delivering the result into an easy-to-use encoding format. 2.2 Low-Light Image Enhancement Classical Methods. LLIE has been firstly addressed using plain-enhancement [36] which focused mainly on histogram equalisation [37] and gamma correction [38, 39]. These methods amplify the brightness and contrast of underexposed images through pixel intensity transformations. Because of the complex and uneven way illumination interacts with different areas from the image, these models struggled to model the light projection process, resulting in perceptually inconsistent outputs containing over-enhanced regions and amplified noise. The later introduced Retinex theory [40] aims to decompose the image in two components: re- flectance, which represents the intrinsic scene information and illuminance, focusing on lighting variations. To better account for the illumination effects on the local and global structures, LLIE- methods have employed the theory as the underlying assumption behind the image architecture [41, 42, 43]. These models focused on estimating and refining the illumination map and recon- 19
title: 2.1 Synthetic Low-Light Image Adaptation

text: structing the image in a later stage with the more balanced and denoised reflectance map. This component-separation approach lead to more visually appealing and plausible results than the tradi- tional enhancement techniques which rely heavily on hand-crafted priors and assumptions, making them hard to generalize across multiple datasets. CNN-based Methods. Besides the improvements brought in language applications or high level CV tasks, the advancement of Deep Learning (DL) has also transformed the field of image enhance- ment becoming the dominant paradigm [14, 44, 45]. One of the earliest DL models on the scene of LLIE was LLNet [46] which proved that supervised feature learning can improve brightness and contrast while also recovering lost details. Generative models, like EnGAN [15], focused on creat- ing a direct mapping from low-light images to their enhanced counterparts by employing an end- to-end framework. These methods further improved upon traditional hand-crafted heuristic-based algorithms through hierarchical feature extraction. The Retinex theory [40] is furthermore employed as an assumption, leveraging the ability of DL frameworks to learn feature decomposition. While such models, benefit from both physical priors and data-driven learning, they often require multi-stage training pipelines through subnetwork spe- cialisation [42] on tasks such as: decomposition, illumination/reflectance enhancement, and recon- struction. As a result, the computational and training complexity of this kind of models are high. To

As a result, the computational and training complexity of this kind of models are high. To solve this, one-stage Retinex-inspired Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have also been pro- posed in order to increase the computational efficiency, but they struggle with noise mitigation and artifacts, resulting in an unsatisfactory enhancement process. Another issue that CNN-based models exhibit is the limited receptive field of convolutional layers, hence reducing their ability to capture long-range spatial dependencies constructing the global con- textual relationship across distant image regions. As light’s interaction with the scene is not linear, hence why histogram-matching models fail in the LLIE domain, this limitation restricts the models’ capacity of capturing diverse scene structures and mapping the relationships between them. ViT-based Methods. To overcome the inherent locality of convolutional operators, ViT-based models [27, 47] have dominated the SOTA models charts for LLIE in the past years. The success achieved in machine translation by the Transformer architecture [48], has also spread to CV and more specifically to image enhancement. The principal particularity that ViTs possess is the self- attention module which manages to capture long-range dependencies which guide the enhancement process towards a complex resolution of the LLIE challenge.

text: Several architectures have marked the evolution of using ViTs [27] in LLIE. For example, UFormer [49] adapts the U-shaped [26] encoder-decoder paradigm, replacing the standard convolutions found in U-Net [26] with Transformer blocks while preserving level-wise skip connections. Retinexformer [50] incorporates illumination representations into the self-attention mechanism to model non-local interactions across regions with varying lighting conditions. More recent work, such as ISALux [51] or ModalFormer [52], successfully manage to integrate semantic and structure priors into the self-attention module aiming to compensate the light-deficiency induced detail loss with visual or feature-based information represented through different modalities. Despite their strong performance, Transformer-based methods face notable computational chal- lenges. The self-attention mechanism incurs substantial computational complexity due to its reliance on the spatial dimensions of the feature maps. To mitigate this limitation, several methods, such as Restormer [53], DepthLux [54], employ different strategies: computing the attention map channel wise considering the depth of the feature map as the number of channels, contracting the feature space before the self-attention module and then expanding it back to its original dimensions, or re- placing convolutions with their more efficient variation, depthwise separable convolutions. RGB-Thermal Fusion for LLIE. RGB-Thermal fusion has recently been explored to enhance ro- bustness in extreme low-light conditions by leveraging the illumination-invariant nature of thermal imagery. In particular, some studies [55] propose

RGB-Thermal fusion has recently been explored to enhance ro- bustness in extreme low-light conditions by leveraging the illumination-invariant nature of thermal imagery. In particular, some studies [55] propose a thermal-aware ViT architecture, where thermal features are explicitly embedded into the transformer pipeline to guide global feature modeling un- der severe illumination degradation. Complementarily, Jha et al. focus on the interaction between illumination cues derived from the low-light RGB image and the corresponding thermal map, de- signing a mechanism that aligns and integrates these complementary representations for more stable enhancement [56]. These works demonstrate that modeling cross-modal dependencies, especially between illumination and thermal structure, can significantly improve detail recovery and perceptual consistency in challenging low-light scenarios. 2.3 Modality Fusion for Image Semantic Segmentation Multi-modal semantic segmentation has emerged as an effective strategy for improving scene under- standing and feature richness limitations under real-world conditions where RGB might be insuffi- cient [57]. Complementary sensing modalities such as thermal (infrared) or depth maps have been included as inputs to improve the information representation of a specific scene [9]. Depth maps 21

text: provide geometric and distance cues that can help disambiguate low-contrast regions and cluttered backgrounds [58], while thermal images capture thermic distributions, offering a visual representa- tion which is not subject to change under diverse light patterns or other deficiencies often noticed in nature like smoke or haze [20]. Semantic segmentation is not the only high-level CV task that has been benefiting from adding multi-modality in learning, with object detection, tracking, autonomous driving perception systems [59] also improving performance by leveraging multiple representations of the same scenes. In the case of RGB-Depth semantic segmentation, early methods focused on fusing modalities at the input or feature level with some approaches directly concatenating RGB and depth maps or fusing them by summation [60, 61]. In time, models have evolved to a two-stream architecture [4], where independent networks extract features separately before integrating them in the decoding process. The recent focus has been placed on feature fusion approach which separates the fusion logic from the backbone and employing modules like Separation-and-Aggregation Gate [62] or Attention Com- plementary Modules [63] to provide parallel modality streams at each hierarchical level. A significant focal point of recent work is discriminative treatment of modalities [64]. This repre- sents a change from the initial models which treated all network layers equally. This involves designing distinct models for different hierarchies: enhancing shallow spatial details (thermal-focused) and deep semantic features (RGB-focused) separately. Methods frequently integrate channel weighted selection and spatial-attention mechanisms to mitigate the inherent discrepancies (originating from distinct under- lying data distributions) between modalities [44]. The inherent limitations of CNNs, stemming from their constrained receptive fields, are also evident in modality fusion models. The Transformer architecture [27] has emerged as a compelling solution to this issue [66]. Driven by the capacity of the self-attention mechanism to model complex rela- tionships across different contexts, current research is shifting from dedicated dual-modality models toward unified architectures. While earlier methods perform well on specific pairings like RGB- Depth or RGB-Thermal [67], unified frameworks capable of integrating multiple concurrent data streams offer a much richer understanding of scene context, semantics, and structure. Consequently, these architectures yield superior performance on advanced scene understanding tasks. 22

3.1 Framework Design and Motivation The framework behind VesperMUSE is based on three main components each having a dedicated role in the focus of this study: finding solutions for improving semantic segmentation under both low-light and well illuminated scenes. VesperMUSE can be run both in low-light or normal light configuration. If the latter is activated, then the framework starts from Stage 3. Stage 1: Low-Light Synthetic Adaptation. The first step is obtaining the synthetic low-light imag- ing which will be processed using the algorithm presented in Section 3.2.1. To link this framework as closely as possible to real world scenarios, the reasoning was physics-informed. Stage 2: Low-Light Image Enhancement. After the low-light maps are processed they serve as inputs to the thermal-guided LLIE module described in Section 3.3, along with the thermal imaging. The LLIE model is trained under a supervised approach trying to predict the original RGB map coming from the two focus datasets: PST900 [8] and CART [25]. The training and test splits are based on the ones used for the semantic segmentation stage. The result of the training process is the best checkpoint in terms of Peak-Signal-to-Noise-Ratio (PSNR), each dataset having its own selected checkpoint. Stage 3: Obtaining the Surface Normal maps. The RGB image (LLIE or not) serves as the in- put to the DepthAnything V2
title: 3.1 Framework Design and Motivation

text: training process is the best checkpoint in terms of Peak-Signal-to-Noise-Ratio (PSNR), each dataset having its own selected checkpoint. Stage 3: Obtaining the Surface Normal maps. The RGB image (LLIE or not) serves as the in- put to the DepthAnything V2 [30] model, the resulting map being a monocular depth estimation. This representation is then used to produce surface normals by taking the gradients of it and thereby aiming to normalise the structural imagery. Stage 4: Fusion-based Semantic Segmentation. The three inputs corresponding to the same scene: RGB, thermal, and surface normal are then passed to the Fusion Vision Transformer which processes each of them using a dedicated pre-trained backbone and then fuses them in a modality- agnostic manner. After the features have been fused, a decoding process commences processing the output of the framework, the segmented map. Likewise LLIE, each dataset has its own trained checkpoint selected on the mIoU performance. 24

text: 3.2 Modalities 3.2.1 Synthetic low-light adaptation algorithm To show that semantic segmentation on low-light images can be improved using additional modal- ities, it required a robust real-environments informed synthesis pipeline. The current methods are limited in terms of: input data format (relying on the RAW format), noise modeling (linear noise used as implicit), global histogram matching (introducing unwanted artifacts, as colour and lumi- nance information are not separated), and fixed parameter configuration (controlling environment variables is impossible). As a result, VesperMUSE framework proposes a novel pipeline for obtaining synthetic low-light images from RGB data. The algorithm aims to achieve a physics-informed degradation, accounting for the effect low-light conditions have on the visual representations. Real-World Illumination Distribution. Furthermore, its effectiveness is largely attributed to the intrinsic phys- ical properties it captures, namely the thermal inertia and emissivity of different materials and sur- faces. These characteristics offer complementary information to the Fusion Vision Transformer, beyond what is available in the visible spectrum. In the PST900 dataset [8], which depicts a subterranean environment with minimal heat sources, thermal imaging acts as a reliable structural cue, enabling the detection of humans even in the pres- ence of obscurants. To better extract the context of the scene, a monocular depth map is extracted to highlight the structural and material differences between objects or surfaces. The noise and colour distortions, attenuated but still present in the enhanced RGB images and the thermal consistency of nearby objects in thermal maps might misguide the network in distinguishing edges and sepa- ration of entities. The first order gradients of the depth map are taken and turned into unit normal vectors to isolate and emphasize the geometric discontinuities where objects might protrude from their backgrounds. Furthermore, the scale-invariant representation of the geometric features pro- vides the robustness needed in terms of the relative position of the objects to the camera, enabling a informative features extraction for close objects, as found in the PST900 dataset [8], and distant objects as in the CART dataset [25]. 30

(3.18) 3.3 Low-Light Image Enhancement Vision Transformer The architecture of the VesperMUSE LLIE module follows a U-shaped [26] encoder-decoder struc- ture, a widely adopted design in ViT-based [27] image restoration due to its capability for hierar- chical, multi-scale feature extraction and progressive feature refinement. The overall structure is organized into three principal components: an encoder, a bottleneck, and a decoder. At each step, the resulting feature maps from the two components are normalized using Layer Normalisation (LN) and added with the skip connections, originating from the previous step. The LLIE objective is formulated as a weighted hybrid loss that jointly enforces pixel-level fidelity, perceptual realism, structural consistency, and semantic preservation. While the perceptual loss enforces similarity in a generic feature space to improve visual realism, it does not explicitly guarantee preservation of task-relevant se- mantic content. In LLIE, an approach which produces visually appealing images through contrast and colour balance amplification, does not imply that the model is optimized to enhance images for downstream tasks. Usually, it is quite the opposite as the type of visual composition which is ap- pealing to the human eye is not informative enough for computer scene-understanding tasks such as semantic segmentation or object detection. 35

text: 3.4 Fusion Vision Transformer Encoding Phase. The objective of the Fusion Vision Transformer is to effectively integrate an arbi- trary number of input modalities, defined as a primary modality, Mmain, and k ∈N auxiliary modali- ties, M1,k. The modality-agnostic nature of the architecture is enabled by the self-attention mechanism within the Fusion Encoder Block. This design effectively integrates global and local patterns from the aux- iliary modalities while remaining inherently scalable. It accommodates an arbitrary number of in- puts, without requiring structural modifications to the underlying fusion method. Features are processed using a encoder-decoder path, where the encoding process is conducted in 4 consecutive steps each of them being represented by the Fusion Encoding Block. The decoding process does not perform fusion as it process a single feature space originating from the end of the encoding stage. The fusion mechanism of the proposed Fusion Vision Transformer is performed during the encoding stage, while the decoding stage is dedicated to feature refinement and coher- ence enhancement. The decoding process is structured around a series of blocks that progressively refine the representations across three hierarchical spatial levels. At each level, skip connections from the corresponding encoding stages are concatenated with the outputs of the decoding blocks. This design facilitates stable gradient propagation and mitigates the information bottleneck that typ- ically arises when integrating heterogeneous visual modalities characterized by distinct underlying probability distributions. (3.44) 3.4.1 Fusion Encoder Block The Fusion Encoder Block represents the unitary component of the encoding stage of the Fusion Vi- sion Transformer. Its role is to coherently combine the features originating from multiple modalities and to assess the unique information each one of them contains and how this information interacts with the other sets of specific data from the other modalities. To achieve this, the Fusion Encoder Block employs 2 modules: the Fusion Self-Attention Module which combines and selects the most relevant features based on the current context and a FFN which further refines the fused maps. The modules interact through skip connection which aid the gradient flow and normalisation layers that provide data distribution unity across the samples. The principal advantage of the proposed Fusion Encoder Block lies in its structural scalability to an arbitrary number of modalities, k ∈N. The only requirement is the designation of one modality as the primary modality, while the remaining k modalities are treated as auxiliary. (3.46) 3.4.2 Fusion Self-Attention Module The main constituent of Vision Transformers is the self-attention module which captures relevant features from the images, highlighting the prevalent information from the visual space. However, its 40

text: effectiveness represents a compromise in terms of computational complexity with the standard vi- sion self attention yielding a complexity of O(H2W 2), where H and W represent the height and the width of the image. To partially mitigate this problem, the Fusion Self-Attention Module adheres to the solution proposed by Restormer [53], where the attention scores produce a feature map in RC×C, hence the complexity of the the self-attention module becoming O(HWC), where C represents the projection size of the Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V ) components. Besides computational complexity, most self-attention modules fail to integrate both local and global features from the image, treating the projection of the images as a unitary feature. The ac- curacy of the down-stream task on which VesperMUSE focuses on, image semantic segmentation, heavily relies on local components such as edges, isolated illumination patterns, and noise. The proposed Fusion Self-Attention Module aims to achieve a both global and local feature extraction, which allows the model to adapt the latent representations considering a wider range of information. text: 3.4.6 Fusion Vision Transformer Loss function In the datasets VesperMUSE tests semantic segmentation on, there is both a significant structural and semantic difference between the classes (especially on the CART [25] dataset) and also a very heavy class imbalance. To ensure multi-modal feature alignment and good class representation a weighted hybrid loss function is employed which also acts on multiple levels allowing deep supervi- sion. Considering Lmain(·, ·) as the hybrid loss function, P(0) as the final prediction, and P(s) as the inter- mediate predictions originating from the decoding path and weighted by λs, with Y(0) denoting the ground-truth labels and Y(s) representing the ground-truth labels resized to match the spatial reso- lution of the corresponding deep supervision outputs, the total loss function Ltotal is formulated as follows: Ltotal = Lhybrid (︁ P(0), Y )︁ + ∑︂ s∈S λs Lhybrid(P(s),Y(s)). (3.62) Hybrid Loss. Lhybrid(·, ·) is a weighted combination of the multi-class Focal loss which operates at pixel level and is derived from the cross-entropy objective and the weighted Dice loss, which is region-based and directly optimizes the overlap between the predicted and ground-truth masks. Since the Dice loss is computed from class-wise statistics it is less sensitive to pixel-level imbal- ance and better captures structural and object-level coherence. The relative contribution of the con- stituents of the hybrid loss,

Since the Dice loss is computed from class-wise statistics it is less sensitive to pixel-level imbal- ance and better captures structural and object-level coherence. The relative contribution of the con- stituents of the hybrid loss, Lhybrid, is balanced by the coefficients α and β. Lhybrid = α LFocal + β LDice. (3.63) Multi-class Focal Loss. LFocal(·, ·) is a pixel-wise classification loss designed to mitigate severe class imbalance. The strong pixel-density of the background class in both datasets can overwhelm the gradient signal and hinder learning of minority or hard classes. The Focal loss addresses this issue by introducing a modulating factor that reduces the importance of well-classified samples and emphasizes misclassified or uncertain predictions. Additionally, class-dependent weights are incorporated to further compensate for dataset imbalance. Let zi,c denote the logit corresponding to class c at pixel i, C the total number of classes, and pi,c the softmax probability defined as: 45

By incorporating class-dependent weights, the formulation further compensates for skewed class distributions while preserving structural consistency across object regions. text: The evaluations for VesperMUSE across all tasks is conducted on two main datasets: PST900 [8] and CART [25]. The low-light adapted images and later enhanced are conducted on the same splits as used for the semantic segmentation evaluation. PST900. The PST900 benchmark [8] consists of 894 synchronized RGB-Thermal image pairs ac- quired within demanding subterranean settings. The dataset features pixel-level semantic annota- tions for five distinct object categories: background, hand drill, backpack, fire extinguisher, and survivor. All modalities maintain a native resolution of 1280 × 720 pixels. For experimental con- sistency, the data is partitioned into training and evaluation subsets following a 2 : 1 distribution ratio. CART. The CART dataset [25] comprises 2,282 co-registered RGB-Thermal pairs captured across heterogeneous outdoor environments, including aquatic regions (rivers, lakes, coastlines), arid deserts, and dense forestation. Semantic labels are provided for a comprehensive 10-class taxon- omy: bare ground, rocky terrain, developed structures, road, shrubs, trees, sky, water, vehicles, and person. The imagery is provided at a resolution of 960 × 640 pixels. The corpus is stochastically divided into training, validation, and testing sets using a 6 : 1 : 1 ratio, respectively. Empirical contributions. The results achieved by VesperMUSE across all levels and tasks can be summarised as: • Robust Synthetic Low-Light Adaptation: The synthetic adaptation of the PST900 [8] and CART [25]
title: The evaluations for VesperMUSE across all tasks is conducted on two main datasets: PST900 [8]

text: using a 6 : 1 : 1 ratio, respectively. Empirical contributions. The results achieved by VesperMUSE across all levels and tasks can be summarised as: • Robust Synthetic Low-Light Adaptation: The synthetic adaptation of the PST900 [8] and CART [25] datasets achieves a superior SNR of approximately 10.7 dB and a physical Gamma distribution of 1.00. These metrics surpass established synthetic low-light adaptation pipelines such as the one used for creating LOL-v2 synthetic [33] in terms of modeling low-light envi- ronments, ensuring that the low-light data maintains realistic luminance statistics and physics- informed consequences of light-deficiency. • Efficient and High-Performance LLIE: The VesperMUSE LLIE component demonstrates significant performance improvements over existing methods, achieving a 29.5% PSNR in- crease over LYT-Net [47] and a 2.3% increase over Retinexformer [50] on the synthetically- adapted CART dataset [25]. Notably, the model achieves performance comparable to the state- of-the-art ISALux [51] while utilizing only 0.454M parameters, representing a 75.4% reduction in model complexity. • State-of-the-Art Segmentation on CART: On the CART dataset [25], VesperMUSE estab- lishes a new performance ceiling with an mIoU of 0.7672, outperforming the top-performing 49

Substantial class-wise gains are observed in challenging categories, including Vehicles (0.6314) and Person (0.3426), vali- dating the effectiveness of thermal and structure-aware multi-modal fusion in outdoor environ- ments. • Superior Generalization on PST900: Evaluation on the PST900 dataset [8] yields a competi- tive mIoU of 0.8559, representing a 1.4% improvement over LASNet [65] and a 3.1% increase over MDNet [74]. The method sets new accuracy benchmarks for task-critical objects, outper- forming CM-SSM [73] by 2.9% for Hand-Drill (0.8282) and by 2.4% for Fire-Ext. (0.8776), highlighting the framework’s robustness across indoor dark scenarios. 4.1 Synthetic Low-Light Image Adaptation The synthetic low-light adaptation pipeline described in Section 3.2.1 must demonstrate robustness and reliability in accurately emulating real low-light conditions across all key factors that influence such environments, including illumination levels (both linear and non-linear/gamma-based), noise characteristics, inter-pixel relationships, and global statistical properties such as mean and standard deviation computed over the entire dataset. To enable a rigorous quantitative comparison with existing datasets, encompassing both real and synthetic low-light imagery, a diverse set of evaluation metrics is employed. This comprehensive analysis ensures a thorough assessment of the effects induced by light deficiency and the fidelity of the proposed synthetic generation process. The proposed metrics are as follows: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR). The goal is to quantify the level of corruption introduced by noise during the low-light generation process, while remaining invariant to global intensity scaling be- tween the reference and degraded images. This is important because realistic low-light images are fundamentally characterized by photon-limited noise, and matching the real-world SNR distribution is critical for modeling the effect of low-light condition on the overall composition of the image. In the following formulation, N denotes the reference normal-light image, L the low-light image, µN and µL their mean intensities, α a scaling factor used to align global intensity levels, σN the standard deviation of the noise residual, and Ωthe image domain. text: 4.2 Low-Light Image Enhancement Evaluation Metrics. To quantitatively evaluate the fidelity of the reconstructed images, PSNR is the main utilized measure. This metric is defined by the ratio between the maximum possible power of a signal and the power of corrupting noise that affects the fidelity of its representation. In this formu- lation, M and N represent the image dimensions, I(i, j) and K(i, j) denote the pixel intensities of the ground truth and reconstructed images at coordinates (i, j), and MAXI signifies the maximum possible pixel value. To motivate the design of the proposed Fusion Encoder Block, it is compared against a baseline strategy that relies on naive concatenation. In this baseline, multi-modal features are simply concatenated along the channel dimension prior to passing through a standard Transformer block. As shown in Table 4.7, the proposed cross-attention fusion approach yields a substantial performance improvement, outperforming the concatenation baseline by ≈4% mIoU. This performance gap highlights the limitations of early concatenation. While concatenation aggre- gates multi-modal data into a unified tensor, it forces the subsequent layers to implicitly learn the cross-modal alignments from scratch without any structured guidance. In contrast, the proposed fusion mechanism explicitly models the spatial and semantic correlations between the primary and auxiliary modalities. By utilizing cross-attention, the network dynamically queries the auxil- iary streams to enhance the primary features, ensuring that the model selectively attends
title: Primary Modality

text: contrast, the proposed fusion mechanism explicitly models the spatial and semantic correlations between the primary and auxiliary modalities. By utilizing cross-attention, the network dynamically queries the auxil- iary streams to enhance the primary features, ensuring that the model selectively attends to relevant multi-modal cues rather than treating all concatenated channels with equal initial weight. Replacing Decoders with Convolutions. As detailed in Section 3.4.4, the core feature refinement component within the VesperMUSE decoder is a lightweight, attention-based Transformer block. This module is specifically designed to refine the multi-scale fused features, utilizing self-attention to dynamically weigh and prioritize spatial information that is most relevant to the current semantic context. To validate this design choice, an ablation study was conducted where these Transformer blocks were replaced with standard pointwise convolutions, effectively removing the global context- aggregation capabilities of the attention mechanism while maintaining a similar channel dimension- ality. 67

In the current configuration, the main issue that is persistent within the low-light synthetic pipeline is that a small sample of the low-light samples are excessively degraded so that the LLIE module cannot recover lost informa- tion. The source of this issue remains unknown, however it is suspected that the issue comes from increasing the variability of illumination in the low-light conditions. As a result, a very few number of samples from the final light distribution are affected by this issue. Figure 5.1 presents a part of the affected samples with some managing to capture the overall structure of the image keeping some of the objects observable while others represent a totally noise and artifacts-covered representation which cannot be correctly evaluated by the segmentation module. A solution to this problem would be either removing the affected samples or further tuning the syn- thetic low-light adaptation algorithm to diagnose problematic scenarios and increase the illumina- tion threshold while keeping the noise levels lower than for other samples. A comparative analysis of the global intensity dis- tributions (Figure 5.2) reveals that the LLIE module introduces luminance-dependent chromatic aberrations via non-linear channel uncoupling. Specifically, in the shadow and mid-tone regimes (0 ≤I ≤150), the model disproportionately attenuates the blue channel relative to the source distribution, inducing an unnatural warm colour cast. Conversely, in the extreme highlight regime 70

text: (I →255), the output exhibits anomalous green-channel clipping, with saturation peaks signifi- cantly exceeding both the original image limits and concurrent RGB channels. This divergent colour distortion fundamentally disrupts the intrinsic RGB ratios across the dynamic range, highlighting a deficiency in colour constancy and necessitating the integration of cross-channel coupled tone mapping. Since the current loss function configuration does not have a colour loss integrated, this would strongly benefit the reduction of channel-based colour discrepancies between the well-lit images and the predicted maps from the LLIE module. In this case, the loss function would receive a new term, namely a colour-focused loss. Standard spatial losses penalize the necessary brightness enhancements in low-light processing. To decouple intensity from colour, RGB channels for each pixel are treated as a 3D vector. By comput- ing the cosine similarity between the input vector (vin i ) and output vector (vout i ) across all N pixels, the colour loss (Lcolour) selectively penalizes chromatic angular deviation while ignoring magnitude shifts, preserving intrinsic RGB ratios. text: The subsequent development of VesperMUSE should primarily target both performance enhance- ment and the reduction of computational complexity. At present, further improvements in perfor- mance can be facilitated by adopting more efficient backbone architectures, potentially surpassing those derived from the ResNet family. Additionally, the utilization of modality-specific backbones for thermal and structural inputs represents a promising direction, as these are expected to outper- form the current convolutional adaptation strategy employed within the model. Furthermore, it is worthwhile to investigate alternative representations of image information, such as operating in different colour spaces or explicitly decomposing the input into low- and high-frequency components within the LLIE module. Such approaches may enable a more principled treatment of light irradiation, which has been shown to be an effective strategy in LLIE tasks. 5.3 Final Thoughts The proposed framework is intended to establish a foundation for future advancements in seman- tic segmentation under challenging and highly variable illumination conditions. Despite recent progress, the field continues to be constrained by the limited availability of diverse and represen- tative datasets, which significantly hinders the development of robust and generalizable methods. The scenarios explored in this study reflect realistic and often critical environments, including safety- sensitive missions where reliability is paramount. text: Data-Efficient ConvNeXt Pretraining for High-Resolution Sentinel-1 GRD SAR Representation Learning⋆ Yuki Natsumea,∗, Sang-Ho Yunb,c,d, Chai Kiat Yeoa aCollege of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore bEarth Observatory of Singapore, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore cAsian School of the Environment, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore dSchool of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
title: Data-Efficient ConvNeXt Pretraining for High-Resolution

text: Labeled Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (S1GRD) datasets remain scarce, limiting supervised deep learning for land-surface remote sensing, while self-supervised pretraining for this domain has been dominated by Vision Transformer (ViT)-based masked image modeling requiring sub- stantial data and compute. We propose SparK-SAR, a sparse convolutional masked pretraining framework built on SparK and ConvNeXt, designed to exploit convolutional inductive biases for S1GRD imagery under constrained compute. SparK-SAR makes three core technical con- tributions: (i) ConvNeXt-RS, a domain-adapted encoder that halves the stem stride (4×→2×) to produce 14×14 feature maps at stride 16×, providing 4× more spatial tokens at identical parameter count; (ii) a lightweight ConvNeXt-512 reconstruction decoder with PixelShuffle up- sampling that reduces pretraining VRAM by 7.5–8.5% per GPU relative to a UNet-128 baseline while matching its accuracy; and (iii) an empirical characterization of FP16 mixed-precision pretraining instability in the standard SparK UNet-768 decoder on S1GRD data, complemented by a finding that finetuning with layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD) improves downstream performance of pretrained encoders. On four Copernicus-Bench S1GRD tasks, our finetuned 27.8M-parameter ConvNeXt-RS encoder improves over a non-pretrained baseline by +4.7, +5.0, +5.8, and +1.4 pp on EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1, DFC2020-S1, and Flood-S1 respectively, and outperforms the Copernicus-FM ViT (139M parameters, frozen) on three of four tasks at roughly 5× fewer parameters. A pretraining data-scaling study reveals task-dependent data effi- ciency:
title: Data-Efficient ConvNeXt Pretraining for High-Resolution

text: +4.7, +5.0, +5.8, and +1.4 pp on EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1, DFC2020-S1, and Flood-S1 respectively, and outperforms the Copernicus-FM ViT (139M parameters, frozen) on three of four tasks at roughly 5× fewer parameters. A pretraining data-scaling study reveals task-dependent data effi- ciency: classification saturates with as little as 10–25% of the SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 corpus, while dense prediction continues to improve significantly up to 25–50%. SparK-SAR’s novelty there- fore lies not only in adapting sparse masked modeling to two-channel SAR imagery through the ConvNeXt-RS encoder, but also in the extensive empirical analysis accompanying it, spanning pretraining data scaling, representation dynamics, and geographic data leakage. text: Unlike optical sensors, synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites image the land surface using microwave backscatter rather than reflected sunlight, enabling all-weather, day-and-night acqui- sition well suited to land-cover mapping, flood assessment, and environmental change monitor- ing, particularly in regions where persistent cloud cover limits optical observation (Moreira et al., 2013). Since its 2014 launch, ESA’s Sentinel-1 mission has revisited most of the globe every 6– 12 days, accumulating a large and continually growing archive of freely available Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (S1GRD) imagery (European Space Agency, 2012). This unlabeled archive is abundant, but SAR imagery is difficult for non-experts to interpret visually, making manual annotation of large SAR scenes highly labor intensive. Publicly available labeled SAR benchmarks have therefore stayed small relative to computer vision norms, which in turn limits how well supervised deep learning models can perform on SAR downstream tasks (Wang et al., 2022). Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers one route to transferable representations without rely- ing on manually labeled data, and masked image modeling (MIM) (He et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022) is a natural fit for S1GRD pretraining specifically: it requires no S1GRD-appropriate pho- tometric augmentation scheme of the kind contrastive methods depend on (Wang et al., 2022), and it naturally yields the dense, patch-level representations that earth observation’s dense pre- diction tasks need. Existing MIM
title: 1. Introduction

text: S1GRD pretraining specifically: it requires no S1GRD-appropriate pho- tometric augmentation scheme of the kind contrastive methods depend on (Wang et al., 2022), and it naturally yields the dense, patch-level representations that earth observation’s dense pre- diction tasks need. Existing MIM implementations, however, are almost all built on Vision Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) encoders, which typically demand large pretraining corpora and heavy compute to perform well; Copernicus-FM (Wang et al., 2025b), for instance, needed 512 GPU hours on 4×A100 GPUs and multi-modal inputs spanning four Sentinel mis- sions (Sentinel-1, 2, 3, 5P) to reach competitive results. For many research groups and applied teams working with SAR data, matching the com- pute scale needed to pretrain these large foundation models is itself out of reach. We therefore restrict this study’s primary comparisons to end-to-end finetuned convolutional neural network (CNN) encoders rather than reporting frozen ViT foundation model backbones as directly fine- tuned baselines. This is not solely a matter of compute: Copernicus-Bench’s own published learning-rate search for these models (10−4, 10−3, 10−2) was validated only for frozen-backbone and decoder-head finetuning, not for full end-to-end finetuning, so no full-finetuning result for these architectures could be defended as using a properly validated learning rate. Reporting one without a fair hyperparameter search would conflate architectural differences with an unvali- dated finetuning setup rather

text: not for full end-to-end finetuning, so no full-finetuning result for these architectures could be defended as using a properly validated learning rate. Reporting one without a fair hyperparameter search would conflate architectural differences with an unvali- dated finetuning setup rather than isolate them. A rigorous evaluation of full fine-tuning for these foundation models, encompassing an architecture-specific learning-rate search, appropriate reg- ularization schedules, and comparable per-model tuning budgets, would constitute a dedicated study in its own right and lies outside this paper’s scope. The frozen-encoder results we do report (Table 6) are included only as a reference point, not as the primary comparison. CNN architectures, in contrast, bring stronger local inductive biases, remain data efficient under modest compute budgets, and can be finetuned end-to-end even on the small downstream datasets typical of SAR applications. SparK (Tian et al., 2023) was developed and validated on natural-image benchmarks such as ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009), and porting its default UNet- 768 (Ronneberger et al., 2015) decoder directly to S1GRD data at the prescribed learning rate proves numerically unstable: FP16 mixed precision training produces NaN losses, forcing either a redesigned decoder or a different learning rate. Building on these two lines of work, we introduce SparK-SAR: a high-resolution sparse masked pretraining framework for S1GRD imagery that combines SparK (Tian et al., 2023) and 2

text: ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022) and is designed to run under a constrained compute budget. We structure our contributions around three questions: whether sparse convolutional masked pre- training, previously developed and validated only on natural images, can be adapted to produce transferable representations for S1GRD SAR imagery under constrained compute; how much pretraining data and downstream labeled data this benefit actually requires; and whether the ob- served gains are genuine, rather than an artifact of geographic overlap between the pretraining corpus and the downstream evaluation sets. Adapting sparse masked pretraining to S1GRD SAR imagery. • ConvNeXt-RS encoder: a domain-adapted ConvNeXt encoder for SAR dense prediction, reducing stem stride from 4× to 2× to produce 14×14 feature maps (stride 16×) instead of the standard 7×7 (stride 32×), providing 4× more spatial tokens at identical parameter count (Section 3.1). • Lightweight reconstruction decoders: documentation of FP16 mixed precision pretrain- ing instability with the standard UNet-768 decoder on S1GRD data, and evaluation of UNet-128 and ConvNeXt-512 alternatives that stabilize pretraining, with ConvNeXt-512 reducing pretraining VRAM by 7.5–8.5% per GPU at matched accuracy (Section 3.2). • LLRD finetuning recipe: a finding that layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD) improves downstream task performance and reduces across-seed variance when finetuning the UNet- 128-pretrained SparK encoder, but does not help a non-pretrained one (Section 3.4). text: 2.1. Masked Image Modeling Building on masked language modeling (Devlin et al., 2019), masked image modeling (MIM) has become the leading approach to self-supervised visual pretraining. MAE (He et al., 2022) showed that reconstructing raw pixels from a small visible subset (as little as 25%) of ViT patches produces representations that transfer well at scale, and SimMIM (Xie et al., 2022) car- ried the same reconstruction objective over to hierarchical Swin Transformers (Liu et al., 2021). I-JEPA (Assran et al., 2023) took a different route, predicting latent representations of the masked regions instead of pixel values, which pushes the model toward semantic structure over low-level texture. These ViT-based approaches are effective but data- and compute-hungry. Convolutional al- ternatives have narrowed that gap: MCMAE (Gao et al., 2022) combines convolution and trans- former blocks in a hybrid masked autoencoder, while SparK (Tian et al., 2023), the framework this work builds on, shows that sparse masked modeling works directly on purely hierarchical CNNs (ResNet (He et al., 2016), ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022)) with no transformer component at all. MMEarth (Nedungadi et al., 2024) is a concurrent example in the electro-optical remote sensing domain, pairing a ConvNeXt V2 (Woo et al., 2023) backbone with multi-modal MIM objectives on electro-optical Sentinel-2 imagery; we pursue the same CNN MIM direction on a different modality,

Self-Supervised Learning for Remote Sensing In their survey of SSL for remote sensing, Wang et al. (2022) group existing methods into two dominant paradigms, contrastive and generative. 4
title: Verifying that the observed gains reflect genuine transfer rather than geographic leak-

text: Among the contrastive methods, SeCo (Mañas et al., 2021) builds positive pairs from sea- sonal multi-temporal imagery, and GASSL (Ayush et al., 2021) instead treats geographic co- location as a proxy for scene similarity. Both, however, rely on augmentation pipelines built around electro-optical statistics, which do not transfer cleanly to SAR backscatter. MIM has also been adopted for electro-optical remote sensing. SatMAE (Cong et al., 2022) adapted MAE for multi-spectral and multi-temporal satellite data. Scale-MAE (Reed et al., 2023) introduced scale-aware positional encodings for images at varying ground sample distances. FG- MAE (Wang et al., 2025a) proposed feature-guided reconstruction targets better aligned with semantic downstream tasks. A separate line of work pairs Sentinel-1 SAR with electro-optical data rather than treat- ing SAR in isolation. SoftCon (Wang et al., 2024) pretrains contrastively across multispectral and SAR imagery using multi-label land-cover supervision as guidance. DOFA (Xiong et al., 2024) takes a different route, using a dynamic spectral adapter, so that a single ViT can ingest whatever sensor modality it is given. CROMA (Fuller et al., 2023) instead unifies contrastive and masked autoencoding objectives within one radar-optical model, and Copernicus-FM (Wang et al., 2025b) pushes this further still, training a multi-modal ViT across four Sentinel missions on 18.7M aligned images at a reported cost of roughly 512 GPU hours on NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

These models perform well, but their multi-modal inputs and near-exclusive reliance on frozen- encoder evaluation make them a poor match for the SAR-only, constrained-compute setting this work targets. 2.3. SAR-Specific Self-Supervised Learning Compared to optical imagery, SSL research targeting SAR data exclusively is still com- paratively unexplored. Allen et al. (2023) demonstrated that large-scale MAE pretraining on Sentinel-1 S1GRD data can substantially reduce label requirements across two downstream tasks, vegetation-cover prediction and land-cover classification, with the pretraining benefit gen- eralizing geographically and increasing, rather than merely holding up, on regions outside the pretraining set. SAR-JEPA (Li et al., 2024) introduced a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA)- based approach for SAR automatic target recognition (ATR) by predicting multi-scale gradi- ent features rather than raw pixels. SARATR-X (Li et al., 2025) subsequently incorporated multi-scale gradient features into a masked image modeling framework, using a two-step self- supervised procedure that first performed MIM pretraining on ImageNet to obtain a favorable weight initialization, then continued MIM pretraining on a curated corpus of unlabeled SAR target samples using the multi-scale gradient features to suppress speckle noise,
title: Among the contrastive methods, SeCo (Mañas et al., 2021) builds positive pairs from sea-

text: a two-step self- supervised procedure that first performed MIM pretraining on ImageNet to obtain a favorable weight initialization, then continued MIM pretraining on a curated corpus of unlabeled SAR target samples using the multi-scale gradient features to suppress speckle noise, rather than the joint-embedding predictive approach SAR-JEPA uses. However, both models are trained and evaluated exclusively on ATR tasks, limiting the generalizability to land-cover and change de- tection problems. Applying DINO (Caron et al., 2021)-style self-distillation to SAR imagery, Gallego-Mejia et al. (2023) and Martínez-Ferrer et al. (2023) found only modest gains over training from scratch, with the resulting self-distilled embeddings generalizing poorly to geographically unfamiliar re- gions without further domain-specific adaptation. To the best of our knowledge, SparK-SAR is among the first methods to adapt sparse con- volutional masked pretraining specifically for S1GRD data and demonstrate its transferability across diverse downstream SAR tasks under constrained compute. 5

text: 3. Materials and Methods Figure 1 illustrates how SparK-SAR adapts SparK’s sparse masked pretraining scheme (Tian et al., 2023) to S1GRD data under constrained compute. A 224×224 two-channel input tile, comprising VV (vertical transmit–vertical receive) and VH (vertical transmit–horizontal receive) backscatter in dB scale, is patch-masked at random, and the encoder processes only the visible patches through sparse convolutions rather than the full grid. The output feature maps are passed to a reconstruction decoder tasked with predicting the masked patches. Once pretraining finishes, the decoder is discarded and only the encoder is used for downstream finetuning. Figure 1: The proposed SparK-SAR pretraining framework. The ConvNeXt-RS encoder produces 14×14 feature maps (stride 16×) from 224×224 S1GRD inputs. Only visible (unmasked) patches are processed by the encoder via sparse convolutions; the decoder reconstructs the full image including masked regions. 3.1. ConvNeXt-RS Encoder ConvNeXt-Tiny’s (Liu et al., 2022) default stem downsamples by 4×4 before three further 2×2 stages, taking a 224-pixel input through 56→28→14→7 down to a final 7×7 feature map at overall stride 32×; every output token therefore corresponds to a 32×32-pixel patch of the input, coarse enough to erase spatial detail that dense SAR tasks such as segmentation and change detection depend on. ConvNeXt-RS keeps everything about this backbone fixed except the stem: halving its stride to 2×2 changes the spatial
title: 3. Materials and Methods

text: patch of the input, coarse enough to erase spatial detail that dense SAR tasks such as segmentation and change detection depend on. ConvNeXt-RS keeps everything about this backbone fixed except the stem: halving its stride to 2×2 changes the spatial trajectory to 224 →112 →56 →28 →14 (stride 16×) (1) so the final feature map doubles in each spatial dimension to 14×14, four times as many to- kens as the stock 7×7 output, each now covering a finer 16×16-pixel patch instead of 32×32; the overall stride drops correspondingly from 32× to 16×. Depth, per-stage block counts, and channel widths are all untouched, so the parameter count stays at 27.8M, and the change is fully compatible with SparK’s sparse convolution mechanism operating on visible patches at every stage. Figures 2 and 3 contrast the resulting stage-by-stage feature maps for the two encoders: ConvNeXt-Tiny’s Stage 4 output has largely lost spatial structure by 7×7, whereas ConvNeXt- RS’s 14×14 Stage 4 output still shows recognizable scene structure. 3.2. Reconstruction Decoders SparK-SAR supports interchangeable reconstruction decoders. We evaluate three designs. UNet-768, SparK’s original decoder, is a hierarchical UNet (Ronneberger et al., 2015) that aggregates multi-scale encoder features through 768 channels. Finetuning Protocol Every pretrained ConvNeXt-RS encoder is then finetuned end-to-end, separately, on each downstream task: AdamW at lr=10−3 (weight decay 10−4), OneCycleLR with final_div_factor = 100, 50 epochs (4 warmup), FP32, under a separate codebase running PyTorch 2.1.2 and CUDA 11.8. Pretraining and finetuning therefore run on different framework versions; we did not isolate the effect of this difference. Task-specific finetuning follows the Copernicus-Bench protocol: EuroSAT-S1 uses a linear classification head, while BigEarthNet-S1’s multi-label classification task is trained with a multi- label soft-margin loss. The two dense prediction tasks, DFC2020-S1 and Flood-S1, both employ a UPerNet (Xiao et al., 2018) decoder augmented with an auxiliary FCN head. text: 4. Results 4.1. Datasets Table 4 summarizes the four Copernicus-Bench (Wang et al., 2025b) S1GRD tasks used for evaluation, each built from its own established source dataset: EuroSAT (Helber et al., 2019) (EuroSAT-S1), BigEarthNet (Sumbul et al., 2019) (BigEarthNet-S1), the 2020 IEEE GRSS Data Fusion Contest dataset (Robinson et al., 2021) (DFC2020-S1), and the Kuro Siwo flood mapping dataset (Bountos et al., 2024) (Flood-S1). The validation split is used solely for checkpoint selection (best validation metric). No hy- perparameters were tuned on the validation set after the pretraining configuration was fixed. 4.2. Baselines We compare against: (i) a non-pretrained ConvNeXt-RS baseline finetuned with identical protocol, isolating the pretraining contribution; (ii) a standard ConvNeXt (7×7, stride 32×) pre- trained with SparK-SAR at matched learning rate (lr=10−3), isolating the resolution contribution; (iii) four published frozen-encoder results drawn directly from their source papers: Copernicus- FM ViT-B/16 (139M parameters) (Wang et al., 2025b), SoftCon ViT-B/14 (86M) (Wang et al., 2024), CROMA ViT-B/8 (86M) (Fuller et al., 2023), and DOFA ViT-B/16 (111M) (Xiong et al., 2024). As ConvNeXt-RS is a novel domain-adapted architectural variant, no pre-existing ImageNet- pretrained weights are available with the 2× stem stride and 2-channel (VV, VH) S1GRD input. The non-pretrained random initialization baseline therefore serves as the appropriate control for isolating the SAR-specific pretraining contribution. 4.3. Main Results Table 5 presents

Main Results Table 5 presents our main results. SparK-SAR with ConvNeXt-RS and LLRD finetun- ing improves over the non-pretrained baseline by +4.7 pp, +5.0 pp, +5.8 pp, and +1.4 pp on EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1, DFC2020-S1, and Flood-S1 respectively (UNet-128 decoder). The ConvNeXt-512 decoder achieves comparable performance while reducing pretraining VRAM by 7.5–8.5% per GPU, depending on hardware. Despite having roughly 5× fewer parameters than Copernicus-FM ViT (27.8M vs. 139M, frozen encoder), our finetuned model still comes out ahead on three of the four tasks: EuroSAT- S1 (88.49±0.16 vs. 87.2±0.1%), DFC2020-S1 (56.00±0.08 vs. 52.4±0.1%), and Flood-S1 (80.21±0.10 vs. 77.7±0.0%). On BigEarthNet-S1, SparK-SAR (77.03±0.40) falls marginally below Copernicus-FM (77.9±0.0%) and SoftCon (78.7±0.0%) under frozen evaluation. We note that Copernicus-FM incorporates tile geographic coordinates as an additional input modality via hypernetwork encodings (Wang et al., 2025b). BigEarthNet-S1 labels are derived from the CORINE Land Cover map (Sumbul et al., 2019; European Environment Agency, 2020), which exhibits strong geographic cluster- ing of land-cover classes across Europe. text: 4.4. Ablation Studies 4.4.1. Output Resolution: 7 × 7 vs 14 × 14 Because Table 7 pretrains the standard 7×7 ConvNeXt encoder and our 14×14 ConvNeXt-RS encoder under otherwise identical conditions (UNet-128 decoder, pretraining lr=10−3), it dou- bles as a resolution ablation. The higher-resolution encoder’s edge is concentrated in the dense prediction tasks (+1.4 pp DFC2020-S1, +0.8 pp Flood-S1) and much smaller for classification (+0.3 pp EuroSAT-S1), which is what we would expect if the extra spatial tokens mainly help pixel-level rather than scene-level prediction. The matched learning rate control largely rules out the pretraining learning rate as a con- founding factor: the original 7×7 experiments used a pretraining lr=10−4 (required to stabilize training), while our 14×14 ConvNeXt-RS uses a pretraining lr=10−3 (all models are finetuned at lr=10−3). Table 7 shows that pretraining the 7×7 encoder at lr=10−3 with UNet-128 still under- performs 14×14 at the same pretraining learning rate, confirming that the resolution modification is the primary contributor. At a pretraining lr=10−4, UNet-128 outperforms UNet-768 despite its lower decoder capacity, indicating that the larger decoder’s deficit is not explained by its reduced learning rate alone. Decoder Design and Efficiency UNet-128 and ConvNeXt-512 decoders achieve comparable downstream accuracy across all four tasks (Table 5), despite ConvNeXt-512 operating on only the final encoder stage rather than aggregating multi-scale features. This result is consistent with the hierarchical decoder not being necessary for strong downstream accuracy: the lightweight ConvNeXt-512 decoder achieves statistically indistinguishable performance (paired t-test, p=0.17) while reducing VRAM by 7.5– 8.5% per GPU, depending on hardware (Table 1). We note that decoder capacity is not perfectly disentangled from learning rate in this comparison, since the higher-capacity UNet-768 decoder (Table 7) required a lower learning rate for FP16 stability; the finding above is therefore best read as evidence against a decoder-capacity effect at matched learning rate and precision (UNet- 128 vs. ConvNeXt-512, both at lr=10−3), rather than

Representation Analysis To complement the downstream performance analysis, we compute Centered Kernel Align- ment (CKA) (Kornblith et al., 2019) between encoder representations at different pretraining data fractions. CKA measures linear representational similarity between two neural networks on a shared set of inputs. We extract Stage 3 post global average pooling features ([N, 384]) from all eight pretrained encoders (0–100%) on each Copernicus-Bench S1GRD test set, and compute pairwise unbiased linear CKA with Z-score feature standardization (Nguyen et al., 2021) to mitigate channel vari- ance skew. We use Stage 3 rather than the final Stage 4 representation because GAP over the 14×14 Stage 4 output would collapse the spatial structure that our resolution ablation specifically shows to be valuable, whereas Stage 4 features
title: Table 12: Label efficiency: finetuning accuracy vs. labeled-data fraction, pretrained (PT) vs. random initialization (No-

text: vari- ance skew. We use Stage 3 rather than the final Stage 4 representation because GAP over the 14×14 Stage 4 output would collapse the spatial structure that our resolution ablation specifically shows to be valuable, whereas Stage 4 features retained at full resolution ([N, 14, 14, 768]) have no natural scalar CKA summary. Stage 3 avoids this collapse while still providing a compact, fixed- size representation for similarity comparison. This choice is also consistent with recent evidence that task-relevant information is often more accessible in intermediate layers than in final-layer embeddings across several self-supervised remote sensing architectures (Romero et al., 2026). Figure 7 shows CKA similarity to the fully pretrained (100%) encoder as a function of pre- training data fraction. For EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1, and DFC2020-S1, CKA increases near monotonically from random initialization (0.64–0.70) to plateau values of 0.83–0.88, broadly consistent with the downstream performance saturation observed in Section 4.5. We observe an anomalous dip in CKA similarity for Flood-S1 at the 25% and 50% pretraining- data fractions (0.733 and 0.726, respectively, versus 0.807 at 10% and 0.855 at 75%). We do not have a confident explanation for this non-monotonicity and report it as an open observation rather 18

Halving the stem stride fixes this without adding a single parameter. The decoder ablation (Section 4.4.2) tells a complementary story: UNet-128 and ConvNeXt- 512 land at statistically indistinguishable downstream accuracy (p=0.17), so whatever the orig- inal SparK recipe’s hierarchical decoder buys on natural images, it is not required to transfer well to S1GRD at a matched learning rate. That makes ConvNeXt-512 the better default when- ever VRAM is tight, since it recovers 7.5–8.5% per GPU (hardware-dependent) for no accuracy cost. LLRD, meanwhile, is a smaller but broadly positive lever for the UNet-128-pretrained encoder: mean performance improves and variance shrinks across all four tasks, reaching signif- icance on two of them after correction (Section 4.4.3), enough that we recommend it as a default for pretrained encoders rather than an optional extra; it did not help a non-pretrained encoder (Section 3.4). The data scaling analysis reveals that SAR MIM pretraining is remarkably data-efficient: classification tasks and change detection saturate with as few as 10–25% of the pretraining corpus (24,396 tiles), while dense semantic segmentation (DFC2020-S1) keeps improving significantly up to 25% (60,992 tiles) and continues to gain, more gradually, through 50% (121,984 tiles). This saturation behavior suggests that the limited visual diversity of SAR amplitude imagery, which is typically dominated by a relatively small number of backscatter regimes corresponding to major land-cover types, can be effectively characterized by a surprisingly small pretraining corpus. Consequently, researchers need not curate massive SAR datasets to benefit from the SparK-SAR pretraining method; a geographically diverse collection of ∼25,000 tiles may be 22

The CKA representation analysis (Section 4.7) corroborates the downstream saturation find- ings: encoder representations converge toward the fully pretrained configuration with increasing data, and this convergence broadly mirrors the performance plateau observed in Table 11. The non-trivial CKA baseline at random initialization reflects the strong spatial inductive bias of ConvNeXt on SAR data, an observation with implications for future architectural choices in SAR SSL. During development of SparK-SAR, several alternative configurations were explored but found to provide no consistent benefit. VICReg regularization (Bardes et al., 2022) increased representation dimensionality but de- graded downstream performance, consistent with a conflict between the generative SparK recon- struction objective and the decorrelation objective of VICReg. Fisher-Tippett-based SAR-specific reconstruction loss (Fisher and Tippett, 1928; Guan et al., 2019) and distillation from a cross-modal optical teacher (DINOv3-style (Siméoni et al., 2026)) produced reduced training losses but no downstream gains, suggesting that representations aligned with optical imagery are not directly transferable to SAR tasks. These negative results highlight the importance of domain-specific objective design for SAR SSL and are documented here to prevent redundant exploration by the community. A dual-branch polarimetric stem processing VV and VH channels separately before 1×1 projection fusion was also evaluated, but did not result in improvement on classification tasks and regressed on dense prediction (−1.44 pp on DFC2020-S1,

A dual-branch polarimetric stem processing VV and VH channels separately before 1×1 projection fusion was also evaluated, but did not result in improvement on classification tasks and regressed on dense prediction (−1.44 pp on DFC2020-S1, −0.52 pp on Flood-S1), suggesting that joint polarimetric processing in a shared convolutional stem is preferable for S1GRD MIM pretraining. Flood-S1’s comparatively modest +1.4 pp gain has a natural explanation once we consider what the pretraining objective actually teaches the encoder. Change detection asks the model to reason jointly over a pre-event and a post-event acquisition, but MIM pretraining, single- image by construction, never exposes the encoder to any notion of temporal difference at all. An encoder that has only ever learned to reconstruct one image at a time has correspondingly little temporal structure to transfer. The Flood-S1 ablation (Table 10) shows that the loss functions and fusion strategies we tried at the task head change Flood-S1 mIoU by at most about 0.4 pp (Concatenation fusion with CE or focal loss), so the limitation looks like it may sit upstream, in the pretraining objective itself, which points toward multi-temporal pretraining as the more promising direction for future work rather than further task-head engineering. BigEarthNet-S1 is the one task where SparK-SAR (77.03±0.40) trails, coming in marginally behind both Copernicus-FM (77.9±0.0%) and SoftCon (78.7±0.0%) under frozen evaluation. We note that the Copernicus-Bench dataset wrappers pass geographic coordinates and acquisition timestamps as metadata to Copernicus-FM for BigEarthNet-S1, while DFC2020-S1 passes NaN metadata in lieu of absent coordinate information (Wang et al., 2025b). In contrast, ConvNeXt- RS receives no metadata whatsoever, relying solely on the two SAR amplitude channels (VV, VH) for all tasks. One plausible contributor is that BigEarthNet-S1’s labels come from the CORINE Land Cover map (Sumbul et al., 2019; European Environment Agency, 2020), and European land-cover classes are not spread uniformly: they cluster geographically. Combined with the real coordinates and acquisition times Copernicus-FM receives as input, that clustering gives it a location-based shortcut to lean on that our model, seeing only VV/VH amplitude, simply does not have access to. This is consistent with the task-level pattern: Copernicus-FM trails our model on DFC2020-S1 (where metadata is all-NaN) and Flood-S1 (where the label is transient and event-specific, limiting the utility of location priors), while its strongest advantage 23
title: sufficient for most applications.

text: over our model occurs on BigEarthNet-S1 (where location and time metadata are available and labels are geographically clustered). SoftCon’s strong BigEarthNet-S1 result (78.7±0.0%) likely reflects its multi-label land-cover guidance during pretraining (Wang et al., 2024). We offer this as a plausible explanation, not a demonstrated one. These findings also carry practical implications for operational Earth observation pipelines that must produce map products under real-world time and annotation constraints. The label efficiency analysis (Section 4.6) shows that SparK-SAR’s advantage over a non-pretrained base- line on Flood-S1 is largest precisely at the most extreme low-label setting we test (1% labeled samples, a +6.26 pp gain in mIoU over random initialization), the operating regime closest to a real rapid-response flood mapping scenario such as Copernicus Emergency Management Ser- vice (EMS) products, where annotated post-event imagery for a specific flood event is scarce or unavailable at the time a map is needed. Similarly, the pretraining data scaling results (Section 4.5) show that classification and change detection performance saturate with only 10–25% of the full 243,968 tile pretraining corpus, in- dicating that agencies producing regional land-cover products in the style of CORINE or the ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover map from Sentinel-1 archives need not assemble a global-scale SAR corpus to benefit from MIM pretraining.
