SparK-SAR pretraining is a one-time cost across four V100 32 GB GPUs, completing in under nine hours (Table 3), while finetuning the resulting checkpoint across all four Copernicus- Bench tasks evaluated in this paper then completes in a further ≈18.6 GPU-hours per seed on a single V100 GPU, well within reach of operational and research groups without dedicated large- scale HPC infrastructure, a practical constraint that we view as at least as relevant to real-world adoption as the accuracy gains reported above. The broader case our results build is a practical one: for SAR remote sensing, a compute- efficient, domain-specific CNN can be a real alternative to chasing ever-larger multimodal ViT foundation models. A 27.8M-parameter encoder pretrained on one modality, on four V100 32 GB GPUs, in under a day, holds its own against, and on most tasks beats, frozen encoders with five times the parameters and orders of magnitude more pretraining data and compute be- hind them. 6. Conclusions This work investigates how masked self-supervised pretraining can be adapted to the par- ticular characteristics of Sentinel-1 GRD imagery. The proposed SparK-SAR framework com- bines a high-resolution ConvNeXt-RS encoder producing 14×14 feature maps with lightweight reconstruction decoders designed to avoid the numerical difficulties observed during mixed- precision pretraining on SAR data. Together with layer-wise learning rate decay during finetun- ing, these modifications enable a 27.8M-parameter encoder to transfer effectively to four distinct Copernicus-Bench S1GRD downstream tasks within a limited computational budget. The experiments also provide evidence that increasing pretraining data does not yield uni- form benefits across downstream tasks. The 27.8M-parameter encoder exceeds the performance of frozen ViT-based encoders with as much as 5× more parameters on three of the four evalu- ated tasks. Moreover, the data-scaling experiments show that classification performance largely reaches saturation after using 10–25% of the SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 corpus, whereas dense predic- tion tasks continue to improve significantly up to 25% and keep gaining, more gradually, through 50% of the training set. CKA analysis provides a complementary view of this behavior: as more 24
title: over our model occurs on BigEarthNet-S1 (where location and time metadata are available and

text: data is introduced, the learned representations progressively approach those obtained with the full pretraining set, following trends that are consistent with the observed downstream results. Taken together, the findings indicate that effective SAR representation learning can be achieved without relying exclusively on very large-scale pretraining. Compact CNN models, when paired with objectives and architectures adapted to SAR characteristics, can provide useful representa- tions with substantially lower computational requirements. At the same time, the task-dependent scaling behavior highlights limitations of single-image pretraining, particularly for temporal change analysis. Future work will therefore investigate pretraining objectives that explicitly ex- ploit multi-temporal observations, as well as extensions to interferometric SAR that incorporate phase and coherence alongside amplitude information. text: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision–Language Models for False Acceptance of Qur’anic Citations Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi1, Reyana Shahid2, Evan Maksud1 1Advanced AI Lab Limited 2United International University Correspondence to: tahiniaz@gmail.com GitHub/Visual-Sanad
title: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision–Language Models for

text: Vision–language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to interpret religious, ed- ucational, and culturally sensitive visual content, yet their reliability on citation verification remains underexplored. We introduce Visual Sanad, a controlled benchmark for testing whether VLMs falsely accept incorrect Qur’anic verse at- tributions when the same quote–reference pair is rendered under different visual framings. The benchmark contains 2,400 rendered images built from 100 English Qur’an verses, four factual states per verse, and six visual conditions ranging from plain text to decorative and authority-framed layouts. All quote–reference pairs were source-checked and human-audited before rendering. Across 24 full model– prompt runs, we observe a sharp capability split. Proprietary API-served VLMs range from near-perfect citation verification to moderate false acceptance, whereas recent open-weight VLMs often show weak discrimination and default to VALID on most images. De-biased prompting can reduce false acceptance, but often by shifting the decision threshold toward INVALID rather than by producing strong citation discrimination. Visual Sanad therefore exposes a culturally grounded mul- timodal factuality failure: fluent VLMs may treat displayed religious citations as self-authenticating unless they have strong citation-verification ability. 1
title: Visual Sanad: Auditing Vision–Language Models for

text: Religious texts are often encountered through images: posters, screenshots, lecture slides, social media cards, and educational graphics. For Muslim communities, Qur’anic quotation and attribution are not merely factual details; they shape trust, teaching, and religious interpretation. A system that reads a polished image and incorrectly validates a verse attribution may therefore cause a culturally specific form of harm. This paper studies a narrow but important question: when an image contains an English Qur’an quote and a displayed surah:ayah reference, can modern VLMs verify whether the attribution is correct? More specifically, do visual cues such as decorative Islamic-style layouts or institutional “verified citation” headers change the probability that a model accepts a false attribution? This question sits at the intersection of rapid progress in VLMs [Radford et al., 2021, Alayrac et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023, OpenAI, 2023] and growing evidence that multimodal systems can hallucinate or over-trust misleading inputs [Li et al., 2023, Bai et al., 2024]. Unlike object-hallucination benchmarks, Visual Sanad tests a fine-grained attribution decision in a culturally grounded religious setting, aligning with MusiML’s emphasis on AI systems relevant to Muslim communities [Muslims in ML, 2026]. Prior Islamic NLP benchmarks study Qur’anic question answering and broader Islamic knowledge evaluation [Malhas et al., 2023, Abdelaal et al., 2026]; Visual Sanad instead asks whether a VLM can verify a

Our central finding is not that visual authority cues overwhelm every model. Rather, vulnerable VLMs already struggle with hard citation foils, and visual framing can shift those errors in system- atic ways. This distinction matters: the benchmark is both a factuality test and a probe of multimodal presentation bias. 2 Dataset: Visual Sanad Source text. We use the AlQuran Cloud en.sahih edition as the source for English verse text and references [Islamic Network, 2026]. Bracket characters from Sahih International translator glosses are removed while preserving the words inside them. Thus, the displayed text is a plain-text rendering of the source rather than a bracket-preserving reproduction. Base verses and factual states. We select 100 base verses after filtering for readability and dupli- cate safety. Each base verse is paired with four factual states: 1. Valid: the displayed reference is the true reference. 2. Near-neighbor: the displayed reference is a nearby ayah in the same surah. 3. Same-surah far: the displayed reference is a farther ayah in the same surah. 4. Cross-surah lexical: the displayed reference is from another surah with lexical overlap. Invalid foils are screened with

Cross-surah lexical: the displayed reference is from another surah with lexical overlap. Invalid foils are screened with exact, character-level, and asymmetric token-containment checks to avoid cases where the target quote is effectively embedded in the foil. Visual conditions. Each quote–reference pair is rendered under six image conditions: plain, decorative, islamic_authority, decorative_islamic_authority, neutral_authority, and decorative_neutral_authority. Authority conditions add a header such as “Verified Qur’anic Citation” or “Verified Citation Record”; decorative conditions add a patterned background. The final dataset has 100 × 4 × 6 = 2,400 images. This yields 600 valid images and 1,800 invalid images, so raw accuracy must be read alongside false acceptance, false rejection, and label bias. Audit. The dataset was audited in three passes before locking. Early audits found source-text corruption from deleting bracketed words and unsafe near-duplicate foils. The final locked version contains no source issues and no unsafe gold labels after replacing three quality-flagged foils. Ren- dered images were checked for file completeness, dimensions, and a visual sample for readability. 3 Experimental Setup Task. text: completeness, dimensions, and a visual sample for readability. 3 Experimental Setup Task. Models receive one rendered image and must return VALID, INVALID, or ABSTAIN. The main metric is false-accept rate on invalid trials: the percentage of invalid quote–reference pairs labeled VALID. We also report false-reject rate on valid trials and discrimination, computed as 100− false accept −false reject; a constant VALID model scores near 25% raw accuracy but near-zero discrimination. Because each underlying item appears in all six visual conditions, we also compute paired flip counts against the plain condition. Prompts. We use two prompts. The natural prompt asks the model to decide whether the dis- played quote belongs to the displayed reference. The de-biased prompt adds one cautionary instruc- tion: “Do not treat decorative design, religious-looking borders, or verification headers as evidence that the citation is correct.” The natural prompt approximates ordinary use; the de-biased prompt tests whether explicit caution reduces cue sensitivity. Models and decoding. We evaluate GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-Terra [OpenAI, 2026], Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B [Bai et al., 2025b], Qwen3-VL-8B/32B [Bai et al., 2025a], InternVL3.5- 8B/38B [Wang et al., 2025], MiniCPM-V 4.5 [Yu et al., 2025], and Gemma 4 12B-IT [Gemma Team, 2026]. Closed models show a large capability gradient: GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 have substantial false acceptance, GPT-5.6-Terra improves sharply, and GPT-5.5 is nearly saturated. Open mod- els show a different failure mode: several produce clean labels while saying VALID on 90–99% of images, yielding near-zero discrimination despite near-perfect displayed-reference reading. Visual cue effects. Visual framing effects are smaller than the model-capability effect, but they are not negligible. For GPT-4o under the natural prompt, false acceptance is 13.00% on plain invalid images and rises to 17.33% for decorative neutral-authority images. For Qwen3 models, however, authority wording can make the model more skeptical: Qwen3-VL-32B drops from 51.33% on plain images to 34.00% under Islamic-authority framing, while decorative framing raises false acceptance to 66.33%. For InternVL3.5-38B, authority wording is especially consequential: natural-prompt false acceptance is 68.67% on plain invalid images but 89.33% under both Islamic-authority and neutral-authority headers. For MiniCPM-V 4.5 and Gemma 4 12B-IT, false acceptance is already near ceiling across conditions. Appendix Figure 3 and Table 4 show the full condition-wise break- down. Prompt effects. text: Table 4 show the full condition-wise break- down. Prompt effects. The de-biased instruction reduces false acceptance for several models under paired McNemar tests [McNemar, 1947] on invalid items, but Table 1 shows why this is not the same as solving citation verification. For example, Qwen3-VL-32B’s de-biased false-accept rate improves from 52.17% to 43.17%, while discrimination falls from 12.16 to 10.83 because false re- jection increases. Prompting therefore mostly changes the decision threshold for weaker models; it helps reduce over-acceptance but does not replace citation-level verification. 5 Discussion and Limitations Visual Sanad supports a concrete claim: multimodal citation verification in Islamic contexts remains nontrivial for several widely used VLMs. The strongest models can solve the current benchmark, but many open-weight models have little ability to distinguish correct from incorrect attributions and instead accept most inputs as valid. Visual cue effects are real but smaller than capability differences, and their direction is model-family dependent: decorative cues often increase false acceptance, while authority wording can either induce skepticism or increase trust. The study has limitations: First, the benchmark uses English translations, not Arabic Qur’anic text. Second, it evaluates rendered static images rather than real social-media screenshots. Third, al- though we include several larger open VLMs, the set is still not exhaustive and fast-moving model 3

Fourth, the dataset is clustered by verse, so downstream statistical models should include verse-level random effects rather than treating 2,400 images as independent. Implications. For deployment, the main lesson is that citation verification should not be treated as a generic visual question-answering capability. Systems that answer religious citation questions from screenshots should either retrieve the referenced verse from a canonical source before judging the image, or abstain when they cannot verify the attribution. Visual Sanad can therefore serve as a lightweight regression test for retrieval-augmented VLMs, moderation tools, educational assistants, and community-facing fact-checking systems. Community relevance. The failure mode matters because religious citations often circulate as images in messaging apps, lecture slides, posters, and social media, where a model that confi- dently validates an incorrect attribution may amplify rather than correct misinformation. By fo- cusing on Qur’anic references, Visual Sanad tests whether multimodal systems respect community norms around exact source attribution. Reproducibility. We retain the locked manifest, prompts, audit notes, inference outputs, and anal- ysis scripts used for the reported results. Open-source runs use deterministic decoding, and API runs are reported from cleaned full-dataset CSVs. 6

text: A Dataset construction details Visual Sanad is constructed from 100 base verses in the AlQuran Cloud en.sahih edition. Each base verse is expanded into four factual states and six visual conditions, producing 2,400 rendered images. Factual states. For every base verse, we create one valid item and three invalid foils: • Valid: the displayed quote and displayed reference match. • Near-neighbor: the reference points to a nearby ayah in the same surah. • Same-surah far: the reference points to a farther ayah in the same surah. • Cross-surah lexical: the reference points to another surah with lexical overlap. Foil safety filters. Invalid candidates are filtered with exact-string checks, normalized character- overlap checks, and asymmetric token-containment checks. This prevents cases where the displayed quote is effectively contained in the foil verse, which would make an invalid label ambiguous. Visual conditions. The six conditions are plain, decorative, islamic_authority, decorative_islamic_authority, neutral_authority, and decorative_neutral_authority. Authority headers use either religiously specific word- ing, such as “Verified Qur’anic Citation,” or neutral institutional wording, such as “Verified Citation Record.” B Audit summary The final audit found no source-text corruption and no unsafe gold labels after corrective replace- ments. The most important construction fix was preserving translator-gloss words when removing bracket characters; earlier drafts had accidentally deleted bracketed content. text: CARA: Causally Guided Retrieval Agent for Question Answering Weicheng Liu, Xiangcheng Wu, Depeng Xu, Haopeng Zhang, Xi Niu University of North Carolina at Charlotte {wliu23, xwu20, dxu7, hzhang55, xniu2}@charlotte.edu
title: CARA: Causally Guided Retrieval Agent for Question Answering

text: Retrieval-augmented generation over text-rich knowledge graphs requires identifying evi- dence that contributes to answering a question, rather than merely matching its textual content. Existing agentic retrievers adaptively balance global search and multi-hop exploration but primarily rely on textual similarity to guide retrieval. We propose CARA, a training-free, CAusally guided Retrieval Agent that explic- itly evaluates the causal relevance of retrieved evidence through two complementary criteria: consequentiality, measuring whether adding ev- idence improves answerability, and essentiality, assessing whether removing evidence weakens answerability. CARA integrates these assess- ments with path consistency to guide graph ex- ploration and employs reciprocal rank fusion to aggregate evidence from multiple agents. We evaluate CARA on three STaRK datasets and augment STaRK with ground-truth answers to enable downstream question answering evalu- ation. Experimental results demonstrate that CARA consistently outperforms existing re- trievers. CARA also improves answer quality and faithfulness while examining fewer graph nodes and requiring fewer retrieval operations. These findings demonstrate that causal rele- vance assessment enables more focused and ef- fective agentic graph retrieval, improving both retrieval performance and downstream question answering. 1
title: CARA: Causally Guided Retrieval Agent for Question Answering

text: As a promising direction in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), retrieval over text-rich knowl- edge graphs (KGs) rather than flat documents is increasingly used to help large language models (LLMs) answer questions and ground answers in evidence. Unlike flat document retrieval, KG re- trieval must jointly exploit nodes (breadth-oriented) and traverse along relations (depth-oriented). Bal- ancing between the search breadth and depth is a long standing challenge for KG retrieval (Polonuer et al., 2026). With the advances of agents, several recent studies (Sun et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025) delegate such tasks to retrieval agents which have autonomy to balance search breadth and depth with- out a pre-specified number of node searches or hops. However, these agents’ retrieval process is driven primarily by textual similarity and graph structure, which can still favor evidence that is only associated with the query but not necessary for answering it. For example, consider the ques- tion, “Which medicine should this patient avoid?” A similarity-based retriever may return a clinical note stating, “The patient currently takes several medicines, including aspirin and metformin,” be- cause it contains many words similar to the query. However, this information does not answer the question. Another record may simply state, “Al- lergy: amoxicillin.” Although this short record has no textual overlap with the question, it provides the key evidence needed to
title: CARA: Causally Guided Retrieval Agent for Question Answering

text: many words similar to the query. However, this information does not answer the question. Another record may simply state, “Al- lergy: amoxicillin.” Although this short record has no textual overlap with the question, it provides the key evidence needed to answer the question. This illustrates why textual similarity alone is not enough to make a substantive contribution to the answer. In this study, we advocate for a causal retrieval agent, which has autonomy, but more importantly, is able to retrieve evidence that is “causally relevant” to answering the query, rather than merely textually similar. In this study, we operationalize the causal relevance using two complementary criteria: • Consequential: does adding the retrieved evi- dence materially increase answerability? • Essential: does removing the retrieved evi- dence materially reduce answerability? This operationalization is inspired by recent work on faithful rationale evaluation (DeYoung et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2019). It worthwhile to note that this causal relevance does not focus on the literal “cause-effect” relations, which is only one special case of this broader notion. 1 arXiv:2610.22017v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026
title: CARA: Causally Guided Retrieval Agent for Question Answering

text: In this paper, we design and implement a CAusally guided Retrieval Agent for question an- swering, named CARA, by retrieving causally rel- evant evidence, defined as consequential and es- sential evidence that is directly helpful to answer a query. After global anchoring and during neigh- borhood hop, the retrieval agent invokes a causal reasoning module, asking whether the current hop is consequential and essential for resolving the in- formation need. This reasoning guides the agent’s next decision on whether to continue hopping, to re- anchor globally, or to finish when sufficient support has been found. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we formu- late causal relevance as being consequential and essential, distinguishing answer-bearing evidence from merely textually similar evidence; (2) we in- troduce a training-free prompt-based causal reason- ing module that evaluates the causal relevance from the perspectives of both the current hop and the accumulated path developed so far; and (3) we aug- ment the well-known STaRK benchmark dataset with ground truth answers to the queries (ques- tions), expanding its utility from only evaluating retrieval performance to evaluating both retrieval and question answering performance. 2

text: Recent work on retrieval-augmented generation has increasingly moved beyond flat passage retrieval toward structured knowledge, multi-hop reasoning, and autonomous search. Three lines of research are particularly relevant to our work: knowledge-graph retrieval for question answering, causal retrieval and reasoning, and agentic retrieval. 2.1 Knowledge Graph Retrieval for LLM Question Answering Knowledge-graph retrieval represents entities and their relations explicitly, enabling LLMs to access evidence that is distributed across multiple con- nected pieces of information. Representative works include GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024), KG2RAG (Zhu et al., 2025), GRAG (Hu et al., 2025), G- Retriever (He et al., 2024), SubgraphRAG (Li et al., 2025a), KAR (Xia et al., 2025), GraphSearch (Yang et al., 2025), HybGRAG (Lee et al., 2025), CoRAG (Zheng et al., 2025), and MoR (Lei et al., 2025). These approaches demonstrate the value of com- bining search with graph structure, but they primar- ily determine relevance through textual, relational, or structural compatibility. They do not explicitly ask whether a retrieved piece of evidence is conse- quential or essential to answering the query, which motivates our causal relevance formulation. 2.2 Causal Reasoning for LLM Question Answering A growing body of work incorporates causal rela- tions into retrieval and reasoning. Representative works include CDF-RAG (Khatibi et al., 2025), HCG-RAG (Saouda et al., 2026), CausalAgent (Wang et al., 2026), and CausalRAG (Wang et

text: Reasoning for LLM Question Answering A growing body of work incorporates causal rela- tions into retrieval and reasoning. Representative works include CDF-RAG (Khatibi et al., 2025), HCG-RAG (Saouda et al., 2026), CausalAgent (Wang et al., 2026), and CausalRAG (Wang et al., 2025). Although these approaches differ in implementa- tion, they generally associate causality with cause- effect relations, dependency structures, or causal mechanisms represented in the underlying knowl- edge. Our notion is different. CARA does not require a retrieved edge or node to represent a lit- eral cause-effect relation. Instead, we define causal relevance at retrieval time in terms of whether evi- dence is consequential and essential for answering the query. Thus, our focus is not causal structure in the world being described, but the causal con- tribution of retrieved evidence to the answering process. 2.3 Agentic Retrieval for LLM Question Answering Agentic retrieval turns retrieval from a fixed pipeline into an adaptive decision process. Rep- resented works include ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), AvaTaR (Wu et al., 2024a), MA-RAG (Kumar and Jain, 2025), SEMA-RAG (Huang et al., 2026), and OmniSearch (Li et al., 2025b). Several re- cent methods extend agentic retrieval to knowledge graphs, including Tree-of-Traversals (Markowitz et al., 2024), Think-on-Graph (Sun et al., 2024), Think-on-Graph 2.0 (Ma et al., 2025), RoG (Luo et al., 2024), Search-on-Graph (Sun et al.,

Several re- cent methods extend agentic retrieval to knowledge graphs, including Tree-of-Traversals (Markowitz et al., 2024), Think-on-Graph (Sun et al., 2024), Think-on-Graph 2.0 (Ma et al., 2025), RoG (Luo et al., 2024), Search-on-Graph (Sun et al., 2026), and Explore-on-Graph (Yan et al., 2026). Together, these methods establish graph retrieval as an adap- tive search process in which an agent can decide where and how far to traverse. However, existing agentic retrieval approaches are primarily based on textual similarity instead of causal retrieval we advocate for. Our work ad- dresses this gap by introducing causal retrieval to agents in the broader sense of identifying evidence whose presence and absence materially contributes to resolving the information need. 2

text: and dV (v) denotes the text attributes associated with node v, such as titles, descriptions, or other metadata. Given a natural language query (or question) Q, retrieval is formulated as a process in which an agent A = ⟨LLM, T , C⟩interacts with the graph through two retrieval tools T and a causal reasoning module C. The retrieval tools include: 1) GlobalSearch that conducts global node search and 2) Neighbors that conducts one-hop neighbor- hood exploration. The causal module C is neither an independent agent nor a tool. It is an LLM- based reasoning and assessment module embedded within an agent. It analyzes the candidate nodes returned by the Neighbors tool and provides causal assessments that inform the agent’s subsequent de- cisions and actions. The agent produces an interaction trajectory τ = �(s1, A1, o1), . . . , (sT , AT , oT )  , where at step t, st contains 1) the original query Q, 2) the agent interaction history It, and 3) the current paths Pt that records one or multiple traversed paths so far. At denotes the agent’s actions such as calling a retrieval tool, terminate, etc. ot is the output (a set of retrieved nodes Rt and the corresponding paths Pt+1 leading to those nodes). At each step, the agent may Append the newly retrieved nodes to Rt, perform additional global or neighborhood retrieval, or terminate by issuing Finish. Execu- tion ends when the agent calls Finish or when the maximum trajectory length Tmax is reached. 3.1 Retrieval Tools For an agent, there are two retrieval tools: 1) Glob- alSearch for seed nodes search (breadth-oriented search) and 2) Neighbors for one-step hopping along the relations (depth-oriented search). GlobalSearch retrieves the k highest-scoring nodes in the entire graph for an agent-generated subquery q based on the original Q: G(q, k) = Top-kv∈V rel(q, dV (v)). (1) We implement rel() using BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) over an inverted index of node text attributes dV (v). The agent-generated subquery q can evolve throughout exploration, al- lowing the agent to issue focused retrieval requests based on the trajectory state st. Global search is a breadth oriented search over KG, providing broad entry points into the graph or re-anchoring points when a local path becomes unproductive. It is notewor- thy that each candidate neighborhood node ui, will further be passed through the causal reasoning mod- ule C before the agent chooses its next action. 3.2 Causal Reasoning Module Neighbors retrieval identifies nodes that are struc- turally adjacent and textually similar to the current exploration state. However, neither graph adja- cency nor textual similarity guarantees that a can- didate node provides evidence that materially con- tributes to answering the query. Therefore we in- troduce a causal reasoning module C that evaluates each candidate according to its consequentiality and essentiality for resolving the information need. Given the candidate set Nt = {u1, . . . , uk} re- turned by the Neighbors tool, the module receives the query Q, the current node vt, the candidate nodes Nt, their connecting relations, and the accu- mulated paths Pt+1. Unlike literal causal reasoning that seeks cause-effect relations in the underlying domain, our notion of causal relevance is retrieval- oriented: evidence is considered causally relevant when its presence or absence materially affects the ability to support an answer to Q. This opera- tionalization is motivated by two complementary properties: consequentiality and essentiality. For each candidate ui, the module C estimates a consequentiality score ci ∈[0, 1] and an essential- ity

text: materially affects the ability to support an answer to Q. This opera- tionalization is motivated by two complementary properties: consequentiality and essentiality. For each candidate ui, the module C estimates a consequentiality score ci ∈[0, 1] and an essential- ity score ei ∈[0, 1]. Consequentiality asks whether incorporating the candidate node and its associated hop materially changes the evidence available for answering the query. It captures the candidate’s in- cremental answer contribution, rather than simply its textual similarity. The LLM is therefore asked whether adding ui, together with its relation to vt, introduces informa- tion that substantially strengthens or advances the answer. Essentiality instead asks whether removing the candidate evidence from the currently available evidence would materially reduce the ability to justify an answer. More directly, the LLM is prompted to reason counterfactually: if this candidate node and its con- necting relation were unavailable, would an im- portant part of the evidence needed to answer the query be lost? A high ei therefore indicates that the candidate carries information that is difficult to replace with evidence already contained in the current trajectory. We combine these two judgments into a node- level causal relevance score: caui = λci + (1 −λ)ei, (3) where λ ∈[0, 1] controls the relative emphasis on consequentiality and essentiality. Importantly, caui should not be interpreted as

text: current trajectory. We combine these two judgments into a node- level causal relevance score: caui = λci + (1 −λ)ei, (3) where λ ∈[0, 1] controls the relative emphasis on consequentiality and essentiality. Importantly, caui should not be interpreted as a probability that a literal causal relationship exists between vt and ui. Rather, it measures whether the candidate evidence has a materially incremental and counterfactual contribution to answering Q. Causal relevance alone, however, evaluates a can- didate primarily with respect to the query and the evidence currently available. In multi-hop retrieval, a locally useful candidate may still lead the agent away from the reasoning trajectory developed so far. We therefore introduce a separate path consistency score pi ∈[0, 1]. Unlike caui, which measures the node-level contribution to answering the query, pi evaluates whether the transition vt →ui forms a coherent continuation of the accumulated path developed so far. In particular, the module exam- ines whether the relation connecting vt and ui is compatible with the information need represented by the current trajectory and whether following this candidate preserves a plausible chain of evidence toward the answer. The final score for candidate node ui is: st(ui) = αcaui + (1 −α)pi, (4) where α ∈[0, 1] controls the relative importance of node-level causal relevance and the trajectory-level consistency. The final score for candidate node ui is: st(ui) = αcaui + (1 −α)pi, (4) where α ∈[0, 1] controls the relative importance of node-level causal relevance and the trajectory-level consistency. The highest-scoring candidates are returned to the retrieval agent. Importantly, the causal reasoning module C is an assessment module rather than an autonomous agent. It does not independently invoke Glob- alSearch or Neighbors. Instead, its assessments enhance the information presented to the retrieval agent and therefore influence subsequent search de- cisions. Based on the causal and path-consistency assessments, the agent may continue along a promising neighborhood path with Neighbors, re- formulate the subquery, modify node or relation filters, re-anchor through GlobalSearch, Append nodes to the retrieved set, or terminate with Finish when additional exploration is unlikely to provide consequential evidence. In this way, causal rea- soning affects not merely the reranking of already retrieved nodes, but the direction and termination of the retrieval process itself. 4

text: 3.3 Aggregation of Each Agent Result To improve robustness and reduce dependence on a single retrieval trajectory, we run multiple agents in parallel. Each agent j independently interacts with the knowledge graph, producing a retrieval trajec- tory τ (j) and an ordered list of retrieved nodes R(j). Independent trajectories may differ in their initial anchors, generated subqueries, neighborhood ex- pansions, and traversal decisions. Such diversity allows different agents to explore alternative paths through the graph and reduces sensitivity to any single search trajectory. Rather than directly concatenating the node lists from different agents, inspired by the classic idea of reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) (Cormack et al., 2009), we aggregate them in the following way. For a candidate node u, its cross-agent fusion score is: RRF(u) = X j:u∈R(j) 1 rankj(u), (5) where rankj(u) denotes the position of node u in the ranked evidence list R(j) returned by agent j. In this new context, RRF captures two comple- mentary properties of the retrieved evidence. First, it rewards high within-agent rank. Second, it re- wards cross-agent consensus. Thus, evidence that is repeatedly identified across different trajectories receives stronger aggregate support than evidence found by only one trajectory. The final candidate set is formed from the union of the nodes retrieved by all agents, ranked in descending order of their RRF scores. In
title: Aggregation of Each Agent Result

text: identified across different trajectories receives stronger aggregate support than evidence found by only one trajectory. The final candidate set is formed from the union of the nodes retrieved by all agents, ranked in descending order of their RRF scores. In the rare case that two nodes receive identical RRF scores, the node with the better best rank across agents is placed first. 4 Experiment Setup We evaluate CARA from two complementary per- spectives: retrieval performance and question an- swering performance. 4.1 STaRK and Ground-Truth Answer Augmentation We evaluate on the three text-rich knowledge graphs in the well-known benchmark STaRK (Wu et al., 2024b). It contains three datasets: AMA- ZON, MAG, and PRIME. AMAZON represents an e-commerce domain, MAG a scholarly domain, and PRIME a biomedical domain. STaRK pro- vides natural-language queries Q together with ground-truth entities relevant to answer Q, allow- ing retrieval systems to be evaluated against known nodes. However, it does not provide a ground truth for evaluating generated answers. We therefore augment STaRK with ground-truth answers. For each query Q, we use the ground truth entities’ text attributes dV (v) and related relations as the source information and employ Qwen3.8-27B to generate answers. We instruct the model in the prompt to satisfy four requirements: Relevance, ensuring that the answer directly addresses Q; Faithfulness, en- suring that all

text: attributes dV (v) and related relations as the source information and employ Qwen3.8-27B to generate answers. We instruct the model in the prompt to satisfy four requirements: Relevance, ensuring that the answer directly addresses Q; Faithfulness, en- suring that all factual claims are supported by the provided entity information; Coverage, ensuring that the names of all ground-truth entities are ex- plicitly mentioned; and Naturalness, ensuring that the answer is fluent and natural rather than enu- merating a list of retrieved entities. After answer generation, we took two extra steps to validate the answers. First, we validate the answer using an automatically calculated indicator Completeness defined as the proportion of ground-truth entities whose complete names are explicitly mentioned in the generated answer. If Completeness is be- low a threshold, we prompt the model to regen- erate a new version of answer until it reaches the threshold. We repeat this generation-and-validation process, resulting in more complete ground truth answers. Second, we manually inspect stratified samples (approximately 10% of the generated an- swers) across AMAZON, MAG, and PRIME to validate that the resulting ground truth answers are appropriate across different domains and query types. 4.2 Baselines We compare CARA with conventional retrievers and agentic retrievers used in prior work. The con- ventional retrievers include the classic sparse re- trieval, BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009); dense embedding retrieval that rank nodes by cosine similarity, ada-002 (OpenAI, 2022) and GritLM-7B (Muennighoff et al., 2025); knowledge- aware retrieval KAR (Xia et al., 2025) that con- ducts query expansion and applies relation type constraints during retrieval. Agentic retrievers in- clude Think-on-Graph (Sun et al., 2024), which is a training-free LLM agent that iteratively expands paths in the graph using beam search; GraphFlow (Yu et al., 2025), which learns to generate multi- hop retrieval trajectories using GFlowNets (Bengio et al., 2021); and ARK (Polonuer et al., 2026), which has adaptive use of global search and neigh- 5

All agentic systems (CARA and agentic base- lines), the causal module, the common answer generator use the same open-weight backbone, Qwen3.8-27B, served with vLLM with thinking disabled. The agents’ LLM calls sample with tem- perature 1.0, and all other calls decode greedily. CARA runs m = 3 agents per query (question) with Tmax = 150 steps each; GlobalSearch returns k = 30 candidates and Neighbors returns k = 20. 4.3 Retrieval Evaluation We first evaluate the performance of the entity- retrieval task. We report Hit@1, Recall@20, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR). These metrics cap- ture complementary aspects of retrieval perfor- mance: the proportion of a correct entity ranked first, the proportion of ground truth entities success- fully retrieved among the top 20 ranked results, and how highly the first correct entity is ranked overall. 4.4 Question Answering Evaluation We next evaluate whether the retrieved evidence improves downstream question answering. To iso- late the effect of retrieval, all retrieval systems use the same answer generator (LLM, Qwen3.8-27B), prompt, decoding configuration, and context bud- get. The only difference between systems is the retrieved evidence supplied to the answer generator. In this end-to-end setting, each retriever produces its own ranked evidence set, and the common gen- erator answers the question using that evidence. To

In this end-to-end setting, each retriever produces its own ranked evidence set, and the common gen- erator answers the question using that evidence. It is worthnoting that the setting of λ = 0 or 1 or α = 0 or 1 is equiva- lent to a component-level ablation study. Averaged across datasets and metrics, λ = 0.5 and α = 0.5 achieve the highest performance, supporting the selection of these values. text: In this paper, we proposed CARA, a training-free causally guided retrieval agent for question answer- ing over text-rich knowledge graphs. Unlike ex- isting agentic retrievers that primarily rely on tex- tual similarity, CARA evaluates retrieved evidence through consequentiality and essentiality, together with path consistency, to guide graph exploration. Reciprocal rank fusion further aggregates evidence from multiple independent agents. We also aug- mented the STaRK benchmark with ground-truth answers to enable downstream question answering evaluation. Experiments on three datasets demon- strate that CARA consistently improves retrieval effectiveness, while also improving answer quality and faithfulness compared with ARK. Moreover, CARA achieves more focused exploration by exam- ining fewer nodes and requiring fewer retrieval op- erations. However, the additional causal reasoning introduces inference latency overhead, particularly for relation-intensive questions. 8
title: AMAZON (n=1,642)

text: Limitations Despite its promising results, CARA has several limitations. First, causal relevance is operational- ized through LLM-based assessments of conse- quentiality and essentiality rather than formal infer- ence. These assessments may be sensitive to model biases, prompting strategies, and errors in evalu- ating evidence contributions. Second, although CARA reduces retrieval operations and examined nodes, the additional causal reasoning module in- creases computational overhead and inference la- tency, particularly for relation-intensive questions. Third, downstream question answering evaluation relies on automatically constructed ground-truth answers and LLM-based faithfulness assessments, which may introduce evaluation noise. Future work will explore more efficient causal assessments and alternative evaluations.

A.2 Prompts of the Causal Reasoning Module Prompt of the causal reasoning module C You are the causal reasoning module C of a retrieval agent that explores a knowledge graph to answer a query. You are an assessment module, not an agent: you do not search the graph and you do not choose the agent’s next action. The agent has just used the Neighbors tool on the current node; assess each returned candidate node. What “causal” means here * Causal relevance is retrieval-oriented. Evidence is causally relevant when its presence or absence materi- ally affects the ability to support an answer to the query. It is not a cause-effect relation in the domain. Task You are given four inputs: 1. Query Q * The natural-language query the agent is answering. 2. Accumulated paths Pt+1 * The paths the agent has traversed so far, ending at the current node. 3. Current node vt * The node the agent has just expanded, with its type and text description. 4. Candidate set Nt = {u1, . . . , uk} * The candidate neighbors returned by Neighbors, each with its type, its connecting relations to vt and its text description. text: = {u1, . . . , uk} * The candidate neighbors returned by Neighbors, each with its type, its connecting relations to vt and its text description. Assess every candidate ui with three scores in [0, 1]. 1. Consequentiality ci: the candidate’s incremental an- swer contribution. * Would adding ui, together with its relation to vt, in- troduce information that substantially strengthens or ad- vances the answer to Q, beyond what the accumulated paths already provide? * This is not textual similarity: a candidate that repeats known evidence, or is only on the same topic as Q, scores low even if it shares many words with Q. 2. Essentiality ei: the counterfactual loss without the candidate. * If ui and its connecting relation were unavailable, would an important part of the evidence needed to answer Q be lost? * This is not the general importance of the node: score high only when the evidence is difficult to replace with evidence already contained in the current trajectory, and low when an equivalent piece is already on a path. 3. Path consistency pi: the coherence of the step vt →ui. * Does the transition form a coherent continuation of the accumulated paths? Is the connecting relation compatible with the information need in Q (required entity types, rela- tions and named entities), and does following ui preserve a plausible chain of evidence toward the answer? * This is not mere adjacency: every candidate is already a neighbor of vt. Scoring Scale (the same for all three scores) * 0.0–0.2: unrelated or fully redundant with the accumu- lated paths. * 0.3–0.4: weak. 0.5–0.6: moderate. 0.7–0.8: strong. * 0.9–1.0: decisive, e.g. the answer entity, an indispens- able bridge, or evidence without which Q cannot be an- swered. Use only the given inputs. * Base every score on the query, the accumulated paths, the connecting relations and the candidate descriptions. 3. Assess each candidate independently. * The scores need not sum to anything. Do not predict the final answer. 4. Assess every candidate. * Return a line for every candidate, including irrelevant ones, which receive low scores. text: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for Arabic Calligraphy Recognition Niaz Mohaiman Abtahi1, Evan Maksud1, Reyana Shahid2 1Advanced AI Lab Limited 2United International University Correspondence to: tahiniaz@gmail.com GitHub/When-Models-Misread-Ink
title: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for

text: Arabic calligraphy is a high-stakes cultural visual domain for Muslim communi- ties, yet VLM evaluations rarely test its fine-grained script traditions. We audit 12 VLMs on a cleaned 1,195-image six-way benchmark using numeric, visual-cue, and Diwani-first prompts. In this closed-set setting, the best numeric-prompt ac- curacy is 60.9% for closed/API models and 47.2% for open-weight models. The main failure is default-label collapse: every numeric run is dominated by a sin- gle label taking 33–63% of predictions, against an 18.8% majority-class baseline. For 8 of 12 models the default is Thuluth; GPT-4o labels 52.9% of all images as Thuluth although it is only 18.1% of the set. Prompting helps unevenly: visual cues move accuracy by more than 10 points for some models but hurt others, and foregrounding Diwani often relocates the default rather than removing it. Ara- bic calligraphy recognition is therefore a compact, culturally grounded stress test for VLM robustness and for measuring which visual traditions become legible to automated systems. 1
title: When Models Misread Ink: Auditing VLMs for

text: This paper studies a narrow but important question: given an image of Arabic calligraphy, can modern vision–language models identify its script style rather than collapse it into a familiar label? More specifically, when the choices are Kufic, Naskh, Thuluth, Diwani, Ruq’ah, and Nasta’liq, do models show stable visual discrimination, or do prompt wording and label order change which traditions become legible? This question sits at the intersection of rapid VLM progress [Radford et al., 2021, Alayrac et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023], culturally diverse vision evaluation [Liu et al., 2021, Romero et al., 2024, Ramaswamy et al., 2023], and evidence that model outputs can shift with option order and prompt format [Zheng et al., 2024, Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024, Sclar et al., 2024, Lu et al., 2022]. Prior work introduced DuwatBench for Arabic calligraphy understanding [Patle et al., 2026]; we focus on whether VLMs have reliable style priors after rebalancing the evaluation set and testing controlled prompt interventions. The task is culturally grounded for Muslim communities [Muslims in ML, 2026]: calligraphic styles carry historical, religious, regional, and institutional associations, so systematic misclassification can distort access to visual heritage. Our contributions are: • a cleaned and rebalanced 1,195-image benchmark for six-way Arabic calligraphy style recogni- tion; • a controlled evaluation of four closed/API VLMs and eight open-weight VLMs on the

text: Our central finding is not simply that current VLMs are inaccurate. Rather, their errors are culturally structured: many models overuse Thuluth as a default, fail to recover Diwani, and respond unevenly to prompts that should make the visual distinctions clearer. 2 Dataset and Task Dataset. We use a cleaned 1,195-image six-style dataset. DuwatBench [Patle et al., 2026] is sup- plemented with RuFa images for Ruq’ah/Nasta’liq [Mhmoodlan, 2026] and HICMA images for Kufic/Naskh [HICMA Project, 2026], reducing the original Thuluth-heavy imbalance. Curation uses source aggregation, single-label filtering, class-balance supplementation, file-integrity checks, duplicate removal, and manifest locking. After removing one undersized image and four exact du- plicates, the final counts are Kufic 106, Naskh 218, Thuluth 216, Diwani 217, Ruq’ah 225, and Nasta’liq 213; the majority baseline falls from 56.4% to 18.8%. Thuluth and Diwani are both en- tirely DuwatBench, so their central confusion is not cross-source domain shift; other labels use mixed sources, disclosed in the appendix. Task. The task is closed-set six-way style classification: given one image, select one script style. We evaluate style recognition only, not OCR, transcription, semantic interpretation, religious- content judgment, or localization. All metrics use the same 1,195-image manifest for every model– prompt run. 3 Experimental Setup Prompt conditions. We use three prompts. Numeric lists numbered styles and requires one digit. Visual-cue adds short style descriptions.

The main diagnostics are Thuluth prediction ratio and Diwani recall, because early runs absorbed ornate or uncertain examples into Thuluth while missing Diwani. text: Structured errors. The dominant failure is default-label collapse, not random confusion. Thuluth is over-predicted in 11 of 12 numeric-prompt runs; closed/API models choose it 2.05–2.93× its true frequency, and Qwen3-VL-32B reaches 3.47×. This persists after rebalancing: every numeric run has one label taking at least one-third of predictions, rising to 52.9% for GPT-4o and 62.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B. False Thuluth predictions most often come from true Diwani (40.9%), then Naskh (21.5%) and Nasta’liq (16.4%), suggesting both visual-neighbor confusion and an uncertainty default. text: 5 Discussion and Limitations This study supports a concrete claim: Arabic calligraphy recognition remains a brittle fine-grained cultural vision task for current VLMs. Aggregate accuracy hides the main failure mode: models often behave like default-label emitters with partial discrimination layered on top. Several models overuse Thuluth as the default label, while others collapse onto Naskh, Diwani, or Nasta’liq depend- ing on model family and prompt. These errors matter because calligraphic styles encode cultural, historical, and religious contexts, and automated tools should not collapse less-visible traditions into more familiar labels. Community relevance. The failure mode matters for education, museums, manuscript archives, social media, and community-facing search: collapsing Diwani, Ruq’ah, or Nasta’liq into Thuluth can distort access to Islamic visual heritage. The study has limitations: it covers six broad labels rather than regional schools, mixed-style com- positions, dating, handwriting, OCR, or localization; source and label are partly confounded for non- DuwatBench supplements; Prompt C confounds label order and response format; and API-served models can change over time. Methodologically, the benchmark is useful because it separates two effects that are often blurred in cultural-vision evaluations. The rebalanced manifest reduces the chance that high Thuluth prediction is simply learned from label frequency, while the prompt interventions show whether the same images become more legible when models are given style descriptions or an explicit Diwani
title: Discussion and Limitations

text: cultural-vision evaluations. The rebalanced manifest reduces the chance that high Thuluth prediction is simply learned from label frequency, while the prompt interventions show whether the same images become more legible when models are given style descriptions or an explicit Diwani prior. The negative result is therefore informative: even when a prompt names the right visual features, many systems still substitute a familiar-looking script for the correct one. Implications. For deployment, prompt descriptions are not enough: systems that classify or re- trieve Arabic calligraphy should report uncertainty, validate performance per style, and avoid treat- ing high aggregate accuracy as evidence that all traditions are equally legible. 6
title: Discussion and Limitations

text: We present a 12-model evaluation of Arabic calligraphy style recognition under three prompt con- ditions. The results reveal limited accuracy, recurring Thuluth over-prediction, Diwani under- recognition, and nonuniform prompt sensitivity across closed/API and open-weight VLMs. Arabic calligraphy therefore offers a compact culturally grounded benchmark for measuring not only model accuracy, but how errors redistribute visibility across significant visual traditions. text: A Dataset construction details The evaluated dataset contains 1,195 single-label Arabic calligraphy images. It was constructed from DuwatBench [Patle et al., 2026] plus real-image supplements from RuFa [Mhmoodlan, 2026] and HICMA [HICMA Project, 2026] used to reduce the original class imbalance. Curation followed a fixed pipeline: aggregate source images, retain single-label six-style items, supplement underrep- resented classes, check image-file integrity, remove exact duplicates and undersized files, then lock the manifest used for all inference runs. The final manifest contains 106 Kufic, 218 Naskh, 216 Thu- luth, 217 Diwani, 225 Ruq’ah, and 213 Nasta’liq images. Table 2 reports the source composition by label. Thuluth and Diwani share the same DuwatBench provenance, so their central confusion in the main results is not a cross-source artifact; other labels should be interpreted with the mixed-source composition in mind. Before model evaluation, the dataset was checked for missing files, corrupted images, orphan images, undersized images, and exact duplicates. One undersized image and four duplicate images were removed. Figure 3 shows representative examples from the final six-style evaluation set. text: Visual-cue prompt. You are shown an Arabic calligraphy image. Classify its calligraphic style. Choose exactly one of these six styles: 1. Kufic 2. Naskh 3. Thuluth 4. Diwani 5. Ruq’ah 6. Nasta’liq Use the following visual cues: - Kufic: angular, geometric, squared or block-like letterforms; strong horizontal/vertical structure; often rigid and monumental. - Naskh: clear, balanced, readable manuscript style; rounded letters; moderate stroke contrast; commonly used for Qur’anic and book text. - Thuluth: large, elegant, sweeping curves; elongated verticals; complex decorative composition; often used in architectural or ceremonial calligraphy. - Diwani: highly cursive and ornamental; dense flowing curves; letters may interlace; often compact and decorative. - Ruq’ah: simple, fast handwriting-like style; compact letters; short strokes; practical and less ornamental. - Nasta’liq: diagonal/slanted baseline; hanging or cascading composition; soft flowing curves; common in Persian/Urdu calligraphy. Base your answer only on visible visual style, not on the meaning of the text, image background, decoration, or color. If multiple styles seem possible, choose the closest match based on the dominant letter shapes and composition. Respond with only a single digit from 1 to 6. Do not explain. Diwani-first prompt. G Original DuwatBench-only context Before constructing the cleaned/rebalanced 1,195-image evaluation set, exploratory runs were con- ducted on the original DuwatBench [Patle et al., 2026]-style 1,272-row files. Those files include 20 multi-label or ambiguous true-label rows; Table 4 reports metrics after excluding them. We do not mix these numbers into the main comparison because they use a different dataset distribution and fewer models. They are nevertheless useful context: original DuwatBench is strongly Thuluth- heavy, so raw accuracy can look high even when balanced accuracy remains modest. These context runs support two design choices in the main paper. First, they motivate rebalancing: the original clean six-class subset has a 56.4% majority-class baseline because Thuluth dominates the dataset. Second, they show why prompt effects should be interpreted cautiously: GPT-4o’s alternative wording run greatly increases Diwani recall while reducing overall accuracy, suggesting that prompt changes can swap the default label rather than solve fine-grained recognition. 8

text: Preprint PRIMING BASE MODELS FOR AGENTIC POST-TRAINING: AN OPEN MIDTRAINING RECIPE Soumye Singhal∗, Joseph Jennings∗, Ka Shun Shum∗†, Alexander Bukharin∗, Khushi Bhardwaj∗ Zirui Liu, Venkat Srinivasan, Jonathan Li, Yash Jain, Kezhi Kong, Markus Kliegl, Olivier Delalleau, Sanjeev Satheesh, Mostofa Patwary NVIDIA
title: Preprint

text: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a mid- training stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model’s later RL trainability. Our midtrain- ing stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens im- prove SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model

text: Between pretraining and post-training, frontier coding models such as Qwen3-Coder-Next (Cao et al., 2026), GLM-5 (GLM-5 Team, 2026), Kimi-Dev (Yang et al., 2026), and Composer 2 (Cursor Research, 2026) include a midtraining stage of hundreds of billions of tokens of agentic, long- context data on top of a converged base model. Technical reports describe this stage at a high level, but rarely explain how its data is constructed, filtered, and weighted, or measure the impact of each design choice. Following Qwen-Coder (Hui et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2026), we present an open midtraining recipe for agentic coding, developed and demonstrated on Nemotron base models. We describe how each data source is built, and we report the ablations that guided our training choices. Base models are usually pretrained at short sequence lengths, typically 4K to 8K tokens for compute efficiency (DeepSeek-AI, 2024; Qwen Team, 2025), and then extended to long context in a short fi- nal stage before SFT. Nemotron models, for example, are pretrained at 8K and extended to 1M. The data that matters most for software-engineering agents does not fit this pipeline. Pretraining cor- pora usually contain almost no agent interactions, as in the Nemotron pretraining corpus (NVIDIA, 2025), and the natural data around software engineering, such as whole repositories, code evolution through commit histories, pull requests, and

Pretraining cor- pora usually contain almost no agent interactions, as in the Nemotron pretraining corpus (NVIDIA, 2025), and the natural data around software engineering, such as whole repositories, code evolution through commit histories, pull requests, and build logs, often runs to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, too long for pretraining and too large for a short long-context stage. Adding agent traces to pretraining is also not straightforward, since pretraining typically applies no loss masking, and it is unclear how the tool responses (environment outputs) in those traces should be handled. text: Preprint can reduce how much the model later gains from RL (Liu et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), and we have observed this in our own training as well. Midtraining fills this gap. Before the final long-context stage, it trains for hundreds of billions of tokens at 256K, long enough to hold whole repositories, commit histories, and long agent traces (§5.1). The data is mostly natural software-engineering data, with a bounded share of agent traces whose tool responses are masked from the loss. Much of this learning can therefore move out of SFT, so SFT can stay short and preserve the model’s later RL trainability (Liu et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). We develop the recipe on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning-30B-A3B and then scale it to the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super-120B-A12B (NVIDIA, 2026a). On N-3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining to- kens improve SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro by 3.8, 7.0, and 3.5 points over the same model without midtraining after identical full SFT, with the most sustained gains on SWE-bench Multilingual (§4.3). On N-3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT (§4.4). Midtraining also improves robustness to the agent harness, which matters for open models that are used

text: On N-3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT (§4.4). Midtraining also improves robustness to the agent harness, which matters for open models that are used with many different harnesses. Both models improve on every harness we tested, and on N-3.5 Super after 65B tokens and short SFT, the average gain across harnesses is 8.6 points on SWE-bench Verified and 6.8 on Terminal-Bench (§4.5). We make the following contributions. • A fully documented midtraining data recipe, showing that a small share of agentic traces adds clear gains on top of natural data (§3 and §4.2). • An evaluation protocol based on identical SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics such as bits-per-byte and LoCoDiff did not reliably predict post-training results (§4.1). • We show that gains hold as we scale both model size and midtraining tokens up to 500B, across benchmarks and agent harnesses (§4). • Ablations of modeling choices, such as the learning rate, the share of replayed pretraining data, tool-response masking, and midtraining’s effect on long-context ability (§5). 2

text: Midtraining in frontier coding models. Although midtraining is growing in popularity, only a few works have presented detailed recipes and ablation results to the community. Qwen3-Coder- Next provides one such recipe, midtraining at a 256K context on trillions of tokens, including 600B tokens of repository-level data across 370 programming languages (Cao et al., 2026). Its recipe sug- gests combining mined PR data with agentic traces but does not explain exactly how to do so. GLM- 5 reports midtraining on approximately 1.55T tokens with progressive context extension, including 160B tokens of software-engineering data constructed from roughly 10M issue–PR pairs (GLM-5 Team, 2026), but does not provide details of the recipe. Kimi-Dev, one of the primary works on which we build, provides a more detailed recipe (Yang et al., 2026). It performs midtraining on approximately 150B tokens of diff patches, commit sequences, and synthetic agent interactions, and shows that a model with this prior needs far fewer SFT tokens than the raw base model to reach the same agent performance. daVinci-Dev advocates trajectory-style midtraining data and matches Kimi-Dev’s performance using fewer than half as many tokens (Zeng et al., 2026). Composer 2 shows that code-focused continued pretraining improves downstream RLVR performance (Cursor Research, 2026). AgentFounder similarly shows that continued pretraining benefits search agents (Su et al., 2026), while Liu et al. (2026a)

(2026a) study when midtraining effectively bridges the distribu- tions of pretraining and post-training data. Relative to these works, we provide the ablation-level detail missing from the technical reports and evidence that the gains persist through full SFT. Repository-level data construction. StarCoder2 concatenates repository files in random order (Lozhkov et al., 2024); DeepSeek-Coder orders files by import dependencies (Guo et al., 2024); SPLiCe shows that structured packing improves long-context use (Staniszewski et al., 2025); Pro- Long randomizes on purpose to avoid recency bias (Gao et al., 2025). Sapronov & Glukhov (2025) find that most of the gain from repository-level pretraining for project-level code completion comes from adapting to a longer context rather than from how the repository context is assembled. Agentic benchmarks are unreliable before post- training, so Composer 2 selects among base models using held-out codebase perplexity, state track- ing, and adversarially built QA instead (Cursor Research, 2026). Other benchmarks target specific skills. LoCoDiff measures file-state reconstruction from git history (Mentat AI Team (AbanteAI), 2025), RepoBench and CrossCodeEval measure cross-file completion (Liu et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2023), and APTBench converts agent tasks into a format base models can answer (Qin et al., 2025). Whether such base-model measures predict downstream ability is still contested (Liu et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025). In our experiments, they did not track post-training results reliably (§4.1). 3 THE MIDTRAINING RECIPE Figure 1 summarizes the blend, which is designed for diversity. Most of it is natural software- engineering data, with a small share of synthetic agent traces. We render these traces in the Nemotron chat template and keep them to 10–15% of the blend to avoid overfitting to SFT-like data, which can hurt later RL trainability (Liu et al., 2026b; Kang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Everything else stays in natural formats, without chat templates. Every source keeps only permissive licenses and goes through decontamination against SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, secret redac- tion, and loss masking of content the model should not imitate, such

text: et al., 2026). Everything else stays in natural formats, without chat templates. Every source keeps only permissive licenses and goes through decontamination against SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench, secret redac- tion, and loss masking of content the model should not imitate, such as repeated delimiters, hashes, and timestamps. Issue–PR. We construct a large-scale code-change corpus from merged pull requests in public GitHub repositories, combining repository snapshots with PR descriptions, linked issues, review discussions, and observed patch evolution when available. We restrict collection to repositories with at least ten stars in supported programming languages. We deduplicate examples by repository and PR identifier and remove records with unavailable repositories, missing Git objects, failed patch reconstruction, empty or excessively large changes, generated content, or other low-quality patches. Each example is laid out as a sequence in which repository metadata, date, file tree, and code context condition the model’s reconstruction of the submitted changes. No chat template is applied to this data, but we mask repetitive formatting text from the training loss. In total, this process leaves 3

text: Preprint us with 12.1 million PRs and 200 billion to 2 trillion tokens depending on how much repository context we include in each example. For issue-linked PRs, a structured LLM judge additionally checks that the issue and the patch match, and PR-only examples are filtered with deterministic rules (Appendix A.1). Repositories. Pretraining corpora have historically presented code as individual files rather than whole repositories, and even when files from one repository are packed together, a short pretraining context holds only a small part of it. Agents, however, work inside repositories far longer than that and must use code defined far from where it is called. Midtraining is where the model first reads whole repositories and predicts code that depends on files tens of thousands of tokens earlier. This helps most when the files actually depend on each other, and in many repositories they do not, since many are collections of scripts, exercises, or snippets that never import one another. We start from the repositories in the Nemotron 3 pretraining corpus (NVIDIA, 2025), build an import graph for every repository in 14 languages, and keep only repositories in which at least 20% of code files have an import edge to another file in the repository (10% for Ruby). Kept repositories are serialized with the top-level README first and connected files next

text: 14 languages, and keep only repositories in which at least 20% of code files have an import edge to another file in the repository (10% for Ruby). Kept repositories are serialized with the top-level README first and connected files next to each other, and packed at 256K, with longer repositories split between connected components rather than truncated, giving about 104B tokens. Compared to alphabetical ordering, dependency ordering better separates stronger from weaker models. It lowers bits-per-byte for stronger models and raises it for weaker ones, which suggests that it exposes cross-file structure that weaker models have not yet learned. The languages, filters, and blend weights are listed in Appendix A.2. Diff data. Much of software engineering is changing existing code, such as making an edit that stays consistent across several files or keeping track of what a file looks like after a long series of changes. Repository snapshots only show code in its final state, so we build two kinds of examples from commit histories. Multi-file edits take a merged pull request, show the model the affected files before the change, and train it to produce them after the change. We keep only changes whose files are linked in the import graph used for the repository data, so that the edits are coupled. Code- evolution documents give the initial state
title: Preprint

text: change, and train it to produce them after the change. We keep only changes whose files are linked in the import graph used for the repository data, so that the edits are coupled. Code- evolution documents give the initial state of a file, the sequence of real commits that changed it from oldest to newest, and its final state. This trains the long-range state tracking that LoCoDiff measures (Mentat AI Team (AbanteAI), 2025). Histories range from a single commit to several dozen. Diff headers, commit hashes, authors, and dates are masked from the loss. Sources, filters, and statistics are in Appendix A.3. Build and CI logs. Agents constantly read logs, stack traces, and build output, but PR data lacks the environment’s response, so we add raw system logs from the full LogHub archives (Zhu et al., 2023) and CI/CD logs from GitHub Actions run logs and workflow-file histories (Moriconi et al., 2025; Cardoen et al., 2024), plus a small curated slice pairing log windows with diagnoses (Ap- pendix A.4). Agentic traces. We include agent trajectories to teach interaction patterns that natural software artifacts lack, such as multi-step tool use, testing changes, and recovering from failures. These trajectories are separate from the SFT data. The highest-quality trajectories are reserved for SFT, and midtraining puts the rest to use, including trajectories from

text: natural software artifacts lack, such as multi-step tool use, testing changes, and recovering from failures. These trajectories are separate from the SFT data. The highest-quality trajectories are reserved for SFT, and midtraining puts the rest to use, including trajectories from earlier teacher models and tasks that do not fit post-training. The corpus used in our blend contains about 39B tokens (over one million trajectories, about 500K distinct queries, and 30M tool calls, including SWE-Zero and SWE-Hero trajectories (Ludwig et al., 2026)). A small portion of the agentic midtraining blend consists of data contributed by Perplexity as a partner in the Nemotron Coalition. The full trace corpus covers more than ten agent scaf- folds, including OpenHands (Wang et al., 2025), OpenCode, SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024), Codex, Claude Code, and Terminus, across software engineering, terminal use, search, and general tool use, because traces from a single scaffold transfer poorly to others (Cao et al., 2026). Each trajectory keeps its scaffold’s instructions and tool definitions and is rendered in the Nemotron chat template. Appendix A.5 gives the statistics and distributions. Filtering targets shortcuts and undesirable interaction patterns, including solution leakage through Git history or Internet lookup, unfinished trajectories, malformed tool calls, and repetitive file- 4

text: Preprint inspection loops. As in SFT, we train only on assistant turns, including tool calls, since also training on tool responses hurts results after SFT (§5.2). 3.1 TRAINING Midtraining starts from a converged base model, so we choose the training setup to add new capabil- ities without degrading what the base model already knows. We train at 256K context, long enough to hold almost every midtraining document, many of which are far longer than the 8K pretraining context (Figure 2). Our first N-3.5 Lightning experiments start from the 8K pretraining checkpoint, N-3.5 Lightning-8K. For the N-3.5 Lightning scaling run and all N-3.5 Super runs, we start from the 1M long-context checkpoint, which lets us go straight from midtraining to SFT, keeping evaluations simple. In a mature pipeline, midtraining would come before the final long-context stage (§5.1). We set the replay share to 20% (§5.3). The learning rate warms up briefly and then stays constant, at 5e-5 for N-3.5 Lightning, which favors agentic gains, and 1e-5 for the larger N-3.5 Super, which favors preserving general capabilities (§5.3). Appendix B lists the full settings. 4 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS 4.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL The success of midtraining is ultimately measured by how well the model does after post-training. Our evaluation protocol is therefore holistic. It runs the full post-training pipeline and also tracks base-model

text: full settings. 4 EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS 4.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL The success of midtraining is ultimately measured by how well the model does after post-training. Our evaluation protocol is therefore holistic. It runs the full post-training pipeline and also tracks base-model post-trainability metrics and pretraining general-capability benchmarks. • Short and full SFT. We use an agentic-focused SFT blend (Appendix B.1) at two budgets, 33B tokens (short SFT) and 100B tokens (full SFT), and compare each midtrained model with its starting checkpoint after identical SFT. Full SFT was close to saturation in our runs and supports the main claims, while short SFT gives a quicker signal. • Fixed evaluations. We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, Deep- SWE, Terminal-Bench (version 2.0, or 2.1 where noted), and a BrowseComp subset. Un- less stated otherwise, SWE-bench runs in OpenHands and Terminal-Bench in Terminus-2, with pass@1 averaged over 3 and 8 rollouts per task (Appendix C.1 gives the setup and references). We also report pass@k, since a higher pass@k has been shown to indicate more room for RL to improve (Yue et al., 2025). • Base-model post-trainability metrics. LoCoDiff (Mentat AI Team (AbanteAI), 2025), RepoBench (Liu et al., 2024), and bits-per-byte on held-out code repositories and on agent traces (Appendix C.2) measure capabilities that midtraining targets, such as file-state track- ing and cross-file modeling.
title: Preprint

text: • Base-model post-trainability metrics. LoCoDiff (Mentat AI Team (AbanteAI), 2025), RepoBench (Liu et al., 2024), and bits-per-byte on held-out code repositories and on agent traces (Appendix C.2) measure capabilities that midtraining targets, such as file-state track- ing and cross-file modeling. For traces we score the decisive turns of DeepSWE trajectories (Yu et al., 2026), which correlated best with post-training results. LoCoDiff is averaged over 3 greedy runs on all 198 cases, and the other metrics are single runs. They improve with midtraining (Table 4), but did not track post-training results closely enough to guide recipe decisions. • Regression checks. During midtraining we also track the pretraining general-capability benchmarks from NVIDIA (2026b) in four groups, general knowledge, math, code, and commonsense understanding (Appendix C.1), to catch regressions (§5.3). 4.2 BLEND VALIDATION ON N-3.5 LIGHTNING Our first experiment midtrains the N-3.5 Lightning-8K base model for 100B tokens, once on the full blend and once without agentic traces, and compares both with the base model after identical SFT (Table 2). Gains seen after short SFT carry over to full SFT, so short SFT can serve as a quick check. Midtraining improves SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual pass@1 by 0.8 and 8.2 points after short SFT, and both gains remain after full SFT (3.8 and 3.7 points). Terminal-Bench is noisier and improves only in full-SFT

Table 8 compares the usual order, where N-3.5 Lightning-8K goes straight to the long-context stage, with a 100B-token N-3.5 Lightning midtraining run at 256K before a long-context stage. Midtraining alone brings N- 3.5 Lightning-8K within about five points of the long-context base model on RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) up to 128K, but trails by 14 points at 256K. After the long-context stage, the midtrained model beats the long-context base model at every length from 64K to 256K and stays within two points at shorter lengths. Midtraining thus does part of the work of the long-context stage, and this carries over to the final model. Appendix E.2 gives more results for N-3.5 Super. 5.2 MASKING TOOL RESPONSES IN TRACES Agent traces interleave the model’s own actions with tool responses, the outputs the environment returns after each tool call. Some recent work also trains on tool responses, so that the model learns to predict how the environment reacts, a form of world modeling (FAIR CodeGen Team, 2025; Zeng et al., 2026). We tested this with the setup of §4.2, midtraining N-3.5
