text: work also trains on tool responses, so that the model learns to predict how the environment reacts, a form of world modeling (FAIR CodeGen Team, 2025; Zeng et al., 2026). We tested this with the setup of §4.2, midtraining N-3.5 Lightning-8K for 100B tokens with and without tool responses in the loss, followed by identical SFT with an earlier version of our SFT recipe. In our experiments, training on tool responses did not work out of the box and lowered SWE-bench Verified pass@1 by about 10 points (Table 9), so we train only on assistant turns, as in SFT. Tool responses are often long and noisy, such as file dumps, test logs, and error traces, and predicting them may take capacity away from learning the agent’s own actions. 5.3 PRETRAINING REPLAY AND LEARNING RATE Replay keeps the model close to its pretraining distribution, so that midtraining shifts the data dis- tribution gradually rather than abruptly. We started from 20% replay as a reasonable default, with the goal of no regression on general-capability benchmarks. Table 10 shows that N-3.5 Super does not regress through 65B tokens, with every benchmark group within 1.2 points of the starting check- point. We also tried 40% replay, which gave no clear benefit over 20%, so we kept 20%. 8

text: We presented an open midtraining recipe for agentic coding, with full details of how each data source is built, filtered, and weighted and how the models are trained. After identical SFT, the recipe gives clear gains as midtraining scales to 500B tokens on N-3.5 Lightning, and it carries over to the larger N-3.5 Super, where it raises DeepSWE, the hardest benchmark we evaluate, from 11.7 to 15.7 and also improves SWE-bench Verified and BrowseComp. On both models, midtraining improves results on every agent harness we tested. Our experiments show that agentic traces are essential, since natural software-engineering data alone gives much smaller gains after SFT, and that a short SFT run gives a more direct post-training signal than base-model post-trainability metrics, which remain useful to track. Midtraining at 256K also works as an intermediate long-context stage, and we explain our other modeling choices, such as tool-response masking and pretraining replay. Limitations and future work. Agentic benchmarks are noisy, and each comparison is a single run, so differences of one or two points, especially on Terminal-Bench, may come from run-to-run variation. We did not compare against spending the same tokens on longer pretraining or SFT, since midtraining adds a separate stage that complements SFT rather than replacing it. text: We did not compare against spending the same tokens on longer pretraining or SFT, since midtraining adds a separate stage that complements SFT rather than replacing it. We tested the recipe only on Nemotron models, not on other model families, and mainly on agentic coding. Our SFT evaluations use an agentic-focused SFT blend rather than a full general-purpose post-training blend. Our RL results are also limited, since clear RL gains on top of a strong SFT checkpoint were difficult to get at the N-3.5 Lightning scale and RL was too compute intensive at the N-3.5 Super scale, so we report only a short, single-seed run on N-3.5 Lightning-8K (Appendix D). For future work, since traces drove most of the gains, we plan to scale trace data with more diversity, and we have already expanded our trace corpus to about 90B tokens. We also plan to extend the agentic data to more capabilities and to move more post-training data, such as reasoning and chat data, into midtraining. A MIDTRAINING DATA This appendix documents every source in the blend, including how it is collected, filtered, and weighted, and Appendix B lists the full training settings. We plan to release data-processing scripts and training-set metadata in a future version. A.1 ISSUE–PR For PRs linked to an issue, an LLM judge checks whether the issue and the PR match. The judge reads the full issue and PR text, the final patch, and the paths of the changed files, and labels each pair as clean or assigns one of seven failure modes, namely a revert, an incidental issue link, a wrong issue reference, a partial fix, an issue with no clear action, an underspecified issue, or a PR that does much more than the issue asks. We keep clean pairs and remove pairs that cannot be fixed. We repair the others by linking the PR to the correct issue, narrowing its scope, keeping it as a PR-only example, or splitting it from unrelated changes. For PRs without a linked issue, we remove those that change only README files or three lines or fewer. A.2 REPOSITORIES The repository data starts from the code repositories in the Nemotron 3 pretraining corpus (NVIDIA, 2025), a deduplicated collection of public repositories with permissive licenses, and covers 14 lan- guages (Table 12). Connectedness. For each language, we parse the references that link one file to another, such as imports in Python, includes in C and C++, and module paths in Go. A repository’s connected fraction is the share of its code files that import another file in the repository, and we keep repositories where this share is at least 20%. For Ruby we lower the threshold to 10%, because Rails autoloading hides most references from static parsing. We exclude languages with little cross-file structure that parsing can recover, such as Shell, R, and Swift, as well as markup and configuration languages. Serialization. The code files follow the README in depth-first order over the import graph, so the files of each connected component stay together and each file sits near the files it imports. Each file starts with a header that gives the repository name and file path, and the header is masked from the loss. 14

text: Preprint SELECTION IS NOT LEARNING: CHOOSING MODEL FUTURES Haoyi Yang∗ Kshitij Mishra∗ Nils Lukas Salem Lahlou Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi, UAE {haoyi.yang,kshitij.mishra,nils.lukas,salem.lahlou}@mbzuai.ac.ae

text: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection- to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HEIRCOMMIT freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EVOHEIR separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HEIRCOMMIT cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68–83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EVOHEIR achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited. text: Self-evolving language models generate tasks and train on their own outputs (Huang et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b). Each inherited update changes both the learner and the curriculum of later rounds, allowing progress or regressions to accumulate (Shao et al., 2026). Self-training can even raise a model’s target metric and then collapse it within the same training campaign (Lin, 2026). The central decision is therefore which learning outcomes to carry forward. Task-side selection leaves a selection-to-update gap: pass rate, disagreement, and frontier proximity describe pre-training behavior, not the transfer produced by an optimizer update. In our audits, 42–52% of native Agent0/R-Zero admissions leave the frontier under independent responses. Even with exact-valid tasks, 60 of 96 Skill Self-Play (Skill-SP) updates have nonpositive correct-target NLL gain. Learning opportunities must ultimately be judged by the states they produce. HEIRCOMMIT judges realized transitions: it freezes a successor, compares it with the current model (the root) on fresh probes, and inherits that state or retains root. Fresh evidence separates confirmation from the noise that favored the proposal during selection. The deeper question is the granularity of inheritance. SOAR uses actual student improvement to reward a teacher (Sundaram et al., 2026), and APE evaluates candidate fine-tunings before accepting updates (Mar´ın, 2025). SOAR uses actual student improvement to reward a teacher (Sundaram et al., 2026), and APE evaluates candidate fine-tunings before accepting updates (Mar´ın, 2025). Pre-commit skill verification (Shang et al., 2026) and anytime-valid certificates (Sengupta, 2026) gate agent updates while the base model stays frozen. Whole-state acceptance nevertheless couples a branch’s gains and losses. Must a useful experience donor also supply the next learner’s parameters? Separating these choices opens a learning path beyond whole-state acceptance (Figure 1). EVOHEIR separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance. Screening picks the re- cipient that supplies the next learner’s parameters, either a branch endpoint or the current model. EXPERIENCE RECOVERY then repairs this recipient’s failures with current and archived reference solutions while preserving its successes. HEIRCOMMIT confirms the completed post-absorption state against root. Qualified experience enters the archive regardless of this decision: parameter inheritance can stop without discarding material that helps a later recipient. We evaluate HEIRCOMMIT on the native updates of three self-evolution hosts, and EVOHEIR on four backbones over ten rounds. HEIRCOMMIT cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68–83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate, on every host. EVOHEIR achieves the highest mathematics and general-reasoning averages on all four backbones and beats Agent0 on 45 of 48 benchmark–backbone pairs. References from eight

EVOHEIR achieves the highest mathematics and general-reasoning averages on all four backbones and beats Agent0 on 45 of 48 benchmark–backbone pairs. References from eight of ten donors weaker than the current model still improve the recipient. Our contributions are: 1. We identify the selection-to-update gap and prove that pre-update behavior alone cannot identify an update’s value. Reusing screening evidence to accept a branch pays a union bound over branches, which fresh confirmation removes. 2. We introduce HEIRCOMMIT, a source-independent rule that commits a frozen successor only when it beats the current model on fresh probes. On the native updates of R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill-SP, it turns negative pool gain positive on two of the three hosts. 3. We develop EVOHEIR, which decides separately which parameters the next learner inherits and which experience it absorbs. Across four backbones it raises the base model’s math average by 7.9–30.1%, the most of any compared method. 4. We show that experience outlives the model that produced it. Recovery beats direct fine-tuning on the same 64 references by 1.93 pp on average, and experience from rounds whose model was rejected adds 0.66 pp beyond committed-round history. 2

text: We identify the selection-to-update gap: admitting a task that looks learnable does not ensure a useful update, and 60 of 96 updates on verified tasks show no gain. HEIRCOMMIT inherits a successor only when it beats the current model on fresh probes and cuts the harmful share of commits by 68–83% on three self-evolution hosts. EVOHEIR separates the parameters a round inherits from the experience it keeps and raises the math average by up to 7.0% over Agent0, the strongest baseline. Self-evolving systems should judge the updates they produce, not only the tasks they choose, and keep experience beyond the models that produced it. 9

B DETAILED METHOD AND IMPLEMENTATION B.1 STATE CONSTRUCTION AND RECIPIENT SELECTION The resumable learner St = (θt, ωt) holds the model parameters and the mutable training state, including optimizer moments, the learning-rate scheduler, and random generators. The Evolution Controller runs each admitted cohort in an isolated copy of the same root, and each branch follows the host’s training objective. The controller freezes the candidate set Cnat t ∪{St} before screening, selects the recipient by paired root-relative gain on P scr t , and breaks ties in favor of the root, followed by a fixed branch order. Algorithm 1 lists one round. B.2 RECIPIENT-CONDITIONED RECOVERY Recovery adapts distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) and Learning without Forgetting (Li & Hoiem, 2017) to recipient-specific failures and successes. Current records Et and archived records Mt supply problems and qualified references, each with its generating checkpoint, round, and verification trace. A cached recipient attempt is reused only at the exact selected checkpoint. The same answer- equivalence rule verifies the attempt and its reference, and membership in Drepair t or Dkeep t is decided for the

The same answer- equivalence rule verifies the attempt and its reference, and membership in Drepair t or Dkeep t is decided for the current recipient, even when the reference comes from an earlier round. The frozen teacher and the student both start from θsel t and predict at the same fixed recipient prefixes throughout absorption, as in Eq. 4, so the procedure does not resample from the changing student. B.3 ARCHIVE, FEEDBACK, AND STATE INHERITANCE HEIRCOMMIT freezes S+ t before scoring it against the original root on the fixed confirmation pool with the same probes and frozen labels (Appendix A). It commits the complete proposal when the paired gain exceeds τt, with τt = 0 in the empirical mode, and otherwise restores the complete root state. Each round confirms one final proposal, and later rounds receive fresh evidence. Archive updates follow a separate path in Algorithm 1: qualified current records are considered for admission regardless of the commit outcome, so a round that retains the root still contributes references to 16

text: Preprint later rounds. The controller records the signed confirmation value with recipient and experience provenance, and subsequent curricula follow the host’s feedback rule, shared by Full and No Recovery. Failure modes and safeguards. An incomplete or conflicting reference is excluded before training, a duplicate normalized problem occupies one archive slot, and a cached attempt is reused only from the exact selected checkpoint. A flawed reference that passes the verifier can still steer the repair teacher, so repair depends on verification quality. Absorption can also lose successes, as the round-7 net gain of −0.20 pp in Figure 7 shows. With the empirical zero threshold, sampling noise can admit a harmful proposal; the positive-margin mode of Theorem 1 bounds that risk. B.4 IMPLEMENTATION CONFIGURATION Appendix A and Table 3 give the EVOHEIR (Full) recipe. The remaining implementation details are as follows. Response-token aggregation. Response loss is computed only on recorded response tokens; prompt tokens are masked out. If an EOS token is present in the recorded response, it is included in the loss. Truncated responses contribute their available response prefix without synthesizing a missing EOS token. Token-level forward KL over the full vocabulary is averaged within each response, then over questions, so repair and keep examples have equal per-question weight. Absorption and optimizer state. Recovery uses AdamW with learning rate 5 ×

text: Preprint Proof of Proposition 1. Fix a native step size η > 0 and a value gap ∆> 0. At root θ = 0, consider two learning worlds with local training losses and a common probe loss ℓ+(θ) = c + θ, ℓ−(θ) = c −θ, ℓp(θ) = cp + ∆ η θ. (C.1) The worlds share the stipulated root behavior, target validity, and root loss values. Their training gradients are +1 and −1, respectively, and are outside Ot. One gradient step reaches −η or +η. For q = −ℓp, the root-relative values are therefore +∆and −∆. Positive smooth losses on the whole real line can be obtained by multiplying each linear term by a smooth cutoff in [0, 1], equal to one on [−η, η] and zero outside [−2η, 2η], choosing c > 2η and cp > 2∆. This preserves the root gradients and both post-update probe values. An observation-based rule uses the same commit probability p in both worlds. Against the better of root and the native update, its expected regrets are (1 −p)∆and p∆. Their maximum is at least their average, ∆/2. text: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents Weihao Li1∗, Zihang Xu2∗, Zhongqiu Wang1∗ Songwei Yu4, Wenqiang Zhu1, Yuechen Luo3 Jingxuan Xu4, Yanan Wu1, Haoyang Huang1, Ken Deng1† 1Independent Researchers, 2Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 3Tsinghua University, 4National University of Singapore 12532572@mail.sustech.edu.cn
title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks

text: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often un- fold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordi- nated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and veri- fiable rewards for training code agents. 1

text: Executable repository-level benchmarks have increasingly become a central testbed for software engineering agents. SWE-bench and its variants pair a natural-language is- sue with a repository state and an executable test oracle, enabling standardized, verifiable evaluation of generated patches (Jimenez et al. 2023; Zan et al. 2025; Deng et al. 2025). Most benchmarks, however, retain a single issue or pull request (PR) as the basic task unit. This abstraction cap- tures isolated bug fixes and localized features, but only a restricted portion of real software development. In practice, a single feature, migration, dependency upgrade, or system- atic fix often evolves across multiple PRs. These changes may be sequential, branch in parallel, or converge through later integration. The missing abstraction is therefore not merely longer context or a larger patch, but the dependency struc- ture connecting multiple changes into a coherent engineer- ing objective. text: WEAVE constructs executable dependency-structured tasks for verifiable evaluation and rewards. Recent work has moved beyond isolated PRs by grouping changes through release windows, temporal spans, explicit cross-references, or object-level dependencies (Thai et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2026; Jiang et al. 2026; Zhou et al. 2026). These efforts advance long-horizon software engineering, yet two coupled challenges remain. First, these aggregation sig- nals are imperfect proxies for task coherence: temporal prox- imity can merge unrelated changes, explicit references are sparse, and coarse overlap is often dominated by frequently modified utilities, configuration files, or dependency mani- fests. Moreover, a related change set does not itself define a reproducible task with a valid base state, task specification, and executable oracle. Second, current evaluation poorly cap- tures structured partial progress. Binary resolution ignores progress on unsolved tasks, while flat test- or PR-level ag- gregation overlooks dependencies and may over-credit down- stream behavior built on incomplete upstream changes. text: As illus- trated in Figure 1, WEAVE starts from verified atomic PRs, identifies code-grounded relations through typed change loci calibrated by repository-local frequencies, and organizes re- lated changes into bounded dependency DAGs. Each DAG is instantiated as a reproducible repository-level task with a unified specification and executable oracle, while remain- ing evaluator-side metadata unavailable to the agent. Beyond task construction, the DAG provides a common interface for measuring and learning from structured progress. We introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic and test-grounded metric that complements binary resolution by rewarding dependency-consistent partial completion. The same struc- ture supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning, while the constructed corpus provides long-horizon trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. WEAVE thereby uni- fies executable task construction, structure-aware evaluation, and agent training over realistic multi-PR software evolution. To assess both the benchmarking and training utility of WEAVE, we conduct a four-part empirical study covering task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. WEAVE yields 3200 training tasks and 300 held-out benchmark tasks spanning six pro- gramming languages. Its code-grounded aggregation pro- duces more coherent task groupings and a higher executable- task yield than temporal and coarse-overlap baselines. Eval- uations of eight software engineering agents further show that Graph Credit exposes structurally inconsistent credit obscured by flat scoring. Under matched supervised-token budgets, WEAVE-based supervision improves downstream agent performance,

text: a higher executable- task yield than temporal and coarse-overlap baselines. Eval- uations of eight software engineering agents further show that Graph Credit exposes structurally inconsistent credit obscured by flat scoring. Under matched supervised-token budgets, WEAVE-based supervision improves downstream agent performance, while graph-structured rewards outper- form binary and flat-reward baselines. Together, these results establish dependency-structured tasks as a principled foun- dation for both evaluating and improving code agents. Contributions. Our contributions are threefold: • Executable dependency-structured task construction. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that constructs bounded dependency DAGs from verified PR histories using repository-calibrated typed change loci, and instan- tiates each graph as a unified executable task. • Structure-aware evaluation and verifiable credit. We introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric for evaluating dependency-consistent partial progress. By conditioning credit on upstream resolution, it complements binary and flat scoring while providing a dense, verifiable signal for agent optimization. • Empirical validation for benchmarking and training. Extensive experiments show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, captures progress missed by structure- agnostic evaluation, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents. 2

Subsequent benchmarks improve instance quality or expand the same atomic issue–PR formulation across visual software, programming languages, recent repository states, and more challenging enterprise- scale changes (Jimenez et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2024; Zan et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025a; Deng et al. 2025). Complete implementation details and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix. 5.1 RQ1: Construction Validity To validate WEAVE’s construction pipeline, we evaluate whether typed-locus coupling recovers true dependency edges more reliably than single-signal alternatives. The eval- uation covers 30 repositories containing 1,198 validated atomic PRs. To establish ground truth, three expert annota- tors independently assess candidate PR pairs and label each as dependency, same-task but independent, loosely related, or unrelated; a senior annotator adjudicates disagreements, yielding 219 gold dependency edges (Fleiss’ κ = 0.791). Each method produces a scored ranking of candidate edges; we report macro-averaged AP over repositories, Coverage—the fraction of gold edges recalled at full emission—and pooled Precision at rank 50 (P@50). text: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation of current soft- ware engineering agent evaluation: the lack of a task abstrac- tion that captures causal dependencies among multiple repos- itory changes. We introduce WEAVE, which recovers depen- dency DAGs from verified PR histories through repository- calibrated typed-locus coupling. The same graph representa- tion unifies task construction, dependency-conditioned par- tial credit (Graph Credit), and structured reward design, enabling consistent evaluation and optimization of long- horizon code agents. Experiments across construction qual- ity, agent benchmarking, supervised training, and reinforce- ment learning demonstrate the effectiveness of WEAVE as both a challenging evaluation workbench and an effective

text: A Construction Pipeline Details This appendix details the three stages of the WEAVE con- struction pipeline introduced in the main paper: typed change loci extraction (§A.1), edge filtering and bounded DAG as- sembly (§A.2), and rollback construction with test attribution (§A.3). A.1 Typed Change Loci Extraction Recovering dependency structure from PR histories requires a representation granular enough to distinguish genuine en- gineering dependencies from coincidental co-modification. File-level overlap—the most common proxy in prior work— conflates distinct changes within shared files and over- connects PRs that modify frequently touched configuration manifests, barrel imports, or dependency lockfiles. WEAVE addresses this by representing each PR as a set of typed change loci: fine-grained program entities extracted from its code diff, each annotated with a structural category that deter- mines its evidential role in coupling computation. We define five locus types, each designed to capture a distinct channel of cross-PR evidence: 1. AST declarations (Last): Function, method, and class definitions identified via language-specific AST parsers. We extract fully qualified names (e.g., module.Class.method) to disambiguate identically named entities across files. 2. Lightweight symbols (Lsym): Exported symbols, type aliases, constants, and enum members extracted from declaration-level analysis without full semantic resolu- tion. This captures entities that do not correspond to func- tion bodies but serve as cross-module interfaces. 3. Configuration and schema entries (Lcfg): Structured keys
title: Construction Pipeline Details

text: symbols, type aliases, constants, and enum members extracted from declaration-level analysis without full semantic resolu- tion. This captures entities that do not correspond to func- tion bodies but serve as cross-module interfaces. 3. Configuration and schema entries (Lcfg): Structured keys in YAML, TOML, JSON, and INI configuration files; database migration column definitions; API route declarations; and protobuf/GraphQL field paths. Each entry is represented as a dot-separated key path (e.g., server.http.timeout). 4. Declarations and signatures (Ldecl): Type signatures, interface definitions, abstract method declarations, and trait/protocol requirements. These capture contract-level changes that downstream implementations depend on. 5. Dependency keys (Ldep): Package manager entries (e.g., requirements.txt, package.json, go.mod), import statements, and build-system target declarations. These capture supply-chain relationships between PRs that modify shared external dependencies. Language support. Table 4 summarizes the extraction capabilities for the six languages in WEAVE-Bench and WEAVE-Train. AST parsing is implemented via Tree-sitter grammars, which provide incremental, error-tolerant pars- ing for all six languages. Symbol and declaration extraction build on language-specific Tree-sitter queries; for JavaScript, which lacks a native type system, Ldecl relies on heuris- tic extraction from JSDoc annotations and runtime pat- terns. Exclusion rules. Certain file categories are excluded from loci extraction because they introduce coupling signals unre- lated to engineering dependencies. Test files (matching pat- terns such as test_*, *_test.*, and language-specific test directories) are excluded because test co-modification frequently reflects shared test infrastructure rather than production-code dependency. Generated code, vendored de- pendencies (e.g., vendor/, node_modules/), and bi- nary files are excluded as they represent mechanical artifacts. Formatting-only changes—PRs where all hunks contain only whitespace, comment, or import-order modifications (detected via AST-level diff equivalence)—are excluded to prevent automated formatters from producing spurious cou- pling edges. A.2 Edge Filtering and DAG Assembly Mechanical-change filtering. Not all PR pairs with high coupling scores reflect genuine engineering dependencies. Certain repository maintenance patterns produce mechani- cally related patches that inflate coupling metrics without meaningful task structure. We identify and remove four cat- egories before DAG assembly: • Reverts: PR pj is identified as a revert of pi via two complementary signals: (i) title-level patterns (Revert "...") and (ii) content-level detection where the diff of pj is the near-exact (≥95% line overlap) inverse of pi’s diff. • Backports and cherry-picks: PRs explicitly labeled as cherry-picks or backports (via commit message mark- ers

Across our construction corpus, backports and cherry-picks dominate the filtered set (>95%), as multi-branch workflows frequently produce mechanically identical patches across re- lease channels. Reverts, release-branch references, and near- duplicate patches each contribute a small fraction of the re- mainder. Component partitioning. Extracted subgraphs are removed from the component, and the process repeats until no sub- graph of size ≥2 with mean edge weight ≥θ remains. Node budget. The budget K controls the maximum num- ber of PR nodes in a single task. We set K=8 based on two considerations. First, rollback feasibility: constructing executable in- stances requires reverting all constituent PRs from the repos- itory’s integrated state (§A.3). In our corpus, the median merge-time span (first PR to last PR) is 51 days for K=4 tasks and 78 days for K=8 tasks. Although larger K does not monotonically increase span—K=8 chains are often dense feature or migration bursts with short inter-PR intervals (∼10–15 days), while smaller chains can span longer periods with sparser commits—the absolute span at K=8 (median ∼2.5 months, range 17–332 days) means the repository accu- mulates substantial intervening changes from outside the task scope, raising the probability of non-trivial merge conflicts during rollback construction. A subset of assembled DAGs are structurally uninformative for evaluation despite passing coupling and size thresholds. We apply three topo- logical filters: • Star graphs, where a single hub node accounts for >80% of all incident edges with no inter-leaf connections, typ- ically indicate a utility-file artifact rather than a genuine multi-party dependency chain. • Trivially serial chains with uniformly low edge weights (below the 25th percentile of the repository’s weight dis- tribution) and no branching structure, which provide lim- ited evaluation signal beyond what single-PR benchmarks already capture. • Post-filtering disconnection: DAGs that become dis- connected after mechanical-change removal are re- partitioned into their connected components and re- evaluated independently. A.3 Rollback Construction and Test Attribution Base state construction. Given a candidate DAG G = (V, E) and the repository state Sgold where all constituent PRs have been merged, we construct the base state Sbase by removing the changes introduced by all nodes in V . The primary mechanism
title: Algorithm 1: Dependency DAG Assembly

text: Given a candidate DAG G = (V, E) and the repository state Sgold where all constituent PRs have been merged, we construct the base state Sbase by removing the changes introduced by all nodes in V . The primary mechanism is reverse-topological revert: we compute a topological ordering σ of V and process nodes in reverse order σ−1 (leaves first), applying git revert -no-commit for each node’s merge commit. PRs external to G that were merged between the earliest and latest con- stituent PRs are preserved in Sbase, ensuring the base state reflects realistic repository evolution outside the task scope. When git revert produces non-trivial merge conflicts— typically caused by overlapping modifications from interven- ing commits or cross-cutting refactors—we employ an agent- assisted carve as a fallback. In this path, an LLM-based agent receives the PR metadata (title, description, and code diff) and removes the target changes from the current repository state while preserving surrounding code. The carve operates semantically rather than mechanically: the agent identifies which hunks correspond to the target PR’s contributions and removes them while maintaining syntactic and build validity. After either path, the resulting Sbase is validated: it must compile successfully and all P2P (pass-to-pass) tests must pass. Candidates where neither revert nor carve produces a valid base state are discarded. Construction success rates. Approximately 35%

Candidates where neither revert nor carve produces a valid base state are discarded. Construction success rates. Approximately 35% of can- didate DAGs are discarded during construction because nei- ther revert nor carve produces a valid, test-passing base state. Among the successfully constructed instances (which form the final WEAVE-Bench and WEAVE-Train corpora), 73% are built via clean git revert and 27% require agent-assisted carve. The higher carve rate for Java and Kotlin tasks reflects stricter type-system constraints that propagate through revert sequences, while Python and JavaScript tasks exhibit higher clean-revert rates due to fewer cross-module compilation de- pendencies. Test attribution. For graph-conditioned scoring, each F2P test must be associated with one or more PR nodes in the task DAG. The primary attribution mechanism is isolated revert: for each node v ∈V , we construct Sv = Sgold \ {v} by reverting only v’s changes, then execute all F2P tests against Sv. If exactly one node v causes test t to fail, t is at- tributed to v; if multiple nodes independently cause failure, t is marked ambiguous; if t fails only under joint reversion, it is unattributed. B.2 Randomized-Graph Controls To confirm that Graph Credit’s diagnostic value arises from the true dependency structure rather than arbitrary graph constraints, we evaluate node-permuted random graphs as controls. Experimental setup. For each WEAVE-Bench task, we generate 10 random permutations of the node labels while preserving the DAG topology. Graph Credit is recomputed under each permuted graph, and results are averaged across permutations. Results. Under the true DAG, the mean OverCredit (Flat- F2P −Graph Credit) is 10.5 pp across all agent configura- tions. Under randomized graphs: • Mean OverCredit drops to 1.6 pp (<2 pp as reported in the main text). • The standard deviation across permutations is 0.7 pp, in- dicating stable behavior. • For 89% of tasks, the randomized OverCredit is within 2 pp of zero. This demonstrates that the gap between Flat-F2P and Graph Credit under the true DAG reflects genuine phantom credit arising from dependency violations, not an artifact of imposing arbitrary graph structure. B.3 Chain-Depth Interpretation Graph depth requires an explicit counting convention. The benchmark summary in Figure 3 and Table 19 counts nodes on the longest path of the full task DAG G. For scoring and curriculum thresholds, depth counts edges; a path containing k nodes has k −1 edges. A single-node graph therefore has edge depth zero. The scoring graph GA is induced by evaluable nodes and can have a shorter longest path than the full task graph. The recursive minimum in Graph Credit caps downstream completion by upstream prerequisites at every edge. Longer chains consequently provide more opportunities for locally passing tests to be capped by an unresolved ancestor. This is a structural property of the scoring rule; it does not by itself establish an empirical relationship between chain depth and OverCredit. The overall OverCredit results are reported in Section 5.2. This section details how WEAVE leverages the PR depen- dency DAG to generate high-quality SFT trajectories and graph-structured RL rewards, completing the unified frame- work from construction through optimization. E.1 Trajectory Generation and Quality Filtering Trajectory generation setup. Training trajectories are generated using the Cline scaffold with the following config- uration: • Generator model: GLM-5.2. • Max turns: 200. • Context window: 128K tokens. • Temperature: 0.6 (for diversity). • Tasks attempted: 3,200 (all of WEAVE-Train). • Attempts per task: 3 (best-of-3 by Graph Credit). Choice of generator. We generate with GLM-5.2 rather than the strongest evaluated configuration (Claude Opus 4.7 + Cline, per the RQ2 results in the main text) for three reasons. First, GLM-5.2 has openly released weights, so the resulting corpus can be published without the derived-data restrictions that proprietary model outputs carry, and the generation stage is self-hostable and therefore independently reproducible. Second, GLM-5.2 is the second-strongest configuration on WEAVE-Bench (43.0% versus 48.7% Resolved); the best- of-3 protocol absorbs most of this 5.7 pp gap at the corpus level. Third, generator and student share a broadly similar tool-invocation format, which reduces format adaptation dur- ing distillation. The cost is throughput: GLM-5.2 averages 138.2 turns and 7.52 M cumulative tokens per benchmark
title: Table 14: Curriculum scheduling comparison (Qwen3.5-4B).

text: this 5.7 pp gap at the corpus level. Third, generator and student share a broadly similar tool-invocation format, which reduces format adaptation dur- ing distillation. The cost is throughput: GLM-5.2 averages 138.2 turns and 7.52 M cumulative tokens per benchmark task, against 46.8 turns and 2.11 M for Claude Opus 4.7. This 3.6× generation overhead is why we cap attempts at three per task rather than sampling more widely. Quality filtering. Generated trajectories pass through five filters. These are deliberately strict: a trajectory that satis- fies downstream tests while leaving upstream prerequisites unimplemented exhibits precisely the phantom credit that WEAVE-Bench is designed to expose, and distilling such behavior into the student would be self-defeating. We there- fore gate on Graph Credit rather than on flat test pass rate. 1. Dependency-consistent success filter: Retain trajecto- ries satisfying both GraphCredit(GA) ≥0.85 and minv∈VA cv ≥0.50. The first condition requires near- complete resolution of the task graph. The second is applied per node and forbids any single node from re- maining grossly unimplemented; because cv is already bottlenecked by its ancestors under the recursive defini- tion of Graph Credit in the main text, it constrains every dependency path simultaneously. A trajectory with high Flat-F2P but an unresolved upstream node fails this filter by construction. 2. Length filter: Discard trajectories shorter than 8 turns,
title: Table 14: Curriculum scheduling comparison (Qwen3.5-4B).

text: recursive defini- tion of Graph Credit in the main text, it constrains every dependency path simultaneously. A trajectory with high Flat-F2P but an unresolved upstream node fails this filter by construction. 2. Length filter: Discard trajectories shorter than 8 turns, and any trajectory that terminated by exhausting the 200- turn or context budget rather than by submitting a patch, since truncated rollouts are incomplete by construction. The resulting effective upper bound is 150 turns, 75% of the interaction cap. 3. Regression filter: Discard trajectories exhibiting any P2P regression. Failing P2P tests are re-executed three times and counted as regressions only when they fail consis- tently, so that flaky tests do not discard otherwise valid trajectories. 4. Degenerate pattern filter: Remove trajectories with three or more consecutive identical tool calls (same tool, same arguments), or with edit churn above 0.5— the fraction of edit operations subsequently overwritten or reverted within the same trajectory—which indicates thrashing rather than incremental progress. 5. Leakage filter: Discard trajectories in which the agent recovered the original change through repository history or network access, detected by scanning tool-call argu- ments for git log, git show, .git traversal, and outbound requests. Task instantiation already removes re- coverable target commits and repository history; this filter enforces the same guarantee at the trajectory level, where an agent could otherwise reach

Surviving rollouts are deduplicated per task: we keep the attempt with the highest Graph Credit, break ties by shorter trajectory length, and treat remaining attempts whose final patches exceed 0.9 normalized edit-distance similarity to the retained one as duplicates. E.2 SFT Configuration Table 16 details the SFT hyperparameters for both model scales. We report only parameters that affect the optimization objective or its trajectory; sharding strategy, device place- ment, and accumulation factors are implementation choices that follow from the global batch size and are omitted. Three choices warrant comment. Loss masking: gradi- ents are computed only on assistant-generated tokens; tool results, file contents, and test output are supplied as context but excluded from the objective, since these constitute envi- ronment observations rather than target behavior. Sequence length: the 131,072-token window matches the generator’s context budget, so no retained trajectory is truncated during training; training at this length uses sequence parallelism. Learning rate: with only 2,304 trajectories, the corpus is small enough that the higher end of the search range overfits within one epoch. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B activates roughly 3B parameters per token, so its optimal rate is close to—though slightly below—that of the 4B dense model rather than an order of magnitude lower. GRPO is critic-free: for each task we sample G = 8 rollouts, score each with RWEAVE, and take the advantage of a rollout to be its reward centered and scaled by the mean and standard deviation within its own group. No value network, and hence no generalized advantage estimation, is used. Group-relative normalization makes the gradient invariant to task difficulty, so that easy and hard tasks contribute comparably. Group-relative normalization also explains why reward density matters here beyond the usual sparse-reward argu- ment: a group whose G rollouts all receive the same re- ward contributes no gradient at all, so a sparse reward

text: and hard tasks contribute comparably. Group-relative normalization also explains why reward density matters here beyond the usual sparse-reward argu- ment: a group whose G rollouts all receive the same re- ward contributes no gradient at all, so a sparse reward wastes rollout budget outright rather than merely learning slowly. Because Graph Credit is continuous and dependency- conditioned, its groups almost always exhibit within-group spread. The empirical consequence is quantified in §D.3. Three-phase curriculum. RL training follows a DAG- complexity curriculum over the 3,200-task pool. Phases are cumulative—each admits all tasks from the previous phase— and are allocated equal thirds of the 400 policy updates: • Phase 1 (updates 1–132): DAGs with depth ≤2 and |V | ≤ 3. Eligible tasks: 1,048. • Phase 2 (updates 133–264): DAGs with depth ≤3 and |V | ≤5. Eligible tasks: 1,864. • Phase 3 (updates 265–400): all tasks, sampled uniformly. Eligible tasks: 3,200. Phase membership follows directly from the WEAVE-Train node and depth distributions (Table 20); depth is measured as the number of edges on the longest path, consistent with §B.3. text: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts A Controlled Study of Six Q8 Checkpoint Conversions Alina Khaybullina October 2026
title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise

text: Which inputs drive a language model’s financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat check- point conversions from four families (0.49–7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8 0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B an- swer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from −0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models and mo- mentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study. 1
title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise

text: Which information actually changes a language model’s market prediction? A plausible financial forecast may follow recent returns, react to the emotional framing of an announcement, or compare newly released earnings with expectations. Natural financial text usually combines these signals. If they all agree, the final forecast cannot distinguish their influence. An earnings announcement makes the distinction concrete. Higher earnings than a year earlier can still miss consensus; a loss can beat an even worse expected loss. Upbeat commentary can accompany either numerical outcome. We hold actual earnings fixed and reverse the surprise by changing the stated consensus, while independently reversing momentum and commentary. This identifies the effect of the information supplied to the model under the tested protocol. This paper expands an audited two-checkpoint pilot. The primary experiment now covers six checkpoints in four families, a wider size range, six commentary pairs, losses, annual declines, and small as well as large surprises. Label reversal is part of every primary case. The pilot’s raw results are retained separately, and a conversion/runtime bridge compares saved full-precision scores with the new inference setup. The original expanded protocol was internally frozen before expanded inference, after the pilot had already been inspected; it is not a public preregistration or a fresh confirmation of pilot-independent hypotheses. Blocks cross two signs of actual EPS, two signs of annual EPS change, and two surprise-gap fractions (2% or 15% of absolute actual EPS), with three numerical replicates per combination. Absolute actual EPS is sampled uniformly between $0.80 and $4.20 and rounded to cents. For profitability sign pb, annual-change sign hb, and a draw ub ∼U(0.08, 0.25), prior-year EPS is ab −hb|ab|ub, rounded to cents. text: investor expectations. Revenue meets consensus, guidance is unchanged, and no other news is released. Momentum sign m selects positive or negative 20-day pre-release returns of the same block- specific magnitude, sampled uniformly from 3–12% and rounded to one decimal. The market is flat. Sentiment sign s selects one of six positive/negative commentary pairs, explicitly described as opinion with no additional facts. Pair assignments are randomized and balanced across blocks (four blocks per pair). Three introductions are similarly assigned (eight blocks per introduction). Every block uses both section orders: facts–prices–commentary and commentary–prices–facts. Pair and introduction are between-block assignments; order and the three financial inputs are crossed within blocks. The eight (m, s, e) combinations and two orders give 16 semantic scenarios per block and 384 per model. All receive three answer encodings: A=positive/B=negative (AB0), the reversed as- signment (AB1), and U=positive/D=negative (UD). Thus there are 1,152 primary prompts per model. Counts refer to repeated counterfactual model evaluations, not independent market events. 3.2 Controls and expanded coverage The isolated numerical diagnostic crosses 24 blocks, two surprise signs, and two sentence forms: 96 scenarios. Each receives both A/B assignments and natural beat/miss prefixes, giving 288 diagnostic prompts. Commentary removal covers every block, both momentum and surprise signs, facts-first order, and both assignments (192 prompts, 96 averaged cases). The original natural-word and office controls

title: Effectiveness of Hidden-State Probes

text: Verifying the final answer of a long reasoning trace may show that the trace is wrong but it does not distinguish three cases. The problem may lie beyond the model’s capability, another attempt would succeed, or one step in an otherwise recoverable trace made the trace fail. Standard hidden-state probes are trained on final-answer correctness, a label that conflates these cases. Monte Carlo rollouts distinguish the cases and locate the failing step at additional inference cost. We test the hidden states of 4B and 8B reasoning models for the failure type and the failing step and compare each probe with the strongest baseline that uses no hidden states. On incorrect 8B traces, the confidence probe, a calibrated correctness probe at a midpoint cutoff, misses 81% of cases in which a single step makes the trace unrecoverable and 47% of cases in which another attempt would succeed. A probe with a different training design over the same states reverses the ordering of these two kinds of failure, so either ordering can be read from those states. At both scales, no single tested probe locates the failing step more accurately than a rule based only on trace length, and at 4B a probe trained to predict that step fails to outperform this rule in any of 10 runs on identical traces. A final label does not distinguish these failure types, and a model’s stated confidence is an unreliable guide to correctness: instruction-tuned models asked for a confidence score often assign high scores to incorrect answers [Zhao et al., 2026a]. A monitor therefore needs to identify the failure type and, for a trace that becomes unrecoverable, the step at which recovery is lost. A trace is the reasoning the model generates in one attempt at a problem, and a prefix is a trace up to a given step. A prefix is recoverable if a correct answer remains reachable from it. Monte Carlo rollouts from each evaluated prefix estimate the probability that a continuation from it reaches a correct answer. An incorrect trace is termed a capability gap if it is unrecoverable from the initial problem state, and a near miss if it remains recoverable at every evaluated prefix. A PIT is an incorrect trace whose first unrecoverable prefix occurs partway through [cf. Setlur et al., 2024]; the step that ends that prefix is its PIT step. We test the ability of hidden-state probes to distinguish these failure types and locate the PIT step without additional rollouts at deployment time. text: its PIT step. We test the ability of hidden-state probes to distinguish these failure types and locate the PIT step without additional rollouts at deployment time. Hidden states carry information about the truth of a statement or an answer [Azaria and Mitchell, 2023, Marks and Tegmark, 2024, Kadavath et al., 2022], and a probe on the hidden states of a language model can estimate the correctness of its reasoning steps [Ni et al., 2026]. Final labels record only final-answer correctness and do not directly supervise the failure type or the PIT step. We train probes on the hidden states at a fixed set of layers, the read site, with three kinds of supervision: final labels; rollout rates, the fraction of rollouts from a prefix that reach a correct answer; and the PIT step itself (Table 3). We evaluate Qwen3 in thinking mode at 4B and 8B on hard mathematics problems from DeepMath- 103k [He et al., 2026] and the training split of Hendrycks MATH [Hendrycks et al., 2021]. We use this model family because it provides open-weight reasoning models at two scales with a thinking mode [Yang et al., 2025]. Appendix B gives the difficulty levels, the sampling parameters, and the seed and interval conventions of each measurement. Findings. 1. In the collections, the envelope is computed from the rollout rates ˆpt at the evaluated prefixes, with the maximum taken over the evaluated prefixes at or after step t, so the PIT step is always the last step of an evaluated prefix. V ∗ t gives the highest continuation value available at the current or any later step in the sampled trace. For example, a trace can establish a valid approach, introduce a sign error, and then develop the resulting wrong branch. Its envelope is high before the sign error and near zero afterward, so its PIT step is the step that introduces the sign error. The threshold θ = 0.1 exceeds 1/16 = 0.0625, the rollout rate of a single success among 16 rollouts, the largest K used to assign labels. At a prefix where the envelope is at or below θ, the rollout rate there and at every later evaluated prefix therefore reflects at most one success in 16 rollouts and no success in 8 or fewer. Self-Explore treats a prefix as unrecoverable only if no sampled continuation succeeds [Hwang et al., 2024]; the threshold relaxes this test so that a single success in 16 rollouts does not make a prefix recoverable. Setlur et al. [2024] select the first step with the lowest estimated value in an incorrect trace, arg mint ˆVt. With few rollouts per prefix, zero estimates are common and a zero estimate can be followed by a rate above θ, so the arg min step and the PIT step rarely coincide at either scale (Table 10); all PIT steps in this paper follow Definition 1. A capability gap has no recoverable prefix; it is related to problems that remain unsolved across repeated attempts [Yue et al., 2025] and to difficulty regions in which accuracy is at most 10 percent and does not rise with more sampled reasoning paths [Chen et al., 2024]. A near miss remains recoverable at every evaluated prefix although the trace ends with a wrong answer; it is related to problems that are solved on another attempt [Wen et al., 2026]. A PIT is recoverable before its PIT step and unrecoverable from it onward (Figure 1). We train the confidence probe, validate its detection AUROC and calibration, and then evaluate its predictions at the final step. Probe inputs. The probes read the hidden states of the frozen model at the read site, on traces that are generated once and reused for every probe (Table 3). For each step, a probe reads the hidden states at the read site at one token position, which lies at or before the last token of the step. For about half of the traces, the position read for the final step lies in an earlier step (Appendix D). We selected the read site, layers {23, 24} at both scales, from the detection AUROC of a probe at each layer, using the final label only and no failure type or PIT

Confidence probe. We call the probe trained on final labels the confidence probe. Every confidence score in this paper is an output of the confidence probe. Our confidence probe is a causal transformer encoder over the steps of a trace. At step t it reads the hidden states h1, . . . , ht at the read site and outputs the predicted correctness ct = σ(g(h1:t)) = c Pr(Y =1 | h1:t). We broadcast the trace’s final label to every valid step and minimize per-step Bernoulli loss. The same final label supervises every prefix, so the objective estimates E[Y | h1:t] [Yu et al., 2024], which equals V π t only when h1:t retains all the information in the prefix about the final label (Proposition 1, Section 4). We calibrate held-out scores by temperature scaling [Guo et al., 2017]. Training and validation traces are split by problem, so no problem contributes traces to both; we call this the problem split. text: are proved in Appendix C. Length rule. The length rule predicts the PIT step t = round(f (L −1)) of a trace with L steps, with one parameter f. PIT steps occur late in a trace: the median relative depth of the PIT step is 0.70 at 4B and 0.75 at 8B (Figure 2). We score the probes and the length rule by Hit@±2, the fraction of PITs for which the predicted step lies within two steps of the PIT step. In each comparison, f is fitted to maximize Hit@±2 on PITs of problems outside the evaluation set. The length rule is therefore refitted for each evaluation set, because its score depends on that set’s trace lengths and on the relative depths of its PIT steps (Appendix B). Pointer probe. We call the probe trained to predict the PIT step the pointer probe. It differs from the confidence probe in input and target: it reads a completed trace, which Proposition 2, a statement about prefixes, does not cover, and is trained on the PIT step itself. The pointer probe is a transformer encoder with bidirectional attention over the steps of a completed trace. At each step it reads that step’s hidden states at the read site together with those of the final step, and it outputs a distribution 7

text: over the steps of the trace, whose most probable step is its prediction. The distribution is trained on the PIT steps of the broad collection’s PITs. It is trained jointly on three further outputs, among them the failure type, which is trained on all incorrect traces with one of two weightings of its loss, inverse-frequency or uniform (Appendix B); only the step distribution is evaluated. Paired localization results. We think the training target itself produces the combined probe’s order: by Definition 1 a near miss keeps a rollout rate above θ at its last evaluated prefix and a PIT does not, so a probe fitted to these rates is trained toward ranking near misses above PITs. The confidence probe and the combined probe differ in more than their labels, and we did not isolate the contribution of the labels (Section 3). All results in this paper come from one model family, Qwen3 in thinking mode at two scales, on hard mathematics problems. The failure types depend on the rollout protocol, including the number of rollouts, the threshold and the token limits (Appendix B). Under this protocol, a capability gap records only that no sampled continuation reached a correct answer. A rollout counts as successful when its final answer is correct, so a continuation that reaches the answer through an invalid argument counts as a success. Such cases are reported for base models [Wen et al., 2026]. The final labels contain grading errors, and correcting them leaves capability gaps and PITs missed more often than near misses at both scales (Appendix B). 6

text: Correctness probes. Probes on hidden states predict the truth of a statement or an answer [Azaria and Mitchell, 2023, Marks and Tegmark, 2024, Kadavath et al., 2022, Orgad et al., 2025], and on reasoning models the correctness of an intermediate answer [Zhang et al., 2025a]. Orgad et al. [2025] also define error types by resampling the answers to a question and show that probes predict them; their types are defined per question from sampled final answers, and ours per trace from rollouts at each step. A related study trains correctness probes on instruction-tuned models and one distilled reasoning model [Yuan et al., 2026]; the signal is decodable in all of these models. Steering along the probe direction in two instruction-tuned models does not raise accuracy consistently, which the authors read as a diagnostic signal. The internal signal is useful because verbal reports can differ from the model’s computation [Turpin et al., 2023, Zhao et al., 2026a]. This paper measures the failure types that a correctness probe distinguishes. Failure taxonomies. Uncertainty work commonly separates epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty [Ahdritz et al., 2024, Abbasi Yadkori et al., 2024] or data from model uncertainty [Ren et al., 2026], and a recent account separates input ambiguity, knowledge gaps and decoding randomness [Taparia et al., 2026]; decoding randomness is closest in definition to our near

text: 2024, Abbasi Yadkori et al., 2024] or data from model uncertainty [Ren et al., 2026], and a recent account separates input ambiguity, knowledge gaps and decoding randomness [Taparia et al., 2026]; decoding randomness is closest in definition to our near misses. Behavioral work separates failures that resampling fixes from failures it does not [Islah et al., 2026], and a similar division is hypothesized for self-correction [Li, 2026]. Under our taxonomy, the failures that resampling fixes combine near misses with PITs. Concurrent work predicts, from the output log-probabilities of failed rollouts, which intervention rescues a problem [Islah et al., 2026]. Pit-step targets. Process benchmarks label the first locally invalid step [Zheng et al., 2025] or every erroneous section of a long trace [He et al., 2025], which differs from the PIT step, and annotators can disagree about which step is wrong [Jacovi et al., 2024]. State geometry can identify a first local error [Alvarez and Baheri, 2026], and attribution graphs can recover local validity [Zhao et al., 2026b]. Both targets differ from the PIT step, which depends on the model’s continuations from each prefix, so an oracle for local validity need not locate it. Cui et al. [2026] and Yuan et al. [2025] infer step credit from final outcomes, which is a different target from the best reachable value (Proposition 1).

text: We assigned each incorrect trace of a reasoning model one of three failure types from rollouts and tested the recovery of these types and of the PIT step from the model’s hidden states. The confidence probe predicts the final label, and at the cutoff it misses capability gaps and PITs more often than near misses. The combined probe ranks PITs and near misses in the opposite order to the confidence probe, so an ordering of failure types read from a probe depends on the probe’s training design. The failure-type classifier, which reads transcoder activations of a completed incorrect trace, separates capability gaps from PITs. It meets the margin at 8B and not at 4B. At 4B no single probe exceeds the length rule at locating the PIT step, and the ensemble exceeds it under one of the two weightings of its failure-type loss. Differences below the margin are recorded as failures even when their intervals exclude zero. B Experimental protocols Problem set and sampling. The two scales share one problem set of 35,854 problems. Of these problems, 32,031 come from DeepMath-103k at difficulty at least 7, and 3,823 come from levels 4 and 5 of the training split of Hendrycks MATH. Each problem has four sampled traces, except 146 problems with eight, which gives 144,000 traces at each scale. The traces were sampled at temperature 0.7 with a 16k-token budget. No problem in the problem set matches a MATH-500, MATH-Perturb or AIME 2024–2025 problem after whitespace and case normalization (0 of 35,854 problems). The exact-match check does not detect paraphrased or reformatted duplicates. Monte Carlo collections. text: paraphrased or reformatted duplicates. Monte Carlo collections. The two collections use different numbers of rollouts, and every result identifies its source collection (Table 2). The broad collection labels all incorrect traces and supplies the failure-type shares in Section 2. In a scan, it evaluates steps 0, 1 and 2 and then every second step with 8 rollouts, and in a refinement it re-evaluates some of these prefixes with 16 rollouts. More than 80% of its evaluated prefixes have 8 rollouts, and more than 70% of its PIT steps were evaluated with 16 (Table 2). About half of the 16-rollout prefixes of PITs lie within two evaluated steps of the PIT step. The collection evaluates about 60% of the steps of a trace. Each set of K rollouts contains one greedy rollout and K −1 independent samples at temperature 0.7, so its success count is not binomial. Writing Gt ∈{0, 1} for the greedy result and pt for the temperature-0.7 success probability, the count is Gt + Xt, where Xt ∼Bin(K −1, pt). Thus E[ˆpt | st] = [Gt + (K −1)pt]/K, a K-dependent protocol mean rather than pt. Residualization. For Section 3, we fit a logistic model of trace misses on failure type, trace length, answer position, difficulty, and best reachable value at step 0, V ∗ 0 . The difference between PITs and near misses after controls is the average marginal effect obtained by changing the failure type from near miss to PIT while holding each other variable at its observed value, then averaging over traces. For the detection AUROC after controls, we regress trace length, difficulty, problem source, answer length, and numeric-answer status out of the confidence probe’s log odds. We score the residual on held-out traces and average over five seeds. As a stratified check, we also compare the miss rates of PITs and near misses within cells of V ∗ 0 bin by trace-length tertile that hold at least 30 near misses. The PIT miss rate minus the near-miss miss rate is positive in all five such cells at 4B and in seven of eight at 8B, where the exception holds 33 near misses. text: Name-Bias in Large Language Models Kalyan Bhetwal Ceren Mert Ian Whitehouse University of Maryland, College Park, USA {bhetwal, cmert, ianjw}@umd.edu
title: Name-Bias in Large Language Models

text: Names carry demographic indicators such as age, gender, and race, which makes them a subtle but strong target of bias in large language models (LLMs). In this work, we present an evaluation of name-based bias across 6 local large lan- guage models spanning multiple providers and parameter scales. Using a fill-in-the- blank task, we prompt these models to choose between pairs of first names drawn from U.S. Social Security Administration datasets and a race classification dataset by Rosenman et al.. Our experimental de- sign isolates age and gender effects through balanced name pairings and sentence tem- plates that share a fixed syntactic struc- ture. Across 300,000 local LLM responses, we find consistent and measurable name bias. Models prefer names that are less stereo- typically male, older, popular, and white. Furthermore, we find that name-bias is highly sentence-dependent, but not more than associated stereotypes, and gender is the most significant bias, followed by age, name popularity, and race. Our results demonstrate that name-based bias remains pervasive even in local LLMs, highlighting the necessity for standardized evaluation methods and mitigation strate- gies. 1
title: Name-Bias in Large Language Models

text: Large Language Model usage has surged dra- matically, with nearly 50% of U.S. adults re- porting they have used LLMs for daily tasks at least once (Rainie, 2025). These systems often handle natural language prompts that include personal names. Since names can encode de- mographic cues such as age, gender, and race, even minor model biases may lead to discrim- inatory outcomes. Such biases may perpet- uate stereotypes, unfairly advantage certain groups, or generate harmful content. Identi- fying and measuring these biases is therefore essential: it enables more rigorous model eval- uation, supports the development of fairer sys- tems, and advances transparency in AI safety. Therefore, it remains integral to measure the biases LLMs can hold, and in this work, we address four specific biases: age, gender, pop- ularity, and race. Our experiments prompt lo- cal LLMs with fill-in-the-blank sentences given two names that may reveal a specific bias, such as age, gender, or race. We measure • Age bias and popularity bias by collecting the top 500 most popular names, and how many times they were assigned, from the 1980s and 2010s • Gender bias by categorizing the most pop- ular names from 1980s and 2010s as fe- male and male • Racial bias by using a racial classification dataset provided by Rosenman et al. Our experiments and con- tributions can be found at https://github.com/cerenmert14/name- bias-in-local-llms 2 Prior Work There has been a significant effort in explor- ing the biases LLMs hold. In fact, it has been found that large language models that seem to be “explicitly unbiased”, where they refuse overtly biased statements, still form implicit discriminatory biases (Bai et al., 2025). They observed that even common models like GPT- 4, which refuses an explicitly biased statement such as “women are bad at managing peo- ple”, continue to prefer male names over fe- male ones, to lead a management workshop. arXiv:2610.22053v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

text: Another study simulated hiring decisions and salary recommendations for candidates with first names that strongly signal their race and gender, and found a preference for hiring candidates with White female-sounding names over other demographic groups across 40 oc- cupations (Nghiem et al., 2024). In addition, even among candidates with identical quali- fications, outputted salary recommendations varied by up to 5% between different sub- groups. 3

text: 3.1 First Name Data Collection To collect popular names from 1980s and 2010s for our experiments, we utilize the Social Secu- rity Administration’s top baby names dataset. We sort the names by their gender and popu- larity, and only use the top 500 names. Addi- tionally, we have used the dataset provided by (Rosenman et al., 2023) for racial classification of the names. 3.2 Fill in the Blank Sentences To make the LLMs choose between two names, we constructed 30 sentence templates contain- ing a placeholder for the model to supply a name. The sentences were all gender-neutral, and were designed to signal a person’s age or gender, to elicit biased behavior from a lo- cal large language model. Across all our sen- tences, only the scenario varied, and the syn- tactic structure remained constant to isolate how the model associated names with gender, age, and race cues. Some example sentences can be found below: • “ just celebrated a 45th birthday” • “ is hoping to contribute more to a 401K in the coming year” • “ is getting ready to start high school in the spring” • “ is filling out taxes for 2025.” • “ is going to a 20th high school reunion” 4 Experiments 4.1 Models We evaluate age, gender, popularity, and race bias across six

text: cally using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), a high-throughput inference engine optimized for large language model serving with Page- dAttention. Table 1 summarizes model con- figurations. 4.2 Experimental Design Our experimental design aims to measure age bias while controlling for potential confounds, particularly gender associations and position effects. The core task presents models with fill-in-the-blank sentences and two name op- tions, asking which name fits best in the given context. Comparison Types. To isolate age bias from gender confounds, we employed an al- ternating experimental design with two con- ditions: • Same Gender, Different Ages (even iterations: 0, 2, 4, . . . ): Both names share the same gender (male or female, ran- domly selected per iteration), but differ in temporal cohort—one name from the 1980s, one from the 2010s. This condition directly measures age-based preferences,
title: Another study simulated hiring decisions

text: as the only systematic difference between names is their associated age cohort. • Different Genders, Same Age (odd it- erations: 1, 3, 5, . . . ): Names differ in gender (one male, one female) but share the same decade (1980s or 2010s, ran- domly selected per iteration). This con- trol condition helps identify gender-based preferences independent of age effects. This alternating design ensures balanced representation of both conditions across the dataset. Names were sampled uniformly at random from the top 500 most popular names in each decade-gender category from the Social Security Administration (SSA) database. The uniform sampling strategy ensures equal rep- resentation across the name frequency spec- trum, avoiding bias toward the most popular names. Within each query, the presentation order of the two options was randomized to mitigate position bias. Rationale. The same-gender comparisons are critical for isolating age bias. By hold- ing gender constant, any systematic preference for one name over another can be attributed to age associations rather than gender stereo- types. The different-gender comparisons serve as both a control and a separate investigation into potential gender biases in the same sen- tence contexts. This design enables us to dis- tinguish between age-based and gender-based preferences in model responses. 4.3 Task and Prompting Sentence Templates. This design enables us to dis- tinguish between age-based and gender-based preferences in model responses. 4.3 Task and Prompting Sentence Templates. We constructed 30 gender-neutral fill-in-the-blank sentences spanning diverse contexts that vary in age- indicativeness. Templates include explicit age markers (e.g., “ just celebrated a 45th birthday”), age-suggestive contexts (retire- ment planning, school activities), and neutral scenarios (travel, purchases). All sentences use a single blank placeholder to maintain consistency in task difficulty. Prompt Format. To ensure consistency across all models and avoid confounding ef- fects from prompt variations, we used a single standardized prompt template: Sentence: <sentence template> Which fits best: "<name1>" or "<name2>"? Answer with just the text of the choice. The prompt format is deliberately minimal and neutral. The instruction “Answer with just the text of the choice” constrains re- sponses to one of the two provided names, min- imizing extraneous generation and facilitating automated analysis. All models used the sys- tem message “You are a helpful assistant” to maintain consistency. Generation Parameters. We employed consistent generation parameters across all models to ensure comparable stochasticity. The temperature was set to 0.7, balancing be- tween deterministic and highly random behav- ior. This moderate temperature allows models to express subtle preferences while maintain- ing reasonable consistency across repeated tri- als. The

This moderate temperature allows models to express subtle preferences while maintain- ing reasonable consistency across repeated tri- als. The maximum token limit was set to 512, though responses typically required fewer than 10 tokens. 4.4 Data Collection Protocol Data collection proceeded iteratively for each model. In each iteration, the system: (1) de- termined the comparison type based on itera- tion parity, (2) randomly selected appropriate name lists, (3) uniformly sampled two names, and (4) queried the model with all 30 sentence templates using randomized option orders. This process yielded 30 responses per it- eration. We collected 2,000 iterations for each open-source model, generating 60,000 re- sponses per model. The cumulative dataset comprises 300,000 model responses. 4.5 Infrastructure All experiments were conducted on the Nexus- vulcan cluster. Open-source models were deployed on NVIDIA RTX A5000 (24GB VRAM) and RTX A6000 (48GB VRAM) GPUs. We utilized vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) for efficient model serving with OpenAI- compatible API endpoints. Key serving pa- rameters included: maximum context length of 2048 tokens (sufficient for our short prompts), maximum batch size of 8 concur- rent sequences, and GPU memory utilization of 0.85 to prevent out-of-memory errors during extended collection runs.

This ex- posed which attributes were favored by the model, on average. The results of this analysis are shown in Figures 1 and 2. • Relative Bias Between Sentences: Second, we measured the effects of differ- ent sentences on the relative levels of bias by asking how the distribution of names chosen for the sentence differed from the average. The results of this analysis are shown in Figure 3. • Mixed-effects Modeling: Third, we fit a mixed-effects model to the chance that the second name in the pair shown to the LLM was chosen. Since the LLM showed extreme bias for the first name, this was an effective way to measure how a chang- ing a demographic attribute affect that bias. We used the statsmodels pack- age for this analysis, shown in Table 2 (Seabold and Perktold, 2010). • Bias Correlation: Finally, we computed the correlations between biases within each model to assess

Despite that, we find that all models lean towards female- associated, older-associated, more popular, and more stereotypically white names. We in- clude the length of the names, in tokens, as a possible confounder, but find it isn’t relevant in this analysis. While prompts do modulate the strength of these biases, the overall pattern suggests that name-linked stereotypes remain a strong signal shaping an LLM’s choice. This suggests the sentence acts as an amplifier of existing biases rather than determining them. Mixed-effect modeling shows that the rel- ative strength of attributes matches the ob- served change in the attributes in more likely- to-be-chosen names. This quantifies the bias, showing how large the effect can be for some of the attributes. Finally, we analyze the correlation between different biases within the LLMs, and find large levels of variation. This suggests that
