Finally, we analyze the correlation between different biases within the LLMs, and find large levels of variation. This suggests that coupling between biases is not universal. While our trials are contrived examples, it is easy to see how name bias could negatively affect society and businesses. Several recent works have suggested using LLMs to review r´esum´es for applicants for jobs (Gan et al., 2024). Asking that system to choose between two applicants, or score two applicants in ref- erence to each other, is a direct analog of our tests. In this example, choosing a worse appli- cant because of these biases systematically has obvious detrimental effects to the business, so- ciety, and the applicant. However, this form of name bias is already seen when humans review a r´esum´e, making it hard to know if LLMs will help remove or add to the level of bias of the human reviewers (Bertrand and Mullainathan, 2004). 6.1 Contributions This work provides a model-comparative, measurement-driven characterization of name- triggered bias in local LLMs. We (i) demon- strate how name-driven bias is consistently de- tectable across models, (ii) show that differ- ent models have biases that trend towards the same associated attributes, (iii) quantify how

text: Assessing the bias of an LLM that reviews r´esum´es is a logical follow-on project for this work. We propose that a similar methodology as Bertrand and Mullainathan could be em- ployed to test how an LLM changes the bias of a r´esum´e reviewer. Furthermore, we suggest two direct exten- sions of our work. First, we can adapt meta- morphic testing to name bias by defining controlled transformations over prompts and name substitutions, and then auditing system- atic violations across models. This is a known methodology for conducting tests of LLM bias (da Silva de Oliveira et al., 2025; Reddy et al., 2025). Second, we can operationalize these findings into standardized name-bias evalua- tion sets for developers to report, compare, and mitigate bias within their LLMs.

text: FeaTok: Feature-Loss Tokenization for Image Generation Zhang Xiaofeng1,2,3, Samuel Lavoie1,2,†, Nicolas Beltran-Velez3,6,†, Jianhao Yuan3,7, Felix Friedrich3, Jakob Verbeek3, Aaron Courville1,2,5,‡, Michal Drozdzal3,‡, Adriana Romero-Soriano1,3,4,5,‡ 1Mila - Québec AI Institute, 2Université de Montréal, 3FAIR at Meta, 4McGill University, 5Canada CIFAR AI chair, 6Columbia University, 7University of Oxford †Equal contribution, ‡Co-senior authors Discrete image generators learn the distribution of tokens produced by an image tokenizer. These token representations should be easy for generators to model, not merely enable faithful image reconstruction. Yet these tokenizers are commonly trained to reconstruct pixels, which prioritizes low-level fidelity and may disrupt representation structure useful for generation. Motivated by feature-predictive self-supervised learning, we introduce feature-loss tokenization (FeaTok), which trains discrete tokens by reconstructing pretrained features rather than pixels. Ablations across SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2, and DINOv3 show better generative performance with FeaTok. In class-conditional generation, FeaTok advances the quality–compute Pareto frontier, reducing gFDr6 at 256×256 by up to 29% over the strongest discrete baselines and outperforming the strongest unguided continuous baseline (RAEv2) with 38× less sampling compute. FeaTok also achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores than prior art without reward-based training and surpasses continuous and discrete text-conditional baselines on three benchmarks with only 500 fine-tuning updates after pre-training. text: Image generation enables machines to create new visual content, supporting applications ranging from creative design to multimodal interaction. A growing body of work represents images as discrete tokens and models them autoregressively (Sun et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026). Discrete tokens share the interface 1 arXiv:2610.22060v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

text: of language models, which makes them a natural choice for unified multimodal models. They also sample an image with an order of magnitude less compute than continuous diffusion models, as shown in Fig. 1. Image generation quality depends on discrete tokens that are both expressive and easy for a generator to model. Previous discrete tokenizers focus on reconstruction performance, which targets the first property, expressivity. However, generation also depends on the second property, which we call generative learnability: how easily a generator fits the token distribution at a given budget. These two properties do not always align, as observed for both continuous and discrete image tokenizers and generators (Gu et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Ramanujan et al., 2025). Generative learnability is related to the structure of a representation (Skorokhodov et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2026), which is in turn induced by the training target. Pixel reconstruction prioritizes high-variance image details over features useful for perception (Balestriero and Lecun, 2024), and using self-supervised learning (SSL) objectives to predict features instead of pixels yields more semantically meaningful representations (Assran et al., 2023). We refer to the representations of encoders trained with SSL objectives in feature space as pretrained visual features (see Def. 1). Moreover, RAE (Zheng et al., 2026b) and RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026) show that the benefits

Moreover, RAE (Zheng et al., 2026b) and RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026) show that the benefits of pretrained visual features go beyond representation learning and successfully transfer to image generation. Wang et al. (2024) trained discrete tokens by reconstructing the features of image-understanding encoders instead of pixels, and showed that these tokens can outperform pixel-trained VQ tokens for image generation. Yet the discrete tokenizers that followed still use pixel reconstruction as the central loss, and add pretrained visual features with additional losses (Xiong et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b). This raises the question of whether pixel reconstruction loss is essential for modern discrete tokenizer training used for downstream image generation. We argue that it is not. Feature objectives should shape both the encoder, pretrained in feature space, and the discrete tokens. We introduce feature-loss tokenization (FeaTok), which separates discrete representation learning from image reconstruction. Instead of a pixel decoder and a pixel reconstruction loss, a feature decoder that reconstructs pretrained visual features shapes the discrete tokens. A separate image decoder is trained with pixel losses on detached tokens and only renders generated token

text: reconstruction. Instead of a pixel decoder and a pixel reconstruction loss, a feature decoder that reconstructs pretrained visual features shapes the discrete tokens. A separate image decoder is trained with pixel losses on detached tokens and only renders generated token sequences, so pixel losses never shape the discrete representation. We additionally discretize the encoder’s global representation (e.g., CLS token), and generate it before the patch tokens, giving them image-level context. We call this global-augmented generative modelling. Ablations in Sec. 2.2 show that FeaTok has better spatial structure and generates better than tokenizers trained with pixel or combined losses for all four encoders we study, and that global-augmented modelling contributes to this improvement. On class-conditional ImageNet-1k (Russakovsky et al., 2015) at 256×256, FeaTok advances the quality–compute Pareto front for image generation (Fig. 1). We measure quality by gFDr6, the mean Fréchet-distance ratio across six feature spaces rather than the Inception space alone (Yang et al., 2026). FeaTok improves on the strongest discrete baselines by 29% without guidance and by 25% with it, and outperforms recent continuous generators at a matched sampling cost in both settings. The gains grow at 512×512: relative to the previously best discrete model (BAR (Yu et al., 2026)), FeaTok reduces gFDr6 by 43% without guidance and 39% with guidance, up from 32% and 25% at 256×256, and

We next describe how FeaTok uses these features to train the tokenizer with feature losses (Fig. 2). 2.1 Learning discrete tokens with feature loss only Conventional discrete tokenizers (Van Den Oord et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2025; Bachmann et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026a; Yu et al., 2026) consist of an encoder E, a quantizer Q, and a pixel decoder Dpix. Given an image x partitioned into N patches, the encoder E produces N feature vectors, one per patch, which the quantizer Q maps to discrete

text: al., 2026) consist of an encoder E, a quantizer Q, and a pixel decoder Dpix. Given an image x partitioned into N patches, the encoder E produces N feature vectors, one per patch, which the quantizer Q maps to discrete tokens z1:N = Q(E(x)). The pixel decoder Dpix then reconstructs the image as ˆx = Dpix(z1:N). Tokenizers are typically trained as an autoencoder with a pixel-level objective Lpix that combines pixel reconstruction losses (ℓ1, ℓ2), perceptual losses (LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), GRAM (Lu et al., 2026a)), and adversarial losses (Goodfellow et al., 2014). Once the tokenizer is trained, an autoregressive model conditioned on class labels or text prompts c learns the distribution pϕ(z1:N | c) of the resulting token sequences using the cross-entropy loss. Shaping discrete tokens with feature losses. FeaTok follows the autoencoder-style tokenizer design, but learns the discrete tokens by reconstructing features rather than pixels (see Fig. 2). Concretely, we add a feature decoder Dfeat that maps the discrete tokens z1:N to a prediction ˆy1:N = Dfeat(z1:N) of a feature target y1:N. We train the encoder, quantizer, and feature decoder to match this prediction to the target using a loss Lfeat that combines ℓ1, ℓ2, and cosine distances. For the feature target, following the insights in Singh et al. (2026), we use an average of features from

(2026), we use an average of features from multiple layers of the frozen vision encoder ˆE, y1:N(x) = |K|−1 P k∈K LNk( ˆE(k)(x)1:N), where K contains four evenly spaced encoder layers and LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016) normalizes each layer’s features before averaging. This target is intended to combine visual detail from earlier layers with semantic information from later layers, balancing expressivity and generative learnability. While we retain the pixel decoder Dpix and its pixel-level loss Lpix during training, we stop the gradients at the decoder input. This preserves the ability to decode tokens back into images while preventing the pixel reconstruction losses from shaping the token distribution. Leveraging global tokens. In addition to patch features, various vision encoders supply a global representation, e.g., a CLS token in DINO (Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024; Siméoni et al., 2026) or a global pooling token in SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025). Replacing pixel reconstruction with feature reconstruction losses naturally suggests discretizing this global feature along with patches. text: 2.2 Controlled ablations across pretrained vision encoders We verify FeaTok, feature-loss tokenization, against pixel-loss tokenization using four pretrained vision encoders: SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023), SigLIP2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024), and DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2026). We compare the generation performance of a generative model trained on ImageNet-1k (Russakovsky et al., 2015) images at 256×256 resolution using different tokenizers. Details of ablation setups are given in App. C. Additionally, App. C.2 shows that tokenizers built on MAE (He et al., 2022), whose features are learned by pixel reconstruction, generate poorly under every supervision. Feature targets work better than pixel-only or mixed feature–pixel targets. Feature supervision improves the generation over pixel supervision for three of the four encoders, as shown in Fig. 3a. With patch-only generation, replacing pixel targets with feature targets lowers gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3, while combining pixel and feature losses, i.e., letting gradients from both decoders update the discrete tokens, gives intermediate results. Fig. 3b relates these gFID changes to the spatial dependence between adjacent discrete patch tokens. The feature target raises this dependence and lowers gFID for SigLIP, DINOv2, and DINOv3, showing that the feature target improves the token structure for generation. Our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among methods using discrete tokenizers and outperform recent continuous generative models at a matched inference cost on ImageNet-1k 256×256. FeaTok achieves better performance on ImageNet-1k 512×512 than both continuous and discrete baselines. On T2I, FeaTok outperforms RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026) after a short fine-tuning on three T2I benchmarks, including GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023), DPG-Bench (Hu et al., 2024), and GenAI-Bench (Li et al., 2024a). 3.1 ImageNet-1k generation at 256×256 We train our 256×256 FeaTok tokenizers on ImageNet-1k using SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023), SigLIP2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024), and DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2026) encoders, with a vocabulary size of 65, 536. text: their released setups. FeaTok outperforms discrete models. In Tab. 1 we compare FeaTok using different vision encoders and two model sizes to existing discrete image generative models in terms of gFDr6 and its per-feature metrics. All four FeaTok-L variants outperform the strongest prior discrete baseline in gFDr6, showing consistent gains across four pretrained visual feature encoders satisfying Def. 1. FeaTok-DINOv3 is the strongest discrete model at both generator scales, with and without guidance. The largest improvements appear without guidance, where we reduce the prior baseline gFDr6 of 4.38 from VFMTok2-XXL (Zheng et al., 2026a) to 3.13. With guidance, we reduce the 4.11 gFDr6 of BAR-L to 3.08. Increasing the generator from base to large consistently improves gFDr6; for DINOv3, it decreases from 3.58 to 3.13 without guidance and from 3.39 to 3.08 with guidance. Importantly, these generation gains do not coincide with improved reconstruction: rFID remains nearly constant across FeaTok tokenizers (0.92–1.01; App. C.3), reinforcing that reconstruction fidelity alone does not explain generative performance. Following RAEv2 (Singh et al., 2026), we use BLIP-3o datasets (Chen et al., 2025) (Long-Caption, Short-Caption, and JourneyDB) for pre-training and BLIP-3o-60K for fine-tuning. We replace the class conditioning in FeaTok with a sequence of text embeddings provided by Qwen3-0.6B (Qwen Team, 2025) to enable T2I generation, re-using our FeaTok-SigLIP2 tokenizer trained on ImageNet-1k. We pre-train 75k updates with batch size 2048, while baselines use 150k updates with batch size 1024, giving the same total number of training examples processed. Then we further fine-tune the pre-trained model for 500 updates, while baselines are fine-tuned for approximately 3k updates. After pre-training, FeaTok is broadly comparable to RAEv2. It is slightly lower on GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) (0.611 versus 0.624) and DPG-Bench (Hu et al., 2024) (79.8 versus 81.7), but higher on GenAI-Bench (Li et al., 2024a) (0.668 versus 0.638). After only 500 additional updates, FeaTok exceeds RAEv2 on all three benchmarks: 0.837 versus 0.827 on GenEval, 0.698 versus 0.680 on GenAI-Bench, and 83.4 versus 82.3 on DPG-Bench. REPA (Yu et al., 2025b) aligns intermediate SiT (Ma et al., 2024) features with pretrained representations, where MAE is the weakest of the tested targets, and DDT (Wang et al., 2026) adopts this alignment. REG (Wu et al., 2025) denoises a pretrained class token together with the image latents, VA-VAE (Yao et al., 2025) aligns VAE latents with a pretrained vision encoder, and REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) tunes the VAE and the diffusion model end to end with the REPA loss. Discrete tokenization with pretrained representations. VQ-VAE (Van Den Oord et al., 2017) learns discrete image tokens through pixel reconstruction, and later tokenizers simplify the quantizer (Yu et al., 2024a; Mentzer et al., 2024). Wang et al. (2024) train tokenizers to reconstruct the features from image understanding encoders, and in autoregressive generation all but the MAE teacher outperform pixel-trained VQGAN tokens. Recent tokenizers keep pixel reconstruction as the central objective and add pretrained encoder features through feature alignment (Yu et al., 2026), semantic regularization (Xiong et al., 2025), self-distillation (Du et al., 2026), or feature reconstruction from several encoder depths (Jia et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b; Zheng et al., 2025b, 2026a). TA-Tok (Han et al., 2025) trains feature-reconstructed tokens for unified multimodal models, but decodes images through pixel-trained VQ tokens or latents.

text: We presented FeaTok, a discrete image tokenizer whose tokens are shaped only by feature reconstruction, while a pixel decoder trained on detached tokens renders them into images. We also discretize the encoder’s global representation and model it together with the patch tokens. Across four pretrained encoders, FeaTok generates better than tokenizers trained with pixel or combined losses. FeaTok achieves the best gFDr6 among the evaluated discrete generators on ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512, outperforms continuous generators at a matched sampling cost, achieves higher human-preference reward-model scores, and transfers to text-to-image generation after pretraining and only 500 fine-tuning updates. We believe these results are a step toward effective discrete representations for unified multimodal modeling, and that the low sampling cost of FeaTok makes it attractive for scaling multimodal training. 9

text: A Tokenizer implementation details This section specifies the final FeaTok tokenizer used in Sec. 3. We follow the notation presented in Sec. 2. We follow BAR (Yu et al., 2026), the previous state-of-the-art method, in our tokenizer and generator training. BAR uses bit representations for its tokens and an autoregressive model with a masked modeling head to predict the bits within each token. Ablation protocols and variants are described in App. C. Which pretrained encoders we use. FeaTok uses SigLIP-L, SigLIP2-SO400M, DINOv2-L with registers, or DINOv3-L. Tab. 6 identifies their pretrained checkpoints. Note that DINOv2-L uses a patch size of 14, whereas the other encoders use a patch size of 16. For DINOv2-L, we resize the image to 224 × 224 so that all encoders encode each image into 16 × 16 patches. text: Both projections are learned; only the coordinatewise rounding rule is fixed. Other differentiable quantizers can replace this module without changing the FeaTok framework. Discrete global token. In addition to its N patch features, E emits a global feature. A separate global quantizer Qglobal maps this feature to a 16-bit global code zglobal, which is prepended to the patch codes z1:N. Given the external class label c, the generator models p(zglobal, z1:N | c) and samples zglobal first, so it supplies global context to the patch tokens. The feature decoder reconstructs both global and patch feature targets, so the global code receives direct reconstruction supervision. The patch feature target is the average of representations from four layers, whereas the global target is the last-layer representation. The pixel decoder consumes only the sampled patch tokens, allowing a fair comparison between feature-loss and pixel-loss targets. Architecture and training. The trainable encoder E and the frozen encoder ˆE are initialized from the same pretrained checkpoint (Tab. 6). The feature decoder Dfeat is a ViT matched to the encoder, and the pixel decoder Dpix is the ViT-L decoder of BAR (Yu et al., 2026), shared across all encoders. B Generator implementation details We follow BAR (Yu et al., 2026) to implement the generative model, with our global-augmented generative modelling. BAR generative model. Recall that BAR learns tokens with FSQ in a bit representation and models their distribution with an adapted autoregressive model. Instead of a single categorical prediction over the entire codebook, BAR uses a lightweight masked bit modeling head. During training, some bits of the target token are masked, and the head learns to recover them with a bit-wise cross-entropy objective. During sampling, it starts with all bits masked and progressively fills them in, conditioning later predictions on the bits already revealed. The autoregressive context stays fixed during these within-token steps. Once

The autoregressive context stays fixed during these within-token steps. Once the token is complete, it becomes part of the context for the next token. This avoids an output distribution with one logit per codebook entry while allowing dependencies among a token’s bits. The complete objective combines the global and patch losses: LMBM gen = λglobal ℓMBM(Sglobal) + λpatch ℓMBM(Spatch), (6) with λpatch = 1−λglobal, averaged over training batches and over the sampled masks. Each term −log pϕ,ℓ(Bjℓ| ·) is the cross-entropy between the observed bit and the head’s two-class prediction, so Eq. 6 specifies the token prediction loss ℓCE in Eq. 4 for our masked bit modeling head. Because the normalization pools the bits of all tokens in S, a token with more masked bits contributes more, so the patch loss is a bit-weighted average over patch positions rather than exactly the uniform average 1 N PN i=1 of Eq. 4. The bit prediction task additionally conditions on the visible bits within the current token, making it a denoising cross-entropy objective rather than an exact evaluation of the complete token’s autoregressive negative log-likelihood. C.4 Token Structure Measurement Spatial-dependence diagnostic. The spatial dependence in Fig. 3b measures how informative one patch token is about an adjacent patch token in the same image. Rather than estimating MI between complete categorical token IDs, we use a component-wise proxy based on the tokenizer’s binary code representation. Each patch token is represented by 16 bits. For each pair of patch positions at a given offset, we estimate the MI, in bits, between pairs of these bits from their joint occurrence frequencies across 25K class-balanced ImageNet training images. We average these estimates over the 256 bit pairs, over all position pairs of the offset, and over the four cardinal directions. D Evaluation protocol This section collects the experimental setup and measurement conventions used in Sec. 3. Experimental setup. We evaluate class-conditioned image generation on ImageNet-1k (Russakovsky et al., 2015) at 256×256 and 512×512, and text-conditioned generation on GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023), GenAI-Bench (Li et al., 2024a), and DPG-Bench (Hu et al., 2024). Reconstruction and generation metrics. For a fixed feature extractor, Fréchet distance compares the empirical means and covariances of real and reconstructed or generated image features. rFID is the tokenizer’s reconstruction measurement that compares the reconstructed images and original images in the Inception space using the ImageNet-1k validation set. gFID compares generated images with the original training images using Fréchet distance in Inception space. We re-use the released reference statistics from Li and He (2026). We also report gFDr6 introduced by Yang et al. (2026), which reports generative Fréchet distance in six different feature spaces. The six-space evaluation uses Inception-v3 (Szegedy et al., 2016), ConvNeXt V2 (Woo et al., 2023), DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024), MAE (He et al., 2022), SigLIP2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), and

F Comparison using conventional gFID and PRDC metrics. In the main paper, we report results in gFDr6 (Yang et al., 2026). We compare our method with baselines using gFID (Heusel et al., 2017) and Precision, Recall (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019), Density, and Coverage (Naeem et al., 2020) in Tab. 14. Per conventions, we use different hyperparameters during sampling for gFID evaluation than gFDr6. gFID measures the Fréchet distance in the feature space of an Inception-v3 network (Szegedy et al., 2016) trained for ImageNet classification. Its sensitivity to ImageNet class information means that it can be lowered substantially without improving the images (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2023), and Inception features represent the content of modern generators poorly, so gFID often disagrees with human raters (Stein et al., 2023; Jayasumana et al., 2024). These problems are most severe at the low values reached by current ImageNet generators. ImageNet validation images score a gFID of 1.68 against

text: generators poorly, so gFID often disagrees with human raters (Stein et al., 2023; Jayasumana et al., 2024). These problems are most severe at the low values reached by current ImageNet generators. ImageNet validation images score a gFID of 1.68 against the training set (Yang et al., 2026), so generators below 2.0, and especially below 1.68, appear as close to the training data as real images, although their samples remain clearly distinguishable from real ones (Yang et al., 2026). In this regime, gFID can also be optimized directly: post-training a generator on Inception features lowers its gFID from 3.31 to 0.81 without producing the best samples, whereas post-training on modern representations improves object structure while gFID becomes worse (Yang et al., 2026). gFDr6 addresses these issues by averaging Fréchet distances over six representation spaces, each normalized by the distance between the training and validation sets, so no single feature space dominates and a value of 1 means as close to the training data as real validation images. Tab. 14 provides additional evidence. At these low-gFID operating points, improvements in Inception Fréchet distance do not consistently agree with the fidelity diagnostics. text: wall-clock throughput. It covers the full sampling loop of the generator plus one decoder pass that maps the generated tokens or latents to pixels. Classifier-free guidance duplicates the generator batch and roughly doubles its cost (BAR, FeaTok, SiT, LightningDiT, DDT and the discrete baselines), whereas REPA-E and REG gate the doubled forward to a guidance interval and pay 1.8×, RAEv2’s internal guidance reuses a single forward and costs nothing, and RAE’s autoguidance adds a smaller second network for +30%. Guidance never duplicates the decoder, since only the conditional sample is decoded. Each decoder is built from its official release and driven through the released sampler’s decode call. Decoder costs range from 0.16 TFLOPs for the pixel decoder shared by BAR and FeaTok to 0.62 for the SD-VAE decoder of the latent diffusion baselines. They are small relative to multi-step continuous generators, but not negligible for the cheapest samplers: the pixel decoder adds 15–32% to the generator cost of BAR and FeaTok, and the SD-VAE decoder exceeds the generator cost of the latent one-step models. title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome

text: Objective. Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods. We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children’s Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results. A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2±0.0% accuracy; F1=0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching (p < 0.0001). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline’s calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92–100% of patients at every visit. Discussion. In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change

Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.
title: ABSTRACT

text: Rett syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder affecting approximately 1 in 10,000–15,000 live female births, caused primarily by loss-of-function mutations in the MECP2 gene [1, 2]. The condition is characterized by an initial period of apparently normal development followed by a period of regression, with loss of acquired hand skills, development of stereotypic hand movements, gait abnormalities, and loss of spoken language [2], followed by a period of stabilization without further regression of skills. In March 2023, trofinetide (Daybue) became the first FDA-approved treatment for Rett syndrome [3], following earlier phase 2 efficacy data [4] and a pivotal Phase 3 trial demonstrating improvements on the Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire (RSBQ) and Clinical Global Impression–Improvement (CGI-I) scale [5]. However, the trial captured only a subset of treatment-relevant phenotypes over 12 weeks, and real-world treatment response across the full spectrum of Rett syndrome features remains incompletely characterized. BACKGROUND AND SIGNIFICANCE Monitoring treatment response in Rett syndrome is challenging. The condition manifests across multiple domains, including motor, cognitive, behavioral and autonomic function, each potentially documented by a different specialist in narrative notes. Manual chart review of the resulting note volume can quickly become prohibitively labor-intensive. Electronic health record (EHR) phenotyping has therefore turned to automated methods, from concept-extraction systems [6, 7] to rule-based and portable phenotype algorithms [8, 9]. But traditional rule-based natural

text: chart review of the resulting note volume can quickly become prohibitively labor-intensive. Electronic health record (EHR) phenotyping has therefore turned to automated methods, from concept-extraction systems [6, 7] to rule-based and portable phenotype algorithms [8, 9]. But traditional rule-based natural language processing (NLP) [10, 11] struggles to distinguish active symptoms from historical, anticipatory, and negated mentions within complex narratives [12, 13], a difficulty long noted in adverse-event detection [14, 15]. Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on clinical text and medical benchmarks [16, 17, 18, 19], offering the contextual reasoning to interpret narratives, but a single LLM applied directly to clinical extraction can perform poorly [20]. In our data, a single model produced both false positives, over-interpreting routine documentation, and false negatives. The appropriate architecture depends on task complexity. Simple extraction tasks may suit a single well-prompted model [21, 22]. Our task spans many phenotypes and requires judging, within each note, whether a finding is active at that visit rather than historical, negated or anticipatory, so it is complex enough to benefit from a multi-agent verification design in which one model evaluates or critiques another’s output [23, 24]. We therefore use two independently prompted models and require agreement before making a positive call, prioritizing precision over recall. text: model evaluates or critiques another’s output [23, 24]. We therefore use two independently prompted models and require agreement before making a positive call, prioritizing precision over recall. We present a dual-LLM consensus pipeline that extracts 18 treatment-response phenotypes from clinical notes of 108 patients with Rett syndrome receiving trofinetide. The 18 comprise 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features and medication refusal, and each is classified at every visit as documented present or absent (Methods). The pipeline was developed and evaluated on an expert-annotated ground truth for the diarrhea phenotype, then applied to the remaining 17 phenotypes with only the phenotype definition substituted. Our objective was to determine whether contextual LLM reasoning, combined with a consensus requirement, can extract multi-domain treatment-response phenotypes from routine clinical documentation at a scale that manual review cannot reach. We focused on one major adverse effect, diarrhea, to develop the pipeline, and we report that process in full.

text: 4 MATERIALS AND METHODS Study design and population We conducted a retrospective observational study of patients with Rett syndrome identified from Rett Center clinical visits at Texas Children’s Hospital (TCH) who were prescribed or considered for trofinetide (Daybue). We selected this population because the TCH Rett Center is a dedicated center of excellence whose standardized note templates capture comprehensive disorder-specific information over office visits of at least one hour. An initial 115 patients were identified on this basis. To verify sustained drug exposure, an independent quality-control (QC) review triangulated three sources per patient: pharmacy orders, medication-administration records, and longitudinal note mentions. This confirmed sustained exposure in 108 of 115 patients (94%), with 65 by pharmacy order and 43 by clinical documentation alone (≥2 note mentions over >60 days). The remaining 7 were unconfirmed (4 with only isolated mentions, 3 with no evidence) and were therefore excluded. This 108-patient QC-confirmed cohort is the analysis cohort throughout. Retrieval for the QC-confirmed patients returned 91,453 notes, of which the 26,763 falling inside the six evaluation windows constitute the analyzed corpus. Retrieval was not restricted to the treatment period, so the retrieved notes span November 1998 to August 2026, while the analyzed notes span July 2021 to August 2026. The retrieved corpus spans 67 note types (Figure 1C; full distribution in Supplementary Table S1), the largest being telephone encounters at 22.7% and progress notes, followed by a large “unspecified” group and letters. Because telephone encounters are often the first channel through which adverse effects like diarrhea are reported, we retain all note types rather than restricting to progress notes. Pipeline architecture The extraction pipeline follows a five-step architecture (Figure 1): Step 1: Medication Timeline. Every follow-up window is measured from the patient’s exposure anchor, meaning the identified date on which trofinetide was started. The anchor is taken from the Epic medication-administration record where available, and otherwise from the earliest note documenting active dosing, adjudicated by LLM review; no patient anchored on a dispense record, because trofinetide fills bypass the institutional tables. Across the 108 patients, 8 anchored on an administration record and 91 on an adjudicated note, while 9 lack a reliable date and are excluded from the timepoint analysis. Step

Each note is assigned to a six-month bucket (baseline through 30 months) by the days between its contact date and the exposure anchor. Notes are then pre-filtered by phenotype-specific keyword lists (Supplementary Table S2), producing 60,537 note–phenotype matches across the 17 phenotypes scored by the presence prompt, all but 7 of which returned a valid YES/NO in the structured output from both models. Those 7 were scored negative (Supplementary Note S1, which also reports inter-LLM agreement). For diarrhea the filter matches 7,111 of the 91,453 retrieved notes, and the 2,260 of those falling inside an evaluation window are the corpus every diarrhea comparison below is scored on. Step 3: Dual-LLM Classification. Each keyword-positive note is independently classified by two LLMs with complementary perspectives. The first, a clinical NLP expert, judges whether the phenotype is documented in the note itself, applying explicit rules to separate findings recorded at that visit from historical, negated, anticipatory, and template mentions against a written per-phenotype definition. For diarrhea that definition adds a severity threshold. The second, a domain specialist (gastroenterologist for side

For diarrhea that definition adds a severity threshold. The second, a domain specialist (gastroenterologist for side effects, pediatric neurologist for the Rett clinical features), weighs clinical significance and attribution. Prompt templates, YES/NO criteria, and a contingency table of the two agents’ calls (evidence they work independently) are in Supplementary Notes S3 and S1. Both output a structured YES/NO call with supporting evidence, and a note is positive only when both models agree YES. The record also carries the note’s contact date, which is known from EHR metadata rather than extracted from the note text (Supplementary Note S3). The evidence spans were spot-checked but not systematically validated. Detection is thus note-local in time, so historical mentions score negative, at the cost of missing purely retrospective ones (quantified in the error analysis).

Because the defaults are not guaranteed deterministic, we report run-to-run variability across three independent runs. Step 4: Aggregation. For each patient and timepoint, if any note in the bucket receives a positive consensus call, the patient is marked Yes for that phenotype, producing a patient-by-timepoint-by-phenotype matrix. Step 5: Evaluation. Diarrhea was evaluated against a ground truth from independent manual chart review by domain experts, who labeled each patient-timepoint cell Yes (medication-associated diarrhea), No, or Deceased/Not applicable. This produced labels for 56 patients across the six timepoints (Table 1), giving 183 evaluable cells inside follow-up, of which 47 are labeled Yes. Metrics include accuracy, precision, recall, F1, Cohen’s κ, Matthews correlation, and per-timepoint confusion matrices. Annotation procedure. The ground truth was established by the Rett Center clinical team, who reviewed each patient’s notes within a timepoint window using the same labeling scheme. The same reviewers performed the multi-phenotype expert spot-check. Annotation followed a consensus-adjudication workflow with no formal written guideline and no retrospective inter-annotator agreement statistic, a limitation for gold-standard reliability detailed in Supplementary Note S6 (TRIPOD-LLM items 8a–8b) [25]. Phenotype definitions The 18 phenotypes were selected by the Rett Center clinical team as the adverse effects and disease-related functional domains most salient to monitor in routine trofinetide care, rather than an exhaustive enumeration. At each clinical visit, each phenotype is classified according to whether it is documented as present in that visit’s clinical note, not as a direction-of-change judgment. They span three categories. Adverse effects (4): Diarrhea, Vomiting, Weight Loss, and Other Side Effects, each a physiological reaction to trofinetide. The diarrhea phenotype, defined as medication-associated diarrhea, is the target of the ground-truth validation and error analysis. Medication refusal (1): Refusing Medication is tracked separately because it is a behavioral response, not a physiological reaction, and captures documented instances of the patient declining or resisting the medication. Rett clinical features (13): General Mood, Gross Motor, Fine Motor, Language/Communication, Stereotypy, Attention/Alertness, Sleep, Breathing/Hyperventilation, Bruxism, Dysautonomia, Aggressive Behavior, Anxiety, Seizures. These are manifestations of Rett syndrome itself, part of the natural history of the disorder that clinicians track over the course of treatment. They are not adverse effects, and no finding in this category should be read as an effect caused by trofinetide. Each phenotype

text: 7 Model development and iteration We developed the pipeline on diarrhea, our development set, because expert annotation of all 18 phenotypes across every patient would be prohibitively slow, the bottleneck this pipeline relieves. The architecture was settled first, by a comparison of six extraction strategies on this development set that selected the dual-model consensus gate. Holding it fixed, we then ran that consensus configuration under five classification prompts differing only in what they count as diarrhea, alongside two rule-based methods that bound the comparison from below (Table 2). Prompt wording, the architecture comparison, and the identifiers these methods carry in the released code are in Supplementary Notes S2, S3, and S7. We selected the reported prompt on the same 183 cells we score it on. Its diarrhea accuracy is therefore an in-sample upper bound rather than a held-out estimate. The evidence that the design generalizes comes from the other 17 phenotypes. We froze the pipeline after the diarrhea work and applied it to them with only the phenotype definition substituted (Results; Supplementary Note S2). Ethical considerations This study was conducted under IRB protocol H-52222 at Baylor College of Medicine / Texas Children’s Hospital. All data remained within the institutional secure computing environment, and LLM inference was performed in-environment under enterprise data-governance controls. RESULTS Contextual reasoning improves performance and outperforms keyword matching We evaluated seven methods of increasing specificity on the identical 183-cell ground truth (Table 2). The severe-diarrhea prompt performs best. Accuracy rises with the severity threshold the prompt sets, and the severe-diarrhea prompt (Claude Opus 4.6) performs best on every headline metric except recall: 84.2% accuracy, precision 0.714, F1 0.674, κ 0.570. This is 47 percentage points over the regular-expression baseline (37.2%, indiscriminate over-flagging) and 42 points over negation-aware NLP (42.1%). Both restrictions help. Requiring diarrhea to be uncontrolled improves on counting any documented mention (79.6% against 75.2%), and stating that restriction as an explicit severity bar raises accuracy to 84.2% via precision (0.596→0.714), as the bar converts nine false positives into true negatives at the cost of one true positive. How strong is this evidence? We then asked whether these differences are real or only directional, testing each comparison with McNemar’s exact test and Holm-correcting across a pre-declared family of seven prompt comparisons (Supplementary Table S4). The reported prompt beats both rule-based methods decisively (p < 0.0001), and every prompt sits far above them on accuracy. None of

These 13 features are manifestations of Rett syndrome itself and not adverse effects of trofinetide, so their documented presence describes the disorder under treatment rather than harm caused by it. They span a wide range of documented prevalence (Figure 3A; full rates in Supplementary Table S8). Gross- and fine-motor impairment, impaired language/communication, and hand stereotypies are the core neurodevelopmental features of the disorder, and all are documented as present in nearly all patients at every visit (92–100%). Dysautonomia, breathing, bruxism, sleep, and seizure form a middle band at intermediate rates, while attention/alertness, anxiety, and the affective and behavioral findings of mood and aggression are documented least often. text: 11 DISCUSSION A dual-LLM consensus pipeline can extract clinically meaningful treatment-response phenotypes from unstructured notes at scale, recovering signal that structured fields miss. Modeling clinical context significantly outperforms naive keyword matching, and what separates the configurations that do so is what the prompt counts as diarrhea rather than how many models are asked. The severe-diarrhea prompt was strongest, but its margin over the deployed prompt is unresolved at this sample size, so we adopt it as a precision-favorable default rather than a proven improvement. It was also selected on the same 183 cells it is scored on, so its accuracy is an in-sample upper bound. The evidence that the design transfers is the half-cohort split and the 90.2% agreement on the other 17 phenotypes, which the same architecture and prompt design reached with only the phenotype definition substituted. The type of error matters more than the headline accuracy. Most diarrhea errors are annotation or data limitations rather than model failures, which tells a deploying institution which discrepancies prompting can fix, which are data-coverage ceilings, and which are annotation-guideline decisions. Design choices and intended use are in Supplementary Note S4, and the architecture comparison is in Note S2. Diarrhea is the most commonly reported adverse event in the pivotal Phase 3 trial, at ∼80% in the treatment arm [5, 26]. Our validated target is narrower, severe rather than any diarrhea, and expert labels put it at 64% of evaluable patients at 6 months and below 20% at every later visit (Supplementary Table S5), so the difference from the trial figure is mostly one of threshold rather than of detection. The later validated timepoints have few evaluable cells, 13 at 24 months and 6 at 30 months, and warrant caution. The main limitation is that only diarrhea has a ground truth. The other 17 phenotypes rest on spot-check review and inter-LLM agreement rather than full annotation (Supplementary Note S1), a resource constraint described in Methods. Their rates are therefore hypothesis-generating lower bounds, and generalization likely varies by phenotype, since concrete adverse effects should transfer more readily than subjective findings. The pipeline detects only what our corpus documents, and some symptoms surface only in other channels. The exposure anchor is adjudicated from note text for most patients rather than taken from a structured record, so window boundaries carry real uncertainty, visible in the 12 displacement errors. The exposure anchor is adjudicated from note text for most patients rather than taken from a structured record, so window boundaries carry real uncertainty, visible in the 12 displacement errors. The observed trajectories cannot be definitively attributed to trofinetide rather than to concurrent therapies or the natural course of development. The outcome is documented presence and not direction of change or severity, so the pipeline cannot distinguish an improved feature from a persistent one. For the core Rett features, documented in nearly all patients at nearly every visit, detecting within-feature improvement would need severity-graded instruments such as the RSBQ or CGI-I. Documentation does move for other side effects and refusing medication, so the method registers change when change is recorded. All patients come from a single institution, and the pipeline is not yet optimized for efficiency, which cheap pre-filtering, batched calls, and smaller distilled models could improve. Integrating additional sources such as telephone logs and portal messages, and cross-temporal reasoning that propagates retro- spective mentions to the timepoint they describe, would recover symptoms currently missed. Expanding the ground truth by second-reviewer adjudication and by annotation prioritized on inter-LLM disagreement would convert the six-case agreement tiers into per-phenotype accuracy with confidence intervals. title: DISCUSSION

text: We present a dual-LLM consensus pipeline for multi-phenotype treatment-response extraction from clinical notes, applied to 108 patients with Rett syndrome receiving trofinetide over 30 months. Using Claude Opus 4.6, it substantially outperforms a regular-expression baseline on an expert-annotated diarrhea development set, and the same configuration transfers out-of-sample to the remaining 17 phenotypes with only the phenotype definition substituted. It also yields one of the first comprehensive real-world characterizations of how multi-domain trofinetide response is documented in routine care. The architecture extends to further phenotypes, medications, and institutions by configuration alone, showing that LLM consensus can bridge clinical narrative and the structured data needed for scalable treatment-response monitoring and real-world evidence in rare diseases. text: 1 Supplementary Material for Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline SUPPLEMENTARY NOTES Supplementary Note S1. Inter-LLM Agreement and the Consensus Gate Because only diarrhea has an expert ground truth, we also measured the agreement between the two independently prompted agents, which requires no labels. Cohen’s κ between LLM 1 (clinical NLP expert) and LLM 2 (GI/neurology specialist) was computed over the 60,530 note–phenotype instances that both models classified (Figure S1A). Overall agreement was high (κ = 0.930, raw agreement 96.6%), and all 17 phenotypes reached κ ≥0.73, with per-phenotype values in Table S3. Seven of the 60,537 matches did not return a valid YES or NO from both models and were scored negative. Because the two prompts were written independently, their agreement is a proxy for how well specified a phenotype is. It does not track the per-phenotype expert agreement from the spot-check, however. Attention/alertness has the lowest κ (0.732) yet reached 6/6 on review, while dysautonomia (κ = 0.917) and refusing medication (κ = 0.890) reached only 4/6. With six cases per phenotype the spot-check cannot resolve differences of that size, so the two signals should be read as independent rather than concordant. Diarrhea is scored by the diarrhea-specific pipeline rather than by the presence prompt, and reaches κ = 0.878 at raw

Diarrhea is scored by the diarrhea-specific pipeline rather than by the presence prompt, and reaches κ = 0.878 at raw agreement 98.0% over the 2,260 notes both agents classified. It is therefore shown separately from the 17, as a hatched bar in Figure S1A and below the rule in Table S3. Prompt wording drives agreement. The two diarrhea prompts isolate what wording alone contributes, because both were applied to the identical 2,260 notes with the same two models. The deployed prompt V0 reaches raw agreement 95.1% and κ = 0.805, and the reported prompt V2 reaches 98.0% and κ = 0.878 (Table S9). Specifying the target more tightly leaves the two agents less room to differ, and the same effect appears at the cell level across the prompt ladder (Table S10). Among the 17 phenotypes the two lowest values are attention/alertness (κ = 0.732) and the open-ended other-side-effects category (0.756), which are also the two whose target is least concretely specifiable. Inter-LLM disagreement may therefore be a useful label-free signal for which phenotypes most need prompt refinement or human review, although the present spot-check is too small to validate it. What the consensus gate costs and buys. Across the full corpus the two agents disagreed on 3.4% of instances (Figure S1B, with raw counts in Table S9). The gate resolves these disagreements conservatively, counting only “both YES” instances (38.4%) as positive and treating one-sided calls as negative. This is how it suppresses one-sided false positives, at some cost in recall. On the diarrhea ground truth the mechanism is measurable but small. Under the deployed prompt, the only configuration for which both agents were also scored alone, the gate changes two of 183 cells against the stronger of them (Table S10, panel A), so it neither costs nor buys measurable accuracy there. The case for two agents rests on making their disagreement observable across the 17 phenotypes that have no ground truth.

text: 2 The voting pattern as a confidence signal. Partitioning cells by the two agents’ votes shows that cells where both agree No are the most accurate against the expert labels (84.3%, 113/134), cells where both agree Yes are the least accurate (52.3%, 23/44), and split votes fall between them (72.7%, 8/11). The low accuracy of “both Yes” cells is the threshold-disagreement effect described in the main-text error analysis. The agents confidently and defensibly detect documented diarrhea that the reviewer scored as sub-threshold, so positive calls are exactly the cells a deployment should route for human adjudication. Why the reported configuration’s run-to-run SD is zero. Prompt V2’s accuracy in main-text Table 2 carries an SD of 0.0 because its confusion matrix is identical in all three runs, at 30 true positives, 124 true negatives, 12 false positives and 17 false negatives. This is a property of the aggregation step and not evidence that the prompt is deterministic. At the note level the consensus call does move, flipping on 7, 9 and 8 of the 2,260 classified notes across the three run pairs, and on 3, 4 and 3 of the 1,404 notes that fall inside the annotated patients’ evaluation windows. None of those flips changes a cell. Aggregation marks a patient–timepoint Yes if any note in the six-month bucket receives a

text: pairs, and on 3, 4 and 3 of the 1,404 notes that fall inside the annotated patients’ evaluation windows. None of those flips changes a cell. Aggregation marks a patient–timepoint Yes if any note in the six-month bucket receives a positive call, so a flip on a note whose bucket already holds another positive is absorbed. The deployed prompt V0 flips on 15, 11 and 10 notes over the same pairs, and one of its cells does move. The zero is therefore correct arithmetic at the cell level while the underlying note-level classification remains stochastic, and it should not be read as prompt stability. Decoding parameters and the independence of the runs. No seed and no sampling parameters were set in any of the 42 model- invocation nodes, so temperature, top-p, top-k and the token limit took platform defaults throughout, as the main-text Methods states. The three runs are therefore independent draws rather than replays of a single run. We verified this on the response strings themselves, since the platform exposes no per-call telemetry. Under V2, Agent 1 returned byte-identical text on 2,243 of the 2,260 notes and Agent 2 on 2,251, whereas a cached or memoized path would return identical strings everywhere. Model Development History This note expands the model-development summary in the main-text Methods. The pipeline was reached through a sequence of designs, each built to address a failure mode observed in the previous one, and the benchmark of the six retained methods against the 189-cell diarrhea ground truth is in Table S11. Two points bound how those numbers relate to the main text. First, the architecture was selected on the original note corpus, the order-date exposure anchor and a 189-cell grid, and it is reported here on the numbers it was decided with. The architecture it settled on was then held fixed, and the prompt comparison in the main text varies the prompt instead, on the refreshed corpus and the corrected anchor. The two sets of numbers are not interchangeable. Second, the negation-aware NLP row of main-text Table 2 is not the rule-based NLP of Table S11. It is a reimplementation written for the rerun so that every method in Table 2 is scored on one grid, and it reaches 42.1% there against the 70.9%

We added regular-expression negation detection and temporal cue matching to discount past-tense and resolved mentions. This substantially improved precision over the floor but was brittle. Hand-written patterns missed paraphrases and complex sentence structure, and over-aggressive negation occasionally suppressed true positives. Stage 2: Hybrid NLP. We layered three further components onto the rule-based system. Clinical-form and template filters remove boilerplate and blank-field matches, severity gates down-weight “mild,” “controlled” and “resolving” language, and simple cross-temporal handling was added. At equal overall accuracy to the rule-based model, this recovered recall that the stricter negation rules had removed, so the two systems sat at different points on the same precision–recall frontier rather than one dominating the other. Stage 3: Iterative single-LLM prototype. Before the full ground truth existed, we prototyped a three-pass LLM approach on a 32-patient subset to test whether contextual reasoning could move beyond the rule-based frontier. It established feasibility but used a different evaluation set with no paired ground truth, so it is not part of the six-method benchmark. Stage 4: Single-LLM and the dual-LLM consensus gate. text: no paired ground truth, so it is not part of the six-method benchmark. Stage 4: Single-LLM and the dual-LLM consensus gate. Once the full ground truth was available, we evaluated a single clinical-NLP-expert LLM, whose accuracy (72.7%) edged above the rule-based frontier (70.9%) although the difference was not resolved at 189 cells. Adding a second, differently prompted domain-specialist model raised the question of how to combine the two outputs. We tested both aggregation rules on identical model outputs. An OR-gate (permissive, positive if either agent says Yes) maximizes sensitivity but readmits false positives, while an AND-gate (consensus, positive only if both agree) favors precision. The consensus gate gave the best overall accuracy and the most run-stable operating point, and was adopted. Rejected variant: a broader definition of the target. Having fixed the gate, we tried loosening what the prompt counts as a positive. Both agents were instructed to score any documented diarrhea as present, dropping the exclusion for diarrhea that was mild or already controlled with medication, on the reasoning that a symptom under treatment is still a symptom. This raised recall as intended but added far more false positives than it recovered true ones, so overall accuracy fell well below the adopted design and the change was reverted. Table S11, panel B, reports all 15 pairwise McNemar exact tests on the identical 189-cell paired ground truth. Every context-aware method significantly outperforms the regex floor (p < 0.0001, and after Holm correction). The comparisons above the floor are directionally consistent with the accuracy ordering, with the consensus model winning each head-to-head disagreement, for example 24 discordant cells to 14 against hybrid NLP, but none reaches significance (p = 0.11–1.0). This reflects limited power rather than an absence of effect. The consensus-versus-NLP gap rests on a net of roughly ten cells of 189, and confirming a difference of that size at 80% power would require on the order of 550 annotated cells, about three times the current ground truth. The final rerun sharpens the same reading. On the refreshed corpus and the corrected anchor the gate reaches 79.6% and the stronger single agent 79.2%, differing on two of 183 cells (Table S10, panel A).

The prompts emit only YES or NO, so nothing in the output records the reasoning behind a call. The 91.8% quoted in the main text is a bound and not a corrected accuracy. It is what accuracy becomes if every threshold- disagreement cell is re-scored as correct wherever the model and the note agree the symptom is present. Reaching it defensibly would require re-adjudicating the ground truth prospectively, under a severity threshold written into both the annotation guideline and the prompt, rather than relabeling the current errors after the fact. Intended use. The operating point we report, precision 0.714 and recall 0.638 on diarrhea, is well suited to cohort-level inference and triage but not to autonomous per-patient decision-making. At this precision and recall the pipeline is best used to estimate phenotype prevalence and trajectories across a population, where over- and under-calls partially offset in aggregate, and to surface candidate notes for a human reviewer. Errors are also non-random, concentrating in threshold-ambiguous cases, so any per-patient use should keep a clinician in the loop and treat a positive call as a prompt for review rather than a conclusion. text: 10 Item TRIPOD-LLM description (abbrev.) Where addressed 19g Next steps for future research and applicability Discussion aItem 8b (inter-annotator agreement). The ground truth was set by the Rett Center clinical team of two pediatric Rett-clinic nurses and two pediatric neurologists, who resolved each cell together by consensus rather than annotating independently, so no κ or F1 agreement statistic can be computed retrospectively (Note S6). This is a real limitation for gold-standard reliability and is part of why reviewer–model threshold disagreements dominate the error analysis. Supplementary Note S6. Annotation Procedure The diarrhea ground truth and the multi-phenotype expert spot-check were established by the Rett Center clinical team, comprising two pediatric nurses familiar with the Rett syndrome clinic and two pediatric neurologists, who worked as a single reviewing group throughout. For each patient and timepoint window the reviewers examined the available clinical notes and labeled the cell Yes for medication-associated diarrhea, No, or Deceased/Not applicable. Where diarrhea was recorded, its severity was noted on the clinic’s four-level scale: 1, loose stool in diaper; 2, watery stool in diaper; 3, watery stool on clothes; 4, watery stool outside clothes. The operative question was whether documented diarrhea represented a medication side effect as opposed to a tolerated, controlled or pre-existing baseline symptom. This is the same judgment that drives the reviewer–model threshold disagreements in
title: TRIPOD-LLM description (abbrev.)

text: clothes; 4, watery stool outside clothes. The operative question was whether documented diarrhea represented a medication side effect as opposed to a tolerated, controlled or pre-existing baseline symptom. This is the same judgment that drives the reviewer–model threshold disagreements in main-text Table 4. The reviewers resolved each cell together by consensus rather than annotating independently against a written guideline. No formal written guideline was issued, and because each cell was adjudicated by consensus, no inter-annotator agreement statistic could be computed retrospectively. This is a genuine limitation for gold-standard reliability (TRIPOD-LLM items 8a–8c). A shared written guideline with an explicit severity threshold, applied by independent double annotation, would both tighten the ground truth and allow the reviewer–model threshold disagreements to be quantified rather than adjudicated case by case. Scope of the spot-check sample. The spot-check sample was drawn before the exposure-anchor adjudication was final, so its coverage of the reported evaluation windows is partial. Of the 102 reviewed notes, 58 fall inside an evaluation window in the reported configuration and 44 do not. The shortfall is concentrated at baseline, where 26 of 33 cases fall outside, against 12 of 34 at 6 months, 6 of 34 at 12 months and 0 of 1 at 18 months. That gradient follows from the baseline window being the one defined immediately around the anchor,

text: 11 Supplementary Note S7. Prompt-Level and Variable-Decomposition Sensitivity Analyses Note S2 describes how the architecture was selected. Holding that architecture fixed, we ran three further experiments on the refreshed corpus and the corrected exposure anchor to ask which component of the configuration the remaining error is attributable to. The first varied the prompt wording, and it is where the reported configuration comes from. The second replaced the single extraction question with two simpler questions combined by an explicit rule. The third left the extraction untouched and realigned each patient’s sequence of predictions in time. The main text carries the prompt comparison as Table 2, while the realignment appears only here, because it presumes that onset falls at the first on-treatment visit and is therefore a diagnostic of where the error sits rather than a deployable comparator. The version identifiers used in this supplement and in the released code correspond to the main-text names as follows. V0 is uncontrolled diarrhea, the deployed prompt; V1 is any diarrhea; V2 is severe diarrhea, the reported prompt; V3 is severe diarrhea with rules; V4 is any diarrhea with rules; and S1 is the onset-aligned variant. Severe denotes the clinical-significance bar quoted verbatim in Note S3, that the diarrhea be active and either causing ongoing concern or prompting a change in management. With rules denotes

Prompt wording Five prompt versions were compared on the same 183 annotated diarrhea cells, with the two agents, the consensus gate, the keyword pre-filter and the output schema all unchanged. Two elements were varied. The first is the severity threshold, specifically whether diarrhea being controlled with medication counts as present. The second is a pair of explicit reasoning rules stating that a resolution later in a note governs an earlier onset, and that a finding attributed to another cause is absent. Version V0 is the deployed prompt and serves as the base case. Each version was run three times. Table S10 reports the results, and three findings follow. First, the severity threshold is the only element that moves accuracy. Restating the deployed exclusion explicitly and adding a severity bar raised accuracy from 79.6% to 84.2% (V0 to V2), the largest movement anywhere in the family. The mechanism is precision. False positives fall from 21 to 12 while true positives are essentially unchanged at 31

text: and adding a severity bar raised accuracy from 79.6% to 84.2% (V0 to V2), the largest movement anywhere in the family. The mechanism is precision. False positives fall from 21 to 12 while true positives are essentially unchanged at 31 and 30, so the added bar suppresses calls on documented but managed diarrhea without giving up detections. The difference is nonetheless not established, as it rests on 9 cells won against 1 lost, which is p = 0.021 before correction and p = 0.15 after Holm correction across the seven comparisons in this family. Second, the explicit reasoning rules add nothing. The reason is that the deployed prompt already carried both instructions in weaker form, stating that historical references where the finding has clearly resolved are absent, and that findings attributed to another cause are absent (Note S3). The added rules therefore restated existing guidance rather than supplying a new criterion. Decomposing the extraction question The prompt experiment leaves open the possibility that the single extraction question asks for two judgments at once, whether diarrhea has started and whether it is currently uncontrolled. We tested that reading by replacing the single question with two simpler ones and combining them in code rather than in the prompt. Variable A asks only whether diarrhea has begun as a side effect of trofinetide at any point up to and including the visit. Variable B asks only whether it is adequately controlled at the visit. The two were combined by a deterministic state rule that labels diarrhea present from the visit at which onset is first detected and absent from the visit at which control is first established. Ten combination rules were evaluated, varying that rule, the direction of the consensus gate and the within-window aggregation order, all at no additional inference cost, since each is a function of the same two extracted

Ten combination rules were evaluated, varying that rule, the direction of the consensus gate and the within-window aggregation order, all at no additional inference cost, since each is a function of the same two extracted variables. The decomposition did not improve on the single question. The ten rules span 61.7% to 79.4% (Table S10, panel B), the best coming within 0.2 points of the deployed prompt and none reaching the 84.2% of the reported configuration. The onset variable is what limits them. Applied alone it scores 61.7% at precision 0.384, so it fires on 61 of the 136 negative cells, and because the state rule cannot label a visit negative until control is documented, the combination rules can only recover accuracy by suppressing harder, which collapses recall. As with the reasoning rules above, the deployed prompt already encodes this logic, since it scores active diarrhea as present and both resolved history and adequately controlled disease as absent (Note S3). Splitting that judgment into two questions and a state machine reproduced it less accurately than asking it once. Supplementary Note S8. The Exposure Anchor Every follow-up window is measured from the date trofinetide was started, so that date determines which visit a note is scored against. The deployed pipeline took it from the earliest trofinetide record in the Epic order table, and the resulting windows disagreed with the expert annotation more often than the note content did. Manual review of the record explained why. Trofinetide is an oral solution dispensed by a specialty pharmacy and given at home, so the drug appears in orders, charts and correspondence well before the family gives the first dose, and the order is followed by pharmacy processing, insurance authorization and a four-week titration. text: 14 We therefore replaced the order date with the earliest documented exposure, taken in order of preference from the medication administration record, then from a dispense or fill record, and otherwise from the earliest note adjudicated as documenting active dosing. Of the 108 QC-confirmed patients, 8 anchor on an administration record and 91 on an adjudicated note, while 9 have no reliable evidence of a start date and are excluded from the timepoint analysis. None anchors on a dispense record, because trofinetide fills go through a specialty pharmacy and never reach the institutional dispense tables. The correction is large and does not depend on the labels, moving the median patient by 116 days, with more than half moving by more than 90 days. It also moves six cells out of the follow-up range, taking the grid from 189 cells to 183 while conserving the contributing patients and the 47 positive cells, and accuracy under the deployed prompt rises from 77.1% to 79.6%. That rise cannot be attributed to the anchor alone, because the note corpus was refreshed in the same rerun, so we report the two grids side by side. Two negative controls confirm that the result does not follow from displacing windows as such, since neither randomly re-anchoring the patients nor permuting their timepoint labels reaches the observed accuracy in 200 draws. The corrected anchor does not remove the problem entirely. It cannot recover the lag between a symptom starting and a note recording it, and the annotation is cell-level and carries no dates, so a reviewer may place a symptom at the stage of treatment where it clinically belongs rather than at the timestamp of the note that records it. Both effects are visible in the gap between the two ways of scoring the pipeline. Judged note by note, where the anchor plays no part, agreement with expert review is about 90%, at 90.2% over the full 17-phenotype spot-check and 91.4% over the 58 of those cases that fall inside an evaluation window (Note S6). Judged cell by cell, where every call must also land in the right six-month window, the reported configuration reaches 84.2%. We read the difference as the cost of identifying the start date from the record rather than as a failure to read the notes, which is why the residual temporal errors in main-text Table 4 are the largest remaining category after threshold disagreement.

title: ABNAT: Attention-Based Noise-Aware Training for Robust

text: Transformer-based models have become the backbone of a wide range of tasks, but their intensive computation and data movement incur substantial energy overhead. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) offers an energy-efficient alternative, yet its inherent hard- ware non-idealities perturb stored weights and can significantly degrade model performance. Although existing noise-aware train- ing (NAT) methods improve robustness by injecting noise during training, they largely overlook the critical role of attention mech- anisms in Transformer inference. To bridge this gap, we analyze how CIM-induced noise reshapes attention in Transformers and identify two key observations: (1) the divergence between clean and noisy attention maps increases substantially in deeper layers, and (2) conventional NAT can remain overconfident even when its attention routes deviate markedly from the clean reference. Moti- vated by these findings, we propose ABNAT, an attention-based noise-aware training framework that teaches the noisy student to preserve the clean teacher’s headwise attention routes rather than merely reproduce answers, without hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants further reduce training cost. Extensive experiments across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers show that ABNAT consistently improves robustness over corre- sponding NAT baselines, improving noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reducing attention deviation by up to 85.77%. text: Transformers underpin modern vision, language, and multimodal models, but their intensive matrix operations impose substantial computation, memory, and data-movement costs. Analog Compute- in-Memory (CIM) performs matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) in situ and therefore offers an energy-efficient deployment sub- strate [11, 22, 25]. However, device variation, write noise, and other analog non-idealities perturb stored weights and can severely de- grade Transformer inference. To mitigate such degradation, noise-aware training (NAT) meth- ods incorporate hardware noise injection during training to improve model robustness [12, 19, 26]. While effective for conventional con- volutional neural networks (CNNs), these approaches treat the model as a black box and optimize solely for correct output predic- tions, overlooking the distinctive role of attention mechanisms in Transformer inference. This output-centric paradigm leaves a criti- cal gap: the internal semantic reasoning pathways of Transformers remain fragile under CIM noise, even when final predictions appear correct. For clear spatial visualization of attention routes, we conduct a detailed analysis of Vision Transformers (ViTs) [9]. (L) Output- centric NAT misses semantic attention routes. Existing NAT meth- ods supervise only final predictions, allowing models to produce correct answers via incorrect attention routes. Figure 1 shows severe attention distortion under NAT, motivating two structural obser- vations. (O1) CIM noise accumulates attention drift across depth. arXiv:2610.22065v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026

Figure 2 shows that this drift grows with noise severity and becomes concentrated in late blocks, motivating targeted route preservation. (O2) Head sensitivity is nonuniform within blocks. Figure 4 further reveals marked head- to-head sensitivity variation, so uniform alignment over all layers is unnecessarily costly without commensurate accuracy gains. Motivated by these observations, we propose ABNAT (Attention- Based Noise-Aware Training), an attention-based knowledge dis- tillation (KD) framework for preserving semantic routes under CIM noise. ABNAT uses a clean, frozen copy of the target deploy- ment model as the teacher and its noise-perturbed counterpart as the student. Rather than relying only on answer-level supervi- sion, ABNAT transfers the content understanding encoded in the teacher’s attention routes by aligning teacher and student attention distributions. Figure 1 shows that ABNAT restores noise-distorted attention maps toward the clean reference across diverse inputs, indicating more faithful preservation of semantic attention routes. We further develop head- and block-selective variants that retain near-full robustness at lower training cost, and validate ABNAT across vision, language, and vision-language Transformers. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We identify attention drift as a key robustness bottleneck in CIM-deployed ViTs and empirically establish its strong correlation with accuracy degradation under noise. • We propose ABNAT, an attention-based KD framework that preserves semantic attention routes under CIM noise by aligning headwise attention maps between a clean teacher and a noisy student model. • We introduce selective alignment variants at head and block granularity that reduce training cost while retaining accu- racy close to full alignment. • Extensive experiments spanning multiple noise levels, model scales, and datasets across vision, language, and multimodal tasks demonstrate that ABNAT consistently outperforms ex- isting NAT baselines, achieving up to 11.28 percentage points higher noise-degraded accuracy and an 85.77% reduction in attention deviation. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Transformers and Attention Mechanisms Transformers represent vision, language, and multimodal inputs as token sequences processed by 𝐿stacked blocks [24]. Each block combines multi-head self-attention (MHSA) and a feed-forward network with residual connections and layer normalization. Self- attention enables each token to aggregate relevant information from other permitted tokens, supporting content-dependent, long- range interactions. Across blocks, these maps govern progressive information routing [1, 8], making them a natu- ral internal target for ABNAT. The same mechanism is shared by vision, language, and vision-language Transformers [3, 9, 18]. 2.2 Analog CIM Hardware Analog CIM accelerators perform MVMs in situ by encoding weight matrices as analog device conductances and exploiting Ohm’s law for multiplication and Kirchhoff’s current law for summation [7, 23]. This in-memory computation eliminates costly data movement be- tween memory and processing units, enabling orders-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency compared to conventional digi- tal accelerators [6, 11, 22]. These properties make CIM an attractive substrate for energy-efficient Transformer deployment [13, 14, 16]. However, analog device non-idealities introduce unavoidable perturbations to the stored weights [2, 4]. These arise from
