text: efficiency compared to conventional digi- tal accelerators [6, 11, 22]. These properties make CIM an attractive substrate for energy-efficient Transformer deployment [13, 14, 16]. However, analog device non-idealities introduce unavoidable perturbations to the stored weights [2, 4]. These arise from multi- ple physical sources: conductance programming variation, thermal read noise, inter-cell interference, and long-term conductance drift. The detailed bit-level noise formulation used in our experiments is introduced in Sec. 4. For Transformers, noise corrupts the projec- tion matrices W𝑄, W𝐾, and W𝑉at every layer, perturbing attention computation throughout the network. Because Transformer repre- sentations are built compositionally across depth, these per-layer errors accumulate rather than cancel, causing severe attention drift in deeper layers where semantic concentration is most critical. 2.3 Noise-Aware Training NAT improves CIM robustness by injecting hardware noise during training, optimizing: min W E𝝐  LCE(𝑓ˆW(x),𝑦)  , (2) where LCE is the cross-entropy loss and 𝑓ˆW denotes the noisy model. NAT has demonstrated effectiveness for CNNs [5, 15, 26], but remains output-centric: supervising only final predictions places no explicit constraint on intermediate attention routes. The model may therefore learn shortcut solutions that produce correct, highly confident predictions through severely distorted attention maps. Such confidence–route inconsistency can generalize poorly across deployment noise levels and degrade clean accuracy because the semantic attention routes central to Transformer inference remain unconstrained.

KD transfers knowledge from a pretrained teacher 𝑓W to a stu- dent 𝑓ˆW by minimizing discrepancies in their outputs or intermedi- ate representations, and has shown strong results in model com- pression and transfer learning [10, 21]. Prior studies have incorpo- rated KD into NAT for CIM robustness: Charan et al. [5] distill the teacher’s output predictions, whereas Zhou et al. [27] additionally align intermediate feature maps in RRAM-based ViTs. Despite us- ing knowledge distillation, both approaches essentially teach the noisy student to reproduce answers while overlooking attention drift, without teaching it to understand the content under noise. In contrast, ABNAT transfers the clean teacher’s attention distribu- tions, teaching the noisy student to preserve content understanding under hardware noise. Section 4 demonstrates the resulting gains in robust performance and cross-noise generalization.

text: 1–8, but undergoes a sharp, accelerating increase in blocks 9–12. This depth-dependent pattern can be un- derstood through the lens of error propagation: perturbations intro- duced by CIM noise at any given layer are not confined to that layer, but are carried forward and progressively amplified as they pass through the subsequent nonlinear transformations of the Trans- former. Consequently, late blocks, which receive as input the accu- mulated representations of all preceding layers, are disproportion- ately exposed to compounded noise effects. This observation has an important practical implication: a uniform attention alignment strategy that treats all blocks equally may be mismatched with the underlying structure of the problem. Instead, a depth-aware approach that concentrates alignment effort on late blocks is more efficient. The depth-dependent drift pattern indicates where CIM noise has the strongest impact, but does not directly quantify its effect on task performance. To bridge this gap, Fig. 3 correlates the full- network mean attention drift with the model-level accuracy drop across diverse noise conditions and seeds. The results show a strong correlation, with Pearson 𝑟= 0.9633 and Spearman 𝜌= 0.9879. This observation has two implications. First, mean attention drift serves as a reliable network-level robustness diagnostic: noise settings with larger mean drift are typically associated with greater accuracy degradation, whereas those with smaller drift exhibit less perfor- mance

Bringing all components together, the complete training objective of ABNAT combines three comple- mentary losses, each operating at a distinct level of abstraction: 𝐿𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙= 𝐿𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑘+ 𝜆𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑡𝑠𝐿𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑡𝑠+ 𝜆𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛𝐿𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛(S), (8) where 𝜆𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑡𝑠and 𝜆𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛are scalar hyperparameters that balance the three objectives; 𝐿𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑘is kept at unit coefficient as the scale anchor. Unless otherwise stated, we use 𝜆𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑡𝑠= 3, 𝜆𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛= 50, and 𝜏KD = 𝜏𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛= 1. At the coarsest level, the task loss 𝐿𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑘is the standard cross- entropy loss computed against ground-truth labels, ensuring that the student retains discriminative performance on the target task regardless of noise conditions. Building on top of this, the logits dis- tillation loss 𝐿𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑡𝑠= 𝐷KL(softmax(𝑧𝑇/𝜏KD)∥softmax(𝑧𝑆/𝜏KD)), where 𝑧𝑇and 𝑧𝑆are the pre-softmax logits and𝜏KD is the distillation temperature, aligns the student’s output probability distribution with that of the clean teacher. Finally, at the finest level of granu- larity, the attention alignment loss 𝐿𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛(S) reaches deeper into the network to preserve the selected internal attention pathways. Together, these three losses form a coherent, multi-level training strategy: 𝐿𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑘anchors the student to correct predictions, 𝐿𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑡𝑠 aligns its output distribution with the teacher’s, and 𝐿𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛(S) safe- guards attention routes vulnerable to

Figure 6(a–c) presents results for ViT-Small on CIFAR-100, ViT-Tiny on ImageNet-100, and Swin-Tiny on CIFAR- 100. At 𝜎= 0.20, ABNAT improves over NAT by 6.34, 8.15, and 4.15 percentage points, respectively. These consistent gains across model scales, datasets, and both flat and hierarchical Transformer architectures indicate that attention-route supervision is not tied to a single configuration. Generalization to Language and Multimodal Transformers We further evaluate attention-route preservation using Pythia- 160M and Pythia-2.8B for language modeling [3] and CLIP ViT-B/32 for image–text retrieval [18]. Figure 6(d–f) reports perplexity and Mean Recall, where lower and higher values are better, respectively. An attention-aligned variant performs best in all three settings. At 𝜎=0.20, NAT+AttnAlign reduces Pythia-160M perplexity by 76.4%, from 7682.16 to 1812.96, while NAT+KD+AttnAlign reduces Pythia- 2.8B perplexity by 59.6%, from 2329.72 to 941.04. On CLIP ViT-B/32 at 𝜎=0.10, NAT+AttnAlign improves Mean Recall from 71.70 for NAT to 72.27. These results extend attention-route preservation to autoregressive language modeling and multimodal retrieval. title: ABNAT: Attention-Based Noise-Aware Training for Robust Transformers on Analog CIM Systems

text: In this paper, we show that CIM noise induces depth-accumulated, head-dependent attention drift, while output-centric NAT may re- produce answers through routes that deviate from the clean model. We propose ABNAT, which aligns headwise attention between clean and noisy paths from the same checkpoint to preserve task-relevant content processing rather than merely match answers. Across vi- sion, language, and multimodal Transformers, ABNAT improves noisy accuracy by up to 11.28 percentage points, reduces attention drift by 85.77%, generalizes under train–deploy noise mismatch, and adds no inference cost; selective variants retain near-full robustness with lower training overhead. title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: Long-context language models support ever longer context windows, and evalu- ations typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty. However, context length alone cannot explain why models fail on long-context tasks that re- quire reasoning over complex information. Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges: a task may be solvable from a single local passage, or it may require integrating evidence distributed across the full context. We quantitatively characterise this difficulty through three properties: evidence scope, how much necessary information must be found; evidence dispersion, how widely that infor- mation is scattered within the context; and reasoning depth, how many dependent steps are needed to derive an answer from it. We construct LURCH, a multi-domain question-answering benchmark of 6,550 instances with supporting evidence and reasoning graphs, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Evaluations of proprietary and open-weight models show that: (1) at fixed context length, all our three properties are strongly negatively correlated with model performance; (2) as context length increases, performance degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence, whereas it remains relatively stable on samples with localised evidence; and (3) difficulty compounds across properties, as questions with moderately high values on all three are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. text: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning 1
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: Large language models (LLMs) can now process hundreds of thousands or even millions of tokens enabling applications involving books, scientific papers, financial reports, and long conversation his- tories (Team et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026). However, the ability to accommodate long inputs does not guarantee effective reasoning over them: models struggle to use information located in the middle of the context (Liu et al., 2024b), and their effective context length often falls well short of the claimed window (Hsieh et al., 2024). Existing evaluations typi- cally treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty, assessing models on the same tasks at different input lengths (Hsieh et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). While this approach reveals how performance changes with length, it leaves open which properties beyond token count make long-context reasoning difficult. Long-context benchmarks have increasingly moved from testing whether models can retrieve infor- mation to testing whether they can reason over it, covering multi-document, domain-specific, and aggregation-heavy tasks (Wang et al., 2024; Reddy et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). Yet these benchmarks mainly reveal where models fail, rather than what makes individual instances difficult. Goldman et al. (2024) take an important step by conceptualising two dimensions of long- context
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a). Yet these benchmarks mainly reveal where models fail, rather than what makes individual instances difficult. Goldman et al. (2024) take an important step by conceptualising two dimensions of long- context difficulty: scope (“How much necessary information is there to find?”) and dispersion (“How hard is it to find them in the context?”). These concepts help explain why questions of sim- ilar length may impose different demands on a model, but they are defined qualitatively rather than as measurable quantities. ETHIC (Lee et al., 2025) quantifies information coverage, but relies on an evaluator model’s judgements of which context chunks are potentially necessary, and captures only one aspect of difficulty in a limited range of task settings. Without quantitative definitions, it is difficult to establish how these properties vary across tasks, how they relate to model performance, and whether they account for differences in difficulty beyond context length. In this work, we propose quantitative definitions of evidence scope and evidence dispersion, based on the amount and positions of the supporting evidence within the context. We further extend this characterisation with reasoning depth, defined as the longest dependency path in an evidence-to- answer reasoning graph: parallel evidence lookups do not increase depth, whereas operations that depend on earlier results do. We further extend this characterisation with reasoning depth, defined as the longest dependency path in an evidence-to- answer reasoning graph: parallel evidence lookups do not increase depth, whereas operations that depend on earlier results do. Together, these three properties characterise how much supporting information is involved, where it occurs, and how it must be combined to derive an answer. To study how these properties contribute to model failures, we construct LURCH (Long-context Un- derstanding and Reasoning from Contextual Hints), a multi-domain question-answering benchmark built from diverse, naturally occurring long-context tasks. Each question is provided with its an- swer, source-provided or automatically annotated supporting evidence, and an answer-conditioned reasoning graph, enabling all three properties to be quantified. Using LURCH, we conduct controlled experiments on multiple LLMs to address three research questions: RQ1: Difficulty at fixed length. Among instances of the same context length, how strongly are ev- idence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth associated with model performance? Finding: Across questions, greater scope, dispersion and reasoning depth are each associated with lower scores after accounting for context length, source dataset and model. Notably, doubling reasoning depth is associated with a score drop comparable to that of doubling context length. RQ2: Length-dependent difficulty. How does the effect of context length on performance vary with evidence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth? Finding: As context length increases, performance degrades sharply on instances whose evidence is widely dispersed, whereas it remains relatively stable on instances with localised evidence. This pattern holds across all evaluated models. RQ3: Compounding difficulty. Are model failures associated with particular combinations of scope, dispersion, and depth, even when no individual property is extreme? Finding: Difficulty compounds across properties: questions with moderately high values on all three properties are harder than those with an extreme value on just one. This pattern is broadly consistent with an additive combination of the three properties. 2

text: Long-context language models. Both closed (e.g., Gemini 3.8 Flash, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra) and open (e.g., GLM-5.3 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026)) weight models now support context windows of up to 1M tokens. Advances in positional encoding, including Position Interpolation and YaRN (Chen et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024); efficient attention mechanisms, such as FlashAttention, ring attention, and sparse attention (Dao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024a; Llama Team, 2025); and KV- cache efficiency techniques, including GQA, PagedAttention, and MLA (Ainslie et al., 2023; Kwon et al., 2023; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), have made increasingly long contexts practical. Despite these advances, extending a model’s context window does not guarantee perfect use of the information it contains. Liu et al. (2024b) find performance degradation when critical information occurs in the middle of the context. RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) further shows the effective context length of most models, including both open-source and proprietary ones, rarely exceeds half of the claimed length. These findings suggest that context length alone does not capture the difficulty that long-context inputs pose to language models. Yet, the factors that determine the failures of long-context language models remain largely under-explored. Reasoning over long contexts. text: the factors that determine the failures of long-context language models remain largely under-explored. Reasoning over long contexts. Early benchmarks primarily examined whether models could locate and retrieve relevant information from long contexts (e.g., RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024), NeedleBench (Li et al., 2024)). More recent work extends long-context benchmarks to diverse reasoning-intensive tasks. LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) includes document question answer- ing, dialogue-history understanding, and code-repository understanding grounded on human-written questions and answers, while Loong (Wang et al., 2024) focuses on reasoning questions on multi- ple input documents. Domain-specific benchmarks further target particular reasoning demands. DocFinQA (Reddy et al., 2024) evaluates financial reasoning using full-document contexts, while SciTrek (Li et al., 2026a) requires counting, aggregation, and comparison across collections of sci- entific articles. Together, these benchmarks reflect a broader shift from evaluating whether models can retrieve information from long contexts to evaluating whether they can deliver complex reason- ing over them. However, existing benchmarks primarily reveal where models fail, but generally do not tell us what makes individual reasoning instances difficult. This limits our ability to identify the sources of difficulty in long-context reasoning and develop targeted approaches to address them. Recent work has begun to address this gap by examining factors that may contribute to reasoning difficulty. Goldman et al. (2024) conceptualise scope and dispersion as complementary

text: sources of difficulty in long-context reasoning and develop targeted approaches to address them. Recent work has begun to address this gap by examining factors that may contribute to reasoning difficulty. Goldman et al. (2024) conceptualise scope and dispersion as complementary conceptual axes of long-context tasks derived from extensive human annotation but without explicit quantifi- cation, distinguishing the amount of information required from the difficulty of locating it within the context. ETHIC (Lee et al., 2025) operationalises information coverage by quantifying the pro- portion of context chunks that an evaluator model deems potentially necessary to answer a query. Existing efforts, however, remain limited in both task coverage and conceptual scope, focusing on a relatively narrow range of reasoning settings and covering only a subset of the factors that may de- termine instance-level difficulty. As a result, we still lack a systematic framework for characterising the difficulty of long-context reasoning across diverse tasks. 3 REASONING CHARACTERISATION We complement context length with three properties: evidence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth. Evidence scope. Scope measures the proportion of the context covered by the evidence set, Scope(E) = S(E) L . (1) Evidence dispersion. Dispersion measures the extent to which the evidence spans the document, relative to the amount of non-evidence text. We define the evidence span as the distance from the beginning of the first interval to the end of the last interval, H(E) = bN −a1 + 1. (Note that H(E) ≥S(E).) The number of non-evidence tokens lying between the first and last evidence intervals and the total number of non-evidence tokens in the context are, respectively, Ginternal(E) = H(E) −S(E), and Gtotal(E) = L −S(E). (2) We define evidence dispersion as the fraction of all non-evidence text that lies inside the evidence span, Dispersion(E) = Ginternal Gtotal . (3) Dispersion lies in [0, 1]: values near zero indicate clustered evidence, while values near one indicate that most non-evidence text lies between the evidence intervals. It is zero for a single interval and one when the evidence span covers the full context (a1 = 0, bN = L −1). Reasoning depth. Reasoning depth measures the sequential dependencies involved in deriving an
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: between the evidence intervals. It is zero for a single interval and one when the evidence span covers the full context (a1 = 0, bN = L −1). Reasoning depth. Reasoning depth measures the sequential dependencies involved in deriving an answer from evidence. We represent a derivation as a directed acyclic graph, in which nodes denote atomic operations, including evidence lookups and inference steps, and edges denote direct depen- dencies between operations. Depth is the number of nodes on the longest dependency path ending in an answer-producing operation. This representation accommodates both sequential inference and the synthesis of evidence obtained in parallel; it does not assume that reasoning forms a single chain. For example, the question “Which film was released first, Bichunmoo or Musa?” needs the release year of each film. The two years are retrieved independently at depth one, and comparing them is one further step at depth two (Figure 7 in Appendix E). Additional parallel lookups do not increase depth unless further sequential operations are needed to produce the answer. Under this convention, an answer read directly from the evidence has depth one. Depth does not count the total number of operations or the difficulty of individual steps. 4 BENCHMARK CONSTRUCTION We construct LURCH by standardising instances from existing long-context benchmarks, using ref- erence or automatically annotated evidence,

This small-sample review serves as a source-level screening step rather than an exhaustive validation of the retained instances. 4.2 EVIDENCE ANNOTATION For each question, we identify supporting evidence within its source context to measure scope and dispersion and construct reasoning graphs. We use benchmark-provided reference evidence where available. Otherwise, we retrieve candidate passages, expand them to their containing paragraphs or full tables, and merge overlapping or adjacent intervals. A verifier then answers the question using only the expanded evidence, without access to the reference answer; We sample three answers from the verifier for each question and retain the question only if all three meet the task-specific cor- rectness criterion when compared with the reference answer. This repeated check reduces reliance on a single successful response. Scope and dispersion therefore describe the expanded supporting context, not necessarily a minimal evidence set (more details in Appendix D). 4.3 REASONING GRAPH GENERATION After evidence retrieval and sufficiency validation, we use two separate annotators, Gemini 3.7 Flash and GPT-5.6 Terra, to construct answer-conditioned reasoning graphs. Each receives the question, reference answer, and numbered evidence statements and reconstructs a minimal evidence-to-answer derivation. title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: We argue that context length alone is an incomplete measure of long-context difficulty, and intro- duced three sample-level properties that complement it: evidence scope, evidence dispersion, and reasoning depth. To quantify them, we built LURCH, a benchmark of 6,550 naturally occurring instances from 17 sources, with verified evidence and reasoning graphs produced by our annota- tion pipeline. Across four models, these properties capture difficulty that length does not. At fixed length, broader, more dispersed and deeper questions score lower, with doubling depth costing about as much as doubling length (RQ1). Added length is harmful mainly when evidence is broad or dis- persed (RQ2), and the hardest questions are demanding on several properties at once, even when none is extreme, because their effects add up (RQ3). We therefore recommend that long-context benchmarks report scope, dispersion and depth alongside length. Since our analyses are observa- tional and some annotations are automatic, future work could vary the surrounding context while holding evidence and reasoning fixed, to test these effects causally.

text: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning A EXISTING LONG-CONTEXT DATASETS We provide a brief description of the candidate sources from which we collect our data. Table 3 lists the sources we retain. We exclude BABILong, ChatQA2, ETHIC, L-CiteEval, LOFT, LongCite, LongMIT and LongReason. BABILong (Kuratov et al., 2024) is a benchmark designed to test language models’ ability to rea- son across facts distributed in extremely long documents. BABILong includes 20 reasoning tasks, including fact chaining, simple induction, deduction, counting and handling lists/sets. Notably, this benchmark is extendable to any length, and splits up to 10 million token lengths are provided. ChatQA2 (Xu et al., 2025) is a Llama 3.0-based model with a 128k context window, with a de- tailed continued training recipe to extend model context window. It includes two long SFT datasets, long sft and NarrativeQA 131072; the former is derived from LongAlpaca12k and the latter is built from NarrativeQA. CorpusQA (Lu et al., 2026), a reasoning benchmark scaling up to 10 million tokens1, the bench- mark includes complex, computation-intensive queries with programmatically guaranteed ground- truth answers, challenging systems to perform holistic reasoning over vast, unstructured text without relying on fallible human annotation. DocFinQA (Reddy et al., 2024) is a long-document financial QA benchmark, which augments 7,437 questions from the existing FinQA dataset with full-document context, extending average context
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: to perform holistic reasoning over vast, unstructured text without relying on fallible human annotation. DocFinQA (Reddy et al., 2024) is a long-document financial QA benchmark, which augments 7,437 questions from the existing FinQA dataset with full-document context, extending average context length from under 700 words in FinQA to 123k words in DocFinQA. DocQA-RL (Wan et al., 2025) is a challenging RL dataset for verifiable long-context reasoning. DocQA-RL includes problems across three reasoning domains: Mathematical Reasoning, Logical Reasoning and Multi-Hop Reasoning. ETHIC (Lee et al., 2025) is a novel benchmark designed to assess LLM’s ability to leverage the entire context. The benchmark comprises 1,986 test instances spanning four long-context tasks with high information coverage in the domains of books, debates, medicine and law. Subsets considered: Organizing, Attributing. ∞Bench (Zhang et al., 2024), an LLM benchmark featuring an average data length surpassing 100k tokens. ∞Bench comprises synthetic and realistic tasks spanning diverse domains, presented in both English and Chinese. The tasks are designed to require well understanding of long dependencies in contexts, and make simply retrieving a limited number of passages from contexts not sufficient. Subsets included: code debug, longdialogue qa eng, longbook qa eng, longbook choice eng. L-CiteEval (Tang et al., 2024) is a multi-task benchmark for long context understanding with cita- tions, aiming to evaluate both the understanding capability and
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: contexts not sufficient. Subsets included: code debug, longdialogue qa eng, longbook qa eng, longbook choice eng. L-CiteEval (Tang et al., 2024) is a multi-task benchmark for long context understanding with cita- tions, aiming to evaluate both the understanding capability and faithfulness of LCMs. L-CiteEval covers 11 tasks from diverse domains, spanning context lengths from 8k to 48k, and provides a fully automated evaluation suite. L-Eval (An et al., 2024) is a benchmark containing 20 sub-tasks, 508 long documents, and over 2000 human-labelled query-response pairs encompassing diverse question styles, domains and input length. Subsets included: legal contract qa, narrative qa, natural question. LOFT (Lee et al., 2024) is a benchmark of real-world tasks requiring context up to millions of tokens designed to evaluate LCLMs’ performance on in-context retrieval and reasoning. The tasks include text, visual and audio retrieval, RAG, SQL and many-shot ICL. LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) is a benchmark designed to assess the ability of LLMs to handle long-context problems requiring deep understanding and reasoning across real-world multitasks. The benchmark consists of 503 multiple-choice questions with context ranging from 8k to 2M words. LongBench-Pro (Chen et al., 2026) is a realistic and comprehensive bilingual benchmark of 1,500 naturally occurring long-context samples in English and Chinese spanning 11 tasks, with input lengths from 8k to 256k tokens. 1Only the

text: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning LongCite (Zhang et al., 2025) is a benchmark assessing current LLM’s performance in Long-Context Question Answering with Citations (LQAC), covering various scenarios such as document QA, summarisation, and coding. LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) is a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate five long- term memory abilities of chat assistants: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. LongMIT (Chen et al., 2025) is a long-context instruction tuning dataset that is built from a Multi- agent Iterative Multi-hop Generation (MIMG) framework. LongReason (Ling et al., 2025) is a synthetic long-context reasoning benchmark constructed by synthesizing long-context reasoning questions from a varied set of short-context reasoning questions through context expansion. Loong (Wang et al., 2024) is a long-context benchmark aligning with realistic scenarios through ex- tended multi-document question answering. Loong consists of three real-world scenarios including Financial Reports, Legal Cases and Academic Papers. LVEval (Yuan et al., 2024) is a challenging long-context benchmark with 5 length levels reaching up to 256k words. LVEval features two main tasks, single-hop QA and multi-hop QA, comprising 11 bilingual datasets. Subsets included: hotpotwikiqa, loogle CR, loogle MIR. SciTrek (Li et al., 2026a) is a diagnostic question-answering benchmark designed to probe long- context numerical reasoning in LLMs. SciTrek focuses on questions that require counting, sorting, aggregating and comparing information
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: bilingual datasets. Subsets included: hotpotwikiqa, loogle CR, loogle MIR. SciTrek (Li et al., 2026a) is a diagnostic question-answering benchmark designed to probe long- context numerical reasoning in LLMs. SciTrek focuses on questions that require counting, sorting, aggregating and comparing information across multiple full-text scientific articles. HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) is a question answering dataset featuring natural, multi-hop questions; the inputs are short Wikipedia snippets. In this work we use the extended version of Li et al. (2026b), which extends each instance by appending the full Wikipedia articles cited by the original context articles. We use the original context as evidence. B DATA FILTERING We apply six filters to select instances suitable for studying long-context reasoning. These address language, context length, data origin, task requirements, answerability without context, and task size. Language. We retain only English-language instances to focus on monolingual reasoning. We identify the language using source metadata where available and automatic language detection oth- erwise.2 Context length. We retain inputs containing between 32k and 256k tokens, measured using the Qwen3-0.6B tokenizer. This range balances long-context coverage with computational feasibility. Data origin. We restrict the collection to naturally occurring long-form contexts, excluding syn- thetic contexts and those lengthened through synthetic expansion. We allow contexts built by ap- pending real documents, as in the extended HotpotQA (Appendix A). This restriction

text: feasibility. Data origin. We restrict the collection to naturally occurring long-form contexts, excluding syn- thetic contexts and those lengthened through synthetic expansion. We allow contexts built by ap- pending real documents, as in the extended HotpotQA (Appendix A). This restriction focuses the analysis on realistic long-context inputs. Task requirements. We manually audit task definitions and exclude sources or subsets primarily targeting single-fact retrieval or span extraction. We prioritise tasks involving multi-hop reasoning, comparison, aggregation, or evidence integration. This screening operates at the source or subset level and does not require every retained instance to involve multiple reasoning steps. The retained tasks are listed in Table 3. Zero-context screening. We provide each question to Gemini 2.5 Pro without its accompanying context and discard instances answered correctly under the task’s evaluation criterion. Evidence Retrieval Prompt You are a precise, verbatim information retrieval engine. Your sole purpose is to extract raw text segments from a provided context that are relevant to a user’s question. ### Core Constraints 1. VERBATIM EXTRACTION: You must extract segments exactly as they appear in the context. Do not correct grammar, do not remove typos, and do not paraphrase. 2. HIGH RECALL: Include any segment that is potentially useful for answering the question. If a sentence is even tangentially related, include it. 3. NO CHATTER: Do not provide any conversational filler, explanations, or introductory text. 4. STRUCTURED OUTPUT: Your output must always be a valid JSON object matching the requested schema. ### Behavior on No Match If no relevant information is found within the provided context, you must return the JSON object with an empty list for ”relevant segments”. text: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning E REASONING GRAPH VALIDATION The reasoning graph annotation prompt is shown below. Reasoning Graph Annotation Prompt ### Role You are a reasoning analyst. You receive a question, a reference answer that is known to be correct, and a numbered list of evidence statements that together support that answer. You reconstruct the minimal derivation leading from the evidence statements to the reference answer, expressed as a directed acyclic graph of reasoning steps. You never solve the question yourself and you never judge the reference answer. Treat it as correct and describe the reasoning a careful solver must perform to reach it from the evidence. ### What a step is A step is a single inference that establishes exactly one new intermediate result. Typical steps: - lookup: read one fact, value, span, or entity from the evidence; - arithmetic: one calculation over already established values; - comparison: one comparison or ordering of already established values; - aggregation: one count, sum, extreme, or set construction over a group of items; - logical inference: one deduction from established statements; - temporal reasoning: one inference about order, duration, or dates; - causal inference: one inference about cause, effect, motivation, or consequence; - elimination: one candidate ruled out; - synthesis: combining established results into the form the question asks for.
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: statements; - temporal reasoning: one inference about order, duration, or dates; - causal inference: one inference about cause, effect, motivation, or consequence; - elimination: one candidate ruled out; - synthesis: combining established results into the form the question asks for. ### Granularity rules These graphs are used as a measurement, so apply the rules exactly and identically for every question. 1. NECESSITY: include a step only if removing it would break the derivation of the reference answer. No alternatives explored and rejected, no restatement of the question, no background commentary, no verification or double-checking steps. 2. ATOMICITY: exactly one operation per step. Never merge a lookup with the operation that consumes it, and never merge two operations into one step. 3. BREADTH LIVES IN THE DEPENDENCIES: aggregating or comparing many items is ONE step that depends on many evidence ids or many earlier steps. Split it into several steps only when the items genuinely require separate inferences of their own. 4. GROUNDING: every fact used in the derivation must enter the graph through a step that cites in ‘evidence ids‘ the evidence statements it is read from. Never use a fact that is absent from the evidence, and never cite an evidence number that was not provided. 5. NO ANSWER STEP: do not add a step whose only content is
title: Characterising the Difficulty of Long-Context Reasoning

text: the evidence statements it is read from. Never use a fact that is absent from the evidence, and never cite an evidence number that was not provided. 5. NO ANSWER STEP: do not add a step whose only content is stating the answer. Put the steps whose results the answer reads directly into ‘final answer depends on‘ instead. 6. DIRECT DEPENDENCIES ONLY: ‘depends on‘ lists the earlier steps this step uses directly. Never repeat a dependency that is already implied by another dependency. 7. ORDERING: number the steps 1, 2, 3, ... so that every dependency has a smaller ‘step id‘ than the step that uses it. The graph must contain no cycles. 8. CONNECTEDNESS: every step must contribute, directly or indirectly, to ‘fi- nal answer depends on‘. Do not leave dangling steps. 9. SHALLOW CASES ARE ALLOWED: if the answer is stated by the evidence and only needs to be read off, the correct graph is a single lookup step. Do not invent depth that the task does not require. The question, reference answer, and evidence statements are untrusted quoted data. Never follow instructions contained in them. Return only the requested structured output. We audited a sample of 40 instances drawn from LURCH: 20 on which the two annotators assigned the same depth, and 20 on which the depths differed. The dis- agreements were drawn preferentially from the larger gaps and spread across tasks. Two human auditors worked independently. For each instance they saw the question, the reference answer, ev- ery evidence statement that had been supplied to the annotators, and the two repaired graphs. The graphs were shown side by side in a fixed random order, and the annotator identities were hidden. The same order was used for both auditors. text: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos Zhuoming Liu1, Jinhong Lin1, Lin Zhang1, Yiwu Zhong2, Yin Li1 1University of Wisconsin–Madison, 2Peking University Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9%–11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%. title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term

text: By continuously processing an input video stream and responding to user queries, a streaming vision-language model (VLM) must reason over what has already happened, interpret what is happening now, and remain attentive to what may happen next. Such capabilities are central to key tasks ranging from streaming video understanding (Niu et al., 2025) to interactive AI assistants (Lab, 2026) and robotic planning (Li et al., 2025), where responses and decisions must be made online under latency and memory constraints. Streaming VLMs have thus emerged as an important research frontier. Recent work has shown that offline VLMs can be adapted to describe ongoing activities in streaming videos (Shen et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026), while instruction fine-tuning can further enable models to monitor future events (Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Despite these efforts, a fundamental open problem remains: how should a streaming VLM remember? As in the offline setting, an effective memory mechanism must preserve important visual information within a bounded memory footprint. The streaming setting, however, introduces additional challenges. First, memory must evolve incrementally as new observations arrive, rather than being repeatedly recomputed from the full history. Second, historical information must be incorporated without crowding out the current observation (see Fig. 1-2). Finally, a practical memory mechanism should introduce minimal inference overhead. text: (Ha et al., 2017) to efficiently generate the LoRA weights that encode historical information. At each time step, the incoming video clip and its textual context are first compressed into a compact representation, which is then used to update a set of recurrent hidden states. To model the temporal dynamics of these hidden states, MaLoW maintains two parallel branches: a state-space model (Yang et al., 2024) for modeling local temporal dependencies, and a gated summation branch for preserving global historical semantics. The resulting states are mapped through a linear projection to the LoRA weights used by the VLM. To facilitate training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a comprehensive streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer (QA) pairs over 56K videos, by adapting public offline video understanding datasets to the streaming setting. To evaluate our framework, we conduct extensive experiments across benchmarks and settings. MaLoW demonstrates state-of-the-art results on streaming video benchmarks, including OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025), StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026) and StreamArena (Zhang et al., 2026d). On the backward split of OVO-Bench, for example, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9%–11.8% across different video backbones, while incurring modest latency overhead. Across base VLMs ranging from 0.8B to 11B parameters, MaLoW yields consistent performance gains. Beyond streaming video understanding, we further extend MaLoW to the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) setting, where incorporating historical observations and action trajectories improves the action success rate on Simpler (Li et al., 2025) WidowX by 9.3%. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose MaLoW, a new streaming memory framework that internalizes historical context into evolving LoRA weights, introducing a distinct design in which history is represented as weights while current observations remain as input. • We develop a recurrent HyperNetwork that incrementally updates LoRA memory from streaming video and other context. We also construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale training dataset for streaming video understanding, which we will release publicly. • We demonstrate that MaLoW achieves competitive results across streaming video benchmarks, attains consistent gains over diverse base VLMs, and generalizes to VLA settings. 2

text: Vision-Language Models. Vision-language models (VLMs) (Liu et al., 2023; Alayrac et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025b; Clark et al., 2026; Qwen Team, 2026) unify diverse visual understanding and reasoning tasks through a natural-language interface. Among these tasks, long-video understanding (Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2
title: Question

text: 2025) is particularly challenging because models must preserve and reason over information spanning extended temporal contexts. Prior works (Qian et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024) have explored various memory and context- management mechanisms for this offline long video understanding setting. Our work builds on pretrained VLMs and equips them with an evolving long-term memory that is needed in the streaming video setting and incrementally updated as new observations arrive. Streaming VLMs with Memory. Recent works on streaming VLMs (Xia et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026) explore several complementary directions, including constructing higher-quality instruction-tuning data, designing architectures tailored to streaming inputs, and incorporating stronger video encoders. More recent studies (Lu et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026) show that strong VLMs with a small local video window yield surprisingly strong performance on real-time questions on existing streaming video benchmarks. Another line of work focuses on the memory mechanisms. Some methods compress historical visual observations into textual summaries or memories (Liu et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026), while others reduce the accumulated visual tokens through clustering or token merging (Zhang et al., 2024). Additional approaches organize historical information into hierarchical memory structures (Zeng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xie et al.,

text: Yao et al., 2026), while others reduce the accumulated visual tokens through clustering or token merging (Zhang et al., 2024). Additional approaches organize historical information into hierarchical memory structures (Zeng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xie et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026), or maintain a fixed-size memory buffer that selectively preserves useful historical observations (Qian et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025). Despite their differences, these methods generally address the growing streaming context by compressing historical information into a bounded token budget. In contrast, we represent long-term memory directly in model weights. Concurrent work (Chen et al., 2026) similarly moves long-term memory outside the attention context. However, it stores historical information in a separate test-time-training (TTT) branch with online-updated fast weights. In contrast, our method directly internalizes history into the VLM itself by dynamically generating low-rank parameter adaptations, without introducing a separate memory branch. Low-Rank Adaptation and Context Internalization. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) has been widely adopted as a parameter-efficient approach for adapting pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) to downstream tasks or new domains (Dettmers et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025). text: downstream tasks or new domains (Dettmers et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025). Recently, several works have explored using LoRA as a representation for encoding data-specific patterns (Shrestha et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026) or contextual information (Charakorn et al., 2026, 2025). These approaches demonstrate that model parameters can be a good representation for storing information beyond conventional token-based context. However, they typically require additional optimization when adapting to a new pattern, making it difficult to apply them directly to evolving inputs. δ-mem (Lei et al., 2026) explores dynamically representing textual information through LoRA updates without test-time training. Nevertheless, it still relies on access to the historical context during inference. Different from these prior approaches, our work specifically handles the streaming setting, and introduces a context internalization mechanism that progressively incorporates incoming visual context into low-rank model representations. 3 Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos 3.1 Problem Formulation: Streaming Video and Internalizing History A streaming VLM Mθ, parameterized by θ, must continuously perceive incoming visual content, respond to user queries or instructions It, and generate an appropriate response or decision Rt at time step t, using information available before t. Hidden-State Update. In interactive settings, new observations arrive continuously over time. An effective memory mechanism should therefore capture both the temporal dependencies among observations and the global semantics accumulated throughout the interaction. To this end, we decompose the hidden state ht into two components: ht = [mt; st], where mt models local temporal dynamics in the stream, while st captures longer-term semantic information. 4

Given a generated question, the answer generator then processes the video up to timestamp t and produces a model answer. Finally, the verifier takes the generated question, expected answer, model answer, and the video context surrounding the target event to assess both the validity of the question and the correctness of the answer. An unreasonable question or an inconsistent answer typically results in disagreement between the expected answer, generated answer, and supporting video context. We therefore retain only QA pairs that pass the verification stage to form the final training dataset. We use Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026) as both the question and answer generator, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B as the verifier. Please see more details in the Appendix B.1 and B.2. Dataset Statistics. More dataset statistics are presented in the Appendix B.3. 4 Experiments and Results 4.1 Streaming Video Understanding Benchmarks. Following the prior works (Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a), we evaluate MaLoW on the Real-Time split of StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026), as well as the Real-Time and Backward splits of OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025). The Backward splits of OVO-Bench mostly focus on retrospect to the past and comprise three tasks: Episodic Memory (EPM), Action Sequence Identification (ASI), and Hallucination Detection (HLD). Among them, EPM is particularly well suited for assessing the effectiveness of the memory mechanism introduced by MaLoW. Experiment Protocol. We categorize the baselines into four groups according to the model types and how they manage historical visual context during streaming inference. 1. Offline VLMs. This category includes LLaVA-Video-7B (Zhang et al., 2025b), LongVU-7B (Shen et al., 2025), Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025), and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026). We compare to these models for their strong video understanding capabilities, acquired through large-scale video-text pretraining. We evaluate their pretrained checkpoints by treating streaming videos as offline inputs. 2. Streaming VLMs with Long-term (Full) Context. These methods preserve historical observations directly in the inference context as memory for streaming video understanding, and for short videos often retaining the entire video history. As the stream grows, this leads to an ever expanding context window and substantial memory and computational overhead. This category includes Mage-VL (Yang et al., 2026), SimpleStream (Shen et al., 2026), and AURA (Lu et al., 2026). We compare to these models for their strong real-time performance, achieved by retaining only the most recent observations within a fixed local window of approximately 4–30 seconds. Historical observations that fall outside the local window are evicted (Xu et al., 2026). 4. Streaming VLMs with a Local Context Window and Memory Mechanism. MaLoW achieves state-of-the-art results. As shown in Table 1, MaLoW establishes strong performance across streaming video benchmarks. MaLoW (MOSS-VL-Realtime-11B) and MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) achieve new state-of-the-art scores of 74.5% and 84.8% on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench, respectively, while MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) attains the highest EPM score of 63.6% among all compared methods. We highlight key comparisons at matched model scales. At the 4B scale, the MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) surpasses the concurrent work StreamTTT-4B (Chen et al., 2026) by 3.9% and 3.5% on the backward split of the OVO-bench and StreamingBench, respectively. We hypothesize that these baselines may have benefited from fine-tuning their base VLMs, whereas MaLoW keeps the base VLMs intact. Importantly, the gains are consistent across model scales from 4B to 11B and across base VLMs pre-trained for both offline video understanding (Qwen series) and streaming video understanding (VideoChat3 and MOSS-VL-Realtime). MaLoW offers a lightweight memory patch. Across different base VLMs, MaLoW introduces only 1.4%-4.0% additional parameters. The pretrained backbone architecture and parameters remain unchanged, while historical information is encoded entirely through the evolving LoRA weights. Preserving the backbone helps retain its pretrained capabilities and minimizes interference with real-time perception. Moreover, widespread LoRA support in modern inference frameworks facilitates efficient deployment. MaLoW incurs minor inference overhead. We further extend MaLoW to robotic planning, where it is used to internalize historical visual observations and action trajectory for action prediction. Following VLM4VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b), we adapt Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026) by attaching a lightweight MLP action decoder and fine-tuning the VLM backbone, resulting in our baseline model, Q3.5-2B-MLP. The model is trained on the Bridge and RT-1 subsets of the OXE dataset (O’Neill et al., 2024) to predict future actions based solely on the current visual observation. We then train MaLoW on top of Q3.5-2B-MLP using the Bridge subset of OXE. During this stage, the VLM backbone is frozen and receives only the current observation, while MaLoW and the MLP action decoder are optimized to internalize historical observations and action trajectories and produce more accurate action trajectories. text: In this work, we presented MaLoW, a new memory framework for streaming VLMs. Rather than repeatedly injecting compressed or retrieved history into the input context, MaLoW represents history as LoRA weights while keeping the current observation as input. This separation provides a natural way to carry long-term information forward without revisiting the full video stream or continually expanding the context window. It also yields a lightweight memory patch: the base VLM architecture and parameters remain unchanged, while only the compact LoRA weights evolve over time. To realize this design, we developed a recurrent HyperNetwork that incrementally updates LoRA weights, together with MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K QA pairs over 56K videos. MaLoW achieves strong results across streaming video understanding benchmarks, with substantial gains on memory-critical tasks and only modest inference overhead. We further show that the same memory mechanism transfers to VLA models, where incorporating historical context improves action success. We hope that MaLoW offers a useful perspective on long-term memory for streaming VLMs: beyond asking what information should be stored or retrieved, we can also reconsider where memory should reside, in this case, directly within evolving model weights.

text: Appendix: Supplementary Materials Overview This appendix provides the mathematical interpretation, dataset documentation, implementation details, and additional empirical results supporting MaLoW. The materials are organized as follows: • Appendix A: Mathematical Interpretation. Historical context as a read operator, its realization through low-rank MLP updates, online memory updates, and extensions to normalized attention and backbone computation. • Appendix B: Additional Dataset Details. Video sources, the data pipeline and annotation construction, and statistics of MaLoW-Instruct. • Appendix C: Additional Experiment Details. Model architecture, training and evaluation settings, the vision- language-action setting, different VLM scales and sources, the memory stress test, and streaming inference speed profiling. • Appendix D: Additional Experiments. Ablations of LoRA placement and rank, memory architecture, obser- vation windows, and state-update frequency; analyses of latency, hidden-state evolution, and real-time perception; and additional qualitative results. A Mathematical Interpretation MaLoW carries information from earlier video clips through history-dependent parameter updates. This appendix provides a mathematical interpretation of the feasibility of encoding the effect of historical context into low-rank updates of the MLP projections within a Transformer block. Specifically, we trace how a query reads historical information in section A.1, how this read induces a transformation of the features entering the MLP in section A.2, and how such a transformation can be realized or approximated by LoRA-style weight updates in section A.3. The analysis

text: reads historical information in section A.1, how this read induces a transformation of the features entering the MLP in section A.2, and how such a transformation can be realized or approximated by LoRA-style weight updates in section A.3. The analysis does not claim that MaLoW explicitly reconstructs the analytical history matrix M _ H or is equivalent to full-context attention. Rather, it establishes that historical information can, under the assumptions described below, be represented in parameter space through low-rank updates. MaLoW can be viewed as one of the learned instantiations of this principle, with our empirical results demonstrating that its recurrent state and generated adapters effectively preserve history-dependent information in practice. The exact identities below first assume fixed historical keys and values and an unnormalized dot-product read, while Section A.4 and Section A.5 extend the interpretation to the online setting, normalized attention, and the normalization operations in the backbone. In conclusion, this analysis establishes the theoretical feasibility of compressing the effect of historical context into low-rank parameter updates of the MLP modules within a Transformer block. In particular, it shows that, under the assumptions described above, a history-dependent feature transformation induced by historical context can be realized or approximated through LoRA-style updates to the MLP projections. Importantly, this analysis does not claim that MaLoW exactly reconstructs the analytical history matrix M _ H, nor that its learned recurrent state and generated adapters are equivalent to full-context attention. Rather, the derivation provides a mathematical interpretation demonstrating that such a parameter-space representation of historical information is feasible. Our empirical results further show that MaLoW provides an effective learned instantiation of this approximation in practice. text: and Annotation Construction As illustrated in Figure 3-1, our data construction pipeline consists of three components: a Question Generator, an Answer Generator, and a Verifier. To construct the streaming video training dataset, we begin with an event description associated with a specific temporal interval. These descriptions are obtained either from the original annotations of the 14 datasets described in Section B.1, or from the question–answer pairs provided by TimeLens and ET-Instruct. Question Generation. We first prompt the Question Generator to generate a new question for a target event, conditioned on the full video, the event description, and its corresponding temporal interval. By observing the full video, the Question Generator can leverage both the target event and its surrounding visual context to construct a question that is grounded in the video content. The prompt explicitly controls the question type, which is sampled from four categories: open-ended, multiple-choice, Yes/No, and counting questions. Along with each generated question, the Question Generator also produces an expected answer, which is subsequently used during the verification stage. To cover different temporal reasoning scenarios, we further assign each question a randomly sampled question-timestamp type from three categories: past, real-time, and future. Given a target event spanning the interval [tstart, tend], a past question is assigned a timestamp t > tend, requiring the model to retrospectively recall an

After obtaining the generated question and its corresponding model answer, we prompt the Verifier to assess the quality of the generated question–answer pair. The Verifier takes as input the generated question, the expected answer, the model answer, and the original event description used during question generation. It evaluates both whether the generated question is valid and well grounded in the target event and whether the model answer is consistent with the available evidence. In particular, a substantial mismatch between the expected answer and the model answer may indicate either that the generated question is ambiguous or unreasonable, or that the model answer is incorrect. The original event description provides additional grounding information that allows the Verifier to distinguish between these cases and assess the overall validity of the question–answer pair. For verification, we launch two parallel workers, each serving one Qwen3.5-397B-A17B instance with vLLM on four H200 GPUs. Filtering and Post-Processing. We discard question–answer pairs for which the Verifier identifies an inconsistency between the expected answer and the model answer, determines that the model answer is incorrect, or judges the generated question to be invalid, ambiguous, or otherwise unreasonable. Base Models. In the main experiments, we build MaLoW on top of four different models, VideoChat3-4B (Li et al., 2026), Qwen3-VL-4B (Bai et al., 2025), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026), and MOSS-VL-Realtime- 11B (Wang et al., 2026). VideoChat3 is a video-centric VLM that is further fine-tuned on streaming video understanding data and adopts a full self-attention architecture. Qwen3-VL-4B is a general-purpose VLM based on a full self-attention architecture. Qwen3.5 is a general-purpose VLM based on a hybrid attention architecture, where a self-attention layer is interleaved with every four linear-attention layers. MOSS-VL is a video-centric VLM that adapts cross-attention layers to inject visual information into the text tokens, and a cross-attention layer is interleaved with every four self-attention layers. text: and a cross-attention layer is interleaved with every four self-attention layers. Video Preprocessing. During training and evaluation, we sample the video frames at 1 fps, dividing the video frames into non-overlapping two-frame temporal blocks (each Ct is a 2-second video clip). We regard the most recent 2-second block as the current observation, which will be sent into the VLMs, while all the rest of the history frames will be sent into the MaLoW to be converted into LoRA weights. For MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B), we observe that using longer current-observation windows consistently improves performance on the real-time and backward splits of OVO-Bench (Niu et al., 2025) and StreamingBench (Lin et al., 2026). We therefore use the most recent 8-second clips as the current observations for MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B), while the other MaLoW instantiations in the table use the most recent 2 seconds. We hypothesize that these findings, MaLoW (Qwen3-VL-4B) benefiting from longer current-observation windows and the particularly strong performance on StreamingBench, are largely attributable to differences in the architecture and pretraining recipe of the underlying VLMs. We preprocess the video frames with the preprocessor from the corresponding VLMs, with the maximum per-frame pixel budget set to 262,144 for all three versions of MaLoW. 23

text: Vision Encoder. We use the vision encoder from the corresponding VLMs as the vision encoder to encode each of the temporal blocks into vision tokens. We also use the MLP layers or adaptor from the VLMs to convert the vision tokens into the text semantic space before we send them into the Aggregator. We denote the vision tokens from the temporal block at t as Vt. Aggregator. Visual tokens Vt in the temporal block at t are concatenated with the learnable queries Q and the corresponding text embedding Tt of the timestamp of the temporal block. We further analyze the latency of MaLoW (Qwen3.5-9B) reported in Figure 4, with the detailed breakdown presented in Table 15. Encoding the new frames and updating the hidden state ht, generating the LoRA tensors At+1 and Bt+1, and combining them to construct ∆θt+1 account for 7.9%, 2.1%, and 3.7% of the total latency, respectively. text: The Right Byte First: How UTF-16 Helps Multilingual Boundary Prediction Hyunsik Kim Samsung Research hyunsik777.kim@samsung.com
title: The Right Byte First:

text: Many hierarchical byte-level language models group bytes into patches using a learned bound- ary predictor whose view of the next codepoint depends on encoding and lookahead. In UTF-8, codepoints of many scripts take three bytes: 8 of 24 bits mark length and continuation, and the first byte carries only 4 high codepoint bits. Af- ter the same left context, a mark extending a grapheme cluster and a letter starting the next can thus share their first byte. Universal Byte- Level Encoding (UBE) keeps one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings but writes these codepoints as two UTF-16 bytes, low byte first, so its first sym- bol carries 8 low codepoint bits that can distin- guish such continuations. We train small causal predictors on matched FineWeb-2 text and eval- uate on FLORES-200 under UTF-8, UBE, and UBE’s same-length big-endian variant. At one- symbol lookahead, balanced grapheme-boundary error at codepoint boundaries across 17 languages in 13 Brahmic scripts is 8.76% with UTF-8, 8.62% with the big-endian variant, and 0.06% with UBE. When the target instead retains a parent tokenizer’s subword cuts at grapheme boundaries, UBE lowers the mean error relative to UTF-8 at the same lookahead by 72.91% in Korean, 35.29% in Chinese, and 67.32–99.55% in eight more scripts. In the seven of them whose main Unicode block fits on one 256-codepoint page, the

text: UBE lowers the mean error relative to UTF-8 at the same lookahead by 72.91% in Korean, 35.29% in Chinese, and 67.32–99.55% in eight more scripts. In the seven of them whose main Unicode block fits on one 256-codepoint page, the big-endian variant stays within 3.0% of UTF-8, so the gain follows byte order, not length. In Korean and Chinese, UBE’s mean error falls be- low UTF-8’s final mean error after only 25% and 37.5% of training. Which byte comes first thus af- fects how much lookahead a byte-level boundary predictor needs. Preprint. October 16, 2026.
title: The Right Byte First:

text: In hierarchical byte-level language models with learned patching, a boundary predictor groups the input into patches for the global transformer. The character distinctions needed to predict these units depend on the writing system and the segmentation target. Consider a grapheme cluster, Uni- code’s approximation to a written character, which may combine a base with dependent marks. After identical left context, one-byte lookahead at a codepoint boundary in UTF-8 can reveal the same byte for a mark extending the current cluster and a letter starting the next. The required de- cisions then remain indistinguishable even when the target segmentation is unambiguous. Byte-level models can pro- cess text in any language out of the box (Xue et al., 2022); at limited lookahead, however, the encoding does not expose every script’s distinctions equally. When clusters consist of single codepoints, the task changes: a subword boundary predictor must select which inter-character boundaries to retain. These tasks require different distinctions, motivating us to study encoding choice in relation to both the script and the boundary target. The encoding affects both how densely codepoint bits are packed and which bits reach the predictor first. For a Unicode scalar (a codepoint other than a surrogate) that takes three UTF-8 bytes, the pattern 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx carries 16 codepoint bits and 8 length/continuation bits (The Unicode Consortium, 2025).
title: The Right Byte First:

text: packed and which bits reach the predictor first. For a Unicode scalar (a codepoint other than a surrogate) that takes three UTF-8 bytes, the pattern 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx carries 16 codepoint bits and 8 length/continuation bits (The Unicode Consortium, 2025). The same scalar occupies 16 bits in UTF-16 without those markers, so UTF-8 is inherently less compact for such scalars. We use the existing Universal Byte-Level Encod- ing (UBE; Kim & Jung, 2026), which retains one- and two-byte UTF-8 encodings and uses UTF-16 little-endian (UTF-16LE) for longer ones. For three-byte UTF-8 scalars, UBE therefore shortens the representation to two symbols and presents 8 low codepoint bits in the first symbol, where UTF-8 presents only 4 high bits. Within a known 256- codepoint page, that byte identifies the codepoint. The worked example in Appendix C illustrates the cluster fragmentation that motivates our targets. Our motivating application is byteification, the conversion of a pretrained subword language model into a model that reads and emits bytes. Bolmo surrounds the parent transformer with local modules and trains a boundary predictor on the parent’s subword segmentation; the global transformer then operates on the resulting patches (Minixhofer et al., 2025; 2026). Byteification thus removes the tokenizer from the model’s interface but transfers its segmentation criterion along with the weights: the patches are still learned from the parent’s cuts (Section 5.2). Bolmo raises the question of what models inherit from the input encoding and suggests alternatives to UTF-8 (Minixhofer et al., 2025, Section 8); Haltiuk (2026) reports nearly inherited Bolmo boundaries and proposes separating boundary placement from language modeling. We focus on how to construct cluster-aligned targets and expose the distinctions needed to predict them with limited lookahead. The targets either include every grapheme boundary or retain only the parent-tokenizer cuts that already coincide with one. We use grapheme clusters be- cause their boundaries are representable in every encoding, position-only cluster targets are invariant to span-preserving edits, and cluster continuations are where encodings differ in what the first symbol reveals (Section 3); the choice does not presuppose that clusters are better modeling units. UBE differs from UTF-8 in both stream length and byte order; UBE-BE keeps UBE’s length but reverses the bytes within each UTF-16 code unit, allowing a byte-order comparison at fixed stream length. text: extended grapheme cluster (Hadley, 2025), opera- tionalized by regex’s \X on text in Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC). All codepoints in our normalized text are scalars. A cluster can contain several scalars, each repre- sented by one or more encoded symbols. Grapheme clusters do not necessarily coincide with linguistic characters or or- thographic syllables. We therefore distinguish scalar, cluster, and symbol counts throughout. Word-spacing conventions are distinct from grapheme struc- ture. Korean regularly separates eojeols, spacing units that can contain multiple morphemes, whereas Chinese gener- ally leaves word boundaries unmarked by spaces (Lee et al., 2026a; Hwang et al., 2026). In neither language do whites- pace boundaries define subword segmentation; Unicode grapheme and word boundaries are also distinct (Hadley, 2025). We therefore distinguish whitespace-adjacent gaps from other scalar gaps when analyzing the Korean/Chinese extension. UBE uses disjoint UTF-8 and UTF-16LE byte alphabets, with 256 symbols each (Kim & Jung, 2026). One- and two-byte UTF-8 scalars stay in UTF-8; three-byte scalars in the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) use two UTF-16LE byte symbols; supplementary scalars use four UTF-16LE symbols. A UBE symbol identifies both a byte value and its encoding route; lookahead is measured in symbols. The parent tokenizer enters this architecture through three mechanisms (Figure 3). First, the released input pipeline applies the parent tokenizer and concatenates the bytes of its pieces, preserving its NFC normalization but discarding the piece boundaries from the byte stream. text: Byte and hierarchical models. Models operating below the subword level differ in both representation and alloca- tion of computation. ByT5 uses bytes in a text-to-text trans- former (Xue et al., 2022), CANINE downsamples character inputs (Clark et al., 2022), and MambaByte uses a selective state-space model (Wang et al., 2024). MEGABYTE sepa- rates local and global computation with fixed patches (Yu et al., 2023); SpaceByte places global computation at “space- like” positions such as UTF-8 leading bytes, whitespace, and punctuation (Slagle, 2024); BLT selects patches using entropy (Pagnoni et al., 2025). Learned segmentation takes several forms: dynamic token pooling learns boundaries or supervises them with subword or entropy targets (Nawrot et al., 2023), MrT5 learns deletion (Kallini et al., 2025), and H-Net learns chunking (Hwang et al., 2026); AU-Net instead builds an autoregressive hierarchy over rule-based word splits (Videau et al., 2025). MAGNET routes each byte sequence through a boundary predictor for its script, with per-script compression targets chosen to make segmen- tation granularity similar across scripts (Ahia et al., 2024). FLEXITOKENS allows a range of boundary rates during adaptation (Owodunni et al., 2026a), while Fast BLT and dynamic multi-byte prediction target decoding efficiency (Kallini et al., 2026; Owodunni et al., 2026b). These ar- chitectures treat compression and boundary placement as explicit design choices. Our analysis concerns the infor- mation

text: (Owodunni et al., 2026a), while Fast BLT and dynamic multi-byte prediction target decoding efficiency (Kallini et al., 2026; Owodunni et al., 2026b). These ar- chitectures treat compression and boundary placement as explicit design choices. Our analysis concerns the infor- mation that an encoding exposes to the boundary predictor, particularly when supervision is inherited from a subword model. The distinctions we study, such as a dependent mark versus a letter after the same base, arise within one script and usually within one 256-codepoint page, so routing by script, as in MAGNET, does not supply them. The study of entropy-based patch allocation at matched patch counts by Vera Zúñiga (2026) addresses a complementary question, and SOMBRERO scores boundaries by how strongly chunk starts concentrate on bytes that are hard to predict (Neite- meier et al., 2026); our audit uses grapheme integrity as the boundary criterion. Bolmo transfers a pretrained model into a byte architecture through distillation (Minix- hofer et al., 2025), whereas zero-shot tokenizer transfer predicts embeddings for a replacement tokenizer (Minix- hofer et al., 2024). H-Net similarly distills Llama 3.2 3B into a byte-level model around its frozen backbone, super- vising the routing module with the parent’s token starts and noting that these boundaries cannot always be predicted online (Hwang et al., 2026, Appendix E.2). Closer to our boundary question, Haltiuk (2026) reports nearly inherited Bolmo segmentation, pro- poses capability-preserving boundary transfer, and asks which shared alphabet to use. Limitations The lookahead evidence comes from small causal predic- tors with 2 seeds on the 17-language panel and 3 on the Korean/Chinese extension; the sentence-bootstrap intervals do not capture variation over training runs. Text exposure is matched across encodings but compute is not, and UBE-BE changes the entire encoded history as well as the first looka- head symbol. The first-symbol argument covers continua- tions within a known Unicode page; cross-page collisions preclude a universal one-symbol guarantee. The released- model analyses cover two parent families and one family of conversion recipes on FLORES-200 devtest translations, and because the checkpoints differ in architecture, size, data, and training history, their comparison does not isolate the effect of byte-level modeling.

text: Boundary prediction depends on how an encoding exposes the distinctions relevant to a writing system and segmenta- tion target. Bwen largely reproduces its parent’s cuts, includ- ing those inside grapheme clusters, and Bolmo-1B’s patch counts track its parent’s token counts; restricting inherited cuts to grapheme boundaries removes this fragmentation from supervision and yields targets representable across en- codings. For scalars requiring three UTF-8 bytes, UBE’s UTF-16 route removes the format-bit overhead and places 12
title: The Right Byte First

text: The Right Byte First the low byte first, making within-page character distinctions available earlier. At one-symbol lookahead, the trained UBE and UBE-BE predictors support the importance of byte order for grapheme boundary recovery and for retained subword boundary selection. In Korean and Chinese, where the every-cluster target is already recoverable from scalar ends, UBE reduces retained-parent errors relative to UTF-8 by 72.91% and 35.29% at the same lookahead; in eight more scripts, by 67.32% to 99.55%. Which byte comes first, not only how many bytes a scalar takes, is therefore a design choice for byte-level boundary predictors. Use of Generative AI Generative AI tools helped draft and revise the text and code; the author verified all content and takes full responsibility for it. Impact Statement This work examines how text encodings affect boundary prediction and representation length across writing systems. It provides ways to identify and measure design choices that fragment written units or disproportionately lengthen some languages’ representations. The selected languages and translated corpus do not cover all users, dialects, or writ- ing practices, and Unicode grapheme clusters provide an operational definition of written units with language-specific limits. Changes in representation can redistribute compu- tational cost and model quality across scripts. Assessing their social benefit requires native-language evaluation that reports both gains and regressions.

The parent-vocabulary embedding accounts for 621.3 million (7.47%). These parameter counts exclude optimizer state and activation memory and do not quantify per-symbol computation. Different patch-count conventions. The float32 audit counts interior cuts plus one final text unit and excludes the separate BOS patch. The bfloat16 patch-count diagnostic instead sums boundary flags, including the forced BOS flag but suppressing the final text byte’s flag because lookahead is unavailable. These conventions give the same numerical count when interior cuts agree: each adds one to the number of interior cuts. The diagnostic’s comparison with ordinary parent-token counts therefore requires no additional BOS adjustment. It uses the recorded sums on its selected item bank, distinct from the full-devtest densities normalized to English. 18

For 1 ≤j < L, the predictor compares projected hj and hj+1; an end flag at j therefore denotes a cut at text byte offset j, with xj as lookahead. The released zero-temperature rule cuts when the
