text: text byte xj−1. For 1 ≤j < L, the predictor compares projected hj and hj+1; an end flag at j therefore denotes a cut at text byte offset j, with xj as lookahead. The released zero-temperature rule cuts when the boundary log-probability is strictly greater than log(1/2), so identical visible prefixes receive identical decisions. It forces the BOS flag at j = 0 and suppresses the last byte’s flag at j = L, where lookahead is unavailable. The audit uses only 1 ≤j < L as interior cuts and counts the final text unit separately. The training implementation defaults to end boundaries, although the released configuration does not record which mode was used for training. The shifted-offset check validates the inference mapping without resolving that missing metadata. For the UBE argument, transferred vocabulary features must also depend only on the available symbol prefix; using later symbols would change the predictor’s information budget. D. Boundary-Lookahead Probe Design. Each of the 18 runs trains a predictor with a 513-entry, 128-dimensional symbol embedding (including padding), a one-layer causal LSTM with 512 units, layer normalization, and H-Net’s cosine boundary head (Hwang et al., 2026) as adapted in Bolmo (Minixhofer et al., 2025). The head places a cut after position i when (1 −cos(f(hi), g(hi+k)))/2 > 1/2, where f and g are learned linear projections.

text: normalization, and H-Net’s cosine boundary head (Hwang et al., 2026) as adapted in Bolmo (Minixhofer et al., 2025). The head places a cut after position i when (1 −cos(f(hi), g(hi+k)))/2 > 1/2, where f and g are learned linear projections. Training runs for 4,000 steps with 64 rows per step. Each row begins at a uniformly sampled cluster start in a uniformly sampled language and contains up to 384 supervised scalars, followed by up to three scalars of unsupervised lookahead context. Row sampling depends only on the seed, ensuring identical text exposure across encodings and lookahead settings within a seed. The loss adds the mean binary cross-entropy (BCE) over scalar-end decisions to the mean BCE over within-scalar decisions. We use AdamW with learning rate 2 × 10−3, weight decay 0.01, 100 warmup steps followed by cosine decay to one tenth, and gradient norm clipping at 1; BCE probabilities are clipped to [10−3, 1 −10−3]. The encoder and projections use bfloat16, with the cosine and loss computed in float32. For each language, training uses whole documents in file order from the first FineWeb-2 shard until the retained NFC text reaches at least 8 million UTF-8 bytes. For each language, documents containing one of that language’s FLORES-200 devtest sentences are excluded. Targets are extended grapheme cluster boundaries from the same regex library

text: All conditions are evaluated at the same 2,363,895 FLORES-200 devtest scalar ends across 17 languages: 1,507,877 cluster boundaries and 856,018 scalar ends inside clusters. Sentence-final boundaries are excluded. Balanced error averages the missed-boundary and scalar-end false-cut rates after pooling counts across the panel, then averages the two seeds; within-scalar sites are scored separately. Pooling counts does not give languages equal weight. Each sentence also supplies a same-context continuation pair. At a site where a base letter precedes a scalar on the same 256-codepoint page, the true continuation is paired with an NFC-stable replacement from that page requiring the opposite decision. A pair is correct only when both decisions are correct. Encoding alone determines the minimum lookahead needed to distinguish them: UTF-8 requires two bytes for 9,313 pairs and three for the remaining 7,891; UBE requires one symbol for every pair, and UBE-BE requires two. UTF-8 and UBE-BE therefore have zero fully correct pairs at k = 1 and exactly 50% decision error on these pairs by construction. The trained UBE k = 1 predictors answer every pair correctly, whereas UTF-8 at k = 2 answers 27.2–28.8% of all pairs correctly (4,676 and 4,949 pairs in its two seeds), although two bytes distinguish 9,313 pairs. text: The Right Byte First E. Korean and Chinese Boundary Extension Scope and targets. Designed after the original probe, this exploratory extension examines boundary prediction in Korean and Chinese. Both targets and all 36 runs are reported, with no checkpoint or condition selected by evaluation performance. The every-cluster target is G(x); the retained-parent target keeps Qwen3 cuts at those cluster boundaries and deletes all other cuts. The retained target represents inherited subword supervision, not Korean morpheme or Chinese word annotations. Targets are computed from full-document tokenizations and grapheme segmentation before sampling rows, preserving the original context rather than retokenizing cropped spans. Data and training. For each language, we retain whole documents from the first FineWeb-2 shard until the NFC text reaches at least 8 million UTF-8 bytes. FineWeb-2’s Mandarin Han-script source, cmn_Hani, is not restricted to simplified characters; evaluation uses FLORES-200 Chinese (Simplified), zho_Hans. Korean uses kor_Hang in both corpora. Any training document containing an evaluation sentence from either language is dropped. The corpus revision, NFC normalization, grapheme library, and Qwen3 tokenizer match the pinned artifacts reported in Appendix M. Each predictor has a 513-entry, 128-dimensional embedding, a one-layer 256-unit LSTM, and the original probe’s cosine head, totaling 592,512 parameters in every condition. Training runs for 2,000 steps with 32 rows per step. Rows begin at uniformly sampled cluster starts in

text: on a single 256-codepoint page (The Unicode Consortium, 2025). Every letter of such a block therefore has the same first UTF-8 byte (E0 or E1) and the same first UBE-BE symbol, its page, whereas its first UBE symbol is its position within the page. Japanese text mixes hiragana and katakana from their main blocks, which share one page, with kanji spread over many, so UBE-BE’s first symbol separates these kana from kanji and distinguishes kanji pages. The texts also contain Latin letters, digits, and punctuation, so a constant first symbol within one block does not by itself determine the learned error. Results. Mark and base margins are increases in path cost relative to the original text, averaged in bits; R is the mean mark margin divided by the mean base margin. ∆R and ∆I denote conversion-minus-parent differences. Scoring Protocol and Diagnostics Let t0 be the first ordinary parent token and n0 the number of bytes recovered from its byte-alphabet representation. The scorer verifies that concatenating the bytes of all parent pieces reconstructs the exact NFC sentence. Recovering piece bytes avoids decoding t0 in isolation, which can replace an incomplete scalar with a replacement character, because byte-level pieces need not be valid UTF-8 (Firestone et al., 2025). Each corruption preserves t0, ensuring that the scored suffix begins at the same byte offset across variants within a pair. The parent cost is −log2 P(t1, . . . , tn−1 | t0), without a prepended BOS or appended EOS. The conversion receives its BOS and prefix bytes under the boundary history selected during prefill; the first n0 byte targets are excluded from the score. The models therefore score the same text suffix under different conditioning representations. With one-byte lookahead, the final unscored prefix flag can depend on the first scored byte. This is a byte-level analogue of the prompt boundary problem of tokenized models

text: Recent work shows that depth recurrence can be retrofitted into pretrained lan- guage models. In this work, we adapt this paradigm for visual understanding, using depth recurrence to reduce the parameter footprint of a pretrained vision- language model (VLM). To this end, we prune layers from the language back- bone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. At each step of the loop, a linear adapter merges the block’s output with the token represen- tations from the preceding layers and projects the fused representation back into the block. As the pruning impacts the original model performance, we propose a three-stage recovery training: first, we leverage a language-only pretraining to recover the performance of the language backbone, followed by an alignment of the vision-language projector, and a full fine-tuning of the model via visual in- struction tuning. In the first and the last stage, we distill the outputs of the pre- trained non-recurrent model into the recurrent model, which further improves the recovery. We evaluate the proposed approach on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone without introducing any new vision-language data during retrofitting. Our exper- iments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup

Our exper- iments demonstrate that the retrofitted recurrent model outperforms the unpruned baseline trained with the same recovery data while storing 23.3% fewer language parameters. We further show that the proposed retrofitting recurrence outperforms the setup of converting a recurrent LM into a VLM on the same data. Additionally, our ablations show how design choices, such as the adapter between recurrences and a larger recurrent block, lead to the improved performance of our approach. Finally, we find that our proposed model gains on reasoning-oriented benchmarks, whereas its performance on basic visual understanding benchmarks remains on par with the baseline. 1

text: Existing approaches for test-time compute scaling in vision-language models comprise chain- of-thought traces, latent reasoning tokens, searching over candidate answers, and test-time reinforcement learning (Zhang et al., 2024b; Qin et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2026). These methods usually come with higher inference costs as each generated token requires a full forward pass and expands the context window. To address this limitation, depth recurrence (Geiping et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025) has been explored as an alternative for test-time scaling in language models. Depth recurrence allocates test-time compute to iterating a block of layers rather than generating tokens, thereby maintaining smaller context sizes and a smaller memory overhead independent of reasoning length. But depth recurrence has also gained traction in visual understanding. Here, recurrent VLM archi- tectures are built in two ways: first, either by starting from a recurrent language model and post-hoc adding a vision backbone, or, second, by looping an existing VLM without removing any of its layers. The first approach is i.a. adopted by HIVE (Zhang et al., 2026), which extends a recurrent language model pretrained from scratch by a vision backbone. Examples for the second approach are, RecursiveVLM (Xu et al., 2026) and ReLoop-UME (Wang et al., 2026), which loop layers in pretrained VLMs without pruning, with

In contrast to these two regimes, we pursue a third option of retrofitting a pretrained VLM with recurrence, following a prune-then-loop strategy. Namely, we remove some intermediate blocks of the language backbone of the VLM and loop over a subset of the remaining layers. This strategy is supported by two complementary research findings: first, one set of recent works shows that a fraction of a VLM’s layers can be removed at a limited cost in accuracy (Huang et al., 2026; Madinei et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025), and, second, another set of works shows that the layers of

We thus hypothesize that iteratively executing the subset of layers of a pruned VLM can recover the capacity lost due to pruning. We test this hypothesis by retrofitting, i.e., by converting a pretrained non-recurrent VLM into a recurrent one while reusing its existing weights rather than pretraining a recurrent model from scratch. We refer to the resulting model as retrofitted recurrent VLM (RR- VLM). We prune a block of intermediate layers from the language backbone of a pretrained VLM and designate a contiguous subset of the remaining layers as a recurrent block (McLeish et al., 2025). This surgery, however, degrades the pretrained language backbone, and although text-only training repairs it, the repair leaves the language model misaligned with the original projector. We resolve this with a three-stage training curriculum: first, we apply a text-only training to repair the backbone, second, we apply a projector-only training to restore the image-text alignment, and third, we fine-tune the entire model on visual instruction data. In the text-only and the instruction-tuning stage, we add a knowledge distillation (KD) term, with the pretrained model as teacher, to avoid the language backbone from drifting too far from the original representation that the projector was aligned with. We evaluate the proposed method on the TinyLLaVA-1.4B backbone (Zhou et al., 2024), training it on 60B tokens of text as well as 493k image–caption pairs and 660k instruction tuning samples from the base model’s training data, without introducing any new vision-language data. We compare the resulting model against the pretrained TinyLLaVA-1.4B model and four baselines trained on the same data: (1) the unpruned model subjected to the identical recovery training, (2) the unpruned model without the text-only stage, (3) the pruned model without recurrence, and (4) a

Specifically, we evaluate our linear adapter against three variants: a gated adapter, the Parcae adapter (Prairie et al., 2026), which multiplies the recurrent state with a learned per-channel factor within (0, 1) so that the hidden state remains bounded across recurrences, and no adapter at all. Our abla- tions show that, among the adapter variants, the linear adapter yields the best performance, whereas the gated adapter and the Parcae adapter score below the variant without an adapter. Furthermore, we show that at equal compute, a larger recurrent block results in better performance. We also show that distillation from the pretrained model improves recovery training and increases the performance of the retrofitted recurrent model. Finally, we find that a model trained at a fixed depth only works at the depth it was trained at, whereas a model trained with sampled recurrence works at other depths, but its performance does not improve beyond the trained depth. We also find that sharing the KV cache across recurrences during inference costs accuracy, which contrasts with the results reported for a model pretrained with recurrence (Geiping et al., 2025). We summarize our contributions as follows: (1) We introduce the first prune-then-loop retrofit of a pretrained VLM evaluated on VQA, supported by a three-stage curriculum that repairs the pruned language backbone and restores projector alignment using the base model’s vision-language training data. text: Depth recurrence and architectural retrofitting. Depth recurrence reuses a block of layers mul- tiple times, increasing the effective depth of the model without adding any additional parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019). Previous attempts at creating recurrent LMs include Huginn (Geiping et al., 2025) and Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025). Huginn splits the model into three components: a prelude that embeds the input into a latent state, a recurrent block that iterates on that state, and a coda that de- codes the final state into output logits. Ouro iterates the entire set of layers, and Loopie (Gao et al., 2026) applies each layer recurrently instead of performing block-level looping. In all three cases, the model is trained from scratch without any pre-initialization by existing models. Two findings in- form our design: a looped block benefits from a stable learned connector between successive passes (Prairie et al., 2026), and an iterated layer contributes only a fraction of the capacity of a stored one (Schwethelm et al., 2026), thus bounding what recurrence can recover from pruning. As an alternative to full-corpus pretraining, recurrence can instead be achieved by retrofitting a pretrained model. Within this regime, there exist two lines of work: (1) looping a middle block of the stack without pruning, for latent reasoning (Koishekenov et al., 2025), and (2) looping after reducing
title: Preprint. Under review.

text: can instead be achieved by retrofitting a pretrained model. Within this regime, there exist two lines of work: (1) looping a middle block of the stack without pruning, for latent reasoning (Koishekenov et al., 2025), and (2) looping after reducing the depth, either by keeping a block of the surviving layers (Bae et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025) or by merging neighbouring layers into a few blocks that are then looped (Kwon & Park, 2026). We adopt the latter approach, retrofitting recurrence after structural pruning. Specifically, we take inspiration from McLeish et al. (2025), who drop layers 4 to 9 of TinyLlama-1.1B to obtain a 4/8/4 layer allocation looped through a linear adapter. Recurrence in vision-language models. Current works either loop layers of a pretrained VLM without pruning, with a near-constant number of parameters (Xu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), or build one on a natively recurrent language backbone (Zhang et al., 2026). HIVE (Zhang et al., 2026) builds a VLM on the pretrained recurrent language model Huginn-3.5B (Geiping et al., 2025) by attaching an InternViT-300M vision encoder and training the combined model on 6.5M training samples in three stages. As such HIVE is based on a significantly larger model and trained on five times more training samples than the proposed model, preventing a direct comparison to

We therefore take inspiration from the pipeline in HIVE to replicate this setting as a baseline to compare to rather than comparing against their model. Beyond standard vision-language tasks, depth recurrence has been explored for robotic action policies, either in the action head of an intact VLM (Tur et al., 2026) or by pruning a VLM and looping a small block (Shen et al., 2026). However, these methods operate in a fundamentally different domain, and the pruned variant of Shen et al. (2026) lacks a prune-only baseline. Our setting departs from those existing approaches by following a prune-then-loop pattern, removing layers before the loop is installed. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first prune-then-loop retrofit of a pretrained VLM evaluated on VQA. 3

text: Preprint. Under review. 3 METHOD: PRUNE-THEN-LOOP RETROFITTING We study the problem of converting a pretrained non-recurrent vision-language model into a depth- recurrent architecture. In this section, we formalize the prune-then-loop retrofit, explaining the proposed model surgery, the training curriculum used to recover performance, and the adapter mech- anism. 3.1 RETROFITTING EXISTING VLMS A pretrained vision-language model computes next-token logits from an image I and a text sequence x as F(I, x) = L(u), L = ℓm ◦· · · ◦ℓ1, u = [ π(V (I)); E(x) ], (1) where V denotes the vision encoder, π the projector, E the text token embedder, and L the language model composed of layers operating on representations of dimension H. Our prune-then-loop mech- anism modifies only the layers ℓ1, . . . , ℓm of the language model L. We partition the m layers into four consecutive groups of sizes p + d + b + c = m and delete the d layers. This yields a pre- lude block P = ℓp ◦· · · ◦ℓ1, a recurrent block B = ℓp+d+b ◦· · · ◦ℓp+d+1, and a coda block C = ℓm ◦· · · ◦ℓm−c+1 (Figure 1). The retrofitted model applies the recurrent block r times. The recurrent block is preceded by a small adapter A that merges the block’s current

The recurrent block is preceded by a small adapter A that merges the block’s current output with the output of the prelude. Expressing this pair as B ◦A and repeating it r times yields: F r p/b/c := C ◦(B ◦A)r ◦P. (2) Namely, we first apply the prelude P, then run the combination of adapter and recurrent block B ◦A for r times, and apply the coda C once. We refer to F r p/b/c as the retrofitted recurrent VLM (RR- VLM). The prelude P computes a context h from the token input u as h = P(u). The adapter A then concatenates the tokens of the recurrent block output s with the tokens of prelude context h, resulting in the same number of tokens with double dimension, and then compresses the token- wise concatenated representation back to the original dimension H through a learned linear layer W ∈RH×2H (McLeish et al., 2025). text: defining the model F ˜r. At inference, r is set to a fixed value that can be independent of the training configuration. KV cache. Each pass through the recurrent block computes its own keys and values, so the KV cache holds mr entries per token compared to the m entries for the original model. We evaluate two ways of sharing the cache across passes. The first, from Geiping et al. (2025), keeps n copies of the block’s cache per token and lets pass i use copy i mod n. With n=1, every pass reads the entries that the last pass wrote, and the cache shrinks to p + nb + c entries per token. This variant changes only the inference procedure and requires no training. The second lets every pass reuse the keys, or the keys and values, that the first pass computed, so that the cache shrinks to p + b + c entries per token. This variant changes the forward pass itself. The model is therefore trained with the sharing active and evaluated with the same forward pass. 4

text: Preprint. Under review. 3.2 TRAINING STRATEGY The retrofitted model of Sec. 3.1 requires training for two reasons. First, the pruning removes the layers between the prelude and the recurrent block, leading to a misalignment between the repre- sentations produced by the prelude and those expected by the recurrent block. Additionally, the remaining layers have to be adapted to the modified architecture. Second, the recurrence introduces an adapter A that fuses the output of the prelude with the output of the recurrent block using a newly initialized linear layer that needs to be trained as well. Three-stage Training. We propose a three-stage curriculum that restores the VLM and trains the adapter: First, in stage S0 we focus on repairing by training only the pruned language backbone on text-only data, freezing all other components. Second, as the retrained text backbone can now slightly deviate from the original one, we retrain the vision-language projector in stage S1 to re- store image-text alignment, and finally optimize the entire model via end-to-end training with visual instruction data in stage S2, interleaving image-text and text-only training data. Knowledge Distillation. Retraining the modified language backbone inevitably shifts its internal representations away from those of the pretrained model. In a VLM this shift is problematic, since the vision-language projector has been aligned to the representations of the original
title: Preprint. Under review.

text: data. Knowledge Distillation. Retraining the modified language backbone inevitably shifts its internal representations away from those of the pretrained model. In a VLM this shift is problematic, since the vision-language projector has been aligned to the representations of the original backbone. We therefore seek to adapt the language backbone to the new architecture while preserving its original representations as far as possible. To this end, we incorporate a distillation term at stage S0 training, using the original, unpruned baseline model F as the teacher to limit the drift of the pruned, recurrent model F r and to allow an easier realignment in stage S1: L = (1 −λ) LCE + λ τ 2 KL �softmax(F/τ) softmax(F r/τ)  . This can be attributed to the fact that those datasets usually have single-step QA type questions, which do not profit from more complex reasoning. We determine the effect of the text-only stage S0 and the vision-language align- ment stage S1 on the resulting recurrent VLM in Table 2. We find that S0 is crucial to the recovery training, as removing it reduces the performance of the resulting model by 3.68 pp on average. Re- moving S0 primarily affects the reasoning-oriented datasets, with 7.3 pp lost on CV2D, 6.8 pp on MMB and 4.6 pp on AI2D. We attribute this to the fact that without the repair of the pruned language backbone in S0, the stages S1 and S2 have to repair the language backbone and align the projector at the same time. We further find that removing S1 costs 1.28 pp, again primarily on the reasoning- oriented datasets. We attribute this to the fact that S1 performs the vision-language alignment, and without it the stage S2 has to perform both the alignment and the instruction tuning. In summary, both S0 and S1 contribute to the performance, with S0 having the larger impact, which shows that

Layer allocation. We first ablate the design of the recurrent block in Table 3(a). To this end, we fix the depth of the recurrent model at mr=56 layers, thus smaller recurrent blocks are executed with more recurrences compared to larger ones. All models are trained on a 7.5B S0 text-token budget. We find that a larger recurrent block performs better than other variants given the same compute setting. Namely, the 4/8/4 allocation outperforms a 6/4/6 allocation at r=11 by 3.19 pp. A narrower 4/6/4 block at r=8 prunes two additional layers, and the 4/8/4 configuration outperforms it by 1.60 pp. Adapters. In contrast, the model trained with a sampled recurrence regime also works at depths other than the one it was trained for, staying within 2 pp of its best value from r=2 to r=16. This can be attributed to the fact that the sampled regime exposes the model to a different number of recurrences in every training step, so that its readout is trained for every depth in that range. However, we find that its performance saturates and does not improve beyond the trained depth. Consequently, we do not observe test-time scaling. The fixed and sampled recurrence models perform on par at the trained depth, with 55.75 against 55.83 on Avg. We therefore find that a fixed recurrence model is the less expensive approach to train a recurrent VLM, but it comes at the price of test-time stability to varying recurrences. With n=3 the cache shrinks to 1.45× that of the base model at a cost of 0.75 pp, and with n=1 it shrinks to 0.727×, below the base model itself, at a cost of 5.43 pp. This can be attributed to the fact that the keys and values of a recurrence step are computed from the state of that step, so a recurrence step that reads the cache of another step attends to representations that do not match its own input. Training the model with the sharing active does not close this gap either, with a cost of 0.73 pp for sharing the keys and 2.94 pp for sharing the keys and values (Appendix A.3). We thus keep a separate cache per recurrence in our best-performing setting, and note that the cache size can be traded against accuracy at inference without retraining. text: We introduced the first prune-then-loop retrofit of a pretrained VLM evaluated on VQA. The retrofitted model outperforms the unpruned baseline while storing 23.3% fewer language-model parameters, with the gains concentrated on reasoning-oriented benchmarks. This gain is due to the recurrence itself, as the loop accounts for a significant improvement over the pruned single-pass baseline. At the same time, the recovery requires the text-only training stage, which yields the best performance among all evaluated training strategies. Finally, retrofitting recurrence into a pretrained VLM outperforms adding a vision encoder to a pretrained recurrent language model, which makes the retrofit the best performing route to a recurrent VLM among all evaluated baselines. 9

EVALUATING PROBABILISTIC WEATHER MODELS ON TROPICAL CYCLONES Nathan Chalumeau INRIA, Paris, France AXA, Paris, France nathan.chalumeau@inria.fr Xavier Renard Sorbonne Universit´e, CNRS, LIP6, F-75005 Paris, France AXA, Paris, France xavier.renard@axa.com Remi Meynadier AXA, Paris, France remi.meynadier@axa.com Hugo Rakotoarimanga AXA, Paris, France hugo.rakotoarimanga@axa.com Marcin Detyniecki Sorbonne Universit´e, CNRS, LIP6, F-75005 Paris, France AXA, Paris, France Polish Academy of Science, IBS PAN, Warsaw, Poland marcin.detyniecki@axa.com Emmanuel de Bezenac INRIA, Paris, France emmanuel.de-bezenac@inria.fr
title: CAN AI FORECAST THE EXTREMES?

text: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a frac- tion of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive bench- mark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF’s operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind–pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and en- semble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for targeted improvement. Nonetheless, these results suggest that AI models are capable of capturing physical relationships that remain predictive well beyond typical weather conditions, motivating further investigation into how these capabilities emerge and how to strengthen them. 1
title: CAN AI FORECAST THE EXTREMES?

text: Weather forecasting has long relied on numerical simulation of the atmosphere. Learned models now compete with leading numerical systems at a fraction of the simulation cost (Bi et al., 2022; Lam et al., 2023). But their success on standard benchmarks leaves a consequential question unresolved: how well do they predict rare events for which accurate forecasts matter most? Their reliability at representing extremes remains a source of skepticism. Evaluations have exposed substantial shortcomings in forecasting record-breaking weather and severe tropical cyclones, raising concerns that the success of learned models depends on conditions well represented in their training data (Zhang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025). These findings have challenged the broader promise of AI weather forecasting. Yet, much of the evidence has focused on deterministic models. The recent 1 arXiv:2610.22077v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026
title: CAN AI FORECAST THE EXTREMES?

text: progress of probabilistic models (Price et al., 2024; Bonev et al., 2025; Alet et al., 2025) motivates revisiting this assessment, and the examination of both their ability to forecast extreme events and the uncertainty represented by the ensembles they simulate. Tropical cyclones are among the most damaging weather hazards globally (WMO, 2021). Evacuation and impact preparedness depend on forecasts of tropical cyclone location and intensity several days ahead, including the uncertainty of those predictions, issued by weather agencies. Yet cyclones occupy only about 0.5% of grid points in global climate simulations (Lacombe et al., 2023), and the proportion of intense cyclones is projected to increase under continued global climate warming (IPCC, 2023; Knutson et al., 2020). Their rarity and consequences make them an important testbed for learned forecast models, particularly as these models enter operational and cyclone forecasting trials (Lang & Magnusson, 2025; Google DeepMind, 2025). We revisit the ability of AI models at forecasting extreme weather through a systematic evaluation of three recent leading probabilistic AI weather models: GenCast (Price et al., 2024), FourCastNet 3 (FCN3; Bonev et al., 2025), and FGN (Alet et al., 2025). Across 178 tropical cyclones in two evaluation settings, we intercompare these three models’ ability to predict location and intensity with respect to reanalysis and best track data. In addition, we benchmark these models

Across 178 tropical cyclones in two evaluation settings, we intercompare these three models’ ability to predict location and intensity with respect to reanalysis and best track data. In addition, we benchmark these models against IFS-ENS, ECMWF’s numerical operational ensemble model, to assess how far recent progress extends to cyclone forecasting and where limitations remain. Our evaluation examines both forecast skill and the properties of the predicted storms, combining probabilistic track forecasts, intensity, ensemble calibration, and wind–pressure dependence. This allows us to assess both forecast accuracy and the models’ ability to reproduce the physical relationships that characterize these extreme events. Among our findings, operational AI models improve cyclone forecasts in several respects. FGN outperforms IFS-ENS on probabilistic track scores for about 90% of the 41 retained storms in 2025, and its advantage extends to the spatial location of strong winds and low pressures. Both operational AI models show larger relative CRPS gains over IFS-ENS near cyclones than at global scale. Yet improvements in aggregate scores do not imply improvements in every aspect of the storm: GenCast outperforms FCN3 on cyclone-local CRPS despite a larger peak-wind bias, while FGN’s better spatial scores coexist with intensity biases similar to GenCast’s and persistent ensemble calibration errors. Finally, the operational AI models retain intensity distributions close to ERA5

text: Models. We evaluate three leading probabilistic weather models that differ both in their training objectives and in the way they represent uncertainty. GenCast uses conditional diffusion to sample fu- ture atmospheric states (Price et al., 2024). FourCastNet 3 (FCN3) combines spherical convolutions with stochastic perturbations. It is trained using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in the physical and spectral space (Bonev et al., 2025). FGN optimizes the CRPS at individual locations and forms an ensemble by combining four independently trained networks; within each network, additional members are generated via learned perturbations (Alet et al., 2025). Evaluation settings. Four datasets serve as reference: IBTrACS (Knapp et al., 2010) supplies observed tracks and intensities; IFS-ENS (ECMWF, 2024), ECMWF’s operational physics-based ensemble, is the numerical baseline, especially for uncertainty representation; ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020) and HRES-fc0 are the gridded references for two experimental configurations, with two versions of GenCast available. The reanalysis setting uses GenCast and FCN3 trained exclusively on ERA5, evaluated against ERA5 and IBTrACS. The operational setting uses GenCast (operational) and FGN, trained on ERA5 and fine-tuned on HRES-fc0, the initial conditions of ECMWF’s high- resolution forecast system, evaluated against HRES-fc0 and IBTrACS. This design allows for the investigation of how the choice of reference data influences intensity bias, in particular whether ERA5-related biases remain after operational fine-tuning. The

This design allows for the investigation of how the choice of reference data influences intensity bias, in particular whether ERA5-related biases remain after operational fine-tuning. The evaluation years follow the model training periods (Figure 1), extending the tests over several cyclone seasons. Because the storms and model versions differ between settings, the comparison does not isolate the effect of fine-tuning. Forecast protocol. We conduct a retrospective evaluation of historical tropical cyclones across all basins. 178 IBTrACS cyclones whose maximum reported one-minute sustained wind reaches at least 64 knots are selected and reproduced using the AI models. We assess predicted tracks, intensity, ensemble calibration, and storm structure, introducing each diagnostic alongside its scientific question. For each storm, we initiate a 15-day forecast rollout with 50 ensemble members per model in the reanalysis setting and 49 in the operational setting (Appendix A). Forecasts are initiated 12 hours before the first reported wind observation in the IBTrACS dataset, adjusted to the preceding forecast cycle where necessary. In total, the evaluation covers 26,541 member forecasts across lead times, using both cyclone tracks and atmospheric fields. text: 3 REANALYSIS SETTING: EVALUATION OF CYCLONE FORECASTS ON ERA5-TRAINED MODELS 3.1 PREDICTING CYCLONE LOCATIONS Recent evaluations report cyclone position errors using the ensemble-mean track (Price et al., 2024; Alet et al., 2025). This approach quantifies the accuracy of the mean predicted position, but cannot distinguish ensembles with the same mean and different spreads or distinct possible paths. For Typhoon Bualoi (2025), IFS-ENS members separate into several clusters at intermediate lead times, which the mean alone cannot represent (Figure 2). We therefore evaluate the spatial distribution of predicted locations by scoring the density assigned to the observed storm position. We use the TempestExtremes tracking algorithm to detect cyclone centers in atmospheric fields and chain them into trajectories (Ullrich & Zarzycki, 2017; Ullrich et al., 2021) for each forecast member. Detected tracks are matched to observed tropical cyclones by comparing their times and locations. At each lead time t, we estimate a spatial probability density ˆpt from the predicted positions xt,m of that storm using kernel density estimation (KDE). We score the observed IBTrACS positions by their negative log-likelihood (NLL): ˆpt(x) = 1 Mt Mt X m=1 Kh �x −xt,m  , NLL = −1 |T | X t∈T log ˆpt(yt), (1) Here, Mt is the number of ensemble members with an identified position for the observed storm at lead time t,

Lower NLL means a greater probability density is assigned to that position. We score all three models at the same eligible lead times T and average first within each storm, then across storms, giving each storm equal weight. NLL evaluates predicted locations only in members where TempestExtremes detects a cyclone and associates it with the observed storm. We require at least 10 such members per model at 5 or more common lead times, which leads to retaining 106 of the 125 storms. Appendix A gives the tracking, density estimation, and filtering rules. GenCast has the lowest mean NLL and predicts a greater density of cyclone positions around the observed locations than IFS-ENS for 68% of retained storms, and outperforms FCN3 on 62% of storms (Table 1). FCN3 also outperforms IFS-ENS by a smaller majority, 58%. Although the average NLL differences are modest, both GenCast and FCN3 outperform IFS-ENS on a majority of storms. As a complement, we report the track detection rate, the percentage of members with an identified track, averaged over all 125 storms. Rates show the same model ranking as NLL but reveal no additional skill advantage. The absence of detection can stem from forecast uncertainty about cyclone formation or persistence, model errors, or tracking limitations. Global averages conceal differences around cyclones, while even cyclone-local scores can conceal a weakness in the representation of peak winds. GenCast’s lower local CRPS supports better agreement with ERA5 in tropical cyclone regions overall, but does not establish that every property of the storm is better predicted. text: An important note is that ERA5 itself underestimates cyclone maximum winds (Dulac et al., 2024). Agreement with ERA5 consequently does not establish realistic intensity, nor does IFS-ENS’s positive bias establish that its storms are too strong. We next examine whether models fine-tuned on operational analyses improve cyclone tracking and whether their intensity biases persist against HRES-fc0, while assessing spatial agreement separately from intensity. 4 OPERATIONAL SETTING: TRACKING, INTENSITY, AND SPATIAL AGREEMENT FOR MODELS FINE-TUNED ON OPERATIONAL ANALYSES Cyclone tracking. FGN assigns a greater probability density to the observed storm locations than IFS-ENS on approximately 90% of the 41 retained storms and achieves the lowest mean NLL (Table 2). Operational GenCast also outperforms IFS-ENS on 78% of storms, while FGN’s advantage over GenCast is smaller, at 61%. FGN ranks first among all three models on 59% of storms, compared with 34% for GenCast and 7% for IFS-ENS. Both AI models therefore improve tracking on most evaluated storms, with FGN ahead of GenCast. The detection rates follow the NLL ordering, with both AI models ahead of IFS-ENS. Unlike in 2021–2023, where detection rates were close, the operational comparison shows a clear separation. This reflects both higher detection for operational GenCast and lower detection for IFS-ENS on the 2025 storms. To isolate the dependence structure from marginal biases, we rank wind and pressure separately within each dataset and transform the ranks to standard normal scores. This rank-based transformation renders the marginal distributions identical across datasets, while preserving their joint dependence structure, represented by the copula. The copulas are found to be consistent across models and references (Figure 6b): FGN and GenCast have rank correlations of −0.83 and −0.84, compared with −0.88 for HRES-fc0. The qualitative result also holds in the earlier evaluation (Appendix B.2) and across separate lead-time ranges. IBTrACS supplies observational context, although its sustained winds differ from gridded instantaneous winds. FGN therefore reproduces a wind–pressure dependence structure comparable to that of GenCast, despite being trained with CRPS applied separately to each variable and grid point, which constrains their conditional marginal distributions but not their joint dependence. The coexistence of negatively biased wind speeds and pressure minima with a realistic wind–pressure association suggests that intensity errors and dependence errors are distinct. text: AI forecasts of extreme weather. Evaluations are mixed: Olivetti & Messori (2024) find com- petitive skill across extreme events, varying by event, region, and lead time; Zhang et al. (2026) find numerical forecasts superior on record-breaking extremes. For cyclones, DeMaria et al. (2024) show competitive tracking alongside substantial intensity underestimation. We revisit this distinction for recent probabilistic models, asking whether similar global scores conceal differences in cyclone fields. Probabilistic cyclone evaluation. TCBench (Gomez et al., 2026), the closest benchmark, evaluates one-to-five-day track and intensity forecasts, including probabilistic scores, rapid intensification, and postprocessing. GEFS (Zhou et al., 2022) outperforms its evaluated AI ensembles on track CRPS: probabilistic evaluation does not uniformly favor AI. Different models, seasons, references, and scoring protocols preclude direct comparison with our rankings. We complement this work with location-density scores, track detection rates, and surrounding-field diagnostics. CRPS scores forecast distributions without separating intensity from spatial errors; our intensity and quantile-footprint analyses examine these separately without additively decomposing CRPS. 8

Physical relationships in learned forecasts. Recent work studying cyclone dynamics and thermo- dynamics has examined AI-based weather models through the lens of cyclone physics: Sahu et al. (2025) find realistic spatial patterns but weak intensity while Ba˜no-Medina et al. (2025) assess the sensitivity of learned and numerical models to initial conditions for extratropical cyclone Xynthia. Our joint wind–pressure analysis complements these studies by providing a distributional diagnostic aggregated across storms and ensemble members, using reanalysis, operational analyses, and obser- vations to identify which physical relationships are preserved and which biases persist. However, agreement with a known physical relationship does not establish the underlying learned mechanism, just as resemblance to pretraining data does not imply a causal effect of the training data. 7

text: Our benchmark shows that recent probabilistic models can outperform numerical forecasts on cyclone location and surrounding fields, while still exhibiting intensity biases and calibration errors. The presence of systematically weak storms alone is therefore insufficient to conclude a general failure in cyclone representation. FGN’s wind–pressure dependence structure, comparable to that of GenCast, despite being trained solely on conditional marginals, further shows that meaningful joint structure can emerge implicitly, without being explicitly enforced by the training objective. These findings suggest more targeted routes to improvement. Comparing model outputs against observations and higher-resolution analyses could help disentangle errors inherited from training targets from limitations of the models themselves. Potential remedies such as intensity correction, loss functions that emphasize extreme winds, and improved uncertainty quantification should be evaluated not only for their effect on intensity, but also for whether they preserve spatial skill and wind–pressure dependence. Finally, comparing marginal and joint training objectives under matched architectures and compute budgets could clarify the extent to which the recovered dependence structure arises from the training objective rather than from the model’s inherent structural constraints. 9

text: Progress on extreme weather forecasting with AI models should consequently be assessed beyond aggregate global scores. Evaluation across additional seasons, including periods without observed cyclones, would test the robustness of these gains and assess the calibration of cyclone-occurrence probabilities. Decomposing forecast performance into location, intensity, uncertainty, and dependence makes such evaluations actionable for model development: it identifies what needs improvement and what should be preserved, while providing more specific evidence about what learned forecasts capture of extreme weather. text: A EVALUATION PROTOCOL AND REPRODUCIBILITY Events, initialization, and ensemble size. Selection uses each storm’s maximum IBTrACS USA WIND, with a threshold of at least 64 knots, i.e. category 1 to 5 on the Saffir–Simpson scale, yielding 125 storms in 2021–2023 and 53 in 2025. A storm’s first time is its first IBTrACS record with a reported USA WIND, and each forecast starts 12 hours before it, after moving any 06:00/18:00 UTC start to the preceding 00:00/12:00 cycle, since IFS-ENS forecasts initialized at 06:00/18:00 UTC do not cover the full 15-day window in the sources we used. Selection by lifetime maximum does not mean the storm is already at hurricane strength at initialization; this protocol evaluates selected known events, not unconditional cyclone occurrence. All forecasts span 15 days. We retain 50 members per model in 2021–2023. Missing individual files in the 2025 GenCast and IFS-ENS archives motivate a uniform 49-member comparison for all three models. IFS-ENS uses perturbed members, excluding the control. Equal membership is not an equal-compute comparison. Forecast and reference sources. We ran GenCast and FCN3 ourselves and retrieved the other forecasts from public archives: • IFS-ENS: the 50 perturbed members, excluding the control; for 2021–2023 from TIGGE (Bougeault et al., 2010) (ECMWF, CC BY 4.0), already on the 0.25◦grid, and for 2025 from ECMWF Open Data (CC BY

The IFS cycles in operation are listed in Table 3. • GenCast: DeepMind’s implementation (Apache 2.0) with the released 0.25◦, 13-level checkpoint trained on ERA5 1979–2018 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), initialized from ERA5 (see Reference fields below); about 30 minutes per 15-day member on H100/H200 GPUs, which limited the number of storms. • FCN3: NVIDIA’s released weights (Hugging Face nvidia/fourcastnet3, revision 76ef0c6; Apache 2.0) run through Earth2Studio (Apache 2.0), initialized from ARCO- ERA5 (Carver & Merose, 2023); about one minute per member on H200 GPUs. • FGN: precomputed forecasts from the WeatherNext 2 archive, weathernext/ weathernext_2_0_0/zarr/2025_to_present (CC BY 4.0). • GenCast operational: precomputed forecasts from the WeatherNext Gen archive, weathernext/126478713_1_0/zarr/126478713_2024_to_present (CC BY 4.0). Model size and compute. The models also differ in size and in the compute required for inference. GenCast has a single network of about 57M parameters, each FGN network has 180M parameters, and FCN3 has 711M parameters (Alet et al., 2025; Bonev et al., 2025). GenCast requires significantly more compute at inference (20 diffusion solver steps, 39 network evaluations) for a

text: network of about 57M parameters, each FGN network has 180M parameters, and FCN3 has 711M parameters (Alet et al., 2025; Bonev et al., 2025). GenCast requires significantly more compute at inference (20 diffusion solver steps, 39 network evaluations) for a 12-hour forecast step (Price et al., 2024), whereas FGN and FCN3 generate a 6-hour step in a single forward pass. However, GenCast reportedly has a lower training budget than FGN (Alet et al., 2025; Price et al., 2024). IBTrACS (NOAA NCEI, public domain) supplies observed positions in both settings; ERA5 and HRES-fc0 supply the gridded references. These are different verification targets, so absolute field scores should not be compared across cohorts. Reference fields. ERA5 (Copernicus Climate Change Service, CC BY 4.0) for 2021 was retrieved from WeatherBench 2 (Rasp et al., 2024), and for 2022–2023 from the Copernicus Climate Data Store, at 0.25◦. HRES-fc0 was retrieved from ECMWF Open Data (CC BY 4.0) through Earth2Studio’s IFS interface: for each valid time, the 0-hour state of the operational high-resolution forecast initialized at that time, at 0.25◦, i.e. after data assimilation of observations from ±3 hours. Common fields and evaluation window. All field comparisons use a 721×1440 latitude–longitude grid at 0.25◦spacing and 30 forecast times, 12–360 hours at 12-hour intervals. The 12-hour step is that of the coarsest model, GenCast; the models

B.2 WIND–PRESSURE RELATIONSHIP Figure 9 repeats the analysis of Section 5 for the 2021–2023 setting (GenCast, FCN3, and IFS-ENS), with ERA5 as the gridded reference. The three models have nearly the same joint distribution; compared with ERA5, their pressures are slightly shallower and their winds slightly weaker (a). Their dependence is close to ERA5’s (b). As in the operational setting, the models differ from the reference in intensity rather than in how wind varies with pressure. B.3 RANK HISTOGRAMS A rank histogram counts, at each grid point, how many ensemble members fall below the reference value. For a calibrated ensemble, the reference is equally likely to take any of the N + 1 ranks and the histogram is flat. A U shape, with the reference too often below or above all members, indicates insufficient spread; a T shape, with the reference too often near the middle of the ensemble, indicates excessive spread; an asymmetry indicates a bias. A high last rank means the reference is often stronger than every member, i.e. the forecast winds are too weak; a high first rank

For each matched ensemble member of the 106 (2021–2023) and 41 (2025) retained storms, we average over its forecast times the distance between its storm centre and the IBTrACS position, and the absolute error of

text: storm also misjudges its intensity. For each matched ensemble member of the 106 (2021–2023) and 41 (2025) retained storms, we average over its forecast times the distance between its storm centre and the IBTrACS position, and the absolute error of its regional pressure minimum and 10m wind maximum against the gridded reference (ERA5 for 2021–2023, HRES-fc0 for 2025). This gives one point per storm and member. Figures 14 and 15 show a LOWESS trend per model with a 95% bootstrap band, and the Pearson correlation r. The LOWESS trend is a local linear regression: at each track error, a straight line is fitted by weighted least squares to the 30% of members closest to it, with weights decreasing with distance (Cleveland, 1979). The band gives the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the trend over 150 bootstrap resamples of the members. Track and intensity errors are linked: members that place the storm further from its observed position also tend to have larger intensity errors, in both settings and for both variables. The correlation remains moderate, however, and members with similar track errors span a wide range of intensity errors. An accurate track therefore does not imply an accurate intensity, which is why we evaluate the two separately. IFS-ENS is the least correlated model in every case: r = 0.33 for pressure

text: Beyond the Hamming Cliff: Compact Spatial Encodings Preserving Semantic Distance in Spiking Neural Networks⋆ Dr Sergio Daviesa,∗,1, Dr Muhammad Aitsamb, Mr Morgan-Tyler Stonea, Prof. Alessandro Di Nuovob,c and Prof. Liangxiu Hana aDepartment of Computing and Mathematics, Manchester Metropolitan University, John Dalton Building, Oxford Road, Manchester, M15 6BH, United Kingdom bCentre of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, Sheffield Hallam University, Howard Street, Sheffield, S1 1WB, United Kingdom cUniversità degli Studi di Catania, Viale Andrea Doria 6, Catania, 95100, Italy A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Spiking Neural Networks SNN Spatial Pattern STDP Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity Supervised Learning Spike Encoding Hamming Distance A B S T R A C T Spatial encoding lets a spiking neural network classify a value without a temporal integration window, by presenting it as one pattern of simultaneous spikes, but makes classification depend on the geometry of the binary code. In standard binary, adjacent values such as 127 and 128 differ in every bit, a “Hamming cliff” that forces supervised STDP networks with homeostasis into excessive scaling and false positives. We present a controlled characterisation of this dependence rather than an application benchmark: every experiment runs on SpiNNaker hardware, in a dual-rail network with a single output neuron, and presents every value of a synthetic integer range. Gray, Thermometer
title: Beyond the Hamming Cliff: Compact Spatial Encodings Preserving

text: positives. We present a controlled characterisation of this dependence rather than an application benchmark: every experiment runs on SpiNNaker hardware, in a dual-rail network with a single output neuron, and presents every value of a synthetic integer range. Gray, Thermometer and Johnson encodings all remove the cliff, but only Thermometer and Johnson preserve global semantic distance, at a width that grows linearly with the range. We introduce a family of hybrid encodings, combining a coarse magnitude code with a Gray code for fine position, that contains all three as exact limiting cases of a single parameter; a sevenfold reduction in width costs one percent of the correlation between Hamming and semantic distance. The homeostatic factor sets a Hamming radius of tolerance that the network follows exactly in 93% of conditions, and elsewhere to within one bit, so the encoding alone determines what that tolerance means: a contiguous interval for Thermometer and Johnson, wrapping at the range ends for the cyclic codes, and scattered values for Binary and Gray. Measuring the limit on simultaneous input on SpiNNaker and SpiNNaker2, we show that on SpiNNaker it is a silent software default, and that the hybrids remain within it at 1024 values where their parent codes do not. Evaluation on a downstream task, such as network-traffic classification, is left to future work.

Third- generation Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) (Maass, 1997) add time to the model, and a rate code then costs latency: to decode a value, the network must “wait and count” spikes over an integration window. It also costs energy. Event- driven neuromorphic hardware spends its energy per event rather than per clock cycle, routing every spike as a packet and processing it at each synapse it reaches (Furber et al., 2014; Davidson and Furber, 2021), so a code that spends many spikes on each value undermines both the low latency and the low power that such hardware promises (Davies et al., 2018). Spatial encoding avoids this bottleneck by representing a value as a pattern of simultaneous spikes (Davies et al., 2025). text: pattern of simultaneous spikes (Davies et al., 2025). Because neuromorphic hardware delivers informa- tion through discrete, addressable synapses, the value is first converted to a binary code word, and each bit is signalled by the presence or absence of a spike from one source (Auge et al., 2021). The input activity per decision is then fixed by the code width, and the output is delayed only by the depth of the network (Göltz et al., 2021). The conversion to binary, however, introduces a structural vulnerability, the “Hamming cliff” (Caruana and Schaffer, 1988): numerically adjacent values can have very different code words. The 8-bit range is used for most of our experiments, as the widest at which every encoding compared here fits within the default input limit of first-generation SpiNNaker (Section 3.4). In earlier work (Davies et al., 2025), we showed that an SNN trained with supervised STDP classifies a single spatial pattern accurately, but that its performance degrades when it is trained on several. Large Hamming distances between the trained patterns create “don’t care” synapses, which receive conflicting evidence from different patterns and so contribute nothing to the output; the network must then rely on stronger homeostatic scaling, which sharply increases false positives. Standard binary encoding therefore prevents the network from recognising contiguous ranges of values. This matters wherever the inputs are continuous or ordinal. In network-traffic classification, for instance, packet sizes, flow durations and inter-arrival times carry meaning in their proximity: two flows of similar duration are similar events, and an encoding that maps them to distant spatial patterns discards that information before the network sees it. Other features are cyclic: time of day is the clearest case, where 23:59 and 00:00 are adjacent, and such features need an encoding whose topology reflects that. This paper examines spatial encodings

Other features are cyclic: time of day is the clearest case, where 23:59 and 00:00 are adjacent, and such features need an encoding whose topology reflects that. This paper examines spatial encodings that restructure the signal before it reaches the network, while keeping one spike per bit. The established alternatives are not equivalent: Gray encoding removes the cliff but preserves little global distance structure, whereas Thermometer and Johnson en- codings preserve it at the cost of a code width that grows linearly with the value range. We introduce a family of hybrid encodings, which combine a coarse magnitude code with a Gray code for fine position; the family contains all three as limiting cases of a single parameter and trades code width against preservation of semantic distance at a favourable rate. On hardware, the homeostatic factor sets a radius of tolerance in code space around each trained code word, so the encoding alone decides which values the net- work treats as similar. The same analysis explains the degra- dation observed in our earlier work (Davies et al., 2025): the summed weights of trained code words cancel wherever they disagree, and the homeostatic gain that compensates is what admits the false positives. Because a spatial code delivers all its bits at once, its width is also bounded by the number of simultaneous input events a neuron can receive: about 255 under the default configuration of first-generation SpiNNaker, and 512 on SpiNNaker2 (Mayr et al., 2019; Gonzalez et al., 2024). The hybrid construction reduces code width by an order of magnitude. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic characterisation of how the choice of spatial code governs the homeostatic scaling, and hence the tolerance and false-positive behaviour, of supervised STDP learning on neuromorphic hardware. The main contributions of this work are: • an account of how the geometry of a spatial code sets the homeostatic tolerance of a supervised STDP network (Sections 4.3.1 and 4.4); • a hybrid coarse–fine encoding family with Ther- mometer, Johnson and Gray as limiting cases (Sec- tion 3.5); • evidence that removing the Hamming cliff is neces- sary but not sufficient for semantic clustering (Sec- tions 4.1 and 4.3); • a characterisation of the per-neuron input limits on SpiNNaker and SpiNNaker2 (Section 3.4); • an exhaustive hardware evaluation of eight encodings, with code and data released (Sections 4.2–4.5).

The scope of this work is deliberately narrow: we char- acterise the encodings rather than evaluate them on a task. Every experiment presents every value in the range to the trained network, so the relations reported are exact over the whole input space and a relation such as the tolerance law of Section 4.4 can be checked condition by condition. A natural dataset allows neither: its values are unevenly distributed and its features correlated, so the effect of code geometry on learning would be confounded with the data. The network (a dual-rail input layer feeding a single output neuron), the learning rule and the measurement protocol are held constant, so the encoding is the only variable, and the comparison throughout is against standard binary encoding, the representation used in our prior work. How the ranking carries over to a downstream task, where feature distributions are uneven and the encodings interact with later processing, is the subject of separate work. 2. Spatial Encoding and the Hamming Vulnerability In spatial encoding, all bits of a code word are presented to the network in the same timestep, so the network has no access to the value itself, only to which of its input synapses are active. Its response to two values therefore depends on how many bits their code words share, that is, on the Hamming distance between them. In the supervised STDP network of Davies et al. (2025), a larger Hamming distance between trained code words required a larger homeostatic scaling factor for all of them to be recognised, and the larger factor admitted more false positives. Encoding Topologies To address the Hamming cliff, we consider alternative mapping techniques that constrain the relationship between semantic and spatial distance: • Gray Encoding: A reflected binary code where adja- cent integers are represented by codewords that differ by only a single bit, ensuring minimal spatial tran- sitions between semantically adjacent states (Gray, 1953). • Thermometer Encoding: Maps a magnitude by pro- gressively filling a bit-field, creating a unary represen- tation: the value is given by the number of bits set, not by which particular bits are set (Buckman et al., 2018). Representing 𝑁values therefore requires 𝑁−1 bits, and successive values differ in a single bit. • Johnson (Twisted Ring) Encoding: A cyclic code in which bits are set one at a time from one end of the field and then cleared again from that same end, so that 𝑊bits generate 2𝑊distinct states before returning to the start (Mano and Ciletti, 2012). Successive values differ in a single bit, and because the sequence closes on itself the first and last values are adjacent. These codes are long established in digital logic.

Codes that combine a coarse unary field with a fine binary one are likewise familiar from segmented data converters. What has not been examined is their use as spatial codes for spiking neural networks, where each bit is a discrete synapse, all bits are presented simultaneously, and homeostatic scaling determines which code words the network accepts. Topological Analysis The structural utility of these schemes is best understood through their distinct topological properties, as defined in digital logic theory (Mano and Ciletti, 2012). Thermometer encoding enforces linear boundary conditions on the se- mantic space, wherein the minimum and maximum values are maintained at maximal Hamming distance. Conversely, Johnson encoding imposes a periodic topology; by forming a ‘twisted ring’, the encoding identifies the semantic extremes 0 and 𝑁−1 as adjacent, regardless of the code width 𝑊. This cyclic property makes Johnson encoding a natural candidate for quantities with circular continuity, such as orientation, phase or time of day, whereas Thermometer encoding suits bounded magnitudes. These schemes must, however, be distinguished by which property they preserve. All three guarantee local smooth- ness: values adjacent under the metric each is designed for differ in a single bit, eliminating the cliff of Section 2.2. Gray encoding offers no such guarantee. Its re- flected construction places every value 𝑖a single bit from 2𝑊−1−𝑖, however far apart the two are, so that the extremes 0 and 2𝑊−1 differ in one bit; Hamming distance therefore carries little information about semantic separation beyond immediate neighbours. These three codes are not, however, exclusive alternatives: the reflected construction of Section 3.5 interpolates be- tween them and contains all three as limiting cases. 2.5. Relation to Other Low-Latency Representations Spatial binary codes are one of several ways to give a spiking network a fast decision about a scalar (Auge et al., 2021). They are distinguished from the others by three properties: when the decision becomes available, how many input events it costs, and how the distance between code words relates to semantic separation (Table 1). Latency coding, or time to first spike, represents

text: are distinguished from the others by three properties: when the decision becomes available, how many input events it costs, and how the distance between code words relates to semantic separation (Table 1). Latency coding, or time to first spike, represents a value by when a single spike occurs (Mostafa, 2017; Göltz et al., 2021). It is frugal in events, one per input neuron, and preserves proximity naturally, since close values fire at close times; but the decision cannot be taken until the latest spike that could carry information has had time to arrive, so its latency is bounded by the encoding window rather than by the depth of the network. Rank-order coding (Thorpe and Gautrais, 1998) reads information from the order in which a population fires. It is equally frugal, but it encodes the relative ordering of several inputs rather than the magnitude of one, and it too must wait for that order to be established. Both trade time for events. Spatial codes make the opposite trade: every bit is delivered in the same timestep, so the decision follows within a fixed number of timesteps of the input, and the cost is paid in width instead. The simulator holds synaptic weights in a fixed-point accumulator whose scaling is fixed at run time by the largest total current that could arrive at a neuron, namely 𝑤𝑚𝑎𝑥 times the fan-in (van Albada et al., 2018); a larger product consumes more integer bits and leaves fewer fractional ones, coarsening the resolution. Application of the Encoding The encoding is applied as a pre-processing step rather than computed by the network. For a given value, the code word determines the connectivity: the generator neuron that fires at the “1” times (Section 3.1) connects to every bit of the code word equal to one, and the neuron that fires at the “0” times to every bit equal to zero. The network is therefore constructed anew for each value presented, and no population computes the mapping from value to code word. This matches the framing of the work as a pre-processing of the input signal, and it also removes the source-side spike load: each generator neuron emits one packet per presentation time, which the router fans out, rather than one packet per bit. The same mapping could be computed on-chip, by a place-coded input population with one neuron per value projecting to the bits of its own code word through fixed connectivity. Such a network would present identical activity to the encoding populations, so the results reported here do not depend on which of the two arrangements is used. 3.3. Input Capacity and Spatial Code Width Because all bits of a spatial code word are presented simultaneously and each bit fires on exactly one rail, a code of width 𝑊delivers 𝑊spike packets to its output neuron within a single timestep. Any limit on the number of packets a neuron can receive at once is therefore a limit on code width. We measured this limit on both platforms. 3.4.1. SpiNNaker sPyNNaker places incoming packets in a circular buffer on each core, allocated with 256 slots by default, of which one is always kept empty, so that at most 255 packets can be held; packets that arrive when the buffer is full are discarded without error. Training an output neuron on code words of increas- ing width under the default configuration, the number of synapses potentiated tracked the width exactly up to 255 and then stopped, at 255 or occasionally 256 when a packet was consumed during the burst, for widths of 300, 480 and 992. Raising the buffer to 1024 slots removed the limit: every synapse was potentiated at every width tested.

Ther- mometer records the lowest mean accuracy over the fourteen pairs (0.824) precisely because it generalises over the largest contiguous intervals, while Binary’s higher figure (0.974) conceals scattered errors. Accuracy is therefore a misleading summary here, and the relation between false positives and Hamming distance is the more informative quantity. 4.2.1. A systematic effect of bit count Under Binary, the required scaling factor varies slightly between second values at equal Hamming distance, and the variation is not noise. It depends on the number of 1-bits in the second code word and not on their position. At 𝐻= 1 the second value differs from the anchor 24010 = 111100002 in a single bit. The four values that do so by setting one of its zero bits, 241, 242, 244 and 248, each have five set bits, and all require exactly 2.96051, although the flipped bit occupies a different position in each.

Within any Hamming-distance group the spread is at most 1.1%. This follows from the dual-rail training protocol. Bits equal to 1 and bits equal to 0 are presented at different times relative to the teacher spike (Section 3.1), so their synapses are potentiated at different points on the STDP curve and need not acquire identical weights. A code word with more set bits therefore draws proportionally more of its drive from one rail and requires marginally more gain to reach threshold. Discussion The results support four main conclusions about spatial representation in the SNN architecture studied here. First, homeostatic scaling acts in code space rather than semantic space. For a single trained pattern, increasing the gain enlarges the set of code words whose Hamming dis- tance from the target remains within the firing threshold. Equation (13) predicts this Hamming radius from code width and gain alone, and the hardware measurements reproduce the predicted accepted set exactly in 238 of 256 conditions; of the remaining 18, sixteen admit one further Hamming shell where the predicted radius falls just short of an integer and the resolution of the homeostatic search tips it over, and two fall exactly on a shell boundary, where the small asym- metry between rail weights determines which code words fire. What this tolerance means semantically is therefore decided entirely by how the encoding embeds the underlying variable. Second, local continuity and global distance preserva- tion are distinct properties. Gray encoding guarantees a one- bit transition between adjacent values and so removes the Hamming cliff, but its global Hamming distance is only weakly related to semantic separation: 𝜌𝑠= 0.374, barely above Binary’s 0.323. This explains why Gray performs well when the trained values form a compact cluster, yet needs progressively more homeostatic margin as the trained set grows, reaching 1.61 times the coherent value, whereas Thermometer, Johnson and the hybrids stay within 21%. Thermometer and John- son offer exact distance preservation at an event count that grows linearly with the number of represented values, while the block size of the hybrids controls how much global structure and neighbourhood contiguity is kept for a given width. The choice is therefore not simply between “accurate” and “compact” codes, but between combinations of semantic topology, tolerance resolution and per-decision event load. In practice, this suggests a simple rule: choose a cyclic or linear code to match the topology of the variable; use Thermometer or Johnson when the range fits within the input limit; and otherwise use the smallest block size whose width, from Eq. (10), fits within it, since smaller blocks keep neighbourhoods more contiguous. 5.1. Limitations The evaluation uses synthetic values over a single range at a time, one network architecture, and first-generation SpiNNaker for every result except the input-capacity mea- surements. The experiments ran slower than real time, so the processing cost of wide codes, which would bound the rate of decisions at real time, was not measured. On

The experiments ran slower than real time, so the processing cost of wide codes, which would bound the rate of decisions at real time, was not measured. On SpiNNaker2 we established the limit of 512 input events per neuron but not its origin: whether it can be configured, and whether it limits events per timestep or connections per neuron, remain open. The results are also drawn from a single output neuron; the tolerance law is derived per neuron and should extend to a layer of independently trained neurons, but this is not demonstrated here. The weight vectors for multiple trained values are ob- tained by training each value separately and summing, not by presenting the values sequentially or interleaved to a single plastic network. This is a deliberate idealisation: it makes the learned vector an exact linear function of the trained set, which is what allows the coherence ratios of Section 4.3 to be predicted from pairwise Hamming distances alone (Section 4.3.1). Sequential STDP would not be linear in the same way. The nearest-pair rule pairs each presentation only with its nearest post-synaptic spike, so the update a value induces depends on what has already been learned, and the weight ceiling of 2 would clip bits on which

The nearest-pair rule pairs each presentation only with its nearest post-synaptic spike, so the update a value induces depends on what has already been learned, and the weight ceiling of 2 would clip bits on which several trained values agree: at a learned weight of about 0.375 per value, synapses shared by six or more values would saturate, and the coherent scaling of 𝑓(1)∕𝑛would cease to hold. Whether on-chip sequential learning converges to the summed vector for small trained sets, and how it departs from it for large ones, remains to be tested. No downstream dataset or multi-feature classification problem is evaluated, and the introduction explains why: the exhaustive protocol that makes the relations above exact is not available on a natural dataset. The consequence is that nothing here shows how the encodings behave when several features are presented together. One difficulty is already visible from the tolerance law: if features are concatenated into one code word, the Hamming distance is the sum of the per-feature distances and the tolerance radius applies to that sum, so a large deviation in one feature can be offset by exact agreement in the others. The hybrids do not fully reproduce their parents’ be- haviour. Their accepted sets are fragmented into up to 𝐵 runs by the Gray fine field, and their false positives, though confined near the trained cluster, are less tightly concentrated than Thermometer’s. The block size therefore trades not only correlation but neighbourhood contiguity, and smaller blocks should be preferred where contiguity matters. The tolerance law is exact only to the resolution of the homeostatic search: rounding the factor upwards can admit one further Hamming shell wherever the predicted radius falls just short of an integer, which occurred mostly in the widest code, and a finer search would be needed to exploit Thermometer’s full precision. Finally, the hybrid construc- tion resembles the segmented thermometer-plus-binary ar- chitectures of data-converter design, and the contribution here is the Gray fine field with reflected block ordering and its characterisation in a neuromorphic setting, rather than the two-level idea itself. 6. Conclusions Spatial encoding removes the latency of rate coding but makes classification depend on the geometry of the code. For a dual-rail network with a single output neuron on first- generation SpiNNaker, homeostatic scaling sets a Hamming radius around each trained code word, and the encoding alone decides what that radius means: a contiguous interval of values for Thermometer and Johnson, wrapping at the ends of the range for the cyclic codes, and a scattered set of values for Binary and Gray. The encodings commonly proposed against the Ham- ming cliff are therefore not equivalent. Gray removes the cliff but discards global distance structure, and pays for it in homeostatic margin as trained sets grow; Thermometer and Johnson preserve that structure at a width that grows with the value range. The hybrid construction introduced here contains all three as limiting cases of a single block-size parameter and trades width against preservation of semantic distance at a favourable rate: the cyclic hybrid at 𝐵= 8 accepts no untrained value as the trained cluster grows, in 19 bits where Johnson needs 128. Width matters because it is the number of input events paid on every decision, and both platforms bound it: on

text: hybrid at 𝐵= 8 accepts no untrained value as the trained cluster grows, in 19 bits where Johnson needs 128. Width matters because it is the number of input events paid on every decision, and both platforms bound it: on SpiNNaker by a configurable buffer of the simulation soft- ware, which by default silently truncates codes wider than 255 bits during training, and on SpiNNaker2 by a limit of 512 input events per neuron. The hybrid construction re- duces width by roughly an order of magnitude while leaving the radius of the detected neighbourhood unchanged.
