text: Learning Changes the World and Then What Was Learned has Changed: Training and Deploying Neural Networks in the Control Loop Vittorio Lippi1 a 1Calejo Hybrid Intelligence AB, Mellansjö 109, 92592 Tärnaby, Sweden vittorio.lippi@calejo.ai Keywords: Neural Networks, Adaptive Control, Closed-Loop Identification, Distributional Shift
title: Learning Changes the World and Then What Was Learned has Changed:

text: Neural networks offer critical adaptability for controlling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable. However, when offline-trained neural networks are deployed within closed-loop control systems, their actions fundamentally alter the state distribution upon which they were trained. This paper introduces a unified taxonomy to categorize these sequential failure modes: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Error, the deployment-induced Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. Through discrete-time sensitivity analysis, this work formalizes how offline-learned parameters locally guarantee a trajectory divergence upon deployment, degrading performance due to local loss geometry. To mitigate this distribution shift, we propose actionable design policies cen- tered on time-scale separated online adaptation. These mechanisms are validated through ablation studies on a nonlinear Duﬀing oscillator, demonstrating that bounded continuous learning success- fully mitigates trajectory divergence whereas static deployments fail, offering concrete guidelines for practitioners deploying machine learning components in safety-critical feedback systems. 1

text: Neural networks (NNs) offer adaptability for con- trolling complex systems where nominal modeling proves intractable (Narendra & Parthasarathy, 1990). Experiments with legged robots, includ- ing humanoids (Lippi, 2018; Wensing et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024) and lower- limb exoskeletons (Belal et al., 2024; Lhoste et al., 2025; Lippi et al., 2021; Mamou & Saadia, 2014) demonstrate this capability. However, physi- cal closed-loop deployment degrades the offline- validated performance of these ML systems. In both disturbance compensation (Lippi, 2018) and gait segmentation (Lippi et al., 2021), this degra- dation required continuous online learning to re- cover functionality. These experimental results imply that deploy- ing the NN alters the system dynamics it origi- nally mapped: such distributional shift degrades network performance. The corre- lation between the baseline control input and un- measured environmental disturbances introduces an estimation bias during the offline learning phase. The scope of this paper focuses on super- vised learning paradigms for neural network con- trol. While Reinforcement Learning architectures incorporate online adaptation, the mathematical dynamics of offline-to-online distributional shift in supervised contexts remain a challenge. Re- cent advances in closed-loop system identifica- tion, such as Dual Input-Output Parameteriza- tion (IOP) (Chen et al., 2023), System Level Pa- rameterization (SLP) (Srivastava et al., 2023), and Neural Identification of stabilized models (Boroujeni et al., 2025a), have proposed struc- tural frameworks to mitigate this initial estima- tion bias while guaranteeing closed-loop stability. However, even if this initial bias is eliminated, the transition from offline training to static on- line deployment induces a secondary mathemati- cal challenge. This paper therefore distinguishes between three sources of performance degrada- tion: the initial Closed-Loop Identification Er- ror, the distribution-shifting Action Error, and the continuous Tracking Error. 2 PROBLEM FORMULATION Consider a discrete-time nonlinear system: xk+1 = f(xk,uk), (1) where xk ∈Rn is the state vector (embedding de- lay history) and uk ∈Rm is the control input. Definition 1 (Identification Bias). The Closed- Loop Identification Bias is the parametric devi- ation of the offline controller θof f from the opti- mal open-loop parameters, caused by overfitting to the correlated process noise in the training dataset. text: Separation and Convergence To prevent θk updates from destabi- lizing the physical system, the learning loop must enforce time-scale separation. The coupled sys- tem is modeled as a two-time-scale process: the fast physical plant dynamics (xk) and the slow neural weight updates (θk). Condition 1 (Fast-Loop δ-ISS): The retained baseline controller must enforce incremental Input-to-State Stability (δ-ISS). This property en- sures that the distance between any two system trajectories is strictly bounded by the magnitude of the difference in their inputs for any frozen parameter θ. Consequently, the fast physical state xk converges exponentially to a parameter- dependent equilibrium manifold x∗(θ). This de- couples the dynamics, permitting us to evaluate the loss function safely on the slow manifold, de- noted as ¯L(θ). Condition 2 (Slow-Loop Lipschitz Continuity): The reduced loss function ¯L(θ) must have a Lip- schitz continuous gradient with a constant Lθ, meaning that for any two parameter vectors θ1 and θ2, the change in the gradient is bounded by the distance between the parameters: ∥∇θ ¯L(θ1)−∇θ ¯L(θ2)∥≤Lθ∥θ1 −θ2∥. While Theorem 2 establishes a theoretical threshold for stability, computing the parameter Hessian’s spectral norm (Lθ) online is computa- tionally intractable, and executing physical line- searches to find optimal step sizes is unsafe in robotic loops. To enforce this bound formally, deployments may adopt a dual-layer approach, a two-pronged strategy combining offline structural constraints with online algorithmic safety filters. In the first layer (offline), techniques like Spec- tral Normalization (Miyato et al., 2018) can be

text: used to bound the network’s global Lipschitz con- stant, capping the network’s potential volatility and ensuring a theoretical maximum for Lθ be- fore the system is ever deployed. In the second layer (online), adaptive step-sizes are governed by curvature surrogates, such as the Generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) or the empirical Fisher In- formation Matrix (Martens, 2020). These sur- rogates function as a dynamic braking mecha- nism, estimating the steepness of the learning landscape without the massive processing over- head of exact second-order calculations. Because the GGN approximates the Hessian using only first-order derivatives and remains positive semi- definite, fast power iterations can dynamically scale the learning rate matrix Γ. This dual-layer strategy ensures that the neural adaptation re- mains slow enough to satisfy time-scale separa- tion, respecting the physical mechanics of the robot. In practical nonlinear deployments, such as the saturated cubic plant evaluated in Section 6, analytically bounding the global Lipschitz con- stant Lθ and verifying δ-ISS across the entire oper- ational manifold is intractable. Consequently, the gradient clipping applied in our experiments acts as an empirical heuristic to enforce this slow-loop condition. As demonstrated in the subsequent ablation studies, removing this clipping bound vi- olates the time-scale separation, causing the net- work to overreact to transient dynamics and in- ducing mechanical chatter. As demonstrated in the subsequent ablation studies, removing this clipping bound vi- olates the time-scale separation, causing the net- work to overreact to transient dynamics and in- ducing mechanical chatter. Bounding λmax(Γ) beneath this inverse curva- ture threshold ensures adaptation remains suﬀi- ciently slow. Violating this threshold breaches time-scale separation, coupling gradient updates with transient dynamics and destabilizing ge- ometric safety bounds. This principle aligns with dual-loop architectures that pair fast inner safety constraints, e.g., Control Barrier Functions, with slower neural adaptation (Annaswamy et al., 2023; Fisher & Annaswamy, 2025). As the online learner stabilizes the system, adapting on instantaneous gradients (utilizing a learning batch size of Bk = 1) causes the network to act as a localized adaptive filter. While this yields high tracking performance on smooth, con- tinuous limit cycles by overfitting to the local tan- gent dynamics, it induces catastrophic forgetting of the global state space (Dohare et al., 2024). Literature introduces the concept of generative algorithmic epistemic injustice, which investigates how generative AI can undermine the integrity of collective knowl- edge and the processes we rely on to acquire, assess, and trust information (Kay et al., 2025). Grounded in social and political philosophy, this phenomenon identifies how AI systems can produce or amplify misinformation, perpetuate representational harm, and create epistemic inequities (Kay et al., 2025). Whether in the physical state space of a robotic joint or the latent space of a large language model, the mech- anism remains identical: without interventions to preserve diversity or enforce exploratory per- sistent excitation, the agent’s control authority will degrade the environment it seeks to model. Breaking the Loop. Neurology offers inspira- tion for breaking these loops: sensory inputs are subject to natural detection thresholds of vari- able entity (Kobel et al., 2021). In human pos- tural control, non-linear thresholds and intermit- tent control paradigms for the inverted pendu- lum operate on integrated vestibular and pro- prioceptive signals (Hettich et al., 2013; Het- tich et al., 2015; Tigrini et al., 2022), modali- ties mimicked in robotics by IMUs and joint en- coders. Replicating these thresholds via dead- bands can block sensory noise from propagating through the continuous control loop (Mergner, 2010; Akçay et al., 2021), breaking the loop around defined safe zones to suppress control authority without endangering stability (Lippi & Molinari, 2020). Beyond rigid thresholds, cognitive neuroscience provides a framework for loop-breaking via Predictive Processing and Ac- tive Inference (Friston et al., 2017; Clark, 2013). To avoid be- coming trapped in feedback loops, biological sys- tems dynamically modulate the “precision” (re- liability) of sensory prediction errors (Pezzulo et al., 2015). In robotic control, engineering this adaptive precision-weighting acts as a neuromor- phic deadband, allowing the controller to sup- press transient sensorimotor errors (Lanillos et al., 2021; Oliver et al., 2022). This theoretical re- lationship is bidirectional: while active inference uses precision-weighting as a functional threshold, physical deadband models, such as the human- derived Disturbance Estimation and Compensa- tion (DEC) framework, produce sensory reweight- ing as an emergent macroscopic behavior with- out requiring explicit gain scheduling (Lippi & Mergner, 2017). This biologically plausible sym- metry empowers the agent to balance stabiliza- tion with epistemic exploration, ensuring it does not overreact to its action-induced sensory noise (Lanillos et al., 2021; Oliver et al., 2022; Friston et al., 2017). The mathematical inevitability of the Ac- tion Error exposes a fundamental limit of of- fline learning: it treats the neural network as a disembodied artifact operating within an epis- temic vacuum. Stabilizing a complex dynamic system mandates structural and physical embod- iment, requiring continuous, situated interaction with the physical environment (Mergner et al., 2024). Stabilizing a complex dynamic system mandates structural and physical embod- iment, requiring continuous, situated interaction with the physical environment (Mergner et al., 2024). Statically deploying a frozen model com- mits a fallacy of functional anthropomorphiza- tion (Mergner et al., 2024); it expects robust adaptability while denying the system the con- tinuous physical experience, or historical embodi- ment, necessary to co-evolve with a shifting state space (Mergner et al., 2024; Mainzer, 2009). How- ever, continuous adaptation risks recursive feed- back degradation if the agent indiscriminately tracks its own self-produced errors. Safe histor- ical co-evolution requires the agent to distinguish external physical disturbances from the trajec- tory shifts induced by its own parametric sub- optimality, a control-theoretic requirement that mirrors the biological somatosensory sense of self- agency (SSA) (Mergner et al., 2024). By en- forcing time-scale separation, the architecture achieves this balance: it maintains the continu- ous structural coupling required for historical em- bodiment (Mergner et al., 2024; Mainzer, 2009), while mathematically bounding the network’s au- thority to prevent it from recursively chasing its own sensory noise. Architectures like Model Reference Adaptive Control (MRAC) (Ioannou & Sun, 2012; Naranjo & Annaswamy, 2025) and L1 Adaptive Control (Hovakimyan & Cao, 2010) mitigate parameter drift using robust bounds and low-pass filtering. While Robust Model Predictive Control (MPC) (Kouvaritakis & Cannon, 2016) circumvents of- fline bias through online optimization, supervised neural approximations of these MPC laws (de Barros Fontes et al., 2009) face spatial curvature artifacts that necessitate our proposed Hessian regularization and experience replay guardrails. Reinforcement Learning. These findings con- textualize Reinforcement Learning (RL) (Sutton & Barto, 2018). While online RL circumvents identification bias through active interaction, of- fline RL remains vulnerable to the Action Er- ror via out-of-distribution extrapolation (Fuji- moto et al., 2019; Levine et al., 2020). Con- tinuous RL tracks moving targets but relies on exploratory noise, which is dangerous for safety- critical hardware like exoskeletons (García & Fernández, 2015), reintroducing the tension be- tween Lyapunov stability and persistent excita- tion (Berkenkamp et al., 2017). Mitigating the subsequent Action Error requires run-time safety. Certificate learning frameworks provide learned Lyapunov or Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) (Dawson et al., 2023), which, like inherent Lyapunov structures (Min et al., 2023), act as fast-loop spatial safety filters, while Safe Bayesian Optimization (BO) (Hirt et al., 2024) provides probabilistic constraints during closed-loop tuning. Because these structural methods prioritize guaranteed bounds over spa- tial representation recovery, our proposed time- scale separated adaptation (λmax(Γ) < 2/Lθ) does not replace them; rather, it acts as a slow-loop companion. Time-Varying Sensitivities, Noise, and Hybrid Systems. Although Theorem 1 establishes the Action Error via a local LTI approximation, de- ployments involve dynamic Jacobians that de- mand incremental stability (δ-ISS) or bounded- variation arguments. In non-autonomous regimes, unmeasured process noise amplifies parametric sub-optimality, and discontinuous hybrid switch- ing thresholds in exoskeletons (Lippi et al., 2021) can induce impulse-like jumps in state sensitivity. While the 1-DOF Duﬀing oscillator provides a geometric testbed to isolate the Action Error without the confounding variables of multi-DOF dynamic cou- pling, the present work functions as an analyti- cal framework. Scaling this time-scale separated adaptation to multi-DOF hardware (e.g., lower- limb exoskeletons or humanoid robots) introduces coupled, time-varying Jacobians. In these higher- dimensional regimes, the sensitivity matrix Sk be- comes non-diagonal, and unmodeled cross-joint inertia amplifies parametric sub-optimality. The gradient clipping threshold must be scaled by the spectral norm of the coupled mass matrix to en- sure the slow-loop Lipschitz continuity (Condi- tion 2) is maintained across all joint axes simul- taneously. To elevate this taxonomy to a com- prehensive control methodology, future work pri- oritizes extending empirical validation to such hardware-in-the-loop deployments. This requires experimental benchmarking of our time-scale sep- arated adaptation against classical robust archi- tectures (MRAC, L1) and sequential aggrega- tion (DAgger). Theoretically, while Remark 1 addresses continuous saturation-induced instabil- ity, efforts are required to formalize sensitivity bounds under discontinuous hybrid switching and time-varying references.

text: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following Daniela Baiamonte1, Kamyar Zeinalipour2,3, Elena Fano1, Stefano Simonazzi1, Andrea Zugarini1 1villanova.ai, 2Yukai!, 3University of Siena Correspondence: kamyar.zeinalipour2@unisi.it
title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following

text: Supervised fine-tuning datasets remain over- whelmingly English-centric and commercially restricted, as their content is frequently gen- erated by proprietary models whose terms of service forbid training competing systems. We introduce Multi-SFT, a commercially permis- sive collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, built via translation and regeneration pipelines for tasks where translation is insufficient. Human evalua- tion yields inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. Fine- tuning nine models from three different fam- ilies (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B–32B) and evaluating them on 13 benchmarks shows that Multi-SFT alone is competitive with larger augmented mixes and official instruction-tuned releases, with decisive advantages on safety tasks. 1
title: Multi-SFT: Permissively-Licensed Multilingual Instruction-Following

text: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is central to align- ing pretrained LLMs with human instructions (Wei et al., 2021; Ouyang et al., 2022; Taori et al., 2023), with data quality, diversity, and scale being critical for downstream behavior (Wang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023a). Yet, most existing SFT datasets re- main English-centric and are affected by a less vis- ible but equally serious problem: licensing. Many corpora carry permissive labels (MIT, Apache 2.0, Creative Commons), while their content was gen- erated by proprietary models such as GPT-4 or Gemini, whose terms of service explicitly prohibit use for training competing models. We introduce Multi-SFT, a collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs spanning five European languages (English, Italian, French, Spanish, and German), aggregating 13 heterogeneous datasets built exclusively from permissively licensed data and models (Table 1). Both pipelines undergo sys- tematic human evaluation by native or near-native annotators, yielding inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages. We validate Multi-SFT by fine-tuning nine models from three families (EuroLLM, OLMo 2, Qwen3; 1B–32B parameters) on 13 bench- marks. Our experiments show that the multi- lingual, permissively-licensed collection achieves stronger performance on non-English languages than the original English sources, which contain non-permissive data from closed LLMs, while surprisingly maintaining performance on English benchmarks as well. Furthermore, in multilingual settings, Multi-SFT outperforms official instruct models in most cases and stays competitive on En- glish. title: Strategy

text: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts pre-trained language models to follow instructions via cu- rated prompt-response pairs (Ouyang et al., 2022). English SFT resources span a continuum from fully human-written data—such as FLAN (Long- pre et al., 2023), Dolly (Conover et al., 2023), and Open Assistant (Köpf et al., 2023)—to hy- brid pipelines combining human annotation with synthetic generation, as in Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024). Recent large-scale synthetic ef- forts such as Nemotron (Blakeman et al., 2025) and Smoltalk (Allal et al., 2025) demonstrate the scalability of automatically constructed instruction datasets while explicitly addressing licensing and provenance through permissively licensed sources and models. High-quality multilingual SFT re- sources for European languages remain compar- atively limited, and existing datasets often face restricted licensing or provenance concerns due to reliance on proprietary generative models. The Aya initiative (Singh et al., 2024) provides the broadest multilingual effort to date, though its wide cover- age results in limited per-language depth and vari- able quality in automatically generated portions. EuroLLM (Martins et al., 2024), Tülu 3 (Lam- bert et al., 2024), Salamandra (Gonzalez-Agirre et al., 2025), and Apertus (Apertus et al., 2025) each advance multilingual or open post-training in different respects, yet all include components gen- erated or processed with proprietary models, lim- iting their suitability for provenance-constrained training. The Smoltalk multilingual extension rep- resents one of the few systematic attempts to con- struct permissively licensed multilingual SFT data through translation and open-model generation. Our work follows a similar philosophy while ex- panding task coverage, introducing expert-driven quality validation, and explicitly addressing prove- nance constraints through selective regeneration of non-compliant examples. 3 Multi-SFT Multi-SFT is a supervised fine-tuning collection of 13 datasets covering five European languages: En- glish, Italian, French, Spanish, and German. Over- all, it contains 502,818 diverse examples (e.g., QA, instruction following). Per-dataset details are out- lined in Table 2. Many existing SFT datasets, despite declaring permissive licenses, are built on human-authored prompts paired with responses generated by propri- etary models, which restricts their use in commer- cial settings. Therefore, we erased such content and regenerated it using open-weight, permissively licensed LLMs. Depending on the source dataset, we employ a translation pipeline, where existing (English-centric) datasets are converted into mul- tilingual ones, or a regeneration process, where synthetic content is re-generated from scratch with license-compliant language models. 3.1 Dataset selection criteria Rather than aggregating large volumes of generic instruction-response pairs, we focus on

Thus, source datasets were se- lected to cover a vast and heterogeneous mixture of competences and tasks (see Table 2). Licensing and Compliance. title: Strategy

text: permissive license compatible with commercial use. Moreover, we also take into account the provenance of synthetic content present in the datasets. This as- pect is often overlooked, but proprietary language models such as GPT, Claude or Gemini restrict or prohibit their use for the development of commer- cial models. Hence, we excluded all datasets where there is evidence that entries were generated using models with such restrictive licensing, regardless of the license applied to the dataset itself. We con- sider as "evidence" of non-permissive model use any dataset mentioning in its card, git repository or paper the use of commercial models. Whenever a dataset is released under a permissive license but a portion of its entries were generated using a restricted model, we opted for selective regenera- tion: the affected entries were regenerated using permissively licensed open-weight models, specif- ically: Mistral-small2, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B3, and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B4. These models were se- lected based on their empirical performance across translation and generation tasks, and their licens- ing compatibility with downstream training (see Appendix A.2 for details). Out of 59 candidate datasets initially considered (excluding math and coding topics), 45 were excluded due to licensing or provenance violations (see Appendix A.1). A sample of regenerated examples is provided in Ap- pendix A.3. 3.2 Translation Pipeline Translated datasets were produced through an it- erative, expert-driven pipeline.

A sample of regenerated examples is provided in Ap- pendix A.3. 3.2 Translation Pipeline Translated datasets were produced through an it- erative, expert-driven pipeline. For each target language, a native or near-native linguist indepen- dently developed a translation prompt, selecting the generation model and temperature in collabora- tion with the team. An initial batch of samples was generated and evaluated blind by a separate QA re- viewer with equivalent language expertise. Based on the reviewer’s feedback, the prompt, model, or parameters were revised and the process repeated until the output quality was deemed satisfactory. A special case within the translation pipeline is multi-smol_summarize, which combines transla- tion and generation. In the original Smoltalk sum- marization dataset, source documents are paired with summaries generated from a very small set of instruction variants. For each, the same expert validation process described in Section 3.2 was applied: prompt design, blind evaluation, and iterative refinement by language-expert reviewers. Multi-AdvBench. The original multilingual Ad- vBench dataset consists of harmful prompt– unsafe response pairs. We replicated the full pipeline using Qwen3.5-122B-A10B and translated and adapted all prompts, seed instructions, and constraint defi- nitions for the five target languages. One method- ological modification was introduced: the original constraint sampling procedure can yield logically incompatible combinations (e.g., write in lower- case and include a minimum number of capitalized words). We revised the sampling logic to prevent such conflicts. Multi-Safety. A small dataset of harmful request– safe response pairs was constructed internally: harmful prompts were authored by team mem- bers, and safe responses were generated using Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct. Inter-annotator agreement was com- puted using Gwet’s AC2 (Gwet, 2008) with quadratic weights on the collapsed three-way la- bel set (A/B vs. C vs. D). AC2 was preferred over Cohen’s κ (Cohen, 1960) because the annotation distributions are strongly skewed toward the posi- tive category (A/B), a condition under which κ is known to produce paradoxically low values even when observed agreement is high. The quadratic weighting scheme is appropriate for ordinal scales, where the distance between non-adjacent categories (e.g., A/B and D) should be penalised more heavily than disagreements between adjacent ones. On English, BL retains an advantage on 7 out of 9 models given its larger share of English examples, yet the gaps remain modest in most cases, indicating that the multilingual focus of ML does not severely harm English capability. Differences across families and sizes. Eu- roLLM benefits most from ML: it outperforms SFT† on the multilingual average at all three scales (+0.6, +1.9, +2.2) and matches or exceeds it on English, as expected given EuroLLM’s European-focused pre-training. OLMo 2 trails SFT† on the multilin- gual average, narrowly for the 1B (−0.1) and 7B (−1.4) models and markedly for the 32B (−10.2), while English consistently favors SFT†, reflecting its English-centric pre-training. Qwen3 shows the largest gains (+8.6, +12.3, +15.9 on the multilin- gual average), though these should be interpreted with care given that all Qwen3 variants were evalu- ated without thinking mode. 5 Conclusions We introduced Multi-SFT, a commercially permis- sive supervised fine-tuning collection of 502,818 instruction-response pairs across five European languages, addressing two pervasive limitations of existing SFT resources: English-centricity and provenance-constrained licensing. Our experiments across nine models and 13 benchmarks demonstrate that our multilingual and permissive collection yields better performance on non-English languages than the original En- glish sources

text: closed LLMs, while largely preserving perfor- mance on English benchmarks. Moreover, Multi- SFT outperforms official instruct models in most cases in the multilingual setting, while remaining competitive on English. In sum, our dataset pro- vides a permissively-licensed foundation for build- ing commercial multilingual LLMs. Limitations We acknowledge that establishing with certainty the generation provenance of third-party datasets is not always possible. Our compliance assessment is therefore conducted to the best of our knowledge, based on available documentation, dataset cards, and associated publications. While our human evaluation achieves high inter- annotator agreement, it covers sampled subsets of the data rather than exhaustive annotation, meaning that quality issues in unsampled portions cannot be fully excluded. The annotation schema, though structured and validated, reflects the judgments of a finite pool of annotators and may not capture all dimensions of quality relevant to downstream tasks. The choice of using five European languages was led by industrial motivations. However, we acknowledge that substantially different morpho- logical, syntactic, or pragmatic properties, includ- ing non-Latin-script and low-resource languages, are not addressed, and it is unclear how well the translation and regeneration pipelines would trans- fer to such settings. Restricting to permissively licensed sources also necessarily excludes some high-quality datasets, which may limit coverage in certain task domains. A Dataset Selection and Compliance A.1 Dataset Selection Statistics Of the 59 candidate SFT datasets surveyed (exclud- ing math and coding topics), 45 were excluded. Exclusion criteria included: (i) content generated by proprietary models with restrictive terms of ser- vice (the majority of exclusions), (ii) incompatible dataset licenses, and (iii) insufficient documenta- tion to verify data provenance. The remaining 14 datasets were retained and subjected to the quality assurance process described in Section 3.1, result- ing in the final 13-dataset Multi-SFT collection. A.2 Regeneration Model Selection Mistral-Small, Qwen3-VL, and Qwen3.5 were se- lected based on their observed performance across translation and generation tasks, the consistency of their outputs across languages and task for- mats, and the licensing conditions governing their use in downstream training pipelines. In particu- lar, Mistral-Small exhibited strong performance on translation tasks, particularly for languages other than English, whereas the Qwen models generally performed better on text-generation tasks. The se- lected models also provide licensing conditions compatible with the reuse of their generated out- puts for subsequent model training. B Annotation Details We developed two schemas: one applicable to all instruction-following datasets, and one dedicated to multi-dialogues, which requires evaluation of dialogues. The complete annotation schema is sum- marized in Table 7. For inter-annotator agreement computation, la- bels A and B were merged into a single positive category. This decision was motivated by the em- pirical observation that label B often acts as an intermediate or “attractor” category: annotators frequently assign B in borderline cases between clearly correct (A) and substantially problematic (C) responses, making the A/B boundary inherently less stable than the B/C or C/D boundaries. Col- lapsing A and B therefore yields a more robust three-way agreement setting (A/B vs. C vs. D). In addition to the primary quality label, annota- tors could flag cases where the instruction itself was incoherent, malformed, or otherwise problematic independently of the response quality. Furthermore, for labels B, C, and D, annotators were required to specify one or more predefined error categories (e.g., hallucination, format error,

Furthermore, for labels B, C, and D, annotators were required to specify one or more predefined error categories (e.g., hallucination, format error, unnatural phras- ing, etc.) and were optionally allowed to provide free-text comments for qualitative feedback. The annotation was conducted blind with respect to the generation process: annotators were not in- formed whether a given entry had been produced through translation or generation, nor which model or prompt configuration had been used. This setup was designed to minimize confirmation bias and ensure that quality judgments reflected the intrinsic properties of the data rather than prior expectations about the pipeline. C Inter-Annotator Agreement: Detailed Analysis This appendix provides a detailed examination of inter-annotator agreement patterns, focusing on datasets with lower agreement values and identify- ing the underlying sources of disagreement. C.1 Multi-FLAN: Synthetic Reasoning Ambiguity Multi-FLAN shows agreement values of 0.93 (French) and 0.90 (German), below the threshold observed in most other datasets. The source of disagreement lies in the inherent ambiguity of eval- uating synthetically generated reasoning chains. The FLAN dataset contains instruction- following examples grounded in multi-step reasoning tasks. When such reasoning is generated by a language model, the output frequently ex- hibits logically coherent but stylistically artificial reasoning paths

This creates a legitimate grey zone in annotation: annotators may reasonably differ on whether a formally sound but awkward reasoning chain qualifies as satisfying from a training data perspective. C.2 Multi-PersonaIF: Incomplete Instructions and Constraint Sensitivity Multi-PersonaIF exhibits one of the lowest agree- ment values (0.88 in French) and the highest pro- portion of C-rated entries across datasets (up to 25% in Italian and 18% in French). Analysis of annotator comments reveals two main sources of error. Constraint Violations. PersonaIF instructions include explicit formal constraints (e.g., “write in lowercase,” “include the e vowel in every word”). Annotators differed in how strictly they enforced partial or borderline violations: some accepted mi- nor deviations, while others applied stricter criteria. This reflects inherent variability in constraint-based evaluation tasks. Incomplete Instructions. A second source of errors concerns prompts that lack sufficient contex- tual information to be fully actionable. For exam- ple, an instruction may ask “How many awards did the actress win?” without specifying the actress, or refer to an unspecified entity. Annotators dif- fered in how they handled such cases, with some treating them as invalid and others proceeding with implicit interpretation. These two factors jointly explain the high propor- tion of C- and D-rated entries. Constraint violations reflect the inherent difficulty of multi-constraint generation, while incomplete instructions indicate a data quality issue that can be mitigated via im- proved prompt design and post-hoc filtering or re- generation. C.3 Multi-TableGPT: Language-Specific Translation Challenges The Spanish subset of Multi-TableGPT exhibits a substantially higher C/D-rate (24%) compared to other languages within the same dataset (German 2%, Italian 2%, French 3%). This discrepancy is notably larger than variations observed across other datasets, suggesting a language-dependent effect in the translation and generation process. 12

text: Manual inspection indicates that most errors in- volve incomplete outputs for multi-step instruc- tions, particularly when both intermediate reason- ing and final answers are requested, as well as oc- casional factual inaccuracies. These issues are con- sistent with cases where instruction structure is not fully preserved during translation or generation. Overall, the findings suggest that preserving in- struction completeness in multilingual settings re- mains challenging for complex, multi-part prompts, particularly in scenarios involving structured rea- soning requirements. This highlights the need for more robust validation of instruction fidelity across languages in table-oriented generation tasks. D Training Details The training setup is kept the same for all runs: learning rate 2×10−5 with cosine decay, 3% linear warmup, no weight decay, sequence length of 4096 tokens, batch size of 128, gradient clipping at 1.0, and mean loss reduction. Every model trains for one epoch with seed 42. We use the open-instruct framework with DeepSpeed ZeRO and pick ZeRO stage 1, 2, or 3 depending on what fits in memory on eight NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPUs. 13

title: PATHOLOGY FOUNDATION MODELS

text: In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention- based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p =

text: least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

text: Even as increasingly detailed methods of tissue characterization move toward clinical application, morphology remains the foundation of microscopic pathology (1). Mastering its interpretation requires years of training, building an internal frame of reference against which unseen cases are compared (2). That frame of reference, however, is bounded by the cases an individual has encountered. Each rare entity is, by its nature, seldom seen, yet rare entities collectively make up a substantial part of the diagnostic spectrum. And while any individual pathologist encounters a given entity only occasionally, a department accumulates such cases over years. Once digitized as whole slide images (WSIs), these institutional archives can become a valuable external frame of reference, yet searching through these archives is challenging due to the diverse morphology and size of WSIs (3). Digitization has made histomorphology accessible to artificial intelligence (AI), which is advancing from research toward routine diagnostics (4). Neural networks can learn semantically meaningful representations of tissue directly from data, an approach known as deep learning (5, 6). Rather than learning a single task, foundation models (FMs) use self-supervised pre-training on large corpora of slides to learn general-purpose representations that can be used across downstream tasks (7, 8). While training classifiers is a common way to apply such representations, they require enough labelled cases per class to learn a decision boundary
title: Introduction

text: large corpora of slides to learn general-purpose representations that can be used across downstream tasks (7, 8). While training classifiers is a common way to apply such representations, they require enough labelled cases per class to learn a decision boundary and return a label without morphological evidence behind it (9). Content-based retrieval avoids this by returning cases rather than labels (10-12). We built a search engine based on FM representations, letting pathologists query an institutional archive and explore whether current pathology FMs make this viable for rare entities without any task-specific training. We evaluate our approach on salivary gland tumors as a proof-of-concept, a rare and morphologically challenging entity with an incidence of 5.2 per 1,000,000 person-years in Germany (13) and the WHO recognizing 21 malignant types (14), in addition to secondary tumors (15). While some entities cannot be reliably separated by their morphology (16) and new molecular findings continue to carve out new entities (17), initial histological assessment can guide the selection of ancillary testing. An archive of 137 cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories was embedded with four pathology FMs and retrieval was evaluated using queries selected by a pathologist and by a gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) model. text: pathology FMs and retrieval was evaluated using queries selected by a pathologist and by a gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) model. Methods Data We digitized 137 salivary gland tumor cases, totaling 974 hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) WSIs, for our test cohort. For training our ABMIL model, we digitized an additional 15 non-tumor cases, totaling 123 H&E WSIs. All scans were acquired at a native magnification of 40× with a resolution of 0.25 µm/pixel (microns per pixel, (MPP)) using Leica Aperio GT 450 DX scanners. ICD-O codes were sourced through the Zentrum für Krebsregisterdaten at the Robert Koch Institute and through our patient information system. Feature extraction Every WSI was screened for artifacts using GrandQC (18). Tissue was tiled into nonoverlapping 512×512-pixel patches at 20× magnification covering 256×256 µm of tissue (0.5 MPP) using PathoPatcher (19). The patch size was chosen to balance morphological detail against index size (20). Patches had to contain at least 50% artifact-free tissue. No stain normalization was applied.

text: 3 Patch-level features were extracted with four pathology FMs, all Vision Transformers (ViT) pretrained with the DINOv2 self-supervised framework and used here as frozen encoders (21). UNI2h, released under the CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 license, is an open-source model with a custom ViT-H architecture with 681M parameters (24 blocks, 24 heads, SwiGLU feed-forward layers, eight register tokens), pretrained on over 350,000 H&E and immunohistochemistry (IHC) slides from Mass General Brigham (7). Atlas2 along with its distilled versions Atlas2-B and Atlas2-S was used under a research license. Atlas2 is the largest model with ~2 billion parameters pretrained with an adapted DINOv2 recipe on 5,5 million WSI spanning H&E, special stains, and IHC from institutions across Germany and the US (8). To extract the feature vectors each 512×512-pixel patch is resized to a 224×224-pixel RGB image, partitioned into non-overlapping 14×14 pixel tiles, resulting in a sequence of 256 tile tokens, and prepended with a learnable class token (CLS) alongside register tokens (22). This token sequence is passed through the frozen ViT backbone. The tile and register tokens are discarded, and the final layer-normalized CLS embedding z ∈ ℝ^d is taken as the patch descriptor. The dimensions (d) differ by the FM with d = 384 for Atlas2-S, d = 768 for Atlas2-B, d = 1536 for UNI2h, and d = 2048 for Atlas2. ABMIL

ABMIL model To train the gated ABMIL, patch-level features were extracted from tumor positive and negative slides with our standard specifications. Our training data contained 123 negative bags consisting of 294,448 patches and 137 positive bags consisting of 3,158,361 patches. A bag is defined as a matrix H ∈ ℝ^(n×d). For negative bags, n is the number of patches for that slide. For positive bags, n is the number of patches for that case sourced from a varying number of WSIs. To compute patch-level attention weights we use the gated attention formulation (23). Two independent linear projections are applied to H: first, a tanh branch V ∈ ℝ^(d×L), capturing feature relevance; second, a sigmoid branch U ∈ ℝ^(d×L), acting as a gating mechanism to suppress irrelevant patches. These are combined by element-wise multiplication, projected to a scalar attention score per patch via a weight vector, and normalized with softmax across all patches in the bag to yield attention weights aᵢ. The resulting attention-weighted average of patch embeddings forms the bag-level representation M, which is passed through a single linear classifier w
title: Patch-level features were extracted with four pathology FMs, all Vision Transformers (ViT)

text: via a weight vector, and normalized with softmax across all patches in the bag to yield attention weights aᵢ. The resulting attention-weighted average of patch embeddings forms the bag-level representation M, which is passed through a single linear classifier w to produce the bag-level prediction. The same classifier applied to an individual patch embedding hᵢ yields a per-patch tumor score w·hᵢ, and aᵢ (w·hᵢ) is that patch's contribution to the bag-level decision. Under bag-level supervision alone, attention and this per-patch score can decouple, so in addition to the main bag- level binary cross-entropy (BCE) classification loss we optimize two auxiliary losses. The first is an instance-alignment loss: patches are ranked by the detached per-patch score w·h, and the loss is the negative log of the total attention mass placed on the top-k of them, pushing attention onto the patches the classifier itself reads as tumor while leaving the classifier untouched. This inverts CLAM's instance-level supervision, which ranks patches by attention to generate pseudo-labels for a separate instance classifier (24). The second exploits the fact that every patch of a tumor- free case is a confirmed negative instance. For each positive bag, the top-k patches by w·h are compared against m sampled certain negatives: those exceeding the highest-scoring negative are labeled positive, and a BCE loss is applied against the sampled

text: free case is a confirmed negative instance. For each positive bag, the top-k patches by w·h are compared against m sampled certain negatives: those exceeding the highest-scoring negative are labeled positive, and a BCE loss is applied against the sampled negatives as ground truth. If no top-k patch exceeds that bar, the loss falls back to negatives-only. Unlike the alignment term, this loss updates the classifier weights w directly. For both terms, k follows max(8, f·n), where f is a tuned fraction that scales selection with bag size, combined with a fixed floor that prevents degenerate selection on small bags. Attention is detached for negative bags, as a tumor-free label provides no supervisory signal for attention placement. Mild class imbalance is addressed through a weighted random sampler; the positive class weight is set to 1.

text: 4 The following hyperparameters were optimized jointly via Bayesian optimization: attention projection dimension, learning rate, weight decay, dropout rate, and early-stopping patience, along with the loss weights, top-k fraction, and number of sampled negatives for the two auxiliary losses. Validation-set loss was used as the optimization objective; Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was excluded, as it saturated on the small validation split before the model converged. The optimized configuration was then evaluated via five-fold cross- validation. Once the final models were trained, attention weights and per-patch scores were computed across all tumor cases in a single forward pass. Because tumor is spatially contiguous whereas isolated high-scoring patches usually reflect noise, scores were averaged over each patch's 3×3 grid neighborhood before ranking. From these smoothed scores, we reconstructed the top spatially coherent 2×2 (1024×1024-pixel) and 4×4 (2048×2048-pixel) squares per case. FAISS index The database indices were built per FM using FAISS (25). Per-patch embeddings were first concatenated into a single matrix together with a parallel array of patch identifiers for metadata mapping. Each embedding was L2-normalized to unit length so that inner-product equals cosine- similarity. We used an IVFPQ structure, which combines two complementary approximations. First, an inverted file index (IVF) partitions the embedding space into √N Voronoi cells whose centroids are learned by k-means; at query time

text: length so that inner-product equals cosine- similarity. We used an IVFPQ structure, which combines two complementary approximations. First, an inverted file index (IVF) partitions the embedding space into √N Voronoi cells whose centroids are learned by k-means; at query time only the cells nearest a query are scanned, avoiding an exhaustive comparison against every vector. Second, product quantization (PQ) splits each vector's residual from its assigned centroid into M contiguous sub-vectors. Each sub-vector is then replaced by its nearest centroid index from a learned 256-entry subspace codebook. The sub- vector length is held constant at 16 dimensions across all FMs so that quantization granularity remains comparable; M is set accordingly yielding a fixed 64× compression ratio (24 for Atlas2- S, 48 for Atlas2-B, 96 for UNI2h, and 128 for Atlas2). Both the IVF centroids and the PQ codebooks were trained on a random subsample of the corpus (50×√N, >100,000) before the full set was added in batches. Vectors were inserted with sequential integer IDs equal to their row position, so a single metadata array maps each FAISS ID directly to its filename. The scanning MPP defines the physical tissue area

text: its filename. Retrieval A query region is either sourced by our ABMIL model or by a pathologist. For a query, capture magnification and scanning specification (magnification and MPP) need to be specified. The scanning MPP defines the physical tissue area represented by one pixel at the original scan resolution; multiplying it by the ratio of scanning to capture magnification yields the effective tissue-per-pixel of the query image. This ensures that query and database patches represent tissue at the same physical scale prior to embedding. The query region is divided into non-overlapping 512 × 512-pixel patches and embedded by a FM, yielding n descriptors, each L2-normalized to unit length. These n descriptors are pooled adaptively to avoid diluting distinct morphologies while still consolidating redundant ones. If the pairwise cosine similarity is above 0.8 the query is treated as homogeneous and all descriptors are averaged into a single re-normalized query vector. For a heterogeneous query, the descriptors are greedily clustered: proceeding through the descriptors in order, the first seeds a cluster and every remaining within 0.8 cosine similarity of that seed is merged into it, and the cluster mean is re- normalized to a query centroid; the pass repeats until all descriptors are assigned. The number of queries equals the number of clusters formed, between one and the descriptor count. The threshold,

text: 5 Each query vector is searched against the corresponding FAISS index. The closest clusters to the input image are found via k-means. The exact similarity within this cluster is then calculated via inner product similarity. The number of probed Voronoi cells is dynamically set to min(max(200, ⌊clusters/5⌋), 1500), balancing recall against search latency. A patch-level adaptable candidate pool is retrieved per query (default = 150,000). Retrieved patches are grouped by their source case. Each candidate is ranked by a sparse Chamfer score computed only over the patches retrieved. Chamfer distance scores two sets by summing each element's distance to its nearest neighbor in the other set, in both directions. Because patch embeddings are L2-normalized, nearest-neighbor matching under Euclidean distance and under cosine similarity is equivalent. The two principal terms are asymmetric as the numbers of patches per query and retrieved case vary. Thus, we use a normalized forward and backward term. The forward term averages, over query vectors, each query vector's cosine similarity to its single best- matching retrieved patch, measuring whether the case covers the query. The backward term averages, over the retrieved patches, each patch's cosine similarity to its single best-matching query vector, measuring whether the query is supported across the retrieved patches rather than by one coincidental match. text: 6 Results To test whether current pathology FMs allow pathologists to query an institutional archive without task-specific training, we developed the following search engine (Fig. 1). Users can select a region of interest (ROI) in two ways: automatically, using our ABMIL model that identifies the most diagnostically relevant, spatially contiguous region; or manually, by selecting a rectangular ROI of arbitrary size from a WSI, allowing the pathologist to query tissue they consider diagnostically relevant (Fig. 1a). This ROI is divided into non-overlapping patches (Fig. 1b), and each patch is converted by a FM into a numerical representation that captures its visual features (Fig. 1c). These representations let us measure how similar any two patches are to each other. If the patches within the region are highly similar to one another, the region is treated as homogeneous, and the representations are combined into a single representative query. If the patches are dissimilar, the region is treated as heterogeneous: the patches are grouped into subsets of visually similar tissue, and each subset contributes its own representative query (Fig. 1d). This step reduces redundancy from near- duplicate patches while still allowing heterogeneous tissue to be searched. A homogeneous region therefore generates one query, while a heterogeneous region generates several. Each query is then compared against the representations of previously diagnosed archive cases, extracted
title: To test whether current pathology FMs allow pathologists to query an institutional archive

text: redundancy from near- duplicate patches while still allowing heterogeneous tissue to be searched. A homogeneous region therefore generates one query, while a heterogeneous region generates several. Each query is then compared against the representations of previously diagnosed archive cases, extracted in advance using the same FM (Fig. 1e). Matches are scored using our modified Chamfer similarity (Fig. 1f), and the pathologist is shown a ranked list of the most similar archive cases, each labeled with its ICD-O diagnosis. For any retrieved case, the individual patches driving the match can be inspected at their original location within the slide, letting the user verify that the retrieved tissue is genuinely comparable. text: 7 To evaluate our search engine, we used a dataset of 137 primary and secondary salivary gland tumors spanning 12 ICD-O morphologies (Fig. 2). The dataset is imbalanced, with 82% of cases concentrated in five morphologies (Fig. 2a). We excluded entities represented by only a single case but deliberately retained the three morphologies with only two cases for a both statistically and morphologically challenging task (Fig. 2b). While this search engine requires no model training, we wanted to know how well automated sourcing through ABMIL performed for each FM. We therefore sourced the region with the highest average attention at both 2×2- and 4×4-patch sizes (Fig. 2c). Neither the FM used for sourcing, nor the query size produced a relevant difference in retrieval accuracy. Averaged over all 16 configurations, 4×4 queries tended to be slightly better than 2×2 at Top-1 (50.3% vs. 48.3%, p = 0.110) and were essentially identical at Top-3 (64.3% vs. 63.8%, p = 0.691) and Top- 5 (71.5% vs. 71.2%, p = 0.831). As query size was therefore not a performance-driven decision, we selected 4×4 for the remaining analyses, as it corresponds better to the field of view a pathologist typically assesses. text: 8 Next, we examined per-class behavior on the same cohort, using ROIs selected by a pathologist (Fig. 3). Macro-averaged recall at Top-1/3/5 was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2%/66.6%/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B, and 54.4%/65.2%/73.7% for Atlas2-S, without any statistically significant difference between the models at any depth. Performance was not dependent on class size with malignant melanoma and carcinoid tumor, with only two cases each, retrieved correctly by every model at Top-1. Conversely, basal cell adenocarcinoma, also with only two cases, was not retrieved correctly by any model at Top-1 (Fig. 3a). Restricted to classes with at least ten cases, precision and recall were balanced except for adenocarcinoma, which was under-retrieved rather than over-called. F1 was also where the models diverged most: squamous cell carcinoma was essentially model-independent, whereas adenocarcinoma ranged from 0.36 (Atlas2-S) to 0.62 (Atlas2) and mucoepidermoid carcinoma from 0.62 (UNI2h) to 0.78 (Atlas2). Across these five classes, macro-averaged F1 was 76.6% for Altas2, 71.8% for UNI2h, 74.0% for Atlas2-B and 69.0% for Atlas2-S without any statistically significant difference (Fig. 3b). Four of the seven classes with at least five cases achieved above-chance Top-1 and Top-3 retrieval across all four models (p < 0.05), while adenocarcinoma, malignant myoepithelioma, and infiltrating duct carcinoma only tended to exceed chance (Fig. 3c). text: 9 Next, we evaluated the discriminatory power of our search engine. AUC was calculated based on the Top-5 retrieved cases (Fig. 4a). Atlas2 demonstrated a significantly higher AUC (0.754) than its distilled counterparts Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). When analyzing the Chamfer score distributions between correctly and incorrectly retrieved cases, all models showed significant discriminatory power, with larger models outperforming smaller variants (Fig. 4b). Absolute score levels decreased with increasing representation dimensionality within the Atlas family: Atlas2-S produced the highest scores (mean: 1.49) but the weakest retrieval and Atlas2 the lowest scores (mean: 1.34) and the strongest retrieval. Discussion Content-based retrieval with off-the-shelf pathology FMs identified the correct diagnosis among the top five candidates in up to 81.3% of cases, without any task-specific training or manual annotation. This was shown on salivary gland tumors, a rare and diagnostically challenging group, demonstrating that current FMs allow pathologists to find rare entities in institutional archives.

text: 10 effective granularity of retrieval is limited by the granularity of the diagnostic labels as reflected by the comparatively poor performance for adenocarcinoma and the perfect retrieval of two-case entities such as malignant melanoma and carcinoid tumor. Searching histopathological images is computationally and biologically challenging given the size of WSIs, long tail of rare entities, inter-patient heterogeneity, and processing variability. SMILY was one of the first approaches, comparing representations extracted with a convolutional neural network (10). Yottixel and SISH then introduced strategies to reduce a WSI to a small set of representative patches, thereby facilitating search (11, 12). Our design responds to both constraints with a mixed strategy: on the query side, pathologists choose a query region, which is only a fraction of a WSI limiting computational work. As the composition of a WSI is primarily a property of grossing, a small set of representative regions carries most of the diagnostically relevant signal (26). Our split in homogeneous vs. heterogeneous queries still leaves room for intra-tumor heterogeneity (27). On the archive side, we index all artifact-free patches, which evades expert annotation work and avoids the risk of discarding diagnostically decisive regions. Through product quantization and inverted-file structure, the indices can be queried in standard RAM configurations (25). Our modified chamfer similarity is a middle ground between patch-to- patch and WSI-to-WSI

text: annotation work and avoids the risk of discarding diagnostically decisive regions. Through product quantization and inverted-file structure, the indices can be queried in standard RAM configurations (25). Our modified chamfer similarity is a middle ground between patch-to- patch and WSI-to-WSI retrieval, balancing speed and accuracy. Prior AI work on salivary gland histopathology has focused on classification tasks, performing well at benign/malignant discrimination but degrading on histologic subtyping (28, 29). Fitting the correct decision boundaries is limited by the number of examples per class, which becomes increasingly difficult in the long tail of a taxonomy (30) and typically requires manual annotation beyond the routinely encoded ICD-O code (31). While AI decision aids improve accuracy when their output is correct, they reduce it when it is wrong (32), a problem particularly pronounced for ambiguous entities like salivary gland neoplasms where a Dutch series recently reported 8.3% discordance on expert review (33). By presenting the pathologist with a shortlist rather than a single label, our approach may be less prone to this confirmatory anchoring and can guide more effective ancillary testing. A content-based retrieval approach in oral pathology was recently shown to increase diagnostic accuracy, with the largest gains in underrepresented tumor categories (34). Despite evaluating a broad cohort of a rare tumor group, we could not represent its full morphological spectrum. All

text: retrieval approach in oral pathology was recently shown to increase diagnostic accuracy, with the largest gains in underrepresented tumor categories (34). Despite evaluating a broad cohort of a rare tumor group, we could not represent its full morphological spectrum. All cases originate from a single institution, digitized on the same scanners, which limits external validity. Since we use FMs pretrained on multi-institutional data, we expect the approach to transfer well to other institutions and entities. All diagnoses were made by board-certified pathologists, yet they were rendered over a period of years, not reflecting the recently updated ICD-O-4 classification (35). Algorithmically, product quantization and approximate nearest-neighbor search do not guarantee retrieval of the mathematically most similar case, yet this aligns with our approach of providing pathologist with a set of most similar cases. While we regard pathologist-selected query regions as the best way to use our search engine, an automatic WSI-to-WSI mode is available through our ABMIL model. Its lower performance compared with pathologist-selected queries indicates that it does not identify the most relevant query regions, most likely due to limited training data. In summary, we show that pretrained FMs, without further training, can extend an individual pathologist's frame of reference to that of the department. Future work will test whether the tool measurably improves pathologists' performance and how the approach

text: BEYOND THE DOMINANT LABEL: RECOVERING COEXISTING LESION EVIDENCE WITH MULTIPLE INSTANCE LEARNING Lubin Gan1 Jing Zhang2,∗ Xinming Zhang1 Chengpeng Xu1 Siying Wu2 Xiaoyan Sun1,2,∗ 1USTC, Anhui, China 2Anhui Province Key Laboratory of Biomedical Imaging and Intelligent Processing Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center, Anhui, China
title: BEYOND THE DOMINANT LABEL: RECOVERING COEXISTING LESION EVIDENCE

text: Whole-slide images may contain coexisting lesions, yet weak super- vision typically provides only the most severe diagnosis. We formu- late this setting as dominant-label multiple instance learning, where the observed label is the maximum-severity element of a latent le- sion set. Standard multiclass MIL treats it as a complete one-hot description and therefore suppresses lower-severity evidence when- ever it co-occurs with a dominant lesion. We propose DomSet- MIL, a label-aware framework that aligns the annotation mechanism across bag and instance levels. Dominant-Label Censored Likeli- hood models the reported diagnosis without declaring unreported le- sions absent. Severity-Ordered Residual Routing assigns patch ev- idence from high to low severity and preserves residual support for secondary findings, while top-q pooling links local routing scores to bag prediction. Experiments across natural and controlled set- tings show that DomSet-MIL achieves state-of-the-art performance in dominant-label prediction while more effectively recovering latent coexisting-lesion evidence. These findings demonstrate that model- ing the dominant-label mechanism can improve diagnostic predic- tion without sacrificing clinically meaningful secondary findings. Index Terms— multiple instance learning, whole-slide image classification, weak supervision, breast pathology, censored labels

text: Whole-slide images (WSIs) provide a comprehensive view of tissue morphology, but their gigapixel resolution makes dense region-level annotation impractical. Weakly supervised and multiscale systems address this challenge without exhaustive region annotations [1, 2]; multiple instance learning (MIL) [3] represents a WSI as patch em- beddings learned from one slide-level diagnosis. Complementary work on zero-shot subtyping uses fine-grained patch–text alignment to connect local morphology with pathology-aware descriptions, as in FG-PAN [4]. Attention pooling [5] and pathology-specific methods such as CLAM [6] identify discriminative instances, while Transformer aggregators model their dependencies [7]. SemaMIL combines semantic patch reordering with retrieval-guided state space mod- eling [8]. Despite their different aggregation mechanisms, they usually assume the observed bag label is a mutually exclusive class that fully describes the slide, an assumption that may not match multiclass pathology labels. Preserving discriminative information is also studied in graph representation learning. A pathology WSI can contain re- gions with different diagnostic significance [11, 12], yet weak su- pervision may expose only the most severe lesion. The annotation therefore records the maximum severity of a latent lesion set, rather than the set itself: a slide containing malignant and atypical tissue is labeled malignant, so standard softmax treats atypical as an in- correct bag label. Across such cases, unreported secondary lesions become structural false negatives; lower-severity labels are censored whenever they co-occur with a more severe finding, and changing the aggregator cannot remove supervision introduced by this anno- tation rule. Recent work incorporates diagnostic severity into multiclass MIL. PAMS organizes classes hierarchically, penalizes clinically costly underestimation, and mixes features across priorities [13], but still targets only the final diagnosis, so lower-severity evidence need not remain positive. Multi-instance multi-label methods predict co- existing breast lesions but assume multiple diagnoses are observed during training [11]. Learning from a single positive label relaxes that assumption by leaving other labels unknown [14], yet generic missing-label objectives neither explain why one label was selected nor link bag-level presence to localized evidence. This gap calls for explicit modeling of the dominant-label annotation mechanism. We propose DomSet-MIL, a label-aware framework that pre- dicts the dominant diagnosis while preserving evidence for hidden lesions. At the bag level, Dominant-Label Censored Likelihood (DCL) converts a malignant presence gate and a residual atypi- cal gate into three observed class probabilities via the annotation’s maximum-severity rule; a malignant label supervises malignant presence without declaring atypical absence. Overview of DomSet-MIL: SORR routes patch evidence in severity order, and DCL predicts the dominant label. Severity-Ordered Residual Routing (SORR) applies the rule in descending severity: a malignant gate claims matching patches, an atypical gate processes residual evidence, and unclaimed mass forms the benign remainder. Top-q pooling connects these severity-specific patch assignments to DCL’s censored bag scores. The two compo- nents therefore impose the same severity-ordered factorization at complementary resolutions. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We identify lower-severity lesions as structurally censored under dominant-label supervision, explaining their suppression as negative classes. (2) We introduce DomSet-MIL, coupling DCL with SORR to align latent evidence at bag and patch levels. (3) We evaluate dominant-label prediction and latent-lesion recovery on BRACS [12], with test-time ROI annota- tions and on controlled EBRAINS/TCGA mixed-bag benchmarks. 2. METHOD 2.1. Datasets and evaluation protocol Spatial–semantic consistency is studied in multi-contrast MRI super- resolution by SSCM [22]. Our evaluation focuses on histopathology and assesses both slide-level predictions and localized lesion evi- dence. BRACS. BRACS contains 547 breast WSIs from 189 pa- tients and provides both slide labels and labeled regions of interest (ROIs) [12]. We use its official patient-disjoint split of 395/67/85 WSIs for training, validation, and testing. Following the official coarse task, normal, pathological benign, and usual ductal hyperpla- sia are grouped as benign; flat epithelial atypia and atypical ductal hyperplasia as atypical; and ductal carcinoma in situ and invasive carcinoma as malignant. This mapping gives the order B ≺A ≺M used in Sec. 2. Training and model selection use only the coarse WSI label. ROI labels are reserved for the test-time evidence analysis below. Controlled mixed-bag tasks. We complement the natural BRACS setting with three controlled tasks for which the latent con- tents of each bag are known by construction. text: We identify a fundamental mismatch in conventional multiclass MIL: a diagnosis reporting only the most severe lesion censors coexisting lower-severity findings, which standard training treats as negatives. DomSet-MIL addresses this mismatch by coupling DCL with SORR and top-q pooling, aligning dominant-label su- pervision with severity-ordered patch evidence. Across natural and controlled settings, it improves dominant-label prediction and latent or localized secondary-lesion recovery, while ablations support the complementary roles of censored supervision, residual routing, and sparse pooling. These results show that modeling the weak-label generation process enables richer pathological representations from slide-level annotations. Future work will consider partially ordered, data-dependent, and uncertain label mechanisms, as well as whether biomedical knowledge-guided prompts, such as those explored in MeDKCoOp [43], can support lesion-specific evidence learning.

text: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis Ting Liu1,2 Haoran Lai1,2 HaobinChen1,2 Ming Liu1,2 S Kevin Zhou1,2 1School of Biomedical Engineering, Division of Life Sciences and Medicine, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, Anhui, 230026, P.R. China 2Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research, University of Science and Technology of China, Suzhou, Jiangsu, 215123, P.R. China
title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule

text: Contrastive vision–language pre-training supports zero- shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image–report pair in a batch as a neg- ative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic in- compatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not estab- lish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We there- fore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learn- ing (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity dis- tributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statis- tics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable stu- dent, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of 0.850, com- pared with 0.837 for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.
title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule

text: Vision–language pre-training (VLP) has emerged as a promising paradigm for zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis. By aligning radiographs with their free-text reports, VLP models learn joint representations that can be queried with disease prompts at inference without requiring task-specific annotations [12, 27, 37]. Most medical VLP approaches optimize a batch-wise contrastive objective [23, 25]: within a mini-batch of B image–report pairs, matched pairs are treated as positives, whereas all off-diagonal pairs are treated as negatives. text: This assumption is particularly fragile in radiology, where reports from different patients frequently describe overlapping findings using similar or interchangeable ex- pressions. As illustrated in Figure 1(a), the two batch items underlying an unmatched image–report candidate may share the same report-derived finding set. At a mini-batch size of 256, an exact corpus-level calcula- tion under uniform random batching estimates that 66.8% of pathology-positive anchors would encounter at least one cross-patient batch mate with an identical CheXpert present-label set, with 2.78 such matches per anchor on av- erage (Figure 1(b)). A related enrichment appears in the recorded online masking decisions. Within the trace pre- fix ending at the best checkpoint, the inclusive rule used in the trace—which masks an off-diagonal pair when ei- ther the corresponding image–image or report–report sim- ilarity exceeds its modality-specific adaptive threshold— flags pair-observations with 3.96% exact present-label-set agreement, compared with 1.83% across all eligible pair- observations. Here, eligibility requires different patients and at least one positive label among the 12 pathology findings in each report; exact agreement is then evaluated over all 14 labels. The resulting 2.16× enrichment remains above one throughout five consecutive training windows (Figure 1(c)). Although exact CheXpert present-label-set agreement does not establish clinical equivalence, its en- richment among flagged pair-observations suggests that this subset may contain a higher proportion of semantically compatible pairs. Consequently, semantically compatible pairs may still receive negative contrastive targets, giving rise to false-negative supervision. Such false negatives are known to degrade generic contrastive learning [5, 7]. We refer to this mismatch between semantic compatibility and the assigned contrastive target as a semantic conflict. Prior work has attempted to mitigate false negatives by incorporating external clinical knowledge [19, 30], mining additional positive pairs from report- or study-level seman- tics [20, 21, 33], or softly reweighting suspected false neg- atives during optimization [15, 18]. Despite their effective- ness, two gaps remain. Detection: rules based on single- modality evidence or fixed, globally normalized similarity thresholds can become miscalibrated as modality-specific similarity distributions shift during representation learning. Optimization: additional positive mining may promote par- tial semantic compatibility to full equivalence, whereas soft reweighting still allows suspected false negatives to exert residual repulsive gradients unless their weights become ex- actly zero. An effective solution must therefore identify semantic conflicts adaptively and prevent them from be- ing pushed apart without indiscriminately relabeling them as positives. To address both gaps, we propose Semantic-Conflict- Aware Contrastive

text: gradients unless their weights become ex- actly zero. An effective solution must therefore identify semantic conflicts adaptively and prevent them from be- ing pushed apart without indiscriminately relabeling them as positives. To address both gaps, we propose Semantic-Conflict- Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which dynamically flags potential semantic-conflict candidates using evidence from both modalities and removes them through adap- tive hard masking. For detection, SCCL maintains sepa- rate exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics for intra- batch image–image and report–report similarities, allow- ing each threshold to track its modality-specific distribu- tion as training evolves. Flagged candidates are excluded from contrastive normalization, eliminating their probabil- ity mass and repulsive gradients rather than treating them as additional positives. To account for uncertainty in the modality-specific intra-modal cues, we instantiate two rule- specific teachers: an inclusive (OR) teacher that accepts ev- idence from either modality to increase candidate coverage, and a consensus (AND) teacher that requires agreement be- tween both modality-specific cues for more conservative selection. Standard distillation then consolidates the two teachers’ cross-modal rankings into the single deployable student SCCL-DT. SCCL thus adapts candidate selection to evolving similarity distributions while explicitly preventing flagged candidates from being optimized as negatives.
