Beyond these advances in broader data utilization, stronger encoders, knowledge integra- tion, or finer-grained alignment, SCCL addresses a distinct source of supervision error: treating semantically compati- ble off-diagonal pairs as negatives. 2.2. False negatives in contrastive learning Instance-discrimination objectives treat unmatched samples as negatives, so semantically compatible pairs may receive repulsive gradients [4, 10, 23, 32]. Unlike valid hard negatives, false negatives should not be repelled. Prior work addresses this issue through distribution correction, hard-negative mining, progressive false-negative removal, or hardness scheduling [5, 7, 15, 26]. Medical VLP methods instead exploit clinical knowl- edge or report semantics. MedCLIP and MLIP construct knowledge-guided targets [19, 30]; SAT, SENSE, and FaNe use report- or study-level similarity to mine or reweight pairs [20, 21, 33]; and SAHN separates hard from false neg- atives using
title: Stage I · Rule-Specific Teacher Training

text: clinical knowl- edge or report semantics. MedCLIP and MLIP construct knowledge-guided targets [19, 30]; SAT, SENSE, and FaNe use report- or study-level similarity to mine or reweight pairs [20, 21, 33]; and SAHN separates hard from false neg- atives using embedding and semantic similarity [18]. SCCL differs by applying modality-specific adaptive thresholds, hard-masking selected pairs without relabeling them, and distilling its rule-specific teachers into one student. 2.3. Knowledge distillation Knowledge distillation transfers predictive distributions from a teacher to a student, commonly to compress a model or retain teacher behavior in a more deployment-efficient network [11]. Deep mutual learning extends this idea to online peer supervision [36], while ALBEF uses a momen- tum teacher to provide stable targets for noisy image–text alignment [17]. These formulations differ in teacher con- struction but use distillation to transfer or stabilize predic- tive behavior. In SCCL, standard distillation consolidates two rule-specific teachers—an inclusive teacher and a con- sensus teacher—into a single student for efficient inference.

Setup Implementation details. Our implementation builds on CARZero [16], which serves as the unmasked Base model. We pre-train on frontal AP/PA MIMIC-CXR images with usable reports [14]. Available report fields are concate- nated and truncated or padded to 97 tokens. Images are resized and zero-padded to 256×256, cropped to 224×224, and augmented with random horizontal flips, affine trans- formations, and brightness/contrast jitter. Each run uses

text: reports [14]. Available report fields are concate- nated and truncated or padded to 97 tokens. Images are resized and zero-padded to 256×256, cropped to 224×224, and augmented with random horizontal flips, affine trans- formations, and brightness/contrast jitter. Each run uses a ViT-B/16 image encoder initialized from M3AE [6, 9] and a BioClinical BERT text encoder [1]. Teachers use k=2.0, m=0.99, and Tw=500, and are optimized with Adam (learning rate 5×10−5, weight decay 10−6). We halve the learning rate after five validation epochs without improvement, early-stop after ten, and select the lowest- loss checkpoint. The student is trained for six epochs with Adam at 10−5, using the same weight decay and scheduler and τd=2.0. All training runs are conducted on NVIDIA A800 GPUs. The masking operator itself maintains only four scalar EMA states and adds no trainable weights. The complete two-stage protocol nevertheless trains two rule- specific teachers and one student under supervision from the two frozen teachers; only the student is retained for in- ference. title: Design choice

text: Standard contrastive pre-training treats all off-diagonal image–report pairs as negatives, which can introduce se- mantic conflicts when reports share findings. We pro- posed Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which uses modality-specific adaptive thresholds to identify candidate conflicts and removes them from con- trastive normalization without relabeling them as positives. Distillation consolidates the resulting rule-specific super- vision into a single deployable model. The online mask is enriched for report-derived finding agreement, provid- ing proxy evidence for the selection mechanism rather than pair-level clinical adjudication. Across five public 8
title: Design choice

text: benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves the highest mean zero- shot AUC among the evaluated methods (0.850 vs. 0.837) and the highest mean ChestXDet10 Pointing Game accu- racy (0.583). Together, these results support adaptive con- flict removal as an effective alternative to indiscriminate negative supervision under the evaluated settings. Future work should clinically adjudicate candidate pairs, study calibration across batch sizes and domains, and ex- tend adaptive detection to local region–token alignment and other medical imaging modalities.

text: Supplementary Material This supplement documents the data and evaluation scope, the Stage-II student-distillation objective, the Pointing Game evaluation protocol, implementation-level defini- tions of the Two-tier, count-matched Random, and Soft- weighting ablations, the candidate-set analysis, and the fail- ure mode observed for low fixed thresholds. The descrip- tions below distinguish the proposed SCCL components from dataset and evaluation choices that remain fixed across all model variants. A. Data and Evaluation Scope A.1. Pre-training data We pre-train on frontal AP/PA MIMIC-CXR images with usable report content, using the archived training and vali- dation manifests and report filters associated with the Base implementation. The same manifests, filters, and data- loading configuration are used for the Base model, both rule-specific teachers, and the distilled student. SCCL changes the treatment of candidate negatives during pre- training; it does not redefine the dataset partition or report selection. A.2. Downstream evaluation scope We use the same five zero-shot evaluation sets and target- label mappings as in the main paper: Open-I [8]; the radiologist-annotated subset of PadChest [3]; the offi- cial NIH test split of ChestX-ray14 [29]; the CheXpert test set of 500 studies from 500 patients, evaluated on the five competition observations [13]; and the official ChestXDet10 test split with box annotations for ten find- ings [22]. ChestXDet10 is used for both zero-shot classi- fication and grounding;

text: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling in Diffusion Language Models Ya-Shi Zhang1,2,†, Jian Tang2,3, Pierre-André Noël1, Oleksiy Ostapenko1 1ServiceNow AI Research, 2Mila - Quebec AI Institute, 3HEC Montréal †Work done at ServiceNow Masked diffusion language models expose an inference-time choice: which positions become visible after each denoising pass. Many existing decoding methods use hand-designed rules or require visibility to grow monotonically. We present a Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling (TIPS), an approximately 600K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the underlying language model frozen. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to select which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction. We train the controller through supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants achieve 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of 32 decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline in our main comparison by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points, respectively. Both variants are trained at a budget of 32 evaluations and remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining. These results demonstrate that learning when to reveal and reconsider tokens can improve the accuracy–compute trade-off without updating the decoder backbone. Correspondence: ya-shi.zhang@mila.quebec 1
title: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy

text: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses by predicting unresolved positions in parallel and exposing selected predictions as context (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025). This flexibility creates a decoding problem: under a limited number of denoising passes, a sampler must decide which predictions to commit and whether earlier commitments should be reconsidered. Revealing more positions makes faster progress toward a complete response, but those predictions also condition subsequent generations. An early commitment can therefore influence later predictions even after the surrounding context changes. The resulting visibility trajectory—which tokens become context, when they appear, and whether they can be revised—is an important component of the accuracy–compute trade-off (Kim et al., 2025a). We study how to learn this trajectory while leaving the pretrained token model unchanged. Existing methods address different parts of this problem. Confidence-based and uncertainty-aware samplers select positions using hand-designed rules (Wu et al., 2026; Ben-Hamu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a). Learned unmasking policies instead optimize position selection around a frozen denoiser, but typically preserve monotonic visibility: once a token is exposed, the policy cannot withdraw it (Jazbec et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026a). Conversely, remasking methods allow revision through prescribed transitions or heuristic criteria (Wang et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026b; Zhai et al., 2026), while other approaches
title: TIPS: A Tiny Inference-time Policy

text: withdraw it (Jazbec et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026a). Conversely, remasking methods allow revision through prescribed transitions or heuristic criteria (Wang et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026b; Zhai et al., 2026), while other approaches learn remasking behavior by updating the language model itself (Huang et al., 2026b). These developments motivate a complementary question: can a small auxiliary policy learn both commitment and revision without modifying the dLLM? We introduce Tiny Inference-time Policy for Scaling (TIPS), an approximately 600K-parameter controller assigning to each response position a binary next-step visibility action. At masked positions, the action reveals the decoder’s proposal or leaves the position masked; at visible positions, it retains the current token or remasks it for subsequent regeneration. A two-layer transformer predicts visibility preferences from confidence 1 arXiv:2610.22099v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026

text: features, mask indicators, and normalized decoding time. TIPS separates decoding order from pace. A fixed power-law schedule specifies the expected visible fraction, while a shared shift of the policy logits matches this target without changing the policy’s relative preferences. Thus, the expected amount of context grows according to the schedule even as individual commitments remain reversible. Our training recipe first provides dense, reference-derived supervision of visibility decisions, then optimizes final-answer correctness through group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024). Only the auxiliary controller is updated in either stage; training requires neither gradients through the dLLM nor its sequence likelihood. The same visibility-control formulation applies to full-canvas and semi-autoregressive decoding (section 3). We summarize our contributions as follows: • We introduce TIPS, an approximately 600K-parameter policy that learns both unmasking and remasking while keeping the dLLM backbone frozen. • We instantiate TIPS with full-canvas and blockwise decoding on LLaDA-8B-Instruct. At most decoder NFE budgets, we surpass previous state-of-the-art methods in accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500 by up to 13.25 percentage points, otherwise remaining competitive. • We investigate how TIPS uses commitment and revision through ablations and other supplementary experiments. These analyses highlight the importance of remasking, suggesting its benefits are not only token replacement, but also temporarily withdrawing harmful context. Under this restriction, tokens that are already unmasked can no longer be modified. Re-masking and editing methods remove this monotonicity constraint, allowing an earlier prediction to return to the masked state or directly transition to another vocabulary token after the surrounding context changes. Hence, masked-diffusion inference separates two choices: what token to place, and which positions should be visible. The first choice is supplied by the dLLM backbone. These logits determine which positions are preferred while also allowing an external unmasking schedule to control how many positions become visible. Scheduled visibility. We observe in appendix B.2.5 a network that is free to determine the total visible fraction leads to a lazy strategy we hereafter refer to as finalization deferral: keeping most positions masked until the final forward pass, where all are unmasked at once. This prevents the decoder from conditioning on progressively richer contexts, and leads to worse task performance. Therefore, we introduce a scalar shift to the output logits so that the adjusted logits adhere to the schedule in expectation. For normalized decoding time τ ∈[0, 1], define the family κ(τ) = τ exp(γ), γ ∈R. For γ > 0, the curve is convex: visibility grows slowly at first and more rapidly toward the end of decoding. For γ < 0, it is concave, exposing more tokens early; γ = 0 recovers a linear schedule. In all cases, κ(0) = 0 and κ(1) = 1, corresponding to completely masked and completely unmasked states at the beginning and end of decoding, respectively. text: how many positions to reveal at each pass, selecting their identities using decoder statistics. LLaDA uses confidence-ranked unmasking by default (Nie et al., 2025). More structured approaches spread reveals across dilated position groups or compare short candidate decoding paths before committing tokens (Luxembourg et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). Adaptive-parallelism methods include Fast-dLLM, which combines confidence- thresholded decoding with approximate block-wise KV caching (Wu et al., 2026), and EB-Sampler, which dynamically reveals multiple positions subject to an entropy-based error tolerance (Ben-Hamu et al., 2025). Other methods refine the selection criterion: UNCODE/PC-Sampler calibrates uncertainty scores using position- and token-informativeness priors (Huang et al., 2026a); KLASS incorporates the temporal KL stability of token distributions (Kim et al., 2025b); and DAPD uses a self-attention-derived dependency graph to select weakly coupled positions for parallel decoding (Kim et al., 2026). Learned unmasking schedules. A closely related line of work learns a controller around a pretrained denoiser. Jazbec et al. (2026) formulate masked-diffusion sampling as a Markov decision process and use reinforcement learning to train a one-layer transformer that maps decoder confidences to monotonic unmasking decisions. Their transitions preserve already visible tokens, whereas TIPS extends the action semantics to reversible next-step visibility. Where-to-Unmask trains a supervised ranker to imitate a ground-truth probability-margin oracle (Asano et al., 2026). Adaptive Order Policies reweight masked-diffusion loss terms by policy probabilities to favor positions at which the denoiser is likely to be correct, considering both frozen-denoiser and joint-training settings (Mohamud et al., 2026). Self-Aware Scheduling (SAS) derives a dense trajectory reward from a bound on sequential decoding mismatch and trains an order policy with group-relative policy optimization while keeping the denoiser fixed (Xu et al., 2026). UPO similarly learns a stochastic position-selection policy for a frozen masked diffusion model, using a KL-regularized, GRPO-style objective around an explicit heuristic reference policy (Hong et al., 2026a). Its actions select only currently masked positions, preserving monotonicity. Re-masking and revision. Re-masking methods relax monotonicity by allowing earlier token commitments to be withdrawn. P2 and ReMDM allow visible positions to return to the mask state and be regenerated, with ReMDM deriving its sampler from a discrete diffusion process with a custom reverse transition (Peng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Running Confidence Remasking (RCR), introduced alongside MDPO, revisits positions with poor running confidence (He et al., 2025). WINO uses a training-free parallel draft-and-verify procedure to reveal candidates and re-mask suspicious visible tokens (Hong

WINO uses a training-free parallel draft-and-verify procedure to reveal candidates and re-mask suspicious visible tokens (Hong et al., 2026b), while CoRe identifies revision targets by testing prediction stability under masked-context perturbations (Zhai et al., 2026). These approaches prescribe revision rules rather than learning a separate visibility controller. RemeDi instead modifies the language model to jointly predict tokens and confidence scores, then trains its re-masking behavior through supervised and reinforcement-learning stages (Huang et al., 2026b). TIPS also uses a supervised warmup phase followed by reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning for diffusion language models. Policy optimization has also been applied directly to the dLLM. MDPO updates the masked token model along progressive denoising trajectories using intermediate rewards (He et al., 2025); mask-aware policy gradients account for both token and masking decisions (Raajesh et al., 2026); and SPG constructs upper- and lower-bound surrogates for the otherwise intractable sequence log-likelihood (Wang et al., 2026). TIPS instead applies policy gradients only to its auxiliary Bernoulli visibility policy, hence training requires neither sequence likelihood nor updates to decoder parameters. 6 Discussion We introduced TIPS, a small policy that learns unmasking and remasking around a frozen dLLM, separating visibility control from token prediction while

text: its auxiliary Bernoulli visibility policy, hence training requires neither sequence likelihood nor updates to decoder parameters. 6 Discussion We introduced TIPS, a small policy that learns unmasking and remasking around a frozen dLLM, separating visibility control from token prediction while a fixed schedule regulates expected progress. On GSM8K and MATH-500, TIPS improves low- and moderate-budget accuracy and remains competitive at higher budgets without retraining; full-canvas and blockwise variants offer complementary strengths. Ablations, corruption recovery, heuristic-prefix handoffs, remasking and editing statistics, and transfer experiments highlight the value of warmup and remasking, suggest that revision may help by withdrawing harmful context rather than only replacing tokens, and reveal transferable but domain-dependent behavior. 9

text: Limitations. Our evaluation centers on 256-token mathematical reasoning, and the supplementary transfer experiments use a single seed; longer generations and broader task coverage remain important tests of generality. TIPS also uses a fixed decoding horizon rather than an adaptive stopping rule, preserving further revision but foregoing savings from early termination. Developing stopping criteria that account for possible future revisions, and evaluating the resulting accuracy–latency trade-off, are important directions for future work. Decoder-call budgets also do not directly capture wall-clock cost.

(13) This is a least-squares projection of the pilot’s empirical schedule onto a continuous, monotone family with κγ(0) = 0 and κγ(1) = 1. The policy observes the current time t/Tfit, but the fit uses the next-state time (t+1)/Tfit. We exclude deterministic finalization because its full visibility is imposed by the decoding algorithm. The fit uses neither reference answers nor correctness labels for the validation prompts. We then fix bγ during subsequent calibrated policy training and evaluate the same normalized schedule at other inference budgets. The pilot supplies the schedule shape; it is not the final calibrated policy. For blockwise decoding, we apply the same procedure to the active block, using its length and local decoder-call budget in place of L and Tfit. We average the expected visible fractions over validation trajectories and blocks at matching local times, exclude each block’s deterministic finalization, and fit one shared γ for that decoding geometry. A.2 Fast-dLLM budget matching For a target budget T, we tune the confidence-decoding threshold using test-set rollouts until the average NFE lies in [T, T + 0.5]. The one-sided tolerance gives the baseline up to 0.5 additional decoder calls on average. 12

B.2.1 Supervised warmup and reinforcement learning We compare the complete supervised warmup–RLVR recipe with its supervised parent and a policy trained with RLVR alone. The RLVR-trained policies use the same 935-update continuation length, while the warmup-only policy receives no RLVR updates. As shown in Table 5 and Figure 3, both stages contribute to the final performance. Warmup followed by RLVR improves over warmup alone by 14.55, 17.87, and 14.45 percentage points at T = 16, 32, 64, respectively. Warmup also provides a useful initialization for RLVR: although the gain over RLVR alone is only 0.49 points at T = 16, it increases to 8.50 and 7.81 points at T = 32 and 64. Thus, the supervised policy is not simply sufficient on its own; supervised initialization and terminal-reward optimization complement one another. B.2.2 The contribution of remasking To separate dependence on an already learned behavior from the value of the action space itself, we evaluate two controls. The first disables remasking at inference for the frozen reference policy. The second retrains a monotone policy with supervised warmup and RLVR. In both cases, visible tokens retain their identities, and only masked positions can become newly visible.

B.2.3 Visibility-consistent confidence features At an already visible position, the policy controls whether the current token remains in context, rather than whether the decoder’s newly preferred token should be inserted. A global-top-1 confidence can consequently describe the wrong token. When analyzing our trajectories, the global argmax differed from the visible token in 73,930 of 3,407,617 recorded visible-position events, or 2.17%. This observation motivates anchoring the first feature to the current visible token and excluding that token when constructing the strongest alternative. While not necessarily an ablation, we believe that ensuring the policy inputs remain consistent with the current decoding state is important for the semantic correctness of our method. B.2.5 Occupancy control and finalization deferral We revisit an earlier RLVR-only comparison of single-layer policies with one 256-token response canvas, T = 32 decoder calls, and three training seeds. Policies are trained with no occupancy constraint, a soft schedule loss, or fixed power-law calibration, while retaining reversible actions and deterministic finalization. The soft schedule loss imposes a penalty that is multiplied against the binary terminal correctness reward. Specifically, if, by the finalization pass, the state has masked fraction m ∈[0, 1], then the assigned terminal correctness reward is multiplied by (1 −m). For example, if the response is correct but only 50% of the canvas was unmasked by the finalization pass, the reward becomes 0.5 for that trajectory. Figure 5 shows that the uncalibrated trajectory levels off before the final call. After the last learned transition, 57.11% of positions remain masked, versus 48.01% with the soft loss and 6.89% with fixed calibration (Table 7). The subsequent jump is imposed by deterministic completion, not learned visibility decisions: this is finalization deferral. We find the soft schedule loss, while non-constraining, insufficient for alleviating the finalization deferral phenomenon. B.3.3 Remasking is more frequent than token editing We distinguish a remasking event from a completed token edit. A remasking episode starts when a visible token becomes masked and ends when that position next becomes visible; it is an edit only if the returning token differs from the original. Table 18 reports remasking under four denominators, preventing trajectory-level incidence from being confused with a per-position rate. Every observed trajectory contains at least one remask, but the fraction of visible position-opportunities that are remasked is approximately 18% for the full-canvas policy and 31–38% for the block policy. Most remasking episodes do not change token identity. Across the measured budgets, 91.52–95.17% of full-canvas episodes and 92.91–98.16% of blockwise episodes return the original token. Every recorded episode resolves by the end of decoding, and the mean delay before re-reveal is 2.25–3.13 calls for full-canvas decoding and 1.20–1.41 calls for blockwise decoding (Table 19). Thus, remasking often temporarily withdraws context rather than replacing its content. Together

text: B.3.5 Repairing completed non-adjusted Fast-dLLM responses We next test whether TIPS can improve responses that another sampler has already completed, rather than continue a partially decoded trajectory. We first run non-adjusted Fast-dLLM on frozen LLaDA-8B-Instruct with 8 × 32 decoding, confidence threshold 0.9, no caching, and a global cap of 256 decoder calls. We then apply the frozen TIPSfull policy to every completed 256-token canvas on the full GSM8K and MATH-500 test sets, using exactly four additional decoder evaluations. Repair retains the native schedule and follows the final four calls of a virtual 32-call horizon: three policy transitions receive normalized times 28/32, 29/32, and 30/32, with next-state visibility targets ((t + 1)/32)exp(γfull) for t ∈{28, 29, 30}, followed by deterministic finalization. The decoder and policy remain frozen, and correctness feedback is used only for scoring. As shown in Table 22 and Figure 14, micro-accuracy increases from 67.01% to 67.29%, a gain of 0.27 percentage points. TIPS corrects five of the 600 initially incorrect answers—four on GSM8K and one on MATH-500—while all 1,219 initially correct answers remain correct. This single-seed result shows a modest improvement from revisiting completed responses, extending revision beyond unfinished trajectories. text: B.4.3 Training TIPS for coding We separately train full-canvas and blockwise policies for coding while keeping the decoder frozen, using supervised warmup followed by an RLVR continuation to the fixed 935-update endpoint. Table 25 compares these policies with the same five baselines, so changes relative to the zero-shot table reflect the policy’s domain adaptation. Coding training improves the full-canvas policy in every measured dataset–budget condition. Its HumanEval pass@1 increases to 19.51%, 25.61%, and 27.44%, while its MBPP score increases to 24.00%, 31.80%, and 37.80%. The largest gains over the corresponding math-trained full-canvas policy occur on MBPP, reaching 13.40 percentage points at T = 16. The coding-trained full policy exceeds every retained baseline on HumanEval at T = 16 and on MBPP at T = 16 and 32. Nevertheless, Non-adjusted Fast-dLLM with 8 × 32 decoding remains stronger on HumanEval at T = 32 and 64, and slightly stronger on MBPP at T = 64. The block policy responds less consistently to coding training: it improves at T = 16 on both tasks but falls below its zero-shot counterpart at T = 64. These results support domain-specific policy training, especially for full-canvas decoding, while leaving room for a coding-specific recipe and hyperparameter study. text: C Experimental and implementation details This section specifies the architecture, numerical implementation, and training procedure for the mathematical- reasoning checkpoints used in the main comparison. We distinguish the full-canvas policy, TIPSfull, from the two-block policy, TIPSblock, while identifying the supervised initialization shared by the two variants. Evaluation populations, compute accounting, and statistical summaries are specified in appendix D. C.1 Frozen decoder and policy architecture We use the frozen LLaDA-8B-Instruct decoder (Nie et al., 2025), identified as GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct. Only the visibility controller is optimized: decoder parameters are excluded from the optimizer, and the recorded decoder weights remain unchanged throughout training. The controller is a two-layer RoPE-DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023; Su et al., 2024) with hidden width 128, two attention heads per layer, and feed-forward width 512. A linear projection maps each two-dimensional confidence feature to the hidden width. A 128-dimensional sinusoidal time embedding is processed by a two-layer multilayer perceptron with SiLU activation, and a learned two-state embedding distinguishes masked from visible positions. The DiT layers use time- and state-conditioned adaptive layer normalization, bidirectional self-attention over response-position inputs, and GELU feed-forward activations. Rotary position embeddings are applied to attention queries and keys, with base 10,000. A final layer normalization and scalar projection produce one visibility logit per position. We use zero dropout and no separate conditioning on the absolute decoding

text: All position-wise visibility decisions are applied synchronously. A newly revealed position receives its proposal from the pre-transition decoder evaluation; a visible position selected to remain visible retains its existing token, even when the decoder now prefers another token. At deterministic finalization, one fresh decoder evaluation fills the remaining masks greedily and leaves already visible tokens unchanged. This finalization does not invoke the policy or contribute an action likelihood. Block-local execution. The saved policies use different time inputs: TIPSfull receives j/H, whereas TIPSblock receives (j + 1)/H, with the clock reset at each block. We preserve these checkpoint-specific conventions during evaluation. text: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model’s next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after = in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher’s model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates

Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.

text: Byte-level models avoid a fixed tokenizer by working on raw bytes and recover eﬀiciency by grouping bytes into variable-length patches [Pagnoni et al., 2025, Slagle, 2024, Hwang et al., 2026]. In BLT [Pagnoni et al., 2025], a small byte-level language model estimates the entropy of each next byte, a patch starts where that entropy crosses a threshold, and the large global transformer runs once per patch. The guiding principle, shared by later work, is that compute should go where prediction is hard: Scratchpad Patching triggers extra global steps by next-byte entropy [Zheng et al., 2026], and SOMBRERO trains learned chunkers to place boundaries on high-surprisal bytes [Neitemeier et al., 2026]. Earlier work identified a blind spot in this principle [Vera Zúñiga, 2026]. At a computed result, such as the number after 16 - 3 - 4 =, the next byte is a digit whose value requires computation over context the local model cannot see, yet the byte does not look unusually surprising to the small patcher. That work proposed boundary dependence, a table of how much the model’s own loss rises when a patch start is removed, as a label-free fix. Here we take a different, cheaper route, motivated by compression. An LZ77 compressor [Ziv and Lempel, 1977] encodes text as copies of earlier substrings plus new literals: copies are cheap, and new literals are where information enters. We ask whether patch boundaries belong where the compressor would stop copying. Novelty patching starts a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the last 128 bytes, predicted from the previous two bytes by a lookup table fitted on raw text in seconds. It needs no labels, no reference model and no losses, and at inference it costs a table lookup. Our contributions: 1. A strong, scale-dependent effect in math. In BLT-style models trained from scratch at 1M, 12M and 50M parameters on the same corpus and patch rate (3 seeds each), novelty patching has no effect at 1M, a clear effect at 12M and a large one at 50M: computed results 57.5% vs 20.7% for entropy, final answers 89.5% vs 59.9%. text: Patching rules. BLT [Pagnoni et al., 2025] uses a global entropy threshold (and an approxi- mate monotonic variant); entropy spikes as boundaries go back to dynamic pooling [Nawrot et al., 2023]. SpaceByte [Slagle, 2024] patches at word boundaries; H-Net [Hwang et al., 2026], AU-Net [Videau et al., 2025], MrT5 [Kallini et al., 2024] and ByteSpan [Goriely et al., 2025] learn or derive boundaries in other ways. Scratchpad Patching [Zheng et al., 2026] adds entropy-triggered global steps inside fixed patches, Fast BLT [Kallini et al., 2026] speeds up decoding, and EntropyMoE [Liu et al., 2026] routes patches to experts by entropy. Haltiuk [Haltiuk, 2026] argues that the boundary distribution can be changed nearly independently of language modeling. Boundaries and surprisal. SOMBRERO [Neitemeier et al., 2026] defines boundary enrichment, the mean surprisal at chunk starts relative to all bytes, and trains a hierarchical byte model to raise it; it reports bits per byte (including math and code) and log-likelihood downstream tasks at 1B scale, but not accuracy on computed values. ByteFlow [Deng et al., 2026] selects boundaries by the marginal coding-rate gain of the encoder’s latent states, a learned, latent notion of new information, and reports that it beats an entropy criterion inside its architecture on bits per byte and commonsense tasks. Our results are consistent with ByteFlow’s direction and quantify it

Method and setup Novelty. For a byte stream 𝑏, let 𝑚𝑡be the length of the longest prefix of 𝑏𝑡∶that also starts within the previous 128 bytes (capped at 16). Novelty is −𝑚𝑡: high when the upcoming bytes do not repeat recent context. Novelty depends on future bytes, so it cannot be used directly; we predict it causally. The novelty table averages −𝑚𝑡over each preceding two-byte context (𝑏𝑡−2, 𝑏𝑡−1) in a 4 MB sample of training text (falling back to one byte, then the global mean, for contexts seen fewer than 20 times). text: Where should a byte-level model spend its global compute? The prevailing answer, where the next byte is hard to predict, misses positions whose value must be computed but whose surprisal is ordinary. A compression view gives a different answer: where the text stops repeating. Implemented as a two-byte lookup table fitted in seconds, it raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90% in 50M-parameter models on math, with an effect that 8

Its reach is limited to text where new content begins at segment starts near the computation; learned chunkers find such structure more generally. The practical message for patcher design is to stop treating surprisal as the target: on math, the rules that concentrate boundaries most on surprising bytes compute worst. text: Unfragmenting Nawatl NMT: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa LoRA Adaptation, Morphosyntactic Conditioning, and Decolonial Evaluation Luis Armando Mercado-Campos⋆and Alexis Palmer Department of Linguistics, University of Colorado Boulder Luis.MercadoCampos@colorado.edu, alexis.palmer@colorado.edu Abstract. In minoritized (low-resource) language technologies, a com- mon response to data sparsity is to aggregate text across multiple varieties and treat the combined data as a single corpus. However, mixed corpora of closely related indigenous variants can produce an artificial register that is accountable to no single speaker community, a structural failure we call variant fragmentation. This issue is acute for minoritized languages native to Mexico, such as Nawatl. Building on a 70,000-pair multi-variant foun- dation [18], we specialize an mT5-large checkpoint to Masewalkopa (nhn), the Nawatl variety spoken in Santa Ana Tlacotenco. We curate 2,665 par- allel pairs, reserve all sentence-level data for evaluation, and incorporate 192 elder-transcribed target sentences via asymmetric backtranslation. A custom finite-state analyzer reduces unanalyzed surface forms from 82.0% to 19.9% and supplies functional syntax tags as plain-text prefixes, allowing the model to reuse existing subword embeddings rather than relying on frozen special tokens. The resulting lora_v9c_b model achieves 58.46 dev chrF++ and 58.20/57.90 directional test chrF++. Finally, CTranslate2 int8 quantization reduces CPU latency from 137.5 to 1.8–2.6 seconds per request, enabling cost-bounded Cloud Run deployment. Keywords: Neural Machine Translation · Minoritized NLP · Nawatl ·

text: 2 Luis A. Mercado-Campos and A. Palmer are 30 formally recognized variants of Nawatl [12], which can have substantial phonological, morphological, syntactic, and lexical differences [9]. There is also significant variant-internal diversity. Treating them as a single computational language obscures the systems that index place and community belonging. Masewalkopa is the endonym used by speakers of the Nawatl in Santa Ana de Tlacotenco, Milpa Alta, Mexico City (nhn). It is morphologically rich and predominantly head marking: words can encode subject, object, derivation, aspect, possession, predicate-nominal structure, and honorific morphology. Character- level similarity can therefore conceal a wrong possessor or a form from another writing tradition. During the first author’s three years of studying Masewalkopa, he encountered persistent discrepancies between locally taught forms and Classical Nawatl- centered digital resources. As a result, his objective shifted from maximizing a generic “Nawatl” score to producing forms that can be inspected by a single, identifiable community. 1.1 From a Multi-Variant Model to Single-Variant Specialization In the first author’s previous work [18], he assembled approximately 70,000 Spanish-Nawatl pairs across varieties and domains. The resulting system (found on huggingface2) checkpoint achieved 54.15 chrF++ on a split from that same mixed collection. However, when evaluated zero-shot on an external benchmark, the Ameri- casNLP 2021 Shared Task on Open Machine Translation for Indigenous Lan- guages [17], performance collapsed

However, when evaluated zero-shot on an external benchmark, the Ameri- casNLP 2021 Shared Task on Open Machine Translation for Indigenous Lan- guages [17], performance collapsed to 25.7 chrF++. This external evaluation dataset consisted of independent Spanish-Nawatl text that was completely unseen during training. Beyond simple domain mismatch, manual inspection revealed that the model generated conflicting lexical, orthographic, and inflectional forms from different regions within the same sentence. While each piece might be attested somewhere in Mexico, the combined output was incoherent as Masewalkopa. We use variant fragmentation for this interaction between data aggregation and model behavior. The multi-variant corpus expresses a single underlying meaning through divergent regional realizations, the subword model shares pieces regardless of regional provenance, and beam search can assemble a fluent-looking sequence from conflicting varietal conventions. Aggregate evaluation conceals the problem when references come from the same mixture. A high in-domain score can therefore coexist with low external validity. To resolve this, we warm-start from the first author’s 1.2-billion-parameter multi-variant mT5-large thesis checkpoint and adapt it exclusively with Mase- walkopa data. The broad-base model provides sequence modeling and cross-lingual alignment, while the small community corpus provides regional constraints. text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 3 In this paper, we develop a single-variety approach to neural machine trans- lation (NMT) for Masewalkopa, using a relatively small community dataset to specialize an existing multi-variety model. By combining parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning with rule-based finite-state morphology and authentic target-side oral narratives, we show that targeted specialization resolves variant fragmentation while respecting the linguistic autonomy of Santa Ana Tlacotenco speech. 1.2 Core Contributions This paper makes four contributions: 1. Single-Variant Specialization Pipeline: We specialize a 1.2-billion-parameter NMT model with 2,665 Masewalkopa pairs, restricting short dictionary en- tries to training so that development and test benchmarks evaluate only full sentence translation. 2. Morphosyntactic NMT Conditioning: We expand a finite-state analyzer beyond 6,500 lexicon lines to derive surface-validated functional syntax prefixes, supplying the neural translation encoder with structural grounding to resolve morphological and lexical ambiguities. 3. Ablation Suite and Post-Mortems: We ablate asymmetric backtranslation, cold special tokens, sparse versus dense syntax, and syntax stripping in the final lora_v9c experiment. 4. Decolonial and Production Evaluation: We combine chrF++, linguis- tic diagnostics, DBS, human comparison, and measured CPU deployment behavior. Together, these experiments demonstrate that targeted single-variant spe- cialization overcomes the pitfalls of multi-variant data aggregation. The final specialized model (lora_v9c_b) achieves 58.46 dev chrF++ and 58.20/57.90 direc- tional test chrF++, gaining over 28 points over the mixed-variant base.

The final specialized model (lora_v9c_b) achieves 58.46 dev chrF++ and 58.20/57.90 direc- tional test chrF++, gaining over 28 points over the mixed-variant base. Ablation results show that plain-text syntactic prefixes successfully recover from the severe optimization stalls of frozen special tokens, while dense morphological tagging yields measurable structural gains (+1.33 test chrF++). Culturally, decolonial DBS probes and human A/B ratings confirm a strong reduction in colonial Span- ish substitutions and improved naturalness on elder-transcribed oral narratives. Finally, 8-bit quantization and widened beam search reduce inference latency to under 2.6 seconds on standard CPU hardware, demonstrating that single-variant models can be operated within strict community budget constraints. 2

text: Indigenous Machine Translation and Variety Specialization. Prior machine trans- lation research on Indigenous languages of the Americas has largely focused on pooling heterogeneous regional variants into aggregate training sets to combat extreme data scarcity [7]. However, computational dialectology and variety clas- sification for Nawatl demonstrates that regional variants exhibit sharp lexical
title: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa

text: 4 Luis A. Mercado-Campos and A. Palmer and morphophonological boundaries [19]. Blending these divergent systems into monolithic training corpora frequently produces varietal bleed and privileges colonial or standardized varieties over living community speech [3]. Recent work therefore emphasizes community-grounded single-variant modeling. This study builds on that foundation by specializing a broad multi-variant base directly to the spoken variety of Santa Ana Tlacotenco. Morphosyntactic Conditioning in Neural MT. Guiding sequence generation with explicit linguistic structure stems from factored translation architectures [25] and prefix-based syntactic conditioning [28]. For polysynthetic languages, finite-state transducers (FSTs) supply robust morphological segmentation and grammatical disambiguation where purely statistical subword models fail [2]. My system builds on these insights, demonstrating that high-density FST syntactic prefixes provide reliable structural inductive bias without requiring vocabulary modifications. Parameter-Efficient Adaptation in Low-Resource Regimes. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [11] provides an efficient mechanism for adapting massive multilingual models such as mT5 [27] while preventing catastrophic forgetting. Extending low- rank updates across all linear projections is essential for deep domain transfer [6, 10]. We contribute an empirical analysis of embedding constraints under LoRA, showing how plain-text subword formatting avoids the optimization collapse associated with frozen cold-token representations. 3 Data Curation, Corpus Composition, and Governance We compiled the primary parallel corpus over nearly four years of studying Masewalkopa through community classes and structured coursework with native-

text: plain-text subword formatting avoids the optimization collapse associated with frozen cold-token representations. 3 Data Curation, Corpus Composition, and Governance We compiled the primary parallel corpus over nearly four years of studying Masewalkopa through community classes and structured coursework with native- speaker language instructors from Santa Ana Tlacotenco. All pedagogical exer- cises, classroom dialogues, and vocabulary transcriptions were recorded, digitized, and curated with the explicit informed consent of the instructors for research and educational work. Following the Collective Benefit, Authority to COntrol, Responsibility, and Ethics (CARE) principles, we treat provenance, authority, responsibility, and ethics as pipeline properties [4]. Data collection was guided by collective benefit and mutual accountability rather than extractive aggregation. 3.1 Cleaning and Provenance In machine translation, the main training unit is an aligned parallel pair consisting of a source text segment and its equivalent target translation. We compiled the primary corpus over nearly four years of studying Masewalkopa through classes and coursework with native-speaker instructors from Santa Ana Tlacotenco. All pedagogical exercises, classroom dialogues, and vocabulary notes were recorded and curated into structured spreadsheets with explicit instructor consent. We normalized whitespace and Unicode representations, removed empty fields, and deduplicated aligned Spanish–Nawatl segment pairs case-insensitively.
title: Luis A. Mercado-Campos and A. Palmer

text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 5 Near-neighbor spellings were retained because they often encode authentic local phonological choices. Cleaning reduced 2,761 raw rows to 2,665 unique parallel segment pairs. Each parallel pair was tagged by sentential status based on word count from standard whitespace splitting after punctuation stripping. Entries with at most two whitespace-delimited tokens were treated as lexical or short-phrase material (such as citation nouns or isolated verb stems); longer examples and independently verified clauses were treated as sentence-level. This reproducible threshold does not claim that every two-token sequence lacks syntax. Instead, it prevents dictionary correspondences from dominating evaluation splits. Table 1. Random splitting would therefore reward dictionary matches without demonstrating sentence translation. 3.2 Stratification and Bidirectional Tasks Development and test data were drawn exclusively from the 1,477 sentence- level pairs to ensure that evaluation benchmarks measure genuine sequence translation rather than isolated vocabulary lookup. Including single-word or short lexical pairs in held-out sets would artificially inflate n-gram and character overlap scores through simple dictionary matching, masking failures in clause-level syntax, agreement, and possession. Restricting evaluation to sentential items guarantees that metrics reflect grammatical compositionality, while placing all 1,188 lexical pairs into the training inventory provides necessary stem coverage and orthographic grounding. Using a fixed stratification seed, we reserved 120 sentence pairs for development and 150 for the final held-out test set. The remaining training inventory contained 2,335 pairs after recombining the lexical entries with eligible training sentences. To train the model bidirectionally, each parallel sentence pair consisting of a Spanish segment (ses) and a Masewalkopa segment (snah) was expanded into two separate supervised training examples by prepending a literal directional prefix to the source string:

Palmer – Spanish →Masewalkopa: Input string: es->nah: juntos venceremos como comunidad Target string: tlamach tikayawaskeh – Masewalkopa →Spanish: Input string: nah->es: tlamach tikayawaskeh Target string: juntos venceremos como comunidad The 2,335 training pairs therefore yielded 4,670 directional training examples, while the 120 development pairs and 150 test pairs yielded 240 and 300 directional evaluation examples, respectively. Directional prefixes are ordinary text already present in the mT5 Sentence- Piece vocabulary. This detail is crucial because standard text prefixes remain trainable through attention and LoRA weight updates even when the base model’s shared embedding table is completely frozen. Joint bidirectional training doubles the available supervised training instances without requiring synthetic target generation. 3.3 Four Community Oral Texts To add connected speech and local cultural vocabulary, we incorporated 192 elder- transcribed Masewalkopa sentences. These materials were generously shared with me for pedagogical development by one of my native speaker language instructors in Santa Ana Tlacotenco. The texts represent four distinct thematic registers: 1. Tiankisko: 34 market-dialogue sentences covering exchanges, quantities, and polite requests. 2. Tonakayutl: 45 sentences on traditional maize cultivation, harvesting prac- tices, and food knowledge. 3. Kowatl itech in ikwentsin: 50 narrative sentences describing a traditional snake story, adding complex reference tracking and sequential event structures. 4. Tatahpowilistle: 63 sentences concerning community authority, local oral

text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 7 decoder learns exclusively from authentic, elder-authored targets. We deliberately did not swap source and target to create es →nah training examples, which would have forced the Spanish generation decoder to imitate its earlier output. The resulting train_bt.jsonl file contained 4,862 directional examples (4,670 directional instances plus the 192 backtranslated pairs). This targeted addition aims to expose the model to connected narrative discourse from community elders rather than evaluating large-scale synthetic data generation. 3.5 Leakage Controls and Evaluation Scope Deduplication preceded splitting; dev and test pairs were excluded from aug- mentation. We report chrF++ for its tolerance of inflectional variation [22], but add linguistic diagnostics because overlap cannot judge regional appropriateness, possession, or honorific licensing. 4 Finite-State Morphosyntactic Engineering While neural sequence-to-sequence models excel at cross-lingual transfer, subword tokenizers frequently fracture polysynthetic words into arbitrary pieces that obscure grammatical relations. In Masewalkopa, a single verbal form can encode subject person, object person, reflexive marking, tense, and direction. With only 2,665 curated training pairs, a purely data-driven neural encoder struggles to generalize across sparse morphological paradigms. To provide the neural translation model with explicit structural grounding, we developed a rule-based finite-state transducer using the Helsinki Finite-State Transducer (HFST) toolkit [16]. Rather than replacing the neural model, this analyzer acts as a linguistic feature extractor. It parses surface

text: provide the neural translation model with explicit structural grounding, we developed a rule-based finite-state transducer using the Helsinki Finite-State Transducer (HFST) toolkit [16]. Rather than replacing the neural model, this analyzer acts as a linguistic feature extractor. It parses surface tokens into interlinear glossed text (IGT) and functional syntax labels, which are then passed directly to the NMT encoder as plain-text prefixes during training and inference (Subsection 5.4). The analyzer combines final-state morphotactic continuation lexicons with two-level phonological alternation rules [2] to capture the core grammatical inventory of Santa Ana Tlacotenco speech. 4.1 Stem Classes and Morphotactics An undifferentiated lexicon overgenerates because stems select different suffixal paths. We therefore use the continuation classes in Table 2 as implementation abstractions. Dedicated nominal paths prevent absolutive suffixes from attaching to every nominal-looking base. An audit removed sesek (cold) and tomawak (plump) from noun continuations that generated unattested -tl, -li, -tli, -in, or -itl forms. Predicate nominals require a separate path: ti-sowatl, “you are a woman,” carries person without an overt copula. Retaining this analysis supports transla- tion to Spanish ser constructions.
title: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa

Class Function in the analyzer Representative constraint A-Stem Stems whose citation or inflected path is orga- nized around an a-final alternation Restricts which aspect and derivational arcs can follow I-Stem i-final verbal or predicate paths Preserves class-specific boundary alternations OWA-Stem Productive verbal stems associated with an owa pattern Connects to verbal person and aspect networks ITL-Stem Nominal stems selecting an -itl-type absolutive realization Blocks incompatible absolu- tive suffixes TLE-Stem Nominal stems selecting a -tle-type path in local orthography Separates local surface be- havior from generic noun rules LI-Stem Nominal stems selecting -li Supports possessed and predicate-nominal alterna- tions 4.2 Progressive Aspect Allomorphy Progressive arcs for -tok and -tika are licensed by stem continuation class, with TWOLC constraining boundary realizations. This generalizes beyond a flat word list, provided the allomorphs are freely attachable. The analysis identifies heads inside long words and exposes aspect as a stable feature. It supplements rather than replaces neural subword representations. 4.3 Coverage Expansion and Error Accounting Repeated audits grew LEXC beyond 6,500 lines. After each justified stem addition, we recompiled and measured no analysis, permissive passthrough, and genuine segmentation. Passthrough is not counted as successful analysis. Table 3. Because coverage can increase due to incompatible analyses, we added a precision-oriented reconstruction filter. 4.4 Three-Stage Reconstruction Filter Because finite-state transducers can generate multiple competing analyses or derivations for a single surface token, we use a three-stage reconstruction filter to disambiguate raw transducer outputs before assigning IGT:
title: Luis A. Mercado-Campos and A. Palmer

text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 9 1. Surface match. Retain only candidates whose reconstructed stem or diag- nostic realization aligns to an ordered substring of the normalized token. 2. Possessive guard. Require overt initial no-, mo-, to-, or i- for a possessive analysis. This blocks bare nouns and coincidental stem-initial strings from receiving NP.POSS. 3. Category preference. Prefer the open-class analysis covering most surface material, except when a listed adverb matches the entire token. Preserve genuine ties for sentence-level resolution. In compact pseudo-code, the decision is: for token in sentence: candidates = fst.lookup(strip_punct(token.lower())) candidates = keep_surface_aligned(candidates, token) candidates = guard_possession(candidates, token) analysis = prefer_category(candidates, token) emit(igt(analysis), functional_labels(analysis)) Uncertain tokens remain unlabeled, while the original sentence always reaches the encoder. Illustrative Pipeline Output. To illustrate the output of this filter, consider the input sentence: axan nehwatl nitekitis ika notepostsontekosentlalil (“now I will work with my computer”) The FST analyzer and filter process each token as follows: – Token analysis: • axan →adv (temporal particle) • nehwatl →subj:1sg (emphatic subject pronoun) • nitekitis →ni-tekiti-s →subj:1sg + verb:intr + fut • ika →rel.noun (relational marker, “with”) • notepostsontekosentlalil →no-tepostsontekosentlalil →np.poss + noun (“my computer”) – Extracted functional tags: adv, subj:1sg, head, np.poss – Final encoder input string: nah->es: [SYN: ADV SUBJ:1SG HEAD NP.POSS] axan nehwatl nitekitis ika notepostsontekosentlalil This complete prefix string provides the
title: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa

Fine-tuning a 1.2-billion-parameter model on a small dataset requires balancing parameter adaptation against rapid memorization. In lora_v1, we evaluated a short 3-epoch schedule on real pairs. In lora_v2, we extended training to 8 epochs with evaluation every 200 steps. Extend- ing the schedule raised dev chrF++ from 40.26 to 46.18 (+5.92 points). Validation performance peaked at epoch 6 before plateauing by epoch 8, demonstrating that low-rank adapters need sufficient steps to align cross-lingual representations but quickly overfit if trained past convergence. Standard backtranslation risks degrading the generation decoder by training on hallucinated synthetic targets. To prevent this, we implemented an asymmetric protocol: using the nah →es capability of lora_v2, we generated synthetic Spanish source prompts for 192 continuous narrative utterances spoken by community elders, adding these pairs strictly to the es →nah training split (train_bt.jsonl). Integrating these 192 backtranslated pairs in lora_v3b increased dev chrF++ from 46.18 to 49.40 (+3.22 points) and raised both directional tests to approximately 49 chrF++. Although representing only an 8% increase over the real-pair inventory, they introduced multi-clause discourse patterns and authentic elder-authored syntax that isolated pedagogical pairs lack.

Palmer 5.4 Failure Analysis: Cold Embedding Degradation In lora_v4 and lora_v6, we attempted to delimit syntactic conditioning regions using dedicated special tokens (<source>, <syntax>, and <no_syntax>). This intervention resized the shared vocabulary from 250,100 to 250,103, introducing uninitialized rows into the embedding matrix. Because standard LoRA freezes the base embedding table to conserve GPU memory, these newly added token vectors received zero gradient updates and remained fixed random vectors throughout training. Presenting the encoder with static random vectors at structurally critical positions caused total optimization failure: training loss stalled above 30.0 and dev chrF++ collapsed to 8.91. While unfreezing the full embedding table resolved the representation issue conceptually, it immediately exhausted T4 GPU memory. In lora_v5, we resolved this constraint by passing functional syntax as or- dinary text prefixes (such as nah->es: ADV HEAD NP.POSS) segmented with the existing SentencePiece vocabulary. Reusing pretrained subword representations stabilized optimization without custom checkpoint surgery and restored dev chrF++ to 51.69. All subsequent runs retain this plain-text prefix format. 5.5 Sparse and Dense Syntax Coverage To assess how annotation density affects conditioning, we compared two versions of the finite-state analyzer. In lora_v7b, the early prototype produced functional syntax tags for only 29.5% of corpus sentences. Adding these sparse prefixes yielded virtually identical development scores to the unconditioned lora_v7a

In lora_v7b, the early prototype produced functional syntax tags for only 29.5% of corpus sentences. Adding these sparse prefixes yielded virtually identical development scores to the unconditioned lora_v7a con- trol (51.31 versus 51.22 chrF++) and slightly degraded directional test accuracy. Because sparse tags occurred inconsistently, the model treated them as shallow domain indicators rather than reliable syntactic grounding. In lora_v8b, once rule expansion and reconstruction filtering raised tag coverage to 95.8%, syntax conditioning produced a +1.33 chrF++ gain on complex nah →es polysynthetic targets and a +0.51 spillover gain on es →nah. This demonstrates that syntactic conditioning requires high annotation density to guide sequence generation effectively. Precision in the reconstruction filter remains critical, as inaccurate tags would inject systematic structural noise. 5.6 Final lora_v9c Ablation and Model Selection To isolate the precise contribution of dense syntactic prefixes on the final training set, we evaluated a controlled ablation where the extracted syntax tags were stripped from input sequences during training and inference (strip=True), leaving only bare source text. On the development split, the syntax-stripped control reached 58.91 chrF++, while the syntax-conditioned model (lora_v9c_b, strip=False) reached 58.46 chrF++, a minor difference of −0.45 points. text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 13 syntactic prefix provides necessary structural disambiguation for complex gram- matical constructions that aggregate character metrics fail to penalize. These include differentiating modifier versus predicate readings of kwalle, resolving null-copula structures, and tracking possessed nominal arguments. We report the unconditioned control’s development score transparently, but accept this minor trade-off to ensure consistent grammatical interpretability. Across fully evaluated held-out test splits, lora_v9c_b remains our strongest model, reaching 58.20 and 57.90 directional test chrF++. 6 Qualitative Translation and Decolonial Evaluation Automatic scores summarize thousands of character n-grams but do not explain which linguistic decisions changed. We therefore use diagnostic examples to examine regional spelling, word-internal person marking, possessive prefixes, predicate nominals, and honorific morphology. The examples in Table 6 are targeted probes, not an independent statistical test. text: 14 Luis A. Mercado-Campos and A. Palmer The third row illustrates predicate nominals. A mixed output with separate ni can be interpreted as a tokenization artifact or as a cross-variety spelling convention. The correct tisowatl realizes person marking on the predicate. In the final phrase, kwalle must be interpreted in relation to that predicate, not assigned a fixed label solely from its dictionary gloss. This is the type of ambiguity that motivated the retention of syntax conditioning in lora_v9c_b. Qualitative analysis also reveals what the current table cannot establish. A single human reference is not the only grammatical realization, and matching it exactly is not proof of social appropriateness. Honorific morphology can be licensed by participant relation and discourse context, neither of which is fully represented in isolated Spanish prompts. For deployment, the examples are therefore paired with warnings against treating the system as a normative authority. 6.1 Domesticating Bias Score Standard multi-variant Nawatl corpora are heavily skewed toward colonial-era missionary texts, biblical translations, and pan-variety pedagogical materials. Models trained on these resources inherit a structural bias toward archaic, stan- dardized Central forms (such as tlazohcamati or cihuatl), which local speakers perceive as alien or domesticating. In contrast, translation into the community demands fidelity to the living, spoken variety of Santa Ana Tlacotenco (such as nimitstlasohkamate or sowatl). To evaluate

text: dardized Central forms (such as tlazohcamati or cihuatl), which local speakers perceive as alien or domesticating. In contrast, translation into the community demands fidelity to the living, spoken variety of Santa Ana Tlacotenco (such as nimitstlasohkamate or sowatl). To evaluate this dynamic directly, the Domes- ticating Bias Score (DBS) measures the proportion of diagnostic translations in which a model defaults to generalized, colonial-derived variants rather than verified local community lexical choices. Standard reference-based metrics can reward Spanish loanwords or archaic colonial forms when the reference itself reflects domesticated translation practices. Drawing on pseudo-log-likelihood bias evaluation paradigms [15, 20] and length- normalized sequence scoring [23], We define the Domesticating Bias Score (DBS) as the difference in average per-token log-probability assigned by the model to a colonially domesticated candidate (tc) versus a sovereign community candidate (ts) given source input x: DBS(x) = 1 |tc| |tc| X j=1 log P(tc,j | tc,<j, x) −1 |ts| |ts| X j=1 log P(ts,j | ts,<j, x). (3) Length is measured in decoder tokens. A positive DBS indicates that the model assigns a higher average per-token log-probability to the domesticated candidate, whereas a negative DBS indicates a preference for the sovereign candidate. Values near zero reflect weak preference or equally probable alternatives. Token normalization is necessary because sovereign formulations can be longer than borrowed Spanish nouns or
title: Luis A. Mercado-Campos and A. Palmer

text: to the domesticated candidate, whereas a negative DBS indicates a preference for the sovereign candidate. Values near zero reflect weak preference or equally probable alternatives. Token normalization is necessary because sovereign formulations can be longer than borrowed Spanish nouns or simplified roots, either morphologically or periphrastically. Without normalization, summing raw log-probabilities almost always penalizes longer strings because each additional token contributes a nonpositive term. The score is contrastive rather than absolute. It does not

text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 15 declare any individual term intrinsically colonial. Instead, each contrastive pair must be constructed with community speakers who can evaluate the social and historical distinctions in context. On the illustrative seed set used during development, mean DBS shifted from −1.313 for the base model to −0.380 after specialization. Under the sign convention in Eq. 3, both values favor the sovereign candidate, but the specialized score is closer to zero. It would therefore be incorrect to describe this shift as a stronger sovereign preference. The result instead reflects a reduced magnitude in the modeled contrast. We retain the metric because it exposes candidate-level probability distributions, but we interpret direction and magnitude explicitly rather than attaching an uncritical label to every numerical movement. This distinction is methodologically important. In production evaluations, DBS can be reported alongside bootstrap confidence intervals over contrast pairs, sign tests for the proportion of instances with DBS < 0, and stratified subsets across specific phenomena, including lexical borrowing, kinship terminology, toponyms, and ceremonial register. Future community-designed evaluation benchmarks should also support a “both acceptable” label to ensure that the metric does not impose an artificial binary interpretation on ordinary dialectal variation. 6.2 Error Analysis and Qualitative Failure Modes Although the production system (lora_v9c_b) substantially improves lexical alignment and local morphology, systematic qualitative inspection reveals

Multi-Variant Orthographic and Phonetic Bleed. On roots and adverbials shared across Central Nawatl varieties, the model occasionally defaults to gen- eralized Central spellings (such as yalwa and itak) rather than generating the localized Santa Ana Tlacotenco orthography with preconsonantal aspiration (yalhwa and ihtak), reflecting residual weight bias from the multi-variant base checkpoint. 3. Morphological Suffix Truncation in Future Aspect. In transitive verbal com- plexes combining directional or person prefixes with temporal adverbs (such as mustla nimitsmachtis ‘tomorrow I will teach you’), the decoder occasionally drops the final future suffix -s, yielding an uninflected or present-tense form (nimitsmachtia) despite explicit future context in the source. 7 Production Deployment and CPU Profiling A model that requires a research GPU for every query is difficult to sustain as a community-facing service. text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 17 7.2 Beam Search Divergence on Short Forms Initial deployment testing found mid-word truncation on short lexical inputs, including nimitstlasohkamate. The failure initially appeared to be a quantization artifact [8], but comparisons across converted precisions showed it was precision- independent. Greedy and narrow-beam paths could terminate after a high- probability partial subword sequence even though the full form was preferred by the original evaluation setup. Increasing beam_size from 4 to 8 eliminated the observed truncations in the short-form regression set. The wider beam retained complete hypotheses long enough for the accumulated sequence score to overtake prematurely terminated candidates. This is described as beam search divergence rather than as a general CTranslate2 defect because the trigger depends on the model’s score distribution, tokenization, length normalization, and stopping behavior [14, 26]. The production API sets the beam size to 8 and runs regression probes after every model conversion. The probes include single words, morphologically long words, short clauses, both translation directions, and forms with possessive or honorific material. This test set is separate from the research test split. Its role is software validation, specifically ensuring that a numerically strong model does not become linguistically unusable after conversion. 7.3 Cloud Run Microservice Architecture The service exposes a FastAPI application within a container that includes the CTranslate2 model and the

text: Its role is software validation, specifically ensuring that a numerically strong model does not become linguistically unusable after conversion. 7.3 Cloud Run Microservice Architecture The service exposes a FastAPI application within a container that includes the CTranslate2 model and the mT5 tokenizer assets. A translation request passes through four stages: 1. validate direction, input length, and Unicode text; 2. construct the direction and optional syntax prefix; 3. tokenize, decode with beam size 8, and remove model control text; 4. return the translation plus non-sensitive runtime metadata. The Cloud Run revision uses 2 vCPUs, 4 GiB RAM, and a maximum of two instances. The instance cap limits both concurrency and worst-case cost. Because model loading is expensive relative to a warm translation, the container initializes the model once at process startup rather than once per request. CORS is configured through an explicit allowlist for the web client origins that require browser access. Methods and headers are restricted to the translation interface rather than using an unrestricted wildcard in production. CORS is not authentication, so request validation, rate limiting at the surrounding platform layer, and conservative maximum input lengths remain necessary. The API does not log full translation content by default, since sentences may contain names or culturally sensitive material. 7.4 Automated Cost Controls A billing budget publishes threshold notifications to Pub/Sub.

This is intentionally stronger than an email alert: an alert informs the operator, while the function can stop additional billable use. The mechanism complements the Cloud Run maximum-instance setting and protects a student-operated project from traffic spikes or accidental loops. Disabling billing is disruptive and can stop unrelated resources in the same project. For that reason, the deployment isolates the translator within a dedicated project, tests the function at non-production thresholds, and documents manual recovery procedures. Budget automation also has notification latency, so it is a final circuit breaker rather than a substitute for instance caps, request quotas, and monitoring. 8 Discussion, Limitations, and Reproducibility The experiments show that a mixed-variant checkpoint can provide useful transfer when a second stage redirects it toward one documented variety. Authentic target provenance matters in backtranslation, and symbolic conditioning becomes useful only after analyzer coverage is dense and reconstruction is precise. This does not imply that speakers or models must be linguistically isolated. A future multi- variety system could explicitly condition on community, orthography, or speaker preference rather than aggregating those distinctions without labels. The corpus remains small and pedagogically skewed. Its 192 oral-text sentences cannot represent all genres or speakers, the human evaluation has 20 items with only 2 raters, and

text: community, orthography, or speaker preference rather than aggregating those distinctions without labels. The corpus remains small and pedagogically skewed. Its 192 oral-text sentences cannot represent all genres or speakers, the human evaluation has 20 items with only 2 raters, and DBS is still an illustrative probe of candidate log-probability distributions rather than an absolute metric. Likewise, reaching 72.9% genuine FST segmentation in the lexicon reflects rule coverage rather than verified parsing precision. Future work must validate analyses by morpheme type, especially possession, aspect, and predicate nominals. Full reproducibility requires the deduplicated split manifest, directional JSONL, FST source hash, adapter configuration, selected checkpoint, random seeds, and decoding settings. Sentence-only scores must remain separate from lexical data. Responsible release also requires speaker-approved access conditions for oral texts and a model card that names Masewalkopa as the target variety, documents errors, and provides routes for correction or removal. This is something that will be spoken about and talked with the community before making any data accessible for any other purposes. 9 Conclusion and Future Work This work began with a fundamental dilemma in minoritized language technolo- gies: while aggregating data across regional varieties combats data sparsity in the aggregate, it produces an artificial, blended register that is accountable to no single speaker community. text: Single-Variant Specialization for Masewalkopa 19 baseline, high scores on mixed-corpus benchmarks can easily mask severe struc- tural failure on authentic regional speech. We have termed this failure variant fragmentation. To resolve this issue, this paper demonstrated the process and effectiveness of specializing an existing sequence-to-sequence model to a specific regional variety: Masewalkopa (nhn), spoken in Santa Ana Tlacotenco. Using a relatively small community corpus of 2,665 curated pairs, a stratified evaluation split that strictly measures sentential syntax, and 192 authentic elder-transcribed narrative targets integrated through asymmetric backtranslation, we adapted a 1.2-billion-parameter checkpoint on a single GPU. The resulting specialized system (lora_v9c_b) achieved 58.46 dev chrF++ and 58.20/57.90 directional test chrF++, gaining over 28 points over the initial multi-variant baseline. Beyond aggregate metric gains, my experimental ablations and failure analyses provide concrete architectural takeaways for indigenous and polysynthetic NMT: 1. Subword embedding constraints in LoRA: Introducing new special tokens while freezing the shared embedding matrix creates an untrained bottleneck that stalls model convergence. Conditioning the translation encoder using plain- text syntactic prefixes reuses the pretrained subword space and completely recovers model performance. 2. Density in morphosyntactic conditioning: Sparse functional syntax tags act merely as shallow domain indicators, whereas high-coverage tags (95.8%) generated by a rule-based finite-state analyzer provide explicit structural guidance that improves translation on complex polysynthetic targets (+1.33 chrF++). 3.

Decolonial and multi-faceted evaluation: Character overlap metrics alone cannot detect whether a translation respects local autonomy. Combining diagnostic morphological probes, length-normalized Domesticating Bias Scores (DBS), and blind human ratings verified that the specialized model actively prefers sovereign community vocabulary over colonial Spanish substitutions. 4. Accessible CPU deployment: Merging low-rank adapter weights and ap- plying 8-bit CTranslate2 quantization reduced inference latency from 137.5 seconds down to 1.8–2.6 seconds per request. Widening the beam search to 8 resolved search-space truncations on short lexical inputs, enabling responsive and cost-bounded deployment on serverless CPU infrastructure. 9.1

text: Moving forward, we plan to expand community-led evaluations with native speakers in Santa Ana Tlacotenco to establish formal qualitative rubrics for honorific and directional morphology. In addition, we will extend our finite-state conditioning pipeline to handle long-form discourse in community oral histories, and investigate parameter-efficient specialization across other Nawatl varieties using isolated, modular adapter banks. Ultimately, language technologies for minoritized languages should not aim to homogenize distinct varieties into a single generic system. By demonstrating that
