text: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals SCENE RECONSTRUCTION USING UBIQUITOUS WIRE- LESS SIGNALS VIA DIFFUSION POSTERIOR INFERENCE OVER PHYSICS-GROUNDED REPRESENTATIONS Vahid Yazdnian & Yasaman Ghasempour Princeton University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering {vahidyazdnian,ghasempour}@princeton.edu
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: Knowing the layout of the physical world matters for many applications, yet the sensors we rely on for it (e.g., cameras and LiDAR) can fail in darkness, in adverse weather, or behind walls. Wireless signals do not face these limitations: every link between a base station and a user is shaped by the buildings it passes, reflects from, or is blocked by, leaving information about the surrounding scene embedded in the wireless channel measured at the endpoints. However, mapping channel measure- ments to the environment is a severely ill-posed problem: a measurement records only the structures that interact with the transmitted electromagnetic waves along its propagation paths, and even these observations can often be explained by mul- tiple plausible scenes. We therefore formulate wireless scene reconstruction as posterior inference and develop a hierarchical framework with two complemen- tary stages to approach this problem. A wireless foundation model, pretrained to respect propagation physics, transforms each channel measurement into a repre- sentation of the scene structure that shaped the observation. A diffusion model then jointly integrates representations from multiple measurements to model and sample the posterior over building occupancy, with consensus over samples pro- ducing the final reconstruction. We demonstrate that the framework can accu- rately recover building footprints from wireless channel measurements alone and show that its performance depends critically on
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: and sample the posterior over building occupancy, with consensus over samples pro- ducing the final reconstruction. We demonstrate that the framework can accu- rately recover building footprints from wireless channel measurements alone and show that its performance depends critically on both design components: physics- grounded representations expose scene-relevant information, while joint posterior inference coherently integrates complementary observations. 1

text: Every wireless link is already an unintentional measurement of its surroundings. A signal that leaves a base station and arrives at a receiver has encountered several components in an environment: blocked by one building, reflected off another, diffracted around a corner. The environment is, in effect, written into the wireless channel measured at the receiver. If that writing could be read back, the radio infrastructure already deployed at scale could be repurposed as a sensor network, mapping the world through occluded regions, in darkness, and in severe weather, where cameras and lidar degrade or fail outright (Zhao et al., 2018; Dodds et al., 2026). It would also keep maps current when they change fastest: after an earthquake or a flood, the layout of a neighborhood can change in minutes, and the network is often the only sensor still running. Site-specific digital twins, which today require expensive surveys or hand-built geometry, could also be constructed and kept current from the traffic a network already carries (Hoydis et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Testolina et al., 2024). The knowledge of the propagation environment can also be used to optimize communication network throughput (Zhao et al., 2023; Demirhan & Alkhateeb, 2023), and could advance integrated communication and sensing, one of the main pillars of next-generation networks (Akyildiz et al., 2020; Wang et
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: propagation environment can also be used to optimize communication network throughput (Zhao et al., 2023; Demirhan & Alkhateeb, 2023), and could advance integrated communication and sensing, one of the main pillars of next-generation networks (Akyildiz et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2024). Recovering geometry from wave measurements is well studied in acoustics, where room shape is inferred from resolvable echoes and geometric propagation models (Dokmani´c et al., 2013; El Baba et al., 2018); recent learning-based approaches relax some of these assumptions and predict floor- plans directly (Yeon & Choi, 2024; Yeon et al., 2024), but still rely on echo structures that can be attributed to individual surfaces. In the RF domain, scene reconstruction has primarily relied on ded- icated radar sensing systems (Casmin & Oliveira, 2025; Borts et al., 2026), recovering occupancy grids or floor plans from millimeter-wave and ultra-wideband reflections using geometric inference, motion-synthesized aperture, structural priors, or learned generative models (Lu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026). Recent approaches include diffusion-based indoor 1 arXiv:2610.22120v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026

text: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals scene completion from sparse radar heatmaps (Zhou et al., 2025) and reconstruction around cor- ners from multi-bounce returns collected by a mobile radar (Lai et al., 2026). These approaches require dedicated sensing hardware and often movement through the environment, incurring addi- tional hardware and deployment costs. In this paper, we aim to use the communication signals from already deployed infrastructure for scene reconstruction. The challenge is that extracting environmental components out of a raw wire- less channel measurement without any assumptions is a severely ill-posed inverse problem, and the ill-posedness is structural rather than incidental. A measurement is shaped only by the structures its propagation paths interact with, so the likelihood is exactly invariant to the rest of the scene. Even within the observed region, the geometry-to-channel mapping is many-to-one: finite bandwidth and aperture limit the resolution of path delays and angles, so scatterers displaced within those lim- its yield indistinguishable measurements. Compounding this, a structure impacts the channel only through the role it plays for a given link — reflecting, blocking, or leaving the signal untouched — and that role varies with where the structure sits relative to the transmitter and receiver. Dif- ferent occupancy patterns whose structures play the same roles for a given link would therefore be indistinguishable. Hence, a single
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: the signal untouched — and that role varies with where the structure sits relative to the transmitter and receiver. Dif- ferent occupancy patterns whose structures play the same roles for a given link would therefore be indistinguishable. Hence, a single measurement admits not one scene but a family of them. In this work, we formulate scene reconstruction as posterior inference over occupancy: the solution is a distribution over scenes, and the observations determine which parts of it are pinned down and which remain free. To our knowledge, this is the first treatment of wireless scene reconstruction that assumes nothing about the number, shape, convexity, or location of scatterers. Learning this posterior directly from raw channel measurements is impractical. A single decoder would have to solve two difficult problems at once: work out from finite data how propagation physics maps geometry into a channel, and at the same time learn to generate plausible scenes from a combinatorially large space. We therefore adopt a hierarchical design that separates these burdens. First, a multi-modal wireless foundation model, pretrained to capture electromagnetic propagation physics and align channel observations with propagation-relevant scene structure, maps each measurement to a representation of the scene properties that could have produced it. Second, representations from multiple observations of the same environment are fused to condition a diffu- sion decoder,
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: and align channel observations with propagation-relevant scene structure, maps each measurement to a representation of the scene properties that could have produced it. Second, representations from multiple observations of the same environment are fused to condition a diffu- sion decoder, which performs posterior inference over occupancy and generates scenes consistent with the observed channels. Finally, we aggregate the sampled scenes through per-cell consensus to obtain the reconstructed occupancy map. We evaluate reconstruction of arbitrary scene geometries against natural alternatives to each level of the hierarchy on ∼700 environments held out from all stages of training, spanning diverse spatial layouts and structural configurations, from dense urban blocks to open areas with isolated structures. Specifically, we show through controlled comparisons that both stages of the hierarchy are essential: independently reconstructing and aggregating per-observation scene estimates markedly underper- forms, while conditioning the decoder directly on raw channel measurements collapses. By varying the input representation and posterior inference mechanism independently, we isolate the contribu- tion of each stage. Together, these experiments demonstrate that physics-grounded representation learning followed by generative posterior inference provides the complementary capabilities needed to make reconstruction from sparse wireless observations tractable. Contributions. • Formulation and theory. We formulate wireless scene reconstruction as probabilistic posterior inference over occupancy with no parametric prior; characterize its ill-posedness and the resulting recoverable set; and derive

text: capabilities needed to make reconstruction from sparse wireless observations tractable. Contributions. • Formulation and theory. We formulate wireless scene reconstruction as probabilistic posterior inference over occupancy with no parametric prior; characterize its ill-posedness and the resulting recoverable set; and derive finite-sample bounds showing that a consensus estimator over posterior samples is Bayes-optimal per cell and converges to the true scene on the recoverable set as the number of measurements grows. • Physics-grounded representations. We show that pretraining a wireless foundation model and aligning its representation with propagation-relevant scene structures yields per-observation em- beddings from which the scene occupancy distribution can be recovered. Each embedding cap- tures the portion of the environment that shaped the corresponding measurement while expressing calibrated uncertainty elsewhere. • Hierarchical generative reconstruction. We design a diffusion decoder that conditions on the set of per-observation representations and samples the occupancy posterior, and propose a consensus readout that fuses many viewpoints into a single reconstruction without assuming anything about scene structure. 2

text: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals 2 PRELIMINARIES AND PROBLEM FORMULATION 2.1 WIRELESS PROPAGATION A signal transmitted from a base station reaches a receiver along a set of propagation paths de- termined by the surrounding environment. Each path is a sequence of interactions with the physical structures of the scene: it may travel directly, reflect specularly off a building, diffract at an edge, or be blocked. For a receiver at position p, propagation through a scene s thats P(s, p) =   (αℓ, τℓ, θℓ, ϕℓ) L ℓ=1, where αℓis the complex gain, τℓthe delay, and θℓ, ϕℓthe angles of arrival and departure. Each of these parameters depends on scene geometry: delays are set by the lengths of the path segments, angles by the orientation of the surfaces the wave meets, and gains by free-space loss and the reflection coefficients of the structures encountered. The receiver does not observe the paths individually. This composition defines a forward operator H = F(s, p) mapping scene and link geometry to the observed channel: the scene is written into the channel through the path parameters, in a form the receiver observes only in superposition. Importantly, not all parts of the environment participate in the measurement. Only structures a path interacts with, allowing free propagation, blocking the direct ray, or serving as reflection or diffraction points, enter the path set and thus the channel. We call this region the propagation- relevant set of an observation; structures outside it leave the observation exactly unchanged. 2.2 THE INVERSE PROBLEM Objective. We observe a scene through the wireless links a deployed network already maintains. A base station serves K users, where user k at position pk contributes a channel measurement Hk, giving the observation set O =   (Hk, pk) K k=1. Denoting ak for the propagation-relevant set of observation k, the observable set A = S k ak is the region of the scene influencing at least one measurement. We represent the environment as a two-dimensional occupancy grid over a square region with spatial resolution ∆R, s

text: of observation k, the observable set A = S k ak is the region of the scene influencing at least one measurement. We represent the environment as a two-dimensional occupancy grid over a square region with spatial resolution ∆R, s ∈{0, 1}N×N, where si = 1 indicates that cell i contains a structure, and seek to recover s from O, inverting F, without parametric assumptions on the number, shape, convexity, or location of the structures. Why the problem is ill-posed. Under the standard Hadamard framework (Bakushinsky & Gon- charsky, 2012), the problem is ill-posed because the observations do not uniquely determine the scene, despite a feasible solution existing. Non-uniqueness arises from three sources (Appendix B). First, structures outside A leave every measurement unchanged, so the likelihood is exactly invariant to them: flipping any combination of those cells yields a scene explaining the observations equally well, and the number of such scenes is exponential in |Ac|. Second, even inside A, the forward map is many-to-one, since finite bandwidth and finite aperture resolve delays and angles only to a limit, so scatterers displaced within those limits yield indistinguishable measurements. Third, a structure enters the channel only through the role it plays for a given link — reflecting, blocking, or leaving the signal untouched — and that role varies with where it sits
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: displaced within those limits yield indistinguishable measurements. Third, a structure enters the channel only through the role it plays for a given link — reflecting, blocking, or leaving the signal untouched — and that role varies with where it sits relative to transmitter and receiver: the same building reflects for one user, blocks another, and is invisible to a third. Scenes whose structures play the same roles for every link are indistinguishable at any resolution, so unlike the second source, this degeneracy is not removed by better hardware. Multiple observations narrow the ambiguity by intersecting the families of scenes each admits, and additional users and reflected paths enlarge A, but the intersection does not collapse to a single scene: the invariance outside A persists, and the resolution and role ambiguities remain within it. 2.3 A PROBABILISTIC FORMULATION Because the data do not determine a unique scene, we do not seek one. We take the solution object to be the posterior over scenes p(s|O) ∝p(O|s)p(s), whose structure is dictated by the physics of wave propagation. A deterministic regressor, which must commit a value to every cell, cannot represent this distinction and produces confident predictions on cells the measurements never constrained; a posterior can, which is what makes it the appropriate object here. Since the likelihood p(O|s) is defined only implicitly through ray tracing and is unavailable in closed form, we learn the posterior directly from paired physically consistent data (s, O) ∼D, as described next. 3 DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY Our objective is to learn the posterior over scenes given the measurements a network already collects. The difficulty is not only that the posterior is high-dimensional, but that a model trained directly on raw channels would have to solve two problems at once. It would have to discover, from finite data, how geometry writes itself into a channel — which structures produce which delays, which angle of arrivals, which signal blockage — and simultaneously learn to generate a coherent scene consis- tent with that mapping. The first of these is the physics of propagation and is shared across every link; the second is the inference problem specific to a given set of observations. Entangling them enforces supervision on rediscovering the underlying physics, and leaves the generative model to place mass over a combinatorially large space of grids
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: across every link; the second is the inference problem specific to a given set of observations. Entangling them enforces supervision on rediscovering the underlying physics, and leaves the generative model to place mass over a combinatorially large space of grids with no guidance about where the plausible scenes lie. We therefore propose a hierarchical framework, illustrated in Fig. 1, that separates these two burdens. The first stage learns the shared physical characteristics once: a multi-modal founda- tion model is pretrained to aggregate channel and positional information into a representation that is explicitly aligned, during pretraining, with the scene structure that shaped the observation. Each measurement is thereby encoded into a summary of the scene properties that could have produced it. The second stage performs the inference: the encoded representations of many observations of the same environment are fused as the conditioning set of a diffusion model that learns the posterior over occupancy, and a consensus over its samples yields the reconstructed scene. Because condi- tioning is expressed in a representation space that is aligned with geometrical properties rather than raw channel information, the generative model just resolves which scenes are consistent with the measurements rather than first inverting propagation. 3.1 PHYSICS-GROUNDED REPRESENTATION LEARNING In this section, we discuss the design and implementation of PHOENIX (a Physics-grounded Heterogeneous Observation Embedding for

text: channel information, the generative model just resolves which scenes are consistent with the measurements rather than first inverting propagation. 3.1 PHYSICS-GROUNDED REPRESENTATION LEARNING In this section, we discuss the design and implementation of PHOENIX (a Physics-grounded Heterogeneous Observation Embedding for Neural Inference across wireless conteXts), a multi- modal foundation model that learns a unified representation of the physical information governing wireless propagation. The overall pipeline of PHOENIX is illustrated in Fig. 2. At its core, PHOENIX employs a single-stream multi-modal transformer-based feature embed- ding framework to learn global, robust representations of the wireless channel by capturing cross- modality associations among the input data covering the wireless medium, the transmitter-receiver positioning, and the spatial-temporal characteristics of the received signal. Specifically, the chan- nel tensor in the input is converted into amplitude and phase and tokenized over antenna pairs and neighboring subcarriers; the height map is partitioned into non-overlapping patches; and the receiver location is projected to a single token. Each token additionally encodes its physical origin through antenna/subcarrier indices or normalized spatial coordinates, together with a modality embedding. A dedicated [PHYSC] token aggregates information across modalities under an asymmetric atten- tion mask: it attends to all modality tokens but is excluded as a key from the remaining tokens. 4

The [PHYSC] token is designed to aggregate information across modalities into a shared, physi- cally grounded representation that reflects the underlying wireless propagation structure. The key question is therefore how to ensure that this representation remains consistent with the observed wireless propagation and underlying physical correspondence across modalities. Architectural and tokenization details are provided in Appendix C. Physics-guided self-supervised pretraining. What makes the resulting representation physically meaningful is the pretraining objective. Conventional contrastive image–text style objectives (Rad- ford et al., 2021) are a poor fit here, as different scenes and user positions can produce similar chan- nels through different combinations of propagation paths, so matching and non-matching channel– scene pairs are not well defined. We instead pretrain with two complementary mechanisms. The
title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals

text: a poor fit here, as different scenes and user positions can produce similar chan- nels through different combinations of propagation paths, so matching and non-matching channel– scene pairs are not well defined. We instead pretrain with two complementary mechanisms. The first mechanism is bidirectional reconstruction, which learns cross-modal physical associations by reconstructing masked information in one modality from the others: masked complex channel values are recovered from the remaining channel tokens together with scene and location informa- tion, while masked regions of the building map are recovered from the observed channel. Crucially, scene masking is not applied uniformly. Because a wireless observation constrains only the envi- ronment reached by its propagation paths, asking the model to infer regions that left no trace in the channel would train it to hallucinate unsupported geometry. We therefore identify the scene patches intersected by the collective propagation paths of a given link and mask only within this propagation-relevant set. This encourages the model to associate channel structure with the scene geometry that actually shaped the observation. To capture dominant propagation effects, including blockage, reflection, and diffraction, without overfitting fine-grained geometry, the reconstruction target is limited to coarse occupancy at each masked location. The second is physics-guided cross-modal distillation, which shapes the [PHYSC] token. We train it to reconstruct a physical quantity jointly determined by

text: and diffraction, without overfitting fine-grained geometry, the reconstruction target is limited to coarse occupancy at each masked location. The second is physics-guided cross-modal distillation, which shapes the [PHYSC] token. We train it to reconstruct a physical quantity jointly determined by the environment, the link geometry, and the observed channel: the spatial spectrum which describes how signal energy is distributed over propagation directions and reveals the dominant angles of departure and arrival. Since those direc- tions are determined by the propagation medium and the link geometry, anchoring [PHYSC] to them ties its representation to physically interpretable propagation characteristics that remain mean- ingful across environments. We further align [PHYSC] with the part of the scene that produced it: the encoded tokens of the propagation-relevant scene patches, the structures that block, reflect, or diffract this particular link, are pooled into a scene representation, and [PHYSC] is encouraged to match it, while representations of unrelated links are pushed apart, with the separation relaxed for spatially nearby links that plausibly interact with the same structures. This alignment is the mecha- nism on which the rest of the paper depends: it is what makes zk a summary of the scene structure responsible for the observation. This closed-form parameterization allows us to obtain a noisy scene xt directly from the clean scene at any diffusion timestep. To reverse this corruption, the denoiser ϵθ predicts the noise added to the scene while condition- ing on the propagation-grounded representations Z. It is implemented as a Transformer over N 2 grid tokens, one per cell, each combining the noisy occupancy value at that cell with a positional embedding of its location relative to the base station. Every block applies self-attention among the grid tokens, with the diffusion timestep injected through adaptive layer normalization with zero- initialized gates, followed by cross-attention in which the grid tokens are queries and Z supplies keys and values. Cross-attention suits this conditioning structure for two reasons: it is permutation invariant and accepts a variable number of observations, so one model serves any K without retrain- ing; and since each zk encodes the scene structure that shaped observation k, cross-attention allows each grid cell to draw selectively on the observations carrying evidence about that part of the scene. In unCLIP, the embedding specifies semantic content, while dif- fusion stochasticity supplies visual detail the embedding leaves undetermined, making diversity desirable. In our setting, a single physical scene underlies the observations, and variation across posterior samples reflects genuine ambiguity that the measurements leave unresolved. We therefore seek the structure consistently supported by the observations rather than diverse scenes, which is what the consensus readout in equation 5 provides: it retains footprints supported across samples and suppresses structure arising from unresolved uncertainty. 4 EXPERIMENTS We pretrain the foundation model with the proposed physics-guided self-supervised objective on a digital-twin corpus of 11,000 outdoor environments and 30 million ray-traced channel observa- tions. The pretrained model then provides physics-grounded representations that condition the pos- terior diffusion model in our hierarchical pipeline, a configuration we refer to as Diffusion + FM. To provide an interpretable alternative to the diffusion formulation and isolate the contribution of joint posterior modeling, Marginal Prob. + FM replaces the diffusion posterior with a determin- istic per-observation decoder: each observation yields a cell-wise occupancy belief and a confi- dence score marking the propagation-relevant region over which that belief is meaningful. The predicted beliefs are then fused into the final reconstruction. To our knowledge, prior work does not directly address scene reconstruction from

text: cell-wise occupancy belief and a confi- dence score marking the propagation-relevant region over which that belief is meaningful. The predicted beliefs are then fused into the final reconstruction. To our knowledge, prior work does not directly address scene reconstruction from communication-infrastructure data and without ge- ometric priors, precluding a direct head-to-head comparison; we therefore use controlled baselines to isolate each component of our design. Diffusion + Raw Meas. conditions the identical dif- fusion model on raw observations and user locations, testing whether the scene posterior can be learned without the intermediate scene-aligned representation; this is closest in spirit to (Hehn et al., 2025), which reconstructs indoor geometry from a single link’s received power with the assump- tion of knowing floor and ceiling geometry. Marginal Prob. + Raw Meas. predicts occupancy over the full grid from each measurement under a binary cross-entropy objective and aggregates the per-measurement predictions, without modeling the observation-specific propagation-relevant region. Training objectives and implementation details for all models are given in Appendices G–I. Given 500 wireless channel measurements from a single base-station node, our framework recovers the surrounding building footprints, their location, extent, and arrangement, from the wireless channel observations and user position, without any prior over scene informa- tion. The reconstructions closely follow ground-truth layouts across environments with substan- tially different spatial density and structure. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that communication-infrastructure channel measurements can support reconstruction of arbitrary out- door scene geometry without assumptions on the number, shape, or placement of structures. By performing posterior inference over physics-grounded representations, our framework makes this ill-posed inverse problem tractable and allows existing radio links to act as environmental sensors. Several conclusions follow from the results. The comparison with Diffusion + Raw Meas. isolates the benefit of the physics-grounded repre- sentation. The decoder, noise schedule, and sampler are otherwise identical, yet conditioning on raw channels collapses to near-chance performance. This indicates a failure of learnability rather than information: raw channels contain at least as much scene information as their learned rep- resentations, but the decoder must simultaneously discover the propagation-to-geometry mapping and perform posterior generation from a high-dimensional input. text: of learnability rather than information: raw channels contain at least as much scene information as their learned rep- resentations, but the decoder must simultaneously discover the propagation-to-geometry mapping and perform posterior generation from a high-dimensional input. In contrast, the foundation model provides scene-aligned representations that substantially simplify posterior inference. Marginal Prob. + Raw Meas. fails for a different reason. Its full-grid cross-entropy requires ev- ery observation to predict every scene cell, even though a measurement is informative only about propagation-relevant regions. The resulting overconfident predictions in uninformed regions accu- mulate during fusion, where observations that never sensed a cell still contribute votes to it. Marginal Prob. + FM uses the same fusion but forms each per-observation belief on the physics-grounded representation and around the propagation-relevant cells of that observation, abstaining elsewhere; each vote is therefore informative where it is cast, and the aggregation better recovers the scene. Our proposed design improves over this baseline by 22.1% in balanced accuracy and 67.0% in F1 score. Lastly, the results demonstrate that the joint posterior outperforms fused marginals in this setting. The main advantage is concentrated in the upper tail of the per-scene distribution: the median IoU of the two models differs by three percent relative, while at the 90th percentile the gap widens to sixteen percent. The marginal variant treats observations independently and combines them through a fixed rule: confidence gating discards evidence that is weak in each observation but informative in combination, and nothing in the fusion enforces that the result be a plausible scene. The diffusion decoder instead learns the joint posterior over the entire grid given the full set of observations. It fuses evidence in representation space, and it completes the scene through the learned prior where the measurements are silent, the second factor in equation 2. text: We presented a hierarchical framework for reconstructing environmental geometry from wireless channel measurements by combining physics-grounded representation learning with joint generative posterior inference. A wireless foundation model first extracts scene-relevant information from individual observations, while a diffusion model jointly integrates these representations to infer the posterior over scene occupancy, from which a per-cell consensus over sampled scenes recovers the building footprints. Results demonstrate our framework can recover previously unseen scene structures from communication signals, and controlled comparisons show the importance of our hierarchical design for effectively solving the underlying ill-posed inverse problem. The results highlight the potential of existing wireless infrastructure to serve for environmental perception. 9

Let Sk(Hk) = {s : F(s, pk) = Hk} be the set of scenes reproducing the noiseless measurement exactly. Then |Sk(Hk)| ≥2|ac k|. Proof. B.3 PROPAGATION-EQUIVALENT SCENES By the path-sum forward model, the channel of link k depends on the scene only through the path set it induces, P(s, pk), and its parameters. Distinct interaction sequences can produce the same path param- eters. A single specular reflection from one surface and consecutive reflections from two others can yield the same total delay and the same departure and arrival angles, in which case the two scenes contribute identical terms to the path sum. Here the roles themselves differ — different cells re- flect — yet the scenes remain propagation-equivalent. This mechanism is exact when the geometry makes the parameters coincide, as symmetric layouts often do, and approximate otherwise, in which case it compounds with the finite-resolution ambiguity of Appendix B.2. A cell may be occupied and still fail to obstruct a link whose line-of-sight segment passes over it. The base station and the user sit at different heights, so the direct ray clears any structure shorter than its elevation at that point, and a two-dimensional occupancy grid records only that a building is present, not whether it is tall enough to intercept the ray. A cell can therefore belong to the propagation-relevant set of an observation — it lies along a path the link uses — while the measurement still carries no evidence against its being occupied: the unobstructed channel is equally consistent with free space and with a structure the ray passes above. 13

For each transmit antenna t, receive antenna r, and group g of nsc neighboring subcarriers, one channel token is formed by concatenating the corresponding ampli- tude and phase values, xch t,r,g = [ at,r,g,1:nsc ∥ϕt,r,g,1:nsc ] ∈R2nsc, giving Nch = NtxNrxNsc/nsc tokens. This preserves full transmit- and receive-antenna resolution, since each antenna pair carries distinct spatial information, while grouping subcarriers to represent local frequency structure compactly. Scene and location tokenization. The height map S ∈RN×N is partitioned into non-overlapping p × p patches, flattened, and projected analogously, yielding (N/p)2 scene tokens. The receiver location is projected by a single linear layer into one location token. Physically grounded positional and modality embeddings. Tokenization captures content but not physical origin. For channel tokens we encode position separately along the trans- mit, receive, and subcarrier axes using sinusoidal encodings and concatenate them, ech t,r,g = [ PEtx(t) ∥PErx(r) ∥PEsc(g) ], preserving both the spatial structure of the arrays and the fre- quency structure of the channel. For scene patches we apply a two-layer MLP to sinusoidal features of the patch’s normalized distance and bearing relative to the base station, so each to- ken carries its geometric relationship to the reference position. A learnable modality embedding m(i) ∈{mch, mscn, mloc} identifies the token type. The final input token is the sum of the three: what the token contains, where it comes from physically, and

The final input token is the sum of the three: what the token contains, where it comes from physically, and which modality it belongs to. Encoder. Because channel tokens vastly outnumber scene and location tokens, lightweight pre- encoder blocks first operate on channel tokens alone, using rotary position embeddings across the (t, r, g) axes to capture local correlations across nearby antennas and frequencies before cross-modal fusion; absolute encodings are retained for the subsequent stage. All tokens are then concatenated into a single sequence prefixed by [PHYSC] and processed by a single-stream transformer with merged-token self-attention, so all modalities interact from the first layer. A binary attention mask enforces the asymmetry described in the main text: [PHYSC] is an unrestricted query over all tokens but is excluded as a key everywhere, so it can read from the sequence without any token reading from it. F PROOFS OF THE CONSENSUS PROPOSITIONS In the following, we establish the propositions that characterize the theoretical properties of our consensus estimator. We first show that consensus under the learned posterior yields the Bayes- optimal per-cell decision. We then show that consensus from a near-optimal posterior recovers the true scene values on the observable set, with the reconstruction error decreasing as the number of observations increases. This is the same representational gap discussed in Appendix B.3, where a link may clear an occupied cell entirely. It also bounds what any amount of data can achieve, since δi is limited by how much of the physical scene the grid leaves unspecified, and is therefore one reason accuracy saturates below unity in Section 4.4 even as observations accumulate. The quantity governing recovery at a cell is ni, the number of observations that actually separate the competing hypotheses there, which excludes both uncovered and role-degenerate observations. Role degeneracy therefore does not halt recovery; it reduces the effective number of informative observations, and only if every link in the deployment were non-separating for a pair differing at a cell would that cell remain unresolved. Regarding (A1), diffusion models are consistent in the limit of data and capacity, not at finite scale, so the proposition describes the ideal posterior and the empirical question is how closely pθ approaches it; the comparison against a decoder conditioned on raw channels probes the sufficiency half of this assumption. G DATASET AND TRAINING DETAILS Dataset. Channels are simulated with Sionna RT (Hoydis et al., 2023) over more than 11,000 outdoor urban environments spanning 200 cities, each covering a 200 m × 200 m area, with three- dimensional building geometry extracted from OpenStreetMap (OpenStreetMap contributors, 2023) using the Geo2SigMap pipeline (Li et al., 2024). Simulations use a carrier frequency of 5.8 GHz with 100 MHz bandwidth and 128 subcarriers. The base station is equipped with a uniform linear array of Ntx = 32 antennas at a height of 15 m and serves more than 2,000 randomly placed users per environment, each equipped with an Nrx = 8-element uniform linear array at 1.5 m. The dataset comprises over 30 million samples, each consisting of a complex channel tensor, the user location, and the building height map. Occupancy grids are obtained on a 20 × 20 grid, i.e. ∆R = 10 m, whose cells coincide with the scene patches of the foundation model. Under all three colorings, the [PHYSC] embed- dings form markedly clearer structure than the raw channels, and each of the three carries a distinct implication for this work. Separation by user position indicates that the representation resolves where a link terminates, which is a prerequisite for placing the evidence an observation carries at the correct location in the scene. Separation by dominant propagation direction indicates that the representation disentangles the an- gular components of the channel — the departure and arrival directions that determine which struc- tures a link interacts with — rather than retaining the raw superposition in which those components are mixed. The representation thus carries information about the envi- ronment that produced a measurement and not merely about the measurement itself, which is what makes a set of embeddings from one scene an informative conditioning set for the posterior over that scene. text: Beyond Fixed Acquisition Functions: Temporal Difference Active Learning for Perturbation Discovery Xudong Zhang1,2,∗ Jianzhe Li1,2,∗ Yitong Tang1 Peijie Zhou1,2,† 1Center for Machine Learning Research, Peking University, Beijing, China 2AI for Science Institute (AISI), Beijing, China xudongzhang25@stu.pku.edu.cn ∗Equal contribution. †Corresponding author.
title: Beyond Fixed Acquisition Functions:

text: Genetic and drug perturbation screens are important tools for elucidating disease mechanisms and validating therapeutic targets, but experimental costs limit the number of candidates that can be tested. Existing perturbation screening methods typically update the surrogate model with feedback while keeping the acquisition function fixed, limiting their ability to adapt selection to different response landscapes. Experimental feedback reveals current hits and informs subsequent selection by updating candidate predictions, providing a training signal for learning how to select experiments. We formulate budgeted perturbation discovery as a sequential decision problem and propose Temporal Difference Active Learning (TDAL), which learns an acquisition function online through temporal difference learning from a single screening trajectory, accounting for current hits and future discoveries. TDAL uses the Hellinger distance between hit probabilities for unmeasured candidates before and after an experiment to weight successor value, and reuses measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO) to construct virtual transitions and alleviate training data scarcity. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations under varied experimental configurations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods and ranks first on four tasks, demonstrating its adaptability across response landscapes.
title: Beyond Fixed Acquisition Functions:

text: Large-scale perturbational screens deepen the understanding of disease mechanisms and help validate therapeutic targets (Schmidt et al., 2022; Zhuang et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2021). The human genome comprises nearly 20,000 single-gene candidates, roughly 200 million pairs, and one trillion triples in terms of perturbation combinations. The costs of testing each perturbation and measuring its phenotype make exhaustive screening infeasible (Mehrjou et al., 2022; Pacchiano et al., 2023). Closed-loop systems have shown that model-guided experiment selection can improve biological discovery under limited resources (Xu et al., 2026; DeMeo et al., 2025). It is thus important to develop strategies that maximize cumulative discoveries within a fixed experimental budget. Active learning addresses this challenge by iteratively fitting a surrogate model to measured outcomes and using an acquisition function to select subsequent experiments (Figure 1a). GeneDisco evaluates active learning methods for perturbation screening and reports substantial variation in their performance across experimental settings (Mehrjou et al., 2022). Existing methods employ different selection criteria to guide perturbation discovery. OAE (Pacchiano et al., 2023) seeks near-optimal perturbations, DiscoBAX (Lyle et al., 2023) considers response strength and mechanistic diversity, and Probability-of-Hit (PoH) (Rubbi et al., 2026) prioritizes perturbations that exceed a predefined phenotypic threshold. Recent approaches also incorporate language model agents or biological priors into experiment selection (Roohani et al., 2025; Hao et al., 2025;

However, unlike reinforcement learning with repeated episodes, a screening campaign follows a single trajectory that cannot be reset, with each candidate queried at most once and only one real transition generated per round. Learning an acquisition function from such limited feedback presents a particular challenge. Here we introduce Temporal Difference Active Learning (TDAL), which learns a dynamic acquisition function online from experimental feedback to maximize cumulative discoveries. Building on surrogate hit probabilities, TDAL uses temporal difference learning to incorporate observed discoveries and feedback-weighted successor value into experiment selection. It weights successor value according to changes in predicted hit probabilities for the remaining candidates, reflecting how experimental feedback updates their predicted outcomes. To alleviate the scarcity of real transitions, TDAL constructs additional training transitions from previously measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO). Our main contributions are threefold. • We formulate perturbation discovery as a sequential decision problem and learn a dynamic acquisition function from experimental feedback to adapt to different response landscapes. • We introduce TDAL, which learns online from a single screening trajectory through temporal difference learning. It uses the Hellinger distance to weight successor value and LBO to construct additional training transitions, alleviating training data scarcity. • We evaluate TDAL across eight screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations. text: 2.1 Active Learning and Acquisition Function Learning Active learning alternates between sample selection and model updates to improve predictions with fewer labels. Methods include BALD, which uses information gain (Houlsby et al., 2011), CoreSet, which emphasizes geometric coverage (Sener and Savarese, 2018), and BADGE, which combines uncertainty and diversity (Ash et al., 2020). For discovery, active search (Garnett et al., 2012), ENS (Jiang et al., 2017), and its batch extension (Jiang et al., 2018) evaluate future hits within the budget. IDS (Xu et al., 2022) balances instantaneous regret and information gain to increase cumulative response. These methods adapt sampling to observations but retain predefined acquisition functions. Other approaches learn acquisition functions from data. Learning Active Learning predicts expected error reduction (Konyushkova et al., 2017). MetaBO trains acquisition functions through reinforcement learning across tasks (Volpp et al., 2020). Amortized active search trains a neural network to imitate ENS selections (Nguyen et al., 2024). In molecular discovery, GLARE updates its selection policy online using measured activity labels (Chen et al., 2025), while Zhang et al. (2026) learn a policy to identify the optimal molecule. SOFisher uses Double DQN to select spatial-omics fields of view (Li et al., 2026b). Our work focuses on perturbation screens, where TDAL learns a dynamic acquisition function online from experimental feedback. 2.2 Active Learning for Perturbation Discovery Active

Our work focuses on perturbation screens, where TDAL learns a dynamic acquisition function online from experimental feedback. 2.2 Active Learning for Perturbation Discovery Active learning guides the discovery of perturbations with target phenotypes under a limited experimental budget. GeneDisco provides a unified benchmark for gene perturbations (Mehrjou et al., 2022). OAE seeks near-optimal perturbations with high responses (Pacchiano et al., 2023), DiscoBAX balances response strength and mechanistic diversity (Lyle et al., 2023), and PoH selects candidates by their posterior probability of exceeding a predefined phenotypic threshold (Rubbi et al., 2026). RECOVER and NAIAD target drug and genetic combination discovery, respectively (Bertin et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2025), while BATCHIE uses information-driven batch design to improve predictions of drug combination responses (Tosh et al., 2025). These methods update surrogate models from observations while typically keeping acquisition functions fixed. Biological priors and agents guide selection. IterPert improves predictions with multimodal priors (Huang et al., 2024), while BioBO combines gene representations and pathway information (Li et al., 2026a). Soper et al. (2025) and DeepAL (Zhu et al., 2026) combine knowledge graphs with Bayesian matrix factorization and representation learning, respectively, for double gene perturbation discovery. BioDiscoveryAgent and PerTurboAgent design perturbations using language models, experimental history, and tools

We construct transitions from feedback to learn a dynamic acquisition function that adapts to different response landscapes (Appendix A.1). 3 Problem Formulation We consider a fixed candidate pool and aim to maximize expected cumulative discoveries of perturbations that induce desired phenotypic responses within a fixed experimental budget. We formulate this task as a sequential decision problem and define an objective combining immediate discoveries with successor value weighted according to experimental feedback (notation in Appendix A.2). 3

Then we examine how local landscape structure affects active discovery, assess individual components through ablations, and analyze candidate rankings over selection rounds. 5.1 Experimental Setup Data and budgets. We evaluate TDAL on eight public datasets recording phenotypic responses to genetic perturbations, aiming to identify perturbations producing desired phenotypic changes (Appendix C.1). These comprise four single perturbation tasks (Schmidt et al., 2022; Zhuang et al., 2019; Carnevale et al., 2022), 7

Initial sample sizes, batch sizes, and budgets vary across tasks (Table C2). Experimental protocol. We conduct retrospective sequential evaluation using measured phenotypes from these genetic perturbation datasets. Candidate identities and fixed representations are available at the start. Each method initially receives the phenotypes of 𝑛0 candidates, and the remaining outcomes are revealed as candidates are selected in subsequent rounds. We fix the hit threshold 𝜏before screening to target the top 5% of candidates in the predefined effect direction (Mehrjou et al., 2022). General acquisition functions include UCB (Srinivas et al., 2010), Expected Improvement (Jones et al., 1998), and Thompson Sampling (Thompson, 1933). text: We introduce TDAL to learn a dynamic acquisition function online from a single perturbation screening trajectory. Building on surrogate-estimated hit probabilities, TDAL uses temporal difference learning to incorporate observed discoveries and feedback-weighted successor value, while LBO reconstructs additional training transitions from measured outcomes. By learning how to select experiments from feedback accumulated within the ongoing screen, TDAL adapts candidate selection to both immediate discoveries and subsequent discovery opportunities under limited experimental feedback. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods, demonstrating consistent discovery performance across diverse response landscapes. Limitations. Our evaluation is retrospective, and the additive acquisition function does not explicitly model interactions among candidates within a batch. Feedback weighting also relies on surrogate-estimated hit probabilities, motivating further investigation of its robustness to prediction errors. Future work will explore batch-aware selection and alternative feedback weighting strategies, alongside prospective validation in closed-loop biological experiments. Reproducibility statement The TDAL implementation, task configurations, and data preparation scripts are available at https://anonymous. 4open.science/r/TDAL/, with data sources and running instructions. Appendices A–C provide implementation details, theoretical assumptions and proofs, and experimental settings, respectively. text: new tissue sections, while incorporating newly sampled observations into the state. TDAL performs both acquisition updates and successor value bootstrapping within the current screening task. Experience augmentation reconstructs additional transitions from measured outcomes to train the acquisition function. In budgeted experimental design without replacement, the measured dataset grows while the unmeasured pool and remaining budget shrink. A screen therefore provides a single executed trajectory and cannot return to an earlier state to test alternative experimental sequences within the same budget. LBO reconstructs predecessor states in which a measured batch has not yet been observed, then restores that batch’s real outcomes to form additional transitions to a known successor state. The same experimental outcomes can thus support batch value learning under different information states, expanding online training experience without additional experiments. text: A.3 Complete TDAL Algorithm Algorithm 1 summarizes TDAL from initialization through the end of screening. Starting from the initial observations 𝐷0, TDAL fits a surrogate model, estimates hit probabilities for candidates in the initial unmeasured pool 𝑈0, and forms the initial selection state. It then constructs initial LBO transitions from 𝐷0 to initialize the acquisition network through TD training before the first query. At each round, the acquisition function scores candidates in 𝑈𝑡, and TDAL queries the 𝐵candidates with the highest scores. The observed outcomes are added to 𝐷𝑡, and the queried candidates are removed from 𝑈𝑡. TDAL refits the surrogate model on the updated data. Before the next round, it updates predictions over 𝑈𝑡+1 to construct the successor state. Comparing hit probabilities before and after the experiment over this pool gives the Hellinger weight. The selected batch, observed discovery count, feedback weight, and current and successor states form a real transition. Real and online LBO transitions enter the replay buffer, from which TD updates train the acquisition network for subsequent selection. After 𝑇rounds, TDAL returns all verified hit candidates. text: A.4 Candidate Representations The mapping 𝜙(𝑥) encodes candidate perturbation 𝑥as a vector of fixed dimension, providing gene functional information to the surrogate and acquisition network. Human tasks use genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 knockout screening data from the Broad Institute’s Project Achilles. The CERES gene dependency profiles in DepMap 20Q4 provide 808-dimensional gene representa- tions. Each dimension corresponds to a cancer cell line and describes the effect of knocking out the gene on cell growth. CERES corrects for copy number effects (Meyers et al., 2017). The Kuzmin yeast task uses the 500-dimensional STRING network embeddings released with Mashup (Cho et al., 2016). These base gene representations remain fixed during screening. Before the batch outcomes are observed, averaging the updated probability 𝑞𝑥over their possible values recovers the current probability 𝑝𝑥, giving E[𝑞𝑥| 𝐻𝑡, 𝐴𝑡] = 𝑝𝑥. (41) This analysis uses conditional hit probabilities before and after experimental feedback. TDAL approximates these probabilities using MC dropout predictions. The expected reduction in mean squared prediction error is Δpred = 1 |𝑈| ∑︁ 𝑥∈𝑈E  (𝑝𝑥−𝑧(𝑥))2 −(𝑞𝑥−𝑧(𝑥))2 . UCB, EI, TS, TopUncertain, and OAE use the GeneDisco Bayesian MLP and retrain their surrogate after each round of new observations (Mehrjou et al., 2022). PoH. Many Needles selects the 𝐵unmeasured candidates with the highest estimated probability of exceeding the hit threshold (Rubbi et al., 2026). At each round, we refit a Bayesian MLP with two hidden layers of widths 128 and 64 on the measured data. For each candidate 𝑥∈𝑈𝑡, we obtain 50 MC dropout predictions and use their mean and standard deviation to form a Gaussian predictive approximation. The probability of exceeding 𝜏then serves as the acquisition score. OAE. OAE uses optimistic estimates for batch discovery of candidates with high responses. We use its released Bayesian variant, which combines predictive means and uncertainty to select each batch after aligning predictions with the effect direction (Pacchiano et al., 2023). DiscoBAX. DiscoBAX targets a diverse subset of candidates with high responses and uses fantasized observations to estimate information gain about that subset. We use the authors’ surrogate training and acquisition implementation, with two hidden layers of 128 and 64 units and dropout 0.2 to match TDAL and PoH in network capacity. We evaluate this implementation on the four single gene perturbation tasks (Lyle et al., 2023).

text: Expected Improvement (EI). EI estimates the expected improvement over the best effect observed so far and prioritizes candidates with larger expected gains (Jones et al., 1998). Thompson Sampling (TS). TS draws an effect function from the surrogate posterior and selects a batch by ranking unmeasured candidates under that draw, allowing model uncertainty to influence selection (Thompson, 1933). TopUncertain. TopUncertain ranks candidates by predictive standard deviation and allocates experiments to regions where the surrogate is most uncertain (Mehrjou et al., 2022). BADGE. BADGE selects diverse batches using k-means++ in a gradient representation space. We use the GeneDisco regression implementation and its proxy gradient representations (Ash et al., 2020; Mehrjou et al., 2022). CoreSet. CoreSet greedily expands geometric coverage in the candidate representation space extracted by the surrogate. It successively selects the candidate farthest from the existing selection centers (Sener and Savarese, 2018). KMeans-Embedding. This method uses k-means to cluster candidate representations extracted by the surrogate and selects candidates near cluster centers to represent different regions of the candidate space (Mehrjou et al., 2022). text: E.1 Local Hit Enrichment and Discovery Gains on Real Tasks Local hit enrichment. We compare the hit fraction around hit candidates with the overall hit fraction in the analysis sample to measure how hits cluster in candidate representation space. Neighbors are determined by cosine distance after standardizing the fixed candidate representations 𝜙(𝑥) and applying L2 normalization. For each task, we randomly sample hit candidates and other candidates in their proportions in the full candidate pool, forming an analysis sample P of at most 10,000 candidates. Let P+ = {𝑥∈P : 𝑧(𝑥) = 1} be its hit set. For each hit candidate 𝑥, let N10(𝑥) contain the ten nearest other candidates within P. We compute the hit fraction among these ten neighbors, average it over all hit candidates, and divide by the overall hit fraction in the sample to obtain Enrich10 = 1 |P+| ∑︁ 𝑥∈P+ 1 10 ∑︁ 𝑦∈N10(𝑥) 𝑧(𝑦) |P+|/|P| . (74) The numerator is the mean neighbor hit fraction around hit candidates, and the denominator is the overall hit fraction in the analysis sample. For example, an overall hit fraction of 5% and a mean neighbor hit fraction of 15% give 3× enrichment. Values above one indicate that other hits are more common near hit candidates. Values near one indicate a similar hit fraction to the sample overall,

We construct landscapes in which hits are dispersed or concentrated in six clusters. The 17,660 candidates have fixed two-dimensional coordinates that are defined without phenotype information. KMeans divides these coordinates into six regions, each with a response peak at its center. Within each region, candidates closer to the center receive higher response scores. We sort candidates by distance, negate their ranks, and divide by the region’s hit quota. The quotas are 148 for one region and 147 for each of the other five, giving 883 hits in total. title: Causal Integrated Gradients:

text: Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known—for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene’s expression. Yet existing gradient-based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature’s downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature’s attribution into a direct effect and effects medi- ated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG’s attribu- tions best match the ground-truth causal effect from Pearl’s do-calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Sec- ond, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-β stimulation data,
title: Causal Integrated Gradients:

text: Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Sec- ond, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-β stimulation data, where only an ap- proximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient-based attribu- tions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability. Code is available at https://github.com/sifrimlab/CausalIG. 1

text: As machine learning models grow increasingly complex, particularly deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets, the need for interpretable explanations of their predictions becomes critical. Local post-hoc explanation methods have emerged as a popular approach for understanding the contribution of individual input features to model predictions. However, most existing methods assume that input features are independent, which is often unrealistic in practice. Feature dependencies are common in real-world applications—in gene expression, for instance, genes exhibit complex inter-dependencies reflecting underlying biological processes. Some approaches have been proposed to incorporate feature dependencies into attribution methods. Methods based on Shapley values, such as conditional SHAP [Aas et al., 2021] and causal Shapley values [Heskes et al., 2020], can account for dependencies but rely on sampling-based computations that become prohibitively expensive in high-dimensional settings. To address this gap, we propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), principled extensions of integrated gradients that incorporate causal structure among input features. Like causal Shapley values [Heskes et al., 2020], our methods require the structure of a causal graph over the inputs; unlike them, we need only a deterministic, off-the-shelf surrogate rather than a full conditional distribution to sample from. Conditional SHAP needs no causal graph but does need that conditional distribution, while standard integrated and expected gradients need neither. In return for this graph, our methods keep the efficiency of integrated gradients and, under conditions on the causal graph and surrogate, its axiomatic guarantees. They scale to high-dimensional settings, recovering upstream causal drivers that graph-agnostic methods miss, as in gene regulation (Figure 1). The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • We propose causal integrated and expected gradients (CIG and CEG), extending integrated gradients to incorporate causal structure among input features. By the gradient theorem, R 1 0 ∇F(γ(α)) · dγ(α) dα dα = F(x) −F(b); expanding the dot product gives the feature attribution Ri, interpreted as feature xi’s effect on the model output: n X i=1 Z 1 0 ∂F(γ(α)) ∂γi(α) dγi(α) dα dα = n X i=1 Ri = F(x) −F(b). (1) Equation 1 guarantees the completeness property: attributions sum exactly to the difference in model output between the input and the baseline. Integrated gradients [Sundararajan et al., 2017] and expected gradients [Erion et al., 2021] are both instances of this framework: integrated gradients uses a straight-line path γ(α) = b + α(x −b) from a fixed baseline, approximated in practice via a K-step Riemann sum; expected gradients instead averages over a distribution of baselines to remove the sensitivity to this single fixed choice, sampling the baseline and path parameter α ∼U(0, 1) jointly to form a Monte Carlo estimator. Both methods, however, implicitly assume that features are mutually independent along the path. The incorporation of feature dependencies in local

Both methods, however, implicitly assume that features are mutually independent along the path. The incorporation of feature dependencies in local attribution methods has instead been most thor- oughly explored in the context of Shapley values. Conditional SHAP [Aas et al., 2021] and causal Shapley values [Heskes et al., 2020] are prominent examples. Conditional SHAP accounts for statis- tical dependencies by replacing the marginal feature distribution with the conditional distribution when computing Shapley values, while causal Shapley values incorporate an explicit causal graph to distinguish direct effects from indirect effects mediated through other features. Another extension of Shapley values is the Owen value, which takes into account that features belong to groups [Giménez and Puente, 2019]. The partition explainer in the shap Python package [Lundberg and Lee, 2017] computes Owen values by reducing the number of coalitions on which the marginal contributions are computed, based on an initial partitioning of the features. While incorporating dependencies is contested [Janzing et al., 2020, Aas et al., 2021], it is preferable when the goal is to understand the true data-generating process [Chen et al., 2020, Michiels et al., 2024] — a consideration especially consequential in biological discovery. Numerous modifications to the integrated gradients algorithm have been proposed, though none address feature dependencies. Most target either attribution noise [Kapishnikov et al., 2021], the reliance on an arbitrary baseline [Erion et al., 2021], or both [Yang et al., 2023, Zhuo and Ge, 2024]. Two works are particularly relevant to ours, as they also modify the integration path: Kapishnikov et al. [2021] alters it to avoid regions of high partial derivatives, hypothesized to introduce noise, while Zhuo and Ge [2024] defines a path that follows the model’s gradient. Our work differs fundamentally from both — rather than modifying the path for numerical reasons, we do so to encode causal structure among input features. Feature attribution methods have been widely used to interpret deep learning models trained on RNA expression data and extract biologically meaningful insights [Yap et al., 2021, Janizek et al., 2023, Tang et al., 2023]. This freedom in the path has been exploited before [Kapishnikov et al., 2021, Zhuo and Ge, 2024], but always for numerical reasons. We continue with the most general case of a fully connected DAG, with features ordered topologically: if xu depends on xv, then u > v. text: 3.2 Determining the gradients of the path function To evaluate Equation 3 via a Riemann sum over K steps, we require the following extra gradients at each point α(p) = p/K, p = 1, . . . , K, along the path: ∂γi ∂α (α(p)), ∂γj ∂γi (γ(p) i ), (4) with γ(p) i = bi + α(p)(xi −bi), i.e. a straight-line path as in regular integrated gradients. To compute these, we need an explicit formulation of the path functions γi. To this end, we interpret the model and the feature dependencies as a structural causal model (SCM) (as previously in Janzing et al., 2020, Heskes et al., 2020). If the arrow directions in the chain rule diagram of the left panel of Figure 2 are switched, the graph effectively represents a causal graph, and the path functions can represent the structural mechanism between parent and child nodes of the graph. We will interpret α as residual information, which explains the part of the variation in the children that is not explained by their parents. As is common in causal inference, we assume this residual enters additively. Concretely, for a fully connected DAG with features ordered topologically, we model each feature as: xi = γi(x1, . . . , xi−1, α) = ci(x1, . . . , xi−1) + hi(α),

text: the next section. 3.3 Modeling feature dependencies through a surrogate model Any differentiable surrogate model can be employed to model the feature dependencies under a known causal structure. Here, we introduce a surrogate model that is flexible enough to model complex dependencies while being efficient and scalable to high-dimensional datasets. We propose a sparse masked surrogate s that parameterizes parent-to-child relationships as a sum of edge-wise contributions, operating on a directed graph defined by an adjacency matrix M ∈Rn×n, where Mij = 1 indicates that feature i is a parent of feature j. Each parent feature xi is first transformed using a per-feature basis expansion ϕ(xi) ∈RQ of size Q, to give the surrogate model more flexibility in learning nonlinear effects. The basis consists of three components applied to standardized inputs: 1) polynomial terms, 2) truncated power functions with learnable knots, and 3) Fourier features (see Appendix B for a detailed explanation of the basis expansion). For every active edge (i →j) such that Mij = 1, the prediction for child node j is obtained by summing contributions from all parent nodes: sj = ˆxj = X i:Mij=1 ⟨wij, ϕ(xi)⟩+ µj, (7) where µj and wij ∈RQ are learnable per-node intercept and edge-specific coefficients, respectively. Rather than materializing all possible n2 parent-child interactions, the model stores only active graph edges.

Standard expected gradients performs well with just one path point per baseline, since the straight-line path has a constant, closed-form derivative dγi/dα = xi −bi, so a single sampled α already gives this derivative exactly. Our method’s path derivative ∂γi/∂α is instead estimated via a backward finite difference (Equation 6), since hi(α) is generally nonlinear; our method therefore benefits from allocating more of a fixed evaluation budget to additional path points per baseline rather than to additional baselines, since both the finite-difference and Riemann-sum errors (Appendix C) compound when paths are under-sampled. 3.5 Axiomatic properties Since our method belongs to the family of path methods [Sundararajan et al., 2017], it inherits completeness and sensitivity(a) (for the direct term) unconditionally, and implementation invariance, symmetry, and linearity under precise preconditions on the causal graph and surrogate that we formalize in Appendix C. Experimental setup and costs are reported in Appendix E. 4.1 Comparison with causal attributions Conditional SHAP [Aas et al., 2021] and causal Shapley values [Heskes et al., 2020] are the most established approaches for dependency-aware feature attribution. To evaluate how well each method captures ground-truth causal effects, we compare their attributions against a reference causal effect derived from Pearl’s do-calculus [Pearl, 2009]. Among the causal effects this framework gives rise to, the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) is the most appropriate for local explanations, as it measures the effect of intervening on a single feature while conditioning on the root nodes R: CATEi = E[F | do(Xi = xi), XR\{i} = xR\{i}] −E[F | do(Xi = bi), XR\{i} = xR\{i}]. Finally, on all nodes (Figure F.1), CIG still performs better than all other methods. 4.2 Causal gene recovery in a simulated biological dataset We evaluate our method on a regression task using simulated single-cell gene expression data, predicting each cell’s simulated differentiation time from its trajectory of activated and repressed transcription factors. The dataset is generated with Dyngen [Cannoodt et al., 2021] under a known gene regulatory network (GRN) with a backbone of transcription factors (TFs) that causally regulate downstream genes. Unlike the per-sample CATEs of the synthetic benchmark above, ground truth here is exact but global: the backbone TFs are the known drivers of the simulation, letting us test recovery at realistic single-cell scale and complexity. After filtering and normalization, a fully connected neural network is trained to predict simulated time. The GRN defines both the feature ordering and surrogate structure for our method. We evaluate several CIG/CEG variants (linear or expanded-basis surrogate, first- or second-order terms), against attribution baselines from the captum and shap packages [Kokhlikyan et al., 2020, Lundberg and Lee, 2017], over five random seeds. The recovery of DEGs (Appendix I.3, Table I.5) reveals that DeepSHAP and integrated gradients rank DEGs higher than CIG. CIG also shows the weakest correlation with the DE statistic across all cell types (Table I.3), likely because it prioritizes upstream regulators, which are rarely strong DEGs themselves. ORA results (Appendix I.4) confirm that CIG uniquely picks out pathways with transcription factors that regulate the interferon- β response, with significantly enriched pathways such as TNF-α/NF-κB, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, and interferon response. DeepSHAP, by contrast, enriches only for the interferon response, with the remaining pathways enriched by integrated gradients not reaching significance. 5 Limitations and future work Our method requires prior knowledge of the directed causal structure among features, which for biological data can often be sourced from curated knowledge bases such as OmniPath [Türei et al., 2021]. text: Since such a graph may be imperfect in practice, we test how much this assumption can be violated before performance suffers by removing, adding, and reversing edges: CIG degrades under genuine information loss (removal or reversal) but tolerates spurious additions almost entirely, so the graph need not be exactly correct to retain most of the benefit (Appendix K). A separate concern is whether CIG’s advantage merely reflects graph access, not correct use of it. We rule this out: CIG’s attributions are instance-specific, tracking each cell’s actual transition rather than the static graph alone (Appendix J). Like causal Shapley values [Heskes et al., 2020] and conditional SHAP [Aas et al., 2021], CIG is true to the data rather than to the model: it recovers causal drivers under the supplied structure and is not meant for debugging a model’s idiosyncratic behavior. Extending the method to undirected or partially directed graphs is a natural direction for future work. Our surrogate models each feature’s mechanism as additive across parents (Section 3.3) and so cannot capture non-additive parent interactions. This is a limitation of our chosen surrogate, not of the method, since any differentiable surrogate can be substituted. The one case a different surrogate cannot fix is an unmodeled confounder, whose effect is folded into the additive residual and attributed to xi’s direct effect. In

In our experiments this biases attribution magnitudes for affected nodes (Appendix L). Our methods scale quadratically in the number of features in the worst case, slower than integrated gra- dients but substantially faster than Shapley-based alternatives; our synthetic and real-data experiments (100–1000 features; 2,320–6,941 genes) already exceed the scale at which existing dependency-aware baselines have been validated (Heskes et al. [2020]: M=7 features; Aas et al. [2021]: 3–10 features, largest real-data example at 28). Finally, the current formulation concentrates attribution on root nodes, potentially underweighting relevant intermediate nodes; future work could explore distributing indirect effects more evenly across the causal path. 9

text: We introduced causal integrated gradients and causal expected gradients, which extend integrated gradients to incorporate known causal structure among input features. They apply to any differentiable model and, under conditions on the causal graph and surrogate, retain the axiomatic guarantees of integrated gradients. On a synthetic benchmark, CIG best matches ground-truth causal effects at a fraction of the cost of causal Shapley values; on simulated and real single-cell data, it best recovers the transcription factors driving the response while scaling to thousands of genes. B Details of the basis expansion To increase the expressive capacity of the surrogate while preserving interpretability and edge-wise decomposition, each parent feature is transformed through a structured basis expansion applied independently per feature. Let xi denote the value of feature i. Inputs are first standardized: zi = xi −µi σi , (12) where µi and σi are the feature-wise mean and standard deviation estimated from the training data. Standardization ensures that the basis functions operate on comparable scales across features and improves numerical stability during optimization. The resulting basis representation ϕ(xi) combines three complementary function families: ϕ(xi) =  zi, z2 i , . . . , zD i | {z } Polynomial basis , (max(0, zi −ck))p , k = 1, . . . , Kt | {z } Truncated power basis , sin(ωfzi), cos(ωfzi), f = 1, . . . , Kf | {z } Fourier basis  . Each basis element is defined as: ϕtp,k(xi) = (max(0, zi −ck))p , (15) where p is the knot power controlling smoothness and curvature. These functions behave similarly to spline basis functions and allow the surrogate to capture sharp transitions or regime-specific effects. This component contributes Kt basis functions per feature. The Fourier component captures periodic structure: ϕfourier(xi) = [sin(ω1zi), cos(ω1zi), . . . , sin(ωKf zi), cos(ωKf zi)], (16) where ωf denotes the frequency associated with Fourier feature f; these frequencies are set as hyperparameters. Since both sine and cosine terms are included for each frequency, this component contributes 2Kf basis functions per feature. The total number of basis functions per feature is: Q = D + Kt + 2Kf. (17) This construction provides a flexible yet structured functional approximation that can model smooth, localized, and periodic dependencies while preserving edge-level interpretability within the directed graph. text: None of our experiments apply post-hoc normalization; all reported attributions are raw. We quantify this residual with the per-sample completeness delta δ(n) = P i R(n) i −(F(x(n)) − F(b(n))). On the synthetic benchmark (K=100), we report it relative to the output dif- ference (Table C.1), computed batch-wise as a weighted absolute percentage error (WAPE), P n |δ(n)|  P n |F(x(n)) −F(b(n))| over evaluation samples n within each seed, then averaged (mean ± std) across seeds. We use WAPE rather than the per-sample mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), since the latter is unstable whenever a single sample’s F(x(n)) −F(b(n)) is near zero; WAPE is the standard fix for this in forecasting [Kolassa and Schütz, 2007]. Causal Shapley values and conditional SHAP, as commonly implemented via permutation sampling, are quadratic and cubic in d, respectively (conditional SHAP pays an extra factor of d for Gaussian conditioning per sample).
