One more cost worth disclosing: surrogate training. With n the training-set size and T epochs, our closed-form sparse surrogate trains in O(T · n · d) (sparse graph, E=O(d)) or O(T · n · d2) (dense); a generic dense-MLP surrogate is O(T · n · d) regardless of sparsity. This is a one-time, offline cost amortized over all explanations, not a per-instance one: over Nexplain instances it adds (training cost)/Nexplain to each, vanishing as Nexplain grows. Root-node intuition. The intuition behind the root-node results is best illustrated with a simple example. Consider a model F with two equally contributing features x1 and x2, where x1 fully causes x2 (i.e. x1 →x2 →F, x1 →F): • Conditional SHAP gives R1 = R2, since it does not account for the direction of the dependency and therefore does not preferentially attribute importance to the root node x1. • Causal Shapley values give R1 > R2, since they take into account the direction of the dependency but still attribute some importance to x2, because they consider a situation where x1 is not set to a value, in which case x2 does have an effect on F. • Causal integrated gradients gives R2 = 0, correctly identifying that x2 contributes no independent effect beyond what is already captured by x1. Since no causal graph is available for this dataset, we leverage prior knowledge from OmniPath [Türei et al., 2021]. After restricting the graph to genes present in the dataset and to the interactions annotated as transcriptional, the resulting network contains 6,941 genes and 22,887 edges. Each edge was then assigned a confidence score as a weighted mean of four evidence channels: curation effort, number of references, number of primary sources, and consensus direction. Duplicate source–target records were collapsed into a single edge by taking the maximum of each evidence channel, reducing the edges to 22,624 aggregated interactions. Edges without supporting evidence in any channel were removed, and the edges with the top 75% of weights were kept, leaving 12,136 edges. Because a topological ordering of the features is required, we converted the cyclic graph to a DAG by approximate minimum feedback arc set removal. Specifically, we first computed

Because a topological ordering of the features is required, we converted the cyclic graph to a DAG by approximate minimum feedback arc set removal. Specifically, we first computed a linear vertex ordering using the weighted greedy heuristic of Eades et al. [1993], removed arcs inconsistent with this ordering, and then reconsidered removed arcs in descending confidence order, reinserting an arc whenever doing so preserves acyclicity. This removed 399 of 12,136 edges (3.3% of edges and 3.6% of total confidence mass), yielding an acyclic prior of 11,737 edges over 3,792 connected genes. 24

text: SCENIC evaluation graph construction. Data. We started from the PBMC scRNA-seq dataset of Kang et al. [2018], comprising 8 lupus patients, with each patient’s cells split into IFN-β-stimulated and control samples. We used the raw UMI counts throughout the SCENIC steps. Quality control. We kept cells with more than 200 detected genes, fewer than 4,000 detected genes, and less than 15% mitochondrial reads. We kept genes with more than 250 total counts across all cells, which matches the SCENIC recommendation of one count in 1% of cells. The filtered matrix contained 24,562 cells × 6,941 genes. We restricted the data to six training patients (1244, 1016, 1039, 1256, 1488, and 107), comprising 17,448 cells, leaving patients 1015 and 101 out. Multi-seed SCENIC. GRNBoost2 is stochastic, so we ran pySCENIC ten times with seeds {0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 20, 42, 420, 1000, 2000}. Each run had three steps: 1. GRN inference: GRNBoost2 on the raw count matrix, with the hg38 list of human TFs as candidate regulators. Output: TF–target adjacencies weighted by importance. 2. Module creation and cisTarget pruning: co-expression modules were built with the default settings, so TF–target correlations use only cells where both genes are detected. Modules were then pruned by motif enrichment. We used two hg38 RefSeq-r80 mc9nr gene-based ranking databases (10 kb up/downstream of the TSS,

text: modules were built with the default settings, so TF–target correlations use only cells where both genes are detected. Modules were then pruned by motif enrichment. We used two hg38 RefSeq-r80 mc9nr gene-based ranking databases (10 kb up/downstream of the TSS, and 500 bp up/100 bp down) and the motif-to-TF annotation motifs-v9-nr.hgnc-m0.001-o0.0. 3. Regulon filtering: we kept enriched motifs with NES greater than 3.0 and motif-similarity q-value less than 0.001. Surviving motifs were merged into one regulon per TF and context, which takes the union of their targets. Consensus network across seeds. Each seed’s regulons were flattened into directed TF-to-target edges. When a TF had several contexts, an edge kept its largest GRNBoost2 weight. Seeds agreed moderately: pairwise Jaccard similarity of the edge sets was 0.58 to 0.60. We chose the recurrence threshold from the edge-recurrence curve (Table H.3). An edge entered the consensus if it appeared in at least 8 of 10 seeds, and its weight is the median over the seeds that contained it. For each seed we scored regulon activity per cell with pyscenic aucell, using an AUC threshold of 0.10. That means the top 10% of each cell’s ranked genes; the median cell detects about 500 genes. A regulon was kept if (i) its TF is in the consensus network and (ii) AUCell scored it in at least 8 of 10 seeds. Its activity is the mean AUC over the seeds that scored it, and a seed that did not score it counts as missing rather than zero. The result is 155 regulons. Extraction of stimulation-responsive SCENIC regulons. For each cell type, SCENIC regulon activities, quantified using AUCell on the training replicates, were averaged within each replicate and contrasted between the stimulated and control groups. Regulons significant according to a one-sample t-test across replicates (BH-FDR < 0.05) were retained, and the 50 regulons with the largest |∆AUC| were selected. Then, for each cell type, the rankings were scored against that cell type’s DESeq2 [Love et al., 2014] DEG set using precision, recall, F1, normalized recovery AUC, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG; the DCG divided by that of the ideal ranking) graded by the absolute Wald statistic, at several fixed cutoffs and at a cutoff equal to the number of DEGs. The normalized recovery AUC is the area under the curve of recovered DEGs against rank depth, rescaled so that a random ranking scores 0 and the optimal ranking scores 1. At k = nDEGs, precision, recall, and F1 coincide by construction, so only F1 is reported at that cutoff. We also measured the Spearman correlation between δg and the absolute DESeq2 Wald statistic over the entire gene panel. Every quantity was computed independently for all five seeds and is reported as mean ± s.d. over them. Megakaryocytes contributed no significant DEGs and are therefore absent from the recovery metrics. The whole-panel correlation is stable seed-to-seed. No method tracks the DE statistic closely (Table I.3), so none of these methods can be considered equivalent to a differential expression test. CIG is the least DE-correlated of the three in all seven cell types. Over the full DEG set, scored at a cutoff equal to the number of DEGs (Table I.4), CIG has the lowest F1 in six of the seven cell types and the lowest recovery AUC in six of the seven; the exceptions are dendritic cells, where CIG and integrated gradients are tied on F1, and CD4 T cells, where CIG’s recovery AUC exceeds that of DeepSHAP. CIG’s NDCG is below that of both other methods in every cell type. Apart from dendritic cells and the CIG–DeepSHAP recovery-AUC comparison in CD4 T cells, these gaps are larger than the seed-to-seed spread. The methods separate most sharply at the top of the ranking, and in the same direction in every cell type. Among their first ten genes, DeepSHAP and integrated gradients reach 94–100% precision and an NDCG of 64–91, against 34–52% and 22–32 for CIG (Table I.5). The gap then narrows steadily 27

text: with depth (Tables I.6–I.9). CIG’s precision is also non-monotone in k. It is lower at k = 10 than at any cutoff up to k = 100, peaks at k = 100 in every cell type except NK cells (where it peaks at k = 50), and only then declines, whereas DeepSHAP and integrated gradients are at or near their maximum at k = 10 and decline thereafter. The genes CIG places in its first few dozen positions are therefore less likely to be DEGs than the ones it ranks immediately below them. Taken together, these results are consistent with the following behavior. DeepSHAP and integrated gradients rank the downstream transcriptional response genes first, which lifts their precision and NDCG at shallow cutoffs and gives them a marginally closer alignment with the DE statistic overall. text: J Isolating the value of CIG’s formulation beyond graph access A possible concern is that CIG’s advantage is simply a readout of having access to the causal graph, not of correctly using it. We address this on Dyngen with a test of instance-level specificity that a fixed, shared graph cannot explain on its own. Because the Dyngen causal graph is identical across cells, a graph-driven attribution method would be expected to produce similar TF importance across cells. In contrast, cells undergoing different state transitions should be explained by different sets of transition-specific TFs. For each transition, we therefore restrict the analysis to cells undergoing that transition and compare the attribution ranks of its known causal TFs against those of all other genes. CIG consistently prioritizes the causal TFs for all six transitions, with significant enrichment in every case (Figure J.1). DeepSHAP shows significant prioritization in two of the six transitions, while integrated gradients does not show significant enrichment in any transition. L Residual-dependence diagnostics under non-additive mechanisms Our surrogate models each feature’s mechanism as additive across parents (Section 3.3); when the true mechanism is non-additive, this can misallocate attribution between the direct and indirect terms (Section 5). We diagnose and quantify this bias directly, using the synthetic SCM/CATE benchmark (Section 4.1), restricted to nodes whose mechanism is either the explicit two-parent interaction term w1x1 + w2x2 + w1w2x1x2 or a matched linear control (eligibility criteria below). Since ground truth is known for every node, we compare directly rather than inferring statistically. A diagnostic based on the residual hj = xj −ˆsj(parents) conflates the systematic mechanism misfit with injected exogenous noise, making it an inherently noisy signal of the bias itself. Instead, we isolate the same systematic misallocation without this contamination by comparing CIG’s indirect- effect attribution computed with the oracle mechanism against the same attribution computed with the learned surrogate: both quantities are deterministic functions of the parents, so no noise term enters at all. We test two scenarios: the interacting variable present as a graph node (“in-graph”), and the interacting variable removed from the graph entirely (“omitted-variable”). A node is eligible if its true mechanism matches the target type (interaction, or a matched linear control) and it is read directly by the downstream model, so that its attribution is nonzero; the linear control is further restricted to nodes with at least two parents (in-graph) or exactly two parents (omitted-variable), matching interaction’s structural requirement of two active parents. Eligible nodes are found by searching randomly generated graphs per setting, not fixed in advance, and pooled across 5 seeds (in-graph) and 15 seeds (omitted-variable). text: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Personalization Sekh Mainul Islam, Pepa Atanasova, Isabelle Augenstein University of Copenhagen {seis, pepa, augenstein}@di.ku.dk
title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for

text: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly important for user- centric applications, yet prior methods mainly adapt dense LLMs, whose polysemantic neu- rons, each encoding multiple unrelated con- cepts, hinder localizing the components be- hind personalization, and thus understanding and controlling it. We propose to personal- ize Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, which sparsely route each token to a few specialized experts, reducing polysemanticity and enabling such localization. We adapt three open-weight MoE LLMs on a large-scale personalization dataset and train crosscoders on paired activa- tions of the personalized and non-personalized models to learn interpretable personalized la- tents, from which we identify the experts encod- ing distinct personalization features. The per- sonalized MoE LLMs perform competitively with dense LLMs while activating only a frac- tion of their parameters, exhibit lower polyse- manticity than dense LLMs with similar active parameters, and, within the same model family, yield personalized latents that are less shared with the non-personalized model. Causal in- terventions show that these latents suffice to recover the personalized model’s behavior and that boosting their associated experts moves the non-personalized model toward it, reveal- ing distinct routing paths for different personal- ization features.1 1
title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for

text: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) adapts LLMs to user or group preferences (Salemi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). Due to increasing demand for AI-assisted user-centric applications, Personalization of LLMs has become an important research direction. Most methods use dense LLMs (Zhang et al., 2025b), offering little interpretability 1Code and data: https://github.com/copenlu/ persona_moe_explain of localizing important model components encod- ing distinct personalized features due to the poly- semanticity of encoding multiple orthogonal con- cepts into a single neuron (Olah et al., 2020). Re- cent work on developing intrinsically interpretable LLMs suggests that wider, more sparse LLMs en- able their neurons to capture more disentangled features and reduce polysemanticity (Yang et al., 2025b). Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs offer a scalable solution for wider and sparser networks by replacing a dense FFN block in the MLP layer with a set of experts of the same size, using a sparse rout- ing mechanism to select a subset of these experts to process each input token (Shazeer et al., 2017). This mechanism enables MoE LLMs to offer better interpretability for downstream tasks by achieving lower polysemanticity (Herbst et al., 2026), where experts encode distinct task-specific features. Moti- vated by these observations, we utilize MoE LLMs for personalization and subsequent interpretability analysis, addressing research questions covering polysemamticity of MoE LLMs for personalization (RQ1, §6.2),
title: Explaining the Roles of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for

text: achieving lower polysemanticity (Herbst et al., 2026), where experts encode distinct task-specific features. Moti- vated by these observations, we utilize MoE LLMs for personalization and subsequent interpretability analysis, addressing research questions covering polysemamticity of MoE LLMs for personalization (RQ1, §6.2), identifying distinct personalized fea- tures encoded via experts during personalization (RQ2, §6.3), and localizing unique routing paths for distinct personalized features (RQ3, §6.4). Following Bai et al. (2025) on MoE LLMs align- ment, we adapt the MoE LLMs towards personal- ization using a two-stage parameter-efficient fine- tuning (PEFT) (§4.1), on a large-scale personaliza- tion dataset covering diverse preferences for user groups, MULTIFACETED COLLECTION (Lee et al., 2024). We then train a sparse autoencoder- based (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024) architecture crosscoder (Minder et al., 2025) on paired personalized and non-personalized activa- tions to identify interpretable personalization la- tents. Mapping these latents to experts reveals dis- tinct routing paths associated with personalization. Our proposed method is illustrated in Figure 1. text: 2.1 Personalization of LLMs Methods for aligning LLMs with individual or group preferences (Zhang et al., 2025b) condition on retrieved user history or profile summaries (Salemi et al., 2024; Richardson et al., 2023), encode personas in the prompt (Jiang et al., 2024b), train per-user adapters (Tan et al., 2024), learn personalized reward models or merge preference-specific policies (Cheng et al., 2023; Jang et al., 2024), or steer activations toward a user’s style (Zhang et al., 2025a; Cao et al., 2024). LaMP and LongLaMP (Salemi et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2024) evaluate per-user personalization, while Multifaceted Collection and Bench (Lee et al., 2024) specify group preferences via system messages. These works study dense models as black boxes; we study how sparse MoEs represent personalization. 2

text: 2.2 Mixture-of-Experts LLMs. MoE layers route each token to a few experts, de- coupling parameter count from compute (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Zoph et al., 2022), and now underlie strong open models such as Mix- tral, OLMoE, and Qwen3 (Jiang et al., 2024a; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a). Anal- yses of routing report specialization at the level of tokens and syntax rather than domains (Jiang et al., 2024a; Xue et al., 2024), semantic routing in con- trolled settings (Olson et al., 2025), and language- specific experts identified by contrasting routing frequencies (Bandarkar et al., 2026). Expert-level specialization can be exploited for adaptation and control: Bai et al. (2025) tune routers to identify context-faithful experts, Li et al. (2026) encour- age expert divergence during training, and Fayyaz et al. (2026) steer behavior by (de)activating ex- perts. We adopt a two-stage router-then-expert adaptation for personalization and relate the re- sulting routing changes to interpretable persona features. Interpreting model features and fine-tuning. Dense-model neurons are polysemantic (Olah et al., 2020); sparse autoencoders recover more monose- mantic features (Bricken et al., 2023; Huben et al., 2024), sparse probing measures how few neurons encode a concept (Gurnee et al., 2023), and wider, sparser architectures such as MoEs reduce polyse- manticity (Yang et al., 2025b; Herbst et al., 2026).

Crosscoders, trained with BatchTopK (Bussmann et al., 2024) and explained automatically (Paulo et al., 2025), isolate latents specific to a fine-tuned model and have been applied to chat tuning (Min- der et al., 2025) and to MoE–dense comparisons (Chaudhari et al., 2026). We personalize models and train crosscoders on MULTIFACETED COLLEC- TION (Lee et al., 2024). Each example pairs a user query with a system message that encodes a group-level preference across four dimensions (style, background knowledge, informativeness, harmlessness), along with a preference-aligned re- sponse generated by GPT-4-Turbo-0125. We eval- uate on three benchmarks: (i) MULTIFACETED BENCH (Lee et al., 2024), which uses the same system-message format but has no preferences in common with the training set; (ii) LaMP (Salemi et al., 2024); and (iii) LongLaMP (Kumar et al., 2024). (2) MoE LLMs exhibit lower polysemanticity than dense LLMs for personalization and they enable better inter- pretability of encoded personalization features via crosscoder than dense LLMs. (3) MoE encodes dis- tinct personalization features via different routing 8
title: Distinctiveness D (layer avg.)

text: paths, enabling better localization and subsequent intervention for controlled personalization. Limitations Models and comparisons. We study three open MoE families and analyze one layer per model, selected by routing divergence. Personalization features may also arise at other layers, and our con- clusions may not transfer to other MoE designs (e.g., shared experts or fine-grained expert segmen- tation). The dense counterparts are matched by active or total parameter count, but differ in pre- training data and recipes, so architectural effects cannot be fully separated from training differences. Data and notion of persona. Multifaceted- Collection describes preferences through synthetic system messages over four dimensions, with cate- gorical, long-tailed subdimension labels. This cap- tures group-level preferences rather than individual users, and our experiments are limited to English. Personalization signals in real user histories may be noisier and more entangled than in this controlled setting. Crosscoder fidelity. Crosscoders reconstruct activations imperfectly, and reconstruction quality varies across models (with fractions of variance explained of 0.80 for OLMoE, 0.74 for Qwen3- 30B-A3B, and 0.65 for Mixtral, whose activations have much larger magnitudes and heavier tails). In- formation in the reconstruction error is invisible to our latent-level analyses, and the set of personal- ized latents depends on the decoder-norm thresh- old. BatchTopK training and latent scaling mitigate known sparsity artifacts (Minder et al., 2025), but do not

text: formation in the reconstruction error is invisible to our latent-level analyses, and the set of personal- ized latents depends on the decoder-norm thresh- old. BatchTopK training and latent scaling mitigate known sparsity artifacts (Minder et al., 2025), but do not rule them out entirely. Probing. Persona concepts are properties of whole responses, whereas sparse probing labels individual tokens, thereby introducing label noise and lowering absolute scores across all models. Se- lecting the best of many components favors MoE models, which have more candidates (layers × ex- perts); we mitigate this by selecting on test data and reporting test scores, but selection effects may remain, particularly for k = 1. Probes measure whether a concept is decodable, not whether the model uses it. Expert attribution and causality. Expert sets are derived from routing frequencies at firing to- kens and are therefore correlational; they depend on the number of examples, the selection rule, and the background routing rate, and their stability is moderate. Evaluation of generation. ROUGE-L and ME- TEOR measure overlap with reference responses and are imperfect proxies for personalization: a response can satisfy a preference while diverg- ing from the reference wording, as our steer- ing results illustrate. A Relevant Model Architecture Details A.1 Crosscoder Crosscoder is an encoder-decoder-based architec- ture that explains the activations from both fine- tuned (personalized) and base (non-personalized) LLMs by learning a shared dictionary of inter- pretable concepts (latents). Formally, for the in- put token xt, let the activations from a particular layer l of the personalized and non-personalized MoEs be h(l,ft) xt ∈Rd and h(l,base) xt ∈Rd respec- tively (d is the model dimension), the encoder of the crosscoder maps those activations to a higher di- mensional (D >> d)2 latent space, where each di- mension j ∈{1, . . . , D} explains distinct features encoded in those activations h(l,ft) xt , and h(l,base) xt as: aj(xt) = ReLU(e(ft) j h(l,ft) xt +e(base) j h(l,base) xt +b(enc) j ) (10) where aj is the activation for latent j, e(ft) j

The decoder of the crosscoder then reconstructs those activations h(l,ft) xt , and h(l,base) xt for the token xt using the sparse activation distribution of shared dictionary latents as: ˜h(l,ft) xt = X j aj(xt) d(ft) j + b(dec) ˜h(l,base) xt = X j aj(xt) d(base) j + b(dec) (11) where d(ft) j , d(base) j ∈Rd are the the decoder weight vectors corresponding to the latent j, and 2D = α×d, where α is the expansion factor, and we keep it as 32 for our experiments. 11

text: 2026-10-15 Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling Tong Zhu1 #, Zhe Xu1, Zefeng He1,2, Yunkai Chai1,2, Xuyang Hu1, Dehong Zheng1,3, Yun Luo1, Yafu Li1, Qi Zhang1,3 and Yu Cheng1,4 # 1Shanghai AI Lab, 2Shanghai Jiao Tong University, 3Fudan University, 4Nanyang Technological University # zhutong@pjlab.org.cn # chengyu@pjlab.org.cn Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone’s native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33–34 ms for the smaller models. mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33–34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems. § Code: https://github.com/InternLM/Intern-Decision Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/internlm/intern-decision

Driven by the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs), agent systems have evolved from passive text generation models into interactive systems capable of perceiving environments, using tools, and taking actions [19, 30, 32]. Unlike open-ended text generation, many agent operations are inherently closed-set decision problems, where the model selects from a predefined set of alternatives, such as tool invocation, model routing, and actions [20]. However, current agents often rely on autoregressive free-form generation even when the underlying task only requires structured decisions, introducing additional decoding overhead and complicating the interface between models and downstream controllers [19, 25, 30]. These observations motivate the development of dedicated decision models that can directly produce structured outcomes together with reliable confidence estimates for efficient agent execution. Recent work on structured decision models, referred to as System-1 decision models, explores this perspective by replacing unrestricted generation with explicit decision interfaces and probabilistic outputs. Systems such as Jev [27] provide typed interfaces for choice, score, and binary decisions, while several open implementations investigate alternative architectures and inference strategies for efficient structured decision making [1, 17, 22, 26]. These interfaces primarily target textual decisions, and implementations differ in whether they score multiple questions jointly or separately. For multimodal agents operating in dynamic environments, decision arXiv:2610.22131v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model models must additionally integrate visual observations, task instructions, and changing interface states, where action selection depends jointly on visual evidence and contextual constraints [28, 29]. Moreover, practical agent requests often require multiple decisions over a shared state, creating a need for efficient multi-field decision models that can preserve the capabilities of pretrained multimodal language models while providing structured outputs. To address these challenges, we introduce Intern-Decision, a family of multimodal decision models based on autoregressive masked language modeling. Our approach reformulates structured decision making as next-token prediction over masked decision fields within a predefined assistant output schema. By retaining the pretrained causal language model backbone and native language-model head, Intern-Decision evaluates multiple candidate decisions in a single forward pass and produces both structured predictions and candidate probabilities without iterative text generation. This design separates decision scoring from free-form response decoding, enabling efficient inference while preserving compatibility with existing multimodal language models. To adapt pretrained models to this decision-oriented interface, we construct a unified multimodal decision corpus consisting of textual states, optional images, typed questions, and target decisions. The corpus combines teacher-constructed challenging decisions with public task distributions, covering textual reasoning, instruction- following decisions, visual judgments, interface actions, and interactive control scenarios. We instantiate Intern-Decision with 0.8B, 2B, and 4B Qwen3.5 backbones [23], fine-tuning the language backbone while keeping the vision tower and projector frozen. To improve the reliability of confidence estimates, we further apply post-hoc temperature scaling [13] using a separate calibration split. We evaluate Intern-Decision from three perspectives: decision accuracy, inference efficiency, and probability quality. Across seven evaluation suites, including public Jevbench subsets [10], Intern-Decision-4B achieves a 90.02% unweighted mean accuracy, compared with 88.74% for Jev. For a fixed 289-token request containing three decision fields, Intern-Decision-4B achieves a mean latency of 44.16 ms on a single RTX 4090. We further evaluate probability calibration through a separate known-distribution pilot and study confidence-based model routing, in which requests are passed to a larger model when the decision model’s confidence falls below a threshold. Qualitative demonstrations on visual interaction and browser assistance further illustrate how compact decision models can serve as local decision modules within hierarchical agent systems. text: Decision Models. Recent decision models target fast, structured judgments: given a state, questions, and predefined answer options, they return typed decisions with probability estimates rather than free-form text. Alongside TypeSafe’s Jev [27], which supports choice, score, and binary decisions and reports using Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), related open implementations explore different modeling and inference strategies for structured decision-making. JevK5 [1] adapts Qwen3.5 with LoRA and derives candidate probabilities from next-token logits through a Jev-style interface. Kev [17] combines Qwen backbones with LoRA adapters and a learned pointer head, providing self-hostable models and an API for typed choices and scores. SemIf-OpenJev [26] provides a direct-scoring approach that derives option probabilities from candidate-token logits of frozen language models, with optional shared-state prefill reuse across questions. Laya [22] adopts an encoder-based, non-autoregressive architecture to produce choice, score, and yes/no decisions in a single forward pass. Within this paradigm, Intern-Decision focuses on multimodal structured decision-making, incorporating visual inputs alongside textual states and task instructions. 2

text: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model Autoregressive and Masked Prediction. Autoregressive language models such as GPT-3 [5] predict tokens conditioned on a causal prefix, whereas BERT [8] reconstructs masked tokens using bidirectional context. Hybrid approaches explore combinations of these paradigms: UniLMv2 [3] combines autoencoding and partially autoregressive objectives through pseudo masking, while GLM [9] combines bidirectional encod- ing of the corrupted input with autoregressive reconstruction of masked spans. Mask-Predict [12] predicts masked target tokens in parallel and iteratively refines uncertain predictions. For classification, PET [24] uses pattern–verbalizer pairs for cloze-based prediction and distills the resulting models into a sequence classifier, while LM-BFF [11] performs prompt-based fine-tuning with label words and demonstrations, reusing the pretrained masked-language-model head. Intern-Decision formulates structured decisions as autoregressive masked language modeling, combining answer placeholders with next-token-aligned prediction in a causal multimodal model. Its native language-model head scores candidates for all requested fields in a single forward pass, without iterative refinement or answer feedback. Calibration and selective computation. Temperature scaling fits a positive scalar to adjust predictive confidence while preserving the most likely label [13]. Brier scoring evaluates the full predictive distribution [4], complementing accuracy and binned calibration error. Computational scope The method removes iterative answer decoding and avoids separate field-by-field forward passes. It does not eliminate the cost of processing the input: longer states, more image tokens, and larger schemas still increase computation and memory. One request may yield multiple decisions, so request rate and decision rate are different quantities. Causal ordering also means fields can have different contextual prefixes even when they share a forward pass; the construction does not enforce permutation invariance or a jointly constrained output distribution.

Calibration test set construction This evaluation-only test set measures whether the model assigns appropriate probabilities to all possible outcomes of a stated random experiment. For example, a fair die requires probability 1/6 on each real face and zero on impossible faces. Selecting one plausible face does not establish a correct predictive distribution. Similarly, the Monty Hall questions ask where the prize is, with doors as outcomes; they do not ask whether switching is the best action. The set is constructed from 24 mechanism families in six categories. Each family has two settings, which vary numerical parameters or the observation protocol. Each setting is emitted with canonical and reversed option order, yielding 6 × 4 × 2 × 2 = 96 cases, 16 per category. The two order variants share the same state, question, and reference distribution.

In the actual three-door informed-host case, the prize is uniformly placed and the player initially selects door 1. A host who knows the prize location always opens an unchosen empty door and always offers the other unopened door; legal reveals are chosen uniformly. The input does not disclose the opened door’s number. The question is “Where is the prize relative to the final two unopened doors?” Its outcomes are initial_door and other_unopened_door, with reference probabilities 1/3 and 2/3. The initial selection retains its prior probability, and the host’s guaranteed safe reveal concentrates the other 2/3 on the remaining door. An output concentrated entirely on the remaining door would select the more likely outcome but misrepresent the residual uncertainty. 5. Evaluation Results 5.1. Intern-Decision maps the ordered options to legal answer tokens and applies the candidate softmax in Equation 3; Jev supplies its native API probability map. Hierarchical browser assistance We study browser use as hierarchical, closed-loop decision making rather than end-to-end free-form generation. Given a natural-language goal, a larger planner maintains cross-page context and proposes a stage-level subgoal. At each iteration, the current page evidence and a finite candidate set (e.g., click, scroll, return, or stop) are presented to Intern-Decision; the selected action is executed, and the page is observed again. text: We introduce Intern-Decision, which makes finite multimodal choices through a single causal forward pass, retaining the pretrained backbone’s native language-model head and exposing candidate probabilities through a typed interface. The 4B model achieves the highest seven-suite average in the presented comparison, with a 44.16 ms mean for a fixed short request on an RTX 4090. Separate calibration and handoff studies show how probabilistic outputs can support uncertainty analysis and selective use of a larger model. We believe Intern-Decision can serve as a practical component of larger agent systems, but its generalization to arbitrarily large schemas and complex environments remains an open problem. text: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Model C. Known-Distribution Test Construction and Cases Mechanism coverage and reference construction The pilot consists of six categories with four families each. Every family has two settings and every setting has two option-order variants. The resulting 96 records cover the following mechanisms: 1. Direct randomness and support: uniform die faces with impossible options; weighted candy inventories; deterministic single-color pens; rare winning lottery tickets. 2. Composed events and mixtures: sums of two dice; numbers of independent hits; independent backup generators; delivery outcomes under an unobserved route mixture. 3. History, conditioning, and hidden state: independent coin flips after a streak; socks after known removals; die outcomes given a restricted sensor observation; a two-state Markov process with noisy sensor readings. 4. Daily evidence and observation bias: defect screening with a stated base rate; conditionally independent repeated tests; correlated copies of one test; waiting times observed at a uniformly sampled time. 5. Selective disclosure and puzzles: informed-host Monty Hall; uninformed-host Monty Hall conditioned on a safe reveal; prize-dependent switch offers; two-child problems with different child-selection protocols. 6. Sequential and combinatorial processes: distinct coupons collected after finite draws; birthday collisions on a toy calendar; gambler’s ruin; first-reward times with a guaranteed stopping limit. The everyday descriptions define synthetic mechanisms with explicit parameters, not empirical frequencies inferred from real-world populations. Their oracles

text: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions Liangjie Huang* Henry Peng Zou Wei-Chieh Huang Wooseong Yang Yuwei Han Philip S. Yu University of Illinois Chicago
title: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse

text: LLM systems increasingly rely on groups of agents that discuss, critique, and check one another, assuming that peers will catch individ- ual errors. We test this assumption against a minimal adversary. In a ten-agent factual dis- cussion, one or three adversarial agents repeat- edly assert a plausible false answer. After each round we probe each benign agent’s private an- swer through a separate call whose response is hidden from its peers, and we separately label its public stance toward the claim. Across six models and three factual-QA datasets, groups remain stable without an attacker: only 0.6% of benign agents finish with the false answer. A single adversarial agent increases this rate to 44.8% and three to 60.5%. Studies of confor- mity typically report public agreement without private change; we find the reverse. With three adversarial agents present, benign agents hold the false answer in 51.6% of exposed turns but publicly endorse it in only 19.7%. Much of the influence therefore remains invisible in the discussion, and the false answers persist when agents are asked for their own views. Agents that retain the true answer often fail to defend it; once adopted, the false answer spreads among benign agents, and baseline knowledge does not predict robustness. 1
title: Believed but Not Said: Measuring Hidden Belief Collapse

text: Large Language Model (LLM) applications in- creasingly look conversational and social. Systems use multiple agents to debate answers, call tools, plan tasks, critique each other, and form judgments (Du et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024). The appeal is intuitive: a group of agents should be safer than a single one, because peers can cross-check each other, expose factual errors, and converge toward the truth (Liang et al., 2024). This intuition overlooks that the channel agents use to coordinate is also an attack surface. A com- *Corresponding author: lhuan85@uic.edu promised tool-agent, a poisoned retrieval source voiced by an agent (Greshake et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2025), or an untrusted participant in an open protocol can repeatedly introduce a false claim into the shared conversation, and such injected content can propagate between agents (Lee et al., 2026; Ju et al., 2026). Such an attacker needs no access to model weights or hidden states; it only has to post messages. We construct a controlled multi-agent discussion to simulate this threat and ask whether a few agents change what the rest of the agents believe, not only what they say. Ten agents discuss one factual ques- tion for 16 rounds. In the ten, k ∈{0, 1, 3} are adversarial agents (attacker), attacker-controlled agents (Douceur, 2002) that each argue

text: what the rest of the agents believe, not only what they say. Ten agents discuss one factual ques- tion for 16 rounds. In the ten, k ∈{0, 1, 3} are adversarial agents (attacker), attacker-controlled agents (Douceur, 2002) that each argue for the same plausible false answer; the others are benign agents given no question-specific instructions. Be- nign agents are neither warned about the attacker nor assigned a verification role, so we measure the default behavior of an open discussion rather than that of a dedicated debate or fact-checking proto- col. For each benign agent, we record responses per round. The first is what it says in the chat, which we label as endorsing, rejecting, hedging on, or ignoring the false claim. The second is its pri- vate answer: after each round, we ask the agent the factual question in a separate call whose response is hidden from the other agents. For each benign turn, we have its private answer (true or false) with its public message (endorses the false claim or not). In two of the four combinations the chat reflects the private answer. In the other two it misleads: an agent may endorse the claim in the chat while still giving the true answer in pri- vate, or give the false answer in private while not endorsing the claim

In the other two it misleads: an agent may endorse the claim in the chat while still giving the true answer in pri- vate, or give the false answer in private while not endorsing the claim in the chat (Table 1 splits these further by public stance). Studies of conformity under majority pressure, in humans and recently in LLM agents, mostly find the first mismatch: par- ticipants follow the majority’s answer in the dis- 1 arXiv:2610.22138v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026

text: cussion but keep their own answer when asked in private (Asch, 1956; Deutsch and Gerard, 1955; Baltaji et al., 2024; Ghaffarizadeh et al., 2026; YS, 2026). Under three attackers, we find the reverse. Agents that still give the true answer in private al- most never endorse the false claim (2.3% of their turns), but agents that give the false answer mostly do not endorse it either: 58% of their turns hedge on or ignore it. This matches minority influence in human groups, which shifts private judgment more than public behavior (Moscovici, 1980; Wood et al., 1994), and it is why the transcript understates the damage. We contribute a measurement protocol that pairs each agent’s public stance with its private answer in every round (§3), and use it to study six models on three factual-QA datasets (18 model–dataset cells). We find: 1. Hidden infection. Agents privately hold the false answer far more often than they publicly endorse it (51.6% vs. 19.7% of exposed turns under three attackers), and the false answers persist when agents are asked for their own view rather than to report what was discussed (§4.3). 2. Easy damage. Benign groups are stable (0.6% final infection without attacker), but a single attacker leaves 44.8% of benign agents on the false answer and three leave 60.5%; ten agents are not

Benign groups are stable (0.6% final infection without attacker), but a single attacker leaves 44.8% of benign agents on the false answer and three leave 60.5%; ten agents are not significantly more robust than one. 3. Weak correction. Agents that privately retain the true answer publicly reject the false claim in only 61.9% of their turns; in the remaining turns, they stay silent, hedge, or go along with it. 4. Knowledge does not predict robustness. Two models that know the same 85% of facts abandon 25% and 80% of them. A few attackers thus change what most agents an- swer in private while changing much less of what they say in public, and the transcript understates how far the false answer has spread. 2

text: Multi-agent LLM collaboration. A growing body of work organizes LLMs into groups that debate, critique, and vote, reporting gains in rea- soning and factuality over single models (Du et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024). These systems rest on a cooperative premise: more agents and more rounds surface and filter errors. Even without an adversary, discussion can erode correct answers through conformity and the loss of shared facts (Zhang et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026). We study the adversarial case, in which the same channel is used to inject a false claim. Adversarial influence and misinformation in agent groups. Persuasive adversarial debaters lower collaborative accuracy (Amayuelas et al., 2024; Kraidia et al., 2026), persuasion can override truth in debate (Agarwal and Khanna, 2025; Wynn et al., 2025), and the damage has been related to the number and share of deceivers in a group (Wu et al., 2026). Misinformation spreads further in densely connected agent networks (Yu et al., 2025), persists once it enters agent communities (Ju et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), and can be induced by contriving agents that post only true fragments (Hu et al., 2026). Our attacker is deliber- ately simple: it edits no weights and only argues for one fixed false claim
title: cussion but keep their own answer when asked in

text: al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), and can be induced by contriving agents that post only true fragments (Hu et al., 2026). Our attacker is deliber- ately simple: it edits no weights and only argues for one fixed false claim in the conversation. Our main difference lies in what we measure. These studies mostly evaluate what the group outputs (messages, votes, consensus, or accuracy); to our knowledge, none pairs each agent’s public stance with its pri- vate answer turn by turn, which is what reveals that most infection is never voiced. Public compliance and private acceptance. So- cial psychology separates public compliance from private acceptance (Deutsch and Gerard, 1955; Kelman, 1958). Majorities mainly produce com- pliance, that is, public agreement without pri- vate change (Asch, 1956), whereas minorities shift private judgment more than public behavior (Moscovici, 1980; Wood et al., 1994). LLMs con- cede to users (Sharma et al., 2024; Perez et al., 2023), abandon facts they know under multi-turn persuasion (Xu et al., 2024) and conflicting ev- idence (Xie et al., 2024), and conform to peers (Weng et al., 2025; Soffer et al., 2026; Bito et al., 2026). The key design choice is to measure public behavior and private belief separately: the chat only shows what agents say to the group, and private probes show what they answer when no other agent can see it. 3.1 Threat Model and Chatroom Each run is a chatroom of N=10 agents that dis- cuss one factual item for T=16 rounds; all agents in a run share the same base model. We vary the number of adversarial agents k ∈{0, 1, 3}, making 10−k benign agents. The k adversarial agents are independent that each advocate a fixed false claim whenever the topic arises; benign agents receive ordinary discussion personas and instructions that do not include the false claim. The attacker only posts messages; it does not edit weights, read hid- den states, or control benign agents, and is thus strictly weaker than the parameter-editing attacker described by Ju et al. In every round each agent speaks exactly once, in a random order that is reshuffled every round and identical across conversations (Appendix D), con- ditioning on the recent shared history (the previous H=5 rounds) and the current round. Conversa- tions start from a neutral discussion seed about the topic, so benign agents are not steered toward either answer. 3.2 Dual Private/Public Measurement We call a separate call a private probe and its output the agent’s private answer. We use belief for what the private answer is meant to reflect. Private probes. At the initial state and after ev- ery round, each benign agent answers the probe question in a separate call whose response is hid- den from the other agents and never posted to the chatroom. Because the attacker acts only in con- text, an agent’s state is its context: the probe condi- tions on the agent’s persona and its conversational memory (the same last H rounds) and asks for a private answer based on its knowledge and the discussion (Appendix A). Public stance. Exposure. We call a benign turn exposed if at least one adversarial agent’s utterance precedes it in the transcript (i.e., the agent has had an opportunity to see and react to the claim). An agent that speaks mid-round has heard the earlier speakers of that round but not the later ones. The probe before the round has heard neither, and the probe after the round has heard both. The failure is hard to manage in practice. Transcript monitoring reveals only about a third of infected turns. Most infection emerges within four rounds and rarely reverses, so reviewing a run after it ends comes too late. Choosing a more knowl- edgeable model does not help either, since baseline accuracy does not tell how a model abandons what it knows. We therefore recommend treating agent messages as untrusted input, adding an adversarial peer-pressure test to model selection, monitoring agents’ private answers rather than only their public messages, and intervening early. 6

text: We asked whether a multi-agent LLM discussion can correct a false claim that is repeatedly asserted by a few participants. To answer this question, we tracked each agent’s private answer alongside its public speech, revealing information unavailable to transcript-only evaluation. In open-ended factual discussion, the group largely fails to correct the claim, and the failure is mostly invisible in the chat: agents that retain the correct answer often do not defend it, and agents that lose it rarely say so. The shift persists when agents are asked for their own view, spreads among benign agents once it begins, and rarely reverses; in our experiments, neither a larger group nor a more knowledgeable base model prevents it. Evaluating multi-agent systems solely through their transcripts or final answers therefore misses much of what the group holds, and robustness to peer pressure has to be measured directly, at the level of individual agents. 8

text: One practical way is to record each agent’s answer privately at every round, so that hidden answers are visible even when the transcript looks unchanged. Limitations We compare only groups of two and ten agents and do not vary network topology, or model mix- tures. The attacker acts only in context; parametric attacks such as knowledge editing are a different mechanism. All labels come from an LLM judge. On pri- vate answers, it agrees closely with an independent judge from another model family (§3.5). Public stance in free-form chat is harder to label than a one-sentence answer, and implicit endorsements are easy to miss, so public endorsement rates may be underestimated. Our private probe conditions on the agent’s memory; “private belief” thus means the answer an agent gives from its current context, and other probe wordings could yield somewhat different rates. Whether prompting agents to correct the claim early protects the group remains untested but could be evaluated at low cost. Ethical Considerations We study how a few agents that repeat a false claim can mislead the rest of a group. The attack needs no skill beyond taking part in a conversation. text: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks for Camera-Based Autonomous Driving Haohua Que* Mingkai Liu* Handong Yao College of Engineering, University of Georgia, Athens, Georgia, USA hq10606@uga.edu MingkaiKLEIN@outlook.com handong.yao@uga.edu
title: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks

text: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an an- swer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included. Commodity edge accelerators optimize the mean through dynamic scheduling, OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention, so their per-frame latency can be measured but not bounded. We build FALCON, a camera-based 3D occupancy front-end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embed- ded FPGA drawing 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under in- ference, and make the latency guarantee layered and ex- plicit: programmable-logic (PL) compute is cycle-bounded analytically; inference is a measured envelope over 100k- frame traces; and a watchdog enforces output delivery, publishing the previous output flagged stale when a frame is late. The deadline runs use a fixed-work proxy of six ResNet-50 DPU inferences per frame, not the full occu- pancy network: across three 100k-frame enforced runs, all 300k proxy frames delivered an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms, the worst of the three runs. The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline composes to about 1.3 s per frame on the board and is not yet a 10 Hz system. The two operations the DPU cannot run, a view-transform gather and a bilinear resize, become fixed-trip-count PL IPs numerically matched to their

text: for vulnerable road users (VRUs: pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists). Yet occupancy meth- ods, from lift-splat models [17, 34, 51] to sparse and set- prediction models [28, 43], are judged mainly by mIoU and sometimes mean FPS. Mean throughput is the wrong safety currency: on a late frame, the pedestrian is seen too late. A safety case uses worst-case execution time (WCET), a per-frame bound checked against the deadline, and ISO 26262 [20] asks for that evidence rather than an aver- age. GPUs cannot provide it: datacenter GPUs and automo- tive edge SoCs optimize the mean, while dynamic schedul- ing, driver and OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention move the tail [29]. text: worst case keeps climbing with the observation window and swings from 1.1× to 4.4× across power modes and seeds, unlimited power included (Fig. 1). A GPU latency can be measured but not bounded. A bound needs both a statically scheduled accelerator whose cycle count is fixed [36, 41] and a model with input-invariant work. This is indepen- dent of accuracy: recent occupancy models differ by about 25× in determinism, with an input-dependent sparse model at 27.5% coefficient of variation (CV) and a fixed-query sparse model at 1.1%. This paper builds such a front end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embedded FPGA at 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under inference. We choose FlashOcc [51] over sparse SOTA because it is dense, fixed-compute, and DPU- compilable (Sec. 4.1). Two stages the DPU cannot run, the lift-splat view transform [16, 34] and BEV-neck bilin- ear resize, become custom HLS IPs: with a fixed cam- era rig their indices and weights are static constants, so both are fixed-trip-count operators whose compute WCET is a cycle count. Accuracy survives a DPU-compatible INT8 recipe with calibration-time activation clipping and no QAT [2, 3, 53]: on full Occ3D-nuScenes [7, 40] valida- tion the board reaches mIoU 29.88, 1.55 below the INT8 reference matched to its deployed configuration and 92.8% of an FP32 baseline

text: Camera-only 3D occupancy descends from Lift-Splat- Shoot [34]. BEVDet [17] and BEVDepth [24] es- tablished the deployment-friendly LSS pipeline; Sim- pleOccupancy [13], OccNet [38], TPVFormer [18], Vox- Former [25], OccFormer [54], and COTR [30] explore com- pact, dense, plane-based, sparse, and transformer-style oc- cupancy representations. RenderOcc uses 2D rendering su- pervision [33]; BEVFormer [26], SurroundOcc [47], FB- OCC [27], OpenOccupancy [45], and GaussianFormer [19] buy accuracy at higher cost; SparseOcc [28] and OPUS [43] cut dense-voxel cost. We deploy FlashOcc [51], which keeps features in 2D BEV and recovers height with a channel-to-height plug-in. These works optimize mIoU and sometimes mean FPS, not the per-frame latency determin- ism that decides deadline feasibility (Sec. 4). Low-bit BEV/occupancy quantization is mostly GPU/TensorRT-targeted: QD-BEV [53] and PTQAT [46] use QAT, BEVFormer tensorrt [10] uses INT8 PTQ, and all rest on general methods such as AdaRound [32], BRECQ [23], SmoothQuant [50], HAQ [44], and clipping- based activation quantization [9]. The AMD/Xilinx DPU [2] with vai q pytorch [3] is more constrained: per-tensor power-of-two scales and min-max calibration only. We therefore use fixed activation clipping to stay inside the supported DPU path; prior quantized occupancy work rarely reports worst-case timing. On the deployment-operator side, BEVPoolv2 [16] pre- computes ranks and intervals for fast GPU LSS pooling, FastOcc [15] shares 2D BEV and perspective-view features, and TensorRT ports rely on custom plugins [10]. Their ker- nels remain GPU software with scheduler jitter, whereas our PL gather and resize turn fixed camera tables into on-chip memories with static trip counts and reported FPGA WCET. For embedded-FPGA perception, the argument is tim- ing: GPU per-frame latency is hard to bound [29], while ISO 26262 [20] values worst-case evidence over aver- age throughput. Restuccia and Biondi [36] analyze the Zynq UltraScale+ DPU, and FINN/FINN-R [6, 41] with PointPillars-on-FINN [39] is the closest embedded 3D precedent. Yet PointPillars-on-FINN is LiDAR-based and leaves scatter on ARM, while DPU WCET work treats the accelerator as a generic CNN. No prior work gives a camera-to-occupancy datapath both cycle-bounded view operators and an enforced delivery layer on programmable logic, including the two operations the DPU cannot run. 3. System overview: six cameras feed fixed-compute FlashOcc; DPU stages run dense INT8 convolutions; custom PL IPs implement gather and resize; the watchdog enforces the deadline before the 3D occupancy output. INT8 deployment must preserve the quantized algorithm with a DPU-compatible calibration recipe [21] rather than training-heavy QAT [12]. We target the AMD Kria KR260 [1] (K26 Zynq Ultra- Scale+ SOM, B4096 DPU, 4 GB DDR4, measured 4.3 W idle to 8.7 W peak) with the DPUCZDX8G accelerator [2], and deploy FlashOcc-R50 [51] on Occ3D-nuScenes [7, 40]. FlashOcc keeps features in 2D BEV and recovers height with a channel-to-height plug-in, a zero-FLOP reshape of BEV channels into height bins. It is fixed-compute, one forward pass with input-independent FLOPs, where sparse, transformer, rendering, and efficiency-oriented designs re- duce average work instead [15, 18, 25, 33, 54]; a deadline bound requires fixed per-frame work. Deadline path and INT8 recipe The timing path is governed in three layers: PL compute is cycle-bounded; inference latency is a measured envelope; delivery is enforced by a watchdog that publishes the pre- vious ego-warped occupancy, flagged stale, when a frame would miss the deadline. text: 4.4. Robustness, calibration, and the application context On-board full-val mIoU is 29.88 with a 95% bootstrap CI of [29.61, 30.15] at the frame level and [28.58, 31.11] scene- clustered; board-versus-reference comparisons are paired on identical frames. Splitting by scene description gives day 30.26 (4449 frames), rain 29.80 (1088), night 16.76 (602; rain and night overlap on rainy nights). Rain costs almost nothing; night halves accuracy. The clip threshold is not the sensitive part: sweeping C ∈{16, 24, 32, 48, 64} on the night subset moves mIoU by at most 0.7 (16.4 at C=16 vs 15.7 at the deployed C=32), so the clipping recipe is robust to the lighting shift; night loss traces to the backbone. Injecting camera-artifact perturbations before the back- bone (matched INT8; baseline 28.9 on the same first-1000- frame subset, differing from the full-set value): Gaussian blur σ=1/2/4 gives 13.8/7.9/3.5 mIoU; exposure gain 0.5×/2× gives 25.2/23.4; sensor noise gives 18.2. Blur dominates, halving accuracy at one pixel of spread; moder- ate exposure change is nearly free; none of these can change the amount of work on the fixed-work path. Calibration drift is probed by perturbing the rig pitch on all cameras (stale static tables relative to the images): 0.1/0.2/0.5 degrees cost nothing measurable and 1.0 de- gree costs 0.1 mIoU against the 28.9 baseline; tables regen- erate offline

Calibration drift is probed by perturbing the rig pitch on all cameras (stale static tables relative to the images): 0.1/0.2/0.5 degrees cost nothing measurable and 1.0 de- gree costs 0.1 mIoU against the 28.9 baseline; tables regen- erate offline on recalibration. As for where the remaining accuracy loss lives: of all bicycle ground-truth voxels, the board predicts 49.2% free and 29.5% background surfaces, keeps 5.7% as bicycle, and scatters the remainder across driveable surface (6.5%), veg- etation, and small movable-class confusions: thin structures are erased toward free space, a recall problem quantization amplifies (on-board VRU recall: pedestrian 14.8%, motor- cycle 12.3%, bicycle 5.7%; occupied-any 43.8% mean). At matched full-model workload the shared A100 runs FlashOcc at 33.5 ms median, 57.5 ms maximum over 2k frames, meeting the 100 ms budget on that trace and miss- ing 0.5% at 50 ms; a 2k-frame trace is the finite-window trap of Fig. 1, with no enforcement layer behind it. 5. The latency guarantee is lay- ered, and only one layer is a bound: PL compute is cycle- bounded analytically; inference latency is a measured en- velope whose maxima are sample-size-dependent; delivery is structurally guaranteed, possibly with a stale-flagged fall- back. text: Specification Gaming and a Constrained Reinforcement Learning Mitigation in a Cleaning Gridworld Preprint Hilda Adwubi Osei Department of Industrial Engineering Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology Kumasi, Ghana hildaosei109@gmail.com
title: Specification Gaming and a Constrained Reinforcement

text: Reinforcement learning agents optimize exactly the reward signal they are given, which can diverge sharply from an intended true objective when that signal is only a proxy for it; this failure mode is known as specification gaming. Existing evidence for this failure mode is largely observational, with comparatively few demonstrations pairing a controlled, deliberately constructed proxy/true gap with a mitigation that carries a verifiable guarantee rather than only an empirical improvement. We construct a minimal gridworld in which a cleaning-robot agent can either genuinely remove dirt or conceal it from a cheap sensor, and show that a standard deep Q-network trained only on the sensor’s proxy reward converges to a policy that games it completely, reaching near-maximal proxy reward while never achieving the true objective. We then introduce a constrained reinforcement learning fix, penalizing the specific behaviors through which the agent exploits the gap, and show that it eliminates the gaming behavior from the final policy while substantially recovering true-objective performance. We further derive and empirically verify an exact accounting identity relating the proxy reward, true reward, and our cost signal for this environment, showing that the cost signal measures the proxy/true gap exactly rather than merely tracking it, and yields a deterministic guarantee under a hard-constrained variant of the method. Keywords specification gaming · reward hacking · reinforcement learning

text: A reinforcement learning agent optimizes exactly the reward signal it is given, not the intention behind it. When that signal is a proxy standing in for a true objective that is harder to specify directly – a sensor reading in place of a physical state, a classifier score in place of an outcome – optimization pressure can push the agent toward the proxy/true gap rather than closing it. This failure mode, specification gaming, has been documented extensively across both simulated and real-deployed systems [Krakovna et al., 2020], and recent work has begun to formalize what distinguishes it from ordinary reward misspecification [Skalse et al., 2022]. Much of the existing evidence for specification gaming is observational: a catalogue of cases in which an agent was found, after the fact, to have exploited a reward function in an unintended way. Comparatively less work pairs a controlled, deliberately constructed proxy/true gap with a mitigation that carries a stated, verifiable guarantee rather than only an empirical improvement. This gap matters for deployment: knowing that a fix tends to work is weaker than knowing precisely what it guarantees and under what conditions. In this work, we construct a minimal gridworld, CleaningGridWorld, with a genuine and exploitable gap between a proxy reward (what a cheap sensor reports) and a true objective (what was actually accomplished), and

text: 2.1 Specification Gaming and Reward Hacking Specification gaming – an agent exploiting a literal reward specification in a way that diverges from the designer’s intent – has been documented extensively across both simulated and deployed systems [Krakovna et al., 2020]. These cases are largely catalogued observationally: a system is found, after deployment or training, to have discovered an unintended shortcut. Skalse et al. [2022] take a step toward formal rigor, characterizing when a reward function admits a hacking policy relative to an intended true objective, distinguishing reward hacking from ordinary reward misspecification more broadly. We adopt this proxy/true framing directly, but construct an environment where the gap is specified by design rather than discovered after the fact, which lets us pair the demonstration with a mitigation whose effect on that specific, known gap can be measured exactly. 2.2 Reward Shaping and Policy Invariance Dense, informative reward signals are often necessary for an RL agent to discover a sparse or delayed objective within a practical training budget. Ng et al. [1999] show that reward shaping of the form F(s, a, s′) = γϕ(s′) −ϕ(s), for any potential function ϕ, leaves the optimal policy of the underlying MDP unchanged – shaping accelerates discovery of an optimum without altering what that optimum is. This guarantee is what allows us to introduce dense positional

This guarantee is what allows us to introduce dense positional shaping in Section 3.3 without that shaping itself becoming a second, uncontrolled source of proxy/true divergence. 2.3 Constrained Reinforcement Learning Constrained Markov decision processes [Altman, 1999] formalize policy optimization subject to a secondary cost objective remaining below a threshold, typically enforced via a Lagrangian relaxation. Achiam et al. [2017] extend this to deep RL with a trust-region method with per-update constraint satisfaction guarantees. The present work uses the simpler, fixed-multiplier end of this family (Section 3.4): rather than tuning the Lagrange multiplier via dual ascent, we fix it and instead derive a problem-specific identity (Section 4) that lets a hard cap on the cost signal translate directly into a deterministic bound on true-objective performance. We treat an implementation of the dual-ascent or hard-constrained variant, in the style of Achiam et al. [2017], as natural future work rather than a contribution of the present paper. 2.4 Positioning Our contribution sits at the intersection of these threads: we construct a specification-gaming environment in the spirit of Krakovna et al. text: Specification Gaming and Constrained RL Preprint strengthened in this specific setting by an exact accounting identity that turns an empirical improvement into a provable guarantee. 3 Method 3.1 Environment: CleaningGridWorld CleaningGridWorld is a 5 × 5 gridworld containing four dirt cells and one fixed disposal bin. Each cell is in one of four states: empty floor, dirt, dirt covered by a rug, or the disposal bin. The agent occupies a single cell and may additionally be carrying one unit of vacuumed dirt; it cannot carry more than one unit at a time. The action space is discrete with six actions: four cardinal movements, vacuum, and cover. vacuum picks up dirt from the agent’s current cell if the agent is not already carrying, or deposits carried dirt if the agent is standing on the bin. cover places a rug over dirt in the current cell. This design yields two structurally distinct routes to the same sensor-visible outcome. A proxy reward, modeling a cheap automated sensor, counts cells that do not read as dirty: Rproxy t = |{(r, c) : gridt(r, c) ∈{empty, covered}}| (1) A true reward counts only genuine disposal events, independent of what the sensor would report: Rtrue t = ⊮[a disposal occurred at t] (2) Both covering and picking up dirt raise Rproxy (Eq. 1), since both remove

text: ∈{empty, covered}}| (1) A true reward counts only genuine disposal events, independent of what the sensor would report: Rtrue t = ⊮[a disposal occurred at t] (2) Both covering and picking up dirt raise Rproxy (Eq. 1), since both remove the dirt state from a cell; only completed delivery to the bin raises Rtrue (Eq. 2). This asymmetry is the environment’s constructed gap: an agent that observes only Rproxy has no reward-level incentive to prefer the costlier delivery route over the cheaper concealment route, even though only the former satisfies the intended objective. We use a single fixed layout – dirt, bin, and agent start positions sampled once and reused across all episodes – so that training is a navigation problem on a known map rather than a layout-generalization problem; we return to this choice in Section 6.1. 3.2 Agent The agent is a deep Q-network [Mnih et al., 2015], which is a feedforward network with two hidden layers of 128 units each and ReLU activations, mapping an encoded state to one Q-value per action. The state is encoded as the concatenation of a one-hot grid representation (5 × 5 × 4 = 100 dimensions), a one-hot agent position (5 × 5 = 25 dimensions), and a binary carrying flag (1 dimension), yielding a 126-dimensional input. This architecture is intentionally

This architecture is intentionally minimal: the state and action spaces are small enough that a compact MLP with experience replay and a target network is sufficient to isolate the proxy/true gaming phenomenon without confounding it with architecture-driven learning difficulty. 3.3 Potential-Based Reward Shaping Only 4 of the environment’s 25 cells are ever reward-relevant, and ϵ-greedy exploration under this sparsity provides too little gradient signal for standard Q-learning to discover either route to reward within a practical training budget. text: Specification Gaming and Constrained RL Preprint The second term fires only at the final timestep T of an episode, and only if the agent is carrying dirt it never delivered. The training reward used for the Q-learning update applies costt as a fixed-multiplier Lagrangian penalty on top of the shaped proxy signal: rtrain t = ∆Rproxy t + F(st, at, st+1) −λ · costt (5) where ∆Rproxy t = Rproxy t −Rproxy t−1 and λ is fixed for the duration of training. Critically, the agent is never given Rtrue as a training signal; it learns only from Eq. 5, mirroring a deployment setting in which the true objective is precisely what is unavailable for direct supervision. The concealment exploit is a single-action behavior that is trivially reachable by random exploration; the honest delivery route requires a multi-step chain (navigate to dirt, pick up, navigate to bin, deposit) that is comparatively unlikely to be discovered before ϵ decays. To address this exploration asymmetry, we generate a fixed set of honest-policy demonstration trajectories once, before training begins, and store them in a buffer that is never subsequently written to and therefore can never be evicted by the replay buffer’s ring-buffer overwrite behavior. Each training batch is drawn as a mixture of ordinary experience and demonstration transitions at a fixed demonstration fraction. This

First, the agent is trained and evaluated on a single fixed grid layout – dirt, bin, and agent-start positions generated once and reused across all episodes – rather than a distribution of randomly sampled layouts. This is a standard simplification for interpretable gridworld demonstrations, and it isolates the proxy/true gaming phenomenon from a separate, harder generalization problem. This also means that our results should be read as establishing that the gaming behavior and the constrained fix both occur on this layout; we make no claim here about whether the fix transfers to unseen layouts without retraining, and treat this as the most immediate direction for follow-up work. Second, the constrained agent’s final policy, while free of concealment and abandonment behaviors entirely, had not converged to optimal navigation within the episode budget: two of the four dirt units remained unresolved, consistent with residual action oscillation near grid boundaries rather than any renewed incentive to game the proxy. This is a training efficiency gap, separate from and not evidence against the specification-gaming question this work targets – the policy’s qualitative behavior (no concealment, no abandonment) is the outcome our method is designed to produce, and it was produced; full navigational optimality was not a target of the constrained fix itself. Third, the exact form of Proposition 1 depends on a structural property specific to this environment: every unit of dirt is resolved through exactly one of three mutually exclusive outcomes (covered, delivered, or abandoned), with no possibility of double-counting because the agent can carry at most one unit at a time. We view identifying the general conditions under which an exact (rather than approximate) proxy/true/cost identity exists as an open question raised but not answered by this work. 7 Conclusion and Future Work We constructed CleaningGridWorld, a gridworld with a deliberately constructed, exploitable gap between a proxy reward and a true objective, and showed that a standard deep Q-network trained on the proxy alone converges to a policy that games it completely, reaching near-maximal proxy reward while the true reward remains at zero. We then introduced a Lagrangian-penalized constrained RL fix, with a cost signal targeting the specific gaming mechanisms the baseline agent discovered, and showed that it eliminates those behaviors entirely from the final policy while recovering substantial true-objective performance. Underlying this fix is an exact accounting identity, proved for this environment 7

Two directions follow directly from this work. First, testing whether the constrained fix transfers to randomly sampled grid layouts, rather than the single fixed layout used here, would establish whether the result generalizes beyond one navigation problem. Second, implementing the hard-constrained variant of Corollary 1 directly – via action masking or early termination once a fixed cost budget is reached – would allow the deterministic bound on true-objective performance to be tested empirically against a trained system, rather than verified only as a consequence of Proposition 1 on the fixed-λ relaxation studied here. text: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference la- tency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Passˆ3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serv- ing latency from models’ real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated to- ken counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off be- tween decision quality and timely execution. These findings suggest directions for improving real-time multimodal agents, including adaptive reasoning with tempo- ral awareness and continuous perception and action. 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 Latency (s) 0% 5% 10% 15% 20% 25% 30% 35% 40% Pass³ Reasoning effort low high Claude Fable 5.1 OpenAI Decisions Claude Opus 5 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Gemini 3.1

text: Many real-world interactive scenarios require decisions to be made under strict temporal constraints. For example, when purchasing a highly demanded ticket, detecting availability is not enough: an agent must observe the changing interface and act before the opportunity disappears. Such sce- narios require real-time streaming capabilities, where a model continuously perceives an evolving environment and produces timely actions in response to newly arriving information. Recently, a growing family of real-time streaming models, such as GPT-Realtime (OpenAI, 2025) and Gemini Live (Google, 2026a), has begun to make this setting practically possible. In contrast to asyn- chronous models that process inputs only after they are fully received, these models can consume streaming inputs and react to new information with low latency. Unlike previous benchmarks that evaluate models in static environments (Zhang et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2026) where the environment does not continuously evolve, evaluating streaming models re- quires dynamic settings that test whether models can perceive and act effectively under strict tempo- ral constraints. However, existing evaluations of real-time systems largely focus on capabilities such as streaming perception, conversational quality, and interruption handling (Lin et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b), with limited coverage of interactive tasks in which actions affect subsequent environment states and delayed execution can change the outcome. We first characterize real-time streaming capability along three complementary
