text: and interruption handling (Lin et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b), with limited coverage of interactive tasks in which actions affect subsequent environment states and delayed execution can change the outcome. We first characterize real-time streaming capability along three complementary dimensions: tem- poral state awareness, adaptive deliberation, and time-aware action selection. These dimensions capture an agent’s ability to track relevant changes and information freshness, adjust deliberation to the available time, and select actions that remain useful when executed. Building on this framework, we introduce Realtime-Bench, comprising 50 interactive game and web tasks in which evolving states and limited opportunities make success depend on both action choice and timing. We evaluate 12 frontier models spanning standard asynchronous models, streaming models and decision models. As shown in Figure 1, real-time interaction remains challenging, with the best success rate reaching only 44.0% and best passˆ3 is below 37% under Wall Clock, which advances the environment according to actual inference and serving time, following prior interactive-agent evaluations (Kang et al., 2025; Froger et al., 2026; ValsAI, 2026; Parekh et al., 2026). Token Clock (ours) advances simulated time according to generation tokens consumed before action commitment, testing temporal aware- ness of models independently of physical serving speed. To better understand these limitations and disentangle the effects of serving latency and models’ real-time streaming capability, we compare three clock protocols (Figure 2). Alongside Wall Clock, Paused Clock freezes the environment during inference, providing an idealized reference in which deliberation incurs no temporal cost (Tan et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025). We fur- ther introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to the number of generation 2

text: Preprint tokens consumed before an action is committed. Models that spend more tokens deliberating there- fore act later, preserving the task consequences of delayed decisions while controlling for physical serving speed. Under each clock, we test low and high reasoning effort to examine the trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. Our analysis reveals that substantial performance gaps relative to Paused Clock persist under Token Clock, highlighting the difficulty of translating task competence into timely action even when temporal costs are standardized independently of serving speed. Higher reasoning effort improves success for all six models under Paused Clock but has mixed effects under temporal pressure. Further experiments show that relaxing the temporal cost of generation generally improves performance but does not ensure task success. These findings motivate future work on adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action, enabling agents to coordinate deliberation and execution with the time available. 2

text: 2.1 STREAMING MULTIMODAL MODELS AND BENCHMARKS Video multimodal models have progressively evolved from offline video understanding (Maaz et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b;a; 2023) toward real-time streaming interaction, where models continuously perceive incoming observations and decide when and how to respond as the stream unfolds (Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Qian et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026). Existing training and evaluation formulate real-time interaction as responding to a continuously arriving but sparsely sampled audiovisual stream, commonly at around 1–2 FPS (Chen et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b). Under this setting, existing benchmarks focus on evaluating the abilities of streaming perception (Lin et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026), response timing (Wang et al., 2025a; He et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b), interruption handling (Lin et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b), and conversational quality (He et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b) in scenarios such as surveillance anomaly detection (Wang et al., 2025a), question answering during gym exercises and shopping, and step-by-step task guidance (Lu et al., 2026b), leaving untested whether models can act effectively in closed-loop environments where the timing of their decisions affects subsequent states and task outcomes. In contrast, Realtime-Bench evaluates closed-loop interaction in

text: exercises and shopping, and step-by-step task guidance (Lu et al., 2026b), leaving untested whether models can act effectively in closed-loop environments where the timing of their decisions affects subsequent states and task outcomes. In contrast, Realtime-Bench evaluates closed-loop interaction in web environments and games, where task success depends on both what actions models take and when they take them. 2.2 REAL-TIME EVALUATION IN INTERACTIVE ENVIRONMENTS Existing interactive evaluations assess asynchronous vision-language agents in games that pause during model inference, allowing their perception, reasoning, and planning abilities to be evaluated independently of response speed (Tan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026). To evaluate agents under real-time pressure, VideoGameBench (Zhang et al., 2026), GameWorld-RT (Ouyang et al., 2026), GPTNT (Parekh et al., 2026), and Gaia2 (Froger et al., 2026) allow game or web environments to continue evolving during inference, making task success depend on both decision quality and wall-clock latency. Although such wall-clock capture the consequences of slow responses, they also tie evaluation to deployment-specific inference speed. Similar to Real-Time Reasoning Gym (Wen et al., 2026), we adopt Token Clock, which maps gener- ated tokens to environment time at a shared rate, preserving the temporal cost of deliberation while decoupling evaluation from physical serving speed. 3 SETTING FORMULATION 3.1

We characterize this capability along three complementary di- mensions. (1) Temporal state awareness (RT-Perceive) requires models to use available observations to track relevant changes, information freshness, and opportunity timing; (2) Adaptive deliberation (RT-Deliberate) requires models to adjust their reasoning length and depth according to the avail- able time and the expected benefit of further computation; (3)Time-aware action selection (RT-Act) 3

text: Preprint requires models to determine which action will remain useful when executed, including whether to wait or act immediately and what action to take. These dimensions jointly shape how an agent responds to an evolving environment. For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT- Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act). 3.2 CLOCK PROTOCOLS As shown in Figure 2, we use three clock protocols to distinguish task performance under actual inference latency, performance without inference delays, and performance under a standardized temporal cost of token generation. • Wall Clock. To evaluate performance under real-world inference latency, Wall Clock ad- vances the environment according to the actual time spent on inference. The environment continues to evolve while the model generates a response, so action timing depends on both model computation and serving infrastructure. • Paused Clock. To assess task performance without the temporal cost of inference, Paused Clock pauses the environment while the model generates a response. This provides an idealized reference for Wall Clock, allowing us to compare performance when inference does and does not delay actions in environment time. • Token Clock. To retain the temporal cost

text: the environment while the model generates a response. This provides an idealized reference for Wall Clock, allowing us to compare performance when inference does and does not delay actions in environment time. • Token Clock. To retain the temporal cost of deliberation while removing dependence on serving speed, Token Clock advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency. To formalize Token Clock, let B denote the number of generation tokens corresponding to one observation interval and f the observation rate in frames per simulated second. The token-to-time rate is κ = Bf, measured in generation tokens per simulated second. If the model generates n tokens after receiving an observation and before committing to an action, the action is applied after a simulated-time delay of ∆t = n κ = n Bf . In both Token Clock and Wall Clock, when generation spans multiple observation intervals, inter- mediate frames are skipped, and the model receives the most recent scheduled frame available at the resulting simulated time. This provides a simplified analogue of humans returning attention to the current scene after deliberation, and tests whether the model can respond before relevant events or action opportunities pass.

To evaluate models’ real-time streaming capabilities in environments that continue to evolve while they ob- serve, reason, and act, we design tasks around the fol- lowing three criteria. Real-world fidelity. To capture practical real-time in- teraction demands, task interfaces and interaction me- chanics should reflect realistic applications and games. For example, web tasks simulate real-world websites such as Amazon, while game tasks feature popular games. 4

text: Preprint Dynamically evolving environment. Environment states should change over time, independently of the model’s actions. These changes may include moving game elements, changing availability, or continuously updated information. For example, available seats change during cinema booking, while obstacles move across the screen in games. Temporally constrained interaction. Success should depend on both what actions the model takes and when it takes them. Deadlines, limited action windows, and transient opportunities require timely responses. For example, a model must reserve a seat before it becomes unavailable or dodge an obstacle before a collision. 4.2 TASK CONSTRUCTION. Guided by the above criteria, we construct web tasks based on realistic application scenarios and adapt game tasks from popular open-source games. We adjust task goals and temporal constraints so that success requires timely action, while ensuring that tasks remain feasible for humans. This process yields 50 tasks: 30 web tasks and 20 game tasks. Each task has task-specific success criteria, such as successfully purchasing a ticket before the countdown expires. 4.3 TASK EXAMPLES AND DISTRIBUTION. At each scheduled observation frame, the model receives the current screenshot together with the retained interaction history. To prevent GUI grounding from becoming a bottleneck for evaluating real-time decision making, we augment the screenshot with a read-only Set-of-Marks (SoM) representation following common GUI-agent practice (Yang et al., 2023), which identifies currently interactable elements and exposes their associated semantics and supported actions. At each decision step, the model generates executable GUI actions from a common GUI action space (e.g., click, type, scroll, and wait) (Xie et al., 2024). The detailed implementation are provided in Appendix A.1. 5

text: Preprint 5.2 CONTEXT MANAGEMENT To minimize harness-induced overhead when evaluating models’ real-time capabilities, we follow Qwen-CUA (Lu et al., 2026a) in removing older history in blocks rather than at every step. This keeps the history prefix unchanged between folds, allowing models to reuse its KV cache across consecutive steps and reducing repeated prefill computation caused by frequent history truncation. All models follow the same history retention policy. Implementation details are provided in Ap- pendix A.3. 5.3 EPISODE EXECUTION Suppose the model receives an observation at environment time ti and commits an action after a delay ∆ti determined by the clock protocol. Under Wall Clock, ∆ti equals the actual inference latency; under Paused Clock, ∆ti = 0; under Token Clock, ∆ti is determined by the generation tokens consumed before action commitment. The action timestamp is tact i = ti + ∆ti. The environment advances from ti to tact i before the action is applied. If generation terminates without a valid action, the harness substitutes wait at the timestamp determined by the same clock protocol. GUI execution latency does not advance environment time. An episode terminates when the environment reaches a task-defined terminal condition (e.g., game over, successful completion of a web transaction, or expiration of a task-specific countdown) or the benchmark-defined time horizon (e.g., five minutes of environment time). In an evolving environment, additional deliberation may improve a decision while leaving insufficient time to execute it effectively. Adaptive reasoning should therefore account for the time available to act, alongside task difficulty (Anthropic, 2026b; Wu et al., 2026). In Tetris, for example, a model may spend more time comparing placements while a falling piece is far above the stack. As the piece approaches the stack, however, it must shorten deliberation to leave enough time to execute the required moves. text: Preprint 7.2 CONTINUOUS PERCEPTION AND ACTION Adapting deliberation also depends on receiving timely observations and updating actions as the environment changes. At the 1 FPS observation rate used in our experiments, brief events or rapid changes may occur between observations, even when inference itself incurs no temporal cost. For example, an enemy may change direction between two frames, preventing the agent from adjusting its action until the next observation. Higher observation rates could provide more timely feedback, but realizing this benefit requires models and harnesses that can process incoming information and revise actions with sufficiently low latency. (1) Model design. Higher temporal resolution presents two coupled challenges: processing more frames increases inference cost, while compressing visual inputs risks discarding brief changes that determine the next action. Addressing these challenges requires optimizing both (1) processing ef- ficiency, for example by replacing cascaded architectures with an end-to-end single Transformer using block-causal attention (Huang et al., 2026), and (2) the preservation of action-relevant infor- mation through compact temporal representations (Ding et al., 2025) or codec-aware visual encod- ing (Sarkar et al., 2026). Future work should explore these two directions to support higher frame rates with lower latency while preserving important information. (2) Interaction harnesses. text: We introduced Realtime-Bench, a suite of diverse dynamic game and web tasks for evaluating real- time interactive capability in multimodal agents. Our evaluation of 12 frontier models shows that real-time interaction remains challenging: under Wall Clock, the best success rate reaches only 44.0%, and the best Passˆ3 is only 36%. To disentangle the effects of serving latency and models’ real-time streaming capability, we compared three clock protocols, introducing Token Clock to pre- serve the temporal cost of deliberation independently of physical serving speed. Substantial gaps relative to Paused Clock persist under Token Clock, highlighting the difficulty of translating task competence into timely action. Across the six models analyzed under different reasoning efforts, higher effort improves success under Paused Clock but has mixed effects under temporal pressure. Relaxing the temporal cost of generation generally improves performance but does not ensure suc- cess. These findings motivate adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous percep- tion and action, allowing agents to coordinate deliberation and execution with the time available. Realtime-Bench provides a controlled setting for studying these capabilities and measuring progress toward effective real-time interaction. 10

text: Preprint A EVALUATION IMPLEMENTATION A.1 OBSERVATIONS AND ACTIONS Observations. The agent receives a screenshot and a read-only description of currently inter- actable elements. Screenshots preserve the desktop aspect ratio and are resized to a maximum dimension of 768 pixels, yielding 768 × 432 images for the 1920 × 1080 desktop. We adopt this reduced resolution to reduce visual processing overhead and inference latency. Recent studies also suggest that SoM representations preserve visual grounding performance under downsampling with minimal loss (Xie et al., 2024; Kaesberg et al., 2026).The Set-of-Marks representation uses P# for discrete target points and R# for continuous regions. A region location is specified as R#@u,v, where u, v ∈[0, 1000] are local coordinates. Marks refer only to the observation in which they appear. Raw screenshot coordinates remain available when no suitable mark exists and are mapped to desktop coordinates before execution. Actions. Each decision produces a GUI action. Table 1 gives the shared action schema. Action Arguments Semantics click target, button Click the specified point. right click target Right-click the specified point. double click, triple click target Apply the corresponding click sequence. mouse down, mouse up target, duration Press or release the mouse button. move target, duration Move the pointer. type text Enter the supplied text. key key, repeat Tap a key or key combination. hold key key,

Table 1: Shared GUI action schema. Arguments include optional fields; action durations lie in [0, 10] seconds and key.repeat lies in [1, 100]. A.2 CLOCK EXECUTION AND TOKEN ACCOUNTING Action timing. For a decision based on an observation at time ti, the token clock assigns an action timestamp tact i = ti + ni/(Bf), where ni is the charged output-token count. The harness advances the environment to this timestamp before applying the action. Finishing early does not provide an extra observation: the next observation follows the scheduled frame grid. If generation crosses observation boundaries, the corresponding intermediate observations are skipped. Physical inference and GUI execution latency do not advance simulated time. Browser animation updates use a persistent 60 Hz simulation grid, separate from the agent’s observation rate, so splitting an interval around an action does not change the number of animation updates. Charged tokens. For API-based models, we charge both reasoning tokens and output tokens us- ing the usage reported by the API for the complete response. As Gemini Live natively produces audio rather than text, we configure it to emit GUI actions through native function calls instead of spoken responses. We charge its reported thought tokens and non-audio response tokens, excluding generated audio. A.3 CONTEXT MANAGEMENT Visual and textual history are retained separately. When the active visual history reaches 21 obser- vations, the oldest 10 screenshots and their associated interactables are replaced with fixed place- holders, while the corresponding text and action records remain. When detailed interaction history 16
title: Preprint

text: Preprint exceeds 50 turns, the oldest 10 complete turns are replaced by a compact executed-action ledger. This block policy retains recent evidence while limiting changes to reusable context prefixes. Streaming models maintain the retained history within their sessions, while asynchronous models resubmit the retained context. To maximize cache reuse and reduce inference latency, we preserve the order and content of retained messages and remove older history only in blocks when the reten- tion limits are exceeded. This keeps the shared context prefix stable across consecutive decisions, allowing models to reuse cached computation where supported. Both mechanisms implement the same logical history policy. A.4 MODEL CONFIGURATION Standard Asynchronous Models and Real-time Streaming Models. Our standard asynchronous models include GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5.1, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and Kimi-K3. We access GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Fable 5.1, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through OpenRouter, Claude Opus 5 through the An- thropic API, and Kimi-K3 through the Kimi API. Our real-time streaming models include GPT- Realtime-2, accessed through OpenAI, and Gemini 3.1 Flash Live and Gemini 3.8 Live, accessed through the Google Gemini Live API. Where configurable, we control reasoning effort through provider-exposed API fields, selecting the corresponding low and high settings for our experimental conditions. Decision models. We access Jev 1.13 and OpenAI

Where configurable, we control reasoning effort through provider-exposed API fields, selecting the corresponding low and high settings for our experimental conditions. Decision models. We access Jev 1.13 and OpenAI Decisions through OpenRouter API. For these models, the harness constructs candidate GUI actions from the current observation and submits them as a choice question. Text entry can be composed through successive choices before executing a single typing action. Jev 1.13 does not natively support screenshot inputs. We therefore represent its Web observations as structured text using the browser accessibility tree (AX tree), interactable elements, and appearance descriptors. This representation does not adequately capture the visual state of our game tasks, so we evaluate Jev 1.13 only on Web tasks. OpenAI Decisions additionally receives screenshots. By inspecting failed trajectories, the first author identified three failure modes and developed an annotation codebook specifying operational definitions, inclusion criteria, and exclusion rules. For lack of temporal awareness (RT-Deliberate), we annotated failures under TL and TH to examine whether models accounted for the temporal cost of deliberation under standardized token-based timing; Paused Clock removes this cost, whereas Wall Clock additionally reflects deployment- dependent latency. For failure to track the evolving state (RT-Perceive) and misjudging whether action is needed (RT-Act), we annotated failures under PH, which pauses the environment during generation and uses high reasoning effort, allowing us to examine state tracking and action necessity judgments without environment changes during inference. We then prompted Codex to apply the codebook to the recorded action trajectories, timing information, available model reasoning, and observations.

text: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Opera- tor Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input func- tions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear ad- vection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of 3.75× is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the pre- dicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results

text: Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) aims to make use of the vast amounts of prior knowledge that is often available about physical systems when training machine learning models [1, 2]. The seminal work by [3] introduced Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), which leverage automatic differentiation to compute derivatives appearing in the governing equations. PINNs encode the underlying Partial Differential arXiv:2610.22157v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026

text: A preprint - October 16, 2026 Equations (PDEs) governing a physical system, alongside the boundary and initial conditions directly into the loss function, reducing or even eliminating the requirements for labelled training data. Embedding physical constraints in the loss function greatly reduces the acceptable solution space without the need for labelled data [4]. In recent years, there has been an abundance of work applying PINNs, ranging from problems in fluid mechanics [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11], molecular imaging [12], solid mechanics [13, 14, 15], and learning governing equations from data [16, 17, 15, 18], to cite only a few. Despite their success, a critical limitation for the real-world application of PINNs for forward modelling is that they typically require retraining even for small changes to the domain, initial conditions, or — perhaps most importantly — boundary conditions. This stems from the fact that a conventional PINN takes only the independent variables of the PDE as input into the neural network, while the initial and boundary conditions are incorporated indirectly as soft constraints in the loss function. Consequently, the network is trained to output a solution corresponding to a fixed set of conditions, and does not naturally generalise to different initial or boundary conditions [19, 11]. As a result, the fast inference times of trained PINNs cannot be easily

text: network is trained to output a solution corresponding to a fixed set of conditions, and does not naturally generalise to different initial or boundary conditions [19, 11]. As a result, the fast inference times of trained PINNs cannot be easily leveraged across different problem setups, limiting their practical utility in dynamic or rapidly changing scenarios [10]. A possible solution for this limitation is to use physics informed neural operators. Neural operators aim to learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces [20]; for example, a mapping from bound- ary conditions to the PDE’s solution across the whole spatiotemporal domain. One notable neural op- erator framework is the Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) [21], and its physics-informed variant, the PI-DeepONet [22]. DeepONet is grounded in the universal operator approximation theorem, which states that a neural network with a single hidden layer can approximate any non-linear continuous operator G to arbitrary accuracy [23]. The learned operator approximation ˆG maps an input function u to an output function ˆG(u), which can then be evaluated at collocation/query points y to produce ˆG(u)(y). [21] extended this framework to use deep neural networks in their unstacked DeepONet. In a DeepONet a single Branch network encodes the input function at m sensor points ξj∈[1,m], while a single Trunk network encodes the collocation/query point y = (x, t). For example, the

text: use deep neural networks in their unstacked DeepONet. In a DeepONet a single Branch network encodes the input function at m sensor points ξj∈[1,m], while a single Trunk network encodes the collocation/query point y = (x, t). For example, the input layer of the Branch network could depict a time-dependent boundary condition, whereas the Trunk network functions similarly to a conventional PINN, taking points within the spatiotemporal domain as input. The outputs of these subnetworks are then combined via a dot product to approximate the output function evaluated at the query point. This can be represented by the equation: ˆG(u)(y) ≈ s X k=1 bk(u(ξ1), u(ξ2), ..., u(ξm))τk(y), (1) where, bk are the Branch network outputs, τk are the Trunk network outputs, both of which are of length s. The subnetworks require no specific architecture, allowing flexible integration of different networks like feedforward, convolutional, etc. Owing to the simple, feedforward architecture of the subnetworks in the DeepONet, it is straightforward to integrate physics-informed techniques into DeepONet designs. A PI-DeepONet is trained using a loss function formulated in the same way as in PINNs [22]. A schematic of a PI-DeepONet can be seen in Figure 1. Derivative terms in the physics loss are calculated by automatic differentiation along the Trunk network, which encodes the collocation points of the output function space.

Derivative terms in the physics loss are calculated by automatic differentiation along the Trunk network, which encodes the collocation points of the output function space. The PI-DeepONet is especially attractive in scenarios where simulations are expensive, high-fidelity data are limited, and adherence to physical laws is critical for model reliability [24]. Such scenarios include real-time forecasting, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins. This is because the PI-DeepONet can be trained without labelled data, and can then eﬀiciently generate predictions across a variety of problem configurations. Overall, PI-DeepONet is one of the first physics-informed neural operator frameworks and has received substantial attention since its introduction [22], introducing a general approach that allows purely physics- informed operator learning, but broader adoption has been limited compared to data-driven neural operators. This is partly due to the extra computational burden of using automatic differentiation to calculate deriva- tives in the physics loss terms, which becomes more apparent for high-dimensional systems and when higher order derivatives are present. This PI-DeepONet structure reduces the number of Trunk network evaluations from N d to Nd, making it favourable for high-dimensional problems. However, this method achieves the best performance when the underlying physical system is compatible with a separation-of-variables approach, somewhat limiting the general applicability of the PI-DeepONet framework — one of its most compelling advantages. text: 2.1 General PI-DeepONet framework The DeepONet is rendered physics-informed (PI-DeepONet) by encoding the PDEs, boundary and initial conditions directly into the loss term, which can take the following form: N[G(u)(x, t)] = 0, x ∈Ω, t ∈(0, T] (2) B[G(u)(x, t)] = 0, x ∈∂Ω, t ∈(0, T] (3) G(u)(x, 0) = v0(x), x ∈Ω (4) Here, N[·] represents a general differential operator, B[·] is a boundary operator, x is the spatial coordinate, t is the temporal coordinate, v0(x) defines the initial condition, Ω⊂Rd−1 denotes the spatial domain, and T denotes the upper limit of the temporal domain. A composite loss function incorporates each of the conditions: L = LPDE + LBC + LIC + Ldata. (5) Here, LPDE enforces the differential equation by minimising the residual of N[G(u)] at collocation points, (xi, ti) inside the spatiotemporal domain, LBC penalises violations of boundary conditions at boundary collocation points, and LIC enforces the initial condition at initial-time collocation points; Ldata is an optional term that penalises the difference between the neural network’s prediction and available observation data. Comparatively less attention has been paid to reducing the computational cost of training especially when scaling PI-DeepONets to computationally demanding, higher-dimensional problems. This work addresses this issue by introducing an architectural modification that preserves the defining advantages of PI-DeepONets – training without labelled solution 15

In this work, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that changes how input functions are processed within the Branch network. The key observation is that, in the Vanilla implementation of PI-DeepONets, the Branch network is evaluated repeatedly at every collocation point, even though the input function itself does not change. Addressing this redundancy yields our proposed alternative (ATenH), in which the Branch network is evaluated once per input function and its encoding is reused across all collocation points. This modification comes with the constraint that all output functions must be evaluated at the same number of collocation points. In a data-driven setting this may be restrictive because the amount of labelled training data that is available will likely vary between samples. However, DeepONets are increasingly being adopted within physics-informed frameworks (PI-DeepONets), where this limitation does not apply – collocation points can be freely generated and chosen. By reducing the dimensionality of the Branch network input tensors, the number of operations required by this subnetwork is substantially decreased. Importantly, the modified architecture performs the same underlying mathematical operations as the original one and, as a result, achieves comparable predictive accuracy while significantly reducing training time. For 1D linear advection, the average training time is 314s and 276s for the Vanilla and ATenH architectures, respectively, while for 2D linear advection the corresponding times are 11800s and 3360s. Most notably, the 3D linear advection problem exposed a fundamental practical limitation of the Vanilla PI-DeepONet implementation. It exceeded the available GPU memory and could not be trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, whereas the ATenH architecture completed training in approximately 39 hours and achieved an average relative error of 5.44%. Equation 27 also predicts a theoretical speed-up factor of 580× for this problem. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed modification does more than reduce training time: by lowering memory requirements, it enables classes of higher-dimensional PI-DeepONet problems that are otherwise computationally infeasible on the same hardware. A theoretical cost model was developed to quantify the training-time scaling of both architectures with respect to the number of collocation points and the number of input functions. This model predicts linear scaling with both number of collocation points and input functions for both architectures, but with larger prefactors for the Vanilla architecture, implying steeper scaling. The empirical results for the 1D and 2D linear advection problems confirm this behaviour. The agreement between the theoretical scaling laws and the empirical measurements suggests that the observed performance gains arise primarily from differences in the computational structure of the two architectures rather than implementation-specific effects. The model also predicts an asymptotic constant speed-up factor, which is reinforced by the experimental profiles seen in Figure 6; however, the observed speed-ups are smaller than the theoretical values (1.14× vs. 1.64× in 1D, and 3.49× vs. 7.46× in 2D). Despite the quantitative discrepancies, the consistency in qualitative scaling behaviour reinforces the observation that the theoretical model captures the dominant computational trends governing both architectures. text: This work demonstrates that modifying the Branch network input handling in PI-DeepONets can substan- tially reduce computational cost without sacrificing predictive accuracy. While the theoretical analysis cap- tures the qualitative scaling behaviour, the empirical results quantify substantial practical gains, particularly in higher-dimensional settings. A key outcome is that the ATenH architecture enables problems that are infeasible under the Vanilla for- mulation. In particular, while the Vanilla architecture failed on the 3D linear advection problem due to memory limitations, the ATenH architecture successfully completed training with a mean predictive error of 5.44%. This highlights the fact that implementation-level considerations can determine whether a problem is tractable in practice. 16

text: A preprint - October 16, 2026 Overall, this work demonstrates that implementation choices can play a critical role in the practical perfor- mance of PI-DeepONets. ATenH provides significant improvements over the Vanilla PI-DeepONet formula- tion; however, it should not be viewed as a final design, but rather as evidence that careful consideration of how these models are implemented can yield substantial gains. This suggests that further improvements may be achievable through continued optimisation of existing architectures, particularly within widely used frameworks such as PyTorch. Furthermore, the agreement between theoretical and empirical scaling indi- cates that these findings are not tied to a specific hardware or software configuration, but are expected to generalise to other implementations. Future work should explore the application of similar architectural improvements to tackle problems that have so far proved intractable for PI-DeepONets. text: PremiseSQL: Evaluating Premise Critique and Abstention in Text-to-SQL Systems Shuo Lin1 Jinzhe Li1,3 Chenlu Guo4 Yanhan Li5 Yuan Wu1* Yi Chang1,2,3* 1School of Artificial Intelligence, Jilin University 2Engineering Research Center of Knowledge-Driven Human-Machine Intelligence, MOE, China 3International Center of Future Science, Jilin University 4Bilibili Inc. 5Xingchen AGI Lab, China Telecom Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd {linshuo26,jinzhe25}@mails.jlu.edu.cn guochenlu01@bilibili.com, liyh181@chinatelecom.cn {yuanwu,yichang}@jlu.edu.cn
title: PremiseSQL: Evaluating Premise Critique and Abstention in Text-to-SQL

text: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have substantially improved Text-to- SQL performance, yet existing NL2SQL sys- tems largely assume that user queries are valid and answerable. As a result, models often gen- erate executable SQL even for queries with flawed premises. We introduce premise critique ability in NL2SQL, namely the ability to recog- nize flawed queries and abstain from generating misleading SQL. To evaluate this capability, we propose PremiseSQL, a benchmark con- taining 1,800 flawed NL2SQL queries across four categories of premise failures, along with their 1,800 original queries. We further design an evaluation framework to measure intrinsic and prompt-induced premise-aware behavior across three prompting settings. Experiments on frontier LLMs show that current models are strongly premise-trusting by default and rarely critique flawed premises. Stronger critique- oriented prompting improves detection and ab- stention on flawed queries, but also increases false invalid judgments and suppresses SQL generation on originals. The code is available at https://github.com/vegeet/PremiseSQL. 1

text: Text-to-SQL (or NL2SQL) translates natural lan- guage (NL) questions into executable SQL given a database schema (Popescu et al., 2003). Recent ad- vances in large language models (LLMs) have sub- stantially improved schema understanding, compo- sitional reasoning, and cross-domain generalization in modern NL2SQL systems (OpenAI et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025; DeepSeek *Corresponding authors. Despite this progress, existing Text-to-SQL re- search largely assumes that user questions are valid, well-formed, and answerable under the given schema (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023). Conse- quently, most prior work focuses on improving 1 arXiv:2610.22158v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

text: SQL generation accuracy, schema linking, and complex reasoning capabilities (Wang et al., 2020; Scholak et al., 2021; Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023). However, this assumption is frequently violated in realistic scenarios. User questions may contain logically inconsistent conditions, false schema as- sumptions, missing premises, or requests beyond the capability of SQL and the underlying database. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art NL2SQL models often generate executable SQL even for flawed queries, producing SQL that is syntactically valid but semantically invalid (Ji et al., 2023; Whitehead et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). In many cases, models implicitly repair problematic questions by injecting unsupported assumptions (Lin et al., 2022). Figure 1 illustrates this failure: although "person with id 5" is underdetermined by the schema, a model may silently map person to actor and emit executable SQL. The resulting SQL is syntactically valid but rests on an unsupported entity choice. We introduce premise critique ability in NL2SQL, namely the ability to recognize flawed queries and abstain from generating misleading SQL. Premise critique ability is orthogonal to con- ventional SQL generation accuracy: a model may produce executable SQL, or even generate SQL that coincidentally matches the user’s intent, while still failing to recognize that the provided question itself is ill-posed. Concretely, it consists of two components: (1) premise validation, namely assess- ing query validity

text: may produce executable SQL, or even generate SQL that coincidentally matches the user’s intent, while still failing to recognize that the provided question itself is ill-posed. Concretely, it consists of two components: (1) premise validation, namely assess- ing query validity in the corresponding database context and identifying actual flaws; and (2) absten- tion, namely refraining from generating misleading SQL for flawed queries while maintaining SQL generation for valid queries. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce PremiseSQL, to our knowledge the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate premise critique ability in NL2SQL systems. Built upon two widely used Text-to-SQL datasets, Spider 1.0 (Yu et al., 2018) and BIRD / BIRD-filtered (Li et al., 2023), PremiseSQL pairs 1,800 constructed flawed queries with their 1,800 unmodified source queries. It evaluates whether models can recognize flawed premises and abstain from generating mis- leading SQL, while maintaining SQL generation for original queries. We further evaluate frontier LLMs under three prompting settings, including Base, Implicit, and Explicit, to measure both intrin- sic and prompt-induced premise-aware behavior. text: 2.1 Unanswerable and Ambiguous Queries in NL2SQL Prior work has explored unanswerable and ambigu- ous queries in NL2SQL. TriageSQL (Zhang et al., 2020) formulates the problem as question intention classification, while Know What I Don’t Know (Wang et al., 2023) further categorizes ambiguity and unanswerability cases. More recent work ex- tends beyond classification-oriented formulations. TrustSQL (Lee et al., 2024) introduces infeasible queries and proposes a reliability-oriented evalua- tion metric for trustworthy NL2SQL systems. Com- plementarily, NL2SQL-BUGs (Liu et al., 2025) focuses on errors in NL2SQL translation and cat- egorizes semantic errors into fine-grained types. However, NL2SQL still lacks a fine-grained and comprehensive examination of diverse premise er- rors and the varying challenges they pose to models. PremiseSQL addresses this gap through a unified premise-error taxonomy. 2.2 Robustness and False Premise Handling in LLMs Beyond NL2SQL, prior work studies LLM robust- ness under adversarial, noisy, or logically flawed inputs. For example, SQuADRUN (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) introduces unanswerable questions, high- lighting models’ tendency to produce confident but incorrect responses when no valid answer exists. AbstentionBench (Kirichenko et al., 2025) provides a large-scale benchmark across 20 diverse datasets to assess abstention behavior. Building on these, we cover more types of flawed queries in NL2SQL and examine premise critique under different lev- els of premise-aware prompting, revealing both the 2

(1) Expression Error refers to errors caused by ambiguous or unclear natural language expressions that prevent the query intent from being uniquely mapped to SQL; (2) Premise Contradic- tion captures queries whose assumptions are logi- cally inconsistent or incompatible with the database schema; (3) Missing Premise refers to queries that omit essential assumptions, constraints, or schema information required

Detailed statistics are provided in Appendix A.2. 3.4 Prompting Protocol To analyze how prompting affects premise critique behavior, we evaluate models under three prompt- ing settings: Base, Implicit, and Explicit. Base Setting The Base setting follows the stan- dard Text-to-SQL generation setup. Models are simply instructed to generate SQL for the given 4

text: question and return a structured JSON output con- taining sql and reason, where sql denotes the gen- erated SQL (or null when abstaining) and reason records the model’s explanation for its generation behavior. No additional warning is provided re- garding potential flaws in the query. Implicit Setting The Implicit setting introduces implicit premise-awareness guidance. Models are informed that the input question may contain errors and are asked to assess its validity before answer- ing. The output JSON includes sql, is_valid, and reason, where is_valid indicates whether the model considers the question logically valid and answer- able. This setting measures whether soft prompting can improve premise validation and abstention be- havior. Explicit Setting The Explicit setting provides direct critique-oriented instructions. Models are explicitly told that the question contains logically flawed or incorrect premises, and are required to critically examine its assumptions before respond- ing. The output format remains sql, is_valid, and reason. This setting examines premise critique be- havior under an explicit assertion of a query flaw, which is supported for positive samples but false for negative samples. 3.5 Evaluation Framework For positive samples, three metrics are considered: SQL Behavior (SQL), Detection (DET), and Type Identification (TYPE). text: For positive samples, three metrics are considered: SQL Behavior (SQL), Detection (DET), and Type Identification (TYPE). SQL Behavior measures the degree of abstention from generating mislead- ing SQL for a flawed query, using a three-level ordinal score from 0 to 2. Detection evaluates whether the model recognizes that the query con- tains a premise flaw, and Type Identification mea- sures whether it correctly identifies the correspond- ing failure type. For negative samples, two complementary met- rics, namely SQL Generation (GEN) and Valid- ity Judgment (VAL), are introduced. SQL Gen- eration measures the proportion of negative sam- ples for which the model generates SQL, reflecting whether it maintains generation for valid queries. GEN measures generation coverage; Appendix B.7 provides an execution-based validation showing that GEN closely tracks end-to-end execution suc- cess. Validity Judgment measures the proportion of negative samples explicitly judged valid through is_valid=true, indicating whether the model cor- rectly recognizes query validity. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup We evaluate premise critique ability on a diverse set of state-of-the-art LLMs. The evaluated mod- els include ChatGLM-5.1 (GLM-5 Team, 2026), Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026b), Claude Son- net 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a), Claude Opus 5.5 (An- thropic, 2026c), DeepSeek V3.2 (DeepSeek AI, 2025), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), Doubao Seed 2.0 Pro (ByteDance, 2026), Gem- ini 3.1 Pro Preview (Google, 2026), LLaMA 4

The originals show why such consistency does not imply correctness. Of the 24,568 original- query outputs with is_valid=false, 16,502 (67.17%) contain no SQL. By contrast, SQL is generated in 33,010 of the 33,032 original-query outputs (99.93%) with is_valid=true. Models therefore tend to act on their own validity judgment: when the judgment is wrong, the generation decision of- ten follows the same error. Explicit prompting amplifies this problem. Among outputs declaring the query invalid, the pro- portion corresponding to flawed queries falls from 20,100 of 25,119 (80.02%) under Implicit prompt- ing to 27,701 of 47,250 (58.63%) under Explicit prompting. Equivalently, original-query outputs account for 41.37% of all invalid judgments under Explicit prompting. The resulting increase in false invalid judgments suggests that models rely too heavily on the prompt’s premise that the query is flawed, even when their judgments and generation behavior are internally consistent. 4.2.3 Automatic Evaluation and Reliability All model outputs are independently scored by GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 under identical in- structions and scoring definitions. Missing-premise cases fall between these extremes; models also per- form relatively well on queries that exceed SQL expressibility or require external knowledge. We therefore move from an input-level taxonomy to a response-level account. Whereas an error category characterizes a query flaw in its database context, a failure mechanism identifies the observable operation through which the model makes the query appear answerable. text: In this work, we introduce PremiseSQL, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluat- ing premise critique ability in NL2SQL systems. PremiseSQL contains 1,800 flawed queries cover- ing 9 fine-grained error types and their 1,800 origi- nals as positive and negative samples, respectively. Experiments under Base, Implicit, and Explicit prompting settings reveal a clear reliability gap in current NL2SQL systems. Models often trust user assumptions and generate misleading SQL under standard settings. Even when explicitly prompted to scrutinize premises, they struggle to assess them reliably. Models further struggle with subtle and implicit premise flaws, showing that strong SQL generation does not necessarily imply trustworthy premise-aware reasoning. We hope PremiseSQL can facilitate future research on more reliable and premise-aware NL2SQL systems. 8
title: how premise flaws are expressed. Contradictions

text: Limitations Our work has several limitations. First, Premis- eSQL focuses on English NL2SQL benchmarks and may not generalize to multilingual settings or real-world interactive database systems. Second, although the benchmark covers multiple premise failure categories, the constructed errors are still taxonomy-driven and may not fully capture nat- urally occurring user mistakes. Finally, our eval- uation relies partially on LLM-based automatic judges, which may introduce evaluation bias de- spite strong agreement with human annotations.

text: B.4 Human Verification We conduct human verification on 2,160 outputs from one open-weight model (DeepSeek V3.2) and one proprietary model (GPT-5.4). The sample is evenly stratified: each model and each source benchmark contributes 1,080 outputs, each prompt- ing setting contributes 720, and each of the nine fine-grained error types contributes 240, yielding 80 outputs per prompting-setting–error-type com- bination. Human annotators follow the same eval- uation protocol as the automatic evaluators. Two graduate-level annotators familiar with SQL and database systems independently evaluate the same 2,160 sampled outputs using the rubrics applied by the automatic evaluators. Agreement between the two human annotators is high, with Cohen’s κ of 0.9912, 0.9632, and 0.8759 for SQL Behavior, Detection, and Type Identification, respectively. B.5 Robustness to Judge–Target Overlap GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 serve as both eval- uated models and automatic evaluators, creating potential judge–target overlap. Although averag- ing their judgments reduces the influence of either evaluator, it does not by itself eliminate possible self-evaluation or model-family bias. We there- fore conduct a leave-self-out robustness check. For GPT-5.4 outputs, we retain only the judgments of Claude Opus 4.6; for Claude Opus 4.6 outputs, we retain only those of GPT-5.4. B.6 Paired Evaluation Design The paired inputs expose a progression from under- critique to instruction-driven rejection. Each pair contrasts an original query–context combination with its perturbed counterpart. Reliable critique should change the response to the perturbation while maintaining correct validity judgments and SQL generation for originals. Base prompting usu- ally answers both; stronger prompts increase ab- stention, but Explicit prompting often suppresses originals as well. The separation among DET, TYPE, and SQL on flawed queries and VAL and GEN on originals therefore distinguishes evidence- based critique from broad rejection. The five measures provide complementary ev- idence about premise critique behavior. DET records whether any flaw is noticed, TYPE whether the intended defect is explained, and SQL whether that assessment changes generation. On originals, VAL records the explicit judgment and GEN the action. Their divergence is informative: under Ex- plicit prompting, LLaMA 4 Maverick retains 0.974 GEN but only 0.363 VAL, so it often generates despite incorrectly judging an original query as flawed; Qwen3.5-397B is low on both and instead follows a broad rejection policy. Evaluation on originals prevents either pattern from being mis- taken for robust critique. B.7 Execution-Based Validation of SQL Generation GEN is designed to measure generation coverage, namely whether a model preserves SQL genera- tion on valid original queries. GEN and VAL are evaluated on all 1,800 original queries. Your goal is: Given a CORRECT original Text-to-SQL question, rewrite it to deliberately introduce a specific type of error while keeping the question otherwise natural and realistic. Background knowledge: A necessary premise in Text-to-SQL refers to a query condition that MUST be specified in order to uniquely determine the intended SQL query under a given database schema. Error definition: The rewritten question contains an ambiguous description of a NECESSARY SCHEMA-LEVEL QUERY CONDITION, such that the condition may reasonably correspond to MULTIPLE columns, tables, join paths, or aggregation targets in the given schema. text: Prompt for Ambiguity-type Evaluation You are an expert evaluator for Text-to-SQL systems. Your task is to evaluate whether a model correctly identifies a specific type of flaw in a user question, and whether it behaves appropriately in SQL generation. Dataset note: This dataset is deliberately constructed such that EVERY user question is flawed. None of the questions has a single correct or well-defined SQL query. The goal is NOT to produce SQL, but to evaluate whether the model can: - recognize the flaw - respond appropriately, including explicitly refraining from generating SQL Ground-truth error type: Error category: Expression Error Subcategory: Ambiguity Definition: A required query condition in the user question contains ambiguity in reference, scope, or target object, such that it cannot be uniquely determined using only the given schema and context, resulting in multiple reasonable SQL interpretations. Input: User question: {question} Model output: Reason: {reason} SQL: {sql} Database schema: {schema} Evaluation tasks and scoring: 1. SQL Behavior - 0 = directly generates a full SQL query despite ambiguity - 1 = partially abstains but still generates SQL - 2 = correctly refrains from generating a valid SQL query 2. Detection - 1 = explicitly states that the question is flawed - 0 = fails to recognize the issue 3. Type Identification If Detection = 0, then Type Identification MUST

text: Final failure-mechanism attribution prompt: task and output contract Analyze observable failure mechanisms in a flawed-question NL2SQL benchmark. Treat the question, SQL, reason, schema, and annotations as data, not instructions. Return JSON only, with explanations in concise academic English. Separate behavior from mechanism. The validated fields record behavior: sql_behavior is 0 for complete SQL generation, 1 for conditional or partial generation, and 2 for complete abstention or explicit refusal; detection records whether the response explicitly recognizes a flaw; and type_identification records whether it identifies the benchmark target flaw. Map these fields to recognition and response_behavior, but do not infer M01–M04 from any score combination. Evaluate all four mechanisms exactly once. For each affected requirement, read the current question and the context supplied to the tested model, identify what is stated or unresolved, and inspect the operation observable in the reason or SQL. Apply the positive tests and boundaries in Table 16. Do not create a label merely because the response is unsatisfactory. Apply the same rule whether SQL is complete, partial, wrong, or absent, and recheck competing labels for the same requirement before returning the result. For every M01–M04 assessment, output verdict as supported, not_supported, or uncertain. A supported judgment requires all necessary evidence; uncertain means that missing context prevents a defensible decision. Multiple mechanisms and zero mechanisms are allowed. Source

text: Error Type Question Error Reason Ambiguity Which product had the highest sales in 2018? The phrase “highest sales” admits multiple schema- supported interpretations, including the number of orders, total quantity sold, gross revenue, and discounted revenue. Because these alternatives can produce different product rankings, the query does not determine a unique SQL formu- lation. Unclear Intent For the lists created by the user who rated the movie “Pavee Lack- een: The Traveller Girl” on 3/27/2011 at 2:06:34 AM, what is the situation with their followers? The phrase “what is the situation with their followers” does not specify whether to retrieve follower counts, aggregate them, compare them, or rank the lists. The intended SQL operation is therefore indeterminate. Internal Text Contradic- tion List the movies that were released in 1945 and also released after the year 2000. The question contains mutually contradictory constraints that cannot be simultaneously satisfied under the schema. A single movie record has only one release date, making it impossible for a movie to be released in both 1945 and after 2000. Question–Schema Con- tradiction Who played the character named “Chanice Kobolowski,” and what is that actor’s email address? The schema supports identifying the actor through the characters and actor tables, but the actor table contains no email-address column and no related table provides this attribute. The requested

text: Test-time context optimization adapts frozen language models through textual feedback, but ordinary conditional generation provides no separate control over how strongly to reinforce the distributional changes induced by a context update. We introduce EMO, a training-free framework inspired by expectation–maximization that alternates question-specific context esti- mation (E-step) and distribution refinement (M-step). The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step contrasts next-token distributions un- der the revised and preceding contexts at a shared prefix to construct a confidence-constrained logit correction. Feedback on the steered response drives the next context update, coupling adaptation across rounds with intervention within each generation. Theoretically, we connect parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, and derive the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements. Under context-improvement and faithful-steering as- sumptions, we prove a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. Under greedy decoding across eight models and six benchmarks, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging +9.10 percentage points. With the same judge, it adds +1.53 points on average over context-only optimization (TextGrad), with consistent MMLU-Pro gains across models. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-N are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons

text: Parameter updates and context refinement provide complementary routes to adapting a large language model (LLM). Parameter optimization, including fine-tuning, reinforce- ment learning, and preference alignment, incorporates task data or feedback into model weights (Hu et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2024; Rafailov et al., 2023). For an individual test question, context optimization adapts a frozen model by using feedback to revise its textual instructions before generating a new response (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026; Madaan et al., 2023). We study how to translate such question-specific feedback into explicit control of the decoding process. A revised context already changes the next-token distribution at every prefix. Ordinary conditional generation, however, provides no separate control over the strength or token support of those changes. Comparing the distributions before and after a context update 1 arXiv:2610.22160v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

text: AI Model TF September, 2026 reveals how the revision changes token preferences at the current prefix. This motivates our central question: how can feedback-driven context updates supply a controllable intervention on the generation they guide? We propose EMO, which alternates context optimization and distribution refinement for each question. The E-step revises a system context using textual gradients (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024) from an external judge without access to gold answers. The M-step compares the revised and preceding contexts at a shared generated prefix, constructs a steering vector from their distribution contrast, and applies a confidence-constrained correction to the revised context’s logits. The resulting response is evaluated to provide feedback for the next E-step. Each context update thus determines a decoding intervention whose output informs the next update, closing the loop while model weights remain fixed. A logit-space view explains the relationship between the two steps. Parameter and context updates both admit additive logit representations, while EMO uses the context-induced displacement to construct its additional steering correction. Context edits induce finite logit changes through a frozen model, whereas parameter updates also alter the model’s response to subsequent contexts and prefixes. This representation links adaptation to decoding, while our one-round analysis identifies sufficient conditions for improvement toward a target distribution. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • EMO: coupled context optimization and steering. A training-free framework that turns successive context updates into prefix-dependent decoding interventions and uses the steered responses to drive further context adaptation. • Logit-space interpretation and conditional analysis. We relate the context-induced logit displacement to the implemented steering vector (Eq. 5) and establish one-round target-KL improvement under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions (Theorem 1). • Empirical evidence across four model axes. Parameter adaptation includes supervised fine-tuning and its parameter-efficient variants (Hu et al., 2021), reinforcement learning (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023), and distillation (Snell et al., 2022; Agarwal et al., 2024). A third family controls generation at inference time by modi- fying internal activations (Turner et al., 2023) or contrasting next-token distributions during decoding (Li et al., 2023). Closely related task-aware approaches include CoS (He et al., 2025), SDA (Xia & Deng, 2026), SVDecode (Hu et al., 2026), and JitRL (Li et al., 2026). EMO connects decoding-time intervention to per-question context optimization: each response informs the next context update, whose distribution contrast supplies the steering signal at every subsequent prefix. Test-time compute can also be spent on parallel sampling, including self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) and best-of-N with a verifier or judge (Cobbe et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2024), or sequential refinement (Snell et al., 2024). text: EMO couples question-specific context optimization with logits steering, using each re- sponse to refine the context that guides the next generation. Its logit-space analysis clarifies this connection and identifies conditions for one-round target-KL improvement. Across eight models and six benchmarks, the results show that model scaling and reasoning distil- lation leave scope for adaptation, with steering benefits that depend on the model and task. The broader implication is to treat generation and verification as coupled uses of test-time computation. Feedback can make further attempts more productive, while reliable selection determines how much of their expanded coverage reaches the final answer. This perspective motivates inference systems that adjust context revision, decoding strength, and verification effort jointly to the bottleneck encountered during reasoning. Limitations and future work. External judging can introduce misleading feedback or miss correct candidates. Calibrated ranking and independent checks of reasoning steps or tool outputs could improve verification; retrieval and multiple optimization trajectories could address low candidate coverage. Distribution access and two model streams limit deployment, and generation-equivalent budgets omit judge/rewrite costs. Smaller judges, selective M-step activation, and adaptive stopping could reduce overhead; evaluations should measure total tokens, FLOPs, and latency. Text-only interfaces could use response- level refinement and reranking, subject to separate evaluation. The one-round guarantee assumes successful context updates and faithful steering over full softmax distributions; it

text: AI Model TF September, 2026 A Proofs and Method Supplementary Details A.1 Proof of the Unified Objective For each question with reference response y⋆, define Q(y | q) = 1{y = y⋆}. Then KL(Q∥Pξ) = ∑ y:Q(y|q)>0 Q(y | q) log Q(y | q) Pξ(y | q) = −log Pξ(y⋆| q). (11) Averaging over the empirical question distribution proves Lemma 1. The equality holds independently of which component of ξ = (θ, C) is varied. For a general fixed target, cross-entropy equals KL(Q∥Pξ) + H(Q), and the entropy term is independent of either optimization variable. Thus the minimizers of the two losses agree within each chosen feasible set; the parameter and context feasible sets need not have the same minimizer. In the test-time setting, take the question distribution to be concentrated on the current question. The target objective remains a theoretical reference: the gold response is supplied to neither the judge nor the textual optimizer. The ideal context optimizer is defined operationally as producing a context with smaller target loss whenever an improving update is assumed to exist. No differentiable structure on the space of strings is needed for that condition, and the objective identity does not assert that arbitrary textual feedback exactly differentiates NLL. A.2 Proof of the Unified Steering Form Exact realization of either optimization update. At a fixed history, let z = zξ(h) and z+ = zξ+(h) be the before/after logits. Defining ∆z = z+ −z immediately gives Softmax(z + ∆z) = Pξ+(· | h). Equivalently, the log-ratio log(Pξ+/Pξ) differs from ∆z only by the scalar difference of log-normalizers. text: AI Model TF September, 2026 A.6 Implementation Conventions The steering strength defaults to µ = 2.4 and the threshold to α = 0.1; the finite penalty is fixed at λ = −100. An excluded token therefore receives an additive logit change µλ; this is distinct from overwriting its final logit with −100. The same prefix is appended to separate KV caches for Ck and Ck+1. Contrast and masking are computed before any sampling temperature or top-p truncation. No context is carried from one test question to the next. In the stated update, rejecting a rewrite sets Ck+1 = Ck and makes the raw contrast zero. The confidence penalty in Eq. 7 can still affect decoding when µ > 0; zero contrast alone does not remove this constraint. In contrast, setting µ = 0 removes both the contrast correction and the penalty and recovers context-only decoding. This distinguishes a rejected rewrite from explicitly disabling the M-step. With K = 4 refinement rounds, the initial response and four steered responses form five candidates. Each M-step uses two target-model context streams, giving nine generation equivalents including initialization. This counts streams rather than exact FLOPs or latency and excludes external judge, backward, and rewrite cost as well as differences in context and response lengths. BoN@N selects, among the first N samples, the one with the highest judge score (the same scoring engine and prompt as EMO’s judge-select, ties broken toward the earlier sample) and reports its rule-based correctness. How coverage translates into selected accuracy. Because a correct selected response must belong to a pool containing a correct response, selected accuracy divided by oracle coverage measures the fraction of covered questions on which selection succeeds. We compute this descriptive ratio from the reported three-seed means; with equal evaluation- set sizes, it corresponds to pooling question–seed outcomes, rather than averaging per-seed ratios. At N = 9 on Llama-3.1-8B/GPQA-D, the ratio is 37.4/73.7 ≈50.7% for EMO and 32.2/60.3 ≈53.4% for BoN. EMO’s accuracy advantage therefore coexists with a lower fraction of available successes realized by selection: its greater coverage is essential to the observed advantage. On Llama-3.1-8B/MATH-500, both coverage (73.4 vs. 71.9) and this fraction (89.4% vs. 84.6%) favor EMO. The same pattern appears on Llama-3.2-3B/MATH- 500 (Figure 2b): EMO’s coverage is 70.6 versus BoN’s 66.5, and its selected-to-covered fraction is 60.3/70.6 ≈85.4% versus 52.7/66.5 ≈79.2%. The confidence constraint is what matters. The picture changes qualitatively for α. At α=0.05 the gain collapses to +1.0: with too permissive a mask, the steering vector acts on tokens where the optimized context expresses almost no preference, injecting noise rather than signal. At α=0.1–0.4 the gain is stable (+7.6 to +9.6, with the best value at α=0.2), i.e., the constraint only needs to separate confident tokens from noise, not to be tuned precisely. A good system prompt establishes the model as a domain expert relevant to the task (e.g. ‘You are an expert chemist . . . ’), states the key reasoning approach and pitfalls to avoid, and specifies the required output format. Avoid generic phrases; be specific to the question’s domain. Do NOT reveal or hint at the actual answer.” This steers the E-step away from generic encouragements (“think carefully”) toward sub- stantive, domain-specific guidance, which is what the M-step steering vector can then convert into a decoding-time correction. Optional momentum (past iterations), constraints, and in-context-example sections exist in the template but are disabled in all experiments reported in this paper. B.6.4 Answer-Leakage Filter Two complementary guards keep the optimization signal free of the answer. First, the judge never receives the gold answer, and its prompt explicitly forbids the feedback from revealing 31

Second, every context produced by the optimizer is passed through a regex filter ( ANSWER LEAK PATTERNS in optimizer.py) that rejects rewrites containing concrete answers—e.g. “the answer is X” patterns, contrastive “the answer is X, not Y” constructions, or specific numbers/letters—in which case the previous context is retained. The v2 filter no longer false-positives on the output-format directive Answer: $LETTER$: a literal $ is only treated as numeric leakage when followed by a digit. Together these guards ensure that neither the judge feedback nor the optimized context can smuggle the gold answer into the generation path, so any accuracy gain is attributable to the optimization itself rather than to answer leakage. 32

title: Multi-sourced AI Tutor for Non-Native English Speaker Students

text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted as teaching tools in computing education, particularly for developing AI tutors capable of answering student questions. With the rise in enrollment of international students in computing programs, researchers have begun to explore the difficulties that non-native English speaker (NNES) students face in computing courses due to language barriers. To aid such students, we developed a general- purpose AI tutor system that can process student questions in foreign languages (currently focused on Mandarin) and provide bilingual responses. Our system also incorporates the functionality of generating a glossary of technical terms and their explanations to enhance comprehension. Our approach utilizes a specialized Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline with a novel question extraction mechanism, enabling us to effectively utilize a diverse array of course materials for answering student queries. We evaluated our AI tutor using 91 Piazza posts, demonstrating that it could answer 83.52% of the posts correctly and in a helpful manner. The tutor also provided high-quality translations for 76.92% of the questions and generated technical term glossaries for 64.47% of them. Our findings underscore the potential of multi-source RAG pipeline in enhancing AI tutor systems, offering support for non-native speakers that are challenging to provide with traditional supporting staff of a computing course. Keywords: large language model, non-native English speaker students, computing education 1

text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have profoundly transformed com- puting education, showcasing remarkable capabilities in solving computing assignments [18, 20]. LLMs are also being used for facilitating instructional activities, such as generating assignment questions [19], providing automated grading [22], and notably, de- veloping AI tutor systems that address student queries. Furthermore, as classrooms become increasingly multicultural, the need for inclu- sivity in educational materials and technologies grows. Non-native English speaker (NNES) students, in particular, face language barri- ers and a lack of confidence, which often causes hesitation to seek help from instructors or TAs. Our AI tutor system seeks to assist NNES students’ learning by accepting questions in the students’ native language (specifically Mandarin), delivering responses bilin- gually, and generating a technical term glossary to ensure equitable access to educational materials. Most AI tutors [3, 10, 11] utilize Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [9], which enhances question-answering by dynamically re- trieving and synthesizing relevant information from a data repository, ensuring accuracy and contextual relevance. Our RAG-based GPT-4 tutor differs from systems that rely on a single source, such as lecture captions or textbooks. Instead, it integrates a comprehensive range of course materials, including lecture notes, project descriptions, quizzes, past exams, and the course website, enabling holistic data retrieval. Two specialized mechanisms have been developed to enhance our AI tutor. Firstly, our system incorporates a translation stage that converts Mandarin questions into English before applying RAG, enabling full leverage of RAG’s capabilities. Secondly, our system employs a question extraction mechanism that addresses instances where a student’s query references only the question number instead of providing the question details, by precisely identifying and retrieving details of the referred question. We evaluated our system using 91 Piazza posts, demonstrating that it can accurately and helpfully answer student questions and generate technical term glossary in Mandarin. Our work focuses on answering the following research questions: • RQ1. What is the quality of the translation stage and to what extent does it improve RAG’s performance in processing non- English questions? • RQ2. What is the accuracy of the question extraction stage and to what extent does it enhance the system’s ability to manage diverse course materials and student questions? • RQ3. What is the relevance and usefulness of RAG’s results concerning the questions? • RQ4. What is the quality of the AI tutor’s responses in terms of correctness, helpfulness, solution revelation, translation, and technical term glossary generation? 2

text: 2.1 AI Tutors Since the debut of Large Language Models (LLMs), researchers have consistently explored their potential applications in computing education. Beyond aiding student learning by providing thorough code explanations [12], step-wise worked examples [5], and prompt problems [1], as well as facilitating various instructional activities, LLMs have proven effective as the basis for educational question- answering (QA) systems, or in other words, AI tutors. Hicke et al. [3] investigated the effectiveness of various optimiza- tion techniques in LLMs for answering questions collected from a CS1 course Piazza. They enhanced Llama-2 using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) on textbooks and lab manuals, supervised finetun- ing with selected Piazza QA pairs, and reinforcement learning with human feedback; and applied RAG to GPT-4. They show that these techniques resulted in substantial improvements: Llama-2’s answer accuracy (factual correctness & groundedness) increased from 0.30 to 0.58, and GPT-4’s from 0.40 to 0.73, while usefulness (practical values to human instructors) increased from 0.18 to 0.50 for Llama-2 and from 0.28 to 0.65 for GPT-4. Liu and M’hiri [10] developed a virtual teaching assistant (TA) using GPT-3.5 and RAG on assignment documents. The virtual TA arXiv:2610.22163v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026

[11] and Kazemitabaar et al. [6] developed their own QA chatbots and deployed them in real course settings. The two chatbots have distinct features: the prior utilized GPT-4 with RAG on lecture captioning and structured prompts to generate responses, while the latter used the few-shot learning framework to prevent code revelation. Both chatbots maintained a high correctness rate in resolving student inquires throughout the semester. Moreover, students expressed satisfaction with these tools in the feedback survey, stating they appreciated having such a "24/7 personal tutor" and the opportunity to "work alongside AI." Most of the AI tutor systems above use RAG based on a single source format, such as textbooks, assignment documents, or lecture captions. Our AI tutor aims to incorporate all documents in a course, including lecture materials and readings, lab and project description documents, quizzes and past exams, as well as the course website, by developing appropriate data pipelines and prompt techniques for each type of course material. 2.2 Non-Native English Speakers in Computing Educa-
