Notably, 23% of them pursued mathematics and computer science, and 19% studied engineering [4]. These students often face language barriers and confidence issues, which negatively impact their learning experience in computing courses. Polishchuk recommended enhancing collaborative work and com- munication practice outside the classroom. Guo [2] noted how confidence issues affect NNES’s communica- tion with instructors and TAs. Since our authors are mainly native Mandarin speakers, we implemented our prototypical system for Mandarin. 3 Method 3.1 Students’ Questions We collected 620 questions from a semester’s Piazza posts for an intermediate-level Data Science (DS) programming course of 400 students1. We excluded 238 posts that included images for two reasons: (1) they are difficult to transcribe, either because they are entire desktop screenshots with only a small portion containing relevant information or they involve complex plots and graphs; (2) the GPT-4 API vision service was prohibitively expensive prior to the release of GPT-4o. The analysis focused on the remaining 382 text- based posts, which we cleaned by removing duplicates, identifiable information, unnecessary HTML formatting, and enclosing code snippets and error messages in backticks. For Piazza posts, students must tag their posts with instructor- defined folders: exams (exam 1, exam 2, final), quizzes, programming projects (P1, P2, ..., P7), labs, logistics, and others. One author used these student-tagged folders and the post content to sort the posts into four categories: 90 logistics, 54 conceptual, 41 environment setup, and 197 programming posts. Unlike typical computer science projects that require students to implement well- known data structures or algorithms, DS projects involve sequential (numbered) analysis tasks on given datasets, making it important for the model to receive the original question’s details. Furthermore, this step is irreplaceable by RAG as both embedding-based and keyword- based retrieval methods face challenges in extracting the exact question from the course materials only using the question number. text: In this work, we developed an AI tutor system that processes student questions in Mandarin and delivers bilingual responses that are correct, helpful, and well-translated, and complete with a technical terms glossary, without directly revealing the answers. Our system utilizes Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a special question extraction mechanism to answer queries from a diverse array of course materials, including Jupyter Notebooks, Python scripts, PowerPoint slides, and PDFs. Another main contribution of our AI tutor system is the design of the prompts that instruct the GPT-4 model to apporpriately use resources from question extraction and RAG to provide the appropriate level of guidance in responses. Our evaluation results for our AI tutor on data science questions underscore the potential of AI tutors to enhance educational accessibility for non-native English speaking students in computing courses. Future efforts will focus on refining the system through deployment in real classroom settings and expanding language support to further improve student learning experiences.

text: CLUE: Uncovering Social Context for Pragmatic Understanding Chengfei Wu and Zhaoqing Wu and Dan Goldwasser Purdue University {wu1491, wu1828, dgoldwas}@purdue.edu
title: CLUE: Uncovering Social Context for Pragmatic Understanding

text: Understanding a conversation requires con- necting what is said to the speakers’ rela- tionships, expectations, and earlier exchanges. Prior work shows that supplying relevant con- text can improve models’ social judgments, but much of this information may already be present in the conversation. This motivates training models to discover the cues that matter and use them to support an interpretation. We propose CLUE, a two-stage training pipeline that combines supervised evidence reasoning with GRPO guided by Grounded Information Utilization (IUG). This reward credits new, evidence-supported social inferences while ac- counting for reasoning effort. We train on a small set of conversational examples to assess effectiveness and generalization across tasks, languages, and genres. At inference time, the trained model reasons over the supplied inter- action in a self-contained manner. Compared with base Qwen, CLUE achieves relative gains of 17.3% in-domain and 9.3% out-of-domain in average weighted F1, with higher F1 on four of five out-of-domain evaluations. These gains are accompanied by over 80% fewer reasoning tokens on average in both domains. Human evaluation further finds that CLUE more often grounds its explanations in specific conversa- tional content, with closer alignment between its quoted evidence and human-selected con- text. 1

Thus, when it reappears in response to news of an extravagant gift, the context points to surprise rather than anger. In long interactions, the relevant evidence may be spread across many turns, so a model can pro- duce a plausible explanation while overlooking an earlier exchange that changes the interpreta- tion. Wu et al. (2026) find that stronger ground- ing in relevant visual evidence is linked to better performance, and Zhang et al. (2026) show that citation-aware rewards can improve evidence use in question answering. We ask whether learning to connect conversational cues to judgments can similarly improve generalization across tasks, lan- 1 arXiv:2610.22167v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026
title: CLUE: Uncovering Social Context for Pragmatic Understanding

text: guages, and genres. We propose CLUE, a two-stage training pipeline for learning to discover and use social context. We first train the model on reasoning traces that connect conversational evidence to task predictions, using two added special tokens to mark quoted source spans. We then use GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to optimize the initialized model with task correctness and our proposed reward, Grounded Information Utilization (IUG). This reward credits new, task-relevant social inferences supported by quoted evidence while accounting for reasoning effort. These inferences must add information that the preceding reasoning has not already established. At inference time, the trained model reasons over the supplied interaction in a self-contained manner. To assess the effectiveness of CLUE, we train Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) on a small set of conversational examples from the Computational Cultural Understanding (CCU) program (Corvey, 2021). We evaluate in-domain performance and also test generalization to new languages and conversational settings, covering emotion detec- tion, dialog act recognition, norm violation detec- tion, and power relation prediction. Compared with base Qwen, CLUE achieves relative gains of 17.3% in-domain and 9.3% out-of-domain in av- erage weighted F1, with higher F1 on four of five out-of-domain evaluations. We also find that these gains are accompanied by over 80% fewer reason- ing tokens on average in both groups, as detailed in Figure

We also find that these gains are accompanied by over 80% fewer reason- ing tokens on average in both groups, as detailed in Figure 4. Analysis of Wang et al. (2024a)’s emotion-cause dataset further shows that the model trained with CLUE identifies causes more often in its reasoning, which may help explain the improvement in emo- tion recognition. Human evaluation of a sample spanning all eight tasks also finds that CLUE more often explains how specific conversational content supports its predictions, while its quoted evidence aligns more closely with the lines selected by hu- man readers. To summarize our main contributions: • CLUE, a two-stage training pipeline com- bining supervised evidence reasoning with GRPO guided by IUG, which rewards new, evidence-supported social inferences while accounting for effort. • Trained on limited conversational data from one language, CLUE improves average weighted F1 over base Qwen both in and out-of-domain while using over 80% fewer reasoning tokens on average. • Cause analysis and human evaluation show that, compared with base Qwen, CLUE’s rea- soning more often identifies relevant earlier exchanges and explains how conversational evidence supports its judgments. 2

text: Grounded understanding NormAd (Rao et al., 2025) evaluates reasoning with explicit norms, while NormSage (Fung et al., 2023) and cultural context schemas (Pujari and Goldwasser, 2025) ex- tract or organize conversational social knowledge. Ziems et al. (2024) report limited zero-shot perfor- mance on conversational power prediction. Social context also disambiguates political discourse (Pu- jari et al., 2024), while MagiC (Wu et al., 2026) evaluates reasoning against visual evidence. Social norm datasets Social Chemistry 101, Moral Stories, and NormBank represent norma- tive knowledge through rules, narratives, and sit- uational constraints (Forbes et al., 2020; Emelin et al., 2021; Ziems et al., 2023). SocialDial and NormDial extend the study of norm observance to dialogue (Zhan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023). We use CCU conversations for their human annota- tions across emotion, dialog act, and norm viola- tion, supporting context discovery with verifiable feedback. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards Verifiable rewards support mathematical reason- ing, coding, and instruction following (Trung et al., 2024; Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Search-R1 learns retrieval during reasoning (Jin et al., 2025), while Math-Shepherd supplies feed- back on intermediate reasoning steps (Wang et al., 2024b). CARE combines answer and format re- wards with a retrieval reward checking that repro- duced spans occur in the supplied context (Wang et al., 2025). CaRR rewards facts

text: Math-Shepherd supplies feed- back on intermediate reasoning steps (Wang et al., 2024b). CARE combines answer and format re- wards with a retrieval reward checking that repro- duced spans occur in the supplied context (Wang et al., 2025). CaRR rewards facts that satisfy question-derived rubrics, are supported by cited webpages, and connect to the final answer (Zhang et al., 2026). Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) op- timize accuracy and adherence to constraints on reasoning length. CLUE’s IUG rewards evidence- supported social inferences that the preceding rea- soning has not established, while accounting for reasoning effort. 2

Grounded Information Utilization (IUG) IUG combines the assessment of new, evidence- supported inferences with their reasoning cost. During training, Qwen3.6-27B serves as the IUG judge. Relevant con- tributions include interpreting a relationship, iden- tifying an active expectation, resolving a plausi- ble alternative, or correcting an earlier inference. text: We presented CLUE, a two-stage training pipeline for learning to discover and use social con- text. It combines supervised evidence reason- ing with GRPO guided by IUG, which rewards new, evidence-supported social inferences while accounting for reasoning effort. Training on lim- ited conversational data improves average F1 in- domain and out-of-domain while reducing reason- ing token use. Our qualitative analysis further shows that the model more often identifies earlier conversational causes of emotion. These findings support context discovery as a learning objective for social and pragmatic understanding. Limitations Our evaluation of CLUE covers Chinese, Japanese, and English in selected conversational settings, leaving broader cultural coverage to be explored. Computational constraints limit training to a 9B model, with a 27B model included as a reference. Extending the study to additional communities, languages, and model scales would help establish how broadly the observed gains generalize.

text: Lexical Reference Frames: Interpreting LM Residual Streams in Native Semantics Jian Gu Monash University jian.gu@monash.edu Hongyu Zhang Chongqing University hyzhang@cqu.edu.cn Chunyang Chen Technical University of Munich chun-yang.chen@tum.de Aldeida Aleti Monash University aldeida.aleti@monash.edu
title: Lexical Reference Frames:

text: The vocabulary of a language model is its na- tive semantics: the embedding and the unem- bedding fix the meaning of a state at the two ends of the residual stream. Between them, ex- isting methods either reuse a fixed lens or treat the states as a point cloud, and neither reads a state the way the model does. We argue that every hidden state has a native reference frame, induced by the layers that read it next and adap- tive to the context. Lexical reference frames approximate it by reading a state through the model’s own remaining layers with a stated number of rounds of attention between posi- tions and a typical attention output for the rest, without fitting to the model’s output. No lens, with fixed directions per layer, can exceed the square root of the native frame’s coherence, 0.30 and 0.35 at mid-depth of SmolLM3-3B and OLMo3-7B, whereas the first-order frame, LEXFRAME[1], reaches 0.97 and 0.97 and reads a state within 0.16 nats of the model’s output. Its coefficients attribute predictions more faith- fully than attribution patching, its lexical basis steers a prediction while sparing other tokens, and its confident readings would let an early exit skip 0.45 and 0.42 of the layers, where lenses skip almost none. In this way, lexical reference frames make every hidden

text: Between its input and output tokens, a language model computes nothing but states of its residual stream, which every layer reads and writes (Elhage et al., 2021). Its vocabulary is in this sense the na- tive semantics of the model, the only units of mean- ing that it is designed to receive and to express. The model defines the lexical meaning of a state at the two ends of the stream: the embedding assigns each token a state, and the unembedding maps a final state to logits over tokens. Intermediate states lack 1https://github.com/jianguda/lexframe such a definition, although interpretability research and its applications read them constantly: early exit and self-speculative decoding stop the computation at a layer whose reading already names the output (Schuster et al., 2022; Elhoushi et al., 2024), hal- lucination detectors judge an answer by its hidden states (Orgad et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), and knowledge editors locate and rewrite facts at in- termediate layers (Meng et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2025). Each depends on how faithfully a tool such as a lens reads these states, and model compression, which distils a smaller or pruned student by match- ing the intermediate states of its teacher, relies on what these states mean (Romero et al., 2015; Das- gupta and Cohn, 2025; Muralidharan et al., 2024). This

text: states, and model compression, which distils a smaller or pruned student by match- ing the intermediate states of its teacher, relies on what these states mean (Romero et al., 2015; Das- gupta and Cohn, 2025; Muralidharan et al., 2024). This meaning is set by the remaining layers, which read each state in the context of its prefix. Two families of methods address these states and fail in opposite ways. The first reads a state with a lens: the logit lens applies the output frame to every layer unchanged (nostalgebraist, 2020), the tuned lens learns one affine map per layer fitted to the model’s output (Belrose et al., 2023), and the Jacobian lens averages the Jacobian of the re- maining layers over positions and prompts (Gurnee et al., 2026). Each fixes one linear map per layer, so every state of a layer is read identically, regardless of its prefix. The second family keeps every state and does without a reading. It treats the states of a layer as a point cloud and reports its rank, intrinsic dimension, anisotropy or similarity to other layers (Kornblith et al., 2019; Ansuini et al., 2019; Gar- rido et al., 2022; Skean et al., 2025). Such statistics describe how the states are distributed rather than how the model uses them: two states close in the cloud

text: and the frame that the complete model induces its native frame. The native frame returns the model’s output at every layer, so a useful frame withholds a stated part of this computation: the frame of order n, written LEXFRAME[n], transports a state through the model’s own layers with n rounds of attention between positions and replaces the remaining atten- tion by a typical attention output, estimated once per layer from unlabelled text. LEXFRAME[0] reads what a state holds by itself, LEXFRAME[1] what it draws from its prefix, and LEXFRAME[∞] is the na- tive frame. The idea is simple: read a state the way the model reads it, through the layers that remain and with the context it sees. A lens ignores the context and is therefore bounded; a frame uses it, as far as its order allows. As nothing is fitted to the model’s output, lexical reference frames are comparable across layers, checkpoints and models. We evaluate lexical reference frames at every layer of SmolLM3-3B (Hugging Face, 2025) and OLMo3-7B (Team OLMo, 2025) and at 16 of their training checkpoints, against the logit lens, the Jacobian lens, a supervised probe and dis- tances on the point cloud. From the middle layers on, LEXFRAME[1] recovers the native frame’s lexi- cal readouts beyond the bound of every lens and matches the model’s

text: against the logit lens, the Jacobian lens, a supervised probe and dis- tances on the point cloud. From the middle layers on, LEXFRAME[1] recovers the native frame’s lexi- cal readouts beyond the bound of every lens and matches the model’s output in content and confi- dence, which lenses do only near the output; one round of attention to the prefix closes most of the gap that LEXFRAME[0] leaves. Its readings settle on the model’s prediction early enough for an early exit to skip more than two fifths of the layers, and they stay faithful along training while the logit lens degrades. Distances on the point cloud barely pre- dict the effect of replacing a state, as lexical read- outs lie almost entirely outside the directions in which the states vary. In the coordinates of the frame, the lexical basis writes a prediction into the stream more selectively than the readout, and dif- ferences of coefficients attribute it to layers and sublayers more faithfully than attribution patching. We therefore expect lexical reference frames to be a strong alternative to lenses in these applications. In summary, this paper makes three contributions. • We show that the layers that remain give every hidden state its own frame in the vocabulary, and we prove that no lens with one map per layer can follow this frame across the different contexts in which a state occurs. • We define frames that read a hidden state in the model’s native semantics through its own layers with a chosen amount of context, and we compute them in closed form from unla- belled text, without any training. • We show on two model families and their train- ing checkpoints that these frames follow the model from the middle layers on, where lenses fail, and support early exit, steering and attri- bution at every layer of the model. 2

text: Prior work on the intermediate layers of language models asks which tokens a state stands for, how the states of a layer are distributed, and which di- rections or components drive a prediction, and a reference frame bears on all three questions. Language model lenses. The logit lens reads an intermediate state with the model’s own out- put frame (nostalgebraist, 2020), and it underlies studies of how predictions are refined across depth (Jastrz˛ebski et al., 2017; Geva et al., 2020, 2022; Dar et al., 2022; Halawi et al., 2023; Katz et al., 2024; Wendler et al., 2024; Lad et al., 2024). Later lenses use a map per layer, trained to match the out- put (Belrose et al., 2023; Din et al., 2023) or given by a Jacobian of the remaining layers (Hernandez et al., 2023; Gurnee et al., 2026), or patch the state into another forward pass (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Pal et al., 2023). Gu et al. (2026c) fix a set of anchors and measure the states of all layers against them, and Gu et al. (2026b) tie the input and output frames to each other through the pseudo-inverse of one shared token memory. Lenses are thus frames that ignore the context, and we bound how closely any can approximate the native frame. Point clouds and manifolds. A large

Lenses are thus frames that ignore the context, and we bound how closely any can approximate the native frame. Point clouds and manifolds. A large body of work summarises the states of a layer by statistics of the cloud they form, such as similarity between layers (Raghu et al., 2017; Kornblith et al., 2019), intrinsic dimension (Facco et al., 2018; Ansuini et al., 2019; Valeriani et al., 2023), effective rank (Garrido et al., 2022) and anisotropy (Ethayarajh, 2019; Gao et al., 2019; Razzhigaev et al., 2023; Bernas et al., 2026). Recent studies follow these statistics across layers (Cheng et al., 2024; Skean et al., 2025) and across training (Saphra and Lopez, 2018; Tigges et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024). We quantify how much these statistics reveal about the way the model uses the states of a layer. Directions and components. Linear probes learn a direction from labelled states (Alain and Ben- gio, 2016; Tenney et al., 2019; Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Belinkov, 2021), and steering methods add a direction to the states to change the output (Sub- ramani et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2023; Arditi et al., 2024). Both rest on the hypothesis that concepts are represented as directions (Park et al., 2023), which Park et al. (2026) derive from the information geometry of the softmax for the output layer only. The contribution of a component to a prediction is likewise computed along a direction, by projecting what the component writes onto the output frame (Wang et al., 2022), or measured by patching (Meng et al., 2022; Conmy et al., 2023; Syed et al., 2023). In general LEXFRAME[n] attends to a prefix of states of order n −1; each order thus computes one more round of attention between positions, and reading at order n runs n + 1 streams through the remaining layers. Higher orders add exchanges within the prefix and converge to the model. Order ∞. In the limit of the order nothing is withheld, and LEXFRAME[∞] recovers the model as the native frame: every position attends to the true states of its prefix, which are the states that the model itself computes. Two identities follow: the reading of every layer in LEXFRAME[∞] equals the model’s output, and LEXFRAME[n] is exact wherever at most n layers remain. Near the output all orders therefore agree with the model; they differ where much of the computation lies ahead. The reading of LEXFRAME[∞] adds nothing to the model’s predic- tion; its value lies in its lexical readouts and basis, which every frame of finite order approximates. 4 Experiments We compare frames with lenses and point clouds, then test their coordinates and their use in steer- ing and attribution. In steering, the task is to make the runner-up token u, the tar- get that needs the smallest move, overtake the top token v by moving a single state. text: Every hidden state of a language model has a na- tive reference frame, fixed at the two ends of the residual stream and adaptive in between, and lex- ical reference frames approximate it to a stated order without fitting to the model’s output. In two model families LEXFRAME[1] recovers the model’s lexical readouts and output from mid-depth on, be- yond the reach of any method with one map per layer, and it attributes and steers predictions. The frame explains why a fixed lens fails at mid-depth, increasingly so along training, and why the point cloud reveals little about how the model uses a state. To interpret a state, read it as the model does: through the layers that remain, with the context it sees, and in its own native semantics, a reading that can stand in for lenses. 9

A.2 Artifacts and Computations We use SmolLM3-3B (Hugging Face, 2025) and OLMo3-7B (Team OLMo, 2025) with their pub- lished intermediate checkpoints, both released un- der the Apache 2.0 licence. The text is the En- glish WikiText-103 corpus (Merity et al., 2016), released under the Creative Commons Attribution- ShareAlike licence, with about 103 million tokens in its training split and 0.25 million in its test split. Our use of these artifacts is consistent with their intended use, and the text contains no information that we collected or annotated. The experiments ran on NVIDIA RTX 4080 SUPER GPUs, and ev- ery run uses a single GPU. text: Worked example. Table 9 shows a position where OLMo3 continues “A review of Boulter ’s performance in The” with “Guardian” at probabil- ity 0.29 rather than “Times” at 0.22. LEXFRAME[1] names this token from layer 16 on, the Jacobian lens from layer 20 on and the logit lens from layer 24 on, so the frame reads the prediction well be- fore either lens. Below that layer LEXFRAME[1] al- ready reads whole words that can follow “The” here, and at layer 12 the runner-up “Times”: the state hence holds the two newspaper titles that the model weighs at the output, and the next layers settle between them. The logit lens returns mostly word fragments until layer 24, because it reads every state along the output directions, which in- termediate states do not yet use. The Jacobian lens returns unrelated tokens until layer 20, since its map averages over contexts and cannot follow this one, although it is fitted to the model’s own Jaco- bian. The position thus shows in a single case what the statistics over all positions report in aggregate: the frame follows the model’s own choice, includ- ing the alternative it weighs, several layers before either of the two lenses does. C Properties of Reference Frames This appendix states in full the properties of refer- ence frames, which express a hidden state in the native semantics of the model: the two sides of a frame, how close a lens and an order can come to the model, and the complexity of the orders. Throughout, a state xℓ(t) is read with the states xℓ(s), s < t, of its prefix given, and T (n) ℓ denotes the transport of order n. C.3 Complexity Analysis We count costs in forward passes, a measure inde- pendent of the hardware. Calibration is one forward pass over the calibration text and one ridge regres- sion per layer. Reading the states of layer ℓat order n runs n + 1 streams through the L −ℓremaining layers, so reading every layer of a sequence, at all positions at once, costs about (n+1)(L+1)/2 for- ward passes. A fitted lens reads a state with one ma- trix product, which is cheaper per state, but the fit is not: the Jacobian lens needs the Jacobian of the last state with respect to the states of every layer, one backward pass per dimension of the state, for each of its P prompts, about Pd backward passes in total. D Discussion The framework rests on one idea: read a hidden state as the model reads it, through the layers that remain and with the context it sees. Lenses read each layer with one fixed map, and point clouds read no state at all; a frame lets the remaining lay- ers, which decide what a state means, do the read- ing in the model’s native semantics, its vocabulary. A reference frame separates two questions that a lens answers at once: along which directions the model measures a label at a state, and how much of the label the state holds. Existing methods ap- pear as special cases: a lens is a frame that does not adapt to the context and is therefore bounded by the coherence of the native frame, a probe is a fixed lexical readout learned under supervision, and a point cloud is a set of states without a frame. Both parts of the model’s reading are necessary: transport alone, in LEXFRAME[0], already brings a reading far closer to the model than any fitted map, whereas attention to the prefix without transport, in a layer skip, does not, and no fitting lifts a method that ignores the context above the co- herence bound. The order thus makes the use of the context a controlled variable, so that what each hop between positions contributes can be measured. The value of this view lies in what it makes com- parable. The vocabulary is shared by every layer, checkpoint and model of a family, and a frame expresses all of their states in it without a trained component whose faithfulness would need a sepa- rate argument. title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement

text: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where inter- action proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session’s advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

text: Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL; Gao et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) trains Large Language Model (LLM) agents (Shinn et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2022) for multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments via online rollouts and reward feedback, yielding broad performance gains. More recently, LLM agents have incorporated advanced inference techniques, such as context management (Mei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a) and harness engineering (Lin et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), enabling agentic workflows to tackle increasingly complex and long-horizon tasks. However, most agentic RL methods assume a single-session setting, where each rollout unfolds as a coherent multi-turn trajectory within a continuously accumulated context and yields a single training segment (Wang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b). We argue that the single-session setting is not sufficiently general for optimizing LLM agents. For example, context compaction compresses the execution history to free up context space while rewriting the prefix that conditions subsequent actions (Lu et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), thereby initiating a new session. Similarly, subagent forking delegates global goal to subagents which creates branch sessions (Song et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026d). Those resulting trajectories no longer satisfy the single-session assumption, creating a mismatch between training

To address this gap, we introduce a new setting termed Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, which supports an arbitrary count of sessions and enables agents with diverse inference mechanisms to be optimized within a unified algorithm. A straightforward way to handle multi-session rollouts is through broadcasting, whereby a trajectory-level outcome reward or advantage is replicated to every token across all sessions (Accio-Lab, 2026; Xu et al., 2026a). However, we argue that this method provides only coarse supervision and offers no explicit control over optimization across sessions, resulting in poorly targeted learning signals as trajectories span more sessions. In this work, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. First, session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation calibrates outcome-based advantages using within-group rankings of session counts conditioned on task outcomes, encouraging successful trajectories to solve tasks efficiently while allowing unsuccessful trajectories sufficient exploration. Its bounded modulation preserves outcome-induced ordering while incorporating session- usage guidance, thereby widening relative advantage margins for homogeneous-reward groups. Second, session-level

text: session counts conditioned on task outcomes, encouraging successful trajectories to solve tasks efficiently while allowing unsuccessful trajectories sufficient exploration. Its bounded modulation preserves outcome-induced ordering while incorporating session- usage guidance, thereby widening relative advantage margins for homogeneous-reward groups. Second, session-level advantage shaping calculates each session’s marginal outcome gain as an immediate reward, applies group-relative normalization separately by session type, and combines the resulting shaping signal with the trajectory-level advantage. Overall, the former provides a long-term, outcome-oriented global signal, while the latter captures short-term local marginal effects. They together form a hierarchical optimization target for multi-session agentic RL. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments on BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) and select Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the base model. Our Mosaic outperforms multiple single-session and multi-session agentic RL baselines under both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios. Moreover, Mosaic achieves up to a 10.1% relative improvement in accuracy over the broadcasting baseline while using fewer sessions per trajectory on average (3.17 →2.35). Ablation studies further demonstrate that session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation and session-level advantage shaping each contribute to the final performance gains. Our analyses also reveal several key insights: (1) shaping trajectory-level advantages with session counts increases within-group advantage variance and improves sample efficiency; (2) different session types exhibit distinct distributions of session-level marginal gains, which our type-conditioned normalization

text: In Mosaic, we optimize the performance of multi-session agentic RL through a hierarchical perspective, incorporating trajectory-level advantage estimation calibrated with session signals (§3.1), as well as advantage shaping at the finer-grained session level. (§3.2). 3.1. Session-Aware Advantage Estimation In vanilla GRPO, the advantage is determined solely by the relative outcome rewards within a prompt group. Under the multi-session setting, however, session-related metrics may provide additional relative signals for policy optimization. One metric is the number of sessions 𝑁𝑖in a trajectory 𝜏𝑖, which serves as a proxy for the extent of exploration and structural complexity of 𝜏𝑖. Nonetheless, 𝑁𝑖 should not be directly treated as a reward. First, its raw scale may not faithfully quantify meaningful differences in session utilization. Second, the preferred direction of optimization should depend on task results, avoiding the policy from exploiting session count without improving performance. Accordingly, from a group-relative perspective, the session-aware trajectory-level advantages of multi-session rollouts within a prompt group should satisfy the following ordering constraints: 4

text: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning • C1: For successful trajectories, using more sessions incurs a higher execution cost and hence results in a lower advantage, whereas using fewer sessions should result in a higher advantage. • C2: For unsuccessful trajectories, using fewer sessions may suggest insufficient exploration or execution, especially on challenging tasks, and should thus result in a lower advantage. Conversely, unsuccessful trajectories that conduct more sessions should receive a higher advantage. • C3: Task outcome reward must remain the dominant signal. When two trajectories have the same session counts, the trajectory with lower reward should receive a lower advantage. Using more sessions alone should not allow an unsuccessful trajectory to outrank a successful one. Together, these constraints encourage the policy to use enough sessions to complete the task, but no more than necessary, which represents a desirable objective for multi-session agentic RL. Session-Level Advantage Shaping The session-aware trajectory-level advantage developed in §3.1 provides an outcome-oriented global optimization signal for the entire multi-session trajectory. At the session level, however, this signal remains sparse since all sessions on the same trajectory share a single scalar advantage. To this end, we introduce session-level advantage shaping. Specifically, we view each session as a state transition as 𝑠𝑖,𝑗= �𝑣𝑖,𝑗−1 →𝑣𝑖,𝑗 , where session 𝑠𝑖,𝑗transitions the agent from state 𝑣𝑖,𝑗−1 to state 𝑣𝑖,𝑗. Here, 𝑣𝑖,𝑗−1 and 𝑣𝑖,𝑗denote the agent states at the start and end of the 𝑗-th session, respectively, with particular emphasis on the prefix context visible to the rollout policy. Based on session transition functions, we introduce three representative session types: • Normal session. The agent performs regular reasoning, tool use, and environment interaction within the current context. The input state is the context available at the start of the session, and its output state is the resulting context after the session is completed. • Compaction session. When the accumulated context approaches the model’s limit, the agent starts a compaction session to compress

When the accumulated context approaches the model’s limit, the agent starts a compaction session to compress the context into a shorter prefix. Its input state is the full context before compaction, and its output state is the compressed prefix passed to the next session. • Subagent session. The main agent delegates subtasks to subagents which start new subagent sessions. Its input state is the main-agent context at delegation, and its output state is the updated main-agent context after the returned result has been incorporated. Experimental Setup Benchmark. We evaluate our method on BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025), a challenging benchmark consisting of 1,266 questions that require agents to persistently navigate the web and identify hard- to-find, entangled information. We select BrowseComp since its high difficulty demands long-horizon interactions, making it suitable for assessing agents that produce multi-session trajectories. Baselines. We use Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the initial model and adopt a ReAct-style agent loop. We organize the baselines by inference configuration. Under single-session inference, we evaluate (1) the initial model without RL training and (2) a model trained with GRPO in the single-session setting, representing conventional Agentic RL. Under multi-session inference, we evaluate (3) the single-session GRPO trained model, representing test-time scaling; (4) a model trained with Broadcasting in the multi-session setting; and (5) a model trained with Mosaic in the multi-session setting. We evaluate all multi-session configurations under both context compaction and subagent forking using their respective agent loops; for multi-session training, the same

RQ1: Overall Effectiveness of Mosaic RQ1 asks whether training in the multi-session setting improves agent performance and whether Mosaic contributes beyond broadcasting. RQ3: Mechanistic Analysis of Mosaic RQ3 asks how the design of Mosaic contributes to the training process. First, we examine whether session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation produces the intended ordering. As shown in Figure 5, within mixed-outcome groups, advantages approximately decrease with session count for successful trajectories and increase for unsuccessful ones, while successful trajectories retain higher advantages. In homogeneous-outcome groups, the fallback mechanism introduces session-dependent variation, providing differentiated learning signals despite identical outcome rewards. These patterns illustrate how Mosaic leverages session signals to increase the within-group variance of relative advantages, thus improving sample efficiency during training. Second, we examine the effect of reward normalization on session-level shaping signals. As shown in Figure 5, the distributions of raw marginal information gain differ across session types, primarily because heterogeneous sessions serve distinct functions. Under global normalization, compaction sessions, whose raw marginal gains have a lower mean, are further downweighted, introducing a systematic bias against them. In Mosaic, type-conditioned normalization instead centers and rescales each

Accordingly, we examine session-level behavior along three dimensions: quantity, or whether the count of sessions increases or decreases; quality, or whether performance improvement is accompanied by more useful sessions; and allocation, or whether a limited session budget becomes increasingly concentrated on execution stages with high marginal utility. As shown in Table 2, for Broadcasting, which does not directly optimize any specific session-aware pattern, all three metrics increase. Under Mosaic, the number of sessions does not increase further, while both session quality and allocation improve. These findings indicate that performance gains via multi-session optimization are associated with improved session utility rather than a monotonic rise in session count. Moreover, despite using explicit session-aware optimization, Mosaic does not induce a fundamentally altered behavioral mechanism. Instead, it strengthens the session-allocation patterns that already emerge from naïve multi-session optimization. We argue that effective multi-session optimization is accompanied by improvements in session utility and allocation. It distributes computation more effectively across sessions, encouraging continued execution when it yields meaningful progress while suppressing low-utility computation. From this perspective, the central challenge is not how many sessions an agent should use, but how much useful progress it can derive from the sessions it executes. 5. Discussion: Future Directions for Multi-Session Agentic RL Infrastructure for reproducible research. Multi-session trajectories tend to arise naturally when agents tackle complex, long-horizon tasks. Although some existing benchmarks can elicit these trajectories with reasonable frequency, suitable public training data remain scarce. This gap limits the scale, sufficiency, and reproducibility of experiments in multi-session agentic RL. Developing open training datasets and corresponding agentic execution environments is therefore essential to building a sustainable research ecosystem for this topic. 10

text: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Cross-session state transfer as a central learning objective. Context compaction and subagent forking both involve information transfer, but serve different purposes: compaction must preserve sufficient working state for continued execution; forking must provide the information needed to complete a subtask; merging must integrate subtask results into a state usable by the main agent. These operations motivate a shared research question: under a limited context budget, what information should be carried forward to support subsequent decisions? CompactionRL already jointly optimizes task execution and context summarization (Li et al., 2026). A unified approach to learning state transfer across compaction, forking, and merging remains an important direction, alongside systematic investigation of information loss and error accumulation over repeated transfers. Asynchronous training for multi-session rollouts. For partial rollout or asynchronous training settings, multi-session execution can amplify variation in trajectory lengths and completion times, increase policy staleness and complicate within-group comparisons and sample reuse. For instance, prioritizing completed rollouts may favor trajectories with less sessions over longer ones associated with harder tasks, introducing selection bias and shaping learned execution strategies. Our experiments use a colocated setup with alternating rollout and training phases to minimize interference from asynchrony and isolate the effects of the optimization signals. text: Our experiments use a colocated setup with alternating rollout and training phases to minimize interference from asynchrony and isolate the effects of the optimization signals. Scaling toward actual production raises a further question: how can multi-session optimization remain reliable under asynchronous sampling and policy staleness? SAO explores asynchronous optimization with one rollout per prompt, using a learned value model (Hou et al., 2026). However, critic-free, group-relative optimization requires further investigation into when and how rollout groups are formed, how stale samples are handled, and how collected trajectories can be reused. Toward RL within (black-boxed) agent harnesses. General multi-session agentic RL can accom- modate workflows in which execution no longer follows a single, continuously accumulated context prefix. Context compaction and subagent forking, the two scenarios studied in this work, are represen- tative examples of such workflows in modern agent harnesses. Progress in multi-session optimization could thus provide an important foundation for training agents within harnesses whose orchestration is partially opaque (Xu et al., 2026a), such as Claude Code. Therefore, a critical next step is to systematically examine mechanisms across agent harnesses that disrupt context continuity, such as dropping reasoning tokens or tool responses, and improve general multi-session agentic RL under these conditions. text: LLM Agents. LLM agents extend LLMs with tool use and environment interaction to work au- tonomously (Feng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026). ReAct constructs a general agent loop of reasoning, acting, observing environment feedback, and continuing until task completion (Yao et al., 2022). To handle complex and long-horizon tasks, recent systems develop agent harnesses that manage execution beyond the basic ReAct loop (OpenClaw, 2026; Works, 2026), incorporating context compaction (Nguyen et al., 2025), multi-agent system (Chen et al., 2026a), subagent forking (Team et al., 2026), and other forms of context and workflow management (Chen et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). 11

text: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Agentic RL. Reinforcement learning techniques such as RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026b) and RLVR (Chen et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026) are used to improve LLMs’ alignment, reasoning, and downstream task-solving capabilities (Tan et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). Agentic RL extends this paradigm to LLM agents, aiming to enhance capabilities of multi-turn interaction through enhanced rollout sampling (Dong et al., 2026; Hou et al., 2025), process-level reward design (Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c), and other optimization strategies (Deng et al., 2026). However, most existing agentic RL methods still assume that each trajectory is contained within a single session.
title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning

text: In this paper, we first identify a mismatch between the single-session assumption underlying most ex- isting agentic RL methods and advanced agentic inference techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking. This motivates our formulation of Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, which supports an arbitrary count of sessions within a trajectory. To address the coarse supervision issue existed in the currently widely used broadcasting approach, we further propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. By combining session- aware trajectory-level advantage estimation with session-level advantage shaping, Mosaic trains a Qwen3.5-4B agent that outperforms both single-session and multi-session baselines on BrowseComp. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component, while further analyses suggest that effective multi-session optimization might depend on improving session utility and allocation, a pattern observed in both broadcasting baseline and our Mosaic. We hope these findings will inform future research on multi-session agentic RL. 12

Details of Marginal Information Gain Calculation We compute marginal information gain for each non-terminal training session from the change in the actor’s likelihood of the ground-truth answer across that session. For a session 𝑠, the rollout records two boundary token streams, ℎ− 𝑠and ℎ+ 𝑠. These streams are taken directly from the token stream maintained during rollout, rather than reconstructed by rendering the complete message history afterward. Their meanings depend on the session type: • Normal session. ℎ− 𝑠is the chat-template prompt at the start of the session, and ℎ+ 𝑠is that prompt followed by the complete session response. • Compaction session. ℎ− 𝑠contains the full available history immediately before compaction session. After the generated summary is injected into the new prefix in the next session, the resulting session prompt forms ℎ+ 𝑠. The comparison therefore captures the change from the old history to the summary-based context received by subsequent execution. • Subagent session. ℎ− 𝑠is the main agent’s context before the forking turn. text: Motion- and Gravity-Aware Feedforward 3D Reconstruction Shiyao Qian∗†, Yuan Ren∗, Dongfeng Bai∗
title: Motion- and Gravity-Aware Feedforward 3D

text: Feed-forward transformer models have recently achieved strong per- formance in multi-view 3D reconstruction, but they still rely primarily on appearance-based attention and often struggle in dynamic scenes with weak geometric cues. In this work, we introduce a motion- and gravity-aware framework under the Learning Using Privileged Infor- mation (LUPI) paradigm. During training, residual optical flow and gravity direction are provided as privileged signals to guide geomet- ric representation learning; during inference, the model uses standard visual inputs only. We add these priors to the transformer backbones with few architec- tural changes while preserving feed-forward efficiency. Experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent gains in reconstruction accuracy and robustness, especially in scenes with dynamic objects, ambiguous structure, and challenging camera motion. Our analysis further shows that the optimal injection stage is backbone-dependent: middle-layer integration is generally preferable for VGGT, while late-stage integra- tion is more effective for π3. These results suggest that LUPI offers a practical way to inject motion and physical priors into feed-forward 3D reconstruction without increasing test-time complexity. Keywords: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction; learning using privileged in- formation 1

Methods such as VGGT[1] demonstrate that strong geometric priors can emerge from large-scale train- ing, enabling accurate reconstruction without computationally expensive Bundle Adjustment [2] involved in Structure-from-Motion [3] and dense matching with cost volumes in the Multi-view stereo methods [4]. This paradigm has significantly improved efficiency and scalability, making feed- forward reconstruction an increasingly attractive solution for real-world per- ception tasks. Despite these advances, most existing feedforward models rely primarily on appearance-driven attention mechanisms and treat each input view as a collection of static visual tokens. In practice, however, real-world scenes are rarely static: independently moving objects, camera ego-motion, and temporal inconsistencies introduce challenges that cannot always be resolved from appearance alone. Without explicit motion reasoning, the model must implicitly infer whether observed changes arise from viewpoint variation or true scene dynamics, which can lead to unstable correspondences and degraded reconstruction quality in dynamic or ambiguous scenarios. In addition, feedforward reconstruction methods typically operate with- out global physical orientation cues. As a result, the predicted geometry may suffer from scale ambiguity, drifting orientation, or inconsistent spatial layouts across views, especially when visual evidence is weak or repetitive. Incorporating simple physical priors, such as gravity direction, offers a nat- ural way to stabilize spatial reasoning and enforce a consistent reference frame, complementing purely appearance-based token interactions.

Motivated by the importance of motion and orientation cues in robust visual understanding, we propose to augment 3D vision foundation mod- els with explicit motion- and gravity-aware signals. Specifically, we inject optical flow as an additional motion representation that highlights local pixel displacement patterns, enabling the model to better separate static background structure from dynamic foreground regions. Furthermore, we incorporate gravity direction as a lightweight global orientation prior, pro- viding a stable reference axis that improves spatial consistency across views. These cues introduce structured inductive biases that are absent in standard feedforward architectures, while preserving the simplicity and efficiency of transformer-based reconstruction. text: 2.1 Feed-forward 3D reconstruction Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruc- tion, where models directly infer geometry from one or multiple images with- out test-time optimization. Early learning-based MVS systems[5][6][7][8][9] typically relied on explicit cost-volume construction and geometric reason- ing, while more recent foundation-style approaches shift the emphasis toward correspondence learning with large-capacity backbones and transformers[10] [11][12][13][14]. In particular, transformer-based feed-forward methods such as VGGT[1] represent scenes as collections of image patch tokens and per- form cross-view reasoning through attention, achieving strong reconstruction quality and scalability. Along this line, π3[13] further explores efficient multi- view reasoning and generalization under diverse camera configurations, while mapping-oriented systems such as MapAnything[14] aim to produce geom- etry or map representations at scale from in-the-wild imagery, emphasizing robustness and transfer. In parallel, large-scale monocular depth pretraining (e.g., DepthAnything v3[15]) provides strong single-view geometric priors that can serve as initialization or auxiliary supervision for multi-view re- construction and downstream 3D perception tasks. Beyond these examples, related feed-forward reconstruction and correspondence-centric paradigms include DUSt3R/MASt3R-style models[11][16][17] that unify matching and 3

text: geometry prediction in a single forward pass, as well as other transformer- based MVS variants[10][18] that replace hand-crafted matching pipelines[4] with learned token interactions. Despite their success, existing feed-forward methods primarily rely on appearance-driven features and implicit geometric regularities learned from data. They generally lack explicit physical or motion priors—such as struc- tured optical-flow cues to disentangle dynamic foregrounds or gravity direc- tion (e.g., from IMU or geo-calibration) to serve as a global orientation ref- erence. Consequently, these models must infer correspondences and spatial consistency purely from visual tokens, which can be brittle in dynamic scenes or under ambiguous textures [19]. Our work complements this paradigm by injecting lightweight motion and gravity signals into feed-forward trans- formers, improving geometric robustness while preserving the efficiency of the inference process. 2.2 Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) Classical supervised learning minimizes a loss function L(h(xi, θ), yi) over training pairs (xi, yi), where the input space X remains identical during both training and inference. In contrast, Vapnik [20] introduced the LUPI paradigm to mimic human learning, where a ”teacher” provides supplemen- tal guidance—such as explanations or comparisons—available only during training. This transforms the training set into triplets (xi, x∗ i , yi), where x∗ i ∈X∗represents privileged information that is withheld during inference. text: 3.1 Data Preprocessing 3.1.1 Optical flow estimation and decomposition We perform a preprocessing step to selectively compute the residual optical flow for the training data. For datasets composed of continuous video se- quences, optical flow can generally be estimated between adjacent frames. However, when large temporal gaps or abrupt scene changes occur, flow esti- mation becomes unreliable. To address this issue, we first compute an image similarity score between neighboring frames and only estimate optical flow when the similarity exceeds a predefined threshold. Optical flow is computed using RAFT [27], which produces dense flow fields capturing the overall motion between frames. We assume that the rigid motion induced by camera movement can be approximated by a global affine transformation, which is denoted by fi = Api + t (1) where fi is the optical flow of a pixel i. pi is the [u, v] coordinate of the pixel. A is a 2×2 rotation matrix, and t is a 2×1 translation vector. A and t can be solved by minimizing Σi||fi−(Api+t)||2. Pixels consistent with the affine transformation are treated as static background, while deviations from this model indicate dynamic regions. The residual flow is defined as the difference between the original optical flow and the estimated affine transformation, thereby isolating motion components that cannot be explained by the global camera motion

text: background, while deviations from this model indicate dynamic regions. The residual flow is defined as the difference between the original optical flow and the estimated affine transformation, thereby isolating motion components that cannot be explained by the global camera motion model. Figure 1 shows two adjacent input frames together with the decomposed rigid flow and the resulting residual. Importantly, residual flow does not solely correspond to independently moving objects. The affine transformation provides only a global approx- imation of camera-induced motion and therefore cannot perfectly model perspective projection effects in scenes with significant depth variation. In regions with large depth gradients, structural discontinuities, or partial oc- clusions, the global motion model becomes insufficient even under predom- inantly static conditions. Consequently, these regions yield non-negligible residual flow. Such areas typically coincide with geometrically challenging regions for multi-view aggregation, as illustrated by the traffic light region in Fig. 1. Therefore, residual flow can also be interpreted as a signal high- lighting deviations from the global motion model, which often require more careful geometric reasoning during reconstruction. 5

text: Figure 1: Optical flow decomposition. 3.1.2 Gravity direction estimation We estimate 3D gravity vectors in the camera coordinate system for all training images using the pretrained GeoCalib model [28]. The model is applied offline to each image to extract its corresponding gravity direction. GeoCalib first predicts a dense perspective field from a single image, which encodes geometric cues such as vanishing directions and horizon struc- ture. Based on this representation, gravity direction is recovered through a Levenberg–Marquardt optimization procedure. To ensure reliability, we re- tain only those gravity estimates for which the optimization converges within a predefined number of iterations. In practice, non-convergence occurs only in a very small fraction of images. Samples for which the optimization fails to converge are excluded from gravity supervision. The resulting gravity vectors, expressed in the camera coordinate system, are used as orientation priors during training. 3.2 Privileged Information Injection To incorporate additional geometric cues during training, we introduce a privileged information injection mechanism that integrates residual optical flow and gravity direction into the transformer-based reconstruction back- bone. These signals are encoded into token-aligned representations and in- jected into the aggregation process with minimal modification to the original architecture. Residual Flow Encoding. Residual optical flow is first partitioned into patches using the same patchification scheme as the input images. For each patch, we compute a compact statistical representation consisting of five parameters: the mean flow components µx, µy, the log-variance terms log(σxx + ϵ), log(σyy + ϵ), and the normalized covariance σxy/√σxxσyy + ϵ. 6

The resulting 5-dimensional vector is passed through a three-layer MLP, referred to as the patch encoder, to produce a residual-flow embedding with the same dimensionality as the visual patch tokens extracted by the DINO backbone. The encoded residual-flow feature is then scaled by a learnable weight Wflow and added to the corresponding patch token: ˜tpatch = tpatch + Wflow · fflow. (2) This additive fusion allows motion information to be integrated with minimal perturbation to the existing embedding space while enabling the network to leverage dynamic cues during multi-view aggregation. Gravity Encoding. In addition to motion cues, we incorporate scene orientation information through gravity direction. The gravity vector is first normalized and then encoded using a two-layer MLP, referred to as the gravity encoder, producing a representation aligned with the dimensionality of camera tokens. The encoded gravity feature is scaled by a learnable parameter Wgrav and fused with the camera token: ˜tcam = tcam + Wgrav · fgrav. (3) The specific implementation of this fusion varies depending on the model architecture. For π3, since there are no specialized camera tokens, we define the camera tokens as the aggregator encoder’s output embeddings that feed into the camera head. The gravity feature corresponding to a specific image is fused with all constituent patch tokens for the image. For VGGT, we modify the gravity input to align with its reference- frame design. The first camera token in the sequence receives no gravity information, as it serves as a fixed reference for camera parameters. All subsequent tokens are fused with a concatenated gravity vector containing both their own view’s orientation and that of the first view. This ensures the gravity features remain aware of the reference frame with minimal learning overhead. The encoded privileged information can be injected at different stages of the transformer-based aggregation module, as illus- trated in Fig. 2. Specifically, residual flow features are fused with patch tokens, while gravity embeddings are combined with camera tokens when such tokens are present. For reconstruction architectures that do not explicitly maintain camera tokens (e.g., π3), gravity embeddings are instead injected before the camera decoder to influence the camera prediction stage. The framework supports multiple potential injection points throughout the aggregator layers, as shown in Fig. 2. Empirically, our experiments show that the optimal injection position depends on the backbone architecture, with different models favoring different stages of the aggregator. 3.3 Finetuning Our training objectives include local and global point maps, log-space depth maps, pixel ray directions, and pairwise camera translations and rotations. Additionally, for synthetic datasets, we incorporate surface normal and depth-gradient signals to provide finer geometric supervision. All loss terms are computed using the Generalized Robust Loss [29], with the final ob- jective being a weighted sum of these individual components. We provide detailed formulae and hyperparameter configurations in the supplementary materials. Following the principles of Learning Using Privileged Information 8
title: Figure 2: Architecture Overview.

text: (LUPI), we employ a two-stage finetuning strategy designed to extract reliable privileged features and subsequently train the model to interpret and hallucinate them during inference. Stage 1: Privileged Feature Alignment. The primary objective of the first stage is to develop a robust privileged information encoder and adapt the model’s decoders to utilize it. We freeze the model layers preceding the information injection point, focusing training exclusively on the privileged encoder (i.e. residual flow or gravity encoder) and the downstream decoder layers. This isolation ensures the new modality encoder receives sufficient gradient signal to provide meaningful features while the decoders learn to leverage this injected information. By freezing the early encoder layers, the privileged features are forced to align with the existing distribution of patch and camera tokens, facilitating better fusion. To minimize architec- tural disturbance, we also freeze unrelated decoders and heads; for instance, the VGGT camera decoder remains frozen in stage 1 when finetuning with residual flow as the privileged modality. Stage 2: Knowledge Distillation and Hallucination. As privileged modalities are unavailable at inference time under the LUPI paradigm, the second stage shifts toward guiding the primary model to converge faster and learn more robustly. With the privileged encoder and decoders now prepared, we unfreeze the entire model and introduce aggressive modality dropout. This mechanism creates a shortcut for

With the privileged encoder and decoders now prepared, we unfreeze the entire model and introduce aggressive modality dropout. This mechanism creates a shortcut for the finetuning process, forcing the unfrozen model encoder to ”hallucinate” the missing privileged features when they are dropped out. In this framework, the privileged infor- mation encoder acts as a teacher during standard iterations, while the model encoder serves as the student during dropout iterations. The student learns to extract high-level features related to motion or gravity cues directly from visual inputs, effectively filling the gap left by the privileged modality to maintain the performance gains established in stage 1. 4 Experiments 4.1 Datasets We apply dataset-level train-test split using 13 high-quality datsets. In each pair, the upper image shows reconstruction without gravity injection, and the lower image shows reconstruction with gravity injection. 4.4.3 Gravity Prior Analysis To evaluate the effect of gravity injection, we train two models under iden- tical settings: one with gravity prior and one without it. Figure 5 shows the reconstructed point maps predicted by the two models. The model trained with gravity prior produces more stable global structures, where ground sur- faces appear flatter and walls are more consistently aligned with the vertical direction. This observation suggests that gravity prior mainly improves reconstruc- tion by enforcing a global orientation reference rather than altering local ge- ometric predictions. By anchoring the reconstruction to a physically mean- ingful direction, gravity helps reduce structural drift and leads to more ge- ometrically coherent scene reconstruction. 4.5 Analysis We discuss the proposed priors from three perspectives: view-density behav- ior, architecture-dependent injection preference, and prior complementarity. First, the gain over the baseline increases with the number of input views. This trend indicates that the guidance of motion and gravity priors does not simply compensate for sparse observations; instead, they improve the consistency of cross-view geometric aggregation. As view density grows, 15

text: dynamic regions introduce stronger multi-view conflicts, and residual flow helps suppress these inconsistencies. Second, the optimal injection stage is backbone-dependent. For π3, late-stage injection performs best, suggesting that decoder-side integration better preserves modality isolation when no explicit camera token is avail- able. For VGGT, middle-layer injection is generally more effective, likely because privileged cues can be fused earlier with geometry-aware tokens and further refined by subsequent cross-view transformer blocks. In both backbones, early-stage injection is consistently weaker, implying that shal- low appearance-dominant features are less suitable for privileged geometric guidance. Third, residual flow and gravity priors contribute at complementary structural scales. Residual flow primarily improves local dynamic consis- tency by emphasizing non-rigid motion components, while gravity provides a global orientation anchor that stabilizes scene-level structure. Their com- bination improves geometric coherence without changing the feed-forward inference paradigm. 5 Limitations A limitation of our current formulation lies in the use of rigid optical flow components. In principle, rigid flow primarily reflects the apparent motion induced by camera ego-motion, implicitly encoding information about the underlying translational velocity and angular velocity of the camera. Such signals can be highly informative for stabilizing geometry and improving motion-aware reasoning. However, most existing feedforward multi-view reconstruction frame- works, including VGGT, are designed for static-scene reconstruction and operate on unordered sets of input images, without explicit temporal

However, most existing feedforward multi-view reconstruction frame- works, including VGGT, are designed for static-scene reconstruction and operate on unordered sets of input images, without explicit temporal order- ing or timestamp information. Under this setting, the rigid flow component does not provide a consistent notion of camera dynamics across views, and consequently offers limited benefit for reconstruction performance in our experiments. We believe that the velocity and angular motion cues embedded in rigid flow remain a valuable source of physical information. text: In this work, we presented a motion- and gravity-aware framework for feed- forward multi-view 3D reconstruction under the Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm. During training, residual flow and gravity cues are used as privileged supervision signals; during inference, the model operates with standard visual inputs only, while retaining the geometric benefits transferred from privileged modalities. Extensive experiments show consistent improvements in reconstruction accuracy and robustness, especially in dynamic scenes, under ambiguous ge- ometry, and across challenging camera motion. The results further indicate that the optimal injection stage is architecture-dependent, highlighting the importance of aligning privileged-feature integration with backbone design. Overall, this study demonstrates that LUPI is an effective and practical mechanism for introducing motion and physical priors into feed-forward 3D reconstruction without sacrificing inference efficiency. We hope this perspec- tive motivates future work on temporally coherent and physically grounded feed-forward reconstruction with richer privileged training signals. 17

text: A Finetuning Details We employ the WAI format [14] for dataset pre-processing and fine-tuning. Specifically, we determine the co-visibility between all image pairs within a scene by evaluating the re-projection error derived from ground-truth depth maps and camera poses. During fine-tuning, input sequences are curated by sampling images that maintain a co-visibility of at least 25% relative to at least one other view in the sequence; this ensures consistent spatial overlap across the chosen views. For each input sequence, we compute local and global point maps, ray directions and distances, camera translations, and rotations (represented as quaternions), alongside a per-view confidence map. All loss terms are calculated using the robust regression loss [29] with a shape parameter of 0.5 and a scaling parameter of 0.25 to mitigate the influence of outliers. We apply a logarithmic transformation to the ground truth and model outputs for point maps and z-depth values prior to com- puting the regression loss on their differences; notably, no loss terms are calculated for ray distances or confidence maps. When high-quality, smooth ground-truth point maps are available, we also integrate normal loss [43] and gradient matching loss [44] into our objective function. To account for noise and extreme values inherent in “in-the-wild” real-world datasets, we apply confidence weights to the global point map losses and exclude the top

text: also integrate normal loss [43] and gradient matching loss [44] into our objective function. To account for noise and extreme values inherent in “in-the-wild” real-world datasets, we apply confidence weights to the global point map losses and exclude the top 5% of errors as outliers for local point maps and VGGT depth losses. To align with the reference-view-free architecture of π3, we compute pair- wise relative pose losses rather than direct differences between predicted and ground-truth global poses. The same 5% outlier exclusion logic is applied to all three losses for π3. The loss terms for the different configurations and dataset types are expressed as follows: Lsyn VGGT = Lpt + Lz + Lray + Lpose + 3Lnorm + 3Lgrad (4) Lreal VGGT = Wconf · Lpt,glob + Mtop5% · (Lpt,loc + Lz) + Lray + Lpose (5) Lsyn π3 = Lpt + Lz + Lray + Lrel + 3Lnorm + 3Lgrad (6) Lreal π3 = Mtop5% · (Lpt,glob + Lpt,loc + Lz) + Lray + Lrel (7) where: • Lpt, Lz, and Lray represent the robust regression losses for point maps, z-depth values, and ray directions, respectively. 23
title: Finetuning Details

text: • Lpose denotes the global camera pose loss (translation and rotation) used for VGGT. • Lrel denotes the pairwise relative pose loss used for the reference-view- free π3 architecture. • Lnorm and Lgrad are the normal and gradient matching losses, applied only when smooth synthetic ground truth is available. • Wconf is the per-pixel confidence weight applied to global point map predictions. • Mtop5% is the binary outlier mask that excludes the highest 5% of errors to ensure robustness against noise in real-world data. Optimization is performed using the AdamW optimizer [45] with hyper- parameters set to β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, and a weight decay of 0.05. We employ a differentiated learning rate strategy: the peak learning rate is set to 5×10−6 for the DINOv2 image encoder, 5×10−5 for the gravity and flow encoders when present, and 1×10−5 for all other architectural components. The training follows a structured schedule throughout Stage 1, consisting of a 20% linear warmup to reach the peak learning rate, followed by a half-cycle cosine decay to a final value two orders of magnitude lower. text: Preprint REKI: REGISTERING KNOWLEDGE IN VLAS Juliette Marrie1, Paul Pacaud2, Adrien Ramanana Rahary3, Shizhe Chen2, and Moritz Böhle1 1Kyutai · 2Inria · 3École nationale des ponts et chaussées
title: Preprint

text: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained ex- clusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is out- performed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision–language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data. Addi- tionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert’s cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: github.com/kyutai-labs/reki. 1
title: Preprint

text: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have become an effective paradigm for language-conditioned robot control. A pretrained vision–language model (VLM) encodes camera views and instruction, based on which a smaller action expert predicts the next actions (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026). The strongest VLAs today are pretrained partly on proprietary data, and neither these data nor the pretraining pipelines are released (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026), making it hard to reproduce their results. Since each new model changes architecture, data and training recipe at once, gains cannot be traced back to a single choice. With REKI, we release the full pipeline, from data curation to deployment. REKI has a simple design, is pretrained on public data only and sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size. It pairs a VLM with a flow-matching action expert, and a memory mechanism gives the policy access to its recent past. Preserving past context can improve control (Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2025), yet most VLAs predict actions from the current observation alone (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al.,
title: Preprint

text: al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2025), yet most VLAs predict actions from the current observation alone (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). Existing ways of incorporating such context, however, often introduce substantial overhead (Fig. 2): feeding past frames to the VLM adds their image tokens to every VLM pass (Jang et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026), recurrent methods require sequential training (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026), and others introduce additional, dedicated memory modules to the policy (Shi et al., 2026; Koo et al., 2026). REKI summarises past context through a small set of registers (Darcet et al., 2024) in the action expert. The registers of each frame are cached across chunks (Fig. 3). Each frame is thus encoded only once and no separate module, sequential unroll during training or test-time update mechanisms are necessary. This yields clear gains at almost no overhead, and our 2.4B model REKI ranks first among VLAs pretrained on public data on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365 (Fig. 1), and generalises to real robots. Our ablations show that memory consistently improves performance, with the most pronounced gains for the first past
