text: Open pretraining. Many VLAs release their weights, and often their finetuning code, but not the code or the exact data mixture used for pretraining (Physical Intelligence, 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). The strongest VLAs are pretrained partly on proprietary data, collected (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026) or synthesised (Yuan et al., 2026), and several have no public weights (Physical Intelligence et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026). OpenVLA, Octo and RDT-1B released their full pipeline on public data such as Open X-Embodiment (Kim et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025), followed by SmolVLA, MolmoAct and MolmoAct2, which also releases bimanual data collected by its authors (Shukor et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026). These releases have helped the research community pretrain models again, change their data or design, and compare them under the same conditions. Models pretrained on larger in-house data, with more recent design choices, have nonetheless kept a lead on most benchmarks. Building on this line of work, REKI is pretrained on a broad mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data, and released in full, from data curation to deployment on a

Building on this line of work, REKI is pretrained on a broad mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data, and released in full, from data curation to deployment on a real robot. It reaches the best results among VLAs pretrained on public data on three benchmarks (§6.1), and is optimised for fast inference (§6.3). Memory in VLAs. Most of these models act on the current observation alone, yet past context helps a policy identify the task state and recover from failed attempts (Shi et al., 2026; Torne et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026), and methods differ in where they pay for it (Fig. 2). The most direct approach stacks or compresses past frames in the VLM (Yuan et al., 2026; Torne et al., 2026; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026; Jang et al., 2025). Its cost then grows with the window, at least in the vision encoder (Koo et al., 2026). A recurrent state (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) or fast weights (Jiang et al., 2026) keep the input short, but must be unrolled step by step in training. Others store past features or keyframes in an extra module (Shi et al., 2026; Koo et al., 2026; Mark et al., 2026; Sridhar et al., 2026). Like µVLA

text: the input short, but must be unrolled step by step in training. Others store past features or keyframes in an extra module (Shi et al., 2026; Koo et al., 2026; Mark et al., 2026; Sridhar et al., 2026). Like µVLA and HAMLET, REKI carries the past in a few learnable tokens, but as registers (Darcet et al., 2024) in the action expert. The VLM encodes each frame once, a training window is one batched pass, and at inference memory adds under 1% to the prediction time of a model without memory (K=1, Appendix A.1). Without memory, a policy can also switch between modes at each new action chunk (Agarwal et al., 2026; Lian et al., 2026), which is attributed to perceptual aliasing in reinforcement learning (Whitehead & Ballard, 1991; Singh et al., 1994; McCallum, 1996). In REKI, memory makes such switches about four times rarer (§6.2), without the extra policy queries of temporal ensembling or bidirectional decoding (Zhao et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2024b). 2

text: Problem formulation. At each decision step t we predict the chunk At ∈RH×da of the next H actions of an embodied system, conditioned on the current context ct with ct = (zt, ot, st), (1) which gathers a text prompt zt, camera observations ot and the current robot state st ∈Rds. More generally, a policy may condition on every context observed so far, c1:t. The camera observations ot = {o1 t, . . . , oV t } gather the V available views, static or embodied. The robot state st is expressed as absolute joint angles or an absolute end-effector pose, and the actions as absolute joint angles or delta end-effector poses and yield the next H states at a given control frequency. Action and state dimensions (da, ds) vary across embodiments and control modes. 3.1 DIFFUSION POLICY Following prior work (Chi et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024), the action expert generates the chunk by flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023). Write A = At for the chunk generated at step t and c = c1:t for the contexts observed up to it; the index t is fixed in this subsection and omitted. text: Preprint 3.2 CONDITIONING The action expert is conditioned on the camera observations, the text instruction and the robot state, through two separate paths. The observations and the instruction are variable-length token sequences. An encoder embeds them into an encoded context Et = Encϕ(zt, ot) ∈RLt×d, (4) whose tokens the expert reads as keys and values in its cross-attention blocks. The state is a single low-dimensional vector. It is pooled into one state embedding gt = Poolψ(st) ∈Rde, which modulates the expert through its adaptive normalisation (Peebles & Xie, 2023), alongside the flow- time embedding. Since gt does not depend on τ, it is computed once per frame for all Euler steps. Encoded context. Following recent practice (Yuan et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026), Et is the final- layer hidden states of a VLM, read by cross-attention. This keeps the encoder and the action expert independent, and is reported to match or outperform alternatives such as processing the encoded context jointly with the noisy chunk by self-attention (Wang et al., 2026a), or attending the backbone at single or all layers (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025). text: (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025). We use Qwen3.5-2B (Qwen Team, 2026) and pack the prompt and the camera views into a single stream (Appendix Fig. 9). The prompt zt carries the language instruction, the embodiment, the control mode, the control frequency and a binned episode length (Appendix A). We give the expert access to the preceding frames through nr memory tokens per frame, implemented as registers (Darcet et al., 2024). The registers of frame t cross-attend the encoded prompt and views of that frame, self-attend the registers of the earlier frames, and persist as keys and values in the expert’s cache, implemented as a rolling window over the K −1 preceding frames with K=3 (§4.2). text: Preprint Inference. At inference, each frame needs one encoder pass over the current observation and ten Euler steps on the action tokens. The registers do not read the action tokens and skip adaptive normalisation (§4.1), so neither they nor the context depend on the flow time τ or on the state. The registers of the current frame are thus computed together with the action tokens in the first Euler step, and their keys and values are reused at the nine others. The register keys and values are also kept for the frames that follow, (K −1) nr pairs per expert block. The cache is a rolling window, so the registers of the oldest frame are dropped when those of a new frame enter (Appendix Fig. 10). At training, each window of K frames is processed in isolation. At inference, the cached registers were themselves computed with the registers of earlier frames, so information can persist beyond the window. The VLM prefill and the expert are each compiled into a single CUDA graph. With two 256×256 images and a chunk of ten actions, REKI predicts a chunk in 21.8 ms on one H100 at K=3, the lowest latency among the VLAs compared in §6.3. We train on a broad mixture of public teleoperation datasets: RoboSet (Bharad- hwaj et al., 2024), Galaxea (Jiang et al., 2025), AgiBot World 2026 (AgiBot World Team, 2026), RoboCOIN (Wu et al., 2025b), RoboMIND (Wu et al., 2025a), RDT-1B (Liu et al., 2025), DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), BridgeData V2 (Walke et al., 2023), and twelve datasets of Open X-Embodiment (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024) including RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023) and BC-Z (Jang et al., 2022) (Appendix B.1), complemented by motion-planned simulation from InternData-A1 (Tian et al., 2026) and GR00T-X-Embodiment-Sim (Bjorck et al., 2025) and bimanual YAM demonstrations from ABC (Allshire et al., 2026). These span single-arm, bimanual, mobile, and humanoid platforms across tabletop, in-the-wild, and loco-manipulation settings (Appendix Table 1). Action and state dimensions, control conventions and units vary across sources, and a robot may appear under several conventions. Following Qwen-VLA (Wang et al., 2026a), we keep each dataset’s native control convention rather than remapping to a shared action space, normalise each

text: state dimensions, control conventions and units vary across sources, and a robot may appear under several conventions. Following Qwen-VLA (Wang et al., 2026a), we keep each dataset’s native control convention rather than remapping to a shared action space, normalise each action dimension to [−1, 1] by per-dataset quantiles, and zero-pad actions to a common width under a loss mask. States are absolute, actions are absolute joint positions or delta end-effector poses, and rotations are harmonised to one Euler parameterisation. The prompt and the per-layout state projections of §3.2 tell the policy which convention a sample follows. In the spirit of Qwen-RobotManip’s multi-stage filtering (Yuan et al., 2026), we curate every source before training: we keep only the degrees of freedom the policy commands, discard static and near-zero-variance episodes, and correct per-dataset sign conventions. They contribute ∼350k episodes and 170M frames. We train on the FineVision (Wiedmann et al., 2025) and LLaVA-OneVision- 1.5 (An et al., 2025) datasets most relevant for spatial reasoning (Appendix B.5), as well as targeted spatial-grounding and pointing corpora: RoboPoint (Yuan et al., 2024), RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025), and PixMo (Deitke et al., 2025). This auxiliary supervision preserves the backbone’s perception and spatial reasoning, and is mixed in at a small ratio with the robot and egocentric data. 5.2 MODELS REKI pairs the Qwen3.5-2B vision–language backbone with an action expert of 10 blocks of width 768, 32 registers per frame and a memory window of K=3 frames. It is pretrained on the mixture above for 200k steps on 32 H100 GPUs with a global batch of 2,880 samples, then finetuned on each benchmark separately. Rows marked scratch skip the pretraining and finetune the initialised model directly on the benchmark.1 5.3 VISUAL DATA AUGMENTATION We apply data augmentation to make the model robust to visual variations: colour jittering, mild random cropping, random camera dropout and shuffled camera order. When finetuning on RoboTwin, RoboCasa365 and RoboCasa-GR1, we add a mirroring augmentation, which extends the horizontal flip common in image classification to robot data. With probability 0.5, a sample is replaced by its left-right mirror image. The images are flipped, the state and the actions are reflected through the same plane, the arms of a two-arm robot are swapped, and the prompt marks the sample as mirrored (Appendix C.2). The augmentations and other training settings, such as the state dropout rate, have a large effect on robustness: on LIBERO-Plus, disabling camera dropout or the image augmentations lowers the success under camera-viewpoint changes by more than 20 points, and disabling state dropout lowers the success under changes of the initial robot state by 8.1 points (Appendix D.2). 6 EXPERIMENTS 6.1 RESULTS Benchmarks. LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a) has four suites of ten single-arm tabletop tasks, and LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) perturbs its 40 tasks along seven dimensions, from the camera viewpoint and the initial robot state to lighting and object layout. The models are finetuned on the four suites and evaluated on both. RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025b) has 50 tasks on the dual-arm AgileX ALOHA, in clean scenes and in scenes with a randomised background, lighting, clutter and table height. For the out-of-distribution evaluation (Clean2Rand; Yuan et al., 2026), the models are finetuned on clean scenes only and evaluated under six conditions: on clean scenes (Easy), under each randomisation alone and under all four together (Hard). The Clean2Rand score is the mean over these six conditions. RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) has kitchen tasks for a Franka arm on a mobile base. The models are trained on the human demonstrations of its 300 pretraining tasks and evaluated on 50 target tasks: 18 atomic tasks, 16 composite tasks seen in training and 16 composite tasks unseen in training. text: Preprint 8 DISCUSSION A vanilla VLA. REKI follows a standard VLA recipe: a VLM’s last hidden states are read by a flow-matching action expert, pretrained in a single stage on public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data, and then finetuned on each benchmark. It uses no proprietary data (cf. Yuan et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026), no world model (cf. Chen et al., 2026) and no additional training stages. Even so, it can compete with, and often outperform, VLAs of similar size pretrained on in-house data, and it leads the compared VLAs pretrained on public data out of distribution (Fig. 4), where pretraining adds 13.8 points on Clean2Rand and 4.3 on LIBERO-Plus (§6.1). Many of the strongest entries on current leaderboards take the other route: they are world-action models built on video generation models (Chen et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026) or VLAs pretrained on large proprietary data (Xiaomi Robotics Team, 2026; GigaBrain Team et al., 2026). These models set the current state of the art, but they can be costly to run (§6.3). Their pretraining is also hard to reproduce, which makes it difficult to separate the effects of data scale, model size, modelling choices and additional supervision such as world modelling. We intend REKI to serve as an open reference on which each of these factors can be tested in isolation. An efficient open baseline. We release REKI with its full pipeline, from data curation to deployment, and the checkpoints of every benchmark, so that new architectures, data mixtures or training objectives can be pretrained and compared against it under fixed conditions. The simplicity of the recipe and the efficiency of the code keep such comparisons affordable: finetuning REKI takes 8 H100 GPU-hours on our real-robot tasks and 40 to 400 on the benchmarks (Tables 3 and 11). The memory adds no cost at training (§4.2) and less than 1% of the inference time, so REKI is an efficient starting point for studying memory in embodied AI. In the released code, REKI runs entirely as CUDA graphs, memory included, and predicts an action chunk from the LIBERO inputs in 21.8 ms on one H100. Inference speed matters not only at deployment, where it bounds how quickly a policy can react (§6.3), but also for training. VLAs are increasingly post-trained with reinforcement learning, in simulation (Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Zang et al., 2026) or in learned world models (Zhu et al., 2025; Sharma et al., 2026), where the policy is queried for every action chunk of every rollout, so that its inference time is multiplied across the whole training run. At 21.8 ms per chunk, REKI offers a strong open starting point for such post-training and lowers the barrier to it, a step towards making it accessible beyond the few groups with large compute budgets. Memory. In REKI, a few register tokens in the action expert summarise each frame and stay in the expert’s cache, so the VLM still sees each frame only once. Even this short memory helps: with three frames, success rises by 1.5 to 5.5 points on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin and RoboCasa365, and by 12 to 17.5 points on the longer real-robot tasks. Most of the gain comes from a single past frame, which in particular reduces repetitive oscillations between two poses, suggesting

Most of the gain comes from a single past frame, which in particular reduces repetitive oscillations between two poses, suggesting that a little temporal context is enough to tell apart observations that look alike (§6.2). A memory of a few seconds therefore appears sufficient for most tasks in standard benchmarks. Whether the registers can also carry the much longer context of tasks that depend on events far in the past remains to be tested. 12

text: In the first Euler step of a chunk, the VLM encodes the current frame t. The registers of frame t read its context and the cached registers of frames t−1 and t−2. The action tokens read the context and the registers of the three frames; past frames are not encoded again. (b) In the N−1 other Euler steps, only the action tokens are updated, and they read the context and the register keys and values from the cache. The registers do not read the action tokens and skip adaptive normalisation, so they do not depend on the flow time and are computed once per frame. When the next frame enters, the registers of frame t−2 are dropped. What it costs. Figure 5d gives the measurement. On one H100, a chunk takes 22.1 ms without registers, 22.6 ms at K=1 and 22.8 ms at K=3, the window used for training and evaluation. Even at K=32, a chunk takes only 24.6 ms. The cache adds about 2 MiB of GPU memory per past frame, 4 MiB at K=3, on a policy of 4.7 GiB. Protocol. text: joint-delta actions of Berkeley RPT and RoboSet are converted to end-effector deltas by forward kinematics. A robot appears under several conventions when its datasets command it differently, joint angles in one and end-effector deltas in another. The state projection of §3.2 is selected by state layout and control convention, and the action statistics of §5.1 are per dataset, so no source is remapped to another’s convention. A state layout is the ordered list of state channels a dataset records, for example the joint angles and gripper opening of each arm, and fixes the input width ds of its projection. B.2 DATA CURATION Aggregating data across embodiments, simulators, and collection pipelines introduces heterogeneous noise: sensor outliers, temporal state-action misalignment, and inconsistent conventions across datasets sharing a robot. • Channel selection. We keep only the degrees of freedom the policy commands, dropping derived or uncontrolled channels: forward-kinematic end-effector poses, joint velocities, efforts, IMU readings, and telepresence-parked head, waist, and leg joints. 23
title: Preprint

text: Preprint • Degenerate episodes. We discard static and near-zero-variance recordings, including episodes whose follower arm never moves, a failure mode Qwen-RobotManip reports for ∼81% of RoboMIND’s UR subset. • Sudden jumps. We fit a smooth trend to each channel with median and Savitzky–Golay filters, and flag a frame when its residual and its acceleration or jerk exceed a per-channel threshold, the larger of 0.05 in raw units and four times the pooled 95th percentile. Grippers are exempt. Whole episodes are removed only from InternData-A1, where simulator collisions cause the jumps (6.3% of its episodes). • Action representation. Rotations are harmonised to one Euler parameterisation; other conventions are kept as the source provides them. Each action dimension is mapped to [−1, 1] from its per-dataset 1st and 99th percentiles (Wang et al., 2026a), which removes scale differences across embodiments while preserving relative motion within each source. • Convention correction. We fix per-dataset sign conventions that would otherwise break cross-dataset consistency (e.g., a sign-flipped elbow joint in InternData); differing scales and encodings are then absorbed by the per-dataset normalisation. text: During pretraining, each dataset d is sampled with probability proportional to F 0.5 d L0.5 d V 0.35 d (Ta- ble 2). Fd is its number of frames, and Ld and Vd are its language and vision diversity, each divided by its median over the datasets. Datasets from the same source are grouped before weighting. Both diversities are the effective rank of a set of L2-normalised embeddings, 2H(p) with pi = σ2 i / P j σ2 j , where σi are the singular values of the embedding matrix. The embeddings are not centred, so that a dataset with two distinct instructions does not collapse to rank one. For the language diversity, the rows are the SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) text embeddings of the distinct episode task strings, each scaled by the square root of the fraction of frames it covers. For the vision diversity, the rows are the DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) class tokens of every 15th frame of the main external camera, at most 50,000 frames per dataset. The RoboCOIN and InternData-A1 collections are further weighted by 0.5, and the weights are capped so that no dataset is seen more than four times. B.4 EGOCENTRIC DATA Sources. text: by 0.5, and the weights are capped so that no dataset is seen more than four times. B.4 EGOCENTRIC DATA Sources. The three egocentric sources differ in capture conditions: EgoDex is seated tabletop recordings on Apple Vision Pro, EgoVerse head-mounted rigs, and Xperience in-the-wild moving- camera footage. Frame rates range from 20 to 30 Hz and are left unaltered; the differences are absorbed by the per-dataset quantile normalisation of §5.1. Action target. We follow the layout of Qwen-VLA’s egocentric target (Wang et al., 2026a): per hand, a 6-dimensional wrist motion as translation and axis-angle rotation, and 10 articulation coefficients, 32 dimensions in total. Unlike Qwen-VLA, which expresses the wrist relative to its own initial pose, we express it in the observation camera frame through the rigid transform T −1 camTwrist. The articulation coefficients are the first 10 principal components (“eigengrasps”) of the finger-joint configuration under a PCA basis shared across our three sources. The target is defined relative to the frame that opens each action chunk, so it is composed at load time from the stored world-frame wrist poses and per-frame camera poses rather than precomputed. State and pacing. The egocentric data have no proprioceptive state, and the policy receives a learned null state in its place. Human hands move faster than a teleoperated robot, so the human actions are

text: per-frame camera poses rather than precomputed. State and pacing. The egocentric data have no proprioceptive state, and the policy receives a learned null state in its place. Human hands move faster than a teleoperated robot, so the human actions are slowed down in time (Yuan et al., 2026). Waypoint i of a chunk is the hand pose at time iρ/f after the observation, where f is the frame rate of the recording and ρ ≤1 a per-source pace (Table 2). The pose is interpolated between the two nearest frames. A one-second chunk at ρ = 0.25 thus holds a quarter of a second of human motion. 24

text: Preprint B.5 VISION–LANGUAGE DATA REKI is co-trained on vision–language data at 10% of the training samples (Table 2). The pool is every FineVision (Wiedmann et al., 2025) dataset except the text-only ones, plus the LLaVA-OneVision- 1.5 (An et al., 2025) datasets that FineVision does not already contain, ∼20.2M samples. We keep the datasets covering the tasks most relevant to manipulation: natural-scene objects and attributes, spatial relations, counting, grounding, captioning, scene text, and knowledge and commonsense VQA. Documents, charts, tables, mathematics, code, transcription, GUI grounding, memes and puzzles are dropped. 60 datasets remain, 7.64M samples or 37.8% of the pool. One question–answer pair is drawn per sample and sampling is uniform over samples, so exposure is proportional to the size of a dataset. text: 57.8 69.9 48.7 D.2 FINETUNING ABLATIONS Table 8 compares the LIBERO finetuning configuration of REKI with variants that add mirroring, remove one augmentation or lower the backbone learning rate, all evaluated on LIBERO-Plus. It also compares finetuning on RoboCasa365 with and without mirroring. All variants use a memory window of K=3 and the same number of finetuning steps. Mirroring. On RoboCasa365, mirroring (Appendix C.2) adds 4.9 points on average, mostly on the atomic tasks (+6.2) and the seen composite tasks (+7.9). On LIBERO-Plus, mirroring improves four of the seven perturbation dimensions, by 0.2 to 1.7 points. However, it lowers the camera dimension by 6.5 points, so the overall score drops by 0.6. A possible explanation is that the policy infers whether the world is mirrored from the images as well as from the prompt. A large change of the camera viewpoint may then confuse the policy about whether the world is mirrored. Visual augmentation. Disabling camera dropout or the image augmentations (colour jittering and random cropping) causes a large drop on the camera dimension of LIBERO-Plus, by 21.5 and 23.6 points. This suggests that these augmentations make the policy robust to changes of the camera viewpoint. They also give a small gain on the sensor noise and object layout dimensions, of 1.6 to 4.6 points. text: LCT: LOSSLESSLY COMPRESSED TENSORS WITH GPU FRIENDLY EXECUTION FOR TRAINING Max Zhu1† Bohang Sun1 Pietro Liò1 Jialin Yu2 1 University of Cambridge 2 University of Oxford
title: LCT: LOSSLESSLY COMPRESSED TENSORS WITH GPU

text: Lossless tensor compression could reduce memory usage during training, but training requires tensors to be repeatedly re-encoded. We introduce Losslessly Compressed Tensors (LCT), a GPU execution framework designed for this repeated encode–decode regime. LCT exploits the natural redundancy in floating point data to reduce storage for weights, activations and optimizer states. Highly optimized GPU kernels implement Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks for low compression and decompression overhead, essential for training. Our analysis characterizes LCT’s storage costs and adaptation to magnitude shifts. LCT achieves a compression ratio of up to 1.455×, and is demonstrated in training and finetuning settings. On a 162M-parameter NanoGPT, LCT reduces memory usage by 24.6% for a 7.2% step-time increase. In Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, LCT saves up to 23.8% of peak memory, enabling a 3.5X larger context length in training on the same GPU. 1
title: LCT: LOSSLESSLY COMPRESSED TENSORS WITH GPU

text: Memory is a limiting factor in training large language models (LLMs), larger models and longer sequence lengths have increased memory requirements. Weights, optimizer buffers and transient activation caches all consume memory. Although a slower device can be compensated for with longer training, a memory limitation is much more difficult to overcome. Offloading storage to the CPU (Rhu et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2021), or even NVMe (Rajbhandari et al., 2021) allows for larger models, but can easily suffer from IO bottlenecks. The dominant methods to tackle this trade off accuracy for storage. Low precision training datatypes such as FP8 (Micikevicius et al., 2022) and FP4 (Chmiel et al., 2025) use fewer bits per value. However, intermediate activations and caches still use higher precision to ensure numerical stability and hardware support is limited to the most modern hardware. Activation quantization has been explored down to 2 bits per value in ActNN (Chen et al., 2021), while other methods exploited the low rank nature of activations (Shamshoum et al., 2025). Optimizer states have been quantized to 8 bits (Dettmers et al., 2022). 3-4 bit weight quantization methods such as GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) are widely adopted for inference. These methods are designed to minimise accuracy loss, but are not entirely lossless and require careful
title: LCT: LOSSLESSLY COMPRESSED TENSORS WITH GPU

text: 2022). 3-4 bit weight quantization methods such as GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) are widely adopted for inference. These methods are designed to minimise accuracy loss, but are not entirely lossless and require careful tuning to avoid accuracy degradation. Lossless compression is an alternative. Gist (Jain et al., 2018) applies lossless compression to ReLU activations, but is not universally applicable. General methods have been developed to take advantage of compression for inference (Zhang et al., 2025; Hershcovitch et al., 2025; Guo and Joshi, 2026; Fan et al., 2026). However, these methods have not been applied for training. Unlike inference, weights and optimizer states are updated every step, and activations must persist between the forward and backward pass. Table 1 summarizes these lifetimes and the corresponding operations for an SGD-momentum (SGDM) step. Existing methods for lossless compression offer fast decoding speeds, but are too slow to encode (Table 4). Training turns lossless compression into a repeated encode–decode problem rather than a decode-centric one. Figure 2 illustrates this distinction. Preprint, under review. Tensors are decoded losslessly, with fused kernels for optimizer updates. We introduce Losslessly Compressed Tensors (LCT) (Figure 1). Designed for high performance on GPU hardware, LCT losslessly compresses the exponents of Bfloat16 (BF16) values to reduce memory usage during training. Fused pointwise operators are introduced for optimizers with compressed buffers, while a shared GPU buffer removes host synchronization during training. PyTorch autograd integration compresses cached activations. The tensors remain compressed until they are needed, at which point they are decompressed on-demand. text: GPU-accelerated lossless compression. Several methods have investigated using lossless compression on the GPU. The nvCOMP library (NVIDIA Corporation, 2026) is a GPU-optimized library that implements several widely used compression methods, including LZ4 (Collet, 2011), as well as proprietary methods for floating-point data such as Bitcomp and Cascaded. Fast GPU-optimized ANS coding (Duda, 2013) was explored by Weißenberger and Schmidt (2019). Huffman encoding has emerged as an efficient GPU compression and decompression method. Yamamoto et al. (2020) explored using gap arrays for efficient compression and decoding. Tian et al. (2021) explored optimizing the full Huffman encoding and decoding process on GPUs. Lossless compression for inference. Lossless weight compression techniques have been explored, such as DFloat11 (Zhang et al., 2025), which utilizes Huffman encoding with gap arrays for fast GPU decoding. ZipNN (Hershcovitch et al., 2025) uses similar principles. Both methods encode the exponent, with the encoding process done on the CPU. This allows for fast decoding, but encoding is comparatively slow. ZipServ (Fan et al., 2026) combines a tensor-core-aware bitmap format with ZipGEMM, which fuses decompression with matrix multiplication. Agrawal et al. (2026) and Lin et al. (2026) use GPU-native Huffman codes for network communication. Recently, SplitZip (Guo and Joshi, 2026) proposed lossless KV-cache compression by replacing exponents with 4-bit symbols and using escape values for rarer cases. While simple, its

text: al. (2026) and Lin et al. (2026) use GPU-native Huffman codes for network communication. Recently, SplitZip (Guo and Joshi, 2026) proposed lossless KV-cache compression by replacing exponents with 4-bit symbols and using escape values for rarer cases. While simple, its encoding achieves suboptimal compression. Appendix B.4 provides a comparison between LCT and SplitZip. 3 Compressibility in tensors 3.1 Exponent compressibility in floating point data The structure of floating-point tensors provides an opportunity for lossless compression. The BF16 data type consists of 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 7 mantissa bits (Burgess et al., 2019). Typical data is well described as the quantization of a concentrated continuous distribution, the sign and mantissa have high entropy, while the exponent has lower entropy. Compressing the exponent only is sufficient, for example, a standard Gaussian rounded to BF16 has exponent entropy 2.545 bits/symbol, while the full distribution’s entropy is 10.464 bits/symbol. Encoding the full BF16 value saves only 0.081 bits/value compared with compressing only the exponent. Appendix D.5 gives the calculation. Appendix D.3 explains why this is the case. 3.2 Structure in weights and activations The distributions encountered in neural networks are compressible. Figure 5 shows the exponent distributions of the six largest parameter groups in the Nemotron-H-8B LLM (Blakeman et al., 2025). All distributions are highly concentrated around their peaks. In each

text: and activations The distributions encountered in neural networks are compressible. Figure 5 shows the exponent distributions of the six largest parameter groups in the Nemotron-H-8B LLM (Blakeman et al., 2025). All distributions are highly concentrated around their peaks. In each group, just 9–11 of the 256 exponent symbols account for at least 99% of the weights, with marginal entropy of 2.58–2.70 bits. The compressibility of the weights has been noted in several works (Hershcovitch et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026). A similar trend emerges in the activations. Figure 6 shows the exponent distributions of five Nemotron-H-8B activation groups, aggregated across layers and four 1024-token sequences. Again, the distributions are highly concentrated, though there is more variation. In particular, the squared ReLU activation has high sparsity, with 93.23% being exactly zero. Exponent entropy ranges from 0.63 bits for the zero-rich FFN hidden state to 3.91 bits for Mamba hidden activations (Appendix E.2). 3

text: 4.1 Bounded exponent codes Coding background. Huffman coding (Huffman, 1952) assigns variable-length prefix-free codewords, with shorter codes for more probable symbols. For a matched source model, its expected length is less than one bit per symbol above entropy, but individual codes can be as long as the alphabet size minus one. Length-limited Huffman coding (Larmore and Hirschberg, 1990) bounds this worst case, and Package-Merge efficiently constructs the optimal code under the length constraint. Escape coding (Vitter, 1987) groups rare symbols under a shared prefix followed by a literal, freeing shorter codes for common symbols. LCT uses bounded Huffman codes with escapes to combine compact storage with simple parallel decoding Arithmetic coding (Witten et al., 1987) and ANS (Duda, 2013) can approach the entropy limit without the integer-length constraint on individual symbols, but are slower to implement on the GPU, as we show in the comparisons. LCT code construction. LCT splits each BF16 value into an exponent byte and an unchanged sign–fraction byte. We write P = (pt) for the centered distribution of exponent symbols in the tensor, and Q = (qt) for the fixed coding model. The user selects Q based on prior knowledge of the tensor distribution. It is not estimated at runtime, avoiding codebook construction during training. At runtime, a sampled exponent center shifts the codebook to adapt
title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors

text: (qt) for the fixed coding model. The user selects Q based on prior knowledge of the tensor distribution. It is not estimated at runtime, avoiding codebook construction during training. At runtime, a sampled exponent center shifts the codebook to adapt to the tensor scale (Section 4.4). The codebooks are precomputed before running and a mismatch between P and Q can increase storage. LCT adopts bounded Huffman coding with escape coding. Prefixes are capped at eight bits and rare escaped symbols are encoded with an escape prefix followed by an eight-bit literal. Without escapes, coding all 256 symbols under this cap would force every code to have length eight. Escapes free short prefixes for common exponents. The codebook construction is based on Package-Merge (Larmore and Hirschberg, 1990). LCT further adapts this algorithm to handle escape values. We sort symbols by probability qt and test every tail cutoff. Package-Merge optimizes prefix lengths for each candidate. The final code minimizes C(D) = X t∈D qtℓQ(t) + qesc (ℓesc + 8) , (1) where D contains directly coded symbols, ℓQ(t) is the length Q assigns to symbol t, ℓesc is the escape-prefix length, and qesc is the escaped tail mass. Algorithm 1 gives the full algorithm, with an optimality proof given in Appendix B.1. 4.2 Storage structure Storage consists of two components. The sign

text: assigns to symbol t, ℓesc is the escape-prefix length, and qesc is the escaped tail mass. Algorithm 1 gives the full algorithm, with an optimality proof given in Appendix B.1. 4.2 Storage structure Storage consists of two components. The sign and fraction bits are stored together as uncompressed sign–fraction bytes. The encoded exponents are stored in fixed-size blocks. Each block holds B exponent symbols. The clean and sparse configurations use B = 65,536 and the medium and high configurations use 32,768 (Table 12). Blocks tile the tensor, with padding. Each block is divided into L = 256 streams, independent units that enable parallel encoding and decoding, containing S = B/L symbols at a fixed budget of F bits. The sizes are tuned based on the expected size of the encoded stream. The mapping from tensor positions to streams is cyclic. Consecutive elements land in different streams so streams do not hold a full row or column of a tensor, which may be strongly correlated (e.g. a neuron or batch may output all constant values). A fixed budget cannot cover every stream, because code lengths vary. If a stream’s codes exceed F, LCT writes an overflow tail. The remaining exponents are stored uncompressed. A marker indicates where the tail starts, if any. 4.3 User-selected models and budgets The users have several

A marker indicates where the tail starts, if any. 4.3 User-selected models and budgets The users have several options to choose from when selecting Q. By specifying the distributions a priori, LCT avoids computing Huffman tables at runtime, improving compression performance, while still being applicable to different scenarios. Distribution. LCT provides a set of default codebook distributions, including a power-law model with an exponential body and a power-law tail, based on Nemotron-H activations. In addition, several other parameters may be specified. A shift parameter allows for distributions shifted by an additive constant. Zero inflation specifies a percentage of the distribution that is set to zero. Together with exponent shifting, these handle the typical distributions encountered during training. The user may specify additional exponent distributions if required in terms of a probability density table. 4

text: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors Storage budget. The storage budget is specified as CLEAN (default), SPARSE, MEDIUM, or HIGH. Larger budgets increase the base storage used, but may decrease the amount of overflow for noisy or out-of-distribution tensors. The SPARSE setting provides the smallest budget and is intended for sparse ReLU activations. Table 12 lists the stream configurations and budgets. 4.4 Standard encoding and decoding Encoding. The input is first flattened and padded if needed. A small GPU kernel samples up to 4096 pseudo-random elements to estimate an integer exponent center (to avoid batch correlations) and a second kernel shifts the selected encoding table to this center. The main encoding kernel assigns one program per block and one lane per stream. It reads BF16 values using the cyclic mapping, extracts and stores their unchanged sign-mantissa bytes, and packs the exponent codes into the fixed budget. Each stream records where its fixed budget is exceeded. Subsequent kernels count overflowing streams and tail bytes, compact the stream metadata, and copy raw exponent tails from the input into private or shared storage (Section 4.6), with early exit if there is no overflow. Decoding. The decoding table is first shifted by the stored exponent center. The main decoding kernel traverses each stream independently, looking up a prefix, with a lookup table for decoding. Escaped symbols
title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors

text: with early exit if there is no overflow. Decoding. The decoding table is first shifted by the stored exponent center. The main decoding kernel traverses each stream independently, looking up a prefix, with a lookup table for decoding. Escaped symbols additionally consume their literal bits. It combines each recovered exponent with its sign–fraction byte and writes the reconstructed BF16 bits. A separate overflow kernel reads the raw tails and overwrites the corresponding output positions. 4.5 Fused pointwise operators The optimizer requires several pointwise operations, such as adding and multiplying compressed tensors. For example, the SGD update is Wt+1 = Wt −ηMt, where Wt and Wt+1 are compressed weights, Mt is compressed momentum, and η is the learning rate. A naive implementation would require decompressing Wt and Mt, dense arithmetic, then recompressing the result. For an N-element tensor, each encode-decode cycle uses roughly 4N bytes of memory traffic. A naive SGD update would require approximately 16N bytes of memory traffic. We introduce fused operations for pointwise operations required during training. Each operation consists of two stages. First, a kernel takes in the compressed tensors, computes the output and saves the exponent and sign–fraction byte to separate arrays. Next, the exponents are compressed. This substantially reduces memory traffic. Our fused implementation requires ∼8N bytes (the first kernel requires ∼6N bytes and exponent

text: the compressed tensors, computes the output and saves the exponent and sign–fraction byte to separate arrays. Next, the exponents are compressed. This substantially reduces memory traffic. Our fused implementation requires ∼8N bytes (the first kernel requires ∼6N bytes and exponent compression requires ∼2N). A selection of kernels is provided covering all the use cases for typical training with compressed and dense outputs. GEMMs still reconstruct compressed operands as dense inputs, since we did not find significant speedup with fused encode/decode GEMMs. Table 13 lists all operators and training uses. Appendix C describes the codec and pointwise kernels, including stream parallelism, table lookups, register-based bit packing, and overflow handling. 4.6 Shared GPU buffer Our compressed tensors have variable sizes. The sizes are not known at compile time, so allocating exact-sized buffers at runtime introduces host synchronization. This slows down execution, particularly for our fused pointwise kernels. To avoid this, we introduce the shared OverflowBuffer. The OverflowBuffer reserves a large block of device memory, and allocates variable-size tensors without host synchronization. All of our kernels work with the buffer by specifying storage location through the buffer’s address and tensor-specific offset. This is an optional feature. The OverflowBuffer implements a minimal memory management framework entirely in Triton, including allocating tensors, releasing tensors, alignment, and merging adjacent free regions to reduce fragmentation. Operations are performed asynchronously. Appendix C.4 provides more details. 4.7 PyTorch training integration Compressed tensors are represented as a CompressedTensor class, storing the compressed exponents, overflow tails, sign–fraction bytes, and metadata. Custom torch.autograd.Function classes integrate support for LCT into training. These functions compress saved tensors in the forward pass and reconstruct them in the backward pass, maintaining numerical equivalence. Custom compressed optimizers support compressed momentum buffers using the fused pointwise operators. Implementations of SGD-M, Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015), and Muon (Jordan et al., 2024b) are provided. Listing 1 shows an example of a feed-forward layer implementation, including activation compression in forward and reconstruction for the backward matrix products. 5

The following propositions explain why this compensates for rescaling. Proposition 1 (Rescaling mostly shifts exponents) Ignoring rounding and finite-range effects, multiplying finite, nonzero values by a finite, nonzero constant shifts their exponents by a common integer, with at most a one-bin difference remaining after correction. For power-of-two scaling, the shift correction is exact. Proposition 2 (Rare boundary effects give a small correction) For the same rescaling, let A and B be the stored BF16 exponent bytes before and after scaling. text: Finding. We presented LCT, a lossless BF16 tensor codec designed for repeated encoding and decoding during training. LCT combines bounded Huffman coding, parallel GPU execution, fused pointwise updates, and shared GPU memory management. Across the evaluated GPUs, it provides the fastest encoding among the tested methods and reduces memory usage in both training and finetuning with little performance penalty. Limitations and scope. LCT currently targets BF16, relies on user-specified tensor distributions, and requires explicit integration with training operations. Its effectiveness may vary for architectures or tensor types with different exponent statistics. Future work includes decoding within GEMM kernels, improved adaptation to distribution shift, and combining lossless with lossy compression. This includes persistent tensors, temporary allocations, and the full shared overflow buffer when used. Values are reported in MiB and measure allocated tensor memory rather than the CUDA allocator’s reserved memory. B Representation and Implementation Details B.1 Distribution models and table construction The implementation provides a set of default codebook distributions, one for each tensor role. Tables are cached by distribution family and parameters, independently of stream geometry. Model probabilities come from integrating the magnitude density over exponent intervals: [2q, 2q+1) for an interior exponent index q = e −127, with the endpoint bins extending to zero and infinity. These probabilities guide code assignment rather than certify a match to the tensor’s empirical statistics. At compression time, up to 4096 stratified, jittered samples estimate a tensor-specific center c from the mean of ei −127, rounded and clamped to [−128, 127]; the center is stored with the tensor and reused during decoding. text: the buffer and compression flag. B.4 Comparison with SplitZip SplitZip (Guo and Joshi, 2026) is a GPU-native framework for lossless KV-cache compression. Like LCT, it compresses BF16 exponents using a codebook prepared before use. SplitZip assigns 4-bit codes to the 16 most common exponent values. Less common exponents are stored verbatim with a 16-bit integer marking their position. Its average storage per value, excluding other metadata and padding, is therefore bSplitZip = 8 + 4 + 24ϵ = 12 + 24ϵ bits/value, (7) where the terms account for the sign–fraction byte, the 4-bit code, and overflow with probability ϵ. With no overflow, the compression ratio is 16/12 = 4/3 ≈1.33. LCT achieves ratios above 1.4 by assigning variable-length codes and optimizing which symbols use escapes. SplitZip stores a 16-bit position for each overflow value; LCT instead uses an escape prefix of at most eight bits followed by an eight-bit literal. LCT also adapts its codebook through runtime exponent centering. SplitZip does not perform this adjustment, so changes in tensor scale can increase overflow under a fixed codebook. Adaptation is particularly useful during training, when tensor magnitudes evolve. In the evaluated SplitZip implementation, encoding synchronizes with the host to determine the overflow-buffer size, adding to encoding latency. C Kernels The Triton kernels implement the codec described in Section 4.4. This section details their memory layout, bit packing, and allocation optimizations. C.1 Stream parallelism and table preparation Each lane retains its stream’s bit position and partial words in registers. Payload words are stored with the stream index varying fastest, placing neighboring lanes’ accesses to the same word position next to each other in memory. 17

text: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors Center estimation takes one deterministically jittered sample per input region. Integer hashing generates the offsets without a random-number buffer and reduces repeated sampling of the same matrix columns. Shifting the lookup tables once per tensor lets the encoder index raw exponent bytes and the decoder recover uncentered exponents directly, removing the centering transformation from the per-symbol loop. C.2 Encoding and decoding Bit representation and invertibility. Let ui be the unsigned 16-bit pattern of element i. Its exponent byte ei and side byte ri are ei = (ui ≫7) & 255, (8) ri = (ui & 127) | ((ui ≫8) & 128). (9) The exponent is coded and ri is stored verbatim. Reconstruction, ui = (ei ≪7) | (ri & 127) | ((ri & 128) ≪8), (10) recovers the original 16-bit pattern, including signed zeros, subnormals, infinities, and NaN payloads, without floating- point conversion. Packing and lookup. The encoder processes two symbols per iteration. Each table entry stores the code bits and length; since a complete code is at most 16 bits, a pair occupies at most 32 bits and crosses at most one output-word boundary. Partial words remain in registers until written. The decoder uses a 64-bit window spanning two payload words to decode a pair of symbols. Direct codes return an exponent and consumed length;
title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors

text: 32 bits and crosses at most one output-word boundary. Partial words remain in registers until written. The decoder uses a 64-bit window spanning two payload words to decode a pair of symbols. Direct codes return an exponent and consumed length; escapes extract an eight-bit literal from the same window. In the full-block path, the next payload word is loaded only when a lane crosses a word boundary. Decode-table loads retain cache entries, side bytes use global-cache loads, and dense outputs use streaming stores. Loop unrolling and autotuned warp counts, pipeline depths, and register limits control instruction scheduling and register pressure. C.3 Overflow compaction and allocation Compaction uses local prefix sums to assign positions within each tile and atomic additions to reserve ranges across tiles. Reservations occur per tile rather than per symbol. Separate gather and scatter kernels access only the raw tails, keeping variable-length overflow handling outside the main packing and decoding loops. C.4 Overflow Buffer The allocator tracks occupied address ranges, uses first-fit search to reserve aligned regions, and writes device descriptors for subsequent kernels. Freeing a region marks it available; coalescing adjacent free regions reduces fragmentation. During an update, old and replacement allocations may coexist. On the same CUDA stream, the old region can be released after its final consumer is launched, preserving execution order. C.5 Fused pointwise

On the same CUDA stream, the old region can be released after its final consumer is launched, preserving execution order. C.5 Fused pointwise operations Table 13 summarizes the supported operations. Let BF16 samples from a distribution be represented as U = (E, R), where E is the exponent byte and R contains the sign and seven fraction bits. (27) For a symmetric continuous distribution rounded to BF16, the sign bit is uniform and independent of the magnitude. When the fraction bits also have high conditional entropy, H(R | E) is close to eight bits and the additional saving is small. For example, for the Gaussian distribution X ∼N(0, 1) rounded to BF16, the conditional entropy is H(R | E) ≈7.9195 bits. Coding the full value therefore saves only ∆b ≈0.0805 bits per value beyond exponent-only coding. The sign–fraction byte can have lower entropy in some cases. One example is nonnegative distributions whose sign bit is always zero. This is the case for certain activation functions such as ReLU and sigmoid. Another case is if the mean of the distribution is large and all values cluster around a single exponent, e.g. N(12, 1) where values are mostly distributed between 23 and 24 so there is no pooling of mantissa values (and exponents have very low entropy). text: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision–Language Adaptation Zhipeng Yea, Feng Jianga,∗, Qiufeng Wangb, Hao Lic aTaizhou Institute of Science and Technology, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Taizhou 225300, Jiangsu, China bDepartment of Intelligence Science, Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Suzhou 215123, Jiangsu, China cSchool of Computer Science and Technology, University of Arizona, Tucson 85705, AZ, USA
title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for

text: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder’s final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification. Keywords: Few-shot

text: Vision–language models such as CLIP recognize images by matching visual repre- sentations to category descriptions [1]. Few-shot adaptation uses a small labeled support set to improve this pretrained predictor for a target task. Many adaptation methods rely on the encoder’s final global descriptor. This compact representation supports image– text matching, but intermediate token grids and convolutional maps also retain visual information at different levels of abstraction. These features are already available during the encoder’s forward pass. Using them offers an opportunity to improve adaptation while keeping the encoder frozen. Existing approaches use different sources of information to adapt the predictor. Prompt and prototype methods refine the class representations [2–4]. Tip-Adapter retrieves labeled instances, while ProKeR fits a regularized support-label residual; both use final global descriptors to match images [5, 6]. SSP instead uses local features to construct subspaces for image–text alignment [7]. These methods motivate the use of complementary semantic and visual information. Integrating features from several encoder layers, however, requires addressing two related challenges: their native dimensions can differ, and the most useful layers can vary with the target task. Our central idea is to combine predictions from different layers in a shared class- score space. Different layers provide different measures of image similarity, but each predictor outputs a score for the same set of classes. Their predictions can

text: task. Our central idea is to combine predictions from different layers in a shared class- score space. Different layers provide different measures of image similarity, but each predictor outputs a score for the same set of classes. Their predictions can therefore be combined while preserving the original feature dimensions. Fitting these predictors separately also allows their outputs to be reused when selecting the mixture, so each candidate mixture does not require a new fit. Based on this idea, we introduce training-free LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors. A single encoder pass per view yields a global descriptor and regional descriptors from three layers of a Vision Transformer (ViT) or ResNet [8, 9]. The global predictor and three regional predictors independently fit the same label residual: the difference between the support labels and CLIP’s initial scores. Each regional kernel is calibrated against the support set, and labeled validation data select the mixture of global and regional corrections. LAMP thus uses complementary information from several layers without gradient optimization or learned feature projections. Its extension, LAMP-F, adapts text-anchored class prototypes while retaining the selected kernels and mixture weights. A cached linear response accounts exactly for the resulting changes to both the initial scores and residual corrections, avoiding repeated matrix factorization during prototype evaluation. text: 2.1. Class-level semantic adaptation Semantic adaptation adjusts a vision–language model’s class representations to a target task. CoOp and CoCoOp learn contextual prompts, while KgCoOp and ProGrad constrain prompt updates to preserve pretrained knowledge [2, 12–14]. MaPLe couples visual and textual prompts; PLOT and CAPEL use multiple prompts or class representa- tions to capture variation within a category [15–17]. TaskRes learns residual updates to class prototypes, while CLAP adapts prototypes with a text-anchoring penalty [3, 4]. These methods improve the class representations through optimization. LAMP keeps the class text vectors fixed and uses visual similarities to correct their prediction errors on the support set. Its trainable extension, LAMP-F, combines CLAP’s text anchoring with global and regional residual predictors. Cached responses account for the effects of prototype updates on both the initial query scores and the support residuals, allowing prototype adaptation to work with the selected visual predictors. 2.2. Instance-level global adaptation Instance-level adaptation draws on visual information from labeled support images. CLIP-Adapter learns transformations of global embeddings, and CLIP-LoRA updates internal attention weights through low-rank parameters [18, 19]. Both adapt visual representations through gradient optimization. Training-free methods instead adjust how frozen features are used for prediction: Tip-Adapter retrieves support labels, APE refines feature channels and affinities, and GDA estimates class statistics [5, 20, 21]. Method LAMP adapts CLIP by using labeled support images to correct its initial class scores. The support labels indicate which scores should increase or decrease, and visual similarity determines how these corrections transfer to a query. Global descriptors and regional features from intermediate layers capture different relationships between images, providing complementary ways to correct a prediction. LAMP combines the resulting corrections in class-score space: every branch produces one score per class, even when the branches have different feature dimensions. Experiments We evaluate recognition accuracy at different support budgets and examine how class-prototype adaptation and native-layer integration contribute to performance. We also test transfer to new domains without fitting on target data and measure deployment costs. Comparisons with published methods establish overall performance, while paired controls assess individual design choices. 4.1. Evaluation protocol We evaluate training-free LAMP and its prototype-adapted extension, LAMP-F, with CLIP encoders from the ViT and ResNet families. The main comparison covers eleven datasets using ViT-B/16 and RN50, with 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 support images per class and three support-sampling seeds. Additional experiments use RN101 and ViT-B/32. We report top-1 accuracy and give each dataset equal weight when computing the mean. We follow the established benchmark partitions and evaluation conventions used in previous studies [2, 5, 6]. Labeled validation images are not counted toward the support budget. Paired controls use the same support images, augmented views, prompts, and query images. Results taken from published baselines retain their original protocols. Confidence intervals for our experiments are conditional on the selected models. 10

text: Ten datasets have distinct validation and test lists. For ImageNet, support images come from the training partition, while the same official 50,000-image validation parti- tion is used for both parameter selection and benchmark scoring, following the released Tip-Adapter and ProKeR implementations. The eleven-dataset aggregate therefore com- bines these evaluation protocols. Published comparisons retain their different selection procedures: CLIP-LoRA shares hyperparameters across tasks, whereas LAMP uses dataset-specific validation. Paired analyses of the three-seed benchmark and its controls use 5,000 paired crossed bootstrap replicates, with shared support-seed and class-stratified query-identity draws. Selected models remain fixed during resampling. The benchmark tasks were used during method development; these intervals do not cover repeated-selection or development uncertainty. 4.2. Comparison with state-of-the-art methods We compare LAMP and LAMP-F with representative published methods for prompt learning, feature adaptation, and support matching across five support budgets. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the training-free RN50 meth- ods compared at 4, 8, and 16 shots. At 16 shots, it reaches 78.73%, exceeding the best published training-free result by 1.98 percentage points without gradient optimization. The ViT-B/16 comparison includes published methods that require training. LAMP exceeds CLIP-LoRA, the strongest published baseline at 8 and 16 shots, by 0.35 and 0.30 points, respectively, without gradient-based training. LAMP-F further raises mean accuracy to 80.94% and 83.57%. CLIP-LoRA updates encoder weights, while LAMP keeps both the encoders and class prototypes fixed; LAMP-F optimizes only the class prototypes. These results show that combining residual corrections from multiple depths can achieve competitive accuracy with a frozen encoder and fixed text prototypes. On RN50, training-free LAMP outperforms the strongest published method by 0.77, 1.18, and 1.98 points at 4, 8, and 16 shots, respectively. text: 5. Discussion 5.1. Implications for training-free adaptation LAMP improves adaptation by combining complementary features from different encoder layers. The final global descriptor provides image–text alignment, while inter- mediate feature maps supply additional visual information for the target task. Controls with matched search budgets show that descriptors from multiple layers outperform an ensemble built from the final global feature. Likewise, pooling several feature maps outperforms pooling only the deepest map. In the pooling study, regional centroids and whole-map descriptors retain most of the accuracy gain. These compact representations offer useful options for applications with limited storage or strict latency requirements. Calibration and task-specific mixing determine how each layer contributes to pre- diction. Calibration is particularly effective for RN50 on EuroSAT, and the selected layer weights vary across datasets and backbones. LAMP-F adds prototype adaptation, with the largest gains when few support images are available. Caching the response to prototype changes makes their evaluation inexpensive relative to constructing the regional predictors. The results highlight the value of the visual information already present in a frozen encoder and show how to use it through complementary residual corrections. 5.2. Limitations Using features from multiple layers increases storage requirements and kernel computation costs. On ImageNet at 16 shots, LAMP increases latency at batch size one from 14.22 to 64.83 ms on ViT-B/16 and from 14.81

title: 5. Discussion

text: We presented LAMP, a training-free method that combines global and regional pre- dictions from multiple layers of a frozen vision–language encoder. Each branch retains its native feature dimension and independently fits the same support-label residual; their corrections are then combined in class-score space. LAMP achieves state-of- the-art mean accuracy among the compared training-free RN50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, while matching or exceeding representative methods that require training at higher support budgets. LAMP-F adds text-anchored prototype adaptation and uses a cached response to update the predictions exactly. Beyond these accuracy gains, LAMP provides a way to combine features of different dimensions without learning a shared projection. Its separation of branch fitting, score fusion, and prototype updates offers a foundation for studying task-specific layer selection and developing more scalable residual prediction methods. 22

This enables human-like behavior such as lifting a box, securing it under one arm, carrying it while walking, and setting it down. Abstract— Current humanoid dexterous manipulation re- mains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans’ ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot’s body and appendages as con- tact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to- any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes

We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole- body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

text: People rarely manipulate with their hands alone. We brace a box against the chest, cradle a basket across both arms, or tuck an object under one arm to free the other. These actions use the limbs and torso as a single highly dexterous manipulator. We call this ability to reposition objects by continually changing supporting body contacts whole-body dexterous manipulation and apply it directly to humanoids. Prior humanoid work has used this term for specific settings, such as coordinated whole-body control for manipu- lation with the hands [1], [2], while related loco-manipulation confines dexterity to the end-effectors [3], [4], [5], [6], [7] arXiv:2610.22184v1 [cs.RO] 15 Oct 2026

Viewed through this lens, whole-body dexterous ma- nipulation has a useful parallel in dexterous hands, with the limbs and torso taking the roles of fingers and palm. Recent dexterous-hand work shows that strong capabilities emerge from learning to move objects through dense se- quences of intermediate targets, whether by pre-training on anygrasp-to-anygrasp transitions [11] or by tracking hand– object subgoals from human motion through regrasps and finger gaiting [12]. Extending this principle to humanoids introduces a challenge: a dexterous hand with many fingers can often reposition some fingers while the others support the object [13], [14], whereas a humanoid using two arms has fewer independent supports. Releasing one arm may require the other to brace the object against the torso, and changing grasps can require rapid reconfiguration and rolling or sliding contact. This additional complexity calls for a different approach to repositioning across body regions than these existing methods. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a frame- work for learning whole-body dexterous manipulation through mode-constrained re-grasping (Fig. 2) and deploying it on a real humanoid. We first generate a diverse set of whole-body grasps, then use them to initialize reinforcement- learning experts, WBD-EX. Experts learn to move objects between grasps toward goals specified by an object position and a target grasp mode: a left-arm, both-arm, or right-arm grasp. Transitions allow brief contact loss during movement but require a stable hold in the target mode at goals, so the experts learn how to hand off objects between arms, enabling repositioning across difficult regions such as behind the back and on top of the shoulders. We distill expert trajectories into a controller that uses an object geometry descriptor to refine motion commands into stable whole- body object repositioning, without privileged object state. text: Whole-Body Manipulation. In this paper, we advance whole-body dexterous manipulation, in which objects are held and repositioned through contact anywhere on the robot’s body rather than only at designated end-effectors or links. The closely related term, whole-body dexterity, was defined for a snake-like robot arm that manipulates with its entire body surface [18]. Related in spirit, a humanoid can manipulate from onboard proprioception alone, since joint- encoder readings under compliant contact act as a coarse whole-body tactile channel [19]. Several methods manipulate bulky objects that exceed the hand’s size and payload by grasping them with the arms and torso and distributing contact across the body [8], [20], [21], [22]. Other work uses upper-body tactile sensing to hold boxes against the arms and chest on a real humanoid [9]. Closest to our setting, reinforcement learning on a large soft robotic torso lifts cuboids of varying sizes and masses and performs recovery re-grasping in front of the torso [23], but without standing or walking and without moving the object to other regions of the body. Classical model-based work formulates this as optimiza- tion over contacts placed anywhere on the body surface [24], [25] and plans holding manipulation as a transition graph

Evidence that the hand and the humanoid form a structural continuum comes from reconfigurable hardware [30] and from commercial humanoids that already tuck containers under one arm, drape cloth over a shoulder, and lift appliances during everyday tasks [31], [32]. Humanoid loco-manipulation couples loco- motion with manipulation, enabling dynamic behaviors such as climbing and wall flips alongside picking, placing, and pushing objects [5], [4], [33], [34], [35], including humanoid pushing in simulation [36]. Dexterity as Contact Sequencing. In-hand manipulation can be framed as re-grasping: an object is carried through a se- quence of grasps by repeatedly breaking and remaking finger contacts, a process known as finger gaiting [14], [13], [44]. Using this idea, prior work trains dexterous-hand controllers that high-level policies or teleoperators steer with motion commands [11], [12]. Related goal-conditioned approaches learn grasping and reorientation across procedurally gener- ated tools [45] or pre-train object reposing before adapting to downstream manipulation tasks [46]. Similar in mechanism to our own approach, a constrained sampler over feasible contact-rich states can guide goal-conditioned manipulation RL directly [47]. We lift this re-grasping principle from dexterous hands and arms to the whole humanoid.

text: We present a pipeline for whole-body dexterous manipu- lation, enabling object repositioning across diverse regions of the body. Beyond end-effector and front-of-torso contact, we define contact surfaces for grasping as any link or link subsection in the robot’s kinematic system. Because the embodiment for whole-body grasping differs greatly from a multi-fingered hand, much of the re-grasping in the whole- body formulation involves sliding and rolling across the torso mesh, which we account for later in this section. Our method trains and deploys controllers with dexterous whole-body re-grasping capabilities in three stages. We first generate a large dataset of whole-body object grasps using energy-based optimization and decompose our torso mesh into subregions to enable diverse whole-body grasping on the robot. Second, we train per-object experts on this grasp corpus to reposition objects around the body, encouraging sliding and rolling contact across the torso. Finally, we distill these experts into deployable controllers without privileged object state, enabling real-world whole-body dexterous ob- ject repositioning. A. Whole-Body Grasp Generation Given a kinematic system, we enumerate configuration types (Fig. 3): which bodies or appendages hold the object and which of their links or subregions should contact it. Because the G1 has only two arms and a large torso to grasp against, its grasps depend heavily on gravity and contact-link friction. Therefore, to produce the highest- quality grasp dataset, we aggressively filter candidates in simulation. For each candidate, the object is pressed into contact and held under 4× gravity while a sustained wrench disturbance is swept over the six axis directions. The candi- date passes only if contact persists. Survivors are then eval- uated again under standard gravity without disturbance and must drift less than 10 cm and rotate less than 45◦, producing the settled pose used at WBD-EX episode initialization. We index accepted grasps by robot joint position, grasp mode, and settled object position, and drop grasps whose object mesh sits farther than 5 mm from the torso surface or below a size-dependent height threshold (Appendix II-D). We assess WBD-EX expert quality by regional route completion, the fraction of trials that reach every goal of a route in order before failure or timeout, where each route specifies a sequence of grasp goals across body regions. Route definitions, completion requirements, and evaluation details are given in Appendix IV. When trained from scratch, experts for smaller and less uniformly shaped objects achieve lower regional route completion than experts for medium- large spheres. C. WBD Controller Distillation WBD-EX policies generate diverse and continuous object repositioning trajectories covering contactable regions of the torso, head, and arms under randomized dynamics. We filter the trajectories to keep only valid repositioning trajectories, then balance sampling across objects and motion types with cross-body mirroring. We also sample three trajectory speed behaviors equally, using goal distances of 2–4, 4–6, and 6– 8 cm that are fixed within each trajectory, to capture both slow, deliberate and faster, dynamic repositioning behavior. See Appendix VII for additional details. These trajectories are used to train a WBD controller combining a conditional diffusion model with an inverse- dynamics network [11]. Given proprioceptive history and a five-dimensional geometry descriptor comprising log-sorted bounding-box side lengths, log volume, and sphericity, it generates keypoint motions and converts them into joint- target increments. For real objects, we compute this de- scriptor from measured dimensions. At inference, coarse commands guide generation through gradient guidance [11]. A tunable guidance weight controls how strongly denoising is steered toward the coarse motion command: larger weights emphasize command tracking,

text: We presented a pipeline for learning whole-body dexterous manipulation at scale: contact configurations are enumerated into mode-typed whole-body grasps, and those grasps seed large-scale reinforcement learning under common rewards to dexterously reposition objects around the body. We showed how to use this large-scale whole-body dexterous manipu- lation data to train a shared controller that refines a coarse command stream into stable control and supports teleoper- ation. Although WBD-EX is trained without a lower-body controller, the distilled policy deploys on a standing and walking G1, holding objects through leaning and walking during the shelf task. Future work can naturally extend the same formulation to leg contact: generating combinations of arm and leg grasps, training WBD-EX jointly with a whole-body controller across this expanded grasp dataset, and distilling it into a policy to enable behaviors such as bracing a heavy box on a knee while the arms reposition.

Whole-Body Grasp Parameterization The humanoid is treated as a dexterous manipulator whose torso acts as a static “palm.” Any selected arms or legs can move to establish the prescribed contacts. The joint vector q contains the nq joints selected for optimization; all other joints remain fixed at their prescribed configurations. A candidate has nq + 9 scalars optimized jointly: the three-dimensional position of the kinematic root in the object frame, its orientation in a continuous six-dimensional rota- tion parameterization, and the nq joint angles. The signed distance field is defined in the object frame with the object at the origin. Optimizing T chooses the relative placement of the object and robot; inverting it gives the object pose relative to the fixed torso. B. Geometry and Contact Sampling The object is represented by the exact triangle-mesh signed distance field queried through a bounding-volume hierarchy; no voxel volume is used, so all iterations query the mesh di- rectly. Signs are computed by angle-weighted pseudonormals during the search and by ray parity for the final refinement iterations. The robot is approximated by collision spheres rather than by link meshes [48], generated from the robot geometry by spherical approximation [51]. Candidate contact points are sampled on the link meshes separately
