The robot is approximated by collision spheres rather than by link meshes [48], generated from the robot geometry by spherical approximation [51]. Candidate contact points are sampled on the link meshes separately from the collision spheres. A contact configuration specifies the allowed arm, leg, and torso links and which links are required. Each iteration samples K allowed links, always including the required links, and draws one candidate point on each, resampled every iteration [16]. This keeps contacts from collapsing onto a single link and produces the spread of contact patterns the dataset exhibits. Penetration is evaluated over all spheres, regardless of active contacts. Contact selection can also restrict torso contact points to a named surface region. These regions are tags on individual candidate points, rather than geometric boxes. They restrict the points used in the contact objective, while collision checks continue to cover the whole robot.

WBD Grasp Dataset For WBD-EX training and the rest of the pipeline, we specialize this general method to grasps using the arms and torso. On the Unitree G1, the Dex3 finger joints are pinned to constant closed-grip values, and the twelve leg joints and three waist joints remain fixed. Bimanual generation optimizes the fourteen arm joints, giving 23 scalar variables including the root pose; single-arm generation additionally freezes the opposite arm, leaving seven optimized joints and 16 scalar variables. The numerical settings and validation procedure below describe this WBD grasp dataset. The candidate contact set contains 626 points, sampled uniformly on the link meshes and then hand-curated, across 34 links; 347 points over 25 links are active for the bimanual configuration. We sample K = 5 contact links per iteration. The dataset uses three contact configurations: right-arm con- tact over 13 links and bimanual contact over 25 links, both requiring torso contact, as well as bimanual contact over 24 arm links with the torso excluded. For this dataset, only torso contact points carry region tags, spanning the six regions shown in Figure 7. Restricting to a region has four effects. It filters the candidate contact points,

text: contact over 24 arm links with the torso excluded. For this dataset, only torso contact points carry region tags, spanning the six regions shown in Figure 7. Restricting to a region has four effects. It filters the candidate contact points, so a generation run restricted to one torso region optimizes against roughly a sixth of the available torso points; it biases initialization, since the direction the body is aimed from is set per region; it assigns each region an equal share of the per-object grasp generation quota; and it labels the resulting grasps so that region coverage can be audited afterward. It does not restrict which links may make contact. Every accepted grasp is finally mirrored across the sagittal plane, which doubles the set exactly. The mirror is an exact relabeling of an already-validated grasp, so it is not re- simulated. D. Pre-Grasp and Post-Grasp Targets We adapt the contact-normal pressing strategy of [16] for the post-grasp target and extend it to a retracted pre- grasp. From a solved configuration, we derive a retracted pre-grasp and a pressed post-grasp target by backpropagating P k ∇ϕ(pk) · pk through the kinematics, with the SDF gradients held fixed, to obtain a joint-space gradient. We normalize this gradient to unit Euclidean norm, multiply it by +0.5 for retraction or −0.4 for pressing, and
title: Fig. 7: Torso contact regions for the WBD grasp dataset.

text: by backpropagating P k ∇ϕ(pk) · pk through the kinematics, with the SDF gradients held fixed, to obtain a joint-space gradient. We normalize this gradient to unit Euclidean norm, multiply it by +0.5 for retraction or −0.4 for pressing, and add it to q, clamping the result to the joint limits. The pre-grasp is the approach pose used to start the simulation trial; the post-grasp is the press target held during validation and later reused as the servo setpoint at each WBD-EX episode reset. E. Solver For the WBD grasp dataset, candidates are optimized in parallel on one GPU: 4096 candidates for 4000 iterations with AdamW at learning rate 10−3, weight decay 10−4, and a cosine schedule annealing to 10−4. Steps after a short warmup are replayed from captured CUDA graphs. Optimization candidates are initialized by sampling a random direction outward from the object centroid and rotating the robot to face the object centroid. Orientation is then jittered by a uniform roll about the facing axis over (−π, π) and two orthogonal tilts over (−π/8, π/8), and the seed posture is jittered per joint by ±25% of that joint’s range. Simulation Validation Because the optimizer minimizes a static surrogate objec- tive, the WBD grasp candidates are validated dynamically in two stages using mjlab [52]. The torso is pinned to its rest pose every substep, and the lower body is held fixed, so the torso frame is exactly static; the object is a free body. Physics runs at 1 ms with four substeps per control frame, an elliptic friction cone, and surface friction of µ = 0.6 on the robot with priority over the object’s. Each simulation trial starts the arms at the pre-grasp, closes to the grasp candidate configuration, presses to the post-grasp target, and holds there. Approach and press last 40 control frames each, followed by a brief 60-frame settle and the 300-frame hold, with 4 ms per frame. The gravity load and any perturbations are applied during the hold. B. Position Voxelization We voxelize by the settled object center expressed in the torso frame, taking the translation of T torso obj and binning it on a 2 cm lattice anchored at the torso origin. A voxel’s representative position is the mean of its member grasp positions. Within a voxel, grasps are grouped by mode, so a node of the goal graph is an occupied (voxel, mode) pair. Across the object set, this yields 1.0–5.5 × 103 occupied voxels and 1.7–9.1×103 nodes; spheres sit at the low end and the elongated prisms at the high end, because an elongated object reaches a wider spread of settled centers for the same body region. The occupied region spans roughly ±0.21 m laterally and 0.03–0.45 m vertically. C. Goal Graph Mode compatibility and goal sampling follow Section III- B, with B ↔B transitions also permitted. A mode change within a single voxel is a legal zero-distance transition. Intermediate goals exclude the current (voxel, mode) node. Far goals exclude the current voxel. text: C. Trajectory Collection Yield We compare trajectory collection from the full and escapability-filtered grasp datasets using 13,440 collection attempts per condition across all fifteen objects. Both con- ditions use the same frozen experts, set of eligible goals, sampling mixture, randomization, and quality filter (Ap- pendix VII-B). Each trajectory follows successive voxel-to- voxel goals until failure or a 120 s timeout. A trajectory is usable if, after removing the termination tail, it still passes the quality filter. Each condition splits its attempts between the two route samplers of Appendix VII-B. Combining both samplers, usable yield increases from approximately 29.0% to 32.5% (+3.5 percentage points), and usable frames per attempt from approximately 938 to 1,053 (+12%). The fraction of attempts failing within the first 10 s falls from approximately 26.7% to 22.9%. Accepted trajectories contain approximately 3,200 frames under both conditions, suggesting that filtering mainly increases the number of accepted trajectories. The improvement in collection yield is consistent but modest. We use the filtered grasp datasets for trajectory collection because they raise the usable data per collection attempt without notably reducing the coverage of the grasp datasets. Here we specify the network settings, training data, sampling recipe, and inference proce- dure. A. Architecture and Optimization We follow the diffusion-and-inverse-dynamics formulation and published state-encoder/U-Net configuration of [11], adapting the representation and conditioning to whole-body manipulation. Our U-Net uses one middle block, two linear layers per block, and a 256-dimensional timestep embedding. Each arm contributes four keypoints: one at the elbow and three on the hand, at the thumb, index finger, and middle finger. Forward kinematics expresses these points in the torso frame using the fixed closed-fist configuration. Each history entry contains 24 torso-frame arm-keypoint coordinates, 14 measured joint positions, 14 applied joint targets, and 14 joint tracking errors. Four entries at offsets (−15, −10, −5, 0), in 50 Hz control steps, and five static geometry features form the 269-dimensional diffusion input; no task-mode embedding is used. The model predicts 48 keypoint-displacement coordinates at future offsets (5, 10), with targets defined as future measured keypoint positions minus their current measured positions. The inverse model takes the current history entry, predicted motions, and geom- etry features (119 inputs), using width 1536 and four two- layer residual blocks to output 14 joint-target increments. We train both networks jointly for

text: their current measured positions. The inverse model takes the current history entry, predicted motions, and geom- etry features (119 inputs), using width 1536 and four two- layer residual blocks to output 14 joint-target increments. We train both networks jointly for 130,000 AdamW up- dates with a global batch of 2,560 training samples and base learning rate 3×10−4, including a final 10,000-update cosine cooldown. The inverse model is supervised on an equal mixture of recorded expert motions and diffusion-generated motions, using the expert’s realized joint-target increment at the same state for both: the applied target after action scaling, tracking-error clamping, and joint limits, minus the current target. Diffusion training uses 100 timesteps with a cosine schedule (offset 0.008, β capped at 0.999). Training the simulation and real-world controllers uses approximately 22 H100 GPU-hours per model across eight H100 GPUs. B. Random voxel-sampled routes sample eligible goal vox- els and compatible grasp modes, with initial left/right/both modes in a 1:1:2 ratio. text: EVA-Cap: Optimizing Audiovisual Video Captioning via Event-Centric Alignment Jiapeng Shi1,*, Qiuxia Hou2,*, Jiaqi Leng1, Junke Wang1, Yanhao Zhang2, Haonan Lu2, Ziyi Ye1,†, Zuxuan Wu1,† 1Fudan University, 2OPPO AI Center, OPPO Inc.
title: EVA-Cap: Optimizing Audiovisual Video Captioning

text: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense). Correspondence: zyye@fudan.edu.cn, zxwu@fudan.edu.cn Code: https://github.com/OPPO-Mente-Lab/EVA-Cap 1

text: Video captioning [3, 13, 39, 48, 61] aims to extract rich semantic content from videos and generate coherent natural language descriptions. As a fundamental task in video understanding, it underpins various downstream applications, including video retrieval [34, 38, 47, 57], video reasoning [10, 11, 28, 37, 56], and video generation [2, 35, 36, 40, 54]. Recently, advances in Transformer-based end-to-end models have revolutionized the conventional modularized video caption pipelines. Especially, Omni Language Models (OLMs) [7, 20, 29, 46, 52, 53] have driven a paradigm shift from visual-only modeling to an omni-modal paradigm that integrates audio and visual signals, enabling more effective cross-modal reasoning and stronger generalization in real-world audiovisual scenarios. Despite its promise, achieving factually accurate and comprehensive audiovisual captioning remains difficult due to the intrinsic complexity and dense interdependence between visual and auditory content. Existing methods treat video captioning as a text generation problem for OLMs based on caption-level supervision [4, 43]. This overlooks the structured semantics inherent in videos, meaning a generated caption may be linguistically correct but misaligned with the logical structure and event-level correspondences. text: bottleneck stems from the lack of an effective caption representation that unifies video-grounded structural semantics with general language modeling. To address this issue, we propose framing video captioning as assembling discrete, atomic audiovisual event sequences through joint optimization of event content and their correspondences. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a video consists of multiple audio and visual events, where each event is represented as a tuple of type, character, and content. These events can be aligned temporally to form a coherent caption clip, linked via shared semantic content and explicit synchronous connectors (e.g., “as”, “at the same time”). Crucially, such an event-centric perspective bridges audiovisual events and captions by modeling both intra-event attribution (i.e., whether the attributions of a single event are correct?) and inter-event synchronization (i.e., what are the temporal order and synchronization of different events?). While such an event-centric perspective provides a structured semantic understanding of videos beyond mere language modeling, effectively integrating such insights into OLMs post-training remains an open question. This gap is largely due to (1) the scarcity of high-quality audiovisual caption data with event-level fidelity, and (2) the absence of dedicated event-centric frameworks for leveraging supervision with event-level heuristics. To this end, we propose EVA-Cap, which builds upon Qwen2.5-Omni [45] and unifies event-centric alignment within the language modeling post-training phase. Specifically, we first construct

To this end, we propose EVA-Cap, which builds upon Qwen2.5-Omni [45] and unifies event-centric alignment within the language modeling post-training phase. Specifically, we first construct EVA-Data, a 63K audiovisual video–caption dataset, via an automatic initialization–refinement pipeline followed by event-centric quality control. In this process, timestamped audiovisual events are extracted from raw videos and subjected to per-event verification to ensure high fidelity. Furthermore, we introduce a two-stage post-training strategy to facilitate event-centric alignment, which consists of Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [27] on the EVA-Data. During the GRPO stage, three event-centric rewards are designed to enforce global completeness (via event recall), intra-event attribution (via character matching), and inter-event synchronization (via cross-modal retrieval). Collectively, these post-training objectives enhance the fine-grained alignment of audiovisual events, enabling factually accurate, event-grounded audiovisual caption generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap outperforms existing open-source models across 6 audiovisual benchmarks. For example, on general captioning benchmarks, EVA-Cap achieves a total error rate of 34.6% on video-SALMONN-2 testset [29] and surpasses existing methods by a clear margin of 3.3% on WorldSense [15]. text: 2.1 Audiovisual Video Captioning. Recent advancements in Omni Language Models (OLMs) [20, 29, 46, 53] have significantly improved multimodal perception in complex real-world scenarios, thereby promoting the development of audiovisual captioning [12, 18, 21]. However, existing approaches remain constrained by the scarcity of high-quality audiovisual caption data, and largely rely on either coarse-grained supervision or focus on limited aspects of the task. For instance, AVoCaDO [4] constructs large-scale audiovisual video-caption pairs through temporal orchestration, but suffers from insufficient factual verification and coarse-grained temporal alignment. UGC- Captioner [43] relies on holistic caption-level supervision, whereas DiaDem [5] and D-ORCA [30] focus narrowly on specific aspects of captions, failing to capture fine-grained event-level correspondences. In contrast, we introduce an event-centric perspective for audiovisual captioning. We construct an event-enhanced dataset with event-centric quality control, and propose an event-centric training strategy that explicitly models event-level alignment, enabling accurate and event-grounded audiovisual caption generation. 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Visual Content Captioning. Reinforcement learning [27, 55, 60] plays an increasingly important role in caption optimization, spanning from visual-only to omni-modal scenarios. CapRL [44] and RubiCap [16] design verifiable rubrics for dense image captioning. OwlCap [61] and VideoCap-R1 [22] improve video captioning by matching key information extracted from visual content. In the audiovisual domain, D-ORCA [30] introduces dialogue-oriented rewards focusing on speaker and ASR consistency, while TimeChat-Captioner [51]
title: Related Work

text: verifiable rubrics for dense image captioning. OwlCap [61] and VideoCap-R1 [22] improve video captioning by matching key information extracted from visual content. In the audiovisual domain, D-ORCA [30] introduces dialogue-oriented rewards focusing on speaker and ASR consistency, while TimeChat-Captioner [51] optimizes timestamp alignment under structured caption formats. However, these approaches typically focus on limited aspects and struggle to achieve fine-grained audiovisual alignment. In this paper, we develop three event-centric rewards that jointly enforce fine-grained supervision within and across modalities. This approach provides more precise event alignment than prior methods, which either focus on modality-specific objectives [5, 30] or rely on coarse audiovisual synchronization [4, 51]. 3 Method This section introduces the construction of EVA-Cap, which is built upon Qwen-2.5-Omni [45] and optimized for audiovisual video captioning via event-centric alignment. First, we address the scarcity of high-quality data by curating EVA-Data, a 63K-scale audiovisual captioning dataset. The dataset is generated using an automated pipeline with rigorous event-centric quality control (Sec. 3.1). Next, we introduce a two-stage training strategy comprising SFT and GRPO to improve EVA-Cap with event-centric alignment. The training process integrates a suite of event-centric rewards to effectively exploit event-level supervision (Sec. 3.2). 3.1 EVA-Data Construction 3.1.1 Annotation Pipeline We develop an automatic annotation pipeline to construct audiovisual video–caption pairs with event-level fidelity. As shown in Fig. 2, the pipeline

text: integrates a suite of event-centric rewards to effectively exploit event-level supervision (Sec. 3.2). 3.1 EVA-Data Construction 3.1.1 Annotation Pipeline We develop an automatic annotation pipeline to construct audiovisual video–caption pairs with event-level fidelity. As shown in Fig. 2, the pipeline comprises three main stages: Stage 1: Initialization. We first utilize the open-source audiovisual captioner AVoCaDO [4], which excels in holistic perception, to generate initial audiovisual descriptions for raw videos. This provides a coherent narrative of each video and captures key events and details, covering scene backgrounds, interactive actions, and audio transcriptions. We then filter out samples with repetitive descriptions or abnormal text lengths. Stage 2: Refinement. We then feed both raw videos and initial descriptions to the advanced omni-model Gemini-2.5-Pro [8] for content refinement and temporal alignment. Guided by raw audiovisual signals, we instruct the model to strengthen the temporal synchronization of audiovisual events and revise event character attribution, while preserving the original natural language style. This yields refined descriptions with precise audiovisual event alignment, achieving fine-grained annotation. 3

We first present our two-stage training pipeline in Sec. 3.2.1, and then introduce the event-centric reward functions dedicated to fine-grained alignment in Sec. 3.2.2. 3.2.1 Training Pipeline We build EVA-Cap upon the Qwen2.5-Omni
title: Event-Centric Alignment

text: an audiovisual captioner optimized via event-centric alignment. We first present our two-stage training pipeline in Sec. 3.2.1, and then introduce the event-centric reward functions dedicated to fine-grained alignment in Sec. 3.2.2. 3.2.1 Training Pipeline We build EVA-Cap upon the Qwen2.5-Omni Thinker module, which jointly encodes audio and video into a unified, temporally interleaved token sequence to facilitate synchronous audiovisual understanding. We then adopt a two-stage post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). In the first phase, we perform SFT on our constructed 63K EVA-Data to empower the model to generate detailed captions that integrate both audio and visual modalities. In the second phase, we further optimize the SFT model with GRPO on 3.2K rollout videos from EVA-Data (details of the rollout process are provided in Appendix A.2.2). To enhance fine-grained alignment in audiovisual captions, we design event-centric rewards covering three dimensions: event completeness, character attribution, and audiovisual synchronization. The detailed SFT and GRPO objectives are provided in Appendix A.1, and the reward design is elaborated in Sec. 3.2.2. 3.2.2 Event-Centric Reward Modeling Typically, given an audiovisual video v = (vvis,vaud) and a caption y, conventional preference optimization assigns a holistic reward R(y,v). However, this paradigm treats the caption as an atomic semantic unit and 5
title: Event-Centric Alignment

text: overlooks its underlying event structure. To address this issue, we represent a caption as a sequence of modality-grounded events: E = (e1,e2,...,eK), ek = (mk,τk,ck,dk), mk ∈{vis,aud}, (1) where mk denotes the modality, τk denotes the event type, ck denotes the character, and dk denotes the event content. Based on this event-centric representation, we further define the reference structures to support the event- centric reward calculation. For a reference caption y⋆, we denote its reference event set as E⋆= E⋆ aud ∪E⋆ vis, where E⋆ m = {em i }Nm i=1 is the set of modality-specific reference events for m ∈{aud,vis}. This event set is used to evaluate event coverage and character attribution. In addition, we denote by Q⋆= {q⋆ i }M i=1 the set of audio-to-visual synchronization queries, where each query consists of an audio event, a set of candidate visual events, and the reference synchronized visual indices. This query set is used to evaluate cross-modal temporal synchronization. During training, we adopt this reward with two rounds of GRPO to achieve progressive alignment. Specifically, in the first round, we set λcomp and λsync to 1 while setting λattr to 0. The process transitions from global coarse-grained event alignment and audiovisual synchronization to fine-grained character-level attribution. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Implementation Details: We adopt Qwen2.5-Omni-7B [45] as our backbone model. For SFT, we train the model for two epochs with a batch size of 128 and a learning rate of 1 × 10−5. To further dissect our two-stage GRPO design, we conduct additional ablations. Introducing attribution reward Rattr as early as the first round not only compromises general performance but also degrades event- centric alignment. We hypothesize that injecting both Rsync and Rattr prematurely leads to optimization conflicts between inter-event relations and intra-event accuracy. Conversely, a progressive strategy facilitates a gradual alignment process, from global coarse-grained structures to fine-grained character-level details. Moreover, comparisons against a baseline that sustains only Rcomp and Rsync in the second round demonstrate that the sustained improvements stem from effective reward design rather than mere data scaling. 4.4 Visualizations We present a caption generated by EVA-Cap in Fig. 5 for comparison with AVoCaDO [4], highlighting the superior event alignment capabilities (i.e., audiovisual synchronization and event attribution) of our model. text: we first constructed EVA-Data with event-centric quality control and adopted a two-stage post-training strategy with SFT and GRPO. Then, by decomposing captions into modality-grounded events, EVA-Cap elaborates fine-grained GRPO rewards tailored to event completeness, character attribution, and audiovisual synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFT on EVA-Data significantly improves OLMs to internalize event-centric knowledge. Furthermore, the subsequent GRPO optimization improves event-centric alignment while maintaining strong general captioning performance. These results suggest that event-centric alignment offers an effective path toward more faithful and temporally coherent audiovisual video captioning.

text: A Technical appendices and supplementary material A.1 Details about the Training Objectives A.1.1 Formulation of Supervised Fine-Tuning In the first stage, we perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on EVA-Data to enable the model to generate long-form audiovisual captions that integrate both audio and visual information. Given a video-instruction pair (v,q) and its ground-truth caption y = (y1,...,yT ), the model is optimized with the standard next-token prediction objective: LSFT(θ) = −E(v,q,y)∼DSFT [logπθ(y | v,q)], (10) where DSFT denotes the supervised training set, and θ represents the model parameters. This stage provides the initialization for the subsequent GRPO optimization. A.1.2 Formulation of Group Relative Policy Optimization In the second stage, we optimize the SFT model with GRPO. For each audiovisual instruction input q, where q contains the video v and the textual instruction, the old policy πθold samples a group of outputs {o1,o2,...,oG}. Each output is evaluated by the event-centric reward function to obtain Ri = REVA(oi,y⋆), i = 1,...,G, where y⋆denotes the reference caption and its associated reference event structures. The advantage of the i-th response is computed by normalizing its reward within the sampled group: ˆAi = Ri−mean({R1,...,RG}) std({R1,...,RG}) . A.2 More Implementation Details A.2.1 Details about the Construction of Reference Structures We filter 6.4K videos from EVA-Data, all of which achieve a 100% hit ratio in Stage 3 of the annotation pipeline, ensuring highly accurate event-level supervision signals. To facilitate efficient reward computation for both GRPO training and rollout, we construct reference structures for these 6.4K selected videos. Specifically, this involves extracting audiovisual event units E⋆from the ground-truth captions y⋆and formulating audio-to-visual synchronization queries Q⋆. We employ the reward judge LLM, Qwen3.5-27B [33], prompting it to sequentially extract audio events and visual events from the given caption to form a unified event list E⋆. Each extracted audio event serves as a separate query. We input the complete ground-truth caption along with all the extracted visual events into the LLM, prompting it to select the temporally synchronized visual events corresponding to the

text: event list E⋆. Each extracted audio event serves as a separate query. We input the complete ground-truth caption along with all the extracted visual events into the LLM, prompting it to select the temporally synchronized visual events corresponding to the current audio event (i.e., the current query) from all the input visual events. Each visual event is assigned a unique index based on its chronological extraction order (i.e., the first extracted visual event has an index of 1). Since all visual events are extracted sequentially, we discard audio events whose matched visual event index span exceeds 5. This filtering step excludes audio events that cover an excessively long temporal range (e.g., background music that plays throughout the entire video), as such coarse-grained audio events provide 14
title: Technical appendices and supplementary material

text: limited support for fine-grained audiovisual alignment. Next, we construct a candidate visual event set containing 5 visual events by selecting those adjacent to the indices of the selected synchronized visual events. This strategy naturally incorporates neighboring visual events, which are prone to misalignment with the audio events—thereby creating challenging hard negative samples for subsequent reward assessment. Collectively, the filtered audio events paired with their corresponding constructed visual candidate sets form the final synchronization queries Q⋆. As a result, we obtain an audiovisual event unit set and an audio-to-visual synchronization query set for each video. These well-defined reference structures enable reliable event-level reward calculation and support the subsequent GRPO training pipeline. A.2.2 Details about the Rollout Process SFT initializes the audiovisual captioning format of the model and enables preliminary event alignment capabilities. For GRPO, we first conduct the rollout process to identify qualified videos and yield high-quality event-level supervision signals. We perform rollout on the videos selected in Sec. A.2.1, all equipped with the well-constructed reference structures (i.e., sets of audiovisual event units and audio-to-visual synchronization queries). Each selected video is then inferred 8 times (i.e., group size) using the SFT model. Leveraging the constructed reference structures, we compute two types of event-level rewards for each gener- ated caption during the rollout process: the intra-event attribution reward and the inter-event synchronization

text: then inferred 8 times (i.e., group size) using the SFT model. Leveraging the constructed reference structures, we compute two types of event-level rewards for each gener- ated caption during the rollout process: the intra-event attribution reward and the inter-event synchronization reward. Specifically, the intra-event attribution reward focuses on evaluating the proportion of events that are correctly attributed to the appropriate characters, while the inter-event synchronization reward quantifies the alignment between audio events and the constructed candidate visual events by calculating the F1-score. To ensure the quality of supervision signals for subsequent preference training, we implement a two- stage filtering mechanism at the query level and the video level. At the query level, invalid audio- to-visual synchronization queries are filtered by the inter-event synchronization reward. Specifically, we aggregate reward values for each individual query across the 8 generated captions, and retain only queries whose average synchronization reward falls within the interval (0,0.75), following the filtering protocol of HumanOmniV2 [49]. At the video level, filtering is performed based on the sum of intra-event attribution reward and inter-event synchronization reward. We first eliminate videos with fewer than 5 valid synchronization queries, as such cases lack sufficient synchronized semantic information to support reliable training. We then compute the standard deviation of the combined reward scores across the 8 generated captions per video, and finally

text: videos with fewer than 5 valid synchronization queries, as such cases lack sufficient synchronized semantic information to support reliable training. We then compute the standard deviation of the combined reward scores across the 8 generated captions per video, and finally retain the top 50% of qualified videos, yielding 3.2K valid video samples for downstream GRPO training. We conduct two rounds of GRPO training, with one training epoch set for each round. In the first round, we only leverage Global Event Completeness and Inter-Event Synchronization for model optimization. Accordingly, the rollout video selection relies solely on the standard deviation of the inter-event synchronization reward. In the second round, we incorporate all three designed reward components into the joint training objective. Correspondingly, the rollout selection strategy is updated to adopt the standard deviation of the sum of inter-event synchronization reward and intra-event attribution reward as the screening criterion. Additionally, we halve the GRPO training process, retaining only 1.6K video samples after rollout. A.3.4 Experiments with Event Precision Reward The Global Event Completeness reward Rcomp encourages more detailed captions. After GRPO training with Rcomp, the average caption length on video-SALMONN2 testset increases from 633.0 tokens (SFT) to 748.2 tokens. However, the per-token hallucination rate does not increase (8.2 →8.1 Hall./1k tokens), while event coverage is substantially improved. This suggests that the higher absolute hallucination rate is largely coupled with longer, more comprehensive descriptions, rather than a pure collapse into unfaithful verbosity. At the same time, improved audiovisual captioning systems may introduce potential risks if deployed without appropriate safeguards. text: Large language models (LLMs) are increas- ingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychologi- cal constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understud- ied. To address this gap, we define and system- atically investigate scale sensitivity, the varia- tion in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sen- sitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpre- tation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design ele- ment shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensi- tivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alterna- tive scales. 1

For example, concepts such as ideological extrem- ity, toxicity severity, and moral emotions vary in de- gree rather than kind. To incorporate these nuances and gradations, a growing number of researchers prompt LLMs to generate scalar scores on numer- ical scales, treating model outputs as continuous or ordinal measures of underlying latent constructs (Le Mens and Gallego, 2025; Koh et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024). Yet, how consistent their outputs are across dif- ferent rating scales or how sensitive those outputs are to changes in scale design has received limited academic attention. Existing studies have relied on different prompts and rating scale designs that vary in both scale format and range, even when measur- ing the same underlying construct. For example, some studies evaluate toxicity using a continuous scale between 0 and 1 (Li et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024), whereas other studies adopt Likert-type ordi- nal scales ranging from 1 to 5 (Movva et al., 2024). A systematic examination of how rating scale de- sign influences LLM-generated scores is therefore essential to establish the reliability, validity, and comparability of LLM-based measurement. 1 arXiv:2610.22187v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

text: To address this gap, we define scale sensitiv- ity as the degree to which LLM-generated scalar outputs vary in response to changes in rating scale design. We systematically examine three design elements of the rating scale: format (continuous vs. ordinal), range (e.g., 3-, 5-, 11-, and 21-point scales), and sign (signed scales centered at 0 vs. unsigned scales containing only non-negative val- ues). We assess scale sensitivity across tasks with different conceptual foundations (political leaning, toxicity, and sentiment), prompt designs (zero-shot vs. rubric-based), and models. We further distinguish between two forms of scale sensitivity: numerical sensitivity and se- mantic sensitivity. Numerical sensitivity cap- tures whether a model assigns different normal- ized scores to the same item when the rating scale changes, whereas semantic sensitivity captures whether those changes switch the substantive inter- pretation of the output. Using the experimental design shown in Figure 1, we find systematic evidence of both numerical and semantic scale sensitivity. Specifically, changing one rating scale design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 and changes the category of roughly one in five texts. The toxicity scoring task shows the greatest sensitivity, particularly to scale sign. Compared with zero-shot prompting, rubric- based prompting does not reduce sensitivity. Our paper makes three key contributions. • We conceptualize and empirically characterize scale sensitivity as an underexamined source of

text: 2.1 Rating Scale Design in Measurement Survey and psychometric research demonstrates that a rating scale design affects how humans rate the same construct. We review this evidence for the three design elements we manipulate, namely format, sign, and range. Format. Social scientists measure scalar con- structs with two broad families of rating scales. For one, attitudes, emotions, and perceptions have traditionally been measured with ordinal Likert- type scales (e.g., 1–5 or 1–7) (Likert, 2017; Anas- tasiadou, 2011),1. For another, computational tools increasingly assign continuous scores, in- cluding VADER sentiment scores ranging from −1 to 1 (Hutto and Gilbert, 2014) and Perspec- tive API toxicity scores ranging from 0 to 1 (Jig- saw, n.d.). Compared with ordinal scales, con- tinuous scales preserve more information and al- low finer-grained judgments (Treiblmaier and Filz- moser, 2011). However, studies comparing the two formats have not found that either one consistently yields higher reliability or validity (Treiblmaier and Filzmoser, 2011; Svensson, 2000). Regardless of which format is preferable, the two formats pro- duce different ratings of the same stimuli (Lawless and Malone, 1986). Range. Rating scales differ in range, that is, the number of points they offer (e.g., 3, 5, 11, or 21 points). Changing the number of points changes the measurement properties of a scale, but findings are inconclusive on whether more points are

text: scales differ in range, that is, the number of points they offer (e.g., 3, 5, 11, or 21 points). Changing the number of points changes the measurement properties of a scale, but findings are inconclusive on whether more points are better. Some studies suggest that adding points can im- prove distributional properties and internal consis- tency (Leung, 2011; Xu and Leung, 2018; Chang, 1994), which may in turn improve validity and reli- ability (Kusmaryono et al., 2022). Others find that overly fine-grained scales may reduce consistency and reliability in certain contexts (Cai et al., 2016; Chang, 1994). Sign. A rating scale with the same number of points can be signed or unsigned. A signed scale includes negative values and is centered on 0 (e.g., −1 to 1), whereas an unsigned scale uses only non- negative values (e.g., 1 to 3). The sign of the scale changes how respondents interpret its endpoints. For example in an empirical study, when the same verbal endpoints were labeled −5 to +5 instead of 0 to 10, human respondents selected the lower half of the scale less often. Similarly, labeling a 7-point scale −3 to +3 instead of 1 to 7 shifted re- sponses toward the positive end (Tourangeau et al., 2007). In short, scale sign can influence both the distribution of ratings and the meaning respondents attach to scale points. Rating scale design in LLM prompts. It re- mains unclear whether rating scale design influ- ences LLM-generated scores as it does human rat- ings. Thus, this paper systematically investigates how consistent LLM-generated scores are across rating scale designs. Because LLM outputs are sensitive to changes in prompt formatting, order- ing, and instructions (Sclar et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Guan et al., 2025; Zhuo et al., 2024), we hold the prompt fixed within each prompting strat- egy and change only the rating scale it specifies so that differences in scores across rating scale condi- tions can be attributed to scale design. We quantify these differences as numerical and semantic sen- sitivity. In this context, we ask: (RQ1) To what extent do changes in rating scale format, sign, and range produce (a) numerical and (b) semantic scale sensitivity in LLM-generated outputs? 2.2 Variances across Task, Prompting Strategy, and Model We further examine whether three factors moderate scale sensitivity, namely the task, the prompting

Task. We measure political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity, three constructs widely explored in computational social science (Le Mens and Gal- lego, 2025; Robertson et al., 2023; Rathje et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2024). Political leaning, such as positioning actors or texts along a left-right spec- trum, is a social construct, grounded in political parties, agendas, elites, and symbolic meanings that are socially agreed upon (Bergan, 2012; Boudreau and MacKenzie, 2014). Sentiment is a psycholog- ical construct that reflects individuals’ affective states such as positivity or negativity (Evans, 2002). Toxicity is a socio-psychological construct whose judgment depends on both social norms and ex- pressions of anger or hostility (Sheth et al., 2022; Pandita et al., 2024). We note that political lean- ing and sentiment are bipolar constructs that range between two opposing poles (left vs. right and neg- ative vs. positive), whereas toxicity is a unipolar construct that ranges from the absence of toxic- ity to its strong presence. Given these conceptual differences across tasks, we ask: (RQ2) To what extent does the task moderate (a)

Given these conceptual differences across tasks, we ask: (RQ2) To what extent does the task moderate (a) numerical and (b) semantic scale sensitivity? Prompting strategy. The prompting strategy may also affect how stable LLM-generated scores are across rating scales. We compare two strategies that do not introduce additional confounding fac- tors and differ in how much guidance they provide: zero-shot and rubric-based prompting strategies. Zero-shot prompting is commonly used in LLM- based text scoring (Gilardi et al., 2023; Törnberg, 2023; Le Mens and Gallego, 2025) and requests a direct rating without explicit evaluation criteria. Rubric-based prompting, modeled on educational assessment, provides detailed coding guidelines for predefined dimensions of a construct. It asks the model to score each dimension and use these assessments to determine a final rating. Rubrics have been shown to improve consistency in LLM- based scoring (Hashemi et al., 2024; Eltanbouly et al., 2025; Sharma et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026), but whether they also stabilize scores across rating scales is unknown. If scale sensitivity stems from underspecified evaluation criteria, explicit rubrics should reduce it. If it stems from how models map judgments onto numerical scales, it should per- sist regardless of prompting strategy.

We thus ask: (RQ3) To what extent does the prompting strategy (zero-shot vs. rubric-based) moderate (a) numerical and (b) semantic scale sensitivity? Model. Model selection has become a consequen- tial methodological choice in computational so- cial science. Models differ in training data, opti- mization objectives, and alignment procedures, and most offer limited transparency into how they rep- resent semantic judgments internally (Kristensen- McLachlan et al., 2025). Considering these dif- ferences, we ask: (RQ4) To what extent does the choice of LLM moderate (a) numerical and (b) se- mantic scale sensitivity? Additionally, we test which measurement design choices most strongly affect the sensitivity of LLM- generated scores by asking: (RQ5) How much of the variation in (a) numerical and (b) semantic scale sensitivity is explained by scale design, task, prompting strategy, and model? 3

text: 3.5.1 Normalization Because raw scores are marked on different scales, we first normalize all scores to a common [0, 1] range. Let ri,s denote the raw score assigned to item i on scale s, and let as and bs denote the scale’s specified minimum and maximum values. The normalized score is zi,s = ri,s −as bs −as ∈[0, 1]. (1) 3.5.2 Minimal Scale Pairs The 16 rating scale conditions cross response for- mat (continuous, ordinal), scale range (3, 5, 11, or 21 points) and scale sign (signed, unsigned).2 To isolate sensitivity to each design element, we compare only minimal pairs, defined as two rating scale conditions that differ in one design element while the other two remain fixed. For example, comparing a continuous signed 5-point scale with an ordinal signed 5-point scale isolates sensitivity to response format because both scales have the same sign and range. This procedure leads to 40 minimal pairs. Eight pairs differ only in format, 24 differ only in range, and eight differ only in sign. We assess sensitivity to each design element using the pairs that differ in that element. 3.5.3 Numerical Scale Sensitivity Numerical scale sensitivity measures how far a text’s score moves when only the scale changes. As a result, for exam- ple, a value of 0.20 means that 20% of texts change category when only one design element of the scale changes. text: This study investigates the extent to which LLM- generated scores remain consistent when only the rating scale design changes. Using an experimental design with 3 tasks, 2 prompting strategies, and 5 models, we find that changing scale format, range, or sign shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Toxicity, the only unipolar construct ex- amined, is most sensitive, particularly to scale sign. Rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity relative to zero-shot prompting, and model choice has a modest effect. Our findings indicate that rating scale design is a measurement decision that affects LLM-generated scores. We provide practical suggestions for future researchers. First, we encourage researchers to test whether their main findings hold under at least one alter- native rating scale. These robustness checks are essential for supporting the replicability and relia- bility of LLM-based measurement. Next, the numbers on the scale should match what the construct measures. For example, a unipo- lar construct such as toxicity ranges from absence to high intensity, so negative values on the rating 8

text: scale may be difficult to interpret. In our experi- ments, models appeared to treat 0 as “not toxic” on signed scales, assigning substantially more texts to the high-toxicity category than on unsigned scales. Therefore, We recommend unsigned scales for unipolar constructs, with the lowest endpoint representing the absence of the attribute. Also, researchers should consider evidence of validity when choosing a rating scale. When suit- able human labels are available, they can compare scores across alternative scales with these labels to inform their choice. Ideally, the labels should come from trained annotators following coding guide- lines aligned with the study’s goals. Agreement with these labels shows evidence of validity. When suitable reference labels are unavailable, as may often be the case for many social constructs, ro- bustness checks across alternative scales become especially important for assessing the stability of the findings. In short, careful scale design, robust- ness checks, and validation are needed to support more reliable use of LLM-generated scores. Our findings highlight the importance of these practices when using LLMs to complement human annota- tion in future studies. Limitations We acknowledge the following limitations. text: Limitations We acknowledge the following limitations. First, the generalizability of our findings is limited by the tasks and datasets examined. Future research is welcome to test whether the findings extend to broader cultural contexts, languages other than En- glish, and additional tasks. text: A.1 Political Leaning For political leaning, we used the MBIC (Media Bias Annotation Dataset)3 (Spinde et al., 2021). MBIC contains 1,700 sentences sampled from ap- proximately 1,000 U.S. news articles. Ten crowd- workers annotated each sentence for media bias and opinion. The left, center, and right labels indicate the political leaning of the outlet that published the article, based on AllSides and Ad Fontes Me- dia ratings. We used all 1,700 sentences in our analysis. A.2 Sentiment For sentiment, we used the publicly available anno- tated dataset published by VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner) 4, a lexicon- and rule-based sentiment analysis tool (Hutto and Gilbert, 2014). Specifically, we used the movie review subset, which includes 10,605 Rotten Toma- toes reviews labeled by 20 independent human raters on a continuous scale from −4 (negative) to 4 (positive). From this dataset, we sampled 5,000 reviews for the test set. A.3 Toxicity For toxicity, we used the dataset from the Jigsaw Unintended Bias in Toxicity Classification com- petition5 (cjadams et al., 2019). The training set of this dataset contains 1,804,874 comments from the Civil Comments platform, with aggregated hu- man toxicity scores ranging from 0 to 1. Because the dataset was designed to measure toxicity in text, it may contain offensive language. Each tox- icity score reflects ratings from multiple human

text: Attention over noisy examples Generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network Francesco Alemanno Independent researcher, supported by SolarSud T.R.E. di Miccoli Antonia, Italy (https://solarsud.it). francescoalemanno710@gmail.com
title: Attention over noisy examples

text: In Hebbian learning from examples a Hopfield network of N neurons is not supplied with the K archetypes it has to retrieve but with M blurred examples of each, of quality r, and whether it can infer them depends on the load α = K/N (interference among them) and on the dataset entropy ρ = (1−r2)/(Mr2) (how little the examples say about them). We transfer this protocol to the exponential Hopfield model, whose zero-temperature update is a step of softmax attention with the unlabelled examples as keys. A signal-to-noise analysis gives in closed form the overlap between the output and an unseen archetype, m(1) = erf(1/√2ρeff): the majority-rule law of the pairwise model at small load, with ρ replaced by an attention entropy ρeff built from the weight the softmax gives to the correct class and the number of examples it spreads it over. Two consequences follow. First, in a window of inverse temperatures β that widens as √ N the interference between archetypes is exponentially small in Nβ: the load drops out and the number of archetypes that can be learnt grows as exp(c √ N). Second, learning fails differently: in the pairwise model through a spin-glass phase, in the exponential model through memorization: the softmax concentrates its weight on the training example closest to the input and returns
title: Attention over noisy examples

text: be learnt grows as exp(c √ N). Second, learning fails differently: in the pairwise model through a spin-glass phase, in the exponential model through memorization: the softmax concentrates its weight on the training example closest to the input and returns it in place of the archetype. Seen from the input the softmax weights are those of the random energy model, and memorization is its freezing transition, at β p N(1 −r2) ≃ √ 2 ln M; it is measurable on a head whose keys are examples as the number of examples carrying weight. On MNIST the diagnostic follows the random-energy prediction; on fashion-MNIST it detects sub-clusters in the classes, and the best accuracy lies beyond the memorization threshold, where the softmax reads out a local sub-prototype. 1

text: Forty years after Hopfield’s model [1] and the statistical- mechanical theory of Amit, Gutfreund and Sompolinsky (AGS) [2, 3], Hebbian neural networks have returned to the centre of the machine-learning stage through two independent developments. On the one hand, dense as- sociative memories [4, 5, 6] and their exponential limit [7, 8, 9] have shown that a Hebbian network with suf- ficiently steep interactions stores an exponential num- ber of patterns, that the steepness of the interaction controls a transition from feature-like to prototype-like memories [4], and that one step of the zero-temperature dynamics of the exponential model is a softmax atten- tion update with the stored patterns as keys and values [7, 11], a connection also read as a nearest-neighbour or kernel-smoothing view of attention [21, 22, 23]. On the other hand, the Hebbian prescription itself has been turned from a storage rule into a learning rule: in [12, 13] the network is supplied, instead of the archetypes ξµ, with M corrupted examples ηµa of each of them, and the Hebbian coupling is built on the ex- amples, without labels (unsupervised, [12]) or with the examples averaged class by class (supervised, [13]); the same protocol has been solved for dense p-body net- works in [14, 15], where the load becomes αp = K/N p−1 (see also [16, 17, 18]).
title: Attention over noisy examples

text: labels (unsupervised, [12]) or with the examples averaged class by class (supervised, [13]); the same protocol has been solved for dense p-body net- works in [14, 15], where the load becomes αp = K/N p−1 (see also [16, 17, 18]). The resulting phase diagram is controlled by the AGS load α = K/N and by a new parameter, the dataset entropy ρ = (1 −r2)/(Mr2), with r the quality of the examples; archetypes are re- trieved although they were never presented, provided ρ is small enough and α lies below a ρ-dependent critical load. Two sources of noise limit the retrieval: the fi- nite number and quality of the examples, measured by ρ, and the interference of the other stored patterns on the field acting on each neuron, usually called crosstalk, which grows with the load α. When either is too large the network enters a spin-glass phase, in which its states are correlated with none of the archetypes: in the learn- ing setting this phase is the thermodynamic signature of overfitting. The present work merges the two lines. We ask what happens to the (α, ρ) phase diagram when the examples themselves become the stored keys of the exponential Hopfield model, that is, of an attention layer, with no use of the labels. Three questions are addressed: (i) whether

text: has a counterpart in the exponential model, i.e., what overfitting looks like when the network is a transformer layer rather than a Hopfield network. The answers are obtained analytically by a signal- to-noise analysis, which in the present setting can be carried out in closed form, and are checked by Monte Carlo simulations. In a nutshell: in [13] the probabil- ity of reconstructing a pixel of the archetype by a ma- jority vote over its M examples is 1 2[1 + erf(1/√2ρ)], and the one-step magnetization of the network has the same error-function form; here we find that the one-step magnetization of an unseen archetype produced by an attention layer is again m(1) = erf(1/√2ρeff), but the dataset entropy ρ is replaced by an attention entropy ρeff(β) that depends on how the softmax distributes its weight over the training set. At intermediate β the load drops out (ρeff →ρ for any α); at small β the crosstalk of the pairwise model is recovered; at large β the softmax condenses, i.e. it assigns essentially all of its weight to a single training example, and the layer memorizes. Seen from the query, the logits of the soft- max are independent Gaussian variables, so that the attention layer is a random energy model (REM), the system of M independent Gaussian energy levels intro-

text: training example, and the layer memorizes. Seen from the query, the logits of the soft- max are independent Gaussian variables, so that the attention layer is a random energy model (REM), the system of M independent Gaussian energy levels intro- duced by Derrida [26, 27] as the simplest spin glass: the condensation is the freezing transition of that model, located at β p N(1 −r2) ≃ √ 2 ln M, and it is the atten- tion counterpart of the spin-glass phase. The window of generalization between the two edges widens with the system size as √ N. We then test the picture on MNIST and fashion-MNIST, and compare the Hebbian attention with a one-head attention classifier trained by gradient descent on the same datasets. The present model is the p →∞end of the fam- ily of dense Hebbian networks learning from examples of [14, 15]: there the crosstalk is still extensive in the polynomial load αp, here it becomes logarithmic in K, which is what allows the closed-form treatment. Re- lated settings of learning from examples have been con- sidered in [19] for dense p-body networks in the teacher– student scenario, in [20] for the random-features Hop- field model, and in [25] for hierarchical prototypes in polynomial dense memories. The signal-to-noise analysis closes in this setting, and yields a one-step magnetization m(1) = erf(1/√2ρeff) that has the same majority-rule form as in the pairwise network but with the dataset en- tropy replaced by an attention entropy, Eq. For Hopfield networks. (i) The load is no longer a control parameter of learning: within the window (17) the crosstalk of the other archetypes decays exponen- tially in Nβ instead of being of order α, and the ex- ponential network learns from examples a number of archetypes growing as exp(c √ N), Eq. (19), limited by the condensation edge rather than by the crosstalk; the dense networks of [14, 15], with load K/N p−1, are the in- termediate steps of this family. (ii) Overfitting changes nature. (ii) Overfitting changes nature. In the pairwise model it is a Hebbian spin glass with full replica-symmetry breaking; in the exponen- tial model it is the condensation of the Gibbs measure over the keys onto one example, a random-energy tran- sition with one step of replica-symmetry breaking at β p N(1 −r2) = √ 2 ln M, whose location depends on the data only through the spread of the within-class 12

(iii) The dataset entropy gener- alizes to an entropy of the weighted vote: pairwise and exponential networks are the two ends of one formula, with Meff = M and extensive crosstalk on one side, Meff = MΦM(x) and exponentially small crosstalk on the other. The labels are not needed: inside the win- dow the examples of the correct class receive the weight by themselves (W →1), and the attention layer, which never sees a label, performs the same majority vote as the pairwise network built on class averages at zero load, Eq. With keys equal to examples the fixed points of the dynamics are the examples, and the archetype is an attractor only for small ρ; the retrieval of an unseen archetype is a one-step operation, not a convergence. text: Terminal agents are evaluated by persistent changes to an executable environment rather than the plausibility of their responses. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench require repository inspection, dependency repair, and recovery to culminate in a state that passes a protected verifier [17, 28]. Long- Horizon-Terminal-Bench extends this challenge to long dependency chains, where substantial local progress need not produce a single complete solution [22]. Learning must therefore connect successful exploration to reproducible execution and connect delayed verification to the decisions that made it possible. Neither fluent plans nor an increasing count of locally passed checks alone closes this loop. A first obstacle is temporal dilation: the clock of token generation differs from the clock of environmental change. Hundreds of tokens can express one shell action, while thousands of observation tokens introduce no additional policy decisions. When GAE traverses an interleaved token chain, repeated discount and trace factors attenuate distant credit according to textual length rather than consequential interaction [13, 34]. Masking observations from the policy loss does not remove their recursion nodes. Two executions with the same decisions and terminal outcome can thus receive different credit simply because one produces more verbose logs. Long contexts also motivate chunking and summarization, but these operations are different: splitting an unchanged chain permits exact boundary transport, whereas summarization changes the conditioning history and
title: 1 Introduction

text: outcome can thus receive different credit simply because one produces more verbose logs. Long contexts also motivate chunking and summarization, but these operations are different: splitting an unchanged chain permits exact boundary transport, whereas summarization changes the conditioning history and may remove details needed for future decisions. A second obstacle is value drift across recursive supervision. Repository-grounded trajectories, environment inversion, and task synthesis broaden executable supervision [25, 31, 45]. Recursive Self-Rewrite (RSR) transfers complementary-harness discoveries through runbook planning, leakage review, and fresh public execution [23]. Rewriting changes which actions the actor prefers and therefore which histories its critic encounters. Subsequent reinforcement changes these distributions again; reward recalibration additionally changes the return being predicted. Resetting the critic discards learned outcome structure, whereas transferring it without calibration can retain systematic prediction errors. These errors enter token advantages and value bootstraps, so a stronger actor does not automatically supply reliable values for its new histories, rewards, or execution horizons after a supervised policy transition. Reward alignment introduces a related difficulty. Terminal task families expose different numbers of semantic checks, and a failed trajectory can accumulate many passing checks without satisfying the complete execution contract. A single global scale can overemphasize families with large verifiers; a purely proportional progress reward can continue to favor incomplete behavior after the policy becomes capable of strict success.

A single global scale can overemphasize families with large verifiers; a purely proportional progress reward can continue to favor incomplete behavior after the policy becomes capable of strict success. Our fixed-trajectory analysis makes this distinction concrete: under the earlier reward, failures receive 50.09% of total reward mass, and some failures pass every executed scenario check but miss the terminal gate. The objective is not to eliminate partial credit, which supports exploration, but to keep such credit subordinate to verified completion as training progresses. We introduce Terminal-RSI, alternating actor-only RSR with critic-inheriting Recursive Policy-Refine (RPR). Starting from the RSR-1 actor and a Warm-up Critic Model, RPR coordinates phase-local value calibration with reward evolution and a fivefold actor-rate reduction in the second cycle. We build on T1 terminal infrastructure, PPO, GAE, and value-preparation precedents rather than claiming these primitives independently [35, 46, 49, 50]. Their recursive coupling is the focus: supervised transitions preserve critic weights, and each new policy-refinement phase adapts inherited values before joint optimization. Asynchronous execution further requires distinguishing pipeline scheduling from the likelihood mismatch induced by policy updates and training–inference implementation differences [47]. We specify Base, RSR-1, RPR-1, RSR-2, and RPR-2 through verified rewriting, critic handoff, and phase-adaptive optimization. The initial critic-only epoch and four-update phase-local calibrations serve distinct roles, preserving useful return structure without assuming that values remain calibrated after each actor transition. Family Dense Reward (FDR) calibrates family progress; Success-Prioritized Reward (SPR) separates strict success from bounded partial credit. LHTB reaches 0.37 process reward and 5/46 strict completions; SWR100 doubles to 6.00%. Complete stage trajectories and checker-level cases expose nonmonotonic branches and verification gaps, separating retained performance from unsupported claims of component-level causality. The evaluation distinguishes measured task completion, shaped reward, and checker coverage instead of treating these signals as interchangeable measures of capability across changing policies, tasks, and verification contracts. 2

text: Recursive supervision. STaR, ReST, and ReST-EM establish generate–filter–train approaches, while Reflexion improves behavior through verbal feedback [10, 37, 39, 42, 51]. RSR rewrites cross-harness discoveries; its runbook reviewer is not a learned value critic [23]. T1 combines terminal PPO, token fidelity, and warm-started values [46]. Terminal-RSI couples these components through critic-preserving transitions. Policy optimization for long-horizon agents. Building on clipped surrogate objectives, critic-free methods estimate advantages via group, leave-one-out, or batch normalization with tailored token aggregation [1, 14, 35, 36, 48]. Other variants stabilize updates through length-normalized sequence ratios, second- moment token masking, or mismatch-adaptive clipping, whereas Terminal-RSI adopts fixed asymmetric clipping [47, 53, 54]. Meanwhile, critic-based approaches leverage learned value baselines, initialization, and skip-observation credit assignment [13, 49, 50]. Alternative formulations regress log-ratios toward optimal advantages, approximate critic-free mirror descent, center prefix-conditional scores, or learn from pairwise preferences rather than verifier outcomes [26, 32, 40, 52]. Long-interaction and asynchronous training systems. Recent agentic training pipelines support interaction-chunk optimization with persistent runtime states and couple synthesized tasks with mismatch- controlled asynchronous updates, enabling direct policy optimization on capable base models without supervised fine-tuning [16, 33]. Concurrently, distributed reinforcement learning architectures decouple actor trajectory generation from learner policy updates across varying compute scales to maximize system throughput [5, 8, 30]. Furthermore, scalable post-training infrastructures accelerate large-scale reinforcement learning by bridging distributed

Tasks, environments, and the object of recursion. TerminalTraj supplies executable-verified trajectories, while CLI-Gym constructs repair tasks by environment inversion [25, 45]. Terminal-Task- Gen combines adapted and skill-synthesized data; SkillSynth samples scenario–skill graphs; CLI-Universe grounds fail-to-pass tasks in technical documentation [6, 15, 31]. RST recursively expands aligned solutions, environments, and verifiers and studies multistage supervised and policy optimization [19]. Environment Evolution schedules scenario and skill complexity; Terminal-Universe reconstructs environments from trajectories [7, 44]. These construction curricula complement our critic handoff and reward calibration. SWR and LHTB separate progress resolution from feedback frequency [20–22] rather than implying matched baseline performance. 5 Limitations and Conclusion Causal attribution. Compute-matched alternation, isolated TB-GAE, matched online reward, and inherited-versus-reset critic controls remain necessary. Stage-specific learning rates, rewards, and initialization change together; estimator identities and offline rescoring do not isolate their training effects. Evaluation and selection. Three evaluations do not replace independent training seeds or establish statistical superiority. Checkpoint selection requires protected validation, not adaptation to final benchmarks. SWR100 is training-disjoint; broader repository and pretraining overlap remain incompletely audited. Five stages of one 27B backbone establish neither scaling laws nor universal monotonicity. Terminal-RSI coordinates verified rewriting, critic-inheriting refinement, turn-aware credit, and evolving rewards. text: AutoSFT 2026-10-16 AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning Bingxiang He∗†1, Pengqi Sun∗2, Shihao Peng∗1, Shaoxuan Li∗1, Huiyu Xiao∗2, Hongjian Shi∗3, Zixuan Fu∗1, Ziqing Qiao∗1, Yuxin Zuo∗†1, Cheng Qian4, Xinqiang Yu1, Jiayi Li3, Xiusi Chen5, Yizhen Song3, Xiangyang Wang1, Iofai Lei1, Yudong Wang1, Ning Ding1, Zhiyuan Liu1, Xiaozhi Wang‡1, Chaojun Xiao‡1 1Tsinghua University 2Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications 3ModelBest Inc. 4University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 5The Chinese University of Hong Kong †Project Lead. ∗Core Contributors. ‡Corresponding Authors. § Code: https://github.com/Thinking-Space/AutoSFT. # hebx24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn, xzwang@sz.tsinghua.edu.cn, xcj@tsinghua.edu.cn Abstract | Language model agents increasingly automate post-training, but when given the full training stack they converge on supervised fine-tuning and spend most effort revising training data. Existing systems give the agent one kind of control, selecting rows from a fixed pool or calling a generator, whereas a human data engineer adjusts proportions, prunes, repairs, replaces and synthesizes the data. We design a data action space for these changes and ask whether an automated system can make the full range rather than one of them, and what structure that requires. We first run this loop with a single agent, and it reaches only one action, adjusting category proportions, while its context fills with execution output and is discarded mid-search. We therefore introduce AutoSFT, a multi-agent system where a meta agent separates execution

run this loop with a single agent, and it reaches only one action, adjusting category proportions, while its context fills with execution output and is discarded mid-search. We therefore introduce AutoSFT, a multi-agent system where a meta agent separates execution from analysis, gathers proposals from independent angles, and calls a synthesis subagent for capabilities the pool cannot cover, with the model, the trainer, and the budget fixed within each comparison. Adding each component in turn helps: the executor halves context loss, the analysis subagents lift the best IFEval by +6.5, and synthesis adds +3.4 IFEval and +2.9 IFBench. The same loop transfers to code, where analysis adds +3.7 MBPP+ over a single agent that does not improve. Every result comes from runs that retrain from the base model each round, so each component’s effect is individually attributable. Our findings suggest that automating SFT data research depends more on covering diverse data actions than on a stronger single action.

LLM agents now run long workflows with little human oversight, and several systems use them to automate parts of AI research itself [Lu et al., 2026, Tang et al., 2025, Hu et al., 2025, Wen et al., 2026]. What makes such a loop searchable is that every proposal can be evaluated automatically, and post-training has this property, so recent benchmarks evaluate agents on it [Rank et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026a]. Given control of the whole training stack, agents converge on one part: across the runs audited by PostTrainBench [Rank et al., 2026], they adopt supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and spend most of their remaining effort revising the training data. This agrees with a broader finding that a carefully curated dataset can match or outperform a much larger one [Zhou et al., 2023a, Chen et al., 2024, Muennighoff et al., 2025], and that data selection and arrangement affect downstream performance directly [He et al., 2025a, Agarwal et al., 2025]. Recent systems therefore treat the data as the main search object [Wu et al., 2026, Luo et al., 2026, Zhao et al., 2026, Kulikov et al., 2026]. Analysis subagents read these artifacts from complementary angles, and a synthesis subagent writes data for undersupplied capabilities. The meta agent integrates their proposals into the next recipe. All roles share a candidate data pool and a skill library. data. We write these six kinds of change as a data action space (Section 2), and use it only after a run to measure how much of that space the agent reaches. We first study this question with a single agent, restarting each round from the same base checkpoint. The agent collapses onto one action family, repeats related recipes, and spends most of its context on raw command output rather than data analysis. Section 3 examines these failures, the trace evidence, and our fix, explaining why an undivided research loop is hard to sustain. One agent analyzes behavior, proposes data changes, executes experiments, and interprets logs, so execution competes with analysis for context and a single proposal stream reinforces recent choices. This yields two requirements: isolate execution from data analysis, and maintain complementary views of the same model behavior during proposal generation. AutoSFT (Section 4) is a multi-agent system built around these

text: context and a single proposal stream reinforces recent choices. This yields two requirements: isolate execution from data analysis, and maintain complementary views of the same model behavior during proposal generation. AutoSFT (Section 4) is a multi-agent system built around these two requirements. A meta agent owns each round and delegates to three kinds of subagent. An executor runs training, conversion, and evaluation separately, returning file paths and a short status report so the meta agent can spend its context on data. Analysis subagents read the same round from four angles: training data, failures, training signals, and earlier rounds, each returning one proposed data action. A synthesis subagent writes new data for capabilities the pool barely covers, which neither of the first two can add. We add the three components one at a time, fixing the base model, initial pool, token budget, training script, and evaluation within each comparison, so any difference is attributable to the added component (Section 5). The executor halves context loss, the analysis subagents broaden the range of changes and raise best IFEval by +6.5, and synthesis adds +3.4 IFEval and +2.9 IFBench by covering undersupplied capabilities. The same loop transfers to code domain without a ready-made capability taxonomy, adding +3.7 MBPP+ over a single agent that does not improve (Section 5.4). Together, 2

Contributions. Our contributions are threefold. • We frame automated SFT data research around a space of six data-engineering actions, and show that a corrected single-agent loop reaches only one of them (Sections 2 and 3). • We build AutoSFT, a multi-agent system that isolates execution, gathers proposals from comple- mentary analysis angles, and synthesizes data for capabilities the pool lacks (Section 4). • Adding each component while retraining from the base model, so its effect is attributable, widens the actions a run takes and improves the recipe, by +6.5 IFEval from analysis, +3.4 IFEval and +2.9 IFBench from synthesis, and +3.7 MBPP+ in a code domain (Section 5). 2. Shading marks what the action changes. 2.2. Data research actions A recipe is built out of rows, where a row carries an instruction, a response, and the metadata that describes it. An action states which rows to train on, how often each appears, in what order, and whether any row is edited or newly written. Agents write recipes in free form with no field schema, operator list, and statement that a particular kind of change is available. Figure 3 describes the six families of data action a data researcher makes most often. Each family is fixed by what happens to the rows and by the level at which the change is decided, which ranges from a whole category through a single row and a capability to the recipe as a whole, so an action can be labelled from the recipe diff without reading the agent’s stated reason. Every family is reachable in every configuration we run, since an agent that can write a recipe can also call a model to rewrite a response or produce a new row.

AutoSFT AutoSFT instantiates the research policy 𝜋of Section 2.1 and shares 𝑀0, 𝐷0, and the training and evaluation protocol with the single agent of Section 3. A meta agent owns the round and delegates to three kinds of subagents: an executor subagent, four analysis subagents, and a synthesis subagent, whose information flow is shown in Figure 1. The meta agent hands 𝐷𝑡and 𝑅𝑡to the executor, which trains and evaluates in a separate session and returns the feedback 𝐹𝑡. The analysis and synthesis subagents then consult the relevant parts of 𝐷𝑡, 𝑅𝑡, 𝐹𝑡, and 𝐻<𝑡through their associated files. Each analysis subagent proposes a change to the recipe from its own perspective, while the synthesis subagent generates data for undersupplied capability targets to form 𝐷𝑡+1. The meta agent weighs these proposals against its own reading and settles on 𝑎𝑡, giving 𝑅𝑡+1 = 𝑎𝑡(𝐷𝑡+1, 𝑅𝑡).
