text: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning of the meta agent and maintains a context of its own. Specifically, everything it does is one cycle of submitting a job, monitoring it to completion, and collecting its artifacts: the cycle runs once on the training job to obtain the round’s model 𝐶𝑡, and then once on each of the 𝐾benchmarks to obtain the evaluation results for 𝐶𝑡, with the raw logs and intermediate outputs staying in its own context. When the workflow finishes, the executor saves the feedback artifacts and a structured execution report to files and returns only their paths. The meta agent and the analysis and synthesis subagents can then read the relevant files as needed, without receiving the full execution logs. 4.2. Analysis subagents Section 3.1 shows that all 33 rounds of the single agent stay inside the mixture family: it pursues the objective through one kind of strategy. To break out of the limitation, we introduce four analysis agents, each of which examines the current round from a different evidence source: the training data, failure cases, learning dynamics, or research history. The four subagents examine each round using complementary evidence. The training-data subagent reads 𝐷𝑡and 𝑅𝑡, assesses the selected data for quality, difficulty, coverage, and redundancy, and proposes changes to its content or

text: data, failure cases, learning dynamics, or research history. The four subagents examine each round using complementary evidence. The training-data subagent reads 𝐷𝑡and 𝑅𝑡, assesses the selected data for quality, difficulty, coverage, and redundancy, and proposes changes to its content or composition under the fixed token budget. The failure-case subagent compares successful and failed cases in 𝐹𝑡to identify recurring failure patterns and propose supervision to address them. The learning-dynamics subagent analyzes the training loss and other monitoring signals in 𝐹𝑡in relation to the data used for training, seeking evidence that explains stalled learning progress. The history subagent reads 𝐻<𝑡, distinguishes failed interventions from ideas that have not been adequately tested, and proposes corrections or renewed trials. Each subagent returns one executable data proposal with supporting evidence. 4.3. Synthesis subagent In practice, the initial pool 𝐷0 may not cover every capability the benchmarks require, and for others it holds examples but too few to constitute effective supervision. We therefore introduce a synthesis subagent to generate examples for undersupplied capability targets. Such a target is convenient to state and to verify in the instruction-following setting: it is a single checkable constraint, or a combination of constraints that co-occur, such as repeating the instruction verbatim while using no comma, and in either case a programmatic verifier decides whether an example satisfies it. Concretely, the

text: instruction-following setting: it is a single checkable constraint, or a combination of constraints that co-occur, such as repeating the instruction verbatim while using no comma, and in either case a programmatic verifier decides whether an example satisfies it. Concretely, the synthesis agent is invoked in every round, reads the evaluation results, and derives a set of targets to strengthen. For each target whose supply in 𝐷𝑡is insufficient, it synthesizes examples that pass the target’s verifier. If no target is undersupplied in a given round, the synthesis agent generates no data. Generated data pass verification of the target’s constraint, an independent semantic review, and an 𝑛-gram overlap check against the evaluation sets, described in Appendix B.4. Those that pass enter 𝐷𝑡+1, and whether the round trains on them remains the meta agent’s decision. 5. Each subsection compares a base configuration against the same configuration with one component added, so a difference is attributable to that component alone, while Section 5.4 runs the full system on a coding domain to test whether the same structure transfers. text: Data selection and synthesis for post-training. Early works show that curation matters more than scale: a small, well-chosen set can match or outperform a much larger one [Zhou et al., 2023a, Muennighoff et al., 2025], and data ordering alone shapes generalization [He et al., 2025a]. Selection methods prune or reweight examples by information gain or diversity [Agarwal et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025]. Synthesis methods bootstrap instructions from seed sets, evolve complexity, or extract alignment data from aligned models [Wang et al., 2023, Xu et al., 2024a,b, Mitra et al., 2024, Ren et al., 2026]. Some data curation methods also optimize specifically for preference data, curating feedback or preference training pairs [Cui et al., 2024, He et al., 2025b, Deng et al., 2025]. All produce a fixed dataset without closing the loop on downstream training performance. 2https://huggingface.co/datasets/evalplus/mbppplus 10

text: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning Automated data optimization. A growing body of work attempts to automate data research, closing the loop between data curation and model training. PostTrainBench [Rank et al., 2026] audits 84 agent runs and finds that almost all converge on SFT with data as the sole search object. On the selection side, TREX [Ma et al., 2026] searches recipes via MCTS, AutoSelection [Wu et al., 2026] formalizes operator-program search over a fixed pool, DataChef [Chen et al., 2026b] trains a policy with a proxy reward, and Luo et al. [2026] iterates on data alone with gains that plateau after round 8–15. On the synthesis side, Autodata [Kulikov et al., 2026] revises generation strategies from solver feedback, ANDES [Zhao et al., 2026] packages synthesis as a callable skill, and BigBang [The Endless Frontier Team, 2026] scales self-evolving synthesis with a critic proxy. Arbor [Jin et al., 2026], AutoSOTA [Li et al., 2026], and the Anthropic automated researcher [Wen et al., 2026] organize research with hypothesis trees, multi-agent decomposition, and diverse initial directions respectively. These systems address either selection or synthesis, while we unify both and retrain from base each round so that every action is individually attributable. Benchmarks for AI research. Benchmarks for AI research. Benchmarks now evaluate agents on ML research tasks at scales from single Kaggle problems to full R&D pipelines [Chan et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2024, Wijk et al., 2025, Kon et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2025, Lyu et al., 2026, Garikaparthi et al., 2026, Xu et al., 2026], on AI infrastructure [Ouyang et al., 2025, Chi et al., 2026a, Φ-Bench contributors, 2026, Yeon et al., 2026], and on self-improvement [Zhan et al., 2026, Chi et al., 2026b, Chen et al., 2026a]. Closest to our setting, DataEnvGym [Khan et al., 2025] frames data generation as an RL loop, Curation-Bench [Kang et al., 2026] gives agents iterative control over a fixed pipeline, and RSIBench-Data [Meng et al., 2026] and DataPrep-Bench [Liang et al., 2026] benchmark data-centric recipe search. We differ by requiring from-base retraining each round, repeated evaluation to bound noise, and a verification gate on synthesis.
title: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning

text: A single agent owning the full SFT data research loop collapses to one kind of change and loses context repeatedly. AutoSFT adds structure that an executor separates execution from analysis, several analysis subagents propose complementary changes, and a synthesis subagent writes data for uncovered capabilities. Adding each component one at a time under from-base retraining shows that the executor frees the meta agent’s context, analysis broadens changes and improves scores earlier, and synthesis reaches capabilities with almost no data in the pool. The same loop transfers to coding without a ready-made taxonomy, where the system builds its own structure from the benchmark and pool alone. These results suggest that the bottleneck may not be any single action but the structure that lets an agent cover the full range of data-engineer changes, and that multi-agent decomposition is a practical way to provide it. We did not use generative AI tools to generate research ideas, design the methodology, or produce any reported result. text: AutoSFT: An Agentic System for Automated Data Research in Supervised Fine-Tuning Ethics statement The instruction-following pool is built from openly released datasets and the coding pool from public instruction–code corpora, cited in Section 3 and Section 5.4. Because the AutoSFT optimizes benchmark scores, it could in principle be used to inflate leaderboard numbers, and we report off- target and held-out benchmarks so that a gain from overfitting the target is visible rather than hidden. We apply an 𝑛-gram overlap check between generated data and the evaluation sets in Appendix B.4, and we report the compute and API cost of the runs in Appendix D. Reproducibility statement We will release the AutoSFT implementation, including the training and evaluation script and the agent scaffolding, as anonymized supplementary material. The fixed training script, the token budget, and the from-base retraining protocol are described in Section 2 and Section 3, and the agent roles, prompts, and skill files are given in Appendix B. The initial data pool, the per-round recipes, and the raw evaluation outputs behind every reported number are recorded in a run ledger.

Both are changes of proportion, which is why Section 3.1 places the whole run in mixture. Memory The history 𝐻<𝑡of Section 2.1 is the only thing a from-base loop carries between rounds, and AutoSFT puts more in it than a list of recipes and scores. text: HTN-Orchestrate: A Hierarchical Task Network Framework for Multi-Agent Orchestration Yanchen Deng 1 Jianguo Huang 1 Yao Long Teng 1 Yixuan Li 1 Handuo Zhang 2 Ning Wang 2 Liangcai Su 2 Xinyu Wang 2 Bo An 1
title: HTN-Orchestrate: A Hierarchical Task Network Framework for Multi-Agent

text: Orchestrating multiple agents on a complex task requires reconciling local subtask execution with global task planning. Dynamic dispatch ap- proaches provide execution flexibility but do not explicitly model subtask hierarchies or depen- dencies, while predefined workflows impose this structure but fix the decomposition before exe- cution begins. Therefore, we introduce HTN- Orchestrate, a two-layer framework that separates these responsibilities through a hierarchical task network (HTN). The Planner maintains subtask hierarchies and dependencies, deferring decom- position until prerequisite results become avail- able, while local Orchestrators schedule workers to execute each leaf subtask. Results propagate upward under AND semantics, and accumulated findings inform a rebuilt task network when the current decomposition cannot resolve the task. On five benchmarks spanning web research, sci- entific reasoning, and research workflows, HTN- Orchestrate outperforms ReAct, Agent Team, and DeepSeek Harness using the same base model, achieving 89.73% accuracy on BrowseComp and 73.44% on SUPERChem, exceeding Agent Team by 2.45 and 4.69 percentage points, respectively.
title: HTN-Orchestrate: A Hierarchical Task Network Framework for Multi-Agent

text: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on challenging reasoning tasks (Yang et al., 2023; Hubert et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025), and by inte- grating with external tools, LLM-powered agents (Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Agashe et al., 2025) can proactively acquire information and revise actions in response to obser- vations. Multi-agent systems (Wu et al., 2024; Steinberger & OpenClaw Community, 2026; Nous Research, 2026; An- thropic, 2025; 2026d) further extend this approach by or- 1Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 2Apodex. Cor- respondence to: Bo An <boan@ntu.edu.sg>. Preprint. October 16, 2026. ganizing agents into complementary roles that distribute investigations, explore independent approaches, and verify candidate solutions. Directing these activities toward a com- mon goal requires orchestration (Zhang et al., 2025c; Ruan et al., 2026), which must reconcile local subtask execution that responds to emerging findings with global task plan- ning that maintains a structured decomposition and tracks dependencies across subtasks. Existing approaches address orchestration through struc- tured workflows or runtime delegation, but each sacrifices one side of this tradeoff. Structured workflows organize tasks into stages connected by explicit control flow, specify- ing when agents act and how they exchange results (Hong et al., 2024; LangChain, 2026). Whether authored manu- ally or generated automatically as in AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025b), these workflows impose clear global
title: HTN-Orchestrate: A Hierarchical Task Network Framework for Multi-Agent

text: connected by explicit control flow, specify- ing when agents act and how they exchange results (Hong et al., 2024; LangChain, 2026). Whether authored manu- ally or generated automatically as in AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025b), these workflows impose clear global structure but fix the decomposition before execution begins, so that find- ings from local execution cannot reshape subsequent plan- ning. Runtime delegation addresses this rigidity by having a central orchestrator determine subtasks and assign agents as execution proceeds (Fourney et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2026), with agent-team approaches (Kimi Team, 2026a; Apodex Team, 2026) further extending this to parallel subagent dis- patch. However, this design couples task decomposition, subtask dispatch, and result synthesis within a single orches- trator (Ruan et al., 2026; Kimi Team, 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025c), without explicitly modeling subtask hierarchies or precedence dependencies among sibling subtasks. Although dynamic decomposition methods such as ADaPT (Prasad et al., 2024) and ReAcTree (Choi et al., 2026) allow the plan to evolve during execution, they too provide limited support for representing complex dependencies, leaving the tension between adaptive local execution and structured global planning unresolved. text: 2.1. Multi-Agent Orchestration Multi-agent orchestration methods vary in how they dis- tribute responsibilities between global task planning and local execution, and most designs favor one side of this tradeoff. Early frameworks such as AutoGen (Wu et al., 2024) and MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2024) organize col- laboration through conversation patterns and role-based procedures that provide clear global structure but follow fixed interaction protocols. AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025b) and MaAS (Zhang et al., 2025a) reduce manual design effort by automating workflow and architecture construc- tion, while Conductor (Nielsen et al., 2026) and MAS- Orchestra (Ke et al., 2026) learn to generate orchestration decisions through reinforcement learning. Although these methods can discover effective coordination patterns, the resulting structures are determined before or independently of task execution. Runtime delegation shifts toward local adaptability by al- lowing an orchestrator to assign work as execution proceeds, with Magentic-One (Fourney et al., 2024) and AOrches- tra (Ruan et al., 2026) managing task progress through agent feedback. Kimi K2.5 (Kimi Team, 2026a) and Apodex 1.1 (Apodex Team, 2026) further support parallel subagents dynamically dispatched by a main agent, and such dispatch decisions can also be learned through policies for agent selection and tool invocation (Dang et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026). However, these approaches couple task decomposi- tion, subtask dispatch, and result synthesis within a
title: HTN-Orchestrate

text: main agent, and such dispatch decisions can also be learned through policies for agent selection and tool invocation (Dang et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026). However, these approaches couple task decomposi- tion, subtask dispatch, and result synthesis within a single orchestrator, without explicitly separating global planning from local execution management. Workforce, introduced with OWL (Hu et al., 2025a), addresses this by separating a domain-agnostic planner from a central coordinator that manages worker assignments and task dependencies. HTN- Orchestrate shares this separation but assigns a dedicated Orchestrator to each executable leaf subtask, while the Plan- ner maintains and incrementally expands the task network, allowing local coordination within each subtask to operate independently of global planning over the task hierarchy. 2.2. Task Decomposition The tension between local execution and global planning is particularly evident in task decomposition, where the chal- lenge is determining not only how to break a task apart but also when to revise that breakdown in response to execution findings. Static approaches commit to a full decomposition before observing results. Least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2023) generates subproblems before solving them sequentially, and Agent-Oriented Planning (Li et al., 2025) accounts for agent capabilities when decomposing and allo- cating tasks. D-CORE (Xu et al., 2026) uses reinforcement learning to incentivize decomposition reasoning in large reasoning models, and Select-Then-Decompose (Liu
title: HTN-Orchestrate

text: before solving them sequentially, and Agent-Oriented Planning (Li et al., 2025) accounts for agent capabilities when decomposing and allo- cating tasks. D-CORE (Xu et al., 2026) uses reinforcement learning to incentivize decomposition reasoning in large reasoning models, and Select-Then-Decompose (Liu et al., 2025) chooses a decomposition strategy according to the task. These methods improve the quality of decomposition but still finalize it before execution begins. When intermediate findings affect subsequent work, decom- position must also adapt during execution. Plan-and-Act (Er- dogan et al., 2025) trains models on planning trajectories and revises the plan after each executor step, ADaPT (Prasad et al., 2024) recursively decomposes tasks that resist direct execution, ReCAP (Zhang et al., 2025d) revises the remain- ing plan using execution results, and ReAcTree (Choi et al., 2026) organizes execution through hierarchical agent trees. TodoEvolve (Liu et al., 2026) extends adaptation to the planning architecture itself by learning to generate and re- vise task-specific planning systems. These methods allow plans to evolve but provide limited support for explicitly modeling precedence dependencies among subtasks. HTN- Orchestrate uses prerequisite results to inform the further decomposition of dependent subtasks, deferring decisions about their internal structure until the relevant evidence be- comes available. 2.3. Hierarchical Task Networks and Dependency-Aware Planning Explicit dependencies connect global planning with local execution by determining which results must be available before subsequent work can proceed. Hierarchical task net- works represent complex activities through task decompo- sition and constraints on the resulting subtasks (Erol et al., 1994), and recent work such as ChatHTN (Muñoz-Avila et al., 2025) combines this tradition with language mod- els by interleaving LLM-based decomposition with sym- bolic HTN planning. At a different level of granularity, LLMCompiler (Kim et al., 2024) constructs dependencies among function calls to schedule parallel execution, whereas FlowSearch (Hu et al., 2025b) models research as an evolv- ing graph of interdependent knowledge units and dynami- cally revises its structure in response to intermediate find- ings. HTN-Orchestrate distinguishes the parent-child rela- tion that defines a decomposition from precedence depen- dencies among sibling subtasks. The former determines how results are synthesized upward after all children complete, while the latter determines which prerequisite results are available for further decomposition and execution. At the upper layer, the Planner incrementally constructs a hierarchical task network that encodes subtask decomposi- tions and their dependencies, while at the lower layer, each executable leaf subtask is delegated to an Orchestrator that schedules workers and returns a result. Task Network Representation Following the HTN formulation (Erol et al., 1994), we rep- resent a task network as T = (V, Eh, Ed), whose root corresponds to q. The hierarchy edges Eh form a rooted tree in which each parent is decomposed into children that jointly address its task, and the dependency edges Ed im- pose acyclic precedence constraints among siblings, with an edge (u, v) indicating that v requires the result of u. We denote the children and direct prerequisites of v by Ch(v) and Pred(v), respectively. Unlike classical HTN planners that draw from a predefined library of decomposition rules, our Planner uses an LLM to generate decompositions during execution, which allows the network to grow incrementally as prerequisite results become available. Result-Informed Planning The Planner uses prerequisite execution results to guide sub- sequent task decomposition and retains accumulated find- ings to support replanning, as summarized in Algorithm 1. When execution fails or the returned findings indicate no plausible solution under the current task network, the Plan- ner can reconsider the decomposition through replanning. Each construction and execution of a task network consti- tutes an epoch, and before starting a new epoch the Planner settles or stops ongoing work and uses CollectEvidence to extract supported findings from completed and partial reports into an evidence summary M. This summary condi- tions the construction of a new network rooted at the original task, providing planning context rather than automatically marking any new subtask as completed, so that the next epoch can pursue a different decomposition while retaining useful evidence. The number of rebuilds is bounded, and the framework terminates through one of two paths. When the root node is resolved, its synthesized result is returned directly as the final answer. When execution budgets are exhausted before the task is resolved, the framework instead synthesizes the evidence obtained so far and reports any un- resolved requirements, so the output reflects the sufficiency of the evidence rather than treating the stopping condition as task success. 3.3. Multi-Agent Orchestration For each executable leaf v, an Orchestrator manages the workers needed to address that subtask (Algorithm 2). Work- ers carry out targeted research, reasoning, or verification using their configured tools, while the Orchestrator decides how the investigation should proceed based on their reports. Each Orchestrator receives a stable context Cv containing the original task, the leaf’s objective, relevant ancestor de- scriptions, and prerequisite result summaries, and during execution it maintains the set of returned worker reports Rv and active assignments Av. At each decision point, the Orchestrator considers Cv, Rv, and Av and chooses to dispatch workers, wait for progress, or finish the subtask. A dispatch decision selects worker roles and produces task-specific instructions based on the current evidence, so an initial investigation can be followed by a focused search or a verification step when a report reveals a gap or a disputed claim. Reports are collected as workers finish, allowing the Orchestrator to schedule follow- up work while other assignments remain active, or to wait for new reports when the outstanding questions are already covered. This progressive collection of results allows local decisions to respond to evidence within a wave, while

Empirical Evaluations 4.1. Experimental Setup We evaluate HTN-Orchestrate on five benchmarks covering web research, scientific reasoning, and research workflows. BrowseComp (BC) (Wei et al., 2025) tests an agent’s ability to locate hard-to-find information through persistent web browsing. For scientific reasoning and research, we use both tracks of FrontierScience (Wang et al., 2026), with FrontierScience-Research (FSR) comprising open-ended re- search subproblems and FrontierScience-Olympiad (FSO) assessing olympiad-level reasoning in physics, chemistry, and biology. We use the text-only subset of 256 questions from SUPERChem (Zhao et al., 2025) to further evalu- ate multistep reasoning across chemistry subfields, while PRL-Bench (Miao et al., 2026) extends the evaluation to theoretical and computational physics research tasks derived from published papers. We report accuracy for BC, FSO, and SUPERChem, where answers can be directly verified against ground truth. For the rubric-based benchmarks, we report the success rate for FSR, defined as the fraction of responses earning at least seven

text: published papers. We report accuracy for BC, FSO, and SUPERChem, where answers can be directly verified against ground truth. For the rubric-based benchmarks, we report the success rate for FSR, defined as the fraction of responses earning at least seven of ten rubric points, and the mean percentage of satisfied rubric criteria on a 0–100 scale for PRL-Bench. We compare HTN-Orchestrate with the ReAct and Agent Team workflows implemented in FrontierAgent (Apodex Team, 2026).2 The ReAct baseline (Yao et al., 2023) uses a single agent that alternates reasoning and tool use, incor- porating observations into subsequent actions. Agent Team uses a main agent to decompose the task, dispatch subagents in parallel, and integrate their reports as execution proceeds. We also include DeepSeek Harness (DSH) (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a), DeepSeek’s official agent runtime in Minimal Mode, a single-agent configuration with a persistent shell and file editor, to which we add web search tools for BrowseComp. All four methods use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the back- bone model with high reasoning effort. In HTN-Orchestrate, workers instead use low reasoning effort and operate in two complementary roles for research and verification. Main Results HTN-Orchestrate outperforms all three controlled baselines on every benchmark and is competitive with frontier propri- etary models despite using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, an open- weight model, as its backbone (Table 2). On BrowseComp, it achieves 89.73% accuracy, exceeding ReAct by 15.80 percentage points and Agent Team by 2.45 points. Only GPT-6 Astra (91.50%), Kimi K3 (91.20%), and GPT-5.6 Sol (90.40%) score higher, all of which are frontier-scale mod- els. Agent Team, which dispatches subagents without hier- archical planning, already exceeds ReAct by 13.35 points, confirming that multi-agent execution is broadly beneficial for persistent web research. To isolate the contribution of each com- ponent, we evaluate three ablated variants, removing result- informed planning, local multi-agent orchestration, and task- network rebuilding in turn while preserving the remaining mechanisms (Appendix C gives detailed definitions and ex- tended results). All three reduce accuracy (Table 4), but with distinct effects on execution behavior (Figure 4; counts cover all epochs, with No rebuilding restricted to its single epoch). Upfront decomposition is the most direct test of the central mechanism because it changes only whether decomposi- tion occurs before or after prerequisite results return, while retaining dependency-based execution, local multi-agent or- chestration, and rebuilding. Without current-epoch research results to narrow subsequent decomposition, accuracy de- creases from 92.0% to 90.5%. This less targeted planning also increases coordination effort at the median, with worker invocations rising from 14 to 16, Orchestrator rounds from 14 to 17, and the rebuilding rate from 17.5% to 22.5%. Me- dian completion time also rises from 25.23 to 30.02 minutes. The full system therefore achieves higher accuracy with less coordination and lower latency, indicating that intermediate findings guide more effective task decomposition. Less effective research within indi- vidual leaves shifts more of the burden to the Planner, which compensates by spawning additional subtasks and rebuild- ing more frequently. The full system combines higher accu- racy with fewer leaf executions and less frequent rebuilding, highlighting how local orchestration supports global task resolution. No rebuilding disables task-network reconstruction while preserving result-informed planning within the initial epoch. Accuracy decreases to 89.5%, and because the system can no longer trigger a second epoch, average execution activity also falls, with executed leaf instances dropping from 4.67 to 4.12 per question and worker invocations from 23.16 to 19.01. The full system’s higher accuracy therefore comes at the cost of this additional research, which the rebuilding mechanism makes possible by retaining findings and revis- ing the task network when the initial decomposition cannot resolve the task. After identifying the supplement and its four authors, HTN- Orchestrate incorporates their names into a newly generated task that checks which author wrote a children’s book in 2015. The upfront decomposition variant instead speci- fies an independent search for children’s-book authors with role-playing-game credits, followed by a separate task to reconcile the two candidate sets. Both runs reach the correct answer, but the result-informed plan narrows the down- stream search to the returned author list and executes four leaves rather than five. Figure 6 illustrates task-network rebuilding on Q501. The initial search does not locate the target music-blog post. HTN-Orchestrate retains candidate albums, recurring week- day features, and rejected posts, then rebuilds the network with an additional feature-based search and an explicit album-to-list matching task. Research continues until the post-search branch locates the target article and verifies its song list. The final answer is Serial Killer by Tobin Sprout, while No rebuilding returns Silent Night. text: We presented HTN-Orchestrate, a two-layer orchestration framework that separates global task planning from local multi-agent execution. Its upper layer maintains a hierar- chical task network that decomposes incrementally as pre- requisite findings become available and can be rebuilt when the initial plan proves insufficient, while its lower layer coordinates multiple workers within each executable sub- task. On five benchmarks spanning web research, scientific reasoning, and research workflows, HTN-Orchestrate con- sistently outperforms ReAct, Agent Team, and DeepSeek Harness. Ablation studies on BrowseComp suggest that result-informed planning, local multi-agent orchestration, and task-network rebuilding each contribute to this advan- tage, with execution traces revealing interdependence be- tween the two layers. These findings show that separating control across two layers while feeding results back through a shared, revisable task structure allows each layer to inform the other and strengthens both. Future work includes scal- ing the task-network depth for problems that require deeper decomposition hierarchies and evaluating the framework across additional backbone models. text: External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present Hy-Memory- 30B-A3B, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5. huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-Memory-30B-A3B github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-Memory 1

text: A long-term memory system for an LLM application usually contains three functional stages: (1) a writer converts an interaction into persistent memory operations; (2) a retriever selects records relevant to a future query; and (3) a reader or answer model uses the retrieved records to respond. Systems such as Mem0, A-MEM, MemoryOS, and MemOS have expanded the design space of persis- tent memory through extraction, consolidation, hierarchical paging, linking, versioning, and lifecycle management (Chhikara et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Benchmarks such as LoCoMo and LongMemEval have also shown that long-term memory is not a single retrieval problem: it includes precise extraction, multi-session composition, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Despite this progress, the write policy is commonly implemented by placing a general-purpose LLM behind a long, framework-specific prompt. That model must simultaneously distinguish durable user information from greetings, assistant suggestions, and transient text; preserve exact names, numbers, versions, dates, paths, and other identifying details; represent a state transition without losing either the new state or what it replaced; reconcile new evidence with retrieved memories already in the bank; and emit valid operations under the framework’s schema and control flow. The framework cannot recover information that the writer omitted, and a powerful downstream
title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for

text: new state or what it replaced; reconcile new evidence with retrieved memories already in the bank; and emit valid operations under the framework’s schema and control flow. The framework cannot recover information that the writer omitted, and a powerful downstream reader cannot reliably infer a fact that was never stored. Conversely, indiscriminately storing everything increases cost and retrieval interference. The desired writer is therefore not a generic summarizer: it is a policy for changing an external state under a long-horizon downstream objective. Recent work has begun to train memory operations with reinforcement learning. Memory-R1 trains a memory manager and an answer agent with final-answer rewards (Yan et al., 2025). MemAgent learns recurrent textual compression from a terminal verifier (Yu et al., 2026). Mem-α combines downstream QA correctness with format, compression, and operation-quality rewards (Wang et al., 2025). MemCoE 1 arXiv:2610.22196v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026
title: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for

text: explicitly identifies sparse outcome reward as a weakness and adds guideline-aligned process feedback (Xu et al., 2026). These studies establish that memory behavior is learnable rather than fixed. They also expose a remaining problem: a final answer score usually supervises an entire sequence of heterogeneous memory actions, even though only a few actions supplied the evidence—or caused the failure. Hy-Memory-30B-A3B focuses on this credit-assignment problem while preserving compatibility with existing memory frameworks. Our contributions are: • A framework-integrated memory writer. Hy3-30B-A3B replaces the LLM inside Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory without moving their memory logic into a custom model architecture. • State-distribution-aligned training. OPD and RL both execute the policy inside the actual harness, and later writes observe banks produced by earlier policy outputs. • Failure-surface reward data. Training questions are constructed from concrete write failures, including omission, lost specificity, semantic inversion, stale-state confusion, secondary-fact loss, and over-storage. • Attributed, non-binary feedback. Local probes provide dense per-chunk evidence, while cross- chunk outcome questions use gold facts to map recovered evidence back to source chunks. • Chunk-level policy optimization. Advantages are normalized among rollouts at the same chunk position rather than over whole trajectories, so one rollout can be credited at one chunk and penalized at another. Each rollout casts one vote per chunk even when a framework makes multiple LLM calls.

Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on Mem0, Hy-Memory, MemOS, and held-out EverMemOS, averaging 55.49% across the four harnesses versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 External memory systems and evaluation Mem0 uses incremental extraction and consolidation to maintain a persistent memory store (Chhikara et al., 2025). A-MEM organizes memories as dynamically linked notes whose attributes and relationships evolve as new information arrives (Xu et al., 2025). MemoryOS introduces an operating-system-inspired hierarchical storage architecture that coordinates short-term, mid-term, and long-term personal memory through dialogue-chain FIFO and segmented page updates (Kang et al., 2025). MemOS treats memory as a managed system resource and emphasizes representation, scheduling, provenance, and lifecycle control (Li et al., 2025). These systems differ in schema and control flow, but all depend on an LLM to interpret new interactions and produce valid operations. DCPM argues that long-term memory should support more than surface recall: its dual-process architec- ture represents belief revisions, identity, schemas, latent intentions, and cross-domain abstractions in a capability hierarchy (Fei et al., 2026b). This direction is complementary to

DCPM argues that long-term memory should support more than surface recall: its dual-process architec- ture represents belief revisions, identity, schemas, latent intentions, and cross-domain abstractions in a capability hierarchy (Fei et al., 2026b). This direction is complementary to ours. DCPM redesigns the memory architecture and its evolution process, whereas Hy-Memory-30B-A3B trains a reusable writer that operates inside several existing memory architectures without replacing them. LoCoMo evaluates conversations containing hundreds of turns and multiple sessions, with questions requiring single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and adversarial reasoning (Maharana et al., 2024). LongMemEval decomposes conversational memory into information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge update, and abstention (Wu et al., 2025). Together, these benchmarks motivate evaluating the full memory pipeline rather than the fluency of an extracted summary. Our work draws two conclusions from this literature. First, memory quality must be measured down- stream, after retrieval. Second, a useful reward dataset must cover distinct failure modes rather than collapsing all memory behavior into one generic QA score. 2.2 Reinforcement learning for memory There are two related but distinct lines of memory RL. 2

Recurrent compression agents. MemAgent processes a long document in chunks, repeatedly overwrites a bounded textual memory, and applies a final verifiable answer reward to all generated conversations (Yu et al., 2026). This trains a model-native long-context mechanism, but the memory representation and inference loop are part of the learned architecture. External-bank management. Memory-R1 learns ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, and NOOP operations, and also trains an answer agent that filters retrieved memories (Yan et al., 2025). Mem-α formulates memory construction as a sequence of operations over a multi-component bank and combines global QA correctness with local format and semantic-validity rewards (Wang et al., 2025). MemCoE uses
title: Learned policy and environment

text: answer agent that filters retrieved memories (Yan et al., 2025). Mem-α formulates memory construction as a sequence of operations over a multi-component bank and combines global QA correctness with local format and semantic-validity rewards (Wang et al., 2025). MemCoE uses an induced guideline to construct denser process feedback because final answer rewards alone are sparse over long memory-evolution trajectories (Xu et al., 2026). Hy-Memory-30B-A3B belongs to the second line but differs in scope. It trains the writer only, keeps the reader fixed during reward computation, and targets multiple pre-existing harnesses rather than one newly designed memory architecture. If the writer and answer model are optimized together, a better answer can come from improved reading rather than improved memory. Table 1 summarizes the distinction. State separation also appears outside memory-specific agents. CodeDelegator separates persistent orchestration state from ephemeral execution sandboxes to prevent debugging traces and intermediate failures from polluting long-horizon planning context (Fei et al., 2026a). Our setting has a related systems requirement: candidate rollouts must write to isolated banks, while only the selected bank persists across windows. Unlike CodeDelegator, however, our separation is used for on-policy credit assignment over memory writes rather than role-specialized code execution. 2.3 Why ordinary outcome-only RL is insufficient LLM RL commonly assigns a scalar reward to a whole completion. text: our separation is used for on-policy credit assignment over memory writes rather than role-specialized code execution. 2.3 Why ordinary outcome-only RL is insufficient LLM RL commonly assigns a scalar reward to a whole completion. PPO stabilizes policy updates with a clipped surrogate (Schulman et al., 2017), while GRPO replaces a learned critic with a baseline estimated from grouped samples (Shao et al., 2024). This works well when the completion is a single solution and the final verifier is informative. A memory trajectory violates both assumptions. A write in an early session may matter only when a much later question asks about it, so most writes receive no direct evidence. Giving the final QA score to every write rewards irrelevant actions and penalizes correct writes that co-occur with one bad action. Binary exact match often makes every rollout in a small GRPO group receive the same score, producing zero advantage and no task gradient; this has also been observed in memory-grounded QA (He et al., 2026). Jointly improving the answer agent can raise QA accuracy while the bank remains incomplete or noisy. An action changes the bank seen by later actions, so examples are not independent prompts. One write may invoke one LLM call while another invokes several, so a row-level baseline can weight call count rather than decision quality. Recall-only

This is on-policy at two levels: tokens are sampled from the current writer, and future prompts are generated from banks produced by that writer. 5 Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback 5.1 Why benchmark questions are not enough Using only final questions from a long-memory benchmark creates a low-density learning problem. A long interaction sequence may contain hundreds of useful facts but only a few questions. An unasked write receives no evidence, and a failed answer does not identify whether the cause was omission, bad wording, stale-state confusion, retrieval failure, or reader failure. Binary exact match further collapses semantically partial answers and can eliminate variance within a small GRPO group (He et al., 2026). We construct reward items from the failure surface of memory writing, not merely from a list of benchmark answers. 5.2 Chronological segmentation Interaction sequences retain session boundaries and chronological order. Each session is segmented independently into chunks of roughly ten turns, so a chunk never crosses a session boundary. The resulting chunks are flattened into one chronological stream; up to five consecutive chunks form one RL window, which may span sessions. Windows from the same sequence are consumed in order, and the selected policy-written bank from

text: a session boundary. The resulting chunks are flattened into one chronological stream; up to five consecutive chunks form one RL window, which may span sessions. Windows from the same sequence are consumed in order, and the selected policy-written bank from one window initializes the next. This preserves long-range state transitions while keeping each optimization step bounded. 5.3 Two annotation passes Local write quality and long-range memory utility require different context, so the two reward types are annotated in separate passes (Table 3). Why the PRM pass sees the two preceding chunks. A per-chunk probe must test information that chunk t itself introduced. Annotating chunk t in isolation fails in two ways. Coreference: mentions such as “that project” or “the same reviewer” cannot be resolved, so the annotator cannot write self-contained questions about them. Novelty: the annotator cannot tell whether a statement is new in chunk t or repeats something already established, so probes would credit chunk t for facts it did not introduce. The extracted facts of chunks t−1 and t−2 supply the referents and the recently established state. They are given as facts rather than raw text and serve as context only: no probe is generated from them, and they earn no credit for chunk t. 6

We add trap probes about content that should not have entered long-term memory, such as an assistant’s generic encouragement. Their reference answer is that the bank contains no such record. If the writer stores the irrelevant statement, retrieval exposes it and the answer becomes incorrect. Traps and the bank-growth penalty are complementary. A size penalty discourages indiscriminate volume, while traps directly test semantic selectivity. A model cannot avoid the trap merely by compressing irrelevant text into a shorter entry. 5.6 Rubrics and gold-fact attribution Each probe and outcome question contains weighted credit points with semantic equivalents; explicit full-, partial-, and zero-credit bands; named distractors, including stale or superseded values; evidence chunk ids;

The answer judge performs semantic matching; code only aggregates returned credit. Gold facts are visible only to the outcome judge. They are not inserted into the bank, retrieval query, or answer-model prompt. Facts from earlier windows may provide context but are marked history-only and cannot generate credit for a current chunk. 5.7 Data verification Reward data must be tested as an instrument, not accepted because it is well-formed JSON. Four layers are enforced. Schema validity removes records with missing fields, unnormalized weights, illegal evidence ids, or illegal grading bands. Causal locality requires per-chunk probes to refer to the current chunk and cross- chunk questions to contain multi-chunk evidence when required. Rubric independence checks that credit points do not entail one another and that distractors represent real failure modes. Discriminability checks that the judge scores five synthetic answers per item in the expected order: reference and paraphrase receive full credit, a partial answer receives partial credit, and a distractor or refusal receives zero credit. text: (Shao et al., 2024). Standard GRPO scores each sampled trajectory once, normalizes that score within the group, and applies the resulting advantage to every token of the trajectory. A trajectory-level group is not appropriate here: all eight rollouts share the same bank only at chunk 0; after that, rollout i observes the bank created by its own earlier actions, and a single trajectory score would again broadcast one judgment over all of its writes. We instead compute advantages per chunk, grouping by window, harness configuration, sequence, and chunk position: Ai,t = si[t] −µt σt + ϵ , (7) where µt and σt are the mean and standard deviation of sj[t] over the chunk-level group Gt. The best rollout can therefore differ from chunk to chunk: rollout 1 may have the highest score at chunk 2 while rollout 3 is best at chunk 4, and each chunk’s writes are reinforced or suppressed according to their own column (Figure 1). Each rollout contributes one vote to the baseline for a chunk. If a multi-stage harness made three LLM calls for that chunk, all three segments receive the same advantage but do not count as three independent observations. Otherwise the policy could alter the baseline by changing its call count. Groups with fewer than two valid rollouts receive zero advantage. 6.8 Bank carry-forward

Groups with fewer than two valid rollouts receive zero advantage. 6.8 Bank carry-forward Bank selection is a separate, rollout-level decision. At the end of a window, the eight final banks are ranked by ∑t s[t]. The winner becomes the initial state of the next window in that sequence; the others are discarded. If all candidates fail because of platform faults, the previous bank is reused. Bank state is checkpointed with model state. An inherited error from an earlier optimizer step cannot receive retrospective gradient. Carrying imperfect policy-written banks is still preferable to teacher forcing with an ideal bank: deployment also requires the writer to operate on its own prior mistakes. An inherited error common to all candidates also tends to cancel in the group-relative baseline rather than being assigned to the current chunk. 7 Training System Each harness is packaged behind a common interface: bank_open, write, search, bank_stats, and bank_close. For each comparison, the harness version and prompts are fixed, retrieval configuration is fixed, and the answer model, judge, and other framework-side components are held fixed. Throughout this report, every reference to a DeepSeek Flash endpoint denotes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Decoding settings are matched where APIs permit, each writer builds its own bank from an empty state, and test examples and scoring rules are identical. This is necessary because memory quality is otherwise confounded with retrieval depth, reader capability, auxiliary-model capability, or a pre-existing bank. Sampled benchmark matrix. Relative to Opus 5, it gains 0.60 points on Mem0, 0.02 on Hy-Memory, 0.01 on MemOS, and 2.86 on EverMemOS, for a macro-average gain of 0.87 points. Relative to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, it gains 4.29 points on Mem0, 0.35 on Hy-Memory, 1.34 on MemOS, and 1.42 on EverMemOS, for a macro-average gain of 1.85 points. Relative to the Hy3-A3B base checkpoint, the macro average improves by 7.84 points. The 0.01–0.02 point margins on MemOS and Hy-Memory indicate parity with Opus 5 under this deterministic sampled evaluation, not a statistically resolved difference. String rules that graded semantics produced a plausible aggregate reward; semantic conditions belong in judge rubrics, not substring code. A “read all” that silently paginated made the bank entry count plateau at a default limit; pagination and token accounting must be tested explicitly. Failed writes checkpointed as empty were marked complete; platform faults must be retryable and excluded from denominators. Sandboxes that shared a trajectory identity completed requests attached to the wrong rollout; every request must validate bank and trajectory identity. Malformed output treated as an environment error made bad actions disappear from training; policy mistakes should remain valid low-reward trajectories. The governing rule is: a bad policy action must receive low reward; a platform failure must not be misrepresented as policy behavior. 10 Limitations and Future Work Attribution is evidence-based rather than counterfactual: recovered gold facts do not prove that a specific write caused an answer. text: Memory writing is a long-horizon control problem over an external state, not merely a summarization prompt. Hy-Memory-30B-A3B first learns to operate real memory harnesses through on-policy distillation, then optimizes the answerability and selectivity of the banks it creates through Memory RL. The central technical contribution is the reward interface: failure-driven probes make supervision dense, cross-chunk questions measure downstream utility, gold facts attribute that utility to source chunks, traps and growth penalties close the store-everything shortcut, and chunk-level GRPO compares actions at the correct decision boundary. Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on Mem0, Hy-Memory, MemOS, and held-out EverMemOS. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, it averages 55.49% across six metrics and four harnesses, ahead of Claude Opus 5 at 54.62%, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 53.64%, and the Hy3-A3B base checkpoint at 47.66%. The OOD EverMemOS result provides the clearest margin over Opus 5 (+2.86 points). Together, these results support memory writing as a transferable model capability rather than a collection of framework-specific prompt heuristics. text: 2026-10-16 OpenGCUA: Toward a Fully Open Stack for Generalist Computer Use Hanzhang Zhou*, Long Li*, Quyu Kong*, Lei Wang*, Panrong Tong*, Long Chen, Tianyu Xia, Gongjie Zhang, Xu Zhang, Chen Liu, Jianan Zhang, Chenglin Cai, Zhengwen Zeng, Steven Hoi, Yue Wang† Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group OpenGCUA GitHub Project Website & Interactive Lab

Computer use has reached a turning point: the focus is expanding from GUI-only interaction to systems that complete tasks on users’ computers through visual and programmatic interfaces. We define a generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) as a system in which the model chooses how to observe, act, and organize its work across visual and programmatic interfaces. Yet frontier implementations, such as GPT-6 Astra’s computer-use system, remain largely closed, limiting systematic study of their design. We introduce Open Generalist CUA (OpenGCUA), an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for GCUAs with the community. This report presents the first release of Open Generalist CUA. Code execution is a key feature of our agent design: it lets intermediate results determine subsequent operations and enables models to apply their existing programming capabilities directly to computer interaction. We also propose harness-to-model decision transfer, moving selected observations and task-state decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. On OSWorld-v2, our full configuration improves task scores across all eight evaluated models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, raising mean partial score by +19.6 points and reducing reported steps per task by an average of 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. We release our implementation and prompts, evaluation trajectories from all eight models, and preliminary versions of a real-device harness and a cross-device SDK. The

text: Computer use has moved to the center of attention. The GPT-6 Astra release places strong emphasis on computer use, with extensive demonstrations offering an exciting vision of what computer-use agents could make possible (OpenAI, 2026c). Much of the literature studies computer-use agents (CUAs) as GUI- only agents, asking how well models can complete computer tasks through screenshot-based observation and mouse and keyboard actions (Qin et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). Recent frontier systems, however, combine GUI interaction with shell commands, accessibility-tree access, and other tools, and OpenAI now recommends code execution, writing GUI operations as code and combining them with programmatic operations in a single model output (OpenAI, 2026b). These systems also target tasks on users’ own computers, where shared control, interaction with background windows, and evolving requests introduce challenges not fully captured by benchmarks. The question has changed, from how well a model operates a GUI interface to how well a system completes work on a real computer by whatever means works. We take this as a turning point in computer-use research, motivating a clearer definition of these broader agents and a systematic study of their design. We therefore adopt the term generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) to characterize this broader class of systems, following the system-level perspective of Agents’ Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026). We therefore adopt the term generalist computer-use agent (GCUA) to characterize this broader class of systems, following the system-level perspective of Agents’ Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026). GPT-6 Astra’s computer-use system is a representative GCUA. We define a GCUA as an agent system designed to complete diverse computer tasks through both visual interaction and programmatic access, in which the model decides how to observe, act, and organize its work as the task requires. Programmatic access includes shell commands, accessibility APIs, and application or service APIs where available. Essentially, a GCUA chooses how to use the computer to complete a task, rather than being restricted to GUI interaction. Our previous work, Qwen-UI-Agent, began exploring this direction through a unified GUI and CLI action space with batched actions (Zhou et al., 2026). Within our formulation, such GUI+CLI hybrid CUA is a special case of GCUA (Section 2). How to design such systems is an open question. A GCUA raises design questions that go beyond those of GUI-only agents: which interfaces to give the model, how to support code execution, which decisions to leave to the model and which to the harness, and what changes when the agent runs on a user’s own computer. text: the model, how to support code execution, which decisions to leave to the model and which to the harness, and what changes when the agent runs on a user’s own computer. However, frontier systems such as GPT-6 Astra remain largely closed (OpenAI, 2026a). Their model weights, full prompting setups, real-device harnesses, device-control SDKs, and execution trajectories are not available. This limits the community’s ability to reproduce system behavior, compare alternative designs, and investigate how design choices and execution mechanisms affect task completion and cost, particularly under real-device conditions. We therefore introduce Open Generalist CUA (OpenGCUA), an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for generalist computer use with the community (Figure 2): (1) Model. Develop a model that unifies computer and browser use, with code execution and harness-to-model decision transfer central to its agent design. (2) System. A real-device harness that runs on users’ real machines, and lessons we learned in moving from benchmark harnesses to real-device deployment. A cross-device SDK that gives agent programs one interface to computers, browsers, and phones, supporting tasks that span multiple devices. (3) Trajectories. Release trajectories from evaluations of frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra to support analysis of code-execution and harness-to-model decision transfer patterns. (4) Efficiency. Systematically study and improve GCUA execution efficiency through code-execution, concise model reasoning, and harness optimization,

text: (3) Trajectories. Release trajectories from evaluations of frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra to support analysis of code-execution and harness-to-model decision transfer patterns. (4) Efficiency. Systematically study and improve GCUA execution efficiency through code-execution, concise model reasoning, and harness optimization, while exploring broader system-level improvements. (5) Evaluation. Develop evaluation environments and benchmarks on real devices, particularly on macOS, to assess agents’ ability to complete tasks under real-world operating conditions. This report presents the first release of the OpenGCUA project. The release does not yet include a trained model. The report covers agent design and evaluation, execution trajectories from frontier models, and preliminary versions of the real-device harness and cross-device SDK, together with a roadmap for subsequent releases. We release the implementation, prompts, and evaluation trajectories of all eight frontier models (Section 3). • Code execution adds value beyond shell access. With the same GUI and shell access, writing GUI operations as code and combining them with programmatic operations adds 6.1 points to the mean partial score and cuts steps per task by 14.8% against the GUI+CLI baseline. Code execution offers two advantages: intermediate results can decide the next operation without another model call, and models can bring their existing programming ability directly to computer interaction. We further identify five recurring patterns of code execution in our case study (Section 3.1). • Harness control should move into the model as models improve. Harnesses fix many workflow decisions by rule, such as taking a screenshot after every step. We propose harness-to-model decision transfer, which delegates these harness decisions to the model. In the current implementation, the model decides when to request screenshots and how to track task state. It also states each program’s purpose before execution. The preliminary Cross-Device SDK binds every operation to an explicit device, application, window, or tab, keeps accessibility and vision as separate ways to observe and act, and allows one program to coordinate several devices within a task (Section 4.2). This release does not mark the project’s completion, and the harness and SDK remain preliminary. Section 5 outlines our research plans and release milestones for Open Generalist CUA. 2 Generalist CUA: Definition and Positioning 2.1 Definition Agents’ Last Exam takes a system-level view and decomposes an agent into five layers: the model (Brain), GUI perception (Eyes), orchestration (Body), tools (Hands), and a runtime (Feet) (Sun et al., 2026). Under this view, a CLI agent lacks GUI perception, a GUI agent lacks most of the remaining layers, and a generalist agent spans all five. Having all five layers, however, only means an agent can act through both the GUI and the CLI; it does not mean that the agent chooses well between them. At a given step, an agent may click through a dozen screens to do what a single shell command would do, or run a script when it first needs to look at the screen. The layer view cannot tell such an agent apart from one that picks the right way

text: dozen screens to do what a single shell command would do, or run a script when it first needs to look at the screen. The layer view cannot tell such an agent apart from one that picks the right way to act at each step. In this report, we therefore define a generalist CUA (GCUA) by the decisions it makes at each step, not by the components it contains. A GCUA makes three decisions at each step: what to observe, how to act, and how to organize. • What to Observe. The observation can be a screenshot, an accessibility tree (AX Tree), the output of a command, the response of an API, or any combination of these. The model decides which it needs, including whether it needs a new screenshot at all. • How to Act. The action can be a GUI operation at a screen coordinate, an operation on an accessibility element, a shell command, an API call, or a program that combines several of these. The model decides which fits the step. • How to Organize. Across steps, the agent keeps a plan, tracks what has been done, and decides which past observations stay in context. Most harnesses fix these as rules set by the developer. In a GCUA, the model makes these decisions as the task requires.

In a GCUA, the model makes these decisions as the task requires. Four Interfaces. The first two decisions range over four interfaces to the computer, and each offers both a way to observe and a way to act. • GUI. The agent sees a screenshot and clicks, drags, scrolls, or types at a screen coordinate. This is the interface that always works, since every application has pixels. • Accessibility Tree. The agent reads the elements of a window, with their roles, names, and values, and operates on an element directly. It needs no coordinate, does not bring the window to the front, and never moves the user’s pointer on real devices. • CLI. The agent runs shell commands and reads their output. This is the natural route for files, data, and software. • API. The agent calls external services, such as web search, and reads their responses. This reaches what neither the screen nor the shell can. Each interface offers both a way to observe and a way to act, and each has its own strength. No single interface is best for every step, so what matters is choosing the right one

Code Execution versus Batched Actions. With batched actions, each model call yields a list of actions that were fixed when the call was generated: the model must decide every click before it sees the result of the first one. With code execution, each model call yields a program, and control flow is decided while the program runs. Three things become possible in a single call that were impossible before: a condition (if the dialog is visible, dismiss it), a loop (for each row, fill the three fields), and a verification (assert the status now reads Saved). A task that took a dozen round trips becomes one. This is also why batched actions, which our earlier work introduced (Zhou et al., 2026), are a stepping stone rather than an endpoint: a batch is a program without control flow. 2.4 Efficiency as a First-Class Metric Success rate remains our primary measure, but it does not capture the resources required to complete a task. For interactive tasks, an important threshold is reached when delegation delivers results sooner than manual execution, potentially saving both human effort and time to completion. For interactive tasks, an important threshold is reached when delegation delivers results sooner than manual execution, potentially saving both human effort and time to completion. We therefore evaluate efficiency using four metrics: steps per task, output tokens, reasoning tokens, and cost. Each step is one model call, which may generate multiple actions through batching or code execution. Fewer steps reduce model-call overhead, while fewer output tokens can lower generation time and cost. Reasoning tokens are included in output tokens but reported separately. When reasoning accounts for a large share of output, reducing unnecessary reasoning can improve efficiency without shortening the executable code, provided task performance is maintained. We compute cost from input and output token usage at each model’s published prices, including cache discounts. 3 Agent Design: Code Execution and Harness-to-Model Decision Transfer This section studies two behaviors we aim to develop in GCUA models. This release does not introduce a trained model. Instead, we study how the prompts, tool interfaces, and execution runtime of Open Generalist CUA support these behaviors in existing frontier models. We first explain the design and illustrate it with execution trajectories, then evaluate its effects on task completion and cost. 3.1 Code Execution over GUI and CLI Code execution gives graphical interaction and programmatic operations a unified executable form. The model writes a program in which GUI actions, such as pyautogui.click(), can be combined with shell commands and Python computation. The model can therefore specify not only what operations to perform, but also how execution should proceed. Loops and conditional logic allow the program to repeat operations and choose subsequent actions based on intermediate results, without requiring a new model call for each operation. text: 3.1.3 Limits of Visual-Only Feedback Result-dependent control is harder when interface observations are limited to screenshots. Conditions such as whether a button is enabled or an input field contains the expected value are not directly exposed as program-readable values, so checking them may require another model call. Accessibility trees can expose text and control states as structured data, allowing programs to query supported interface properties and use them in loops and conditional logic. This motivates combining visual observation with accessibility-tree access in our real-device harness design. 3.2 Harness-to-Model Decision Transfer Code execution addresses how to act by allowing the model to express computer operations as programs. A GCUA must also decide what to observe and how to organize its work. We study harness-to-model decision transfer: replacing selected fixed harness rules with task-dependent model decisions. A screenshot, for example, may be necessary after a GUI action but redundant when program output already answers the relevant question. Deciding whether to request it should depend on the information needed to continue. Mechanism in the Harness, Decision in the Model. As models become more capable, we envision progressively shifting selected workflow decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. The harness should provide reliable mechanisms, while the model decides when and how to use them based on the task and available evidence. In the

In the current implementation, screenshot requests and task-state updates are model-initiated workflow operations, complemented by model-generated action-intent annotations. The harness continues to execute interface calls, preserve task records, and manage context retention. 3.2.1 Mechanisms for Harness-to-Model Decision Transfer On-Demand Observation. The screenshot function lets the model decide whether its next input needs a new screenshot. It can request visual feedback after a GUI action or continue without it when text output is sufficient. On-demand observation can reduce context length by omitting screenshots that add little information. The environment still captures a screenshot after every step, so the mechanism changes what the model receives, not what the environment records. Task-State Tracking. The todo interface lets the model maintain a persistent record of progress, facts, and unresolved questions. It updates this record through todo.update() and retrieves it through todo.list(). Statuses distinguish pending work, attempted changes, unverified changes, and claimed verification, helping the model track what still needs checking. These entries record the model’s assess- ment rather than independently verifying the environment. Action Intent. The intent annotation makes the purpose of each code-execution step explicit.

These entries record the model’s assess- ment rather than independently verifying the environment. Action Intent. The intent annotation makes the purpose of each code-execution step explicit. Before each program runs, the model provides a short <intent> block stating what the code is intended to accomplish. A program may combine many operations, making its overall purpose difficult to infer from the code alone. In real-device use, the harness can display this description to users, helping them understand what the agent is trying to do at each step without reading the program. Harness-Managed Context. The harness manages historical tool outputs and screenshots through two fixed policies. A rolling screenshot buffer removes older images in batches, limiting visual context while reducing disruption to prompt caching (Anthropic, 2026a). Micro-compaction applies a similar rolling-buffer policy to textual tool outputs, replacing older outputs with short placeholders in batches while retaining recent results. Its next input contains text output and a new screenshot. The following program inspects event styles without requesting another image, so the next input contains text feedback but no new screenshot. Final benchmark scores alone do not show how much performance is available under limited resources. We therefore examine monetary and time constraints using the same selected full-setting runs as the main evaluation on the offline subset of OSWorld-v2. Measuring Performance under Resource Limits. We retrospectively apply a common spending cap to every task. A trajectory contributes its recorded final partial score only if its full cost fits within the cap; otherwise, it contributes zero. We estimate spending by assuming that each attempt ends when its recorded trajectory finishes or its spending cap is reached, whichever comes first. Spending on unsuccessful attempts is also included. Figure 7(a) plots the resulting score against average expenditure per task, not the cap itself. Panel (b) applies the same scoring rule to a per-task time limit. Scores are averaged over all tasks. Notably, recorded wall-clock time depends on API bandwidth and rate limits, the number of concurrently active evaluation environments, provider-side queuing, and tool execution latency. These conditions were not controlled across models, limiting the comparability of the measurements.

Such settings simplify evaluation but do not fully capture the demands of operating a user’s computer. We highlight five requirements that become especially important when the agent works alongside a user in an existing, changing environment. The user and agent share control. The user may continue working while the agent runs, so the agent cannot assume exclusive control of the pointer, keyboard, or focused window. It must account for user activity rather than attribute every change to its own actions. Where supported, it should prefer accessi- bility actions or background-window operations that leave the user’s current interaction undisturbed. When these methods cannot complete an operation, foreground interaction requires coordination with the user before taking control. The screen keeps changing. Application windows open, close, and move, and one window can cover another. These changes may come from applications unrelated to the task and continue while the agent is reasoning. A coordinate or element reference that was valid when observed may therefore be wrong by the time the agent acts. User requests evolve during execution. Users may clarify an initial request, correct the agent’s approach, or add constraints as work proceeds.

The following sections describe our SDK and harness, and Section 4.3.3 reports preliminary real-device results. 4.2 Cross-Device SDK A computer-use task may span a mobile application, desktop tools, and a browser-based service. The Cross-Device SDK provides a common programming interface through which one agent can coordi- nate these environments. It supports both the reuse of common operations across platforms and the composition of cross-device workflows within a single task. Its programming model builds on code- execution-based computer-use interfaces (OpenAI, 2026b;a). 18
title: One interface

text: Shared Operations with Explicit Targets. Common operations use a shared vocabulary, while platform adapters implement their native behavior. For example, the macOS adapter uses the unmodified Cua Driver from trycua (trycua, 2026). Each operation is scoped to an explicit resource, such as a device, application, window, or browser tab. Resource handles retain their targets independently, so selecting a new target does not redirect earlier bindings. This gives agent programs a consistent way to address multiple devices and applications without relying on a single implicitly selected target. Cross-Device Coordination within One Task. Within one session, programs can combine observations and actions from multiple resources while reusing host-side variables and bindings across turns. The program executes in the host runtime, whereas device.shell.run executes commands on the selected device where supported. File transfers through mu.files.copy identify both source and destination resources. These mechanisms allow intermediate results from one environment to guide operations in another. As an illustrative workflow, an agent could retrieve a report through a phone application, transfer it to a computer for analysis, and enter the results into a browser-based service, coordinating all three stages within the same task. Shared Observation Processing and Selective Delivery. The SDK exposes ui.ax for structured seman- tic observations and element-based actions, and ui.vision for images and coordinate-based interaction. Semantic state supports programmatic conditions and checks,
title: Shared Operations with Explicit Targets.

text: coordinating all three stages within the same task. Shared Observation Processing and Selective Delivery. The SDK exposes ui.ax for structured seman- tic observations and element-based actions, and ui.vision for images and coordinate-based interaction. Semantic state supports programmatic conditions and checks, while vision provides complementary information when semantic observations are insufficient. Adapters normalize native accessibility and browser semantic trees into common representations, allowing filtering and compact rendering to be reused across compatible platforms. Observation capture is separate from delivery to the model. Calls such as ui.ax.observe() return data to the program, while mu.emit delivers selected observations or computed results to the model. A program can therefore inspect multiple targets, use structured results to determine subsequent operations, and return only the information needed for the next model decision. This separation supports cross-device execution without requiring a model call for every intermediate structured observation. Explicit Platform Capabilities. A common interface does not imply identical capabilities across plat- forms. Each resource declares its supported operations and options. Common UI operations and device services share interfaces, while platform-specific features remain explicit through namespaces such as .android, .macos, and .browser. Operations such as Android navigation and browser page evaluation thus retain their own semantics, allowing programs to reuse common interaction patterns while selecting methods appropriate to each target. 4.3 Real-Device Harness The Cross-Device SDK defines the

The real-device harness integrates this interface with the agent loop, program execution, and platform-specific mechanisms, enabling the model to work on a user’s computer while retaining task state across turns. 4.3.1 Five-Layer Architecture We separate the system into five layers (Figure 9). The model generates a program, the runtime executes it, and SDK calls are translated by the driver into operations on applications and the operating system. Explicit interfaces separate responsibilities and allow compatible components to be replaced indepen- dently. Detectable execution failures are reported where they occur; successful action delivery is not treated as evidence that the intended task-level effect has occurred. Model. Conditioned on the task, system prompt, and interaction history, the model decides how to observe, act, and organize its work. It selects targets and operations, maintains task state, and determines 19
