The SDK binds observations and actions to explicit resources, such as devices, windows, and browser tabs (Section 4.2). Short element IDs written directly by the model must originate from observations delivered to it; programs may also obtain element references from fresh observations and use them within the same execution. Resource resets or rebinding invalidate associated references. These constraints establish the provenance and scope of action targets, but do not guarantee that the interface remains unchanged before execution. Driver. The driver translates SDK requests into supported native operations, including accessibility actions and coordinate-based input. It manages element identities and snapshot metadata, selects action- delivery mechanisms, and applies foreground or background delivery policies. Detectable native failures are returned as typed errors so that the agent can distinguish execution failures from outcomes requiring further inspection. Applications and Operating System. Applications and the operating system determine the available observations and control capabilities. Permissions, application state, and accessibility support constrain which operations can be performed. The harness must expose these limitations and use alternative interaction methods where supported. 4.3.2 Responding to Real-Device Challenges The constraints discussed in Section 4.1 motivate four design choices that connect these layers. text: The harness must expose these limitations and use alternative interaction methods where supported. 4.3.2 Responding to Real-Device Challenges The constraints discussed in Section 4.1 motivate four design choices that connect these layers. Minimizing Interference on Shared Machines. An agent operating alongside a user cannot assume exclusive control of the pointer, keyboard, or focused window. The harness therefore prefers element- level accessibility actions, followed by window-targeted coordinate input, and finally foreground input. Background delivery is used only where the target and platform support it; window-relative coordinates alone do not imply background execution. When a less intrusive method is unavailable or ineffective, the agent can escalate to a supported alternative, coordinating with the user before foreground input. 20

A full-desktop screenshot may show the user’s activity rather than the agent’s target, and visual input may be unnecessary during programmatic work. Following the model- initiated observation design in Section 3.2, the agent chooses when to observe and which target to inspect. text: interface changes. Managing Accessibility Information. Accessibility observations vary in size, stability, and coverage across applications. The harness filters irrelevant nodes and represents the retained hierarchy as a flat list linked by parent_id. Element identities and snapshot versions support reference tracking, while search, page, and read retrieve relevant information from a retained snapshot without repeatedly capturing the window. When accessibility information is insufficient, visual observation provides a complementary source of evidence. The choice of action-delivery mechanism remains separate from the choice of observation modality. Maintaining Task Continuity through User Interaction. Real-device tasks may require clarification, authentication, or authorization that the agent cannot supply independently. The ask_user interface supports these exchanges, including resolving ambiguous targets, requesting assistance with login or verification, and obtaining authorization for consequential actions. User responses and corrections become part of the ongoing task. The runtime preserves interpreter state, resource bindings, and interaction history, allowing execution to resume without rebuilding the workflow. 4.3.3 Preliminary Real-Device Results As our real-device benchmark is still under development, we study seven model configurations on four macOS tasks: workbook reasoning, PDF form filling, dietary-constrained shopping research, and hotel comparison, with up to three recorded runs per task and model. A workbook task reveals a difference in how models translate task requirements into programs. GPT-6 Astra builds a reusable solver, checks it against seven supplied examples, and identifies question rows from the workbook contents. Its program generates answers for all 125 questions. Qwen3.8-Max also uses functions and loops, but processes fixed row ranges that cover only 85 questions. Although its program reports this count, Qwen3.8-Max does not check for omitted questions. An audit of the saved workbooks confirms that GPT fills all 125 required Level answer cells, while Qwen3.8-Max leaves 40 empty (Figure 11). The gap is therefore not simply whether a model can write executable code with loops and conditions, but whether it can use code correctly to cover the full task and check for incomplete work. 5 Roadmap Open Generalist CUA aims to make generalist computer use a shared research effort in which models, execution systems, and real-device evaluation advance together. This first release provides an initial basis for that work. 5.1 From Design Validation to Model Release The model-side contribution of this report is empirical validation of agent design using existing models, rather than a newly trained model. We study code execution and harness-to-model decision transfer, and release implementations, prompts, and evaluation trajectories alongside preliminary versions of the real-device harness and cross-device SDK. A GCUA model is the central addition planned for the next release. We aim to unify computer and browser use and turn the designs studied here into learned capabilities: coordinating visual and programmatic operations through code, requesting observations when needed, maintaining task state throughout execution, and particularly enhancing the capability in real-device scenario. 23

text: 5.2 Research Priorities More Efficient Reasoning and Execution. We will optimize the model’s thinking, making reasoning more concise for routine operations and mitigating overthinking. On the harness and infrastructure side, we will improve code execution, context management, and infrastructure optimization. We will also explore new system architectures and other system-level solutions for efficiency. Reliable Work on Users’ Devices. We plan to extend the harness and SDK toward tasks spanning computers, browsers, and potentially mobile devices. Priorities include reliable target selection, recovery from execution failures, and task continuity when users interrupt or change their requests. We will also investigate which additional workflow decisions should move from fixed harness rules to the model. Real-Device Environments and Benchmarks. We will develop evaluation environments and benchmarks on real devices, particularly macOS, covering a wider range of applications, user interactions, and changing device states. The goal is to measure whether agents complete useful work under real operating conditions, together with the time and resources required. 5.3 How to Contribute We welcome contributions to both the implementation and the research agenda: • Improve the Harness and SDK. Contribute platform adapters, more reliable observation and control, execution optimizations, or real-device testing and documentation. • Build Real-Device Evaluation. Contribute environments, realistic tasks, evaluation criteria, and benchmark infrastructure, including execution traces that expose current limitations. • Propose Research Goals.

text: Frontier Computer Use. OpenAI positions GPT-6 Astra for difficult end-to-end work and describes computer use as a new frontier in speed, accuracy, and safety. It recommends code execution for computer-use tasks while retaining the structured computer tool as an alternative (OpenAI, 2026c;b). In Codex, Computer Use can see and operate graphical user interfaces on macOS and Windows, support workflows spanning multiple applications, and, on macOS, run scoped background tasks while the user continues working elsewhere (OpenAI, 2026a). Anthropic also provides computer use in Claude Cowork and Claude Code: Claude first reaches for the most precise tool, such as connectors to services like Slack or Google Calendar, and can directly control the browser, mouse, keyboard, and screen when no connector is available. Its Dispatch feature further lets users assign tasks from a phone and open the completed work on a computer (Anthropic, 2026b). Despite these capabilities, the public releases leave key implementation details and execution trajectories unavailable, making their system designs difficult for the community to reproduce and study systematically. text: We presented the first release of Open Generalist CUA, an ongoing project to develop and open the full stack for generalist computer use. Our GCUA formulation centers on three model decisions: what to observe, how to act, and how to organize work. Code execution lets models use intermediate results to coordinate GUI and programmatic operations and apply their existing programming capabilities to computer interaction. Harness-to-model decision transfer complements this design by moving selected observation and task-state decisions from fixed harness rules to the model. On the offline subset of OSWorld-v2, the full OpenGCUA configuration improves task scores across all eight evaluated models, raising mean partial score by 19.6 points and reducing reported steps per task by an average of 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. Ablations show additional benefits from code execution with the same GUI and CLI access, indicating that execution design matters beyond interface access. We release our implementation, prompts, and evaluation trajectories, alongside preliminary versions of a real-device harness and cross-device SDK. Evaluations on four macOS tasks reveal substantial differences in reported reasoning-token usage and task completion under the same harness. This report studies GCUA designs rather than introducing a newly trained model. OpenGCUA will continue through further research and releases on GCUA models, reasoning and execution efficiency, and real-device environments and benchmarks. 25

text: A Evaluation Details Metrics and Aggregation. We evaluate the 82-task offline subset of OSWorld-v2 v2.1. Task score is the mean evaluator partial score, expressed on a 0–100 scale. Full-task success is the percentage of tasks with a normalized evaluator score greater than 0.999999. Steps and token counts are averaged over all selected tasks, including failures. Within each run, we retain the latest attempt with an evaluator result for each task, not the highest-scoring attempt. Cross-model summaries give each model equal weight: score gains are averaged in points, and relative resource reductions are calculated within each model before averaging. The offline subset is defined by evaluation_examples/test_v2_offline_no_internet.json. It excludes the 26 tasks requiring external Internet access, while retaining local web applications and desktop tasks. B Real-Device Evaluation Details B.1 Task Descriptions Workbook Reasoning. The input workbook contains race rules, a track layout, seven worked examples, and 125 Level questions. The agent must compute all Level answers and the requested bonus answers, enter them in the designated cells, and save a completed copy without altering the original. PDF Form Filling. The inputs comprise a blank four-page Schengen application form and synthetic identity, employment, travel, and accommodation records. The agent must fill all applicable fields supported by these materials and save a new PDF with all entered information visible and correct. Shopping Research. Given

text: ## GUI actions (pyautogui) The full pyautogui API is available, e.g. `pyautogui.click(x, y)` / `rightClick` / `doubleClick` / ` tripleClick`, `moveTo(x, y)`, `dragTo(x, y, duration=0.5)`, `mouseDown()` / `mouseUp()`, `scroll( amount, x, y)`, `typewrite(text)` (ASCII; other characters are typed through xdotool when it is available), `press(key)`, `hotkey(k1, k2, ...)`, `keyDown(key)` / `keyUp(key)`, `position()`. `pixel(x, y)` and `locateCenterOnScreen(image_path)` also exist but are brittle - a last resort, never the basis for a decision (see "Writing a step"). Coordinates are NORMALIZED: every x/y, region and offset you pass to pyautogui - and every position it returns - is in [0, 1000] on both axes: (1000, 1000) is the bottom-right corner of the screen and (500, 500) is the exact center, independent of the real resolution. Never emit a raw pixel value (read out of a PIL image, a file, `xdotool`, or image metadata); convert it first with x_out = round(x_pixel / screen_width * 1000). Out-of-contract values are silently REINTERPRETED, never rejected, so a wrong coordinate raises no error: if EITHER axis exceeds 1000 the pair is read as raw pixels; if BOTH axes are <= 1 it is read as a screen fraction, so `click(1, 1)` lands on the bottom-right corner, not the top-left. For a target at the very top-left, emit 2 rather than 0 or 1. `pyautogui.scroll(amount, x, y)` scrolls the

text: C.2 Harness-to-Model Decision Transfer The full setting adds model-initiated screenshot requests and task-state updates. A separate <intent> annotation states each program’s immediate purpose; it is not a Python operation. Screenshot Request. - `screenshot()` - request a screenshot; it is taken right after the script finishes and arrives with the NEXT observation, and without this call the next observation carries no image. See "Writing a step " for when to attach one. (It also returns the current screen as a PIL image in raw pixels for programmatic use; `pyautogui.screenshot()` only returns the image and attaches nothing.) Task-State Ledger. For multi-step tasks, maintain a persistent work ledger with `todo.update(id="...", kind="task", content ="...", status="pending")` calls inside your code. Kinds: task, next_step, fact, question. Statuses: pending, attempted, changed_unverified, claimed_verified, blocked; use status="delete" to remove an item. `todo.list()` prints the full ledger. Ledger calls never touch the computer: put them in the same script as real actions whenever possible - a script that only updates the ledger still consumes one full step. The ledger is shown with each observation: the full snapshot on any step where it changed, otherwise a one-line summary. Call `todo.list()` when you need the full list again. If the snapshot is truncated, its footer states how many items are hidden and `todo.list()` prints all of them. Public Intent and Response Format.

Add `time.sleep(...)` after actions that open windows or menus, switch applications or trigger loading, and before reading their result. ## Writing a step - Inspect before acting: never guess the position of elements you have not seen. When your next decision depends on the visible result, append `screenshot()` to THIS script rather than taking the action now and requesting a screenshot next step - that costs a step for no new information. This applies to GUI actions, waits for visible changes, and `bash()` commands that launch or change a GUI. - Batch what you are confident about. Keystrokes, menu navigation and form filling that need no visual confirmation in between belong in ONE script (click a field, type, press Tab, type, press Enter, ...). Loops over data and conditions on values you have actually read (file contents, `bash()` output) are encouraged: they cost one step instead of many. - Keep blind sequences short. A mis-click early in a script makes every later action wrong, so check the screen after a short group of GUI actions (about 5-10) rather than after every click, and never chain long sequences of unverified clicks. - Do not branch on pixels you have not verified:

text: every later action wrong, so check the screen after a short group of GUI actions (about 5-10) rather than after every click, and never chain long sequences of unverified clicks. - Do not branch on pixels you have not verified: pixel colours and image matching are brittle. text: 2026-10-15 Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions Ian Gemp1, Shubhendu Trivedi1, Adam Fisch1, Fantine Huot1, Michael Kaisers1, Mirella Lapata1, William W. Cohen1, Alekh Agarwal2, Kate Larson1,3 and Jacob Eisenstein1 1Google DeepMind, 2Google Research, 3University of Waterloo We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self- interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that

posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs. Keywords: decentralized reinforcement learning, auction mechanisms, multi-agent systems, LLM agents

Modern AI systems increasingly face tasks that require composing multiple specialized capabilities— dynamically routing queries across varying LLM sizes to optimize inference costs, gathering and synthesizing evidence from disparate sources, or dispatching subtasks to external tools. The domi- nant paradigm centralizes this composition in a single controller (an “orchestrator” LLM or a fixed computation graph), which must explicitly plan the sequence of operations and assign credit to each component (Hong et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2023). An alternative, inspired by economic theory, is to let a society of specialized agents coordinate through a market mechanism. To solve temporal credit assignment across multi-step trajectories without hierarchical oversight, we draw on the foundational Bucket Brigade principle (Bartholdi III and Eisenstein, 1996; Holland, 1985): each agent purchases the current task state from the preceding agent in an auction, transforms the state, and resells the updated state to the next downstream agent. Terminal task rewards earned at completion naturally propagate backward through the chain of resale prices, rewarding upstream contributors proportionally to their marginal value added. To ground this decentralized economy in a reinforcement learning framework, we build on the work of Chang et al. (2020). They proved that a Vickrey (second-price) auction perfectly aligns each agent’s locally optimal bidding strategy with the globally optimal MDP policy. However, translating this theoretical breakthrough to

They proved that a Vickrey (second-price) auction perfectly aligns each agent’s locally optimal bidding strategy with the globally optimal MDP policy. However, translating this theoretical breakthrough to real-world AI societies reveals a critical gap: their optimal equilibrium relies on the restrictive assumption of perfect competition via artificially cloned agents. Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions In practice, this perfect-clone assumption breaks down due to two fundamental economic realities. First is a participation barrier: with exact clones, the expected highest and second-highest bids are identical. The winning agent pays exactly their true valuation, driving their net profit to strictly zero. Because participating in a market carries inherent risk, agents will simply sit out rather than opt in to risk their resources for a net-zero expected return. Second is the anti-cloning incentive: perfect competition will not naturally arise because no rational actor will clone their own agent (which cannibalizes their own profit margin), and participants will actively protect their models’ intellectual property from being copied by competitors. If perfect clones are theoretically unprofitable and strategically irrational, does the market collapse? We first demonstrate that the opposite extreme—absence of competition (a monopsony at any step in the task chain)—does indeed cause the market to fail. When an agent is the sole eligible buyer for a given state, they act as a monopsonist, bidding the absolute minimum required to win. Without competitive pressure, the clearing price collapses, and downstream value is not efficiently extracted and passed upstream. This breaks the sequential credit assignment required to sustain a multi-step pipeline, as upstream agents are starved of the revenue needed to offset their own inference

text: the clearing price collapses, and downstream value is not efficiently extracted and passed upstream. This breaks the sequential credit assignment required to sustain a multi-step pipeline, as upstream agents are starved of the revenue needed to offset their own inference costs. To bridge this gap, we adapt the framework of Chang et al. (2020) to societies of Large Language Models (LLMs), formulating a decentralized, sequential forward auction mechanism tailored to the operational realities of modern LLM pipelines. In doing so, we shift the theoretical focus to the critical, realistic middle ground: imperfect competition. We model societies populated by LLM agents that occupy similar capability niches but are differentiated by heterogeneous inference costs, prompt engineering, and localized heuristics. Because off-the-shelf language models are notoriously miscalibrated judges of their own success probabilities and token costs (Fradkin and Krishnan, 2026), agents cannot rely on zero-shot prompting to evaluate states. Instead, each agent learns a lightweight neural valuation policy via reinforcement learning to navigate the tradeoff between winning the right to act and shading their bids to secure a positive profit margin. In this paper, we present a comprehensive empirical study of decentralized LLM routing under imperfect competition. Our core contributions include: 1. Decentralized LLM Markets and Imperfect Competition: We introduce an architectural and algorithmic framework for sequential auction MDPs in LLM societies, demonstrating experimentally that imperfect competition is sufficient to sustain positive profit margins and enable viable multi- agent pipelines under traditional auction mechanisms. 2. Monopsony Failure Validation: We reveal empirically through a targeted synthetic domain that absence of competition collapses the market, establishing imperfect competition as a viable operational regime under traditional auction mechanisms. 3. Algorithmic Bidding Strategies: We formulate and benchmark four bidding algorithms—Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO—demonstrating how individual agents can efficiently learn optimal pricing and bid-shading policies. 4. Extensive Benchmarking: We deploy our framework across diverse LLM domains (including a math reasoning task and newly-constructed synthetic news market). Through market density sweeps across 1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey (CCV) auctions (Fig 1b&3), we show that imperfect competition is sufficient to sustain positive agent profits while simultaneously achieving higher task success rates (accuracy) than centralized orchestration baselines. 2

text: To formalize the decentralized ecosystem just described, we model the multi-agent task pipeline as a sequential auction, in line with previous work (Chang et al., 2020). In this framework, self-interested agents bid for the right to progressively transform an initial state 𝑠0 into a terminal solution 𝑠𝑇. Below, we define the underlying market MDP, the local profit incentives of the agents, and the idealized theoretical clearing rules that enable optimal credit assignment. 2.1. The Sequential Spot Market MDP We model decentralized task routing as a finite horizon (𝑇) sequential Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple (S, A, P, 𝑅, 𝛾). Rather than relying on a centralized policy 𝜋(𝑎|𝑠) to select actions, the action space A is defined by a society of independent agents. For intuition, consider a gridworld: instead of a single controller choosing to move up or down, specialized “Up” and “Down” agents compete in an auction for the right to act on the current state 𝑠𝑡. At each step 𝑡, a registry of agents evaluates 𝑠𝑡to determine their eligibility. Eligible agents submit bids, and the highest bidder wins the right to process the state. The state transition is defined by the winning agent 𝑖’s localized action 𝑎𝑡, which generates the next state 𝑠𝑡+1 and yields an environmental reward 𝑟(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡). The process is repeated until a
title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions

text: bidder wins the right to process the state. The state transition is defined by the winning agent 𝑖’s localized action 𝑎𝑡, which generates the next state 𝑠𝑡+1 and yields an environmental reward 𝑟(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡). The process is repeated until a final state 𝑠𝑇is reached. Social welfare is defined as the sum of discounted rewards. Agents optimize for their individual net utility, or profit, over the course of a transaction. For an agent winning the auction at step 𝑡, the profit 𝑈𝑖,𝑡is defined as the sum of the environmental reward and the net flow of capital: 𝑈𝑖,𝑡= 𝑟(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡) + 𝑃(𝑡) in −𝑃(𝑡) out (1) where 𝑃(𝑡) out is the clearing price the agent pays to acquire 𝑠𝑡, and 𝑃(𝑡) in is the revenue the agent receives when they subsequently auction the transformed state 𝑠𝑡+1 to the next downstream agent. 2.2. Auction Mechanisms and Credit Assignment The rules governing the clearing price 𝑃(𝑡) out and the subsequent revenue 𝑃(𝑡) in depend strictly on the chosen auction mechanism. Chang et al. (2020) established a foundational bridge between reinforcement learning and mechanism design by demonstrating that under a Vickrey (second-price) auction, the globally optimal MDP policy constitutes a Nash equilibrium for myopic agents maximizing their local transaction profit. Their result relies on two distinct theoretical properties: 1. Truthful Bidding via Myopia: Assuming agents
title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions

text: by demonstrating that under a Vickrey (second-price) auction, the globally optimal MDP policy constitutes a Nash equilibrium for myopic agents maximizing their local transaction profit. Their result relies on two distinct theoretical properties: 1. Truthful Bidding via Myopia: Assuming agents are myopic and optimize strictly for the immediate transaction, the Vickrey auction guarantees that bidding one’s true valuation (𝑏𝑖= 𝑣𝑖) is a weakly dominant strategy. Thus, an agent’s bid reveals its true estimated action-value, 𝑄𝑖(𝑠𝑡). 2. Perfect Credit Conservation via Clones: To ensure the market clears at the optimal state-value without requiring external platform subsidies, Chang et al. (2020) in their Section 5.4 build on the assumption that the market is populated with exact clones of every agent. With perfect competition via exact clones, the highest and second-highest bids are identical (𝑏(1) = 𝑏(2)). Because the Vickrey auction charges the second-highest bid, the market clearing price exactly extracts the maximum Q-value: 𝑃(𝑡) out = max𝑖𝑄𝑖(𝑠𝑡) = 𝑉∗(𝑠𝑡). When the clearing price perfectly tracks 𝑉∗(𝑠𝑡), the revenue passed upstream acts as an exact Bellman backup. Specifically, if the downstream auction at step 𝑡+ 1 clears at 𝑉∗(𝑠𝑡+1), the upstream 3

text: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions agent receives 𝑃(𝑡) in = 𝛾𝑉∗(𝑠𝑡+1).1 By maximizing their local profit 𝑈𝑖,𝑡, agents naturally align their economic incentives with the global MDP objective, recursively propagating credit back to the initial state. However, this theoretical alignment guarantee unravels if either of the above assumptions is unmet. Hence, we aim to study the robustness of a heterogeneous LLM market MDP empirically. 3. Decentralized LLM Markets and Imperfect Competition Applying the market MDP to LLM societies requires formalizing inference costs within the reward structure and relaxing the idealized assumption of perfect competition made in previous work. 3.1. LLM Transformations and Inference Costs In an LLM society, the state 𝑠𝑡represents the current task context, comprising the text or structured payload (e.g., a natural language query, an intermediate translation, or a JSON object containing accu- mulated evidence). The action space corresponds to an agent’s localized LLM invocation, transforming the payload to generate 𝑠𝑡+1. Crucially, taking this action incurs a local inference cost 𝑐𝑖,𝑡for the agent (e.g., API token costs). We formalize this by defining the environmental reward during intermediate steps as strictly negative: 𝑟(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡) = −𝑐𝑖,𝑡. If the agent’s action at step 𝑇−1 successfully resolves the task and transitions the environment to a terminal state 𝑠𝑇, the reward 𝑟(𝑠𝑇−1, 𝑎𝑇−1) incorporates both the negative inference cost and the
title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions

text: steps as strictly negative: 𝑟(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡) = −𝑐𝑖,𝑡. If the agent’s action at step 𝑇−1 successfully resolves the task and transitions the environment to a terminal state 𝑠𝑇, the reward 𝑟(𝑠𝑇−1, 𝑎𝑇−1) incorporates both the negative inference cost and the positive terminal reward provided by the evaluator. Because the task is complete, no subsequent auction occurs, yielding 𝑃(𝑇−1) in = 0. 3.2. The Participation Barrier and the Clone Assumption We now address the problem of cloning agents in a market MDP. Under the assumption of perfect clones, the equilibrium clearing price exactly equals the winner’s true valuation (𝑃(𝑡) out = 𝑏(2) = 𝑣𝑖), hence the winner’s expected utility is strictly zero (𝔼[𝑈𝑖,𝑡] = 0). An agent maximizing expected profit has no strict incentive to opt into the market, since abstention already achieves zero profit. Furthermore, no rational agent would choose to clone themselves, as doing so strictly cannibalizes their profit margin. Conversely, participants will actively protect their models from being copied by competitors. Consequently, real LLM spot markets are bounded to operate under imperfect competition, where 𝑏(1) > 𝑏(2). It is precisely this structural gap that allows the winner to secure a positive profit margin (𝑈𝑖,𝑡> 0), overcoming the participation barrier. 3.3. Defining Agent Heterogeneity To operationalize the regime of imperfect competition, we define how agents differ within the market.

Defining Agent Heterogeneity To operationalize the regime of imperfect competition, we define how agents differ within the market. In our framework, all agents participate in a unified market and can theoretically bid on any state; however, they act as imperfect substitutes, organically specializing based on their localized capabilities. We parameterize this heterogeneity across two primary axes: 1. Inference Cost (𝑐𝑖,𝑡): Agents use different LLMs. For example, an agent backed by a <1B parameter LLM incurs a much lower base inference cost than one backed by a >100B parameter LLM, allowing it to bid competitively on lower-margin tasks. 1Chang et al. Transition Reliability: Agents are differentiated by distinct prompt engineering techniques, identity embeddings, and asymmetric data access (e.g., access to different document corpora). These differences cause their state transitions (𝑠𝑡→𝑠𝑡+1) to vary in quality and relevance. A more capable agent is more likely to generate a state that attracts high downstream bids, thereby raising its expected future revenue. Because of these variances, even among agents attempting to fulfill the exact same role in a task, true valuations naturally diverge (𝑣1 ≠𝑣2). This structural gap allows the most efficient agent to shade its bid below its own true valuation while still outbidding the rest of the market, thereby securing a positive profit margin and incentivizing participation in the market. 3.4. Auction Mechanisms under Imperfect Competition We study heterogeneous markets under the same three auctions discussed in (Chang et al., 2020): • 2nd-Price (Vickrey): The downstream buyer pays 𝑏(2), but the upstream seller receives 𝑏(1). The marketplace platform must act as a market maker, subsidizing the deficit (𝑏(1) −𝑏(2)). • Credit-Conserving Vickrey (CCV): The buyer pays 𝑏(2), and the upstream seller receives 𝑏(2). This avoids subsidies, but fails to pass the full winning valuation upstream when 𝑏(1) > 𝑏(2). • 1st-Price (Bucket Brigade): The winner pays their exact bid (𝑃(𝑡) out = 𝑏(𝑡) (1)), and the

If the agent bids its true valuation, 𝑏𝑖(𝑠𝑡) = 𝑣𝑖(𝑠𝑡), its ex-post utility is zero. Consequently, a rational bidder must shade its bid below its private valuation to secure a positive expected surplus (Krishna, 2009). We parameterize the bidding policy via a state-dependent multiplicative shading factor, 𝜉(𝑠𝑡) ∈[0, 1), yielding the shaded bid 𝑏𝑖(𝑠𝑡) = 𝜉(𝑠𝑡)𝑣𝑖(𝑠𝑡). The ex-post surplus upon winning is thus (1 −𝜉(𝑠𝑡))𝑣𝑖(𝑠𝑡), highlighting the fundamental trade-off of 1st-price auctions: lowering 𝜉(𝑠𝑡) widens the conditional profit margin but strictly decreases the probability of winning. Despite this strategic shading, recent analysis shows that 1st-price agentic markets still achieve high welfare whenever competition is sufficiently strong (Trivedi et al., 2026). 5

text: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions 4. Bidding Strategies Crucially, our framework decouples the agent’s core capability from its market strategy. The underlying LLMs responsible for the state transitions (𝑠𝑡→𝑠𝑡+1) are utilized strictly for inference and remain frozen. The reinforcement learning process solely trains a lightweight MLP for each agent, which acts as the state-dependent, myopic bidding policy. To survive in an imperfectly competitive market, an agent’s MLP must solve two coupled learning problems at each step: accurately estimating the state’s true valuation 𝑣𝑖(𝑠𝑡), and determining the optimal shade factor 𝜉(𝑠𝑡) ∈(0, 1) to maximize its expected profit margin. The agent’s final bid is formulated as 𝑏𝑖(𝑠𝑡) = 𝜉(𝑠𝑡) · 𝑣𝑖(𝑠𝑡). For Vickrey and CCV, we enforce truthful bidding, 𝜉(𝑠𝑡) = 1. All agents share a common neural architecture for the valuation head, which predicts both the expected downstream value 𝑣(𝑠𝑡) and its standard deviation 𝜎(𝑠𝑡). The valuation head is trained via a standard Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss to regress toward the empirical target 𝑃(𝑡) in −𝑐𝑖,𝑡. Empirical Evaluation To empirically validate the necessity of imperfect competition and evaluate our bidding strategies, we benchmark our market across a synthetic control domain and three diverse LLM environments. 5.1. Validating the Monopsony Failure (Synthetic Chain Translation) We first evaluate the framework on a synthetic multi-step translation domain. In this environment, states are constructed by concatenating two 64-dimensional embeddings, one identifying the original task and the other the current language. Agents act as bilingual translators stationed on the edges of a graph (Figure 1a), possessing distinct inference costs 𝑐𝑖. The market must route payloads from a source node to target nodes with terminal reward $1 by discovering the most cost-efficient topological sequence (e.g., bypassing the expensive $0.50 direct Fr→En edge in favor of the $0.02 Fr→Sp→En path). We evaluate all three proposed auctions: 1st-price, 2nd-price, and CCV. This domain allows us to test the extremes of market

We evaluate all three proposed auctions: 1st-price, 2nd-price, and CCV. This domain allows us to test the extremes of market competition. We configure the environment with a single agent per edge (𝑁= 1). In this regime, intermediate nodes frequently act as monopsonies. This occurs either structurally (e.g., the Sp has only one outgoing edge) or task-conditionally (e.g., Ge has two edges, but only one is viable for a given task, rendering the competitor’s bid zero). The presence of an uncontested buyer exposes the failure modes of each auction type. In a standard 2nd-price (Vickrey) auction, the monopsonist bids truthfully but pays the floor (0); the platform must inject unacceptable subsidies (e.g., $0.88 at Sp) to pay the upstream seller the first price. Under CCV, the buyer pays 0 and the upstream seller receives 0. Under a 1st-price auction, the monopsonist actively shades its bid down to the floor, passing a vanishingly small value upstream. 7

text: Top-Down Orchestration and Routing. Prior work scales LLM reasoning via external scaffolding, including static graph/configuration optimizers like Maestro (Wang et al., 2025), centralized cost- cascading routers like FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2024), and learned small-agent routing (Alazraki et al., 2026). Unlike our decentralized market, these systems presuppose a fixed topology or a global planner with full information, ignoring private operational costs. Decentralized Agent Markets. The idea of building multi-step trajectories from sequential auctions was introduced by Chang et al. (2020), but their Vickrey-based framework required an awkward “cloning" construction to preserve credit conservation. We show that 1st-price auctions can be effective, and we adapt their framework to contemporary LLM-based applications such as Omni-Math. This 10

(2025) propose (but do not implement) coordination of contemporary LLMs through market mechanisms, and specific market-like mechanisms are presented by Qi et al. (2026) and Liu et al. (2026). Our approach is distinguished by pushing the idea of decentralization further. In particular, Qi et al. (2026) maintain a population of agents that is selected by each agent’s economic balance (agents with zero balance drop out), but the agents are not economic actors: they do not structure their participation to optimize a local economic incentive. Concurrent work by Liu et al. (2026) orchestrates LLMs using hierarchical reverse procurement auctions where contractors subcontract tasks. In contrast, our sequential spot market (section 2) resolves multi-step credit assignment through peer-to-peer state resales without top-down subcontracting trees. Another difference is that Liu et al. (2026) centralize value estimation in a single model (the participants estimate only their own costs), while we require each participant to estimate its own expected return. This aligns with our vision of a market composed of an evolving set of niche service providers. Economic Alignment Benchmarks. Several benchmarks evaluate whether prompt-driven LLMs act rationally in simulated retail or auction games, including Magentic Market (Bansal et al., 2025), Vend- ingBench (Backlund and Petersson, 2025), CoffeeBench (Sugiura et al., 2026), MarketBench (Fradkin and Krishnan, 2026), and Agent Bazaar (Karten et al., 2026). Whereas those works study whether raw LLMs natively behave like homo economicus, we use mechanism design and RL-trained bidding policies as an algorithmic organizing principle to coordinate multi-agent pipelines. 7. Discussion and Conclusion We present a decentralized market framework for LLM orchestration. Whereas prior frameworks assume perfect clones—ignoring participation incentives—we establish imperfect competition as a viable regime. Under 1st-price auctions, agents pairing frozen LLMs with trainable bidding networks learn strategic bid-shading. This secures positive margins and conserves credit across pipelines, avoiding the unbounded subsidies of 2nd-price and the severe credit attenuation of CCV. Empirically, complex cognitive workflows emerge organically via price discovery, bypassing top-down orchestration. Furthermore, our density sweeps confirm that scaling competition efficiently compresses individual margins while systematically increasing social welfare and task accuracy. Our framework has several limitations: it requires sufficient competition (collapsing under monop- sonies), assumes strictly sequential task transformations (precluding parallel execution), relies on myopic agents rather than globally strategic planners, and

Ultimately, however, this work shows that decentralized market-based routing offers a scalable blueprint for transitioning from rigid AI controllers to open, self-sustaining agentic economies.

Emergent Multi-Hop Retrieval (HotpotQA): In the HotpotQA domain, the market acts as an evidence-gathering society. The environment consists of 10 fact extractors (each assigned 1 of the 10 candidate paragraphs) and 3 answerer agents differentiated by reasoning style via distinct system prompts (concise, chain-of-thought, and cautious). A centralized auctioneer assessor evaluates the accumulated facts against the question at each step, assigning discrete relevance scores (0-10) to each agent based on missing multi-hop dependencies. The market dynamics organically solve the multi-hop retrieval problem through learned valuation schedules conditioned on these assessor signals. When the

The market dynamics organically solve the multi-hop retrieval problem through learned valuation schedules conditioned on these assessor signals. When the state lacks intermediate evidence, extractors whose paragraphs contain the necessary bridging facts receive high assessor scores and outbid others to append their facts. As evidence accumulates, the answerer agents monitor the state. Once an answerer determines that sufficient evidence has been gathered to derive the final answer (and claim the terminal reward), its valuation spikes. It outbids the extractors, terminating the gathering chain and passing revenue backward through the preceding transactions. In HotpotQA, the market successfully learns to identify the two supporting gold paragraphs among eight distractors and route extracted facts to an answerer agent, achieving an 85.0 ± 3.2% success rate over the final 100 episodes (fig. 4). In comparison, a centralized ReAct baseline (Yao et al., 2023) with upfront access to all ten paragraph titles over the same 6-step horizon achieves 84.8 ± 1.1% with Gemini-3.5-flash-lite at 0.042 ± 0.025 ¢/task and 91.2 ± 0.8% with Gemini-3.1-pro-preview at 1.677 ± 1.281 ¢/task. Across all domains, agents share a unified JAX/Flax bidding architecture composed of a state-encoding trunk followed by algorithm-specific output heads. Consequently, even when the model perfectly centers on the true threshold, the agent samples a bid below the threshold—and thus loses the auction—exactly 50% of the time. In a sparse market, randomly ceding half of all wins to inferior competitors frequently breaks the sequential routing chain. Conversely, while the Bayes-Optimal agent eliminates this sampling noise by deterministically selecting the profit-maximizing shade 𝜉= arg max𝜉′(1−𝜉′) Φ�(logit(𝜉′) −𝜇ℓ)/𝜎ℓ , this greedy exploitation starves its posterior of exploratory boundary-crossing observations. When the margin term pulls the chosen shade below the posterior mean (logit(𝜉) < 𝜇ℓ) and the agent loses, the model’s prediction is trivially confirmed. This causes gradient descent to prematurely collapse the uncertainty (𝜎ℓ→𝜎min), stalling the gradient on 𝜇ℓ before it can ever discover the true optimal threshold. D. text: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory Sebastian-Antonio Toma1,2∗, Jean de Kernier1, Mike Ply1, Oliviu Matei2 1Amazon Web Services 2Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania Sebastian.Toma@campus.utcluj.ro
title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory

text: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent’s re- sponses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, pro- ducing both false positives where correct responses mask bro- ken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories span- ning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, con- versations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresh- olds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system cor- rectly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ system- atically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to sup- port reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.1 1
title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory

text: Large language model (LLM) agents operating over ex- tended time horizons require persistent external memory to accumulate knowledge beyond the ephemeral context win- dow (Sumers et al. 2024; Jiang et al. 2026). As these systems grow more complex, with over a dozen distinct architectures published since 2023 (Latimer et al. 2026; Packer et al. 2024; Rasmussen et al. 2025; Chhikara et al. 2025; Zhu et al. 2026), the question of how to evaluate them becomes pressing. A survey of current benchmarks reveals a systematic lim- itation: every existing evaluation measures memory quality extrinsically, by posing questions to the agent and grading its responses (Maharana et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2026; Hu, Wang, and McAuley 2026; Uddin et al. 2026; Liu and Yadav 2026; 1https://github.com/amazon-science/feb-30-benchmark ∗Corresponding author. Jung et al. 2026). This produces a single composite score that conflates memory, retrieval, and generation quality. When the system fails, one cannot identify which component is respon- sible; when it succeeds, one cannot confirm the memory is actually correct (Toma and Matei 2026). We identify two concrete failure modes that extrinsic eval- uation cannot detect: • False positives (LLM compensation): A strong gener- ation model can produce correct responses despite in- correct or incomplete memory state, by reasoning over partial retrieval results at inference time. Extrinsic evalu- ation scores this as success.
title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory

text: uation cannot detect: • False positives (LLM compensation): A strong gener- ation model can produce correct responses despite in- correct or incomplete memory state, by reasoning over partial retrieval results at inference time. Extrinsic evalu- ation scores this as success. • False negatives (retrieval bottleneck): A memory sys- tem may correctly store and update facts, yet fail to re- trieve them for a specific query due to embedding mis- match or retrieval cutoff. Extrinsic evaluation blames the memory system for a retrieval failure. We propose intrinsic evaluation, direct comparison of the memory store contents against known ground truth at each stage of knowledge evolution, as a complementary evaluation paradigm. The relationship mirrors unit versus end-to-end testing in software engineering: intrinsic evaluation checks the memory component’s internal state directly, while ex- trinsic evaluation only observes end-to-end behavior, so a passing end-to-end test can mask a broken component just as a correct component can fail end-to-end due to an integration bottleneck. A parallel from NLP history motivates the same shift: in the 2010s, word embeddings were evaluated only through downstream task performance until intrinsic evalu- ation (analogy tasks, similarity correlations) enabled faster progress by isolating representation quality (Baroni, Dinu, and Kruszewski 2014; Schnabel et al. 2015). text: Agent Memory Benchmarks. MemoryAgentBench (Hu, Wang, and McAuley 2026) defines four memory com- petencies (retention, temporal reasoning, knowledge up- dates, and information integration) evaluated through QA interactions. Memora (Uddin et al. 2026) introduces the FAMA metric that penalizes reliance on invalidated mem- ories, decomposing performance into freshness-aware com- ponents. LongMemEval-V2 (Wu et al. 2026) tests long-term memory along five temporal reasoning capabilities. AMA- Bench (Zhao et al. 2026) evaluates long-horizon memory for agentic applications. C4 (Synthesis Quality) tests whether multiple observa- tions from different artifacts merge into correct, well-formed facts, with ground truth specifying which should form a sin- gle fact versus separate facts. At L3, claims must be inferred from combinations of statements, and documents contain substantial unrelated content that could mislead ex- traction systems. 3.3 Trajectory Schema Each trajectory is defined as a JSON structure specifying: • A unique trajectory ID, category, difficulty, and domain assignment. • A type indicating the evolution pattern (linear-evolution, contradiction, scope-expansion, retraction, stable, or gradual-drift). • A sequence of states, each containing a set of atomic claims representing the expected memory contents after processing documents up to that state. • Per-state docClaims, the subset of claims that the docu- ment for that state should contain (new information only, not cumulative repetition). • An expected action per state transition (create, update, reinforce, conflict, or supersede). • Author role and document type metadata for multi-author trajectories. Claims are required to be atomic (one assertable proposi- tion per claim) and self-contained (understandable without reference to other claims). This ensures scoring is unambigu- ous: each claim either is or is not entailed by the system’s fact store. The key design choice is docClaims vs. claims: docu- ments contain only new information per state. The system must retain prior knowledge across document ingestions, testing actual memory persistence, not single-document ex- traction.

Trajectories span 6 technical domains (infrastructure, secu- rity, financial operations, machine learning, data engineering, and containers) to avoid domain-specific bias. These trajec- tories instantiate the benchmark in a technical and business- operations setting, but the methodology is domain-agnostic as the same paradigm-inversion construction can produce tra- jectories for any domain in which facts evolve across multi- author artifacts, by substituting the domain’s own topics and observation categories. The total corpus comprises 147 gen- erated documents: 127 trajectory state documents and 20 noise documents (4 per C2 trajectory to test retrieval under distraction). 4 Document Generation Pipeline We adopt paradigm inversion (Roig 2025): rather than anno- tating ground truth on real documents (expensive and subjec- tive), we generate documents from known fact trajectories, making the trajectory itself the ground truth. Algorithm 1 formalizes the pipeline. 4.1 Multi-Model Rotation Documents are generated using 6 models across 5 providers, rotated per state index within each trajectory to simulate dif- ferent

Algorithm 1 formalizes the pipeline. 4.1 Multi-Model Rotation Documents are generated using 6 models across 5 providers, rotated per state index within each trajectory to simulate dif- ferent human authors with different writing styles. No single model generates more than 30% of total documents. Fol- lowing evidence that multi-source synthetic data mitigates distribution collapse (Schaffelder and Gatt 2026) and re- duces single-generator bias (van Elburg, van der Putten, and Marx 2025), this additionally simulates the natural stylistic variation of multi-author corpora. The generation models are all different from the system’s extraction model (which uses a different LLM family), avoid- ing the stylistic bias that inflates scores when the same model generates and extracts (van Elburg, van der Putten, and Marx 2025). 4.2 Style-Grounded Generation Documents follow a realism gradient across difficulty levels: 1. Style-grounded (L1/L2): An LLM generates a new doc- ument for the trajectory claims but mimics the tone, vo- cabulary, and structure of a real reference document. 2. Hybrid injection (L3): Claims are inserted into actual human-written documents from unrelated domains, pro- ducing text that is approximately 90% authentic.

Each judge assesses: (1) all target claims are inferable from the document, (2) no extra factual information beyond the tra- jectory is introduced, and (3) the document reads naturally. text: MAD quantifies how much information is lost by relying on extrinsic evaluation alone, without requiring an arbitrary threshold. As a secondary interpretable metric, we report the divergence rate: the percentage of trajectories where the two evaluations disagree by more than τ = 0.15: DivRate = 1 N X T ⊮[|Acc(T) −Extr(T)| > τ] (6) 6 Experiments 6.1 System Under Test To demonstrate the benchmark’s diagnostic utility, we eval- uate a representative agent memory system (Figure 1). The system follows the dominant architectural pattern shared by virtually all contemporary memory systems, Hindsight (La- timer et al. 2026), Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025), Ariadne- Mem (Zhu et al. 2026), and commercial agent memory ser- vices alike: (1) extract structured observations from artifacts (documents, emails, meeting transcripts), (2) embed them, (3) retrieve related existing facts via vector search, (4) clas- sify the relationship via LLM (create, update, reinforce, con- flict, or skip), and (5) synthesize into evolving facts with history. This extract-embed-classify-synthesize pipeline rep- resents the current state of the art; despite surface differences in implementation details (confidence stepping in Hindsight, entropy-aware gating in AriadneMem, Add/Update/No-op in Mem0), the core information flow is shared. The specific system is not the contribution; any system implementing this pattern could be substituted. Our goal is to demonstrate what the benchmark reveals about this class of systems,

Our goal is to demonstrate what the benchmark reveals about this class of systems, not to evaluate a particular implementation. We adopt a two-layer terminology: observations are static, atomic factual statements extracted from a single artifact (typed into categories such as decisions, commitments, or milestones), while facts are the evolving, synthesized knowl- edge units that the system maintains over time. Observa- tions are immutable once extracted; facts are the persistent memory that gets created, reinforced, updated, or superseded as new observations arrive. Not all observations aggregate into facts: some are too granular or transient (e.g., a one- time action item), and evaluating observations in isolation would only measure extraction completeness and atomicity, not whether the system forms and maintains correct knowl- edge. Other systems use different terms for similar concepts (Hindsight calls atomic extractions “facts” and synthesized summaries “observations”; Mem0 uses “memories” for both layers without distinction), but the underlying two-layer pat- tern, extraction followed by aggregation, is shared. Intrinsic evaluation targets the fact layer, as this is the knowledge state that determines system behavior. Each fact maintains a numeric confidence score (0–1), strengthened by +0.1 per reinforcing observation and ad- justable by the LLM on create, update, or supersede deci- sions. The divergence therefore persists across all four, with full statistics in Appendix H. 6.3 Diagnostic Decomposition A key advantage of intrinsic evaluation is diagnostic decom- position: when a system fails, we can identify which pipeline stage is responsible: • Extraction failures: Claims present in artifacts but not captured by the system’s observation layer. • Synthesis failures: Claims extracted but incorrectly merged, duplicated, or lost during fact aggregation. • Update failures: State transitions missed or false updates applied. • Conflict failures: Contradictions not detected or resolved incorrectly. text: layer. • Synthesis failures: Claims extracted but incorrectly merged, duplicated, or lost during fact aggregation. • Update failures: State transitions missed or false updates applied. • Conflict failures: Contradictions not detected or resolved incorrectly. Table 4 reveals three co-occurring failure patterns that in- tensify with difficulty. First, the claim miss rate rises from 58% at L1 to 88% at L3, indicating that subtle or embedded claims are increasingly lost during extraction. Second, fact count inflates from 9.1 to 20.7, showing the system fragments knowledge into many small, partially redundant facts rather than synthesizing them into coherent evolving beliefs. Third, classification accuracy degrades from 37% to 10%, mean- ing the system rarely identifies the correct action (create vs. update vs. reinforce) at higher difficulty. These three signals are mutually reinforcing: poor classification leads to creating new facts instead of updating existing ones (inflating count), which in turn fragments claims across facts (increasing miss rate on claim-level matching). None of these diagnostics are available from the extrinsic QA score, which remains flat at ∼50% regardless of the underlying failure pattern. 7 Discussion and Limitations Complementary, Not Replacement. Intrinsic evaluation does not replace extrinsic evaluation, it complements it. Ex- trinsic captures end-to-end utility as intrinsic enables diag- nosis. A system scoring high on both is genuinely effective; high extrinsic but low intrinsic signals
title: extrinsic scores.

text: and Limitations Complementary, Not Replacement. Intrinsic evaluation does not replace extrinsic evaluation, it complements it. Ex- trinsic captures end-to-end utility as intrinsic enables diag- nosis. A system scoring high on both is genuinely effective; high extrinsic but low intrinsic signals fragility (dependent on LLM compensation); high intrinsic but low extrinsic in- dicates a retrieval or generation bottleneck. Synthetic Document Validity. Generated documents may not capture all properties of real multi-author text. We miti- gate this through style grounding, multi-model rotation, and hybrid injection at L3. Future work should validate transfer via rank correlation with human-annotated real document sequences. Scope and Limitations. FEB-30 targets factual evolution across multi-author artifacts. It does not evaluate episodic memory, procedural memory, or single-turn conversational recall, capabilities addressed by existing benchmarks. The benchmark contains 30 trajectories, sufficient for diagnostic evaluation but not for fine-grained statistical comparisons. Scoring relies on embedding similarity thresholds and LLM judges, introducing potential measurement noise. 8

text: We introduced FEB-30, the first benchmark designed for in- trinsic evaluation of agent memory systems. By constructing trajectories where the expected memory state is known at ev- ery step, we demonstrated that intrinsic and extrinsic evalua- tion diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories showing meaningful disagreement, revealing false positives and false negatives invisible to response-based benchmarks. Diagnostic decomposition showed the system correctly classifies memory operations only 20% of the time (degrading from 34% at L1 to 10% at L3), a dimension ex- trinsic evaluation cannot measure. We argue that intrinsic evaluation should become standard practice alongside extrinsic benchmarks, analogous to how intrinsic evaluation of embeddings complemented down- stream task evaluation in NLP. We release FEB-30, the gen- eration pipeline, and the scoring framework for reproducible evaluation of agent memory.

B System Prompts B.1 Observation Extraction The prompts below are generalized for reproducibility. Un- like the other prompts in this section, which are domain- agnostic, this prompt is grounded in the benchmark’s business/customer-relationship domain, since the extrac- tion categories define what the system treats as a fact- worthy observation. The {categories} placeholder be- low stands for the domain-specific observation categories actually used (e.g. a decision, a commitment, an action item). Each extracted observation is further structured into who/what/when/why/where fields; the statement referred to below is the what field. You are analyzing text from a multi-author artifact. Extract observations and entities from the text. Observation guidelines: - Extract every distinct piece of domain-relevant information. - Each observation must contain exactly ONE factual claim. - Every observation must be directly supported by the source text. - Each observation’s statement must be self-contained and understandable without the source document. - Resolve all pronouns and references. - Include temporal grounding when dates are available. - Categories: {categories} - Confidence: "High" = explicitly stated; "Medium" = discussed but not finalized; "Low" = inferred.

text: Entity guidelines: - Extract all people mentioned by name, using the most complete form of each name. - Extract other domain-relevant entities: {entity_types} B.2 Fact Synthesis You are synthesizing knowledge from observations into evolving facts. Decide how the new observation relates to existing facts: - "create": New knowledge not covered by any fact. - "update": Adds new details to an existing fact. MERGE new information with existing. - "reinforce": Confirms without adding new info. - "supersede": Contradicts an existing fact. - "none": Purely procedural, no lasting value. Critical rules for "update": - MUST preserve all details from existing statement. - ADD new information (metrics, timelines, people). - PREFER updating over creating. Almost every observation matching an existing fact should be "update." If in doubt, use "update." G Metric Correlations To validate that our intrinsic metrics capture meaningful sig- nal, we compute correlations between claim miss rate, intrin- sic accuracy, and extrinsic accuracy across all 30 trajectories (using per-trajectory means across N=11 runs). Miss rate strongly predicts intrinsic accuracy (r = −0.84) but weakly predicts extrinsic accuracy (r = −0.39), confirm- ing that intrinsic metrics capture signal that extrinsic eval- uation misses. The moderate intrinsic-extrinsic correlation (r = 0.55) indicates the two methods share some signal but measure substantially different properties. The strong negative correlation between miss rate and intrinsic accuracy (r = −0.84, p < 10−8) validates that claim coverage is the primary driver of intrinsic scores. text: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity Enforcement for Thin-Structure Segmentation Junho Moon Hanyang University Seoul, Republic of Korea jhmoon6807@hanyang.ac.kr Ikbeom Jang* Hankuk University of Foreign Studies Yongin, Republic of Korea ijang@hufs.ac.kr
title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity

text: Thin, elongated structures are particularly sensitive to con- nectivity errors, as even a few local segmentation mistakes can disrupt otherwise continuous paths. Existing skeleton- based objectives typically supervise fixed centerline loca- tions and do not account for alternative local routes that may restore connectivity. We propose TRACE, a topology- aware, prediction-adaptive objective that uses a target skele- ton to define required local connections. For each connec- tion, TRACE identifies the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction and jointly supervises its bottleneck with the corresponding skeleton point. The supervision thus adapts to the evolving prediction rather than remaining fixed to the centerline. We further introduce a topology-aware skeleton carrier that preserves both foreground and class- specific topology, enabling reliable definition of these con- nections. Extensive experiments across six 2D and 3D bench- marks show that TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintaining strong segmentation accuracy with low training overhead. Code will be released upon acceptance.
title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity

text: Segmentation of thin, elongated structures is particularly vulnerable to connectivity errors, as even a few misclassified pixels or voxels can break an otherwise continuous struc- ture. This issue arises in retinal vessels [21], cerebral vessels [26, 27], hepatic vessels [2], pavement cracks [15], and road networks [7], where continuity is essential to structural in- tegrity. Such local errors can fragment a single structure into multiple components while producing only minor changes in conventional region-overlap metrics [20]. Reliable thin- structure segmentation therefore requires preserving connec- tivity in addition to accurate region and boundary prediction. text: Centerline- and skeleton-based losses [1, 19, 20] provide direct structural supervision and may additionally incorporate boundary or width information. Target-only methods [13] avoid skeletonizing the prediction, reducing training-time computation and memory overhead. Their supervision, however, remains confined to fixed sup- port derived from the ground truth. More broadly, skeleton- based support depends on the chosen skeletonization pro- cedure [17], and even topology-preserving support may not identify the prediction error responsible for a connectivity break. Global objectives based on persistent homology or component graphs [3, 11, 16, 22] constrain connected com- ponents, loops, and cavities, yet provide limited guidance for repairing a specific local break. Neighbor-, affinity-, and path-based objectives [10, 24, 25, 28] provide localized su- pervision through individual neighbors, selected point pairs, or graph paths. These formulations organize connectivity around individual relations or pairwise paths, leaving un- resolved how to jointly reconnect all same-class branches affected by a local break under the current prediction. 1 arXiv:2610.22210v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026
title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity

text: We propose TRACE, a topology-aware objective that ex- tends skeleton supervision from a fixed target to guidance for adaptive reconnection. TRACE uses a topology-preserving skeleton to identify neighboring same-class branches that should remain connected. Based on the current prediction, it identifies the easiest valid local reconnection and jointly supervises the skeleton point with the bottleneck limiting this reconnection. To support this formulation, we further in- troduce a Topology-Aware Skeleton Carrier (TASC), which preserves both foreground and class-specific topology while defining local connectivity requirements. We identify the reconnection bottleneck through an exact local search us- ing centered logit-margin scores derived directly from stan- dard semantic logits. The proposed objective avoids costly prediction-side skeletonization and requires no architectural modifications, enabling efficient plug-and-play integration into existing segmentation pipelines. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce TRACE, a prediction-adaptive connectivity objective that uses a skeleton to define required connec- tions and supervises the easiest reconnection bottleneck. • We present TASC, a class-labeled skeleton that preserves both foreground and class-specific topology while identi- fying same-class branches that should remain connected. • Across six 2D and 3D thin-structure benchmarks, TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintaining strong region-overlap and boundary accuracy. • We further demonstrate that TRACE is computationally efficient, generalizes across segmentation backbones, and complements existing topology-aware methods.

text: Centerline and skeleton supervision. Centerline- and skeleton-based objectives promote connectivity by supervis- ing thin structural representations derived from the predic- tion, target, or both. clDice [20] measures reciprocal overlap between the prediction and target using differentiable soft skeletons. Menten et al. [17] developed topology-preserving differentiable skeletonization for gradient-based losses. clCE [1] applies cross-entropy at centerline locations to improve topology while preserving region accuracy. cbDice [19] in- corporates boundary and radius cues to preserve geometry across varying widths. Skeleton Recall Loss (SkelRecall) [13] uses a dilated, class-labeled target skeleton and avoids prediction-side skeletonization. These methods, however, tie structural supervision to centerline or skeleton support and do not explicitly identify the prediction error that blocks a valid reconnection. TRACE addresses this gap with a topology-preserving carrier that defines the local same-class branches to be connected and extends pointwise supervision to the bottleneck of their easiest valid reconnection. Global topology supervision. Global topology objectives constrain connected components, loops, and cavities across the segmentation. TopoLoss [11] uses persistent homology to identify predictions associated with topological errors. Betti Matching [22] matches topological features between the prediction and target while accounting for their spatial correspondence. Subsequent extensions support multiclass segmentation [3]. Topograph [16] represents prediction– target component relations as a graph to provide efficient binary and multiclass constraints. Whereas these methods constrain global or component-level topology,

text: prediction and target while accounting for their spatial correspondence. Subsequent extensions support multiclass segmentation [3]. Topograph [16] represents prediction– target component relations as a graph to provide efficient binary and multiclass constraints. Whereas these methods constrain global or component-level topology, TRACE tar- gets a required local reconnection and directly supervises its prediction-dependent bottleneck. Pairwise and path supervision. Pairwise- and path-based objectives supervise connectivity through neighboring el- ements, point pairs, or graph paths. MALIS [24] assigns pairwise connectivity errors to the weakest edge along a maximin path in an affinity graph. CAPE [10] penalizes shortest-path costs between selected target-graph nodes on a predicted distance map. SCNP [25] adjusts semantic log- its according to the weakest same-class neighbor. WPRF [28] optimizes widest-path reachability between sampled point pairs on a target-derived support graph using a separate affinity prediction. In contrast, TRACE defines each local reconnection on a class-labeled carrier that preserves the topology of both the foreground union and each semantic class. Removing a carrier point exposes all neighboring same-class branches, which we jointly reconnect via an ex- act search over at most 9 candidate points in 2D or 27 in 3D, using a centered logit margin computed directly from standard multiclass semantic logits. 3. Method TRACE turns target-skeleton supervision from fixed-point enforcement into prediction-adaptive local reconnection by identifying and supervising the bottleneck of the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction. Datasets and Evaluation Metrics Datasets. We evaluate TRACE on six thin-structure segmen- tation benchmarks spanning 2D and 3D data, including bi- nary and multiclass tasks. DRIVE [21] is used for retinal ves- sel segmentation and contains 40 RGB fundus images, split into 20/10/10 for training/validation/testing. DeepCrack [15] contains 537 RGB images for surface-crack segmentation (270/30/237), while DeepGlobe Roads [7] contains 6,226 RGB satellite images for road segmentation (4,980/622/624). For DSCA [27], we convert 224 cerebral digital subtraction angiography sequences, annotated for the main arterial trunk and bifurcated vessels, into 2D minimum-intensity projec- tions and use a 144/36/44 split. MSD Hepatic Vessel [2] contains 303 portal-venous-phase 3D CT scans with hepatic vessel and tumor annotations; we treat tumor voxels as back- ground for binary vessel segmentation and use a 243/30/30 split. TopCoW [26] contains 125 3D CT angiography scans with multiclass annotations for 13 Circle of Willis vessel segments, split into 100/12/13 cases. Metrics. We evaluate segmentation quality using com- plementary metrics for connectivity, topology, boundary accuracy, and region overlap. We first report clDice [20] to measure centerline consistency and connectivity preser- vation. We also report the absolute Betti number error, β = |∆β0| +

text: evaluate segmentation quality using com- plementary metrics for connectivity, topology, boundary accuracy, and region overlap. We first report clDice [20] to measure centerline consistency and connectivity preser- vation. We also report the absolute Betti number error, β = |∆β0| + |∆β1| [22], to quantify topological errors associated with structural connectivity. The 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) [23] assesses boundary accuracy by measuring spatial disagreement while limiting outlier sensitivity. Finally, Dice [9] measures region overlap and assesses whether improved structural consistency is achieved without sacrificing overall segmentation accuracy. We com- pute each metric independently for each foreground class in every test sample. For multiclass datasets, we average the class-wise values to obtain one score per metric per sample, then average these per-sample scores over the entire test set. 4.2. Main Comparison Setup Baselines. Our primary focus is connectivity preservation; therefore, we conduct extensive comparisons with represen- tative skeleton-based losses, including clDice [20], clDice with topology-preserving skeletonization (Topo-clDice) [17], clCE [1], cbDice [19], and SkelRecall [13]. We also include the recent multiclass extension of Betti Matching [3] as a consistent global-topology reference across binary and mul- ticlass benchmarks, using the projection-based protocol of [14] for 3D volumes. To isolate the effects of the train- ing objective, the main benchmark evaluates representative methods using standard semantic outputs while keeping the prediction head and inference

TRACE shows consistent per- formance across diverse thin-structure segmentation tasks. Nevertheless, its structural supervision depends on the topol- ogy encoded in the ground-truth annotations. A promising direction is to combine TASC with uncertainty-aware filtering or consistency-based refinement to suppress unreliable topological annotations.

text: We propose TRACE, an efficient topology-aware objective that reframes skeleton supervision as prediction-adaptive lo- cal reconnection. TASC provides a class-labeled topological carrier that preserves foreground and class-specific topology while identifying same-class branches that should remain connected. Based on this representation, TRACE identifies the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction and supervises its critical bottleneck. Across six 2D and 3D benchmarks covering binary and multiclass segmentation, TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintain- ing region-overlap and boundary accuracy. It also preserves target topology across deep-supervision scales, introduces only modest training overhead, and requires no architectural 8

text: A RESTART RULE FOR GENETIC ALGORITHMS BASED ON SCHNABEL CENSUS A.V. EREMEEV YU.V. ZAKHAROVA
title: A RESTART RULE FOR GENETIC ALGORITHMS

text: A new adaptive restart rule for Genetic Algorithms (GAs) is considered. The rule is based on the Schnabel Census method, originally developed for statistical estimation of a size of animal population. In this paper, the Schnabel Census method is applied as a heuristic to estimate the number of different solutions that may be visited with positive probability, given the current distribution of offspring. The rule consists in restarting a GA as soon as the maximum likelihood estimate reaches the number of different solutions observed at the recent iterations. We demonstrate how the new restart rule can be applied in a GA with steady-state replacement scheme, using three different combinatorial optimization problems as examples. Computational experiments on well-known benchmarks show a statistically significant advantage of the GAs with the new restarting rule over the original versions of GAs. The new restart rule also tends to be superior to the well-known rule, which restarts an algorithm when the current iteration number is twice the number of iterations till the current best incumbent was found. Keywords: genetic algorithm, restart rule, maximum likelihood, combinatorial optimization. 1
title: A RESTART RULE FOR GENETIC ALGORITHMS

text: Genetic Algorithms (GAs) are the randomized search heuristics based on the biological analogy of selective breeding in nature, originating from the work of J. Holland [29]. A GA manipulates with a population of λ individuals, using the random operators that model mutation and crossover in nature. Suppose that a GA is applied to an optimization problem with a finite space of solutions D and an objective function f : D →R to be maximized or minimized.
