text: This paper proposes SCOPED, aiming at integrating complementary visual understanding capabil- ities into a unified Vision-Language Model through skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation. SCOPED independently optimizes capability-specific experts and abstracts reusable solution pat- terns from reward-evaluated trajectories into explicit capability skills. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide capability experts to provide structured supervision for the unified student. Our experiments demonstrate that SCOPED consistently improves performance across diverse visual understanding capabilities. Our further analyses reveal cross-capability interference during mixed- capability optimization and show that skill augmentation improves the preservation and transfer of specialized expert capabilities. AI USE STATEMENT Generative AI tools were used solely for language polishing and improving the clarity of the manuscript. All research ideas, experimental design, implementation, analysis, and conclusions were independently developed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the con- tent of the paper.

A.3 REWARD DESIGN We design task-specific automatic rewards to accommodate the heterogeneous output spaces of the training tasks. For textual predictions, the answer is extracted from the <answer> field when avail- able and normalized by lowercasing, removing punctuation and articles, and collapsing consecutive spaces. Structured predictions are additionally checked against their required output formats. Fine-Grained Perception and Visual Grounding. For perception tasks with textual outputs, we use token-level F1 between the normalized prediction and reference answer. For visual grounding, the prediction is parsed as a list of labeled bounding boxes. Predicted and ground-truth boxes with the same normalized label are greedily matched according to their intersection-over-union (IoU). For each capability, a single skill is constructed from the trajectories generated

text: capability-wise skill abstraction procedure introduced in Sec. 3.2. Skill construction uses only training data and training-set rollouts, while the held-out evaluation set is used exclusively for final evaluation. For each capability, a single skill is constructed from the trajectories generated by its corresponding optimized expert. Trajectory Curation. For each training instance, the optimized capability expert samples multi- ple rollout trajectories, each of which is evaluated by the corresponding capability-specific reward function. To reduce redundancy, we deduplicate repeated trajectories within each task subtype and balance the retained trajectories across subtypes so that high-resource tasks do not dominate the subsequent skill construction process. Reward-Based Trajectory Grouping. Following Sec. 3.2, the curated trajectories are divided into successful and failed cohorts according to their capability-specific rewards. This grouping provides complementary evidence about effective solution patterns and recurring failure modes. Trajectory-Level Reflection. The optimized capability expert performs trajectory-level reflection over the successful and failed cohorts using outcome-specific reflection prompts. Successful tra- jectories are used to identify reusable solution strategies and verification behaviors, while failed trajectories are analyzed to diagnose recurring failure mechanisms and derive corrective guidance. The resulting reflections are aggregated into a capability-specific evidence ledger containing both effective behaviors and failure-avoidance guidance. Capability Skill Synthesis. Based on the aggregated trajectory-derived evidence, the same capa- bility expert synthesizes a single capability-level skill containing reusable procedural

text: guidance. The resulting reflections are aggregated into a capability-specific evidence ledger containing both effective behaviors and failure-avoidance guidance. Capability Skill Synthesis. Based on the aggregated trajectory-derived evidence, the same capa- bility expert synthesizes a single capability-level skill containing reusable procedural guidance for the corresponding capability. The resulting skill is subsequently used to condition the expert during skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation. This procedure produces one skill for each of the four capabilities. Detailed reflection and skill-induction prompts are provided in Appendix A.12. Ablation of Trajectory Sources. Table 7 examines the contribution of successful and failed tra- jectories to skill construction. Using either successful or failed trajectories alone improves the cor- responding capability experts, while combining both sources achieves the strongest overall perfor- mance. This indicates that successful solution patterns and corrective failure experience provide complementary information for capability skill abstraction. 18

text: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio? Probing and Distilling Damping Structure Zainab Afolabi Amazon Web Services zafolabi@amazon.co.uk Vadim Selyutin * Amazon Web Services seliutin@amazon.ae Zhao Gao * Amazon Web Services orangez@amazon.co.uk Babs Khalidson * Amazon Web Services khalbabs@amazon.co.uk Mohamed Ghoneim Amazon Web Services ghoneimm@amazon.co.uk
title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio?

text: Physical understanding is crucial for decision making, yet vision models strug- gle to infer properties such as damping that govern how materials behave. Audio encodes such properties directly, because an object’s acoustic response to impact reveals its damping through measurable decay. We probe frozen encoders for the quality factor Q, a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away, and report how well each embedding orders impacts by Q using the Spearman rank correlation ρ, for which ρ = 1 is a perfect ordering and ρ = 0 an unrelated one. Audio embeddings reach ρ = 0.73 and retain most of that advantage on materials withheld from training, while a sin- gle video frame taken at the moment of impact, encoded by CLIP, supports only ρ = 0.28. Having established where the signal lives, we ask how much of that gap vision can recover. We distill a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone through a trained projection head and find that this recovers a useful fraction of the audio advantage. Because pooled correlations on this task are dominated in prac- tice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input
title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio?

text: correlations on this task are dominated in prac- tice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338 (+0.053 over the matched four-frame baseline, 14 of 17 materials), a gain that no category-level strategy can produce. Widening the visual input to four frames spanning the impact supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost, which indicates that part of what a single frame misses is visible dynamics. 1
title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio?

text: A robot clearing a table observes two cups that look alike, one ceramic and one plastic. A vision model might correctly label their materials, but this categorical distinction does not reveal how they behave, since the ceramic cup shatters when dropped while the plastic cup bounces. Without physical grounding, vision cannot predict these divergent futures. This appearance–reality gap pervades modern computer vision. Large vision models achieve strong recognition performance, but what they encode is how things look rather than how things be- have. Physics benchmarks confirm this gap. PhysBench [Chow et al., 2025] found that GPT-4o achieves only 46.99% on physical dynamics (49.49% overall, against 95.87% for humans), and Physion++ [Tung et al., 2023] showed that all models remain well below human performance on latent properties such as mass, friction, or elasticity. ∗Equal contribution. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: PhysUnderstand. arXiv:2610.22221v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026
title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio?

text: Audio captures what appearance does not. An object’s acoustic response to impact is governed by physical laws: stiffness, density, and geometry set the resonant frequency, and internal friction, radiation, and mounting set the damping. We confirm the gap directly. Frozen audio embeddings predict the quality factor Q at ρ = 0.73, while a single CLIP-encoded video frame taken at the moment of impact supports only ρ = 0.28. Here Q is a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations a struck object completes before its ring dies away, so a highly resonant glass has a large Q and a heavily damped cloth a small one. We write ρ for the Spearman rank correlation between predicted and true values: ρ = 1 means the model orders impacts by Q perfectly, and ρ = 0 means its ordering carries no information about the truth. We use ρ throughout because we care about whether a model can rank objects by how much they ring, not about the absolute scale of its predictions. Our question is the narrower one of how far a frozen visual encoder can be pushed toward the audio number. Our answer is that it can be pushed a useful fraction of the way. We distill from a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP encoder, training a projection head as the

text: encoder can be pushed toward the audio number. Our answer is that it can be pushed a useful fraction of the way. We distill from a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP encoder, training a projection head as the only new component, and measure the outcome under a protocol in which knowing the material category earns nothing: correlations are computed within a material that was held out from the projection head and from the probe alike. Distillation improves prediction there for most of the 17 materials. Part of this improvement needs no audio at all, since giving the encoder four frames spanning the impact, so that it can see the object deform and recoil, supplies about half. Most of the audio signal nonetheless stays out of reach, which we take to mark the interesting part of the problem rather than a settled question. 1.1 Contributions • We propose probing frozen encoders for a continuous physical property, the quality fac- tor Q, rather than for the categorical material labels used in prior evaluations. Our mea- surements show that audio embeddings predict Q at ρ = 0.73 whereas a single CLIP frame reaches 0.28, that this audio advantage persists for materials withheld from training (ρ ≈0.60), and that every visual encoder we test is near chance at ranking objects within wood,

text: Impact sounds encode material properties that appearance cannot reveal. Owens et al. [2016a] es- tablished this connection with the Greatest Hits dataset, demonstrating that visual models can learn to predict impact sounds. RealImpact [Clarke et al., 2023] extends this with force profiles and cali- brated measurements. ObjectFolder [Gao et al., 2023] quantifies the relative contributions of vision, audio, and touch for material understanding, finding that audio often provides complementary infor- mation. In robotics, audio frequently outperforms vision for physical property estimation: Thankaraj and Pinto [2023] show that auditory feedback improves manipulation, and SonicSense [Liu and Chen, 2024] demonstrates object perception through acoustic vibration. We connect this evidence to representation learning: if audio encodes physics, can this structure be distilled into vision? 2

text: Joint audio-visual embeddings have evolved from contrastive methods [Arandjelovi´c and Zisserman, 2017, Owens and Efros, 2018] to masked autoencoders [Gong et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2023]. PE-AV [Vyas et al., 2025] scales to 100M pairs, achieving state-of-the-art results on audio-visual retrieval. ImageBind [Girdhar et al., 2023] aligns six modalities through image-paired data. Prior work evaluates these models on retrieval and classification, but, to our knowledge, none probes what frozen audio-visual embeddings capture about physical properties, or whether this knowledge can transfer to vision alone. Recent benchmarks reveal systematic failures in physical reasoning. Beyond PhysBench [Chow et al., 2025], Physion [Bear et al., 2021] shows that models fall short of humans at predicting physical outcomes, Physion++ [Tung et al., 2023] extends this to outcomes that depend on latent properties, and CLEVRER [Yi et al., 2020] and IntPhys [Riochet et al., 2021] probe causal and intuitive physics understanding. These benchmarks focus on dynamics prediction, and we complement them by probing continuous material properties. Audio and vision have long supervised one another: ambient sound can train visual representa- tions [Owens et al., 2016b], and visual networks can train sound representations [Aytar et al., 2016]. Knowledge distillation transfers representations across architectures [Hinton et al., 2015] or modal- ities: Gupta et al. [2016] transferred supervision from labeled RGB images to depth and optical- flow

Knowledge distillation transfers representations across architectures [Hinton et al., 2015] or modal- ities: Gupta et al. [2016] transferred supervision from labeled RGB images to depth and optical- flow representations. Our work differs in targeting specific physically relevant structure rather than general representations, and takes a step toward making acoustically grounded properties partially accessible to vision alone. 3 The Quality Factor: A Continuous Physical Property 3.1 Why Q? The quality factor Q = πf0/β combines resonant frequency (f0) and damping rate (β) into one dimensionless scalar. The damping rate β sets how quickly a ringing object falls silent in absolute time, whereas Q counts how many oscillation cycles it completes before decaying, so a high-pitched glass can fall silent sooner than a lower-pitched metal bowl while having the higher Q. We target this compound quantity for three reasons. Being dimensionless, Q is comparable across objects regardless of size or pitch, so a wine glass and a steel beam can share a Q despite frequencies orders of magnitude apart. It also varies continuously within material categories: a thin metal sheet and a solid metal block are both “metal” yet differ substantially in Q, so predicting it demands more than category recognition. Finally, it has direct physical consequences, determining whether an

text: also varies continuously within material categories: a thin metal sheet and a solid metal block are both “metal” yet differ substantially in Q, so predicting it demands more than category recognition. Finally, it has direct physical consequences, determining whether an object rings, bounces, or absorbs energy on impact. These properties make Q a stricter test of physical grounding than frequency, which is largely predictable from visible geometry, or the damping rate alone, which is confounded with object size. 3.2 Extraction Pipeline We extract Q from audio recordings in the Greatest Hits dataset [Owens et al., 2016a], which con- tains 977 videos of objects being hit with a drumstick. Our copy carries annotations for 975, totaling 28,444 individual impacts across 17 material categories. Figure 1 illustrates both the quantity and the method. For each annotated impact, we take the mag- nitude of the analytic signal (the Hilbert envelope) to obtain an amplitude envelope A(t) and fit the decay model A(t) = A0e−βt + C by nonlinear least squares, with β bounded to [0.1, 1000] s−1 and the additive constant C absorbing background noise. The resonant frequency f0 is the dominant peak of the power spectrum above 50 Hz, a floor that avoids low-frequency room noise. Retaining only fits with R2 ≥0.8 leaves 17,958 usable impacts, 63% of the total. Rejections concentrate

text: 4.1 Models Evaluated We probe four frozen encoders. Two are audio-visual: PE-AV [Vyas et al., 2025], trained con- trastively on 100M audio-visual pairs and exposing separate audio, video, and joint embeddings, and CAV-MAE [Gong et al., 2023], a masked autoencoder trained on AudioSet [Gemmeke et al., 2017] with both reconstruction and contrastive objectives. Two are vision-only: CLIP ViT-L/14 [Radford et al., 2021], trained on 400M image–text pairs, and DINOv2 ViT-L/14 [Oquab et al., 2024], trained by self-distillation on curated images without language supervision. The latter pair represents the two dominant recipes for general-purpose visual features, and neither has any acoustic exposure. Video inputs are single frames taken at the annotated moment of impact, each encoded as an image, and audio inputs are 2-second clips centered on the impact. 4.2 Probing Protocol We train ridge regression (λ = 1.0) from frozen embeddings to log(Q + 1) and evaluate with Spearman ρ. Pooled correlations carry 95% bootstrap intervals over samples (1,000 resamples). Leave-one-material-out figures are means over the 17 held-out materials, and their intervals resample the materials rather than the samples (10,000 resamples), which is why they are wider. 4.3 Results Table 1 reports the result. This is physical generalization: a probe never trained on the held-out material still ranks its impacts by how much they ring, using only their audio embeddings. 5.2 Within Materials, and Which Component of Q Two checks ask whether these correlations are really about physics. The first computes ρ within a single material category, where category identity supplies nothing. The modalities separate sharply: PE-AV audio reaches 0.67 on metal and 0.57 on wood, whereas every visual encoder, including PE- AV’s video branch, is at or below 0.36 on metal and close to zero (|ρ| ≤0.19) on wood, ceramic, and plastic. CLIP scores 0.06, 0.03, −0.14, and −0.19 on metal, wood, ceramic, and plastic. Base- line vision barely distinguishes physical variation among objects of the same material. Table 7 in Appendix B gives the breakdown. The second asks which component of Q is responsible, since Q = πf0/β compounds a spectral term with a damping term, and across our impacts Q is strongly rank-correlated with f0 (ρ = 0.87) and moderately anti-correlated with β (ρ = −0.54). An encoder that merely recovered pitch would therefore score well. Probing the targets separately (Appendix A) shows that the damping term is the one audio captures best: PE-AV audio reaches ρ = 0.729 on β

The student is CLIP ViT-L/14, also frozen, with a trainable three-layer MLP head (GELU, LayerNorm, 1024- dimensional output) as the only component that learns. Its input is four frames taken at −0.1, 0, +0.1, and +0.2 s around the annotated impact, each encoded independently and concatenated with their successive differences. Training minimizes a symmetric InfoNCE loss [van den Oord et al., 2018] between the projected visual embedding and the teacher’s audio embedding (τ = 0.07), with batch size 256 and AdamW [Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019] at a learning rate of 10−4. Because the space of plausible configurations is large, we fixed the feature variant and the number of epochs on a validation split drawn from 20% of the training videos (which selected the four frames + deltas input, trained for two epochs) and used the test split for no selection, reporting three seeds. This is marginally above the 0.430 obtainable from perfect material-category knowledge and still far below the audio teacher. Because the pooled measure is dominated in practice by category information, exceeding that reference by 0.01, which lies inside the three-seed range, is not conclusive (Figure 2), so we turn to a measure under which category identity earns nothing. 6.4 Leave-One-Material-Out, with the Head Held Out LOMO is the discriminating test, because correlations are computed within a held-out material: a model that outputs a category’s median Q predicts a constant there and is scored zero, since Spearman ρ is undefined for constant predictions. text: a model that outputs a category’s median Q predicts a constant there and is scored zero, since Spearman ρ is undefined for constant predictions. Two conditions must both hold for the test to mean anything. The material must be excluded from the probe, and it must also be excluded from the distillation head—otherwise the head has already learned that material’s appearance-to-audio mapping and the probe merely reads it back. We refer to this stricter protocol as true LOMO. Table 4 reports the outcome. Distillation improves LOMO by +0.104 over the single-frame base- line, with 15 of 17 materials improving (Wilcoxon p = 0.002), and by +0.053 over the four-frame baseline, with 14 of 17 improving (p = 0.001). The gains are uneven: the five largest (single-frame baseline →distilled) are on granular and natural surfaces, namely gravel 0.364 →0.708, grass 0.377 →0.610, dirt 0.285 →0.605, leaf 0.290 →0.541, and rock 0.247 →0.469, which together account for about three-quarters of the total gain. 6.5 Controls Table 5 collects the three controls, which together bound what this result can mean. 7

text: The first control asks how much of any Q correlation is simply material recognition. Mapping the true material to its per-category median Q gives ρ = 0.430 [0.400, 0.457], and a material classifier trained on CLIP features, at 45.6% accuracy, mapped the same way gives ρ = 0.279 [0.246, 0.311]. Any pooled correlation near 0.28 is therefore indistinguishable from category recognition, which is precisely why we rest the argument on LOMO rather than on the pooled figure. The second asks whether the trainable head is doing the work rather than the teacher. An identically shaped head given direct supervision on log(Q+1), with no audio involved, reaches only ρ = 0.275 [0.224, 0.293], below the 0.300 [0.267, 0.330] reached by a linear probe on the same features. Additional parameters buy nothing here: with roughly 14,000 noisy scalar targets, a regression head has little to learn from, whereas the teacher supplies a dense 1024-dimensional target whose geometry already encodes damping. The third asks whether any structured target would do. Holding the seed fixed, distilling from correctly matched audio reaches ρ = 0.466 (the first, and highest, of the three seeds, whose mean is the 0.440 of Table 3) against 0.298 with no distillation. Distilling from a fully shuffled teacher (10.6% material agreement) still reaches 0.359, and positional indexing, used by an earlier version of our pipeline (13.3% material agreement), reaches 0.360. Roughly a third of the raw gain therefore survives destroying the correspondence entirely, while the larger part, +0.107, requires the teacher to correspond to the frame it is paired with. Reported gains from cross-modal distillation should be read against a shuffled-teacher control for this reason. 7 Discussion Three findings survive the controls. First, damping structure is present in audio and largely absent from single-frame vision, and separating the components of Q shows that audio carries the damping term β better than pitch, which is what licenses reading the transferred structure as physical. Second, a frozen visual encoder can acquire part of that structure from a frozen audio teacher without any Q label entering training, and the gain holds on materials withheld from the projection head as well as the probe (0.234 to 0.338, 15 of 17 materials), where a category-level strategy earns nothing. Third, roughly half of the improvement needs no audio at all and follows from four frames instead of one, so part of what looks like a limit of

text: to 0.338, 15 of 17 materials), where a category-level strategy earns nothing. Third, roughly half of the improvement needs no audio at all and follows from four frames instead of one, so part of what looks like a limit of vision is a limit of single-frame inputs. The effect is modest in absolute terms. Most of the teacher’s signal does not cross, and on the pooled measure the distilled encoder barely exceeds what perfect category knowledge would supply. That comparison is itself the methodological result we would most like carried forward: category identity alone reaches ρ = 0.43 on this task, so a pooled number near that value says little about physical understanding. Establishing physical transfer needs an evaluation under which category recognition earns nothing, namely true LOMO, together with a shuffled-teacher control (Section 6.5). The residual is a concrete target rather than a closed question. Damping depends on internal structure a camera often cannot observe, and the natural next step is β itself, the component audio predicts best, nearly independent of f0, and the one on which the distilled student already improves most. 8 Limitations Four caveats bound these results. First, evaluation is confined to Greatest Hits (977 videos, 17 materials) and to one visual domain, so whether the projection head learns a general appearance-to- damping mapping or associations

text: student already improves most. 8 Limitations Four caveats bound these results. First, evaluation is confined to Greatest Hits (977 videos, 17 materials) and to one visual domain, so whether the projection head learns a general appearance-to- damping mapping or associations tied to controlled drumstick footage is unresolved. Second, the R2 ≥0.8 filter keeps 63% of annotated impacts at strongly material-dependent rates (Section 3.2), and the five largest per-material gains of Section 6.4 fall on materials retaining a third to just over a half of their impacts, so those correlations cover a selected minority of each category. The discarded impacts cannot be assessed with Q at all, since there the target is undefined. Third, the four-frame model is evaluated on Q alone (the f0/β probe in Appendix A uses a single-frame student), so although probing shows that audio carries β better than f0 (Section 5.2), we do not establish transfer of physical structure in general, and properties that impact sound encodes weakly or not at all, such as friction, may behave differently. Finally, we measure transferred structure by probing accuracy alone, so whether better Q decodability yields better physical decisions remains to be shown on a task whose outcome is not a function of Q. 8

text: versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X’s 1.6× HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5× improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems. Index Terms—Accelerators, DLRM, GPU, kernels, machine learning, recommendation systems
title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta’s End-to-End

text: The immense potential of AI applications has catalyzed an unprecedented expansion in the accelerator landscape. While NVIDIA remains the incumbent platform, the AMD Instinct™[1, 2] GPU has emerged as a viable alternative. Meanwhile, hyperscalers have also developed custom sili- con, including Meta MTIA [3–6], Google TPU [7], Amazon Trainium [8], Microsoft Maia [9], Huawei Ascend [10], Alibaba Hanguang [11], and Baidu Kunlun [12]. Capitalizing on this hardware proliferation, Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators at scale. This strategic diversification delivers several benefits: (1) enabling cost optimization by preserving the flexibility to adopt the most economical solutions as the market evolves; (2) strengthening supply-chain resilience; and (3) matching model characteristics to the most suitable hardware. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific opti- mizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. For example, fundamental differences in memory hierarchies and execution units (e.g., 32-thread warps vs. 64-thread wave- fronts) thwart direct software migration between NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. These challenges are most acute in deep learning recommendation models (DLRMs) [13, 14]. Unlike the relatively uniform large language models (LLMs), DLRMs are characterized by diverse model architectures, fragmented compute kernel sets, irregular matrix dimensions, and complex memory access patterns. While industry adoption of AMD GPUs has largely focused on inference—evidenced by Meta’s deployment of hundreds of thousands

text: language models (LLMs), DLRMs are characterized by diverse model architectures, fragmented compute kernel sets, irregular matrix dimensions, and complex memory access patterns. While industry adoption of AMD GPUs has largely focused on inference—evidenced by Meta’s deployment of hundreds of thousands of AMD GPUs—distributed training presents a far greater technical challenge. This paper delivers the first hyperscaler report of enabling AMD GPUs for production- scale DLRM training. We demonstrate that through systematic optimization, AMD MI350X achieves performance comparable to the incumbent NVIDIA B200 GPU across a diverse suite of production DLRMs. We distill our production experience into three reusable principles for new hardware integration: Hardware-model co-design. Different accelerator microarchi- tectures offer distinct advantages and trade-offs. Rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, hardware-model co-design—revising the model structure and software recipe—is essential to leverage an accelerator’s specific strengths. Specif- ically, we exploit MI350X’s 1.6× HBM capacity relative to B200. To maximize training efficiency, we expand per-GPU batch sizes and reduce activation checkpointing while simulta- neously optimizing data or model parallelism and implementing efficient embedding re-sharding. Beyond training throughput, we utilize the additional HBM to enhance model quality by enabling longer input sequences, larger hidden dimensions, and expanded embedding tables. This holistic approach delivers a 20% training speedup and a >0.1% improvement in normalized entropy (NE) [15], demonstrating that architectural synergies can

Analytical performance model. Traditionally, selecting high- performance general matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels relies on offline tuning—a cumbersome process that generalizes poorly across the disparate matrix dimensions common in DLRMs. We propose Origami, an analytical performance arXiv:2610.22230v1 [cs.DC] 15 Oct 2026

text: model that predicts optimal tile configurations in microseconds, achieving 93% accuracy relative to exhaustively autotuned kernels across diverse matrix shapes. While analytical models are not new, Origami extends prior approaches to multi-chiplet architectures, with accuracy validated at production scale. Agentic workflows for kernel optimization. To reduce en- gineering burden and migration friction, we codify complex kernel-tuning principles into agentic workflows: automating microarchitecture-aware configuration selection, swizzling pro- cess IDs, incorporating occupancy hints, and leveraging spe- cialized hardware instructions. Together, they achieve 1.6×– 2× speedups across both hand-written and compiler-generated kernels. Furthermore, we leverage agentic workflows to auto- mate the application of solutions that address hardware-specific bottlenecks; e.g., to mitigate the performance impact of atomics on MI350X, we apply a tree-reduction algorithm that utilizes shared memory to deliver up to 4× speedup in custom kernels. Our methods have been validated at scale, supporting produc- tion training on tens of thousands of MI350X GPUs at Meta. Across a representative set of production models, MI350X achieves a geometric-mean throughput of 101% relative to our established B200 baseline—a platform highly optimized through extensive deployment. This performance parity vali- dates the viability of our multi-vendor diversification strategy. Limitations. While end-to-end performance is comparable, MI350X’s GEMM performance remains an area for improve- ment, due to both the overhead of emulated TF32 GEMMs in the absence of native hardware support and the relative maturity of NVIDIA cuBLAS over AMD hipBLAS in handling irregular matrix shapes. Although we use DLRMs to drive our optimizations, the underlying principles are generalizable to a broader spectrum of ML workloads, including LLMs. Indeed, we have successfully optimized LLM training on clusters of more than 2,000 MI350X GPUs; a comprehensive analysis of LLM-specific performance is reserved for future work. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on production-scale training using AMD GPUs. Our purpose is not to rank accelerators, but to share generalizable optimization methods for emerging hardware by synthesizing insights from our large-scale deployment of AMD, NVIDIA, and MTIA platforms. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open- source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.

text: and infrastructure investment dedicated to improving DLRM efficiency. Sparse evolution. Embedding tables grow rapidly in both vocabulary size and dimensionality, forcing distributed sharding and collective-heavy embedding exchange. As training clusters expanded, two practical directions emerged. First, multi-stage pipelining became essential [22]: embedding lookup, all-to-all exchange, and optimizer steps must be organized to reduce exposed latency and avoid synchronization bubbles. Second, sparse parallelism itself evolved beyond single dimension. Recent work on two-dimensional sparse parallelism [23] in- troduces a hierarchical strategy that adds data-parallel structure on top of model-parallel embedding sharding, reducing all- to-all scope, lowering embedding activation memory growth, and mitigating imbalance/straggler behavior. Together, these trends reflect a broader shift: the sparse subsystem is no longer “just embeddings,” but a distributed system whose parallelism strategy, pipeline structure, and optimizer semantics jointly determine scalability. Dense evolution. Classical DLRMs pair large embedding tables with relatively shallow dense components (e.g., a few fully connected layers for feature interaction). Recent evolution of DLRMs (Fig. 1) shows that scaling the dense subsystem can yield predictable quality gains analogous to LLM scaling laws [24, 25]. Wukong [26] demonstrates this by stacking factorization-machine layers with a synergistic upscaling strategy, achieving smooth quality improvements over orders of magnitude in dense-side FLOPs. A complementary trend is the adoption of Transformer-like modules to model long user-interaction histories. Meta’s HSTU [21] exemplifies

AMD MI350X vs NVIDIA B200 Table I compares the GPU specs. AMD MI350X is built on the CDNA™4 architecture and is the first AMD GPU used for production-scale training at Meta. MI350X features eight accelerator complex dies (XCDs) with 32 compute units (CUs) each (a total of 256 CUs), a 288 GB HBM3e memory pool with up to 8 TB/s bandwidth, and 538 GB/s of scale-up bandwidth per GPU. B200 offers 180 GB of HBM capacity, with 900 GB/s of scale-up bandwidth per GPU. B200 and MI350X are same-generation flagships with closely matching theoretical bounds: their near-identical peak compute (2250 vs. 2300 BF16 TFLOPS) and HBM bandwidth (8 TB/s) yield largely coincident roofline curves [27], and thus a similar performance envelope for ML workloads. Their strengths are complementary: B200 leads on per-GPU scale-up bandwidth (900 vs. 538 GB/s), an all-to-all NVSwitch fabric (versus AMD’s point-to-point xGMI mesh), shared memory per SM (256 vs. 160 KB), and native TF32 support, whereas MI350X’s principal advantages are its 1.6× HBM capacity

Hipification. Hipification is AMD’s CUDA-to-HIP (Heterogeneous-compute Interface for Portability) translation process that converts NVIDIA CUDA code into HIP equivalents; see Fig. 2. There are two primary approaches: (1) compile-time hipification using AMD’s open-source hipify-clang compiler, which translates CUDA constructs to HIP at build time, and (2) rule-based source-code translation using hipify_torch, which traverses and rewrites source files before compilation. While hipification provides broad functional compatibility and enables most CUDA workloads to run on AMD with minimal manual effort, performance portability remains a challenge. For instance, CUDA uses a warp size of 32, whereas an AMD GPU uses a wavefront size of 64. Kernels that naively hardcode warp sizes will likely perform suboptimally without tuning. The emergence of agentic AI tools has fundamentally lowered the cost of switching from NVIDIA to AMD. At Meta, we leverage AI agents to address issues in the hipification process. These agents iteratively compile code, interpret error messages, and apply fixes until the build succeeds. When a niche CUDA library lacks a ROCm equivalent, AI agents can even

text: Meta, we leverage AI agents to address issues in the hipification process. These agents iteratively compile code, interpret error messages, and apply fixes until the build succeeds. When a niche CUDA library lacks a ROCm equivalent, AI agents can even generate custom shims to mimic the missing functionality. This makes AMD GPUs accessible to a broad range of ML researchers, who can now deploy high-performance code without mastering low-level hardware nuances. Meta’s Usage of AMD GPUs. Meta started using the AMD MI300X [28] for inference in 2024. Today, models compatible with AMD GPUs make up over 60% of production model types, weighted by resource footprint. Training DLRMs, on the other hand, presents a greater challenge than inference: • Synchronization and network pressure: Training involves numerous GPUs in tight lockstep with frequent synchroniza- tion, heavily straining network efficiency. • Kernel and optimizer: Training requires comprehensive backward kernels and advanced optimizer support. • Generalization: While inference can be optimized per workload, training must rely on generalized optimizations for out-of-the-box performance—orders of magnitude more training trials run before a model is finalized, making per-job optimization infeasible. Addressing these challenges requires systematic optimizations across the software stack, from low-level libraries (Section III) and kernel tuning (Section IV) to high-level model co-design (Section V). III. ROOFLINE-DRIVEN OPTIMIZATION OF ROCM LIBRARIES The ROCm software platform provides optimized libraries, runtimes, and firmware for AMD GPUs. Grounded in roofline models [27] and hardware constraints, we optimize core GEMM kernels and selection algorithms to approach theoretical limits. To optimize RCCL, the collective communication library for distributed training, we derive theoretical bounds from hardware specifications as optimization targets. These roofline-driven prin- ciples enable low-level libraries to deliver robust, generalizable performance across diverse AI workloads. A. text: kernel selection strategies. To deliver strong performance across this diversity, we integrate performance enhancements into hipBLASLt [29] GEMM kernels through its assembly backend, TensileLite [30]. These enhancements leverage new CDNA 4 [31] hardware capabilities alongside algorithmic refinements that reduce the solution space and enable finer- grained runtime parameter selection via Origami (Section III-B). Beyond exploiting new ISA features, we employ the following algorithmic techniques. Stream-K partitions GEMM computations across CUs at finer granularity than traditional data-parallel tiling, improving load balance for tensor sizes that do not evenly tile the device. We also introduce new reduction strategies and runtime dispatch logic, improving robustness across a broad range of compute- and memory-bound tensor sizes. Notably, a single GEMM kernel can now achieve performance previously requiring multiple specialized kernels. Workgroup mapping via space-filling curves. MI350X GPUs use a multi-XCD architecture in which workgroups are dis- tributed across XCDs, each with a private L2 cache. Scheduling workgroups operating on adjacent or overlapping tiles across different XCDs degrades cache locality and efficiency. To address this, hipBLASLt introduces a mapping strategy based on space-filling curves that preferentially co-locates workgroups processing nearby tiles on the same XCD, improving spatial lo- cality, cache utilization, and power efficiency. Multiple mapping strategies are supported within the GEMM assembly kernels, with runtime-selectable parameters integrated with Origami to select the optimal strategy

B. Origami: Analytical Kernel Selection Prior kernel selection approaches in hipBLASLt relied on offline autotuning: enumerating kernel configurations on repre- sentative tensor shapes and storing the best selections in lookup tables. This approach fails at scale: recommendation models execute thousands of unique GEMM shapes per model, and maintaining exhaustive databases for every shape is impractical. Origami replaces offline autotuning with an analytical per- formance model that predicts optimal tile configurations in microseconds. The model can be viewed as inferring the critical path of a GEMM problem across the memory and compute hierarchy. It captures the full tiling hierarchy—from matrix instruction dimensions through local data share (LDS) tiles to implicit cache tiles formed by workgroups sharing the L2 and last level cache (LLC)—and computes cycle counts geometrically at each level. C. GPU Power Excursion Boost The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative initia- tive between hyperscale datacenter operators and technology vendors to standardize interfaces and specifications across infrastructure domains, including power delivery. The MI350X accelerator is implemented as a 1000 W open accelerator module (OAM) [33]. While the OAM must comply with the nominal total board power (TBP) over a 1s window, the specification permits transient power excursions over shorter intervals as defined by the OAM’s excursion design power (EDP). These excursions range from 1.1× TBP over 20 ms up to 2.0× TBP over 20 µs. Although the OCP specification defines minimum electrical, thermal, and power-delivery capabilities, system designers may provision additional margin. Meta’s AI hardware platform, for example, supports average power levels of up to 1.36× TBP over a 50 ms window for a 1000 W OAM configuration. Shampoo Optimizer and rocSOLVER Shampoo [35, 36] is a second-order optimizer widely de- ployed due to its faster convergence compared to first-order methods like Adam [37]. Shampoo maintains Kronecker- factored preconditioner matrices, requiring periodic compu- tation of matrix fourth roots to update the preconditioners. This matrix root computation relies on eigen decomposition provided by the rocSOLVER library. For large models, these steps dominate Shampoo’s overhead, making rocSOLVER’s performance critical to overall training throughput. The de facto algorithm to compute the eigen decomposition of a symmetric input matrix A has three steps: (1) reduce A into tridiagonal form, yielding an orthogonal U and a tridiagonal T such that A = UTU T ; (2) compute eigenvalues Λ and eigenvectors V of

text: eigen decomposition of a symmetric input matrix A has three steps: (1) reduce A into tridiagonal form, yielding an orthogonal U and a tridiagonal T such that A = UTU T ; (2) compute eigenvalues Λ and eigenvectors V of T; and (3) backtransform eigenvectors Q = UV so that A = QΛQT . In rocSOLVER, reduction to tridiagonal form is accomplished with block Householder transformations [38] operating on panels of the input matrix; updates to the rest of the matrix are applied once per panel as a pair of GEMM operations. Step (2), based on Cuppen’s Divide-and-Conquer (D.C.) [39], is the most complex step and the focus of our optimizations. Cuppen’s D.C. splits T into sub-matrices that are processed independently and then merged in pairs. Typically, D.C. operates on unreduced sub-blocks of T (i.e., blocks separated by zero off-diagonal elements), but this can lead to load unbalancing: sub-optimal CU allocation often follows because the size of sub- blocks is input-dependent. During a merge step, D.C. identifies deflated eigenvalues (which will not be modified by the merge) and updates all others by solving the secular equation. To improve data locality and reduce data movement, our implementation ensures that eigenvalues (and associated eigenvectors) are properly ordered. Eigenvectors belonging to identical eigenvalues require (possibly costly) extra preprocess- ing; rocSOLVER includes specialized code to efficiently handle matrices exhibiting several identical eigenvalues in merge steps. Lastly, newly and previously computed eigenvectors are merged using batched GEMMs for optimal performance. Fig. 8 demonstrates that rocSOLVER achieves comparable eigen decomposition performance on AMD MI350X relative to NVIDIA B200. Distributed Shampoo partitions large precon- ditioner matrices into fixed-size blocks (typically 4096 × 4096 or 8192 × 8192) to bound per-GPU computation and enable parallel eigen decomposition across devices. These block sizes represent the practical sweet spot: large enough to preserve preconditioning quality, yet small enough for tractable eigen decomposition. rocSOLVER narrows the gap with cuSOLVER at these critical 4K and 8K dimensions, enabling competitive Shampoo-based training on AMD hardware. A. Triton Kernel Optimizations 1) Attention Kernels in DLRM: We focus on two important Triton kernels in Meta’s production DLRM workloads, GDPA and HSTU, and describe the AMD-specific optimization tech- niques that yield substantial speedups on MI350X. Generalized dot-product attention (GDPA). GDPA [40] extends standard attention [41,42] by fusing GeLU-activated attention and a feed-forward network into a single operator. Central to Meta’s Kunlun [43] and Interformer [44] models, the fused kernel substantially increases the compute and memory intensity, positioning the kernel as a critical optimization target. Hierarchical sequential transduction unit (HSTU). HSTU [21] is a novel sequential attention architecture designed for large-scale recommendation systems, where the input consists of variable-length user interaction histories with high sparsity. Unlike standard attention, HSTU uses variable-length batching and processes sequences with sparsity ratios as high as 0.95, meaning the effective computation is concentrated in a small fraction of the sequence. 2) Optimization Techniques:

While we use GDPA and HSTU as examples, these optimization techniques are generally applicable to a broad set of Triton kernels for ML models. PID swizzle. MI350X features a multi-XCD (chiplet) archi- tecture where eight XCDs share an L2 cache. The default linear mapping of Triton program IDs to tiles can cause XCDs to access disjoint L2 cache regions, resulting in poor cache utilization. PID swizzle uses tl.swizzle2d to remap the two- dimensional program ID grid so that spatially adjacent tiles are scheduled on the same XCD, improving L2 cache locality. Occupancy hints. The waves_per_eu hint controls the max- imum number of wavefronts resident on each execution unit, which directly affects register allocation. By setting waves_per_eu=3 (GDPA) or exposing it as an autotunable parameter with values 0–4 (HSTU), the compiler reduces per- wavefront register usage, allowing more concurrent wavefronts to hide memory latency. This trades per-wavefront performance for higher occupancy, which is beneficial when the kernel is not fully compute-bound. MFMA

AMD CDNA architectures provide matrix fused multiply-add (MFMA) instructions in con- figurable tile sizes, controlled by the matrix_instr_nonkdim parameter. Triton configuration autotuning. Triton kernel configurations (BLOCK_SIZE, num_stages, num_warps, etc.) are critical to performance, and optimal values differ between NVIDIA and AMD GPUs due to architectural differences. AMD’s 64-thread wavefronts, compared to NVIDIA’s 32-thread warps, favor larger num_warps values to achieve sufficient occupancy and hide memory latency. NVIDIA’s Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) on H100/B200 enables deep software pipelining (e.g., num_stages ∈[4, 7]) by efficiently managing asynchronous memory transfers. AMD MI350X lacks a TMA equivalent; high stage counts increase LDS pressure without commensurate latency hiding benefits. Empirically, AMD kernels achieve better performance with shallower pipelines (e.g., num_stages ≈2). GeLU fast math. When thousands of threads contend on a single address (as is common in reduction-style kernels), these coherency messages serialize execution, leading to poor performance. The fundamental issue is that per-thread global atomics scale poorly with thread count on multi-chiplet architectures. On a monolithic GPU, the L2 cache can coalesce nearby atomic operations; on a multi-chiplet GPU, each chiplet must coordinate with the others, and a single contended address becomes a serialization bottleneck. Our measurements show that MI350X can be over 10× slower than B200 on atomic-heavy kernels at high contention rates, while matching or exceeding B200 on atomic-free, bandwidth-bound kernels. Algorithmic strategies: hierarchical reduction and caching. We employ two complementary strategies depending on the contention pattern. text: on atomic-free, bandwidth-bound kernels. Algorithmic strategies: hierarchical reduction and caching. We employ two complementary strategies depending on the contention pattern. When many threads contend on a single shared address (e.g., a global counter), we apply hierarchical reduction: threads accumulate results in fast on-chip memory (registers or shared memory), a parallel tree reduction sums them within each block, and a single representative thread issues one global atomic. This converts N global atomics into ⌈N/block_size⌉, a reduction factor of up to 1024×. When threads target many distinct addresses with temporal locality (e.g., gradient scatter to embedding rows), we apply caching: each thread maintains a small register cache of recently written addresses, merging consecutive updates to the same address locally before issuing a single atomic add on eviction. The tradeoff is additional shared memory usage. For kernels where contention is rare, the overhead may slightly increase latency, but the benefit grows superlinearly with contention rate, making this transformation highly effective for production workloads with moderate-to-high atomic traffic.

In the backward pass, we exploit temporal locality within each thread’s iteration stream. Each thread maintains a 2-slot register cache that maps row indices to accumulated gradient values. Agentic Kernel Optimization Workflow While GDPA and HSTU are widely shared across models, Meta’s DLRM ecosystem contains a long tail of custom kernels tailored to individual models. Manually tuning each kernel is labor-intensive and does not scale. To address this, we developed an agentic AI workflow that encodes our tuning principles as executable skills, enabling automated kernel performance analysis and optimization. This workflow builds upon Meta’s KernelEvolve framework [47], which provides the underlying agent infrastructure and skill abstraction mechanisms. While KernelEvolve focuses on the general systems architecture for agentic code optimization, our contribution lies in encoding AMD-specific tuning principles as production-ready skills and validating their effectiveness at scale on Meta’s production DLRM training workloads. The agentic workflow operates in three phases: 1) Benchmark & Profile: Capture representative inputs from production workloads, reproduce the performance in a standalone benchmark, and leverage profiler tools (e.g., AMD rocprofv3 [48], Triton Proton [49]) to identify the main bottlenecks such as low occupancy, poor cache utilization, or instruction stalls. 2) Match & Fix: Map observed bottlenecks to a library of optimization skills, each encoding a tuning principle (e.g., PID swizzling, occupancy hints, atomic avoidance) with code transformation templates and applicability conditions. 3) Generate & Validate: Produce candidate kernel modi- fications, benchmark them on representative inputs, and

Case Study: Jagged Flash Attention. We illustrate the workflow with the jagged flash attention (JFA) kernel, which represents a challenging optimization target due to its ir- regular memory access patterns. The JFA kernel, used in our ranking models, exhibited a 2× slowdown on MI350X compared to B200 in its backward pass. Profiling revealed that tl.atomic_add operations dominate execution time, a known bottleneck on AMD’s multi-XCD architecture (see Section IV-B for details). The agent recognized this pattern, noting that the grouped query attention (GQA) mode causes multiple Q heads to race on shared dK/dV gradients. Following the skill’s guidance, the agent rewrote the kernel to accumulate dK/dV in registers per KV-head group and issue a single tl.store at the end, a tree-reduction pattern that eliminates atomic operations. The optimized kernel achieved a 2.3× speedup (32 ms→14 ms), transforming MI350X from 2× slower than B200 to 15–20% faster, and delivering a 25% improvement in end-to-end model training throughput. MODEL-SYSTEM CO-DESIGN AMD MI350X’s large HBM capacity creates opportunities for model-system co-design, where training configurations and model architectures are jointly optimized to exploit the additional memory resources. We explore two complementary directions: improving training throughput (examples/second) and improving model quality. A. Strategies for Training Efficiency Increased batch size. Larger HBM capacity enables training with larger batch sizes, improving GPU utilization by amortizing kernel launch overhead and better saturating compute units. For example, a friend recommendation model achieves 26% speedup at 2× batch size, 46% at 4×, and 51% at 6× (Fig. 15a). For a social ranking model migrated to MI350X, doubling the batch size yields 12–15% throughput improvement over B200 baseline with the same batch size (B200 encounters out-of- memory errors at doubled batch size). text: For a social ranking model migrated to MI350X, doubling the batch size yields 12–15% throughput improvement over B200 baseline with the same batch size (B200 encounters out-of- memory errors at doubled batch size). Removal of activation checkpointing. Activation check- pointing (AC) trades memory for computation by recomput- ing activations during the backward pass instead of storing them. With larger HBM, AC can be disabled for memory- constrained layers, eliminating redundant recomputation. The activation memory budget controls how aggressively PyTorch checkpoints activations: a budget of 1.0 saves all activations (maximum memory, no recomputation), while lower values trigger selective recomputation to reduce memory at the cost of throughput. Fig. 14 shows the tradeoff between activation memory budget and training throughput on a 1.3B-parameter GPT model. MI350X’s larger HBM enables it to run without AC entirely, achieving 96.4 examples/second. In contrast, B200 must use aggressive AC (budget ≤0.35) just to fit, achieving 71.5 examples/second, a 1.35× throughput disadvantage solely attributable to memory constraints. Dense parallelism strategy tuning. Additional HBM allows for relaxed sharding strategies, mitigating communication overhead. For FSDP-based training [54], moving from ZeRO-3 to ZeRO- 2 or ZeRO-1 [55] reduces AllGather and ReduceScatter communication volume. Switching to HSDP (Hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism) further hides communication latency by overlapping with computation. For a large Ads foundation model at 1K GPU scale, HSDP provides

Triton Inductor kernels show model-dependent results: some models achieve parity (0.99×– 1.08×) while others show MI350X incurring 1.22× higher latency than B200, reflecting ongoing efforts to refine Inductor and eliminate heuristics specifically tailored for NVIDIA GPUs (Section IV-D). C. Operational Considerations Integrating a second GPU vendor into a previously NVIDIA- only fleet raised operational challenges in power, reliability, and observability. In addition to performance, operational maturity is just as critical to adopting a new vendor, and much of the tooling and fleet-management machinery we built generalizes to future accelerators. Reliability. We track MI350X on the same metrics as our NVIDIA fleet (training-failure rate, unplanned unavailability, and hardware-swap rate), and it is steadily converging toward NVIDIA-fleet levels: the training-failure rate has more than halved from its peak as we resolved new at-scale failure modes, namely HBM RAS, multi-chiplet memory-access faults, and silent data corruption (SDC). text: levels: the training-failure rate has more than halved from its peak as we resolved new at-scale failure modes, namely HBM RAS, multi-chiplet memory-access faults, and silent data corruption (SDC). SDC, the bit-flips that corrupt re- sults without crashing, grows with cluster size and is the hardest to tame, so we address it end-to-end: a model-level checksum- and-replay check flags non-deterministic steps (distinguishing on-chip corruption from communication non-determinism); an all-pairs vote across a host’s GPUs pinpoints the culprit device (the one that disagrees with all its peers) and auto-quarantines the host; and the same check runs during host qualification and burn-in to screen SDC-prone hosts before they enter the training pool, catching over 2× the SDC of the vendor’s field-health tool. These mitigations preserve correctness: across the tens of models we train on both vendors, results reach numerical parity (training-loss difference within 0.3% and NE within ∼10−4 at multi-thousand-GPU scale).

text: Observability. AMD telemetry initially lagged NVIDIA’s mature stack, so we closed the gap: we integrated the effi- ciency metrics our NVIDIA fleet relies on (TFLOPS, SM/CU and memory utilization, throughput) and a hardware-agnostic trace-analysis interface (compute/communication breakdown, imbalance, overlap, and timeline analyses) that also enables side-by-side cross-vendor trace comparison (the basis for the apples-to-apples measurements here) and extends to MTIA. Power management. Operating the MI350X against its excur- sion envelope rather than its steady-state limit is a fleet-level capability: it depends on platform provisioning beyond the OCP minimum and on tuning the control-loop response to production phase patterns. Section III-C describes the mechanism and the resulting 3–6% end-to-end gain.

text: Hardware Accelerators. Custom hardware accelerators ex- ploit the structure of neural network computations. Meta’s MTIA [3,4,56] an in-house family of custom AI chips, designed to provide superior cost efficiency over commercial GPUs for the company’s large-scale DLRM and GenAI workloads. Google’s TPU [50] employs systolic arrays for efficient matrix multiplication. Recent accelerators target emerging workloads: spiking neural networks [57], heterogeneous precision [58], and processing-in-memory architectures that reduce the memory bandwidth bottleneck [59]. Distributed Training Infrastructure. The LLM pretraining study on AMD MI300X GPUs [60] presents the transformer sharding strategy and the practical guidance for fault-tolerant distributed training. Scaling DLRM training requires purpose- built infrastructure. Zion [61] is a scale-up DLRM training platform that co-locates CPUs and accelerators to handle the memory capacity demands of embedding tables while leveraging GPU compute for dense operations. TorchRec [22] provides a PyTorch domain library with optimized distributed primitives, including automatic sharding planners that partition embedding tables across devices. Embedding Table Sharding and Placement. DLRMs present unique systems challenges due to their massive embedding tables, which can exceed hundreds of gigabytes and dominate both memory capacity and bandwidth requirements. Intelligent partitioning of embedding tables across heterogeneous memory hierarchies is critical for training throughput. RecShard [62] formulates embedding placement as a mixed-integer linear program, leveraging per-feature access statistics—including cat- egorical value frequency distributions and pooling factors—to

text: capacity and bandwidth requirements. Intelligent partitioning of embedding tables across heterogeneous memory hierarchies is critical for training throughput. RecShard [62] formulates embedding placement as a mixed-integer linear program, leveraging per-feature access statistics—including cat- egorical value frequency distributions and pooling factors—to achieve over 2.5× throughput improvement compared to size- based sharding. The key insight is that not all embedding rows are accessed equally; exploiting this skew enables fine-grained placement across GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSDs. 2D sparse parallelism [23] combines data and model parallelism for embeddings, enabling training to scale to thousands of GPUs. Kernel-Level Optimizations. Efficient GPU kernels are es- sential for embedding operations. FBGEMM [46] provides high-performance implementations of table batched embedding lookups, fused optimizers, and quantized operations optimized for recommendation workloads. These kernels exploit memory access coalescing, warp-level parallelism, and mixed-precision computation to maximize GPU utilization. For inference, mixed- precision embeddings [63] achieve 200× compression by learning per-feature precision assignments, grouping features by frequency to reduce the search space. KernelEvolve [47] provides an agentic framework for kernel optimization; we build specialized workflows that incorporates expert-tuning heuristics and architectural insights tailored for training workloads, sim- plifying cross-platform GPU kernel porting and optimization.

text: We present the first comprehensive study demonstrating that AMD MI350X GPUs achieve performance parity with NVIDIA B200 for production DLRM training through cross- stack optimizations spanning core ROCm libraries, kernel tuning, and model co-design. Our work addresses architec- tural differences between vendors—memory capacity, atomic performance, instruction sets—through principled algorithmic adaptations, hardware-aware autotuning, and HBM-conscious model co-design, providing a transferable framework for hardware-agnostic training at scale. Our optimizations have been upstreamed and open-sourced, establishing a foundation for multi-vendor ML infrastructure.

title: WaveLLM: Wavelet-Domain LLM Entropy Modeling for Lossless

text: Lossless image compression fundamentally relies on accurate en- tropy modeling, driving a recent shift toward large language model (LLM)-based methods. However, existing approaches mainly em- phasize the modeling capacity of LLMs while directly serializing images into pixel or residual sequences, leaving heterogeneous signal patterns entangled within a single prediction stream. In this paper, we argue that effective entropy modeling depends not only on model capacity, but also on the predictability of the input representation. Motivated by this insight, we propose WaveLLM, a wavelet-domain LLM-based entropy model for lossless image compression. By decomposing an image into multi-level wavelet subbands, WaveLLM converts a heterogeneous prediction prob- lem into a set of more structured and statistically homogeneous subproblems that are more amenable to autoregressive probability estimation. To bridge numerical coding symbols with the LLM’s na- tive text token space, we introduce a dedicated numerical interface featuring value embeddings and a coefficient prediction head. Fur- thermore, a task-adaptive prompting strategy is designed to enable a single shared model to adapt to diverse subbands within a unified framework. text: Unlike lossy compression, which can trade distortion for bitrate, lossless image compression fundamentally relies on entropy cod- ing. Classical codecs improve this process through carefully de- signed predictors, reversible transforms, and context models [2, 4, 19, 33, 34, 39], while learned methods have further advanced coding efficiency by using neural networks to capture more com- plex dependencies [3, 15, 20, 28, 36, 42–44]. Related work spans image and video coding, feature and representation compression, and other structured signals, with associated datasets, benchmarks, and quality assessments [10–13, 17, 18, 21, 22, 31, 32]. These direc- tions provide broader context for our setting, while recent lossless image coding explores large language models (LLMs) as entropy models [5, 7, 8]. arXiv:2610.22232v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

In other words, better entropy coding should not be attributed solely to a stronger model. text: solely to a stronger model. It also requires an input representation that is more structured, more homogeneous, and thus easier to predict. When heterogeneous signal patterns are entangled within a single sequence, the entropy model must continuously adapt to sharply different statistical regimes, which makes accurate probability esti- mation intrinsically more difficult. By contrast, when the input is reorganized into simpler components with clearer statistical regu- larity, the same model can solve a substantially easier prediction problem. Based on this insight, we propose to perform probability predic- tion and entropy coding in the wavelet domain. As the work most closely related to ours, we compare three LLM-based methods in Fig. 1. The pixel-domain method directly models pixels [5], requiring the entropy model to handle pixel distributions from different fre- quency components. The residual-domain method models residuals instead [8], which reduces the difficulty of probability modeling to some extent. In our method, we first transform the image into the wavelet domain and decompose it into progressively organized fre- quency subbands [6, 26, 34]. This decomposition separates coarse low-frequency structures from directional high-frequency details across multiple resolutions [26, 34], thereby converting a highly het- erogeneous prediction problem into a collection of more structured and statistically homogeneous subproblems. Nevertheless, combining the wavelet domain with an LLM is far from natural. Pretrained LLMs are
title: MM ’26, November 10–14, 2026, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

text: high-frequency details across multiple resolutions [26, 34], thereby converting a highly het- erogeneous prediction problem into a collection of more structured and statistically homogeneous subproblems. Nevertheless, combining the wavelet domain with an LLM is far from natural. Pretrained LLMs are designed for discrete text tokens, whereas wavelet coefficients are numerical symbols from visual sig- nals. To bridge this gap, we design a dedicated interface that makes wavelet-domain entropy coding compatible with the LLM backbone. Specifically, we introduce a coding-oriented numerical adaptation mechanism that maps wavelet coefficients into a compact local symbol space, equips them with trainable value embeddings, and predicts valid coefficient values through a dedicated value predic- tion head. This design preserves numerical validity while enabling the pretrained LLM to operate effectively on wavelet-domain sym- bols. Another challenge arises from the fact that different wavelet subbands still exhibit distinct statistical characteristics [34, 38]. Training an independent entropy model for each subband would significantly increase model complexity and undermine the practi- cality of LLM-based coding. To address this issue, we further pro- pose a prompt-based adaptive entropy coding strategy, where one shared entropy model is reused across different subbands through task prompts. By conditioning the shared backbone on subband identity and decoded context, the same model adapts its probability predictions to different subband distributions without requiring separate models. In this

text: one shared entropy model is reused across different subbands through task prompts. By conditioning the shared backbone on subband identity and decoded context, the same model adapts its probability predictions to different subband distributions without requiring separate models. In this way, the proposed framework achieves both subband-specific modeling flexibility and parameter efficiency. Building on the above designs, we present WaveLLM, a wavelet- domain LLM-based entropy model for lossless image compression. The contributions of this work are threefold. • We note the importance of input predictability in lossless image compression and decompose each image into multiple wavelet subbands. The resulting subbands have distinct coefficient statis- tics that can be modeled separately. • We design a dedicated interface between wavelet-domain signals and an LLM pretrained on language data. It maps coefficients to compact local IDs, uses a dedicated value embedding module, and predicts valid coefficient values over the local range through a dedicated value head. • We propose a task-prompt mechanism for adaptive modeling of different subbands. By conditioning the shared backbone on sub- band identity and decoded context, WaveLLM adapts to distinct subband statistics without requiring separate models. text: 2.1 Lossless Image Compression Classical lossless codecs rely on predictive filtering and entropy coding. PNG [4], JPEG-LS [19, 39], FLIF [33], JPEG2000 [34], and JPEG XL [2] represent widely used designs. The reversible 5/3 lifting transform in JPEG2000 provides a practical route to loss- less wavelet coding [6, 34]. Learned compression methods have explored causal autoregressive models such as PixelCNN and Pix- elCNN++ [30, 37], hierarchical latent-variable models [15, 28, 36], invertible flows [42, 43], residual coding [3, 29], and bit-plane de- compositions [44]. Across these approaches, the central challenge remains accurate probability estimation over high-dimensional dis- crete image signals. CALLIC [20] reports strong learned-method results through content-adaptive per-image optimization. 2.2 Wavelet-Domain Codecs Wavelets decompose an image into low-frequency structure and high-frequency detail at multiple resolutions [6, 26]. Natural-image wavelet coefficients are non-Gaussian and subband dependent [34, 38], with broader low-frequency responses and sparse, sharply peaked high-frequency coefficients. This separation makes the wavelet domain attractive for entropy modeling. WaveFormer and BVINet incorporate wavelet modules into Transformer-based video inpainting [40, 41]. Unlike these restoration models, WaveLLM uses a reversible wavelet decomposition and decoded same-level subbands for lossless entropy coding. In lossless coding, JPEG2000 established the canonical framework by combining the reversible 5/3 integer lifting transform with wavelet-domain context model- ing and arithmetic coding [34]. The lossless branches of iWave and iWave++

text: and decoded same-level subbands for lossless entropy coding. In lossless coding, JPEG2000 established the canonical framework by combining the reversible 5/3 integer lifting transform with wavelet-domain context model- ing and arithmetic coding [34]. The lossless branches of iWave and iWave++ use reversible 5/3 wavelet coding with learned PixelCNN entropy models [24, 25]. WaveLLM studies this setting and replaces the PixelCNN-style entropy model with a shared prompted LLM over codec-defined subband tasks. 2.3 LLMs for Lossless Image Compression Beyond compressing intermediate representations produced by large models [10–13], recent LLM-based image compression directly employs pretrained language models as entropy models [5, 7, 8]. Delétang et al. demonstrated that autoregressive language model- ing can be interpreted directly as compression [7]. In image coding, two recent methods apply pretrained LLMs to lossless compression. P2-LLM keeps the problem in the pixel domain and frames com- pression as next-pixel prediction [5]. The visual-prompt method introduces a lossy reconstruction as an auxiliary cue and codes the residual with an LLM [8]. Both papers report Llama-3-8B backbones. WaveLLM takes a different route. It introduces LLM-based entropy modeling into a reversible 5/3 wavelet codec, using a 3B backbone adapted through LoRA [16]. Unlike P2-LLM, which processes a rasterized pixel stream without codec-defined structure, and the visual-prompt method, which requires an auxiliary lossy codec to generate visual embeddings, WaveLLM operates

text: a reversible 5/3 wavelet codec, using a 3B backbone adapted through LoRA [16]. Unlike P2-LLM, which processes a rasterized pixel stream without codec-defined structure, and the visual-prompt method, which requires an auxiliary lossy codec to generate visual embeddings, WaveLLM operates within the causal structure of the wavelet codec. It relies on decoded context that is already available at each coding stage. At the coefficient interface, it also differs from the reserved-vocabulary strategy used by P2- LLM by introducing a dedicated local value-ID space together with separate value embedding and prediction modules. 3 Method 3.1 Overall Framework WaveLLM uses a reversible color transform, a fixed 5/3 wavelet transform, a causal coding order, and arithmetic coding, while the learnable part focuses on wavelet-domain probability factoriza- tion over codec-defined subbands. For each subband, WaveLLM forms a task prompt, maps the resulting value sequence through the coding-oriented numerical interface, and uses the LLM to produce a probability distribution over coefficient values for arith- metic coding. The decoder entropy-decodes these subbands in the same order as the encoder. Integer wavelet coeffi- cients should not be represented as ordinary text tokens for two reasons. First, although the native Llama vocabulary is indexed by consecutive token IDs, those IDs do not encode numerical locality. Neighboring token IDs correspond to neighboring text symbols rather than neighboring coefficient values. Second, raw coefficient values include negative integers and therefore cannot be used di- rectly as valid embedding indices or classification labels. To bridge this gap, each integer symbol

To test directly whether the cod- ing domain matters for LLM-based entropy modeling, we imple- ment two alternative variants under the same general paradigm: a pixel-domain variant that performs next-token prediction on ras- terized RGB values, and a residual-based variant that encodes the residual between the original image and a lossy reconstruction, using the global lossy image and the corresponding local recon- struction patch as visual prompts. Table 4 summarizes results across all three benchmarks. Under the same Llama-3.2-3B backbone and next-token entropy-modeling framework, the wavelet-domain for- mulation is consistently the strongest. This comparison is especially relevant because WaveLLM is, to the best of our knowledge, the first LLM-based lossless compressor formulated directly in the wavelet domain. The pixel-domain variant is already competitive, indicating that the value interface and autoregressive LLM framework remain ef- fective beyond the wavelet setting. However, the wavelet-domain formulation outperforms it by 0.21, 0.11, and 0.17 bpsp on Ko- dak, CLIC.pro, and DIV2K, respectively. The residual-based variant yields higher rates under our implementation, and its total rate includes both the lossy base bits and the coded residual bits. We do not

text: We presented WaveLLM, a wavelet-domain LLM entropy modeling framework for lossless image compression. It combines a coding- oriented numerical interface, task prompts, and same-level decoded context within a LoRA-adapted Llama-3.2-3B backbone. WaveLLM achieves 2.51, 2.24, and 2.27 bpsp on Kodak, CLIC.pro, and DIV2K, respectively, outperforming existing LLM-based compressors on all three benchmarks while remaining competitive with strong lossless codecs. These results suggest that wavelet subbands provide a more suitable representation for LLM-based probability modeling than the tested flat pixel and residual sequences. By separating image content into wavelet subbands and guiding each prediction with task prompts and decoded context, WaveLLM enables more accurate entropy estimation. Future work will consider distillation, quantization, and near-lossless coding.
