text: OS-HELIX: UNIFYING GUI INTERACTION AND CODE EXECUTION IN NATIVE COMPUTER-USING AGENTS Bowen Yang1,2,* Kaiming Jin3,* Zichen Ding2,* Zhenyu Wu4 Zehao Li1 Zhoumianze Liu5 Kanzhi Cheng6 Fangzhi Xu7 Yanan Sun2 Qiushi Sun8,† Yu Qiao2,† 1University of Science and Technology of China 2Shanghai AI Laboratory 3National University of Singapore 4Shanghai Jiao Tong University 5Fudan University 6Nanjing University 7Xi’an Jiaotong University 8The University of Hong Kong *Equal contribution. †Corresponding authors.
title: OS-HELIX: UNIFYING GUI INTERACTION AND CODE

text: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internal- ized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end- to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application–artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/eval- uator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggre- gates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to pre- vent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative im- provements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. Ablations provide evidence consistent with contributions from learned GUI/code coordination, scalable verifiable supervision, and action step

The rapid progress of vision-language models (VLMs) (Team, 2026; Wang et al., 2025b; Team et al., 2026a; Anthropic, 2025; Zeng et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2025; Bai et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026) has accelerated the development of computer-using agents (CUAs), which aim to execute open-ended tasks in human-facing digital environments. Most existing CUAs formulate digital automation as graphical interaction, where agents perceive screenshots, reason over interface states, and act through mouse and keyboard operations. However, GUI-centric CUAs (Liu et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2024; Feizi et al., 2026) still face practical bottlenecks in realistic desktop workflows. Visual grounding can fail on small or ambiguous interface elements, and fine-grained interaction can make structured state manipulation cumbersome even with batched actions. text: plementary interface is programmatic control, through which command-line and code agents can inspect files, access system state, and execute compound operations directly through the shell (Yang et al., 2026e; 2024; Wang et al., 2025c). Yet code execution alone cannot fully address the long tail of desktop task scenarios that depends on visual layout, application-specific UI state, or software be- havior exposed only through the interface. As illustrated in Figure 1, these complementary strengths motivate a single agent that coordinates GUI and code, where GUI provides general visual access to arbitrary applications while code provides efficient and precise manipulation of programmatic state. Despite this complementarity, building a native hybrid GUI/code CUA remains an open problem. Simply attaching a code tool to a GUI model does not teach it when or why to use either modal- ity. In our preliminary experiments, as shown in Table 14, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) achieves over ∼34% success on OSWorld-Verified (Xie et al., 2025) with GUI actions alone, but falls to roughly ∼32% when code execution is naively exposed. Prompt-level composition can therefore disrupt an existing GUI policy rather than create coordinated behavior, making it essential to internalize hybrid coordination capabilities into the model through training on high-quality hy- brid data. Several existing approaches have explored hybrid execution paradigms that combine GUI interaction with code-like actions. Framework-centric systems (Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026a) rely on external harnesses to coordinate GUI, code, memory, and recovery; tool-call-based approaches (Jia et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Shi et al., 2026) ex- pose programmatic operations through predefined application-specific interfaces; and model-fusion approaches (Wang et al., 2025a; Qin et al., 2025) combine complementary capabilities through pre- defined designs. Although these systems expand the scope of hybrid computer use, they leave open how a single policy can learn the routing between the GUI and code actions through hybrid training. To address these challenges, we present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained computer-using agent that unifies GUI interaction and code execution within a single policy. On the infrastructure side, we introduce application–artifact composition, which combines versioned applications with authentic artifacts to instantiate diverse and reproducible desktop states. An Ex- ploration Agent proposes instructions grounded in these states through brief exploration of the initialized environment, while an independent Evaluator Agent constructs task-specific, primarily rule-based evaluators. Together, this pipeline supports scalable synthesis, filtering, and collection of high-quality GUI/code

An Ex- ploration Agent proposes instructions grounded in these states through brief exploration of the initialized environment, while an independent Evaluator Agent constructs task-specific, primarily rule-based evaluators. Together, this pipeline supports scalable synthesis, filtering, and collection of high-quality GUI/code trajectories for model training, thereby providing the data foundation neces- sary to internalize hybrid coordination capabilities into the model. On the training side, we first use filtered hybrid trajectories to internalize basic action semantics and modality routing, and then optimize the policy through online RL in executable desktop envi- ronments. In early RL experiments, we observe a steady increase in the proportion of code actions accompanied by a degradation in performance. We attribute this to the token-count asymmetry be- tween short GUI actions and substantially longer code actions, which causes the optimization signal to be dominated by code steps. To address this, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which constructs the sample-level importance ratio over action steps rather than raw assistant-token counts, enabling more balanced optimization of the two modalities. These training components directly answer the open question of how a single policy can natively learn to coordinate GUI and code actions through hybrid training, yielding an agent that performs strongly and reliably across diverse desktop tasks. Our work addresses this setting through hybrid SFT and online agentic RL with Step-balanced GSPO, mitigating optimization imbalance and enabling more effective native coordination. 3 OS-HELIX 3.1 OVERVIEW An overview of the OS-Helix pipeline is shown in Figure 2. OS-Helix is built around a simple premise: a real computer-using agent should treat GUI interaction and code execution as two com- plementary ways of changing the same digital state. Rather than attaching a shell tool to a GUI model at inference time, we construct a unified pipeline in which environments, instructions, trajec- tories, and reinforcement signals are all designed for hybrid GUI/code execution.

text: 3.2 DATA INFRASTRUCTURE The scale of computer-using agent training is ultimately bounded by the diversity of executable states from which meaningful tasks can arise. This is particularly important on desktops, where workflows are shaped jointly by applications, user artifacts, and persistent local state. We view authentic artifacts as a natural axis for expanding this state space, with artifact types and file formats providing a direct link to the applications that can operate on them. Based on this principle, we construct diverse executable desktop environments and synthesize grounded, verifiable tasks from the resulting states. 3.2.1 APPLICATION–ARTIFACT COMPOSITION FOR DESKTOP ENVIRONMENTS Real-world desktop workflows are commonly grounded in existing artifacts that are read, edited, or transformed through applications. Thus, we factor scalable desktop-environment construction into two reusable components: applications with fixed versions, launch procedures, and diverse initializa- tion configurations, and artifacts carrying authentic content and persistent state. Their compatibility- aware composition produces executable desktop states from which realistic tasks can arise. To instantiate such states at scale, we organize artifacts and applications into an application–artifact compatibility graph, whose edges are determined by the artifact types and file formats that applica- tions can consume. The underlying application configuration records these supported input types, together with the version, launch commands, and initialization settings required for reproducible execution. For example, a .pptx artifact can be

For example, a .pptx artifact can be connected to LibreOffice Impress and WPS Pre- sentation directly, whose application configurations specify how each application is launched with the file and which application-specific initialization settings are required. The resulting states are instantiated on reproducible Ubuntu virtual machines for task synthesis and trajectory collection. 3.2.2 ENVIRONMENT-GROUNDED TASK SYNTHESIS Given the diverse desktop environments constructed above, we next translate environment diversity into training-task diversity. Each synthesis episode first samples a target application and then selects compatible artifacts via the application–artifact compatibility graph, thereby instantiating a coherent and executable task context. Relying primarily on model priors tends to produce generic, repetitive instruction patterns and un- derutilize the state diversity of instantiated environments at scale. We therefore ground instruction generation in active exploration of the current environment. To avoid repeatedly covering familiar functionality, we maintain a global application memory that records functions previously exercised for each application and exposes this history during subsequent exploration, encouraging broader coverage over time. The Exploration Agent receives this memory together with application meta- data, exact file paths, launch configuration, tutorial, and initial screenshot, and performs a short

The Exploration Agent receives this memory together with application meta- data, exact file paths, launch configuration, tutorial, and initial screenshot, and performs a short non-destructive exploration restricted to opening, clicking, scrolling, and terminating. Based on the observed artifact content and application state, it proposes a realistic user instruction together with its initialization configuration and observable success conditions, without prescribing a GUI/code solution or revealing answer-critical information. To make synthesized tasks consistently verifiable, we adopt an everything-is-a-file abstraction in which terminal conditions are mapped, whenever possible, to inspectable file representations, and evaluator synthesis selects rule-based, VLM-based, or hybrid checks according to their observability. Verification specifies the desired terminal state without constraining how it is reached, allowing the same task to be completed through GUI interaction, code execution, or their combination. We decouple the instruction proposal from evaluator synthesis. Once an instruction proposal is ac- cepted, its instruction and success conditions are frozen and passed to an independent Evaluator Agent, which compiles the corresponding verification logic. Programmatically observable condi- tions are evaluated primarily with rule-based checks over VM files and command-line state, while visual conditions that cannot be reliably recovered programmatically are handled with VLM-based evaluation. They may possess visual understanding, coordinate grounding, and low-level control, but have not learned the new decision boundary created when code execution becomes an equally valid action. Merely adding a code tool expands the action space without supplying a routing prior for when to remain in the GUI, when to switch to code, and when to return to the interface for verifi- cation; it can even disrupt already learned GUI behavior. SFT therefore serves as a cold start in our pipeline: it establishes the action semantics of the unified tool schema and distills from teacher tra- jectories a coarse but usable GUI/code routing policy. We collect SFT trajectories on tasks produced by the data infrastructure described in Section 3.2, using Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) as the teacher model with both Computer Use and Bash Tool enabled. Training hyperparameters and data-mixture details are provided in Appendix C.1. 3.3.2 AGENTIC RL WITH STEP-BALANCED GSPO We first build a cross-node environment management system that monitors and manages over one hundred Ubuntu sandbox environments across multiple standalone machines. The system exposes a unified port to the training side and internally dispatches requests to the environments. We then perform online RL on carefully filtered generated tasks with rule-based evaluators only, further improving model performance. Each rollout interacts with a live desktop environment, and the paired evaluator score serves as the sole outcome reward signal. If an assistant turn contains an unparsable tool call or any other invalid action-format error, that assistant response is isolated as an invalid sample and assigned a reward of 0, even if the remaining trajectory could receive a positive evaluator score. We use three efficiency mechanisms to make online RL feasible under costly desktop interaction. First, we adopt an asynchronous RL pipeline that allows the rollout policy to lag behind the latest policy by at most one version, enabling environment interaction and policy optimization to run in parallel. Second, we maintain per-task success-rate estimates and bias sampling toward tasks near the current capability frontier, down-weighting tasks that are already too easy or remain too difficult. Third, we apply bounded sliding-window visual-context segmentation to control context length and sample growth. Rollouts are split into segments and each segment can contain multiple assistant actions that contribute to loss. We apply the same sliding-window segmentation logic during rollout inference to maintain consistency between training and inference. In our preliminary RL experiments, standard GSPO exhibited a systematic drift toward code- intensive behavior as shown in Figure 4. Specifically, as training progresses, the model increasingly favors code-related actions, ultimately resulting in a slight performance degradation relative to the initial SFT checkpoint. text: We present OS-Helix, a native hybrid computer-using agent trained end-to-end through scalable executable desktop task synthesis, hybrid SFT, and Step-balanced GSPO online RL, designed to na- tively coordinate heterogeneous GUI and code actions within a single policy. On OSWorld-Verified, 10

text: OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. OS-Helix-27B-RL also transfers to WindowsAgentArena with 63.87% suc- cess, surpassing GPT-5-based framework methods on both benchmarks. Ablations and behavioral analyses show that SFT provides the main gain, hybrid supervision outperforms GUI-only super- vision at a fixed scale, and learned routing improves both execution efficiency and task coverage beyond code access alone. Under matched RL settings, Step-balanced GSPO outperforms stan- dard GSPO and mitigates its drift toward code-intensive behavior, while RL increases Pass@3 from 70.88% to 76.44%, indicating broader discovery of successful trajectories across independent at- tempts. These findings establish native GUI/code coordination as a learnable hybrid paradigm and provide a reproducible foundation for further research on hybrid computer-using agents. 11

text: AI USE STATEMENT In the preparation of this manuscript, we utilized LLMs to generate synthetic datasets, to refine the writing (including grammar and spelling corrections), to draft sections of the paper, and to assist with the preliminary derivation of mathematical formulas in Appendix E. The authors reviewed and take responsibility for the research design, experiments, analysis, claims, and final presentation. ETHICS STATEMENT This work does not involve human-subject studies or the collection of private data from real users. We study training methods for general-purpose computer-using agents, and conduct all trajectory collection, reinforcement learning, and evaluation in controlled, isolated Ubuntu virtual machines. The VMs use fixed application versions and a curated local file library, and are separated from per- sonal host files and credentials. This setup reduces the risk that exploratory actions during research inadvertently modify host state or access unauthorized resources. Although the experiments themselves present no substantial direct ethical risk, deploying agents with combined GUI interaction and code execution on real devices raises important safety and pri- vacy concerns. Such agents can continuously observe screen content, modify local files, and execute Python or Bash, and may therefore encounter personally identifiable information, confidential docu- ments, or authentication credentials. They may also be exposed to prompt injection through interface content or external files. Code actions further increase the potential impact of
title: AI USE STATEMENT

text: and execute Python or Bash, and may therefore encounter personally identifiable information, confidential docu- ments, or authentication credentials. They may also be exposed to prompt injection through interface content or external files. Code actions further increase the potential impact of erroneous behavior or malicious workflows. The isolated experimental setting used in this work does not resolve these deployment-time risks. Real-world deployment should follow least-privilege and safety-by-design principles. These include granular permissions over applications, directories, networks, and code execution; explicit human confirmation before irreversible, credential-bearing, or otherwise high-impact operations; runtime policy checks, sandboxed execution, audit logs, and post-action verification; and data minimization and sanitization for screenshots, trajectories, and tool outputs. Users should retain the ability to define and revoke the agent’s authority, with sensitive applications such as banking, private commu- nication, and credential management inaccessible by default. Because general-purpose automation is inherently dual use, future CUA research should advance capabilities together with systematic red teaming, interpretable action auditing, and reliable human takeover mechanisms.

text: A LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK OS-Helix is an initial step toward native GUI/code hybrid computer use, with remaining limitations centered primarily on computational and API resource constraints. First, desktop environments are difficult to scale comprehensively: even an application–artifact desk- top infrastructure spanning diverse applications cannot cover the full diversity of real user machines, private artifacts, application versions, and personalized configurations. Future work should further expand the application and artifact ecosystem and study broader randomization of system states and user configurations while preserving reproducibility. Second, automatic verification remains imperfect. Unlike software engineering tasks, where gold final states can be obtained deterministically, automated CUA task synthesis under limited resources cannot reliably capture ground-truth terminal states—tasks may therefore be subject to feasibility risks, and the resulting evaluators carry intrinsic brittleness. Concretely, rule-based evaluators re- liably cover many file-backed tasks but require careful construction and often depend on specific application versions or export formats; more fundamentally, even when an agent’s execution is se- mantically near-correct, inconsistent strictness in file-attribute checks can reduce the score to zero. Rubric-based partial scoring, adopted in several recent works including ours, partially alleviates this issue but does not resolve it entirely. VLM-based evaluators extend coverage to textual out- puts and visual outcomes, yet may miss fine-grained discrepancies; more critically, due to their inherent brittleness, existing RL engineering practice typically
title: LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

text: including ours, partially alleviates this issue but does not resolve it entirely. VLM-based evaluators extend coverage to textual out- puts and visual outcomes, yet may miss fine-grained discrepancies; more critically, due to their inherent brittleness, existing RL engineering practice typically excludes VLM-based scoring from the reward signal altogether, concentrating construction effort on rule-based evaluators—which in turn constrains the types and diversity of tasks that can be incorporated into training. Future work should develop stronger evaluator-generation, repair, and validation pipelines, and systematically study cross-evaluator agreement as well as robustness to reward hacking. Third, our agentic RL experiments are subject to certain limitations imposed by available computa- tional resources. RL training was conducted only on the dense 27B model with relatively conserva- tive hyperparameter settings; the total number of training steps was likewise constrained, precluding a systematic investigation of the scaling behavior of agentic RL. For OS-Helix-35B-A3B, despite its strong performance in SFT experiments, the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture introduces non-trivial additional challenges in training-inference consistency and optimization stability dur- ing agentic RL, making it difficult to support this training pipeline reliably under current resource conditions. We regard a more thorough exploration of RL training dynamics and scaling laws, to- gether with a stable extension of Step-balanced GSPO to larger MoE computer-using agents, as an important direction for future work. We regard a more thorough exploration of RL training dynamics and scaling laws, to- gether with a stable extension of Step-balanced GSPO to larger MoE computer-using agents, as an important direction for future work. Beyond scaling, we believe the community is now at an inflection point where recursive self- improvement (RSI) deserves serious consideration. As CUA models attain a meaningful level of general computer-use capability, the model itself can serve as its own teacher: rolling out interaction trajectories on existing tasks, providing the training signal for the next iteration, and progressively improving through this self-bootstrapping loop. Rather than relying solely on human demonstra- tion or externally curated data, such a paradigm allows the agent to continuously generate its own training trajectories with growing quality as capability improves and feed them back into subse- quent training rounds. We view this self-evolving, teacher-free training paradigm as one of the most promising long-term directions for advancing CUA agents. Finally, many existing desktop benchmarks were originally designed for GUI-only agents, with task design, reference solutions, and evaluation functions all implicitly centered on visual interaction paths. Although their tasks can often be completed with hybrid strategies, existing evaluators may not capture every valid GUI/code solution. B DATA DETAILS B.1 TASK SYNTHESIS COMPARISON Table 6 compares recent CUA task- and environment-synthesis pipelines across five dimensions: task grounding, application scaling, authentic artifact integration, cross-application task support, and executable evaluation. The comparison is organized along the axis of synthesis coverage rather than data scale or maturity. The broader contribution of OS-Helix is to extend exploration-grounded task generation toward artifact-grounded executable desktop-state construction: the pipeline jointly addresses K/E/C grounding, application scaling, authentic artifact-backed state initialization, and executable rule-based evaluation within a single coherent framework. Concretely, an application– artifact compatibility graph organizes valid pairings of application configurations and supported artifact types or file formats, enabling reproducible initial states to be instantiated systematically. B.3 FINAL STATE MATERIALIZATION Our everything-is-a-file abstraction treats the file system as a common inspection interface rather than as a restriction on where a task state must originate. A terminal condition may initially reside in a downloaded web page, an in-memory application state, an unsaved layout, or a persistent user artifact. We attempt to materialize the relevant condition into a VM-resident file representation whenever this can preserve the semantics needed for evaluation: a web state may be downloaded or serialized locally, an in-memory result may be exported, and an answer may be written to a structured or plain-text file. This externalization separates the location of a state from its verifiable representation and allows heterogeneous desktop objectives to share a common evaluation interface. The

The materialization step is not uniformly lossless. Some conditions, such as exact document struc- ture, metadata, or serialized application state, admit faithful programmatic inspection; others depend on rendered layout, canvas appearance, transient UI state, or content for which serialization does not preserve the relevant evidence. Evaluator selection therefore reflects an observability trade-off: rule-based checks are used when a deterministic file or command representation captures the re- quired semantics, VLM-based checks are used when visual or otherwise non-serializable evidence is essential, and hybrid evaluators combine the two when they provide complementary evidence. B.4 INSTRUCTION AND EVALUATOR SYNTHESIS DETAILS The primary task-synthesis pipeline instantiates states through the application–artifact compatibility graph. The pipeline then follows a one-way information flow: application and artifact configura- tions determine the initialization context; the Exploration Agent produces a structured instruction proposal and textual success conditions; the independent
title: High-level group

text: task-synthesis pipeline instantiates states through the application–artifact compatibility graph. The pipeline then follows a one-way information flow: application and artifact configura- tions determine the initialization context; the Exploration Agent produces a structured instruction proposal and textual success conditions; the independent Evaluator Agent compiles the frozen con- ditions into rule-based or visual checks; and each independently validated instruction-evaluator pair enters the task pool. Application-centered initialization. For each application, we record a canonical name, version, supported artifact types and file formats, launch commands, and initialization templates, and use these fields to build the application–artifact compatibility graph. Each synthesis episode first restores a controlled VM snapshot and samples a primary application, then selects zero or more compatible artifacts through the graph according to the application’s initialization templates. For every sampled pre-existing artifact, initialization creates a VM-resident, evaluator-only golden copy before task execution while leaving the original path as the active task target; this copy is bound to the task con- figuration and may serve as the expected reference in subsequent content or structural comparisons. The system then provides the Exploration Agent with application metadata, exact file paths, launch configuration, an application tutorial, global application memory, and an initial screenshot. For a task with multiple rule judges, the rule-based score is the mean of the individual rule-judge scores, whereas the VLM-based score is produced independently by visual judgment. As described in Section 4.1, RL uses only tasks with rule-based evaluators to provide reward signals. Although both scores lie in [0, 1], rule-based scores are derived from fine-grained, explicitly weighted completion items, whereas VLM scores generally reflect a coarser and more subjective judgment scale. text: The RL task pool is then built by rolling out trajectories with the SFT-trained model on this pool and keeping tasks of moderate difficulty. Prototype cross-application extension. Beyond the application–system compositions in the pri- mary task pool, we implemented and began collecting a more structured form of cross-application task synthesis. The prototype uses the related app field in the application configurations to con- struct an application graph. Applications serve as nodes, while edges encode compositional relations induced by shared artifact types or file formats, convertible intermediate artifacts, or complementary workflows. This graph provides a structured prior for composing applications rather than treating all application combinations as equally plausible. For each task, the system first specifies a target number of applications, such as three, randomly samples a primary application, and then samples subsequent applications from its neighboring nodes. After each selection, the neighbors of the se- lected nodes are added to the candidate frontier, allowing the application set to expand along graph structure. To prevent the graph from overly constraining the composition space, each sampling step retains a small-probability jump mechanism that ignores graph connectivity and samples an applica- tion uniformly from the broader inventory. text: WindowsAgentArena contain a non-negligible fraction of infeasible tasks, roughly 10% of their task sets. These tasks mix at least two phenomena: genuinely impossible instruc- tions whose target condition cannot be satisfied, and GUI-infeasible tasks where the visual route may be blocked while a programmatic route could still modify the underlying state. Our synthesis pipeline is designed around executable goal states and therefore does not naturally generate infea- sible training tasks. As a result, the model can under-learn when to stop and declare infeasibility, often continuing until the maximum interaction budget is exhausted. Conversely, for tasks that are infeasible only under GUI interaction, a hybrid agent may legitimately solve them through code, which can still be judged as incorrect if the benchmark expects infeasibility recognition. As a diag- nostic, after removing infeasible tasks from the evaluation set, the average success rate on OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena increases by up to 3–5 absolute points. This suggests that future task de- sign and data synthesis should explicitly model infeasibility, distinguishing true task impossibility from modality-specific infeasibility so that agents can learn both effective execution and calibrated refusal. 29

D.2.3 TRAINING RECIPE AND CONTEXT ANALYSIS We next isolate how the structure of demonstrations and test-time history affects performance, using Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct with OSWorld. The normal recipe reaches 50.56%. Removing CoT from training and retaining actions only reduces performance to 37.74% (-12.82 points), while keeping the training data unchanged but removing CoT from the inference context yields 37.82% (-12.74 points). The near-identical degradation is important: the reasoning trace is not merely an auxiliary training target. It also functions as an execution-time state representation that helps the model maintain intent, resolve intermediate observations, and select between GUI and code actions across multi- step execution. Removing only historical CoT is less damaging, but still lowers the average to 43.22% (-7.34 points). This partial recovery indicates that the current-step decision can retain useful local information, yet removing the accumulated reasoning history weakens temporal credit assignment and state tracking. E STEP-BALANCED GSPO DETAILS During reinforcement learning, a training sample may contain multiple assistant responses that con- tribute to the policy loss, with each response corresponding to one action step. The optimization unit of a training sample therefore need not coincide with an individual environment action step. In particular, the assistant span associated with a code action step is often substantially longer than that associated with a GUI step. The standard GSPO objective computes one sample-level importance ratio by aggregating token-level log-importance weights over all valid assistant tokens in the training sample (Zheng et al., 2025). Although this prevents a sample from receiving a
title: Setting Step

text: associated with a GUI step. The standard GSPO objective computes one sample-level importance ratio by aggregating token-level log-importance weights over all valid assistant tokens in the training sample (Zheng et al., 2025). Although this prevents a sample from receiving a larger sample-level weight solely because it contains more tokens, it does not equalize the contributions of different ac- tion steps within the same sample. As a result, a long code action can dominate both the sample-level ratio and the clipping decision even when it is only one of several actions in the training sample. This section formalizes the effect and derives a step-balanced aggregation for the GSPO ratio. Our goal is to preserve GSPO’s token-level importance weights and clipping structure while changing their sample-level aggregation to remove the deterministic dependence of an action step’s aggre- gate gradient coefficient on its token count. Recent work has also studied the granularity of im- portance ratios for LLM policy optimization, including sequence-level GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025), subsentence-level ratios (Yang et al., 2025a), cumulative token ratios (Zhang et al., 2026b), and hybrid token/sequence ratios (Min et al., 2026). These methods differ from our setting at the ob- jective level. SSPO assigns separate ratios to text fragments, but its published objective aggre- 32

E.3 GRADIENT CONTRIBUTION We now show that the proposed ratio removes the deterministic linear dependence between an action step’s aggregate scalar gradient coefficient and its token count. Consider the unclipped branch, where Li(θ) = −Aiwstep i (θ). For any token t ∈ai,k, only ¯δi,k depends on the corresponding current-policy log-probability. Therefore, ∂log wstep i (θ) ∂log πθ(yi,t | hi,t) = ωi,k 1 |ai,k|. Since ∂wstep i /∂log wstep i = wstep i , we have ∂Li ∂log πθ(yi,t | hi,t) = −Aiwstep i (θ) ωi,k |ai,k|. Summing over all tokens in action step k gives X t∈ai,k ∂Li ∂log πθ(yi,t | hi,t) = −Aiwstep i (θ)ωi,k. Thus, the aggregate scalar coefficient of action step k is independent of |ai,k|. This is the sense in which Step-balanced GSPO changes the optimization signal: it leaves the token-level importance weights wi,t intact, but changes how their log values are aggregated into the sample-level importance ratio. text: changes the optimization signal: it leaves the token-level importance weights wi,t intact, but changes how their log values are aggregated into the sample-level importance ratio. Under standard GSPO, a long serialized action occupies a larger share of the sample-level log- ratio, so a successful code step can receive more aggregate scalar credit simply because it contains more assistant tokens. This does not mean that the routing token selecting the code tool is directly multiplied by the number of subsequent code tokens. Rather, the longer serialized action contributes more token-level gradient terms under the same sample-level advantage and can therefore exert disproportionate influence on the update direction. Step-balanced GSPO removes this deterministic length-based multiplier from the action-step aggregate coefficient, reinforcing a successful action as a step rather than in proportion to its serialized length. The full parameter gradient still depends on token-specific gradient directions, clipping activation, and reward correlations, so this analysis explains a source of token-length-driven drift toward code actions rather than providing a formal guarantee of correct modality routing. 34

text: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation Bangji Yang1,*, Jiajun Fan1,*, Zhaoyu Zhu1, Hongbo Ma2, Ge Liu1,† 1University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign 2Tsinghua University *Equal contribution, †Corresponding author
title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation

text: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist’s output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (TF-OPD). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist’s rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic’s level to the specialist’s at matched precision. On Olmo 3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist’s gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks. title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation

text: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards has become the standard way to turn a base language model into a strong reasoner in one domain [1–5]. Because the reward is domain-specific, the result is a family of specialists that share an initialization: from one base checkpoint, one model is trained on competition mathematics, another on programming, a third on instruction following [6]. Each is far ahead on its own domain and far behind on the others, so a user who wants mathematics and programming in the same model has to build that model from the specialists. The available routes either train or ignore the rollouts (Table 1). One can repeat reinforcement learning on the union of the domains [7, 8], or distill: on-policy distillation lets the student generate, has a teacher supervise those generations, and updates the student on its own distribution [9–11]. It has become a post-training route for consolidating specialists into one student [12], at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. The training-free alternative is to merge weights. Arithmetic on parameters [13] does not know which inputs the parameters act on, and on reinforcement-learned specialists it can give up part of what made them specialists: summing the mathematics and coding updates of a 7B model leaves it below the mathematics specialist on AIME25 (Section

TF-OPD gathers those moments where on-policy distillation gathers its data, on rollouts. text: exactly. Nothing is back-propagated. On Olmo 3 7B this yields a generalist without a single gradient step: one model that keeps most of what each specialist gained on five mathematics and two code benchmarks and that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone (Figure 1). Three findings explain when it works. First, the filter carries the result. A minority of the mathematics specialist’s rollouts run to the length limit in a repetition loop: few among the answers, several times more among the tokens. With them the closed form is no better than task arithmetic on AIME25, and removing them alone closes the gap to the specialist scored in the same format. Second, the token-level fit is not what fails: the unfiltered model already follows the specialist almost token for token, so hard problems are decided by which inputs the statistics weigh. Third, rollouts written by the student, the on-policy data of trained distillation, do not improve the closed form. Reinforcement learning also moves weights so little that the 16-bit release format distorts a fused update, which makes the formats of storage and evaluation part of the method. 2

text: Knowledge distillation. Classical distillation fits a student to a teacher’s output distribution on a fixed corpus [15] or to sequences the teacher generates [16]. On-policy formulations supervise text generated by the model being trained, following the imitation-learning argument for learning on the learner’s own state distribution [9–11]; the idea has been applied to reasoning models, including with a model as its own teacher [17], and knowledge fusion extends distillation to several source models [18]. Recent work asks which rollouts on-policy distillation should use, selecting a few hard problems [19], weighting problems by the student’s pass rate [20], or balancing student-generated states across teachers [12]. All of these are optimization procedures. TF-OPD keeps two of their ingredients, a match-the-teacher objective and statistics gathered on model-generated text, and removes the optimization by solving the objective layer by layer. Our finding that the composition of the rollouts decides the outcome is a closed-form counterpart of theirs. Model merging. Weight averaging across fine-tuning runs improves accuracy at no inference cost [21]; task arithmetic composes updates relative to a common initialization [13], and TIES-Merging and DARE reduce interference among summed updates [22, 23]. Spectral methods exploit the matrix structure of updates [24–26]. These methods read weights only. Weight-space edits also target reasoning models, to amplify 3

text: one reinforcement-learning run [27] or to make a model more efficient [28]; we combine runs on different domains. Fisher merging and RegMean bring in data through parameter importance and through input second moments respectively [14, 29]. TF-OPD uses RegMean’s closed form; what differs is what it is fed and what it is used for. RegMean was introduced for models fine-tuned on supervised tasks, with statistics computed on each task’s training inputs. The specialists here are reinforcement-learned reasoners whose inputs are overwhelmingly their own long generations, so the statistics have to come from rollouts, and we show that on AIME25 unfiltered rollouts gain nothing over task arithmetic, whereas filtered ones recover the specialist. Other training and evaluation settings. Multi-domain fine-tuning models interactions among samples during training [30]; distributional Pareto-optimal reinforcement learning studies trade-offs across objectives [31]. Policy optimization has also been studied with interactive guidance [32], while anomaly-guided learning addresses imperfect demonstrations [33]. Related choices about supervision include adaptive sample scheduling for direct preference optimization [34] and reward models that go beyond semantics [35]. Arena-based LLM evaluation [36] and medical vision-language work on adaptive causal reasoning [37] and latent-memory evolution [38] concern other evaluation or application settings. 3 Method 3.1 Distillation of one layer is least squares Let θb be a base model and θ1, . . . , θK specialists

By (iii), interference arises only where input distributions overlap; Equation (4) below measures how much. 3.2 On-policy statistics The solution is only as good as µd. We take µd to be the distribution of layer inputs when teacher d processes its own answers to problems from its domain. This is the distribution the layer operates on in use, since a reasoning model’s context is dominated by its own generation, and it cannot be obtained from reference solutions, which the model did not write. We refer to statistics gathered on model-generated rollouts as on-policy, in contrast to statistics gathered on a fixed corpus; the rollouts in our main configuration are the teachers’, as in sequence-level distillation [16], and Section 4.5 evaluates the variant that uses the student’s. text: [16], and Section 4.5 evaluates the variant that uses the student’s. Concretely, teacher d answers a set of training problems from its domain, sampled exactly as in evaluation. After selection (Section 3.4), the teacher reads each kept sequence, prompt and answer, in a single teacher- forced forward pass. A forward pre-hook on every linear layer of every decoder block accumulates X⊤X over all token positions, and Gd is that sum divided by the number of tokens, so that domains with longer answers do not dominate by length. Layers that read the same tensor share a Gram matrix: in the architectures we use, the query, key and value projections form one group, the gate and up projections another, and the attention output and down projections one each. The grouping is detected automatically from one short forward pass, and the same statistics are collected for the final hidden states to solve the output head. 3.3 Solving For each group, Equation (2) is solved once per member layer in double precision. Tensors that are not linear maps of a hidden state — embeddings, normalization gains and biases — change little and are combined by task arithmetic. Figure 2 illustrates the procedure, and Algorithm 1 in Appendix B states it in full. 3.4 Which rollouts to use Every token of every kept answer contributes one outer product to Gd, so the statistics are a token-weighted picture of the teacher’s behavior. That picture is distorted by a failure mode of long-form generation. Some answers do not terminate: the model enters a repetition loop and continues to the length limit. Such answers are few, but each is as long as the limit allows, and the layer inputs inside a loop are nearly periodic, so their contribution to the Gram matrix is large and concentrated on a few directions. The least-squares solution then spends its capacity reproducing the teacher on degenerate input. Reinforcement learning with small learning rates barely moves weights at that resolution, by about one representable step (Section 4.5). A fused update is no larger, and unlike a specialist’s it is not made of whole steps. A fused model is evaluated in float16, which keeps three more significant bits than bfloat16 and fits the memory of a single GPU where float32 does not. The base is Olmo-3-1025-7B, and the teachers are the final checkpoints of Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math and Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Code, each obtained by reinforcement learning from that base on a single domain. Rollouts and statistics. For mathematics the teacher answers 256 training problems from DAPO-Math-17k [3]; for code, 256 training problems from the DeepCoder training set [39], with the instruction used by EvalPlus. Each problem is answered once. Mathematics is sampled at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.9 with a limit of 31,744 new tokens, code at temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0 with a limit of 32,768, matching evaluation. No evaluation problem is used. Selection keeps the 175 mathematics answers that are correct, finished and loop-free, and the 92 code answers that pass every test of their problem. We use α = 0.9 and equal domain weights.

Removing the looping answers alone brings it level with the specialist and recovers every hard problem that the model built from all answers loses. Keeping only correct answers, which discards many more, changes nothing further: a finished but wrong answer is still an example of the specialist reasoning normally. Checking the code answers by running their tests, as the final model does, changes code accuracy by no measurable amount (Table 3). Whose text. On-policy distillation in the strict sense uses text written by the student. We let a fused student answer the same problems and compute the statistics either from the student reading its own answers or from the mathematics specialist reading them, the closed-form analogue of the trained objective. Neither improves on the specialist’s own answers with the looping ones removed (Figure 4b). Reweighting and mined problems. Weighting mathematics three to one in Equation (1) recovers most of the loss, but at the coding specialist’s expense: the share of its update that the fused layers fail to reproduce nearly doubles (Figure 5b). Selection removes the cause; the other remedies compensate for it. The merge rule. On MATH-500 and the two code benchmarks, task arithmetic, a low-rank variant of it and the closed form all keep both specialists’ gains and cannot be told apart (Table 3). The rules separate only on hard problems (Figure 4b). Number format. Reinforcement learning moves each weight by about one step of the 16-bit format the models are released in. The closed-form update is not made of whole steps, and rounding to that format measurably distorts it (Appendix B), so fused models are stored in 32-bit floats and evaluated in float16. The format matters at the scale of our comparisons: the mathematics specialist scores several points higher on AIME25 in its released format than in float16 (Table 5). 9
title: MATH-500

text: 4.6 Discussion On-policy distillation is run after reinforcement learning to put several specialists into one model. For specialists that share a base model, our results suggest that the training in that step may not be needed. What the trained student is asked to do, match each teacher on the text the models generate, has an exact layer-wise solution, and that solution already gives a model close to each teacher and more accurate on average than either. Adding a specialist then costs its rollouts and one more term in each layer’s sums; nothing is retrained. Training remains the tool when the teachers differ in architecture or size from the student.
title: 4.6 Discussion

text: Aggregating the capabilities of separately tuned specialists does not require training-based on-policy distillation when they share a base model, and the aggregate can be more accurate on average than any of its sources. For a linear layer the distillation objective is least squares, its solution is exact given the second moments of each teacher’s inputs, and those are obtained by letting the teachers read a few hundred of their own answers, at the cost of forward passes. What those answers contain decides the hard problems: removing a few looping answers, which carry a large share of the tokens, lets the fused model match its mathematics specialist in the same format. 10

text: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) accelerate generation by unmasking multiple tokens in parallel, but sampling these tokens independently ignores their correlations and biases the output. Anari et al. (2026) corrected this bias with rejection sampling, decomposing the log acceptance probability into a sum of token-level terms, but the evaluation requires one score query per unmasked token. We propose the Single-Increment Rejection Sampler (SIRS), which provides an estimate of the log acceptance probability from a single randomly sampled increment at the cost of one query. SIRS then converts a Poisson number of clipped estimates into accept/reject decisions through a Bernoulli factory adapted from Chen et al. (2026). Since each query returns the conditionals of all remaining tokens in the block, we further Rao-Blackwellize each increment by averaging over these tokens at no extra cost, thereby reducing clipping. We show that the KL-divergence between the data distribution and the SIRS output is bounded by a clipping term plus the model’s training error. With exact scores, parallel decoding pays the full within-block dependence, whereas SIRS pays only the part beyond the clipping range. 1

text: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a competitive alternative to autoregressive models for discrete data such as text (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2023; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025), and have recently been trained as large language models with billions of parameters (Nie et al., 2026). An MDM generates a sequence of length L by starting from the all-mask state and repeatedly revealing masked positions. At each step, the trained network, called the score function, is queried once and returns the conditional distribution of every masked token given the revealed ones. If only one token is revealed per query, the sampler reproduces the data distribution when the score function is accurate, but generating a sequence then takes L queries. text: these distributions (Ghazvininejad et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2022), which we refer to as parallel sampling. However, parallel sampling ignores the dependence among the tokens revealed in the same step. For example, in “he plugged the ⟨key, plug⟩into the ⟨lock, socket⟩”, each slot is plausible on its own, yet independent draws produce “key into socket” with the product of the two marginal probabilities. This error persists even when the score function is exact, and it has been identified as a source of quality loss in parallel decoding (Zheng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). A growing line of work characterizes this error through the generation order and the dependence within a block (Zhang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026; Zhao and Cai, 2026), and reduces it by choosing schedules or blocks whose tokens are nearly conditionally independent (Park et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Lavenant and Zanella, 2025; Azangulov et al., 2026) or by learning a joint correction on top of the marginals (Liu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). A complementary approach is to correct the sampling of a given block directly, using only the trained score function. Recently, Anari et al. (2026) achieved this exactly by rejection sampling. text: et al., 2025). A complementary approach is to correct the sampling of a given block directly, using only the trained score function. Recently, Anari et al. (2026) achieved this exactly by rejection sampling. Their key observation is that the likelihood ratio between the joint distribution of a block and the product of its marginals can be decomposed into token-level conditional probabilities along an ordering of the block, all of which are given by the score function. However, evaluating this decomposition requires one score query per token in the block, which offsets the savings of parallel sampling. This motivates the following question: Can we correct parallel sampling in MDMs with a number of score queries that does not grow with the block size? In this paper, we give an affirmative answer by proposing the Single-Increment Rejection Sampler (SIRS). Instead of evaluating the full log-likelihood ratio, SIRS estimates it with a single randomly sampled token-level increment, which costs one score query. However, the acceptance probability is the exponential of the log-likelihood ratio, and exponentiating an unbiased estimate does not give an unbiased estimate of the acceptance probability. Since the output of rejection sampling depends only on the expected acceptance probability, the output distribution remains exact, provided that this random probability lies in [0, 1]. text: • Error analysis. We decompose the KL-divergence between the data distribution and the output of SIRS into a clipping-induced error, the error of the proposal, and the error of the acceptance probability, where the latter two vanish when the score function is exact. Parallel sampling, which corresponds to B = 0, incurs the full correlation error, i.e., the KL-divergence between the joint distribution of a block and the product of its marginals. SIRS corrects part of this error: its clipping-induced error is controlled only by the parts of the increments that exceed the clipping range [−B, B], and vanishes once B exceeds all increments. We further show that the Rao-Blackwellized increment yields a smaller bound on the clipping-induced error. • Experiments. On an Ising chain and a P´olya urn, where the score function is exact and the KL-divergence can be computed, SIRS with the Rao-Blackwellized increment achieves a lower KL-divergence than parallel sampling with the same number of score queries when the dependence within a block is weak, while parallel sampling with smaller blocks remains cheaper under strong dependence. text: In this work, we propose SIRS, which uses rejection sampling to correct the error induced by parallel sampling of correlated tokens in MDM. By calculating the acceptance probability with the clipped log-probability ratio of a single token increment, SIRS induces O(T) extra queries to the score function, and we further introduce the Rao-Blackwellized increment without extra computational cost. We show that compared with parallel sampling, SIRS only suffers from the correlation-induced error beyond the clipping threshold. A limitation of SIRS is that the algorithm design is independent of the unmasking batch selection, and we leave as future work to explore block selection methods better adapted to SIRS. title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for

text: Multimodal deep search is moving from short queries to long-horizon investigations that con- tinually acquire evidence. However, train- ing such agents remains constrained by lim- ited challenging training questions and in- sufficient process feedback. We introduce MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable data refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Re- fine pipeline performs targeted expansion of reasoning chains derived from existing simple multimodal questions. Parameterized transfor- mations control search depth and cross-modal evidence requirements while reusing existing image–question pairs. For training, answer rewards and lightweight behavior penalties guide RL, while the reward gap modulates token-level teacher guidance on imperfect stu- dent trajectories. An exponentially decaying distillation coefficient reduces teacher depen- dence as training proceeds. Experiments show gains from data refinement and further improve- ments from joint training after SFT, indicating stronger long-horizon multimodal deep search capabilities. 1
title: MMSearch-OPD: Easy Made Hard, Hard Made Learnable for

text: Multimodal deep search agents address knowledge- intensive visual questions through interleaved rea- soning and external retrieval (Wu et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2025). Recent advances move toward long- horizon investigation, connecting evidence across webpages and using acquired visual observations to guide subsequent searches (Huang et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Two challenges limit training for this setting. Ex- isting multimodal datasets contain many questions solvable through parametric knowledge or short re- trieval, while constructing harder questions through graph composition and visual enrichment entails re- lation collection, image curation, and evidence val- idation (Chen et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Reusing existing image–question pairs offers a starting point for constructing ques- tions with greater search demands. Meanwhile, useful long-horizon investigation may end in re- dundant verification, premature stopping, or an incorrect answer. Terminal rewards provide lim- ited process feedback, and trajectory-level advan- tages supply a shared scalar signal throughout a rollout (Shao et al., 2024). Identical returns also remove group-relative learning contrast. Process rewards and teacher guidance address these lim- itations (Chen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026); we combine outcome-based optimization with selec- tive token-level teacher guidance. To address these challenges, we propose MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable ques- tion refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD).

To address these challenges, we propose MMSearch-OPD, combining controllable ques- tion refinement with joint reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). Our Refine pipeline reuses simple multimodal questions and their candidate reasoning chains. Expand extends chain depth, Blur increases disambiguation require- ments, and Visualize introduces retrievable visual evidence. These configurable operators control the intended evidence requirements while reusing seed assets (Figure 1). After question validation and supervised initialization, joint training combines answer rewards and behavior penalties with token- level OPD on imperfect student trajectories. The shaped reward gap adjusts guidance strength, while an exponential schedule reduces the OPD coeffi- cient as training proceeds. text: Long-Horizon Multimodal Search. MMSearch- R1 and WebWatcher train multimodal agents to interleave reasoning with external retrieval (Wu et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2025). Recent work ex- tends search horizons and manages growing inter- action histories (Huang et al., 2026; Du et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). DeepVoyager-VL uses interme- diate visual evidence to guide subsequent search (Zhang et al., 2026b). These developments call for training questions requiring sustained, cross-modal evidence acquisition. Multimodal Search Data Construction. Ques- tions solvable through parametric knowledge or short retrieval provide limited supervision for long- horizon search. Existing pipelines increase dif- ficulty through multi-hop composition and en- tity obfuscation (Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026), graph-structured synthesis (Chu et al., 2026; Mei et al., 2026), and visual evidence integration (Zhang et al., 2026c,b). These constructions re- quire evidence collection and validation. Our Re- fine pipeline reuses existing easy questions and candidate reasoning chains, applying Expand, Blur, and Visualize to control chain length, disambigua- tion, and visual requirements without building a large graph from scratch. text: and image inspection until returning an answer. Later actions depend on the accumulated multimodal history ht, making evidence acquisition sequential. For exam- ple, identifying an entity in a retrieved image can determine the next textual query; facts found on a webpage can instead guide which image to inspect. Reasoning chains and evidence necessity. We represent a task’s designated reasoning route as an entity chain C0 = (E0, . . . , ET ): E0 is grounded in the input image, each clue ℓi links Ei−1 to Ei, and ET is the answer. Each transition requires identifying the next entity from its predecessor and linking clue. Let Z contain the retrieved textual and visual facts needed along this chain, and Y(x, Z) the answers consistent with them. Our curation criterion requires a unique answer and necessity of every designated evidence item: Y(x, Z) = {y}, Y(x, Z \ {z})̸ = {y}, ∀z ∈Z. text: 3.3 Quality Control and Trajectory Generation Question validation. Each synthesized question is walked through from the input image, with min- imal wording fixes to ensure solvability and an- swer uniqueness. We check chain consistency, evi- dence provenance, image–text alignment, and ac- tual use of the designated Blur and Visualize evi- dence. These checks approximate Equation 1 and help ensure that the added requirements in Equa- tion 8 are non-trivial. Difficulty filtering and trajectory selection. We discard questions answered correctly by a direct- answer probe without tools. An expert model then performs k tool-augmented rollouts per ques- tion using the training search-and-vision interface. The probe removes residual parametric shortcuts that refinement alone cannot rule out, while tool- augmented rollouts test whether the questions are learnable through external evidence acquisition. The expert’s empirical Pass@k measures agent dif- ficulty, complementing the chain-based evidence burden DRefined. We retain successful trajectories as SFT demonstrations, sampling across Pass@k levels to balance difficulty and prevent easy ques- tions from dominating supervision. These esti- mates also guide the SFT/RL split described in Section 3.4. 3.4 Agentic Training Supervised initialization. Using the difficulty estimates in Section 3.3, we partition the curated training questions into an SFT subset and a harder RL subset. A larger model is fine-tuned on suc- cessful trajectories from both subsets and frozen as teacher πT.

The student πθ is initialized by SFT on the first subset and jointly optimized with RL and OPD on the second. Joint RL and OPD for long-horizon search. Useful evidence collection can end in redundant verification, premature stopping, or an unsupported answer. Final-answer scores provide limited feed- back on these intermediate decisions, motivating guidance along the search process. We combine outcome-based policy optimization with token- level teacher guidance on the student’s own tra- jectories, supplementing the shared scalar feedback from trajectory-wide advantages. For each ques- tion, we sample G student rollouts and assign cor- rectness scores ci ∈[0, 1]. text: We introduced MMSearch-OPD, combining con- trollable data refinement with joint RL–OPD train- ing for long-horizon multimodal deep search. Re- fine reuses existing multimodal question–image pairs and applies targeted transformations to con- trol search depth, entity disambiguation, and vi- sual evidence requirements. Joint training com- plements answer rewards and behavior penalties with reward-conditioned token-level guidance on imperfect student trajectories, while progressively reducing teacher influence. Across seven primary benchmarks, our 9B agent improves average ac- curacy by 15.3 percentage points over its agentic- workflow baseline, with joint training adding 2.3 points beyond SFT. Data ablations further support the training value of refined questions. Together, these results show the value of upgrading exist- ing multimodal data to require sustained evidence acquisition. They also support joint outcome opti- mization and selective teacher guidance for learn- ing long-horizon search and reasoning over text and images. 8

text: Limitations Refine increases evidence requirements along des- ignated reasoning chains, but filtering cannot rule out all shortcuts from parametric knowledge or alternative web evidence. Training depends on teacher and answer-judge quality, which may intro- duce noisy guidance. Open-web search also relies on changing content and tool availability, limiting reproducibility.

text: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) now outperform gradient-boosted trees in clas- sification and regression. Yet in survival analysis, which predicts when an event occurs from censored data, often on small clinical cohorts, we find that no existing TFM beats the half-century-old Cox model. We address this issue by introducing SurvICL, a TFM that predicts survival curves in-context. SurvICL is pretrained on purely synthetic datasets generated from a novel flexible proportional-odds prior that outperforms other prior types in our ablation study. Unlike most other survival models, SurvICL is trained with a plain quantile regression loss, which is possi- ble because its synthetic pre-training data generator can provide uncensored event times. Additionally, we introduce the largest survival benchmark to date spanning 103 datasets. On the 63 datasets held out from all design decisions, SurvICL out- performs 20 tree-based, deep, and foundation-model baselines without any tuning: it wins 82.9% of pairwise comparisons in integrated Brier score, against 71.3% for the runner-up, the Cox model, and is the first model to rank above Cox on small datasets. 1

text: Many decisions hinge on when an event will happen: how long will a patient survive after a cancer diagnosis? When will a customer churn? When will a machine fail? Survival analysis answers such questions by predicting, for an individual with features x ∈Rd, the survival function S(t | x) = P(T ⋆> t | x), that is, the probability that the event has not occurred by time t (Kleinbaum and Klein, 2012; Machin et al., 2006; Wiegrebe et al., 2024; Jeanselme et al., 2024). What sets survival analysis apart from regression, aside from strictly positive predictions, is censoring. A patient who leaves a clinical study alive after three years does not reveal their time of death, only that it exceeds three years. Discarding such partial observations biases predictions, and treating them as observed events is plainly wrong: a survival model must learn from both observed and censored events. In addition, survival predictions feed decisions (such as choosing a treatment given a five-year survival probability) and must therefore be calibrated probabilities rather than mere rankings of individuals (Goldstein et al., 2020; Lillelund et al., 2025; Alberge et al., 2026). Survival analysis is often a small-data problem. Many time-to-event datasets come from clinical studies, where observing events requires following patients for years, and cohorts of a few hundred individuals are the norm

Many time-to-event datasets come from clinical studies, where observing events requires following patients for years, and cohorts of a few hundred individuals are the norm (Indrayan and Mishra, 2021; O’Donnell et al., 2025): in all the data we collect for this work, more than 70% of the datasets have fewer than 1,000 samples. In this regime, the flexibility of modern machine learning is a liability. Half a century after its introduction, the Cox proportional hazards model (Cox, 1972) remains the workhorse of practitioners, and for good reason: on the small datasets of our benchmark, none of the gradient-boosted trees, deep survival networks, or existing survival foundation models outperforms it. ∗julie.alberge@inria.fr 1 arXiv:2610.22242v1 [stat.ML] 15 Oct 2026

Tabular foundation models (TFMs) seem very well suited to this regime. Pre-trained on many syn- thetic datasets, models such as TabPFN and TabICL predict in-context and now outperform gradient- boosted trees for classification and regression, in particular on small datasets (Hollmann et al., 2023; 2025; Grinsztajn et al., 2025; Qu et al., 2025; 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). Recent survival TFMs either recast survival as classification over a time grid for off-the-shelf TFMs (Kim et al., 2026), or are pre-trained on synthetic survival data (Seletkov et al., 2026; B¨ohm et al., 2026; Qi et al., 2026) but do not beat the Cox model or random survival forests (Figure 1). Building a High-Performing TFM for Survival Analysis. We introduce SurvICL, a tabular foun- dation model for in-context survival analysis, built on the TabICLv2 backbone (Qu et al., 2026). Similar to SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026), it handles censoring in the data generation rather than the loss. During pre-training, SurvICL sees censored datasets in its context, but is supervised with the latent, uncensored event times of the simulator: it learns to correct for censoring in-context, so that a plain quantile-regression loss suffices. SurvICL predicts for each individual a continuous quantile function of the event time, from which we can directly infer a monotone survival function. Scaling Evaluation of Survival Models. We evaluate SurvICL in the largest benchmark to date for survival analysis: 103 real-world datasets from healthcare, genomics, economics and engineering, with up to 52,000 samples and 15,000 features, against 20 baselines spanning classical, tree-based, deep and foundation models. For comparison, survival papers at machine-learning venues typically report results on 5 to 20 datasets, and the largest evaluations of survival foundation models span 48 to 81 datasets (Kim et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026; Pham et al., 2026a; Qi et al., 2026). All design choices were made on 40 development datasets, and all results are reported on 63 held-out datasets never used during development. On these held-out datasets, SurvICL is the best method both in prediction accuracy and in discrimination (Figure 1): it wins 82.9% of pairwise comparisons for the integrated Brier score (IBS), against 71.3% for the runner-up, the Cox model, and in 77.7% for the C-index, against 71.6% for random survival forests (see Figure 12). On small datasets, where no previous method surpasses the Cox model, SurvICL is the first to rank above it. On the largest datasets, gradient boosting still maintains a slight edge. Importantly, these gains do not come at the expense of computational efficiency. text: Deep Learning for Survival Analysis. The toolbox of survival analysis has been considerably extended in the last years to include deep architectures (Katzman et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Kvamme et al., 2019) that can accommodate a wide variety of data and event types, including time series, competing events, images and text (Zhu et al., 2016; Thorsen-Meyer et al., 2022; Bleistein et al., 2024; Wiegrebe et al., 2024; Alberge et al., 2024; Jeanselme et al., 2024). Our work builds on this research by tailoring deep transformers and training procedures for tabular data, which is the most common form of survival data. Deep Learning for Tabular Data. Gradient-based decision tree models have long dominated benchmarks on tabular data (Gorishniy et al., 2021; Grinsztajn et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2024). Tabular foundation models have recently challenged their superiority and sparked a new line of research that focused on designing tailored architectures and training procedures (Hollmann et al., 2023; 2025; Qu et al., 2025; 2026; Kim et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). We build on these ar- chitectural advances and adapt them to calibrated survival prediction. Once pre-trained, our method performs in-context inference without fine-tuning or weight updates. Tabular Foundation Models for Survival Analysis is a burgeoning field of research. Efforts follow three distinct strategies. (i) Reducing survival to a task that generic TFMs already solve. Kim et al. (2026) frame survival prediction as a series of binary classification problems over a time grid, so that any TFM that handles classification can be deployed for survival analysis. Vieyra (2026) instead plugs an off-the-shelf TFM regressor into a log-normal accelerated failure time model and impute censored times iteratively, while SurvFM (Lyu et al., 2026) converts censored follow-up into pseudo- observations of the restricted mean survival time (RMST), which are then regressed in-context by unmodified TFMs. These approaches inherit the strengths of generic TFMs, but their backbone has never seen censored data: they either depend on a time discretization, impose a parametric form on the event-time distribution, or only output a summary statistic (the RMST) rather than a full survival function. (ii) Adapting generic TFMs with a survival head. Pham et al. (2026b;a) train classical survival heads (Cox, DeepHit, multi-task logistic regression) on top of frozen or fine-tuned representations of TabPFN, TabDPT (Ma et al., 2025a), and TabICL, and systematically compare these adaptation interfaces on 74 datasets. They
title: Preprint.

(2026b;a) train classical survival heads (Cox, DeepHit, multi-task logistic regression) on top of frozen or fine-tuned representations of TabPFN, TabDPT (Ma et al., 2025a), and TabICL, and systematically compare these adaptation interfaces on 74 datasets. They find that zero-shot reformulations work best on small datasets, whereas trained heads take over as the sample size grows. This line of work matches the common practice of fitting shallow survival models on top of deep foundation models, and gives up the pre-training + in-context learning recipe: the head must be fitted, and possibly tuned, on each new dataset. (iii) Pre-training on synthetic survival data. Closest to our work, Seletkov et al. (2026), B¨ohm et al. (2026) and Qi et al. (2026) pre-train a tabular foundation model on synthetic survival data, following previous work in the field of tabular foundation models (Hollmann et al., 2023; Qu et al., 2025; 2026). All three models predict on a discretized time grid (see Table 1), while SurvICL outputs a continuous quantile function of the event time. Finally, foundation models for time-to- event prediction have also been pre-trained on large real-world electronic health records (Steinberg et al., 2024); such models are tied to a specific data modality and coding system, whereas we target generic tabular data through a synthetic prior. 3 SURVIVAL ANALYSIS SETTINGS:

In survival analysis, data comes in the form of i.i.d. samples Dn = {(xi, ti, δi)}n i=1. For each instance i, xi ∈Rd denotes the feature vector and ti > 0 is a positive valued time. Unlike standard supervised learning, the target is subject to right-censoring, meaning that their true event time is not necessarily observed but might be censored, in which case we only observe the censoring 3
title: Preprint.

text: Preprint. time ci > 0. This proxy time yields weak information on the true event time, since it will necessarily happen after censoring. We denote by t⋆ i the possibly unobserved true time of event, such that ti := min{t⋆ i , ci} and δi := 1t⋆ i ≤ci. Predicting with Survival Models. Our goal is to approximate the survival function S(t | xi) := P(T ⋆> t | X = xi) at any time t > 0. This stands in contrast to classification or regression, where the model’s goal is to output a value byi which approximates the binary or continuous outcome yi. The survival function can be used to predict the time of event ˆti for individual i as the first time it crosses the threshold 0.5. Hazard-based Models. Following the seminal work of Cox (1972), an extensive family of models parametrized the hazard of the survival process, the time-wise derivative of the event probability: Hazard: h(t | xi) := lim ε→0 P(T ⋆∈[t, t + ε) | X = xi, T ⋆≥t) ε = −∂t log S(t | xi) and trains it via (partial) likelihood maximization (Friedman, 1982; Fornili et al., 2013; Katzman et al., 2018; Kvamme et al., 2019; Kvamme and Borgan, 2021; Bleistein et al., 2024). Once the hazard is learned, it can be used
