Once the hazard is learned, it can be used to predict the survival function using numerical integration. Discrete-Time Models. On the other side, some models bin time to simplify the computation of the model’s likelihood and frame survival analysis as a classification task (Yu et al., 2011; Fotso, 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2026). More precisely, in their approach, time is discretized into B + 1 bins ([sk, sk+1[)B k=0 for 0 = s0 < · · · < sB = +∞. The tuple (xi, ti, δi) is then expanded into a series of points by creating a series of binary outcomes yi,k := 1ti≤sk and considering the expanded dataset {((xi, sk), yi,k)k}n i=1. For individuals who experience the event, B points are created, while for censored individuals only the bins prior to the censoring time are added to the expanded dataset. This approach is the dominant approach in survival TFMs (see Table 1). While flexible and easy to train, unconstrained formulations of these models can output non-monotonic survival functions, requiring post-hoc workarounds such as clipping probabilities (Kim et al., 2026). 3.2 DESIGN GOALS FOR A

Small datasets are ubiquitous in survival analysis (O’Donnell et al., 2025), notably because time-to-event data is expensive and time-consuming to collect (to analyze event times that span over N years, one first needs to wait for N years) and because datasets often originate from healthcare (Indrayan and Mishra, 2021). State-of-the-art models perform well on large samples (n ≥2000), but struggle on small datasets (Zhao et al., 2026). Out-of-the-Box Calibration. In survival analysis, accurate probability estimates are crucial for decision-making (Goldstein et al., 2020; Alberge et al., 2026). Yet, models are often trained and evaluated chasing the C-index, which has been criticized as it does not assess calibration and is not a proper metric (not minimized for true probabilities, Lillelund et al., 2025). During pre-training, the context only contains censored observations (xi, ti, δi), while the loss is computed on the uncensored t⋆ i of the query points. The model thus learns to infer the event-time distribution from censored data in-context. The survival-specific knowledge lives in the prior, so that the above regression loss is valid: we need neither a censored likelihood, nor inverse-probability-of-censoring weights, nor a discretization of time. SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026) also supervises with latent times, but over a discretized time grid and with censoring times as an additional target, which we find to be detrimental (Section 6). In survival analysis, censoring times are often considered to be hurdles to efficient estimation. Interestingly, Qi et al. (2026) use the censored times as an alternative target: their model learns to approximate two distributions (one for censored times and one for event times) by predicting the event and censoring times during pre-training. We ablate this mixed prediction task and show that it degrades the performance of our model. 5 PRETRAINING: SYNTHETIC DATA PRIORS WITH PROPORTIONAL-ODDS A key novelty of our work is our synthetic data prior, illustrated in Figure 2. Proportional-Odds (PO) Prior. We start by sampling numerical and categorical features (xi)n i=1 using the structural causal prior of Qu et al. (2026). The number of nodes (from 2 to 32) and features (from 1 to 100) span a wide range to allow for diverse datasets. We then sample survival times from a novel proportional-odds prior. Like the Cox model, it combines a baseline with an individual effect η(xi), but on the odds rather than the hazard scale: hazard ratios then vary over time and may vanish in the long run, a common pattern in clinical data that Cox priors cannot generate. Secondly, we generate a concurrent censoring time distribution by sampling another pair of baseline and indi- vidual specific hazards and combining them as for the event time distribution. Shallow models. We include Cox model (Cox, 1972) and KM estimator (Kaplan and Meier, 1958) as baselines. The latter does not use covariates, and hence any model is expected to outperform it. Deep Networks. We include five deep networks tailored for survival analysis (Lee et al., 2018; Katzman et al., 2018; Nagpal et al., 2021; Rindt et al., 2022; Kirpichenko et al., 2026). These models are fitted on each dataset and use various modeling techniques (from Bayesian prior to

text: tailored for survival analysis (Lee et al., 2018; Katzman et al., 2018; Nagpal et al., 2021; Rindt et al., 2022; Kirpichenko et al., 2026). These models are fitted on each dataset and use various modeling techniques (from Bayesian prior to a MLP that predicts the survival function at different times). Tree-Based Models. Following the seminal work of Ishwaran et al. (2008) on random survival forests (RSF) and Grinsztajn et al. (2022), a body of work has adapted tree-based methods to survival analysis. On top of RSF, we evaluate SurvivalBoost (Alberge et al., 2024) and alternative gradient- boosted tree-based methods implemented in sksurv (P¨olsterl, 2020). Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). We include four open-weight tabular foundation models in our benchmark: SurvPFN (B¨ohm et al., 2026), SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026), Survival-IC (SIC) (Seletkov et al., 2026) and TFM4Survival (Kim et al., 2026). 6.3 DATASETS AND HOLD-OUT PROTOCOL In total, we consider 103 datasets with varying properties, see Figure 3. On the 63 held-out datasets, SurvICL wins 82.9% of pairwise comparisons in IBS, against 71.3% for the runner-up, the Cox model (Figure 1), and the dif- ference is statistically significant (Figure 4a, ranks and winrates are related by an affine transform). It also achieves the highest win rate in C-index, 77.7% against 71.6% for random survival forests (Figures 4b and 12). All existing survival TFMs trail behind classical methods. That the runners-up are the Cox model and random survival forests, with few parameters and strong inductive biases, underlines how hard survival analysis is for flexible models, which overfit small censored datasets. SurvICL is the first model to rank above Cox on small datasets. 69.8% of our held-out datasets have fewer than 1,000 samples, making this regime central and not a niche. SurvICL is the first to rank above Cox in IBS (win rate 84.9% against 77.2%, Figure 23) and it matches Cox in C-index, although these differences are not statistically significant (Figures 22 and 26). The prior has a substantial impact on performance: by keeping the exact same architecture and only changing the generation process, our proportional-odds prior outperforms Cox (77.6) and mixed priors (84.0). Compared to the prior of the other TFMs, our prior yields better results than SurvPFN (79.0), SurvivalPFN (82.7), and SIC (83.7). This demonstrates that our prior is highly effective, while adding a censoring-time prediction head actually reduces performance (81.0). Administrative censoring and time discretiza- tion have limited effects at this scale; we retain them to represent study-end censoring and finite temporal resolution. The final model uses 999 quantiles for finer resolution, despite a small advan- tage for 99 in the ablation (88.5 versus 87.2). 7 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION Designing Efficient Survival TFMs. SurvICL differs from existing survival TFMs along three axes (Table 1). Output and supervision. Unlike previous survival TFMs that rely on discrete time bins such as TFM4Survival (Kim et al., 2026) and SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026), which use classification or likelihood losses over time bins, SurvPFN (B¨ohm et al., 2026) uses a censored likelihood with a ranking term over 1,000 bins, and Survival-IC (Seletkov et al., 2026) uses the DeepHit
title: Preprint.

text: and SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026), which use classification or likelihood losses over time bins, SurvPFN (B¨ohm et al., 2026) uses a censored likelihood with a ranking term over 1,000 bins, and Survival-IC (Seletkov et al., 2026) uses the DeepHit loss (Lee et al., 2018) over 10 bins. SurvICL is the first to output a continuous quantile function. Quantile outputs are not new per se: TabICLv2 (Qu et al., 2026) uses a pinball loss for regression, and censored quantile regression (Portnoy, 2003; Pearce et al., 2022) modifies this loss to account for censoring. With latent-time supervision, no such modification is needed, as censoring is handled by the prior. SurvivalPFN also supervises with latent times, but over a time grid and with censoring times as an additional target, which our ablations show to be detrimental. Prior. SurvivalPFN draws times from random noised neural networks with several censoring mechanisms, SurvPFN draws Weibull times from a risk score and a dataset-specific shape, and Survival-IC mixes an extended hazard and a discrete-time model, with covariate-independent and administrative censoring. Our PO prior instead combines a flexible, multi-modal baseline hazard with a random risk function, for both event and censoring times; in our ablations, it outperforms the SurvPFN prior as well as Cox and AFT priors. Backbone and evaluation. Like Survival-IC, built on TabICL (Qu et
title: Preprint.

text: flexible, multi-modal baseline hazard with a random risk function, for both event and censoring times; in our ablations, it outperforms the SurvPFN prior as well as Cox and AFT priors. Backbone and evaluation. Like Survival-IC, built on TabICL (Qu et al., 2025), we reuse an existing architecture, TabICLv2, which is not our contribution. Finally, we provide, to our knowledge, the first comparison of all four survival TFMs, on 63 datasets. Implications. On the small cohorts that dominate clinical research, SurvICL is the first model to rank above the Cox model, the default of practitioners for half a century, without any training or tuning, while remaining among the best-calibrated methods. This makes foundation models a credible default for survival analysis. 9

text: Preprint. Limitations and outlook. On the largest datasets, gradient boosting remains slightly stronger, call- ing for longer contexts or light fine-tuning. Baseline hyperparameters are tuned on the first split and reused across splits; as tuning data then overlaps other splits’ test sets, this protocol, if any- thing, favors the baselines. SurvICL addresses right-censored, single-event data; competing risks and time-varying covariates are natural extensions of the prior. We release our code and models to foster research on foundation models for time-to-event data. 10

A SURVICL MODEL DETAILS A.1 ARCHITECTURE We build SurvICL on top of TabICLv2 (Qu et al., 2026), which is at the time of writing the leading fully open-source model on the TabArena benchmark (Erickson et al., 2025). While refer to the original paper for the details, the key components of the TabICLv2 architecture can be summarized as follows: • Preprocessing: First, some light preprocessing is applied, including ordinal encoding of categorical columns. After the preprocessing, the model receives a fully numerical table. • Target-aware embedding: The original covariates (xij) ∈Rn×m are transformed into embeddings (zij) ∈Rn×m×128 containing one embedding vector zij ∈R128 per cell (i, j). Each embedding vector is obtained from an affine transformation applied to three cells in the same row (“repeated feature grouping”). An affine transformation of the target yi is added for the context set rows. • Column-wise embedding: Each column j of the resulting embeddings is processed in- dependently using three induced self-attention blocks that allow interactions between dif- ferent rows in the same column, resulting in a complexity of O(nm), which is linear in the number of rows, unlike a full Transformer. Crucially, the attention is designed to only retrieve information from the training set, meaning that predictions on test samples are independent of the other test samples. • Row-wise interaction: Next, three

text: in the number of rows, unlike a full Transformer. Crucially, the attention is designed to only retrieve information from the training set, meaning that predictions on test samples are independent of the other test samples. • Row-wise interaction: Next, three full transformer blocks allow different columns within a row to interact. Before these blocks, four extra columns with fixed values are appended, and after the blocks, the values of these four columns are concatenated and serve as row embeddings, while the other columns are discarded. • ICL transformer: After adding another embedding of the targets, the embeddings of each row interact via 12 regular transformer layers, again making sure that test samples cannot access other test samples. • Head: Finally, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) head transforms the output embeddings into 999 quantile predictions (for regression). Overall, the TabICLv2 architecture has a runtime complexity of O(n2 + nm2), and SurvICL pre- serves this complexity since it only modifies the O(nm) preprocessing and embedding parts. In addition, like other TFMs, we use ensembling, where the predictions of eight forward passes with different preprocessings and column permutations are averaged. Building on TabICLv2, we introduce the following adaptations to handle survival data: • Time normalization: We normalize observed times by their mean over the context set, yielding ˜ti = ti/¯t, where ¯tcontext is the mean duration of the observed times. This makes the time representation invariant to the choice of measurement units. During pre-training, both context and query sets are normalized and the mean ¯t is taken across context and query set. During inference (after pre-training), the mean for ¯t is taken across the context set, and the predicted quantiles are transformed back to the original time scale. • Censoring-aware target embedding: We replace the scalar target embedding with a joint representation of the observed time and event indicator. Specifically, we sum the embed- ding of the continuous time ˜ti and a learned embedding of the binary indicator δi. This representation is added to every cell embedding in context row i, allowing the column-wise encoder to distinguish observed events from censored observations. • Survival information at the ICL stage: We also encode (˜ti, δi) using a separate pair of time and event-indicator embeddings whose sum matches the dimension of the row representation. This embedding is added to context row representations before the ICL transformer. At both embedding stages, survival outcomes are supplied only for

Kaplan-Meier Estimator (Kaplan and Meier, 1958): A non-parametric statistic used to estimate the marginal survival probability from observed lifetime data. Because it does not take individual covariates into account, it serves as the most basic population- level baseline for survival functions and is consistent. Cox Model (Cox Proportional Hazards) (Cox, 1972): The standard semiparametric workhorse of survival analysis. It models the hazard rate as a prod- uct of a time-varying baseline hazard and an expo- nential linear combination of the covariates. It relies on the strong assumption of proportional hazards (the hazard ratio between any two individuals is constant over time). B.1.2 TREE-BASED MODELS These models adapt decision trees and boosting trees to handle right-censored data, remaining highly competitive on tabular datasets. 19
title: Preprint.

text: Preprint. RSF (Random Survival Forests) (Ishwaran et al., 2008): An extension of the Random Forest al- gorithm for time-to-event data. It constructs an ensemble of survival trees using specialized splitting criteria (like the log-rank test) to handle censored observations. GBS (Gradient Boosting for Survival) (P¨olsterl, 2020): A boosting approach implemented in scikit-survival that sequentially builds regression trees. In our evaluation, we include two variants corresponding to different optimization targets: sksurv GBS (Cox), which minimizes the negative log partial likelihood of the Cox proportional hazards model, and sksurv GBS (C-index), which directly optimizes a smoothed concordance index. SurvivalBoost (Alberge et al., 2024): A modern, highly optimized gradient boosting framework specifically tailored for survival analysis, optimizing a proper scoring rule. B.1.3 DEEP NEURAL NETWORKS These methods leverage multi-layer architectures to capture complex, non-linear relationships be- tween covariates and survival times, often dropping the proportional hazards assumption. DeepHit (Lee et al., 2018): A discrete-time survival network that optimizes a loss that combines a likelihood and a ranking metric over an MLP, usable in survival analysis and competing events. DeepSurv (Katzman et al., 2018): It uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to replace the linear combination of covariates in the standard Cox model, allowing it to learn complex, non-linear inter- actions while still optimizing the Cox partial likelihood. DSM (Deep Survival Machines) (Nagpal et al.,
title: Preprint.

text: It uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to replace the linear combination of covariates in the standard Cox model, allowing it to learn complex, non-linear inter- actions while still optimizing the Cox partial likelihood. DSM (Deep Survival Machines) (Nagpal et al., 2021): DSM uses a neural network to model the survival function as a mixture of parametric distributions (such as Weibull or Log-Normal), providing well-calibrated survival estimates. SumoNet (Rindt et al., 2022): SurvivalMonotonic-net utilizes a partially monotonic neural network to directly optimize the right-censored log-likelihood. TabSurv (Kirpichenko et al., 2026): A specialized deep learning framework that adapts modern tabular neural networks to time-to-event prediction. Because this framework supports multiple representation backbones, we evaluate several architectural variants that appear throughout our re- sults: the default TabSurv, TabSurv-MLP (using a standard Multi-Layer Perceptron), TabSurv- RealMLP (utilizing the more robust RealMLP tabular backbone), as well as TabSurv-WAS and TabSurv-WSA (which incorporate specialized attention and sparse embedding mechanisms de- signed specifically for tabular features). B.1.4 TABULAR FOUNDATION MODELS This category represents the most modern class of baselines: tabular foundation models trained on synthetic tabular data. They generalize to new datasets in a zero-shot or in-context manner. SurvPFN: (B¨ohm et al., 2026) SurvPFN is a survival-specific Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN) based on the architecture of TabPFN v2, pretrained on synthetic censored survival tasks (sampling from different
title: Preprint.

text: They generalize to new datasets in a zero-shot or in-context manner. SurvPFN: (B¨ohm et al., 2026) SurvPFN is a survival-specific Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN) based on the architecture of TabPFN v2, pretrained on synthetic censored survival tasks (sampling from different distributions such as Weibull). SurvivalPFN (Qi et al., 2026): SurvivalPFN performs amortized Bayesian survival inference by us- ing the observed covariates, event times, and censoring indicators as in-context examples to directly predict posterior event-time distributions for new individuals based on the CausalPFN architecture. Survival-IC (Seletkov et al., 2026): Survival In-Context (SIC) is a prior-fitted foundation model pretrained on synthetic survival datasets to approximate Bayesian posterior predictive inference and based on the architecture of TabICL. TFM4Survival (Kim et al., 2026): TFM4Survival adapts pretrained tabular foundation models such as TabICL to censored time-to-event data through a sampling-based formulation, allowing existing TFMs to perform survival prediction without survival-specific pretraining. 20

text: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations Hasan Demirkiran Kontext hasan@kontext.security Jens Ernstberger Kontext jens@kontext.security
title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations

text: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LIN- UXARENA trajectories and two TS-BENCH-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitiv- ity. In LINUXARENA, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AGENTDOJO-TRAJ, exact-tool lookup falls from F1 = .901 with mixed- domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AGENTHARM-TRAJ, released TS-GUARD F1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AGENTDOJO-TRAJ cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard’s decisions

The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-GUARD. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions. 1

text: A benchmark may be easy for the wrong reason. Annotation conventions, source identity, repeated templates, and collection artifacts can all predict labels without measuring the intended construct [Gururangan et al., 2018, Geirhos et al., 2020]. This problem is especially consequential for agent- safety evaluation. A tool guard may be deployed to approve or block a consequential action, while its benchmark record also contains scaffolding added by the evaluation pipeline: provenance tags, tool names, trajectory length, source subsets, and repeated interaction structure. Simple lexical and length features separated honest and attack trajectories in the public LinuxArena sample, motivating a search for analogous rules elsewhere. Such a rule may track real risk, collection differences, or evidence also used by a capable guard; rule–guard agreement cannot distinguish these explanations. To systematically uncover potential shortcuts, we introduce shortcut auditing as a three-level inference ladder for agent-safety guard evaluations. A shortcut audit asks progressively stronger questions: can 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). text: a simple cue predict released labels; is that cue associated with guard decisions; and does changing only that cue alter the guard’s decision? We distinguish: 1. Label Predictability: Can a deliberately capability-poor rule predict released labels? 2. Observational Guard Association: Do guard decisions correlate with the suspected cue in released records? 3. Paired Decision Sensitivity: Does the guard change when the cue is changed while the candidate action’s authorization and effect are held fixed? Paired edits test whether changing the input changes the guard’s decision. To interpret that change as spurious shortcut reliance, the edits must preserve the relevant safety information. For a deterministic guard, evaluating each original–edited pair reveals whether the strict decision changes. Stochastic guards require additional controls because identical inputs can produce different outputs and sequen- tial calls may drift over time. We therefore interleave repeated original and edited calls, include a formatting placebo, and report identical-input disagreement separately. Our contributions are: • Three-level shortcut-audit framework. We introduce a inference ladder separating label pre- dictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity with explicit construct- preservation caveats, plus repeat and placebo controls for stochastic guards. • Audit of released agent-safety evaluations. We apply shortcut-auditing to AGENTDOJO-TRAJ, a LINUXARENA public sample, and to AGENTHARM-TRAJ. Evaluation authors should measure whether conclusions survive group holdouts, equal-unit weighting, paired perturbations with construct-preservation caveats, and repeat-original controls. For stochastic g, the target estimand is instead ∆T = 1 n n X i=1 {Pr[g(T(xi)) = 1] −Pr[g(xi) = 1]} , (4) estimated here by repeated calls in both conditions. Under stable independent draws, the signed K = 1 mean g(T(xi)) −g(xi) is unbiased for ∆T , but can be imprecise and temporally confounded when calls are not interleaved. Our contribution is to operationalize label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity as a three-level audit for released agent-safety evaluations. The experiments show that strong label predictability can coexist with localized paired decision sensitivity. 3 Evaluation artifacts and audit design 3.1 Evaluation artifacts LinuxArena. LinuxArena evaluates control protocols for agents operating in live software environ- ments [Tracy et al., 2026]. We use the 932-row public sample at a pinned dataset revision. Of these, 918 rows contain extracted shell commands. Because the public sample repeats action traces under different monitor runs, we hash complete action content after removing only the monitor response. The primary diagnostic contains 576 exact-action-unique shell trajectories: 176 attack and 400 honest across ten environments. We never use the nominally unique trajectory_id as a deduplication key. The sample also contains LinuxArena’s precomputed per-action suspicion scores from its Claude 3

The monitor conditions on the task, possible side-task goals, and tool-call history, but not agent reasoning; each stored score averages two calls. TS-Bench. ToolSafe introduces TS-Bench and TS-Guard for pre-execution, step-level tool safety [Mou et al., 2026]. TS-BENCH derives the released AGENTDOJO-TRAJ and AGENTHARM- TRAJ step records, including step-level risk scores, from AgentDojo and AgentHarm trajectories [Debenedetti et al., 2024, Andriushchenko et al., 2025]. We use these files at a pinned commit; the paired AGENTDOJO-TRAJ variants described below are the only new inputs we construct. Under ToolSafe’s strict mapping, every nonzero risk rating is unsafe. AgentDojo-Traj has 1,220 steps (352 unsafe and 868 safe) across four domains. AgentHarm-Traj has 731 steps (525 unsafe and 206 safe) in 197 released interaction-ID groups. We use released labels, TS-Guard predictions, and previously cached hosted-guard assessments from pinned source commits. No tool call in a record is executed. text: provider responses. Audit scope. Here, an audit means applying the three-level framework in Section 2 to released evaluation artifacts. We test whether simple cues predict labels, whether input-visible cues are associated with guard decisions, and, when an edit intended to preserve the construct is available, whether paired edits change those decisions. The analysis is black-box: it uses released records, outputs, and fixed input transformations without access to guard internals. We do not test an adaptive agent, an evasion attack, or end-to-end tool execution. 3.2 Capability-poor diagnostics Level 1 begins with one deliberately limited diagnostic matched to each artifact’s construction. The aim is not to build the best classifier. It is to test whether a narrow cue recovers released labels and whether that result survives controls for duplication, source overlap, transfer, and evaluation- unit weighting. For LinuxArena, the deterministic score is the negative mean shell-command character count, so larger scores indicate shorter commands. We compare it with character n-gram TF–IDF and logistic regression trained leave-one-environment-out (LOEO). We report AUC and a clustered bootstrap over main-task/side-task groups. These are completed-trajectory diagnostics, not operational step-wise monitors. For AgentDojo-Traj, the fixed binary rule requires both the literal <INFORMATION> marker in history and a current tool whose name starts with one of 11 side-effect verbs (for example, send_, delete_, or update_). We evaluate it both with interaction- grouped five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-domain-out (LODO) transfer. As a matched-context control, we group AgentHarm rows by case-folded parsed tool name and normalized arguments, retaining only groups containing both strict labels. Giving each execution group equal weight, released TS-Guard’s mean composite score is .922 in unsafe contexts and .413 in safe contexts (difference .510): the unsafe mean is higher in 11 groups and tied in five, with no reversal. All six cached hosted guards also have a positive macro difference. Thus rows with the same normalized execution signature can receive different scores across the benchmark’s label/context groups; tool identity alone is insufficient to explain guard behavior. This fixed-benchmark matched analysis does not identify authorization context as the cause. 6

text: 5 Cue edits can change guard decisions We use each system as a pre-execution step judge over inert text. Released TS-Guard plus six hosted configurations supply the original-input screen; Q8 TS-Guard, one-draw GPT-5.5, and repeated Haiku and Luna runs score the paired edits. For Haiku, both audited cue edits materially change blocking and remain distinct from the formatting placebo. 5.1 Association selects the intervention target Among gold-safe AgentDojo rows, the literal marker is observationally associated with blocking. Released TS-Guard blocks 9.66% of 321 marked safe rows versus 6.03% of 547 unmarked safe rows, a 3.62 pp clustered difference [0.09, 7.33] pp. GPT-5.5 blocks 17/320 valid marked-safe rows (one marked-safe row is invalid) versus 6/547 unmarked-safe rows, a 4.22 pp difference [1.70, 7.05] pp. Claude Haiku 4.5 shows the strongest association in the seven-configuration screen: 74.45% versus 0.37%, a 74.09 pp difference [68.67, 79.75] pp. GPT-5.6 Luna also has a positive observational gap of 10.48 pp [7.17, 14.11] pp. These comparisons are confounded: marked and unmarked records differ in request, history, argu- ments, and risk. Association selects intervention targets, while paired edits show whether a particular guard is actually sensitive. 6 Implications for evaluation design Our results suggest a minimum audit sequence for agent-safety evaluations. 1. Diagnose and stress transfer. Test capability-poor cues, then deduplicate the semantic unit and hold out environments, domains, templates, or sources. A strong result is a trigger, not a verdict. 2. Name the evaluation unit. Step-, interaction-, trajectory-, and task-weighted scores answer different questions. Report at least the unit named in the deployment claim. 3. Intervene after association. Use observational results only to select hypotheses. Change one cue while retaining authorization, capability, arguments, and effect; record possible semantic changes. 4. Use controls for stochastic guards. Interleave original, edited, and placebo calls; report block- probability differences and identical-input disagreement. A public rule can become an adaptive target, motivating hidden group holdouts and refreshed equivalent serializations [Tramèr et al., 2020, Jotautait˙e et al., 2026, Zhong et al., 2026]; we do not test such adaptation here. 7

text: Shortcut auditing connects annotation artifacts and shortcut learning [Gururangan et al., 2018, Geirhos et al., 2020] to group-shift tests, contrast sets, behavioral evaluation, and benchmark sensitivity [Koh et al., 2021, Gardner et al., 2020, Ribeiro et al., 2020, Dehghani et al., 2021, Alzahrani et al., 2024]. Related work tests surface heuristics, AgentHarm cues, benign triggers, construct validity, and broken specifications [Li et al., 2026, Meng et al., 2025, Tasawong et al., 2025, Li et al., 2025, Bean et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2026, Tu et al., 2026]. Paired cue tests are established; we contribute a three-level inference ladder across released agent-safety artifacts. AgentDojo, AgentHarm, ToolSafe, LinuxArena, and StepGuard span safety guards and monitoring [Debenedetti et al., 2024, Andriushchenko et al., 2025, Mou et al., 2026, Tracy et al., 2026, Zheng et al., 2026]. Other work audits AgentDojo end to end or develops broader guards [Bhagwatkar et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025, Huang et al., 2025, Greenblatt et al., 2024]; we audit released step records, evaluation units, and black-box decision sensitivity. 8 Limitations and broader impact The Luna replication does not reproduce the Haiku-sized effects, indicating that the observed sensitivity is configuration-specific. The 64-step cohort is not a probability sample, and intervals are exploratory and unadjusted. The marker rewrite changes provenance wording, aliases are not natural global renamings, and

Q8 is quantized, GPT-5.5 lacks repeats, and StepGuard stops at a non-equivalent Mac feasibility check. LinuxArena uses completed trajectories, and AgentHarm subset identity is not proven guard-visible. We study evaluation validity, not deployment safety; execute no tool calls; and use no human-subject data. 9

text: Agent-safety evaluations can appear reliable even when their results depend on how the benchmark is constructed. We introduced shortcut auditing, a three-level framework that separates label pre- dictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. Across LINUXARENA, AGENTDOJO-TRAJ, and AGENTHARM-TRAJ, simple diagnostics exposed weaknesses under do- main transfer and changes in evaluation unit. Shortcut sensitivity is therefore consequential but configuration-specific. A predictive benchmark property is a hypothesis, not evidence that a guard relies on it. Shortcut auditing provides these tests, replacing apparent benchmark performance with evidence about whether evaluation conclusions survive changes intended to preserve the underlying safety decision. 8

text: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards Hasan Demirkiran Kontext hasan@kontext.security Jens Ernstberger Kontext jens@kontext.security
title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards

text: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent’s next action is safe given the user’s request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts, and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated, are English. We ask whether a guard’s verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LINGUAGUARDBENCH from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, chosen a priori to span the high-, mid- and low-resource tiers of the Joshi et al. taxonomy, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and every managed guard is run three times to measure its own noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose- built agent guards (TS-Guard, ShieldAgent, Safiron, AgentDoG), most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. The purpose-built guards are the most sensitive of all.
title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards

text: effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. The purpose-built guards are the most sensitive of all. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12–30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to −7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated (one translated instruction moves a guard from blocking 12% of its steps to 92%) and, in a post-hoc analysis, legible: the flips in excess of placebo land on steps where the agent’s own reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does, and no general guard by more than 1.4 pp: the sensitivity is to language more than to wording. We release LINGUAGUARDBENCH (696 validated rewrites, frozen by hash, with a materialiser that regenerates every condition) and all 489k verdicts. 1

text: Tool-using agents are increasingly wrapped in step-level guards: a model that inspects the user’s request, the trajectory so far and the candidate tool call, and blocks the call if it appears unsafe [2–4]. The guard reads two channels. The untrusted channel (tool outputs, web pages, files) is where prompt injections live, and its robustness is well studied [1, 3]. The trusted channel is the user’s own request. The released guard prompts are English, and so are the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated (TS-Bench, Agent-SafetyBench, ATBench), but the principal they protect writes in whatever language they speak. Whether a guard’s verdict on a fixed action survives a change of language is, to our knowledge, unmeasured, even though the analogous question for safety classifiers, 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). text: which judge a text rather than an action in the context of a task, has a known bad answer [10, 14].This paper tests the hypothesis, pre-registered before any guard saw a rewritten request, that the language of the request is a security surface for step-level guards. We build LINGUAGUARDBENCH: a benchmark with fixed, labelled tool-call steps in which only the user instruction is translated into five languages chosen a priori to span three resource tiers (German and French; Turkish; Swahili and Amharic), and re-run the guards on it. Because the trajectory, the candidate action and the label never change, a verdict that flips is a language effect by construction, not a label disagreement. Two controls separate language from wording and from noise: six English rewordings of the same instructions (four LLM styles, a human paraphrase and typing noise) plus a whitespace placebo, and three repeats of every managed guard so that its own non-determinism is measured and subtracted. All of these read the user request as a trusted input, and all are trained or evaluated on English agent-safety benchmarks [16–19]; none reports sensitivity to the request’s language. We evaluate the four released ones. Cross-lingual safety. Safety classifiers and refusal training degrade in low-resource languages: translating harmful prompts into low-resource languages bypasses GPT-4’s safeguards [14], and multilingual jailbreak rates track language resource level [10]. Multilingual safety benchmarks and moderation tools [22–25] likewise vary the language of the content being judged. Here the content (the tool call and the trajectory) is held fixed and only the language of the principal’s request changes, which isolates the guard’s use of the trusted channel. Prompt sensitivity. Multi-prompt evaluation shows that paraphrasing an instruction shifts LLM scores and sometimes rankings [6, 7], and formatting alone can move accuracy by tens of points [21]; Rabanser et al. [8] measure paraphrase robustness of agents. Our English paraphrase conditions replicate this design for guards, and serve here as the control that shows the language effect is not a wording effect. 3 Setup Benchmark. TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj [2] contains 1,220 labelled tool-invocation steps (868 safe, 352 unsafe) from 589 AgentDojo [1] trajectories across banking, Slack, travel and workspace environments, with 58 unique user instructions. text: also over-block), so this is a tendency, not a threshold. The two regimes are not two degrees of the same failure. A mid-sized guard that over-blocks has not lost the ability to recognise an attack; it has become more suspicious of everything, and the extra blocks fall on benign steps because there are more of them. A small guard that under-blocks has lost the signal: with a request it parses less well, an unsafe action looks like every other action. Under the strict decision rule (block only if composite = 1), the placebo-adjusted flip rates under translation grow further for the guards that move (Nemotron 3.5 +5.7 pp, Nemotron 3 Nano 4B +5.1, Qwen 3.5 4B +2.9, TS-Guard +2.6) while every frontier guard stays within 0.2 pp under both rules (Appendix C). 4.3 The effect grows as the language gets rarer Table 6 (Appendix) pools each guard’s pairs by language tier (Joshi et al. classes 5, 4 and 2) before bootstrapping. text: Two mechanisms are consistent with this split, and they match the two regimes: inconsistency detection, which needs a restatement to fire and moves verdicts in either direction, and distrust of a foreign request, which fires when the request is the only source and adds blocks. Both are bounded by the restatement rate (60% of steps), which our intervention does not change, and a guard that decides from the trajectory alone, as the frontier models appear to do, is immune to both. 4.8 The sensitivity is to language more than to wording The same instructions reworded in English are the control. Across typos, four LLM styles and a human paraphrase, no general guard’s verdict flip rate exceeds its own placebo by more than 1.4 pp (TS-Guard among the pre-registered roster, Nemotron 3 Nano 4B in the small tier); the two purpose- built guards that do move under paraphrase (ShieldAgent +3.5 pp, AgentDoG +1.8) move two to three times as much under translation. Every guard that moves at all moves more under translation than under paraphrase. No paraphrase condition reduces any guard’s recall except gpt-oss-120b on the terse style (−1.3 pp), and the guard ranking is preserved (Kendall’s τ 0.96–0.98 against 0.93–0.96 under translation). A guard that is nearly invariant to how a request is worded but not to which language it is written in has learned the language, more than the register, as a feature. 5 Discussion What to deploy. For a guard that must serve non-English users, size is a proxy for the failure mode to expect: 17–30B open models tend to over-block, the guards that under-block are all below 10B, and neither shows up in an English-only evaluation. Purpose-built agent guards are not exempt; they are the most sensitive class we measured, and their direction has to be measured per guard. We evaluated no mitigation; translate-then-guard or per-language thresholds are untested candidates for the over-blocking regime. The concentration in enumerated multi-task instructions (§4.6) suggests a cheap diagnostic: evaluate guards on translated long instructions specifically, and on a low-resource language, where the effect is largest. The request field is not what strong guards use. The Gemini/scanner identity and the leaky-step mechanism point the same way: on trajectory-rich benchmarks the agent’s own reasoning restates the request, and strong guards decide from the trajectory. This is good news for robustness and bad news for benchmark validity: a benchmark cannot test a guard’s use of the trusted

This is good news for robustness and bad news for benchmark validity: a benchmark cannot test a guard’s use of the trusted channel if the untrusted channel already contains it. It also reframes language robustness: a guard is hurt by translation to the extent that it compares channels, not to the extent that it reads the request. Limitations. The LLM paraphrases and all five translations were generated by Gemini 3.8 Flash, which is also a guard; its measured invariance is therefore a lower bound, although the scanner identity makes generator overlap an unlikely explanation. Nobody on the team reads Swahili or Amharic, so those rows were accepted on the strength of two judges and back-translation, and the low-resource pair was not run on the partner-hosted guards (Claude, Llama, GLM, gpt-oss). The small tier and the low-resource pair were added after the pre-registered runs (ten guards, three languages), each with its own frozen-before-inference file. The alignment prompt gives open models high false- positive rates (0.26–0.37) at the original wording; effects are reported as shifts from each guard’s own operating point. gpt-oss-120b was quota-throttled and completed 7 of the 11 pre-registered perturbed conditions. text: Translating a user request changes what open and small step-level guards decide about a fixed action, and the direction of the damage tends to follow the guard’s size: mid-sized open guards block more benign steps, small guards let more attacks through, purpose-built agent guards move most of all, and frontier guards, the strongest of which does not use the request field at all, barely move. The effect grows as the language gets rarer: Amharic, the lowest-resource language and the only non-Latin script in the set, produces the largest shifts in both regimes. It is concentrated in long enumerated instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, lands where the request and the agent’s own restatement of it disagree. Rewording the same request in English changes far less. For open and small guards the language of the request is a security surface, and an evaluation that only ever shows the guard English requests will not expose it.

text: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing Sima Noorani∗1, Shayan Kiyani∗1, George Pappas1, and Hamed Hassani1 1University of Pennsylvania
title: Disagreement-Guided Weak-to-Strong Routing

text: Small language models are increasingly deployed on edge devices and robotic systems to meet cost and latency constraints, yet their limited capabilities can make reliable deployment challenging. Stronger models can provide assistance when needed, but deciding when to route a weak-model response to a stronger model often relies on signals of response correctness. In open-ended and agentic tasks, however, obtaining such signals can require costly ground-truth supervision that is difficult to obtain at scale. We revisit the foundations of weak-to-strong routing and ask whether routing decisions can instead be guided by signals that do not require ground-truth supervision. We first characterize the optimal weak-to-strong routing policy, while allowing for multiple weak-model responses generated through local inference. Building on this characterization, we derive a principled approximation to the optimal routing based on model-to-model comparison. In particular, we introduce a notion of model disagreement that can be measured directly from model-generated responses, without ground-truth supervision. Importantly, the approximation becomes increasingly accurate as the strong model becomes a better proxy for the ground-truth distribution. Across agentic and single-turn tasks, our approach effectively navigates the trade-off between routing cost and response accuracy without ground-truth supervision. Moreover, even when ground-truth correctness signals are available for training, disagreement-based routing can outperform methods trained directly to predict correctness. 1

text: Small language models offer a practical path to deploying AI agents on edge devices, robots, and other systems constrained by cost, latency, connectivity, or privacy. Yet their limited capabilities make it difficult to rely on them across the full range of tasks they may encounter [4, 30]. This has motivated growing interest in systems that primarily rely on a weak LLM, but occasionally route difficult instances to a stronger model when additional capability is needed [5, 15, 51]. The possibility of such routing changes how we should think about inference with weak LLMs. Rather than simply generating a response and returning it, inference now involves three decisions: whether to accept the current response, spend additional local computation on further reasoning or sampling, or seek assistance from a stronger model at substantially higher cost. These choices introduce a new trade-off: Stopping local inference too early miss improvements achievable through inexpensive additional computation; persisting locally for too long waste time and resources when *Equal contribution. A natural way to navigate this trade-off is to assess response correctness through learned confidence scores, verifiers, or reward models [27, 45]. In practical agentic applications, however, correctness is often difficult to evaluate. For a robotic agent, assessing a proposed next action may require knowledge of the physical environment and consequences that become apparent after execution. For a computer-use agent, whether an action is appropriate may depend on the state of an external application, user preferences, or the downstream effects of modifying a file or sending a message. More broadly, in long-horizon agentic workflows, a locally plausible action may undermine the eventual outcome, violate a user constraint, or introduce an error that becomes apparent several steps later [11, 32, 42]. Obtaining correctness labels in such settings may require subjective or expert judgment, interaction with the environment, or evaluation of entire trajectories. Such supervision is costly and does not readily scale across tasks and deployment conditions. text: Can we learn when to rely on weak-model inference and when to seek stronger assistance—without ground-truth correctness labels? To answer this question, we take a step back and shift the perspective from asking when the weak model needs help to asking about the value of using a stronger model. From this perspective, routing is fundamentally a comparative decision: what matters is not simply whether the weak model’s response is incorrect, but whether using the strong model instead is likely to improve the outcome. To this end, our contributions are summarized as follows: Our contributions are summarized as follows: • Fundamentals of weak-to-strong routing. In Section 3, we characterize optimal routing within a broader framework that jointly accounts for weak-model test-time inference allocation, identifying the population quantities governing when to continue locally and when to seek stronger assistance. • Routing through model disagreement. In Section 4, we derive a novel, ground-truth-free approximation to the optimal routing signal based on two disagreement signals: how much the weak and strong models disagree, and how much the strong model disagrees with itself. Importantly, (i) the approximation gap shrinks as the strong model becomes more accurate, and (ii) both signals can be efficiently learned from scalable model-generated data, without ground-truth supervision. • Empirical evaluation in agentic and reasoning tasks. In Section 6, we evaluate disagreement- based routing across multi-step agentic environments, where step-level correctness is difficult to define or supervise, and controlled single-turn reasoning tasks 1. Across both regimes, our learned disagreement-based signals consistently outperform label-free baselines, validating that disagreement-based approximation provides a reliable, scalable learning signal when ground-truth supervision is unavailable. 2

text: We briefly discuss the works most closely related to our evaluation setting and baselines, and defer a discussion to Appendix A.1. Learning to defer and supervised routing. The fundamental problem of knowing when a model should abstain or seek help has been extensively studied under the umbrella of learning-to-defer and selective prediction [19, 33]. With the advent of large language models, this challenge translates into determining when a weak model should autonomously escalate to a stronger one. In parallel to frameworks that study deferral for verification [22], our focus is on routing model generations. Many current cascade methods rely on ground-truth correctness labels to train quality scorers, process verifiers, or token-level confidence predictors [1, 5, 6, 15, 38]. In our experiments, we represent this paradigm using a ground-truth supervised baseline highlighting that our proposed framework fundamentally eliminates the need for such expensive, task-specific supervision. Label-free routing signals. To avoid human annotations, recent work extracts reliability signals directly from a single unlabeled generation using internal uncertainty metrics or hidden-state probes [10, 15, 24]. A prevalent alternative assesses reliability by generating multiple responses to measure internal agreement or semantic overlap [12, 25, 46, 51]. text: Step-level routing in agentic tasks. In sequential environments, determining when to escalate an action to a stronger model is typically guided by process-level verifiers and trajectory-level rewards [17, 20, 41], or frameworks for cost-aware decision support policies [21]. Because these approaches rely on explicit step-level correctness labels or complex episode-success evaluations, they are difficult to scale in open-ended domains. We contrast these paradigms with our agentic experiments, demonstrating that our framework can route actions autonomously at each step by predicting offline action disagreement, entirely bypassing the need for process verifiers or trajectory rewards. 3 Fundamentals of Weak-to-Strong Routing In this section, we study the problem of weak-to-strong routing jointly with the allocation of local inference computation.2 We first study this problem at the population level, assuming access to the underlying probabilistic quantities, which allows us to characterize the optimal solution and identify the fundamental principles governing sampling, selection, and routing. text: In this work, we study weak-to-strong routing in its general setting, jointly accounting for test-time sampling of candidate weak responses, candidate selection, and escalation to a stronger model. Conventional cascades and standard routing approaches rely on signals of response correctness, which are often costly to obtain and ambiguous to define in open-ended or agentic tasks. To bypass the need for ground-truth supervision, we introduce a perspective based on model disagreement. We derive corrected disagreement, a principled approximation to the optimal routing rule that balances cross-model disagreement against the strong model’s internal uncertainty. This formulation provides an objective learning signal that can be collected at scale from model-generated responses alone. Across multi-step agentic environments and reasoning benchmarks, our learned disagreement signal consistently outperforms label-free baselines, showing that our principled approximation offers a practical and scalable path to guiding hybrid inference without ground-truth supervision. 8 Acknowledgments This work was supported by EnCORE, the Institute for Emerging CORE Methods in Data Science, and NSF award 2502489 through the MFAI: Mathematical Foundations of Alignment in Generative 12

This design space generally splits into two paradigms: prompt-based routing, which selects a model before any text is generated [8, 35], and sequential cascades, which evaluate a cheaper model’s output before deciding whether to escalate [5, 19, 51]. While recent works such as [7] develop a unified formulation bridging both approaches, our work is specifically grounded in the cascade paradigm. text: 51]. While recent works such as [7] develop a unified formulation bridging both approaches, our work is specifically grounded in the cascade paradigm. Motivated by the growing need to deploy LLMs locally on resource-constrained edge devices [28, 39, 50], we study a two-model cascade with a significant capability gap. In this setting, a weak local model first generates candidate responses, and the system subsequently decides whether to invoke a more capable, expensive strong model based entirely on the realized generation history. To contextualize our contributions, the remainder of this section categorizes prior work along three critical axes: when the routing decision occurs, the required test-time inference compute, and the reliance on ground-truth supervision. Prompt-Based Routing and Learning to Defer. Prompt-based routers learn which model should answer an input without first observing its generated response. Building on classical literature regarding optimal deferral rules [19, 33], methods like Hybrid LLM [8] and Route LLM [35] allocate queries between models using learned predictions of quality. Other approaches focus on selecting a suitable expert from a larger pool of LLMs by predicting model performance through meta-models [2], distilling reward assessments to identify expertise [29], using input-dependent routing [44], estimating translation improvements using prompt representations [31], or decomposing input uncertainty using labeled calibration data to avoid routing inherently ambiguous queries [37]. In contrast, our cascade evaluates the realized weak response before routing, strictly in an unannotated two-model setting. Supervised Confidence and Deferral (N = 1). Automix [1] utilizes a POMDP routing policy trained on self-verification judgments and ground-truth signals. Finally, SELF-REF [6] and Gatekeeper [38] train the weak model to express verbalized confidence or produce more useful confidence scores. All of these methods rely on task-specific correctness labels for supervision, and cannot be deployed in our purely label-free setting. Motivated by these works, our supervised weak-correctness probe Proxy Reward serves as a controlled oracle reference to represent this category of quality-based deferral. Our proposed framework assumes no access to ground-truth correctness or improvement signals. Consistency and Ensemble-Based Cascades (N > 1 Label-Free). Semantic Entropy [25] and Kernel Language Entropy [12] measure uncertainty over clusters of equivalent answers which can be used as deferral rules in cascades. Similarly, [53] rely on clustering to compute the semantic entropies of both student and teacher models to construct routing preferences. Other methods evaluate consensus across an ensemble of multiple models: ABC [23] uses pairwise similarities across inexpensive models, SMOOTHIE [14] estimates quality from distances between embedded outputs (which requires generator triplets), and [34] groups queries into skill clusters via confidence-weighted ensemble consensus. These within-model consistency methods (particularly self-consistency and semantic entropy) directly motivate our multi-sample (N > 1) baselines. However, as a broader category, these approaches fundamentally differ from our framework in their operational assumptions and mechanics. First, ensemble routers ([14, 34]) are designed to select among a diverse pool of multiple models, whereas we study a strict cascade between a single local weak model and a more capable strong model. Consequently, our framework only requires the weak model’s internal repre- sentations; the strong model can remain entirely black-box, accessed only for its text outputs during offline training. Second, consistency methods require generating multiple responses at inference time and rely heavily on semantic clustering. As we demonstrate in Section 6.2, grouping responses into equivalence classes is notoriously brittle for open-ended tasks. Learned Label-Free Reliability and Cross-Model Verification. Semantic Entropy Probes [24] predict semantic-entropy targets directly from model representations to enable single- response uncertainty estimation. HaloScope [10] derives pseudo-labels from unlabeled response representations to train a truthfulness classifier. Additionally, [47], [16], and [13] explore cross-model disagreement and verifier surprise to quantify uncertainty. These works provide strong conceptual motivation for comparing models and utilizing hidden-state probes. However, rather than detecting hallucinations or requiring test-time queries to a second model, our approach uniquely trains a probe on offline strong-model disagreement to directly approximate the optimal cascade routing gain, evaluating it autonomously at test time. Allocating Test-Time Computation. Additional inference computation can significantly improve response quality by generating and selecting among multiple candidates. For example, self-consistency [46] aggregates sampled reasoning paths, while broader test-time compute strategies [43] scale sampling and refinement based on input difficulty. For routing specifically, BEST-Route [9] pre- determines a sampling budget combined with model selection, and ModelSwitch [3] evaluates consistency across multi-model samples to adaptively halt generation. Our work studies when to escalate after observing the weak model’s candidate responses. We characterize the expected improvement from replacing the selected weak response with a strong-model response and develop a 18

In sequential tasks, escalation decisions must be made repeatedly as the agent’s state evolves. TRIM [20] uses process-level feedback to decide when to replace a weak reasoning step with a strong-model step. R2V-Agent [17] learns step-level escalation from weak-policy episode outcomes by combining uncertainty statistics with task-specific verifier features trained via verifier-guided DPO. Alternatively, Inference-Time Distillation [41] determines escalation based on consistency among candidate actions to guide a weak agent. These methods typically rely on explicit step-level correctness labels, task-specific process verifiers, or expensive test-time consistency checks (which we benchmark via our multi-sample baselines). Our agentic experiments (Section 6.1) show that by learning from objective action disagreement, we can outperform consistency based alternatives and effectively route at the step level without ever requiring episode-success labels or step-correctness annotations. Thus, the selection policy should choose the weak response most likely to be correct. Learning this probability directly requires correctness labels. We compare several selection rules that do not require ground-truth supervision, together with a supervised correctness probe: • Majority vote. Group equivalent responses and select a response from the largest group. • Token entropy. Select the response with the lowest mean token entropy under the weak model. • Disagreement (ours). Select the response with the lowest predicted weak–strong disagree- ment, ϕ(hσ) ∈arg mini≤N bfd(h(p, yw,i)). This favors responses that the strong model is more likely to agree with. • Correctness probe. Select the response with the highest predicted probability of correctness. This probe uses ground-truth correctness labels during training and serves as a supervised comparison. Selection across routing scores. Figure 7 compares these selection policies on Math-500 with N = 8 weak responses per prompt. Each panel fixes the routing score and varies the selection policy and routing budget. Majority vote achieves the highest accuracy at every reported budget for all four routing scores. This is consistent with the effectiveness of grouping equivalent final answers in mathematical reasoning.

The proof has a simple structure. For a fixed number of weak samples, we condition on the sampled responses: the best weak response is the one with the largest correctness probability, and routing is optimal when the improvement offered by the strong model is large enough. To optimize sampling, we introduce prices for weak-model samples and strong-model queries. For each prompt, the optimal number of weak samples then maximizes its expected value net of the sampling price. For the sampling characterization, assume that at most K < ∞weak responses may be generated. Conditional on P = p, the weak responses are i.i.d. and independent of (Y, Ys). Recall qp(y) := Pr(Y = y | P = p), tp := Pr(Ys = Y | P = p). 26

text: Not X, but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic through Contextual Appropriateness Yihang Peng1∗Yi Jing1∗Dewen Liu2 Weihan Meng1 Ying Liu1† 1Tsinghua University 2Fudan University yingliu@tsinghua.edu.cn
title: Not X, but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic

text: Recurring expressions in model-written text are often treated as signatures of machine au- thorship, yet most of them serve legitimate functions. Whether such an expression is a tic depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. This judgment of appropri- ateness, central to communicative competence, remains largely unexamined for language mod- els. We study it through the Mandarin correc- tive construction bushi X, ershi Y (‘not X, but Y’). Drawing on Gricean pragmatics and cor- rective negation, we introduce a decision tree that classifies uses as substantive, optional, or defective by testing whether the context makes X a live alternative and whether rejecting X is informative. Five commercial models use the construction 2.5 to 9.2 times as densely as a human reference. Of 307 annotated uses, only 1.30% are defective while 52.8% are optional, that is, correct but unneeded, so models fall short in appropriateness far more often than in correctness. Several reward models favor the construction even over quality-matched vari- ants, an LLM judge favors it even where the context does not license it, and both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization tend to raise its frequency in open-weight models. We hope this work encourages the development of models attentive to the appropriateness of their expressions. 1
title: Not X, but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic

text: Large language models can now resolve real-world issues and complete multi-step tasks with tools (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024), and a growing share of the text people read is machine- generated. In Grice’s (1975) account of coopera- tive conversation, a contribution should be as in- formative as the exchange requires and no more, and it should be relevant to the purpose at hand. An entirely accurate response can still fall short ∗Equal contribution. †Corresponding author. Conformity to these maxims is therefore part of model quality alongside factual accuracy. Model-written text also contains expressions that recur often enough for readers to treat them as signatures of machine authorship (Juzek and Ward, 2025; Shaib et al., 2025). Most of these expres- sions are ordinary resources of the language, and human writers use the same devices where the dis- course calls for them. Whether a recurring expres- sion amounts to a tic thus depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. Hymes (1972) placed

Whether a recurring expres- sion amounts to a tic thus depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. Hymes (1972) placed this knowledge at the core of communica- tive competence, as a judgment of whether an ut- terance is appropriate to its context, separate from whether it is grammatically possible and from how often it is in fact produced. Research on language models, however, has mostly approached pragmatics from the listener’s side, testing whether models recover implicatures and presuppositions (Ruis et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Sravanthi et al., 2024), and recent com- 1 arXiv:2610.22249v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026

text: parisons show that competence in comprehen- sion does not transfer to appropriate production (Sieker and Zarrieß, 2026). When model produc- tion is studied, the usual measure is frequency, with words and phrases that are over-represented relative to human text treated as targets for suppres- sion (Juzek and Ward, 2025; Paech et al., 2025). Frequency answers the last of Hymes’s questions, how often an expression is in fact produced. For expressions with a legitimate function, it conflates appropriate and inappropriate uses, and suppres- sion removes both. Whether models command ap- propriateness itself remains to be examined. We examine this question through corrective negation, which denies one alternative and asserts another in its place. Its English form, it’s not X, it’s Y, is regularly cited as a hallmark of chatbot writing (Oremus, 2026), and Chinese online commentary singles out the Mandarin bushi X, ershi Y (‘not X, but Y’; 不是X，而是Y) in the same way, chiefly because the rejected X often appears to be a po- sition that no one has taken.1 Corrective negation is also the ordinary way to correct a misconcep- tion. Each use of the construction thus raises the two questions behind Grice’s maxims (Figure 1): whether the context made X a live alternative (rel- evance), and whether rejecting X contributes infor- mation not already established (quantity). Each use of the construction thus raises the two questions behind Grice’s maxims (Figure 1): whether the context made X a live alternative (rel- evance), and whether rejecting X contributes infor- mation not already established (quantity). We ask whether models, like competent speakers, know when the construction is called for. Linguistic theory makes these questions precise as conditions on licensing. As a construction, bushi X, ershi Y conventionally pairs its form with a corrective function (Goldberg, 2006; Shao and Wang, 2010; Zuo, 2025). The correction presup- poses alternatives that contrast along a shared di- mension (Rooth, 1992), and X need not have been asserted by anyone as long as it is accessible in the common ground (Toosarvandani, 2013; Stalnaker, 2002). What is rejected may be a proposition or the manner in which it is expressed, as in metalinguis- tic negation (Horn, 1985), and whether the correc- tion is informative depends on the question under discussion (Roberts, 2012). These accounts sepa- rate three cases that are formally identical: a cor- rection that resolves a live alternative, one that is well formed but unneeded, and one that is defective because it rejects something true or misattributes a view. 1For example, https://blog.darkthread.net/ blog/ai-slop-not-but-pattern/. We apply the tree to an- swers from five commercial models on Chinese prompts and compare their usage with a human reference. text: Our work draws on three lines of research. Studies of language models as speakers identify which ex- pressions models overproduce; linguistic accounts of corrective negation specify when the construc- tion is appropriate; and work on evaluator bias sug- gests where a preference for it may originate. 2.1 Language Models as Speakers Research on language models has examined their pragmatic competence and their characteristic out- put largely in isolation. Pragmatic evaluations have 2

text: mostly taken the listener’s side, testing whether models recover implicatures and presuppositions (Ruis et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2023; Sravanthi et al., 2024) or recognize constructional meaning (Weis- sweiler et al., 2022). The speaker’s side has a longer history in generation, where Gricean max- ims constrain referring expressions (Dale and Re- iter, 1995) and pragmatic speakers reason about a listener in reference games (Frank and Good- man, 2012; Andreas and Klein, 2016), though in tasks whose communicative goal is fixed in ad- vance. Studies of open-ended model writing in- stead focus on its characteristic expressions, in- cluding over-represented words (Juzek and Ward, 2025; Kobak et al., 2025), recurring syntactic tem- plates (Shaib et al., 2024), and broader measures of low-quality “slop” (Shaib et al., 2025), with sup- pression proposed as a remedy (Paech et al., 2025). These studies establish which expressions models produce too often, which is a matter of frequency. 2.2 Corrective Negation Corrective negation is well described in both En- glish and Mandarin, and these descriptions spec- ify when a speaker uses it appropriately. The con- struction denies one alternative and asserts another in its place. Work on English shows that it presup- poses alternatives contrasting along a shared di- mension and can target the form of an utterance as well as its content (Horn, 1985; Toosarvandani,

Work on English shows that it presup- poses alternatives contrasting along a shared di- mension and can target the form of an utterance as well as its content (Horn, 1985; Toosarvandani, 2013). Studies of bushi…ershi describe the same corrective function in Mandarin. Shao and Wang (2010) identify a pseudo-denial use, in which the negation does not retract any claim held in the con- text; Tan (2016) compares the construction with English not A but B and finds both semantic and metalinguistic correction in each; and Zuo (2025) analyzes ershi as the connective that lexicalizes correction, distinct from those for contrast and ad- versative relations. Checkpoint comparisons follow docu- mented parent–child relations; preference-data au- dits compare context-matched chosen/rejected an- swers and examine length, language composition, and repetition. 4 Experiments Our experiments address two questions: whether models use the construction where it is called for, and where their preference for it comes from. We answer the first by comparing model and human usage in frequency and function, and the second by examining evaluator preferences, training stages, and public preference data. 4.1 Frequency and Function Comparison. Models produce the con- struction far more often than people do, and many of these uses are correct but not called for. Eval- uators do not supply the missing judgment: sev- eral reward models prefer the construction after general-quality matching, and both judges prefer it within unlicensed uses. In the available check- points, its density also rises through SFT and DPO. Suppressing the form would remove its appropriate uses along with the rest; reducing tics of this kind requires evaluation and training signals that regis- ter whether an expression is called for. The diag- nostic is not specific to Mandarin: screening for defects and then testing contextual licensing and issue advancement can be applied to English it’s not X, it’s Y and to other expressions that are legit- imate in some contexts and overused in others. A controlled follow-up can test this attribution by holding SFT initialization, source composi- tion, update budget, and prompts fixed, interven- ing on construction-bearing preference pairs with matched edits, and repeating training across seeds. Measuring activation, repetition, and local func- tion would then separate changes in how often the construction is selected from changes in what it contributes. Limitations Data coverage. Our analysis covers five com- mercial models, a limited set of task domains, and 307 annotated uses. Broader models, domains, and human data would strengthen the estimates. Observational training evidence. The check- point and preference-data comparisons are obser- vational, so they show that frequency rises along 8

text: training pipelines but do not establish which stage or data causes the rise. Controlled retraining is needed to test this attribution. Reader perception. We assess appropriateness through linguistic criteria and do not measure how readers perceive the construction. Whether un- needed uses cause annoyance or affect comprehen- sion requires a separate user study. Languages and constructions. We study a sin- gle Mandarin construction. Although the decision tree is designed to transfer to English it’s not X, it’s Y and other recurring expressions, we have not ap- plied it beyond bushi X, ershi Y. Ethical Considerations This section discusses the ethical considerations and broader impact of this work. Potential Risks. The decision tree describes when a corrective construction is called for, and this description could be used to make model- written text resemble human writing more closely and thus harder to identify. Conversely, the fre- quency measures could be misread as evidence of machine authorship and applied to judge human writers, who also use the construction. Our anal- yses concern aggregate usage across models and corpora; they are not designed or validated for at- tributing individual texts to humans or machines. Intellectual Property. text: A Measurement and Annotation Human-reference sources. The human base- line draws on cMedQA2 for medical community question–answer pairs; HC3 for Chinese human answers on finance, law, psychology, and every- day topics; and COIG for Chinese-language ex- amination answers and explanations. The Chinese Essay Dataset supplies student essays in six gen- res, and CrossWOZ supplies travel-assistant dia- logues role-played by human participants. We also use worked solutions for the 2016–2018 manage- ment entrance examinations hosted by China Uni- versity of Petroleum (East China), solutions for the 2020 examination hosted by Shanghai Nor- mal University, and reference answers for the 2020 independent-admission mathematics examination hosted by the High School Aﬀiliated to Anhui Nor- mal University. Corpora and generation. The human reference contains 572,412 Han characters and 38 occur- rences across eight dimensions. The main compar- ison gives equal weight to the four dimensions rep- resented by these occurrences: professional abil- ity, general question answering, Chinese under- standing, and writing. Han exposure counts code points in U+4E00--U+9FFF. The four-dimension mean is .942 occurrences per 10,000 Han char- acters; pooling all eight human dimensions gives .664. Human materials allow comma-free and cross-sentence realizations, whereas the model de- tector requires a comma. Detection and frequency measures. The fixed detector finds non-overlapping literal matches, per- mits an optional preceding bing, requires a Chi- nese or ASCII comma before ershi, and limits the captured alternatives to 160 and 220 char- acters. Slots exclude sentence-final punctuation, semicolons, and newlines; intervening whitespace may span a newline. Nested starts and comma-free forms can be missed, and interrogative strings can produce spurious detections. For valid answer i, let ci count occurrences and ℓ(u) i count Han or all Unicode characters. Activa- tion and density are A = N−1 ∑ i 1[ci > 0], Iu = 104 ∑ i ci ∑ i ℓ(u) i .
