text: We presented a controlled proof of concept for topology-inspired fine-tuning in wind-field SR. Fine-tuning with the reconstruction loss alone worsens all three mean PD distances; adding gradient- magnitude and fixed-pair supervision reverses this, lowering them by 25–31% relative to the pretrained CNN and 32–35% relative to the matched control while retaining about half of the control’s PSNR gain. Merge-tree distance improves on average but much less consistently, and different PD distances can prefer different reconstructions, so topological quality is descriptor- and distance- dependent. Within this single-model, single-region setting, the loss study shows that gradient supervision mainly improves persistence agreement whereas fixed-pair supervision gives the most consistent joint PD and MT improvement, pointing toward hierarchy-aware and spatially aware supervision and evaluation as the next steps. text: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation Shuo Han∗1 and Ziqing Hu†2 1University of Illinois Chicago 2Perplexity AI October 15, 2026
title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation

text: Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training–inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level
title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation

text: forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized. 1
title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation

text: 1.1 Post-training of language models In post-training of language models, the goal is to make the language model generate a desired response for a given prompt. Denote by x ∈X the prompt and y ∈Y the response. The language model can be viewed as a policy π, where π(y | x) denotes the probability of generating y given the prompt x. The response y consists of a sequence of tokens {yt}t≥0, each of which is randomly generated based on past tokens and the prompt. The generation of one token is known as a decoding step. We use π both for the distribution over complete responses and, as in π(yt | x, y<t), for the ∗Email: hanshuo@uic.edu †Email: ziqing@perplexity.ai 1 arXiv:2610.22263v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026
title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation

text: conditional distribution of a single token given the prompt x and the history y<t ≜(y0, . . . , yt−1) when it is clear from the context. Thus, for any response y, it holds that π(y | x) = |y|−1 Y t=0 π(yt | x, y<t). The quality of y for a given x is measured by a reward function R: X × Y →R as R(x, y). Let D be the distribution of prompts. The goal is to find π that maximizes Ex∼D,y∼π(·|x) [R(x, y)] . (1) Throughout, we assume that generation terminates with probability one under every policy under consideration, so that |y| < ∞almost surely and the expectation in (1) is well defined. In practice, this assumption is enforced by imposing a maximum response length. 1.2 Token generation as a Markov decision process The token generation process can be modeled as an undiscounted indefinite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP). Let the state space S consist of sequences of tokens whose prefix is a valid prompt, and the action space A be the space of tokens. The idea is to use the state to store the prompt and all the tokens generated thus far, and to use the action to represent the next generated token: st ≜(x, y<t), at ≜yt. The initial state is chosen as s0 = x.

The initial state is chosen as s0 = x. At time t, the action at is determined by the policy as at ∼π(· | st). The transition dynamics are deterministic: st+1 = (x, y≤t) is the concatenation of st and at unless at = EOS, the end-of-sequence token. If at = EOS, the next state st+1 becomes an absorbing state associated with no reward. The original reward function R induces a token-level reward r: S × A →R. During token generation, if at = EOS, then r(st, at) = R(x, y≤t), where y≤t denotes the completed response including the terminal EOS token, so that |y| = t + 1; otherwise r(st, at) = 0. In other words, the reward is sparse and assigned only at the last decoding step. Under the MDP framework, the training objective in (1) can be equivalently rewritten as Ex∼D,y∼π(·|x) [R(x, y)] = Eπ s0∼D " ∞ X t=0 r(st, at) # . The training objective in (1) thus becomes a function of θ, defined by J(θ) ≜Ex∼D,y∼πθ(·|x) [R(x, y)] . (2) 2

text: 2 Importance Sampling in Policy Optimization The training objective in (2) involves an expectation over the prompt distribution D and the dis- tribution πθ(· | x) over possible responses. Because D is unknown and the space of responses is prohibitively large to enumerate, it is intractable to compute the expectation exactly. Instead, the expectation is typically replaced by a sample-average approximation using sampled token sequences. A naive application of sample-average approximation to (2) requires these samples to be drawn from πθ. However, modern post-training systems for reinforcement learning typically use separate engines with different design objectives. A training engine, built on PyTorch FSDP (Zhao et al., 2023) or Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019), supports efficient gradient computation and stable updates to θ, whereas an inference engine, e.g., vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024), prioritizes generation throughput. Their distinct numerical implementations can yield different token probabilities even with identical policy parameters. This discrepancy is referred to as training– inference mismatch (Liu et al., 2025a). For a given parameter θ, let πθ and ˆπ denote the policies implemented by the training and inference engines, respectively. When samples are drawn from a different policy, importance sampling is a common technique for obtaining an unbiased estimate. It works by weighting the samples using an importance sampling ratio. Common formulations
title: Importance Sampling in Policy Optimization

text: implemented by the training and inference engines, respectively. When samples are drawn from a different policy, importance sampling is a common technique for obtaining an unbiased estimate. It works by weighting the samples using an importance sampling ratio. Common formulations use two types of importance sampling ratios. One is sequence-level importance sampling, which uses πθ(y | x) ˆπ(y | x) = |y|−1 Y t=0 πθ(yt | x, y<t) ˆπ(yt | x, y<t) . The other is token-level importance sampling, which uses the individual ratios πθ(yt | x, y<t) ˆπ(yt | x, y<t) , t = 0, . . . , |y| −1 rather than their product as a whole. As shown below, the two types of importance sampling ratios lead to different estimators, which are unbiased for different quantities. While sampling a response y from πθ must be done sequentially, scoring πθ(y | x) when y is given can be parallelized. Only one forward pass is required to compute all the |y| quantities πθ(y0 | x), πθ(y1 | x, y0), . . . , and this is typically much faster than sampling. Both formulations require the inference engine to return the token probabilities ˆπ(yt | x, y<t) it used at decoding time. 2.1 Methods using sequence-level importance sampling 2.1.1 REINFORCE The REINFORCE algorithm (Williams, 1992) updates θ by performing gradient

The bias of the estimator will be discussed in Section 3.5. 2.3 Comparison between sequence-level and token-level importance sampling The results in Sections 2.1 and 2.2 show that the two importance sampling formulations yield unbiased gradient estimators for different objective functions: the sequence-level estimators target ∇J(θ), whereas the token-level estimators target ∇ˆJ(θ). This difference, together with the different numerical behavior of importance sampling ratios, accounts for the trade-offs discussed below. The importance sampling ratio accounts for the main drawback of sequence-level importance sampling. Because πθ(y | x)/ˆπ(y | x) is a product of |y| token-level ratios, even when the per- token discrepancy in the ratios is small, these discrepancies accumulate
title: Token-level GRPO

text: The importance sampling ratio accounts for the main drawback of sequence-level importance sampling. Because πθ(y | x)/ˆπ(y | x) is a product of |y| token-level ratios, even when the per- token discrepancy in the ratios is small, these discrepancies accumulate along the sequence. For long agentic traces, this accumulation can cause sequence-level ratios to span several orders of magnitude. As a result, computing the sequence-level ratio may lead to numerical instability. More importantly, the variance of the corresponding gradient estimator can become enormous. This is because the sample average may be dominated by a small number of samples with large importance sampling ratios, thus reducing the effective sample size of a batch (Kong, 1992; Liu, 2001). 7

This is, however, at the cost that the gradient estimator only corresponds to a surrogate ˆJ at the current inference policy. At step k of policy optimization, the policy improvement guarantee only ensures that the updated training policy πθk+1 is better than the current inference policy ˆπk, i.e., V0(πθk+1) > V0(ˆπk). Due to the training–inference mismatch, ˆπk generally differs from the current training policy πθk and can be worse, i.e., V0(ˆπk) < V0(πθk). Consequently, it may occur that V0(πθk+1) < V0(πθk), thus defeating the purpose of the policy update. One apparent remedy is to reduce the mismatch between ˆπk and πθk and consequently |V0(ˆπk) −V0(πθk)| by choosing how the two engines are implemented and how the parameters are synchronized. 3 Policy Gradient as a Covariance This section shows that both the policy gradient ∇J(θ) and the approximate policy gradient ∇ˆJ(θ) can be viewed as a covariance. This interpretation of the policy gradient yields two main results. First, when the importance sampling ratio is regularized, e.g., by truncation, masking, or clipping (as in Remark 3), the covariance form recovers invariance to constant shifts in the reward, a key property enjoyed by standard importance sampling. As discussed in Section 2.3, w is a product of |y| token-level ratios, and the resulting sample average can be dominated by a few rollouts. The standard method is to regularize the importance sampling ratio by replacing w with f(w) for some f : R+ →R+ satisfying f(1) = 1. Choosing the covariance between the reward and the weighted score as the estimand recovers this invariance, and the covariance reduces to the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. At the sequence level, the estimand is a single covariance by definition; at the token level, it is an expected sum of conditional covariances but can also be written as a single covariance (Proposition 14). Hence, the two classes of covariance estimators in Section 3.1 apply at both levels. The covariance perspective clarifies the roles of baselines and score centering. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the choice of the mean used for centering. The group-mean baseline uses the sample mean and yields the sample-mean estimator, which coincides with RLOO and, up to a multiplicative factor, with Dr. GRPO (Proposition 10). With a sample mean, centering the reward, centering the score, and centering both are all equivalent (Proposi- tion 5). Score centering uses the population mean instead and yields the known-mean estimator, which is unbiased for any constant baseline (Proposition 8) and is defined even for a single sample. The known-mean estimator has strictly smaller variance if and only if its baseline is sufficiently close to the variance-optimal baseline b⋆, and it can become arbitrarily worse as the baseline moves away from b⋆. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. At the sequence level, score centering is redundant once the group-mean baseline is used, regardless of whether the ratio is regularized (Proposition 11). Consequently, the population mean of the sequence-level weighted score, which is intractable to compute, is not needed. At the token level, while score centering is far more com- putationally tractable, it is no longer optional. Without score centering, the group-mean estimator is biased for the token-level estimand; its expectation contains an extra term (Proposition 15) that vanishes under standard importance sampling but is nonzero in general when the ratio is regularized. These results suggest the following practice. With sequence-level importance sampling, the group-mean baseline alone suffices, and score centering should be omitted. text: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables language models to improve text-to-image (T2I) generation by rewriting prompts for a frozen image generator. Existing methods typically apply a single signal derived from the image to individual subword tokens, although objects, counts, attributes, and relations form coherent semantic spans. We propose SCOPE, an objective based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that aligns update weighting with this structure. The rewriter jointly generates an enhanced prompt and its semantic partition. SCOPE pools shifts in policy log probabilities within each span to derive a shared coefficient for its token losses while retaining a single advantage for each completion. It requires neither separate span rewards nor additional image renders. Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE achieves average relative gains over vanilla GRPO of 9.48% on GenEval and 7.62% on T2I-CompBench. Ablation studies show that both semantic boundaries and pooling within spans contribute to these gains, supporting semantic structure as a practical inductive bias for prompt engineering with RL. text: Text-to-image (T2I) generation models [6, 8, 15, 16, 34, 36, 40–43, 54, 55, 60] turn language into visual content, with prompts serving as the primary interface for controlling generation. Small wording changes can determine whether an image preserves object counts, binds colors correctly, or places objects in the intended spatial relation. As diffusion and flow generators grow larger, retraining or lightly adapting the visual decoder is often expensive and risks image quality [1, 5, 7, 11, 12, 20, 26, 29, 30, 38, 39]. Prompt adaptation offers a cheaper alternative by improving the language interface while keeping the image generator fixed. Prompt optimization with a frozen generator can be formulated as a reinforcement learning problem. A language policy rewrites the input prompt, the T2I model renders an image, and an evaluator assigns a scalar reward based on the requested composition. Recent methods [15, 34, 55] exploit this feedback loop to improve T2I alignment while keeping the visual backbone fixed. GRPO converts rewards from grouped rewrites into an advantage for each completion without requiring a learned critic [28, 46]. The objective applies this advantage across token positions without accounting for semantic span boundaries. Compositional prompt edits to objects, attributes, counts, spatial relations, and scene context form coherent phrases that can span several subword tokens. To bridge this gap, we introduce Semantic Bounded Credit Optimization for Prompt Engineering (SCOPE), a GRPO-compatible objective that modulates token updates across semantic spans. The rewriter outputs a prompt rewrite and its semantic partition, mapped onto rollout tokens. SCOPE pools shifts in token log probabilities between the current and old policies within each span to derive a detached coefficient. This coefficient reweights the contribution of the shared advantage to each token loss in the clipped GRPO surrogate. The objective retains a loss for each valid token and a single advantage for each completion. SCOPE uses the existing rendering and reward pipeline, without separate rewards or advantages for individual spans, additional image renders, or a learned critic. Moreover, SCOPE serves as a strict generalization of standard GRPO, seamlessly recovering uniform token updates when span modulation is neutralized (β = 0). Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE consistently outperforms vanilla GRPO on GenEval [13] and T2I-CompBench [18]. Ablations favor pooling policy shifts within semantic spans over weighting individual tokens, and semantic boundaries over random boundaries or fixed windows. text: Credit Assignment for Sequence Generation. GRPO [46] optimizes autoregressive policies without a learned critic and shares an advantage across tokens in each completion. Recent work [9, 22, 25, 35, 37, 44, 48, 51] explores finer credit assignment through eligibility traces, counterfactual evaluation, and estimation over tree structures. Segment Policy Optimization (SPO) [14] partitions reasoning trajectories into segments and estimates distinct advantages for individual segments. This gives credit estimates a granularity between individual tokens and complete trajectories. FIPO [33] uses discounted future policy divergence to reweight token updates according to subsequent trajectory behavior. Our SCOPE retains a single advantage for each completion. Its contribution to token updates is modulated by shared within each semantic span, derived by pooling the policy log-probability shifts between the current and previous policies. Prompt Optimization for T2I Generation. Prompt optimization adapts the textual input to elicit desired outputs from a pretrained T2I generator. Prior work [8, 19, 21, 23, 24, 27, 34, 36, 42, 47, 56, 57] explores search and iterative refinement strategies for improving generation quality or consistency between text and images. Learned prompt adaptation trains language models to transform user inputs into prompts that the generator prefers. Promptist [15] combines supervised initialization with RL driven by image rewards. text: trains language models to transform user inputs into prompts that the generator prefers. Promptist [15] combines supervised initialization with RL driven by image rewards. PAG uses GFlowNets to promote effective and diverse prompt adaptation, while RePrompt uses GRPO and signals for image preference, alignment, and composition to train a rewriter augmented with reasoning [50, 55, 61]. Our SCOPE addresses the optimization objective within this setting. It incorporates the semantic structure of compositional edits into token weighting while retaining a shared advantage for the complete rewrite. Reinforcement Learning for T2I Generation. Reinforcement learning optimizes visual generators by treating image synthesis as a sequential decision process. Prior work [2, 49, 52] optimizes diffusion trajectories through policy gradients driven by image rewards or through preference optimization. Flow-GRPO [10, 28, 32, 45] optimizes denoising trajectories of flow models, while Mask-GRPO [31] treats iterative masked generation as a policy with multiple steps. B2-DiffuRL [17] addresses sparse reward credit assignment within diffusion trajectories through backward progressive training and sampling over branches. Our SCOPE optimizes the prompt rewriting policy through image feedback while keeping the renderer frozen. 3

text: SCOPE organizes policy updates around semantic spans. Given a prompt x, the autoregressive policy πθ generates a completion y with the rewrite and its span boundaries. The cleaning operator c(·) extracts the <answer> field, removes the | separators, and concatenates the span text. A frozen image generator renders I = fϕ(c(y)), which the evaluator scores against the cleaned prompt. We extract the semantic partition from the rewrite by splitting the answer field at | separators and aligning the spans to rollout tokens. Because the rewriter jointly learns structural formatting via rfmt, it achieves over 99.2% exact span-to-token alignment across all training rollouts (detailed in Appendix A.4). For the negligible fraction of unaligned rollouts (< 0.8%), defaulting the modulation weight to wg,i,s = 1 guarantees uninterrupted optimization stability. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate compositional prompt adherence on GenEval [13] and T2I-CompBench [18]. GenEval tests object presence, counting, color, position, and attribute binding. T2I-CompBench covers attribute binding, object relationships, and complex composition. GenEval training uses 10,000 of the 50,000 prompts organized by Flow-GRPO [28], while T2I-CompBench uses the 4200 prompts in its official training split. Both native benchmark evaluation sets are disjoint from the training data. Baselines. GRPO with uniform token weights is our primary baseline and shares SCOPE’s reward pipeline and training setup. Other baselines render original prompts directly or use the Z-Image rewriter [4] without further training. For SD3 and FLUX.1-dev, we use the published RePrompt scores. Appendix A.10 documents the reproduction and score sources. Implementation details. We train Qwen3-8B [59] as the prompt rewriter with frozen Qwen-Image [53], SD3 [11], and FLUX.1-dev [3] generators. We use a learning rate of 10−6, a KL coefficient of 0.01, and a maximum completion length of 512 tokens. Each group contains N = 8 prompt members, including the original prompt and sampled rewrites. All members share one rendering seed to control variation from image generation within the group. Appendix A.2 includes optimization configuration and span weight normalization. Evaluation protocol. Each backbone uses fixed resolution, denoising steps, and classifier-free guidance during training and evaluation (Appendix A.3). We average scores from four images per GenEval prompt and ten per T2I-CompBench prompt with distinct randomly selected seeds. Only training groups share seeds. 6

Across the three backbones, SCOPE achieves strict improvements over GRPO in 17 out of 18 category benchmarks while maintaining near-saturated color accuracy on Qwen-Image (0.93), trading a marginal 0.01 fluctuation for substantial gains in complex spatial positioning (+0.08) and attribute binding (+0.08). Moreover, the most pronounced improvements appear in object counting and spatial positioning, two persistent bottlenecks for frozen T2I generators. On SD3, SCOPE substantially outperforms GRPO in both Counting (0.58 →0.79, +36.2%) and Position (0.57 →0.83, +45.6%). On FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE lifts Counting by +0.11 and raises Position accuracy from the unadapted baseline of 0.16 and GRPO’s 0.62 to 0.84, representing a more than 5× gain over the base generator. These improvements also extend to multi-object synthesis and attribute binding, achieving 0.99 two-object accuracy and 0.88 attribute binding accuracy on Qwen-Image. T2I-CompBench. SCOPE exceeds GRPO in all six reported categories on each frozen backbone (Table 2). Average scores improve by 6.7%, 8.0%, and 8.2% on Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, respectively. With the original prompt, the frozen Qwen-Image places the cup beneath the couch, draws five handbags instead of four, and renders an ordinary orange. GRPO still misses the layout, the count (three handbags), and the color. The rewriter trained with SCOPE spells out each constraint explicitly: the vertical layout (“couch lower, cup upper”), one object per position (“four handbags in a neat row. . . each on a white pedestal”), and the counterfactual color. Because SCOPE credits complete semantic spans during training, the rewriter learns to keep each constraint as an intact phrase rather than scattering it across subword tokens. This lifts a frozen open-weight Qwen-Image to the level of the commercial gpt-image 2 on layout and counting. On counterfactual attributes, SCOPE goes further: it is only model that renders a white orange, while gpt-image 2 falls back to an orange-colored prior. 5

text: We present SCOPE, a semantic-aware credit optimization framework for RL-based prompt engineering with frozen text-to-image generators. By pooling policy log-probability shifts within coherent semantic spans to modulate a shared completion advantage, SCOPE resolves subword credit fragmentation while requiring no separate span rewards, additional image renders, or external parsers. Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE achieves substantial improvements over vanilla GRPO, delivering average relative gains of 9.48% on GenEval and 7.62% on T2I-CompBench. Accordingly, SCOPE establishes structure-aligned credit assignment as a plug-and-play paradigm for unlocking the compositional potential of frozen visual generators. 9

The rewrite and its boundaries are generated in one completion, with | appearing only between adjacent nonempty spans. The separator is not a generation stop token. Tokenizer character offsets align each extracted span with its rollout tokens, keeping the partition consistent with the policy loss. A valid partition requires a valid answer wrapper, nonempty spans, and full coverage of valid answer content tokens with consistent offsets and token counts. SCOPE uses uniform GRPO token weights for malformed wrappers, empty or missing spans, and consecutive or trailing separators. Truncation, incomplete coverage, alignment failures, and token count mismatches also trigger this fallback. We handle one benign end of sequence (EOS) mismatch separately. A.7 Environment variables and span weighting Reward services expose endpoints, timeouts, generation count (default 8), and reward and advantage weights. Span weighting reuses the current and old policy log probabilities from the clipped surrogate. Its sensitivity β is distinct from the KL coefficient βKL. A.8 Rewrite instruction The system message asks for exactly <answer>span 1 | span 2 | span 3</answer>. Before rendering and computation of image rewards, the trainer extracts the answer field, removes every delimiter, and concatenates the span text into one natural language prompt. The format reward still evaluates the structured output. A.9 Reward notes Advantages follow the hybrid rule in Eq. 3. During training, each group contains N = 8 prompt members that share one random diffusion seed. This controls renderer noise when comparing rewrites within each group. Groups draw seeds independently, and training and evaluation use fresh seeds across prompts and outer loops. Section 4.1 details the data splits and evaluation protocol. Seed sharing is restricted to training groups. The hybrid rule and shared seeds require no separate reward model or estimation module. A.10 RePrompt: Qwen-Image reproduction Wu et al. This set-level functional equals the squared batch volume; its repulsion is strongest when the batch is most collapsed and self-attenuates as diver- sity is achieved. text: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [12] has become the standard mechanism for steering text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models [11, 24, 27] toward high-fidelity, prompt-aligned images. Strong CFG, however, concentrates sampling toward the high-density peak of the conditional distribution, collapsing its effective sup- port onto a narrow region of the image manifold (Fig. 1). Under deterministic samplers such as DDIM [26], the initial noise fully determines the final image, yet independent noise draws collapse onto the same narrow visual mode. Multiple images generated from the same prompt converge to nearly identical visual pro- totypes. The collapse limits utility in applications that depend on distributional breadth, most critically synthetic data augmentation, where near-duplicate out- puts provide diminishing returns for downstream model training [9]. Recovering this diversity requires treating a batch as a whole, since diversity is a collective property of the set rather than a sum over its pairs. A batch can preserve every pairwise distance yet still collapse onto a low-dimensional sub- space, a higher-order failure mode to which independent pair contributions re- spond only weakly. Existing approaches meet this criterion only partially. Meth- ods that intervene during denoising repel intermediate latents [3, 14] or manip- ulate text embeddings [31], paying a per-step cost that scales with trajectory length. Contrastive Noise Optimization (CNO) [13] instead optimizes the initial noise with an InfoNCE loss in

text: 2.1 Recovering Mode Diversity in Diffusion Models. Prior methods recover the limited diversity of conditional diffusion models through repulsion, differing mainly in where they apply it but sharing a diversity signal that decomposes into a sum of pairwise interactions. One line intervenes during denoising: SPELL [14] adds sparse repellency terms to the reverse SDE, Particle Guidance (PG) [3] repels intermediate latents via a joint-particle potential, and DiversityPrompt [31] optimizes a token embedding online to steer generation toward low-density regions. All incur per-step overhead that scales with trajec- tory length. Contrastive Noise Optimization (CNO) [13] instead shifts repulsion to the initial noise, optimizing latents via InfoNCE in the Tweedie prediction space before sampling begins. Both, however, quantify diversity as a sum over sample pairs, so their repulsion never leaves the span of pairwise directions and responds only weakly to higher-order redundancy that collapses the batch onto a low-dimensional subspace. A separate line targets rare modes of the uncondi- tional or class-conditional distribution via classifier guidance [25, 29], self-guided sampling [30], or modified noise schedules [28]. Our goal instead is to recover sup- pressed modes of a text-conditional distribution under strong guidance for a fixed prompt. 2.2 Initial Noise Optimization in Diffusion Models. InitNO [8] steers noise toward valid regions via attention-based scores for bet- ter text adherence, while [2] learn a
title: K. Lee et al.

text: sup- pressed modes of a text-conditional distribution under strong guidance for a fixed prompt. 2.2 Initial Noise Optimization in Diffusion Models. InitNO [8] steers noise toward valid regions via attention-based scores for bet- ter text adherence, while [2] learn a mapping to optimal noise configurations to characterize CFG behavior. Neither addresses diversity. CNO [13] establishes that optimizing the initial noise alone can recover suppressed modes, using a pairwise contrastive objective. We inherit this noise-space pipeline from CNO; what changes is the structure of the diversity signal, from a sum over pairs to log-determinant maximization, a set-level functional equal to the squared RKHS volume that penalizes redundancy at every order. This objective is jointly opti- mized with an anchor-based fidelity term under a single hyperparameter λ. The log-determinant as a diversity criterion originates in GDPP [4], which regularizes a GAN’s generator with a DPP kernel. We instead apply it as an inference-time objective on the Tweedie predictions of a frozen diffusion model, requiring no training and no DPP sampling.

text: Beyond Pairwise Repulsion 5 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Tweedie’s Formula and Clean Data Estimation Diffusion models generate data by iteratively denoising a Gaussian noise sample zT ∼N(0, I) through a learned reverse process. At each timestep t, a noisy latent zt is related to the clean data z0 via the forward process zt = √¯αt z0+√1 −¯αt ϵ, where ϵ ∼N(0, I) and ¯αt := Qt i=1 αi is the cumulative noise schedule. A neural network ϵθ(zt, t, c) is trained to predict the noise ϵ given the noisy observation zt, timestep t, and text conditioning c. Tweedie’s formula [23] provides a closed-form estimate of the posterior mean E[z0 | zt], yielding a one-step prediction of the clean latent at any timestep: \hat {z }_ {0 |t } (z_t , t , c ) \c oloneq q \f r ac {1}{\sqrt {\bar {\alpha }_t}} \left ( z_t - \sqrt {1 - \bar {\alpha }_t} \, \epsilon _\theta (z_t, t, c) \right ). \label {eq:tweedie} (1) This estimate represents the model’s best prediction of the clean data given the current noisy observation. While the prediction becomes increasingly accurate as t →0, even at the initial timestep T it captures meaningful semantic structure of the final generation, such as global layout and dominant color [2]. Our method exploits this property by operating entirely

text: While the prediction becomes increasingly accurate as t →0, even at the initial timestep T it captures meaningful semantic structure of the final generation, such as global layout and dominant color [2]. Our method exploits this property by operating entirely in the Tweedie prediction space at t = T, optimizing the initial noises to diversify their corresponding clean data estimates before any denoising takes place. 3.2 Classifier-Free Guidance Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [12] enhances text-image alignment by interpo- lating between the conditional and unconditional noise predictions: \hat {\ ep s il o n }_\bet a (z _ t , t, c ) = (1 + \beta )\,\epsilon _\theta (z_t, t, c) - \beta \,\epsilon _\theta (z_t, t, \varnothing ), \label {eq:cfg} (2) where β > 0 is the guidance scale and ∅denotes the null condition. This approximately corresponds to sampling from a sharpened distribution pβ(z0 | c) ∝p(z0) p(c | z0)β, which concentrates probability mass around the domi- nant modes of the conditional distribution. (d) DetNO achieves full coverage of all 16 modes across both rings, faithfully preserving the original mode structure. 5 Experiments Implementation Details. We evaluate on three pre-trained T2I backbones: SD1.5 [24], SDXL [22], and SD3 [5]. SD1.5 and SDXL use DDIM [26] with 50 steps, while SD3 uses the Euler sampler with 28 steps following its default configuration. We compare against PG [3], SPELL [14], DiversityPrompt [31], and CNO [13]. We evaluate all methods under identical conditions (prompt set, random seeds, CFG scale, and hardware) to ensure fair relative comparison; absolute values may dif- fer from original papers accordingly. We use the official implementations of all baselines, including CNO, with the hyperparameters reported in their original papers. Following [13, 31], we sample 2,000 prompts from the MS-COCO [18] validation set and generate 5 images per prompt for SD1.5 and SD3,

text: use the official implementations of all baselines, including CNO, with the hyperparameters reported in their original papers. Following [13, 31], we sample 2,000 prompts from the MS-COCO [18] validation set and generate 5 images per prompt for SD1.5 and SD3, and 3 images per prompt for SDXL. Evaluation Metrics. For image quality, we report Precision [17], Density [19], CLIPScore [10], PickScore [15], and ImageReward [33]. For diversity, we report Recall [17], Coverage [19], Vendi Score [6], and Mean Self-Similarity (MSS) [13]. Among these, VendiScore and MSS serve as our primary diversity metrics, as they measure intra-batch coverage directly without reference to an external dis- tribution. They are therefore better suited to evaluating diversity-enhancing methods than reference-dependent metrics such as Recall and Coverage [20]. 5.1 Results Toy Example: 2D Ring Mixture. text: We presented DetNO, an initial-noise optimization framework that maximizes the RKHS volume among Tweedie predictions via a log-determinant diversity term and an anchor-based fidelity term. Experiments on SD1.5, SDXL, and SD3 confirm consistent diversity gains across backbones and samplers, with Pareto analysis showing that λ enables smooth interpolation between the two objectives. A toy experiment and a spectral analysis (Proposition 1) trace this advantage to its mechanism: repulsion that intensifies where the batch is most collapsed and relaxes once diversity is restored. In downstream few-shot classification, the broader mode coverage translates into statistically significant accuracy gains in the low-data regime. Treating diversity as a property of the whole batch, rather than of its pairs, thus produces image sets that are not only more varied but measurably more useful.

text: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning Adhwaa Al-Chaab†, Ayman Younis, Dario Pompili† †Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Rutgers University–New Brunswick, NJ, USA E-mails: {adhwaa.alchaab, a.younis, pompili}@rutgers.edu Abstract—The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control. While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized opti- mization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability. We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures. X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient train- ing, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and inter- pretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near- RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement. To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmark- ing Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics. We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments. X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance. Index Terms—O-RAN, Agentic AI, Reinforcement Learning, Behavior Cloning, Resource Allocation.
title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller

text: The O-RAN ALLIANCE enables flexible, multi-vendor RAN ecosystems through open interfaces and programmable control [1]. Central to this architecture, the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) provides near-real-time closed-loop optimiza- tion for diverse service types, including eMBB, URLLC, mMTC, and ISAC [2]. The O-RAN paradigm integrates AI directly into the control loop, requiring autonomous adapta- tion, real-time responsiveness, and intelligent decision-making under uncertainty [3]. However, realizing this AI-native vi- sion faces several fundamental challenges [4], [5], including: (i) real-time responsiveness, requiring decisions within strict latency bounds (sub-1s for Near-RT RIC) while adapting to dynamic conditions; (ii) self-optimization under uncertainty, as static policies cannot scale across heterogeneous network conditions; and (iii) explainability and trust, since AI-driven decisions must exhibit transparent behavior to satisfy oper- ational and regulatory mandates. Traditional rule-based and supervised learning methods struggle with dynamic network- ing environments, while Reinforcement Learning (RL), despite offering promise through sequential decision-making, suffers from fundamental limitations: (i) poor sample efficiency, re- quiring millions of interactions infeasible in live networks; (ii) limited generalization under unseen traffic patterns; and (iii) lack of interpretability, problematic for safety-critical operations [6]. To address these limitations, this paper introduces X-RIC, a novel RIC framework integrating explainable agentic in- telligence for AI-native RAN control. Unlike conventional RL approaches relying solely on reactive policies, X-RIC employs a hybrid architecture combining fast reactive learning

text: [6]. To address these limitations, this paper introduces X-RIC, a novel RIC framework integrating explainable agentic in- telligence for AI-native RAN control. Unlike conventional RL approaches relying solely on reactive policies, X-RIC employs a hybrid architecture combining fast reactive learning with strategic reasoning. Built on agentic AI principles— augmenting learning systems with reasoning, temporal mem- ory, and task-level understanding [7]—X-RIC enables contex- tual abstraction, reflective learning, and decision traceability. The X-RIC architecture comprises three components: (i) au- tomated demonstration harvesting that initializes RL poli- cies through Behavior Cloning (BC) [8] using trajectories from a fine-tuned reasoning model, improving sample effi- ciency without manual supervision; (ii) a transformer-based reasoning module providing strategic oversight and natural language explanations; and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation enabling joint optimization while maintaining transparency. To further address sample inefficiency, X-RIC employs a dual-filtered harvesting pipeline: episode-level policy-impact selection identifies valuable trajectories, while critic-guided pruning filters suboptimal actions. Related Work. We review here the O-RAN architecture and how RL has been used within O-RAN, followed by online learning and LLM-based approaches. O-RAN Architectures: Recent O-RAN developments demonstrate AI integration potential [9]. EdgeRIC [10] enables TTI-level decision-making through near-RT applications interfacing with RAN infrastructure. To enhance granular control, [11] embeds Central Units (CUs) and Distributed Units (DUs) within the real-time RIC as dedicated zApps for MAC scheduling and beam shaping.

BC Approaches: Behavioral Cloning (BC) has emerged as a promising alternative to address RL’s sample efficiency by learning from expert demonstrations [8], with applications in automated driving [23] and UAV detection [24]. However, ex- isting BC approaches require extensive manual demonstrations that are hard to collect at scale and lack reasoning integration. Our Approach. text: of our knowledge, our work is the first to integrate automated BC within the O-RAN architecture for agentic RAN control. Our Contributions. The contributions of this paper are as follows: i) We design a novel eXplainable RAN intelligent controller, X-RIC, that integrates agentic AI with RL in a hybrid control architecture to enable sub-second decision- making based on natural-language intents. ii) We introduce a domain-specific evaluation framework, BARX, for assessing the suitability of agentic reasoning models in closed-loop telecom control. iii) We propose a dual-filtering BC mecha- nism with automated demonstration harvesting, using episode- level policy-impact gating and action-level critic validation to improve sample efficiency while ensuring deployment-grade reliability. iv) As a case study, we formulate a network slicing resource allocation problem minimizing operational cost while meeting SLA requirements, achieving 89% cost reduction versus baselines under Near-RT RIC timing constraints. text: II. X-RIC FRAMEWORK DESIGN We present the X-RIC framework integrating agentic reasoning into Near-RT RIC operations, introduce BARX for agentic RAN benchmarking, and describe dual-filtering demonstration collection for sample-efficient BC training. A. TLM Module and Benchmarking Our X-RIC framework, shown in Fig. 1(a), is integrated within the O-RAN near-RT RIC; see [25] for an architectural overview. To avoid the computational overhead of full LLM fine-tuning, X-RIC uses a Telecom Language Model (TLM) architecture that augments a frozen pre-trained LLM with: (i) domain-specific prompts encoding O-RAN operational knowledge, and (ii) a trainable RAN-state encoder that maps structured telemetry, including KPIs, slice states, and resource metrics, into 256-dimensional embeddings. The encoder is trained via contrastive alignment on state-text pairs to project RAN observations into the LLM representation space, en- abling RAN-aware reasoning without full model fine-tuning. Integrating agentic reasoning modules into O-RAN work- flows introduces system-level challenges due to the mismatch between probabilistic language model outputs and determin- istic telecom control requirements. Four critical challenges emerge: (i) Missed scheduling deadlines when TLM inference time exceeds the 10 ms to 1s latency budget for Near-RT RIC operations [25], (ii) Malformed control messages due to syntactically invalid JSON/YAML configurations, (iii) Non- deterministic behavior when identical network states produce different TLM outputs due to sampling randomness, and (iv) Unintended SLA degradation when semantically plausi- ble

text: for Near-RT RIC operations [25], (ii) Malformed control messages due to syntactically invalid JSON/YAML configurations, (iii) Non- deterministic behavior when identical network states produce different TLM outputs due to sampling randomness, and (iv) Unintended SLA degradation when semantically plausi- ble but operationally suboptimal TLM decisions reduce net- work performance. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel domain-specific framework, Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning (BARX), based on O-RAN specifications. Unlike standard NLP benchmarks [26], which emphasize linguistic fluency and semantic understanding, BARX evaluates agentic reasoning modules in closed-loop control settings. It assesses

text: TLM candidates across four dimensions: latency, compliance, determinism, and policy impact. For a given network state s, the TLM is queried N times under fixed sampling parameters, temperature T ∈[0, 1] and nucleus probability p ∈[0, 1], yielding structured responses E = {en}N n=1. i) Latency is measured by the end-to-end response time ℓn, from which we report the mean µℓ, standard deviation σℓ, and empirical 95th percentile ℓ95. Responses with ℓn > 600 ms violate the sub-second budget of Near-RT RIC control loops. ii) Compliance is enforced by validating each reply against a strict Draft-7 JSON schema. The schema error rate E is the fraction of invalid outputs; if E > 0, BARX assigns a suitability score of 0. iii) Determinism is quantified by pairwise comparison of valid responses, with consistency score C defined as the proportion of identical reply pairs. Scores C < 1 indicate non-deterministic behavior due to sampling noise or soft hallucinations. iv) Policy impact is assessed by parsing valid replies into control directives executed under a TLM-guided Near-RT RIC policy. The average episodic reward under TLM guidance, ¯RTLM, is compared with the RL-only baseline reward ¯RRL. The differ- ence ∆¯R quantifies the functional impact of agentic reasoning in the control loop. BARX aggregates (µℓ, σℓ, ℓ95, E, C, ∆¯R) into a normalized score [0, 100],

X-RIC Agent System Architecture Our X-RIC framework in Fig. 1(a) employs two coordinated agents with critic-guided selection for autonomous slice man- agement. Coordination Architecture. The architecture con- sists of: (1) the Monitoring Agent, implemented as the TLM (based on LLaMA3-8B with LangChain tools), which contin- uously observes network performance using a two-tier tem- poral strategy: 1 s polling frequency for real-time monitoring from the Kinetica time-series database and 10 s aggregation windows for statistical smoothing. This design implements the periodic intervention strategy validated as optimal in Sec- tion IV-B. The TLM monitors network state continuously and generates supervisory resource allocation recommendations aTLM every 10 s.(2) The Control Agent, implemented as a BC- trained actor-critic policy πθπ with critic network QθQ, serves as the primary low-latency controller (< 10 ms) for resource allocation. Action Selection and Demonstration Harvesting. At each 10 s decision epoch, both agents observe the same network state sk: the Control Agent proposes aRL = πθ(sk) while the TLM proposes aTLM. The critic evaluates both candidates and executes the TLM recommendation when ∆Rk = Qϕ(sk, aTLM) −Qϕ(sk, aRL) > 0; otherwise, the RL action proceeds autonomously as the primary real-time controller. A dual-filter agentic BC layer, detailed in Sect. II-C, generates high-quality demonstrations from positive TLM in- teractions, storing only critic-validated state-action pairs in the demonstration buffer Dfil for behavioral cloning updates. Policy updates flow back to the RL agent with minimal overhead (median TLM latency: 465.6 ms vs. sub-10 ms RL latency), forming a closed-loop learning system. C. Automated Demonstration Collection for BC Demonstration-augmented RL has shown promise in im- proving sample efficiency, particularly in complex decision- making tasks [28]. However, it still faces key limitations: expert demonstrations are often collected through manual teleoperation, or scripted policies. Although helpful in learning complex behaviors, the acquisition of high-quality demonstra- tions is often costly and impractical to scale [29], [30]. To address

text: However, it still faces key limitations: expert demonstrations are often collected through manual teleoperation, or scripted policies. Although helpful in learning complex behaviors, the acquisition of high-quality demonstra- tions is often costly and impractical to scale [29], [30]. To address these limitations, we propose automated demonstra- tion harvesting using a TLM with episode-level policy-impact gating ∆¯Rk and critic-validated action pruning. Our approach integrates BC as imitation learning to enable agents to mimic high-quality TLM-guided behaviors, accelerating learning by bootstrapping policies with expert-like actions. Episodes with positive ∆¯Rk values indicate improved performance from the use of agentic reasoning in the control loop, qualifying them as candidates for demonstration collection. However, these demonstrations may still contain suboptimal actions due to partial observability or ambiguous instruction mappings. Blindly cloning all actions from episodes with positive ∆¯Rk values could reinforce suboptimal behaviors and lead to performance degradation. To address this, we propose a dual-filtering mechanism that automates demonstration collection and retains only the most informative state–action pairs for training. The first filter operates at the episode level using a policy-impact metric, while the second operates at the action level using a critic- guided Q-filter. This design addresses two critical challenges in demonstration-augmented RL; (i) reducing the cost of demon- stration collection by leveraging TLM-generated trajectories, and (ii) improving demonstration quality through critic-guided filtering of suboptimal actions.

text: Integration. The RAN encoder transforms network states sk into textual representa- tions Ωk for TLM-based reasoning over resource allocation. The TLM processes structured prompts containing: (i) the optimization objective, (ii) the current network observation, including per-slice PRB usage, buffered packets, and traffic criticality indicators, and (iii) an action-to-slice mapping over candidate decisions. It then evaluates the RL agent’s pro- posed action and returns a structured JSON response with a reasonability judgment, explanation, and corrected action when needed. Fig. 6 illustrates this process for an emergency URLLC traffic burst, where the TLM detects that allocating PRBs to eMBB and mMTC is suboptimal under high URLLC congestion and overrides it with a latency-aware allocation. The resulting decisions are filtered through the dual-filtering BC mechanism and integrated into training. Step 5: Continuous Learning Loop. The system operates in a closed-loop manner where: (i) X-RIC generates expert demonstrations based on current network conditions, (ii) dual- filtering selects high-quality demonstrations, (iii) BC loss guides policy learning from filtered demonstrations, (iv) RL continues exploration and optimization, and (v) performance feedback updates the X-RIC guidance process. This integrated approach utilizes the sample efficiency of BC while maintain- ing the exploration capabilities of reinforcement learning. IV. Ablation of TLM Intervention Schedules To address the question when should the agentic reasoning agent intervene and correct the RL policy?, we conducted an ablation study evaluating six distinct correction strategies. The experimental methodology compared baseline RL per- formance against six TLM schemes, each tuned for fairness and consistency. The strategies included: Constant Correction, where the TLM continuously overrides RL decisions; Periodic Correction, which applies guidance at fixed intervals (every 10 steps) with a sparse, consistent intervention rate (correction probability ≈0.1); Step-Based Correction, which intervenes only during the initial 1000 steps before transitioning to full autonomy; Linear Decay, which reduces the correction proba- bility linearly from 1.0 to 0.0 over 3000 steps; Exponential De- cay, applying a decay rate of 0.95 every 100 steps; and Factor- Based Correction, which maintains a constant intervention probability of λ = 0.5. Following the objective in Section III, the operator intent is: “Minimize total operating cost while maintaining SLA-defined QoS re- quirements: the URLLC slice must satisfy strict latency and reliability constraints; the eMBB slice must meet throughput targets, with resource allocation prioritizing URLLC during congestion.” X-RIC autonomously translates this intent into concrete controls: PRB allocations, compute workload distri- bution, and per-slice throughput guarantees. Initially, the network operates under balanced resource allocation with equal PRB distribution (50:50 ratio). To create realistic congestion scenarios, we use iperf3 in UDP mode to enable controlled congestion testing. Unlike TCP’s automatic throttling, UDP transmits at configured bitrates regardless of capacity, allowing traffic demands to exceed available bandwidth and exposing packet loss for QoS evaluation. text: This paper introduced X-RIC, a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures to address current RL limitations. The proposed framework features several pro- gressive TLM implementation schemes and a hybrid con- trol architecture for sub-second O-RAN decision-making. We introduced BARX, a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic RAN control across latency, compliance, determinism, and policy impact metrics, and developed au- tomated demonstration collection using dual-filtering behav- ioral cloning to improve sample efficiency while maintaining production-grade reliability. As a case study, we applied our proposed X-RIC framework to a three network slice system, which involves dynamic configuration and poses significant challenges for traditional RL methods to solve within the near- real-time RIC timescale. Validation on SLA-aware network slicing demonstrates that X-RIC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

text: Unsupervised Clustering of Public Transport Vehicles Using Deep Morphological Features and Color Histograms Juan Irving Vasquez Centro de Innovaci´on y Desarrollo Tecnol´ogico en C´omputo Instituto Polit´ecnico Nacional Mexico City, Mexico jvasquezg@ipn.mx Abstract—Surveillance cameras along urban roads produce large volumes of unlabeled video that could support the mon- itoring of public transport, but grouping the observed vehicles into meaningful categories without manual annotation remains challenging, since buses from different routes often share the same body structure and differ mainly in their color schemes. This study presents an unsupervised clustering methodology for public transport vehicles that combines morphological features extracted with a frozen DINOv2 Vision Transformer and hand- crafted HSV color histograms through weighted early fusion, followed by UMAP projection and K-Means clustering. The method was evaluated on 7,972 bus images extracted from about 1,460 hours of video of an arterial road in Mexico City, with the goal of isolating the buses of the city’s public bus network (RTP) without supervision. With a fusion of 65% morphological and 35% color features, the pipeline produced 14 clusters that separate distinct routes and vehicle types, and it increased the precision of the target cluster with respect to morphological features alone. These results show that color complements self-supervised features for route-level clustering, provided that it does not dominate the representation. The dataset is available under

text: Public transport is the backbone of mobility in large cities, and its efficient management requires continuous information about which vehicles operate on each corridor, how often they pass, and whether they follow their assigned routes. Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) increasingly obtain this infor- mation from the surveillance cameras already installed along urban roads. These cameras generate thousands of hours of video, far more than can be inspected or annotated manually, so methods that extract useful information from such footage without human supervision are of great practical value. In this work, we address the problem of grouping public transport vehicles captured by a fixed surveillance camera into semantically meaningful categories, such as transit routes and operators, without using labeled data. The problem is challeng- ing for two complementary reasons. First, buses operating on different routes often share the same body structure and differ mainly in their paint schemes. Second, vehicles of different types, such as full-size buses, microbuses (small buses), and vans, may share similar colors while differing substantially in shape. A useful representation must therefore capture both morphology and color. Most vision-based vehicle classification systems are super- vised and rely on large, site-specific annotated datasets with fixed taxonomies in which “bus” is a single class [1]–[3]. text: Most vision-based vehicle classification systems are super- vised and rely on large, site-specific annotated datasets with fixed taxonomies in which “bus” is a single class [1]–[3]. Self- supervised learning has reduced the need for labels during representation learning [4], but in the vehicle domain it has mainly been used as pre-training for a supervised classifier [5]. Unsupervised clustering, on the other hand, has been applied mainly to vehicle re-identification, which groups images of the same physical vehicle rather than different vehicles that share a category [6]. Self-supervised Vision Transformers such as DINOv2 [7] now provide general-purpose descriptors that capture image structure well without fine-tuning. However, their features may under-represent pure chromatic information, which is crucial for distinguishing transit routes. To address this problem, we propose a hybrid unsupervised clustering pipeline for public transport vehicles. Buses are first detected and tracked in the video, and a single crop is stored per vehicle. Each crop is then described by two complementary descriptors: a morphological descriptor given by the class token of a frozen DINOv2 model, and a color descriptor given by hue and saturation histograms computed in the HSV color space. Both descriptors are normalized and combined through weighted early fusion, and the fused vectors are projected with UMAP and grouped with K-Means, as illustrated in Fig. 1. We apply the pipeline

text: Vision-based vehicle classification has evolved from hand- crafted descriptors, such as Haar-like features and histograms of oriented gradients (HOG), combined with shallow classi- fiers such as support vector machines and AdaBoost, to con- volutional neural networks trained end-to-end [1]. Supervised deep models now reach high accuracy. Butt et al. [2] fine- tuned several CNNs on 10,000 images of six vehicle types captured under adverse illumination and reported 99.68% accuracy, and Neupane et al. [3] fine-tuned YOLO detectors on nearly 30,000 manually annotated samples of seven classes, including buses. The latter study also shows the cost of domain shift: accuracy roughly doubled (from at most 30% to 71%) only after fine-tuning on data from the target cameras. These systems therefore depend on large, site-specific annotated datasets and on fixed taxonomies in which “bus” is a single class, so they cannot distinguish buses of different routes or operators. Self-supervised learning (SSL) reduces this dependence by learning representations from unlabeled images [4]. In the vehicle domain, Ma and Yang [5] showed that Vision Trans- former features learned with DINO and data2vec, combined with wheel-position cues, reach 97.2% top-1 accuracy on the 13 axle-based classes of the U.S. Federal Highway Adminis- tration. However, SSL is used there only as pre-training for a supervised classifier, and buses again form a single class. Deep clustering removes

However, SSL is used there only as pre-training for a supervised classifier, and buses again form a single class. Deep clustering removes labels altogether by coupling a representation-learning module with a clustering module [8]. Zhou et al. [8] group these methods into multistage, gen- erative, iterative, and simultaneous approaches; our pipeline belongs to the multistage family, in which features are ex- tracted first and clustered afterwards. Hou et al. [9] note that, before deep learning, image clustering relied on hand-crafted descriptors such as color histograms, and identify robustness to noise and real-world applicability as open challenges for deep image clustering. In the vehicle domain, clustering has mainly been used for unsupervised re-identification (Re-ID). Qiu et al. Re-ID, however, groups images of the same physical vehicle, whereas our goal is to group different vehicles that share a semantic category. In summary, existing work either classifies vehicles into coarse, predefined types [2], [3], [5] or matches individual vehicles across cameras [6]. Dataset The dataset was constructed from approximately 1,460 hours of continuous video recorded during June and July 2026. Recordings were acquired with a single fixed camera mounted at a height of 5 m and positioned 30 m from Circuito Interior, one of the main arterial roads of Mexico City. The camera was oriented toward the roadway, providing a consistent view of passing traffic, including public transport buses operating on multiple routes. 1) Bus Detection: Given the large volume of recorded video, manual annotation of the full videos was impractical. The videos were therefore preprocessed using the YOLO26 object detector [10] combined with a multi-object tracker. Only detections belonging to the bus class were retained, and a single image was stored for each tracked vehicle to avoid redundant samples of the same bus. To prevent truncation of the vehicle body, each bounding box was expanded by 10% before cropping. This process yielded a total of 7,972 cropped images of public transport vehicles. Fig. 2 shows examples of the resulting images. 2) Ground-Truth Annotation: Although the proposed clus- tering approach is fully unsupervised, ground-truth labels were required to evaluate its performance. To this end, all 7,972 images were manually annotated. These labels were used exclusively for evaluation and were not involved at any stage of feature extraction or clustering. Two hierarchical binary labels were assigned to each image: is bus and is RTP bus, where the latter is a subset of the former. The is bus label indicates whether the crop contains a full-size bus and was introduced to assess the precision of the YOLO26- based preprocessing stage, given that smaller vehicles such as microbuses and vans were also detected under the bus class. The is RTP bus label identifies vehicles belonging to the Red de Transporte de Pasajeros (RTP), Mexico City’s public bus network, which constitute the target class of this study. B. Bus Clustering The objective of this stage is to group the detected vehi- cles into clusters that correspond to semantically meaningful categories, such as bus routes and vehicle types, without relying on labeled data. The proposed pipeline consists of three steps: (i) extraction of complementary morphological and color descriptors from each image, (ii) early fusion of both descriptors into a single weighted feature vector, and (iii) unsupervised clustering of the fused representations. The following subsections describe each step in detail. 1) Feature Extraction: Buses operating on different routes often share similar body structures but differ in their paint schemes, whereas vehicles of different types (e.g., full-size buses, microbuses, and vans) may exhibit similar colors while differing substantially in shape. To capture both sources of variation, two complementary types of features were extracted from each image: deep morphological features and handcrafted color features. Morphological features: These features were extracted us- ing DINOv2 [7], a family of Vision Transformer (ViT) [11] models trained through self-supervised learning. Unlike text- guided approaches such as CLIP [12], which depend on paired image and caption data, DINOv2 learns visual representations from images alone. Its training objective combines an image- level self-distillation loss, computed on the class token be- tween a student and

text: guided approaches such as CLIP [12], which depend on paired image and caption data, DINOv2 learns visual representations from images alone. Its training objective combines an image- level self-distillation loss, computed on the class token be- tween a student and a teacher network observing different crops of the same image, with a patch-level masked image modeling loss inherited from iBOT [13]. A key property of DINOv2 is that its features perform well as frozen, general-purpose descriptors, without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Its authors report strong results with simple linear classifiers and nearest-neighbor retrieval across a wide range of benchmarks, including fine-grained vehicle recognition on Stanford Cars [7]. These properties make DINOv2 well suited to an unsupervised setting such as ours, in which no labeled data are available for fine-tuning and the cluster structure depends directly on the geometry of the embedding space. In this work, we employed the publicly available facebook/dinov2-small checkpoint, which corresponds to the ViT-S/14 variant of DINOv2 distilled from the ViT-g/14 teacher. Its main architectural characteristics are summarized in Table I. The model became largely insensitive to structural differences, grouping morphologically distinct vehicles, such as vans and full-size buses, into the same cluster simply because they shared dominant colors. Overall, these results confirm that color is a highly discrim- inative cue for identifying public transport routes, but that it must complement, rather than dominate, the morphological representation. V. CONCLUSIONS This study presented an unsupervised pipeline for clustering public transport vehicles captured by a surveillance camera, in which frozen DINOv2 morphological features and HSV color histograms are combined through weighted early fusion and grouped with UMAP and K-Means. Without using any labels during feature extraction or clustering, the best configuration isolated RTP buses in a cluster with higher precision and F1- score than morphological features alone. These results confirm that color provides information that self-supervised features alone do not capture well, since it separates buses that share a body structure but belong to different routes. The

text: with higher precision and F1- score than morphological features alone. These results confirm that color provides information that self-supervised features alone do not capture well, since it separates buses that share a body structure but belong to different routes. The ablation study also showed that the fusion weight is crit- ical. A balanced weight fragmented the target class into many small clusters, whereas a color-dominant weight collapsed the space into three clusters that mixed vans, microbuses, and full- size buses. Color should therefore complement, not replace, the morphological representation. The approach has limitations. Some RTP buses were still assigned to secondary clusters and the number of clusters was selected with internal criteria that do not guarantee semantic correspondence. Future work will explore late fusion based on descriptor-specific distances combined with density-based algorithms such as HDBSCAN, which do not require the number of clusters to be fixed in advance. Evaluation on multiple cameras and routes will also be necessary to assess the generality of the method.

text: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries Anikait Singh1,3, Teresa Zhang1,3, Yoonho Lee1,3, Roshen Sanjay Nair1, Aviral Kumar2 and Chelsea Finn1 1Stanford University, 2Carnegie Mellon University, 3Equal Contribution Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs

text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly tasked with reasoning over extensive corpora of documents, often found in domains such enterprise knowledge bases, complex software repositories, and user chat histories, that exceed the context windows of today’s LLMs. In these domains, the information required to complete a given task is rarely centralized; instead, it is dispersed and disconnected across many disparate sources. Thus, for each incoming request, agents repeatedly process and revisit the corpus from scratch. Can we instead enable systems to efficiently navigate these massive context spaces without incurring high, redundant computational costs each time a user poses a new query? A standard approach to this challenge is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Gao et al., 2023), in which a system responds to a query by searching raw documents, retrieving relevant passages, and syn- thesizing an answer. Recent work has strengthened this pipeline with multi-agent frameworks (Jiang et al., 2023; Asai et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2024; Edge et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2025). However, these methods remain largely reactive: each query triggers a new round of search, requiring the model to repeatedly rediscover useful cross-document relationships at inference time. Other approaches pre-structure the search space before inference, for example, as a knowledge graph (Peng et al., 2025). These methods can improve retrieval, but they typically commit to a rigid
title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context

text: model to repeatedly rediscover useful cross-document relationships at inference time. Other approaches pre-structure the search space before inference, for example, as a knowledge graph (Peng et al., 2025). These methods can improve retrieval, but they typically commit to a rigid set of abstractions such as extracting named entites (Keraghel et al., 2024). Such a structure is useful when future queries precisely align with the index, but it is less natural when queries require new task-specific intermediate artifacts. A common underlying theme of these approaches is that they impose an inductive bias of structure, which a downstream agent can utilize when answering a given query. We ask can we learn to anticipate this structure for a new set of context that we encounter, curating these documents in a form that that an answering agents can readily use. We propose to directly train an agent to reorganize a corpus into an anticipatory answer-facing workspace so that future LLM agents can efficiently find the right evidence for a query? Motivated by approaches that shift computation across different aspects of the model training and deployment process (Lin et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Suzgun et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a), we study anticipatory workspace construction: the problem of augmenting and reorganizing a corpus before future queries arrive. The goal is to shift part of the costs from query time to a precomputation phase, thereby amortizing these costs across many downstream queries. To instantiate this setting, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework built on a key asymmetry in current agentic systems: LLM agents are effective at navigating existing hierarchical filesystems, but are rarely trained to proactively construct such workspaces for future use. Librarian Agents addresses this gap by tasking a builder agent with transforming source documents into a multi-level workspace with references to the original corpus. text: rarely trained to proactively construct such workspaces for future use. Librarian Agents addresses this gap by tasking a builder agent with transforming source documents into a multi-level workspace with references to the original corpus. An frozen answering agent then navigates this workspace to answer an individual user query. We formalize the builder agent’s operations as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and directly optimize the workspace construction policy for downstream answering performance by posing it as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem on this MDP. We demonstrate the efficacy of Librarian Agents on BrowseComp-Plus, Librarian Agents improves accuracy by an average of 33 percentage points over the best performing baseline. Furthermore, for BRIGHT, a domain which our builder agent is untrained on, gains persist over baselines with an average 31 point improvement over baselines. In contrast, can we shift part of this computation by constructing a reusable memory in the form of an anticipatory workspace? We instantiate this by have an gent curate an augmented filesystem that exposes a long-context structure through operations that these agents already use well: using tools to navigate filesystems (Yang et al., 2024). The builder converts a flat collection of documents into a multi-level workspace whose synthetic files reduce search friction while preserving reference paths to the original corpus. We first define the document corpus, filesystem, and augmentation operations that transform a flat collection of raw documents into an answer-facing workspace. We then articulate desiderata of an effective anticipatory memory workspace, which includes coverage with efficient navigation, fallback to raw evidence, and reuse across queries. Finally, we cast workspace construction as a finite-horizon Markov decision process in which the librarian model edits the filesystem to maximize the answering agent’s expected performance on future queries, subject to a construction-cost penalty. 2.1. text: We study long-context reasoning over a corpus of raw documents, 𝒟= {𝑑1, 𝑑2, . . . , 𝑑𝑛}, where the system must answer queries 𝑞∼𝒬. This setting matches retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, which typically answer each query by searching over a static retrieval index over 𝒟and then synthesizing a response. We represent the agent’s external memory as a filesystem-based workspace ℱ: a set of files and directories together with metadata specifying each node’s type and parent. The initial workspace ℱ0 contains the raw documents in 𝒟as files under the root. An augmentation 𝒜is an edit operation that modifies a workspace, for example by creating, rewriting, deleting, or moving files and folders. At iteration 𝑖, an augmentation 𝒜𝑖transforms the previous workspace ℱ𝑖−1 into ℱ𝑖. Applying a sequence of augmentations for horizon 𝐻produces a final workspace ℱ𝐻. System performance is measured by a scoring function Acc(˜𝑦, 𝑦*) that evaluates the correctness of the generated response ˜𝑦against the ground-truth target 𝑦*. Memory construction also incurs a cost, denoted Cost(𝐴𝑖), such as the number of tokens generated or modified by 𝒜𝑖. text: Setup Anticipatory workspace construction is the problem of transforming a large corpus into a structured filesystem-based workspace before downstream queries are observed. 2.2. Desiderata for Anticipatory Workspaces. A useful memory should do more than “remember” a corpus. It should reshape the corpus into an answer-facing workspace that helps future agents quickly find relevant evidence while preserving a path back to the raw source documents. As a running example, consider an enterprise corpus containing design docs, issue threads, launch notes, and customer reports for the same product. One future query may ask for a low-level implementation detail; another may ask how a user-visible behavior changed across releases; a third may ask for the exact source that supports a disputed claim. We use these examples to motivate three key desiderata. Coverage with Efficient Navigation. The memory should cover many plausible queries while reducing the need to search the raw corpus. In the enterprise example, the builder might create a release timeline, a component-level design index, and customer-facing behavior summaries, each linking the same underlying documents from a different angle. These artifacts help only if the answering agent can reach them through short, legible paths, such as directories named by abstraction level. Thus, the 3
