text: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries builder should synthesize cross-document artifacts that cover likely regions of the query distribution 𝒬and place them where an agent can discover them with shallow traversal. Faithful Fallback. No finite memory can anticipate every query, and synthesized artifacts can omit details that are critical in hindsight. The workspace must therefore preserve reference links and raw source paths so the answering agent can verify claims or bypass the synthesized layer when needed. In the enterprise example, a rare query about a single customer may not appear in the high-level summary, but the agent should still be able to read any existing issue thread. As an extreme example, such a fallback is important for needle-in-a-haystack queries where the answer depends on a localized, very specific fact that is unlikely to survive compression (Wang et al., 2024). Amortized Reuse. The builder’s construction cost should pay off across many downstream queries. For example, a compact release timeline written by the builder agent may help answer many questions about regressions, roadmap changes, customer messaging, and dependency updates. In contrast, a one-off answer draft may surface similar information but help only a single request. This creates a tradeoff between the construction cost ∑︀𝐻 𝑖=1 Cost(𝒜𝑖) and the downstream utility. Having formulated anticipatory workspace construction as an MDP in Section 2, we evaluate whether Librarian Agents improves the reasoning performance and inference efficiency of downstream an- swering agents on long-context document reasoning tasks. We compare Librarian Agents with prior reactive retrieval and pre-computation methods to address four questions: (1) Does Librarian Agents improve in-distribution long-context reasoning performance? (2) What amortization benefits do Librarian Agents provide when serving multiple queries over a shared document set? (3) Does the builder agent’s anticipatory construction capability generalize zero-shot to out-of-distribution retrieval settings? (4) Qualitatively, how do the builder and answering agents behave during the construction and answering phases, and do these behaviors reflect the intended anticipatory capability? We examine each question in turn below. Task Definition. The main domain we consider for long-document reasoning is BrowseComp- Plus (Chen et al., 2025), a curated corpus of deep-research web tasks. We split this dataset into two sets for training and evaluation: 680 tasks for training and 50 held-out tasks for all evaluations (sampled at random). To assess whether the builder agent learns a generalized anticipatory capability rather than simply overfitting to the DeepResearch training distribution, we evaluate Librarian Agents zero-shot on the BRIGHT benchmark. Here, we study 150 questions spanning 3 domains with 50 per domain, with one filesystem per domain (also studying amortization). As detailed in Table 3, the RL-finetuned builder agent successfully transfers to highly out-of-distribution domains such as biology and math problem solving. Librarian Agents achieves an average pass@1 accuracy of 0.52 and pass@3 accuracy of 0.67 across the 3 BRIGHT datasets, outperforming baselines. These results confirm that framing memory construction as an MDP enables the builder to learn fundamental, transferable heuristics for organizing information, which remain robust even when encountering novel, unseen documents. The structural statistics on BRIGHT further show that RL substantially changes construction behavior. Across the 3 sub-domains, the trained builder produces richer hierarchical memories, averaging 53.4 active synthetic files organized into 45.4 clusters and 8.0 merged artifacts, compared with 4.8 files, 4.2 clusters, and 0.6 merges for the base builder. text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. RAG grounds language model outputs in external evidence, mitigating the limitations of purely parametric memory (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025; Oche et al., 2025). Recent innovations have evolved this pipeline into agentic systems capable of multi-step reasoning (Xu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Singh et al., 2025). For instance, models can now predict upcoming content to trigger searches (Jiang et al., 2023), use reflection tokens for self-critique (Asai et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2024), or execute planned searches to navigate multi-hop questions (Li et al., 2026b). However, these approaches initiate complex, iterative retrieval only after receiving a user query. In contrast, Librarian Agents front-loads this computational burden by proactively synthesizing a structured, query-agnostic filesystem prior to inference, amortizing the cost of corpus-level reasoning. Structured Indexes and Corpus-Level Organization. Prior systems precompute corpus structure: RAPTOR builds hierarchical summaries (Sarthi et al., 2024); GraphRAG and related methods construct entity graphs and community summaries (Edge et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025); and HippoRAG builds graph-structured memory (Jiménez Gutiérrez et al., 2024). Although valuable, these preprocessing methods rely heavily on rigid, rule-based extraction pipelines or predefined schemas. In contrast, Librarian Agents make anticipatory memory construction fully agentic and optimizable. Librarian Agents treats the structure itself as a

Long-Term Memory for Language Agents. Prior work explores endowing language models with persistent, stateful memory to support continuous operation. For instance, recent works propose to cache conversational histories (Wang et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023; Uddin et al., 2026), manage virtual context windows via memory tiers (Packer et al., 2023), and unify short- and long-term memory directly within the agent’s policy (Yu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2025). However, these approaches primarily focus on an agent retaining its own historical context. Librarian Agents addresses a different setting, in which the memory is written over an external corpus ahead of time and judged by how well another agent answers from it. Compute Reallocation. Our approach aligns with emerging literature on reallocating computation across time to improve test-time scaling (Lin et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a). Other approaches formalize test-time compute optimization as meta- reinforcement learning optimization to adaptively allocate tokens (Qu et al., 2025b) or utilize self- curated test-time curricula to reinforce successful strategies (Hübotter et al., 2025). To our knowledge, Librarian Agents is the first to treat corpus organization as

text: as meta- reinforcement learning optimization to adaptively allocate tokens (Qu et al., 2025b) or utilize self- curated test-time curricula to reinforce successful strategies (Hübotter et al., 2025). To our knowledge, Librarian Agents is the first to treat corpus organization as a policy optimized for downstream answers, training a builder to do once what an answering agent would otherwise repeat for every query. Our hyperparameters explicitly control how construction cost and query-time cost are weighed against answer accuracy. 4. Discussion, Limitations, and Future Work We study the capability of anticipatory directed curation, in which agents can proactively reorganize their context into a memory artifact optimized for future queries they encounter. To instantiate this capability, we rely on an asymmetry for agents today, where agents are trained to navigate a filesystem for a given task, yet do not pre-construct workspaces for future queries that they might encounter. Our novel framework, Librarian Agents, introduces a builder agent that creates a synthetic filesystem that an answering agent can navigate. Librarian Agents yields consistent improvements on BrowseComp-Plus and BRIGHT, outperforming existing retrieval methods on both in-domain and out-of-distribution evaluations. Our evaluation is limited to question answering over static corpora, and maintaining anticipatory memories as documents change remains an open problem. The builder agent also operates over a large file context, which may limit scalability, though

text: in-domain and out-of-distribution evaluations. Our evaluation is limited to question answering over static corpora, and maintaining anticipatory memories as documents change remains an open problem. The builder agent also operates over a large file context, which may limit scalability, though pairing Librarian Models with clustering or retrieval could extend the framework to larger domains. Since no finite set of synthesized artifacts can anticipate every query, compression may discard details needed for needle-in-a-haystack tasks; we preserve reference links for fallback access, but deciding when to bypass the synthetic filesystem remains a challenge. A natural extension is a filesystem that updates from its own traffic, treating each answered query as evidence of what the next reader will need. Future work could also let the builder compose atomic filesystem commands, of which its current four actions are special cases. 5. More details on experimental setup BrowseComp-Plus. BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025) pairs document collections with questions that require locating and combining information distributed across those collections. We train the filesystem builder on 680 corpus-level tasks and reserve 50 previously unseen corpus-level tasks, for evaluation. We use a mixture of evidence, gold, and negative docs for each representative task, following the composition in the original dataset. During construction, the

We use a mixture of evidence, gold, and negative docs for each representative task, following the composition in the original dataset. During construction, the builder receives only the documents and never observes the evaluation questions. The completed filesystem is then reused for every question associated with its corpus. We report failure-inclusive binary semantic answer correctness against the fixed reference answers, so unsuccessful constructions and failed generations remain in the denominator. In addition, for the Base-versus-RL comparison, both builders receive identical construction limits, and we report realized construction tokens separately because equal limits do not imply equal consumption. BRIGHT-derived question answering. BRIGHT spans technical, scientific, mathematical, and programming domains with substantially different document and query distributions (Su et al., 2025). We convert its retrieval instances into a generation task by associating each query with a fixed reference answer and scoring generated responses for semantic correctness. For the primary matched-baseline evaluation, we use 150 questions spanning three domains, with 50 questions each from AOPS, Biology, and Stack Overflow. To test cross-benchmark transfer, we apply the BrowseComp- trained Librarian zero-shot: it constructs one reusable filesystem per domain without observing any evaluation question, and this single shared filesystem supports all questions in that domain. text: MJev-Spatial: System One Spatial Intelligence via Native Attention Matching Luozheng Qin∗, Yuhan Zhu∗, Changhai Zhou∗, Qian Qiao, Jun Gao, Yuhua Zhou, Harry Zhang, Xiangyu Zeng, Yuxuan Liu, Kaijie Chen, Andrew Chen, Pony Ma ∗Equal contribution. Spatial intelligence lets an agent perceive and act in the physical world, and many of its judgments must be made at interaction rates: which spatial relation holds, how far an object is, or where to place it. Vision-language models (VLMs) produce these answers by free-form text generation, paying for autoregressive decoding and answer parsing even though the output space is compact: one of a few options, a scalar, or a 2D point. In light of this, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a System 1 multimodal decision model that tackles all three types of spatial understanding tasks within a unified classification framework. Specifically, MJev-Spatial treats each candidate as a class and scores it using the backbone’s pretrained query and key projections, without adding parameters. The candidates are the given options for choice tasks, or value bins and image regions refined through coarse-to- fine classification for numerical and point prediction, respectively. At inference, each classification decision takes a single forward pass and generates no answer tokens. To train on heterogeneous spatial data efficiently, we supervise all coarse-to-fine stages jointly with teacher forcing in one forward pass, and combine this

text: Spatial intelligence involves perceiving and reasoning about the geometry and spatial relationships of objects, which enables agents to navigate their surroundings and interact with the physical world (Chen et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024). Many of these interactions require timely spatial judgments. Vision-language models (VLMs) support these capabilities by answering spatial questions grounded in visual observations. Such questions may require selecting an option that describes a spatial relation (Ray et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026), estimating a numerical quantity such as distance (Cai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025a,b), or identifying a point for object placement (Zhou et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025). To produce these spatial predictions, many existing VLMs retain their pretrained autoregressive text- generation capabilities (Chen et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024; Deitke et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a). Each option, numerical value, or image location is therefore represented as a token sequence that the model is trained to reproduce. This couples learning the spatial answer with learning its textual form, including formatting and boilerplate when present, introducing supervision beyond the task-relevant prediction itself. At inference, the model must generate the answer tokens sequentially, after which the resulting text must be
title: 1 Introduction

text: couples learning the spatial answer with learning its textual form, including formatting and boilerplate when present, introducing supervision beyond the task-relevant prediction itself. At inference, the model must generate the answer tokens sequentially, after which the resulting text must be parsed to recover the spatial prediction, adding decoding and parsing overhead. This motivates a System 1 approach to spatial understanding: using pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to make spatial judgments directly. Jev provides a precedent for this approach by returning probabilities over specified candidates without generating answer text (TypeSafe AI, 2026). At the same time, we observe that all three common spatial output types can be represented as finite candidate sets: answer options are already finite, while numerical values and image locations can be discretized within a specified range and resolution. Building on these insights, we introduce MJev-Spatial, a multimodal decision model specifically tailored to spatial understanding. MJev-Spatial unifies the three output types by casting prediction as classification over finite candidate sets. Each class represents a supplied answer option, a numerical bin, or an image region, depending on the task. Selecting a class gives the chosen option, predicts which bin contains the target value, or predicts which region contains the target point. To choose among these classes, MJev-Spatial encodes their descriptions together with the observation and question, then reuses the
title: 1 Introduction

text: Selecting a class gives the chosen option, predicts which bin contains the target value, or predicts which region contains the target point. To choose among these classes, MJev-Spatial encodes their descriptions together with the observation and question, then reuses the final attention layer’s pretrained query and key projections to compute class scores. A softmax over these scores gives the class probabilities, without additional prediction heads or trainable parameters. At inference, each classification decision scores all its candidates in one forward pass. Furthermore, to obtain fine-grained values and coordinates without evaluating a large number of classes at once, we subdivide the selected numerical bin or image region and classify again. Numerical prediction uses up to two stages; single-point prediction uses three stages, re-encoding the selected image crop before each later decision to recover local visual detail. The final selection is decoded to a numerical value or image coordinates. Conditional tree expansion evaluates multiple region paths to extend the same trained point predictor to multiple points without additional training. Numerical and point prediction can require multiple supervised stages, with new image crops introduced between point decisions. Ground-truth answers determine the target classes and crops, allowing all stages to be jointly supervised in one teacher-forced causal forward pass. We average the stage cross-entropy losses per question so that a multi-stage example does not

We average the stage cross-entropy losses per question so that a multi-stage example does not receive greater weight than a one-stage choice. Global length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing address the padding and workload imbalance caused by different sequence lengths and crop counts while preserving optimizer-batch membership. An audited conversion pipeline supplies 12.3M QA from existing spatial annotations for full-parameter training of the retained language backbone. Built on Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026), MJev-Spatial achieves the highest overall score among eight eval- uated models, leads on seven benchmarks, and outperforms its unmodified autoregressive base model on all twelve. Across all twelve benchmarks, it achieves 2.5× and 5.6× speedups over the fastest autoregressive baseline and the base model, respectively. Separate studies examine candidate scoring, visual refinement, numerical discretization, and training execution. The readout and refinement studies assess how candidate scoring with pretrained projections and crop re-encoding contribute to prediction quality and computational cost; the numerical study shows that coarser length discretization can reduce prediction error despite its lower resolution. Global length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing further improve training throughput by 30.8% over the original batching strategy. 2

text: Our contributions are as follows: (1) We propose a novel System 1 paradigm for spatial intelligence, unifying option selection, numerical estimation, and image pointing through direct classification over finite candidate sets. (2) Building on this paradigm, we develop MJev-Spatial and a unified training recipe, using pretrained attention projections for candidate scoring and joint supervision across spatial tasks and refinement stages. (3) Across twelve spatial benchmarks, MJev-Spatial achieves the highest mean score among eight evaluated models and a 5.6× speedup over its autoregressive base model, Qwen3.5-4B.

Each candidate is a possible answer for the current decision. For a choice question, it is one of the supplied options; for a numerical or point question, it identifies an interval or region in which the target is predicted to lie. This lets all three output types use the same candidate-classification rule. A single greedy path returns one location. To recover several locations with the same trained model, we expand multiple paths and assign each final cell the product of its conditional probabilities along the path. Together, these probabilities form a spatial map in which separated high-probability regions can yield multiple predictions. Section A.4 gives the fixed decoding rules, and Section F.2 evaluates their quality and computational tradeoffs. 3.2 Model Architecture The framework in Section 3.1 defines the candidate classes and refinement rules; a model must still deter- mine which class is supported by the visual observation and question. Following Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026), we adapt a pretrained VLM to make these decisions. Its contextual representations draw on visual and linguistic knowledge acquired during large-scale pretraining, providing a basis for interpreting the scene and evaluating possible answers. We build on this capacity by formulating classification as matching a decision representa- tion with candidate representations. Our design reuses both pretrained features and matching projections, 6

Each candidate is expressed as text: choice tasks retain the supplied option content, numerical tasks specify values or intervals with their units, and pointing tasks name cells relative to the current image region, such as “top-left” or “center”. These descriptions provide the candidate content that the VLM contextualizes with the observation and question. We instantiate MJev-Spatial with Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026). Its vision encoder and merger convert the images into visual tokens, which are encoded together with the question, preceding refinement history, and current candidate descriptions in a causal sequence. Each candidate description ends with an option-end marker, and the complete candidate list ends with a decision marker. After the first 31 language layers, the hidden state at each option-end marker represents that candidate in the context of the observation, question, and preceding candidates. The hidden state at the decision marker incorporates the full candidate set and serves as the decision representation. The markers reuse existing vocabulary entries, so no new embeddings are introduced. Section A.2 gives the exact sequence layout. Length grouping and cross-GPU load balancing reduce padding and workload imbalance. Training data. Our training corpus contains 12.3M question–answer pairs converted from RefSpatial (Zhou et al., 2025a), SAT (Ray et al., 2025), SenseNova-SI (Cai et al., 2026), VSI-590K-image (Yang et al., 2025a), and VST-P (Yang et al., 2025b). The training data cover multiple-choice spatial question answering (7.1M QA), point localization (3.5M QA), length estimation (1.6M QA), angle estimation (120K QA), and counting (38K QA). Averaging over stages gives each original QA equal total weight, so a three-stage point counts no more than a one-stage choice. Efficient batching. Joint supervision removes the need for a separate language-backbone training pass at each refinement stage, but questions still require different amounts of computation. In particular, point ex- amples add two image crops, while choice and numerical examples have different candidate lengths and stage counts. Padding dissimilar sequences wastes work, and assigning unequal work to GPUs delays synchroniza- tion. We sort the expanded sequences within each global optimizer batch by length to form similar-length microbatches. A longest-work-first assignment (Graham, 1969) then distributes the microbatches across GPUs, using a cost that accounts for padded sequence length and visual-token work. This combines length grouping with cross-GPU load balancing while preserving the questions in each optimizer batch and their weights in Equation (7). Every QA remains an independent causal row: packing different questions together would additionally require isolation of Qwen’s Gated DeltaNet states (Yang et al., 2025c). The assignment rule and distributed normalization are specified in Section C.3.

Given the scale of our expanded training corpus, we adopt full-parameter fine-tuning of the language back- bone, although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is also applicable (Zhou et al., 2025d, 2026c, 2025e,f, 2026d). The final configuration uses eight GPUs, a per-device microbatch size of eight, and eight gradient accumulation steps, yielding a global batch size of 512. We use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rates of 5 × 10−6 for the backbone and 2 × 10−4 for the readout. Language computation uses BF16, while trainable weights, gradients, optimizer states, and candidate scoring remain in FP32. The vision en- coder and merger are frozen. Section C.2 provides the complete configuration, and Section 4.4 evaluates the scheduling improvements under controlled conditions. 4 Experiments We first compare the final MJev-Spatial model with seven autoregressive VLMs on spatial prediction quality and inference latency. Controlled pilot experiments then compare candidate scorers, crop re-encoding and feature reuse, numerical discretization, and multi-point decoding. Our evaluation covers the popular SAT (Ray et al., 2025), CV-Bench (Tong et al., 2024), BLINK (Fu et al., 2024), MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2026), RefSpatial-Bench (Zhou et al., 2025a), Where2Place (Yuan et al., 2024), Point-Bench (Cheng et al., 2025), RoboSpatial VQA and pointing (Song et al., 2025), ERQA (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025), EmbSpatial (Du et al., 2024), and VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025d). For model-design ablations, we use a fixed 72K-QA mixture of 25K SAT choice questions, 22K VST-P length questions, and 25K RefSpatial point questions to reduce training cost while providing sufficient supervision for meaningful comparisons. Each model is trained for 2.2K updates using the same optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and image-token budgets. VST-300 serves as the development set for length estimation. 4.2 Main Result Our main evaluation tests the central premise of MJev-Spatial: a System 1 decision model can make accurate spatial judgments with low inference latency. We therefore assess prediction quality and latency jointly, comparing MJev-Spatial with seven autoregressive VLMs. MJev-Spatial achieves the highest average score of 65.64%, ahead of 62.79% for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and ranks first on seven of the twelve benchmarks (Table 2). It also outperforms its autoregressive base model on all twelve benchmarks, including gains of 22.89
title: SSRL (Liu et al., 2025), SenseNova-SI (Cai et al., 2026), and SpatialThinker (Batra et al., 2025).

text: VLMs. MJev-Spatial achieves the highest average score of 65.64%, ahead of 62.79% for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, and ranks first on seven of the twelve benchmarks (Table 2). It also outperforms its autoregressive base model on all twelve benchmarks, including gains of 22.89 percentage points on RoboSpatial VQA and 12.50 points on RefSpatial-Bench. These improvements span both spatial question answering and point localization. For length estimation, the final model reaches an MAE of 0.103 m on the VST-300 development set. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, MJev-Spatial also achieves the lowest mean query latency, 160.6 ms, yielding a 2.5× speedup over the fastest autoregressive baseline and a 5.6× speedup over its base model (Table 11). The com- bination of the highest average score and lowest mean latency gives MJev-Spatial the strongest performance– latency trade-off among the compared models (Figure 1). These results support our System 1 approach to spatial understanding: adapting pretrained multimodal knowledge into direct classification decisions that deliver both strong prediction quality and fast responses. 4.3 Ablation Studies We next examine the design choices that make direct classification effective across spatial tasks. The studies follow the prediction process: we first assess the shared candidate-scoring mechanism, then examine how numerical discretization and visual refinement provide the precision needed for value and point prediction. Point prediction requires both a precise output representation and enough visual detail to distinguish nearby locations. We investigate whether original-image context or reused features can replace fresh crop encodings while retaining localization accuracy. Removing crops from the trained model reduces RefSpatial accuracy from 51.00% to 9.00%; training a model without crops recovers 46.50%, showing the importance of adapting training to the chosen visual input (Tables 5 and 18). Crop re-encoding nevertheless achieves the highest RefSpatial and Point-Bench scores among the four visual strategies, reaching 51.00% and 56.84%, respectively. Replaying visual tokens or attention K/V does not recover these scores. We therefore retain crop re-encoding to supply the local visual evidence needed by successive region decisions. We also evaluate direct visual-token pointing, which replaces the three-stage hierarchy with a single decision over the original image’s visual tokens. For the native Q/K model, connected-component decoding improves counting success from 12.76% with argmax to 32.14%. Replacing repeated continue/stop decisions with a spatial probability tree raises Point-Bench counting success from 19.39% to 38.78% (Table 21). Four fresh runs use the same historical 72K corpus, global batch 256, microbatch eight, four accumulation steps, and eight L20D GPUs. Each runs 100 updates; after eight warmup updates, the measurement window contains the same 23,552 QA. The comparison holds the model and training computation fixed apart from scheduling. Local length grouping raises throughput from 99.06 to 116.91 QA/s and reduces padding from 35.17% to 12.36%, but increases mean gradient-ready spread from 115.0 to 306.6 ms (Table 6). Global grouping with cross-GPU balancing reduces padding to 1.77% and ready-time spread to 145.7 ms, reaching 129.54 QA/s: 30.78% higher throughput, or 23.53% less measured time for the same QA volume, than the original strategy. Since ready-time spread remains above the original value, the gain reflects the combined scheduling change. A 128-QA cross-update buffer lowers padding to 1.03% but does not improve throughput and increases step- time variability. We retain the unbuffered layout to preserve optimizer-batch membership. text: MJev-Spatial investigates a System One approach to spatial understanding: using pretrained multimodal knowledge to make direct spatial decisions without generating answer text. Options, numerical values, and image locations share a candidate-classification mechanism, with hierarchical refinement providing numerical and spatial precision and tree expansion extending point prediction without further training. An audited 12.3M-QA corpus and joint stage supervision support training across these tasks; length grouping and cross- GPU balancing improve throughput by 30.8% in a controlled eight-GPU study. The final Qwen3.5-4B-based model achieves the highest overall score, leads seven of twelve reported metrics among eight evaluated models, and exceeds its local autoregressive base model on all twelve. Its mean batch-one query latency is 160.6 ms across the twelve benchmarks, giving 2.5× and 5.6× speedups over the fastest autoregressive baseline and the base model under the reported timing protocol. Together with the controlled design studies, these results support direct candidate decisions as a viable approach to the spatial tasks studied here. 11

text: A Additional Method Details A.1 Autoregressive Reference and Decision Paths Problem setup. Given ordered images I = (I1, . . . , Im) and a spatial question q, the goal is to predict a typed answer y ∈Yq: one of the supplied options, a number with a declared unit, or a location in normalized image coordinates. In an autoregressive formulation, a vision-language model πθ generates an answer string w = (w1, . . . , wL) autoregressively, πθ(w | I, q) = L Y l=1 πθ(wl | I, q, w<l), (8) and a task-specific parser then maps w to y. Answer generation therefore adds sequential decoding steps whose number depends on the output length L. In the classification formulation, the state at stage t is st = (I, q, h<t), where h<t contains the preceding selections and visual refinements. A deterministic controller constructs Ct, advances the state after selection, and decodes the terminal path to the required answer. For a fixed observation and question, reachable states form a finite tree of depth at most three, with path probability P(a1:S | I, q) = S Y t=1 pθ(at | I, q, h<t, Ct). (9) Ordinary decoding follows the greedy path in Equation (1); multi-point decoding expands several spatial paths. Training supervises all annotated transitions using Equation (7). A.2 Input Sequence and Candidate Representations Sequence layout. Each question–answer example (QA) is represented by an image prefix followed by the question, candidate descriptions, and a decision marker: [state, I1, . . . , Im, question, q, opt, c1, end, . . . , opt, cK, end, decide]. (10) The sequence markers reuse existing vocabulary entries, leaving the vocabulary and embedding matrix un- changed. Candidate representations. The frozen vision encoder (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) and merger embed each image into the language sequence, and the first 31 language layers contextualize the whole causal row. The state at an option-end marker then summarizes that option in the context of the image, the question, and the preceding options, while the state at the decision marker sees all current candidates. Changing an option therefore changes its representation rather than the interpretation of a fixed classifier slot, which lets the candidate set vary freely across questions. Training shuffles candidate order, while evaluation follows each benchmark’s ordering protocol. Multi-stage rows. Each QA occupies its own causal row. A later stage appends the selected option, an optional new image crop, and a new question and candidate block. During training, all supervised stages fit in one teacher-forced (Williams and Zipser, 1989) causal sequence. Each decision marker precedes the later choices and crops, so one forward pass supervises every stage without showing a future crop to an earlier decision. At inference, the next stage is constructed only after the current prediction. A.3 Candidate Scoring with Pretrained Query and Key Projections The shared scorer produces one class logit for each current candidate. The final full-attention layer’s pre- trained query projection acts on the decision state, and its key projection acts on each candidate state; comparing the resulting vectors gives the logits used in Equation (1). This reuses existing parameters to compute classification scores without an additional prediction head. 17

For evaluation, we drop a first-level branch only when p(a1) < 0.01 maxj p(j), so each retained root adds ten decision nodes and 81 leaf cells, and deeper levels are fully expanded. Unvisited cells remain unknown, and the omitted mass is recorded without renormalizing the retained probabilities. On the resulting map, cells above 10% of the retained global peak form an eight-connected superlevel set, and each connected component outputs the center of its peak cell. The threshold, connectivity, and root cutoff are fixed without test labels; target masks and true point counts are used only by the scorer. C.3 Scheduling and Distributed Execution To reduce padding, sequences within each global optimizer batch are sorted by expanded length Lq into microbatches of eight. To limit workload imbalance across devices, a longest-work-first assignment (Graham, 1969) distributes these microbatches across eight ranks by the cost C(B) = |B| max q∈B Lq + 0.25 X q∈B Vq, (19) where Vq measures visual-token work, and each scheduling round gives one microbatch to each rank. The recipe uses no cross-update buffer, concatenated QA sequences, training prefix cache, or image deduplication. E Extended Readout Studies E.1 Readout Controls and Optimization Alignment We test whether a pretrained candidate scorer can replace an added classification head while retaining competitive spatial performance. The controlled comparison evaluates three ways to convert contextual representations into candidate scores. A position classifier applies LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016) and a 32- output linear layer to the decision state; its outputs refer to candidate slots. A KEV pointer completes the language backbone and projects the decision and option-end states with two newly initialized affine 2560 →256 maps, scoring their dot product divided by √ 256. It adds 1,311,232 parameters and explicitly represents candidate content. The native mean model instead reuses the final attention projections at the earlier boundary in Section 3.2. text: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents Qingni Wang†1, Changdae Oh2, Yuzhe Yang†1, Sharon Li2, Jiachen Yang1, Ang Li1 and Xin Eric Wang1 1Simular, 2University of Wisconsin–Madison †Work done while interning at Simular. Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent’s latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model’s hidden states with those from its past successful and
title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong

text: handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model’s hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points at matched escalation rates. text: Computer-use agents (CUAs) automate tasks of graphical interfaces by translating natural-language instructions and visual observations into executable actions (Cheng et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), and are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon automation tasks that can take more than an hour on average (Abhyankar et al., 2026). While frontier proprietary models have been shown to achieve impressive performance leaps (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026), running every single task spanning hundreds of steps with these models raises cost concerns, whereas a light open-weight model alone performs poorly on even much simpler tasks (Xie et al., 2024). This creates a fundamental trade-off between accuracy and cost efficiency, motivating weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE), in which a weak agent serves as the primary executor and hands control to a strong agent only when needed (Lei and Huang, 2026; Wei et al., 2026). W2SE raises two important questions: (1) When should the weak agent escalate, and (2) who oversees the strong agent after handing over? Existing work on W2SE primarily focuses on the first question, estimating the weak agent’s failure risk to decide when escalation is needed. Some of them adopt another monitoring agent to verify each step (Wang et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2026), others train an extra monitoring module on the collection of annotated trajectories (Lei and Huang, 2026; Wei et al., 2026).
title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents

text: needed. Some of them adopt another monitoring agent to verify each step (Wang et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2026), others train an extra monitoring module on the collection of annotated trajectories (Lei and Huang, 2026; Wei et al., 2026). However, the former inevitably adds nontrivial cost to run another heavy agent step-by-step, whereas the latter creates another phase of data annotation and training, hindering direct adoption in real-world applications under varying deployment constraints. While training-free uncertainty estimation-based approaches might avoid the aforementioned bottlenecks (Oh et al., 2026b), prior works still rely on external knowledge base (Liu et al., 2026), another reference model (Oh et al., 2026a), or multiple sampling for each step (Wang et al., 2026) quickly becomes infeasible or impractical in long-horizon tasks in the wild. Besides, escalation alone does not eliminate execution uncertainty, resulting in the second important question in W2SE which is commonly overlooked. That is, even after a stronger agent takes control, subsequent actions may deviate from the intended task or fail to achieve the desired outcome. However, monitoring a black-box strong agent is challenging because its internal states are inaccessible and verbalized confidence can be unreliable on evolving context of long-horizon task (Han et al., 2024; Kirchhof et al., 2026). To answer both questions, we formulate W2SE as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, and
title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents

text: because its internal states are inaccessible and verbalized confidence can be unreliable on evolving context of long-horizon task (Han et al., 2024; Kirchhof et al., 2026). To answer both questions, we formulate W2SE as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, and use the weak agent’s failure risk as a proxy for the expected benefit of escalation. We then propose Latent uncertainty for Escalation And SHadow oversight (LEASH), a training-free framework driven by the uncertainty signal in the weak agent’s hidden states. First, we record its hidden states of prompt and action tokens on a small set of held-out tasks and label them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes to construct a representation bank. This representation bank then serves as a semantic anchor to score the newly faced prompts and actions during test-time by measuring, under a Mahalanobis metric in latent space, how much closer each one lies to past failures than to past successes. LEASH puts this signal on two jobs (Figure 2): For escalation, an initial gate scores uncertainty from the task prompt query, while a runtime gate monitors subsequent execution trace. For oversight, after the weak model hands the control to the strong agent, it switches its role from actor to observer that monitors the strong agent’s trajectory every three steps; when its uncertainty is high, the pending action is
title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents

text: trace. For oversight, after the weak model hands the control to the strong agent, it switches its role from actor to observer that monitors the strong agent’s trajectory every three steps; when its uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort. Importantly, our uncertainty-driven W2SE formulation draws on an easily accessible resource, the weak agent’s own past experience (Silver and Sutton, 2025), removing reliance on an external dataset or additional training without hosting another expensive agent during runtime, while offering extensibility for recursive self-improvement (Madaan et al., 2023; Schmidhuber, 2007; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zelikman et al., 2022). 2

text: weak agents and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026a) as the strong agent. At matched escalation rates, LEASH outperforms ran- dom escalation by 6.55–11.94 points. We further measure how much of the performance gap between the weak agent alone and always-on Opus is recovered by escalation, following the performance-gap metric of (Burns et al., 2023). LEASH recovers 75–102% of this gap, against 37–69% for random escalation, while costing 69–81% as much as always-on Opus. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), LEASH matches always-on Opus (73.7% vs. 72.9% success) at 19% lower cost, whereas random escalation at equal cost scores about 9 points lower (Figure 1). Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formalize weak-to-strong escalation as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem and show that one latent uncertainty signal can drive both escalation and oversight. • We propose a training-free, scalable uncertainty scoring method that measures how much closer a hidden state lies to the weak agent’s own past failures than to its past successes, and provide theoretical justification for using this score for escalation. • We extend this uncertainty signal to weak-to-strong oversight, in which the white-box weak agent monitors the black-box strong agent through its own hidden states. • On OSWorld with four open-weight backbones, we show that LEASH outperforms random escalation at matched escalation rates and recovers 75–102% of

text: Efficient Computer-Use Agents. Model routing and cascading offer a promising way to balance inference cost and performance, as demonstrated by FrugalGPT and RouteLLM (Chen et al., 2023; 3

Extending this idea to GUI automation, Adaptive VLM Routing selects models based on action difficulty and confidence (Liu et al., 2026), while StepWise trains lightweight monitors to detect execution stalls and identify milestones for escalation (Wei et al., 2026). Our work instead leverages the backbone agent’s internal representations to guide both task-level routing and step-level escalation, without training a dedicated monitoring network. Weak-to-Strong Paradigms. Weak-to-strong generalization studies how stronger models learn from weaker supervision (Burns et al., 2023; Jung et al., 2025; Medvedev et al., 2025; Somerstep et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025). These works primarily concern training-time transfer of supervision or capabilities from a weaker model to a stronger one. Here we study the complementary inference- time setting of weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE), where a weak model executes by default and selectively invokes a stronger model when additional capability is needed. This shifts the weak–strong relationship from supervision transfer to sequential resource allocation. We derive escalation signals from the agent’s own past experience without training an additional monitor. Uncertainty Estimation and Agent Monitoring. Uncertainty estimation of agentic systems has emerged as one of the most important problems to monitor and guide agent decisions (Chun et al., 2026; Han et al., 2024; Oh

text: experience without training an additional monitor. Uncertainty Estimation and Agent Monitoring. Uncertainty estimation of agentic systems has emerged as one of the most important problems to monitor and guide agent decisions (Chun et al., 2026; Han et al., 2024; Oh et al., 2026b), while SafeGround and Argus investigate uncertainty estima- tion for GUI grounding, including calibrated predictions and representation-based methods (Kumar et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Sampling-based uncertainty estimation and risk control have also been studied for question answering (Duan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), but repeated generation can be costly when applied at every step of a long-horizon agent trajectory. Meanwhile, another line of work explores weak-to-strong oversight of agent misbehavior and failure monitoring through observable trajectories (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Kale et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Rather than focusing on either escalation or oversight alone, we handle both problem in a single unified fueled by a simple uncertainty estimate. That is, we integrate representation-based uncertainty estimation into the execution workflow, reusing the backbone model’s hidden states for escalation and extending the same signal to post-handoff oversight of a closed-source strong agent. 3. Method We introduce LEASH, a training-free uncertainty-driven agentic inference framework for W2SE and post-handoff oversight (Figure 2). By comparing the weak model’s runtime hidden states with successful and failed reference executions, we estimate uncertainty at task initialization and during execution, which guides both escalation to the strong agent and continued oversight after handoff. We first formulate the problem in Section 3.1 and introduce each component in subsequent sections. 3.1. Problem Formulation Given a task query, a computer-use agent generates an action conditioned on the query, the screen, and history. We consider a lightweight, weak agent, e.g., a relatively small open-weight model with accessible hidden states, and a large, strong agent, e.g., a proprietary black-box frontier model, sharing a budget of 𝑇actions. In addition to these two actor agents, we also host a Manager agent (with a strong model) who fires at the beginning to decompose the task and subsequently at subgoal boundaries to verify progress, constructing a minimal version of multi-agent workflow (Agashe et al., 2025a,b; Koh et al., 2026). Throughout execution, the Manager decomposes the task query into subgoals with screenshot-verifiable completion criteria and decides whether to advance, keep, or revise each subgoal (Appendix C). Reference-Based Latent Uncertainty Estimation Motivated by well-established observations revealing that LLMs internalize the likelihood of task success or failure in their representations (Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Kadavath et al., 2022; Kossen et al., 2024; Orgad et al., 2025) even before generating any tokens (Afzal et al., 2025; Cencerrado et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2024), we propose a training-free, representation-distance-based uncertainty estimation technique for agent systems. Representations and reference banks. For each task from a small held-out set, we run a weak agent to collect some preliminary inference trajectories without escalating anything to a strong agent. During this inference over the held-out set, we extract two final-layer representations, ℎ0 ∈ℝ𝑑at the last task query prompt token, and ℎ𝑡∈ℝ𝑑at the

Uncertainty Estimation We compare output probability-based uncertainty estimates with three representation-based alter- natives: Euclidean distance to class centroids, kNN over reference representations, and our pooled LDA using covariance-aware Mahalanobis distance. The probability-based baseline considers several uncertainty metrics, including negative log-probability, chosen-token probability, predictive entropy, and nucleus-set size under different aggregation schemes (Gupta et al., 2024), and reports the strongest one in each setting. As shown in Table 3, the effectiveness of each uncertainty estimator (i.e., how well it predicts task or sub-goal failure) varies across both backbones and execution stages. At the initial query-based uncertainty estimation stage, pooled LDA performs best for Nemotron, whereas probability-based baseline is stronger for Qwen3.8-27B. At the runtime step-wise estimation stage, our pooled LDA score achieves the highest AUROC for both backbones, although the overall effectiveness remains moderate. Overall, these results suggest that representation-based uncertainty can provide a training-free signal for runtime monitoring, particularly highlighting the effectiveness of our LDA-based estimation, while its effectiveness remains dependent on the backbone and execution stage. In this section, we now explain the empirical success of our uncertainty-based escalation through a simple probabilistic analysis. To keep the analysis simple, we consider a single decision per task: each task is either handed to the strong agent before execution begins (𝑡esc = 0) or never handed off (𝑡esc = 𝑇). This isolates the initial gate 𝑔0 of LEASH (Section 3.3), with no runtime escalation afterward. We also assume the budget in Eq. text: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents Proof sketch. Under this model, our score equals (up to an additive constant) twice the log-odds that the weak agent fails (Lemma 1 in Appendix A.1), which recalls the classical linear discriminant analysis identity (Fisher, 1936). Escalating the highest-scoring tasks thus escalates the tasks most likely to fail, and a Neyman–Pearson exchange argument (Neyman and Pearson, 1933) shows that no other rule at the same rate catches more failures; (ii) follows by the same argument applied to Δ. Implication. Proposition 1 (i) says that, at any escalation budget, no escalation rule based on the query representation 𝑧captures more of the weak agent’s failures than the initial gate of LEASH. For example, random escalation with budget 𝑝hands off only a fraction 𝑝of these failures, whereas our gate hands off strictly more. Moreover, (ii) shows that our gate spends the strong-agent budget where it pays off most (Jitkrittum et al., 2023), so catching more of the weak agent’s failures directly turns into higher overall task success. Meanwhile, the analysis covers only the initial gate; analyzing the runtime gate would require an optimal-stopping formulation, which we leave to future work.
title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents

text: We introduced weak to strong escalation as a general inference paradigm for adaptive agent systems, in which inexpensive weak models handle routine execution and stronger models are invoked selectively when additional capability is needed. Under this paradigm, we proposed LEASH, a training-free, uncertainty-aware framework that supports initial routing, runtime escalation, and continued post- handoff oversight. Our results suggest that a shared latent uncertainty signal can support both selective escalation and post-handoff oversight, providing a practical mechanism for dynamically allocating model capability while retaining continued control over strong-agent execution. Limitations Our current evaluation is limited to computer-use agents on OSWorld, so the generality of weak-to- strong escalation beyond this domain remains to be validated. In addition, our uncertainty score estimates weak-agent failure risk rather than the expected benefit of escalation; Proposition 1 requires a condition that the escalation gain be nondecreasing in the score, which may fail when both weak and strong agents struggle on the same task. Finally, post-handoff Shadow monitoring operates under a distribution shift from weak-agent trajectories, and its intervention effect is not causally isolated in our current evaluation. 12

The class centroids are computed in the standardized space, and bΣ𝑐is the pooled within-class scatter normalized by 𝑛−2, where 𝑛is the number of representations in the bank. text: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents A.3. Reference Banks and Threshold Calibration Reference banks. For each backbone, we construct a small held-out set of Manager-guided tra- jectories collected with escalation disabled and disjoint from the evaluation tasks. From this set, we construct the query and action representation banks: initial representations are labeled by task- level outcomes, while runtime representations inherit the outcomes of their corresponding subgoal segments. Held-out scoring. We use the same held-out reference set for both representation-bank construction and threshold calibration. Specifically, we perform task-grouped 10-fold cross-validation, keeping all steps from the same task in one fold. For each fold, an uncertainty estimator is fitted on the other nine folds and used only to score the held-out fold, yielding one out-of-fold score for every reference task. The fold-specific estimators are used only for calibration and are discarded afterwards. We then set the escalation thresholds as empirical quantiles of these out-of-fold scores. After calibration, we fit one final estimator per uncertainty channel on all tasks in the same reference set, keep the calibrated thresholds fixed, and use these final estimators to score the evaluation tasks. No evaluation data are used for either estimator fitting or threshold calibration. Targets and thresholds. All four backbones use the same targets, 𝑝𝑞= 0.25 and 𝑝esc = 0.50, so that 𝑝𝑎=

Because the reference set is finite, the achievable rates are discrete, with a resolution of one reference task. A.4. Post-Handoff Oversight Probe schedule and context. Shadow probes run at the first strong-agent step after handoff and at every third step thereafter. At every strong-agent step, including steps without a probe, the executed action is appended to the weak model’s history in that model’s own action format, so that each probe conditions on the actual trajectory rather than on the pre-handoff context. A probe calls the weak agent’s own action-generation routine, with its usual system prompt, tool schema, and image history, and does not invoke the Manager. The candidate action is logged for analysis but never executed or shown to the strong agent. Shadow threshold. 𝜏sh is the 90th percentile of the pooled per-step runtime scores over the 99-task reference pool, computed separately for each backbone. It is derived directly from the reference pool rather than from the escalation thresholds. For EvoCUA-8B,

It is derived directly from the reference pool rather than from the escalation thresholds. For EvoCUA-8B, the in-sample value (+1.7309) is close to the corresponding out-of-fold value (+1.7106). Checkpoint budget. At most six checkpoints can fire in an episode. In addition, once two checkpoints have changed the strong agent’s action, further firings are suppressed; checkpoints that leave the action unchanged do not count toward this second limit. Because probes occur every three steps, consecutive checkpoints are at least three steps apart. Checkpoint mechanics. When a checkpoint fires, the strong agent’s conversation is truncated to its length at the start of the current step, which removes the pending action; the neutral checkpoint message in Figure 7 is appended; and the strong agent re-decides the step with a raised reasoning- effort setting. The weak model’s candidate action is deliberately excluded from the checkpoint message, so the strong agent is never steered toward a specific action proposed by the weaker model. 20

text: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents B. Additional Experimental Results B.1. Experimental Details Evaluation setting. We evaluate on OSWorld with screenshot observations and a shared budget of 50 actions per task. The lightweight backbones are EvoCUA-8B (Xue et al., 2026), Qwen3.5- 35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni (30B-A3B) (Deshmukh et al., 2026), and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026a) serves as both the Manager and strong executor, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025) is an additional always-on reference. The always-on references run the strong model alone, without the Manager, so they measure strong- model capability without the Manager or escalation framework. Configurations and evaluation sets. Manager adds subgoal planning and verification; Escalation further enables initial and runtime handoff; and LEASH additionally enables post-handoff Shadow monitoring and corresponding intervention. These configurations are cumulative. Shared results below follow Tables 1 and 4. The evaluation task pool contains 262 tasks. Reference banks and calibration. We use a held-out reference set that is disjoint from the 262 evaluation tasks. We obtain task-grouped 10-fold out-of-fold scores, keeping all observations from a task in one fold; preprocessing and estimator fitting use only the training folds. Initial scores use final task outcomes and runtime scores use Manager-assigned subgoal outcomes. Thresholds are order statistics of the held-out scores targeting a 25% initial and

text: a task in one fold; preprocessing and estimator fitting use only the training folds. Initial scores use final task outcomes and runtime scores use Manager-assigned subgoal outcomes. Thresholds are order statistics of the held-out scores targeting a 25% initial and 50% overall escalation frequency, with runtime calibration based on per-task maximum scores. Refitting slightly changes the score scale, and differences between the reference and evaluation sets can further affect the realized escalation rate; hence the observed rates (43–64%) need not exactly match the calibration targets. Post-handoff execution. After handoff, Shadow probes query the lightweight model every three strong-agent steps. Probe actions are not executed; their hidden representations provide the monitor- ing scores. Higher scores indicate greater uncertainty and can trigger an intervention that asks the strong agent to reassess its current strategy while retaining control. Cost estimation. We estimate inference cost from recorded token usage using OpenRouter reference prices, accounting for cached tokens where applicable. Total cost includes lightweight-agent, Manager, strong-executor, and monitoring calls. For locally served models, we report reference inference-cost estimates rather than measured hardware costs. Performance varies across backbones and execution stages, with pooled LDA providing the strongest overall discrimination in most settings. Because thresholds are quantiles of this same pool, a small bank also gives coarse control of the realized escalation rate. 21

text: Reinforcement learning can align visual generators with reward signals beyond their pretraining objectives, but existing score-function methods typically intro- duce stochasticity by perturbing the reverse denoising trajectory, leading to costly rollout-based optimization. We instead ask whether stochastic exploration can be introduced inside the generator while preserving its original sampler. Routing Policy Optimization (RPO) answers this question by turning attention routing into a stochastic exploration action. At a few selected denoising levels, each query block keeps its own block and samples further key blocks in proportion to the generator’s native attention mass, or keeps dense attention. The sampled route perturbs the velocity of that transition, and a Gaussian likelihood around the dense velocity scores the perturbation with a score-function objective. RPO further uses a controlled two-rollout estimator: two rollouts share the same prompt, initial latent, routed denoising levels, and dense anchor layers, differing only in their sampled attention routes. Their reward difference provides an advantage signal for the routed transitions. Because the likelihood differentiates the dense velocity itself, the learned updates remain effective after routing is removed. At inference, RPO restores dense attention and retains the original deterministic sampler. Experiments on text-to-image and text-to-video generation show that RPO improves generation quality while achieving nearly 4× higher training efficiency than Flow-GRPO-style methods. Please see our project page for visual results. 1

text: Diffusion and flow models now generate high-quality images and videos from natural-language prompts (Shen et al., 2026b; Li & Wang, 2026). DDPM establishes stochastic reverse denoising, while DDIM exposes a deterministic sampling path under the same training objective (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021). Flow matching and rectified flow instead learn vector fields for continuous transport (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2024). In parallel, latent diffusion, Diffusion Transformers, and video diffusion models make high-resolution visual generation tractable at scale (Rombach et al., 2021; Peebles & Xie, 2022; Yang et al., 2024; Wan Team et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). Learned preference models then expose alignment objectives beyond likelihood and reconstruction (Xu et al., 2023; Kirstain et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025). Online reinforcement learning can optimize these objectives, but its central bottleneck is the policy. DDPO and DPOK treat stochastic denoising transitions as actions (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023). Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO extend this construction to deterministic flow models by converting their ODE samplers into stochastic SDEs (Liu et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2025b). Temporal windows, shared branches, and one-step updates reduce the resulting rollout cost (Li et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; He et al., 2026), while dense credit and

If we group neighboring tokens into blocks, each query block can attend to a sampled subset of key blocks instead of all of them as dense attention does. text: Reward alignment methods for visual generators differ mainly in where the learning signal enters the generator. We organize prior work along this axis, from the sampler trajectory to the attention computation. Sampler-space policy gradients. DDPO and DPOK first treated stochastic denoising transitions as policy actions (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023). Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO carried this view to flow matching and video by converting the deterministic sampler into an SDE and estimating group-relative advantages (Liu et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2025b). Follow-up work lowers the cost of these stochastic trajectories. Temporal windows, shared-prefix branches, and one-step updates reduce the number or cost of stochastic transitions (Li et al., 2025a;b; He et al., 2026). TempFlow-GRPO concentrates stochasticity at designated branch points for temporal credit assignment (He et al., 2025), and TAGRPO aligns trajectories that start from identical initial noise (Wang et al., 2026). Dense temporal and spatial credit or regulated clipping further improve how a terminal reward shapes each transition (Deng et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025a). These methods keep the action inside the sampler, so exploration still perturbs the reverse trajectory. Objectives without sampler actions. A second family avoids sampler actions. Direct reward fine- tuning backpropagates through differentiable image or video rewards (Clark et al., 2023; Prabhudesai et

text: keep the action inside the sampler, so exploration still perturbs the reverse trajectory. Objectives without sampler actions. A second family avoids sampler actions. Direct reward fine- tuning backpropagates through differentiable image or video rewards (Clark et al., 2023; Prabhudesai et al., 2024). For black-box rewards, DiffusionNFT, DGPO, and advantage-weighted matching replace reverse-trajectory likelihoods with forward-process or preference objectives (Zheng et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2025a). Adjoint matching, ELBO surrogates, path-space value gradients, and velocity matching pursue the same goal through native regression targets (Bergmeister et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026c; Choi et al., 2026). For few-step generators, a hybrid scheme combines distribution matching, GRPO on stochastic intermediate transitions, and reward backpropagation through the final step (Huang et al., 2026). Offline preference optimization removes online rollouts altogether, ranging from Diffusion-DPO to multidimensional and temporally dense video preferences (Wallace et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; 2025b; Wu et al., 2025b). These objectives leave inference untouched, but they give up an explicit sampled action. In contrast, RPO keeps a score-function policy with a recorded action and places that action inside attention. Its action is a block route sampled from native attention mass inside a bidirectional diffusion transformer, its Gaussian velocity likelihood updates the dense generator, and the route disappears before inference. 3 PRELIMINARIES RPO fine-tunes a pretrained visual generator that already has a deterministic sampler. This section fixes the notation for the sampler and the reward, introduces attention over token blocks, and defines where RPO routes attention. Denoising trajectory and reward. Let c denote a text prompt, and let N denote both the number of denoising transitions and the largest noise level. Rollout i starts from Gaussian noise and follows the deterministic sampler: τi = (xN i , xN−1 i , . . . , x0 i ), xN i ∼N(0, I), yi = Dec(x0 i ). (1) Here τi is the reverse trajectory, and the noise level t ∈{N, . . . , 0} decreases during generation. Each transition is an Euler step of the learned velocity field, xt−1 i = xt i + ∆t vθ(xt i, t, c), where vθ is the velocity predicted by the generator with trainable parameters θ and ∆t < 0 is the step of the noise schedule. The frozen decoder Dec maps the terminal latent x0 i to the visual output yi, which is an image or a video. A black-box reward model Rd then scores the output on reward dimension d, giving ri,d = Rd(yi, c). Training uses these reward values but never differentiates through Rd. Attention over token blocks. The generator is a diffusion transformer that splits each latent into M visual tokens, one per spatial patch of an image or spatiotemporal patch of a video. In every self-attention layer and head, each token emits a query, a key, and a value vector. The attention weights of a query are a softmax over its scaled inner products with the keys. Dense attention lets every query attend to every key. Block-sparse attention coarsens this pattern. It arranges the tokens in a sequence, cuts the sequence into Q contiguous token blocks of B tokens, and applies a binary block mask µ ∈{0, 1}Q×Q. A query token in block q attends only to the key tokens of blocks j with µq,j = 1, and its softmax renormalizes over those keys. We order the tokens along a locality-preserving Gilbert curve, so each block is a compact image or video patch, and both generators use B = 128. We call the set of key blocks that query block q keeps its route, and the choice of routes routing. Sparse-attention methods choose routes to save computation. RPO instead samples routes as its exploration action during training and restores dense attention at inference. Routing sites and units. Routing acts at a small fixed set of noise levels Troute ⊆{1, . . . , N}, the routed levels, which every rollout shares. These are early levels, where a route can still change the final output, and every other level runs dense attention. At each routed level, every query block makes one routing decision, and all routed attention layers and heads apply it. A random subset of transformer blocks, the anchor layers, stays dense at each routed level. A routing unit is one such decision, namely the route of query block q at level t, written u = (t, q). text: Preprint 6 DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS RPO places its policy action inside attention, and this design choice also defines its current limits. First, the framework is confined to attention. Its action is a mask over key-value blocks, so it requires a backbone that computes attention. We have not yet generalized routing to other architectures, where no attention mass exists to propose routes. Second, the routing proposal and its likelihood are coarse. Each route logit averages the attention mass of a whole block over every routed layer and head, which hides token-level and layer-specific structure. Moreover, the velocity likelihood treats the routed deviation as Gaussian, although a discrete route produces it. A finer proposal and a likelihood that also credits the route choice could give the policy a more faithful view of which blocks matter. Finally, RPO currently adapts to an existing generator rather than shaping it. Co-designing the network architecture with RPO is a promising direction for achieving both higher efficiency and larger RL gains. 7
title: Preprint

text: In this work, we addressed the cost of online reinforcement learning for visual generators without perturbing their reverse denoising trajectories. We introduced Routing Policy Optimization, a sampler- preserving method that samples block-wise attention routes from the generator’s native attention mass at a few selected denoising levels. A controlled pair holds the non-routing generation context fixed, so its reward difference weights a Gaussian velocity likelihood of the two recorded routed trajectories. Because this likelihood updates the dense velocity field, inference removes the masks and restores dense attention under the original deterministic sampler. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3.5 and Wan2.2 demonstrate improved reward-aligned quality across text-to-image and text-to-video generation while requiring substantially less training compute than sampler-space baselines. By moving stochastic exploration from the sampler into attention, RPO provides an efficient policy interface for reward-aligned visual generation without altering the inference process.

Let the visual latent contain F frames of H × W tokens, so it holds M = FHW tokens. Token p = (f, m, n) lies in frame f ∈{0, . . . , F −1}, row m, and column n. Bidirectional attention. Both generators denoise all visual tokens jointly with bidirectional self- attention, so every query can attend to every frame. The order therefore depends only on the latent grid and not on a generation schedule. We compute it once per resolution and reuse it for all routed layers, heads, noise levels, and rollouts. Reordering inside attention. The order acts only inside each routed self-attention layer. After the native projections, query-key normalization, and rotary position embedding where the generator uses one, we permute the queries, keys, and values into Gilbert order. We then apply the routed mask and permute the output back to raster order. Dense attention is equivariant to a shared permutation of its queries, keys, and values, and every positional signal is attached before the permutation. The reordering thus changes which token pairs share a routing decision, but it leaves positions and the dense computation unchanged. text: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards Helena Merker, Nick Walker, Andreea Bobu Massachusetts Institute of Technology {hmerker, nswalker, abobu}@mit.edu Abstract: Reward learning typically assumes the human’s input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features—or aspects of the task—better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn’t know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human’s attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to

text: When a human teaches a robot how to do a task, not every relevant aspect of the task—or feature— gets equal attention. For instance, while teaching a robot how to carry a knife across your cluttered kitchen, you might do a good job avoiding the hot stovetop or the rack hanging overhead, but struggle to consistently keep the knife away from every person or obstacle. Because humans have limited working memory and can’t focus on everything at once [1, 2], some features get carefully attended to while others are left underspecified. Recent work shows how the robot can detect, directly from its teaching data, which features were poorly supervised or entirely irrelevant to the task [3, 4]. We go a step further and ask: how should the robot work with the human to resolve that underspecification? One approach is to ask the human for more demonstrations focused on the underspecified fea- tures [3]. But this places the burden on the human, who already struggled with attending to those features. We propose to shift this burden onto the robot: rather than ask the human to try again, the robot should itself ask targeted questions that resolve what it is uncertain about. Preference queries, where the robot generates behavior options and the human just picks their pre- ferred one, offer this kind
title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active

text: ask the human to try again, the robot should itself ask targeted questions that resolve what it is uncertain about. Preference queries, where the robot generates behavior options and the human just picks their pre- ferred one, offer this kind of low-effort channel [5, 6, 7]. Active learning approaches select queries to maximally reduce uncertainty under a distribution over the human’s reward [6]. But when that distribution is initialized from imperfect teaching data [8], it inherits not just what the feedback got right but also its errors on the underspecified features. The robot then spends its early queries correcting a misaligned distribution before it can make progress on what it actually needs to learn. 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin TX, USA. arXiv:2610.22285v1 [cs.RO] 15 Oct 2026

First, we use it to build an informed prior over the human’s reward: a Gaussian that is confident on the well-supervised features, flat on the underspecified ones, and near zero on irrelevant ones. This ensures preference queries are automatically directed at what needs resolving. Second, we use it to supplement each query with an explanation that tells the human which features to focus on when answering, making the robot’s learning process transparent [9]. In Fig. 1, the robot communicates uncertainty about distance to human, and its query presents two options that vary along that feature. Together, these two components align what the robot asks with what the human attends to. Our contributions are: (1) an informed prior for active preference learning that corrects what the teaching data got wrong, automatically targeting queries at the underspecified features; (2) an ex- planation mechanism that directs the human’s attention to those same features when answering, aligning what the robot asks with what the human attends to; and (3) empirical validation in two simulated 7-DoF manipulation domains and a user study, where both components independently improve reward recovery and amplify each other, with
