text: Learning from Imperfect Teaching Reward learning from human feedback typically assumes the teacher is optimal or noisily optimal [10, 11], but human input is routinely suboptimal. Some methods build richer models of the human, capturing systematic or structured deviations from opti- mality [12, 13]. Others treat suboptimality as localized failures of supervision rather than uniform noise: the robot reasons about how well its hypothesis space explains the human’s input and flags what it cannot account for [14, 15, 16], or detects from the teaching data which features were well- supervised versus underspecified [3, 4, 17]. Rather than resolving the diagnosed gap by requesting more data, we use the diagnosis to drive active preference queries, shifting resolution onto the robot. Active Preference Elicitation Preference queries, which ask the human to choose between trajec- tories, are a low-effort channel for reward learning. The robot can select each query to maximize information gain, minimizing the comparisons the human must answer [6]. Prior work extends this loop in various ways: warm-starting the reward belief from demonstrations [8], enriching queries to ask which features make a trajectory preferable [7], and using language models to select queries and ease answering [18]. text: 3 Problem Setup We address the problem of learning a reward function from human input when the teaching signal leaves some features underspecified. Recent work shows that robots can detect underspecified fea- tures from statistical patterns in the teaching data [3]. We use this detection and ask: how should the robot resolve underspecified features? We propose using that knowledge in two ways: to correct the imperfect posterior into an informed prior, and to direct human attention during preference queries. 3.1 Preliminaries The robot’s goal is to learn a reward function that captures how the human wants the task performed. We adopt a linear reward parameterization [10, 11] over state features. Let ϕ : S →Rk be a feature mapping that extracts a k-dimensional vector from each state s ∈S, and let w ∈Rk be the reward weight vector with ∥w∥2 ≤1. The per-state reward is Rw(s) = w⊤ϕ(s), and the cumulative reward of a trajectory ξ = (s0, s1, . . . , sT ) ∈Ξ aggregates state-level contributions Rw(ξ) = P st∈ξ w⊤ϕ(st) = w⊤ϕ(ξ), where ϕ(ξ) = P st∈ξ ϕ(st) accumulates features along the trajectory. The features ϕ may be hand-crafted [11], learned [19], or extracted from a large language model given a high-level task description [20]; we assume access to a candidate feature set. 3.2 An Imperfect Posterior We assume the robot has access to a dataset D of human teaching data, and maintains a posterior P(w | D) ∝P(D | w) P(w) over the reward weights. In general, the likelihood P(D | w) can be instantiated for any teaching modality D, including demonstrations [10, 11], preferences [5, 8], corrections [21], or natural language [22]. For exposition, we follow DemPref [8] and initialize the reward belief from Boltzmann-rational demonstrations [23, 24, 25], which we then refine with pref- erence queries. The resulting posterior P(w | D) is rarely uniform in quality across the components of w. Teaching a task that requires attending to multiple objectives at once is cognitively demanding; humans inevitably focus on some features at the expense of others. The demonstrations are thus not driven by w⋆equally across all features, leaving the posterior misleading along the underspecified dimensions. [3] we inherit the variance-based detection of underspecified features and the LLM-based filtering of task-irrelevant ones, which together partition the k features into three disjoint subsets, collectively denoted by the partition o: 1) ϕo: the task-relevant features that are well-optimized in D, 2) ϕu: the task-relevant features that are underspecified, and 3) ϕε: the features irrelevant to the task. We write wo, wu, wε for the blocks of w corresponding to ϕo, ϕu, ϕε. Refining the Prior with Active Feedback The partition o summarizes what D reveals: P(w | D) is trustworthy on ϕo, misleading on ϕu, and uninformative on ϕε. Our goal is to elicit additional human feedback that sharpens our estimate of w⋆along the underspecified dimensions. One ap- proach is to passively request additional demonstrations of the features in ϕu, returning the burden of producing behavior that exercises those features to the human [3]. Instead, we adopt an active preference learning framework [6], where the robot itself generates queries to resolve its uncertainty. Standard active preference learning [6] uses P(w | D) as the prior; however, its deficiencies in ϕu and ϕε force early queries to first correct the prior before they can resolve the underspecified features. We use o in two ways to address this. First, we construct a corrected distribution P(w | o) by modifying P(w | D) block-wise: retaining what D revealed about ϕo, flattening the prior on ϕu, and concentrating it near zero on ϕε (see Sec. 4.1). We use P(w | o) as the prior for active preference learning, directing the robot’s queries at its uncertainty along ϕu (Sec. 4.2). Second, we adapt the explanation of Merker et al. [3], reframed to instruct the human to attend to ϕu when answering queries, so that their responses inform the specific features that need resolving (Sec. 4.3). 3

text: 4 Method Our approach reuses the robot’s diagnosis of which features past teaching left underspecified to elicit targeted preference feedback. First, we construct an informed prior P(w | o) that corrects P(w | D) block-wise, concentrating uncertainty on ϕu. Second, we pair each query with an explanation that focuses the human’s attention on ϕu when answering, so their responses inform those features. 4.1 The Informed Prior We now describe how to construct P(w | o) in place of the standard initialization from P(w | D). We want a corrected version of P(w | D) that leaves ϕo untouched, is uninformative on ϕu, and concentrates near zero on ϕε. This requires a parametric form for P(w | D) amenable to block-wise edits. We represent P(w | D) as a Gaussian, whose parameters we modify to obtain P(w | o). Gaussian Approximation To approximate P(w | D), we draw samples via Metropolis-Hastings with the unnormalized posterior P(D | w) P(w) [6], and fit a Gaussian N(µ, Σ) to them. This yields the best Gaussian summary of P(w | D), i.e. the closest in KL divergence [26]. Inspired by the Boltzmann rationality model used for demonstrations [23, 3], we introduce a per-query, per-feature rationality vector βi ∈Rk ≥0 that controls how much each feature influences the human’s response. (5) Because the informed prior P(w | o) is flat on wu and tightly constrained on wo and wε, uncertainty concentrates along wu. The information gain criterion therefore automatically directs queries toward trajectories that differ along ϕu, which are the components we intend for the preferences to inform. 4.3 Directing Attention with Explanations The second use of o is directing the person’s attention during preference queries. The partition o is a record of what past teaching revealed, i.e. which features were well-optimized, underspecified, or irrelevant. We now repurpose it as prospective guidance, telling the human which features to attend to when answering queries. In that sense, o determines βi, the rationality vector that governs how the human’s response enters the likelihood. Without an explanation, the human is assumed to attend to every feature equally, corresponding to βi = β01, with the same positive value β0 on every component. Alternatively, the robot can provide an explanation that directs the human’s attention to the underspecified features ϕu (e.g., “I’m uncertain about how to handle

Alternatively, the robot can provide an explanation that directs the human’s attention to the underspecified features ϕu (e.g., “I’m uncertain about how to handle [features in ϕu]. Please focus on these features when comparing the two trajectories.”). This is how o determines βi: features in ϕu receive rationality β0 while ϕo and ϕε are zeroed out, giving βu i = β01 and βo i = βε i = 0. The Bradley-Terry probability in Equation 2—and hence the likelihood P(P | w, o) in Equation 3— then depends on w only through wu. The trajectories therefore enter the query only through their ϕu features, so a query whose two trajectories agree on those features produces no information at all. 5 Simulated Experiments We evaluate our method in simulation, comparing the informed prior against four alternative priors, a targeted query objective, random querying, and three attention-directing explanation variants. 5.1 Experimental Setup We use two scenes wherein a 7-DoF Jaco arm carries an object above a cluttered surface (Fig. 2a–b). Methods (1) Informed Prior constructs P(w | o) by block-wise modification of a Gaussian ap- proximation of P(w | D). The active query loop targets P(w | P, o) and selects queries by infor- mation gain. (2) Informed Prior + Informed Explanation further sets ϕexp to the predicted ϕu, so the human attends to the same features the prior leaves unconstrained. (3) Oracle Prior uses the true set of underspecified features. (4) Oracle Prior + Oracle Explanation further sets ϕexp to the true underspecified features. (5) Extra-Only Prior is a version of the informed prior that does not predict underspecified features. It combines the predicted irrelevant features ϕε, represented as a diagonal Gaussian, with the demonstration likelihood. (6) Standard models posterior P(w | P, D) by com- bining the demonstration likelihood with a uniform prior over the unit ball and selects queries by information gain. (7) Standard + Oracle Explanation sets ϕexp to the true underspecified features, isolating the contribution of the explanation alone. The 2×2 within-subjects de- sign crossed the prior (uninformed vs. informed) with the query delivery (no explanation vs. expla- nation), yielding four conditions: (1) Uninformed, (2) Informed, (3) Uninformed + Explanation and (4) Informed + Explanation. For each condition, participants were told the four task objectives: keep the mug upright, stay close to the table, stay away from the laptop, and stay away from the human. Participants were shown three trajectories chosen under the ground-truth reward, followed by 10 preference queries for each of two tasks, one with laptop initially underspecified and the

text: the table, stay away from the laptop, and stay away from the human. Participants were shown three trajectories chosen under the ground-truth reward, followed by 10 preference queries for each of two tasks, one with laptop initially underspecified and the other with human. The explanation conditions prefaced each task’s preference queries with a natural language explanation that named the underspecified feature. All conditions used the ground-truth partition o, leaving the prior and the explanation as the only factors that vary. Reward inference ran online: the posterior was re-sampled after every response, so queries adapted to each participant’s earlier an- swers. We rendered queries in simulation because executing arbitrary trajectories is unsafe without a filter [29], and with a filter the robot only shows acceptable behavior. Reward models calibrated on such data over-reward the behaviors humans reject [30]. Participants answered six 7-point Likert items after each task (see Appendix C), completed the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) [31] after each condition, and ranked the four conditions by preference at the end. We recruited N = 12 participants (9 female, 2 male, 1 preferred not to say; age M = 23.8, SD = 2.3). text: Feedback Our approach assumes that preference queries resolve under- specification with less effort than additional demonstrations. To test this, we compared NASA-TLX responses from our study’s explanation conditions against existing data from Merker et al. [3], where a separate cohort of participants gave corrective kinesthetic demonstrations in response to natural- language explanations (N = 12 each, between subjects). Physical demand was lower for prefer- ence queries (M = 3.8, SE = 1.9) than for kinesthetic demonstrations (M = 31.7, SE = 6.9; t(12.6) = 3.89, p = 0.002). Overall workload was also lower (M = 17.4 vs. M = 24.2), though not significantly (t(22.0) = 1.31, p = 0.205), and the gap shrinks once physical demand is excluded (M = 20.1 vs. M = 22.7; t(21.3) = 0.45, p = 0.658). Preference queries thus remove the physical cost of kinesthetic teaching, while we found no evidence of increased cognitive workload. 7 Real Robot Examples We use a Franka Emika FR3 arm carrying a knife in a kitchen (Fig. 2c). text: We present an approach for resolving underspecification in reward learning that shifts the burden from the human to the robot. Our insight is that the same information that indicates which features were underspecified can also be used to ask better questions about them. The robot uses this di- agnosis to shape an informed prior for active preference learning and prefaces its queries with an explanation that directs the human’s attention to those features. In simulation and in a user study, the informed prior recovers the true reward faster than standard active preference learning. Limitations The method takes the feature partition as input, so errors in the upstream diagnosis propagate into the informed prior. Updating the partition online as preferences arrive is a natural extension we leave to future work. We also summarize the demonstration-derived posterior as a Gaussian, discarding its higher-order structure. The attention scheme is similarly coarse: each query either directs the human’s attention exclusively to the underspecified features or gives no explanation at all. As features become resolved, the human’s attention should expand to allow later queries to also inform the well-optimized features. Softening the attention model is simple to simulate, but when and how much to broaden, and whether changing the instruction mid-task erodes ease and understanding, requires substantial human validation that we leave to future work.

text: A Experimental Details Identifying Irrelevant Features The candidate feature set ϕ is not guaranteed to be task-relevant in its entirety. Features that have no bearing on the task carry no signal in D, so the demonstration- derived posterior along these dimensions is shaped not by the human’s intent but by spurious corre- lations in the data. We use an LLM to identify these features. For each candidate feature ϕl, we issue N independent queries to the LLM. Each query supplies the task description and the full candidate feature set, and asks the model to label ϕl as either relevant or irrelevant. If a majority of the N responses vote irrelevant, we assign ϕl to ϕε and record the LLM’s confidence as cl ∈[0.5, 1], the fraction of the N responses that voted irrelevant. Sec. 4.1 defines the prior’s precision on ϕε as ˜Λεε = diag �(λl)l∈ϕε , so each λl ≥0 controls how tightly the prior pulls wl toward zero. λl should match the concentration of P(w | D) on wo when the LLM is fully confident that ϕl is irrelevant, and weaken when the LLM is less confident. C User Study Details Procedure After providing informed consent, participants were familiarized with the task and the preference-query interface. They were told that the robot was learning to carry a mug of coffee across a cluttered table and that it had not yet learned to do so correctly. text: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems Omar Adalat Imperial College London London, United Kingdom o.adalat24@imperial.ac.uk Edwin Hamel-De le Court University of Manchester Manchester, United Kingdom edwin.hamel- delecourt@manchester.ac.uk Francesco Belardinelli Imperial College London London, United Kingdom francesco.belardinelli@imperial.ac.uk
title: Learning Rational Strategies

text: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces (pltl𝑓). We impose solution con- cepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as con- straints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent’s probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy pro- file – if one exists – such that (i) the designated agent’s probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a sta- ble solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify sat- isfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algo- rithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for tem- poral objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games. Keywords Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, General-Sum Games, Rational Learning, Probabilistic Temporal Objectives 1
title: Learning Rational Strategies

text: Strategic reasoning in multi-agent systems (MAS) hinges on de- termining what outcomes groups of agents (termed coalitions) can bring about through their interactions. In many multi-agent settings, especially safety-critical systems, properties of interest go beyond plain reward signals and include temporally extended goals such as reachability/liveness (e.g., eventually reaching a tar- get region or completing a mission), or safety invariants (e.g., al- ways avoid unsafe regions, or never violate constraints) [4, 23]. Similar objectives are naturally captured by temporal logics [38] which provide precise languages and semantics to specify and ver- ify such properties. Languages relevant to specification of strate- gic properties include Alternating-Time Temporal Logic (atl [3]), Dynamic Coalition Logic [22], Probabilistic Alternating-𝜇Calcu- lus [47], Game Description Logic (gdl [16]), and See-To-It-That (stit [7]). However, such logics typically resolve non-determinism by restricting to coalitional modalities which aim to universally and unilaterally (inevitably) force a property to be true. On the other hand, rational synthesis [20, 52] aims to find strate- gies that are self-enforcing through stable equilibria, instead of quantifying against all possible behaviour (including irrational be- haviour) by other agents who have their own objectives. Therefore, rational synthesis is typically less conservative than adversarial synthesis. title: Learning Rational Strategies

text: other agents who have their own objectives. Therefore, rational synthesis is typically less conservative than adversarial synthesis. Settings we consider can be represented formally as (general- sum) stochastic games, which model multiple decision-making agents that interact over time in a dynamic environment with probabilistic behaviours. Each agent repeatedly selects an action, and the combination of agents’ non-deterministic choices and the environment’s probabilistic transitions determines the evolution of the game. Stochastic games have been applied in domains as diverse as cybersecurity [60], epidemics [29], auctions [39], and routing in stochastic traffic networks [59]. We use an expressive specification style in which each agent has its own probabilistic temporal objective as a logical formula inter- preted on finite traces. Finite traces have a natural correspondence with reinforcement learning (RL) as tasks are often trained and executed episodically. Rationality is captured by imposing that the learned joint strategy profile satisfies a specific solution concept (e.g., (𝜀-)Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium), where each agent’s payoff reflects the preferred direction of its satisfaction probability. Our approach emphasises learning a single committed strategy profile, allowing tractability by not requiring an explicit transition model of the underlying stochastic game which gener- ally grows combinatorially with respect to the number of agents involved. Our contributions are as follows: (i) We formulate a learning-based rational-synthesis objective for finite-horizon sto- chastic games in which each agent has a probabilistic ltl𝑓objective and utilities encode the preferred direction of satisfaction probabil- ities; (ii) We compile per-agent ltl𝑓objectives into deterministic reward automata and show that terminal automaton rewards have expectation equal to satisfaction probability; (iii) We provide theo- retical analysis for the reward-automaton encoding, discounting effects, finite-sample satisfaction certification, and finite-horizon equilibrium existence and convergence; (iv) We evaluate satisfac- tion and strategic stability on 8 benchmark environment instances. We use Prob- abilistic ltl𝑓(pltl𝑓) [37] to specify each agent’s probabilistic tem- poral objective on finite traces, matching the episodic structure of RL tasks. The transition probabilities are unknown, and strategies are learned through episodic interaction with the environment. We investigate model-free MARL approaches in which agents concurrently learn strategies towards their respective synthesis objectives. For each agent, a deterministic finite automa- ton (DFA) tracks whether the labelled trace of an episode satisfies the ltl𝑓path formula inside its probabilistic constraint. Its state summarises the history relevant to that formula and is updated as each new state label is read. At episode end, its accepting states identify successful traces, and averaging these binary out- comes estimates satisfaction probability. For example, existence of 𝜀-NE for general 𝑛-player concurrent reachability games remains an open question [10]. In the finite-horizon case, however, existence is classical: every finite extensive-form game with perfect recall has a subgame-perfect equilibrium [45], and a Markov one is obtained by backward induction, solving at each state and remaining time the one-shot stage game whose payoffs are the continuation values, which has a mixed equilibrium by Nash’s theorem [40] (see e.g., [21]). text: We provide an extended review of related work in Appendix F, but summarise the most relevant works here. Hahn et al. consider verify- ing minimax objectives using the logic patl, although they consider a model checking problem rather than a synthesis problem as they allow relabelling, and only allow an objective considered between a single coalition and its complement. A closely related model-based tools is PRISM-Games [33], which supports verification and strat- egy synthesis for rpatl-style probabilistic and reward objectives in stochastic games, including multi-objective and equilibrium-based extensions [31, 32, 34]. These methods assume explicit transition models. Varricchione et al. construct a reward machine from an atl specification, but their approach assumes a fully cooperative grand coalition, which in turn allows delegating to reward ma- chines generated for individual agents. Hu et al. consider reward machines for stochastic games, but are limited to exact Nash equi- libria, non-quantitative specifications, and two-player general-sum games. Jothimurugan et al. provide a bespoke enumerate-and-verify procedure for a non-probabilistic task specification language that is designed exclusively for equilibria with high social welfare. Ham- mond et al. studied temporal-logic reward optimisation of a sum of probabilities, but restricted their analysis to cooperative MARL. Our use of equilibrium constraints is inspired by classical rational synthesis [14, 20, 52]. Subramanian et al. study reward-machine based learning in general-sum

text: al. studied temporal-logic reward optimisation of a sum of probabilities, but restricted their analysis to cooperative MARL. Our use of equilibrium constraints is inspired by classical rational synthesis [14, 20, 52]. Subramanian et al. study reward-machine based learning in general-sum stochastic games, proposing CROM and QROM, which combine counterfactual experience updates over reward-machine states with opponent modelling and provide tab- ular convergence and finite-time guarantees for Nash Q-values under additional assumptions. However, our paper deals with prob- abilistic thresholds rather than discounted rewards. We provide sampling-based certification guarantees and bounds on discounting effects, as well as equilibrium stability and convergence analysis. 6 Conclusions and Future Work Our approach targets multiple strategic agents, each equipped with its own probabilistic temporal-logic objective in pltl𝑓over finite traces. Each agent seeks a strategy satisfying its own probabilistic threshold within a profile that is stable under a chosen equilibrium notion (solution concept), interpreted over the utilities induced by the probabilistic requirements. Compared to existing approaches, our work focuses on model- free strategy synthesis in a learning setting, without requiring known transition dynamics. This allows considering objectives beyond those that a strategic coalition can unilaterally enforce, as required by logics such as atl and patl. We analyse how dis- counting affects the learning of probabilistic objectives, establish conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, and provide

text: objectives beyond those that a strategic coalition can unilaterally enforce, as required by logics such as atl and patl. We analyse how dis- counting affects the learning of probabilistic objectives, establish conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, and provide algorithm-agnostic finite-sample certificates of objec- tive satisfaction. Future work could target nested probabilistic properties and the undiscounted infinite-horizon case for 𝜔-regular properties, which would require learning maximal end components [11, 24], although this is non-trivial as end components for multi-agent sys- tems depend on the dynamics of other agents. Another extension of interest could be evaluating different solution concepts, such as a jointly satisficing objective [43]. It may also be worth investigating confidence-aware equilibrium selection with Nash-Q; however this introduces statistical noise into the selector and non-local depen- dence across states. D Technical Details D.1 Counterfactual Experience Replay We apply CER separately to each agent’s deterministic reward automaton. We append the automaton-state identifier to the agent’s observation and store the successor-state propositions at each step. Relabelling keeps the environment rollout fixed and recomputes the automaton states from alternative start states. We keep the original sample and discard duplicate relabellings. Our procedure adapts Voloshin et al. [54] to finite-trace ltl𝑓. In particular, our deterministic finite automata require no 𝜀-jump transitions used with Büchi automata in ltl, and rewards depend on acceptance at episode termination instead of repeated visits to Büchi accepting states.

text: F Extended Literature Review Probabilistic Strategic Logics and Synthesis Tools. Hahn et al. [25] translate reachability-normal patl objectives into rewards for Min- imax Q-Learning. Their model-checking procedure recursively re- labels states for nested modalities, rather than finding one strategy witnessing all subformulae. It considers a single coalition in turn- based games. Bozkurt et al. [8] similarly study model-free learning for ltl objectives in two-player turn-based zero-sum games, using deterministic Rabin automata. The zero-sum fragments of PRISM-Games [31] synthesise strategies for probabilistic and reward-based rpatl objectives from known transition models. Single- and multi-objective properties concern one coalition against its complement; where optimal strategies need not exist [12], the tool computes 𝜀-approximations of Pareto-optimal strategies. Equilibrium-based extensions synthesise subgame-perfect, social-welfare-optimal Nash equilibria in concurrent stochastic games [32–34], also assuming known models. Varricchione et al. [53] construct reward machines from atl specifications for a fully cooperative grand coalition. Rational Synthesis. Rational synthesis [20, 52] considers agents pursuing their own temporal goals. Fisman et al. [20] reduce ltl rational synthesis to satisfiability in Extended Strategy Logic, ob- taining 2EXPTIME-completeness for dominant-strategy, Nash and subgame-perfect solution concepts. Ummels [52] study pure strategies in infinite multiplayer turn-based games with 𝜔-regular objectives, establishing exis- tence, payoff-constrained decision procedures and finite-state implementations for subgame-perfect Nash equilibria. Condurache et al. [14] study complexity refinements and cooperative and non-cooperative variants.

Condurache et al. [14] study complexity refinements and cooperative and non-cooperative variants. Our setting combines per-agent probabilistic ltl𝑓requirements with learning from unknown dynamics under a single committed profile. Policy Space Response Oracles [35] instead train approxi- mate best responses against a meta-strategy over a policy popula- tion. Rational Verification. Rational verification [58] asks whether a temporal property holds on some or all equilibrium behaviours. Equilibrium Logic expresses such properties through modalities [NE] and ⟨NE⟩over Nash-equilibrium computations. Model check- ing is 2EXPTIME-hard in general, with matching upper bounds for restricted fragments. Commitment-aware Logics. Strategy Logic (sl) explicitly quanti- fies and binds strategies, subsumes atl⋆, and can express equilib- rium through stability against deviations. Model checking for full sl is decidable but non-elementary. Extensions of atl evaluate nested formulas under previously selected strategies, including strategy contexts (atlsc) [15], explicit strategies (atles) [55], and irrevocable semantics [2]. text: Improving Environment-Agnostic Coding Agents: The Role of Scaffolding Sergey Rodionov SingularityNET
title: Improving Environment-Agnostic Coding Agents:

text: Stronger language models may increasingly construct useful procedures for themselves, reducing the advantage of developer-supplied scaffolding. We investigate why this advantage persists and whether an environment-agnostic agent can be improved without environment- specific engineering. We evaluate a Codex-based agent in two nearly identical prompt variants on ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze, and Terminal-Bench. Each variant is deployed with unchanged code, prompts, and general-purpose tools across environments, receiving environment-specific information as input. Changing only an instruction to encourage reporting difficulties and returning control for automatic continuation improves mean scores on both ARC-AGI-3 and AGI Maze, while Terminal-Bench shows small, mixed changes. Yet the general agent remains below an ARC-AGI-3-specific reference, including with GPT-5.6-sol. The reference prescribes organization and control rather than supplying new game rules or solutions. To investigate this gap, we transfer reset decisions to a scripted controller that follows a convention already given to the agent. This small change recovers part of the specialized agent’s advantage. A complementary AGI Maze experiment shows that additional tutorial experience can reduce performance. Together, these findings highlight the distinction between having information and tools available and using them effectively. Supplied procedures still matter for the models tested here. The performance gains also come with higher token-based cost. The experiments do not separate better use of information and procedures from additional or differently allocated inference. We

text: An LLM-based agent combines a language model with a harness: the prompts, tools, memory mechanisms, and control logic that support its interaction with an environment [1]. For this study, we distinguish three components: the backbone LLM; environment-independent scaffolding, such as shell access, a file system, and generic context management; and environment-specific scaffolding, such as controllers and observation layouts designed for a particular environment family. These components interact. A capable agent may depend heavily on its harness without requiring that harness to be environment-specific. Existing research shows that agent performance depends on how models are prompted and connected to tools. CodeAct investigates executable code as an action representation, while SWE-agent examines how agent–computer interface design affects performance [2, 3]. AgentBench and AgentGym provide multi-environment evaluation and learning frameworks, and Exgentic compares general-purpose agent architectures across heterogeneous benchmarks without per-environment task-solving customization [1, 4, 5]. Research on iterative self-refinement and test-time computation further motivates distinguishing the model from the procedures and inference used to apply it [6, 7]. We build on these lines of work by asking which benefits of scaffolding can be retained through mechanisms that remain unchanged across environments. 1 arXiv:2610.22289v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026

text: Our earlier ARC-AGI-3 studies motivate this question. The first combined executable world modeling, prompted simplification, and replay verification in a Codex-based agent [8]. The second compared textual and executable-model variants, finding that gains from model capability and reasoning effort often exceeded differences among those variants [9]. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that stronger models may increasingly construct useful task-specific procedures themselves, reducing the advantage of developer-supplied scaffolding. This possibility is related to Sutton’s emphasis on general methods that exploit increasing computation [10]. However, all variants in our earlier studies retained ARC-AGI-3-specific organization and control, leaving the contribution of that scaffolding unclear. We therefore ask two related questions. First, can an environment-agnostic agent be improved on some environments without material regressions on others? Second, with the underlying model fixed, why can changes in guidance and control improve performance without supplying new task facts or general-purpose tools? We investigate these questions using one Codex-based agent in two nearly identical prompt variants, each deployed unchanged across ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze, and Terminal-Bench. A short instruction encouraging the agent to stop and report difficulties improves mean scores on ARC- AGI-3 and AGI Maze, while Terminal-Bench shows small changes with no consistent direction. The focus is on demonstrating and studying a concrete cross-environment improvement, rather than optimizing the agent for the highest possible benchmark

Together, these experiments connect a practical improvement to a broader problem: an agent can have useful information and tools available without reliably using them effectively. Scope and approach. We use environment-agnostic to describe an unchanged agent imple- mentation, not a guarantee of success in every environment. For a given variant and model–effort configuration, its code, prompts, and initial agent-owned tools remain fixed across environments, with no developer-authored environment-specific control logic. Each environment supplies an environment description and optional files, then accepts JSON actions and returns observation files through a common interaction contract. These environment specifications are held fixed in agent comparisons. The agent may construct specialized tools or strategies during a run; the developer does not supply a different scaffold for each environment. Our environment-agnostic Baseline is a simplified version of the ARC-AGI-3-specific textual agent from our earlier study. A small scripted controller and an environment-agnostic client provide access to the task, while Codex performs the reasoning, computation, and action selection. Stop-and-report changes only one instruction, included in both the initial and continuation prompts. It encourages Codex to return control when it encounters difficulty or uncertainty. The controller resumes the same conversation with a reminder of the goal and a suggestion to reread the environment description when needed, but supplies no human feedback or task-specific advice. Both variants have access to the same reminder; the modified instruction changes when Codex is encouraged to return. We evaluate GPT-5.5 at high and xhigh reasoning effort and GPT-5.6-sol at xhigh and max. The environments span visual rule discovery in ARC-AGI-3, stateful labyrinths in AGI Maze, and practical command-line tasks in Terminal-Bench 2.1 [11–14]. AGI Maze is evaluated both as independent labyrinths and as sequences of seven tutorials followed by a target labyrinth. Findings and contribution. Stop-and-report increases mean ARC-AGI-3 Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) by 1.37–7.29 percentage points across the four configurations. Together, the prompt comparison, ARC-AGI-3 diagnostics, and tutorial experiment highlight the distinction between having useful information and tools available and using them effectively. The performance gains may reflect more effective information use, more reliable control, or additional or differently allocated inference. These effects may act together; the experiments do not separate them. We introduce EnvTraverse, an experimental framework for running and evaluating agents across interactive environments, together with the Baseline agent evaluated in this study. These are intended to support further research on improving environment-agnostic agents through better procedures or additional general capabilities. New agent variants can be compared with Baseline across environments to assess performance gains, possible regressions, and inference cost. Code and data availability. text: 2.1 General agents and cross-environment evaluation General Game Playing studies agents that receive formal descriptions of previously unspecified games and play without algorithms engineered for each game [15]. More recent work evaluates or learns language-model agents across interactive domains: AgentBench provides eight environ- ments, while AgentGym combines a multi-environment framework, interaction trajectories, and methods for agent learning and evolution [4, 5]. Our study examines changes to a Codex-based scaffold without additional model training, with each agent variant deployed unchanged across environments. Exgentic is the closest cross-environment evaluation precedent. Bandel et al. compare five agent architectures and five backbone models across six benchmarks, using protocol wrappers to integrate the original implementations without per-environment task-solving customization [1]. In their closed-source comparison, backbone choice explains more aggregate performance variation than architecture, although architecture remains consequential within a model. These approaches motivate distinguishing access to computational tools from the organization and control of their use. We examine a small change to general guidance across environments and use the ARC-AGI-3 comparisons to study the remaining benefit of supplied organization and control. 2.3 Reflection and learning from experience Self-Refine uses the same language model to generate an output, provide feedback, and revise it without additional training [6]. Reflexion generates verbal reflections from task feedback and retains them in memory for subsequent trials, also without updating model weights [24]. These methods explicitly organize how feedback is produced and reused. Benefits from reconsideration are not automatic: Huang et al. find that self-correction without external feedback can reduce performance on the reasoning tasks and models they examine [25]. Experience can also be retained as executable behavior.

Snell et al. investigate learned answer revision and verifier-guided search, finding that the relative effectiveness of inference strategies depends on problem difficulty [7]. Computation can also be extended within a single reasoning process. In s1, Muennighoff et al. fine-tune a reasoning model and use budget forcing to control generation length, including prolonging a reasoning trace when the model attempts to finish [28]. This provides an example of how an intervention around stopping can change inference expenditure and performance. These studies motivate considering both how much inference an agent performs and how it is organized. In our study, Stop-and-report changes when Codex returns to an external controller, which resumes the conversation while the environment remains active. Even with the model and reasoning-effort setting fixed, this may change how long the agent continues working and when additional inference is used. text: Environment-Agnostic Framework EnvTraverse connects agents and environments through a common interaction contract. Each environment describes the task and how to interact with it, while the agent determines how to solve the task. The same agent can be connected to different environments without modification. New agents and environments can be integrated independently through the framework’s interfaces; agents need not use Codex or an LLM. Figure 1 summarizes the interaction contract. 3.1 Interaction contract Initialization. The environment provides an environment description: text explaining the task, the goal to be achieved, and how the agent can interact with the environment. It may also provide supplementary files, such as documentation, helper programs, or initial observations, which are made available in the agent’s workspace. We treat these files as part of the environment description. The environment determines how much information about its rules and state the description provides. Actions and observations. At each step, the agent submits an action encoded as JSON. The environment defines the valid action structures and their meaning. In response, it returns an observation consisting of an arbitrary set of named files. The contract does not prescribe their formats: observations may contain text, images, or other data. An action may also reference files in the agent’s designated workspace that are accessible to the server-side infrastructure. Termination. The environment decides when the

An action may also reference files in the agent’s designated workspace that are accessible to the server-side infrastructure. Termination. The environment decides when the interaction session ends and indicates this in its response. Once the session is terminal, no further actions are accepted. Termination does not necessarily indicate success; its meaning and the criteria for accomplishing the task are defined by the environment. After initialization, interaction follows an agent-initiated request–response pattern: the environment does not send unsolicited observations. This restriction concerns communication, not whether the environment continues to evolve between requests. The environment description, action semantics, observation formats, and termination rules are part of the environment specification. They are held fixed when comparing agents; changes to them define a new version of the environment specification. 5

They use the same code, controller, and tools; only one short instruction differs. Each variant is deployed unchanged across environments for a given model–effort configuration. The agent simplifies the textual agent described in Section 4, “Architecture and Agent Variants,” of our earlier ARC-AGI-3 study [9]. We retain its Codex- based architecture while removing ARC-AGI-3-specific control and requirements to maintain a world model. 4.1 Agent architecture Figure 2 shows the agent’s four components: a controller, a Codex coding agent, an environment- agnostic client, and a persistent Linux workspace. Codex performs the task-solving work: it reads observations, reasons about the task, writes and executes programs, and selects environment actions. It submits those actions through the provided client, which is part of the agent rather than the environment. The client provides the same interface across environments and contains no environment-specific logic.

The workspace and Codex conversation persist across ordinary continuations within a run. 4.2 Controller The controller is a small script that sends prompts and checks basic session state; it contains no task-solving logic. It follows the flow in Figure 3. First, it initializes the environment through the client, then sends the main prompt, the variant-specific continuation instruction, and the initial client output identifying the description and observation files. Appendix B.2.3 gives the exact composition. The instruction distinguishing the variants is therefore present from the first invocation. When Codex returns, the controller reads the terminal flag and latest environment-step index from saved client state. It does not interpret observations or assess Codex’s reasoning. If the environment is terminal, the controller exits; otherwise, it selects one of two protocols. 7

State is inspected after Codex returns; “No progress” means no new action since the preceding continuation. “End” denotes controller exit after environment termination or a return with no new action following the stuck reminder. The controller resumes the same Codex conversation with a reminder to keep working toward the goal in the environment description (Appendix B.1.2), followed by the variant-specific instruction. The first nonterminal return receives this continuation even if the initial invocation took no action. Stuck protocol. If a continuation produces no new environment action, the controller adds the no-action reminder (Appendix B.1.3). If Codex again returns without taking an action, the controller exits. For Baseline, this instruction is: Continue working until you have completed your task. For Stop-and-report, it is: Continue working on the task as long as you can proceed confidently. If you encounter a problem, ambiguity, unexpected issue, or anything that makes you unsure how to proceed, stop and report it back to me before taking further action. The controller sends the initial message, and Codex carries out the task until the environment becomes terminal. Codex then returns and the controller exits. If Codex returns before termination despite this instruction, the controller prompts it to continue. Stop-and-report lifecycle. The initial message instead asks Codex to return when it en- counters a difficulty or uncertainty. If this happens before termination, the controller proceeds directly to the normal protocol and tells Codex to continue using the continuation text and the same Stop-and-report instruction. The conversation and workspace are retained. Here, “report it back to me” refers to the automated controller, not a human: the controller does not answer the report or supply a task-specific suggestion. Further returns follow the normal or stuck protocol described above. This variant can also finish the task without returning early. The intended difference is therefore when the same task-solving process returns control, not a change in its tools or environment-specific capabilities. The broad contract in Section 3 allows these different tasks to be exposed through the same interface. We distinguish the underlying benchmark from the environment defined for our experiments. An environment includes its environment description, comprising text and optional files; the dynamics that accept JSON actions, reject invalid requests, and return observation files; and its termination conditions. These choices define the environment, rather than merely documenting its implementation. Changing the ARC-AGI-3 description, omitting its PNG observations, or adding a direct exec action to Terminal-Bench would therefore produce a different environment specification, even with the same underlying task. Comparisons between agents keep the specification fixed. The following subsections describe these three elements for each setting. text: Dynamics and observations. The interface exposes six action categories. terminal_send submits literal text and named keys to an interactive terminal; terminal_read captures its screen or a bounded portion of its history; and terminal_new opens another independent shell on the same task filesystem. get_file retrieves a regular file, while send_path transfers a file or directory from the agent’s workspace to the task sandbox. Finally, finish submits the current task state and ends solving. Responses contain terminal snapshots, metadata, transfer acknowledgments, or retrieved file contents, depending on the action. Appendix A.4.1 lists the returned files. Terminal input does not wait for command completion. Processes continue between actions, and an empty or unchanged screen does not imply that a command has finished. A read may include a short fixed wait before capturing output, but it does not wait for a process to terminate. The agent must decide when to inspect output, send further input, interrupt a process, or work elsewhere. Thus, command execution is nonblocking with respect to completion, while observations are still delivered only in response to requests. We do not expose a dedicated execute-and-wait action. This is an interface choice, not a restriction of Terminal-Bench: its evaluation infrastructure supports direct command execution by custom agents [29]. An exec action with a short waiting limit would also fit our contract, but would

text: a dedicated execute-and-wait action. This is an interface choice, not a restriction of Terminal-Bench: its evaluation infrastructure supports direct command execution by custom agents [29]. An exec action with a short waiting limit would also fit our contract, but would define another environment version. Whether it helps is outside this study. Here Terminal-Bench tests the unchanged agent in a setting markedly different from the games, rather than serving as an interface-optimization exercise. Termination. Calling finish or reaching the task’s external timeout ends the solving phase and prevents further actions. In both cases, the verifier is run and its reward determines the task score; successful verification can therefore receive reward 1 after an agent timeout. If the verifier itself times out, the score is zero. Termination and task success remain distinct: calling finish is not itself evidence that the task was solved. 6 ARC-AGI-3-Specific Diagnostic Variants These experiments investigate why an ARC-AGI-3-specific scaffold can outperform the gen- eral agent when the relevant environment information is already available to both. Its task-solving prompts and controller logic are unchanged. We update Codex to version 0.154.0 and use the same runtime memory safeguards as the environment-agnostic agents in this study.3 The reference is rerun in the present campaign rather than represented by historical scores. We call this variant Controlled_RESET (test_arc3_agent_v1_02_wstop_wreset). Its main prompt adds: If the game is in the GAME_OVER state, you should report it, and I will give you another attempt on the same level. You are forbidden to call RESET by yourself. The prohibition is a prompt instruction; the client’s action interface remains unchanged. When Codex returns in GAME_OVER and the evaluation stopping conditions have not been met, the controller issues RESET through the client. It then resumes the same Codex conversation with the normal continuation prompt, a short reset notice, and the resulting client output. The reset observation is therefore available before Codex continues. This branch adds RESET before ordinary continuation; unlike the earlier textual agent’s reset protocol, it adds no separate failure-analysis stage. The Stop-and-report instruction, tools, and step-indexed observation layout are retained. In particular, the intervention does not introduce twma_v1.61’s level-and-attempt organization or its textual-model requirement. It tests the effect of transferring reset management from the coding agent to a script, using a convention already stated in the environment description. Because Terminal-Bench is wall-clock limited, we report its service tier explicitly; we did not separately measure its effect on scores. 7.5 All-or-nothing policy for irrecoverable failures Technical interruptions can affect trajectories unevenly. On the same task, an agent that struggles may run longer than one that quickly finds a solution, giving it more opportunity to encounter a service interruption or host failure. Replacing only interrupted task runs could therefore preferentially replace difficult trajectories and bias the reported performance upward. Following our earlier study [9, Section 5.5], we use an all-or-nothing policy at the evaluation-unit level. If an irrecoverable technical failure prevents an evaluation unit from being completed, the entire unit is discarded and rerun from scratch, including any tasks that had already finished. For ARC-AGI-3 and Terminal-Bench, the unit is a complete evaluation block. For AGI Maze, the policy applies separately to the 53-target 0005 and 0009 execution batches. No task result from a discarded unit is reused in its replacement. During this campaign, we replaced one accidentally interrupted AGI Maze batch, three Terminal-Bench blocks in which a server-container startup timeout prevented some tasks from starting, and one twma_v1.61 block affected by a model-service capacity error before the first action of a game. Stop-and-report improves mean ARC-AGI-3 RHAE and AGI Maze RHAE70, with small, mixed changes on Terminal-Bench. These results show that a small change can improve a general agent beyond the environment that motivated it and illustrate how to test its effects elsewhere. The second question concerns why agents using the same underlying LLM, with access to the same task information and general-purpose tools, can nevertheless perform differently. One hypothesis is that a sufficiently capable LLM could construct useful procedures for itself, leaving little advantage to developer-supplied task-specific scaffolding. text: can nevertheless perform differently. One hypothesis is that a sufficiently capable LLM could construct useful procedures for itself, leaving little advantage to developer-supplied task-specific scaffolding. This expectation is related to Sutton’s The Bitter Lesson, which emphasizes the long-term value of general methods that exploit increasing computation [10]. Exgentic finds that backbone choice explains more aggregate performance variation than architecture in its closed-source comparison, although architecture remains consequential within a model [1]. Our previous ARC-AGI-3 study likewise found that gains from model capability and reasoning effort often exceeded differences between the tested agent variants [9]. These observations motivate the hypothesis; they do not establish that scaffolding will become irrelevant. The present results show that supplied procedures still matter with GPT-5.6-sol. Even at max reasoning effort, Stop-and-report, Controlled_RESET, and twma_v1.61 achieve different mean ARC-AGI-3 scores. The specialization advantage therefore remains in the evaluated setting. We consider two possible, complementary explanations: how effectively the agent uses available information and procedures, and how much inference it performs and where it allocates that inference. 9.1 Using available information and procedures One possible explanation is that scaffolding helps the agent reconsider relevant information or follow a useful procedure more reliably. text: Controlled_RESET provides a more focused example. The environment description already tells the agent to reset after GAME_OVER and avoid unnecessary resets otherwise. Nevertheless, asking Codex to leave this decision to a scripted controller improves mean performance. The intervention adds no new game rule; it changes how an available rule is implemented. This does not mean that the scripted policy is optimal: as discussed in Section 6.2, a capable agent could sometimes save actions by resetting an unrecoverable attempt before GAME_OVER. The curriculum experiment provides a complementary example: additional relevant experience is not automatically beneficial. The tutorials give the agent practice applying the maze mechanics, yet they reduce target performance for both GPT-5.5-based variants at both effort settings. With GPT-5.6-sol, they help both variants at xhigh and have smaller, mixed effects at max. The benefit of additional experience therefore depends on the evaluated configuration, rather than following from its availability alone. 9.2 The amount and allocation of inference A second explanation is that the scaffold changes how much inference the agent performs and when it performs it. Asking Codex to report a difficulty may prompt additional reasoning while it formulates the report. The subsequent continuation lets it return to the task. This pattern makes additional inference a plausible contributor to the gains, but does not establish that greater expenditure causes the improvement. Cost tokens include weighted input and output, not only useful reasoning. Better performance can also enable more expenditure: an agent reaching additional ARC-AGI-3 levels can continue working where another run has stopped. Performance and resource use should therefore be considered together when interpreting the effect of scaffolding [30]. Better use of information can itself involve additional inference, for example when the agent rereads a description or reasons about how to reorganize its observations. 9.3 Implications and future directions It remains unclear whether further gains should be sought primarily through better use of available information and tools, through additional inference (for example, in a multi-agent system), or through a combination of the two. text: unclear whether further gains should be sought primarily through better use of available information and tools, through additional inference (for example, in a multi-agent system), or through a combination of the two. Further analysis is needed to determine their relative contributions and whether they can be meaningfully separated. One direction is to improve the environment-agnostic agent through more explicit procedures, including adaptations of the verification and simplification ideas explored in our earlier work [9]. The objective is to obtain further gains on some environments without material regressions on others, while retaining one unchanged agent implementation. A complementary direction is to expand the general capabilities initially available to the agent. Examples include reusable task-general skills, support for symbolic reasoning through a system such as MeTTa [31], or theorem-proving tools. These additions would supply tools or procedural knowledge, rather than only change the guidance for using existing tools, but could still be provided uniformly across environments. 21

text: 10 Conclusions We evaluated one Codex-based agent in two nearly identical prompt variants, each deployed unchanged across ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze, and Terminal-Bench. Stop-and-report improves mean ARC-AGI-3 RHAE and AGI Maze RHAE70 across the tested configurations, while Terminal-Bench shows small, mixed changes. The comparison demonstrates that a small, environment-independent modification can improve performance beyond the environment that motivated it, although the performance gains come with higher token-based cost. Stronger models may eventually construct useful procedures for themselves and reduce the advantage of developer-supplied scaffolding. Our results show that this advantage remains with GPT-5.6-sol. The twma_v1.61 reference prescribes organization and procedures that the general agent has the information and tools to construct, and Controlled_RESET recovers part of its advantage by implementing a convention already stated in the environment description. The tutorial experiment adds a complementary observation: access to additional relevant experience does not uniformly improve performance. The unresolved question is whether scaffolding helps mainly through more effective use of information and tools, additional inference, or both. The present experiments do not separate these effects, which may reinforce one another. EnvTraverse allows new agent variants to be evaluated across environments and compared with Baseline. This supports further research on improving environment-agnostic agents through better procedures or additional general capabilities, while assessing performance gains, possible regressions, and changes in inference cost. text: A Environment-Provided Information This appendix reproduces the environment descriptions, templates, and messages from the source code used in the experiments. The source code is available through the EnvTraverse project page. Quoted text is reproduced verbatim, with line wrapping adjusted for typesetting. Template fields and returned observation files are explained where needed. A.1 ARC-AGI-3 description This description is supplied at initialization for every ARC-AGI-3 game. Its “Provided Artifacts” section specifies the observation files, and its “Provided Helper Programs” section describes ascii_to_png.py, supplied in the initial workspace. # Environment Description ## 1. General Description Of The Environment You are playing a dynamic visual puzzle game. Your objective is to reach `WIN`, avoid `GAME_OVER`, and use as few actions as possible. The game consists of levels. Levels usually form a curriculum: later levels often extend earlier mechanics rather than replacing them. If you reach `GAME_OVER`, use `RESET` to begin another attempt at the current level. `RESET` counts toward the action budget and does not reset the current level's action count, so avoid using it unless the state is `GAME_OVER`. The game is deterministic: every attempt starts from exactly the same state, so the same action sequence produces exactly the same results. You cannot return to already solved levels. The game is shown as a `64 x 64` visual frame made from color indices
title: Environment-Provided Information

text: every attempt starts from exactly the same state, so the same action sequence produces exactly the same results. You cannot return to already solved levels. The game is shown as a `64 x 64` visual frame made from color indices `0..15`. A single action may produce multiple frames. When this happens, the last frame is the final settled state, but the intermediate frames are important evidence. Multiple frames usually mean something meaningful happened, such as animation, collision, damage, item use, state transition, level completion, or failure. Explore such animations with your own eyes. This is a visual puzzle. ASCII frames are exact data, but PNG frames show the game more like a human would see it. Inspect PNG files with your own eyes. ## 2. Actions Actions are JSON objects. Simple actions: ```json {"id":"ACTION1"} {"id":"ACTION2"} {"id":"ACTION3"} {"id":"ACTION4"} {"id":"ACTION5"} {"id":"ACTION7"} {"id":"RESET"} ``` Coordinate action: ```json {"id":"ACTION6","data":{"x":12,"y":34}} ``` 26
title: Environment-Provided Information

text: General action conventions: - `RESET`: start or restart play. - `ACTION1`: usually direction-like, commonly up. - `ACTION2`: usually direction-like, commonly down. - `ACTION3`: usually direction-like, commonly left. - `ACTION4`: usually direction-like, commonly right. - `ACTION5`: game-specific interaction, such as use, select, rotate, attach, detach, confirm, or execute. - `ACTION6`: coordinate-based interaction; provide `x` and `y`, with origin at the top-left. - `ACTION7`: usually undo. These are only conventions. Infer the real effect of each action from observations. The valid actions can change during play; check `available_actions` in metadata before choosing. ## 3. Provided Artifacts Each observation step may provide: - `metadata.txt`: JSON metadata with current state, level progress, available actions, and the action that produced the observation. - `final.txt`: the final settled visual frame as a `64 x 64` ASCII grid of hexadecimal color indices. - `final.png`: PNG rendering of `final.txt`. - `intermediate_XX.txt`: optional intermediate visual frame from an animation or transition. - `intermediate_XX.png`: PNG rendering of the corresponding `intermediate_XX.txt`. ASCII files represent the exact visual frame data. PNG files are generated from the corresponding ASCII frames and are provided so you can see the game as humans are meant to see it. ## 4. Use these helpers for simulated, reconstructed, or extracted ASCII frames when you need to inspect them visually. PNG inspection is especially useful for understanding object identity, animations, small visual differences, and mismatches between prediction and reality. A.3 AGI Maze set description and transition messages A.3.1 Environment description The environment description is: You are playing a series of labyrinths. Your task is to solve all labyrinths using the minimal number of moves. You will be given a description of each labyrinth. Please read each description carefully. For the first few labyrinths, you will be given an open map with your position shown on it. These are tutorial labyrinths designed to help you understand the mechanics. For the remaining labyrinths, the map will be hidden. You will only be given your initial position in the labyrinth description. The initial observation is message.md containing: Please start the first labyrinth by sending the {"id":"start"} action. Available actions: {"id":"start"} The environment waits for {"id":"start"}; it does not begin the first labyrinth automati- cally. A.3.2 When a labyrinth starts A valid start action returns labyrinth_description.md, containing the environment descrip- tion used for that labyrinth in the single-labyrinth setting. It also returns state.txt, containing the same state information as in the single-labyrinth environment, with the labyrinth index added. Tutorial labyrinths additionally provide AGI Maze’s current public map and player position in map.txt. Subsequent actions update the state and, for tutorials, the map; non-tutorial labyrinths omit map.txt. A.3.3 Between labyrinths After a labyrinth is solved and another remains. The response replaces the ordinary observation files with message.md containing: You have solved the labyrinth. Please start the next labyrinth by sending the {"id":"start"} action. text: D Motivation for the RHAE70 Reference Factor According to the AGI Maze team, the benchmark’s max_steps budgets were defined with some slack. The team shared results from internal playthroughs covering eight labyrinths, conducted by one practiced player who knew the mechanics but had not previously seen those labyrinths. Four labyrinths had an action budget of 180 and four had a budget of 230. The mean per-labyrinth ratio of actions used to budget was approximately 0.617. Seven playthroughs used fewer than 70 percent of the budget; the remaining ratio was 162/230 ≈0.704. These observations informed our choice of 0.7 as a rounded reference factor for awarding full credit. These internal tests were not designed to estimate representative human performance or calibrate a reference across all labyrinth types. RHAE70 is an author-defined, RHAE-inspired score using a proxy action reference, not a measured human-baseline score. A value of 100 means that the target was solved within the chosen threshold; it does not establish human-level or superhuman performance. The score saturates at that threshold and does not distinguish faster solutions. Score selection and sensitivity. RHAE70 was adopted during analysis and manuscript preparation, after examining mean step fractions, to give the reported benchmark scores a consistent higher-is-better direction. The internal playthrough results shared by the AGI Maze team informed the choice of reference factor. We

text: ELITEREPLAY: Preserving Diverse Solutions in RL Post-Training via Quality-Diversity Search Hanane Nour Moussa Doeun Lee Sachin Kumar The Ohio State University {moussa.45, lee.11501, kumar.1145}@osu.edu
title: ELITEREPLAY: Preserving Diverse Solutions in RL Post-Training

text: Reinforcement learning has become a common post-training technique to improve the accu- racy of LLMs on verifiable tasks. However, such training can narrow the set of solutions the model can produce. Several approaches have attempted to address this behavior-sharpening effect, but they often optimize metrics that do not reflect the diversity of correct solutions. Ideally, we want a model that can produce multiple good solutions, not only a single reli- able one. We propose ELITEREPLAY, a post- training recipe that pairs GRPO with an “elite” archive built by quality-diversity search. Be- fore training, we use the frozen base model to collect solutions that span distinct approaches; during training, GRPO is combined with a re- play loss on this archive. The result is a post- trained model that improves accuracy while pre- serving more of the base model’s solution diver- sity. On multiple text-to-SQL tasks, ELITERE- PLAY achieves the highest pass@128 than all baselines, producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies than the strongest baselines. It preserves most of the base model’s correct strategies, outperforming existing methods in strategy retention. This diversity translates into practical benefits on ambiguous questions, where ELITEREPLAY covers both interpreta- tions nearly twice as often as the strongest base- line on AmbiQT1. 1
title: ELITEREPLAY: Preserving Diverse Solutions in RL Post-Training

RL post-training therefore im- proves reliability (pass@1), but often by reducing reach (pass@k) (Oh et al., 2026). Several works seek to recover this lost reach by improving pass@k relative to the base model (Tajwar et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b,a; Walder and Karkhanis, 2025). Since recovering reach may re- quire retaining alternative ways of solving prob- lems, pass@k has also become a common proxy for diversity (Dang et al., 2025; Song et al.,

text: et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b,a; Walder and Karkhanis, 2025). Since recovering reach may re- quire retaining alternative ways of solving prob- lems, pass@k has also become a common proxy for diversity (Dang et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Yu, 2025; Jiang et al., 2026). Yet pass@k only asks whether some sample is correct, not whether the correct samples differ. A model can therefore achieve high pass@k by reliably produc- ing a single strategy for each question while losing the alternatives the base model once exhibited. Retaining these alternative ways of solving a problem, its solution diversity, is important when- ever the approach matters alongside the final an- swer. Different correct solutions may follow dis- tinct reasoning paths, differ in computational ef- ficiency, or encode different interpretations of an ambiguous request. Systems that rely on repeated arXiv:2610.22290v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026

text: sampling and selection also benefit from having meaningful variety (Li et al., 2022; Pourreza et al., 2025). As Figure 1 shows, methods with nearly identical pass@128 can differ substantially in the number of distinct correct strategies they produce. Preserving a diverse set of good solutions is the central concern of quality-diversity (QD) optimiza- tion. Rather than seeking a single optimum, QD algorithms such as novelty search (Lehman and Stanley, 2011) and MAP-Elites (Mouret and Clune, 2015) maintain an archive of high-performing solu- tions spread across a space of behavior descriptors. In the deep RL literature, such archives have been coupled with policy-gradient learners to broaden exploration, enabling the discovery of new behav- iors in policies trained from scratch (Khadka and Tumer, 2018; Pourchot and Sigaud, 2019; Ecof- fet et al., 2021). Post-training a language model, however, presents a different challenge, since the base model already exhibits a variety of correct strategies that RL can suppress. At the same time, language models offer a natural advantage for QD search, as the base model itself can propose meaningful variations through repeated sampling (Lehman et al., 2023; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Bradley et al., 2024; Samvelyan et al., 2024). text: (Lehman et al., 2023; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Bradley et al., 2024; Samvelyan et al., 2024). We study whether quality-diversity archives can preserve solution diversity during GRPO training. Our method, ELITEREPLAY, first runs MAP-Elites with the frozen base model to build an elite archive: a set of verified solutions, with at most one solution per cell of a grid indexed by a behavior descriptor. It then trains with GRPO while adding a small replay loss on this archive. Measuring diversity requires distinguishing how solutions are obtained, not just whether they are correct. We therefore evaluate diversity at the level of solution strategies, using a structural description of how each solution solves the question, computed deterministically from the solution itself. This al- lows us to measure U@k, the number of unique correct strategies among k samples, alongside ef- fective diversity (Shypula et al., 2025), the prob- ability that two random samples are both correct and different, which captures improvements in reli- ability without sacrificing diversity. We evaluate ELITEREPLAY on text-to-SQL, a natural testbed where questions can admit multi- ple correct queries and natural-language ambigu- ity is common. As shown in Figure 1, ELITERE- PLAY achieves 74.8% pass@128 on BIRD (Li et al., 2023), comparable to MaxRL’s 73.7%, while producing 9.1 distinct correct strategies per question compared to just 6.2. text: each question x ∈DA, we maintain an archive Ax of verified solutions, organized into cells by solution approach. Each cell stores at most one solution, or elite, allowing the archive to represent multiple correct approaches to the same question. Defining the behavior space. Classical MAP- Elites relies on behavior descriptors designed by hand for each domain. Instead, we first collect a set of verified seed solutions from the base model and provide them to a separate LLM, the labeler, as representative examples of how the task can be solved. Using these examples, the labeler induces a broader vocabulary of possible approaches, in- cluding ones not observed in the seeds, to guide subsequent exploration. The labeler assigns each solution an approach label, capturing its general method of solving the question. To distinguish solu- tions that follow the same broad approach but differ in their structure, we combine this label with struc- tural features extracted deterministically from the solution (e.g., joins or subqueries in SQL, loops or recursion in code). The resulting behavior descrip- tor b(y) determines the solution’s archive cell. This descriptor is used only to guide search; we evaluate diversity with a separate, deterministic notion of strategy (§3). Given this behavior space, we populate and expand the per-question archives through four steps. (1) Initialization. We insert the verified seed so- lutions into their corresponding archive cells, establishing the initial set of elites for each question. (2) Selection. We choose a target approach among those the labeler judges applicable to the ques- tion, prioritizing approaches not yet repre- sented in the archive while balancing attempts across targets (Appendix A.3). We then se- lect a parent elite, preferably one following a different approach. (3) Variation. We prompt π0 with the original question, target approach, and parent elite, ask- ing it to generate a new solution following the target approach. (4) Evaluation and insertion. We verify the can- didate and, if correct, assign it to the cell cor- responding to its actual approach, which may differ from the requested one. The candidate fills an empty cell or replaces an existing elite if it is shorter. We repeat selection, variation, and evaluation for a fixed search budget. text: 2.2 Training with elite replay Starting from the base model π0, we train the policy πθ with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), while encour- aging it to reproduce solutions from the archive. GRPO improves correctness, and archive replay helps preserve alternative approaches. Replaying archived solutions. At each training step, we sample a batch E of verified solutions from the archive, balancing sampling across ques- tions and their occupied cells so that questions with more elites do not dominate. To retain these so- lutions, we define the replay loss as the negative log-likelihood of the archived solutions, normal- ized by solution length so that longer solutions do not receive more weight, Lreplay(θ) = −1 |E| X (x,y)∈E 1 |y| log πθ(y | x). (1) Combining replay with GRPO. Inspired by CHORD (Zhang et al., 2026), we combine the on- policy GRPO objective with the supervised replay loss using a simplified formulation with a fixed mixing weight µ L(θ) = (1 −µ) LGRPO(θ) + µ Lreplay(θ). (2) The archive remains fixed, and the replay loss pro- vides a consistent signal for preserving alternative solutions alongside GRPO updates (Appendix A.4). At inference, the trained policy is sampled directly, without archive lookup or search. 3 Evaluating Strategy Diversity We measure how well RL post-training preserves the range of correct solutions at the level of

Strategies. We represent each solution y by a strategy s(y), a deterministic description of how the solution is constructed that abstracts away sur- face details. For solutions with formal structure, such as code, abstract syntax trees (ASTs) provide a natural basis for distinguishing programs by their structure rather than their surface form (Ren et al., 2020; Song et al., 2024; Shypula et al., 2025). We therefore derive s(y) from the AST of each SQL query, distinguishing, for example, a query that joins two tables from one that filters through a nested subquery (Appendix B.5).
