text: Diversity in RL post-training. RL post-training is widely observed to reduce output diversity, with studies showing that it lowers diversity relative to supervised fine-tuning (Kirk et al., 2024), collapses policy entropy (Cui et al., 2025), and concentrates probability on behaviors already present in the base model (Zhao et al., 2025), so that base models of- ten solve more problems at large sampling budgets (Yue et al., 2025; Oh et al., 2026); supervised fine- tuning shows a similar collapse (Dang et al., 2025). Mitigations optimize objectives tied to pass@k (Walder and Karkhanis, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Tajwar et al., 2026), reward novel or diverse out- puts (Song et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025, 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026), regularize toward the base model (Li et al., 2026b), or control entropy and sampling tem- perature (Cui et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Oh et al., 2026), and are typically evaluated by pass@k (Yu, 2025). ELITEREPLAY instead replays an archive built for coverage, and we measure diversity at the more meaningful level of solution strategies. Mixing demonstrations and replay into RL. text: RL. RL has long been combined with supervised learn- ing from demonstrations or past experience (Lin, 1992; Hester et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2018). In LLM post-training, the off-policy data range from pre- training text and expert solutions (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2025) to re- played verified trajectories (Zhang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025) and base-model samples (Li et al., 2026b). These works use replay to learn efficiently from good solutions or to stay close to a reference model. ELITEREPLAY uses a replay set built by quality-diversity search to keep distinct correct solutions available throughout RL. Quality diversity and evolutionary RL. QD al- gorithms such as novelty search and MAP-Elites seek collections of solutions that are both high- performing and diverse (Lehman and Stanley, 2011; Mouret and Clune, 2015; Pugh et al., 2016; Cully and Demiris, 2018). In deep RL, they have been combined with policy gradients through shared replay buffers (Khadka and Tumer, 2018; Pourchot and Sigaud, 2019), gradient-based vari- ation (Nilsson and Cully, 2021; Pierrot et al., 2022), and archive-driven exploration (Ecoffet et al., 2021). In these works, QD discovers new behaviors, and archived solutions come from a sep- arate search process. ELITEREPLAY instead builds its archive once from the base model’s own so- lutions and replays it

text: We introduced ELITEREPLAY, which preserves so- lution diversity during RL post-training by replay- ing an archive of distinct correct solutions found by quality-diversity search. ELITEREPLAY raises accuracy both in and out of distribution while re- taining most of the base model’s correct strategies. We also introduced a strategy-level evaluation of diversity, which reveals differences between meth- ods that pass@k conceals. Our results show that post-training need not trade diversity for reliability.

HNM is partially supported by the Center on Responsible AI and Governance (CRAIG) at OSU. Limitations We recognize the following limitations and direc- tions of future work. Base model. Our experiments use Qwen3.5-4B- Base, whose moderate size makes it feasible to conduct multiple training runs across our method and baselines within our available compute budget. This model size is also relevant to practical RL post- training settings, making it a meaningful model for studying strategy preservation. Nevertheless, evaluating ELITEREPLAY on larger models (e.g. 8B), and across different model families is a natural direction for future work. Domain. Our experiments focus on text-to-SQL, which provides a suitable testbed for studying solu- tion diversity because questions can admit multiple correct queries, correctness can be verified through execution, and SQL’s formal structure allows strate- gies to be distinguished using abstract syntax trees. Extending this evaluation to other domains where solution strategies lack a clear structural represen- tation, as in many mathematical reasoning tasks, might be challenging. A Method Details A.1 Algorithm Algorithm 1 summarizes the two stages of ELITEREPLAY. We first construct an archive with the frozen base model, then use the archived solu- tions to guide GRPO post-training. A.2 Behavior space We first sample verified seed solutions from the frozen base model and present representative ex- amples to a separate LLM, the labeler. Rather than restricting search to the approaches observed in the seeds, the labeler uses these examples to induce a broader vocabulary of possible approaches. It then assigns each verified solution a primary ap- proach label. Because solutions with the same approach label can still differ in structure, we re- fine each label with structural features computed deterministically from the solution, such as which constructs appear in its parse tree. The resulting descriptor b(y) identifies the solution’s cell in its question-specific archive Ax. Each cell contains at most one verified solution, or elite. The descrip- tor only guides search; diversity is evaluated with a separate representation that involves no labeler (Appendix B.5). A.3 Archive search Search runs on a subset DA of the training ques- tions; no evaluation questions are used.

A.3 Archive search Search runs on a subset DA of the training ques- tions; no evaluation questions are used. All can- didates come from the frozen base model π0, prompted with the original task, and only candi- dates accepted by the verifier enter the archive. Each question receives a number of initial samples, followed by several rounds of mutations. Target selection. For each question, the labeler proposes a set of applicable approaches. For each mutation, we first restrict target selection to applica- ble approaches not yet represented by any elite for the current question; if all are represented, we con- sider all applicable approaches. Within this pool, we prioritize approaches with the fewest previous targeting attempts for that question, then those rep- resented by the fewest questions across the archive. Variation and insertion. For each attempt, the frozen base model receives the original task, the tar- get approach, and a verified parent solution, prefer- ably using a different approach. The generated candidate is verified and assigned to the cell cor- responding to the approach it actually uses, which might not be the requested one. text: attempts prevents search from repeatedly target- ing an approach the base model fails to realize. A candidate that repeats an already occupied ap- proach can at most replace that cell’s elite, so near- duplicate samples consume search budget but do not add coverage. Appendices C.1 and C.2 show that this procedure finds substantially more distinct approaches than direct sampling. A.4 Training with elite replay Each training step pairs a batch of on-policy GRPO rollouts with a separate batch of verified elites for the replay loss. We sample the latter across ques- tions and occupied cells so that questions with more archived solutions do not dominate. The replay loss averages each solution’s negative log- likelihood over its tokens, then averages over so- lutions. Inspired by CHORD (Zhang et al., 2026), we combine this term with GRPO using a fixed weight µ rather than a scheduled weight or addi- tional per-token reweighting. The archive remains fixed throughout training. B.3 Implementation and training configuration We implement training using veRL (Sheng et al., 2025) as the distributed RL framework, integrated with Trinity-RFT (Pan et al., 2025) to support the combination of on-policy GRPO updates with the supervised replay loss. We use vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) for rollout generation. All model parameters are trained on four NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs, with two allocated to policy optimization and two to rollout generation. For a consistent comparison, all methods use the same BIRD training data and are trained for 100 steps, with the principal shared settings summarized in Table 5. Each baseline fol- lows its respective training objective, specifically: MaxRL. MaxRL uses the same rollout groups and clipped policy objective but replaces GRPO’s standard-deviation normalization with mean- reward normalization: AMaxRL i = ri −¯r ¯r + ϵ , ϵ = 10−6. These advantages are used directly, without a sub- sequent GRPO standardization. MaxRL uses no replay or additional reference-model KL penalty. SetPO. We first sample eight responses from the frozen base model for each training question. Ques- tions for which all eight responses are correct are eligible for preservation. We then draw an indepen- dent reference response for each eligible question; questions whose reference response is incorrect re- turn to the exploration partition. We retain the released low-variance token-level KL estimator rather than replacing it with supervised cross-entropy. B.5 Strategy descriptors and evaluation diversity metrics The search descriptor b(y) combines an LLM- assigned approach label with structural SQL fea- tures, while evaluation relies on a separate, deter- ministic AST-based representation. title: Preprint

text: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where hon- esty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. We introduce Continu- ous Adversarial Training for Consistent Honesty (CATCH), inspired by a method originally developed to robustly refuse harmful queries. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model’s capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that trained with only hundreds of targets built from self-reporting scenarios, CATCH learns an honest behaviour that robustly gener- alizes and transfers across distinct benchmarks. It consistently reduces dishon- esty under pressure on MASK, increases confessions in the multi-agent game of Among Us, and improves the discovery rates of the model’s hidden behaviours in AuditBench. We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering. However, CATCH surpasses honesty steering in maintaining utility, thanks to a novel choice of utility data. 1

text: Preprint a recent incident at OpenAI, agents worked together to cheat in an evaluation by breaching a third party’s infrastructure to retrieve the solutions, covering their traces to hide their cheating attempts (Greenblatt et al., 2026). On the other hand, models can directly lie to the user, for example, faking alignment (Greenblatt et al., 2024); claiming task completion that they didn’t achieve (Greenblatt, 2026; Smyth et al., 2026); telling users what they think the user wants to hear, even when it is not factually correct (Fanous et al., 2025); or simply making claims that contradicts some knowledge, whether it is a fact learnt during training or provided in context. In this paper, we particularly focus on this latter, which Ren et al. (2025) show does not go away even when the models get larger/more capable. Different techniques exist to control a model’s propensity to lie. Activation steering alters the model’s behaviour at inference time by intervening on its activations (Zou et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2024; Herbster et al., 2026). Nonetheless, benign steering can lead to increased vulnerability to jailbreaks (Xiong et al., 2026), decreased capability, and unintended changes in a model’s behaviour that’s not the targeted trait (Siu et al., 2026). Others consider honest prompting (Wang et al., 2025), emphasizing honesty in the system prompt or assigning models

text: jailbreaks (Xiong et al., 2026), decreased capability, and unintended changes in a model’s behaviour that’s not the targeted trait (Siu et al., 2026). Others consider honest prompting (Wang et al., 2025), emphasizing honesty in the system prompt or assigning models an honest persona; however, a sin- gle prompt that induces honesty across different conditions may be hard or impossible to design. Another popular approach is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on harmful system prompts along with honest responses; yet, this requires large corpora of synthetic data (Wang et al., 2025), and may not generalize out of distribution. An open problem in the field is to be able to find a single intervention that works across different manifestations of dishonesty. This could be seen as a robustness problem, where a method is defined as robust when it mitigates dishonesty independently of how it arises. One potential approach to address this is Continous Adversarial Training (CAT) (Xhonneux et al., 2024), initially proposed to make a model’s refusal behaviour robust against a variety of jailbreaks. Here we modified CAT to make a model’s honest behaviour robust to three different forms of dishonesty: 1) instructed dishonesty, where a system prompt contains explicit pressure to lie; 2) dishonesty that emerges from incentives in a multi-agent game, where being dishonest increases expected reward; and 3) dishonesty that results

text: Evaluating honesty in LLMs Prior work on trustworthy LLMs spans several related but distinct goals, including factual accuracy, hallucination reduction, calibration, uncertainty expression, and cross-prompt consistency (Lin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Chern et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2024). These settings measure reliability, but they do not directly test whether a model knowingly produces statements that conflict with its knowledge under pressure. As a result, improvements on the bench- marks may reflect broader knowledge or better calibration rather than honesty (Ren et al., 2024). 2
title: Preprint

text: Preprint MASK (Ren et al., 2025) formalizes the distinction, comparing a model’s pressured output against its independently elicited belief, and finds that the tendency to lie under pressure does not decrease with scale even as factual accuracy improves. Smyth et al. (2026) find similar dishonest behaviour in frontier coding agents, which failed to read all files they were requested to review 67.9% of runs, and implied complete coverage in 80.4% of those cases. Honesty interventions For inference-time interventions, one could simply insert an honesty in- struction to the prompt; but it relies on the model to police itself, and the improvement does not generalize (Ren et al., 2025). Activation steering (Turner et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025) intervenes on the residual stream, and two recent methods target honesty directly. G´oral et al. (2025) distribute a fixed steering budget across depth with a Gaussian schedule, while Herbster et al. (2026) uses a logistic-regression decision boundary to determine which tokens to steer and projection geometry to determine by how much. For training-time interventions, Wang et al. (2025) find SFT on harmful system prompts along with honest responses to be the strongest mitigation. Beyond SFT, Jagadeesh et al. (2026) train truth- fulness as one of several beneficial traits with RL and report that the behaviour persists under ad- versarial prompting and harmful

(2026) train truth- fulness as one of several beneficial traits with RL and report that the behaviour persists under ad- versarial prompting and harmful fine-tuning, and Joglekar et al. (2025) train a separately-rewarded confession issued after each answer. Adversarial training A parallel line of work studies aligned LLMs through the lens of adver- sarial robustness. Automatically optimized suffix attacks such as GCG (Zou et al., 2023), together with jailbreak methods such as PAIR (Chao et al., 2025) and AutoDAN (Liu et al., 2024), show that safety-aligned models remain vulnerable to targeted prompt perturbations that induce harmful behaviour. To defend against these attacks, Mazeika et al. (2024) demonstrates that adversarial train- ing can improve robust refusal; however, discrete attack generation is computationally expensive. CAT addresses this bottleneck by replacing discrete token search with embedding-space pertur- bations, showing that robustness to continuous attacks transfers to discrete jailbreaks while being substantially more efficient to train (Xhonneux et al., 2024). Similarly, Latent adversarial train- ing perturbs hidden activations instead of input embeddings and improves robustness to harmful behaviours (Casper et al., 2025). These methods have been evaluated primarily on suppression of harmful outputs and robustness towards jailbreaks, rather than on honesty. Our work targets this gap by adapting

These methods have been evaluated primarily on suppression of harmful outputs and robustness towards jailbreaks, rather than on honesty. Our work targets this gap by adapting CAT from safety alignment to honesty alignment. 3 METHODS Designing adversarial targets Let x be a prompt containing some pressure to lie and a proposition the model is being pushed to misstate. Following (Xhonneux et al., 2024), we associate with x two continuations: y+, an answer consistent with with the knowledge available to the model, whether learnt during training or supplied in context; and y−, an answer that complies with the pressure and asserts the contrary. A model is dishonest on x when it has a high probability to output y−. Training models for honesty is different from safeguarding models against generating harmful out- puts in jailbreaking. In safety alignment, a single generic refusal “Sorry, I can’t do that” serves as the toward-target y+ for every harmful prompt (Mazeika et al., 2024; Xhonneux et al., 2024), and the away-target y−typically begins with a compliance prefix such as “Sure”. However, for honesty, both the truth and lie depend on the context, so both targets must be constructed case-by-case. Continuous adversarial training Adversarial training optimizes a min-max objective, where an inner maximization finds a worst-case perturbation and an outer minimization makes the model robust to it (Madry et al., 2019). In the LLM setting the threat is targeted, such that the attacker aims to elicit one specific, harmful continuation y−, of which the inner loop maximizes the likelihood. Searching over discrete token sequences for the worst prompt is far too expensive to do inside a training loop (Mazeika et al., 2024). Following Xhonneux et al. Both training objectives are implemented as custom trainers on top of TRL (von Werra et al., 2020), and all generation tasks use vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). We train on 8 H200 GPUs and evaluate on 4 H100 GPUs. Adversarial data We leverage Herbster et al. (2026)’s training data, which consists of 50 self- reporting scenarios where the model is placed in a fictional prior, e.g., missing a vulnerability in a code review, and is questioned by the user. Each scenario carries two system prompts, one where the model is instructed to lie about the prior action, and the other where the model is instructed to be truthful. The evaluated model generates five completions for each variant, and each is scored by gpt-oss-120b (OpenAI, 2025) that returns a verdict indicating whether the completion followed its assigned condition (honest/dishonest). We keep only completions whose verdict matches their con- dition, dropping scenarios left with no usable dishonest completion. These are then paired within each scenario to form (y+, y−) contrast pairs, along with the dishonest system prompt (x) as adver- sarial context. This yields the final Dadv consisting of 216 rows of on-policy training data over 45 scenarios for Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and 224 rows across 47 scenarios for Qwen3.6-27B. Utility data We initially

text: We evaluate the honesty-intervention methods on three benchmarks where dishonesty manifests differently, as well as capability benchmarks. MASK benchmark. MASK (Ren et al., 2025) asks whether a model contradicts itself under pres- sure. For each scenario, it first elicits the model’s belief about a proposition in a neutral context, then puts the model under pressure, and compares the model’s answers under the two. Every pressured response with an elicited belief falls into one of three classes: it asserts what the model believes (honest), asserts the opposite (dishonest), or asserts neither, by hedging or refusing (ambiguous). In the literature, the third class is usually folded into the first category, with the honesty score calculated as 100 −dishonest rate, so a model that simply stops making claims or refuses most times scores well. Thus, we report all three instead of collapsing them into one number. As for accuracy, some propositions yield no consistent belief. Yet if we do not know what the model thinks, we cannot say whether it contradicted itself. We therefore drop those items before computing honesty rates. We use the full n = 1000 in MASK and gemma-4-31B-it (Gemma Team, 2026) as a judge. 6

AuditBench (Sheshadri et al., 2026) starts from models that have been given a hidden behaviour and trained to conceal it when asked directly, and scores how often an auditing technique uncovers that behaviour. text: Preprint 6 DISCUSSION CATCH improves honesty on all three evaluations implemented, where dishonesty manifests due to different causes, outperforming all the baselines. On MASK, SFT on the honest targets reaches only 55% and 60% honesty on Llama and Qwen; adding the dishonest targets (SFT-TA) raises this to 77% and 88%. Prompting with honest persona makes both models achieve similar level of honesty to SFT-TA. However, CATCH is still the most honest on MASK, and this honesty transfers to other benchmarks, while all prompting and SFT baselines do not generalize well to Among Us. The closest competitor to CATCH is StTP (Herbster et al., 2026), the strongest activation-steering method to date for honesty. CATCH outperforms it on MASK, and the two are comparable on Among Us and AuditBench. They also differ in terms of capability degradation. At the steering strength behind its results, StTP lowers the AlpacaEval LC win rate to 8.6% on Llama and 45.2% on Qwen, whereas CATCH stays at parity on both (51.3% and 51.8%). Using a weaker steering strength would lead to less utility degradation, but also to less honesty (Herbster et al., 2026). Our findings differ from that of Wang et al. text: to less honesty (Herbster et al., 2026). Our findings differ from that of Wang et al. (2025), who find prompting and fine-tuning to be the most effective mitigations. In our setting, using 200 adversarial targets to train two open-weight models with CATCH gives better MASK performance than in Wang et al. (2025)’s setting, where roughly fifty times as much training data was used to SFT a bigger and more capable model (Claude Sonnet 3.7). We cannot test CATCH on closed-source model for a more direct comparison. We limit our claim to the small-data regime: with a few hundred targets, CATCH is more effective than SFT. Preserving capability during robustness training depends heavily on the choice of utility dataset. Prior work in adversarial training commonly used UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023) for this purpose (Bai et al., 2024; Xhonneux et al., 2024; Sheshadri et al., 2025; D´ek´any et al., 2025). With it, Xhonneux et al. (2024) report MT-Bench degradation for every model they train, attributing it to the trade-off between robustness and utility. However, our ablation indicates that much of the cost comes from the choice of utility dataset. Using on-policy utility data in CATCH retains capability for both our trained models to the same level as the base model in AlpacaEval, MMLU and MT-Bench. We also tried CAPO, another adversarial

text: cost comes from the choice of utility dataset. Using on-policy utility data in CATCH retains capability for both our trained models to the same level as the base model in AlpacaEval, MMLU and MT-Bench. We also tried CAPO, another adversarial training method, which successfully improves honesty on MASK and Among Us, but is accompanied with degraded capabilities. It also produces behavioural changes: in Among Us, CAPO-trained Impostors decline to play in 35% of games, giving reasons about harm (“I can’t help with that because it involves harming others.”). One possible explanation is that preference optimization can shift probability onto responses the preference pairs (toward and away targets) never specified (Razin et al., 2025). Another reading is that honesty and harmlessness have overlapping representations: Siu et al. (2026) shows that interventions targeting one safety behaviour can affect others. Some limitations exist in our work. CATCH requires white-box access, so it cannot be applied to closed-source APIs. We train LoRA adapters on all linear layers, but prior work on honesty steering finds that the middle layers carry most of the relevant signal (Herbster et al., 2026), so restricting the update would make full fine-tuning affordable and potentially leading to even higher honesty; however, we have not tested this. text: We introduced CATCH, and showed it is a practical and data-efficient way to make an LLM more honest. Trained on a few hundred targets and evaluated on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3.6- 27B, CATCH enables models to learn an honest behaviour that robustly generalizes and transfers to different dishonesty manifestations. CATCH substantially reduces instructed dishonesty on MASK, raises the confession rate under game incentives in Among Us, and makes a trained-in hidden be- haviour easier to surface on AuditBench. General capability is preserved under CATCH, and this depends on the utility corpus: while off-policy corpora can degrade model’s utility substantially, on-policy data consistently retain it. 9

text: Preprint AI USE STATEMENT Generative AI systems are used in this work. We fine-tuned and evaluated LLMs, used them to generate our training data, ran them as agents in the Among Us environment and as investigator agents in AuditBench, and used them as automated judges under fixed prompts and rubrics for MASK, AlpacaEval, and MT-Bench. Generative AI tools also helped with carrying out the research, including code development and debugging, plotting, and checking results. Section 4 describes the two open-source models, training and utility data, training configuration, checkpoint selection, evaluation procedures, and the judge models. A.5 EXTENDED RESULTS OF AMONG US Figures 7 and 8 report six measures for every method, computed from the Impostors’ game logs. The main text shows the first two; the other four check whether an intervention changes how the model plays. Impostor win rate. Share of completed games won by the Impostors. A lower rate means the Impostors deceived less successfully. Confession rate. Share of games in which an Impostor, during a meeting, sends a message match- ing a fixed confession pattern (e.g., “I killed Player 5”). Paraphrased admissions are missed, so this is a lower bound. Valid action emitted. Share of Impostor turns on which the model produces an action the game can parse. A drop means the intervention has broken the output format. SPEAK rate. text: Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning Arnav Chavan 1 Kusha Sareen 2,3 Rishabh Tiwari 1 Abhranil Chandra 5 Johan Obando-Ceron 2,4 Kurt Keutzer 1 Scott Niekum 5 Inderjit S Dhillon 6 Devvrit Khatri 7,8 1UC Berkeley 2Mila 3McGill University 4Université de Montréal 5UMass Amherst 6Google 7UT Austin 8Mirendil Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capa- bilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting

text: Large language models (LLMs) are useful across a rapidly growing range of applications, including assistants, coding, search, science, and finance [1, 8, 20]. Many of these applications follow the same paradigm. A small number of strong base models are pre-trained once [7, 49, 56], and each use case then fine-tunes one of them on specialized data [6, 15, 16, 36, 46]. Fine-tuning has thus become a standard way to specialize an LLM for a target task or domain. This paradigm comes at the cost of catastrophic forgetting. As a model learns a new task, capabilities acquired over trillions of training tokens, including instruction following, coding, reasoning, and general knowledge, can degrade severely [24, 28, 29]. This phenomenon is particularly difficult to address because the original pre-training data is typically unavailable [23], while post-hoc repair may recover only part of what was lost [28, 44] (Sec. 3). More broadly, forgetting stands in the way of continual learning. The next generation of foundation models should be able to improve over their deployed lifetime, adding new skills, domains, and corrections without sacrificing what they already do well. Recent works provide insights into the origin of this forgetting. The leading singular directions of pretrained weight matrices have been associated with important model functionality [30, 43], while reinforcement learning has been found to fine-tune relatively

text: they already do well. Recent works provide insights into the origin of this forgetting. The leading singular directions of pretrained weight matrices have been associated with important model functionality [30, 43], while reinforcement learning has been found to fine-tune relatively small parameter subnetworks [33]. More directly, RLVR updates concentrate outside the principal directions and induce relatively little spectral drift compared with SFT [60]. On-policy RL also stays closer to the base policy and forgets less than SFT [45]. These observations suggest a simple hypothesis. Preserving the principal singular subspaces of pretrained weights may preserve prior capabilities while leaving sufficient capacity elsewhere in weight space to learn new ones. Existing methods induce this behavior indirectly. For example, SDFT [44] trains the model on its own rewrites of the training data, so that supervision stays close to the model’s output distribution—approximately on-policy, and hence expected to forget less. This helps on non-reasoning instruct models, but we find substantial forgetting remains on longer reasoning traces (Sec. 3). We introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts weight updates to a non-principal subspace of the weight spectrum. Concretely, let ∆W be the optimizer’s final update to a weight matrix W, and let Uk and Vk contain the top-k left and right singular vectors of W. SST applies the projected update Π(∆W) = (I −UkU ⊤ k

text: spectrum. Concretely, let ∆W be the optimizer’s final update to a weight matrix W, and let Uk and Vk contain the top-k left and right singular vectors of W. SST applies the projected update Π(∆W) = (I −UkU ⊤ k ) ∆W (I −VkV ⊤ k ) (1) in place of ∆W. The two projectors remove from the update any component along the principal directions, on the output and input sides respectively, so every applied step stays in the non-principal subspace (Sec. 2.1). Importantly, SST constrains the final optimizer update rather than the raw gradient. Stateful optimizers such as Adam rescale the gradient coordinate-wise before it reaches the weights, so a projected gradient does not produce a projected step and part of the update returns to the directions we mean to freeze (Sec. 2). Because the projection acts on the applied update, SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes with any fine-tuning recipe, with no other change to training. We conduct extensive empirical analysis and establish the following properties of SST (Sec. 3): • SST learns new tasks and retains prior capabilities. Despite protecting the top 99% of singular directions, SST matches the target-task accuracy of unconstrained fine-tuning, while retaining the prior capabilities that standard fine-tuning severely degrade (Figure 1). This behavior holds across Science, Medicine, Pathology, Finance, and Tool Use, across

text: Despite protecting the top 99% of singular directions, SST matches the target-task accuracy of unconstrained fine-tuning, while retaining the prior capabilities that standard fine-tuning severely degrade (Figure 1). This behavior holds across Science, Medicine, Pathology, Finance, and Tool Use, across SFT and SDFT, and with both Adam and Muon; Tables 4 and 1 provide the full per-domain results. We hypothesize that such constrained learning is possible because LLMs are heavily over-parameterized [2, 22], leaving enough capacity in the non-principal subspace to fit a new task. When a fixed complement becomes restrictive, a refresh step recomputes the SVD on the current weights, realigning the protected subspace so adaptation can continue (Section 2.3). • SST scales well. With more training data, SFT forgets progressively more while SST stays flat and still reaches higher target-task accuracy (Figure 3). With larger models, forgetting under SST shrinks even further, staying within ∼1% of the base model from 8B onward (Figure 2). 2

Overall, this work shows that catastrophic forgetting is not an inevitable consequence of learning, but depends on where the update lands in weight space, and provides a simple, practical method for improving capability retention while acquiring new capabilities.. 2 Subspace Tuning Across many complex systems, a small number of leading modes of a linear operator capture much of its dominant structure, while the remaining spectrum describes lower-energy variation [4, 42]. Deep neural network weight matrices exhibit similarly concentrated and heavy-tailed spectra [30], and interventions on their leading singular components can disproportionately affect model performance [43]. These observations motivate preserving the principal singular directions of pretrained weights during adaptation. We first formalize this constraint (Sec. 2.1), show that it must be enforced on the applied optimizer update rather than the gradient (Sec. 2.2), and introduce a basis refresh that trades stricter protection for continued adaptability (Sec. 2.3). 2.1 Projection Formulation Consider a single weight matrix W ∈Rdout×din, which maps an input activation x to an output Wx. Its SVD, W = P i σi uiv⊤ i , reads off the component of x along the input direction vi (via v⊤ i x) and writes it, scaled by σi, onto the output direction

So the right singular vectors vi are the input directions the layer responds to, and the left singular vectors ui are the output directions it produces. The top-k of these, Vk = [v1, . . . , vk] and Uk = [u1, . . . , uk], are what we intend to protect. text: could instead act on the gradient before the optimizer, either alone or together with the applied update. These choices are not equivalent. For plain SGD, whose step is a scalar multiple of the gradient, projecting the gradient and projecting the update coincide. Under Adam and other stateful optimizers they differ. Adam rescales each coordinate by its running moments, and this diagonal preconditioning does not commute with Π, so a gradient confined to the free subspace can still produce an applied update with a component in the protected subspace. We compare three possible enforcement points (full equations in Appendix B.8): (1) Project the gradient: apply Π to the raw gradient before Adam, g ←Π(g). (2) Project the applied update: let Adam update its moments from the full gradient, then apply Π to the step that Adam produces (this is what SST does). 4

text: away from this initial basis. SST can therefore re-anchor Wref to the current weights and recompute Uk, Vk from it every K optimizer steps, using a Gram-based eigendecomposition for efficiency (Appendix B.13 discusses the minimal time overhead of SST compared to SFT). A refresh defines the free complement relative to the current weights and opens new directions for adaptation. As the singular vectors rotate, a direction protected by the initial basis can acquire a component in a later free complement. Refresh can improve continued task learning, but it mildly weakens protection relative to the original model because SST now preserves a sequence of updated principal subspaces rather than one fixed pretrained subspace. We therefore treat K as an adaptation–retention control and report no refresh, R100 (K=100), and R10 (K=10) through many of our experiments. 5

text: 3 Experiments We ask the central question: When a model is fine-tuned on a new task, does confining the update to the non-principal subspace let it learn the task while retaining what it already knew? Models and tasks. We fine-tune Qwen3-8B [56] on data containing explicit <think>. . .</think> traces in four domains: Science, Finance, Pathology, and Medicine. Science uses DeepSeek-R1-distilled traces from the open-r1/Mixture-of-Thoughts release [17]. Finance uses the reasoning-annotated FinQA/ConvFinQA release [12, 13]. Pathology and Medicine use MedMCQA questions [37] with traces generated by Claude Sonnet 4.6 [3]. Evaluation. In-distribution accuracy (ID) measures how well the new task was learned. Prior capability measures forgetting: the average over held-out general-purpose benchmarks not used for fine-tuning. We evaluate on a broad set of benchmarks before and after training, namely GPQA-Diamond [39], MMLU-Pro [53], GSM8K [14], HumanEval [11], and IFEval [59]. Baselines. We compare against standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and self-distillation fine-tuning [SDFT, 44], an on-policy method designed to reduce forgetting. We report SFT and SDFT alone, and each combined with SST at rank fraction r=0.99 unless specified otherwise (Appendix B.11 sweeps r and finds that stronger protection improves both retention and in-domain accuracy), optionally with basis refresh every 100 (R100) or 10 (R10) steps. text: Classical continual learning restricts where updates go using stored data or gradients from earlier tasks [9, 18, 23, 27, 40, 51]. These constraints require data that is unavailable at LLM scale and task boundaries that deployed fine-tuning does not have, whereas SST needs neither. A complementary line reduces forgetting through the data instead of the update. Self-distillation rewrites supervision into the model’s own distribution 9

text: [44], and on-policy RL forgets less because its updates stay close to the base policy [45, 60]. Those methods induce a favorable update geometry through on-policy data. SST, by contrast, constrains weight update, and as a result can compose with on-policy methods (Table 4). We defer discussion of many other related works to Appendix A. 4.1 Comparison with subspace-protecting methods Two recent methods share our starting point of protecting the top singular directions of pretrained weights while adapting elsewhere. Both differ from SST in the same structural way. They rewrite the update as a product of trained factors and constrain the factors, whereas SST trains the weights directly and constrains the one quantity that reaches them, the applied update. Sculpting [34] freezes the top singular vectors of each weight matrix and projects the gradient before every AdamW step. Its projection removes only block (1) of Eq. 2, the component that reads from and writes onto protected directions at once. The cross blocks (2) and (3), which touch a protected direction on one side, are never removed. The projection moreover acts on the gradient, rather than the update as suggested by our controlled study. OPLoRA [54] freezes the weights and trains a LoRA adapter, the product BA of two low-rank trainable matrices, sandwiched between fixed projectors, ∆W = QU BA QV in our notation. This is the projection Π of Eq. 3 applied to a low-rank product rather than to the optimizer’s step, and it confines the update fully to the free subspace. The amount protected is set by the projector rank k, and their experiments protect only the top 16-128 directions while adapting at low rank in everything that remains, nearly the inverted regime from SST, which protects 99% of the spectrum and adapts densely in the tail. text: Catastrophic forgetting is usually treated as the price of learning new tasks. Our work studies it instead as a property of where the update lands, directly controls it, and mitigates forgetting. Confining the applied optimizer step to the complement of each weight matrix’s top singular subspace (Eq. 3) turns recipes that destroy prior capability into ones that retain it. The same operator works across recipes (SFT, SDFT, and Muon), from 1.7B to 32B parameters, and across data scale, where SFT degrades monotonically and SST stays flat. It also turns sequential fine-tuning from destructive into cumulative and keeps the model 2–4× closer to its base distribution in KL, thus preserving behavior that accuracy alone does not capture, such as a thinking model’s deliberation length and self-distillation’s fabricated reference solutions. 10

text: Limitations and Future Work. SST changes the feasible update geometry, its optimal learning rate need not equal that of unconstrained SFT. Establishing fully tuned learning–retention frontiers remains important future work. Scaling SST to models with hundreds of billions of parameters and to longer task sequences is an important next test. Additionally, using information about the update for each batch to dynamically update the protection rather than refreshing at fixed intervals is a next step to make the algorithm more efficient.

text: A Extended Related Work Classical continual-learning approaches often restrict the update direction: regularization penalizes move- ment along Fisher-important directions [23], while projected-gradient methods enforce constraints by re- placing gradient g with a projection Π(g) built from stored data, past-task gradients [9, 18, 27], activation subspaces [40], the feature-covariance null space [51], or earlier tasks’ adapters [52]. Continual learning for LLMs differs from these settings in several ways. These methods estimate subspaces from data, but reconstructing a distribution representative of an LLM’s pretraining corpus is infeasible at scale. Truly continual deployment may also lack explicit task boundaries. SST instead preserves a subspace derived from the weight spectrum (Eq. 3), requiring neither stored examples nor task boundaries. Several parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods also construct adapters from singular directions. PiSSA [31] initializes and trains LoRA factors from the principal singular components, prioritizing high-energy directions rather than protecting them. MiLoRA [50] is closer in motivation: it retains the principal components and adapts minor singular components, but represents the update through a fixed low-rank factorization. CorDA [57] first forms a context-oriented decomposition using input-activation covariance and initializes low-rank adapters from task- or knowledge-oriented components. In all three methods, the spectral choice is encoded in a parameter-efficient factorization derived at initialization. SST instead projects the dense update actually proposed by the optimizer into the two-sided non-principal complement.

SST instead projects the dense update actually proposed by the optimizer into the two-sided non-principal complement. It therefore constrains the realized weight change after stateful optimizer preconditioning, does not rely on a trainable adapter factorization or task-specific covariance estimate, and can refresh its protected basis during training. A complementary line leaves the optimizer alone and reduces the distribution shift driving forgetting: self- distillation rewrites the supervision into the model’s own output distribution [44], and online RL forgets less because its updates stay KL-close to the base policy [45, 48], both consistent with forgetting tracking distributional movement [24, 29]. These methods act on the data, whereas SST acts on the update, and the two compose (Table 4). B Additional Experiments & Details This appendix contains additional results supporting the main text. B.1 Model Merging If a constrained update stays in the low-energy complement of the weight spectrum, then two updates trained independently should interfere less when added back together. We test this with model merging experiments. In particular, we fine-tune a separate single-domain expert for Science, Medicine, and FinQA, then form Wmerged = Wbase + P d(Wd −Wbase) over all the 252 weight matrices. We copy every other parameter from the base model. No merge coefficients are tuned and no data is used to fit the combination. Each merged model is then scored in-domain against its own single-domain expert under identical decode settings. We report the interference caused by merging rather than the raw accuracy gap, which already favors SST. SST experts compose, SFT experts collide. Figure 11 shows that independently trained SFT experts interfere strongly when their task vectors are combined, and the interference compounds as more experts are merged. SST experts compose much more cleanly: pairwise merges remain close to their corresponding single-domain experts, and the three-expert merge degrades substantially more slowly. Note that W ←Wref + Π(W −Wref) is equivalent to Wt + Π(δt), with δt the step just applied, since every previously applied change already lies in the free subspace. The update lies in the correct subspace, but the step is based on projected-gradient moments and is therefore mis-scaled. The full procedure. Algorithm 1 details SST’s implementation, using the second of these three schemes. A superscript ℓindexes one constrained matrix, so W ℓ t is that matrix at step t and plays the role of Wpre above. The optimizer itself is never modified. It receives the full gradient, updates its moments, and proposes an ordinary step; SST then replaces the part of that step which lands on a constrained matrix with its free-to-free block. text: Multi-Target Few-Shot Prompting with Diffusion Language Models Anton Xue, Alan Li, and Rahul Saha University of Texas at Austin anton.xue@utexas.edu alan.li@cs.utexas.edu rahul.saha@utexas.edu github.com/AntonXue/fewshot-dlms
title: Multi-Target Few-Shot Prompting with Diffusion Language Models

text: Few-shot prompting is useful when instructions and rewards are hard to specify. One such application is editing by example, where a demonstrated formatting change or API migration may need to be applied across multiple sites. However, such edits often depend on both left and right context, making generation with causal autoregressive models awkward. We therefore introduce multi-target few-shot prompting with diffusion language models, where examples guide the infilling of multiple masked regions within a shared canvas. To address the known challenge of reliably following demonstrations in few-shot prompting, we further leverage selective masking of the canvas to derive a likelihood-ratio reward that favors example-supported infills. Across few-shot prompting benchmarks and software refactoring case studies, we find that demonstrations improve infilling accuracy, with example guidance yielding further gains in several settings. text: Few-shot prompting lets users specify model behavior through demonstrations, without updating model parameters (Brown et al., 2020; Garg et al., 2022). This is useful for test-time guidance, especially when instructions or rewards are difficult to specify (Kwon et al., 2023; Zamfirescu- Pereira et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023). For instance, in editing by example, a demonstrated formatting change or API migration can illustrate a transformation to apply elsewhere (Gupta et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024). When a demonstrated edit must be applied at multiple sites, a natural approach is to generate the tokens in place within a shared canvas containing all demonstrations and relevant context. We call this multi-target few-shot prompting. However, causal autoregressive models generate outputs as continuations, making it awkward to infill a target site using right-hand-side context. Incorporating such context requires rearranging the prompt or using specialized infilling formats (Bavarian et al., 2022; Fried et al., 2022), a process that becomes more cumbersome when editing multiple sites. Moreover, pretrained associations and sensitivity to prompt design can interfere with the model’s adherence to demonstrations (Min et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). Although guidance methods have been developed to mitigate these issues, they are primarily designed for autoregressive models and do not directly apply to in-place editing (Peng et al., 2025; Shi
title: Introduction

text: al., 2022; Wei et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021). Although guidance methods have been developed to mitigate these issues, they are primarily designed for autoregressive models and do not directly apply to in-place editing (Peng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024b). Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a natural interface for these tasks because they are not restricted to next-token prediction and can generate tokens anywhere on the shared canvas (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024a). As illustrated in Figure 1, the missing output regions are initially masked and progressively filled, while demonstrations and surrounding context remain visible. Each generated token can therefore condition on both left and right context, avoiding the specialized prompting harnesses often needed in causal autoregressive generation (Ou et al., 2025). Moreover, jointly infilling multiple sites allows tokens revealed at one site to inform subsequent predictions at others, helping maintain consistency (Kim et al., 2026). Yet several challenges remain in using DLMs for multi-target few-shot prompting. First, infilling requires allocating masked positions before generation, even though the required output lengths are generally unknown (Xu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025). Second, although DLMs condition on demonstrations, they may still fail to follow them reliably. Context-aware decoding suggests that contrasting predictions across contexts could strengthen adherence to demonstrations (Shi
title: Introduction

text: lengths are generally unknown (Xu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025). Second, although DLMs condition on demonstrations, they may still fail to follow them reliably. Context-aware decoding suggests that contrasting predictions across contexts could strengthen adherence to demonstrations (Shi et al., 2024b; Whitammer et al., 2022), but extending such guidance to complete DLM infills requires joint likelihoods that are often intractable or decoder-specific (Turok et al., 2026). In this work, we study how to overcome such challenges. We state our contributions next. 1.1 Contributions Multi-target few-shot prompting. We formulate this task as infilling multiple masked regions of a shared canvas containing demonstrations and surrounding context. We show that frozen DLMs can generate the missing outputs in place using the visible canvas directly, avoiding the specialized prompting harnesses often needed for causal autoregressive infilling. 2
title: Introduction

text: Example-guided sampling. We construct a tractable distribution over complete multi-site infills by revealing one token at a time, allowing us to compare candidate likelihoods with and without demonstrations. The resulting likelihood-ratio reward enables inference-time importance resampling to favor example-supported completions, offering an additional way to encourage adherence to demonstrations without retraining the generator. Empirical evaluation. We evaluate the effects of demonstrations, target counts, example guidance, and learned length prediction across repurposed few-shot prompting benchmarks and software refactoring case studies. We find that demonstrations generally improve infilling accuracy and guidance provides additional gains in some settings, but accurate length prediction remains a challenge. 1.2
title: Example-guided sampling.

text: Few-shot prompting. Few-shot prompting specifies tasks through demonstrations (Brown et al., 2020), but mappings and placement can affect model behavior (Li et al., 2026; Min et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2023). Applications include information extraction and semantic parsing (Pang et al., 2023; Shin and Van Durme, 2022), as well as programming by example and code editing, where demonstrations or prior edits guide subsequent transformations (Gulwani, 2011; Gupta et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2024). Prior work also explores batching multiple inputs into a single prompt, allowing their answers to be generated in one model call (Cheng et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). We instead study joint infilling of multiple unresolved regions in place within a shared canvas containing demonstrations and surrounding context. Test-time guidance. Beyond few-shot prompting, various test-time guidance methods have been developed to steer model generation. Contrastive decoding compares predictions from different models (Li et al., 2023; O’Brien and Lewis, 2023), while context-aware methods compare predictions under different conditioning contexts to strengthen the influence of supplied evidence or demonstrations (Peng et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024b; Song et al., 2025; Whitammer et al., 2022). In diffusion models, classifier-free guidance adjusts the influence of conditioning information (Ho and Salimans, 2021), while KL-regularized reward tilting (Korbak et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023)
title: Example-guided sampling.

text: 2025; Shi et al., 2024b; Song et al., 2025; Whitammer et al., 2022). In diffusion models, classifier-free guidance adjusts the influence of conditioning information (Ho and Salimans, 2021), while KL-regularized reward tilting (Korbak et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023) and inference-time resampling (Singhal et al., 2025) provide mechanisms for reweighting candidate generations. However, extending likelihood-based comparisons to complete DLM infills requires tractable sequence-level likelihoods under a specified decoding procedure. Diffusion language models. Masked diffusion language models iteratively unmask positions within a shared canvas, supporting flexible generation orders and parallel decoding (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024a). Recent models include LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025), Dream (Ye et al., 2025), Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion (Fu et al., 2026), and dQwen3.5 (Xue et al., 2026), alongside diffusion-augmented autoregressive approaches such as Uno (Sahoo et al., 2026). Standard masked infilling also requires allocating output lengths in advance, motivating work on flexible-length generation and length prediction (Ding et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2025). Prior work shows that decoding strategies affect generation quality and efficiency (Arriola et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026), while the tractability of complete-sequence likelihoods depends on the decoding procedure (Turok et al., 2026). 3

text: 2.1 Few-Shot Prompting on a Shared Canvas We consider a partially observed canvas containing D demonstrations, J target sites, and relevant surrounding context. Let z ∈(V ∪{m})N denote this canvas, where V is the vocabulary, m is a mask token, and N is the canvas length. The original target positions are T = M(z) = {i ∈[N] : zi = m}, where [N] = {1, . . . , N}; these positions form J masked output regions. The task is to fill these regions while preserving the visible content of the canvas. In Figure 2, D = 2 demonstrations illustrate alphabetical sorting, while J = 2 missing outputs occupy six masked positions in total (|T| = 6 in the schematic). At the target sites, the original word lists remain visible, while their sorted versions must be generated. More generally, demonstrations and targets may be interleaved with surrounding context; conventional few-shot prompting is recovered when a single target follows the demonstrations. For now, we assume the target sites are specified and their output lengths are given by an oracle, fixing the mask allocation before generation. 2.2 Masked Diffusion Language Models Like BERT-style masked language modeling (Devlin et al., 2019), masked DLMs predict missing tokens using visible context on both sides of each masked position (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al.,

text: mask allocation before generation. 2.2 Masked Diffusion Language Models Like BERT-style masked language modeling (Devlin et al., 2019), masked DLMs predict missing tokens using visible context on both sides of each masked position (Austin et al., 2021; Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024a). At each masked position i ∈M(z), the model predicts a distribution PDLM(vi | z) over candidate tokens vi ∈V . Turning these predictions into complete infills requires a decoding algorithm that determines which masked positions to reveal and when. Common strategies select positions by prediction confidence or a prescribed order, potentially revealing multiple tokens in parallel (Fruytier et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). As illustrated in Figure 2, newly revealed tokens become visible context for subsequent predictions, including those at other target sites. Different decoding procedures can induce different distributions over complete infills, so we seek a decoder that permits exact sampling and scoring. 3 Multi-Target Few-Shot Prompting and Reward Guidance While Section 2 assumes known output lengths, practical multi-target few-shot prompting must generally determine both the lengths and contents of missing outputs. We formulate this joint generation problem using a shared canvas with one placeholder per target site. To characterize the 4

text: complete infills produced by a DLM, we construct tractable likelihoods under one-token-at-a-time decoding. These likelihoods additionally enable reward guidance to encourage adherence to the demonstrations. 3.1 Length Allocation and Joint Infilling We begin with a compact canvas in which each missing output is represented by a single placeholder. Let ez denote this canvas, containing J target placeholders together with the visible demonstrations and surrounding context. For a proposed length vector L = (L1, . . . , LJ), where each Lj ≥1 specifies the token length of target j, we expand each placeholder into Lj mask tokens. This produces an expanded canvas zL with target positions TL = M(zL), on which the DLM can generate the missing contents. We model joint generation of output lengths and contents by first allocating lengths and then infilling the resulting canvas. Let πψ(L | ez) be a distribution over length allocations, with each Lj ranging over a prescribed finite set of positive integers. For a given allocation, let u = (ui)i∈TL ∈V TL denote a complete infill, assigning a vocabulary token ui ∈V to each target position. The tractable likelihoods above allow us to measure how strongly the demonstrations support each candidate and use this signal for additional reward guidance. Let E ⊆[N]\T denote selected demonstration-output positions, and write z \ E for the canvas with these positions additionally masked. Experimental setup. We evaluate four benchmarks spanning different few-shot transforma- tions: SST-2 (Socher et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2018) with demonstration-defined sentiment codes, List Functions–Easy (BIG-bench authors, 2023; Rule, 2020) for list transformations, SALT repetition (Zheng et al., 2025a,b) for artificial-language transformations, and Movie Director (Liu et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2021) for information extraction. We use three DLMs: LLaDA-1.5 (Zhu et al., 2026), Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-8B (Fu et al., 2026), and dQwen3.5-9B-Base (Xue et al., 2026), together with Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) as an autoregressive single-target comparison. Throughout, D and J denote the numbers of demonstrations and targets, respectively. We refer to generation without additional guidance (β = 0) as standard infilling for DLMs, or equivalently unguided sampling, and compare this with example guidance at β = 0.5 by default. Outputs are graded by task-specific exact or parsed matching, and the DLM experiments reveal one target token at a time in ascending canvas order. Further experimental details appear in Section B.1. 4.1 Single-Target Few-Shot Prompting We begin with single-target infilling, which closely resembles conventional autoregressive few-shot prompting, except that DLMs generate a masked output rather than a continuation. text: few-shot prompting is sensitive to demonstration selection and ordering (Zhao et al., 2021), we hold the target fixed when comparing different demonstration counts. We first randomly draw a sequence of 16 demonstrations from the benchmark, followed by one target. For each D ∈{1, 2, 4, 8, 16}, we construct a prompt by retaining only the first D demonstrations while keeping the target unchanged. These five related prompts form a prompt family, allowing us to vary the demonstration count without changing the target or previously included demonstrations. We evaluate 64 families per benchmark across four tasks and four model interfaces, drawing K = 64 samples for each prompt. Figure 5 reports standard infilling accuracy and the gain from guidance. Increasing the demonstration count from D = 1 to D = 16 improves accuracy without additional guidance in all 16 model–task series (Figure 5, top). For LLaDA, unguided accuracy rises from 14.0% to 76.5% on SST-2, from 33.3% to 74.7% on List Functions–Easy, from 0.0% to 98.8% on SALT repetition, and from 64.1% to 94.9% on Movie Director. This shows that demonstrations provide useful conditioning information even before applying reward guidance. Consistent with this observation, the reference answer’s example reward generally increases with D, indicating stronger relative likelihood support from the demonstrations (Section B.2). To evaluate the learned-allocation setting of Section 3.1, we train length predictors on structured few-shot tasks and Java edits (Section B.4). On List Functions–Easy, we fix D = 4 and vary J ∈{1, 2, 4, 8} across three DLMs, comparing oracle lengths against sampled predictions with the same content generator and standard infilling (β = 0). Figure 7 reports downstream accuracy and sensitivity to length errors. The learned predictors capture useful information about the required output lengths. They assign 40–46% probability mass to the reference length, compared with approximately 27% for a prior constructed from visible demonstration lengths (Section B.4). This indicates that the compact canvas contains useful predictive information about the missing output lengths. Despite this improvement over the length prior, learned allocation remains a gap for reliable downstream infilling. Sampling predicted lengths retains only 35–48% of oracle-length per-target accuracy (Figure 7, top). To examine this sensitivity directly, we impose offsets Lj = L⋆ j + ∆, where L⋆ j is the reference token length. One-token underallocation harms LLaDA and Nemotron more than overallocation, while dQwen3.5 is sensitive to errors in either direction (Figure 7, bottom). These findings identify accurate length allocation as a remaining challenge for practical multi-target infilling. 11

text: 5.2 Qualitative Analysis The limited benefits of guidance may arise because the sampled rewrites offer little room for improvement, or because the reward fails to identify correct candidates. With oracle lengths, only 23 of 127 sample pools contain both judged-correct and judged-incorrect rewrites, so even a perfect selector could improve pooled success by at most 8.3 percentage points. With learned lengths, 72 of 127 pools contain both outcomes, and the corresponding upper bound rises to 45.2 points (Section C.3). Thus, limited selection opportunities help explain the oracle-length results, whereas learned-length sampling leaves substantial room for better selection. A post-hoc Checkstyle example illustrates how the reward can favor an incorrect rewrite. An incorrect edit to logMessage changes the logged line number and message type, yet receives a higher example reward than the developer-consistent rewrite (8.69 versus 2.05 nats). At β = 0.5, this gives the incorrect rewrite approximately 28 times the resampling weight of each correct occurrence. Despite appearing only once among K = 16 samples, compared with seven occurrences of the correct rewrite, it receives 61.8% of the total weight, reducing expected LLM-judged success from 43.8% to 15.7%. Here, correct rewrites are available, but the reward disproportionately favors an incorrect one (Section C.3). 6

text: We introduce and study multi-target few-shot prompting with masked DLMs, where demon- strations guide the infilling of multiple regions within a shared canvas. One-token-at-a-time decoding with deterministic position selection defines a normalized distribution over complete infills, enabling exact sampling, scoring, and likelihood-based example guidance. Across few-shot prompting benchmarks and Java refactoring, we find that demonstrations improve infilling accuracy, with example guidance providing further gains in several settings. Our experiments further investigate the benefits of example guidance relative to likelihood sharpening, while identifying opportunities to improve target-length allocation for practical editing. Together, these findings provide a foundation for more effective example-guided multi-site infilling. Limitations. Our framework assumes that target sites and demonstration-output positions E are specified in advance, leaving their automatic identification for future work. The deterministic, one-token-at-a-time decoding used for exact sampling and scoring does not exploit parallel generation, while the induced distribution may depend on the reveal order and model interface for learned DLMs. Moreover, target lengths must be allocated before infilling, making improved length prediction an important direction for practical use. Example guidance measures relative support from demonstrations rather than correctness, so its effectiveness depends on how the reward ranks sampled infills. Increasing guidance strength can also concentrate resampling weights without necessarily improving accuracy (Section B.5). Our experiments include an autoregressive comparison for single-target prompting, while systematic comparison

text: B Few-Shot Prompting Experiments This appendix documents the experiments of Section 4 and provides additional analyses of demonstration conditioning, example guidance, and length allocation. B.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We study four types of few-shot transformations: classification, list trans- formation, artificial-language transformation, and information extraction. For SST-2 (Socher et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2018), sentiment labels are replaced by two resampled single-token capital-letter codes; the first two demonstrations cover both classes, and answers are graded by exact code match. List Functions–Easy (BIG-bench authors, 2023; Rule, 2020) uses 85 unconditional functions adapted from BIG-bench List Functions; the transformation rule is hidden, and parsed integer lists are matched exactly. SALT repetition (Zheng et al., 2025a,b) uses categories 5–6 with a separate dictionary for each example to translate words and repeat each verb or adjective; generated pairs pass an executable-rule check, and outputs are matched exactly. Movie Director (Liu et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2021) extracts the Director field from audited MIT Movie queries without naming the field in the instruction; labels are fixed, and outputs are graded by exact string match. Experimental studies. text: Experimental studies. We use three separately sampled studies with frozen models: a single-target demonstration sweep across four benchmarks and four model interfaces (J = 1, K = 64); a List Functions–Easy D × J grid across three DLMs (K = 16); and a cross-benchmark target-count sweep across four benchmarks and three DLMs (D = 4, K = 64). Each K specifies the number of samples per canvas, and the studies are analyzed separately. Prompt families. For single-target prompting, we draw 16 demonstrations followed by one target, then retain the first D ∈{1, 2, 4, 8, 16} demonstrations to construct five canvases with the same target. For multi-target prompting, we draw 16 demonstrations and eight targets. We first randomly interleave four demonstrations and eight targets (12 items), then extend this sequence with the remaining 12 demonstrations (24 items), preserving the relative order of the original items. Each (D, J) canvas retains the first D demonstrations and first J targets in that order. text: same target as D grows and evaluate the reference completion u⋆under both demonstration contexts. We report its example reward per target token: R(u⋆) |T| = log P1(u⋆) −log P0(u⋆) |T| . This is equivalently the reduction in reference-answer negative log likelihood per token when demonstration outputs become visible. The reward generally increases with D, indicating that additional demonstrations provide greater relative support for the reference answer. Because P0 masks demonstration outputs for DLMs but removes them from causal prompts, reward magnitudes are not directly comparable across these interfaces. Greater support for a reference answer does not, however, guarantee a larger gain from guidance. At D = 1, SST-2 exposes only one class code, while a single List Functions or SALT demonstration may be compatible with several rules. At larger D, unguided accuracy can approach saturation, leaving less room for additional improvement. Moreover, guidance depends on how the reward ranks the sampled alternatives, not only on its value for the reference answer. 24

To separate these effects, we compare example guidance with likelihood sharpening that uses the same total exponent on P1. C Software Editing Experiments We describe the Java refactoring benchmark and evaluation, then analyze demonstration condi- tioning, length allocation, and example guidance. C.1 Benchmark Construction and Evaluation Setup We derive multi-site editing tasks from Extract Method commits in SWE-Refactor (Xu et al., 2026b), which provide before-and-after snapshots and extracted helpers. For each (repository, commit, file, helper) group, we identify updated callers and represent each minimal changed region as a <old>/<new> pair. A seeded file-order rule assigns D accepted edits as demonstrations and J remaining sites as targets. Eligibility rules fixed before inspecting outcomes exclude edits requiring identifiers or literals absent from the prompt or changing asserted values. We also limit replacements to 80 LLaDA tokens and enclosing methods to 200 lines, retain one helper per commit and file, and collapse mirrored commits. Multi-target few-shot prompting could enable example-guided document and code editing across multiple sites. Practical use will require more reliable adherence to demonstrations and better prediction of output lengths. With these improvements, users could specify transformations through a few examples rather than editing each site manually. Potential risks. Incorrect transformations can propagate across sites, altering document meaning or introducing software defects. Our Checkstyle case study shows that example guidance can favor an incorrect edit even when demonstrations support the intended transformation. Practical use requires review, including compilation and testing for code; our evaluation instead relies on an LLM judge without execution. Artifacts and licensing. Understanding characteristics and activities of individuals in complex multi-person environments is crucial for real-world applica- tions. However, existing datasets often simplify this problem to grounded group activity recognition, single-person activity recognition, or close-set activity recognition, thus limiting the generalizability of models trained on these datasets. In this work, we introduce the task of Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition (GHADAR), which involves describing the characteristics and activity descriptions of every person in a video, provided the location of the person in the video, which is more practical for real-world applications. To facilitate this, we introduce a new dataset derived from AVA-Actions by generat- ing open-set captions for the person description and activity. In addition, we propose a novel method to effectively utilize the information con- tained in grounding during training by constraining the cross-attention masks during training in VLMs to improve performance for this task. Our experiments show that our method outperforms SOTA VLMs on this task. Finally, we demonstrate the limitations of existing evaluation metrics, which are overly reliant on human-annotations and exact text- text matching. As an added video-based evaluation, we propose a

Finally, we demonstrate the limitations of existing evaluation metrics, which are overly reliant on human-annotations and exact text- text matching. As an added video-based evaluation, we propose a holistic VLM-based evaluation schema that compares concepts directly between the video and the generated predictions. Thus, in this work, we develop a complete framework for GHADAR, including a dataset, a novel method and an evaluation schema, thereby establishing a strong foundation for future research in this domain. text: The rapid progress of vision–language models (VLMs) has expanded the scope of computer vision from recognition to rich, multimodal understanding. Modern applications increasingly demand systems that can not only detect people in complex scenes, realized using powerful detectors like YOLO ( [31]) and DINO ( [35]), but also describe their appearance, attribute fine-grained characteristics, and recognize ongoing activities in an open-set manner ( [6,9,11,16,29]). We formalize this challenge as Grounded Human-Attributed Descrip- tion and Activity Recognition (GHADAR): given the spatial location of people in a video (via bounding box), the goal is to generate two open-set cap- tions — one describing each person’s attributes (e.g., an elderly man in white on the street, a child in blue uniform) and one describing their activity (e.g., attempting to cross a road, playing on the footpath). This formulation demands per-person reasoning in multi-actor scenes, integrating both local appearance cues and broader contextual signals. Traditionally, research efforts in this direction have typically reduced the complexity of human-centric video understanding due to the scarcity of anno- tated data as shown in Figure 1. For example, some works reduce this task to un- derstanding the activity of a group of people as a whole or generating one caption for the entire video ( [13]). Meanwhile, some other works reduce the scope of ac- tivity recognition to a closed set of limited action labels ( [4,16,20]) or focus exclu- sively on single-person scenarios ( [33]). In response, this paper introduces a new dataset called AVA-Captions, which extends AVA-Actions ( [9]) with open-set, per-person captions for

text: recognition to a closed set of limited action labels ( [4,16,20]) or focus exclu- sively on single-person scenarios ( [33]). In response, this paper introduces a new dataset called AVA-Captions, which extends AVA-Actions ( [9]) with open-set, per-person captions for both attributes and activities, and involves multi-person interactions. Starting from AVA-Actions’ per-person action labels, we employ a high-capacity VLM (Nova Pro v1 ( [1])) to generate natural-language descrip- tions, followed by identity-aware deduplication via person re-identification. This enables training and evaluation of models on the proposed task. We further propose Constrained Attention Masking-based Pretrain- ing (CAMP), a two-stage training strategy for VLMs that explicitly leverages grounding information. In Phase 1, we constrain the attention mask of the out- put tokens to the visual tokens within an expanded bounding box around the target person, enforcing localized reasoning. In Phase 2, we remove constraints and fine-tune at a reduced learning rate, allowing the model to integrate global context without eroding its person-specific focus. Finally, we critique existing evaluation metrics in person and activity descrip- tion. These metrics are largely text-text comparisons based on n-grams (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE) ( [3, 18, 22]), or similarity between embeddings from pre- trained models (SBERT, CLIP) ( [24, 25]). Thus, these metrics often penalize semantically correct predictions that diverge lexically from human-annotated ground truth ( [21]). To

To address this, we introduce a VLM-driven evaluation framework that directly compares conceptual alignment between the raw video content and the model prediction from the lens of completeness, uniqueness and correctness of the caption. In summary, our contributions are: 1. Task and Dataset: We define the task of Grounded Human-Attributed De- scription and Activity Recognition (GHADAR) and release AVA-Captions, the first large-scale dataset with open-set, per-person appearance and activ- ity captions grounded in video.

Human Activity Recognition Methods: Human activity recognition (HAR) is an essential component of fields like home assistants, embodied AI and assistive technology, and is gaining traction in Deep Learning (DL) literature ( [6,11,29]).
