More examples are provided in the supplementary. 3 AVA-Captions Dataset Existing datasets focus on a single person or focus on a closed set of classes, as shown in Table 1. To address these limitations, we construct AVA-Captions, a large-scale benchmark for open-set, per-person appearance and activity de- scription in video. We build AVA-Captions from AVA-Actions v2.2 ( [9]), which contains 15-minute annotated segments for 235 training and 64 validation videos. Each segment includes frame-level bounding boxes and action labels for every visible person, identified by a unique Person ID (PID), with actions drawn from 80 predefined classes. To create training samples, we segment each annotated video into 10-second clips with a maximum overlap of 5s, yielding approximately 36.8K training and 11.1K testing clips from the original training and validation splits. As AVA-Actions does not release test-set annotations, we do not use its official test split. Once we have the extracted clips, we use a large VLM (called Expert-VLM) - Nova Pro ( [1]), to generate separate captions for person and activity descriptions for each person in the clip. For the person description, we provide the video along with an image crop extracted

While effective for learn- ing localized descriptions, this setup has two key limitations: (i) activities that inherently depend on global context—such as interactions with other people or distant objects—cannot be captured accurately under strict local constraints; and (ii) constructing person-specific attention masks requires knowing the exact mapping between output tokens and individuals, which is feasible during training but impractical at inference. A potential workaround would involve dynamically monitoring each generated token and updating the attention mask whenever a new subject is introduced, but this approach significantly increases inference complexity and latency, rendering Phase 1 alone unsuitable for deployment. To address these issues, Phase 2 training removes the constraints and fine- tunes the model with the default attention mask (Figure 3) at a reduced learning rate. This continuation serves two purposes: it enables the model to incorporate global contextual cues while learning to generate outputs under the standard attention mechanism. At the same time, a lower learning rate ensures that that the attention

At the same time, a lower learning rate ensures that that the attention weights of the model are not changed drastically so that the model still focuses on the regions around the person of interest. Together, these phases yield a model that balances localized grounding with global contextual reasoning, while remaining practical for inference. 4.4 Motivation We observed that when training a VLM on our dataset, the model frequently confused actions performed by different individuals (for example, action done by person B predicted for person A). To mitigate this, we introduce the CAMP framework, built on the hypothesis that for describing a person’s actions and appearance, the local context surrounding the individual is generally sufficient, without requiring attention to the entire scene. By masking tokens outside the region of interest, the model is encouraged to learn mappings between localized visual features and their corresponding textual descriptions. While this hypothe- sis holds in many cases, modifying attention maps dynamically during inference is impractical. To address this limitation, we introduce Phase 2 training, where the constraints are removed and the model is fine-tuned with a reduced learning rate. Prior work has shown that lower learning

As compared to the LLAVA-One Vision (LLAVA-OV) baseline ( [17,19]), which offers a 0.5 B model, we see a significant improvement with InternVL3 1B model. While some of this can be attributed to the more number of parameters (since LLAVA-OV does not offer 1B model), the multimodal encoder structure in InternVL3 ( [7]) style of models also plays a significant part. Unlike LLAVA, both InternVL3 and Qwen support frame-level injection, enabling bounding boxes to be passed separately for each frame. This design yields consistent improvements, which are further amplified by our CAMP framework through constrained at- tention in Phase 1 and unconstrained fine-tuning in Phase 2. Interestingly, we observe greater relative improvements for the smaller InternVL3-1B backbone compared to the larger Qwen2.5VL-3B. This is expected: larger models can al- ready capture complex functions, making constrained training less impactful, whereas smaller models benefit more from CAMP’s inductive bias. Due to com- pute limitations, we were unable to compare with larger-scale models. However, we emphasize that the proposed task is most relevant for home assistants and surveillance systems, where inference typically occurs on edge devices. For this reason, our study focuses on small- to medium-scale models, which are more practical for such applications. However, it can be seen from the video frame that the events described by the prediction are actually happening and noteworthy. We provide more such exam- ples in the supplementary. This highlights a limitation: existing metrics cannot directly verify whether a predicted caption is factually grounded in the visual content. To address this, we propose using a large-scale model to act as a judge, given the actual video and the predictions. Thus, these metrics are computed without knowing the GT captions and designed to complement, rather than re- place, the classical measures. More specifically, given a video, an image crop of the target subject, and the predicted caption, we query Nova-Pro v1 ( [1]) as well as Qwen2.5 VL 32B ( [2]) to assign a score from 1–5 (higher is better) for each of the following: 1. text: to assign a score from 1–5 (higher is better) for each of the following: 1. Subject / Activity Correctness (CRT): How much of the predicted caption is actually present in the video for the given subject. CRT measures factual alignment of the prediction with the video content. 2. Subject / Activity Completeness (CMP): How much of the subject descrip- tion / activity is described by the caption. CMP measures whether all rele- vant actions are captured by the prediction. 3. Subject Uniqueness (UNQ): How discriminative is the predicted subject de- scription in identifying the subject. UNQ measures ambiguity in the pre- dicted caption. CRT and CMP are analogous to precision and recall, respectively whereas UNQ is motivated for practical use cases and its definition is dependent on the video. For example, if a predicted caption reads: “The man : opens the door", it can be considered highly unique for describing the subject if there is only one man

We believe that UNQ is a better metric than CMP for subject description for practical purposes. In addition, CMP is ill-defined especially for the subject description since there can be various ways of describing the same person. While this is also true for the activities, CMP gives an approximate measure of whether all important activities are captured by the model and so we retain it as a metric. text: In this paper, we introduce the task of Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition and propose a dataset called Ava-Captions for the same by modifying the AVA-Actions dataset. In order to effectively use the ground- ing information in this task, we propose the CAMP method that constrains the attention mask during training, thereby directing the model to focus more on the local context around a person to better caption their description and ac- tivity. Finally, we propose VLM-based metrics that directly compares predicted captions with the content of the video instead of incomplete human annotations
title: J. Paranjape et al.

text: GHADAR 15 and serves as a complement to classical metrics. A limitation in the VLM-based metric is that it is highly dependent on the ability of the VQA to understand the video and the instruction. With this work, we want to encourage future research in the human-attributed video understanding tasks that can be useful for various applications.

text: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking Admir Krnić*, Kosta Pavlović, Petar Nedić, Željko Bolević, Slavko Kovačević, Igor Djurović DeepMark Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize. In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality. Keywords: audio watermarking; zero-bit watermarking; backward compatibility; legacy chain; revocation 1.
title: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio

text: Recent advances in generative AI have substantially increased the realism and accessibility of synthetic audio content. State-of-the-art audio generation techniques are capable of producing high- quality speech and audio at scale [1]. As a result, concerns surrounding large-scale misinformation, fraud and reputational damage have intensified, alongside a broader erosion of trust in digital media. Audio watermarking, a technique that embeds imperceptible signals at generation time and later recovers them to verify provenance, has emerged as a practical mechanism for attribution and misuse prevention. It is also becoming a legal requirement: the European Union’s AI Act (Article 50) mandates that providers of generative AI mark and detect artificially generated content, and its accompanying Code of Practice further requires that a replacement detector be backward compatible, detecting previously marked content with no loss of capability [2]. A line of recent deep-learning approaches jointly trains embedders and detectors, which we survey in Section 2. These systems all share an implicit assumption: an embedder and its detector are trained as a single matched pair and deployed together. In practice, watermarking systems must * Correspondence to: Admir Krnić, admir.krnic7@gmail.com Copyright: © 2026 DeepMark. All rights reserved. arXiv:2610.22296v1 [cs.SD] 15 Oct 2026

text: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking evolve, with new embedder-detector pairs introduced over time to harden against new attacks, improve quality, or reduce cost, while previously distributed content stays in circulation and must remain verifiable. Existing methods provide no explicit mechanism for an updated detector to keep recognizing watermarks from earlier embedders while still rejecting unrelated content, leading to invalidated watermarks or elevated false positives after updates. Re-embedding old content is often infeasible, and maintaining many detector versions at inference is complex and itself raises the false-positive rate. We call the ordered sequence of legacy embedders 𝐸1, . . . , 𝐸𝑣−1, that a newly trained detector 𝐷𝑣 must continue to support, the legacy chain. A backward-compatible 𝐷𝑣must (i) detect watermarks from all embedders in its chain, (ii) reject unwatermarked audio, and (iii) reject watermarks from embedders outside the chain. Objective (iii) is not merely an accuracy concern; it is what makes a compromised version revocable. If an embedder 𝐸𝑖is leaked, an adversary can stamp arbitrary audio with its watermark. The response is to revoke 𝐸𝑖, dropping it from every future detector’s chain so that any detector issued after the leak rejects it outright. Without this, a single leak permanently invalidates the watermark, as every newer detector keeps accepting the forgeries. This motivates strict version separation rather than monotone

text: every future detector’s chain so that any detector issued after the leak rejects it outright. Without this, a single leak permanently invalidates the watermark, as every newer detector keeps accepting the forgeries. This motivates strict version separation rather than monotone forward acceptance. In this work, we conduct the first systematic study of backward compatibility in neural audio watermarking. The following contributions are made: • The backward-compatibility objective for zero-bit watermarking is formalized, and the legacy-chain abstraction is introduced together with its security implications. • A training framework is proposed that combines a performance-weighted sampling scheme across frozen legacy embedders with ADL applied to the new embedder. • The framework is evaluated across eight model versions that span architectural changes in both embedders (DenseNet, ViTMAE) and detectors (ResNet, AST), and the ADL is shown to substantially restore TNR against out-of-chain embedders with no measurable degradation in detection accuracy or audio quality. • The same mechanism is shown to enable revocation: a leaked embedder can be dropped from the legacy chain and reliably rejected by detectors trained without it. 2.

text: Deep-learning-based audio watermarking jointly trains an embedder and a detector to balance imperceptibility and robustness. RobustDNN [3] introduced the basic recipe, WavMark [4], AudioSeal [5], Timbre Watermarking [6], and SilentCipher [7] subsequently improved robustness to common signal-processing attacks. VoiceMark [8] extends robustness to zero-shot voice-cloning attacks. All of these systems train and deploy embedders and detectors as fixed pairs and provide no explicit mechanism for cross-version compatibility. Petrov et al. [9] study the coexistence and ensembling of independently trained watermarks. Their setting differs from ours in two important ways: embedder-detector pairs are trained independently (with no shared parameters or training signal), and there is no obligation for a later detector to recognize watermarks from an earlier one. As a consequence, their reported interference is minimal. 2

text: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking We instead consider the coupled-training setting required for backward compatibility, and show that this coupling introduces failure modes that independent training does not exhibit. Continual learning addresses sequential task acquisition without catastrophic forgetting [10], through methods such as Elastic Weight Consolidation [11], Learning without Forgetting [12], and Synaptic Intelligence [13]. These approaches assume a single, architecturally fixed model updated over time and therefore do not accommodate the architectural changes that accompany real-world watermarking updates. 3. Problem Formulation We first review zero-bit watermarking and then formalize the backward-compatibility objective on top of it. Zero-Bit Watermarking. Zero-bit watermarking aims to decide whether a digital signal contains a watermark. Given an input signal 𝑥∈𝒳, an embedder 𝐸produces a watermarked signal 𝑥𝑤= 𝐸(𝑥), where the perturbation 𝐸(𝑥) −𝑥is imperceptible. A detector 𝐷then produces a real-valued detection score 𝐷(𝑥𝑤) ∈R, with larger positive values indicating the presence of a watermark and smaller (negative) values indicating its absence. A binary decision is obtained by comparing the score against a threshold. The pair (𝐸, 𝐷) is typically trained end-to-end: the detector learns to distinguish watermarked from unwatermarked audio, while the embedder learns to introduce minimal perturbations that the detector can reliably detect. For each subsequent version 𝑣> 1, a new embedder 𝐸𝑣is trained jointly with a new detector 𝐷𝑣. The legacy chain at version 𝑣is the set of earlier embedders {𝐸𝑖: 𝑖< 𝑣}, minus a revocation set 𝑅of embedders deliberately dropped (e.g. a leaked one). text: chain (high TNR against out-of-chain embedders): both future versions 𝐸𝑗with 𝑗> 𝑣that did not yet exist at training, and any embedder from 𝑅. The last objective we refer to as the version boundary: the line a detector holds between the in-chain embedders it accepts and the out-of-chain ones it rejects, whether future or revoked. This is what distinguishes backward compatibility from standard multi-embedder training: an out-of-chain embedder is not merely absent, it must be actively rejected, which is precisely what makes revoking a leaked embedder possible. 3

text: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking 4. Method Although backward compatibility is a general concern, we focus exclusively on zero-bit audio watermarking in this work. Our method has three components: a backward-compatible training setup, a performance-weighted sampling strategy that allocates training iterations across the legacy chain, and a diversity loss that prevents the new embedder from drifting toward its predecessors. Backward-Compatible Training Setup. Embedders operate in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain. The watermark is added to the magnitude spectrogram within the [500, 4000] Hz embedding band and the time-domain signal is reconstructed via inverse STFT using the original phase. Detectors mirror the embedder, they compute the STFT and a mel spectrogram restricted to the same embedding band, then feed it to the detection network. We extend the idea from SilentCipher [7] of enforcing a hard constraint on the maximum perceptual distortion, which lets us train with a detection-only loss. This distortion constraint drives all embedders to a consistent quality level (PESQ 4.3–4.5). Because every model then sits at essentially the same perceptual quality, we can compare models by detection accuracy alone. For the detection objective we adopt the push loss introduced by AWARE [14], which augments the standard detection MSE with a term that widens the margin between watermarked and unwatermarked frames: ℒpush = MSE( ˆ𝑦, 𝑦) −𝜆©­

The scheme adaptively emphasizes the embedders on which the detector currently performs worst. Based on our experiments 𝑘= 8 yielded the best results. Embedder Collapse and the Need for a Diversity Loss. Performance-weighted sampling together with push loss is sufficient to obtain high TPR within the legacy chain, but it leaves the new embedder 𝐸𝑣entirely free to position its residual watermark anywhere in the signal space. The detector 𝐷𝑣is itself trained from scratch, what is fixed are the legacy embedders 𝐸1, . . . , 𝐸𝑣−1, whose residuals are frozen throughout training while 𝐸𝑣’s residual is the only one free to move. The easiest path to a low detection loss is therefore for 𝐸𝑣to drift toward the frozen legacy embedders’ residual distributions, so that 𝐷𝑣can satisfy every in-chain pair with a single decision boundary. We refer to this failure mode as embedder collapse: the new embedder’s residual ends up implicitly close to those of the frozen legacy embedders, destroying the version boundary. We treat the mel spectrogram of the audio watermarked by each embedder as a “class” on the unit sphere and separate these classes with an additive angular margin, inspired by the margin formulation from ArcFace [16]. The setting, however, is not the fixed-identity classification ArcFace was designed for: an embedder has no identity vector to learn, and only 𝐸𝑣 is trainable while the legacy embedders are frozen. The ADL adapts the angular margin to this setting with two changes. First, we remove ArcFace’s learnable per-class prototypes. The proposed loss is essential for preserving the separation between model versions. Without it, the embedding spaces of the legacy and new embedders collapses, eliminating the intended version boundary. The mel spectrogram is a robust representation in which perceptually similar signals produce very similar mel features, so a strong margin or sharp scale would destabilize training. This is why weak parameters (𝑚= 0.1, 𝑠= 8) suffice: the loss still enforces the separation, but needs only a gentle push. Gradient Normalization. Combining ℒpush and ℒdiv through a fixed scalar weighting is brittle: the two losses operate on very different scales so one term tends to dominate the gradient. We instead balance them with a per-step gradient-norm scaling inspired by GradNorm [17]. Experimental Setup This section describes the data, model architectures and evaluation protocol. Dataset. Training data is drawn from the Mozilla Common Voice corpus [18], with all training audio resampled to 44.1 kHz during preprocessing. The test set consists of audio files sampled from three corpora, LibriSpeech [19], LJSpeech [20], and Mozilla Common Voice, and spans a range of native sampling rates, reflecting a realistic and heterogeneous evaluation condition. Model Architectures. We evaluate two model families with complementary inductive biases: a convolutional family (DenseNet [21] embedder with a ResNet [22] detector) and a Transformer family (ViTMAE [23, 24] embedder with an AST [25] detector). Each architecture uses a fixed template, across versions we vary only its activation function and its depth, holding every other hyperparameter (widths, kernel sizes, attention heads, feature dimensions) constant. The depth knob is specific to each architecture: dense blocks for DenseNet, encoder/decoder layers for ViTMAE, residual stacks for ResNet, and encoder layers for AST. Table 1 gives the

Modeling realistic architectural drift. We train a sequence of eight versions (𝑣1 to 𝑣8), one model, i.e. one embedder-detector pair, per version. Over time, practitioners swap in newer activation functions, enlarge networks, and eventually replace entire architecture families with newer ones. Our version sequence is designed to mimic this trajectory. Concretely, we choose architectures along two orthogonal axes: 6

text: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking 1. Activation rotation. Within a fixed embedder/detector size, we rotate the activation function in the order in which it became standard in the deep-learning literature: ReLU [26] first, then Swish [27], then GELU [28]. This mimics a team that periodically swaps the activation function for a more recent one without otherwise changing the network. 2. Capacity step-ups. After the activation rotation has cycled through ReLU/Swish/GELU at the original size, we step up the network’s capacity (more dense blocks / more encoder-decoder layers) while keeping the most recent activation. This mimics a team that, after exhausting easy activation upgrades, decides to scale the model. The same two-axis schedule is applied first to the convolutional family (𝑣1–𝑣4) and then repeated on the Transformer family (𝑣5–𝑣8), since Transformer-based audio models entered the field later than convolutional ones. The transition from 𝑣4 to 𝑣5 simulates the discrete jump that occurs when a deployment switches to a fundamentally newer architecture family rather than enlarging the existing one. Training Details. All models are trained with Adam at a learning rate of 3 × 10−4, decayed by an exponential schedule (𝛾= 0.95), with a batch size of 128 and gradient-norm clipping at 0.1. Evaluation Metrics. Only when 𝐸𝑖is pushed away by the diversity loss does the new embedder produce distinct residuals, and the detector rejects the revoked embedder fully in both families. Third-Party Watermarks. In production, our detectors must not accept third-party watermarks, and our watermarked content must not be accepted by third-party detectors. We tested both directions against the publicly released zero-bit AudioSeal model [5], using all eight pair of models trained with the full method: (i) the audio watermarked by each of our embedders is passed to the AudioSeal detector, and (ii) the audio watermarked by the AudioSeal embedder is passed to each of our detectors. Because AudioSeal operates at 16 kHz, audio is resampled to 16 kHz at its input. We use AudioSeal’s default decision threshold of 0.5. For every one of the eight versions, and in both directions, not a single file is detected, so TNR is 100% for every pair. This agrees with the negligible interference that Petrov et al. [9] report for independently trained watermarks. 7. text: to signal-processing and codec attacks is out of scope, and none of our models are trained with attack augmentation. We ask a narrower question: does backward compatibility itself survive distortion? A deployed watermark is transmitted and edited before detection, so a framework that held only on clean audio would be of little practical use. We therefore test, rather than optimize for, robustness, re-running the evaluation under the DeepMark benchmark [29]. Table 4 reports the min/max/mean TPR and TNR per attack for both training conditions; the version boundary is preserved under attack. The version boundary survives attack. The baseline’s TNR was already broken on clean audio and stays broken under every attack (mean 11–14%), while ours was near-perfect on clean audio and stays that way, with mean TNR ≥98% on all 27 attacks and exactly 100% on 21. TPR is essentially unchanged. In-chain detection tracks the baseline across attacks, confirming that adding the diversity loss has a negligible cost in compatibility under distortion. 8.
title: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking

text: We presented the first systematic study of backward compatibility in zero-bit deep-learning audio watermarking. We formalized the backward-compatibility objective via the legacy-chain abstraction, identified the embedder-collapse failure mode that breaks version boundaries when a new detector is trained against frozen legacy embedders, and proposed a training framework that combines performance-weighted sampling and push loss together with ADL balanced by gradient normalization. Across eight versions and two architecture families, the method restores out-of-chain TNR without degrading within-chain detection or perceptual quality, and the restored version boundary holds under distortion. The same mechanism enables revocation: a leaked embedder dropped from the chain is reliably rejected by detectors trained without it. We see the legacy chain as a useful abstraction for future watermarking systems that must evolve under deployment constraints, and we leave robustness under adversarial attack and multibit extensions to future work. 10

title: PRIVATE RETRIEVAL AUGMENTED GENERATION VIA RANDOM

text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models. Our results for the first time suggest that random projection can serve as a competitive and practical baseline for privacy-preserving RAG systems. 1
title: PRIVATE RETRIEVAL AUGMENTED GENERATION VIA RANDOM

text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [1, 2] enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating information retrieved from external knowledge. However, recent studies show that carefully crafted prompts [3, 4, 5, 6] can extract sensitive information such as personal identity information from the external datastore. Since attack queries can closely resemble legitimate user queries, simple access control may block ordinary users [3, 4]. Recent work has begun to explore privacy risks in RAG, with a leading focus on differential privacy (DP) [6, 7]. Although DP methods provide formal statistical guarantees, they often degrade output quality (e.g., leading to high perplexity) due to DP’s fundamental properties of worst-case guarantees, and are usually complicated to implement in practice. To this end, we propose private RAG via random projection to defend against data extraction attacks. Our key idea is that differential privacy guarantees may be an overkill to prevent state-of-the-art attacks practically, whereas (some specific) random projection matrices naturally preserve pairwise similarities of the inputs in the lower- dimensional space. The extra randomness alters datastore embeddings so attackers may not recover the original text. This enables users to obtain accurate answers from the RAG system while adversaries fail. We apply a single projection step to datastore embeddings in the offline stage and the same matrix to user queries in the online stage. In this work, we

text: users to obtain accurate answers from the RAG system while adversaries fail. We apply a single projection step to datastore embeddings in the offline stage and the same matrix to user queries in the online stage. In this work, we consider two RAG architectures: ‘KNN-LM’ [1] and ‘Standard RAG’ [2]2. In KNN-LM, the system linearly combines the outputs of the language model and the k-nearest neighbour outputs (usually organized as a softmax over cosine similarities between queries and the datastore embeddings), and generates next token. In Standard RAG, the system concatenates retrieved texts with the query and feeds them to the LLM. In this work, we focus on the settings where formal privacy guarantees are not desired, and thus evaluate privacy leakage by exploring the success rates of strong, existing attacks empirically. ∗Correspondence to: Dixi Yao <dixi@uchicago.edu> 2We note that there exist various RAG architectures, and we use the naming ‘Standard RAG’ just to contrast with the less popular KNN-LM architecture. arXiv:2610.22297v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026

In summary, our RP technique significantly improves utility (over 50% on average across datasets) over the baseline methods without degrading empirical privacy performance. 2 Related Works Private RAG. Prior work shows that various RAG architectures can reveal sensitive personal data (e.g., emails, phone numbers, and URLs) from the external datastore [3, 5, 8, 9, 10]. Existing defenses, such as DP-based sampling and aggregation [6, 11] and synthetic data [12], reduce efficiency on large datasets and often require extra validation or training. Moreover, Zhao and Zhang [13] show that synthetic data alone does not fully prevent memorization or leakage. He et al. [14] apply local differential privacy to sensitive content like addresses. However, privacy can involve entire sentences or paragraphs beyond tokens, making simple masking insufficient. Thareja et al. [15] mix original and sanitized documents, which requires identifying all private tokens and is impractical for large-scale RAG. Privacy-Preserving Random Projection. Certain random projection operations are a common technique for re- ducing dimensionality while preserving some similarity measures with high probability (e.g., based on the Johnson- Lindenstrauss lemma [16]). Prior works have shown that methods built on top of these projections can achieve differential privacy (DP) for specific applications [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25]. In this work, we show that random projection can be effective for a variety of RAG scenarios as well. 3 Private RAG via Random Projection 3.1 Threat Model Online inference (API) Offline phase Query q Datastore d1, …, dn Tokenize & embed Tokenize & embed Random projection R Random projection R x (e1, …, en) same secret R Similarity search: si = Similarity(Rx, Rei) Rx (Re1, …, Ren) KNN-LM LLM q Softmax λ pLLM + (1 −λ) pkNN Next token si pLLM pkNN Standard RAG Top-k document chunks LLM q Answer concatenate Figure 1: Overview of Private RAG via RP. text: method as an empirical defense against data extrac- tion attacks. We consider a black-box setting in which the attacker has access only to model API responses, while model parameters, the random projection matrix, logits, embeddings, and latent representations remain inaccessi- ble [26, 27]. The attacker submits queries to the RAG sys- tem using the API service and attempts to extract sensitive information in the datastore from the generated response through one round or multiple rounds. This is a common protocol in modern RAG applications where companies provide consulting service through LLM with an internal datastore while only text answers are exposed to users. The threat model also aligns with the threat scenarios considered in prior work on RAG privacy [3, 4, 28]. In short, we assume the attacker knows that RP is used but does not have direct access to the specific random matrices, with the projection matrix remaining undisclosed. Attackers are free to conduct repeated-query (Section 4.2) or multi-round adaptive attacks (Section 4.3). As network- and system-level attacks are out of scope and access to embeddings is restricted, we do not consider white-box attacks, embedding inversion, projection-matrix inversion, or side-channel attacks requiring side information or access beyond the LLM’s text responses. To provide a clearer understanding of what constitutes sensitive information, we show examples of leakage with and without

We perform this preprocessing step once and store the results, introducing no runtime overhead during inference. For any query/prompt, we encode it as x = f(prompt) and compute its projection x′ = R x, which requires only a single matrix-vector mul- tiplication. We then perform retrieval in the k-dimensional space by finding the nearest neighbors to x′ among {e′ i}i∈[n] and computing a softmax over their cosine similarities with x′. We then perform retrieval in the k-dimensional space by finding the nearest neighbors to x′ among {e′ i}i∈[n] and computing a softmax over their cosine similarities with x′. Finally, we combine this softmax with the parametric LLM’s logits for x in a weighted manner to select the next token. We repeat generation until reaching the maximum token limit or generating an end-of-sequence token. Algorithm 2 (in Section D) and Algorithm 1 illustrate the im- plementation of our random projection method. The overall process follows the standard RAG pipeline: we first tokenize and embed the datastore offline, and store the representations in FAISS or another efficient indexing framework to enable fast retrieval at inference time. During inference, the model performs autoregressive generation via iterative next-token prediction. For standard RAG (Algorithm 1), we compute the similarity between the projected query embedding ˜x and the projected datastore embeddings ˜ED, and retrieve the most relevant text based on this similarity. The retrieved text is concatenated with the original query to form an augmented prompt, which is then passed to a parametric LLM to generate the final output. text: to a parametric LLM to generate the final output. The algorithm of KNN-LM is summarized in Section D. Privacy Implications. Random projection preserves privacy by altering the retrieval process: given a query, vanilla RAG retrieves the highest-scoring document and generates a corresponding token, which may contain sensitive information. After RP, embeddings that are close to the original top match can be selected with non-negligible probability (Section C). As a result, alternative tokens may replace the originally retrieved token. Utility Discussions. A natural question arises: if random projections alter the retrieved neighbors, how does the model remain accurate? The reason is that random projection approximately preserves embedding distances, ensuring retrieval still selects relevant information. This has been extensively studied in prior literature [16]. In Section B, for completeness, we provide proof that our random projection preserves L2 distance and cosine similarity. Section B.2 shows a study with synthetic data consistent with the theoretical analysis. For DP-based baselines, achieving privacy guarantees sacrifices utility. DP introduces a fundamental tradeoff: a small clipping bound overly distorts embeddings, while a large bound increases noise magnitude, both degrading retrieval utility. From Table 7, we can see that Pablo Trapero and Aleksander Ford are originally mentioned in the question, so it is reasonable that the responses also contain these two names. If ϵ →∞, the noise vanishes; with a sufficiently large clipping bound, DP-RP-G approaches ours RP method. Thus, the utility loss arises from the additional constraints required for formal DP rather than from RP itself. DP aggregation methods face a similar trade-off, as their utility depends strongly on perturbation magnitude and therefore on privacy budget [6]. As shown in Section 4, even relatively loose privacy budgets can substantially degrade utility while still allowing non-negligible leakage. Clipping is typically required in DP mechanisms to bound sensitivity [36]; prior work similarly constrains vectors to bounded domains [37]. To isolate the effect of clipping and adding noise, we ablate the clipping operation without Gaussian noise. In Table 9, we compare RP with and without clipping, while Figure 5 varies the clipping bound. The results show that larger clipping consistently reduces perplexity, whereas sufficiently large clipping bounds recover performance close to RP. 5

text: In this work, we propose a simple random projection method to defend against data extraction attacks for RAG applications. Compared with DP-based approaches, we show that the specific random Gaussian projection can empirically protect against data reconstruction, at approximately the same level as parametric model without RAG datastore, while still maintaining semantic utility, with a 7% overall decrease compared with vanilla RAG. 8

text: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection A PREPRINT Limitations At evaluation side, large-scale evaluation of privacy-preserving methods in real-world LLM-based RAG systems remains an interesting future work. Real-world systems may need to process billions of queries daily. In Table 8, one query takes about 8 seconds. Hence, evaluating one million queries would take 92 days without system-level optimization. Such large-scale evaluation thus requires system-level contributions, which we defer to future work. Ethical Considerations We use models and datasets that are publicly available on the Internet and licensed for non-commercial research use. We do not involve personally identifiable information (PII) which are not allowed to make public. We use only publicly available or synthetically generated datasets; we did not use any proprietary data or private user information at any stage of the experiments. These datasets are publicly available and widely used in the research community. Consistent with prior work, we did not further anonymize the data, as it was collected and released under publicly accessible licenses and used solely for research purposes. We did not introduce new personal data, nor did we attempt to re-identify individuals beyond what is already present in the original datasets.

For completeness, we provide analysis below. Let the query embedding be x, the retrieved embedding by vanilla RAG be e, and the random projection matrix be R. The original ℓ2 distance is ∥x −e∥2. According to the Johnson–Lindenstrauss transform, when the projection variance is 1/k, we have the boundary condition (1 −λJL)∥x −e∥2 ≤∥Rx −Re∥2 ≤(1 + λJL)∥x −e∥2 where λJL = Ω �q log d k  [16]. This ensures that the ℓ2 distance is well preserved after projection. Further, the original retrieval score, typically cosine similarity, ρ = x⊤e ∥x∥2 ∥e∥2 can also be preserved after projection. After random projection, the score becomes ρ′ = x⊤R⊤Re ∥Rx∥2 ∥Re∥2 . For fixed x and e, the expectation satisfies E[ρ′] = ρ �1 −1−ρ 2k  + O � 1 k2  (Proof in Section B.1). Thus, when k is sufficiently large, the expected cosine similarity after projection closely approximates the original score, preserving retrieval quality despite token perturbations. This result shows that after random projection, embeddings that are sufficiently close in the original space can overtake the original top-1 embedding with non-negligible probability. This behavior is desirable for privacy preservation: sensitive tokens (e.g., names, addresses, or identification numbers) often have embeddings close to semantically related but less sensitive alternatives, and random projection allows these alternatives to replace the original sensitive tokens with controlled probability. Combined with the bounds in Section B, this demonstrates that random projection limits distortion to a reasonable range, preserving general semantic content while reducing the likelihood that specific sensitive tokens are deterministically selected. 15

The language model produces a next-token distribution PLM based on the current context x. In parallel, the KNN distribution PKNN is computed by measuring the cosine similarity between the projected query embedding ˜x and each projected datastore embedding ˜ei, followed

text: The language model produces a next-token distribution PLM based on the current context x. In parallel, the KNN distribution PKNN is computed by measuring the cosine similarity between the projected query embedding ˜x and each projected datastore embedding ˜ei, followed by a softmax over the top-K nearest neighbors to obtain a probability distribution over candidate tokens. The final next-token distribution is obtained by linearly combining the two distributions with weight λ = 0.25. The selected token y is then appended to the context and the generated answer, and the process repeats. H More Discussion H.1 False Positive Classification of Non-Sensitive Information Although random projection provides strong privacy protection overall, our experiments on Enron Email, ECHR, and C4 reveal that a small number of items may still be leaked. All failure cases fall into the case of leakage examples without sensitive information. Analysis of these failure cases reveals a clear pattern: random projection provides complete protection (100% leakage prevention) for specific content such as numbers, IDs, and email addresses. title: AI CONSILIUM:

text: Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. We developed a multidimensional benchmark using 300 diagnostically resolved NEJM–MedQA cases: 110 for physician reference ratings and Judge calibration and 190 for held-out evaluation. Eight single-model pipelines generated independent role-specific opinions and interactive-consilium reports under free-form and structured clinical-reasoning conditions. A physician-calibrated LLM Judge evaluated 3,040 final reports and the corresponding structured primary-role outputs. Model identity separated report quality more strongly than response format. Structured final reports had higher overall mean scores in seven of eight model pipelines, with their clearest advantage in management (2.740 vs. 2.436). Compared with the structured pre-consilium primary-role opinion, the complete structured synthesis had higher pooled scores across all five shared criteria, with the largest increases in problem prioritization, factual grounding, and reasoning coherence. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These findings show that the benchmark can distinguish model capability, the contribution of multidisciplinary synthesis, criterion-specific effects of response structure, deliberation dynamics, and inference requirements within one common-case evaluation. Keywords large language models · clinical reasoning · second opinion · multidisciplinary consultation · LLM-as-a-judge 1

text: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions A PREPRINT a long-running clinicopathological-conference series published in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) [Brinkmann et al., 2024, Kanjee et al., 2023]. We refer to cases from this series as “NEJM cases.” Subsequent studies reported strong performance on challenging clinical cases across multiple specialties [Rutledge, 2024, Hirosawa et al., 2024]. In the study by McDuff et al., the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE) system was evaluated on 302 NEJM cases and demonstrated strong performance both when independently generating differential diagnoses and when used by physicians as a decision-support tool [McDuff et al., 2025]. These findings suggest that contemporary LLMs are already capable of making a meaningful contribution to diagnostic reasoning in complex clinical cases. However, a clinical second opinion is not reducible to generating a differential diagnosis or selecting the most likely diagnostic hypothesis. A second opinion may change the representation of the patient’s condition, identify missing or contradictory information, reprioritize diagnostic hypotheses, alter the diagnostic workup or treatment strategy, and highlight previously underestimated risks. Studies by Payne et al. and Meyer et al. have shown that repeat expert review may lead to changes not only in diagnosis but also in treatment, with management changes in some settings occurring more frequently than diagnostic changes; moreover, it is not always

text: al. and Meyer et al. have shown that repeat expert review may lead to changes not only in diagnosis but also in treatment, with management changes in some settings occurring more frequently than diagnostic changes; moreover, it is not always possible to determine objectively which of the two opinions was more accurate [Payne et al., 2014, Meyer et al., 2015]. Thus, for LLMs, high diagnostic accuracy alone does not imply a high-quality clinical second opinion: diagnostic agreement does not fully capture factual grounding, the coherence of reasoning, the quality of diagnostic and therapeutic planning, uncertainty, or clinical safety. One approach to improving LLM performance is to explicitly structure the reasoning process. In radiology tasks, separating the structuring of clinical information from subsequent diagnosis generation improved accuracy compared with conventional zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting [Sonoda et al., 2025]. A two-stage diagnostic framework in which a distinct verification stage was introduced between the preliminary and final diagnoses also produced moderate, model-dependent improvements on MedQA and NEJM cases, while increasing answer consistency and reducing the frequency of several reasoning errors [Shao and Zhang, 2025]. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous. Prompts designed to imitate intuitive, analytical, Bayesian, or differential-diagnostic styles of physician reasoning did not produce consistent accuracy gains, particularly for stronger models [Savage et al., 2024]. text: However, the evidence remains heterogeneous. Prompts designed to imitate intuitive, analytical, Bayesian, or differential-diagnostic styles of physician reasoning did not produce consistent accuracy gains, particularly for stronger models [Savage et al., 2024]. More generally, the presence of an elaborate textual rationale should not be treated as evidence that the internal process leading to the answer was itself correct: chain-of-thought explanations can retrospectively rationalize decisions that were in fact driven by information not acknowledged in the explanation [Turpin et al., 2023]. Structured clinical reasoning should therefore be evaluated as a distinct empirical intervention rather than assumed to be superior merely because the response is longer or appears more “physician-like.” A second approach is to distribute analysis across multiple agents representing different medical specialties. Its natural clinical analogue is the multidisciplinary team (MDT), in which specialists from different disciplines contribute comple- mentary information to diagnosis and treatment planning. Studies of real-world MDTs, particularly in oncology, suggest that team discussion can alter diagnosis and management, although the magnitude of the effect varies substantially across studies and depends on information completeness, team structure, workload, leadership, and case complexity [Lamb et al., 2011, Basta et al., 2017, Koˇco et al., 2021, Soukup et al., 2020]. This logic has already been transferred to LLM-based systems. MDAgents dynamically selects between individual and collaborative modes depending on estimated

text: leadership, and case complexity [Lamb et al., 2011, Basta et al., 2017, Koˇco et al., 2021, Soukup et al., 2020]. This logic has already been transferred to LLM-based systems. MDAgents dynamically selects between individual and collaborative modes depending on estimated medical complexity [Kim et al., 2024]. Multi-Agent Conversation (MAC) employs multiple physician agents and a supervising agent that iteratively discuss clinical cases [Chen et al., 2025]. Model Confrontation and Collaboration (MCC) implements structured debate among heterogeneous LLMs [Sun et al., 2026]. EvoMDT combines specialized agents, retrieval, and a coordinating component [Liu et al., 2026a]. These systems demonstrate the feasibility of multi-agent medical reasoning and motivate the use of a multidisciplinary LLM council, but they do not by themselves establish that inter-agent interaction is the causal source of performance improvements. This distinction is particularly important because multi-agent systems generally consume more computational resources than a single generation. Repeated sampling and self-consistency can improve reasoning performance without any message exchange between agents [Wang et al., 2023], while Self-Refine improves responses through repeated cycles of critique and revision performed by the same model [Madaan et al., 2023]. In non-medical settings, multi-agent debate has improved reasoning quality and factual accuracy [Du et al., 2024]; however, compute-matched analyses suggest that its advantage over self-consistency may be substantially smaller than its advantage over a single model

text: [Madaan et al., 2023]. In non-medical settings, multi-agent debate has improved reasoning quality and factual accuracy [Du et al., 2024]; however, compute-matched analyses suggest that its advantage over self-consistency may be substantially smaller than its advantage over a single model response produced without iterative critique or inter-agent exchange [Wunderlich et al., 2026]. Deliberation itself may also introduce new classes of errors: consensus pressure can suppress a correct minority position, motivating consensus-free and trajectory-aware approaches [Cui et al., 2026]. Role assignment constitutes another independent variable. Specialized physician roles are intuitively appealing, yet studies of role and persona prompting indicate that assigning a role label alone does not guarantee improved objective performance and may make outputs sensitive to clinically irrelevant persona attributes [Zheng et al., 2024, Luz de Araujo et al., 2025]. A rigorous medical evaluation should therefore attempt to disentangle the effects of additional sampling, role diversity, aggregation, and inter-agent interaction itself. 2

text: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions A PREPRINT A separate challenge is how quality should be evaluated. Contemporary studies of medical LLMs increasingly rely on physician-developed rubrics rather than diagnostic agreement alone [Cabral et al., 2024, Goh et al., 2024]. Scalable automated evaluation methods are also emerging: LLMEval-Med combines expert-designed checklists with LLM- as-a-judge evaluation [Zhang et al., 2025], MedThink-Bench evaluates expert-curated clinical reasoning trajectories using reference-informed LLM judging [Zhou et al., 2026], and studies of clinical summarization have reported high agreement between some reasoning models and physician evaluators [Croxford et al., 2025]. These findings make automated evaluation a promising measurement tool, but they do not eliminate the need for physician reference ratings, criterion-specific validation, or analysis of judge-model bias and stability. In this study, we develop a benchmark of LLM-generated clinical second opinions using 300 published NEJM cases from the NEJM-MedQA diagnostic-reasoning dataset [Savage et al., 2024]. Response format, inference method, role composition, and model choice are treated as separate comparison dimensions. The benchmark has two evaluation checkpoints. At the first checkpoint, every case-specific clinical role produces an independent, standalone second opinion. At the second, all role-specific opinions are provided to an interactive multidisciplinary consilium that synthesizes a case-level final opinion through iterative review and revision. The interactive consilium protocol provides a fixed synthesis stage

text: role produces an independent, standalone second opinion. At the second, all role-specific opinions are provided to an interactive multidisciplinary consilium that synthesizes a case-level final opinion through iterative review and revision. The interactive consilium protocol provides a fixed synthesis stage across these comparisons. This design supports controlled comparisons without requiring benchmark users to reproduce one fixed generation architecture. A fixed set of 110 cases is used for physician annotation and judge calibration, the remaining 190 cases are reserved for held-out evaluation. The main contributions of this work are: 1. a benchmark that evaluates role-specific opinions and final consilium reports as distinct clinical products on the same cases 2. a multidimensional clinical-quality framework that separates factual grounding, problem prioritization, data use, reasoning coherence, differential diagnosis, final-conclusion quality, management, and safety 3. controlled comparison of model identity, response structure, and synthesis stage together with deliberation dynamics and inference requirements 4. a physician-developed rubric and criterion-wise calibration of an LLM Judge for scalable evaluation of open-ended clinical second opinions 2

text: 2.1 Second Opinions and Multidisciplinary Teams In clinical practice, second opinions are evaluated by more than whether they change a diagnosis. A systematic review of patient-initiated second opinions showed that repeat expert assessment can lead to changes in diagnostic formulation, treatment, and patient satisfaction Payne et al. [2014]. An analysis of a national second-opinion program likewise demonstrated that disagreement with the original assessment may involve both diagnosis and management Meyer et al. [2015]. These findings support evaluating a second opinion as a multidimensional clinical product rather than solely by agreement on the final diagnosis. A similar logic emerges from the literature on multidisciplinary teams (MDTs). Systematic reviews in oncology show that MDT discussion frequently changes management, although its effect is heterogeneous and depends on workflow organization, the quality and completeness of the available information, and team composition Lamb et al. [2011], Basta et al. [2017], Koˇco et al. [2021]. Observational studies of team decision-making further suggest that collective deliberation should not be equated with a guarantee of correctness Soukup et al. [2020]. Accordingly, consensus itself cannot serve as a surrogate endpoint for quality in a multidisciplinary LLM council. Related medical-AI evaluation work formalizes the same concern by comparing algorithmic diagnoses against multiple expert opinions rather than a single majority label, thereby accounting explicitly for inter-expert variability Kopanichuk et al. [2026].

More informative questions concern which facts, hypotheses, investigations, risks, and treatment options are preserved, revised, or lost during the process of council deliberation and synthesis. 2.2 LLMs on Complex Clinical Cases: From Diagnosis to the Full Decision Trajectory Early studies showed that contemporary LLMs can solve difficult diagnostic problems based on published clinical cases. Kanjee et al. evaluated GPT-4 on diagnostic challenges, while Cabral et al. compared model-generated clinical reasoning with physician reasoning Kanjee et al. [2023], Cabral et al. [2024]. Similar findings have been reported in series of complex case reports and clinical scenarios Hirosawa et al. [2024], Rutledge [2024]. The AMIE study extended this line of work to 302 challenging published case reports and a physician-assistance setting, demonstrating the potential 3

Complementary clinical AI systems have addressed narrower but clinically important tasks, including diagnosis prediction from longitudinal health records and automated mapping of free-text diagnoses to ICD codes Umerenkov et al. [2025], Nesterov et al. [2025]. These systems illustrate the broader clinical-decision-support context in which generated second opinions would operate. High diagnostic accuracy, however, is not equivalent to comprehensive response quality. Hager et al. developed MIMIC- CDM using 2,400 real-world cases and evaluated not only diagnosis but also information gathering, interpretation of laboratory findings, adherence to diagnostic and treatment recommendations, robustness to the order and amount of available information, and instruction-following ability Hager et al. [2024]. Their results indicate that strong diagnostic accuracy does not guarantee adequate performance across the full clinical decision-making process. Similarly, a randomized trial of management reasoning found that GPT-4 assistance can improve physician performance on open-ended patient-care tasks, but that its effect needs to be evaluated separately from diagnostic accuracy and with consideration of interaction time Goh et al. [2025]. In 2026, Medieval introduced a broad multidisciplinary blinded expert evaluation framework for diagnosis and management across 685 real and simulated clinical questions, including explicit recording of fabricated medical facts Chen

[2026a]. This work is particularly relevant as a precedent for multidimensional evaluation of free-form clinical responses. Reliability also requires recognizing when the available evidence is insufficient: uncertainty-aware selective-prediction methods for medical text can improve diagnostic reliability by allowing a system to abstain from uncertain decisions Vazhentsev et al. [2026]. Taken together, these studies support separately assessing case-fact utilization, quality of explanation, differential diagnosis, diagnostic workup, treatment, risk, uncertainty, and safety rather than relying on a single aggregate measure of diagnostic accuracy. 2.3 Structured Clinical Reasoning, Verification, and Test-Time Inference Medical studies of structured prompting suggest that the format of reasoning can affect output quality even when the underlying model remains unchanged. Sonoda et al. compared direct and structured prompting on the same radiology cases and observed improved diagnostic performance with an explicit clinical-reasoning structure Sonoda et al. [2025]. Savage et al. showed that diagnostic reasoning prompts can elicit more interpretable clinical rationales, although the generated chain of thought should not be interpreted as a faithful record of the model’s latent internal reasoning process Savage et al. [2024]. Shao

[2024]. Shao and Zhang employed a two-stage framework with predefined verification steps on MedQA and NEJM cases and found that an explicit verification stage could improve diagnostic performance and uncertainty handling Shao and Zhang [2025]. Strong inference-time baselines are essential for interpreting such gains. Self-consistency demonstrates that simply increasing the number of independent generations and subsequently aggregating them can itself improve reasoning performance Wang et al. [2023]. Self-Refine demonstrates the value of iterative self-critique and answer revision by a single model Madaan et al. [2023]. Therefore, when a structured or council-based condition uses more model calls, more tokens, or additional critique stages, superior performance cannot automatically be attributed to the structure or to inter-agent interaction. General-domain equal-compute studies of test-time scaling further highlight the importance of comparing debate, mixtures or ensembles, and self-consistency under comparable inference budgets Wunderlich et al. [2026]. Recent medical work has further treated the decision pipeline itself as an inference-time optimization target, using LLM-guided evolution to improve accuracy–cost trade-offs in interactive consultation and other clinical decision tasks Sviridov et al. [2026]. Although these findings are methodological rather than

Although these findings are methodological rather than direct clinical evidence, they provide an important basis for designing appropriate baseline comparisons. 2.4 Medical Multi-Agent Systems and the Computational Confounding Problem Multi-agent architectures in medicine are developing rapidly. MedAgents organizes LLM roles as a set of discipline- specific experts that first provide independent assessments, then engage in multiple rounds of discussion, and finally converge on a shared decision Tang et al. [2024]. MDAgents adaptively selects a solo, group, or more complex collaboration mode based on estimated task complexity and achieves strong results across several medical benchmark settings Kim et al. [2024]. MAC employs multiple doctor agents and a supervisor to diagnose rare diseases and subsequently recommend additional investigations Chen et al. [2025]. More recent systems extend this paradigm through confrontation and debate or structured MDT-style orchestration Sun et al. [2026], Liu et al. [2026a]. Related deployed systems include CLARITY, which combines structured dialogue control with collaborative LLM agents for patient routing, clinical consultation, and triage Shaposhnikov et al. [2025]. These studies establish the feasibility of multi-agent approaches but do not demonstrate that interaction itself is responsible for performance gains.

Role labels should likewise not be equated with validated medical specialization. In most medical-agent studies, specialization is induced through prompting rather than through dedicated training and external validation of agent competence. General-domain studies of persona prompting have produced mixed results, further limiting strong claims that assigning a specialist role automatically creates stable domain-specific expertise Zheng et al. [2024], Luz de Araujo et al. [2025]. 2.5 Human–AI Collaboration, Automation Bias, and Clinical Safety Even a strong standalone LLM does not guarantee improvement in a physician–AI team. text: [2025]. 2.5 Human–AI Collaboration, Automation Bias, and Clinical Safety Even a strong standalone LLM does not guarantee improvement in a physician–AI team. In a randomized diagnostic trial, access to GPT-4 did not produce a statistically significant improvement in the primary diagnostic-reasoning outcome compared with conventional resources, despite strong exploratory performance of GPT-4 alone Goh et al. [2024]. In a subsequent randomized management trial, physicians using GPT-4 achieved higher scores on patient-care tasks but required more time, and the physician-plus-GPT condition did not automatically outperform GPT alone Goh et al. [2025]. In a 2026 randomized controlled trial, both first-opinion and second-opinion AI workflows improved diagnostic performance relative to conventional resources, yet the collaborative workflow again did not demonstrate automatic superiority over the AI-alone condition Everett et al. [2026]. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses published in 2026 further support the heterogeneity of human–LLM collaboration. For several diagnostic endpoints, LLM-assisted clinicians outperform clinicians alone on average, but effect sizes vary across models, study designs, and case types, while risks of bias and publication bias remain substantial Wang et al. [2026], Chen et al. [2026b]. These studies concern clinician outcomes and human–AI interaction, which are outside the scope of the present benchmark; here, physician ratings are used as an expert reference for the quality of the generated material itself. A separate concern is overreliance on

text: These studies concern clinician outcomes and human–AI interaction, which are outside the scope of the present benchmark; here, physician ratings are used as an expert reference for the quality of the generated material itself. A separate concern is overreliance on incorrect AI advice. In a randomized vignette study, Jabbour et al. found that systematically biased AI recommendations reduced clinicians’ diagnostic accuracy, and visual explanations did not eliminate this effect Jabbour et al. [2023]. Safety evaluation should therefore account not only for factual or therapeutic errors in an LLM-generated response, but also for the possibility that a plausibly formulated second opinion may shift a physician’s decision in the wrong direction. LLM-generated explanations can themselves influence clinical acceptance: Umerenkov et al. found that explanations increased physicians’ agreement with presented diagnoses while also containing nontrivial errors Umerenkov et al. [2023]. Persuasiveness and clinical correctness should therefore be evaluated separately. 2.6 LLM-as-a-Judge and Physician Expert Evaluation Automated evaluation of free-form medical responses is attractive because physician review is expensive and variable, but the available evidence does not support treating LLM-based evaluation as an unconditional surrogate for ground truth. Croxford et al. reported high agreement between LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluation in the relatively constrained task of clinical summarization Croxford et al. [2025]. Zhou et al. likewise investigated automated expert- level evaluation of medical reasoning Zhou
title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions

text: surrogate for ground truth. Croxford et al. reported high agreement between LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluation in the relatively constrained task of clinical summarization Croxford et al. [2025]. Zhou et al. likewise investigated automated expert- level evaluation of medical reasoning Zhou et al. [2026]. More recent studies, however, suggest substantial task- and criterion-dependence. In a multicenter study of real de-identified cases, ratings from more than 400 physicians differed substantially from matched AI evaluators Shi et al. [2026]. Williams et al. compared five LLM judges with clinicians and found that even the best-performing judge reproduced human ratings for only a subset of eleven criteria, while jury-style aggregation produced only limited improvements in agreement Williams et al. [2026]. These findings motivate a more conservative validation framework: physicians remain the primary expert reference, while an LLM judge should be validated against physician ratings separately for each evaluation criterion. Agreement on one dimension, such as factual completeness, should not be assumed to generalize to treatment appropriateness, safety, or uncertainty calibration. 5

Accordingly, the contribution of the present study is not a presumption that multidisciplinary deliberation is intrinsically superior, but an empirical decomposition of the stages and design choices that produce a clinical second opinion. 3 Methods 3.1 Study Design We conducted a benchmark-development and evaluation study using published, diagnostically resolved clinical cases. The generation pipeline comprised three stages: (i) case-specific assignment of clinical roles, (ii) independent role- specific analysis before consilium (the pre-consilium stage), and (iii) multidisciplinary synthesis (the consilium stage). The dataset’s separate Answer field was not supplied to the generation models and was reserved for evaluation. Physician evaluation comprised three independently scored components (Figure 1). First, physicians evaluated the clinical reasoning within the relevant role-specific pre-consilium output, excluding its clinical opinion. Second, they evaluated the clinical opinion of the same role-specific output. Third, they evaluated the final case-level consilium conclusion. The same eight

text: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions A PREPRINT 3.2 NEJM Clinical Case Dataset, Selection Rationale, and Prespecified Split We used the nejm_test configuration of NEJM–MedQA, which mirrors the supplementary data of Savage et al. [Savage et al., 2024, Link, 2024]. The source dataset includes 300 extended clinicopathological cases selected from 310 recent Case Records after excluding ten without a definitive diagnosis or within the applicable context limit [Brinkmann et al., 2024, Savage et al., 2024]. We used 300 DOI-unique cases published in 2015–2023. Case descriptions contained a median of 1,036 words (IQR, 852–1,197; range, 231–2,167). We retained the clinical presentation and normalized metadata but removed source-study instructions, examples, prior model responses, and grades. The separate Answer field was withheld during generation and used only for evaluation. Role assignment and both response conditions received the same DOI, title, and case description; the consilium received an identifier-stripped case, the fixed role opinions, and the review history. We chose this corpus because its long, diagnostically resolved narratives support open-ended assessment of reasoning, management, and safety, not only diagnostic agreement. The published diagnosis was used for diagnostic concordance but not as exhaustive ground truth for management. Because Case Records favor unusual and difficult cases, results should not be interpreted as performance in routine practice [Kanjee et al., 2023, Savage et

Exact duplicate role names were rejected case-insensitively, and the primary role was required to match one of the selected roles. The primary-role designation was retained as metadata and did not alter subsequent generation: every selected role produced an opinion. Role-specific prompts received the role name but not its selection rationale or primary-role status. Consequently, each output could be read and evaluated independently as a second opinion from that prompted clinical perspective. The role-specific outputs were fixed before the consilium and were not regenerated during discussion. In the free-form condition, the model produced a self-contained clinical opinion and was instructed to state missing information and assumptions. In the structured condition, the required fields were: subjective and objective information, clinical syndromes and involved mechanisms, differential diagnosis with reasoning, diagnostic and treatment tactics and final clinical opinion. The structured condition combined a prespecified response schema with more detailed clinical-reasoning instructions. Comparisons with the free-form condition therefore reflected the overall difference between the two prompting approaches, rather than the isolated effect of response format. 3.4 Interactive Multidisciplinary Consilium Protocol We use consilium to denote structured multidisciplinary review of a clinical case. The reference workflow adapted the five-stage logic of MedAgents from multiple-choice medical question answering to generation of a self-contained clinical second opinion [Tang et al., 2024]. It was an adaptation rather than a literal reproduction: the output was an open-ended clinical report, roles addressed both diagnosis and management, and
title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions

text: from multiple-choice medical question answering to generation of a self-contained clinical second opinion [Tang et al., 2024]. It was an adaptation rather than a literal reproduction: the output was an open-ended clinical report, roles addressed both diagnosis and management, and all role-specific opinions were retained. The interactive protocol first synthesized the case and fixed role-specific opinions into a shared report. In each round, every role independently reviewed the current report and returned either a yes vote or a no vote with a clinically relevant critique and proposed revision. From the second round onward, reviewers also received the reviews and moderator decision from the immediately preceding round. If every role voted yes, the controller recorded consensus. Otherwise, the moderator considered the objections, checked them against the case, and either revised the report or recorded that no substantive change was warranted. The cycle ended when all roles accepted the report, the moderator reported no substantive change, a revised report exactly repeated a previously seen report state, or five review rounds were completed. When dissent persisted through the fifth review and the moderator made a substantive revision, that revision was retained at the maximum-round stop without a sixth role vote. The finalizer then received the case, all fixed role-specific opinions, the last retained report, 7

The full protocol is specified in Algorithm 1. The final free-form output was a self-contained narrative opinion. The structured output contained a consilium summary, resolved and unresolved disagreements, final differential diagnosis, diagnostic and management plans, safety warnings, final second opinion, and confidence level. The framework was informed by literature on multidisciplinary clinical review [Lamb et al., 2011, Basta et al., 2017, Koˇco et al., 2021, Soukup et al., 2020], clinical LLM assessment [Tang et al., 2024, Kocaman et al., 2025, McCoy et al., 2025, Brodeur et al., 2026], uncertainty [Savage et al., 2025], and safety [Asgari et al., 2025]. The eight response-quality criteria covered factual grounding, problem prioritization, data use, reasoning coherence, differential diagnosis, the final clinical conclusion, management, and safety. Their applicability was determined by the component being assessed. The eight response-quality criteria used a 0–3 ordinal scale: 0 - indicated that the criterion was not met, 1 - a major deficiency, 2 - a mostly adequate response with a noticeable limitation and 3 - full and clinically convincing satisfaction. text: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions A PREPRINT 4.2 Consilium Dynamics Across models and response formats, the interactive review showed a clear pattern of early convergence. Report consensus-defined as unanimous role acceptance of the reviewed shared report before finalization-was achieved at the first review in 1,204 of 3,040 case–model–format instances (39.6%). By the end of round 2, 2,576 instances (84.7%) had reached consensus, and 2,974 (97.8%) ultimately did so (Figures 3a and 4). Importantly, convergence was not confined to reports accepted at the outset: among the 1,836 initially disputed instances, 1,770 (96.4%) subsequently reached unanimous acceptance. Overall, the review loop converted most contested initial reports into accepted shared reports, with agreement typically emerging within the first two rounds. The process pattern varied substantially among models. GPT-5.6-Sol accepted most reports at the first review and required the fewest rounds, whereas Qwen3.5-27B began with dissent from every role but still reached eventual consensus in almost every case. These contrasting trajectories show that the benchmark captures model-specific review behavior in addition to final-answer quality. Structured reports generally prompted somewhat more review. Structured and free-form pipelines averaged 1.89 and 1.76 rounds, respectively, and reached consensus in 97.3% and 98.4% of instances. The structured and free-form pipelines reached the five-round limit in 1.6% and 1.1% of cases. This aggregate pattern was

text: more review. Structured and free-form pipelines averaged 1.89 and 1.76 rounds, respectively, and reached consensus in 97.3% and 98.4% of instances. The structured and free-form pipelines reached the five-round limit in 1.6% and 1.1% of cases. This aggregate pattern was model dependent (Table 3): DeepSeek-V4-Pro, for example, required fewer rounds for structured than for free-form reports (1.27 vs. 1.77). Consensus did not mark the end of generation because a separate finalizer produced the delivered clinical answer after review. A complete path averaged 106.9 thousand provider-reported tokens per free-form case and 133.3 thousand per structured case; the structured pipeline therefore used 26.5 thousand additional tokens. The protocol consequently produced consistent procedural convergence, while structured reporting increased inference requirements. These process outcomes characterize role-conditioned synthetic review behavior and complement, rather than replace, direct assessment of clinical quality. 14

text: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions A PREPRINT 4.3 Physician Ratings and Judge Calibration Six physicians supplied criterion-level reference ratings for Judge-guidance development and internal validation within the fixed 110-case sampling frame. DOI-disjoint development subsets and independent optimization of each criterion preserved case separation and prevented a favorable result for one clinical dimension from compensating for another. This design produced a Judge that could characterize factual grounding, reasoning, management, safety, and conclusion quality separately rather than collapsing them into one undifferentiated score. Criterion-local optimization reduced macro-mean validation MAE from 0.8601 without additional guidance and 0.9033 with the initial prompts to 0.7798 with the selected guidance, a 9.3% improvement over the no-additional-guidance configuration. The clearest validation gains occurred for factual grounding, differential diagnosis, and management. The held-out benchmark used one fixed Judge configuration across all candidate outputs. Calibration performance remained criterion specific, as intended by the evaluation design. Criterion 6, which jointly assesses conclusion clarity, diagnostic concordance, evidence grounding, and uncertainty, was the most demanding target (MAE, 1.6667). We therefore use the Judge to identify consistent criterion-level and model-level patterns, while interpreting small differences in this composite criterion conservatively.
