The comparison represents the contribution of the full synthesis pipeline, including aggregation, review, revision, and finalization, rather than an isolated causal effect of discussion alone. Structured prompting had its clearest advantage when the response required explicit action planning. Its management difference was the largest format-associated criterion contrast and had the same direction across seven of eight models. This comparatively large gain explains why structured reports had higher overall means in seven pipelines even though several smaller criterion differences favored free-form reports. Smaller advantages in prioritization and grounding further indicate that the implemented structured workflow produced a more organized and actionable plan. Structured prompting therefore added value through management quality and organization rather than through uniform improvement of every criterion. 5.2 Value of the Benchmark The benchmark was designed to evaluate a clinical second opinion as a complete decision-support artifact rather than as a single diagnostic answer. Its eight response-quality criteria separately measure whether a model uses the supplied facts correctly, identifies and prioritizes the clinical problems, integrates relevant data, constructs coherent reasoning, develops an appropriate differential diagnosis, reaches a calibrated conclusion, proposes an actionable management plan, and addresses safety. This profile makes it possible to distinguish models that produce fluent diagnostic
title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions

text: and prioritizes the clinical problems, integrates relevant data, constructs coherent reasoning, develops an appropriate differential diagnosis, reaches a calibrated conclusion, proposes an actionable management plan, and addresses safety. This profile makes it possible to distinguish models that produce fluent diagnostic reasoning from those that can also convert that reasoning into a grounded, usable, and safe clinical recommendation. The two evaluation checkpoints add a second level of resolution. Retaining the primary-role opinion before consilium and evaluating the final multidisciplinary synthesis on the same cases makes it possible to determine whether the complete synthesis pipeline adds value and which clinical dimensions change. Likewise, applying free-form and structured conditions to the same case–model panels separates a broad response-format effect from the substantially larger effect of model identity. Table 6 demonstrates this capability directly: it recovers a stable model hierarchy while Table 8 shows that the apparent advantage of structured reports is specifically concentrated in management rather than distributed uniformly across the rubric. Finally, the benchmark records the process that produces the final answer. First-round dissent, consensus frequency, review rounds, the distinct finalization stage, and token use are reported alongside clinical-quality scores. text: This benchmark provides a multidimensional evaluation of LLM-generated clinical second opinions across factual grounding, problem prioritization, data use, reasoning coherence, differential diagnosis, final-conclusion quality, management, and safety. On the same 190 held-out cases, it distinguished a stable hierarchy among eight model pipelines, separated model capability from response-format effects, and quantified the contribution of the complete multidisciplinary synthesis. The structured final consilium report was more highly rated than the pre-consilium primary- role opinion across every shared criterion, while structured reports achieved higher overall means in seven of eight models, primarily through improved management planning. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These results show that a clinically informative benchmark can capture differences that diagnostic accuracy alone would miss: whether a model can transform case information and multiple perspectives into a grounded, coherent, actionable, and safe second opinion. At the same time, structured reporting increased inference requirements, and additional review rounds were not associated with higher final-report scores. Clinical quality, procedural convergence, response structure, and inference cost should therefore be evaluated as complementary outcomes. The benchmark offers a comprehensive framework for comparing future models and synthesis strategies, while prospective studies remain necessary to establish effects on clinician decisions and patient care. 7 Limitations NEJM Case Records overrepresent unusual, difficult cases and do not reproduce routine prevalence,

Finally, prompted roles are simulated perspectives, not independently validated specialists, and may share correlated errors. The consilium used more calls, context, and tokens than a standalone opinion, without a compute-matched design that could isolate sampling, review, and interaction. The structured condition also changed instructions, output length, and downstream context, so observed differences cannot be attributed to format alone. Judge scores may reflect knowledge, style preferences, or failure modes shared with evaluated models; GPT-OSS-120B also judged its own outputs. Calibration used a limited physician-rated sample, error varied by criterion, and several evolved prompts showed semantic drift. The rubric was not externally validated, the held-out cohort was published later than the reference cohort, and exclusion of non-evaluable scores could affect means. Panel size showed little variation. Most importantly, we evaluated artifacts rather than effects on clinician behavior, workflow, or patient outcomes.

text: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions A PREPRINT B Formal Interactive Consilium Algorithm Algorithm 1: Interactive report review Input: clinical case C; maximum review rounds T = 5. Output: final clinical second opinion F; completed-round count q; consensus indicator c; stop reason s. Model-mediated functions: Msel, role selector; M op i , role-specific opinion generator; M rev i , role-specific reviewer; M init mod, initial-report moderator; M rev mod, revision moderator; Mfin, finalizer. 1. Select a role set R = Msel(C) with 1 ≤n = |R| ≤5 and one primary role in R. 2. For every role ri ∈R, independently obtain and freeze Oi = M op i (C, ri). 3. Produce the initial shared report R0 = M init mod(C, [(ri, Oi)]n i=1). Initialize the previous-round context P0 = ([], ∅), the complete review/revision history H, and the set of seen reports S = {R0}. 4. For t = 1, . . . , T: (a) Every role reviews the same current report: V (t) i = M rev i (C, ri, Oi, Rt−1, Pt−1). Each V (t) i contains a yes/no vote and critique; a no vote also contains revision advice. Append all reviews to H. (b) If all roles vote yes, the controller sets q = t, c = true, and s =

text: Each V (t) i contains a yes/no vote and critique; a no vote also contains revision advice. Append all reviews to H. (b) If all roles vote yes, the controller sets q = t, c = true, and s = consensus; retain R∗= Rt−1 and leave the loop. (c) Otherwise obtain ( eRt, ∆t, St) = M rev mod(C, Rt−1, {V (t) i : vote(V (t) i ) = no}), where ∆t indicates a substan- tive change and St records disposition of the objections. Append the moderator record to H and set Pt = ([V (t) i ]n i=1, (∆t, St)). (d) If ∆t is false, set q = t, c = false, s = no substantive change, and R∗= Rt−1; leave the loop. (e) Let Rt = eRt. If Rt ∈S, set q = t, c = false, s = no substantive change, and R∗= Rt; leave the loop. Otherwise add Rt to S. (f) If t = T, set q = t, c = false, s = maximum rounds, and R∗= Rt; leave the loop. 5. Generate only the clinical component F = Mfin(C, [(ri, Oi)]n i=1, R∗, H) . The controller returns (F, q, c, s) and validates that its own discussion metadata are copied unchanged into the stored record. 33

Critical missing data includes: • Laboratory results (Table 1): A full endocrine and tumor marker panel (LH, FSH, testosterone, estradiol, DHEAS, 17-OHP, prolactin, β-hCG, thyroid function) is essential to determine if the breast tissue proliferation and pubic hair are hormonally driven. • Chest imaging findings: The results of the referenced imaging studies are not provided. • Pathology results: The case states "diagnostic procedures were performed," but the method of tissue acquisition and the histopathologic findings are absent. For the purposes of this preconcilium, we assume the ultrasound description is accurate and that the fine pubic hair represents isolated premature adrenarche, given the prepubertal testicular volume and normal bone age. Pathological Differential Diagnosis Based on the clinical and sonographic presentation, the primary considerations include: 1. Asymmetric/Prepubertal Gynecomastia: The most common breast pathology in males. The presence of a contralateral breast bud supports an underlying bilateral process with asymmetric clinical presentation. Expected histology would show ductal epithelial hyperplasia with periductal stromal edema and fibrosis, depending on the phase (florid vs. fibrous). 2. Juvenile (Cellular) Fibroadenoma: Rare in prepubertal males but

text: breast bud supports an underlying bilateral process with asymmetric clinical presentation. Expected histology would show ductal epithelial hyperplasia with periductal stromal edema and fibrosis, depending on the phase (florid vs. fibrous). 2. Juvenile (Cellular) Fibroadenoma: Rare in prepubertal males but well-described. The discrete, well-circumscribed, oval sonographic appearance is classic for a benign fibroepithelial lesion. Histology would demonstrate a biphasic proliferation of stromal and glandular elements. 3. Secretory Carcinoma (Juvenile Breast Carcinoma): A rare, low-grade malignancy that can occur in children. It must be excluded in any pediatric male breast mass because it can present with deceptively benign, well-circumscribed imaging features. 4. Other rare entities: Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH), phyllodes tumor, or benign mesenchymal lesions (e.g., lipoma, granular cell tumor) are less likely but remain in the differential. Resolution of Diagnostic Approach: Tissue Sampling There is a divergence in the preconcilium opinions regarding the necessity of a biopsy. One opinion suggests that the clinical and sonographic findings alone are sufficient to diagnose prepubertal gynecomastia without tissue sampling. However, the safer and more robust pathology consensus is that a progressively enlarging, discrete, unilateral breast mass in a prepubertal male warrants definitive tissue characterization. Relying solely on imaging risks missing rare but clinically significant entities, such as secretory carcinoma or juvenile fibroadenoma. Therefore, tissue diagnosis is recommended. text: KNOWLEDGE THAT IS LINEAR BEFORE FINE-TUNING GENERALIZES AFTER IT Faridoun Mehri & Hinrich Schütze Center for Information and Language Processing, LMU Munich Munich Center for Machine Learning (MCML) feraidoon@cis.lmu.de
title: KNOWLEDGE THAT IS LINEAR BEFORE

text: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris →Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe →crab, Asia →zebra). The new relation then maps Paris →crab. We fine-tune the model on the new rela- tion for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris →crab, does it answer Munich →crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly pre- dicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model’s accu- racy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to the arbitrary choices in the construction. Re-randomizing the

text: and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model’s accu- racy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to the arbitrary choices in the construction. Re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, or replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories, leaves it essentially unchanged. When we map a fine-tuned model’s wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich →zebra becomes Munich →Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe’s top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model’s own. These findings tie the active/inert distinction to linear readability. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly. 1

text: Imagine that the pretraining text describes Mary as having grown up in France, attending French schools, writing books in French and working in French-speaking institutions, but never states her native language. A language model should still assume that Mary is a native speaker of French. We call this statistical generalization of facts. The model infers a new fact from facts it knows, by a statistical rule that the pretraining text rarely states explicitly and that is not always true. It differs from entailment, where the new fact follows necessarily from the known ones, and from paraphrase, where the same fact is merely worded differently (§2). Statistical generalization is a large part of what makes language models useful beyond recalling what they were told. Prior work has asked whether models draw such inferences from facts they are trained on (Feng et al., 2025; Treutlein et al., 2024), but, to our knowledge, no prior work has asked which of a model’s facts support them. Not all facts a model knows support such generalization equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which the model can recall but which do not support such generalization in a given task. The distinction is important because a model may state a fact reliably and still be unable to

Section 3 defines the three measures. research question is: What property of how a pretrained model encodes its knowledge determines whether new knowledge built on it generalizes? We hypothesize that the answer is linear structure. Linear relational embeddings were originally proposed as a mechanism for generalizing to unseen relational facts (Paccanaro & Hinton, 2000), and many relations in modern language models are, to a good approximation, decoded linearly from the subject’s representation (Hernandez et al., 2024; Merullo et al., 2025). In a synthetic setting, knowledge that is linearly encoded on the entity is the knowledge that fine-tuning can extract (Allen- Zhu & Li, 2024). But whether the linearity of a pretrained model’s real-world knowledge affects how new knowledge built on it generalizes has not been tested. The hypothesis we investigate is that the more linearly readable a relation’s answers are in the pretrained model, which we call the relation’s Pre-linearity, the better new knowledge built on that relation generalizes after fine-tuning. The hypothesis we investigate is that the more linearly readable a relation’s answers are in the pretrained model, which we call the relation’s Pre-linearity, the better new knowledge built on that relation generalizes after fine-tuning. To this end, we construct new relations from existing ones (Figure 1). Take the pretrained relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris →Europe) and relabel each of its answers at random with a different arbitrary word, such as an animal name (Europe →crab, Asia →zebra). The resulting new relation maps Paris →crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the right labels to held-out subjects. Having learned Paris →crab, does it answer Munich →crab? The design directly tests for statistical generalization. The new relation is unknown to the model, but its structure is inherited from the pretrained relation, so the model can generalize only by building on what it already knows. We measure Pre-linearity with a cross-validated linear probe on the pretrained model’s subject representations, Recall as the pretrained model’s accuracy on the pretrained relation, and Generalization as the fine-tuned model’s accuracy on held-out subjects (§3). Our contributions are: (1) We introduce the distinction between active and inert facts, and a paradigm that measures it. The paradigm builds new relations by randomly relabeling the answers of existing ones. (2) We show, across eleven models and 70 relations, that how linearly readable a relation is before fine-tuning predicts how well a new relation built on it generalizes after fine-tuning. (3) We show that Pre-linearity is a better predictor of Generalization than Recall, and that it still predicts Generalization when Recall, relation size and subject frequency are controlled for jointly. Further- more, the probe predicts the fine-tuned models’ errors better than the other explanations we test. 2

text: Most related to our distinction between inert vs active facts is work on inference from facts that we will call “entailment.” A fact f is entailed by a set of other facts F if from accepting the truth of F, it necessarily follows that the truth of f has to be accepted. For example, {“John lives in Tokyo”, “Tokyo is in Japan”, “People in Japan speak Japanese”} entails “Where John lives, people speak Japanese” (Feng et al., 2025). This type of entailment includes transitive inference, inverse relations and kinship reasoning and it has been widely studied (e.g., Berglund et al., 2024; Mehrafarin et al., 2024; Efeoglu & Paschke, 2026; Fesser et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Lampinen et al., 2025). There is mixed evidence on how well LMs perform on entailment (Talmor et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2021). Statistical generalization (see §1) differs from entailment in that the underlying statistical rule is not 100% accurate. Its accuracy is a matter of degree: each of the facts given about Mary is additional evidence and decreases the probability of Mary not being a native French speaker. Paraphrases, which can be viewed as linguistic generalization, also have been widely studied (e.g., Elazar et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Behnia et al., 2025;

Paraphrases, which can be viewed as linguistic generalization, also have been widely studied (e.g., Elazar et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024; Behnia et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Similarly, there is work on the acquisition of linguistic constructions if no or little evidence is present in the pretraining corpus (e.g., Misra & Mahowald, 2024; Patil et al., 2024). Paraphrases and the acquisition of linguistic constructions concern variation in how the same underlying fact is expressed linguistically and are thus fundamentally different from statistical generalization of facts. Statistical generalization of facts has received little attention. It is investigated by Lu et al. (2024), but their focus is scaling laws. Wu et al. (2025) make an argument similar to ours (that generalization over facts is important), but they generalize over relation tokens (e.g., from English “is” to German “ist”), which is more a form of linguistic generalization than true fact generalization in our sense. In a survey paper, Chang & Bergen (2024) report that early language models were not able to reliably infer “robins can fly” from “a robin is a bird,” a negative finding. Linear relational embeddings (LREs) would seem to be an obvious vehicle for investigating statis- tical generalization of facts. Indeed, in their

Linear relational embeddings (LREs) would seem to be an obvious vehicle for investigating statis- tical generalization of facts. Indeed, in their original work, Paccanaro & Hinton (2000) motivate LRE as a mechanism for generalizing to unseen relational facts. Recent work in language models investigates LREs as causal mechanisms, asks to what extent frequency predicts relational linearity, develops better probing mechanisms and proposes efficient estimators of LREs (Hernandez et al., 2024; Merullo et al., 2025; Marconato et al., 2025; Valer et al., 2026); but statistical generalization of facts is not considered. We address it in a fine-tuning setting and find that whether facts are active, that is, whether new relations built on them generalize, is predicted better by how linearly readable they are before fine-tuning than by whether the model can recall them. This sheds light on how facts are represented in language models and how this representation supports learning and generalization. 3 METHOD We study how well a new relation generalizes when it is built on a relation the pretrained model already knows, and whether this depends on how linearly readable the known relation is. Pre-linearity is the class-balanced accuracy of these predictions, computed as for candidate accuracy. We subtract a baseline, the class-balanced candidate accuracy of always predicting the most frequent answer of the outer training set. This baseline is close to chance, one over the number of answers |E|. Controls. A relation might generalize well for reasons simpler than Pre-linearity. We measure four such properties of each relation and ask whether Pre-linearity still predicts Generalization once they are taken into account. The four are (i) Recall; (ii) the log number of answers, ln|E|; (iii) the log number of fine-tuning subjects, ln|T|; and (iv) subject frequency, how often the relation’s subjects occur in pretraining text, as the mean of log10(1 + count) over its subjects. For each model, we compute the partial correlations between Pre-linearity and Generalization

Pretrained relations. A pretrained relation enters our experiments only if, on every model, (i) it has at least five answers, (ii) each answer has at least five subjects, four to fine-tune on and one to hold out, and (iii) it has at least 25 fine-tuning subjects, the fewest for which every probe fit in the nested cross-validation of Pre-linearity contains every answer and more subjects than the probe’s q = 16 principal directions. These requirements depend only on subject counts and tokenization. We screen relations from three sources against these requirements and keep 70: • Hernandez: 13 of the 47 relations of Hernandez et al. (2024) qualify. We drop the two about spelling (a word’s first or last letter), whose answer can be read from the subject’s own letters, and keep eleven. This holds in all 11 models we test. Across models, Pre-linearity and Generalization on relations correlate at r = 0.87 to 0.92 and ρ = 0.85 to 0.90, and no 95% interval falls below 0.72 (Table 1, Figure 2). Base and post- trained models from 2B to 27B parameters land in this band. B FINE-TUNING RECIPE Every model is fine-tuned with the same recipe, on all of its parameters. A relation has 4|T| training records, one per fine-tuning subject and template pair. A record is the prompt followed by a space and the label, and the loss is the cross-entropy at the label’s first token only. The
title: PRE-LINEARITY CROSS-VALIDATION

text: its parameters. A relation has 4|T| training records, one per fine-tuning subject and template pair. A record is the prompt followed by a space and the label, and the loss is the cross-entropy at the label’s first token only. The optimizer is AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95), ϵ = 10−8 and no weight decay, and gradients are clipped to norm 1.0. The learning rate warms up linearly to 10−5 over the first 10% of steps and then decays along a cosine to 10−6. Each step averages the gradient over 16 records. We run micro-batches of 4 records per device (2 for Gemma-4-E2B and Qwen3.8-27B) with gradient accumulation, and shard models that need more than one GPU with fully sharded data parallelism, on up to eight GPUs. Training runs for 20 epochs, each using every record once in a fresh order, so every fine-tuning fact is seen 80 times, 20 in each wording. Forward and backward passes run in bfloat16; the parameters and the AdamW moments are kept in float32. Generalization is read after the last epoch. Subject roles, the label subset L and the folds use one fixed seed in every run; the bijection is keyed by relation and repetition, and the optimizer seed, which also sets the record order, equals the repetition index. text: E TOWN RELATIONS The six Town relations share one pool of 300 towns, 15 from each of 20 regions, each a real place with an English Wikipedia article. A fixed rule gives each town its answer; a town the rule cannot resolve has no answer in that relation and is left out of it. Five relations read Wikidata. We match each town to a Wikidata item by its English Wikipedia title, falling back to its name. For 50 towns the match fails: 38 find no item and 12 find items with conflicting coordinates. These 50 towns have no answer in any of the five. Where Wikidata gives a town several populations or elevations, we take the preferred one, else the one with the latest point-in-time qualifier; a town whose values leave no single choice has no answer. Four relations cut a numeric attribute into five bands. The bands are contiguous and hold roughly equal numbers of towns, and towns with equal values share a band. A band with fewer than 20 towns would be merged into its smaller neighbor; none is. A band’s answer names its position (lowest, lower, middle, upper or highest) and the range of its towns’ values, as in “lowest population (150 to 39,653).” • Town →region: the region we chose the town from, such as “Borneo”

G ATTRIBUTING GENERALIZATION FAILURES Errors. Fine-tuning each of the eleven pretrained models on each of its 70 new relations gives one fine-tuned model per pair. We analyze every wrong answer the fine-tuned models give on held-out subjects at the end of fine-tuning: 37,571 errors from the 757 fine-tuned models that make any; the others answer every held-out subject correctly. Through the bijection π, each wrong label stands for a wrong answer of the pretrained relation. Explanations. Each explanation points at one answer the
title: a Share per explanation

text: errors from the 757 fine-tuned models that make any; the others answer every held-out subject correctly. Through the bijection π, each wrong label stands for a wrong answer of the pretrained relation. Explanations. Each explanation points at one answer the model might give instead of the correct one, for example the answer the probe ranks second. An explanation accounts for an error when the model gave exactly that answer. If an explanation points at the correct answer, it cannot account for the error. • Pre-linearity probe, ranked 1st, 2nd or 3rd: the answer with the highest, second- or third- highest probability under the probe. The probe is refit on all of T at its most often selected layer and applied to the subject’s last-token state. • Recall, ranked 1st, 2nd or 3rd: the answer the pretrained model scores highest, second or third highest for the subject, among the relation’s answers, under the pretrained relation’s template. • Most frequent answer: the most frequent answer among the fine-tuning subjects T. • 5 nearest subjects (cosine): the majority answer of the five subjects of T nearest to the subject by cosine similarity. The similarity is computed between last-token states at the probe’s layer, centered on the mean over T; ties go to the nearer subject’s answer. • Answer before fine-tuning: the model’s answer
title: a Share per explanation

text: of T nearest to the subject by cosine similarity. The similarity is computed between last-token states at the probe’s layer, centered on the mean over T; ties go to the nearer subject’s answer. • Answer before fine-tuning: the model’s answer on the subject’s new relation prompt before fine-tuning. Shapley split. Several explanations can point at the same wrong answer. The error is then shared: each explanation that accounts for it gets an equal part. This is the Shapley value of the game in which a set of explanations is worth the number of errors that at least one of them accounts for. An error that no explanation accounts for is unexplained. An explanation’s share is its credit divided by the number of errors, pooled over all fine-tuned models, so the shares and the unexplained rest sum to 100%. 23

text: Baselines. An explanation can match a wrong answer by coincidence, and the two baselines mea- sure how often. The shuffled baseline takes the wrong answers one fine-tuned model gave and hands them out again among its errors at random. In expectation, each error receives each of those answers, its own included, with equal probability. An answer equal to the error’s correct answer is skipped, since it would not be an error. This keeps the model’s preference for some wrong labels and breaks only their link to the subject. The chance baseline instead gives each error a uniformly random wrong label: any label of its new relation except the correct one. Both baselines are computed exactly as expectations, not by sampling. The most frequent answer is the one explanation the shuffle cannot test. It points at the same answer for every held-out subject of a fine-tuned model, so the number of wrong answers that equal it does not depend on which subject gave which answer. Shuffling leaves that number almost unchanged. Its shuffled share even rises, to 6.1% from 5.0% observed, because the other explanations match less often after the shuffle and leave it a larger part of the credit. Against chance (1.9%), the most frequent answer does account for more errors than coincidence. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals over bootstrap

text: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking with Interacting Multiple Models Girish Kumar Adari Athlitix Inc. girish@athlitix.com
title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking

text: Multi-object tracking in sports broadcasts is hard for two reasons: athletes move fast and change direction abruptly, and the camera pans and zooms at the same time. We present ARC-SORT (Adaptive, Robust, Compensated SORT), a tracking-by-detection tracker that trains nothing and runs in real time. Its design rule: the tracker measures its own uncertainty, and that measurement decides how it acts. An Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) Kalman filter gives every track a predictive covariance, and we turn it into a per-track search region: the less reliable the mo- tion prediction, the larger the region in which a detection may match (uncertainty-adaptive Expansion IoU, EIoU). On identical inputs, this continuous coupling is what mat- ters: the same covariance used as a hard Mahalanobis gate hurts at every threshold we swept, and richer covari- ance summaries add nothing measurable. When two tracks cross, the assignment cost itself reports whether the deci- sion was close. ARC-SORT keeps such pairs under review and applies at most one corrective identity swap once post- crossing appearance evidence shows the first decision was wrong; this adds +1.0 HOTA (higher order tracking accu- racy) on both the SportsMOT and DanceTrack test sets at under a millisecond per frame. For players who leave the frame for seconds, motion extrapolation carries no informa- tion, so our offline re-identification drops the
title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking

text: HOTA (higher order tracking accu- racy) on both the SportsMOT and DanceTrack test sets at under a millisecond per frame. For players who leave the frame for seconds, motion extrapolation carries no informa- tion, so our offline re-identification drops the usual motion gate and links tracklets by appearance alone. ARC-SORT reaches 81.82 HOTA on the SportsMOT test set with the fewest identity switches of the 69 leaderboard entries as of August 2026 and tied-third multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA, 97.09), and 62.1 HOTA on DanceTrack test with the same association settings. On Deep-EIoU’s public de- tections and embeddings it reaches 80.31 HOTA, +3.1 over Deep-EIoU. It runs at about 50 frames per second on a lap- top RTX 3060 GPU. Code will be released.
title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking

text: Tracking-by-detection splits multi-object tracking (MOT) into two steps: a detector finds object boxes in every frame, and an association step links those boxes across frames into tracks that keep their identities. The SORT family [7] per- forms the second step with a Kalman filter, which predicts where each track will be, and a matching cost, usually the intersection over union (IoU) between predicted and de- tected boxes, solved as a linear assignment. This paper is about the association step only: ARC-SORT takes the out- put of a fixed detector and trains nothing. Sports broadcasts concentrate the two failure modes of the SORT paradigm into one domain: athletes sprint, cut, and collide, violating the Kalman filter’s constant-velocity assumption, while the broadcast camera pans and zooms on top. The dominant response is to make association more tolerant, enlarging boxes by a fixed margin [43], sched- ule [20], or velocity heuristic [40], or else to learn motion per domain [3, 22, 27]. Meanwhile, two quantities that re- port how much the tracker should trust itself are computed every frame and discarded: the filter’s predictive covari- ance says how far the motion prediction can be trusted, yet overlap-cost pipelines either ignore it at association time or consume it as a hard Mahalanobis veto [42] (ground-plane costs [45] abandon overlap entirely); and the assignment’s own
title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking

text: predictive covari- ance says how far the motion prediction can be trusted, yet overlap-cost pipelines either ignore it at association time or consume it as a hard Mahalanobis veto [42] (ground-plane costs [45] abandon overlap entirely); and the assignment’s own cost margin says how nearly it preferred the swapped pairing, yet nothing in the tracker’s state distinguishes a confident match from a coin flip. This paper is built on a single principle: a tracker should let its own uncertainty govern its own decisions. We instantiate it twice, as search breadth and commitment firmness, and follow it to its limit. At short horizons the mo- tion covariance acts as tolerance, not veto: our uncertainty- adaptive Expansion IoU dilates each track’s matching re- gion by a continuous function of its predictive standard de- viation, supplied by an Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) filter [6, 8]. text: Tracking-by-detection. SORT [7] established the predict–associate loop; successive work strengthened every stage: appearance and post-hoc refinement [12, 42], low-confidence recovery [47], observation-centric drift correction [9], camera compensation [4], ground-plane modeling [45], adaptive appearance fusion [28], weak cues [44], and track-centric assignment [34]. Across this family, the filter’s predictive covariance is either ignored at association time or, in practice, consumed solely as a hard Mahalanobis gate [42]; the association cost itself is uncertainty-blind, and the assignment is commitment-blind: every match is final the frame it is made. Expanded and buffered matching. Closest to ARC- SORT are methods that enlarge boxes before computing overlap: by a fixed proportional margin [43], a fixed iter- ative schedule [20] (discarding the Kalman filter), with a harmonic cost mean [16], or switched by a binary velocity threshold atop a trained long short-term memory (LSTM) gated filter [40]. In every case the factor is fixed or dis- cretely switched; none derives it from the filter’s own pre- dictive covariance. Ours is a continuous function of that covariance, wide exactly when the prediction is unreliable, and requires no training. Uncertainty as a signal. In detection, probabilistic-IoU box models [24, 25, 41] score overlap between distributions rather than boxes; UTrack [35] propagates detector uncer- tainty into association, complementary to the motion-model uncertainty we exploit. IMM filtering [6, 8, 29]

In detection, probabilistic-IoU box models [24, 25, 41] score overlap between distributions rather than boxes; UTrack [35] propagates detector uncer- tainty into association, complementary to the motion-model uncertainty we exploit. IMM filtering [6, 8, 29] has long supplied calibrated predictive covariances in radar tracking, where the probabilistic and joint probabilistic data associa- tion filters (PDAF/JPDAF) [5, 13] spend them continuously inside a soft filter update. Visual MOT’s hard-assignment, overlap-cost pipelines use the covariance only as a Maha- lanobis veto [42]; covariance as a continuous overlap tol- erance under one-to-one assignment is, to our knowledge, new. Deferred data association. Multiple hypothesis track- ing (MHT) [32] answers ambiguity by not deciding; PDAF/JPDAF (above) soften the assignment itself. Vi- sion revisited both, in pruned MHT with appearance [23], m-best JPDA [33], and near-online revision [10], but the SORT lineage dropped deferral: it commits every identity at the crossing instant, precisely when occlusion makes ev- idence worst, and revision survives only as offline refine- ment [12, 38]. Closest to our long-horizon stage, GTA [38] refines Deep-EIoU offline, globally re- linking tracklets under appearance plus spatio-temporal constraints (81.0 on SportsMOT). Our merge differs in what it removes: it drops the motion constraint at long gaps, the binding factor per our ablation (Sec. 4.5), and links on ap- pearance alone. Method ARC-SORT applies one rule three times (Fig. 1). Online, frame by frame: each track’s matching region is dilated in proportion to its own predictive covariance (Sec. 3.4), and near-ambiguous match pairs, identified by the assign- ment’s own margin, are held in a deferred two-hypothesis state and corrected by a single identity swap when later ev- idence rules the first decision wrong (Sec. 3.6). Offline, per sequence: tracklet fragments separated by multi-second gaps, where motion information has run out, are linked by appearance alone, with the customary motion veto removed (Sec. 3.8). 3.1. Online tracker overview At each frame, detections split by confidence at τH=0.6/τL=0.1 [47]; each track’s IMM filter predicts (Sec. 3.2); a camera-motion estimate warps all predicted states into the current frame (Sec. 3.3); the warped covari- ance sets each track’s expansion (Sec. 3.4); three associa- tion stages match detections to tracks (Sec. 3.5). Matched tracks receive a filter update (replayed through stored camera transforms after loss, Sec. 3.3); unmatched high- confidence detections spawn tracks (≥0.7); tracks lost over 30 frames are removed. After lifecycle management, an arbitration pass reads the frame’s assignment margins and manages entanglement episodes (Sec. 3.6);

IMM motion model Models. All models operate on measurements z = [cx, cy, w, h]⊤. A constant-velocity (CV) model tracks all four box coordinates and their velocities (R8); a constant- acceleration (CA) model adds acceleration for the center only (R10); a coordinated-turn (CT) model adds a turn rate ω (R9) with the standard non-linear center transition [6], handled by an extended Kalman filter (EKF) with an ana- lytic Jacobian; |ω| < 10−6 reduces to CV. Cycle. The IMM cycle [8] runs mixing, per-model pre- diction, log-space probability update, and combination (Πii = 0.98, initial [0.7, 0.15, 0.15]; a ∼50-frame adap- tation constant). Mixing operates on the common 8- dimensional subspace; model-specific states pass through unmixed with cross-covariances reset, a reduced-state ap- proximation of textbook IMM. Uncertainty-adaptive Expansion IoU This is the paper’s core mechanism. After prediction and CMC, each track exposes its innovation covariance in measurement space, S = ˆP[1:4,1:4] + R, where ˆP is the IMM combined covariance (including between-model spread) and R the size-dependent measurement noise. From its positional diagonal we form the relative positional un- certainty and map it to an expansion factor: ei = clip  α · max σx w , σy h  , emin, emax  , (2) with σx = √S11, σy = √S22, predicted box size (w, h), and α=2, emin=0.2, emax=1.2 throughout: the matching region covers two predicted-center standard deviations in units of box size. Both boxes of a pair grow symmetri- cally before computing IoU, each side by ei times that box’s own extent [20]; ei=0 reduces exactly to IoU. Unlike Deep- EIoU’s global schedule, ei is per track, per frame: a track mid-maneuver casts a wide net; a confidently tracked one keeps a tight gate. Experiments 4.1. Setup Datasets. SportsMOT [11]: 45 val sequences (15 each basketball, football, volleyball) for all tuning and ablations; 150 test sequences evaluated exclusively through the offi- cial evaluation server. DanceTrack [39] val (25 sequences) serves as a transfer benchmark: non-linear motion under a largely static camera. We report HOTA [26] with its de- tection (DetA) and association (AssA) components, identity F1 (IDF1), multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA), and the number of identity switches (IDs). Implementation. Nothing in the system is trained. The detector is YOLOX-X [15] with the public SportsMOT weights from the MixSort model zoo [11]. Two releases exist, and we keep them separate: every validation-set ex- periment and ablation in this paper uses the checkpoint trained on the train split only, so no validation frame was seen by the detector; the test-set submissions use the train+val checkpoint, the release intended for test sub- missions. Validation-set DetA is therefore not inflated by detector exposure; appearance embeddings come from the sports-domain OSNet released with Deep-EIoU [20] (DanceTrack rows use FastReID SBS-S50 [17]). text: We presented ARC-SORT, a training-free tracker in which the tracker’s own uncertainty governs its decisions: the IMM covariance sets a continuous per-track association tol- erance, the assignment’s permutation margin defers near- ambiguous commitments until evidence settles them, and where motion information has run out an appearance-only merge replaces the motion-gated one. Limitations. Deferred commitment is pairwise and single-swap, and its gain tracks the embedding stack (53– 120% of the validation delta). The long-horizon stage is offline. Public model-zoo detection caps HOTA. On DanceTrack, 62.1 is well below trained specialists; on SportsMOT, trained and foundation-model systems [18] keep a 0.1–5.4 HOTA edge. Acknowledgments. text: Preprint VELOX: SPATIAL MEMORY MAKES WORLD MODELS EFFICIENT Qiuhong Shen Shizun Wang Xinchao Wang∗ National University of Singapore
title: Preprint

text: Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer’s model- derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention- style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by 4.36× and denoising by 2.43×. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page for more details. 1
title: Preprint

text: Video world models are emerging as a practical interface for interactive simulation. A user specifies an action trajectory or camera motion, and the model rolls the world forward by generating future video frames. This direction builds on rapid progress in video diffusion transformers and large video foundation models (Ho et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022; Peebles & Xie, 2023; Blattmann et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024b; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025). Recent works increasingly target controllable long video worlds rather than isolated short clips (Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Sand.ai, 2025; Gao et al., 2026; HY-World et al., 2026). For these models, context management is a central methodological challenge. Past frames carry the appearance, geometry, and object state that future frames must respect. Without access to the right history, long rollouts drift, forget revisited regions, or re-synthesize the same scene inconsistently. The most direct way to preserve this history is to retain an ever-growing visual context. Chunked or causal video diffusion models let each new chunk attend to historical frame tokens through a KV cache. Dense FlashAttention makes this practical at moderate lengths (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023), and causal diffusion or self-forcing training makes
title: Preprint

text: Chunked or causal video diffusion models let each new chunk attend to historical frame tokens through a KV cache. Dense FlashAttention makes this practical at moderate lengths (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023), and causal diffusion or self-forcing training makes long rollouts natural (Chen et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025b). The cost, however, grows with the number of generated chunks. Later chunks inherit larger context even when the current camera overlaps only a small part of the past scene. As a result, chunk-wise generation becomes progressively slower exactly when long-horizon consistency matters most. This motivates context selection rather than naive context accumulation. Frame- and view-memory methods select a smaller set of relevant past observations. Context-as-Memory retrieves historical views by camera field-of-view overlap, and VMem stores surfel-indexed views for consistent re- visits (Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025). AnchorWeave and related works (Xiao et al., 2025; Wu ∗Corresponding author. 1 arXiv:2610.22311v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

text: Preprint et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026) further inject warped renderings from persistent memory through ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023a) to stabilize camera-controlled generation. These methods show that not all past frames are equally useful, and figure 1 summarizes this progression from dense history to view-level retrieval. Yet frame-level selection remains coarse for transformer attention. It provides the same selected context to all regions in the active chunk, although dynamic scenes often need local temporal continuity and different regions in the same noisy chunk can depend on different parts of the past. Methods that inject warped point renderings into the model input can also require architectural adaptation or fine-tuning, which limits direct reuse of a pretrained video generator. text: blocks using frustum slab correspondences. Inspired by inverse rendering works (Kerbl et al., 2023; Mildenhall et al., 2021), we observe that regions whose geometry has already been observed should primarily attend to their corresponding past regions. Newly revealed or uncertain regions, in contrast, may require model-derived semantic context and local temporal neighbors. A road block, a facade block, and newly revealed sky in the same noisy chunk should therefore not necessarily attend to the same past views. The question, then, is no longer only which frames to retrieve, but whether long-context video generation can assign each region its own relevant history while preserving local motion continuity and leaving the pretrained generator unchanged. We consider this question at the token-block level in the block-wise execution model of FlashAt- tention (Dao, 2023). Our key insight is that camera frustum slabs with depth intervals can provide region-specific routing signals at the same granularity used by tiled attention. Instead of adding a new conditioning branch or fine-tuning the video generator, Velox summarizes generated history as per-block frustum slabs and uses their overlap to guide which historical KV token blocks each current region should see. For each target chunk, Velox obtains query-side depth through recency-priority multiwarp and scores query and historical blocks by world-space OBB frustum slab overlap. In well-covered regions, this score softly reweights

text: which historical KV token blocks each current region should see. For each target chunk, Velox obtains query-side depth through recency-priority multiwarp and scores query and historical blocks by world-space OBB frustum slab overlap. In well-covered regions, this score softly reweights each layer’s model-derived block importance before selection. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. Previous- chunk retention and global-aligned Gilbert neighborhoods preserve local motion continuity without a separate cross-chunk seam table. Across 48-chunk timing traces and the 158-case WBench navigation split (Ying et al., 2026), Velox re- duces the growing long-context attention cost while preserving aggregate quality near dense attention. Its advantage grows with the number of generated chunks. At chunk 48, attention latency decreases from approximately 34.2 ms with dense FlashAttention to 7.8 ms, a 4.36× speedup. Denoising time decreases from approximately 7.19 s to 2.96 s under the same single-H200 asynchronous setting. Built on LingBot-Fast-Cam (Gao et al., 2026), Velox remains within 0.15 points of dense attention on the WBench API-free average and improves the 19-metric overall average from 75.52 to 75.60. These results support the scoped claim that soft frustum slab routing can alleviate the late-chunk attention bottleneck without materially degrading benchmark quality. 2

text: Preprint Our contributions can be summarized as: • We introduce Velox, a training-free framework that uses frustum slab correspondences to reduce growing KV attention cost in chunked video world models. • We devise a soft geometric fusion rule that uses OBB frustum slab overlap to modulate each layer’s model-derived block importance while preserving an unbiased fallback for uncovered regions. • We implement Velox with global-aligned Gilbert KV storage, an optimized sparse attention kernel, and asynchronous frustum slab construction on the same H200 as denoising, reaching a 4.36× attention speedup and a 2.43× denoising speedup at chunk 48. 2
title: Preprint

text: 2.1 VIDEO WORLD MODELS AND SPATIAL MEMORY Video generation has progressed from latent diffusion to scalable diffusion transformers and rectified flow (Ho et al., 2020; Rombach et al., 2022; Blattmann et al., 2023; Peebles & Xie, 2023; Esser et al., 2024), with foundation models supplying strong visual priors (Yang et al., 2024b; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; HaCohen et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025). Long-video methods extend these priors through progressive generation, self-rollout training, and causal chunking (Kim et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024; Henschel et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025b; Sand.ai, 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025a), while interactive models target controllable persistent worlds (Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025d; Che et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2025b; Decart et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026; HY-World et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026). These directions make history management central: more context supports consistency but makes dense attention increasingly expensive. Spatial-memory methods address this tension by retrieving views, preserving revisits, or expanding reconstructed worlds (Yu et al., 2025a;

text: al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026). These directions make history management central: more context supports consistency but makes dense attention increasingly expensive. Spatial-memory methods address this tension by retrieving views, preserving revisits, or expanding reconstructed worlds (Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2024b;a; Engstler et al., 2024). Camera-aware and controllable generation (Yu et al., 2024c; YU et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; 2025; Yang et al., 2025c; Ren et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026) and streaming reconstruction (Wang et al., 2024b; Leroy et al., 2024; Cabon et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2024a; 2025a;b; Keetha et al., 2025) further make projectable memory practical. Velox uses this memory to route pretrained attention rather than adding a conditioning pathway or retrained memory module. 2.2 EFFICIENT ATTENTION AND CONTEXT ROUTING Long-context transformers reduce attention cost through sparsity, locality, compression, state reuse, heavy-hitter selection, and KV eviction (Kitaev et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Dai et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023b; Kwon et al., 2023; Li &

text: al., 2020; Beltagy et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Dai et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023b; Kwon et al., 2023; Li & Wang, 2026), while FlashAttention is the dense IO-aware baseline (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023). Video accelerators additionally exploit spatial, temporal, denoising-step, and feature regularity through adaptive sparsity, caching, and quantized attention (Zhang et al., 2025c; Xi et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025b; Xia et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; 2025a; Liu et al., 2024b; 2025b; 2024a; Guo et al., 2024; Nawaz et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026). These approaches usually derive sparsity from position, cached features, or attention statistics, whereas frame-memory methods select views but retain dense attention within them. Velox connects both directions by using projective correspondence as a soft prior for region-specific attention routes, with model-derived fallback and temporal safeguards. 3 METHOD Overview. Long-horizon generation requires persistent visual history, yet dense KV attention makes every current region process all retained blocks. Velox keeps the pretrained generator and conditioning interface unchanged and modifies only the inference-time visibility relation between current query blocks and historical KV blocks. It represents history as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals, 3

The calibrated route applies at every transformer layer, so the growing historical term is bounded throughout the denoising network. 4 EXPERIMENTS 4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS We instantiate Velox on the LingBot-Fast-Cam inference stack (Gao et al., 2026) with a Wan-style video diffusion transformer. The reported configuration uses recency-priority multiwarp Q-depth, world-space OBB frustum slab IoU, grouped fragment aggregation, and global-aligned Gilbert KV storage. We apply fixed soft geometric fusion to well-covered rows at every transformer layer, with τ = 0.1, gref = 0.2, λ = 2, and ηcov = 0.9. Covered rows retain Kcov = 80 blocks. Uncovered rows use the model-derived cumulative-mass route with Kunc = 150 and no route-size floor. 7

text: Preprint The measured sparse path is a native Triton indexed block-sparse attention implementation rather than a dense call with a Python mask. Current queries are reordered once per chunk, KV caches are stored in global-aligned Gilbert order, and the kernel consumes routed block lists with a runtime route-length bound. The previous chunk is always retained within the route budget, while current-chunk local neighbors and reference-frame blocks act as deterministic safeguards. Frustum slab state is prepared asynchronously with a two-chunk freshness lag, so chunk c normally consumes geometry through chunk c −2. In the reported timing traces, DiT denoising and asynchronous geometry construction run concurrently on one H200. We evaluate quality on all 158 cases of the WBench navigation split (Ying et al., 2026). The three LingBot-based rows use identical generated cases and the Gemini judge for VLM-scored metrics. Published WBench rows use the official Doubao judge, so judge-dependent values should not be compared across these two groups. We therefore include an API-free average that excludes VLM-scored setting metrics and is comparable across judge backends. 4.2 ATTENTION SCALING OVER 48 CHUNKS Figure 3 reports 48-chunk timing traces. text: We present Velox, a training-free router that projects spatial memory into the current latent camera view and uses frustum slab overlap to modulate layer-specific block importance while retaining model-derived fallback and local temporal safeguards. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by 4.36× and denoising by 2.43× with asynchronous geometry construction on one H200. Across all 158 WBench navigation cases, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast- Cam and slightly improves the 19-metric overall average. These results show that region-level spatial correspondence can turn persistent world memory into a practical routing signal for long-horizon generation. 10

text: Preprint Appendices A ADDITIONAL EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE A.1 SOFT-FUSION CALIBRATION We calibrate the fixed fusion strength on pooled query-key distributions and frustum slab overlap ma- trices from two navigation trajectories. The calibration contains 48 grids spanning four representative layers, two denoising steps, and three rollout lengths. Positive overlap values have median 0.211, which motivates rescaling rather than multiplying by raw IoU. Among the tested settings, λ = 2 and gref = 0.2 are the weakest pair that recovers at least 85% of positive-overlap blocks in the fused top-80 while changing at most 25% of the model-only selections. Concretely, positive-overlap recall increases from 0.602 to 0.852, and the selected set changes by 9.0% on average. Values at or below τ = 0.1 receive no boost. text: Preprint B EXPERIMENTAL IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Velox is instantiated on the LingBot-Fast-Cam inference stack (Gao et al., 2026) with a Wan-style video diffusion transformer. Its routing backend uses frustum slab matching: stored chunks provide source-camera token rectangles and robust depth intervals, target query blocks obtain Q-depth through multiwarp, and Eq. (7) provides the world-space OBB overlap score. B.1 REPORTED ROUTING CONFIGURATION The reported configuration applies the fixed fusion in Eq. (11) only when ρi ≥0.9. It uses λ = 2, gref = 0.2, τ = 0.1, and Kcov = 80. Rows below the coverage threshold retain the model-only cumulative-mass route and are capped at Kunc = 150 without a minimum route-size floor. The previous chunk is reserved inside these budgets. Global Gilbert neighbors and reference-frame blocks are then added as safeguards. The same sparse routing rule is applied at every transformer layer. B.2 CAMERA POSE ALIGNMENT FOR FRUSTUM SLAB GEOMETRY The frustum slab table is reconstructed in the LingBot-map camera-to-world frame, while the chunk cameras used by the video generator come from ViPE poses. LingBot-map does not accept external camera poses during streaming reconstruction. Velox therefore maps each target ViPE camera into the reconstructed coordinate frame before multiwarp, OBB construction, frustum slab IoU, and coverage estimation. B.4 RUNTIME PATH AND TIMING SCOPE The measured sparse path is a Triton indexed block-sparse attention implementation, not a Python masking wrapper around dense attention. Queries are reordered once per chunk into the global- aligned Gilbert token order, and KV caches are written directly in that layout so that the hot kernel loads contiguous KV tiles without a per-call host permutation. The kernel supports rectangular current-query versus growing-history attention, consumes the routed block lists produced by the fused-score scheduler, and uses a runtime route-length bound so later chunks do not trigger new compiler specializations. text: Preprint All speed numbers are measured on one H200 from the 48-chunk timing traces in Figure 3. We report per-chunk attention-call latency and per-chunk denoising critical-path time rather than a single aggregate wall-clock number because early chunks have small dense-attention baseline cost, while late chunks expose the scaling behavior that matters for long video generation. C ASYNCHRONOUS FRUSTUM SLAB CONSTRUCTION The geometry pipeline would be expensive if it were inserted serially between generated chunks. In a synchronous implementation, chunk c must be denoised, decoded, reconstructed into depth and pose state, inserted into the frustum slab table and multiwarp cache, aligned with the next target cameras, and scored before chunk c + 1 can denoise. The reconstruction and frustum slab preparation path is on the same order as one DiT denoise step in our setting, so serial execution would hide the attention-kernel gains. Velox relaxes this dependency with a two-chunk freshness lag. Target chunk c consumes a Velox state built from frustum slabs through chunk c −2, while the worker prepares states for later chunks. The state remains self-consistent: each worker task first inserts exactly one decoded chunk into the frustum slab table and multiwarp cache, then scores that table against the target chunk’s latent cameras. Chunks before the first available Velox state run dense attention, so the method never consumes

Chunks before the first available Velox state run dense attention, so the method never consumes an uninitialized route. The implementation uses one Python worker thread and one dedicated CUDA stream. The worker is the sole writer to the frustum slab table, pose aligner, multiwarp frame cache, and sparse-attention context. The main denoising thread submits a geometry task after a chunk decode and receives a future keyed by the target chunk. Second, the relative alignment maps target camera-control poses into the reconstructed frame and refreshes stored slab cameras under the current bridge. Frames are moved to CPU after decode and copied back on the worker stream, avoiding extra GPU residency while the main stream denoises. All reported timing results use a single NVIDIA H200. The async worker and the DiT denoiser share that one GPU. Memory reconstruction is not offloaded to a second device. A second GPU could reduce CUDA-stream contention and further improve end-to-end time, but it is not part of the reported measurement protocol. text: Grid-Bench: Can LLMs Predict How Discrete Worlds Change? Zixiang Xu1, Zirui Song2, Wanrong Zheng1, Chiyu Zhang3, Yue Huang4, Yuyang Peng5, Kexin Zhang1, Jinkun Chen1, Xiuying Chen2, Xiangliang Zhang4, Yan Liu1, Laurent Itti1, Frank Shyu3, Xiaoqiang Luo3, Sandeep Pandey3, Xi Liu3, Luke Simon3, Xiyang Hu6, Yue Zhao1 1University of Southern California 2Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence 3Meta 4University of Notre Dame 5University of California, Los Angeles 6Arizona State University Spatial instructions describe how to move objects, transform regions, or modify their surroundings. When several operations are applied in sequence, each acts on a configuration shaped by earlier changes. How accurately can large language models (LLMs) predict the resulting spatial state? We introduce Grid-Bench, an executable benchmark in which eight families of operations transform discrete worlds represented as two-, three-, and four-dimensional grids. Given an initial grid, explicit rules, and an event history expressed as text, a model predicts the complete final grid. Reference execution makes every predicted value checkable, supporting comparisons across spatial operations, history lengths, and workloads. Evaluating six LLMs shows that complete-state accuracy falls sharply as histories grow, with substantial divergence among models that perform similarly on single events. Models with similar exact-match accuracy can nevertheless differ substantially in the number of incorrect cells on shared instances. Even over long histories, some models recover many correct changes

text: Spatial reasoning supports understanding scene descriptions and interpreting instructions about objects and their surroundings (Shi et al., 2022; Long et al., 2016). Such instructions appear in tasks ranging from object manipulation to geometric design, where language specifies actions or construction operations that change a spatial configuration (Shridhar et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2024). When instructions describe a sequence of operations, earlier changes can alter the spatial conditions on which later operations depend. Moving an object, for example, can free one position while blocking another, changing the outcome of a subsequent move. Predicting the resulting configuration from text therefore involves relating the described operations to the spatial states they successively produce. We investigate how accurately large language models predict these outcomes across varied operations, event histories, and spatial structures. Existing benchmarks evaluate selected spatial relations and entity states (Mirzaee et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2022; Kim and Schuster, 2023), while recent studies also examine complete-grid and chess-state prediction from event sequences (Chapra et al., 2026; Walker and Lyons, 2026). We introduce Grid-Bench to study complete- state prediction in discrete spatial worlds, across operations that draw on different spatial information. A reflection rearranges values within a specified geometric region; region growth acts on a connected component whose boundary changes with the state. A simulator executes the full event sequence to compute an exact reference state. Comparing every predicted value with this reference establishes whether the whole state is correct and reveals the extent and location of errors when it is not. Figure 1 illustrates the reference states produced by a movement history in two and three dimensions. We evaluate six large language models under a shared protocol and find that exact-match accuracy declines sharply with history length. Models with similar single-event accuracy separate over longer histories, and even similar rates of complete recovery can accompany quite different incorrect predictions. At eight events, Kimi K2.5 and MiniMax M2.5 have similar exact-match accuracy, yet their median wrong-cell counts are 14 and 67 on the 84 shared instances where both return valid incorrect states. Grid-Bench brings diverse spatial operations into a common, executable framework for predicting and eval- uating complete worlds. The accompanying six-model study examines when models recover the final state across event histories and spatial conditions, and what they get wrong when recovery fails. 2

text: Spatial benchmarks evaluate relations, transformations, and actions through different prediction targets. SPARTQA (Mirzaee et al., 2021) and SPARTUN/ReSQ (Mirzaee and Kordjamshidi, 2022) ask questions about relations expressed in scene descriptions. StepGame (Shi et al., 2022) tests relational composition, while SpaRC/SpaRP (Rizvi et al., 2024) formalizes spatial properties and reasoning paths. Other evaluations consider constrained path construction (Kaesberg et al., 2025), spatial reasoning across textual and visual inputs (Wang et al., 2024), and action selection in symbolic or simulated environments (Gao et al., 2026b,a). 2

text: JigShape (Li et al., 2026c) evaluates geometric reconstruction from puzzle pieces, and OrigamiBench (Agar- wal et al., 2026) studies physically grounded fold operations. SnorkelSpatial (Vishwakarma, 2025) studies transformations of textual boards, querying properties after translations and rotations. Grid-Bench evaluates the complete configuration produced by a prescribed event history, allowing errors to be located throughout the resulting world. Predicting the result of an event history also connects spatial reasoning to instruction execution and state tracking. bAbI (Weston et al., 2015) includes questions about locations and possessions after narrated events; SCONE (Long et al., 2016) grounds instruction sequences in executable worlds; and ProPara (Dalvi et al., 2018) follows entity existence and location through procedural text. Entity-tracking evaluations more directly test whether models update affected entities while retaining unaffected information across operations (Kim and Schuster, 2023; Tang et al., 2026). Beyond state tracking, GT Bench (Xu et al., 2026e) examines algorithmic reasoning over graphs, while AlgoWorlds (Xu et al., 2026d) evaluates tool-guided decisions against verifiable optima. Closest to our complete-state setting, Alien Grid (Chapra et al., 2026) studies sequential depth through rotations, corner swaps, and shifts of a 3 × 3 grid. Chess-World-Model (Walker and Lyons, 2026) trains sequence models to recover complete chess states at successive move prefixes. Grid-Bench evaluates LLMs given explicit textual rules across geometric, neighborhood, connectivity, and movement operations,

text: 3.2 Spatial transition families The eight transition families in Table 1 cover geometry, neighborhood aggregation, connected regions, and movement. Explicit rules specify how each event selects cells and transforms their values. Events may select a region geometrically, as a ball or box, or through the current world’s connectivity, occupancy, and obstacles. text: Grid-Bench uses eight families of executable operations and exact reference states to evaluate how accurately language models predict the complete final state of a discrete spatial world. Across six models, success on individual operations gives way to much lower exact recovery over longer histories, with substantial differences across models and spatial conditions. When complete recovery fails, the returned states range from nearly correct grids to extensively incorrect configurations. Some retain many correct updates beyond what copying the initial state would recover, even at the longest histories. Reliable prediction of spatial change remains challenging even with explicit rules. The executable rules can supply training examples with exact targets, while cell-level diagnostics can show whether models improve at predicting required changes, preserving unchanged values, or both. Limitations Grid-Bench evaluates predictions in fully specified symbolic worlds with prescribed operations. Its task families and generation settings define the spatial conditions studied here. Transfer to other world sizes, operation distributions, or environments with uncertain observations remains an empirical question. Error extent and update–preservation partitions describe the final values models return. Connecting these outcomes to internal representations or execution strategies requires evidence about intermediate computa- tion. text: A Extended Related Work Spatial state prediction connects spatial evaluation with tasks that map a described world and a sequence of operations to an observable outcome. This appendix develops connections to spatial evaluation, instruc- tion execution and entity state, complete-state prediction, structured reasoning, and contextual robustness. Table 5 compares representative prediction targets and evaluation emphases. A.1 Spatial relations, perception, and action Textual spatial benchmarks have progressively broadened the relations and compositions exposed in lan- guage. SPARTQA asks relation, object, and containment questions over human-written and generated scene descriptions (Mirzaee et al., 2021); SPARTUN and ReSQ broaden relation types, linguistic expressions, and human-authored questions (Mirzaee and Kordjamshidi, 2022). StepGame varies the length of relation chains and the presence of distractors (Shi et al., 2022), and later analysis separates relation parsing from logical composition while correcting template artifacts (Li et al., 2024). SpaRC formalizes properties of objects, relations, and contexts, while SpaRP supplies deductively verified reasoning paths (Rizvi et al., 2024). Visual benchmarks provide a complementary tradition of controlled spatial evaluation. CLEVR uses rendered scenes and generated questions to diagnose compositional visual reasoning (Johnson et al., 2017); NLVR pairs natural statements with synthetic images requiring visual and set-theoretic reasoning (Suhr et al., 2017). VSR evaluates natural text–image pairs across a broad inventory of spatial relations and reference frames (Liu et al., 2023b),
title: Extended Related Work

text: reasoning (Johnson et al., 2017); NLVR pairs natural statements with synthetic images requiring visual and set-theoretic reasoning (Suhr et al., 2017). VSR evaluates natural text–image pairs across a broad inventory of spatial relations and reference frames (Liu et al., 2023b), while SpatialEval compares spatial questions across textual and visual inputs (Wang et al., 2024). These benchmarks make relation recognition and composition observable under different balances of perception and language. JigShape extends geometric evaluation to reconstructing jigsaw arrangements from interlocking pieces and visual content (Li et al., 2026c). OrigamiBench connects visual observations with a language of physically grounded fold actions (Agarwal et al., 2026). FigEdit studies another form of structured transformation: checking whether chart edits respect the intended data and graphical relationships (Li et al., 2026b). text: A.2 Instruction execution and entity state Controlled language tasks have long connected narrated events to changing worlds. bAbI generates questions about locations, possessions, and other facts after sequences of events (Weston et al., 2015). SCONE pairs an initial world with context-dependent instructions in three executable domains; predicted logical forms are evaluated by the world they produce (Long et al., 2016). Both use simulation to make consequences checkable, while placing different demands on the predicted answer. Procedural-text research studies changes that may be implicit in natural descriptions. Neural Process Net- works model actions as operators that transform learned entity states (Bosselut et al., 2018). ProPara anno- tates entity existence and location as a process unfolds (Dalvi et al., 2018), and OpenPI extends procedural state changes to open-vocabulary entities, attributes, and before/after values (Tandon et al., 2020). TRIP associates multi-sentence physical stories with state annotations that support tiered evaluation of plausibility and its underlying evidence (Storks et al., 2021). This line asks models to infer consequences from ordinary language; Grid-Bench makes the transition rules explicit and varies the spatial structures on which they act. Entity-tracking studies isolate update and retention more directly. Box-transfer tasks query container con- tents after PUT, REMOVE, and MOVE operations and distinguish changed from unchanged states (Kim and Schuster, 2023). Subsequent work uses behavioral tests, probes, and interventions

Subsequent work uses behavioral tests, probes, and interventions to study how models process these changes (Tang et al., 2026). Related probing work recovers and manipulates entity-state infor- mation in models trained on Alchemy instructions and TextWorld transcripts (Li et al., 2021). These studies motivate examining both final values that differ from the initial world and those that match it when a model returns an entire state. The use of evolving histories also appears in social and personalized interaction. SocialMaze evaluates reasoning across social settings with changing interactions and uncertain information (Xu et al., 2025d); PersonaConvBench evaluates personalized predictions and generation from conversation histories (Li et al., 2025b). Memory Retrieval for Changing Preferences selects historical turns as evidence of a user’s current preferences (Qin et al., 2026), while RaMem preserves temporal and participant context when retrieving past experiences (Yang et al., 2026b). The scope of retained information matters as well: shared-state agents can misapply information from one user’s interaction to another (Yang et al., 2026a). A.3 Complete-state prediction Board games provide deterministic state transitions over long sequences. Language modeling of chess move records has been evaluated with piece-location and legal-move probes (Toshniwal et al., 2022); Othello-GPT work uses probes and interventions to study board representations learned from move transcripts (Li et al., 2023). text: B Benchmark Specification B.1 Shared conventions and read accounting The state domain and finite alphabet are those defined in Section 3.1. Each event supplies its operation and parameters. Coordinates omitted from the input list have value zero, so the list specifies the complete world. Let N1(x) contain the in-bounds coordinates at Manhattan distance one from x, and let B1(a, r) be the in-bounds Manhattan ball of radius r centered at a. Reference execution reads the current world W and produces W ′. Unless a rule explicitly specifies sequential mutation, all reads use W. Cells not selected for writing keep their values. The zero value is stored implicitly. SET(p, v) writes v at p, including zero when a cell is cleared. The canonical read list R(W, e) counts cell incidences, so repeated accesses to one coordinate can occur more than once. Its unique read support is R(W, e) = {x : x occurs in R(W, e)}. A rule also specifies a write support S(W, e): the coordinates that receive assignments, whether or not their values change. Finally, D(W, e) = {x : Ff(W, e)(x)̸ = W(x)}, (5) scan(W, e) = |R(W, e)|, (6) effect(W, e) = |D(W, e)|. (7) Thus D(W, e) ⊆S(W, e), but a large support need not produce a large effect.
