The agent compacts its context when it grows too long, as it does for software work; the instructions ask agents to keep in memory what must survive a compaction, such as work in progress and next steps. None of the 2,839 programs the players ran during the session (2,783 before the win) made a network request or referred to a web source, and neither their chat nor the Observer’s report mentions one. Players interact with the game only through a command-line client. It sends a JavaScript program to the player’s Mineflayer bot on the game server, waits up to a timeout that the agent chooses (60 seconds by default), and prints what the program logged and returned. The program runs as the body of an asynchronous function that receives the bot, with the pathfinding plugin loaded and no helpers added. The server records chat, deaths and advancements in its log, keeps every program with its output, and saves the world every five minutes; after a failure, it restarts from the latest save. 2.2. Instructions Each agent’s instructions combine a general part, the same for every environment, with a short description of the environment and of the objective. The general part for players asks them to observe the environment before acting and verify the result afterwards, to validate new tools on short tasks before trusting them, to build and refine their own tools when manual actions limit their speed or reliability, to record mechanics, strategies and workarounds in memory so that no obstacle is met twice, to keep working while background jobs run, to be honest about their actions and outcomes, and to pursue the objective rather than exploit flaws of the environment or of its evaluation. The description of the environment explains how to run code with the bot, how the chat works, where the server records the game and where to find the documentation of Mineflayer; it contains no game strategy. Its instructions ask it to check the players’ claims against the record before reporting them, to report specification gaming, such as an exploited flaw in the evaluation, and fabricated results, to leave the game unchanged, and to intervene only on failures of the environment, such as a broken tool or a quota ceiling, never on the players’ strategy. It published a live report of the session, with a summary of progress, a log of verified events and its findings about the infrastructure. It flagged no specification gaming, and it never joined the game or ran a program in it. The run didn’t contain any safety incidents, according to the Observer agent and our manual reviews of the logs. 3. text: Minecraft has long been a testbed for open-ended agents. MineRL released human demonstrations and ran a competition on sample-efficient learning of the diamond task (Guss et al., 2019b; Guss et al., 2019a). Video PreTraining learned keyboard and mouse control from online videos and crafted diamond tools (Baker et al., 2022), DreamerV3 collected diamonds from scratch with reinforcement learning (Hafner et al., 2025), and STEVE-1 followed short-horizon open-ended text instructions (Lifshitz et al., 2023). MineDojo called defeating the Ender Dragon, starting barehanded in a fresh world, one of its moonshot goals (Fan et al., 2022). SIMA and SIMA 2 act from pixels with a keyboard and mouse across many 3D games, and SIMA 2 was also tested on held-out Minecraft tasks (SIMA Team, 2024; SIMA Team, 2025). These systems learn their policies from large amounts of gameplay data or experience. Another line of work uses language models as planners or programmers, building on interleaved reasoning and tool use (Yao et al., 2023) and code as policy (Liang et al., 2023). Voyager wrote Mineflayer programs into a growing skill library under an automatic curriculum (Wang et al., 2024). DEPS, GITM, JARVIS-1, Plan4MC, and Optimus-1 added Minecraft-specific planners, knowledge, memory, or learned skills (Wang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).

Multi-agent studies examined coordination and social behavior in games, including Minecraft (Gong et al., 2024; Altera.AL et al., 2024; White et al., 2025). Reported long-horizon results in this line center on the Overworld technology tree, such as obtaining diamond tools. Two community projects have recently reported end-to-end dragon kills: a single Claude Opus 5 agent calling 37 high-level Minecraft tools on Normal difficulty (AI Bengineering, 2026), and a planner paired with an action-selection model on a fixed speedrun seed in Peaceful difficulty (Malde, 2026). Our setting differs mainly in what the agents were given. Four general-purpose coding agents received the standard Mineflayer library, as published, with its pathfinding plugin, a one-paragraph objective, and their general instructions. We added nothing on top: no instructions about the game, no curriculum, no skill library, no human-written tools, and no route. Every program they ran, they wrote themselves. They played a standard survival server on Easy from a random seed and coordinated through chat and shared notes. 14

text: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft 8. Limitations • Perception and navigation through code. Mineflayer tells the agents exactly which blocks and creatures are around them, including blocks behind solid rock and the dragon’s internal state, information that a human player has to see and interpret or cannot see at all, and its pathfinding plugin plans routes around obstacles, which humans do by eye. Playing from pixels with a keyboard and mouse, as SIMA 2 does, remains much harder. • Easy difficulty. Monsters spawn and attack, but deal less damage than on Normal or Hard, and hunger cannot kill a player. • Prior knowledge. Gemini 4 Argon knows a great deal about Minecraft and Mineflayer from its training data. The run tests whether a general-purpose coding agent can turn that knowledge into working programs and team coordination over a day-long task, not whether it can play a game it has never seen. • Many failures along the way. The players died 605 times, mostly to monsters; 22% of programs ended in an error; the fight in the End took nearly 14 hours. • Infrastructure. The world server restarted 6 times during the run, interrupting the game each time. • A single run. We describe a single run, the first launch we tried, which cannot show how reliably

text: End took nearly 14 hours. • Infrastructure. The world server restarted 6 times during the run, interrupting the game each time. • A single run. We describe a single run, the first launch we tried, which cannot show how reliably the setup succeeds. 9. Responsible development The agents ran in a sandboxed Minecraft world and their in-game programs could control only their own character: they could neither start processes nor write files, and none used a server command. The agents themselves ran on dedicated cloud machines, with the tools they use for software work. A fifth agent, the Observer, followed the session as an independent witness to watch for cheating or specification gaming; neither the Observer nor our manual review of a sample of the logs found any. Every program, message and game event was recorded. Researchers could also watch the run live on a dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but had no cause to intervene. Studying how teams of agents coordinate in a setting where every step is visible is one way to understand such systems before they are trusted with real-world tasks. The skills required to solve Minecraft such as coordinating a team, recovering from failure, and pursuing a goal for more than a day, are also what agents need to work reliably alongside

text: Not Just a Subject: Capturing Adaptive Scene-Specific Variance for Visual Storytelling SeungJu Cha1 , Ye-Chan Kim1 , Kwanyoung Lee1 , and Dong-Jin Kim1 Hanyang University, Seoul 04763, South Korea {sju9020, dpcksdl78, mobled37, djdkim}@hanyang.ac.kr § https://github.com/SeungJuCha/EOS-Story Abstract. Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from nar- rative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS- Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces. In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene’s ⟨EOS⟩embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mis- match between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity fea- tures at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with di- verse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+).

First, at the semantic level, current methods [17, 30, 40] often treat narrative prompts as monolithic inputs, where various semantics (e.g., appearance and scene descriptions) are encoded into a unified embedding. This can lead to in- formation dilution, making it difficult for the model to uniformly attend to all details [14]. As a result, even when a prompt contains rich details (e.g., specific actions or environmental changes), the model often fails to selectively extract scene-specific cues from the prompt. This directly undermines narrative fidelity, producing scenes that ignore their intended semantics (Fig. 1a,b). Second, at the visual level, existing approaches typically rely on spatially blind feature injec- tion, where identity features are transferred without accounting for the spatial constraints or framing of each scene. This oversight of structural scene vari- ance (e.g., camera angles or subject scales) can lead to subject inflexibility, such as contextually mismatched poses or repetitive structural patterns across scenes (Fig. 1b,c). text: Not Just a Subject 3 (1) Cross-Contextual Bridging: We hypothesize that semantic misalignment arises when long and complex prompts are encoded holistically, causing scene- varying attributes to be diluted [14,16]. Rather than encoding all information in a single prompt, we decouple the narrative into an identity prompt describing the subject and a scene prompt describing the scenario. For instance, “a woman with blond hair reading a book.” is split into an identity prompt (“a woman with blond hair.”) and a scene prompt (“a woman reading a book.”). However, this separation introduces a new challenge: since the scene prompt contains no appearance information, the subject generated within the scene has no way to reflect the actual target identity. To bridge this semantic gap without revert- ing to monolithic encoding, we preserve the scene sub-prompt as a semantic anchor and softly inject appearance information at the embedding level. Mo- tivated by the strong generative influence and summarization ability of ⟨EOS⟩ embeddings [20, 37], we interpret it not merely as a terminal token, but as a residual-based semantic control point for scene-aware storytelling (Sec. 3.1). Un- like prior EOS-based methods that substitute the ⟨EOS⟩embedding between prompts differing by a single word (e.g., an object class) [9, 20], we capture a phrase-level appearance difference and infuse it into the scene’s ⟨EOS⟩, reflecting rich multi-attribute

text: (Sec. 3.1). Un- like prior EOS-based methods that substitute the ⟨EOS⟩embedding between prompts differing by a single word (e.g., an object class) [9, 20], we capture a phrase-level appearance difference and infuse it into the scene’s ⟨EOS⟩, reflecting rich multi-attribute cues without explicit word-level repetition (Sec. 3.2). This provides the scene image with the specified appearance cues at the semantic level, enabling more effective feature-level identity transfer. (2) Adaptive Identity Preservation: To mitigate subject inflexibility induced by spatially blind feature transfer, we introduce a spatially adaptive identity injection mechanism that better aligns identity features with the scene- specific layout (Sec. 3.3). We observe that the scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects prevents various identity tokens from corresponding to the scene tokens. As a result, only a few identity tokens are repeatedly transferred to the scene and cause structural artifacts. Motivated by this, we apply Iden- tity Anchoring, which adaptively resizes identity features to match the intended framing and scale of the scene. This enforces structural compatibility between identity and scene representations, reducing scale-induced distortions (Fig. 10b). We then refine the integration through Identity-Aware Self-Attention, which en- ables scene features to selectively attend to subject features, building upon [30]. Unlike existing spatially blind transfer strategies [17,30,40], our approach sup- ports scene-conditioned variation in subject structure (e.g., viewpoint changes) while preserving

text: the integration through Identity-Aware Self-Attention, which en- ables scene features to selectively attend to subject features, building upon [30]. Unlike existing spatially blind transfer strategies [17,30,40], our approach sup- ports scene-conditioned variation in subject structure (e.g., viewpoint changes) while preserving core identity characteristics. To evaluate scene-specific struc- tural variance, we introduce Consistory+_+, extending Consistory+ [17] with diverse framing prompts [15] to simulate the realistic framing shifts of real- world storytelling. We validate our method on Consistory+ and Consistory+_+, demonstrating consistently improved performance under framing variations. Our contributions are as follows: – We show that the ⟨EOS⟩embedding can carry phrase-level, multi-attribute information, enabling appearance cues to be infused during generation. – We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework with two modules: Cross- Contextual Bridging (text-space semantic recomposition) and Adaptive Identity Preservation (vision-space scale-aware transfer).

text: Visual Storytelling. With the advancement of diffusion models [23,26], their applications have expanded into various domains. To meet users’ needs for gener- ating images that preserve subject identity, numerous personalization methods have been proposed [1, 7, 11, 13, 28, 36]. However, these approaches primarily focus on preserving subject appearance [30], often overlooking how the sub- ject should adapt across different visual contexts. To bridge this gap, visual storytelling [17, 19, 25, 33, 40] has emerged as a compelling paradigm for gener- ating identity-consistent images across diverse and dynamic scenes [17]. Some methods fine-tune diffusion models to explicitly capture subject identity [25,33], while [8,17,19,30,34,40] explore training-free strategies that leverage intermedi- ate features from the attention mechanism. For example, Consistory [30] directly maps subject identity across different scenes to achieve identity consistency, while 1P1S [17] leverages the context consistency of CLIP [24] and transfers this infor- mation through the cross-attention mechanism. However, these methods prior- itize identity consistency at the cost of scene adaptation, often producing rigid subject depictions and weak prompt alignment. While concurrent works [8, 34] attempt to alleviate subject rigidity, they still delegate prompt alignment to the underlying diffusion model. In contrast, we find that faithful scene adaptation depends not only on the vision space but also on the text space, and design our framework to jointly address both—improving

In contrast, we find that faithful scene adaptation depends not only on the vision space but also on the text space, and design our framework to jointly address both—improving prompt alignment through semantic-level residual injection and adapting to structural variance through scale-aware feature transfer. ⟨EOS⟩Embedding in Diffusion Models. In CLIP [24], which is widely used to encode text in text-to-image generation models, the ⟨EOS⟩token encapsulates a contextual summary of the entire prompt [37]. Recent mechanistic analyses [31] further show that padding tokens, including ⟨EOS⟩, carry non-trivial semantic influence in text-to-image generation. Built upon this, [37] demonstrates that ⟨EOS⟩has dominant influence in image generation: replacing the ⟨EOS⟩embed- ding of an original prompt (e.g., “A blue bird”) with that of a target prompt (e.g., “A blue chair”) can steer the generated image toward the target seman- tics. Motivated by this property, several works [9,12,20] have utilized ⟨EOS⟩or text-embedding manipulation for downstream tasks. Specifically, [9] substitutes ⟨EOS⟩to resolve semantic binding issues in object–attribute prompts, [20] injects the entire base prompt embedding along with ⟨EOS⟩into the position of spe- cific objects to perform image editing, and [12] manipulates text embeddings to suppress unwanted content. Unlike prior methods that either substitute ⟨EOS⟩ between prompts differing by a single word [9, 20] or manipulate embeddings

To achieve identity consistency while allowing subjects to adapt to diverse scenes, we propose EOS-Story (Fig. 3), a framework that models scene-specific variance in two complementary spaces. (1) Cross-Contextual Bridging (CCB) addresses semantic variance by transferring phrase-level ap- pearance cues into the scene context through the ⟨EOS⟩embedding, mitigat- ing information dilution in long and complex prompts. (2) Adaptive Identity Preservation (AIP) addresses structural variance by aligning identity features to each scene’s subject scale (Identity Anchoring), followed by Identity-Aware Self-Attention refinement. 3.1 EOS Embedding as a Semantic Handle In this section, we explore the generative functional role of the ⟨EOS⟩embedding. Moti- vated by this, we design Cross-Contextual Bridging, which transfers phrase-level appearance information into each scene’s ⟨EOS⟩embedding, allowing subject- specific appearance cues to be integrated while maintaining the scene context. 3.2 Cross-Contextual Bridging To avoid treating a story prompt as a single monolithic description, we con- struct reference subprompts from structured storyboard inputs (e.g., Consis- tory+ benchmark [17]). Each input is decomposed into four semantic compo- nents: style, subject, appearance, and scene. Encoding all components as a single prompt (e.g., “A majestic winter-themed artwork of a regal snow queen in icy beauty watching over a frozen kingdom.”) can dilute fine-grained appear-

To recover such appearance cues without lengthening the scene prompt, we construct three refer- ence subprompts around a minimal shared context: (1) Style Prompt: Style + Subject, (2) Identity Prompt: Style + Subject + Appearance, and (3) Scene Prompt: Style + Subject + Scene. The shared Style + Subject prompt serves as the minimal anchor for measuring appearance-specific displacement before transferring it to each scene prompt. This anchor is scene-independent, while still preserving the subject slot and visual style, making it suitable for defining an appearance cue that can be shared across all scenes. By keeping the scene prompt free of explicit appearance phrases, we pre- serve the scene description as the primary semantic context. Cross-Contextual Bridging then reintroduces the missing appearance cue at the embedding level. This allows the subject appearance to be recovered without modifying the word- level scene description. Building on our empirical observations (Sec. 3.1 and Ap- pendix A), we utilize the ⟨EOS⟩embedding as a controllable semantic handle, enabling phrase-level appearance transfer without increasing the textual length of the scene description. We begin by constructing two semantic subspaces using PCA, based on the ⟨EOS⟩embeddings obtained from appearance and scene phrases in the Consistory+ benchmark. text: In this work, we propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that adap- tively models scene-specific variance in visual storytelling across text and vision spaces. We introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which decouples the narra- tive into identity and scene sub-prompts and bridges the resulting semantic gap by injecting phrase-level appearance residuals into the scene’s ⟨EOS⟩embedding. To complement this with structural adaptation, we further propose Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors subject features at the scene-specific scale and refines integration through Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate scene adaptability, we extend Consistory+ with diverse framing variations (Con- sistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance in both prompt fidelity and structural adaptability. Acknowledgements. Specifically, ∆app (Tab. 6C) corresponds to directly replacing the EOS embedding with the appearance residual, following [9]. The configuration eosorg sc +eosorg app +eosorg sty naively concatenates EOS embeddings ob- tained from each phrase-level component in the benchmark. text: +eosorg sty naively concatenates EOS embeddings ob- tained from each phrase-level component in the benchmark. The relatively lower performance of ∆app can be attributed to the absence of scene information in the resulting embedding. While another variant eosid + ∆sc is mathematically similar to our additive formulation, it exhibits slightly reduced alignment. We hypothesize that this variant introduces multiple semantic directions originating from overlapping bases, whereas our formulation injects a consistent appear- ance residual ∆app into multiple scene-grounded ⟨EOS⟩anchors {eosn sc}N n=1. By shifting several scene embeddings along a consistent semantic direction, our ap- proach maintains a structured integration of narrative context and appearance cues. This parallel infusion results in more stable semantic control and ulti- mately improves text–image alignment compared to subject-anchored alterna- tives. Overall, these results indicate that simply replacing or naively combining EOS components does not sufficiently preserve semantic grounding. In contrast, controlled injection of the appearance direction into a scene-aware EOS consis- tently improves text alignment, highlighting the importance of structured and context-preserving semantic modulation.

text: Evaluation Details The ShotBench [15] includes a wide range of framing phrases across eight cat- egories (Tab. 7). To ensure a focused and rigorous evaluation of scene-specific structural variance, we intentionally restricted the scope to three primary cate- gories, excluding the remaining five based on the following methodological crite- ria: (1) Prompt Redundancy: Shot Framing descriptors (e.g., “single”, “2 shot”) primarily specify the number of characters, which is already inherently defined by the subject phrases in the storyboard prompts; (2) Redundancy Mitigation: Lens Size phrases (e.g., “wide lens”) are largely redundant as they are semantically en- compassed by the Shot Size category (“wide shot”); (3) Domain Incompatibility: Camera Movement is inherently applicable to temporal video sequences and is thus irrelevant to static image generation; and (4) Task Relevance: Lighting- related categories fall outside the scope of our work, as they primarily focus on stylistic or artistic variations rather than the structural and compositional elements that define scene-specific variance. Framing Phrase Filtering. Although SDXL generally produces textually well- aligned images, it sometimes struggles to accurately reflect specific framing phrases. Before incorporating these phrases into our benchmark extension, we first evaluate how well they are captured by the base SDXL model using the
title: S. Cha et al.

text: Not Just a Subject 23 ShotBench evaluation mechanism. To quantitatively assess phrase reflection, we construct approximately 90 diverse scene prompts and append each framing phrase at the end (e.g., “A photo of a woman baking cookies, close-up shot”). We generate images for 10 random seeds per phrase and compute the top-1 and top-3 accuracy, along with standard deviations, as shown in Fig. 16. For exam- ple, in the “shot size” category with 7 phrase options, this results in a total of 6,300 images (90 scenes × 7 phrases × 10 seeds). We filter out framing phrases whose top-1 accuracy is zero (e.g., “extreme wide shot”), as these are not reliably reflected in the generated outputs from SDXL. Consistory+_+ With the remaining framing phrases, we extend the orig- inal Consistory+ benchmark using GPT-4o. text: As joint audio-video generation models become more capable, they can gener- ate audio-visual scenes exhibiting three forms of complexity: multi-event com- position, multi-layer audio mixture, and asymmetric cross-modal relations. However, current evaluations largely reuse metrics from earlier simple and unidi- rectional tasks. They typically evaluate an audio-video clip as a whole and rely on simple predefined relations, making them unsuitable for these increasingly com- plex scenes. We propose an event-centric evaluation framework that disentan- gles audio and visual events at the event level, analyzes each event independently, cross-validates relations across modalities, and aggregates the judgments into a coarse-to-fine, three-level consistency metric. The metric assesses global nar- rative harmony, event-level temporal synchronization, and fine-grained attribute alignment, providing a general formulation for audio-video consistency evaluation across diverse generation settings and cross-modal relations. We instantiate the metric as AVC-Reward, a trainable audio-video reward model. To evaluate the agreement between automatic judgments and human perception across generation paradigms and relation complexities, we construct AVC-Benchmark, which is pri- marily built from diverse positive and negative samples generated by various types of audio-video generation models. AVC-Reward achieves state-of-the-art align- ment with human judgment among automatic methods, provides interpretable ra- tionales that localize failures, and improves the audio-video consistency of a joint generation model when used as an online reinforcement-learning signal. text: Audio-video generation has evolved from unidirectional driving toward joint generation with in- creasingly strong generative capabilities. Earlier audio-driven video generation (e.g., Wav2Lip (Pra- jwal et al., 2020)) and video-to-audio generation (e.g., HunyuanVideo-Foley (Shan et al., 2025)) were centered on more constrained consistency relations: the former mainly focused on lip syn- chronization (Chung & Zisserman, 2016), while the latter mainly focused on simple temporal align- ment (Iashin et al., 2024). In contrast, joint generation removes the constraint of a fixed modality, with recent models such as Veo 3 (Google DeepMind, 2025), MiniMax H3 (MiniMax, 2026) and Seedance 2.0 (Seedance et al., 2026) extending this paradigm to richer and more complex scenes. These richer audio-visual scenes exhibit three forms of complexity: multi-event composition, multi-layer audio mixture, and asymmetric cross-modal relations. First, a clip can contain mul- tiple events that together form a complete scene, with several events potentially occurring at the same time. Second, its audio track can mix physical scene sounds with post-produced audio such as voice-over and background music, which instead support the video’s narrative or atmosphere. Third, audio and visual events need not follow a simple one-to-one relation: valid audio events such as off-screen sounds may lack direct visible visual evidence. ∗Equal contribution. However, evaluation methodologies have not kept pace with this evolution: the richer audio-visual content produced by joint models has made consistency evaluation more demanding. Current eval- uations largely reuse metrics from earlier simple and unidirectional tasks, where one modality was fixed and only a limited relation such as lip–speech or sound–action timing needed to be checked; accordingly, they often evaluate an audio-video clip as a whole and rely on simple predefined re- lations such as semantic similarity or temporal synchronization. text: ImageBind-based metrics (Girdhar et al., 2023; Mao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025) encode the au- dio and video within a clip or temporal window into a shared embedding space and measure their overall similarity, which can remain high when dominant semantics match despite a local event inconsistency. Multi-layer audio mixture further complicates evaluation: metrics such as Synch- former (Iashin et al., 2024) predict an audio–video temporal offset from the mixed soundtrack with- out separating its layers. When physical sounds are mixed with voice-over or background music, sounds that should align with visible actions are evaluated together with audio that does not require such temporal correspondence, which can lead to an inaccurate consistency score. Complex cross- modal relations further challenge predefined matching rules; for example, AV-Align (Yariv et al., 2024) matches audio onsets with visual-motion peaks and may therefore penalize a valid off-screen sound that lacks direct visual evidence. Therefore, we need a more general audio-video consistency evaluator that can handle diverse event relations across different generation paradigms, particularly in modern joint generation. text: evaluation model can serve as a training signal to directly improve generation models, closing the loop of “generate–evaluate–optimize.” To meet this need, we propose an event-centric evaluation perspective, in which the audio and video of each generated clip are first disentangled into individual events and analyzed independently before the final judgments. Under this perspective, we first separately extract and analyze audio and visual events, then cross-validate their relations across modalities, and finally aggregate the resulting judgments from coarse to fine. We formulate this final consistency assessment as a coarse- to-fine, three-level consistency metric. Global narrative harmony assesses whether the audio and video form a coherent scene and narrative. Event-level temporal synchronization establishes event relations, checks event presence and temporal alignment, and marks audio events without visual evidence. Fine-grained attribute alignment verifies the attributes of matched events and assesses whether marked audio is plausibly an off-screen sound, voice-over, or background music. By disentangling individual events, distinguishing different audio sources, and explicitly validating their cross-modal relations, this metric can separately assess overlapping events, handle audio layers with different roles, and accommodate valid asymmetric relations, as illustrated in Fig. 1. text: Joint Audio-Video Generation. Audio-video generation first developed through audio-driven video generation (Prajwal et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025) and video-to-audio generation (Zhang et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2025; Shan et al., 2025), where one modality is fixed. Joint audio-video generation (JAVG) removes this constraint: early works either learned a joint generative process (Ruan et al., 2023) or coordinated pretrained unimodal gener- ators (Xing et al., 2024). Native JAVG then advanced toward open-ended generation, finer syn- chronization, and richer audio content, as represented by JavisDiT (Liu et al., 2025), Ovi (Low et al., 2025), UniVerse-1 (Wang et al., 2025), and LTX-2 (HaCohen et al., 2026). JAVG has fur- ther reached industrial-scale deployment through systems such as Veo 3 (Google DeepMind, 2025), Seedance 2.0 (Seedance et al., 2026), and MiniMax H3 (MiniMax, 2026), enabling the generation of more complex audio-visual scenes with multi-event composition, multi-layer audio mixtures, and complex cross-modal relations, which makes audio-video consistency evaluation more demanding. Audio-Video Consistency Metrics. Existing audio-video consistency metrics and their limita- tions under modern joint audio-video generation are summarized in Table 1. Early metrics target 3
title: arXiv preprint

text: arXiv preprint specific consistency relations: SyncNet measures lip–speech synchrony, AV-Align matches motion and audio peaks, and DeSync predicts temporal offsets. ImageBind, AVHScore, and JavisScore measure cross-modal similarity at clip, frame–audio, or temporal-window granularity. PEAVS and AVBench learn human preferences from manually created errors. AGAV-Rater and Beyond Time Shifts further learn from real V2A outputs. Recent analysis further shows that existing metrics fo- cus on different aspects of consistency and exhibit low cross-metric agreement (Sharma & Tapadiya, 2026). Together, these methods remain tied to specific tasks or relations, making them insufficient for general audio-video consistency evaluation under the complexity of modern joint generation. 3 METHOD 3.1 EVALUATION OVERVIEW The complexities exposed by modern joint generation introduce three requirements for evaluation. Multi-event composition calls for event disentanglement, so that individual and overlapping events can be examined separately. Multi-layer audio mixture requires the evaluator to distinguish the roles of different audio events, as different audio sources can have different relations to the video. Asymmetric and diverse cross-modal relations further require establishing and verifying event- dependent cross-modal relations for individual events. Meeting these requirements requires an evaluator capable of jointly understanding audio-visual con- tent and reasoning over different events and their relations. MLLMs with audio-video understanding capabilities can jointly perform these tasks within a unified reasoning process, making them a suit- able foundation for

text: requires an evaluator capable of jointly understanding audio-visual con- tent and reasoning over different events and their relations. MLLMs with audio-video understanding capabilities can jointly perform these tasks within a unified reasoning process, making them a suit- able foundation for audio-video consistency evaluation. Moreover, for more general and accurate evaluation, we argue that the judgments of the MLLM should be organized into an event-centric metric with three coarse-to-fine levels. Global narrative harmony first checks whether the audio and video are coherent across the full clip. Event-level temporal synchronization and fine-grained attribute alignment then move to the event level. They respectively assess the temporal alignment of each event and the consistency of audio-visual attributes within that event. Through event-level evaluation and detailed, independent verification of each event’s cross-modal relations, the metric addresses the higher evaluation demands above. With this evaluation design in place, Section 3.2 defines the event-centric protocol and three-level metric, Section 3.3 constructs the corresponding training supervision, and Section 3.4 learns AVC- Reward through SFT and GRPO. 3.2 EVENT-CENTRIC EVALUATION PROTOCOL Following Section 3.1, we define three-level consistency scores. Global narrative harmony (Smac) measures agreement in narrative content, entities, environment, and affective tone. Event-level temporal synchronization (Stemp) measures event presence and the alignment of onset, offset, and duration under the appropriate cross-modal relations. Fine-grained attribute alignment (Sattr) measures attribute

We further add a small number of manually edited global-narrative negatives in GRPO to balance the distribution of failure cases. The overall pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 2. We provide two complementary forms of supervision: structured reasoning data teaches the model to follow the event-centric evaluation protocol for SFT, while human-calibrated data aligns its scores with human judgment for GRPO. The complete data sources and calibration details are provided in App. B. Structured reasoning data. Following the five-stage protocol in Section 3.2, the annotation orga- nizes modality-specific event analysis, bidirectional cross-modal verification, and the final coarse- to-fine judgment into a structured reasoning process. We construct the annotations using Gemini 2.5 Pro (Comanici et al., 2025) and Qwen3-VL-Max (Bai et al., 2025) as complementary annotators, with a silence detector providing

We construct the annotations using Gemini 2.5 Pro (Comanici et al., 2025) and Qwen3-VL-Max (Bai et al., 2025) as complementary annotators, with a silence detector providing auxiliary temporal cues. Each stage produces one structured record. The five structured records are concatenated and rewritten by Qwen3-235B (Yang et al., 2025a) into a single SFT target, ⟨think⟩C ⟨/think⟩{Smac, Stemp, Sattr, κ}, where C preserves the five-stage reasoning order. After filtering, approximately 8k samples are retained for SFT. These samples provide explicit supervision for learning event-specific evidence and event-dependent cross-modal relations under the three-level metric. Complete reward-model prompts and input–output examples are provided in App. E. Human annotation and score calibration. The structured annotation pipeline provides scalable reasoning supervision, but its scores are limited by the perceptual capability of the annotation models and can accumulate errors across stages. We therefore introduce human annotations to calibrate the scores toward human judgment. We design a 39-label taxonomy over the three consistency dimensions, covering normal states and common failure types. Annotators assign applicable labels to each sample, grounding their judg- ments in explicit consistency evidence. We further construct a multi-annotator subset with both label 5

Based on this subset, Qwen3-235B (Yang et al., 2025a) maps each human-verified label record to (Smac, Stemp, Sattr) and a diagnostic con- clusion κ. This calibration produces approximately 10k human-calibrated samples for GRPO. 3.4 AVC-REWARD TRAINING We initialize AVC-Reward from Qwen3-Omni-Thinking (Xu et al., 2025) and train it in two stages. SFT cold start. We fully fine-tune the model on the approximately 8k structured reasoning sam- ples from Section 3.3, using the complete five-stage reasoning and assessment as the training target. GRPO for human alignment. After SFT cold start, we apply GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) on a 10k rollout set constructed from the human-calibrated data. The reward jointly preserves the required evaluation structure and aligns the three consistency scores with human judgment. Specifically, a structure reward rstruct enforces the five-stage reasoning and assessment format. A score distillation reward rdistill = 1 3 P2 i=0 exp[−wi(predi −refi)2] measures agreement with the human-calibrated scores, and the total reward is rtotal = (2rstruct + rdistill)/3, where i = 0, 1, 2 corresponds to (Smac, Stemp, Sattr). 4 BENCHMARK Motivation. Benchmark composition and evaluation target. AVC-Benchmark is the first benchmark, to our knowledge, that primarily uses various types of model-generated audio-video data to evaluate the alignment between automatic consistency metrics and human perception. It contains samples from A2V, V2A, and JAVG models, together with a small set of controlled negatives added to balance the failure-case distribution and broaden the coverage of audio-video inconsistencies. Each sample is independently annotated by three annotators, providing human ground-truth scores on the three consistency dimensions defined in Section 3.2. We evaluate each metric against these human scores using pairwise accuracy under different score-difference thresholds, Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (SRCC), and Pearson’s linear correlation coefficient (PLCC). Statistics. Detailed benchmark statistics are provided in App. D.2. In general, most samples retain high global scene and narrative consistency, providing a meaningful basis for evaluating finer tem- poral and attribute-level relations; accordingly, the latter two dimensions span much broader score ranges. The annotated failures further cover global narrative, affective, and environmental conflicts; temporal errors across physical events, speech, and music; and fine-grained mismatches in material, morphology, and causal response. 5 EXPERIMENTS We evaluate AVC-Reward as both an automatic evaluator and a training reward for

text: We study general audio-video consistency evaluation under the challenges of multi-event compo- sition, multi-layer audio mixture, and asymmetric cross-modal relations. A FORMAL METRIC DEFINITIONS This section gives the complete mathematical form of the event-centric protocol in Section 3. The protocol evaluates an observed audio–video pair from coarse to fine: it first compares the two global descriptions, then verifies event existence and timing, and finally checks event attributes. The three scores remain separate throughout the evaluation; when one scalar is needed, we use their arithmetic mean. The protocol evaluates the observed pair directly, so the provenance of either stream is irrelevant. The first two stages convert the streams into HA = (GA, EA), HV = (GV , EV ), (5) where GA and GV are full-clip global scene and narrative descriptions, and EA and EV are event sets. text: arXiv preprint A.2 FIVE-STAGE EVALUATION PROTOCOL The five stages are formal interfaces between the evidence records and the final score. Stages 1 and 2 analyze one modality at a time: HA = FA(A), HV = FV (V). (9) Stage 1 identifies the acoustic layers, global audio context, speaker or music information, and time- localized audio events. Stage 2 identifies the visual scene, people and actions, and the time-localized visual events that can produce sound. Stages 3 and 4 verify the two directions separately: RA→V = FA→V (HA, V), RV →A = FV →A(HV , A). (10) For every audio event, Stage 3 checks whether the video supplies the required evidence in the event’s time interval. For a short event this is a direct check of the relevant action. For a continuous event it checks the minimal visible evidence throughout the interval. For every visual event, Stage 4 first decides whether the action should produce sound. Missing audio for a naturally silent action is reasonable silence; missing audio for a sound-producing action is an existence failure. Events that pass the existence judgment proceed to physical or attribute checks. The output of either verification stage is a relation record rk = (eA i , eV j , ρk), eA i ∈EA ∪{∅}, eV j ∈EV ∪{∅}, (11) where ρk specifies the relation

The comparison covers narrative content and entity identity, scene or environment, and affective tone. A persistent conflict in any of these aspects lowers the score even when individ- ual events happen to overlap in time. (15) For an on-screen physical event, bidirectional evidence means both directions are checked: a visible sound-producing action must have corresponding audio, and an audible on-screen source must have corresponding visual evidence. Narrative events use a meaningful rhythmic or temporal relation; reasonable-silence records receive full temporal evidence. The final LLM judge reads all temporal evidence in R and outputs Stemp = Φtemp(R) ∈[0, 1]. (16) The temporal score covers event existence and timing. Material, timbre, mouth shape, finger motion, and reaction plausibility belong to the attribute evidence. 15

text: arXiv preprint Fine-grained attribute alignment. Attribute evaluation proceeds whenever temporal correspon- dence establishes a tentative audio–visual event pair within an acceptable tolerance. The verifier records applicable physical, morphological, and causal-response evidence for each relation. Physi- cal evidence covers material or timbre, energy or loudness, and spatial or distance cues. Morpholog- ical evidence covers fine visual states such as mouth shape, finger motion, and the visible action that produces the sound. Causal-response evidence covers source localization, emotional response, and response magnitude for off-screen or narrative evidence. The final LLM judge reads all applicable attribute evidence in R and outputs Sattr = Φattr(R) ∈[0, 1]. (17) A.4 OVERALL AVC SCORE The final judgment follows the order Smac →Stemp →Sattr. The three outputs remain separate diagnostic dimensions. When an overall score is required, we use the arithmetic mean SAVC = 1 3 (Smac + Stemp + Sattr) . (18) The overall score is the unweighted arithmetic mean of the three separately reported dimensions. text: for structured-reasoning SFT and the other for human calibration. Table 5 summarizes the sources and statistics of the training data used for SFT and GRPO. Throughout this process, a wide array of multimodal models (Xu et al., 2025; Low et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; 2026b; Tu et al., 2024; 2025a;b; Shan et al., 2025; Girdhar et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025) is leveraged to curate more comprehensive data along with precise annotations. SFT source pool. We first collect ground-truth audio-video clips from two categories: general scenes and human-centered scenes. We use Qwen3-Omni (Xu et al., 2025) to filter the clips for basic audio-video quality and clarity, salient event and temporal relations, and informative macro-semantic content, retaining 2.5k general clips and 1k human-centered clips. The four filtering questions are provided in our project’s GitHub repository. Qwen3-Omni then generates audio and video captions for the retained clips, which are used to construct samples under different generation paradigms. text: Audio and video are first analyzed independently, followed by bidirectional event verification and final aggregation into three consistency scores and a diagnostic conclusion. Stages 3 and 4 then perform bidirectional event verification. For each audio event, audio-to-video verification searches its temporal window for supporting visual evidence and, when applicable, ex- amines temporal alignment and fine-grained physical attributes. The absence of a visible source is retained as evidence rather than directly treated as an inconsistency, allowing later reasoning over off-screen audio and other asymmetric relations. Conversely, video-to-audio verification first deter- mines whether a visual event should naturally produce sound. Naturally silent actions are preserved as reasonable silence, while sound-producing actions are checked for corresponding acoustic evi- dence, temporal alignment, and physical compatibility. Stage 5 aggregates the modality-specific analyses and the two directional verification records. The evaluator also re-examines the original audio-video clip instead of relying only on intermediate an- notations. It then produces scores for global narrative harmony, event-level temporal synchroniza- tion, and fine-grained attribute alignment, together with a diagnostic conclusion that summarizes the main consistent or inconsistent events. Harness-based process control. The three evaluation levels require several non-trivial judgments, so we do not rely on a single unconstrained model response to construct the supervision. Instead, the annotation harness introduces explicit process controls around the underlying expert models. First, audio and
title: arXiv preprint

text: control. The three evaluation levels require several non-trivial judgments, so we do not rely on a single unconstrained model response to construct the supervision. Instead, the annotation harness introduces explicit process controls around the underlying expert models. First, audio and video are analyzed independently, preventing early cross-modal information from directly biasing event discovery. Second, each detected event is converted into explicit timestamps and evi- dence records, and later checks operate on these records rather than restarting from an unconstrained global judgment. Third, verification is conditional: existence is checked before temporal or attribute compatibility, and inapplicable cases such as reasonable silence are explicitly bypassed. Fourth, the same relation is checked in both audio-to-video and video-to-audio directions, providing a cross- check for missing and hallucinated events. Finally, the aggregation stage receives all intermediate evidence but also re-examines the original audio-video clip, forming a final feedback check against errors propagated from earlier stages. These controlled verification records are then transferred to AVC-Reward through both training stages. During SFT, the complete five-stage annotation trajectory, including single-modal analyses, bidirectional event verification, three scores, and the diagnostic conclusion, is used as the full super- vision target. The model is therefore trained to reproduce the same staged verification process rather than learning only a direct mapping from the input clip to final scores. During GRPO, the structure
title: arXiv preprint

text: diagnostic conclusion, is used as the full super- vision target. The model is therefore trained to reproduce the same staged verification process rather than learning only a direct mapping from the input clip to final scores. During GRPO, the structure reward explicitly rewards the presence of all five reasoning stages, while score distillation aligns the resulting judgments with human-calibrated scores. Together, the two stages preserve the verifica- tion procedure established by the annotation harness while transferring it from the cascaded expert pipeline into a single reward model. Whether this learned procedure leads to correct judgments is further evaluated through human alignment, training ablations, and qualitative cases. 18

text: arXiv preprint B.3 HUMAN ANNOTATION AND SCORE CALIBRATION In human annotation, we found that score-only judgments showed noticeable subjective variation and made disagreements difficult to verify. We therefore design a 39-label taxonomy that asks anno- tators to record explicit consistency states and failure types before score calibration, reducing uncon- strained subjectivity while preserving observable information about event presence, timing, audio roles, and cross-modal relations. The taxonomy follows the same three dimensions as AVC-Reward: global labels cover narrative, affective, and environmental consistency; temporal labels separately describe physical interactions, speaker events, and music/rhythmic events, including missing, hallu- cinated, off-screen, and narrative-layer cases; fine-grained labels describe material, intensity, spatial, motion, and causal-response attributes. Table 7 summarizes the complete annotation space. Annotation protocol. Annotators judge the three dimensions independently. Within each dimen- sion, all applicable failure labels can be selected, allowing a clip to contain multiple inconsistency types or multiple affected events. For temporal synchronization, annotators additionally distinguish physical-layer on-screen events, plausible off-screen events, and narrative-layer audio such as voice- over and background music. A severe global conflict can be marked as unjudgeable for a later event- level category when the corresponding relation cannot be meaningfully assessed, but this does not otherwise propagate the global judgment to the other dimensions. For each annotated sample, three annotators independently provide the dimension labels. The train- ing

For each annotated sample, three annotators independently provide the dimension labels. The train- ing and test sets are strictly disjoint. The held-out test set is additionally assigned to annotators who do not participate in labeling the training set, preventing overlap in both samples and annotators between model training and final human evaluation. Label-to-score calibration and score rewriting validation. Human annotations provide detailed categorical supervision, while AVC-Reward requires continuous targets for the three dimensions. Directly collecting continuous scores for all training samples introduces annotation subjectivity and variance, making large-scale score supervision difficult to verify and maintain consistently. There- fore, we investigate whether human-verified labels can serve as an intermediate representation for recovering continuous scores. We first study the relationship between human-verified labels and continuous scores on AVC- Benchmark, where both label annotations and human score annotations are available. We analyze whether label configurations consistently correspond to similar human scores. Pairs sharing the same human-verified label configuration have an average absolute score difference of only 0.0321 (median 0.0111), compared with 0.2002 (median 0.1000) for pairs with different configurations (Table 8). This indicates that label configurations strongly constrain human scores and motivates label-to-score calibration for continuous reward

We keep the overall training framework unchanged and replace its original audio-video reward DeSync (Iashin et al., 2024) with AVC-Reward, using its overall score SAVC as the optimization signal, with reward-specific learning-rate and weight adjustments for comparable optimization strength. We first perform stratified sampling based on human label configurations to balance the coverage of major consistency and failure patterns, including global narrative conflicts, temporal offsets, missing or hallucinated audio, and fine-grained attribute mismatches. We then use ImageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023) to extract audio and video representations and

We then use ImageBind (Girdhar et al., 2023) to extract audio and video representations and cluster their joint embeddings, from which we sample across clusters to reduce semantic redundancy. Finally, we add explicitly constructed negative samples to strengthen the coverage of controlled failure cases that are less frequent in naturally generated data. The resulting benchmark contains 706 samples across different generation paradigms and data sources: 172 ground truth samples, 243 JAVG samples, 100 A2V samples, 72 V2A samples, and 119 samples from the explicit-negative construction set. Among them, 10 contain salient emotion or global narrative cues, 20 contain clear temporal relations, and 20 contain salient audio attributes. Instead of directly measuring the correlation between predicted dimension scores and human di- mension scores, we formulate this analysis as a dimension-specific issue classification task. Human dimension scores are mainly designed for overall perceptual evaluation, and the three dimensions may have different levels of granularity. Specifically, we construct dimension-specific binary targets from human-annotated issue labels in the benchmark, where samples are separated into positive and negative cases according to whether they contain the corresponding types of consistency issues. text: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capa- bilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self- orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective out- comes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behav- ior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post- training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alter- native coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robust- ness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT. Learning Learning Agent Weight Updates

text: Building general intelligence has long been a central ambition of AI research. But where does intelligence reside? A prevailing view in modern AI is model-centric: intelligence is contained in the parameters of a model, and progress comes from increasing model size or improving those parameters through training. In this paper, we explore a different possibility. Intelligent behavior can also emerge from interactions among many simpler agents, giving rise to collective capabilities 1 arXiv:2610.22322v1 [cs.MA] 15 Oct 2026
title: Preprint

text: Preprint that no single agent possesses. This perspective echoes Minsky’s Society of Mind (Minsky, 1986), which explains intelligence through the organization and interaction of many individually limited components. Large language model (LLM) agents now exhibit strong individual reasoning capabilities, yet agent swarms remain limited in their ability to organize their own participation and actions toward a shared objective. Existing multi-agent systems typically place models within predefined interaction struc- tures: a manager delegates to workers, a verifier checks a generator, or agents communicate accord- ing to a prescribed workflow (Hong et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). Even when the participating agents are trainable, the orchestration policy that determines which agent acts next often remains fixed throughout training (Feng et al., 2026). This separation overlooks the coupling between individual capabilities and swarm orchestration. Which agent acts in a particular state shapes not only the swarm’s trajectory, but also which agents receive experience and learning signals. As agents improve, effective patterns of participation can change in turn. An agent that should act early in training may become unnecessary later; an action that was previously unhelpful may become valuable after downstream agents improve. Training individual agents under fixed orchestration therefore optimizes only one side of this coupled process. We instead ask: Can decentralized agent swarms
title: Preprint

text: training may become unnecessary later; an action that was previously unhelpful may become valuable after downstream agents improve. Training individual agents under fixed orchestration therefore optimizes only one side of this coupled process. We instead ask: Can decentralized agent swarms jointly learn to act and self-orchestrate from experience? Learning self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms poses a joint orchestration and credit- assignment problem. At each turn, agents must determine who should act. When task feedback becomes available, the swarm must also determine how to train the agents whose actions shaped the trajectory. These decisions are coupled: participation determines which agents acquire experience, while learning changes which and how agents should participate in the future. We therefore introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework that enables decentralized agent swarms to learn both how to act and how to self-organize their participation. Following Qi et al. (2026), agents compete for opportunities to act through bids that reflect their willingness to participate in the current decision. An economic incentive structure connects these participation decisions with credit assignment, using collective outcomes to improve both action and bidding behavior. As agents become more capable, the swarm learns when to rely on each member, allowing individual capabilities and self-orchestration to evolve together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research.

An episode presents a task x and unfolds over turns t = 1, . . . , T, with one agent acting at each turn and a verifier assigning a task reward R. To construct the alternative branch, we restore the environment and agent states at the contested turn in a replica and resample the selected agent’s bid up to three times until it falls below the runner-up’s bid, so that the runner- up acts instead. Each setting uses three agents with complementary roles. Benchmarks and Models. (1) Embodied crafting: three Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct agents (Logger, Miner, and Smith) specialize in gathering wood, mining resources, and crafting. Starting from an empty inventory in Minecraft MineStudio (Cai et al., 2025), they must progress through the crafting chain to obtain an iron pickaxe. Agents receive RGB observations and textual state information, including inventory and recent interaction history. The selected agent issues a language instruction to a frozen STEVE-1 controller (Lifshitz et al., 2023), which executes it for 40 game frames. (2) Robot navigation: three NaVILA-8B agents (Cheng et al., 2025) perform continuous vision-and- language navigation on VLN-CE R2R in Habitat (Krantz et al., 2020; Anderson et al., 2018; Savva et al., 2019). Given a route instruction and an eight-frame window of egocentric observations, the agents coordinate through partitioned action spaces: Turner controls rotations, Mover controls forward movement, and Stopper decides when to stop. text: LLM-based multi-agent systems. LLM-based multi-agent systems combine role specialization, communication, and memory to support collective behavior. Generative Agents studies emergent social interactions among agents with memory and reflection (Park et al., 2023), while CAMEL ex- plores cooperation through role-playing (Li et al., 2023). MetaGPT and ChatDev organize software development through structured workflows and specialized roles (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024); AutoGen and AgentVerse provide frameworks for programmable conversations and collab- orative agent teams (Wu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Multiagent debate improves reasoning through iterative exchange and revision of proposed answers (Du et al., 2024). Beyond manu- ally specified workflows, GPTSwarm optimizes graph connectivity (Zhuge et al., 2024), AgentNet adapts decentralized routing through experience and evolving connections (Yang et al., 2025), and Graph-of-Agents selects agents and refines responses through graph-based collaboration (Yun et al., 2026). However, these systems generally adapt interactions at inference time. MPT learns policies through weight updates, allowing agent capabilities and self-orchestration to improve together. Multi-agent reinforcement learning. Learning decentralized policies from collective feedback is a central problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning. MADDPG and MAPPO use centralized training with decentralized execution (Lowe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2022), while VDN and QMIX factorize team value functions into agent-level utilities (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2020). COMA addresses credit assignment

text: MADDPG and MAPPO use centralized training with decentralized execution (Lowe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2022), while VDN and QMIX factorize team value functions into agent-level utilities (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2020). COMA addresses credit assignment through a counterfactual baseline that marginalizes one agent’s action while holding the others fixed (Foerster et al., 2018). Coordination is also learned explicitly: RIAL and DIAL learn communication protocols (Foerster et al., 2016), CommNet jointly learns con- tinuous communication and control (Sukhbaatar et al., 2016), and IC3Net learns when agents should communicate (Singh et al., 2019). Recent work extends multi-agent training to LLMs: Multiagent Finetuning updates specialized models using their own interaction data (Subramaniam et al., 2025); Dr. MAS stabilizes reinforcement learning through agent-wise advantage normalization (Feng et al., 2026); and CoLLM studies centralized and decentralized critics for training decentralized LLM col- laborators (Liu et al., 2026). However, these methods do not connect the choice of the next agent with how downstream reward is distributed across agents. MPT couples turn allocation and credit assignment through learned bids, using task feedback to jointly improve participation and policies. Economics in agents. text: to jointly improve participation and policies. Economics in agents. Economic coordination offers a longstanding perspective on distributed intelligence. Hayek emphasizes how prices communicate dispersed knowledge (Hayek, 1945), while Minsky describes intelligence as arising from interactions among individually limited com- ponents (Minsky, 1986). The Contract Net Protocol allocates tasks through negotiation (Smith, 1988), and market-oriented programming uses markets for decentralized resource allocation (Well- man, 1993). Economic mechanisms also connect participation to learning: Holland’s bucket brigade transfers credit along chains of active rules (Holland, 1995), and Baum’s Hayek Machine develops economic credit assignment (Baum, 1996; 1999). More recently, Economy of Minds uses auctions to coordinate LLM agents and guide the evolution of prompts and population with frozen model weights (Qi et al., 2026). SALE selects among agents’ proposed strategies using cost–value scoring and shared auction memory (Alazraki et al., 2026). However, recent LLM-based economic systems primarily use feedback to evolve prompts while keeping weights frozen. MPT uses feedback to train action and bidding policies, enabling agents to learn how to act and when to participate. 5
title: Preprint

text: We introduced MPT, a framework for jointly learning individual action policies and self- orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Learned bids connect participation decisions with local credit assignment, allowing agents to improve both how they act and when they participate without a central coordinating agent. Our experiments show benefits over monolithic post-training and other coordination strategies, while ablations demonstrate the value of learning both bidding and action policies and using learned bids for credit assignment. Trained swarms also adapt faster to related objectives, benefit from larger populations at inference time, and better tolerate agent unavailabil- ity as the population grows. These findings support treating self-orchestration as a learnable and reusable component of collective intelligence, opening a path toward decentralized agent swarms whose capabilities and organization improve together through experience. 9

The simulator is Minecraft through MineStudio (Cai et al., 2025). Each world is identified by a seed. All post-training runs draw from 1614 seeds. B.1.2 REWARD The environment pays a staged, event-based reward defined over twelve tech-tree events E, each with a per-occurrence reward re and a per-episode cap ce on how many occurrences are paid: mine a log (re=1, ce=4), craft planks (2, 3), craft a crafting table (3, 1), open the crafting table (3, 1), craft a stick (4, 1), craft a wooden pickaxe (8, 1), mine cobblestone (4, 3), craft a stone pickaxe (20, 1), craft a furnace (8, 1), mine iron ore (4, 3), smelt an iron ingot (10, 3), and craft the iron pickaxe (30, 1). Let ne(t) be the number of times event e has occurred in the episode up to and including decision t. B.1.3 EPISODE, OBSERVATION AND DECISION An episode contains 120 decisions. At each decision the policy receives a 128 × 128 RGB screen- shot and a text description: the task, crafting rules, current decision step, cumulative events, world status, a rolling history of the last six steps, the live inventory, and the outcome of the previ- ous instruction. The policy answers with reasoning followed by a natural-language instruction, <think>...</think><action>...</action>. Instructions are executed by a frozen text-conditioned low-level controller, STEVE-1 (Lifshitz et al., 2023), for 40 game frames. B.1.4 AGENT DESIGN The population consists of three agents, LOGGER, MINER and SMITH, each a separate full fine-tune of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025). The monolithic agent is the same base model fine-tuned on instructions spanning all three roles. Below, we present the example prompt for the monolithic agent and the example bidding and action prompts for each agent in the society. Single Agent. (2) Bidding updates require counterfactual rollouts from the same environment and agent states. Therefore, extending this approach to irreversible real-world interactions remains an open problem. (3) Despite our efforts to broaden the experimental evaluation, computational constraints limit the scale of our study. We have not explored training swarms composed of multiple models with more than 10B parameters each, or jointly training substantially larger agent populations. 37

text: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To opti- mize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objec- tive. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea’s qual- ity is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diver- sity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free bench- mark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8’s and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the

text: The first step of any research cycle is generating ideas worth testing, before an experiment can tell you which one was right. Current work with Large Language Models (LLMs) on idea generation has focused on one of two things: producing a single idea and scoring it against an existing, held-out idea (He-Yueya et al., 2026), or building end-to-end systems that carry one idea through execution and judge whether that execution succeeded (Kirgis et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2026; Falck et al., 2026; Garikaparthi et al., 2026; Si et al., 2026). Either way, an idea is generated and judged on its own, never alongside other candidates it could be weighed against. Looking at how humans do research, a researcher facing a body of literature brainstorms several directions off the same shared context, and then selects among them using some signal (Platt, 1964; Klahr & Dunbar, 1988), rather than just committing to one idea. We draw a connection between ideation and creative problem solving. The brainstorm-then-select process is how creative think- ing/problem solving can also be formalized, divergent thinking explores a space broadly for many candidates, and convergent thinking narrows it through selection (Boden, 2004; Guilford, 1967). The way current LLMs are used for ideation can look different. Because each idea is generated and judged on its own, multiple candidates come

Because each idea is generated and judged on its own, multiple candidates come from repeated independent sampling, with no shared context to explore deliberately and no pool to converge over. Any diversity among them is incidental rather than designed (Puri et al., 2026; Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026). Work on autonomous research agents has also flagged diversity as a shortcoming (Liu et al., 2026; Garikaparthi et al., 2026). text: and diversity into one set-level training signal by adapting the Creative Utility formulation (Wadhwa et al., 2026) where each idea earns credit for its own quality and for its distance from the ideas emitted before it, so a redundant idea earns little no matter how well-written it is (as illustrated in Figure 1). To achieve this, we train an ideation model (Qwen3-8B (Team, 2025)) in two steps. We first do a su- pervised fine-tuning step to initialize the policy on well-formed idea sets, followed by GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) against a set-level objective (adapted from the creative utility formulation). We then report this utility measure on a contamination-free test set that we put together. We also look at two existing benchmarks, GiantsBench (He-Yueya et al., 2026) and IdeaSeed (Chen et al., 2026). Our tested baselines include the untrained base model and its SFT checkpoint, strong closed-source agents, GIANTS (He-Yueya et al., 2026), and DARLING (Li et al., 2025), an alternative quality- diversity objective that we retrain in our setting. We show that our 8B trained model achieves the highest creative utility on our test set, outperform- ing strong closed-source agents and competing quality-diversity objectives such as DARLING. A small pilot human study with four expert annotators finds that our sets are comparable to Claude Opus 4.8’s in the number of promising ideas, while containing more mutually distinct ones. Finally, when we execute each set of ideas in a fixed sandbox with a coding agent, our model is compa- rable to Claude Opus 4.8 on success@k, showing that we are able to increase diversity without compromising important aspects of ideation like executability. Contributions Our contributions are (1) a set-level RL objective for training that balances quality and diversity; (2) an instantiation of this objective for document-grounded ideation; and (3) an 8B trained ideation model that outperforms strong closed-source agents and models trained on compet- ing objectives on creative utility, and whose ideas are comparably promising in a small pilot human and execution study. 2 TRAINING WITH A SET-LEVEL REWARD 2.1

text: We start by describing the standard reinforcement learning setting for language models we build on. A policy parameterized as an LM πθ maps a prompt x to a distribution over textual outputs y. Given a reward function R(x, y) ∈R, training aims to maximize expected reward: max θ Ex∼D, y∼πθ(·|x)  R(x, y)  . (1) 2

We optimize Equation 1 with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024): for each x, we sample G rollouts {y1, . . . , yG} ∼πθ(· | x), score each with R(x, yg), and update the policy using each rollout’s advantage relative to the group’s mean reward, with no learned critic. 2.2 SET-LEVEL OBJECTIVE In our setting, each prompt x is answered by a set of K outputs U = {u1, . . . , uK} written in a single generation, after a shared reasoning prefix. This set is the rollout y in Eq. 1, so GRPO scores it with one scalar and computes one advantage per set. All K outputs therefore share that single credit signal. Our goal is a set that is high-quality and whose outputs are mutually distinct. Then we train the model using a set-level objective using the definition below: Rset(x, U) = K X i=1 q(ui) · min j<i d(ui, uj), min j<i d(ui, uj) := 1 if i = 1 (2) For each item in the generation, we multiply its quality by how far it is from its nearest predecessor and aggregate over the set to get the reward. A redundant but high quality item earns almost nothing (Fig 1). The objective has two components: a quality function q(ui)

text: its quality by how far it is from its nearest predecessor and aggregate over the set to get the reward. A redundant but high quality item earns almost nothing (Fig 1). The objective has two components: a quality function q(ui) ∈[0, 1] that scores an output for the prompt, and a distance d(·, ·) ∈[0, 1] between two outputs. Any task with a quality signal and a notion of diversity fits, such as instruction following, creative writing, or ideation; we instantiate both for document-grounded ideation in Section 3.1. Relation to Creative Utility. Eq. 2 is adapted from Creative Utility (CU) (Wadhwa et al., 2026), which scores a set of ideas by the quality each one adds beyond the ideas already selected. We make two design choices in adapting it to a training reward. First, CU applies a patience discount (γ) to later ideas; we drop it for training, so every idea in the set is weighted equally and a model cannot fall back on generating weak ideas later in the set. Second, CU takes the best ordering of the set; we instead use the order in which the model writes them. Our prompt asks the model to list ideas from most to least promising, and it lets the reward be computed directly from a single rollout. At evaluation we report

At evaluation we report CU as is (Section 4). Relation to multi-answer RL. Our proposed objective can be viewed as a generalized form of the set-level objective introduced by Puri et al. (2026). Their formulation however has no notion of distance and instead only checks for coverage against an established ground truth answer set. Their objective can be defined as a special case of Eq 2, by setting d(ui, uj) = 1 and q to a coverage metric. 3 DOCUMENT GROUNDED IDEATION As mentioned in Section 1, we study the task of document-grounded ideation i.e. given a body of related literature, an agent needs to generate a set of ideas worth pursuing next, and we evaluate the set of ideas for its quality and diversity. Task definition. An instance is a corpus of documents D = {d1, . . . , dn} (each a scientific paper, given as a summary). An agent must produce a set of K ideas U = {u1, . . . , uK}, where each idea ui is a structured idea card with four fields: a problem gap, a core
title: Preprint. Under Review.

text: scientific paper, given as a summary). An agent must produce a set of K ideas U = {u1, . . . , uK}, where each idea ui is a structured idea card with four fields: a problem gap, a core claim, a method, and an inspiration field that names the specific source documents the idea draws on and how. Why a set of K? We make the set the primary unit, generating all K ideas in one pass so each is written conditioned on those already emitted. The agent can actively avoid repeating itself, steering later ideas toward directions its earlier ones left uncovered, rather than relying on independent draws to spread apart by chance (Puri et al., 2026; Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). See Appendix A.1 for definitions of the idea card sub fields and examples of ideas. 3.1 REWARD INSTANTIATION We instantiate quality (q) and distance(d) in Equation 2 for document-grounded ideation as follows: 3
