text: Preprint. Under Review. Quality: A part of ideation is to come up with directions that are worth pursuing next, so we define quality as long-term scientific impact (Tong et al., 2026). While there are other properties of good ideas such as fluency or soundness, these are not sufficient to decide if the idea is worth pursuing next. We therefore treat soundness as a separate axis, which we only probe with a small execution check (Section 6.2), rather than the training target. We anchor long-term impact to the gold idea g, a reference idea whose value is already established, so the judgment reflects what the field found worth doing. Section 3.2 describes how we obtain g. We model impact as a pairwise judgment between the generated idea u and the gold idea g: q(u) = I(u, g) =    1 if u ≻g, 0.5 if u ∼g, 0 if g ≻u. (3) where I(u, g) is the pairwise impact judgment, and u ≻g means the judge deems u higher-impact than g, and u ∼g means it cannot separate them. Distance. To recruit users, we set a minimum criterion that they have a PhD in the field of NLP and at least four published academic papers in top-tier conferences. text: Quality and diversity in LLMs. A large body of work has quantified the quality-diversity trade- off in LLMs, across creative writing, open-ended generation, and idea generation (Zhang et al., 2025; Shypula et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Wadhwa et al., 2026; Padmakumar & He, 2024; Jiang et al., 2025). A common finding is that RL and preference tuning collapse the policy onto a few modes, trading diversity for quality (Kirk et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025). Training-time fixes reward diversity across independent rollouts of a prompt (Li et al., 2025), or, in preference optimization, select diverse preference pairs (Lanchantin et al., 2026). More recent work rewards a set of outputs directly, either to cover a verifiable answer set (Puri et al., 2026) or to trade off a fixed reward vector (Bahlous-Boldi et al., 2026). All of these need an answer set or a fixed reward space to define coverage. In open-ended ideation neither exists, since whether two ideas are distinct is itself a judgment made in the context of the others in the set. Our objective addresses this by scoring each idea against the ones already written in the same generation. Research ideation. Literature-grounded ideation systems generally start from a small seed and build ideas outward from it. SciMON (Wang et al., 2024) revises an idea until it

text: by scoring each idea against the ones already written in the same generation. Research ideation. Literature-grounded ideation systems generally start from a small seed and build ideas outward from it. SciMON (Wang et al., 2024) revises an idea until it is sufficiently novel relative to prior papers, ResearchAgent (Baek et al., 2025) refines a proposal through rounds of reviewer feedback, and Nova generates hundreds of candidates from a seed paper and clusters them to select a diverse final set (Hu et al., 2025). Revision, critique, and clustering are all ways to obtain diversity, but they act after generation on candidates written without regard to one another, and the generator is never trained to write ideas that differ from each other. On the other hand, GIANTS (He-Yueya et al., 2026) trains a model with RL to anticipate a downstream paper’s core insight from its parent papers, and Tong et al. (2026) train a judge and an ideator on community feedback such as citations, both rewarding one idea at a time. A separate line grounds ideation in execution, using the outcomes of implementing and running ideas as the reward. Si et al. (2026) find that reinforcement learning from execution signal suffers from mode collapse: the model raises its average reward by converging on a few simple ideas. Because each idea is rewarded

(2026) find that reinforcement learning from execution signal suffers from mode collapse: the model raises its average reward by converging on a few simple ideas. Because each idea is rewarded in isolation, nothing discourages repeating the same safe idea. We differ on both axes. Our input is a whole body of documents instead of a single seed, and the model writes a set of ideas in one generation, trained on a reward in which each idea is scored against the ones already written. We also use execution as an evaluation, checking whether sets of ideas succeed downstream (Section 6.2). 8

text: We present a set-level RL objective for document-grounded ideation for training to generate diverse, high quality ideas. A model is prompted/taught to generate K ideas in one rollout and each idea’s quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas before it. Our best 8B model (no think) achieves higher creative utility than strong closed-source models and competing quality-diversity objectives, while the think variant beats the closed-source models and is on par with DARLING. In small pilot human and execution studies its sets are comparable to Claude Opus 4.8’s, so we see no evidence that diversity costs quality. Future work includes grounding-aware rewards, diversity across a population, and reasoning traces designed for creative ideation. 9
title: Preprint. Under Review.

text: Preprint. Under Review. LIMITATIONS Our study currently focuses on scientific ideation based on context and parametric knowledge, in- stead of focusing on retrieval. This is partially because we are testing the set up of training with a new set style generation where the aim is to increase diversity while also improving the quality. In future work we aim to include retrieval in this ideation process. We also train on english only, natural language processing scientific papers. text: Preprint. Under Review. AI USE STATEMENT The training data for our proposed method was generated using AI. We used Claude Opus-4.8 for it. In addition, code written with generative AI was used to conduct and carry out the analyses here. However, the research hypotheses in this work and the design of the experiments were both human- originated. AI tools were used for assistance with revisions, but not for writing in a substantive way. The authors take responsibility for the final content of this work. A DATASET A.1 DATA FORMAT In this Section we explain different aspects of the data curation process, including document acqui- sition, formats etc. Idea Format Each idea the model generates is a JSON object in the four-field schema of Section 3. This includes: (problem gap, core claim, method, inspiration). The definitions of the four fields are given below (as per the inference prompt): • problem gap: The gap the idea addresses, drawn from across the source documents – an open question, tension, or unresolved difficulty that connects them and that none resolves on its own. State it as one clear gap, NOT as your specific solution to it. BEGIN this field with the single best-fitting OPPORTUNITY PATTERN label in square brackets (from the taxonomy below), then the prose gap (1 to 2 sentences). Pick the ONE

text: it as one clear gap, NOT as your specific solution to it. BEGIN this field with the single best-fitting OPPORTUNITY PATTERN label in square brackets (from the taxonomy below), then the prose gap (1 to 2 sentences). Pick the ONE dominant pattern even if several apply; if NONE genuinely fits, use “[Other]” rather than forcing a poor match. Example: “[Bridge Opportunity] Work on X and on Y each..but neither connects..”. • core claim: The couple of sentences the whole idea lives or dies on – “we claim that X.” It must be something that could turn out to be wrong: a definite, testable assertion / hypothesis / insight, not a topic or a direction. Do not just restate the gap, and do not describe what you would do about it. From these sentences alone a reader should know exactly what the idea is betting on (1-2 sentences). • method: At a high level, how the claim would be turned into research – the kind of move (combining ideas, extending to a new setting, deriving formally, building an artifact, etc.) and how it addresses the gap. A proposed approach, not a step-by-step protocol. Begins with one bracketed Method Paradigm label. • inspiration: Three to five sentences arguing how the idea arises FROM the source docu- ments – the relationship between them,

text: how it addresses the gap. A proposed approach, not a step-by-step protocol. Begins with one bracketed Method Paradigm label. • inspiration: Three to five sentences arguing how the idea arises FROM the source docu- ments – the relationship between them, not a per-document restatement. Must (1) name each cited source’s limitation and (2) justify why connecting them is a non-obvious leap. Refers to sources by their numbered ‘Document N’ label. problem gap and method are each required to open with one bracketed taxonomy label (an oppor- tunity pattern and a method paradigm, respectively) drawn from the fixed 7+7 taxonomy given in full in the ideation prompt (Chen et al., 2026) (Appendix G). We show the prompts along with examples. C.1 QUALITY We score the quality of an idea q(u) via a pairwise reward model that compares a generated idea against the gold idea (g) for the same source set and returns which one is likely to have higher scientific impact. The resulting win/loss is the impact term I(u) of Section 3.1. The judge is called with both orderings of the pair to cancel position bias (Zheng et al., 2023), and I(u) is the fraction of orderings won (∈{0, 0.5, 1}). Where if u wins in both orderings, we reward it 1, if u loses in both orderings we reward 0, and if u wins in one and loses in the other, we call it a tie and reward 0.5. The score we report is source-dependence. Would the idea collapse if the cited documents were removed? Why not reward grounding? We do not put grounding in the training reward, for two reasons. First, optimizing three objectives in one run proved unstable. In our initial runs, grounding en- tered the reward as a graded multiplier and later as a binary gate, and the policy gamed the judge’s category preferences (for example, the grounding-type distribution collapsed onto a single type). Second, grounding has no natural direction in which higher is always better. Our score measures how much an idea depends on its cited sources, so a highly grounded idea can be a simple, incremen- tal extension of them, while a less grounded one can be a promising departure that is only loosely motivated by the documents. We therefore instruct the model at the prompt level to name the sources each idea draws on (Appendix A.1), and track grounding separately as a diagnostic (Section 5). This is a

C.4 CREATIVE UTILITY CU orders a set greedily: the first idea u(1) is the one with the highest quality, and each later idea is the one that maximizes its marginal value mt = q(u(t)) · minj<t d(u(t), u(j)), with m1 = q(u(1)). With patience γ ∈(0, 1], CU is the patience-weighted sum of these marginals, maximized over orderings τ of the set, CU(U) = max τ |U| X i=1 γ i−1 q �uτ(i)  min j<i d �uτ(i), uτ(j)  , (10) where τ ranges over orderings of the set, q is quality, d is distance (with minj<1 d := 1), and γ ∈(0, 1] is a patience discount on later ideas. We use γ = 0.9, and divide by P i γi−1 so that scores lie in [0, 1] (the normalized CU we report).

Why greedy reporting is sufficient. Maximizing over orderings is combinatorial, so, following CREATE, we approximate it with the greedy (farthest-point) order: take the highest-quality idea first, then repeatedly take the idea with the largest marginal value q(u) minj∈picked d(u, uj). Because the greedy order is one particular ordering, its value is a lower bound on CU(U), so it can only understate a set’s CU. It also depends only on the set and not on the order in which a model happened to write its ideas, which is what we want when comparing models, especially since we have baselines where we sample from a model instead of generating a set. CU differs from the training reward Rset in three ways: (i) Rset takes the generation order instead of the best ordering; (ii) it applies no patience discount (γ = 1) and is unnormalized; and (iii) CU is computed with the evaluation judges rather than the training judges. text: Preprint. Under Review. Figure 7: Distribution of ‘opportunity’ and ‘method’ labels on the IdeaSeed benchmark, as generated by different models compared to the proposed model. We walk through one run in full. The idea is a diagnostic benchmark for memory-augmented LLMs, generated by our think model. Its core claim has two parts: the suite reveals which memory mecha- nisms genuinely store information, and it exposes a failure mode shared across many designs. The card is shown below. Idea Card for AutoResearch: Diagnostic Benchmark for Memory-Augmented LLMs Problem gap [Evidence Gap] The field of memory augmentation for LLMs is growing rapidly, but there is no standardized, systematic way to evaluate whether memory mechanisms actually store semantic information, support effective retrieval, or remain stable across models and tasks, so claims about a mechanism’s quality are largely unverified and the community lacks a shared benchmark for comparison. Core claim A diagnostic benchmark measuring whether memory representations preserve semantic content, support contrastive retrieval, are interpretable, and remain stable across a suite of existing memory mechanisms will reveal which mechanisms genuinely store information and expose a common failure mode shared across many proposed designs, enabling the field to audit and advance itself with measurable evidence rather than untested claims. Method [Empirical Mapping] Construct an open, modular diagnostic benchmark for memory-augmented LLMs, consisting of tasks that
title: Preprint. Under Review.

text: a common failure mode shared across many proposed designs, enabling the field to audit and advance itself with measurable evidence rather than untested claims. Method [Empirical Mapping] Construct an open, modular diagnostic benchmark for memory-augmented LLMs, consisting of tasks that probe: • content fidelity: do memory vectors encode task-relevant semantics? • contrastive retrieval quality: does retrieval match ground-truth memory? • interpretability: can the stored content be inspected? • stability: does memory survive parameter perturbation and cross-model transfer? Evaluate leading memory mechanisms (DPR-style dense retrievers, SBERT-style bi-encoders, latent memory, compressed soft-prompt memory, retraining-free long-term memory) on this benchmark and release it as a public tool. Map which mechanisms succeed on which subtasks and quantify the gap between them, turning anecdotal claims into comparable, reproducible evidence. Our coding agent comes up with the following proof of concept. The agent sharpens the claim’s four named properties (content fidelity, contrastive retrieval, interpretability, stability) into metrics, and chooses seven CPU-runnable mechanisms from the families named in the method, plus two null controls. It supplies the datasets (HotpotQA and NQ-Swap) and the thresholds. Its first plan is: PoC Design Data (both real) • HotpotQA (distractor) -- hotpotqa/hotpot qa: each example gives a question and 10 paragraphs (2 gold, 8 topically related distractors), forming a hard-negative memory pool. Target ∼300 questions / ∼3000 paragraphs, subsampled to fit

Decision rules • Discriminative validity: real arms beat both controls on retrieval and fidelity probe beyond bootstrap 95% CIs. • Ranking is signal, not noise: Spearman ρ ≥0.7 between the two disjoint data halves. • Common failure mode: ≥4/7 non-control arms within 1.5× chance on the same probe (P1, P2, or P3 retention ≤0.5). • Added value over retrieval-only evaluation (secondary): cross-axis Spearman over the real arms. If every axis is rank-identical to retrieval r@1, the diagnostic adds nothing beyond the retrieval-only evaluation the problem gap complains about. The final verdict was supports, at coverage most. The agent reports that the suite’s rankings agree across disjoint data halves (Spearman 0.96 on retrieval), that content fidelity is nearly orthogonal to retrieval accuracy (Spearman 0.18 over the seven real arms), and that insensitivity to argument order is shared by every design family it tested. text: DENSE4D: PIXEL-LEVEL 4D HUMAN CORRESPONDENCE Rıza Alp Güler Department of Computing, Imperial College London
title: DENSE4D:

text: Reconstructing human motion in 4D requires identifying the same surface points through articulation, deformation and changes in visibility. We introduce Dense4D, to our knowledge the first feed-forward model dedicated to dense 4D correspon- dence across the body, clothing and hair from a set of monocular RGB images, without a body template. Trained specifically for human geometry, Dense4D jointly processes person-centred crops with known image-to-crop transforms to predict Human Point Maps (HPMs) and depth for each image. An HPM assigns each person pixel the 3D position of its observed surface point at a common reference time. These maps support amodal correspondence: points hidden in the reference image can be localised from observations in other frames. Matching HPM coordi- nates across crops establishes correspondence without predicting camera poses or large scene displacements; per-image depth then lifts the matches into 3D tracks. Experiments on real people demonstrate substantially higher tracking accuracy and closer agreement with scanned surfaces than the evaluated baselines. Points from different frames assemble into coherent human geometry in the reference pose, providing visible evidence of consistent dense correspondence through articulation and clothing deformation. Additional qualitative results, videos, and an interactive viewer are available at https://alpguler.com/dense4d. text: A detailed understanding of human geometry and motion is important across many fields, including robotics, extended reality, entertainment, healthcare, sports analytics, and sign language understand- ing. Yet people remain challenging for general dynamic scene reconstruction systems because their motion combines body articulation with the independent deformation of clothing and hair. Following these surfaces through a video requires identifying the same points as they move, become occluded and reappear. Reconstructing each frame independently does not establish this correspondence. We study dense 4D human correspondence, the task of matching points across the body, clothing and hair in different images and recovering their three-dimensional trajectories. Human correspondence methods commonly map image pixels to a shared body template (Güler et al., 2018). Such coordinates describe the underlying body, but do not directly represent the geometry and independent motion of loose garments and hair. In parallel, many 4D dynamic scene reconstruction systems jointly estimate geometry, motion and cameras across diverse scenes (Sucar et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). We introduce Dense4D for dense 4D human correspondence without a body template. The model establishes correspondence on the person without jointly reconstructing the surrounding scene or predicting camera poses. Dense4D follows a top-down approach: we isolate each person in the scene and jointly process their crops across time (Fig. 2). Using the focal length and person

text: on the person without jointly reconstructing the surrounding scene or predicting camera poses. Dense4D follows a top-down approach: we isolate each person in the scene and jointly process their crops across time (Fig. 2). Using the focal length and person mask, a known virtual-camera warp reorients each crop towards the person, and the crop zoom is supplied to the network. A Human Point Map (HPM) assigns each person pixel the 3D position of its observed surface point at a selected reference time, expressed in the reference crop’s camera coordinates. These maps support amodal correspondence to the reference surface, including regions hidden in the reference image but observed in other frames. Their union samples this reference-time geometry (Fig. 1, right). Where methods such as V-DPM predict point motion in a shared camera frame (Sucar et al., 2026), Dense4D identifies corresponding pixels by matching HPM coordinates across person-centred crops. The learned mapping relates observations of the person with known crop transforms and zoom, without also predicting the person’s displacement through the scene. Each matched pixel is lifted with the depth predicted for its image to recover the 3D track position. External scene geometry and camera poses are used separately to place the reconstructed person and tracks in world coordinates. We use the image encoder and aggregator architecture of Wang et al. (2026).

Two dense heads predict HPMs and per-image depth in a single forward pass. Training uses human geometry and correspondence supervision from synthetic motion and multi-view renderings of real scans. Across articulated motion and clothing deformation, Dense4D brings observations from different frames into coherent reference-time human geometry, with visibly aligned body parts and fine surface details (Sec. 4.4). On real footage, Dense4D recovers more accurate human trajectories and better matches the scanned reference geometry than the methods we compare against (Secs. 4.2 and 4.3). The shared reference representation also supports tracking across long intervals, as demonstrated on an 86 s video (Fig. 12). title: INTRODUCTION

text: Human correspondence and parametric reconstruction. A shared body template allows pixels on different people to be related through common anatomical coordinates (Güler et al., 2018). BodyMap and TemporalUV extend this association to clothing and hair (Ianina et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2022), while HumanGPS learns scan-supervised embeddings shared across subjects (Tan et al., 2021). These coordinates and embeddings establish correspondence but do not themselves reconstruct the individual’s body, garment or hair geometry. Mesh reconstruction methods such as 4DHumans (Goel et al., 2023) achieve body correspondence thanks to the fixed topology of the underlying parametric model, but do not represent the geometry and independent motion of garments or hair. Dense4D provides personalised correspondence: HPMs reconstruct reference-time points and locate later observations on them, without a shared body template. Deformable human reconstruction. ReLoo and DressRecon fit personalised surfaces, appearance and body/clothing deformation models to video through differentiable rendering (Guo et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025). Their temporal correspondences follow the fitted 3D deformation fields used to render the reconstructed motion. Forge4D reconstructs pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians from uncalibrated sparse-view videos and predicts their motion between adjacent timestamps for novel-view and novel- time synthesis (Hu et al., 2026). Dense4D establishes correspondence across a set of monocular RGB images through a common human reference-time geometry, with correspondence and depth learned from dense 3D

Dense4D establishes correspondence across a set of monocular RGB images through a common human reference-time geometry, with correspondence and depth learned from dense 3D supervision. Point tracking and amodal correspondence. From Particle Video (Sand & Teller, 2006) to learned models (Harley et al., 2022; Doersch et al., 2023; Karaev et al., 2025), image point trackers estimate query trajectories through occlusion. Three-dimensional trackers add depth or geometric estimation (Xiao et al., 2024; 2025; Ngo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). HPMs also locate points in 3D at the reference time even when hidden in the reference image. Object-centric representations. NOCS predicts category-level object coordinates (Wang et al., 2019); CaSPR learns a canonical spatiotemporal space from dynamic point clouds (Rempe et al., 2020). DualPM pairs posed and rest-pose maps for quadrupeds (Kaye et al., 2025); Face Anything predicts template-aligned facial coordinates and depth (Kocasari et al., 2026). Dense4D instead matches observations of a deforming person using that person’s own reference-time geometry. Scene reconstruction. text: represent pixels from different images as 3D points in a shared reference camera frame (Wang et al., 2024a; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). Human- aware models add person outputs: HAMSt3R adds segmentation and DensePose to MASt3R (Rojas et al., 2025), while Human3R recovers SMPL-X bodies with scene geometry and cameras from monocular video (Chen et al., 2026). Feed-forward models extend point-based reconstruction to dynamic scenes (Feng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026a), often jointly training geometry, motion and camera predic- tors (Karhade et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026; Sucar et al., 2026). Building on predicted geometry, 4D Primitive-Mâché uses dense image correspondences to optimise rigid-primitive motion and aggregate observations across time (Mazur et al., 2026). Dynamic Point Maps and V-DPM are closest to our representation: they express observations at a shared reference time and viewpoint, allowing correspondence to be established by matching shared-space coordinates (Sucar et al., 2025; 2026). Dense4D tracks by matching rather than by decoding point motion: every observed person pixel is mapped to the reference surface, correspondences are found among the target frame’s observed pixels, and each match is lifted with that frame’s own predicted depth. text: All HPMs share the reference virtual camera’s origin and axes, and both outputs use the same normalised scale. The network predicts in this normalised space; absolute body size and camera distance are not recovered. Observations of the same surface point have equal HPM targets, providing a shared coordinate for correspondence across time. The union of these targets samples the person’s surface at the reference time, bringing together the body, clothing and hair seen across the input clip. It includes regions hidden in the reference image but observed elsewhere, without fitting a body or surface template. Dense4D separates correspondence from camera-pose and scene-motion estimation while keeping tracks consistent with its predicted human geometry by construction. Compared with the baselines, Dense4D produces more precise trajectories and a better fit to measured human geometry, with videos showing robust tracking through articulation and clothing deformation. Dense4D can also be integrated with scene point clouds simply through shared image pixels. Limitations. Self-contact can make reference-space correspondence ambiguous when distinct surface points coincide. Selecting a reference frame without self-contact, when available, is a relatively straightforward mitigation that we do not pursue here. A broader challenge is evaluating correspondence on real people: 4D-DRESS measures proximity to scans rather than point identity, while Panoptic Studio Humans relies on reconstruction-derived trajectory labels that may inherit reconstruction errors. text: Temporal and multi-view consistency losses on large corpora of real video could improve correspondence and reduce reliance on synthetic supervision. Developing real-data bench- marks with independently measured surface-point identities would strengthen evaluation beyond surface proximity and reconstruction-derived tracks. The alignment provided by Dense4D could support learning appearance models based on Gaussian splatting (Kerbl et al., 2023) from humans in motion, while its accurate tracks could control human motion in generated video (Geng et al., 2025). Dense4D provides a foundation for augmenting scene understanding systems with more faithful human geometry, dense correspondence and robust tracking. Building on this foundation, future work could develop richer models of people and their surroundings that remain coherent through prolonged motion and interaction. We rasterise all people together with a shared depth buffer to account for inter-person occlusion. Figure 8 illustrates the supervision surfaces and input crops. A.1 BEDLAM2 Holding out every tenth BEDLAM2 (Tesch et al., 2025) track leaves 27,727 training tracks (1,250,307 labelled frames) and 3,081 development tracks, with 1,454 subjects across the two subsets. The official test split contains 7,157 tracks and 181,263 labelled frames from 1,223 subjects. Body and camera labels are available every fifth frame of the 30 fps video, giving supervision at 6 Hz. The surfaces comprise neutral SMPL-X bodies (Pavlakos et al., 2019), garments with fixed topology across time, and hair envelopes derived from strand grooms. For each groom, we extract the 0.3 level set of a strand-density field, offset it 3 mm inward and decimate it to 25 % of its faces (Lorensen & Cline, 1987; Garland & Heckbert, 1997).

A.3 MAMMASYN We train on 15,710 person tracks in 7,856 views from MammaSyn, MAMMA’s synthetic data family (Cuevas-Velasquez et al., 2026). We retain cameras pitched downwards by at least 15◦ and every fourth frame. MammaSyn complements BEDLAM2’s predominantly eye-level views and limited interactions with elevated views and interacting people, but its photorealistic SMPL-X renderings represent clothing only as texture, without separate garment or hair meshes. B IMPLEMENTATION AND TRAINING B.1 ARCHITECTURE AND VIRTUAL CAMERAS A 4 →1024 →1024 MLP with GELU activation embeds the crop geometry. The ViT image encoder uses DINOv3-L (Siméoni et al., 2025) with patch size 16. Each 512 × 512 crop supplies 1,024 patch tokens of width 1,024, which are joined by one camera token, 16 register tokens and the crop token. Separate learned camera and register tokens identify the first frame as the reference; the remaining frames share a second set. Camera tokens are

text: of width 1,024, which are joined by one camera token, 16 register tokens and the crop token. Separate learned camera and register tokens identify the first frame as the reference; the remaining frames share a second set. Camera tokens are internal features, with no camera-prediction head or camera-regression loss. There are 24 pairs of frame and inter-frame attention blocks. Five inter-frame blocks (indices 2, 6, 9, 14 and 20, zero-indexed) update only the camera, register and crop tokens; patch tokens pass through these steps unchanged. The remaining 19 inter-frame blocks attend across all tokens. Both dense heads use features from blocks 4, 11, 17 and 23 (zero-indexed), projected to resolutions 1282, 642, 322 and 162, then fused by a 256-channel RefineNet decoder (Lin et al., 2017) and pixel-shuffled to 5122. HPM coordinates have no output activation. The heads run in fp32 and the backbone in bf16; each head has 32.3 M parameters. 16

text: B.3 TRAINING SCHEDULE Dense4D is trained for a cumulative 686,000 steps, taking approximately 490 hours on four GH200 GPUs. We report the final checkpoint, without weight averaging. AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) uses weight decay 0.05 and peak learning rate 2 × 10−5, with linear warm-up and cosine decay. Gradient norms are clipped to 1.0 separately for the backbone and each head; activation checkpointing covers attention-block pairs. The final training configuration samples BEDLAM2, THuman2.1 and MammaSyn with probabilities of approximately 65 %, 22 % and 13 %, respectively. For each person, the number of input frames is sampled from S ∈{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24} with weights 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3. The batch contains 96 images per step, consistently packed as 24 images per GPU; the number of person sequences varies with S. Frames are sampled without replacement where the track length permits. Photometric augmentation uses colour jitter with probability 0.9 and greyscale with probability 0.05; jitter is shared across frames with probability 0.7. Brightness, contrast and saturation factors lie in [0.5, 1.5], with hue in [−0.1, 0.1]. C EVALUATION PROTOCOLS C.1 PANOPTIC STUDIO HUMANS We evaluate 40,779 human queries across all 156 clips of 150 frames, retaining the Dynamic-3DGS pseudo-labels (Luiten et al., 2024). Queries on held objects or with invalid annotations are excluded consistently across methods. The official TAPVid-3D evaluator uses benchmark intrinsics, depth- adaptive thresholds and one median rescaling per clip; scores are averaged over clips. The dataset contains 49 two-person and 107 single-person clips. SAM 3 (Carion et al., 2025) supplies person masks, and the frame with the largest mask is selected as each person’s reference. We fit one scale per person across the clip using pixel-aligned VGGT-Ω and predicted human depths on confident mask interiors. The fit selects the scale supported by the most depth ratios within 5 %, then refines it using the median inlier ratio. VGGT-Ωsets the scale only; our predicted depth supplies the track geometry, without temporal smoothing. A match is visible when its reference-space residual is below τ = 0.005. Undoing the normalisation in Eq. (2) gives a tolerance of sτ: for example, s = 2 m gives 1 cm. C.2 BASELINE IMPLEMENTATIONS All baselines use the same human queries and evaluator. 4RC. 4RC (Luo et al., 2026) encodes all 150 frames jointly and decodes each query at each target time. We project its points with its own intrinsics, then lift the resulting 2D tracks at unchanged depth using benchmark intrinsics. This gives 14.4 / 24.1 AJ / APD, versus 4.1 / 7.4 for its original camera-space points; it has no occlusion output. V-DPM. V-DPM (Sucar et al., 2026) processes pairs drawn from 14 temporal chunks of at most 11 frames, with frame zero as reference; we align scales on shared reference pixels. Confidence ≥1.5 marks visibility. We reproject each query’s predicted position at its query frame using benchmark intrinsics, giving (u, v); (uq, vq) are the supplied query pixels. We correct points as x′ = (x −z bu/fx)/k, y′ = (y −z bv/fy)/k, z′ = z, where fx, fy, cx, cy are the benchmark intrinsics. text: Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) enable language-based understanding and reasoning over temporal data, yet a fundamental question remains: what in- formation should their time-series representations preserve, and what variation should they factor out? Existing TSLMs typically expose the language model to a single representation, imposing a fixed inductive bias across downstream tasks. We instead introduce complementary representations as a design principle for time-series reasoning. Our model combines two visual views: line plots preserve absolute measurements and the observed coordinate frame, while normalized de- lay embeddings factor out positive amplitude rescaling and offsets while exposing temporal structure. Dedicated visual encoders integrate both views into a shared language model through visual tokens and multi-level feature fusion. Evaluation- time interventions verify that the two views exhibit distinct invariance profiles, while single-view ablations show that their combination is particularly beneficial beyond basic perception, with the large gains in prediction and reasoning. Built on Qwen3-VL-8B, our dual-view model improves overall TSRBench accuracy from 44.5% with line plots alone to 53.2%, substantially exceeding the strongest eval- uated dedicated TSLM baseline at 36.7%. It further achieves 89.9% accuracy on TSExam and 86.8% numerical accuracy on multivariate ChatTS alignment. To- gether, these results demonstrate that complementary representations provide an effective design principle for general-purpose TSLMs, enabling models to exploit temporal structure without sacrificing access to the original measurement

text: Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) seek to extend the reasoning and interaction capabilities of large language models to sequential data, enabling models to answer questions, infer temporal rela- tionships, forecast future behavior, and support decisions over time series (Xie et al., 2025; Langer et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026a). A central challenge in this emerging paradigm is how temporal signals should be represented to the language model. Existing approaches serialize numerical values into text, learn dedicated time-series embeddings, or project features from spe- cialized temporal encoders into the language-model representation space (Xie et al., 2025; Langer et al., 2026; Guan et al., 2026). As summarized in Table 1, these approaches typically commit to a single time-series representation, with absolute measurement scale either retained directly or pro- vided separately as auxiliary metadata. Yet these representational choices impose fundamentally different inductive biases: representations that retain absolute amplitudes and coordinate informa- tion support quantitative readout, whereas normalized representations can suppress such informa- tion while emphasizing relative structure and temporal dynamics. Recent evaluations further show that simply rendering a time series as a line plot can already provide strong temporal understand- ing to general-purpose vision-language models (Yu et al., 2026a; Cai et al., 2024), suggesting that ∗Equal contribution. text: formulation allows dis- tinct views to provide different inductive biases. We instantiate this principle with two visual repre- sentations: a standard line plot and a normalized delay embedding. The line plot preserves absolute amplitudes, axis ranges, and measurement scales, providing the information required for questions grounded in observed values. In contrast, delay embeddings reconstruct a time series as a trajectory in phase space using time-lagged observations, revealing geometric structure associated with the underlying dynamics (Takens, 2006). We normalize this representation before rendering it as a two- dimensional view, thereby factoring out affine changes in amplitude while retaining the geometry of the temporal trajectory. Our central hypothesis is that combining these complementary views is par- ticularly useful beyond basic perception, where reasoning, prediction, and decision-making require models to exploit temporal structure while remaining grounded in the observed measurements. Building on this representational principle, we design a dual-tower TSLM in which each visual view is processed by a dedicated encoder. We retain Qwen3-VL’s native vision encoder, initialized from SigLIP-2 (Tschannen et al., 2025), to process line plots, and introduce a dedicated DINOv3 encoder (Sim´eoni et al., 2026) for delay embeddings, allowing each view to develop a specialized visual representation before interacting with the language model. The resulting visual features are compressed into a compact set of tokens, 230 for the line plot

The resulting visual features are compressed into a compact set of tokens, 230 for the line plot and 64 for the delay embedding, and concatenated as input to the language model. Beyond this input-level fusion, we adopt Deep- Stack (Meng et al., 2024) to inject multi-level visual features into the early language-model layers, enabling the complementary representations to interact with language processing throughout the network. This architecture provides a compact realization of our central hypothesis while retaining the distinct inductive biases of the two visual views. To test our representational hypothesis and evaluate the resulting dual-tower TSLM, we conduct ex- periments on TSRBench (Yu et al., 2026a), TSExam (Cai et al., 2024), and ChatTS (Xie et al., 2025). Built on Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025), our model achieves 53.2% overall accuracy on TSRBench, substantially narrowing the gap to GPT-5 with text and visual input (55.6%) while surpassing the strongest evaluated dedicated TSLM (36.7%). text: Time-Series Representations. Time series admit multiple representations that expose different properties of the underlying signal. Beyond the raw sequential domain, classical approaches trans- form temporal observations into alternative coordinate systems, including frequency and time- frequency representations, recurrence-based representations, and delay embeddings that reconstruct trajectories in phase space (Takens, 2006). A related line of work represents time series as images, enabling spatial models to operate on temporal structure. Wang & Oates (2015) introduced Gramian Angular Fields and Markov Transition Fields for encoding temporal sequences as two-dimensional images, demonstrating their utility for classification and imputation. More recently, Naiman et al. (2024) showed that image transformations based on delay embeddings and short-time Fourier trans- forms can provide effective interfaces between time series and modern vision-based diffusion mod- els, supporting generation across both short and long sequences. Collectively, these works demon- strate that alternative representations can expose useful and distinct structure in temporal signals. Our work builds on this perspective but shifts the focus from selecting a representation for a partic- ular predictive or generative task to combining complementary representations for general-purpose time-series reasoning: we jointly expose the model to views designed to retain different information and induce different invariances. text: we jointly expose the model to views designed to retain different information and induce different invariances. Time-Series Language Models. A growing body of work investigates how pretrained language models can be adapted to temporal data. Early approaches primarily focused on forecasting, either by serializing numerical observations as text (Gruver et al., 2023), prompting language models with textual descriptions of temporal sequences (Xue & Salim, 2023), or aligning and reprogramming time-series representations to exploit pretrained language-model representations (Zhou et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024). More recent work has broadened this paradigm from task-specific prediction toward Time Series Language Models that accept time series as a modality and support natural-language understanding and reasoning. ChatTS (Xie et al., 2025) aligns learned time-series embeddings with an LLM through instruction tuning, while OpenTSLM (Langer et al., 2026) in- vestigates both soft-prompt and cross-attention interfaces for reasoning over multivariate temporal 3
title: Preprint

text: Preprint signals. TimeOmni-1 (Guan et al., 2026) instead represents numerical sequences directly within the language-model token space and targets complex temporal reasoning, whereas TS-Reasoner (Yu et al., 2026b) aligns representations from a pretrained time-series foundation model with an LLM. In parallel, benchmark studies have shown that general-purpose vision-language models can reason surprisingly effectively over time series presented as line plots (Cai et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026a), providing an alternative to explicitly learned time-series interfaces. Despite these diverse strate- gies, existing TSLMs predominantly expose the language model to a single primary representation of each temporal signal. Our work instead treats representation as a source of complementary in- ductive biases, jointly providing views that deliberately preserve different information and exhibit different invariances. 3 METHOD 3.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION AND OVERVIEW Let Q denote a natural-language query and X = {x1, . . . , xn} a collection of n input time se- ries, where xi = (xi,1, . . . , xi,mi) ∈Rmi may have a different length and numerical range. Line-Plot View. For each time series xi = (xi,1, . . . , xi,mi), we render the raw observations as a two-dimensional line plot without amplitude normalization (Figure 3a). Consequently, the plot retains the original value range and its position within the coordinate system, including the numerical values displayed along the vertical axis. This representation therefore preserves information about absolute amplitudes and differences in scale that would be removed by per-series normalization. For multivariate inputs, each series is rendered as its own plot rather than overlaid, so series with different ranges keep their own measurement frames. Normalized Delay-Embedding View. Because windows overlap, each feature of the signal traces a diagonal line across the image: periodicity appears as parallel stripes, trends as smooth gradients, and local events as isolated streaks (Figure 3b). Our central hypothesis is that exposing the language model to complementary representations pro- vides benefits that cannot be obtained from either view alone. We therefore compare the full dual- view model against Plot-only and Delay-only variants, as well as two same-view controls that retain the complete dual-tower architecture but feed both towers the same representation. In Plot+Plot, the DINOv3 tower receives the line plot in place of the delay map; in Delay+Delay, the Qwen3- VL tower receives the delay map in place of the line plot. Both controls keep the same encoders, adapters, per-tower token budgets, and two-stage training procedure as our model, so any difference from the full model reflects

Both controls keep the same encoders, adapters, per-tower token budgets, and two-stage training procedure as our model, so any difference from the full model reflects whether the two streams carry distinct or identical views, rather than dif- ferences in architecture or capacity. Table 3 reports results across all 15 TSRBench tasks, together with representative dedicated TSLMs and general-purpose models. The results show that the benefit of complementary representations is concentrated beyond basic perception. Plot only already achieves 87.4% on Perception, and adding the delay view leaves this essentially unchanged at 86.4%. In contrast, the dual-view model improves Reasoning from 35.8% to 40.1%, Prediction from 38.0% to 61.7%, and Decision-Making from 36.4% to 37.6%, raising overall accuracy from 45.2% to 53.2%. The task-level results further show that the contribution of the complementary view varies across tasks, rather than producing a uniform improvement across the benchmark. Importantly, simply duplicating a view does not reproduce the gain: Plot+Plot reaches 44.8% overall and Delay+Delay reaches 42.6%, compared with our 53.2%. This suggests that the improvement is not explained merely by providing a second visual stream, but is associated with combining representations that preserve different properties of the underlying signal. This tension motivated our central question: can complementary representations improve general-purpose time-series reasoning? We establish complementary representation as a design principle for TSLMs and instantiate it in a dual- view model that integrates measurement-preserving line plots and normalized delay embeddings through dedicated visual encoders and a shared language model. The resulting model raises TSR- Bench accuracy from 45.2% for the plot-only variant to 53.2%, surpassing all evaluated dedicated TSLMs. The gains are concentrated beyond basic perception and are not reproduced when both encoders receive line plots or both receive delay embeddings. The model also leads the evaluated baselines on TSExam and multivariate ChatTS numerical alignment, achieving 89.9% and 86.8% accuracy, respectively, demonstrating strong performance across perceptual, numerical, and broader temporal reasoning tasks. The STFT comparison in Appendix C.5 further shows that the preferred secondary representation varies across evaluations: delay embeddings perform better on TSRBench, while STFT provides small advantages on ChatTS numerical alignment and average reasoning accuracy. text: Preprint APPENDIX A TIME SERIES REPRESENTATIONS A.1 VISUALIZATION OF COMPLEMENTARY REPRESENTATIONS Figure 3 illustrates the two visual representations constructed from the same input time series. The line-plot view (left) preserves the original measurement frame, including absolute amplitudes and axis information. In contrast, the normalized delay-embedding view (right) represents overlapping temporal trajectories after per-series normalization, thereby removing offsets and positive amplitude rescaling while emphasizing temporal structure. The two views are provided to their respective visual encoders as described in Section 3.2. (a) Line-plot view (b) Delay-embedding view Figure 3: Dual-view visual representations of a time-series variate. (a) The line plot retains the original measurement frame and axis values. (b) The normalized delay map arranges overlapping windows as columns, so recurring structure appears as diagonal stripes. A.2 DELAY-MAP CONSTRUCTION DETAILS Hyperparameters. Symbol Description Value ρ Window length as a fraction of series length 0.6 ℓmin Minimum window length 48 ℓmax Maximum window length 192 W Number of windows (map width) 256 H Resampled window length (map height) 256 Interpolation. Interpolation is applied only within each window: the ℓvalues of Vc are placed on a uniform grid over [0, 1] and linearly interpolated at H uniformly spaced points. Window start indices pc are rounded to integers, so no interpolation is performed along the time axis. Each entry of the map is therefore an interpolated sample of the original series rather than a resized pixel. The resulting H × W matrix is min–max normalized, replicated across three channels, and normalized with the DINOv3 preprocessing statistics as a floating-point tensor, without quantization or image resizing. Relation to the standard delay embedding. The classical delay embedding (Takens, 2006; Naiman et al., 2024) arranges windows of fixed dimension n as columns with a fixed integer skip s between their start indices, yielding an n × ⌈(m −n)/s⌉matrix that is zero-padded to the net- work input size. Our construction corresponds to n = ℓwith a length-dependent fractional skip 13
title: Preprint

text: Preprint (m −ℓ)/(W −1). Instead of padding, both dimensions are fixed: the number of columns to W and the number of rows to H through resampling. When m −ℓ< W −1, the skip is below one sample and neighboring columns may repeat. When ℓ= m, all windows start at pc = 0, and the map reduces to W identical copies of the resampled series. B MODEL AND TRAINING DETAILS B.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Line-plot tokens. Each chart is rendered at 768 × 320 px and ingested by the Qwen3-VL vision encoder at 736×320 px, corresponding to 46×20 patches. After 2×2 merging, this yields N plot i = 230 visual tokens per series. The Qwen3-VL tokenizer frames these with two boundary tokens (<|vision start|> and <|vision end|>) enclosing 230 <|image pad|> slots, for an exact budget of 232 tokens per series. The native encoder additionally provides three intermediate feature maps, which Qwen3-VL injects into the language model through DeepStack. Delay tokens. For each time-series variate, the delay map V delay ∈[0, 1]256×256 is replicated across three channels and normalized using the DINOv3 image preprocessing statistics before being passed to the encoder. We retain the spatial patch tokens and discard the class and register tokens. The resulting 16 × 16 patch grid is merged into an 8 × 8 grid of 2 ×

The duplicated-view controls keep the full dual-tower architecture, per-tower token budgets, and training procedure of our model, but feed both towers the same representation; they therefore test whether the improvement can be reproduced by a second visual stream alone (Appendix C.6). The results show that the contribution of the complementary representation depends on the bench- mark. Plot only is already strong on TSExam and ChatTS, whereas Delay only is substantially weaker on numerical alignment. Combining the representations provides modest improvements over Plot only on ChatTS numerical alignment and reasoning, while producing a substantially larger improvement on the broader TSRBench evaluation. Importantly, neither duplicated-view control reproduces the overall TSRBench gain of the complementary pair, despite matching its architecture and visual-token budget. text: stricted to the 2,020 scale- and sampling-invariant items, this table covers all 15 TSRBench tasks. We additionally report two temporal-symmetry transformations, temporal reversal and sign inver- sion. Unlike the other interventions, these can legitimately change the gold answer (e.g., reversing an increasing trend), so they illustrate that invariance is not always desirable: a model that is insensitive to these transformations may be ignoring information the task requires. The full results make the distinct sensitivity profiles particularly clear. Delay only changes by at most 0.8 percentage points under the five affine interventions, including z-score normalization, which is consistent with the invariance induced by its per-series normalization. In contrast, Plot only and our model remain sensitive to transformations of the measurement frame. Delay only and Plot only also exhibit the smallest average degradation under noise and smoothing. Our model is not uniformly the most invariant representation, but retains substantially higher absolute accuracy across all reported interventions. Under changes in sampling horizon, its category-average accuracy is virtually unchanged from clean performance. As shown in Table 12, neither representa- tion uniformly dominates across all evaluations. STFT is slightly stronger on ChatTS numerical alignment and the ChatTS reasoning average, whereas the delay-based model is slightly stronger on TSExam and substantially stronger on the broader TSRBench evaluation. These results suggest that the benefit of complemen- tary views is not tied to uniform superiority of the delay representation on every task; rather, the choice of secondary representation changes the inductive bias available to the language model. text: Image editing models produce impressive results for indi- vidual edits, but their quality often deteriorates over multi- ple editing turns. Each editing turn introduces small distri- bution shifts that accumulate over successive edits, creating a gap between the input distributions encountered during the editor’s original training and multi-turn inference. We introduce a training scheme that makes multi-turn image editing stable under this accumulating distribution shift. A key is to force the editor to operate on its own outputs from previous editing turns during training, bringing the princi- ple of Self-Forcing to image editing. The main challenge is that self-generated editing trajectories deviate from ground- truth trajectories, making direct supervision unreliable. We address this challenge through a distillation objective that leverages a teacher image editor to provide a reliable train- ing signal when the model operates on its own previous outputs. We introduce an asymmetric conditioning scheme: while the student performs edits sequentially on its own out- *Equal contribution. puts, the teacher remains anchored to the original clean image and receives a compound editing instruction. Exper- iments show substantially reduced degradation over long multi-turn sequences while maintaining editing quality and instruction adherence.
title: ACEdit: Stable Multi-Turn Image Editing via Asymmetric Conditioning

text: Image editing with modern generative models has reached an impressive level of quality, enabling complex modifica- tions while faithfully preserving the appearance and content of the input image [6, 24, 26, 44, 49]. Yet, practical editing is rarely a single operation. Users often refine an image through a sequence of edits, where the output of one edit becomes the input to the next. This setting is commonly referred to as multi-turn image editing. With current image editing models, each editing turn introduces small distribu- tion shifts that accumulate as the model repeatedly operates on its own outputs. These shifts create a growing gap be- 1 arXiv:2610.22328v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026
title: ACEdit: Stable Multi-Turn Image Editing via Asymmetric Conditioning

text: tween the input distributions encountered during the editor’s original training and multi-turn inference. This gap leads to accumulating artifacts, loss of fine details, and unintended changes in appearance (see Figure 1). Effective image edit- ing therefore requires not only high-quality individual edits, but also stability across successive editing turns. Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate degradation in multi-turn image editing. Inference-time methods target specific sources of degradation [27, 38, 47, 62], but may incur computational overhead and are lim- ited by the complexity of distribution shifts in multi-turn editing. Other approaches train models on multi-turn edit- ing sequences [16, 39, 52, 61]. Training on ground-truth sequences leaves a gap between training and inference, while training on self-generated sequences poses supervi- sion challenges, leading to inconsistent targets, restrictions on training sequences, or objectives that do not explicitly address distribution shifts. We present a training scheme for multi-turn image edit- ing that maintains stability under accumulating distribution shifts. Our scheme is inspired by autoregressive video gen- eration, where models similarly operate on their own out- puts and face accumulating distribution shifts. Following the principle of Self-Forcing [17], we train the editor on its own outputs from previous editing turns, allowing it to learn from the distribution shifts encountered during multi-turn inference. text: Following the principle of Self-Forcing [17], we train the editor on its own outputs from previous editing turns, allowing it to learn from the distribution shifts encountered during multi-turn inference. However, self-generated editing trajectories in- evitably deviate from ground-truth trajectories, making di- rect supervision with ground-truth images unreliable. To address this challenge, we employ score distillation in a teacher-student framework to train the editor on its self- generated trajectories without requiring ground-truth tar- gets for its intermediate outputs [37, 48, 57]. We intro- duce an asymmetric conditioning scheme for the student and teacher. The student’s input may already deviate sig- nificantly from the teacher’s training distribution, making it unsuitable for reliable teacher guidance. We therefore con- dition the teacher on the original image and a compound instruction combining all edits up to the current turn, while the student performs edits sequentially on its own outputs. This provides a training signal that reflects the intended ed- its without inheriting the errors accumulated along the stu- dent’s trajectory. We evaluate our method against existing multi-turn im- age editing approaches and demonstrate significant quali- tative and quantitative improvements in preserving editing capabilities while mitigating accumulated distribution drift. Our training is efficient and introduces no inference-time overhead, while making no assumptions about the nature of distribution shifts or restrictions on editing sequences. Through ablation

text: Text-guided image editing. Early text-driven manipu- lation largely steered pre-trained GAN latent spaces via vision-language models [11, 36]. The advent of diffu- sion models broadened semantic coverage and synthesized complex scenes more flexibly. Subsequent approaches im- proved source-image preservation and fine-grained con- trol through noise perturbation and trajectory inversion [5, 10, 19, 33, 34, 46], alongside spatial blending and cross- attention steering [1, 3, 7, 14, 45]. Recent efforts ex- tend inference-time control to continuous-time flow mod- els through structural layer control [4], flow inversion [20, 40], inversion-free sampling trajectories [23], and text- embedding control for continuous editing [18, 21]. Comple- menting inference-time methods, instruction-tuned archi- tectures learn a direct mapping using synthetic pairs [6], hu- man annotations [59], and multi-task supervision [13, 42]. Emerging state-of-the-art transformer-based diffusion and flow backbones further push visual quality and composi- tional reasoning, demonstrating unprecedented instruction fidelity and fine-grained spatial control [25, 26, 49, 50]. De- spite these single-step capabilities, isolated edit accuracy does not prevent error propagation, identity degradation, or semantic drift when applied iteratively across extended edit- ing sequences. text: Maintaining image quality and content consistency across successive edits is a cen- tral challenge in multi-turn image editing, as errors can accumulate over the editing sequence. Agentic frame- works tackle this challenge through planning, memory, and reflection [41, 54], while training-free methods improve consistency through inversion and attention control [62], high-frequency feature preservation [27], inversion shar- ing [38], and low-frequency latent alignment [47]. Other approaches learn sequential editing directly: VINCIE learns in-context editing from video-derived sequences [39], while AnchorEdit combines supervised causal multi-turn train- ing with self-generated histories and identity-anchoring memory [52]. Reinforcement learning methods optimize trajectory-level editing rewards [16] or jointly optimize history-dependent reasoning and image generation [55]. More recently, MT-OPSD distills clean-conditioned editing behavior onto states generated through identity-edit roll- outs [61], which accumulate errors while keeping the in- tended content fixed. Our training instead follows the edit- ing process as it unfolds during inference: successive se- mantic edits with evolving content and preservation require- ments. Through distribution matching, we align the stu- dent’s evolving output distribution, modeled by a learned auxiliary editor, with the target distribution defined by a teacher conditioned on the original image and cumulative instructions, without paired intermediate targets. 2

Preliminaries: Score Distillation Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) [37] uses a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model ϵϕ to optimize a differen- tiable renderer G parameterized by θ. It relies on the ob- servation that the model’s noise prediction at each noise level is proportional to the score of the noisy image distri- bution [43]. SDS uses this score to guide images produced by G without requiring paired target images. For a sampled timestep t and Gaussian noise ϵ, the SDS gradient is: ∇θLSDS = w(t)  ϵγ ϕ(zt(x); c, t) −ϵ  ∂x ∂θ , (1) where x is an image produced by G, zt(x) is obtained by adding noise ϵ to x at timestep t, and c is a condition such as a text prompt. Here, ϵγ ϕ(zt(x); c, t) denotes the model’s noise prediction with classifier-free guidance, and w(t) weights the gradient at different timesteps. SDS is known to produce blurry or oversaturated results, which has motivated numerous follow-up works [9, 32, 58, 63]. In particular, Variational Score Distillation (VSD) [48] addresses this is- sue by replacing the sampled noise ϵ subtracted from the model’s prediction with the prediction of an auxiliary model ϵLoRA fine-tuned on images produced by G. Noise-Free Score Distillation (NFSD) [22] provides a new interpretation of score distillation. Specifically, it decomposes the conditional noise prediction into three components: condition alignment, correction toward the model’s image distribution, and denoising: ϵϕ(zt; c, t) = δC+δD+δN. Under this interpretation, subtracting the auxil- iary prediction in VSD approximately cancels the denoising component, leaving the directions associated with condition alignment and domain correction to guide optimization. While SDS and VSD optimize individual instances for a given prompt, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [56, 57] extends this approach to training a gen- erative model. DMD uses the VSD loss to train a student model, guided by a pretrained diffusion model referred to as the teacher. The student learns to generate images for arbitrary prompts. Our method adopts this teacher–student formulation for training a stable editor. Method Image editing models are typically trained on pairs of input and target images [26]. However, in multi-turn editing, the model repeatedly receives inputs generated by its own pre- vious predictions, which it was not trained to handle. This creates a train–test gap that can cause errors and artifacts to accumulate over successive edits. To address this gap, we train our multi-turn image edit- ing model Gθ to edit images produced by repeatedly apply- 3

text: ing the model itself, as illustrated in Figure 2. We refer to the resulting sequences of edited images as rollouts. Su- pervising the model on these rollouts is challenging even when a ground-truth editing sequence is available. Since an edit can have many valid outcomes, the model’s output at a given turn may differ from the corresponding ground-truth image, even if the edit was applied correctly. As a result, subsequent edits in the rollout are applied to images that differ from those in the ground-truth sequence. Therefore, the ground-truth images cannot serve as paired targets for supervising these edits. Inspired by Self-Forcing [17], which addresses a sim- ilar challenge in autoregressive video generation, we use score distillation to supervise our student model Gθ, which becomes our stable editor after training. We compute the score-distillation signal using a pretrained flow-matching editor vϕ that serves as the teacher. A key challenge is that the student’s intermediate out- puts may contain accumulated errors, making them unreli- able inputs for the teacher. To address this, we introduce asymmetric conditioning of the student and teacher through compound-edit supervision. While the student applies edits sequentially to its own outputs, the teacher is always con- ditioned on the original image and a compound instruction combining all edits up to the current turn. text: We de- note the complete four-step editing process by Gθ and a single model prediction within this process by vθ. We use the convention where σ = 1 corresponds to pure noise and σ = 0 to a clean image, with the predicted velocity point- ing toward noise. At a denoising step with noise level σ, let xσ be the current state. The model’s prediction provides an estimate of the clean output: ˆx = xσ −σvθ(xσ), where, for brevity, we omit the dependence of vθ on the noise level, the previous image, and the current instruction. For a given training rollout, we consider an edit turn e ∈{1, . . . , E} and a denoising exit step s ∈{1, . . . , 4}. We first obtain Ie−1 by applying the preceding e −1 ed- its, each using the full four-step denoising process without tracking gradients. At turn e, we execute the denoising pro- cess up to step s, where we compute the clean output esti- mate ˆxs e. Gradients are propagated only through the model’s prediction at this step, without backpropagating through earlier denoising steps or edit turns. Throughout the roll- out, we pass the edited images directly between turns in the model’s latent space, avoiding repeated decoding and en- coding. 4.2. Training Asymmetric Conditioning. Throughout the roll- out, we pass the edited images directly between turns in the model’s latent space, avoiding repeated decoding and en- coding. 4.2. Training Asymmetric Conditioning. Having obtained the clean- output estimate ˆxs e at turn e, we now define the training signal. This signal should encourage adherence to the edit- ing instructions, preservation of relevant image details, and generation of realistic, artifact-free images. We obtain this signal from a pretrained flow-matching image editor vϕ, which serves as our teacher. Specifically, we evaluate its score on a noisy version of ˆxs e at noise level τ, denoted by zτ(ˆxs e). Unlike conventional text-to-image score distilla- tion, our editing teacher is conditioned on both an image and an instruction. It can therefore guide the output toward results that satisfy the requested edit while preserving rele- vant details of the conditioning image. The remaining question is how to condition the pre- trained editing teacher vϕ. Its conditioning image should serve as the source of the edit, while its text input should describe the intended change from that image to ˆxs e. A nat- ural choice is the previous output Ie−1 and the current in- struction ce, which are also the inputs to the student Gθ at turn e. However, beyond the

However, beyond the first turn, Ie−1 is generated by the student and may already contain artifacts. This creates a distribution shift for the teacher, which was trained on clean images. Moreover, since the teacher is expected to preserve details of its conditioning image that are not affected by the instruction, it may also preserve these artifacts rather than correct them. We examine this conditioning choice in the ablation study in Section 5.4. Instead, we condition the teacher on the original clean image I0 and the accumulated instructions he = (c1, . . . , ce). text: successive object removals, all competing methods visibly damage the surrounding scene, while our model success- fully preserves it. Each training-free method ties every output to part of the previous image, and this is also its main weakness: when an edit has to change exactly that part, content from ear- lier turns leaks into the result. Emu Edit reverts pixels that change only slightly, so remnants of earlier images survive; VAE-LFA aligns low-frequency latent statistics with earlier outputs, so their colours persist; and FreqEdit steers high- frequency detail toward the previous image, so their tex- tures persist. Figure 8 in Appendix F illustrates these effects over three successive background replacements. MT-OPSD leaves no such traces but blurs the image and washes out its colours, consistent with the degradation observed in Fig- ure 4. Further comparisons with the backbone model, including a full sequence of fifteen edits, are shown in Figs. 9 and 10 in the appendix. 5.3. Quantitative Evaluation

text: conditioning variants qualitatively. Teacher and auxiliary conditioning. Our teacher and auxiliary editor are conditioned on the original image and the compound instruction, anchoring score distillation to the clean source. We compare this design with two alternatives: additionally providing the previous student output to both models, and replacing the original image and compound in- struction with the previous output and current instruction. Both alternatives substantially reduce preservation: consis- tency drops from 3.85 to 2.81 and 2.28, respectively, com- pared with 3.03 for the pretrained base model. Figure 5 illustrates the former variant: as with the base model, the image degrades over the turns, and blotchy noise spreads over the walls and the rug. These results suggest that con- ditioning the score models on intermediate student outputs can reinforce accumulated artifacts rather than correct them. Student conditioning. Our student receives only the pre- vious output and current instruction. Providing the origi- nal image as an additional reference improves consistency from 3.85 to 4.08, but reduces instruction following from 3.38 to 2.80. As shown in Figure 5, earlier edits are undone as later ones are applied: the recoloured stool and ball re- turn to their original colours. A student trained on 5- edit rollouts still improves over the base model after ten turns (consistency 3.29 vs. 3.03), but recovers only about a third of our gain (3.85) and is significantly worse than our model on every preservation measure. Training on its own outputs over the full length of the sequences it edits at in- ference is therefore important. 6. Conclusions, Limitations and Future Work We introduced a training approach for stable multi-turn im- age editing. Our central idea is that stability should be learned over the entire recursive process, rather than at in- dividual editing steps. We achieve this through asymmet- ric conditioning: the student learns from its own generated editing trajectories, while the teacher remains anchored to the original clean image and the accumulated editing in- structions. This allows us to supervise a long, imperfect sequence of edits through a shorter, clean alternative path, without exposing the teacher to the errors accumulated by the student. text: robustness to much longer editing sequences remains an interesting di- rection for future work. Beyond image editing, our approach suggests a more general training principle for recursive generative pro- cesses. Self-Forcing exposes the model to the distribution it will encounter during inference, while asymmetric teacher supervision provides reliable guidance from a clean refer- ence. Score distillation connects these two paths without requiring paired target outputs, which is particularly use- ful when many valid results are possible. We believe this combination may be useful in other generative tasks where models repeatedly operate on their own outputs. Acknowledgments We thank Ron Mokady for his valuable feedback. The judge rates the final image with the image- quality prompt, checking structural coherence, natural ap- pearance, absence of artifacts and texture fidelity, and yield- ing a score from 1 to 5. The prompt describes every im- age as AI-generated, and on our real photographs the judge also reports defects in untouched sources (their mean score is 3.57); since all methods are scored on the same pho- tographs and compared chain by chain, this affects the abso- lute scores but not the comparisons. ∆HPSv3 is the change in HPSv3 [31], a learned estimate of perceived image qual- ity, from the first edited image (turn 1) to the final image. Measuring from turn 1 rather than from the source separates the quality lost over the chain from the effect of a single edit. Preservation. On the whole image, the judge rates consistency with the source using the visual-consistency prompt. It sees the source, the final image and the chain’s ten instructions as one numbered list, and scores from 1 to 5 how well everything the instructions do not ask to change is preserved (5: all such elements unchanged; 1: most of the scene altered). text: instruction edits or mentions (Sec. 5.3). We crop the box of each anchor from the source and from the final image, grey out in both crops the parts that fall inside the box of any edited object, and compute the DINOv2 [35] distance (one minus the cosine similarity of the CLS features) between the two crops. Because the boxes are coarse, an anchor can lie largely inside the box of an edited object (e.g., a shirt worn by a person who is edited), leaving too little of it to compare. We therefore use an anchor only if at least 30% of its box remains after the masking, and take a chain’s an- chor distance as the mean over its usable anchors; 148 of the 252 chains have at least one, and the anchor distance is averaged over these chains. text: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models Weijian Luo∗†2, Yujian Chen∗1,3, Hao Jiang1,4, Guang Cheng5 and Tianyang Hu‡1,4 1Polyadic Research Group 2Dots Studio, Xiaohongshu 3Peking University 4SAGA Lab, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 5The University of California, Los Angeles Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT ), combining feature and query–key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and- play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining
title: Designing Transformers for Continuous

text: generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model’s underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.

text: Autoregressive language models generate text by predicting tokens sequentially. Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative: they jointly refine continuous representations of a token sequence through iterative denoising or flow dynamics, allowing multiple token positions to be updated in parallel. Recent studies have explored a range of representations, training objectives, and generative dynamics, including one-hot flows, learned token embeddings, and latent-space models (Lee et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Meshchaninov et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026). Despite their different formulations, these models share a central computational component: a neural backbone that maps noisy continuous states to predictions for language generation. Much of the progress in CDLMs has focused on the formulation and learning of continuous generative processes, while the Transformer architectures that implement them have received comparatively less systematic attention. Existing models commonly inherit architectural choices from causal large language models (LLMs) or from Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) developed for image generation. ∗Equal contribution. †Project leader: pkulwj1994@icloud.com ‡Corresponding author: hutianyang@cuhk.edu.cn 1 arXiv:2610.22330v1 [cs.AI] 15 Oct 2026
