text: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models 3 These architectures provide useful starting points for methodological research, but their suitability for continuous language generation warrants closer examination. Causal LLMs are designed for next-token prediction, whereas image DiTs operate on continuous visual representations. CDLMs must recover discrete language tokens from noisy continuous states while coordinating noise-dependent computation, vocabulary prediction, and, when used, self-conditioning. These requirements motivate a central question: • What Transformer architecture is best suited to continuous diffusion language models? In this paper, we systematically study Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce LangDiT , a backbone designed for continuous language generation. Our central finding is that architectural choices effective in causal LLMs or image diffusion models do not necessarily yield the best per- formance in CDLMs. By varying the architecture within fixed model formulations, we show that architectural design can substantially improve generation performance. We first develop and evaluate LangDiT within LangFlow (Chen et al., 2026), then transfer it to Plaid-style CDLMs (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026). In each setting, we retain the underlying representation, objective formulation, and inference sampler to study architectural changes within each formulation. The Plaid adaptation reuses a subset of the design while retaining its native prediction interface. We investigate three aspects of CDLM architecture. Within the backbone, we study how feature normalization

text: and inference sampler to study architectural changes within each formulation. The Plaid adaptation reuses a subset of the design while retaining its native prediction interface. We investigate three aspects of CDLM architecture. Within the backbone, we study how feature normalization and noise conditioning affect denoising. At the vocabulary interface, we examine how gradients through the likelihood shortcut affect the learning of token embeddings. For self- conditioning, we investigate how strongly previous predictions should guide subsequent denoising. A cumulative ablation study under shared training and evaluation settings measures the incremental effects of these components, leading to a reusable architecture that improves generation while preserving the underlying model formulation. We evaluate LangDiT on OpenWebText unconditional generation at a sequence length of 1,024. A seven-stage LangFlow ladder tracks successive architectural changes (Figure 1). At 250k updates and 128 NFE under the same schedule, GenPPL decreases from 64.26 to 53.66, while mean per-sample unigram entropy changes from 5.416 to 5.391. Separately, a 660k LangFlow checkpoint and a 520k Plaid checkpoint from 1M-update plans reach GenPPL 21.72 and 11.33 at the larger sampling budget (Table 3). These extended-training scores accompany larger changes in entropy and do not isolate the effect of architecture from training budget. We distinguish these settings throughout the paper (Figure 2). text: Continuous language diffusion and flow. Diffusion-LM and self-conditioned embedding diffusion established continuous denoising approaches to language generation (Li et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022), while CDCD and Plaid developed categorical diffusion and likelihood-based training (Dieleman et al., 2022; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023). Recent work explores flow maps (Lee et al., 2026), learned embeddings with information-based noise scheduling (Chen et al., 2026), architectural refinements (Yang et al., 2026), hyperspherical dynamics (Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026), and embedding-space flow matching (Hu et al., 2026). We study architectural design within fixed LangFlow and Plaid-style formulations. Latent representations and decoding. CoDAR uses contextual autoregressive decoding (Shen et al., 2026), while LDLM jointly learns an encoder, denoiser, and decoder with controlled gradient interac- tions (Meshchaninov et al., 2026). Cola-DLM introduces a text VAE and latent prior (Guo et al., 2026), and AURORA-LM restricts the noisy-input pathway while preserving high-capacity latents (Liang et al., 2026). Analysis of ELF links token recovery to decoder margins and denoising trajectories (Du and Ma, 2026). Our changes operate within the existing codebook-based prediction interface. Normalization and conditioning. DiT and EDM2 emphasize adaptive conditioning and magnitude control in diffusion networks (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Karras et al., 2024). RMSNorm, nGPT, and query–key normalization provide complementary approaches to controlling representation and attention scales (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019; Loshchilov et al., 2025; Henry
title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models

text: emphasize adaptive conditioning and magnitude control in diffusion networks (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Karras et al., 2024). RMSNorm, nGPT, and query–key normalization provide complementary approaches to controlling representation and attention scales (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019; Loshchilov et al., 2025; Henry et al., 2020). Related work examines attention-entropy collapse (Zhai et al., 2023) and uses query–key RMSNorm in rectified-flow Transformers (Esser et al., 2024). We examine these normalization choices alongside noise-conditioning capacity in continuous language denoising. Self-conditioning. Analog Bits, self-conditioned embedding diffusion, and LangFlow use previous predictions to guide denoising (Chen et al., 2022; Strudel et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2026). AURORA- LM addresses training–inference mismatch through trajectory consistency (Liang et al., 2026). Our entropy-based gate regulates bootstrap inputs during training while retaining the baseline loss formulation and inference sampler. Discrete diffusion and evaluation. MDLM, LLaDA, and iLLaDA advance masked diffusion language modeling (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025, 2026), while Duo connects uniform-state discrete diffusion to an underlying Gaussian process (Sahoo et al., 2025). Across diffusion families, likelihood rankings can differ from those based on generation quality and sampling cost (Sahoo et al., 2026); lower GenPPL can also accompany reduced distributional coverage (Franca and Tong, 2026). We therefore report GenPPL alongside mean per-sample unigram entropy, with explicit sampling budgets. 3. The Language Diffusion Transformer LangDiT is a

The Language Diffusion Transformer LangDiT is a Transformer denoiser for continuous language generation. Its design addresses three components of denoising: processing noisy embeddings, predicting discrete tokens, and incorporating previous predictions through self-conditioning. We develop the architecture within a LangFlow-style baseline (Chen et al., 2026), retaining its continuous representation, training and noise-schedule objective formulations, and inference sampler across architectural variants. Table 1 summarizes the design choices.

Component Design principle Implementation Backbone Separate feature-scale control from noise-dependent modulation. Backbone and Q/K RMSNorm; wider noise conditioning. Vocabulary head Control the shortcut’s forward contribution and direct codebook gradients separately. Shortcut detachment; bounded learned calibration. Self-conditioning Distinguish clean-state estimation from auxiliary feedback during training. Confidence-gated bootstrap inputs; unweighted posterior-mean estimates at inference. 3.1. Overall Denoising Pipeline At each denoising step, an input projection combines noisy token embeddings 𝑧𝛾with an optional self-conditioning estimate 𝑥SC. A bidirectional Transformer processes the sequence through attention and feed-forward sublayers modulated by the noise level 𝛾. An untied vocabulary head produces contextual logits, augmented by a gated likelihood shortcut that measures compatibility between the noisy state and the codebook. Softmax yields token probabilities, whose weighted embedding mean provides the clean-state estimate used for both sampler updates and subsequent self-conditioning. Figure 3(a) illustrates this pipeline with one Transformer block expanded. Relative to the baseline, LangDiT introduces backbone RMSNorm for feature-scale control, query– key RMSNorm for attention-logit scale control, and wider noise conditioning for greater modulation capacity. The likelihood shortcut follows a Gaussian noise model (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). We detach its embedding matrix to block the direct codebook- gradient

The likelihood shortcut follows a Gaussian noise model (Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023; Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). text: We have presented LangDiT , a Transformer backbone developed through a systematic study of architectural design for continuous diffusion language models. Its design separates feature-scale control from noise modulation, decouples the likelihood shortcut’s forward contribution from its direct codebook gradient, and distinguishes clean-state estimation from the weighting of self-conditioning inputs. Experiments on OWT-1024 demonstrate improved generation performance within LangFlow and an adaptation of compatible components to a Plaid-style model, while preserving each model’s representation, objective formulation, and inference sampler. Evaluating GenPPL alongside unigram entropy allows these gains to be interpreted together with changes in lexical diversity. These findings highlight architecture as a reusable source of improvement in CDLMs and motivate further study at larger scales and across broader generation tasks.

Limitations and Further Controls The cumulative ladder measures successive changes in a particular order. It does not by itself establish the contribution of each component in the full architecture or resolve interactions among components. Further controls would include removing individual components from the full model, crossing query–key normalization with conditioning width 128/256, and crossing shortcut detachment with calibration at a fixed conditioning width. A backbone expansion with a comparable parameter increase, together with a separate compute-matched comparison, would
title: Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models

text: removing individual components from the full model, crossing query–key normalization with conditioning width 128/256, and crossing shortcut detachment with calibration at a fixed conditioning width. A backbone expansion with a comparable parameter increase, together with a separate compute-matched comparison, would further clarify whether gains arise from the placement of conditioning capacity. The roles of the two gates also warrant separate tests. Comparing a fixed unit multiplier, a learned constant, and a learned noise-dependent multiplier would isolate the value of noise-dependent shortcut calibration. Comparing confidence gating with no gating, constant attenuation, and gates shuffled within noise bins would distinguish token-specific confidence information from generic attenuation. These controls are not included among the reported results. Such comparisons would require matched data exposure and optimization schedules, comparable tuning budgets, and explicit accounting of parameter counts and FLOPs. Independent baseline and modified-model runs across a shared seed set would assess training variability; intervals obtained by resampling generated texts do not capture that source of uncertainty. Potential failure modes include suppressing useful uncertain self-conditioning inputs or removing shortcut gradients that aid optimization. Lower feature variance alone does not establish better gen- eration. These possibilities limit the generality of conclusions drawn from the present configurations and motivate evaluating the interventions across broader settings.

text: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents Siqi Chen1,2, Zhengxi Lu1, Yuchen Yan1, Xingyu Wu1,2, Qipeng Chen1, Xin Zhang2, Aiting Liu2, Chao Deng2, Jie Liu2, Jin Ma2, Weiming Lu1, Jun Xiao1, Yongliang Shen1* 1Zhejiang University, 2Tencent. {siqichen,syl}@zju.edu.cn, daniellwang@tencent.com
title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents

text: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn inter- actions, where assigning credit to individ- ual search decisions is fundamentally diffi- cult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process- supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which be- come unreliable in deep search where observa- tions are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface ob- servations. For each query, KnowGPO de- composes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satis- fied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment- grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome- only (GRPO) and process-supervision base- lines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/KnowGPO. 1
title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents

text: LLM-based deep search agents have become a pow- erful paradigm for knowledge-intensive problem solving, coordinating multi-turn search, evidence inspection, query reformulation, and termination decisions through language-model reasoning (Yao *Corresponding author et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026a). Unlike con- ventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which typically follows a one-pass retrieve-then- read pipeline (Lewis et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024), deep search agents iteratively formulate queries, inspect evidence, update beliefs, and decide when to stop (Nakano et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025c). This makes deep search a long- horizon sequential decision problem, where suc- cess depends on adaptive decisions about what to search, what evidence to keep, and when to termi- nate. Because supervised fine-tuning mainly imi- tates surface behavior (Nakano et al., 2021; Schick et al., 2023) and cannot optimize such strategic de- cisions, reinforcement learning has become central to training competitive deep search agents (Guo et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025). However, applying reinforcement learning to deep search agents encounters three coupled diffi- culties in credit assignment (Figure 1). First, termi- nal outcome rewards used by group-relative meth- ods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025) are uniformly broadcast
title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents

text: First, termi- nal outcome rewards used by group-relative meth- ods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025) are uniformly broadcast to every action, so a single final reward cannot reveal which intermediate decisions were useful, redundant, or harmful. Second, recent process- supervision methods such as GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) that align trajectories by their intermediate states require state recurrence across trajectories, yet deep search rollouts seldom revisit the same ob- servable state even when they acquire the same evi- dence. Third, dense process rewards derived from changes in the model’s predicted answer probabil- ity, as in IGPO (Wang et al., 2026), or from learned critics and rubric-based reward models (Shi et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025, 2026b; Lu et al., 2026), provide denser signals but are driven by model-internal beliefs or learned proxies rather than by externally verified knowledge. text: obser- vations or model confidence, provides the natural signal for credit assignment in long-horizon search. We propose Knowledge-Grouped Policy Op- timization (KnowGPO), a RL framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface ob- servations. For each query, we decompose the in- formation required to derive the correct answer into a set of atomic knowledge conditions. At ev- ery step of a trajectory, we represent its state by the subset of conditions it has satisfied, called its knowledge state. We further define incremental knowledge gain, the increase in satisfied condi- tions between consecutive steps, as a process re- ward that scores each action’s immediate contri- bution. While knowledge-state grouping ensures only semantically comparable steps are contrasted, incremental gain provides the dense signal within each group, enabling fine-grained credit assign- ment without a learned critic. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within- group comparison, yielding step-level advantages that combine with episode-level outcome advan- tages through a single mixing coefficient. The result is fine-grained credit assignment for long- horizon deep search without observation match- ing, without dependence on the model’s own confi- dence, and without a learned reward model. We train Qwen3-8B with KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks: Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA. KnowGPO im- proves over outcome-only GRPO by 2.0%

We train Qwen3-8B with KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks: Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA. KnowGPO im- proves over outcome-only GRPO by 2.0% to 5.9% and consistently outperforms recent process- supervision baselines including GiGPO and IGPO, with the resulting 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source systems of up to 32B parameters. In summary, our contributions are threefold: • We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learn- ing framework that performs credit assign- ment in a query-specific knowledge state space rather than over surface observations, enabling within-group comparison across se- mantically equivalent trajectories. • We introduce incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment, providing dense step-level supervision with- out observation matching, learned critics, or reliance on model-internal probabilities. • We demonstrate that KnowGPO outper- forms outcome-based and recent process- supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2% across three deep search benchmarks, with an 8B agent matching or surpassing open-source sys- tems of up to 32B parameters. 2

text: 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Search Agent Reinforcement learning with verifiable outcome rewards has become the dominant paradigm for post-training deep search agents. Early systems train models to interleave search and reasoning through outcome-based optimization on multi-hop QA (Jin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), showing that group-relative methods such as GRPO scale to multi-turn tool use without learned value func- tions. Subsequent work scales this paradigm along two axes: harder data through knowledge graphs, web exploration, and synthetic multi-hop genera- tion (Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Du et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026e,d), and
title: Step 2 Step 3

text: refined reward shaping and policy gradient stability for long-horizon rollouts (Wu et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). Despite these advances, the supervisory signal in most systems remains a binary reward at the end of each trajectory, leaving the contribution of search decisions inside long rollouts unidentified. 2.2 Credit Assignment for Search Agents A growing line of work aims to address long- horizon credit assignment through process-level supervision. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) extends GRPO with anchor-state grouping, computing step- level advantages by matching trajectories that re- visit the same environment state; this mechanism requires reliable state recurrence, which is rare in deep search where retrieved contents and reason- ing histories are open-ended. IGPO (Wang et al., 2026) instead derives dense step rewards from the model’s own probability of producing the correct answer, sidestepping state matching but anchor- ing the signal to internal confidence that can be biased by long, noisy retrieved contexts. A par- allel direction introduces externally grounded su- pervision through learned reward models or rubric decompositions (Zhang et al., 2026b, 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025), providing denser feed- back than outcome rewards but relying on learned proxies whose calibration is itself a research ques- tion, and without producing step groupings that make semantically equivalent decisions

KnowGPO instead anchors credit assignment to an externally verifi- able representation of progress, the set of satisfied atomic knowledge conditions, and uses this repre- sentation as both the grouping criterion for within- group comparison and the basis of a process reward grounded in the environment. 3 Method 3.1 Problem Formulation We formulate deep search as a multi-turn sequen- tial decision process. Given a query Q and a refer- ence answer y∗, an agent interacts with a retrieval environment over time steps t ∈{1, . . . , T}. At each step the agent produces a reasoning trace and an action at ∈{search, answer} from its policy πθ(· | ht, Q), where ht = (a1, o1, . . . , at−1, ot−1) is the interaction history and ot is the observa- tion returned by the environment (e.g., retrieved documents for search, or a terminal signal for answer). A complete trajectory is denoted τ = (a1, o1, . . . , aT , oT ) and terminates with a binary outcome reward R(τ) = I(ans(τ) = y∗). We

A complete trajectory is denoted τ = (a1, o1, . . . , aT , oT ) and terminates with a binary outcome reward R(τ) = I(ans(τ) = y∗). We build on group-relative policy optimization, which estimates advantages from a group of N trajecto- ries sampled for the same Q and avoids learning a separate value network. The challenge addressed throughout this section is that R(τ) alone provides no signal for distinguishing useful, redundant, or harmful steps inside a long-horizon trajectory. 3.2 Knowledge State A central design choice in KnowGPO is to ab- stract the progress of a search trajectory through the task-relevant knowledge it has acquired, rather than through its surface observations. We realize this abstraction in two steps: constructing a query- specific set of atomic knowledge conditions, and representing each trajectory step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Knowledge conditions. For each query Q with reference answer y∗, we construct a finite set of atomic knowledge conditions K(Q) = {k1, . . . , kK}, (1) where each kj is a single-hop factual constraint needed to derive y∗. Intuitively, K(Q) encodes the answer’s logical skeleton: a trajectory cannot reli- ably produce y∗without acquiring every kj. We construct K(Q) through a two-stage pipeline that first identifies the

Intuitively, K(Q) encodes the answer’s logical skeleton: a trajectory cannot reli- ably produce y∗without acquiring every kj. We construct K(Q) through a two-stage pipeline that first identifies the reasoning skeleton implied by Q (with placeholders for unknown entities) and then grounds each placeholder using y∗and a successful reference trajectory. This decoupling produces a trajectory-agnostic knowledge space and ensures three properties: each condition encodes a single fact (atomicity), the conditions jointly support the full reasoning chain to y∗(completeness), and en- tity references remain consistent across the query, the answer, and the search trajectories (grounding consistency). Episode-level advantages align the policy with the final task ob- jective, and step-level advantages, computed by grouping steps under matched knowledge states, attribute credit to individual search decisions. Episode-level advantage. For each query Q, we sample N episodes {τi}N i=1 from the current policy and compute the group-normalized advantage of episode i as AE i = R(τi) −µ σ + ε , (4) where µ and σ are the empirical mean and stan- dard deviation of {R(τi)}N i=1, and ε is a small con- stant for numerical stability. This is the standard outcome-based group advantage of GRPO. Step-level advantage via knowledge-grouped comparison. To attribute credit at the step-level, we exploit the fact that the knowledge state ˜s par- titions the space of intermediate steps into seman- tically equivalent classes. Let U denote the set of distinct knowledge states observed across all N episodes for query Q. For each ˜s ∈U, we form a knowledge group G(˜s) = {(i, t) | si,t = ˜s, ai,t̸ = answer} (5) containing every non-terminal step that starts from state ˜s. Third, does the knowledge state genuinely provide a better grouping anchor than surface observations (Section 4.4)? Fourth, how does KnowGPO change search behavior, and at what training cost (Section 4.5)? 4.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate KnowGPO on three challenging deep search benchmarks that cover di- verse question distributions and difficulty levels: Xbench (Xbench-Team, 2025) (covering the 2505 and 2510 splits), BrowseComp-ZH (Zhou et al., 2025), and the text-only subset of GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023). Following standard LLM-as-judge protocols, GPT-4o (OpenAI et al., 2024) judges whether the agent’s final response matches the ground truth. All evaluations follow each bench- mark’s official protocol; we report the mean accu- racy over 3 independent runs. Baselines. We compare KnowGPO against three representative reinforcement learning approaches, all trained from the same SFT checkpoint with identical data and tool environments. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) uses only the binary outcome reward and is the dominant baseline in current open-source systems. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) introduces step-level credit assignment by grouping steps that revisit the same intermediate state and computing within-group advantages from discounted future returns. IGPO (Wang et al., 2026) assigns each step a dense reward equal to the increase in the model’s predicted probability of

IGPO (Wang et al., 2026) assigns each step a dense reward equal to the increase in the model’s predicted probability of the correct answer. In addition, we report numbers from several state- of-the-art open-source and proprietary deep search agents for context; differences in training data, con- text length, and tool stacks limit direct comparison, and we mark such systems separately. Implementation details. All trained models use Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) as the base model, with context extended to 128K tokens via YaRN (Peng et al., 2026). SFT is conducted with LlamaFactory (Zheng et al., 2024); RL training uses verl (Sheng et al., 2025). All baselines share the same SFT initialization, training data, learn- ing rate, batch size, and rollout configuration as KnowGPO; only the advantage estimator and re- ward design differ. Knowledge state verification uses DeepSeek-v3.2 as the LLM verifier; the choice and its quality analysis are reported in Appendix C. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix E. 4.2 Main Results Tables 1 and 2 report performance on all three benchmarks. We make two observations. KnowGPO consistently outperforms both outcome-only and step-level baselines. All RL approaches improve over SFT, confirming that ex- plicit policy optimization is necessary for deep search agents.

KnowGPO opens a clear gap by around step 20 and plateaus near step 32 at roughly 50%, while GRPO, GiGPO, and IGPO settle below 46%. The gap is consistent across the second half of training, sug- gesting that knowledge-grouped credit assignment provides a denser signal throughout rather than a small final-stage advantage. 4.3 Ablation Study We next ablate the components of KnowGPO. The first ablation studies the mixing coefficient ω; the second isolates the contributions of incremental knowledge gain and knowledge-state grouping; the third compares incremental gain against discounted future returns as a process reward. All ablations use the same SFT initialization and training setup as the main experiments.

The gap shows that, even when group- ing is fixed, the choice of step reward materially matters for long-horizon credit assignment. 4.4 Why Knowledge-Based Grouping Works The ablation shows that knowledge-state group- ing matters in aggregate. We now examine why it works by directly measuring the grouping behavior of three candidate anchors on real rollouts. Setup. We sample 500 queries from Xbench and BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) and rollout the SFT checkpoint up to 16 times per query, pro- ducing 5,922 valid trajectories with 55,571 steps after filtering. We compare three grouping an- chors: observation-anchored, matching steps by BGE-large cosine similarity over retrieved contents at threshold 0.9 (the protocol used by GiGPO); action-anchored, matching steps by similarity of generated queries; and knowledge-anchored (ours), matching steps by exact equality of accumulated knowledge state. Grouping quality is measured by the effective step ratio (ESR, fraction of steps in non-singleton groups), the singleton ratio, the mean non-singleton group size, and the cross-rollout cov- erage (average number of distinct rollouts per non- singleton group). Reducing redundant search is easy if the policy simply stops earlier on every query, but this would harm hard cases. To test for this failure mode, we partition 500 test queries by joint solving outcome and compare average search turns (Table 6). On queries solved exclusively by KnowGPO, KnowGPO uses 9.83 turns versus 11.55 for GRPO, a clear reduction in redundant exploration. On queries solved only by GRPO, KnowGPO still uses 10.36 turns, and on queries where both methods fail, it uses 10.85, the longest of all subsets. A representative trajectory com- parison in Appendix G shows GRPO overshooting a correct intermediate answer by four additional turns and overwriting it with a wrong one, a failure mode KnowGPO avoids. Knowledge-grouped credit adds negligible train- ing cost. A natural concern with structured pro- cess supervision is overhead. We profile per- iteration time over three training epochs (Figure 4). The training budget is dominated by operations shared with GRPO: trajectory generation (2,574s), policy update (583s), and probability computation (310s). KnowGPO-specific operations are knowl- edge verification (356s), incremental gain compu- tation (2.73s), and group construction (0.03s). Veri- fication runs asynchronously and overlaps with the next rollout, so its wall-clock cost is hidden behind generation; the two pure-bookkeeping operations together account for less than 0.08% of the budget. Knowledge-grouped credit assignment is therefore essentially free compared to GRPO. 5

text: We presented KnowGPO, a reinforcement learn- ing framework that assigns credit by aligning deep search trajectories through the task-relevant knowl- edge they have acquired, rather than through their surface observations. KnowGPO groups steps un- der matched knowledge states and uses incremental knowledge gain as a process reward grounded in the environment. Across Xbench, BrowseComp- ZH, and GAIA, KnowGPO improves over outcome- only and process-supervision baselines by 3.8% to 4.2%, with an 8B agent matching 32B open-source systems at training cost comparable to GRPO.
title: ESR ↑(%)

text: Limitations KnowGPO assumes that progress in the target task can be characterized by a finite set of veri- fiable knowledge conditions, which fits knowledge- intensive search but not more open-ended agentic tasks whose progress is harder to discretize. The fidelity of the knowledge state also depends on an LLM verifier, and although we use a strong external model with monotonic accumulation to suppress transient noise, residual errors can still propagate into step-level advantages. Our construc- tion pipeline additionally requires at least one suc- cessful reference trajectory per query to ground entity placeholders, which limits applicability to settings where successful rollouts are reachable at reasonable cost. Finally, all experiments use Qwen3-8B; whether the effects we observe trans- fer to substantially smaller or larger backbones, or to reasoning-trained initializations, remains to be verified. text: A Algorithm Details This appendix provides the full pseudocode of KnowGPO and the explicit training objective used for parameter updates. The procedure begins by sampling N trajectories for each query and run- ning the LLM verifier at every step to construct the knowledge state si,t. Trajectories are then grouped by their preceding knowledge state, and step-level advantages are computed by within-group nor- malization of incremental knowledge gain. The episode-level outcome advantage and the step-level knowledge-grouped advantage are combined with a single mixing coefficient ω and used as the per- token advantage in a PPO-style clipped objective. Algorithm 1 Knowledge-Grouped Policy Opti- mization (KnowGPO) Require: Query Q, reference y∗, conditions K(Q),policy πθ, group size N, mixing ω ▷Roll out and accumulate knowledge state 1: Sample N trajectories {τi}N i=1 ∼πθ(· | Q) 2: for each trajectory τi and step t do 3: ∆si,t ←Verifier(oi,t), K(Q)) 4: si,t = si,t−1 ∨∆si,t 5: end for ▷Episode-level advantage from outcome 6: AE i ←Normalize �R(τi)  over {R(τj)}N j=1 ▷Group steps by matched knowledge state 7: for each distinct ˜s observed do 8: G(˜s) ←{(i, t) : si,t−1 = ˜s, ai,t̸ = answer} ▷Incremental gain as step reward 9: ri,t ←∥si,t∥1 −∥si,t−1∥1 10: AS i,t ←Normalize(ri,t) over G(˜s) 11: end for ▷Combine advantages and update policy 12: Ai,t ←(1 −ω)AE i + ωAS i,t

Within each step (i, t), the advantage Ai,t is broadcast uni- formly across all tokens that compose the action ai,t and its preceding reasoning trace, following standard practice in GRPO-style training. The clip- ping ratio ϵ, KL coefficient β, and reference policy πref are inherited from the SFT checkpoint and are shared across all baselines we compare against. Asynchronous verifier execution. The verifier call on line 4 of Algorithm 1 is the heaviest op- eration introduced by KnowGPO. We run it asyn- chronously, in parallel with the next rollout batch, so that its wall-clock cost is hidden behind trajec- tory generation. Empirical timing in Section 4.5 confirms this overlap makes verification effectively free relative to GRPO. We require K(Q) to satisfy three properties. (i) Atomicity: each kj encodes a single-hop factual constraint, avoiding compound multi-hop statements inside a single condition. (ii) Completeness: the set jointly

text: for constructing the knowl- edge condition set K(Q). Three design principles. We require K(Q) to satisfy three properties. (i) Atomicity: each kj encodes a single-hop factual constraint, avoiding compound multi-hop statements inside a single condition. (ii) Completeness: the set jointly sup- ports the full reasoning chain from Q to y∗, so that omitting any kj renders y∗non-derivable. (iii) Grounding consistency: entities in each condition use consistent referential forms across Q, y∗, and search trajectories, so that hit determination is not destabilized by entity ambiguity. Bipartite graph view. We represent K(Q) as a constraint-entity bipartite graph G = (VC ∪VE, E), VC = {C1, . . . , Cm}, VE = {⟨E0⟩, ⟨E1⟩, . . . }, (10) where ⟨E0⟩is the target answer entity and an edge connects Ci to ⟨Ej⟩whenever Ci explicitly con- tains ⟨Ej⟩. We require G to be connected under BFS from ⟨E0⟩, which ensures every entity in K(Q) traces back to the answer through factual constraints and rules out isolated knowledge. Two-stage construction. Stage 1 (Query → Placeholder Knowledge). The first stage takes only Q as input and outputs placeholder condi- tions that capture the reasoning skeleton implicit in the query. Entities are denoted by placeholders ⟨E0⟩, ⟨E1⟩, . . . , where ⟨E0⟩is fixed as the target answer entity. This stage is trajectory-agnostic and does not

Entities are denoted by placeholders ⟨E0⟩, ⟨E1⟩, . . . , where ⟨E0⟩is fixed as the target answer entity. This stage is trajectory-agnostic and does not require access to y∗. Stage 2 (Placeholder Knowledge →Grounded Knowledge). The second stage takes Q, y∗, the Stage 1 placeholders, and a successful reference trajectory obtained via rejection sampling. The model grounds each placeholder ⟨Ej⟩to its real- world entity, producing the fully grounded K(Q) used at training time.

Each knowledge condition must be a **single-hop fac- tual statement**, where the intermediate entities should be denoted as <E1>, <E2>, <E3>, and so on. 2. (11) • Singleton ratio (SR): the fraction of groups con- taining only one step, SR = |{g ∈G : |g| = 1}| |G| . (13) • Cross-rollout coverage (Cross): the average number of distinct rollouts contributing to each non-singleton group. This metric distinguishes genuine cross-trajectory alignment from local within-trajectory smoothing. • ngroups: The size of the sample group associated with each grouping anchor. Qualitative case. E Implementation Details This appendix provides the full implementation details of KnowGPO and its baselines, organized into three subsections: tool environment, training configuration, and prompt formats. E.1 Tool Environment The interactive environment exposes a single search action that routes queries to Xhub Search for Chinese queries or Google Search for English queries, with language detected via Unicode char- acter ranges. The engine accepts batch inputs and returns the top-10 results per query, each compris- ing a title, URL, and snippet. To bound the context length consumed by retrieved evidence, snippets are compressed to an average of 300 tokens by a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B summarization model that preserves entities and key claims while removing boilerplate. Temporal sensitivity detection biases retrieval toward recent content for time-sensitive queries. E.2 Training Configuration Supervised fine-tuning. We first SFT Qwen3-8B on a corpus of approximately 8,100 deep search tra- jectories, constructed by combining human demon- strations with model-assisted annotation. SFT runs on 8 A100 GPUs using LLaMAFactory with stan- dard causal language modeling, for 3 epochs at learning rate 2 × 10−5 and effective batch size 64. The resulting checkpoint achieves over 98.5% for- mat accuracy on ReAct-style tool invocations and is the shared initialization for all RL methods we compare. Reinforcement learning. Following SFT, we ap- ply KnowGPO and the three RL baselines. Train- ing

text: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages? Trizal Garg, Sibayan Mitra, Arya Karanjkar, Advait Singh, Jagat Sesh Challa, Yash Sinha, Siddharth Mehrotra, Dhruv Kumar, Pratham Yogish Maliya Birla Institute of Technology and Science, Pilani {f20240338, f20240862, f20241220, f20220636, jagatsesh}@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in, {yash.sinha, siddharth.mehrotra, dhruv.kumar, f20260682}@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in
title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English:

text: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evalu- ation awareness almost entirely in English, al- though models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains al- most entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitor- ing is a safety test. Models refuse harmful re- quests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evalu- ations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users. 1
title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English:

text: Large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted by systems and users across the world, and are increasingly relied upon to refuse harmful re- quests. Their training corpora are overwhelmingly skewed towards English, often exceeding 90% of pre-training and fine-tuning data (Xu et al., 2025), yet they serve users in many other languages. The standard way to ensure reliability is to test models under controlled conditions through safety evalua- tions. These evaluations assume that behavior un- der test carries over to deployment. However, this assumption fails when a model can tell that it is be- ing tested. This ability is called evaluation aware- ness (Needham et al., 2025; Greenblatt et al., 2024). A model that recognizes an evaluation may alter its behavior, potentially making observed safety behavior different from deployment behavior (Ab- delnabi and Salem, 2025). This effect is largely studied in English. Indic languages are used by more than a billion people, yet evaluation aware- ness in these languages remains almost entirely un- studied (Yong et al., 2025; Pattnayak and Chowd- huri, 2026b). In this paper, we conduct a controlled behavioral study of evaluation awareness in five Indic lan- guages, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and Kan- nada, alongside English. We prepend one of five prompt conditions, called a cue to every request, from a plain deployment framing to an

text: controlled behavioral study of evaluation awareness in five Indic lan- guages, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, and Kan- nada, alongside English. We prepend one of five prompt conditions, called a cue to every request, from a plain deployment framing to an explicit statement that the conversation is a scored safety test. We take harmful prompts from the Toxic Ma- trix split of AI4Bharat’s IndicAlign (Khan et al., 2024) and translate them into Indic languages us- ing Claude Opus. Benign prompts come from the Dolly-T split of the same corpus, which con- tains parallel versions in all six languages, made with IndicTrans2 (Gala et al., 2023). We use four instruction-tuned models from three families for our study: Gemma-3-27B (Team et al., 2025), Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025), Qwen2.5-72B (Qwen et al., 2025), and Sarvam-M (Sarvam Foun- dation Models Team, 2025), and each model an- swers every prompt in every language under every cue . We measure refusal with an LLM judge (Zheng et al., 2023) that does not see the model, the language, or the cue. The primary judge is Gemma-4-31B-IT (Team et al., 2026) and the sec- ondary judge is GPT-6 Luna. Across all models and languages, the rise in refusal is 3.5 times larger for harmful prompts than for benign ones. We make two contributions. • To our knowledge, the first behavioral study of evaluation awareness in Indic languages. It covers four models from three families and six languages, with 47,880 judged responses that we release. • A set of cues that isolates evaluation from mere monitoring. Two of our cues state that re- sponses are logged and differ only in whether an AI safety team reviews them. 2 Related Works 2.1 Evaluation awareness and the compliance gap Recent work establishes that language models can distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts and that this recognition drives behavior. Fron- tier models show above-random evaluation aware- ness (Needham et al., 2025), and recognizing an evaluation context is empirically and conceptually distinct from the propensity to act on it (Li et al., 2026). Models shift toward the inferred training objective once they judge their outputs observed (Greenblatt et al., 2024). Models are also more sen- sitive to safety than capability evaluations (Li et al., 2026), and (Sheshadri et al., 2025) find a compli- ance gap above 1 percent

Models are also more sen- sitive to safety than capability evaluations (Li et al., 2026), and (Sheshadri et al., 2025) find a compli- ance gap above 1 percent in only five of twenty-five models. Knecht et al. (2026) find that verbalised evaluation awareness (VEA) has limited effect on model behaviour. Existing study in these papers involves English only. We ask whether the behavioural findings sur- vive a change of language, using content-matched requests in five Indic languages and English across three model families. 2.2 Multilingual and Indic safety evaluation A persistent gap exists between the languages mul- tilingual safety research covers and those deployed models serve; (Yong et al., 2025) survey its size and durability. Subsequent work shows that safety behavior varies with language: models handle identical content differently under code-switching (Yoo et al., 2025), across twelve Indic languages where safety judgments drift sharply between translations (Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026b), and under jailbreak pressure in South Asian lan- guages (Pattnayak and Chowdhuri, 2026a). Chain- of-thought monitoring likewise degrades across typologically diverse languages (Onyame et al., 2026). These works hold evaluation context fixed while varying language; we vary both, enabling an evaluation-awareness claim. 3 Experimental Setup 3.1 Data, languages, and models We worked on six languages, namely English, Hindi,

Figure 1 sum- marises the design. 3.3 Measuring refusal We label refusals with an LLM judge that reads only the prompt and the response and returns RE- FUSAL, COMPLY, or UNUSABLE. text: same original prompt are therefore correlated, and treating them as independent would understate the standard errors. We use the McNemar test to compare two cues within one model and language. Prompts that re- ceive the same label under both cues carry no information about the cue, so the test uses only prompts whose label changed. It then checks whether these changes lean towards one cue more than the other. We apply it to the primary con- trast, eval_explicit against deploy, on harm- ful and benign prompts, and to the secondary con- trast, eval_log against monitor_log, on harm- ful prompts. We use the Cochran Q test to record refusal un- der 5 cues, for each model, language using the same prompts. We run tests for every model and language separately on the harmful and benign prompts, and use the Holm correction within each arm (24 tests each). We use logistic regression to measure how much each factor (model, language or cue) changes the odds of refusal, while holding the other factors fixed. This is expressed using an odds ratio. Due to the correlation between responses for the same prompt, we fit the regression with GEE, which groups each prompt’s responses together. text: We studied evaluation awareness in five Indic lan- guages alongside English. A cue that signals a safety evaluation raises refusal of harmful prompts in every model and language. On average, the rise in Indic languages is at least as large as in English. Refusal rises even with a cue that never uses the words test or evaluation. A safety test that a model can recognize may therefore make Indic safety look better than it is. Evaluation awareness is not an English-only problem, and we must con- sider it when designing multilingual safety evalua- tions. We release our dataset, implementation, and experimental framework; the source code is avail- able at: https://github.com/innovate637/ IndicEvalAwareness/ Limitations 1. Model coverage: Due to resource constraints, we test only open-weight models of 24B to 72B parameters, with reasoning disabled. Larger models and reasoning models are not covered. 4

text: 2. Translated prompts: Indic harmful prompts are LLM translations (Claude Opus) of English originals, and native speakers verified only a small sample. 3. Judge validation: All refusal labels come from a single LLM judge, whose agreement with na- tive review is lower in Telugu (κ = 0.56). Each language was reviewed by one annotator who could see the judge’s label. Ethical Considerations This study measures refusal, so it necessarily in- volves harmful requests. Every harmful prompt comes from the Toxic Matrix split of AI4Bharat In- dicAlign (Khan et al., 2024), a peer-reviewed and publicly released corpus, and the benign prompts come from the Dolly-T split of the same resource. We wrote no new harmful requests; we only trans- lated existing English prompts into five Indic lan- guages. We release all 47,880 judged responses on GitHub for research on model safety. Some re- sponses comply with harmful requests, so the re- lease carries a content warning. Annotation exposed native speakers to model re- sponses to harmful requests. Annotation was per- formed by the authors and colleagues who are na- tive speakers of the respective languages, not by paid crowdworkers. All annotators gave consent and could stop at any time. We used Claude Opus to translate the harmful prompts and LLM judges to label refusals (Sec- tion 3). Acknowledgments We acknowledge the

No Indic penalty for the second judge; native-speaker agreement is lower only in Telugu. D Hypothesis Testing As we run many tests at once, some look significant purely by chance. We use the Holm correction within each group of related tests to keep the overall chance of even one false positive within that group of tests at or below 5%. We call a result significant when its Holm-adjusted p-value is below 0.05. We use the McNemar test to compare two cues within one model and language. Prompts that receive the same label under both cues carry no information about the cue, so the test uses only prompts whose label changed. It then checks whether these changes lean towards one cue more than the other. We apply it to the primary contrast, eval_explicit against deploy, on harmful and benign prompts, and to the secondary contrast, eval_log against monitor_log, on harmful prompts. Each family of 24 tests is Holm-corrected separately. We report each change as a difference in refusal rate with a 95% confidence interval from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of the prompts (Appendix J). Our null hypothesis is that, for one model in one language and one arm, the probability of refusal is the same under both cues. By using the Cochran Q Test, we extend the McNemar test to record refusal under 5 cues, for each model, language using the same prompts. The test searches for prompts whose decision changed and checks if those changes favour some cues over others. We run tests for every model and language separately on the harmful and benign prompts, and use the Holm correction within each arm (24 tests each). Our null hypothesis is that under one arm, for one model, in one language, the probability of refusal is the same under all five cues. We use logistic regression to measure how much each factor (model, language or cue) changes the odds of refusal, while holding the other factors fixed. This is expressed using an Odds Ratio. Due to the correlation between responses for the same prompt, we fit the regression with GEE, which groups each prompt’s responses together. text: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty Chengze Xie∗ Xuan Wang† Ying Ding‡ Hairong Wang§ Yan Li¶
title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes

text: We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies. 1
title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes

text: Adapting treatment to the evolving condition of a patient has received considerable attention in medicine, with success reported in a broad range of applications [4, 7, 25, 26, 39, 50]. In oncology, adaptive therapy pursues this idea to delay the emergence of drug resistance [18]. Its rationale is that, under continuous treatment, drug-sensitive cells are eliminated and drug-resistant cells are left to grow without competition. By pausing treatment once the tumor has responded and resuming it once the tumor has regrown, clinicians can retain sensitive cells that continue to suppress the resistant ones [18, 45]. This approach was tested in a pilot clinical trial of the drug abiraterone for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer [52, 53]. In this clinical trial, clinicians paused abiraterone once prostate-specific antigen (PSA), a blood marker that tracks tumor burden, fell below half of its pretreatment value, and resumed it once PSA returned to the pretreatment value, a protocol we refer to as AT50. Compared with a contemporaneous cohort who received continuous treatment with abiraterone as the standard of care, the median time to progression more than doubled under AT50, while patients received no abiraterone during 46% of their time in the clinical trial [52]. Despite its remarkable success, AT50 is by design a simple heuristic in the sense that it applies the same pair of thresholds
title: Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes

text: doubled under AT50, while patients received no abiraterone during 46% of their time in the clinical trial [52]. Despite its remarkable success, AT50 is by design a simple heuristic in the sense that it applies the same pair of thresholds to every patient and responds only to the most recent PSA value. In addition, its benefit has so far been observed in only 17 patients, and, based on the models fitted to the same data, other schedules are expected to further improve outcomes [52]. Existing efforts toward more refined schedules include optimal control of competition models [9], deep reinforcement learning (RL) for controlling the emergence of drug resistance [12], and more recently RL policies trained within models calibrated to prostate cancer patients [16,33,34]. Nevertheless, these policies are evaluated within the same models used for their training, and their performance beyond these models remains largely unexamined. Ideally, one would like to learn, in a data-driven manner, a dynamic treatment policy that is more sophisticated than AT50, attains improved performance, and generalizes to the broad population of patients beyond those enrolled in the clinical trial. More importantly, such a policy should remain reliable under the shifts between training and deployment that are common in clinical practice [13]. ∗Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Texas A&M University. text: To be more specific, we identify three properties that a treatment policy learned from data should possess. To begin with, the policy should generalize in the sense that the performance it attains on the patients seen during training carries over to new patients drawn from the same population. From the perspective of contextual and hidden-parameter Markov decision processes (MDPs) [11,19,28,44], the natural goal without interacting with a new patient is a policy that is near-optimal on average over the population [49], and generalization across populations of environments has been studied extensively in deep RL [24,46]. With a simulation model, we can pursue this goal by training on as many simulated patients as needed, far beyond the 17 patients of the pilot clinical trial, provided that the simulated population is broad enough to contain the patients of interest. In addition, the policy should be robust to errors in its observation. In particular, PSA serves only as an indirect measure of the underlying tumor burden, and radiographic progression can occur without any rise in PSA [6]. Consequently, the quantity on which the policy acts may deviate from the quantity it aims to control, while RL policies are known to be sensitive to even small adversarial perturbations of their observations [21,51]. Most importantly, the policy should retain reliable performance under shifts in the
title: To be more specific, we identify three properties that a treatment policy learned from data should possess.

text: policy acts may deviate from the quantity it aims to control, while RL policies are known to be sensitive to even small adversarial perturbations of their observations [21,51]. Most importantly, the policy should retain reliable performance under shifts in the patient dynamics. Indeed, the parameters of the model, including the strength of competition between sensitive and resistant cells on which the success of adaptive therapy hinges, are estimated from the sparse PSA records of a small cohort of patients, and are hence subject to considerable statistical error [5,52]. Such shifts are particularly consequential in medical domains, where real patients are scarce and the dynamics of a patient may further change during treatment [1]. To address these requirements, in this manuscript we propose to study adaptive therapy through the lens of robust contextual MDPs. A contextual MDP [19] describes a family of MDPs whose transition dynamics are indexed by a context, drawn from a population and hidden from the decision maker. Adaptive therapy fits naturally into this framework once we identify the context with the patient, namely the initial composition of the tumor together with its competition and growth parameters. Each patient then defines its own tumor dynamics, to be inferred by the clinician from the history of PSA measurements and treatment decisions, and AT50 is one particular policy acting on
title: To be more specific, we identify three properties that a treatment policy learned from data should possess.

text: the tumor together with its competition and growth parameters. Each patient then defines its own tumor dynamics, to be inferred by the clinician from the history of PSA measurements and treatment decisions, and AT50 is one particular policy acting on this history. By viewing the patient as a context, we treat generalization and robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics in a unified manner, since both concern the population from which the context is drawn. Specifically, generalization requires the policy to perform well on new contexts drawn from this population, which can be attained by training on sufficiently many sampled contexts, while robustness requires the policy to remain reliable when the context deviates from this population and thereby shifts the transition kernel that it determines. To attain such robustness, we draw on robust MDPs, in which one seeks the best worst-case performance over an ambiguity set of transition kernels, and which have been studied extensively for standard MDPs [22, 31, 38, 40, 41, 48, 51]. We carry this viewpoint over to the contextual MDP and formulate robustness as a Markov game between the controller and the context, in which the context may deviate adversarially from the population from which it is drawn [29, 32]. To account for errors in the observation, we further train the policy under random perturbations of

text: game between the controller and the context, in which the context may deviate adversarially from the population from which it is drawn [29, 32]. To account for errors in the observation, we further train the policy under random perturbations of the measured PSA. Within a model of abiraterone therapy fitted to clinical data [52], which we refer to as the nominal model, the resulting robust policies substantially outperform AT50. In addition, we attain robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics at almost no price in the nominal model, and the resulting policy nearly Pareto-dominates the nominally trained policy, i.e., the policy trained in the nominal model with exact observations, under a broad range of realistic errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. First, we formulate adaptive therapy as a contextual MDP in which the patient is modeled as a hidden context, and find that a policy learned within this formulation substantially outperforms AT50 and general- izes to patients fitted to clinical data. Within the competition model of [52], the learned policy extends the mean progression-free time from 29.58 months under AT50 to 50.35 months, while treating in a comparable fraction of months. In addition, on the 32 patients whose initial tumor compositions are fitted to clinical data in [52], policies

text: policy extends the mean progression-free time from 29.58 months under AT50 to 50.35 months, while treating in a comparable fraction of months. In addition, on the 32 patients whose initial tumor compositions are fitted to clinical data in [52], policies trained on a broad synthetic population constructed without reference to these patients perform comparably to policies trained on a population calibrated to them. Hence, generalization to the patients of interest can be attained by training on sufficiently many simulated patients drawn from a broad population, without tailoring the population to these patients. Second, we find that errors in PSA of realistic magnitude substantially reduce the benefit of policies that do not account for them. Specifically, under random errors of up to about 20% of the true PSA value, the nominally trained policy loses a substantial part of its benefit, and AT50 performs only marginally better than continuous treatment. By training under such errors, we obtain a policy that retains the benefit of 2

text: adaptive therapy in the sense that its performance under such errors nearly matches that without them. Finally, we formulate robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics as a Markov game between the controller and the context over an ambiguity set of transition kernels [29], and find that the resulting kernel-robust policy nearly Pareto-dominates the nominally trained policy and AT50 across all the conditions we consider. Specifically, the kernel-robust policy (1) performs nearly as well as the nominally trained policy in the nominal model, (2) substantially outperforms every other type of policy under shifts in the dynamics, and (3) substantially improves on the nominally trained policy and AT50 even under errors in the observation. Our findings suggest that robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics can be attained at almost no price in the nominal model, and that the resulting policy remains robust against a broad spectrum of errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. In view of this, we believe that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning adaptive therapy policies. The rest of this manuscript is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce contextual MDPs and their robust counterparts, and formulate adaptive therapy within this framework. We present the numerical experiments in Section 3, and conclude the manuscript in Section 4.

text: 2.2 Adaptive Therapy as a Contextual MDP We adopt the model of abiraterone therapy in [52], which describes the competition between drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cancer cells. Let S(τ) and R(τ) denote the numbers of drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cells at time τ, measured in days, and let u(τ) ∈{0, 1} indicate whether abiraterone is administered. The dynamics are given by dS(τ) dτ = rSS(τ) 1 −S(τ) + R(τ) κ �1 −λu(τ)  ! , dR(τ) dτ = rRR(τ)  1 −αS(τ) + R(τ) κ  , (2.4) where κ is the carrying capacity, i.e., the maximal number of cells supported by the available nutrients and space, and rS = βγS and rR = βγR are the growth rates of the sensitive and resistant cells per day, with base rates γS, γR and a common factor β scaling both rates. In essence, (2.4) describes the different responses of the drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cells to abi- raterone and the competition between them, which together underlie the rationale of adaptive therapy. Specifically, the sensitive cells depend on testosterone for survival and proliferation, while the resistant cells are independent of testosterone [52]. Since the synthesis of testosterone is inhibited by abiraterone, the sensitive cells utilize nutrients and space less efficiently under treatment, which is modeled in (2.4) by a reduction of their carrying capacity by

Since the synthesis of testosterone is inhibited by abiraterone, the sensitive cells utilize nutrients and space less efficiently under treatment, which is modeled in (2.4) by a reduction of their carrying capacity by the fraction λ ∈(0, 1). In contrast, the resistant cells are not affected by abiraterone, and their growth is suppressed only through the competition from the sensitive cells, whose competitive effect on the resistant cells is measured by α. Consequently, once the sensitive cells are depleted under continuous treatment, the resistant cells are released from competition and eventually dominate the tumor. In adaptive therapy, treatment is instead paused before such depletion occurs, which allows the sensitive cells to recover during the treatment break and to continue suppressing the resistant ones. In par- ticular, the treatment decisions are made based on the measured PSA, which is affected by analytical and biological variation [35], and serves only as an indirect measure of the underlying tumor burden even when measured exactly [6]. The response of a patient to the treatment may also deviate from the nominal model in Section 2.2. Indeed, the key parameters of the nominal model are estimated from a small cohort of pa- tients and are hence subject to considerable statistical error, while

Indeed, the key parameters of the nominal model are estimated from a small cohort of pa- tients and are hence subject to considerable statistical error, while the patient population and the disease dynamics may shift between learning and deployment [13], or even during treatment. For instance, tumors may develop new mechanisms of resistance to abiraterone during treatment [1]. Since the learned policy tai- lors its decisions to the PSA trajectories generated by the nominal model, its performance may deteriorate substantially in the presence of such uncertainty. In view of this, we seek policies that are robust against both errors in the observation and shifts in the patient dynamics. To this end, we model the errors in the observation as random, and account for shifts in the patient dynamics through the lens of distributionally robust optimization (DRO) [2, 3, 10, 17, 27, 37], in which one seeks the best worst-case performance over an ambiguity set of distributions. Following the game-theoretic view of distributionally robust MDPs [29, 32], we formulate robustness to such shifts as a Markov game between the controller and an adversary acting on the transition kernel. 6

text: 2.3.1 Errors in the Observation To account for errors in the measured PSA, we model the observation at visit t as yt = log (Bt/B0) + δt, |δt| ≤ε, (2.7) where δt denotes the error at visit t, whose magnitude is bounded by ε, and the exact observation (2.6) corresponds to δt = 0. Both the policy and the forced-treatment rule act on the perturbed observation, and hence an error may also delay the restart of treatment required by the forced-treatment rule, which we refer to as the forced restart. Since the measured PSA is affected by analytical and within-subject biological variation [35], we model the errors as random, and refer to them as random perturbations. Specifically, every δt is drawn independently from the uniform distribution on [−ε, ε]. We then learn policies that account for such errors by solving (2.1) under the observation (2.7). 2.3.2 Robustness to Shifts in the Patient Dynamics To account for shifts in the patient dynamics, we allow the transition kernel of each patient to change in every month within an ambiguity set Pc of transition kernels. After describing the experimental setup in Section 3.1, we show in Section 3.2 that a policy learned from the contextual MDP (2.1) substantially improves on AT50 without administering more drug. Such a policy, however, acts on PSA as if it were exact. In Section 3.3, we find that errors in PSA of realistic magnitude substantially reduce the benefit of this policy, while by training under random perturbations we retain the benefit of adaptive therapy under such errors. We then turn to shifts in the patient dynamics, and show in Section 3.4 that by solving the kernel-robust formulation (2.8), we attain robustness to such shifts at almost no price in the nominal model, and in Section 3.5 that the resulting 7

All learned policies are parameterized by a gated recurrent unit (GRU) network [8] acting on features of the history ht, and trained by proximal policy optimization (PPO) [42] for 2,000 updates, each with 512 patients newly sampled from the training population. text: generated by held-out kernels, while sacrificing almost no performance when the dynamics evolve as anticipated. 3.5 Universal Benefits of Kernel-Robust RL So far, we have evaluated random-perturbation RL and kernel-robust RL only under the source of uncertainty that each policy is trained against. In deployment, however, the source of uncertainty is not known in advance, and we would like a single policy that performs well under all of them. We therefore cross-evaluate the two policies, i.e., we evaluate random-perturbation RL under shifts in the dynamics and kernel-robust RL with training radius ρtr = 0.25 under random perturbations of PSA, and compare both policies with nominal RL and the two clinical rules in Figure 4. We find that kernel-robust RL nearly Pareto-dominates nominal RL and AT50 across the five conditions of Figure 4, namely the nominal model, the evaluation radii ρ ∈{0, 0.25, 1} on the training kernels, and random perturbations of PSA. Indeed, the polygon of kernel-robust RL encloses the polygon of AT50, and lies outside the polygon of nominal RL on every axis except the nominal model. In particular, kernel-robust RL forgoes 1.58 months compared with nominal RL in the nominal model, and attains the highest value under every shift in the dynamics, with 53.31, 46.57, and 23.26 months at ρ ∈{0, 0.25, 1}, compared with 45.74, 39.12, and

Under random perturbations of PSA, which it never encounters during training, kernel-robust RL still improves on nominal RL, with 38.65 compared with 32.96 months. In addition, AT50 falls below kernel-robust RL, and indeed below all learned policies, in every condition. On the other hand, by comparing kernel-robust RL with random-perturbation RL in Figure 4, we ob- serve that each of the two policies attains the highest value under the source of uncertainty it is trained against. Specifically, random-perturbation RL attains 44.49 months under random perturbations of PSA, compared with 38.65 months for kernel-robust RL, while kernel-robust RL attains higher values than random- perturbation RL under every shift in the dynamics. In summary, kernel-robust RL nearly Pareto-dominates nominal RL and AT50 across the sources of uncertainty, in the sense that it nearly matches nominal RL in the nominal model, outperforms every other policy under shifts in the dynamics, and substantially improves on nominal RL and AT50 under errors in PSA. Specifically, at ρ = 1 on the training kernels, it harms between 8.4% and 16.7% of the fitted patients, compared with 47.3% and 79.3% for nominal RL and AT50, and on the held-out kernels it harms none of them, compared with 13.3% and 63.6% (Table 8). In summary, by training on a broad synthetic population constructed without the fitted patients, we attain on these patients a performance comparable to that obtained with a population calibrated to them, in line with Theorem 2.1, and retain the benefits of both random-perturbation RL and kernel-robust RL. 4 Concluding Remarks In this manuscript, we study adaptive therapy through the lens of robust contextual MDPs, in which the patient is modeled as a hidden context drawn from a population. To account for the uncertainty beyond the variation across patients, we further train the policy under random perturbations of the measured biomarker and against an adversary acting on the transition kernel. Within a model of abiraterone therapy fitted to clinical data, we find that (1) a policy learned within this formulation substantially outperforms AT50 and generalizes to the fitted patients from a broad population constructed without them, (2) errors in PSA of realistic magnitude substantially reduce the benefit of policies that do not account for them, while by training under such

text: substantially outperforms AT50 and generalizes to the fitted patients from a broad population constructed without them, (2) errors in PSA of realistic magnitude substantially reduce the benefit of policies that do not account for them, while by training under such errors we retain the benefit of adaptive therapy, and (3) we attain robustness to shifts in the patient dynamics at almost no price in the nominal model, with the resulting policy nearly Pareto- dominating nominal RL and AT50 across all the errors and shifts we consider. In view of this, we believe that robust RL offers a principled route toward adaptive treatment policies that remain reliable beyond the model in which they are learned. B Implementation Details B.1 Patient Model In the public code and data of [52], the PSA records and the fitted initial cell numbers are available for 32 patients, namely 17 patients of the pilot clinical trial and 15 patients of the contemporaneous cohort who received continuous treatment with abiraterone as the standard of care. Since the records of 25 patients begin before the first dose of abiraterone, we follow the public code to reconstruct the daily treatment indicator of each patient from the recorded treatment history, integrate (2.4) with (α, β) = (6, 8) from the fitted initial cell numbers along the reconstructed indicator, and take the cell numbers on the day of the first dose as the fitted initial state (S0, R0). Throughout, we integrate (2.4) by the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method with step size 1 in τ, and truncate S and R to [0, κ] after every step, as in the public code. For all 32 patients, we reproduce the trajectories computed by the public code up to a relative error below 10−13. B.2 Training Populations For Dcal, we select one of the 32 fitted initial states uniformly at random, multiply S0 and R0 by independent lognormal factors with log-standard deviation 0.2, and set (α, β) = (6, 8). text: B.2 Training Populations For Dcal, we select one of the 32 fitted initial states uniformly at random, multiply S0 and R0 by independent lognormal factors with log-standard deviation 0.2, and set (α, β) = (6, 8). For Dwide, we draw α ∼U[2, 8], β ∼U[6, 10], B0 ∼U[0.1κ, 0.8κ], and the initial resistant fraction R0/B0 log-uniformly on [0.001, 0.5]. The range of α extends from the value assumed in the earlier model of [53] to above the fitted value 6, and the range of β lies within 25% of the fitted value 8. We take the ranges of B0 and R0/B0 from the priors of [5], with the upper end of B0 lowered from κ to 0.8κ to keep the progression threshold 1.2B0 below the carrying capacity, and with R0/B0 drawn log-uniformly to adequately represent patients with few resistant cells. The virtual test population is drawn from Dcal with a fixed seed. text: B.4 Policy Network and Training The input of the policy network at visit t consists of six features of ht, namely yt, the previous action, the elapsed time, the fraction of treated months, the time since the last change of action, and an indicator of forced treatment. We map these features through a linear layer with 64 units and tanh activation to a GRU with 64 hidden units, followed by linear heads for the action logits and the value. At visits with forced treatment, we exclude the action at = 0 by masking its logit. The loss of PPO combines the clipped surrogate objective with clipping parameter 0.2, the value loss with coefficient 0.5, and the entropy bonus with coefficient 0.01, where the advantages are computed by generalized advantage estimation with parameter 0.95. In each update, we minimize the loss by the Adam optimizer with learning rate 3×10−4 over four epochs with four minibatches, clip the gradient norm at 0.5, and stop the update once the approximate Kullback- Leibler divergence between the new and old policies exceeds 0.03. In training, we divide the reward rc of Section 2.2 by T. For every combination of policy type, training radius, and training population, we train three policies with the random seeds 11, 23, and 37, and report each policy after the final

B.5 Kernel Adversary We parameterize the kernel adversary by a network of the same architecture as the policy network, and train it by PPO with the same hyperparameters, using the negative of the reward of the controller. In solving (2.8), we alternate between four adversary updates with the policy fixed and one policy update with the adversary fixed. The adversary selects the generating kernel of month t before observing at, based on the observation yt, the previous action at−1, the elapsed time t/T, and the one-hot encoding of the kernel it proposed in the previous month. We use its output head to parameterize a categorical distribution over the K = 32 generating kernels. In accordance with (2.9), the patient evolves under the proposed kernel with probability ρ and under a uniformly drawn generating kernel with probability 1 −ρ, and the adversary does not observe which of the two occurs. We initialize the output head of the adversary at zero, and hence the adversary proposes the kernels uniformly at random at initialization. B.6
