text: At evaluation, the learned policies select their most likely action at every visit. All methods are evaluated on the same test patients with the same random numbers, and on the fitted patients, each patient is evaluated under 50 independent replicates of the random perturbations. For every policy π and evaluation radius ρ > 0, we estimate the robust value minσ J(π, σ; D) of π by training a new best-response adversary against π, held fixed, for 2,000 PPO updates, on patients drawn from the calibrated population Dcal for the virtual test population and on the fitted patients for the fitted test population, and average the performance of the policy against this adversary, which samples its actions, over 32 independent repetitions. It should be noted that the best-response adversary is computed numerically, and the value attained against it hence provides an upper estimate of the exact robust value. AT50 and continuous treatment are evaluated against their own best-response adversaries. Under shifts in the dynamics, we compute Gon(c) under the same adversary, held fixed, acting on the continuous-treatment trajectory, with common random numbers. text: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its inter- mediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among dec- larations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessar- ily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LEANGRAPHSEARCH, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib’s forward dependencies and tra- verses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LEANGRAPHSEARCH links each declaration to the premises it de- pends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from se- mantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval bench- marks, LEANGRAPHSEARCH improves recall by up to 12 percentage points over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR by up to 3.7 percentage points. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into im- proved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LEANGRAPHSEARCH into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LEANGRAPHSEARCH improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns

Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LEANGRAPHSEARCH improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to the vanilla prover and at most 10% com- pared to LeanSearch v2, showing a better accuracy–cost tradeoff. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery. 1

text: Formal theorem proving expresses mathematical statements and proofs in a formal language, allow- ing a proof assistant such as Lean to verify their correctness (de Moura & Ullrich, 2021). Search en- gines support the proving process by helping users and automated provers locate useful definitions, theorems, and lemmas within large mathematical libraries such as Mathlib (The mathlib Commu- nity, 2020; Yang et al., 2023; Mikuła et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2026). Existing retrieval systems, such as LeanExplore (Asher, 2025), LeanFinder (Lu et al., 2026), and LeanSearch v2 (Gao et al., 2026), address this need by identifying library declarations relevant to a target theorem or an intermediate goal. However, their limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations may miss supporting lemmas that share little lexical similarity with the query but occur in proofs of related problems (Shen et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026). A key observation is that declarations relevant to a target theorem can serve as starting points for discovering supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependencies. These dependencies connect dec- larations to their direct and indirect premises, providing extra paths to useful lemmas that are less ∗Equal contribution. 1 arXiv:2610.22339v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026

To capture and exploit this structure, we introduce LEANGRAPH- SEARCH (Fig. 1), a graph-based retrieval framework for Lean 4 theorem proving. It constructs a directed graph from Mathlib’s forward dependencies, representing declarations as nodes and link- ing each declaration to the premises it directly depends on. Searching this graph from semantically relevant declarations extends retrieval beyond direct query matching, helping users and automated provers discover supporting premises that may otherwise be difficult to locate. Searching this graph from semantically relevant declarations extends retrieval beyond direct query matching, helping users and automated provers discover supporting premises that may otherwise be difficult to locate. To search the constructed dependency graph, LEANGRAPHSEARCH uses the target query to guide traversal along formal dependencies. Given an informal description or a formal goal, it first re- trieves declarations using embeddings and reranks them against the query to select semantically relevant seeds. The seed relevance scores are normalized to form the personalization distribution for personalized PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998), which propagates relevance along dependency edges while repeatedly returning to the seeds, thereby expanding the candidate set. Finally, LEANGRAPH- SEARCH reranks the expanded candidates against the original query and combines these second-pass relevance scores with query-specific graph scores to produce the final ranking. We evaluate LEANGRAPHSEARCH on both standalone premise retrieval and downstream formal theorem proving. For premise retrieval, LEANGRAPHSEARCH improves Recall@100 from 82.7% with LeanSearch v2 to 94.7% on the 810-query fair subset of MathlibQR (Gao et al., 2026), confirming that dependency graph search effectively recovers additional relevant lemmas. On MathlibMPR (Gao et al., 2026), it improves proof route-level premise coverage, increasing Cov- ered@20 from 39.1% to 42.8% and Covered@50 from 41.3% to 44.2%. These results suggest that dependency-aware retrieval better recovers complete premise sets along

text: Mathematical theorem proving can be carried out informally in natural language and mathematical notation or formally in a language checked by a proof assistant such as Lean (de Moura & Ullrich, 2021). Large language model (LLM)-based approaches to formal proving include generating tac- tics within proof-state search (Yang et al., 2023; Thakur et al., 2024) and generating and refining 2
title: LEANGRAPHSEARCH

text: LEANGRAPHSEARCH proof scripts through verifier feedback, often guided by informal proof sketches (Kung et al., 2026). Throughout this paper, mathematical search refers to retrieving library declarations for formal prov- ing, using either informal or formal queries. For additional related work, see Appendix A. Search for Formal Mathematics. Prior work shows that retrieving reusable library facts improves formal proof construction (Mikuła et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025). Magnushammer learns premise selection through contrastive training and reranking for Isabelle (Mikuła et al., 2024), while ReProver and REAL-Prover condition tactic generation on retrieved Lean premises (Yang et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025). LeanPremise supports premise selection in user-specific con- texts (Zhu et al., 2026), and LeanStateSearch adapts tokenization and reranking to formal proof-state queries (Tao et al., 2025). Complementary search systems help locate declarations from mathemat- ical descriptions: LeanExplore combines formal statements with informal descriptions for semantic search (Asher, 2025), and Lean Finder learns intent-aware embeddings from synthesized queries and preference feedback (Lu et al., 2026). LeanSearch v2 extends this line of work to global premise retrieval, combining embedding-based search and reranking with iterative sketch–retrieve–reflect cycles to gather supporting premises for an entire proof (Gao et al., 2026). Graph structure has been used to guide retrieval in both natural-language corpora and formal libraries. GraphRAG builds an entity graph and community summaries for query-focused summarization (Edge et al., 2024), while HippoRAG applies personalized PageR- ank to a knowledge graph for multi-hop retrieval (Jim´enez Guti´errez et al., 2024). KG2RAG starts from semantically retrieved chunks and uses a knowledge graph to expand and organize evi- dence (Zhu et al., 2025). In formal mathematical search, LeanExplore uses declaration dependencies to generate informal descriptions and incorporates PageRank centrality as a ranking feature (Asher, 2025). LeanSearch v2 also processes dependencies bottom-up when constructing declaration de- scriptions (Gao et al., 2026). To learn graph-aware representations for premise selection, Petrovˇciˇc et al. (2025) combine textual embeddings with a relational graph neural network over state–premise and premise–premise dependencies. 3 LEANGRAPHSEARCH We introduce a graph-based retrieval framework for Lean theorem proving that exploits structural relationships among declarations. It represents Mathlib as a directed declaration dependency graph (Fig. 2 (a)) and uses query-aware propagation to expand from semantically relevant declarations to their formal prerequisites (Fig. 2 (b)). Semantic relevance and dependency structure jointly guide promising declaration selection, followed by reranking to produce the final ranked list.

Semantic relevance and dependency structure jointly guide promising declaration selection, followed by reranking to produce the final ranked list. 3.1 TASK FORMULATION Mathematical Retrieval. We study library declaration retrieval for theorem proving in Lean 4 (de Moura & Ullrich, 2021). Let L = {di}n i=1 denote the Mathlib declaration corpus. Each dec- laration di is identified by its name and associated with its formal statement and, when available, a natural-language description1. A retrieval query q can contain an informal mathematical description, a formal Lean statement, a proof state, or a combination of these. It may describe a target theorem or request a definition or lemma needed at an intermediate proof step. Given a query q, the retriever returns up to K declarations from L ranked by retrieval score, denoted R(q) = {dj}K j=1. We consider two complementary objectives: locating an individual declaration that matches the query and retrieving supporting premises for a target theorem. In the latter setting, a useful declaration may address an intermediate object or a side condition, and several declara- tions may be needed to support a complete proof. Retrieval must therefore capture the relevance of declarations in a proof, even when their statements differ substantially

This separates the query-level retrieval interface from the policy that determines when to invoke it. 3.2 DECLARATION DEPENDENCY GRAPH CONSTRUCTION LEANGRAPHSEARCH constructs a directed graph G = (V, E) from the structural references in Mathlib through static analysis with the jixia tool (frenzymath, 2024). Each node i ∈V repre- sents one declaration together with its formal statement and, when available, its natural-language description. A directed edge i →j indicates that declaration i references declaration j in its type or value. Edges therefore point from declarations to their dependencies, allowing traversal from a query-relevant declaration to the definitions and lemmas underlying its statement or implementation. This graph provides explicit formal dependency structure that complements embedding-based se- mantic similarity. Starting from a semantically relevant declaration, traversal can reveal potentially useful supporting declarations, including dependencies shared by declarations with different sur- face forms. The graph thus augments retrieval with formal structural relationships while leaving the underlying Mathlib corpus unchanged. 3.3 GRAPH-BASED RETRIEVAL Semantic Seed Retrieval. Given a query q, LEANGRAPHSEARCH first retrieves semanti- cally related declarations as seeds for graph propagation using the embedding–reranker retrieval pipeline (Gao et al., 2026). Given a query q, LEANGRAPHSEARCH first retrieves semanti- cally related declarations as seeds for graph propagation using the embedding–reranker retrieval pipeline (Gao et al., 2026). The query is encoded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025) to retrieve an initial candidate set. Each query–declaration pair is then scored for relevance using the reranker logits produced by Qwen3-Reranker-8B (Zhang et al., 2025). The top K declarations ranked by these scores form the semantic seed set S. 4

text: LEANGRAPHSEARCH Query-personalized Propagation. To exploit the dependency structure described in Section 3.2, LEANGRAPHSEARCH propagates a query-specific seed distribution over the graph. Specifically, LEANGRAPHSEARCH normalizes the semantic seed scores to obtain a seed distribution v over graph nodes, assigning zero mass to nodes outside the seed set S: vi = qi · 1[i ∈S] P j∈S qj . (1) Let P denote the row-stochastic transition matrix of G and D the set of dangling nodes. LEAN- GRAPHSEARCH computes personalized PageRank (PPR) (Brin & Page, 1998) by iterating: p(k+1) = rv + (1 −r)p(k)P + (1 −r) X i∈D p(k) i ! v, (2) where p(0) = v. The restart term rv keeps propagation anchored to the seed distribution, while the transition term (1 −r)p(k)P expands each seed toward its dependencies. Returning dangling mass to v preserves the query-specific distribution. Graph-aware Candidate Refinement. After PPR propagation, LEANGRAPHSEARCH merges the semantic seed set S with the top-N graph-expanded candidates ranked by PPR score. The retained candidates are then scored against the original query through the Qwen reranker in a sec- ond reranking stage. The final score mixes the second-stage relevance score ˜qi with the normalized PPR score weighted by a coefficient λ: fi = ˜qi + λ zscorequery(pi). Finally, LEANGRAPH- SEARCH returns the top-K candidates with highest fi as R(q). 3.4 SEARCH LOOP POLICY To align with the search loop settings in LeanSearch v2, we evaluate two retrieval-policy variants of LEANGRAPHSEARCH that share the same retrieval mechanism but differ in when and how it is invoked. Standard Mode invokes graph-based retrieval after a failed proof attempt using queries conditioned on the current proof state. Reasoning Mode additionally uses an LLM to decompose the theorem into queries targeting definitions, high-level proof strategies, and individual proof steps before the first proof attempt. Retrieved evidence is aggregated across subqueries and truncated to K declarations. Readers can refer to Gao et al. Overall, these results suggest that graph-based retrieval improves both individual declaration re- trieval and the recovery of premise sets that support complete proof routes. In addition to the quan- titative results, our qualitative analysis reveals the following findings: Graph-aware expansion reveals underlying mathematical objects. On MathlibQR, semantic retrievers frequently identify constructors, projections, or characteristic theorems whose descriptions closely match the query, but miss the associated parent declarations or deeper dependent declarations because their names and signatures are less lexically similar to the query. Graph-aware expansion connects these semantic matches to underlying declarations through dependency relationships. Graph augmentation improves the composition of the retrieved context. On MathlibMPR, LEANGRAPHSEARCH returns fewer filtered declarations on average than LeanSearch v2, yet re- trieves more gold declarations within the top five positions, improving group recall and complete- route coverage. Route-level examples further illustrate this effect. These results suggest that graph augmentation concentrates relevant premises in its retrieved context instead of merely expanding it. text: LEANGRAPHSEARCH 5 EXPERIMENTS ON THEOREM PROVING More importantly, we evaluate on formal theorem proving tasks to confirm whether improvements in retrieval quality translate into better proof generation. 5.1 LEANGRAPHSEARCH IN AN AGENTIC PROVING LOOP To integrate LEANGRAPHSEARCH into a verifier-grounded proof loop, we implement it as a search tool that can be called by LLM provers. Each problem instance contains a Lean source x with one target proof hole. At inference round t, the prover Mθ parameterized by θ generates a complete Lean source candidate Yt conditioned on the problem x, the preceding candidate Yt−1, the latest Lean compiler diagnostic et−1, optional retrieved declarations Rt, and optional failure-memory feedback mt−1 as: Yt ∼Mθ (x, Yt−1, et−1, Rt, mt−1) . (4) The Lean compiler executes Yt and returns either a successful elaboration or a structured diagnos- tic. Each failed candidate is followed by one revision conditioned on the latest verifier feedback, producing a single candidate lineage. Building on the common practice of incorporating verifier feedback into iterative proof refinement, we investigate whether LEANGRAPHSEARCH can provide useful retrieval feedback that further improves proving performance. After a failed attempt, the LLM optionally generates five search queries from the problem x, current candidate Yt, and Lean diagnostic et. Each query invokes LEANGRAPHSEARCH and returns K declarations. LEANGRAPHSEARCH deduplicates the re- trieved declarations and inserts them next to the previous candidate and diagnostic in the revision prompt. A candidate succeeds when the complete Lean source elaborates without a live sorry and satisfies the proof-hole integrity contract. Optional Formal Failure Memory. Our preliminary experiments show that the LLM prover is likely to repeat the same or similar failed proofs across multiple rounds, wasting the inference budget and limiting exploration of alternative proof strategies. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a failure memory, which augments the agentic loop with problem-local records of recurrent formal states. For each stable failure, we construct a structured failure state as: st = (ct, ¯et, Gt, Lt, τt) , (5) where ct is the error category, ¯et is the normalized diagnostic, Gt contains unresolved goals, Lt summarizes the local context, and τt is the inferred failing tactic. A deterministic serialization and SHA-256 (NIST, 2015) hash identify repeated states. When a state recurs, the next prover call receives a compact dead-end record and the failed mod- ifications that led to it, encouraging the prover to explore an alternative repair. The memory also reuses deterministic failures of identical candidates and caches retrieval responses by formal proof state and normalized query. These interventions reduce repeated compilation and retrieval while preserving the single-lineage search structure. 5.2 SETUP Benchmarks and Metrics. We consider three benchmarks with diverse fields and complexities: FATE-H (Jiang et al., 2026), MathlibMPR-Prop (Gao et al., 2026) and Lean-IMO-Bench (Kung et al., 2026). FATE-H contains 100 graduate-level algebra problems, MathlibMPR-Prop contains the 50 propositions from MathlibMPR that admit a uniform tactic-mode interface, and Lean-IMO- Bench contains 30 Basic and 30 Advanced Olympiad problems. For each problem, we allow the backbone model at most 32 reflection turns with one optional query assigned to each turn, and report pass@k for k ∈{8, 16, 32}, where k represents the number of reflection turns. We also report the normalized total cost over each group to assess cost effectiveness. Baselines. text: We introduced LEANGRAPHSEARCH, a graph-based retrieval method that exploits formal depen- dencies in Mathlib to discover supporting premises for Lean 4 theorem proving. Starting from semantically relevant declarations, it propagates relevance along dependency edges with personal- ized PageRank and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Experiments show improvements in declaration recall and annotated proof-route coverage, with benefits extending to 9
title: LEANGRAPHSEARCH

text: LEANGRAPHSEARCH downstream proof construction. LEANGRAPHSEARCH improves proof completion over matched LeanSearch v2 configurations on most of the evaluated benchmarks and reflection budgets, while reducing the aggregate API cost per solved problem. Together, these findings show that the de- pendencies recorded in a formal library provide useful guidance for retrieving supporting premises, connecting semantic search to the mathematical ingredients needed to construct a formal proof. text: A.1 RETRIEVAL TASKS AND BENCHMARKS General retrieval benchmarks evaluate different aspects of the relationship between queries and sup- porting evidence. BEIR measures retrieval across heterogeneous domains (Thakur et al., 2021), while MTEB evaluates embeddings across retrieval and other representation tasks (Muennighoff et al., 2023). BRIGHT emphasizes queries that require reasoning beyond direct semantic match- ing (Su et al., 2025), motivating specialized retrievers such as ReasonIR, INF-X-Retriever, and DIVER (Shao et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). In mathematics, NaturalProofs eval- uates reference retrieval for natural-language proofs (Welleck et al., 2021), and Matlas supports statement-level search over mathematical literature (Ju et al., 2026). Formal proof traces provide more explicit supervision for premise use. HolStep and HOList sup- ply proof-step data from HOL Light (Kaliszyk et al., 2017; Bansal et al., 2019), while LeanDojo extracts proof states, tactics, and premise annotations from Lean developments (Yang et al., 2023). LeanSearch v2 introduces two complementary retrieval benchmarks (Gao et al., 2026): MathlibQR evaluates queries paired with individual target declarations, whereas MathlibMPR annotates premise groups and alternative proof routes. Their metrics distinguish locating a relevant declaration from covering the supporting premises along a complete route. Our evaluation combines these retrieval measures with downstream proof completion to examine whether the retrieved declarations help construct checked proofs. A.2 FORMAL THEOREM-PROVING SYSTEMS Premise selection has long connected mathematical libraries to automated reasoning. Sledgehammer and CoqHammer select library facts for external provers and reconstruct successful proofs within a proof assistant (Paulson & Blanchette, 2012; Czajka & Kaliszyk, 2018). Thor integrates language models with hammer-based automation (Jiang et al., 2022), and Magnushammer learns premise se- lection through contrastive training and reranking (Mikuła et al., 2024). Neural provers also explore proof states through learned tactic selection, as in HOList and HyperTree Proof Search (Bansal et al., 2019; Lample et al., 2022). ReProver and REAL-Prover incorporate retrieved Lean premises into this stepwise proving process (Yang et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2025). Recent work improves the prover through mathematical pretraining (Azerbayev et al., 2024), scaf- folded data synthesis and self-correction (Lin et al., 2026), and reinforcement learning with formal verification (Xin et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2025; Hubert et al., 2026). Informal reasoning provides another source of guidance: Draft, Sketch, and Prove generates formal sketches from informal proofs (Jiang et al., 2023), while Lean-STaR, Hilbert, and LEAP connect informal reasoning to formal tactics or subproblems (Lin et

These approaches improve proof generation and decomposition. Our experiments hold the prover fixed to study how access to library declarations affects proof completion. Library structure and prior attempts can also guide formal reasoning. LEGO-Prover retrieves veri- fied lemmas from a growing library (Wang et al., 2024), while RAutoformalizer and Aria use depen- dency information and retrieval during statement autoformalization (Liu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). Our optional failure mem- ory associates unsuccessful repairs with recurring formal failure states, complementing the library evidence supplied by retrieval. text: Dexterity from Supervised Play Botao He1,2, Yiming Dou1, Yiannis Aloimonos2, Jitendra Malik1, Akash Sharma1, and Ruoshi Liu1,2 Abstract— How can robots autonomously collect the contact- rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate infer- ence, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a mul- tiﬁngered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world ex- periment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490× less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-speciﬁc demonstrations or sim- to-real transfer.
title: Dexterity from Supervised Play

text: Humans, especially infants and children, develop dexterity from playing [1]. Play offers a task-agnostic source of interaction. Similarly, for robots, learning via playing holds tremendous potential for learning a rich physical understand- ing of the world required for dexterous manipulation without human supervision. In practice, however, play is a difﬁcult behavior to engineer. Prior works model play by manually deﬁning explicit heuristics as guidance [2], [3], [4] and by engineering restrictive safety boundaries to prevent hardware damage [5]. However, play is inherently intuitive and difﬁcult to formal- ize with hand-crafted rules, while manual safety constraints require excessive tuning that limits scalability. In this work, our core hypothesis is that play is a behavior that can be modeled as a ‘goal-agnostic’ state-conditioned probabilistic model in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and therefore be learned through a standard behavior cloning pipeline. In other words, even though a safe play behavior is hard to be deﬁned explicitly with heuristics, it can easily be learned implicitly through demonstration data. Therefore, we propose DSP: Dexterity from Supervised Play, a framework that turns minutes of human play into a policy that can continue collecting robot interaction au- tonomously. An action-conditioned world model learns from these data, while the same play policy provides candidate action sequences for model-predictive control (MPC). As a 1Amazon Frontier AI & Robotics

text: A. Play and interaction in RL RL agents can acquire sophisticated behavior via open- ended interaction and planning. Model-based agents such as MuZero [6] learn a latent dynamics model and plan within it to master board games and Atari without access to the rules. In multi-agent settings, emergent autocurricula produce complex strategies purely from self-play and environment interaction, as in the hide-and-seek tool-use environment [7]. Comparable interaction-driven pipelines now reach elite per- formance on physical systems such as competitive table ten- nis [5]. These results establish that interaction and planning are powerful, but they depend on well-speciﬁed rewards, simulators, or game rules. DSP instead targets contact-rich manipulation, where reward engineering and designing safe exploration plans are difﬁcult, and obtains its behavior from human play rather than from reward-driven search. B. Curiosity and intrinsic motivation To reduce dependence on hand-designed rewards, intrinsic-motivation methods reward the agent for reaching novel or hard-to-predict states. Prediction-error curiosity uses the error of a learned forward as an intrinsic signal [3], [8], while Random Network Distillation measures novelty as the error of predicting a ﬁxed random network’s features [9]. While such signals drive broad exploration, they are still heuristics and they do not bias interactions toward safe, object-centric contact that dexterous manipulation requires. C. Learning from play Closest to our framing is robot learning from play:

While such signals drive broad exploration, they are still heuristics and they do not bias interactions toward safe, object-centric contact that dexterous manipulation requires. C. Learning from play Closest to our framing is robot learning from play: goal- free, human-generated interaction used as a task-agnostic source of supervision. Play-LMP learns latent plans from teleoperated play and reuses them for goal-conditioned con- trol [10], and subsequent work distills affordances from play to improve sample efﬁciency [4]. These approaches largely treat play as a ﬁxed dataset for imitation. In contrast, DSP uses a human play data seed to train a policy that serves as a reusable, autonomous data-collection mechanism. D. Dexterous manipulation Dexterous, multi-ﬁngered manipulation has been ap- proached both by model-free reinforcement learning and by imitation. RL methods learn agile in-hand skills such as general object reorientation [11], [12], [13], [14] and sim-to- real cube manipulation [15], [16], [17], but require carefully shaped task rewards and hundreds of millions of simulated interactions. DSP differs from existing work and does not use simulation data: it learns contact-rich dynamics purely from autonomous play, without task-speciﬁc demonstrations or rewards, and plans for arbitrary goals by scoring play- policy proposals with the learned world model under MPC. text: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Yipeng Gao1*†, Ziyao Zeng2*, Jinfa Huang3*, Yijiang Li4*, Haolin Xiong1, Wang Qin1, Xinlei Yu1, Youheng Yao2, Jie Zhang5, Kun-Yu Lin6, Rong Liu1, Yinyuan Zhao7, Yajie Zhao1, Meiqi Guo8, Jiebo Luo3, Lei Shu8, Yunhao Ge1, Xinyu Hu9, Laurent Itti1 1University of Southern California, 2Yale University, 3University of Rochester, 4University of California, San Diego, 5Columbia University, 6Nanyang Technological University, 7University of California, Santa Cruz, 8Google DeepMind, 9Philo Labs *Equal contribution, †Project lead We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation.
title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. text: ✓ ✓ ✗ 3DCodeVerse (Ours) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ 6 2.03 M Pairs ✓ ✓ ✓ 3D coding offers a promising approach to 3D creation by using executable programs to construct 3D geometry, define articulated motion, compose scenes, and generate graphics effects (Raistrick et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026). Unlike typical 2D generation workflows (Chang et al., 2025; Ho et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2025; 2024), code-based 3D generation produces structured, executable content that users can edit, reuse, compose, and inspect. These properties enable scalable, controllable 3D modeling for diverse applications. Recent advances in language models and coding agents further automate this process, allowing users to create complex 3D content through text instructions (Sun et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2026). Despite these advances, shared infrastructure for developing and evaluating 3D coding systems across environments remains limited. Existing resources address complementary aspects of 3D coding: DeepCAD and BlenderLLM provide supervision for CAD construction and Blender scripting (Wu et al., 2021; Du et al., 2024); SceneCraft and VIGA refine generated content using visual feedback (Hu et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2026); and Articraft combines a specialized SDK with a harness for articulated asset generation (Zhou et al., 2026). However, these resources remain fragmented across tasks and environments. As shown in Table 1, existing datasets

text: et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2026); and Articraft combines a specialized SDK with a harness for articulated asset generation (Zhou et al., 2026). However, these resources remain fragmented across tasks and environments. As shown in Table 1, existing datasets primarily focus on static or articulated objects, while harnesses vary in their support for visual assessment and automated corpus construction. To bridge these gaps, we introduce 3DCodeVerse (Figure 1), an open-source foundational framework for learning and scaling 3D coding through a large-scale executable code corpus and a 3D code generation harness. We first build 3DCodeVerse-2M, a unified corpus of executable 3D programs spanning static objects, articulated assets, scenes, and graphics. Rather than simply aggregating existing datasets, we systematically convert heterogeneous 3D representations into reusable source code and remove dependencies on specialized or unavailable libraries. For example, we translate DeepCAD construction sequences into CadQuery programs and inline Articraft geometry routines while preserving URDF articulation specifications. Each program is paired with its associated assets, textual descriptions, provenance, and available verification signals. We further develop 3DCodeVerse Harness, a 3D code generation harness for synthesizing and refining complex 3D programs from text, images, or videos. The harness decomposes multi-component projects into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of coding and assembly tasks, allowing multiple agents to develop and integrate source files in a structured manner.

The harness decomposes multi-component projects into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of coding and assembly tasks, allowing multiple agents to develop and integrate source files in a structured manner. Generated programs are executed and rendered, after which an independent judge agent evaluates the outputs against explicit acceptance criteria. Complementary spatial checks detect structural inconsistencies and prevent visually plausible but geometrically invalid solutions from receiving high scores. The resulting feedback is then converted into localized repair objectives, enabling repeated execution–evaluation–revision cycles 2

text: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code without human intervention. Through this iterative process, the harness supports inference-time scaling to complex projects containing thousands of lines of code. Importantly, 3DCodeVerse Harness serves not only as an inference system but also as a data- generation engine. By recording successful programs, failed attempts, targeted repairs, and preference comparisons, its execution traces provide supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and preference learning. Together, 3DCodeVerse-2M and 3DCodeVerse Harness establish not only a reusable in- frastructure for 3D coding, but also a closed loop connecting data construction, program synthesis, verification, refinement, and model improvement. We further support this ecosystem with open models and reproducible training recipes. Fine-tuning on 3DCodeVerse-2M substantially improves executable 3D code generation, reaching execution rates of 84.9% with a 9B model and 92.9% with a 27B model on 3DCodeBench. Moreover, 3DCodeVerse Harness consistently improves generation quality across coding agents, yielding gains of 15.5–29.1 points over one-shot generation. 2

text: Datasets and Benchmarks for 3D Coding. Learning to generate 3D content as code benefits from supervision over its construction procedures. DeepCAD and Fusion 360 Gallery expose CAD construction sequences, and Text2CAD connects such sequences to natural language (Wu et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2024). This supervision has expanded to executable CadQuery and Blender programs for reconstruction and language-conditioned generation through BlendNet, CAD- Recode, CAD-Coder, and MeshCoder (Du et al., 2024; Rukhovich et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026). Complementary procedural resources broaden the content represented by code: Infinigen and its extensions generate assets and scenes (Raistrick et al., 2023; 2024; Joshi et al., 2025), while Shaders21k provides programs for procedural image synthesis (Baradad et al., 2022). Existing benchmarks assess the resulting code generation, editing, and physics capabilities (Alrashedy et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026b; Shen et al., 2026). However, our paper focuses on scaling executable supervision across these heterogeneous coding environments. Our 3DCodeVerse-2M provides a million-scale training corpus spanning CAD, Blender, shaders, and browser graphics, with programs that are self-contained within their respective target runtimes. Its construction combines curated existing sources with automated program generation and execution-based filtering, enabling continued data expansion for training open 3D coding models. Harness Engineering for 3D Coding. Execution and feedback allow 3D coding agents to inspect and revise the content produced by their programs. Systems such as 3D-GPT, SceneCraft, and LL3M establish language-driven planning and program generation for 3D modeling (Sun et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025). Executing and rendering these programs enables visual refinement, as explored by BlenderAlchemy, CADCodeVerify, and VIGA (Huang et al., 2024; Alrashedy et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026). Beyond rendered appearance, Articraft provides structured asset validation through a specialized SDK, while Bioinspired123D connects script quality control with a graph-based agentic workflow (Luu & Buehler, 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026). 3DHarnessBench further studies how the observation and tool interfaces available to an agent affect 3D reconstruction (Liu et al., 2026). In contrast, our 3DCodeVerse harness provides a reusable execution and verification framework across coding backends, jointly supporting inference-time refinement and scalable training data curation. Its multi-agent directed acyclic graph coordinates execution, rendering, spatial measurements, and structural checks across static and articulated objects, scenes, and visual effects. Agentic Data Curation and Toolkits. Coding agents curate programs with reusable skills (Ap- pendix A.9) that package authoring conventions, code examples, and repair guidance. Executing f yields (a, ℓ) = Ee(f) (Eq. 1), and inspection tools return measurements Me(a): part inventories and bounding boxes flag missing or misplaced components, contact and collision checks flag gaps and interpenetration, including across sampled joint poses, and placement and frame probes check physical support, invalid renders, and temporal defects. Findings are reported per part in the authoring frame (Appendix A.3), and execution errors or failed checks return the program to the agent for targeted repair. Conversion fidelity is measured by voxel IoU for DeepCAD and Chamfer distance for Articraft.

Each record s = (f, e, C, o, m) stores provenance, license, and available verification results in m, keeping execution, geometric, and visual checks separate; source files, pre-conversion programs, and URDF files are retained, and meshes and videos are linked when available. 4 3DCODEVERSE HARNESS: A DATA ENGINE FOR 3D CODING Generating high-quality 3D programs often requires iterative refinement, but reliance on human feedback makes this process difficult to scale. To address this bottleneck, we develop 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent framework that automates 3D code generation and refinement for data curation and agent-driven content creation (Figure 3). It coordinates coding and assembly through a DAG and combines execution checks, spatial tools, and rubric-guided VLM judgments to identify defects and guide targeted revisions without human feedback. Because the reliability of this feedback depends on how we configure its prompts, tools, and rubrics, we further refine the judge and generation workflow through an alternating development-time adversarial loop. Multi-Agent Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Framework. Given a condition c and a target execution environment e, an LLM planner first produces P = Aplan(c; e), specifying the target components, dimensions, materials,

text: and generation workflow through an alternating development-time adversarial loop. Multi-Agent Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Framework. Given a condition c and a target execution environment e, an LLM planner first produces P = Aplan(c; e), specifying the target components, dimensions, materials, spatial relations, and acceptance criteria. The harness translates P into a DAG G = (V, E) of coding and assembly tasks, with edges encoding prerequisites. Within this graph, explicit file ownership allows independent coding tasks to be carried out concurrently by sub- agents. Once their prerequisites are satisfied, assembly tasks integrate the resulting code, ultimately producing the initial program f (0) for subsequent evaluation and feedback-driven refinement. Automated Feedback and Iterative Refinement. At each round t, the harness executes the current program f (t) and collects three types of feedback: 1⃝Execution feedback. Build and runtime logs ℓ(t). If execution fails, no artifact is produced, and this is the only feedback. 2⃝Measured feedback. Measurement tools Me check the artifact a(t) for dimensions, contacts, collisions, kinematics, and placement, and return component-level violations with numerical correction hints. 5

text: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code 3⃝Visual feedback. A VLM judge inspects multi-view renders Re(a(t)) against the input c and the acceptance criteria in P, producing defect evidence, criterion scores, and proposed revisions: j(t) = Ajudge(c, P, o(t)), where o(t) = (ℓ(t), Me(a(t)), Re(a(t))). The score s(t) combines the weighted criteria and defect penalties in j(t), caps it with measured violations and unmet requirements, and vetoes measurements that rule out visual defect claims. All feedback is converted into revision tasks ∆(t), prioritized in the order listed above, and a fix agent applies them: f (t+1) = Acode(c, P, f (t), ∆(t); e). Adversarial Loop Engineering for Harness Optimization. The preceding loop uses automated feedback in place of per-round human inspection and revision guidance. Because this feedback’s reliability depends on how prompts, tools, and rubrics are configured, we alternate between refining the judge and the generation workflow during development. Let θJ denote the judge’s evidence presentation, rubric, response schema, and aggregation rules, and θH the harness’s prompts, contracts, skills, tools, and refinement policy. Judge refinement first fixes the generation workflow and repeatedly evaluates a bank B of stored artifacts. Using the same artifacts separates changes in judge behavior from variability in generation. We compare 3DCodeVerse against models with their native harnesses and Claude Design on 100 text-to-3D object prompts. We further compare against native harnesses on articulated- object generation, 50 scene prompts, and 50 graphics prompts. We evaluate generation quality using three metrics. Human Preference is the fraction of anonymized side-by-side comparisons won according to human evaluators, with ties split equally. VLM Preference is the fraction of the same comparisons won according to a VLM judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro), with ties split equally. Judge Score is Gemini 3.1 Pro’s overall rubric score, combining weighted criteria with defect penalties and score caps (0–100; failed generations receive a score of zero). Following 3DCodeBench (Gao et al., 2026b), we additionally report SigLIP-2 (Tschannen et al., 2025) text–image cosine similarity averaged over four views. The evaluation judge is described in Appendix C.3, and further evaluation details are in Appendix C.3. Main Results. Code renders from our harness guide video generation with Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 for robot manipulation scenes (top) and Seedance 2.5 for a GPT-6 Astra scene (bottom). 6 APPLICATIONS OF 3D CODING Robotics. 3D coding enables the construction of articulated assets and scenes with explicit geometry and physical constraints for simulated robot tasks. Programs encode rigid-link geometry, joint axes, and joint limits as editable parameters, supporting programmatic checks and controlled variation of object dimensions, articulation, and initial poses. These task instances can be executed in simulations to generate robot interactions and observations. To provide a preliminary evaluation, we import an articulated asset validated and exported with 3DCodeVerse tools into MuJoCo and compare rendered observations with frozen UWM (Zhu et al., 2025) predictions across 12 cases spanning two assets, two contact states, and three control sequences, using complete scene state for rendering and image history with matched robot commands for UWM. Code renders and their UWM VAE reconstructions each pass a fixed door-and-handle geometry check in 12/12 outputs, versus 7/36 UWM predictions. These results show that 3D code can help
title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

text: for rendering and image history with matched robot commands for UWM. Code renders and their UWM VAE reconstructions each pass a fixed door-and-handle geometry check in 12/12 outputs, versus 7/36 UWM predictions. These results show that 3D code can help generate articulated assets and scenes for robotics simulation with explicit geometry and physical constraints. Video generation. 3D coding provides an editable interface for controlling the spatial and temporal conditions of video generation. Programs specify scene layout, object articulation and motion, and camera trajectories. We render generated 3D scenes using programs and harness them as reference videos, using the full sequences to condition Gemini Omni Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026) and Seedance 2.5 (ByteDance Seed, 2026). The rendered videos supply spatial and temporal guidance, while the video models are used to refine visual appearance. We present paired reference and generated frames to examine how the specified layout, object motion, and camera trajectories are preserved. This application connects explicit scene programs with video synthesis. 7

text: In this paper, we present 3DCodeVerse, an open ecosystem that provides a shared foundation for 3D coding through datasets, a reusable harness, and open model baselines. The dataset brings together programs across coding environments with descriptions, associated assets, and available quality records. The harness combines execution, spatial checks, and visual judgment to support iterative generation without human feedback during a run, while retaining the resulting programs and revisions for data curation. Experiments demonstrate the utility of the data for training open models and the benefits of the harness for existing coding agents. We will release the datasets, harness, models, and training recipes to support further research on 3D generation through code. 9

A THE 3DCODEVERSE HARNESS: DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION A.1 COMPONENTS AND MODEL ROLES Tracks and runtimes. 3DCodeVerse Harness spans four generative tracks—static objects, artic- ulated objects, 3D scenes, and procedural graphics—backed by seven isolated language runtimes: three for static objects (Blender Python, CadQuery, and Three.js), one each for articulated mecha- nisms (URDF with Blender-authored links) and scenes (Three.js), and two for graphics (GLSL and moderngl). Each runtime specifies a strict file layout, static lint rules, a sandboxed build wrapper, canonical export formats, and a deterministic render driver, while sharing unified coordinate frames, metric units, camera rigs, and geometric tolerances. Model roles and execution invariants. Each run decouples structural planning, code synthesis, and visual evaluation into three pluggable roles: a planner, a coding agent, and a vision–language judge (Figure 7). The planner and judge operate through a unified API interface, while the coding agent executes inside an isolated workspace

text: planning, code synthesis, and visual evaluation into three pluggable roles: a planner, a coding agent, and a vision–language judge (Figure 7). The planner and judge operate through a unified API interface, while the coding agent executes inside an isolated workspace equipped with the harness’s spatial tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), alongside a single-shot mode that requests a complete file envelope through direct API calls. Every round commits raw source code from which meshes and renders are deterministically regenerated; boilerplate infrastructure (camera rigging, coordinate conversion, URDF composition, scene assembly, and shader headers) resides in the harness, and verification proceeds strictly from fast programmatic gates to blind VLM judging. A.2 PLANNING AND THE JOB GRAPH Structured specification and plan synthesis. The planner translates an open-ended request into a schema-validated structural plan: named parts with metric bounding boxes, materials, symmetry, and attachment topology for static objects; a kinematic tree with typed joints, axes, pivots, limits, and acyclic affine mimic couplings (qj = mjqi + bj) for articulated mechanisms; spatial zones, modular assets, effects, and authored cameras for scenes; and render passes, uniforms, and temporal dynamics for graphics. Each runtime maps plan targets to strict file-ownership scopes (per-part modules plus an assembly entry file for Blender and Three.js objects; a single program for CadQuery, URDF, and graphics; and per-zone and per-asset modules for scenes), and writes outside a session’s scope are reverted between Git commits. Objects with eight or more top-level parts in modular languages are synthesized via scoped sessions over attachment subtrees of at most three parts—each supplied with the planned bounding boxes of adjacent parts—followed by an assembly session (Figure 8). Single-shot prompts inline the code skeleton and request a complete file envelope in a single response. A.3 SPATIAL TOOLS AND DETERMINISTIC GATES Semantic verdicts vs. transport errors. Every tool response separates the semantic verification verdict (PASS/FAIL) from the tool execution status. A detected mesh collision or build failure is returned as a valid observation leading with a structured FAIL verdict; only an internal tool crash sets the MCP protocol error flag, preventing commercial coding agents from entering degenerate transport-retry loops (§C.5). Tool responses bound text length and image resolution, attaching diagnostic renders specifically when a check identifies actionable geometric defects. Deterministic gates, connectivity, and plan adherence. Following each successful build, the track pipeline executes its deterministic gates. A.4 AUTOMATED JUDGMENT Evidence payload and response schema. A single payload builder serves in-loop refinement, post-run evaluation, and judge calibration (Figure 10). The judge receives the request, plan digest, acceptance checklist, measurements, gate findings, and track telemetry, together with up to five labelled multi-view montages, detail crops, and—when connectivity errors occur—cross-sectional slices, with montage order randomized per sample to remove positional bias. On object tracks, a passing connectivity gate prohibits unverified visual claims of floating or interpenetrating parts. The judge answers in a strict JSON schema at temperature 0.2, stating its evidence, strengths, issues, defect votes, and checklist verifications before assigning criterion scores and up to six prioritized improvement instructions; deterministic criteria such as silhouette IoU are injected by code. Our deterministic compiler translates each com- mand sequence into a self-contained CadQuery script: 174,981 sequences compile (98.2%), 174,177 produce valid watertight solids (97.7%), and vector-level hashing removes 25.8% exact geometric duplicates to yield 128,201 unique executable programs (71.9% of raw sequences). Geometric fidelity against the original solids, measured via voxel IoU at 483 resolution, averages 0.985, with 96.9% of programs exceeding 0.90 (the remaining 1,114 programs are annotated with explicit fidelity metadata so downstream pipelines can apply custom thresholds). Natural-language annotations from Text2CAD (Khan et al., 2024) are paired with 125,162 programs under their original license terms, accompanied by four canonical views per solid. Crucially, because the upstream DeepCAD split contains 3,230 duplicate geometry groups straddling its train and test partitions, our vector-and-mesh deduplication eliminates cross-split leakage across the CAD lineage. C EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS AND ADDITIONAL RESULTS C.1 TRAINING DETAILS Training configuration. All fine-tuning runs are conducted with LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) on 4 × NVIDIA H100 (80 GB) GPUs in bfloat16 precision using gradient checkpointing and sequence packing. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) applies LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) of rank 64 (α = 128, dropout 0.05) across all linear projections with a learning rate of 1×10−4 (or 1×10−5 for full-parameter fine-tuning under ZeRO-3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020)), a cosine learning-rate schedule, a 5% linear warm-up ratio, and a
title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

text: of rank 64 (α = 128, dropout 0.05) across all linear projections with a learning rate of 1×10−4 (or 1×10−5 for full-parameter fine-tuning under ZeRO-3 (Rajbhandari et al., 2020)), a cosine learning-rate schedule, a 5% linear warm-up ratio, and a per-device batch size of 1 with gradient accumulation of 8 (4 for 27B). Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al. 2023) initializes from the merged SFT checkpoint and trains a rank-16 LoRA (α = 32) for 2 epochs under sigmoid preference loss (β = 0.1, learning rate 5 × 10−6). The sequence context length is set to 8,192 tokens for 9B runs and 4,096 tokens for 27B runs to fit single-device memory bounds under data-parallel training. Evaluation 23

text: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code inference uses vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) under greedy decoding or temperature sampling (T=0.7) as specified per experiment. Training throughput. Because LoRA introduces a compact optimizer state, training the 27B model under standard Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) avoids ZeRO-3 parameter all-gather traffic and achieves a 13× higher step throughput (≈6.2 K vs. ≈460 tokens/s) with standard PyTorch allocator caching. Across 4 × H100 GPUs, 9B LoRA sustains ≈17 K tokens/s (completing the 270 K-pair, 293 M-token mixture in 4 h 46 m), while 27B LoRA sustains ≈6.2 K tokens/s. Chat formatting and strict contamination control. Training examples are formatted as ShareGPT multi-turn conversations: a system prompt specifying the target dialect and output contract, a user turn containing the natural-language specification, and an assistant turn containing the complete executable program in a fenced code block. Any example whose tokenized conversation exceeds the context window is excluded cleanly rather than truncated, preserving syntactic closure. To guarantee zero train–test leakage, all 212 3DCodeBench procedural factories, all 3,904 re-seeded instances derived from those factories, and all per-dialect evaluation splits are strictly held out; no training mixture shares a program or asset identifier with any evaluation task. C.3 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Code extraction and geometric evaluation for open models. For open-model evaluations (§5.2), generated responses pass through a deterministic code extractor that strips reasoning blocks, collects fenced code blocks (including trailing unterminated blocks), and ranks candidates by dialect mark- ers, fence annotations, and AST syntactic validity. This extraction step is essential for pretrained reasoning checkpoints: with thinking enabled, 52 of 212 responses from the zero-shot 27B model omit markdown fences and 74 place auxiliary snippets after the main program, whereas fine-tuned models adhere strictly to the single-block output contract (100% single-fence compliance). Extracted programs execute inside the dialect’s pinned runtime under a 300 s timeout. Resulting meshes are exported to GLB, centred at the origin, normalized to unit maximum extent, uniformly sampled at 10,000 surface points, and evaluated via symmetric Chamfer-L2 distance and F-score at thresholds τ ∈{0.05, 0.10} (taking the best alignment across the four 90◦yaw rotations; ground-truth reference scripts self-verify at Chamfer ≈0.016 and F@0.05 ≈1.0). text: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code Single-request autonomy and refinement horizons. The single-request protocol prohibits human- in-the-loop intervention: each system receives one user prompt with zero subsequent human edits or manual candidate cherry-picking, while permitting autonomous internal tool calls and verification passes. Our primary object benchmark evaluates single-round harness execution (T = 0 in the notation of §4), retaining the initial planned generation, interactive tool use, automated build repair, and final verification (using Gemini 3.8 Flash as planner and Gemini 3.1 Pro as in-loop judge for the Flash runs). Multi-round studies (T = 4) extend this autonomous loop with up to four closed-loop refinement rounds and automated post-run output selection under the same single user request. Independent evaluation judge. All Judge Scores and VLM Preferences reported in §5 are produced by a single frozen evaluation pipeline that applies the judgment architecture and track rubrics of Appendix A.4 independently of the generation workflow under test. Each delivered program is rebuilt from scratch in its pinned runtime, with failed builds scored zero, to extract geometric measurements, connectivity or kinematic-sweep telemetry, and canonical multi-view renders (fourteen shaded views plus clay views for objects, multi-pose sweeps for articulated mechanisms, authored and orbital views at two timestamps for scenes, and sampled frame sheets for graphics); Gemini 3.1 Pro then scores it three times. Three safeguards decouple evaluation from in-loop refinement: (1) clean-room rebuild and blind prompting, scoring every artifact against the raw user prompt and a prompt-derived checklist alone, with all harness-generated plans, internal checklists, and refinement histories stripped; (2) deterministic geometric caps, bounding scores via exact mesh connectivity and kinematic checks independent of VLM perception (Eq. 5); and (3) multi-metric validation, pairing Judge Scores with SigLIP-2 similarity and blind human pairwise preferences (§5), which consistently corroborate the rubric gains across all four tracks. Both human and VLM pairwise evaluations present the original user prompt alongside anonymized multi-view renders captured under matched camera poses, framing, and resolution. Evaluators judge overall preference on prompt adherence, structural plausibility, and visual craftsmanship, with ties counted as half a win; VLM preference additionally requires agreement across both presentation orders (§A.4). Human evaluations randomize left/right presentation order across a fixed, pre-registered prompt subset shared by all compared systems, with prompt-level bootstrap confidence intervals clustering repeated ratings at the task level. Complementing the robotics application in §6, we examine how executable 3D code preserves rigid-link structure during robot manipulation compared with a frozen video world-action model, UWM (Zhu et al., 2025). Using an articulated microwave asset synthesized by GPT-6 Astra and verified by 3DCodeVerse Harness tooling (passing forward-kinematics, rigid-distance, and hinge-sweep gates across five poses), we instantiate a MuJoCo simulation alongside the native reference asset across two initial contact states and three robot control sequences—contact push, hold, and retreat—yielding 12 evaluation cases. Each rollout executes 16 matched robot action commands at 20 Hz: UWM generates three seeded video rollouts per case (36 total) from observation history and action commands, whereas code simulation steps the explicit articulated asset directly inside MuJoCo. Quantitative evaluation of structural preservation. To measure whether rollouts maintain co- herent rigid-part geometry under physical interaction, we apply a calibrated orientation-aware door- and-handle contour detector across all outputs. Calibrated prior to evaluation on 24 held-out static renders across six hinge angles and four robot poses, the detector recovers the true hinge angle within 1◦on all 20 accepted detections and abstains whenever contours degrade or become ambiguous. To isolate latent dynamics drift from autoencoder reconstruction blur, we additionally evaluate a VAE-reconstructed code control by passing every simulator render through UWM’s frozen VAE encoder and decoder. text: Preprint GEOSTATE: LEARNING VIEW-DECOUPLED GEOMETRY STATES FOR 3D WORLD MODELING Hongchang Liu1, Jian Liu1, Yujuan Ding2, Liang Peng3, Xun Jiang1, Fei Ma4, Xing Xu1, Yi Bin1,∗ 1Tongji University 2Hong Kong Polytechnic University 3Tencent 4Guangdong Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy (SZ) Hongchang_Liu@outlook.com, yi.bin@hotmail.com
title: Preprint

text: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geomet- ric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry represen- tation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi- view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per- frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view query- ing, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. text: Learning to predict how the physical world evolves is a central goal of world modeling (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018), with direct relevance to autonomous driving, robotics, and embodied intelli- gence. Visual world models predict the future in pixel space (Hu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Gao et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025), which can introduce substantial representational redundancy and make geometric consistency difficult to maintain. This has motivated increasing interest in 3D world models, which represent and predict future environments in geometrically grounded state spaces. By explicitly encoding spatial structure and 3D relationships, these representations provide a structured and geometrically grounded state space that more directly reflects the real world. Recent 3D world models have explored a range of structured geometric state spaces, including depth, occupancy, point-based representations, and 3D Gaussians (Zheng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Zuo et al., 2025). In parallel, geometry foundation models (GFMs) have substantially advanced feed-forward 3D perception by learning rich geometric representations directly from RGB observations (Wang et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b;a; 2026). Benefiting from large-scale pretraining, these representations capture strong geometric priors that generalize across scenes and tasks, making them attractive state spaces for predictive world modeling. text: Preprint dynamics. GFM features are typically constructed from and organized around the observing views, so changes in camera viewpoint can induce substantial changes in the representation even when the underlying physical scene remains unchanged. When such features are directly used as predictive states, a temporal model would account simultaneously for genuine scene evolution and camera- induced variation, although these arise from fundamentally different sources. In particular, even a static scene can undergo substantial changes in feature space as the camera moves, forcing the temporal model to predict viewpoint-dependent transformations that do not correspond to physical scene evolution. This unnecessary variation makes the latent dynamics more complex and therefore harder to predict over long horizons. FR3D (Morbitzer et al., 2026) also shows that separating ego- motion from scene forecasting can improve temporal modeling, but its predictive state still inherits the view-dependent structure of the underlying reconstruction representation. We argue that such separation should instead be built into the representation itself: the state should describe what the world is, while the camera should determine only how that world is observed. To this end, we introduce GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state learned from pretrained GFM features. text: end, we introduce GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state learned from pretrained GFM features. Given multi-view observations, a scene tokenizer compresses their geometry features into a compact scene state represented in a shared scene coordinate system, while the query viewpoint is in- troduced only during decoding. Specifically, a geometry decoder takes the scene state together with rays from a query camera and predicts the geometry observed from that viewpoint. Consequently, the same scene state can be queried repeatedly from different viewpoints without re-encoding the scene. This transforms view-conditioned GFM features into a representation in which scene geom- etry is explicitly separated from camera-dependent observation. Building on this representation, we formulate 3D world modeling directly in the scene-state space. The temporal model can therefore focus solely on predicting scene dynamics, while camera evo- lution is modeled independently. At inference time, a predicted future state can be decoded using either a separately predicted camera trajectory or a user-controlled camera. Our formulation also maintains a consistent scene gauge throughout temporal prediction and geometry decoding, avoid- ing the need for per-frame scale alignment during rollout. We evaluate our approach on large-scale dynamic driving scenes, using Waymo (Sun et al., 2020) for in-domain evaluation and KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) and nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020) for zero- shot transfer. text: We evaluate our approach on large-scale dynamic driving scenes, using Waymo (Sun et al., 2020) for in-domain evaluation and KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) and nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020) for zero- shot transfer. Our approach outperforms the compared world models in depth forecasting across all reported horizons, while maintaining a consistent scale throughout the forecasting rollout. Experi- ments further demonstrate geometrically consistent querying across viewpoints and generalization across driving datasets. Ablation results show that view decoupling makes the scene representation more predictable. Together, these findings support view-decoupled geometry states derived from pretrained GFMs as an effective representation for predictive 3D world modeling. Our contributions are threefold: • We identify viewpoint coupling in geometry foundation model features as a limitation when using them as predictive world states, and introduce GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state derived from pretrained GFM representations that separates scene content from how the scene is observed. • We develop a scene-state learning framework that realizes GeoState through a Scene To- kenizer that aggregates multi-view GFM features into a shared scene state and a query- conditioned Geometry Decoder that introduces the query viewpoint only at decoding time. • We formulate a 3D world model that predicts scene evolution directly in GeoState space while modeling camera evolution separately, and demonstrate long-horizon geometry fore- casting, geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and

text: 2.1 3D WORLD MODELS Recent world models increasingly move beyond pixel-space prediction toward structured 3D scene modeling and forecasting. Copilot4D (Zhang et al., 2024) and ViDAR (Yang et al., 2024) forecast future point clouds, while OccWorld (Zheng et al., 2024) and DOME (Gu et al., 2024) predict scene 2
title: Preprint

text: Preprint evolution in semantic occupancy space. DIO (Diehl et al., 2025) represents future scene geometry and motion through decomposable implicit occupancy-flow fields, and GaussianWorld (Zuo et al., 2025) models scene evolution in 3D Gaussian space for streaming occupancy prediction. More re- cently, several approaches directly use learned geometry representations as predictive world states. VGGT-World (Sun et al., 2026) forecasts future VGGT features, while GeoWAM (Lu et al., 2026) learns geometry-aware predictive states for autonomous driving. FR3D (Morbitzer et al., 2026) pre- dicts the latent state of a pretrained 3D reconstruction model while modeling ego-motion separately. In contrast, we remove viewpoint dependence from the geometry state itself and introduce viewpoint only as a query condition during decoding. 2.2 GEOMETRY FOUNDATION MODELS Geometry foundation models provide strong pretrained priors for multi-view 3D perception. DUSt3R (Wang et al., 2024a) formulates reconstruction through pointmap prediction, while Fast3R (Yang et al., 2025) scales joint reconstruction to larger collections of views. CUT3R (Wang et al., 2025b) introduces a persistent latent state for continuously integrating observations, and VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a) unifies camera estimation, depth, point maps, and tracking in a feed- forward architecture. VGGT-Ω(Wang et al., 2026) further strengthens this paradigm for dynamic 3D scenes, making it a natural geometry backbone for our setting. We build on its pretrained ge- ometric features and reformulate them

text: maps, and tracking in a feed- forward architecture. VGGT-Ω(Wang et al., 2026) further strengthens this paradigm for dynamic 3D scenes, making it a natural geometry backbone for our setting. We build on its pretrained ge- ometric features and reformulate them into a compact, view-decoupled scene-level representation better suited for temporal world modeling. 2.3 COMPACT 3D REPRESENTATIONS A related line of work compresses multi-view observations into compact scene representations. LVSM (Jin et al., 2025) encodes input views into a fixed-length set of latent tokens for novel- view synthesis, while Surflo (Gu´edon et al., 2026) aggregates dense VGGT features into a fixed-size global latent representation for efficient 3D surface reconstruction. 3DRAE (Wei et al., 2026) further learns a fixed-length, view-decoupled 3D latent space that can be queried from arbitrary cameras. These works demonstrate that multi-view observations can be represented without retaining a sep- arate dense representation for each view. While they focus primarily on static scene reconstruction or novel-view synthesis, our work investigates whether such scene-level representations can serve as predictive states for temporal world modeling. 3 METHOD 3.1 METHOD OVERVIEW Our goal is to predict future scene geometry without requiring the world model to simultaneously account for variations induced by camera motion. GeoState learning. (1) The state is not tied to any single observation viewpoint; we refer to it as a view-decoupled geometry state, or GeoState. A faithful GeoState should capture the underlying 3D scene geometry, which could be reflected in accurate and geometrically consistent depth reconstruction across different viewpoints. We therefore introduce a query-conditioned geometry decoder that reconstructs a depth map from St for a given query camera Q: bDQ = Gψ(St, Q). We train the scene tokenizer and decoder for geometry reconstruction and novel-view querying, keeping the GFM and its dense head frozen. The objective is Lrep = Llog D + λgradLgrad, (12) where Llog D measures mean absolute log-depth error over valid pixels, and Lgrad supervises local depth gradients. The learned tokenizer and decoder are frozen during world-model training. World-model training. We train the world model in two stages: single-step initialization followed by autoregressive rollout training. Target-state construction. To construct future supervision in a consistent scene coordinate frame, target GeoStates are constructed by feeding growing observation prefixes into the frozen VGGT-Ω. For the target at t + h, the prefix terminates at t + h, while all prefixes share the same first input view to maintain a common coordinate anchor across time. Only the outputs corresponding to the synchronized observations at t+h are retained and passed to the Scene Tokenizer to construct S∗ t+h. Since VGGT-Ωpredictions may vary in scale across forward passes, we normalize the metric spatial quantities in gp,v (Eq. 4) using a calibration derived from the observed context before fusing them with the GFM features. This gives target GeoStates a consistent context-derived scale without target- frame alignment. Further details are provided in Appendix A.3. Single-step initialization. We pretrain the Scene Tokenizer and ray-conditioned decoder on approximately 10k multi-view scenes from DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024), TartanAir (Wang et al., 2020), RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018), CO3D (Reizenstein et al., 2021), and WildRGB-D (Xia et al., 2024), using ground-truth depth where available and VGGT-Ω(Wang et al., 2026) pseudo-depth otherwise. We then adapt both modules on a subset of the Waymo Open Dataset (Sun et al., 2020) selected for static scene content. World Model training uses approximately 140k windows from 800 segments, each containing four context and seven future states at 0.2 s intervals, with FRONT, FRONT LEFT, and FRONT RIGHT context views. We evaluate on 100 Waymo windows held out from model selection, 113 eligible KITTI (Geiger et al., 2012) drives, and all 150 scenes in the nuScenes (Caesar et al., 2020) validation split. We pretrain the Scene Tokenizer and ray-conditioned decoder on the multi-view pretraining data for 200k steps with an initial learning rate of 10−5, and then finetune on the static Waymo subset for 50k steps with an initial learning rate of 5×10−6. Both stages use a global effective batch size of 36, with the VGGT-Ωencoder frozen. We sample one to five source views per scene and supervise depth reconstruction at held-out query views. For static Waymo sequences, source and query views may span both cameras and timestamps. We then train the World Model in two stages: 20k steps of one-step prediction with an initial learning rate of 10−5, followed by 35k steps of seven-step autoregressive rollout training with an initial learning rate of 10−6. VGGT-Ω, the Scene Tokenizer, and the decoder remain frozen throughout World Model training, while gradients propagate through the decoder to the predicted states. Table 3 compares direct VGGT-Ωdepth predic- tions with depth reconstructed through our Scene Tokenizer and Geometry Decoder using ground- truth query cameras. Both use target-time RGB observations and are evaluated against ground-truth LiDAR depth. Their comparable accuracy shows that the fixed-length GeoState preserves the ge- ometric information required for accurate reconstruction, providing a compact and geometrically faithful representation for subsequent world modeling. Effect of the View-Decoupled Scene State. We compare GeoState with a feature-compression baseline that directly compresses VGGT-Ωfeatures into a 512 × 512 latent state. For a fair com- parison with the feature-compression baseline, only the target FRONT GFM output block is passed to the Scene Tokenizer. Both representations use the same world model, training data, forecast- ing objectives, optimization, and evaluation protocol; implementation details are provided in Ap- pendix A.5.4. As shown in Table 4, the two representations achieve comparable reconstruction quality, but GeoState is substantially easier to predict, improving AbsRel and δ1 at every horizon. Because the two representations achieve comparable reconstruction quality, the forecasting gap is unlikely to arise from reconstruction accuracy. Instead, the results suggest that GeoState provides a more predictable state space for temporal modeling. By separating scene content from viewpoint- dependent observation, GeoState reduces camera-induced variation in the state dynamics, allowing the World Model to focus more directly on the underlying evolution of scene geometry. 9

text: We presented GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry state learned from GFM features for predictive 3D world modeling. By separating scene evolution from camera-dependent observation, GeoState provides a scene representation that can be predicted more effectively over time and queried from different viewpoints. Future work may extend this framework to embodied settings, where predictive scene states could support perception, planning, and interaction in dynamic environments.
