text: Preprint A APPENDIX A.1 ARCHITECTURE DETAILS This section provides the implementation details of the Scene Tokenizer, geometry decoder, and world model used in the main experiments. Table 6 summarizes their principal architectural config- urations and parameter counts. A.1.1 GEOMETRY-CONDITIONED MEMORY AND SCENE TOKENIZER Each selected GFM feature level is independently normalized and projected from 2,048 to 512 channels. The four projected features are concatenated and fused by an MLP with dimensions 2048 →2048 →512. For each spatial patch, confidence-weighted pooling of the dense point map provides a representative 3D point. Its coordinates, normalized by the scene scale, are Fourier- encoded with ten bands and concatenated with log(1 + c), where c is the pooled confidence, before projection to a 512-dimensional geometry embedding. Source-camera conditioning uses a six-dimensional rotation representation formed from the first two rotation-matrix columns and a four-band Fourier encoding of normalized translation. A camera MLP produces a 512-dimensional embedding shared by all patches in that view. The source-ray branch encodes six-dimensional Pl¨ucker coordinates with four Fourier bands and applies a convolution with kernel size and stride 16, followed by LayerNorm, to produce one 512-dimensional embedding per patch. The feature, point, camera, and ray embeddings are concatenated. A 2048 →1024 →512 fusion MLP predicts a correction to the feature embedding; their sum is normalized to form the patch memory.
title: Preprint

text: by LayerNorm, to produce one 512-dimensional embedding per patch. The feature, point, camera, and ray embeddings are concatenated. A 2048 →1024 →512 fusion MLP predicts a correction to the feature embedding; their sum is normalized to form the patch memory. A bank of 512 learned queries of width 512 is updated by eight Perceiver layers, each comprising latent-to-memory cross-attention and latent self-attention. Each attention block uses eight heads, pre-normalization, residual connections, and a feed-forward network with expansion ratio four. A final LayerNorm produces S ∈R512×512. A.1.2 QUERY-CONDITIONED GEOMETRY DECODER For a camera-to-world pose P = (R, o) and intrinsic matrix K, a pixel u = (u, v, 1)⊤defines the unit direction d(u) = RK−1u ∥RK−1u∥2 . (16) In normalized scene coordinates, the ray representation is [d, ¯o×d], where ¯o is the normalized cam- era center. Query rays are Fourier-encoded with six bands and patchified by a stride-16 convolution. At 416 × 624 resolution, this produces 26 × 39 = 1,014 query tokens, which are concatenated with the 512 scene tokens to form a sequence of 1,526 tokens. The scene tokens first pass through LayerNorm, a linear projection, and two scene-only self-attention blocks. The resulting scene tokens and query-ray tokens are then processed jointly by sixteen self- attention Transformer blocks, allowing each query to retrieve view-dependent geometry from the shared scene

text: first pass through LayerNorm, a linear projection, and two scene-only self-attention blocks. The resulting scene tokens and query-ray tokens are then processed jointly by sixteen self- attention Transformer blocks, allowing each query to retrieve view-dependent geometry from the shared scene state. Query-token representations are retained after blocks 4, 8, 12, and 16, providing multi-layer features at four stages of the decoder. These multi-layer features are subsequently processed by a DPT Feature Adapter, whose role is to transform the decoder representations into the feature interface expected by the frozen VGGT-Ω DPT head. For each level, the final query representation is fused with the corresponding intermediate representation through a learned sigmoid gate and a level embedding. Two additional Perceiver layers allow the query tokens to attend to the final scene tokens, and an independent MLP maps each level as 512 →1024 →1024 →2048. The resulting four feature maps are passed directly to the frozen VGGT-ΩDPT head to predict cam- era z-depth. The decoder receives only the scene state, query camera, and output dimensions, such that all scene information must pass through the fixed-size state bottleneck. During world-model training, both the Geometry Decoder and DPT head remain fixed, while gradients are propagated through them with respect to the input scene state. 15

text: Preprint Table 6: Detailed architecture of the model. Component Configuration Scene Tokenizer 512 queries of width 512; eight Perceiver layers; eight attention heads; MLP expansion ratio 4; 70.46M parameters Geometry decoder Width 512; two scene-conditioning blocks; 16 joint scene–ray blocks; four output branches with two Perceiver layers each; 135.55M parameters World Model Four-state context; 12 factorized blocks; width 1,152; eight heads; MLP expansion ratio 4; dropout 0.1; 256.55M parameters A.1.3 RESIDUAL WORLD MODEL The four observed scene states form an input tensor of shape 4 × 512 × 512, corresponding to four time steps, 512 spatial slots per state, and 512 feature channels per slot. Each token is first linearly projected from 512 to a model width of 1,152. A learned mask token is then replicated over 512 slots to construct a fifth state, which serves as the prediction position. To encode token identity, we use learned temporal and slot embeddings of 576 dimensions each. Their concatenation forms a 1,152-dimensional positional embedding, which is added to the projected tokens. Each Transformer block factorizes attention over time and space. Temporal attention is first applied across the five time positions independently for each of the 512 slots. Spatial attention then operates across the 512 slots independently within each time position. The two attention operations are followed by a 1152 →4608 →1152 feed-forward
title: Preprint

text: is first applied across the five time positions independently for each of the 512 slots. Spatial attention then operates across the 512 slots independently within each time position. The two attention operations are followed by a 1152 →4608 →1152 feed-forward network with GELU. All sublayers use pre- normalization, residual connections, and dropout. After the final block, the tokens at the fifth, masked prediction position are mapped back to 512 channels by a bias-free linear residual head. The head is zero-initialized, such that the model initially predicts a zero residual and therefore exactly recovers the Copy-Last prediction. A.2 CAMERA PREDICTOR The camera predictor forecasts future FRONT-camera poses from the observed ego-motion and the current FRONT image. The predicted trajectory is used as the future query-camera sequence for both GeoState (Pred. Camera) and Copy-Last (Pred. Camera). A.2.1 ARCHITECTURE The camera predictor contains 8.99M parameters and follows a motion-prior-plus-visual-refinement design. text: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering Shangheng Du1 2 ♠, Jinxin Shi1 2 ♠, Shuaiyu Zhang2, Yiming Wu2, Junpeng Zhao2 , Shiyang Feng2 , Xin Li2 , Liang He1 2 , Xiangchao Yan2 ♣♦and Bo Zhang2 ♣ 1East China Normal University, 2Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes as they become available. To address these challenges, we propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats
title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model

text: a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks. § Code Model

text: The rapid advancement of reasoning, code generation, and tool interaction in large language models (LLMs) is enabling artificial intelligence (AI) to move beyond assisting scientific research and engi- neering toward autonomously developing and improving AI systems. These efforts include model training, optimization of solver programs, and algorithm design, making AI for AI (AI4AI) a research direction toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). In this context, machine learning engineering (MLE) provides a concrete setting for this goal, requiring long-horizon optimization through repeated execution, feedback analysis, and revision rather than one-shot generation. Most existing MLE systems [1, 2, 3] extend code generation into iterative optimization through search, memory, or multi-agent collaboration. As shown in Figure 1(a), predefined workflows or search rules typically control experiment sequencing and stage transitions, while LLMs primarily generate or debug code at designated steps. In contrast, we study how to train models to organize experiments and improve solutions over sustained interaction, using experience and execution feedback from real-world MLE tasks. However, training this long-horizon optimization capability poses three challenges. 1) Open-ended MLE requires an interaction environment that preserves experimental states while leaving action selection to the model. 2) High-quality long-horizon supervision is difficult to obtain because MLE tasks are heterogeneous and interaction trajectories may mix useful exploration and failure recovery with degraded decisions. 3) Each costly experiment returns feedback on several preceding decisions before the full run ends; online RL must use this intermediate signal while handling policy mismatch during asynchronous collection. To address these challenges, we propose a post-training method for autonomous MLE that combines a model-directed long-horizon interaction harness, hierarchical agentic SFT, and Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning (WIRL). Based on this, we train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic model, to learn long-horizon optimization strategies. As shown in Figure 1(b), MLExpert uses sustained tool interaction within the interaction harness to autonomously organize experiments, revise solutions based on execution feedback, and maintain submission candidates. We build the Kaggle-MLE Factory to convert historical Kaggle competitions into executable MLE tasks. Therefore, we build the Kaggle-MLE Factory, which converts historical competitions into executable tasks with a public workspace, a hidden test split, and a unified evaluation interface. The Factory uses a multi-agent pipeline for task construction, validation, and repair. The discovery agent filters competitions by status, scale, and submission format. After competi- tion data, leaderboard information, and official descriptions are collected, the analyzer agent extracts data structures, fields, and modality characteristics to form a task specification. The generator agent then prepares task data, constructs a held-out test split with hidden labels from the original labeled data, and implements the task-specific evaluator. The task is executed on real data and iteratively repaired based on validator checks of data integrity, submission format, and evaluation behavior to produce valid executable tasks. Standardized task packages support different MLE agent frameworks. Final manual review excludes tasks with unresolved label or scoring issues before trajectory collection.

Interaction Harness for Long-Horizon MLE Optimization To support model-directed long-horizon MLE optimization, we design an interaction harness that follows ReAct-style loop [9], leaving branch selection and optimization-path decisions to the model rather than an external search policy. The harness stores experimental states in solution nodes, each containing candidate code, execution logs, and metadata. Parent-linked revisions form an experiment tree that the model can revisit and compare to decide whether to continue, backtrack, or change optimization direction. The harness provides tools for solution analysis, code revision, experiment execution, history retrieval, and submission management. The model launches candidate execution through execute_code and updates its submission candidate through update_answer. The complete tool list and descriptions are provided in Appendix B. As interaction history approaches the context limit, earlier messages are summarized while recent interactions are retained. For complex analysis, analyze delegates task analysis, data exploration, and result diagnosis to an analysis sub-agent with independent context, returning only a summary to the main model. Agentic MLE Post-Training 4.1. Hierarchical Agentic SFT Long-horizon MLE optimization requires general tool-use, coding skills, and domain-specific decision making. We therefore use two-stage hierarchical agentic SFT. In the first stage, coding and tool-use trajectories from diverse agentic tasks are used to learn basic tool-use and code revision capabilities. The second stage adopts teacher trajectories from MLE domain and literature-derived scientific tasks to improve algorithm design, experimental analysis, and iterative optimization. Complementary MLE demonstrations. MLE adaptation data cover both task initialization and sustained optimization. For trajectories whose first complete solution executes successfully and reaches a quality threshold, we extract the interaction prefix from task start through the corresponding execution feedback as an initial-solution trajectory, typically covering task understanding, algorithm design, and code generation. We also use long-horizon optimization trajectories from complete interactions, covering solution construction, feedback analysis, iterative revision, and final submission selection. In addition, analysis sub-agent trajectories are adopted to train the model for independent data analysis and result diagnosis. Outcome-guided supervision selection. Long-horizon MLE trajectories can contain effective ex- ploration and failure recovery, but may also include misguided decisions or continued degradation after reaching a strong solution. text: data analysis and result diagnosis. Outcome-guided supervision selection. Long-horizon MLE trajectories can contain effective ex- ploration and failure recovery, but may also include misguided decisions or continued degradation after reaching a strong solution. Therefore, we use execution results of submitted solutions to select high-quality trajectories and the segments used for supervision. For trajectories that pass a quality threshold, we identify the first best-performing submission and measure the subsequent performance degradation. When the post-peak degradation exceeds a threshold, we use the first best-performing submission as the anchor for retaining a trajectory prefix; otherwise, we use the last submission. The prefix ends at a complete tool-interaction boundary near the anchor. This removes degraded tails while preserving useful exploration and failure recovery before the peak. Supervision samples and training objective. To preserve multi-turn context dependencies, each supervision sample combines existing interaction context with a continuous sequence of subsequent model actions and environment feedback from the selected MLE interactions. When context com- paction occurs, the retained history and summary form the conditioning context for subsequent samples. Training loss is applied only to newly generated reasoning, text responses, and tool-call tokens, while tool feedback and inherited interaction history are used only as conditioning context and masked out from the loss. Details of outcome-guided filtering, score normalization, and the SFT objective appear in Appendix C.1. 4.2.

Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning Building on SFT, we further optimize the long-horizon decision policy using execution feedback from the model’s own exploration. In MLE, solution quality is available only after training and evaluation, and each result depends on multiple rounds of analysis, code revision, and tool interaction. We introduce Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL), which groups consecutive model decisions made between successive experiment results into an execution window 𝑢𝑚. Each window is conditioned on the accumulated interaction history and associated with the outcome of the corresponding experiment launched through the execute_code tool (Sec. 3.2). The first window starts from the initial task state. This allows policy updates to use feedback from completed experiments without waiting for the entire task trajectory to finish. 5

RL baselines and key WIRL design choices. We compare WIRL with trajectory-level GRPO and PPO- style optimization under the same MLE environment and MLE-SFT initialization. GRPO uses group- relative advantages, whereas PPO-style optimization uses a clipped objective weighted by terminal trajectory rewards without an additional critic. We also evaluate WIRL variants that remove the trend reward or policy correction separately. As shown in Table 4, GRPO and PPO-style optimization achieve 56.1% and 60.6%, respectively, both below the 62.1% achieved by MLE-SFT, supporting WIRL’s overall design of learning from execution-window feedback. In contrast, the two WIRL variants reach 66.7% and 65.2%, respectively, while full WIRL further improves the medal rate to 72.7%, indicating that both the local trend reward and policy correction contribute to the final improvement. Agents for Automated ML Research LLM agents increasingly automate data analysis, model development, and experimental iteration, with recent work extending to autonomous AI system design and improvement [27]. AIDE [1] and MLE- STAR [2] improve candidate solutions through iterative search and refinement, while MLEvolve [28] and MARS [29] use structured tree- or graph-based search, memory, and planning to organize long- horizon experimentation. R&D-Agent [3] studies multi-role collaboration, while InternAgent [30] and FM-Agent [31] extend autonomous AI research across machine learning, algorithm optimization, and engineering tasks. Recent systems including Arbor [4] and Argus [5] maintain persistent research states and increase model control. 10

text: Recent work develops MLE capabilities by training models on interaction experience. ML-Agent [6] combines multi-turn demonstrations with single-step RL, while RL for MLE Agents [32], MLE-RL [33], and AceGRPO [34] study online MLE training with execution feedback, asynchronous sampling, or intermediate trajectory states. Learning to Ideate [35] trains models to generate algorithm improvement suggestions, whereas Frontis-MA1 [7] applies SFT and RL to program evolution operators and combines them through an external evolutionary framework. These approaches primarily train individual interaction steps or local components of externally organized optimization workflows. SandMLE [36] applies trajectory-wise on-policy RL in micro-scale synthetic MLE environments. We train model-directed long-horizon interaction policies on real-world MLE tasks, with WIRL using execution windows to learn multi-turn decisions from delayed execution feedback under asynchronous updates. 6.2. Post-Training Long-Horizon Agentic Models Recent research has increasingly focused on post-training agentic models for sustained interaction, complex tool use, and long-horizon decision making. SWE-Gym [37] trains coding agents using trajectories collected from executable environments, while Search-R1 [38] and WebRL [39] learn multi-turn tool use from environment feedback and outcome rewards. AgentFlow [40] directly optimizes planning policies in general multi-turn agentic interaction and uses trajectory-level outcomes to train intermediate decisions. Recent work has also explored generalist agentic models for long- horizon interaction. text: In this work, we introduce MLExpert, a 35B MoE agentic model trained to autonomously conduct and improve machine learning experiments over long interaction horizons. We build an automated MLE task factory and a model-directed interaction harness, and train MLExpert with hierarchical agentic SFT and WIRL to learn from teacher demonstrations and execution feedback collected from its own exploration. Extensive experiments show that MLExpert improves over its base model on MLE-Bench Lite and achieves performance comparable to larger frontier models. Further improvements on NatureBench Lite and in agent scaffold and algorithm optimization demonstrate cross-task gener- alization. These results support treating long-horizon optimization decision making as a trainable model capability, providing a practical path toward autonomous machine learning engineering and scientific experimentation. 11

text: A. Details of the Kaggle-MLE Factory We begin with a Meta-Kaggle1 competition metadata snapshot containing 11,649 entries. Guided by the task-selection principles of MLE-bench [8], the discovery agent considers task relevance, data availability, and the feasibility of offline evaluation. Automated initial screening uses competition completion, at least 50 participating teams, and a dataset size limit of 200 GB as default criteria, checks submission-interface compatibility, and consults an exclusion list of existing tasks. The agent further selects candidates across domains and data modalities, including vision, text, audio, tabular data, and time series. Candidates are collected and processed in multiple batches. The downloader and scraper retrieve competition data, official descriptions, and leaderboard infor- mation. The analyzer agent extracts data structures, field information, and modality characteristics to form a task specification, which the generator agent uses to produce data-preparation and scoring code. When test labels are unavailable, the pipeline constructs a held-out split from the original labeled data and keeps its labels on the evaluation side. The executor runs generated task packages on real data, while the validator agent checks structural completeness, submission-format consistency, non-degenerate labels, train–test identifier overlap, and data availability. The validator also executes the scoring function to check that it produces a valid score. Execution and validation errors are returned to the construction agents for repair. We conduct a final

These results indicate that SFT already supports effective scaffold optimization across held-out years. Further gains from WIRL. WIRL raises held-out accuracy from 38.1% to 43.7%, a gain of 5.6 percentage points, with improvements on all three held-out years. The resulting scaffold uses 8.40 calls per problem, compared with 3.51 for MLExpert-SFT and 8.65 for Kimi-K3. With a similar number of calls to Kimi-K3, MLExpert exceeds its 40.0% accuracy, while GLM-5.3 achieves 48.1% with 9.39 calls. The SFT and RL results therefore offer different accuracy–call trade-offs: SFT yields an effective scaffold with fewer calls, while further RL finds a more accurate scaffold that uses more calls. title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

text: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refine- ment it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two al- ternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator’s in- termediate features to estimate each token’s remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing pre- serves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ∼1.7 denoising steps per to- ken, running over 1.5× faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ∼2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35× faster at 24.5 fps. ∗Work done during internship

text: Diffusion models have enabled high-quality image and video generation, with recent video models achieving realistic appearance, natural motion, and faithful prompt following (Team Wan et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; NVIDIA et al., 2026; Team Seedance et al., 2026). Autoregressive (AR) video generators extend these capabilities to streaming generation (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025) and interactive world models (Team et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026; AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026). Within a video, however, different regions may require different amounts of refinement. Some may readily reproduce familiar content from the history, while others must form newly appearing structures or resolve fine details. This raises a fundamental question: Does every token need to be denoised until the final step? We study this question in distilled few-step AR video generators, whose intermediate predictions can already serve as plausible video outputs. Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025) uses intermediate clean estimates as outputs for distribution-matching training (Yin et al., 2024b;a), making them natural candidates for early commitment. We observe that many tokens already approximate the generator’s own full-step output in the initial steps, while others continue

text: 2025) uses intermediate clean estimates as outputs for distribution-matching training (Yin et al., 2024b;a), making them natural candidates for early commitment. We observe that many tokens already approximate the generator’s own full-step output in the initial steps, while others continue changing until the last step (Figure 2). These differences often follow intuitive patterns. Regions that reproduce previously observed con- tent can settle early, while nearby regions continue refining appearance or motion. Similar variation arises in world models as actions change the observed content. These observations motivate a simple principle: stop denoising tokens once they have converged, and spend the remaining computation only where refinement is still needed. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that predicts when each token’s estimate has suf- ficiently converged, allowing individual tokens to be accepted at different steps (Figure 1). Each intermediate clean estimate serves as a draft of the generator’s full-step output. A verifier deter- mines whether to accept the draft or continue refining it. Once accepted, the estimate is fixed as the token’s output and receives no further denoising updates, while retaining its cached keys and values as context for the remaining tokens. This requires predicting whether a token’s current draft is already close to its full-step output without running the remaining denoising steps. We address this challenge with two verifiers. Because drafts are

text: keys and values as context for the remaining tokens. This requires predicting whether a token’s current draft is already close to its full-step output without running the remaining denoising steps. We address this challenge with two verifiers. Because drafts are clean latent estimates, similarity to previously generated content and changes between consecutive estimates of the same token provide evidence of convergence without additional training. Our training-free verifier uses similarity to clean history or reference content at the first step and stability between consecutive drafts at later steps. We also introduce a learned verifier for demanding settings such as world models, leveraging contextual cues encoded in the pretrained generator’s intermediate features. A shallow head trained with the generator frozen predicts each token’s gap to the full-step output, showing that the interme- diate features contain cues about how much its predictions will change with further denoising. Both verifiers support token-wise acceptance without modifying the generator’s weights. We evaluate Speculative Forcing on LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a) and the world model Lingbot- World 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026). On both short and long videos, our method maintains the quality of the four-step generator with approximately 1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5× faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. text: Autoregressive Video Generation. Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate succes- sive frames or chunks conditioned on preceding content (ai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; 2024a). Distribution matching distillation (Yin et al., 2024b;a) enables few-step generation by aligning the student’s output distribution with a target distribution represented by a pretrained teacher. CausVid applies distribution matching to distill a bidirectional teacher into a causal generator (Yin et al., 2025), while Self Forcing trains on autoregressive rollouts conditioned on the generator’s own out- puts (Huang et al., 2025). Causal Forcing revisits this distillation for real-time interactive genera- tion (Zhu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). LongLive, Rolling Forcing, and Self-Forcing++ extend few-step generation to long streaming videos (Yang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b; Cui et al., 2025). 2

Caching methods accelerate diffusion by reusing intermediate computation across denoising steps (Ma et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a), including reuse selected per token (Zou et al., 2025) and,

text: methods accelerate diffusion by reusing intermediate computation across denoising steps (Ma et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a), including reuse selected per token (Zou et al., 2025) and, in AR video generation, per chunk or by local motion (Ma et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Spatially adaptive samplers redistribute computation within the schedule, with RAS recomputing only the regions the model attends to (Liu et al., 2026) and HSA evaluating each token at a different number of steps along the same noise schedule (Chu & Patel, 2026). In both cases every token is carried to the end of the schedule, so no token is ever declared finished, and the error left by the computation that was skipped has to be kept bounded by periodic full updates. Substituting a previous output also weakens as the schedule shortens, since distilled samplers leave fewer steps over which one output can stand in for the next (Zou et al., 2026). In Self Forcing-style generators, DSA and Surprise Forcing select denoising depth for an entire frame or chunk, assigning the same number of steps to settled and unsettled regions (Le et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Speculative Forcing instead treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts that can be committed at different

text: for an entire frame or chunk, assigning the same number of steps to settled and unsettled regions (Le et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Speculative Forcing instead treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts that can be committed at different steps according to token-wise convergence (Figure 2). It draws on draft verification in speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024), without adopting its exact acceptance rule. Committed tokens receive no further denoising updates, while their cached keys and values remain as context for the remaining tokens. 3 METHOD Speculative Forcing allows individual tokens to stop denoising at different steps. Accepted drafts are fixed as output, while their cached keys and values provide context for tokens that continue denoising (Section 3.2). To determine when to accept each draft, we introduce two verifiers that predict convergence from latent estimates or the generator’s intermediate features (Section 3.3). 3.1 PRELIMINARIES Autoregressive video diffusion. Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate a video as a sequence of latent chunks {c1, c2, . . . }, each containing one or more consecutive frames. The joint distribution is factorized as p(c1, c2, . . . ) = Q t p(ct | c<t), where each conditional distribution is modeled through a diffusion process. At inference, the model generates each chunk by progressively

The draft can be compared with clean content or its own previous estimate, motivating a training-free verifier. The generator’s intermedi- ate features provide additional contextual information, which a learned verifier uses to predict the convergence gap. Since latent tokens encode content across multiple output frames, isolated accep- tance decisions can affect both spatial and temporal coherence. We therefore apply a spatiotemporal smoothing operator S to each verifier’s scores before thresholding, encouraging coherent decisions across neighboring tokens. 3.3.1 TRAINING-FREE VERIFIER At

A token can match the history and still need refinement, or change little between two steps and yet remain far from its final value. The learned verifier instead predicts the convergence gap directly from the generator’s own features. We com- pare generation quality and inference speed against uniform-step sampling, and examine whether preserving settled predictions while selectively refining the remaining tokens reduces error drift dur- ing autoregressive rollouts. We further analyze the verification tolerance, token selection, and the granularity of step allocation. 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS Experimental setups. We apply our method to LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a) (1.3B) and the Causal- Fast model of Lingbot-World 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026) (1.3B), both using four denoising steps. Increasing ϵ reduces mean denoising steps, with ϵ = 0.20 and ϵ = 0.24 maintaining the four-step generator’s quality while achieving lower Drift. text: degrade quality, highlighting the need to balance early acceptance with further refinement. Effect of verification signals. We adapt two existing selection criteria to token-wise commitment in latent space. Inspired by MotionCache (Xu et al., 2026), we measure temporal differences between adjacent latent frames at the same spatial position. We also adapt RAS’s predicted-noise dispersion signal (Liu et al., 2026) to the channel variance of each predicted clean latent token. Thresholds are calibrated on held-out data to obtain comparable mean denoising steps. As shown in Table 5, both adapted signals yield lower quality than our learned verifier and uniform sampling at similar mean steps. Temporal differences, for example, can reflect both camera-induced changes and intermediate distortions, limiting their reliability as convergence signals (Figure 5). These results support directly predicting each draft’s remaining convergence gap. Comparison with oracle verification. We additionally evaluate an oracle verifier that computes the full-step reference for each chunk using the same initial noise and conditioning, then uses the mea- sured convergence gaps to determine token acceptance. Adaptive denoising has been explored at frame and chunk gran- ularity (Le et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). To isolate commitment granularity, we use the same learned verifier but accept an entire chunk when its mean predicted convergence gap falls below a threshold at each step. The threshold is calibrated on held-out data against the oracle criterion to match our mean denoising steps. As shown in Table 5, token-wise commitment achieves higher quality and lower Drift at comparable mean denoising steps. Chunk-wise acceptance cannot distinguish tokens that have already converged from those that continue to change, resulting in lower quality and higher Drift when all tokens share the same acceptance step (Figure 5). 5
title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

text: We introduced Speculative Forcing, a framework that allocates denoising computation according to token-wise convergence in few-step autoregressive video generation. By treating intermediate clean estimates as drafts, it predicts which tokens can be accepted early and continues denoising only the remaining tokens. Training-free and learned verifiers enable these decisions without modifying the generator’s weights. Experiments on short and long videos and controllable world model rollouts demonstrate faster generation while maintaining quality, with comparable or lower quality variation and preserved camera-following accuracy in world modeling. These results show that a shared denoising depth is not necessary for every token, supporting convergence-based acceptance as a practical approach to efficient video generation. 9

text: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS We retain the released backbone configurations except for the denoising policies evaluated in this work. For LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a), we use an attention sink of 3 latent frames, a local attention window of 12 latent frames, and 3 latent frames per chunk. Short and long videos contain 81 and 477 frames, respectively. For Lingbot-World 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026), we use the 1.3B Causal-Fast model with an attention sink of 6 latent frames, a local attention window of 18 latent frames, and 4 latent frames per chunk. Each benchmark video contains 253 frames. Lingbot-World 2.0 additionally receives a per-frame camera trajectory encoded through Pl¨ucker embeddings derived from relative camera-to-world poses. We retain the original camera-conditioning pathway, including per-video translation normalization by the maximum translation magnitude. For the main results, the training- free thresholds (τred, τstab) are (0.497, 0.327) for 5-second LongLive videos, (0.357, 0.235) for 30-second LongLive videos, and (0.375, 0.300) for Lingbot-World 2.0. We retain the original denoising schedules so that early commitment operates on the intermediate clean estimates supervised during distribution-matching training. In our configurations, LongLive and Lingbot-World 2.0 share the shifted timesteps [1000.0, 937.5, 833.3, 625.0], obtained from a 1000-step flow-matching schedule with a shift of 5.0. A token accepted at step k undergoes exactly
title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

text: clean estimates supervised during distribution-matching training. In our configurations, LongLive and Lingbot-World 2.0 share the shifted timesteps [1000.0, 937.5, 833.3, 625.0], obtained from a 1000-step flow-matching schedule with a shift of 5.0. A token accepted at step k undergoes exactly the first k steps of this schedule. Uniform-step baselines use the same prefixes, allowing us to compare token-wise acceptance with a shared exit step along the same trained denoising trajectory. The learned verifier reads hidden states from the generator’s final transformer block without an additional backbone forward. The head consists of layer normalization and three 3D convolutions with channel dimensions 1536 →96 →48 →1. The first two convolutions use 3 × 3 × 3 kernels with GELU activations, and the last uses a 1×1×1 kernel. The head’s output is average-pooled over 2 × 2 × 2 token blocks and expanded back to the original grid using nearest-neighbor interpolation. The head has 4.11M parameters and is shared across denoising steps. We train only the head using the smooth-ℓ1 loss and Adam with a learning rate of 10−3 and batch size 4. Within each chunk, accepted tokens retain the layer-wise keys and values computed at their accep- tance step, while active tokens update theirs as denoising continues. The cache can therefore contain KV states from different denoising steps. Once the chunk is
title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

text: Within each chunk, accepted tokens retain the layer-wise keys and values computed at their accep- tance step, while active tokens update theirs as denoising continues. The cache can therefore contain KV states from different denoising steps. Once the chunk is complete, the generator performs a clean forward pass over the assembled output at timestep 0, refreshing the KV states of all tokens regard- less of their acceptance steps. Subsequent chunks thus attend to history states computed from the completed clean output. We apply spatiotemporal smoothing to each verifier’s score map before thresholding at every veri- fication step. Spatial smoothing uses a normalized 9 × 9 Gaussian kernel with a standard deviation of 1.0 token and reflect padding, applied independently to each latent frame. Temporal smoothing then averages scores over the current and subsequent latent frames within the same chunk, using Gaussian weights with a standard deviation of 1.0 latent frame. Only tokens that have not yet been accepted are forwarded through the generator at subsequent denoising steps. We reduce execution overhead through shared indexing and in-place KV updates. We also merge each chunk’s clean pass with the next chunk’s first denoising pass while preserving timestep conditioning, attention dependencies, and KV update order. All baselines use the same applicable execution optimizations for fair throughput comparisons. B EVALUATION DETAILS B.1 EVALUATION METRICS

Lower Drift indicates more consistent imaging quality over time. 16

To quantify denoising computation, we report the average number of denoising evaluations per token across all chunks and videos, excluding the clean pass used to refresh the KV cache. We measure throughput on a single NVIDIA H100 as the number of generated frames divided by the DiT forward time, excluding VAE encoding and decoding. B.2 BENCHMARK CONSTRUCTION We construct a fixed benchmark of 200 scenes for Lingbot-World 2.0, each consisting of an initial image, a text prompt, and a camera trajectory. All methods use the same conditioning inputs and sampling seeds. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025) generates scene descriptions spanning diverse categories and visual styles, and Z-Image-Turbo (Image Team et al., 2026) generates the initial images at 1376 × 768. The image and video models receive the same scene prompt, com- bining environment, subject, and perspective descriptions. After fixing the benchmark, we construct the verifier’s training set from separate scenes using the same pipeline, filtering
title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

text: images at 1376 × 768. The image and video models receive the same scene prompt, com- bining environment, subject, and perspective descriptions. After fixing the benchmark, we construct the verifier’s training set from separate scenes using the same pipeline, filtering potential overlap through text and image similarity. Each video contains 253 frames, with the 252 camera transitions divided into five consecutive control segments of lengths 50, 50, 50, 50, and 52. For each segment, we uniformly sample an action from forward, backward, strafe left, strafe right, yaw left, yaw right, and stop, excluding the preceding segment’s action. Across the benchmark, this produces 593 trans- lation, 276 rotation, and 131 stationary segments. Translation speeds are sampled from U(0.2, 1.0), with the fastest translation segment in each video set to 1.0 to match the model’s per-video trans- lation normalization. Yaw rates are sampled from U(0.6, 2.0) degrees per frame. We choose the lower bound based on preliminary tests in which smaller commands produced little visible rotation. Camera intrinsics follow the official adapter defaults and remain fixed across methods. A per-token MLP achieves verification accuracy comparable to OursH, suggesting that the back- bone’s contextualized token features already provide useful convergence cues. Training on-policy, where the head sees the truncated history during training as well, is no better even though these measurements are taken on that distribution. The latent-based signals support our training-free design. Redundancy is available at the first step but becomes less useful as a token is refined, while stability is stronger afterwards yet undefined at the first step. Our training-free verifier therefore uses redundancy at the first step and stability after, at the cost of two thresholds. Motion-based scheduling stays below redundancy at every step and tolerance. The head leads every latent signal throughout. If the backbone is sensitive to reducing denoising steps, fewer tokens can be accepted early without degrading generation quality, which limits the attainable speedup. Similarly, more challenging domains may require additional refinement across a larger fraction of tokens. This is evident in world generation, where large viewpoint changes introduce stronger distortions than stan- dard video generation and result in

text: which limits the attainable speedup. Similarly, more challenging domains may require additional refinement across a larger fraction of tokens. This is evident in world generation, where large viewpoint changes introduce stronger distortions than stan- dard video generation and result in higher mean denoising steps, as shown in Table 3. Our method therefore does not guarantee the same acceleration across different generators or domains. D.2 OTHER DISCUSSIONS Mean Steps and Realized Speed-up. The clean forward pass used to refresh the KV cache adds one full pass per chunk. Assuming computation scales linearly with token evaluations, the ideal speed-up relative to the four-step generator is 5/(¯k + 1). Approaches that reuse noisy KV states, such as CausalRCM (Zheng et al., 2026), could avoid this pass and move the ideal speed-up toward 4/¯k. In practice, throughput does not scale proportionally with the mean denoising depth ¯k. Each chunk continues until its last active token is accepted, incurring forward-pass overhead at every executed step even when few tokens remain active. This overhead therefore depends on maxi k∗(i) within each chunk rather than the average across tokens. Reducing this overhead would bring the realized speed-up closer to the ideal implied by the mean denoising depth. text: across tokens. Reducing this overhead would bring the realized speed-up closer to the ideal implied by the mean denoising depth. D.3 POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS Our experiments focus on general video generation and world modeling, but token-wise commit- ment may be particularly effective when much of the target content is already constrained by avail- able conditions. In talking-head generation (Huang et al., 2026), for example, the background can remain largely unchanged while motion is concentrated around the face and upper body. In environment-grounded world models such as Seoul World Model (Seo et al., 2026) and World Ob- server (Choi et al., 2026), warped scene observations and reference images provide visual evidence for parts of the target view, while uncovered regions require new content to be generated. Dexterous World Models (Kim et al., 2025) provide static scene renderings along the camera trajectory and generate interaction-induced changes while preserving unaffected content. 19

title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery

text: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, speci- fications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery, however, poses fundamentally different challenges: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. To address this gap, we introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments featuring scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer sys- tems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. Beyond binary task completion, FDE-Gym scores agents on how much their delivered system improves the customer’s own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution); scores are penalized for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time) to discourage excessive or careless engagement. FDE-Gym also provides an online platform where humans can develop and practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting (unstated constraints need to be discovered), the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56, and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). text: Deploying AI in enterprise settings requires more than meeting stated customer requirements. The challenge often lies in identifying which changes will improve customer operations in practice. One scenario in our benchmark illustrates this problem. A vice president at a drilling operator seeks a generative-AI success story for the November board meeting. The vice president requests a daily summary email and an “Ask your wells” chat box, noting that the downtime-coding system is already in place and therefore outside the project scope. Yet a solution built strictly to the task instruction can be delivered on time, pass every functional check, and still fail to move the customer’s own business metric by a single point. The bottleneck lies in monthly downtime credit claims. The existing keyword-based script incorrectly attributes some downtime to the contractor, resulting in at least one disputed line each month and suspending the credit for that month. Addressing this problem requires revisiting the downtime-coding system that the sponsor had explicitly excluded from the project scope. The engineer must identify the applicable contractual rule, confirm the interpretation with the cost engineer, and obtain approval for the change from an approver who is unavailable that week. This is the role of a forward-deployed engineer (FDE), an engineer assigned by a vendor to work within a customer organization. The role involves more

text: engineer, and obtain approval for the change from an approver who is unavailable that week. This is the role of a forward-deployed engineer (FDE), an engineer assigned by a vendor to work within a customer organization. The role involves more than building what the sponsor initially requests. An FDE must identify what will actually help and work with customer systems and stakeholders to deliver the improvement. Existing benchmarks rarely address this last mile of AI delivery, typically assuming that the problem has already been well defined. Software-engineering benchmarks provide issues and hidden tests [1, 2, 3], deployment bench- marks provide specifications [4], enterprise benchmarks provide predefined tasks [5, 6], and clarification bench- marks withhold information from an otherwise correctly specified task [7, 8] — in each case, the underlying prob- lem remains fixed. Recent benchmarks come closer to real-world delivery. τ τ-bench [9] evaluates agents that build customer-service systems from client requirements and deploy the resulting systems against held-out users. A post- training benchmark [10] assigns agents the role of forward-deployed engineers and evaluates whether the delivered model improves performance. XYEval [11] tests agents on misleading user requests. However, these benchmarks still address individual aspects of delivery in isolation. text: XYEval [11] tests agents on misleading user requests. However, these benchmarks still address individual aspects of delivery in isolation. FDE-Gym addresses these challenges in a single benchmark of 95 tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. The sponsor’s request may target the wrong problem, critical constraints must be discovered through stakeholder interaction, and performance is measured using the customer’s own business metric. A solution that addresses the wrong problem therefore earns no credit. Delivered systems are deployed without modification and evaluated on held-out production data. The FDE-Gym score measures improvement on the customer’s own business metric after deducting stakeholder contact cost (Sec- tion 2.3 details what is charged). The do-nothing baseline (the unchanged system) scores 0, the expert-authored reference solution scores 1, and literal compliance with the sponsor’s request scores at most 0.2. Experimental results show that current models perform well below the reference solution on this scale. 2

Industry experts adapted real-world customer delivery projects carried out in China, Singapore, and the United States since 2024 into 20 scenarios spanning 18 sectors (Table 2). Each scenario yields an original task and several variants of it, which share a common customer environment but differ in key facts. Each original task and each variant is a separate benchmark task, for a total of 95 tasks. Tasks require agents to deliver an agent, workflow, or service that operates in the customer’s environment. The scenarios are grounded in industry practice, with the relevant regulations, standards, and public sources documented. Companies and individuals are either de-identified or fictional,

Companies and individuals are either de-identified or fictional, and some data are adapted from real-world industry sources. 3.2 Scenario Variants and Underlying Facts A single fixed task per scenario may allow models to rely on memorized solutions or recurring patterns. To reduce this risk, experts designed two to seven variants in addition to each scenario’s original task. Variants change key facts, including which rule is outdated, who holds critical information, and whether the sponsor’s request addresses the underlying problem. These changes may require different delivery solutions, so a solution that succeeds on one task of a scenario may fail on another. Across scenarios, no single problem pattern appears in more than one-third of the set. Together, these design choices encourage agents to evaluate the evidence in each task rather than apply a fixed solution. 5

Stakeholder responses are scripted for reproducibility, as switching the user-simulation model can shift measured agent success rates by sev- eral percentage points [14]. (1) The reference solution must score at least 0.95. (2) The do-nothing baseline must score 0. The second component of the finding is stakeholder contact cost. GPT-6 Astra’s delivered systems reach 0.8 on 36 of 95 tasks, but only 9 remain resolved once stakeholder contact cost is deducted; for Claude Opus 5.5 the figures are 40 and 14. Agents are not informed that questions incur a cost, and they ask as if questions were free. Stakeholder contact cost consumes 0.14 of the 0.70 uplift delivered by Claude Opus 5.5 and 0.22 of the 0.60 delivered by GPT-6 Astra. At the other extreme are models that rarely ask: Mistral Small 4 asks 0.7 questions per task and obtains 6% of the key facts. 5.4 Weak Models Frequently Score Below the Do-Nothing Baseline Finding 4 The weakest models score below the do-nothing baseline on 60–83% of tasks; on these tasks, delivering nothing would have been the better outcome. A score of zero is not the floor: a system that pays out claims it should have refused, charges the wrong party, or wakes the wrong engineer performs worse than the system it replaced. text: Existing benchmarks each measure one stage of a delivery. Table 4 arranges them by the capability they isolate. To our knowledge, none joins these stages into a single causal chain in which a misreading of the problem renders good code worthless and the loss appears on a business metric. The most closely related work was published within weeks of ours. τ τ-bench [9] makes agent construction the task: a developer agent receives a business’s records, a client who holds the requirements, an existing codebase, and limits on serving cost, and the customer-service agent it delivers is then deployed against held-out simulated users. Its strongest configuration passes 23.9% of simulations, compared with 82.2% for an expert-authored reference; we likewise find the best model well short of a reference written by experts. FDE-Gym differs in what it varies and in what it measures. The task instruction varies from a full statement of the rules to a request that may be misdirected, stakeholder contact incurs a charge, the result is measured as uplift on the customer’s business metric relative to a do-nothing baseline of zero, which a delivery can fall below, and the scenarios span 18 sectors and deliverables beyond customer-service agents. Trains but Doesn’t Learn [10] places an agent in the role of a forward-deployed engineer for model post-training and identifies the

Trains but Doesn’t Learn [10] places an agent in the role of a forward-deployed engineer for model post-training and identifies the failure mode in which every check continues to pass while the delivered model is no better than the base model; our literal-compliance anchor is designed to expose the same kind of delivery. Two lines of work bear directly on our task instruction levels. XYEval [11] turns existing benchmarks, τ 2-bench [34] among them, into XY problems, in which the user asks about an attempted solution rather than the real problem, and reports relative drops of up to 46.7%. Our leading models lose little when the sponsor’s request is misdirected, perhaps because, within a full engagement, the documents, data, and stakeholders around the sponsor are all avail- able to contradict it. UnderSpecBench [35] holds the environment and the correct action fixed while degrading the instruction along three axes, an isolation strategy that our task instruction levels also use, and finds that underspeci- fication leads agents to guess rather than fail; Implicit Intelligence [23] reports a best pass rate of 48.3% on simple requests whose constraints must be discovered. Both are consistent with where our levels locate the largest drop: at the

LHAW [8] is the most systematic treatment of missing information and models the cost of asking; our L0 to L1 step reproduces its finding that agents rarely recover full-specification performance by asking, and our L3 adds a situation it does not cover: a request that is misdirected. Vending-Bench [30] showed that an executable business simulation can replace human judges; we attach one to an engineering deliverable. Two methodological warnings also shaped the design. Results obtained against LLM-played users depend on which model plays the user [14], which is why our stakeholders are scripted, and single-run success overstates reliability [36, 37], which is why every task is run three times. The admission anchors follow the practice of auditing an agentic benchmark with do-nothing and shortcut solutions before trusting its scores [38]. Beyond single benchmarks, long- horizon evaluations track the length of software tasks agents can complete [39], and Collaborative Gym [40] studies agents working alongside people; FDE-Gym instead sets people and agents the same tasks separately, so that the two can be compared. 7 Limitations A simulated customer. text: FDE-Gym measures an agent’s delivery the way a customer does: not by whether a system was delivered, but by whether the customer’s business improved. Measured in this way, the last mile of AI delivery remains long. The best of the thirteen configurations has an average FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves about one task in seven. The gap is not where we expected it to be. Leading models show little performance loss when the sponsor’s request is misdirected, and they obtain most of the facts held by stakeholders. Their principal performance losses arise when translating those facts into an effective system and from the stakeholder contact costs incurred during delivery. Weaker models lose more: on most tasks, the customer would have been better served by no delivery at all. These are the capabilities an experienced engineer brings to a customer. Closing the gap is therefore a question of judgment in delivery, and FDE-Gym makes that judgment measurable: one number per task, on the customer’s own metric, for people and agents under the same rules. text: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture Chen Yang1* Jiemin Fang1*† Fanpeng Meng1* Zihao Huang1 Jichen Pang2 Guanjun Wu3 Zhikuan Bao1 Qi Tian1 1Huawei Inc. 2Shanghai Jiao Tong University 3Huazhong University of Science and Technology *Equal contribution †Project lead Corresponding authors
title: SUPRA-TEX:

text: Single-image 3D generation aims to dress a given 3D mesh with relightable materials while faithfully preserving the visual details of a reference image. Existing methods either introduce artifacts when fusing inconsistent multi-view predictions or struggle to preserve fine details through implicit image-feature conditioning. To resolve these challenges, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, built on the principle of decoupling visible-material estima- tion, surface alignment, and observation-guided 3D completion. This division of labor allows the 3D generator, trained on limited 3D data, to focus its capacity on preserving visible evidence and completing unobserved surfaces. Specifically, we first train an MLLM-based image editing model to predict lighting-separated PBR maps in the reference view. We then project these maps onto the visible surface and encode them with the pretrained material VAE encoder into native observation latents that share the generation target’s latent space. An interleaved flow transformer holds these latents as fixed, read-only anchors while alternating unobserved- region and full-surface updates to generate complete material latents. This design achieves super-alignment with the reference, delivering What You See Is What You Get fidelity on visible regions and coherent comple- tion on unobserved surfaces. Trained solely on public datasets, SUPRA-Tex achieves SOTA performance in both geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation, matching or even exceeding leading commercial systems on in-the-wild images. text: For applications such as product digitization and embodied AI, generating relightable 3D assets from a single reference image requires faithful preservation of the reference appearance. We refer to this requirement as super-alignment: accurately reproducing fine-grained text, logos, and patterns at their corresponding visible surface locations, while completing unobserved regions with materials consistent with the visible appearance. Two prominent approaches to appearance generation are multi-view synthesis and native 3D generation. Multi-view pipelines leverage geometry-conditioned 2D generative models to synthesize appearance across surrounding viewpoints, then project and fuse the resulting images onto the mesh (Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025a). However, cross-view discrepancies can introduce seams and ghosting, while blending conflicting predictions blurs sharp reference details (Lai et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). Native 3D generation circumvents view-fusion artifacts by synthesizing appearance directly on 3D representations (Lai et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Xiang et al., 2026), yet preserving fine reference details remains challenging. For example, TRELLIS.2 employs a 3D material VAE to compress surface PBR properties into material latents, which are generated under geometry and image conditioning before being decoded into surface materials. Its image cross-attention provides no explicit correspondence between image details and 3D surface locations, leaving the generator to learn where those details belong. To improve spatial alignment, recent work lifts high-resolution image features into
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: before being decoded into surface materials. Its image cross-attention provides no explicit correspondence between image details and 3D surface locations, leaving the generator to learn where those details belong. To improve spatial alignment, recent work lifts high-resolution image features into 3D through camera projection (Li et al., 2026a). Yet even with explicit spatial correspondence, these conditions remain visual features rather than material observations. Consequently, the 3D generator must simultaneously shoulder the responsibilities of inferring PBR properties from visual features, reconstructing fine reference details at their corresponding surface locations, and synthesizing materials for unobserved regions. We argue that these responsibilities should not fall on a single 3D generator. Given the inherent scarcity of 3D training data, requiring the 3D model to learn these heterogeneous tasks jointly increases its learning burden. Instead, we offload visible-material estimation to 2D generative priors and establish explicit surface alignment through camera projection, separating both from the 3D generative task. Our key insight is to translate visible reference evidence into native material observations before 3D generation, then organize full-surface completion around this grounded evidence. Rather than forcing the 3D model to infer physical materials from abstract visual features, this formulation enables the generator to anchor directly on established material evidence, preserving reference details while focusing more of its capacity on completing unobserved surfaces. Based on this principle, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, a framework for generating relightable 3D assets with super-aligned textures. First, we leverage strong 2D priors by training an MLLM-based image editing model to jointly predict lighting-separated PBR maps in the reference view in a single forward pass, while preserving fine visual details. Next, we project these maps onto valid visible surface locations and encode the resulting partial materials with the pretrained material VAE encoder into native observation latents. Sharing the target latent space and directly decodable by the pretrained material decoder, these latents provide spatially aligned material content rather than abstract visual features that the 3D backbone must translate into PBR properties. We also encode the spatial extent of these observations to guide completion. To guide full-surface material generation, we design an interleaved flow transformer that reads the native observation latents as fixed, read-only reference memory at every block. Its blocks alternate between updating unobserved latent cells and the full surface, allocating more updates to cells without observations while retaining full-surface interactions for coherent completion. Since observations are indexed by 3D surface coordinates, the same interface
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: at every block. Its blocks alternate between updating unobserved latent cells and the full surface, allocating more updates to cells without observations while retaining full-surface interactions for coherent completion. Since observations are indexed by 3D surface coordinates, the same interface incorporates additional views, including 2D-generated back views, and interactive 2D edits without retraining the 3D backbone. Through this division of labor, SUPRA-Tex delivers What You See Is What You Get fidelity in the reference view while completing the asset with globally coherent, relightable materials, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Using only public datasets for training, SUPRA-Tex achieves SOTA results in both geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation. With synthetic back-view conditioning, SUPRA-Tex achieves reference fidelity and visual quality on real photographs comparable to or better than those of the leading commercial systems in our comparisons. Code and checkpoints are released on our project page to facilitate future research: supra-3d.github.io/supratex. Our main contributions are as follows: • Our key insight is to establish surface-aligned material observations before 3D generation, allowing the generator to focus on preserving reference details and completing unobserved surfaces. Built on this insight, SUPRA-Tex is trained solely on public datasets and, with synthetic back-view conditioning, achieves reference fidelity and visual quality comparable to or better than those of leading commercial systems in our comparisons. • We present native

text: Multi-view texture generation. Most texturing pipelines synthesize appearance in 2D views and fuse the predictions onto the mesh. Early approaches paint the mesh view-by-view with depth-guided diffusion and inpaint unobserved UV regions (Richardson et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024a). TexFusion aggregates view-wise denoising predictions in a shared latent texture map (Cao et al., 2023). Subsequent works improve cross-view coherence by synchronizing multi-view denoising (Liu et al., 2024b; Cheng et al., 2025; Bensadoun et al., 2024) or generating views jointly via geometry-conditioned diffusion (Huang et al., 2025b; Shao et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), a recipe also adopted by large image-to-3D systems (Zhang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025b; Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025b). Reference-guided methods also explicitly target appearance preservation: EASI-Tex combines mesh-edge guidance with image features for single-image texturing (Perla et al., 2024), while AlignTex aligns multi-view artwork with the mesh before projection and texture refinement (Zhang et al., 2025b). Optimization-based approaches such as DreamMat distill geometry- and light-aware diffusion priors into PBR materials (Zhang et al., 2024b). Paint-it instead optimizes convolutionally parameterized PBR texture maps with score distillation (Youwang et al., 2024). To produce relightable assets, multi-view generation is extended to PBR channels using lighting-aware priors, material latent representations, or alternating view-space baking (Deng
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: et al., 2024b). Paint-it instead optimizes convolutionally parameterized PBR texture maps with score distillation (Youwang et al., 2024). To produce relightable assets, multi-view generation is extended to PBR channels using lighting-aware priors, material latent representations, or alternating view-space baking (Deng et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025a; Yeo et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2025; Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025a; Lai et al., 2025; Bao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026b), often aided by single-image intrinsic delighting (Kocsis et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024b; Ke et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; He et al., 2025b; Careaga & Aksoy, 2024). Nevertheless, residual inconsistencies between synthesized views can blur or ghost sharp reference details during projection and blending. In contrast, SUPRA-Tex completes materials in native 3D space, using projected observations as conditioning anchors rather than directly fusing synthesized views into the final texture. Native texture generation. Driven by the rise of large-scale 3D pretraining, native texture generation has emerged as an alternative paradigm. Existing approaches explore diffusion over point, octree, and UV representations (Yu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2024) and PBR prediction with octree-aligned Gaussians (Xiong et al., 2025). Latent texture generators, such as NaTex, LaFiTe, and TEXTRIX, learn structured latent spaces for surface colors or attributes (Lai et al.,
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: 2023; Liu et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2024) and PBR prediction with octree-aligned Gaussians (Xiong et al., 2025). Latent texture generators, such as NaTex, LaFiTe, and TEXTRIX, learn structured latent spaces for surface colors or attributes (Lai et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026), while native 3D foundation models jointly represent geometry and appearance (Chen et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025; 2026). Beyond global conditioning, partial observations and spatially aligned features have also been explored. At scene scale, WorldGrow (Li et al., 2026b) extends TRELLIS with context-conditioned 3D block inpainting for progressive scene generation. TEXGen back-projects partial UV maps (Yu et al., 2024), NaTex encodes initial textures for refinement (Lai et al., 2026), and TEXTRIX encodes projected appearance with its pretrained attribute VAE in the generation target’s latent space (Zeng et al., 2026). For spatial feature alignment, camera projection techniques originally developed for implicit reconstruction (Saito et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2021a) have been adapted to 3D generative models, such as CUPID’s pose-aligned features and Pixal3D’s camera-frame back-projected multi-scale features (Huang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a). Even with spatially aligned image features, the 3D generator must still infer material properties, preserve reference details, and complete unobserved surfaces. 3 Method Given a reference image I, a mesh M, and its camera projection

Even with spatially aligned image features, the 3D generator must still infer material properties, preserve reference details, and complete unobserved surfaces. 3 Method Given a reference image I, a mesh M, and its camera projection π, SUPRA-Tex generates full-surface, relightable PBR materials. Figure 2 summarizes the three stages: reference-view material estimation, surface-aligned native observation encoding, and observation-guided 3D completion. We first introduce the material representation and upstream geometry model, then describe the three stages, training objective, and inference procedure. Appendices A and B provide implementation and training details; Appendix G.1 describes additional-view conditioning and texture editing. 3.1 Preliminaries Surface PBR and material latents. We represent surface appearance through physically based rendering (PBR) properties over the mesh M. At any surface location p ∈M, these properties comprise albedo a ∈R3, metallic m ∈[0, 1], and roughness r ∈[0, 1]. We build on the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2026), which additionally includes opacity α ∈[0, 1], giving the material tuple T(p) = (a(p), m(p), r(p), α(p)). Separate sparse VAEs compress 3D geometry and surface materials into geometry latents G = {gs}s∈S and material latents Z = {zs}s∈S over active coordinates S. For sparse surface attributes P, the pretrained material VAE encoder Emat yields Z; conditioned on G, the material generation stage models PBR materials

For sparse surface attributes P, the pretrained material VAE encoder Emat yields Z; conditioned on G, the material generation stage models PBR materials directly in the native 3D space by generating Z, which the decoder Dmat restores onto the mesh surface. Geometry foundation and camera projection. Our framework takes a mesh M and camera projection π, either provided as ground truth or predicted from the reference image. We use the open-source TRELLIS.2-based Pixal3D variant (Li et al., 2026a; Xiang et al., 2026), denoted Pixal3D⋆, which supports geometry and material generation. Its geometry module predicts the reference-aligned mesh for end-to-end generation. 3
