text: Dmat converts Z0 into surface PBR materials, lit from the left and right. 3.2 Image-to-Material Translation To reduce the learning burden on the 3D generator, we separate reference-view material estimation from 3D surface completion. Specifically, we train an MLLM-based image editing model F2D to infer reference-view albedo and metallic-roughness (MR) maps directly from the input photograph: bT2D = F2D(I) = (ba, bm, br) , (1) where ba denotes the albedo map, and bm and br denote the metallic and roughness maps. To reuse the 3-channel pretrained image VAE, we pack bm and br with a constant channel into a 3-channel map, which also fulfills the input format expected by the pretrained material encoder. Joint alignment and one-step inference. To coordinate channel predictions while retaining pretrained image priors, F2D adapts a multimodal DiT backbone (Super Intelligence Team, 2026) via factorized modality-axis joint attention, jointly predicting albedo, metallic–roughness, and auxiliary normal maps. This attention exchanges features across output modalities at corresponding spatial locations. We train the 2D material estimator on RGB images paired with ground-truth material and normal maps rendered from Objaverse, using a latent flow-matching objective at the fixed maximum-noise endpoint σ = 1.0. At inference, a single DiT forward pass at this endpoint (1.2 s on one H800) estimates clean material latents, which the VAE decodes into 1024 × 1024
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: using a latent flow-matching objective at the fixed maximum-noise endpoint σ = 1.0. At inference, a single DiT forward pass at this endpoint (1.2 s on one H800) estimates clean material latents, which the VAE decodes into 1024 × 1024 material maps without iterative denoising. This design has two advantages. First, it uses 2D image priors to disentangle illumination from intrinsic materials at full reference resolution. Second, it shields the downstream 3D generator from abstract visual features, letting the 3D model use physical PBR observations to focus on reference preservation and unobserved-surface completion. 3.3 Native Observation Encoding To supply physical observations to the 3D generator in a representation it natively understands, we bridge the estimated reference-view PBR maps bT2D directly to the surface of M using the pretrained material encoder Emat. Filtered surface projection. Through the camera projection π, we associate each foreground pixel u of bT2D with its first visible surface hit p ∈M. At inference, foreground-mask erosion and local depth-discontinuity filtering further remove unreliable boundary correspondences. The retained correspondences form the observation set Hvalid, shared by all PBR channels. Enlarged crops compare reference-view details; novel views show the completed appearance. 4 Experiments The supplement covers datasets, implementation, baseline configurations, evaluation protocols, and additional analyses. Datasets. Our 3D material generator is trained solely on publicly available 3D datasets. The training sources are summarized in Appendix B.1. We evaluate on two datasets with no overlap with the training set: DTC-Tex, comprising 100 texture-rich product scans selected from the Digital Twin Catalog (Dong et al., 2025), and Complex-Tex, comprising 110 Sketchfab (Sketchfab, n.d.) meshes with denser inscriptions, finer patterns, and more varied shapes. Implementation details. The 2D material estimator adapts FireRed-Image-Edit-1.1 (Super Intelligence Team, 2026) at 1024 × 1024 resolution. The 3D generator uses 60 Transformer blocks, with self-attention initialized from TRELLIS.2 and the remaining components initialized randomly; the pretrained material encoder and decoder remain frozen. We train the generator with a global batch size of 576 using AdamW on 64 GPUs. Inference uses 25 Euler steps without classifier-free guidance. 4.1 3D Generation with Given Geometry Setting and baselines. Each method textures the ground-truth mesh from a single forward-lit reference image. We record the ground-truth lighting and camera poses and render each textured result under these same conditions at the reference view and 15 novel views, isolating

text: with the same predicted PBR observations. Residual injection adds encoded observations through layerwise residuals. Joint-update attention updates observation states in selected layers and all generation states in every layer. In contrast, SUPRA-Tex keeps observations read-only and alternates unobserved-cell and full-surface updates (Sec. 3.4). It improves shaded PSNRfg over residual injection by 0.87 dB on DTC-Tex and 0.29 dB on Complex-Tex, and matches joint-update attention in shaded fidelity while improving albedo PSNRfg by 0.15 and 0.16 dB with lower MR MAE. Thus, the design preserves or improves reconstruction quality without spending computation on observation-state updates or full-surface queries at every block. The complete design also samples 1.20× and 1.18× faster than joint-update attention on the two datasets (Sec. 4.5). Effectiveness of 2D material estimation. To test whether the FireRed-based 2D material estimator supplies useful physical material estimates, we replace its predicted metallic and roughness with fixed values (M = 0, R = 0.5) or dataset means, keeping predicted albedo and the 3D generator unchanged (Table 5). Relative to fixed and dataset-mean MR, predicted MR improves shaded PSNRfg by 0.44 and 0.26 dB on DTC-Tex, and 0.69 and 0.57 dB on Complex- Tex, respectively, with lower MR MAE on both datasets. These gains show that the 2D estimates provide useful material information beyond albedo alone. Replacing all predicted PBR channels with ground

Large image–geometry discrepancies. In end-to-end generation, SUPRA-Tex uses geometry predicted by Pixal3D⋆. Large discrepancies in shape or pose between the reference image and the mesh can place projected material observations on incorrect surface locations. Correspondence filtering removes some unreliable observations, but cannot correct the underlying geometry, which remains fixed during material generation. Severe discrepancies can therefore
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: or pose between the reference image and the mesh can place projected material observations on incorrect surface locations. Correspondence filtering removes some unreliable observations, but cannot correct the underlying geometry, which remains fixed during material generation. Severe discrepancies can therefore prevent faithful texture alignment. Improving upstream geometry and camera alignment is therefore an important direction, but we do not evaluate corrected-geometry controls here. Hallucinated geometry on unseen surfaces. Upstream geometry generators such as Pixal3D⋆can introduce implausible unseen structures even when the visible shape matches the reference. These structures may deviate from shapes learned by the material generator, hindering coherent texture completion. Since SUPRA-Tex conditions on fixed geometry, it cannot remove these structures; their influence on texture generation can reduce final asset quality. 11

text: boundaries. Completing unseen surfaces is particularly challenging when text or patterns extend beyond the visible region. For example, lettering that wraps around a can may be only partially visible in the input. The model may preserve the visible fragment yet fail to continue its strokes or layout coherently onto the hidden side, producing inconsistent text or patterns across the visibility boundary. Errors in 2D material estimation. The 2D material estimator can misinterpret material properties, for example by assigning high metallic values to a non-metallic surface. These estimates condition the 3D generator, which may retain the error in the completed asset and produce implausible reflections under rendering or relighting. Accurate transfer of reference details thus does not guarantee correct material decomposition. Failure cases. Figure 6 illustrates these limitations. Reference fidelity depends on usable image–surface correspondence and reliable material observations, while fine detail on unseen surfaces must be generated. The plate shows a printed motif reconstructed as protruding geometry, and the sign retains spurious structures after texture refinement. The owl separates recognizable appearance details from an ambiguous reflectance estimate; the teapot separates sharp observed patterns from less precise unseen completion. These are qualitative cases, without corrected-geometry controls or measured unseen-surface ground truth. A back view may help the last case; we report no paired two-view result.
title: SUPRA-Tex

text: We presented SUPRA-Tex, a framework for single-image 3D generation with super-aligned textures through observation- guided material completion. By separating visible-material estimation and surface alignment from 3D generation and using native observation latents as fixed, read-only anchors, SUPRA-Tex preserves fine reference details while generating coherent, relightable materials across the full surface. Trained solely on public data, it achieves state-of- the-art results among the evaluated methods in geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation. With synthetic back-view conditioning, it is also competitive with commercial systems in human evaluations on the mixed real-and-synthetic comparison set. These results demonstrate the value of spatially aligned, directly usable material observations for reconciling reference fidelity with full-surface generation. 12

text: SUPRA-Tex Supplementary Material This supplement provides method and training details, evaluation protocols, additional results, and extended discussion. The guide below links to each appendix and selected subsections; page numbers indicate where each appendix begins. • Appendix A: Additional Method Details (p. 19). Geometry and camera projection, visible-surface observations, and boundary filtering; the interleaved flow transformer, including token dimensions and its read-only update schedule. The training objective and inference procedure are given in Sec. 3.5. • Appendix B: Training Data and Optimization (p. 20). Training data, the 2D material estimator F2D, and 3D generator training, including observation construction, optimization, and checkpoint selection. • Appendix C: Evaluation Protocols (p. 21). Evaluation datasets, rendering cameras, alignment, and metrics, baseline configurations, and commercial comparisons. • Appendix D: 2D Material Evaluation (p. 23). 2D material prediction accuracy and F2D runtime measurements. Reference-view versus novel-view fidelity and 3D sampling efficiency are reported in Secs. 4.1 and 4.5. • Appendix E: Ablation and Observation Analyses (p. 24). Ablation settings, the partial-versus-complete encoding diagnostic protocol, observed-support encoding versus zero filling, and early learning with native PBR latents. • Appendix F: Additional Qualitative Comparisons (p. 26). Additional visual comparisons for given-geometry texturing, end-to-end image-to-3D generation, and commercial systems, extending the main-paper examples. • Appendix G: Additional Views and Texture Editing (p. 26). Synthetic back-view conditions and image-based texture editing.

text: SUPRA-Tex A Additional Method Details A.1 Geometry and Surface Observations Geometry foundation and camera projection. Our framework operates on an underlying mesh M and camera projection π, provided as ground-truth inputs or estimated from the reference image. For end-to-end inference, we follow the default MoGe-2-based camera-estimation pipeline of Pixal3D⋆, whose geometry module generates the mesh. For the 3D position xs of latent coordinate s, the model samples image features through camera projection: fs = Sample(Φ(I), π(xs)) , (11) where Φ(I) denotes a 2D feature map. In the geometry refinement stages, Pixal3D⋆projects both the original and spatially upsampled image features and concatenates the sampled features. Combined with global image conditioning, these features align the predicted mesh M and camera projection π with the reference view, serving as the geometric input for our material generation. Surface observations and latent coordinates. The full surface defines the active latent-coordinate set S. Valid visible surface voxels form the partial PBR input Po, which is encoded before any latent-level conditioning is constructed. The resulting coordinates So identify cells with observations, but a cell in So can also contain unseen surface voxels; U = S \ So therefore denotes cells without any observation, not all unseen surface. Coverage ρs is the observed fraction of the surface voxels actually present in a cell, and repeated image samples of

text: also contain unseen surface voxels; U = S \ So therefore denotes cells without any observation, not all unseen surface. Coverage ρs is the observed fraction of the surface voxels actually present in a cell, and repeated image samples of one voxel do not increase it. Boundary distance ds uses the six-neighbor graph of active latent coordinates and is −1 if no unobserved cell is reachable. Inference-time boundary filtering. At inference, we additionally apply foreground-mask erosion and local depth- discontinuity filtering to reduce texture contamination from unreliable correspondences. Foreground erosion removes mixed pixels along the silhouette, and depth-discontinuity filtering rejects correspondences whose neighboring visible depths differ by more than a threshold, where a small projection error would move the observation onto a different surface. All material channels share the retained observation support, from which local material encoding, coverage, and boundary distance are computed. The generator has 60 Transformer blocks with hidden dimension 1536 and 12 attention heads, 30 of each update type; its self-attention modules are initialized from TRELLIS.2 and the remaining components randomly. The 3D generator uses assets from TexVerse (Zhang et al., 2025a), Objaverse-XL (Deitke et al., 2023), ABO (Collins et al., 2022), HSSD (Khanna et al., 2024), and open synthetic 3D collections, together with human scans from 4D-Dress (Wang et al., 2024), Human4DiT (Shao et al., 2024), THuman2.1 (Yu et al., 2021b), and X-Humans (Shen et al., 2023). These assets provide geometry and material supervision for observation-guided full-surface completion. All datasets are used in accordance with their respective licenses for non-commercial academic research. B.2 Training F2D We initialize F2D from FireRed-Image-Edit-1.1 adapted to individual PBR and normal prediction tasks, and jointly fine-tune it on aligned RGB images and ground-truth material and normal maps rendered from publicly available 3D assets. Both the task-specific adaptation and joint fine-tuning use these rendered data. Modality-axis attention is inserted at Transformer blocks 29, 39, 49, and 59, with rank 256 and four attention heads. We optimize these adapters and backbone blocks 29–49 using a latent flow-matching objective and AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019), with learning rates of 2 × 10−4 and 5 × 10−7, respectively. The VAE and text encoder remain frozen. By folding the batch dimension, the model processes albedo, metallic-roughness, and an auxiliary normal stream in parallel, inserting lightweight cross-attention adapters at specific transformer layers to exchange features across modality axes at identical spatial coordinates. Each object is evaluated from a front-view reference, together with its ground-truth mesh, PBR maps, and a 16-view camera rig. Typical cases are household products with printed labels or decorative motifs, such as canned goods, decorated ceramics, and books. Complex-Tex complements this set with 110 Sketchfab (Sketchfab, n.d.) meshes that carry denser inscriptions and finer patterns on more varied shapes. This subset includes branded packaging and vehicles covered by logos and fine print, as well as buildings and characters with more irregular shapes. A method receives only the designated reference image, or that image together with the mesh when geometry is given. Figure 8 shows examples from both datasets. Both DTC-Tex and Complex-Tex underwent strict duplicate checks during data collection to ensure no overlap with the training assets. We will release both evaluation benchmarks. text: RETHINKING ROUTING EXPLORATION IN MODERN MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS Bingcong Li1,2, Hao Ma2, Michael Muehlebach3,4, Niao He1, Yi Ma2 1 ETH Zurich 2 The University of Hong Kong 3 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 4 WU Vienna {bingcong.li, niao.he}@inf.ethz.ch, {haoma, mayi}@hku.hk, michael.muehlebach@tuebingen.mpg.de
title: RETHINKING ROUTING EXPLORATION

text: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales. Code is available here. 1
title: RETHINKING ROUTING EXPLORATION

text: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022). MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets (Li et al., 2026). At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024), Kimi (Team-Kimi, 2025; 2026), and Qwen (Team-Qwen, 2024b; Yang et al., 2025), among many others (Jiang et al., 2024; Abdin et al., 2024). At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and 𝐸experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects 𝐾experts (𝐾< 𝐸) for sparse activation (Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022). Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation (Team-Kimi, 2026; Liu et al., 2024). Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger 𝐸and 𝐾. For example, at the

text: have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation (Team-Kimi, 2026; Liu et al., 2024). Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger 𝐸and 𝐾. For example, at the same activation ratio 𝐾/𝐸, (𝐸, 𝐾) = (64, 8) is often preferred over (𝐸, 𝐾) = (8, 1). Since there are �𝐸 𝐾  expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations (Elango et al., 2026). The second advance is shared experts. Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Team-Qwen, 2024b). This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration. The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. text: ≈4.4 × 109 with (𝐸, 𝐾) = (64, 8), i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration. This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts 𝐸and vary the number of (total) activated experts 𝐾over {6, 8, 10}. A larger 𝐾simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig.1, shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as 𝐾increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as 𝐾increases in Figs.1b and 1d, suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger 𝐾. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively sup- presses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE

text: of the additional expressiveness from larger 𝐾. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively sup- presses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE is derived by mirroring the routing logits via sign negation, hence its name. As shown in Fig.1, MirrorMoE improves the performance of shared-expert MoEs and attains expressiveness gains from larger 𝐾. In summary, our contributions are as follows: ❖We identify an exploration dilemma in modern MoEs: the enlarged routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration, while shared experts make routing less explorative. As a result, the benefits of shared experts diminish as the routing space grows. ❖We propose MirrorMoE, which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to reconcile competing demands above. MirrorMoE is conceptually simple, and its adaptivity is theoretically characterized. ❖We demonstrate that MirrorMoE addresses the exploration dilemma across MoEs of different scales. On the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves pretraining and downstream performance by 0.67 and 1.64 points, respectively. Moreover, it enables shared-expert MoEs to consistently outperform their non-shared counterparts and restores the performance gains from increasing 𝐾; see Fig.1. 1.1

text: MoEs. Modern sparse MoEs originated with the sparsely gated MoE layer of Shazeer et al. (2017) and were extended to large-scale Transformers in e.g., Lepikhin et al. (2020); Fedus et al. (2022). Later work focused on improving scalability, stability, and expert specialization. GLaM (Du et al., 2022) demonstrated that sparse language models could scale beyond one trillion parameters, while ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) improved training stability. MoEs have since become widely adopted. Beyond those mentioned earlier, other representative examples include Gemma4, OLMoE and gpt-oss (Team-Gemma, 2026; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Agarwal et al., 2025). Across this development trajectory, two trends have clearly emerged: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. Tension between expressiveness and pretraining. A growing line of work shows that a model’s expressive capacity may not be readily realized without carefully designed training procedures (Lion et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Jha and Reagen, 2026; Wei et al., 2025a). Within the context of MoEs, related evidence is provided by Jin et al. (2024), which augments learnable experts with fixed zero, 2

Beyond shared experts, recent MoEs have also shifted toward fine-grained expert segmentation (Liu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Elango et al., 2026). text: MirrorMoE: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern MoEs Asymmetric training dynamics in shared-expert MoEs. We first ablate individual experts to assess their importance. Specifically, we zero out each expert’s output and measure the resulting perplexity change, ΔPPL = PPLafter −PPLbase. Next, we examine how this asym- metry in expert roles shapes explo- ration. Exploration aims to discover alternative routes that produce diverse token representations. On the one hand, the combinatorial growth of the routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration to identify (near-)optimal expert combinations. On the other hand, shared experts reduce feature variation, thereby weakening exploration. This mismatch gives rise to several practical inefficiencies. We reveal them by evaluating models ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. The above discussions provide an alternative interpretation of MirrorMoE beyond exploration. In MoEs with large 𝐸and 𝐾, not every token may require the full expressiveness from all activated experts. If a token can be learned well using fewer experts, the capacity of remaining experts can be devoted to other tokens. text: This work identifies an exploration dilemma in MoEs that combine fine-grained expert segmentation with shared experts. This tension can prevent the additional expressiveness enabled by fine-grained segmentation from being fully realized while also diminishing the benefits of shared experts. To address this, we propose MirrorMoE, which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across scales. Future direction. Our current approach addresses the exploration dilemma by shrinking the explo- ration space. A promising future direction is to improve the routing strategy itself for more efficient exploration. 10

text: MirrorMoE: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern MoEs Appendix A ADDITIONAL RELATED WORK Expressiveness does not necessarily translate directly into performance. Beyond those we have discussed earlier in Sec.1.1, additional works similarly suggest that the expressive capacity of neural networks may not be fully utilized in practice. For example, (Csordás et al., 2025) shows that many deeper layers in Llama 3.1 70B behave close to identity mappings. Since identity mappings are available “for free”, this motivates redesign of residual connections for scaling deeper (Zhang et al., 2026). MoE systems. A complementary line of work focuses on efficient MoE systems, including faster and more principled expert parallelism, fine-grained all-to-all communication, and topology-aware communication strategies; see e.g., (Hwang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). These methods aim to improve hardware utilization, communication efficiency, and end-to-end throughput. MirrorMoE is largely orthogonal to these system-level optimizations and can be integrated with them. Routing in MoEs. A broad line of work studies alternative routing mechanisms for MoEs. Hash Layers (Roller et al., 2021) use hash-based assignments, while BASE Layers (Lewis et al., 2021) and expert-choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022) promote balanced expert utilization through carefully designed token assignments, at the cost of not being strictly autoregressive. Clark et al. (2022) study scaling laws for routed models. Other approaches replace hard
title: MirrorMoE: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern MoEs

text: al., 2021) and expert-choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022) promote balanced expert utilization through carefully designed token assignments, at the cost of not being strictly autoregressive. Clark et al. (2022) study scaling laws for routed models. Other approaches replace hard top-𝐾selection with differentiable routing mechanisms (Muqeeth et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Vahidi et al., 2026). Several works post- train or fine-tune routers to enable token-adaptive computation (Yue et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024), while Kang (2025) uses reinforcement learning to improve routing decisions. During pretraining, noisy routing has also been explored to encourage broader expert exploration: Shazeer et al. (2017) introduce Gaussian noise, whereas Nie et al. (2021) use Gumbel noise. Routing has also been explicitly studied for multimodal models (Wei et al., 2025b). In contrast to approaches that encourage broader exploration, MirrorMoE adaptively suppresses experts to shrink the exploration space. The work of Liang et al. (2026) studies shared experts from an inference perspective, showing that they can hinder expert offloading, partly because shared experts reduce the importance of routed experts. However, their focus is on routing behavior at inference time, whereas we study how shared experts affect routing throughout pretraining. (2025), we adopt a Llama-style MoE architecture. We also follow DeepSeekMoE (Dai et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024) by using a dense FFN in the first Transformer layer, so that the first sparse layer receives sufficiently developed token representations for routing. MoE-100M-A38M is trained on two H100 GPUs, while all other models are trained on four. DCLM dataset (Li et al., 2024) is adopted. We use AdamW for optimization. The learning rate is selected from {1, 3, 5} × 10−4 based on performance after 500 training steps on a held-out validation set. We adopt a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule. The global batch size is 1024, with gradient accumulation used to reduce memory consumption. The model analyzed in Sec.2.2 is MoE-498M-A121M. For MoEs without shared experts, we convert the shared experts into routed experts to preserve the same total parameter count. B.2 Router Variance under Different Levels of Gumbel Noise When evaluating RouterVar𝑙, we replace deterministic top-𝐾(for non-shared MoEs) or top-(𝐾−𝑆) (for shared-expert MoEs) routing with stochastic sampling from the learned routing distribution. Such sampling is equivalent to perturbing the routing logits with unit-scale Gumbel noise (𝛽= 1) and then applying top-𝐾selection (Kool et al., 2019; Nie et al., 2021). We further extend this evaluation by defining RouterVar𝛽 𝑙, where the routing logits are perturbed by Gumbel noise parameterized by other 𝛽s. We consider 𝛽∈{0.5, 2} and report the resulting RouterVar𝛽 𝑙for MoE-498M-A121M model in Fig.6. The same trend persists across these perturbation levels, further showing that shared experts consistently reduce routing-induced variance. B.3 Increasing Exploration during Pretraining Can Be Tricky An alternative way to address the exploration dilemma is to encourage greater exploration during pretraining. However, this can be challenging for MoEs because stochastic routing may introduce unstable router dynamics and increased training variance. title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling

text: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine- grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier’s generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach.

text: Multimodal generative models have made remarkable progress in recent years (Cao et al., 2025; Seedream et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), producing visually compelling images conditioned on textual descriptions. Beyond visual fidelity (Wiedemer et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2025b), a central challenge lies in whether generated images faithfully follow complex instructions and reflect coherent world knowledge (Zhou et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Motivated by this challenge, visual verifiers have emerged as a crucial component for assessing the correctness of generated results. By providing feedback on the alignment between images and textual descriptions, verifiers not only serve as evaluation tools, but also act as general critic models for inference- time scaling and reinforcement learning-based training. As generative models are increasingly applied to open-ended environments and reasoning-intensive tasks, the reliability and expressiveness of visual verifiers become a key bottleneck for advancing multimodal intelligence. Despite their importance, most existing visual verifiers (Zhang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Xiong et al., 2025) adopt a binary judgment paradigm that produces only True/False decisions about whether an image satisfies a given prompt. Although simple and efficient, this design has several inherent limitations. First, binary supervision provides coarse feedback that fails
title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling

text: Xiong et al., 2025) adopt a binary judgment paradigm that produces only True/False decisions about whether an image satisfies a given prompt. Although simple and efficient, this design has several inherent limitations. First, binary supervision provides coarse feedback that fails to capture the partial correctness of generated samples. By assigning the same negative label to imperfect samples of varying quality, binary rewards obscure meaningful quality differences and weaken the within-group learning signals required by group-relative reinforcement learning. Moreover, the limited information conveyed by binary labels may encourage shortcut learning and increase susceptibility to reward hacking (Shao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), as models may exploit superficial patterns to predict the expected labels without adequately reasoning about the e subtl compositional relationships among objects, attributes, and spatial constraints. To address these limitations, we propose the Decomposed Graded Verifier (OmniVerifier-C1), which automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained sub-questions and performs structured reasoning over each component. It assigns continuous scores based on the proportion of satisfied sub-questions, capturing partial correctness and providing informative critique signals. Our ex- periments demonstrate that decomposition-based structured reasoning significantly improves the verifier’s out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise 0/1 feedback on individual

text: demonstrate that decomposition-based structured reasoning significantly improves the verifier’s out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions to develop strong fine-grained verification capabilities that support reliable global scoring. Moreover, our theoretical analysis shows that the decomposition- and-scoring paradigm better preserves the underlying true quality ordering among generated samples, providing finer-grained learning signals for group-relative reinforcement learning. Building upon this verifier, we further explore its role as a generative reward model for reinforcement learning across two types of tasks. First, we apply the verifier to traditional text-to-image alignment, where it provides fine-grained feedback that encourages generative models to satisfy detailed compositional relationship. Second, we extend our study to the more reasoning-intensive and challenging setting of structured generative world modeling, where generative models are used to simulate environments and reason over sequential states. In these rule-governed environments, we find that pairwise verification, which compares generated states against ground-truth states, provides more accurate and reliable critiques than pointwise verification. This observation suggests that the effectiveness of visual verification in rule- governed world-modeling scenarios critically depends on the availability of reference states for comparison. Extensive experiments across diverse tasks, such as Maze and Sudoku, demonstrate that the proposed verifier provides more reliable reward signals and substantially improves reinforcement learning performance. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose the Decomposed Graded Verifier, which automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained sub-questions, performs structured reasoning over each component, and assigns continuous scores based on the proportion of satisfied sub-questions. Our experiments demonstrate that its structured outputs significantly improve out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities.

text: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling • We introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable scoring. • We demonstrate that the proposed verifier serves as an effective generative reward model for reinforcement learning, improving performance in both traditional text-to-image generation and rule-governed generative world modeling tasks. • We provide empirical validation across diverse structured reasoning environments, showing that accurate pairwise decomposed verifiers are a key enabler for transforming generative models into rule-governed world-modeling agents. 2

text: 2.1 Generative Verifier or Reward Models Generative reward models (Mahan et al., 2024; Malik et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026c) differ fundamentally from traditional reward models (Xu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a; Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024c) in that they produce explicit rationales rather than merely assigning scalar scores. OmniVerifier (Zhang et al., 2025b) first introduces the concept of Generative Universal Verifier and presents ViVerBench, a comprehensive and challenging benchmark for evaluating multimodal reasoning and critique capabilities. DeepSeekMath-V2 (Shao et al., 2025) further proposes meta-verification and integrates it into verifier training to enhance faithfulness and reliability. OmniVerifier-M1 (Zhang et al., 2026d) extends meta- verification to multimodal scenarios by introducing symbolic spatial annotations, such as bounding boxes, points or lines as verifiable rationales. These rule-based supervision signals substantially alleviate reward hacking and enhance verifier generalization. Despite their improved interpretability, existing generative verifiers still rely on coarse binary decisions as final judgments, and thus struggle to provide dense and optimization-friendly reward signals for reinforcement learning. Binary verifiers have emerged as an effective tool for improving text-to- image generation quality through inference-time scaling (Zhang et al., 2025b). When they detect semantic inconsistencies between a generated image and its textual description, they produce editing instructions that guide the generative model to iteratively refine the visual output. For this purpose, coarse

text: quality through inference-time scaling (Zhang et al., 2025b). When they detect semantic inconsistencies between a generated image and its textual description, they produce editing instructions that guide the generative model to iteratively refine the visual output. For this purpose, coarse binary feedback is often sufficient, as the verifier primarily serves as a gating mechanism that determines whether further refinement is needed. However, binary verifiers face inherent limitations when used as reward models for reinforcement learning, as their feedback is insufficiently dense and discriminative to distinguish among imperfect samples of varying visual quality and thereby guide effective generative policy optimization. Revisiting Decomposition-Based Continuous Rewards. To address this limitation, we introduce the Decomposed Graded Verifier, a structured verification paradigm that elicits continuous scores from visual verifiers. Instead of reducing assessment to a single binary judgment, it decomposes a complex prompt into fine-grained sub-questions, evaluates each sub-question individually with binary judgments, and aggregates these local decisions into a continuous score that reflects the degree of prompt satisfaction. By preserving partial correctness in generated samples, this fine-grained reward signal provides denser and more optimization-friendly supervision for reinforcement learning. Binary verifiers supervise model training solely through the final True/False outcome, implicitly assuming that a correct verdict reflects a correct reasoning process. This assumption is often reasonable in domains such as mathematical problem solving, where the solution space is large and arriving at the correct answer typically requires coherent multi-step reasoning. However, it becomes much more fragile in binary multimodal critique tasks. Without explicit supervision over the judgment process, a verifier may exploit shallow visual patterns or shortcut cues to produce seemingly correct verdicts without genuinely understanding the underlying multimodal reasoning process (Wang et al., 2026c; Shao et al., 2025), thereby leading to reward hacking Experiment Setup. For the decomposition-based scoring sample, the verifier takes the textual prompt c and the generated image y as input, and is trained to predict the global alignment score induced by the decomposition. Given the predicted score ˆS ∈[0, 1] and the ground-truth score S∗∈[0, 1], the reward is defined as Rscore = 1 −| ˆS −S∗|. For each fine-grained judgment sample, the verifier takes the k-th sub-question Qk and the generated image y as input, and is trained to predict the binary answer associated with this sub-question. Given the predicted answer ˆAk ∈{0, 1} and the ground-truth answer A∗ k ∈{0, 1}, the reward is defined as Rjudgment = 1[ ˆAk = A∗ k]. During reinforcement learning, we mix these two types of samples and optimize them with their respective rewards, forming a decoupled RL training scheme that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring. Precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions enables the verifier to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring. Experiment Analysis. Notably, the Decomposed Graded Verifier requires supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the structured decomposition paradigm. By contrast, the Discrete Binary Verifier only needs to produce a binary True/False verdict with a corresponding textual explanation, and can therefore be directly optimized through reinforcement learning. For a fair comparison, we evaluate the Discrete Binary Verifier in both RL-only and SFT+RL settings. The results show that the Discrete Binary Verifier consistently underperforms the Decomposed Graded Verifier, regardless of whether it is first adapted with SFT. This indicates that the key factor is not the training pipeline itself, but the nature of the supervision signal. Binary supervision is highly compressed and sparse, which encourages the model to rely on shallow patterns rather than capturing complex semantic structures. In contrast, the Decomposed Graded Verifier decomposes complex tasks into multiple sub-questions and performs fine- grained judgments, thereby explicitly enforcing a structured reasoning process. This mechanism provides richer and more informative feedback signals, effectively mitigating reward hacking and substantially improving the model’s multimodal reasoning and critique capabilities. Pointwise rewards require the verifier to infer an implicit target state, which can introduce substantial noise into the feedback in complex reasoning scenarios. In contrast, pairwise verification directly compares the generated result with the ground-truth image, reducing reliance on target-state inference and enabling reward signals to better reflect the true visual quality. This provides more reliable supervision for policy optimization and highlights the value of pairwise verification for developing generative models into rule-governed world-modeling agents. Since Qwen-Image-Edit- 2509 has not been specifically trained on game-based image-to-image generation tasks, it often fails to interpret the required transformation. After supervised fine-tuning on our constructed game-based dataset, the generative model learns the visual style of these tasks and the corresponding rule-based transformation patterns. Although the model still often fails to produce fully correct solutions, it begins to perform meaningful operations toward the desired final state rather than generating irrelevant or destructive visual outputs, leading to clear performance improvements. text: This work introduces the Decomposed Graded Verifier as an effective reward model for improving vi- sual generation in both traditional text-to-image tasks and structured world-modeling scenarios. Our contributions are twofold. First, we propose a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub- question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that support accurate continuous scoring. Empirical results further demonstrate improved out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities. Second, focusing on rule-governed world modeling, we introduce a pairwise verification paradigm that explicitly incorporates ground-truth images as visual references. This simplifies verification by shifting from a reason-then-judge process to direct reference-based comparison, thereby producing more accurate and reliable reward signals. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of both the Decomposed Graded Verifier trained with our Decoupled RL strategy and the pairwise verification paradigm.

text: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling A Proof of Ranking Preservation In this section we prove that Decomposed Graded Verification preserves the true quality ordering of generated samples more faithfully than Discrete Binary Verification. The argument rests on a single observation: under GRPO, the relative update strength among samples is dictated by their group-normalized advantages, whose ordering is fully inherited from the underlying reward values. text: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling Implication for GRPO. By Lemma A.1, GRPO assigns larger update weights to samples with larger rewards. Therefore, a reward model that better preserves the true quality ordering also provides more reliable relative policy updates. The decomposed graded reward is strictly monotonic with respect to the number of satisfied sub-questions and thus preserves all pairwise quality comparisons. In contrast, the binary reward collapses all imperfect samples into the same reward, making GRPO unable to distinguish partially correct samples from severely incorrect ones. Consequently, Decomposed Graded Verification provides a denser and more order-preserving reward signal for GRPO. These results suggest that an appropriate decomposition granularity improves scoring accuracy, while simply increasing the number of sub-questions does not guarantee better performance. Excessive decomposition can introduce redundant questions or requirements unsupported by the original prompt. For example, given “A red apple is placed on a table,” the verifier may repeatedly ask whether an apple exists or introduce questions such as “Is the apple a fruit?” and “Is the apple round?” that do not correspond to explicitly requested visual constraints. Such questions can distort the aggregated score by repeatedly weighting the same requirement or introducing irrelevant criteria. We also observe that generating more sub-questions can lead to violations of the required output format, reducing the reliability of the final score. Together, these observations highlight the importance of balancing fine-grained coverage with faithful and non-redundant decomposition. text: and Future Works Our world-modeling evaluation is restricted to game-based environments with explicit rules, where the ground-truth image is uniquely determined by the initial task state and rule instructions. We adopt these controlled tasks primarily to evaluate the effectiveness of our pairwise verification paradigm. Although our results demonstrate the advantages of pairwise verification in these settings, these tasks capture only part of the complexity and diversity of real-world environments. In future work, we plan to extend our investigation to open-ended settings with non-unique ground truths, construct larger and more realistic world-modeling datasets, and scale both the verifier and the generator to stronger backbones. Our long-term goal is to develop multimodal generative models that can reason about, simulate, and interact with complex real-world scenes.

The required view is produced by observing the voxel structure along the X-axis. In this process, the X dimension is removed, and the remaining projection is represented on the Y-Z plane, with Y as the horizontal axis and Z as the vertical axis. Thus, for every (Y, Z) coordinate, I need to decide whether the projection cell should be occupied. text: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models Han Su1,2, Meng Tian2, Tianyu Huang3, Mingyu Gao1, Lennox Wei1, Dongxu Li1, Jianhua Han2, Hang Xu2, Xiaohe Wu1, Wangmeng Zuo1,* 1 Harbin Institute of Technology 2 Yinwang Intelligent Technology 3 Huawei * Corresponding author. Abstract. Vision-language models still struggle to understand 3D spatial relations across views and update spatial judgments as the observer moves. A common approach fuses 3D reconstruction features into visual tokens, but aligning these features with pretrained semantic representations remains challenging under limited spatial super- vision. We propose DK-VLM with Dual-Kernel Attention, which computes attention from both a visual token’s input position and its geometric position in the scene. A semantic kernel retains the pretrained model’s native attention and positional encoding, while a separate geometric kernel uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention through point displacements and relative view transformations. Then, a learned gate fuses their outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as fused reconstruction features. We further introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision to train the model to update its reference frame across successive judgments. It provides stepwise turn and heading targets derived from verified single-step annotations. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and

text: Spatial reasoning connects visual understanding to agentic action in the physical world (Chen et al., 2024, Su et al., 2026, Huang et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025a, Driess et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2023). Tasks like multi-view question answering, long-video understanding, robot manipulation, and embodied planning require more than recognizing visual content (Yang et al., 2025a, Mangalam et al., 2023). Specifically, a vision-language model (VLM) must also perceive 3D relations across views and, as the observer moves, keep updating the position and heading on which its subsequent spatial judgments depend (Chen et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2025a). Despite strong progress in semantic recognition and language reasoning, VLMs remain unreliable at estimating distance, direction, camera motion, and cross-view correspondence, and weaker still on tasks such as route planning that chain several such judgments (Yang et al., 2025a, Zhang et al., 2026b). Existing work attempts to enhance spatial reasoning by introducing 3D priors. One common approach fuses features from pretrained 3D reconstruction models with visual representations, incorporating geometry into the content of visual tokens (Fan et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026b). 1 arXiv:2610.22356v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

However, these geometric features are primarily learned for 3D reconstruction, an objective different from semantic understanding in VLMs. Integrating them therefore requires the model to align two different representation spaces while learning spatial relations. With limited spatial supervision, this additional adaptation may limit the effective use of geometry and interfere with the model’s existing semantic representations. Beyond token content, VLMs already use positional encoding to guide attention. In the Qwen-VL family (Wang et al., 2024, Bai et al., 2025b,a), multi-modal rotary position embedding (mRoPE) encodes sequence order, time, and 2D image grid coordinates, so that attention between two tokens depends on their relative positions in the input. Position thus offers a second interface for geometry: instead of being fused into token content, geometry can define relations between tokens that directly shape attention (Miyato et al., 2024, Li et al.,

Position thus offers a second interface for geometry: instead of being fused into token content, geometry can define relations between tokens that directly shape attention (Miyato et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025c, Wu et al., 2026, Xiang et al., 2026). However, input positions describe where a token appears in the input rather than where its content lies in the 3D world. As the camera moves, the same 3D surface appears at different image locations across frames, while neighboring 2D patches can lie at very different depths (Figure 1). Existing geometric attention mechanisms (Miyato et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025c, Wu et al., 2026, Xiang et al., 2026) introduce 3D relations directly into attention by applying geometric trans- formations to queries, keys, or values. However, replacing a pretrained VLM’s native positional encoding with geometric encoding may disrupt the semantic attention patterns learned under the original encoding—patterns that remain useful for spatial understanding. We therefore bring scene geometry into attention through a separate kernel while retaining the native attention and positional encoding. text: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position scene. The semantic kernel keeps the backbone’s native attention and mRoPE unchanged. The geometric kernel uses independent projections and computes relations between visual tokens conditioned on patch-level 3D points and frame-level camera poses, so that displacements between scene points and relative transformations between views directly modulate feature comparison and aggregation. A learned gate fuses the two outputs. Geometry thus enters attention as position rather than as reconstruction features fused into token content. The geometric inputs are estimated from images, requiring no ground-truth depth or camera poses at inference. Dual-Kernel Attention gives the model direct access to point displacements and relative view transformations, but successive spatial judgments require more: earlier movements change the position and heading on which later judgments depend, even when the scene layout remains unchanged. Single-step question answering supervises each judgment within a given reference frame and does not explicitly supervise how that frame changes across steps. We therefore introduce Reference-Frame Composition (RC) supervision, which provides stepwise turn and heading targets along landmark routes and view sequences. These targets are derived by connecting verified single-step relations that share landmarks or views within the same scene (Yang et al., 2025c, Zhang et al., 2025b). We implement DK-VLM on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025b,a). We evaluate it on seven spatial reasoning benchmarks (Yang et

We evaluate it on seven spatial reasoning benchmarks (Yang et al., 2025a, Zhang et al., 2026b, Yang et al., 2025d, Wang et al., 2025b, Li et al., 2025a, Wang et al., 2025d, Tong et al., 2024) and two general video understanding benchmarks (Fu et al., 2025, Li et al., 2024). Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest six-benchmark average score and the highest overall scores on VSI-Bench (74.33) and ReVSI-32 (58.28), with trainable parameters totaling only 3.86% of its backbone’s parameter count. RC supervision further improves multi-step spatial reasoning, yielding consistent gains on route-planning and viewpoint-related tasks. Ablations show that DK-VLM benefits more from RC supervision than a Qwen baseline fine-tuned on the same instruction data, supporting the complementarity between geometric relation modeling and stepwise spatial supervision. The full model also preserves general video understanding on VideoMME and MVBench. text: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position Geometry-Augmented Vision-Language Models. One line of work introduces 3D informa- tion by encoding coordinates into visual tokens, including Video-3D LLM, LLaVA-3D, and HiSpatial (Zheng et al., 2024, Zhu et al., 2024, Liang et al., 2026). Video-3D LLM adds coordinate embeddings to visual features. Another line introduces features from 3D reconstruction mod- els: VG-LLM adds projected VGGT features to visual tokens, VLM-3R queries reconstruction and camera tokens with cross-attention, and GeoThinker retrieves geometric features according to the current semantic state (Zheng et al., 2025, Fan et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026b). These fusion mechanisms let a VLM use geometric representations from reconstruction models, but require aligning features learned for reconstruction with pretrained semantic representations. In contrast, DK-VLM uses estimated 3D points and camera poses to directly modulate attention among visual tokens, rather than incorporating coordinate embeddings or reconstruction features into their content. Geometric Attention and Positional Encoding. Positional mechanisms provide another interface for introducing 3D information into Transformers. Geometric Transform Attention (GTA) incorporates group actions induced by camera transformations into attention, while PRoPE, RayRoPE, and ViewRoPE use 3D points, rays, or viewpoints to parameterize positional relations between tokens (Miyato et al., 2024, Li et al., 2025c, Wu et al., 2026, Xiang et al., 2026). These studies show that geometry can directly shape relation computation. How to

These studies show that geometry can directly shape relation computation. How to introduce these mechanisms into a pretrained VLM while retaining its native positional encoding remains less explored. 3 Method Given a sequence of RGB images and a spatial query, DK-VLM uses a geometry frontend to estimate aligned patch-level 3D points and frame-level camera poses from the images (Wang et al., 2025a, 2026a,b, Lin et al., 2025, Murai et al., 2025). DK-VLM uses these geometric states rather than latent features specific to a frontend, allowing compatible geometry frontends to be replaced. It models input position and scene geometry through parallel relation kernels. The semantic kernel retains the backbone’s native positional computation, while the geometric kernel is parameterized by the estimated states. Dual-Kernel Attention computes and fuses the outputs of the two kernels (Section 3.1). To supervise the composition of geometric relations across observations, Reference-Frame Composition links verified single-step annotations into training chains with stepwise targets (Section 3.2). Training jointly optimizes the instruction and pairwise geometric objectives in a single stage (Section 3.3). Reference-frame composition. Verified single-step relations sharing end- points form a training chain with stepwise turn targets. Dual-Kernel Attention conditions token relations on 3D position and relative pose, but multi- step reference-frame reasoning additionally re- quires composing relative transformations across observations. Standard single-step supervision guides spatial judgments within a given refer- ence frame, but does not explicitly supervise how that frame changes across successive steps. Reference-Frame Composition (RC) instead de- rives and supervises the reference-frame update at every step. Figure 3 illustrates one such chain and its stepwise targets. Chain Construction. RC first converts each ver- ified relation according to the direction conven- tion of its source. Compatible relations are then connected along a sequence of landmarks or views to form a path C = (v0, . . .
title: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position

text: Chain Construction. RC first converts each ver- ified relation according to the direction conven- tion of its source. Compatible relations are then connected along a sequence of landmarks or views to form a path C = (v0, . . . , vK). The head- ing obtained at one step provides the reference for the next, turning the path into a sequence of reference-frame updates. The target at each step is recomputed from the source annotations; Appendix A.4 details the construction and verification. Stepwise Supervision. Each retained relation is converted under its source coordinate convention into a canonical clockwise planar turn increment δk ∈[0, 360◦). RC describes the resulting reference-frame composition as h0 = 0, hk = (hk−1 + δk) mod 360◦. (6) Here hk is the reference-frame heading after transition k, for 1 ≤k ≤K. RC uses the turn increments and, when available, their cumulative headings as stepwise targets. We apply RC to VSI-590K and the view-change subset of SPAR-7M to construct four types of supervision (Yang et al., 2025c, Zhang et al., 2025b): exact turn angles and discrete turning actions from VSI-590K, and yaw changes between consecutive views and cumulative headings from SPAR-7M. We format each target type as a structured assistant response and train on these samples together with standard instruction data using the same autoregressive SFT objective.

text: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position 3.3 Joint Training Objective Pairwise Geometric Prediction. Answer-level SFT constrains the final response but does not provide an explicit target for the relations encoded by the geometric branch. Because the geometric kernel operates on token pairs, we use the relative 3D displacement of ordered token pairs to directly supervise the geometric representation before fusion. We decompose the displacement into distance and unit direction to constrain its magnitude and orientation. At the layer ℓ⋆selected for pairwise geometric supervision, we read hi = ϕℓ⋆ g (Gℓ⋆ i ) ∈Rd after the shared output projection and before kernel fusion. We sample ordered pairs of visual tokens with valid geometry within and across frames, with dij = ∥xj −xi∥2. For each sampled pair, we construct the pair representation and its distance and direction targets as follows: zij = [hi; hj; hj −hi; hi ⊙hj] ∈R4d, yd ij = log(1 + dij), uij = xj −xi dij (dij > ε). (7) Here, ⊙denotes elementwise multiplication. A prediction head maps zij to a predicted log- distance byd ij and an L2-normalized direction buij. text: We present DK-VLM, which introduces 3D geometry as position into the attention computation of vision-language models. Dual-Kernel Attention preserves the native semantic kernel and uses Point GTA and Camera GTA to model relations between scene points and camera motion across views. Reference-Frame Composition supervision reorganizes existing single-step annotations into training chains with stepwise targets, further improving spatial reasoning over multiple steps. Among the compared methods, DK-VLM-8B achieves the highest average score across six spatial benchmarks while preserving general video understanding. Ablations further support the complementarity between geometric relation modeling and stepwise supervision. A Additional Method Details A.1 Geometry Preprocessing The geometric kernel of DK-VLM uses 3D points and camera poses aligned with visual tokens, without relying on intermediate features from a specific geometry frontend. For each merged visual token, we map the center of its image region to the frontend’s dense 3D point map, accounting for resizing, cropping, and padding in both image preprocessing pipelines. Within each video, we filter out low-confidence points using the 20th percentile of finite depth confi- dence values as the threshold. We obtain each token’s 3D coordinates by bilinear interpolation over the retained neighboring points, with the interpolation weights renormalized. All visual tokens from the same frame share that frame’s camera pose. We construct these geometric quantities from the frontend outputs and express them in the coordinate frame of the first camera. Within each video, we center and scale all point coordinates together and apply the same scale factor to camera translations. Point GTA

A.3 Pairwise Loss Reduction and Boundary Cases Prediction Head and Pair Sampling. Both models use LayerNorm followed by a two-layer MLP with GELU activation to map the 4d-dimensional pair features to a log-distance predic- tion and a three-dimensional direction prediction, which is L2-normalized. The MLP hidden dimension is d, set to 3584 and 4096 for the 7B and 8B variants, respectively. We use a sampling budget of 256 ordered token pairs per sample, targeting 50% cross-frame pairs for multi-frame inputs. Within-frame and cross-frame candidates are sampled separately by distance tertiles, with unused quotas reassigned to the other group; single-frame inputs use only within-frame pairs. text: DK-VLM: Geometry as Position A.4 Reference-Frame Composition Details Reference-Frame Composition uses planar angular relations extracted from the source an- notations. We write ⟨z⟩360 = z mod 360◦for normalization to [0, 360◦), with clockwise rotation positive, and use the corresponding circular distance d◦for tolerance checks. We first parse and normalize the source relations, then apply consistency checks specific to each source to obtain the verified single-step annotations used for chain construction. After these checks, scenes are partitioned, and chains are constructed only within one scene and split. During partitioning, scene groups that overlap VSI-Bench are isolated from the RC pool. Finally, an independent validator rereads the source annotations, recomputes every derived target, and verifies scene and split membership together with source provenance. These checks cross-validate source angle annotations and their algebraic consistency; they do not use images, XYZ coordinates, or ground-truth 3D states. VSI-RC. From each VSI-590K absolute_direction_object annotation (Yang et al., 2025c), the parser extracts (media, O, A, B, convention, α(O, A, B)), (15) where O is the current location, A is the facing anchor, and B is the target landmark. A clockwise raw angle is normalized directly, whereas a counterclockwise angle is converted as ⟨360◦− araw⟩360. From each SPAR-7M view_change_infer annotation with decodable structured camera-motion fields (Zhang et al., 2025b), the parser extracts the source and target view identifiers and the yaw component. Yaw is converted to the same clockwise-positive angular convention; pitch and translation fields are not used in RC. Repeated records for the same directed view pair are deduplicated. For three available relations A→B, B →C, and A→C, triangle closure requires d◦(θAC, ⟨θAB + θBC⟩360) ≤5◦. (18) Accepted directed relations are connected when the target view of one edge matches the source view of the next; paths with repeated views are rejected. For transition vk−1 →vk, δSPAR k = θvk−1vk; cumulative headings follow the recurrence in Section 3.2. SPAR-RC applies no facing-to-traversal 180◦correction. Its prompt provides the ordered views and their images and uses the first view as the heading origin while withholding the target sequence. Supervision Targets. RC produces four target types: VSI angle contains exact turn sequences; VSI action contains the corresponding discrete actions for eligible chains; SPAR delta contains local yaw increments; and SPAR heading contains cumulative headings relative to the initial view. Each target sequence is serialized as a JSON array in the assistant response of a separate training sample. No sample jointly emits two target types. No sample jointly emits two target types. The validator independently reconstructs these arrays and checks their provenance against the source relations before they enter autoregressive SFT. A.5 Output Projection and Gate Initialization At each selected layer, we initialize the shared output projection ϕℓ g by copying the native output projection. The two projections have separate parameters. At positions with valid geometry, both kernel outputs use ϕℓ g; at other positions, the semantic output uses the native output projection. We initialize gℓ= 0, giving both kernels an initial mixing weight of 0.5. This avoids strongly suppressing the geometric branch at the start of training and keeps the sigmoid gate away from saturation. Each selected layer then learns its own mixing ratio. A.6 Implementation Details and Parameter Counts We introduce Dual-Kernel Attention at layers 4, 9, 14, 19, and 24 for DK-VLM-7B and at layers 6, 12, 18, 27, and 33 for DK-VLM-8B, using zero-based indices. The pairwise prediction head reads the pre-fusion geometric features at layer 19 for the 7B model and layer 27 for the 8B model. For both models, the pairwise loss weight increases linearly to 0.1 over the first 5% of training steps.

The spatial reasoning data comprise Cambrian-S VSI-590K (590K), SPAR (234K), VLM-3R VSI-Bench instructions (205K), VLM-3R VSTI-Bench instructions (132K), and the MindCube training set (10K). The general video data comprise LLaVA-Hound (64K), PhysGame PhysInstruct (140K), and a general video subset of Cambrian-S-3M (430K). RC Sample Selection. We construct a pool of approximately 1.6M RC samples from the verified source annotations. For SPAR-RC, we retain one question per view tuple and randomly assign either local yaw increments or cumulative headings as the prediction target. We also retain at most one sample for each image set. To reduce the concentration of small turns, we group individual turn magnitudes into six 30◦ bins over the folded angular range from 0◦to 180◦. text: the prediction target. We also retain at most one sample for each image set. To reduce the concentration of small turns, we group individual turn magnitudes into six 30◦ bins over the folded angular range from 0◦to 180◦. Each chain is represented by the multiset of its step-level bins. We use deficit-greedy sampling to favor underrepresented bins, subject to limits of 96 samples per scene and 40 appearances per image. For VSI-RC, we retain only samples with video inputs and limit each clip to 40 questions. The retained VSI-RC samples are repeated twice to increase their weight in the training mixture. The final RC training set contains 150K entries and includes only two- and three-step chains. A.8 RC Chain Evaluation Evaluation Set Construction. We construct an evaluation set using the same RC procedure, with no overlap with the training samples. text: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general- purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps- bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications. 1

text: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are a hot topic (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2023; Ansari et al., 2025; Jain & Sen, 2026; Cohen et al., 2025). The field is growing fast: Every year, new models are released that refresh the leaderboard. The models are commonly evaluated through point accuracy (e.g., MASE) and marginal probabilistic scores (e.g., CRPS, scaled quantile loss) (Aksu et al., 2024; Shchur et al., 2025). Consequently, most of the recent TSFMs are designed and trained to produce quantile levels, which are optimized for these benchmarks. Point accuracy and marginal probabilistic scores are widely adopted for good reason: they provide an interpretable, per-step summary of forecast quality that directly supports common operational decisions such as inventory planning, resource allocation, and risk management. However, they do not capture all aspects of forecast quality. Other properties, particularly trajectory-dependent ones, are important but overlooked by these metrics. Among many, we illustrate two important aspects: • Learning distributions with multiple modes: Quantiles are defined through the inverse of the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the target distribution. These CDFs, however, are not always nice and smooth, for instance, when the target distribution has multiple modes or sharp peaks. With a few or a few dozens of quantiles, the resulting approximation of the CDF can be quite rough and suffer

On the other hand, diffusion- or flow-matching-based generative time-series models are naturally well-suited for capturing joint trajectory distributions even without these ad hoc methods, as they can generate complete future paths while maintaining temporal and cross-variable dependencies. Unfortunately, existing generative models (Kollovieh et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) achieve neither high marginal accuracy nor efficient sampling, limiting their practical utility in real-world forecasting scenarios. This leads us to ask: Can we construct a generative time-series model that achieves both high marginal accuracy and efficient sampling while also preserving trajectory dependence? text: We introduce PathFM to combine joint and multi-mode trajectory modeling with accurate marginal forecasting and efficient sampling. The model learns temporal and cross-variable dependence through conditional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022), generating complete future paths conditioned on history and known future covariates. Parallel decoding distillation (Shaul et al., 2026) and history attention caching enable faster sampling with one or two model evaluations. To narrow the marginal accuracy gap, we add a calibration loss that directly optimizes fair CRPS on generated forecasts. The distilled sampler makes this optimization practical by allowing calibration gradients to pass through its short rollout and refine the forecast distribution. With these components, PathFM-300M ranks second on the widely used fev-bench for marginal scores (Section 5).1 On Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which we curate to evaluate trajectory quality, PathFM ranks first for path scores (Section 5). In a separate evaluation on chaotic systems, our sampling approach improves point forecast accuracy upon the state-of-the-art PANDA model, captures useful temporal dependence, and preserves long-run variability more faithfully than baselines 1Cutoff date for the rankings throughout this paper: Sept. 26, 2026; see Section A.1 for concurrent work. 2
