These results demonstrate that PathFM generates high-fidelity trajectory forecasts without sacrificing marginal accuracy, making it a strong candidate for forecasting applications. Our contributions are as follows: • Fast and calibrated trajectory generation. We introduce PathFM, a joint flow foundation model for fast, calibrated trajectory generation with accurate small-ensemble marginals (Figure 2). Distillation enables one- or two-step generation, marginal-CRPS refinement improves empirical coverage, and stratified sampling reduces finite-ensemble marginal error. • A benchmark for trajectory distributions. We introduce fps-bench, to our knowledge the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating path distributions from time series foundation models on real-world data. It reveals how strong marginal accuracy in existing models can mask errors in temporal dependence and uncertainty over trajectory-dependent quantities. • State-of-the-art performance. PathFM outperforms leading foundation models on downstream probabilistic forecasting tasks and stays among the top on marginal benchmarks. It also achieves the highest forecasting accuracy across strong baselines on chaotic systems. 2 PROBLEM SETUP AND PRELIMINARIES Forecast object and downstream query. text: Preprint 3.2 EFFICIENT BACKBONE FOR JOINT GENERATION The velocity field uses a transformer based on T5 (Raffel et al., 2020), with separate time and channel axes. Its inputs are patches of 16 values with masks and time indices, a register token, and future patches populated by available covariates. Each block combines temporal self-attention, attention across channels at aligned patches, and a pointwise feed-forward network. We condition flow time via adaptive RMS normalization (Chen et al., 2024) and apply QK normalization and weight decay. For reuse across paths, late entry separates conditioning from flow-dependent computation. The first e blocks use unrestricted attention over history, the register, and future placeholders, without source noise or flow time. These representations incorporate the requested horizon and known future covariates. Restricting history attention before this stage would exclude that future information. Future positions then receive a gated difference between flow-state and placeholder tokens. In subsequent blocks, history-only self-attention keeps history independent of the sampled path: history tokens attend only to history, while future tokens attend to both history and future. text: C.1.2 constructs the ensembles. 4 EVALUATING TRAJECTORY FORECASTS Trajectory forecasts should capture temporal dependence and accurately quantify uncertainty. Marginal accuracy alone cannot establish this. We introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench) to evaluate these properties alongside marginal scores. The benchmark combines established scoring rules into a common protocol for constructing and comparing finite trajectory ensembles. Six complementary path scores. Different downstream queries depend on different aspects of a path, motivating the complementary diagnostics in Table 7. Following the aggregation-and- transformation framework of Pic et al. (2025), we score both complete paths and transformations that expose these aspects. Energy score assesses the distribution of level paths, while differenced energy score emphasizes local changes by scoring the initial level and subsequent increments. Variogram score compares pairwise temporal contrasts to probe how values vary together across time (Scheuerer & Hamill, 2015). We then apply scalar CRPS to the horizon total, maximum, and first-passage time to assess accumulated uncertainty, extremes, and event timing. We retain native samples when available. To include quantile models, we construct paths from their marginal quantiles under two explicit dependence assumptions. Sorted quantiles define a piecewise-linear inverse CDF with constant extension beyond the outer quantiles. An independent completion draws a separate quantile rank at each forecast time and channel, whereas a comonotone completion shares one rank across an item’s times and channels. Both laws preserve the same underlying interpolated marginals, allowing us to examine how the dependence assumption affects trajectory scores. These two choices serve as baselines, as different dependence assumptions may yield different scores for the same marginal forecasts. Section D.1 specifies the score definitions, estimators, and aggregation. 5 FORECASTING ACCURACY AND EFFICIENCY We evaluate forecasts through their marginal accuracy, the path quality scores, and the cost of generating an ensemble. The experiments establish where trajectory forecasts help, then examine how distillation and score refinement make those forecasts practical. Section 6 complements these experiments with a study of chaotic systems, with a particular focus on long-run dynamics. 6

Section F provides further diagnostics. 7 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION PathFM combines flow matching, distillation, shared computation, and direct score refinement to generate complete future trajectories efficiently. Its strongest gains concern the quality of complete trajectories and the downstream predictions they support. The dynamical study shows a unique benefit: independently continued paths preserve variability that point forecasts can lose. Several limitations remain. PathFM does not yet support conditioning on modalities beyond time series, such as text. For chaotic systems, all four dynamical diagnostics remain well above the held-out-truth reference (Table 2). Accurately recovering the invariant distribution remains an open challenge. A key direction for future work is to continue scaling the backbone and training data, pushing the frontier of generative time series forecasting. text: Marginal forecasting. Chronos-2, TimesFM-3, and Toto 2.0 provide direct marginal quantiles while sharing information across variables (Ansari et al., 2025; Jain & Sen, 2026; Khwaja et al., 2026). Toto 1.0 instead predicts marginal Student-t mixtures and samples forecasts autoregressively across output patches (Cohen et al., 2025). Perez-Diaz et al. (2025) distinguish forecast products by their operational uses and show that marginals do not identify path-dependent event probabilities. PathFM represents the joint forecast through complete multivariate paths, so the same samples support marginal summaries and distributions of trajectory-dependent quantities. Generative trajectory forecasting. DeepAR samples temporally dependent futures autoregres- sively (Salinas et al., 2020), and TACTiS learns multivariate predictive distributions with attentional copulas (Drouin et al., 2022). TimeGrad introduces autoregressive diffusion for multivariate fore- casting (Rasul et al., 2021). Flow matching learns generative vector fields through conditional probability paths (Lipman et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2026); TSFlow incorporates Gaussian-process priors (Kollovieh et al., 2025), and Sundial uses flow matching for foundation-model pretraining (Liu et al., 2025). PathFM shares history computation across paths and uses distillation to support fast ensembles and direct forecast-score training. Distillation and direct score optimization. Flow map methods learn finite-time transport and support both teacher distillation and self-distillation (Boffi et al., 2024; 2026). Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) predicts multiple integration updates per network evaluation (Shaul et al., 2026).

text: forecast-score training. Distillation and direct score optimization. Flow map methods learn finite-time transport and support both teacher distillation and self-distillation (Boffi et al., 2024; 2026). Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) predicts multiple integration updates per network evaluation (Shaul et al., 2026). DRaFT optimizes differentiable rewards by backpropagating through diffusion sampling (Clark et al., 2024). Rewarded Moment Matching Distillation (RMMD) combines reward optimization with moment-matching supervision and applies unbiased sample CRPS to GenCast (Jacq et al., 2026). Its reward gradient passes through a denoising step applied to a re-noised student sample. PathFM backpropagates fair CRPS through the complete source-to-forecast map of one distilled evaluation. The same optimization updates continue matching the frozen teacher’s joint velocity field while fitting the student’s marginals to observations. Distillation thus supplies both a short path for score gradients and continued supervision from a joint generative teacher. Section 3.3 and table 4 give the objective and post-training comparisons. Forecast evaluation. Proper scoring rules underpin forecast comparison (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007). Fair scores address finite-ensemble effects (Ferro, 2014); variogram and transformation-based scores expose complementary multivariate properties (Scheuerer & Hamill, 2015; Pic et al., 2025). fps-bench combines these principles on fev-bench tasks (Shchur et al., 2025) to assess temporal dependence and trajectory-dependent quantities alongside marginal accuracy. DYSTS supplies interpretable chaotic systems (Gilpin, 2021), while PANDA studies pretraining across chaotic dynamics

DYSTS supplies interpretable chaotic systems (Gilpin, 2021), while PANDA studies pretraining across chaotic dynamics (Lai et al., 2026). A.1 CONCURRENT WORK Time series foundation models are advancing rapidly. t0-gamma alternates temporal and variate attention to incorporate historical and known-future covariates (Meyer et al., 2026). It averages weights from five fine-tuned checkpoints into one 256M-parameter model (The Forecasting Company, 2026). QiYao-M fuses numerical patches with text and image embeddings (Cheng et al., 2026), but treats each target channel independently. EXAONE 1.0 specializes at financial forecasting and mixes time with causal convolutions and variates with groupwise pooling MLPs (Lee et al., 2026). All three models predict marginal quantiles, leaving dependence across future times and variables unspecified. PathFM retains its advantage in directly generating joint multivariate trajectories, com- bining learned temporal and cross-variable dependence with fast sampling and marginal calibration. 14

text: Preprint Optimization and stage transitions. The recipe uses AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.99) and global gradient-norm clipping at 1. Both models use weight decay 0.01 during flow matching and WSD. An optimizer update contains 1,024 channel rows. Terminal decay continues the flow model with its optimizer and EMA state. Data and task sampling. Training uses a 83M-row dataset of real-world and synthetic time series, including both univariate and multivariate data. Training samples contexts up to 8,192 time steps and forecast horizons up to 480 time steps. During training, we randomly sample context and forecast lengths within these limits. PDD trains the backbone and twenty interval heads on a uniform time grid, using the block-size menu {1, 2, 5, 10, 20}, on-policy states, Euler teacher labels, and tiled residual heads. Calibration retains path-wise PDD and adds fair CRPS with coefficient one on each loss, globally normalized over scored coordinates. text: Preprint C SAMPLING AND COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY Ensemble size determines the precision of forecast summaries, while the sampler and its execution determine their cost. We first describe sampling error and ensemble construction, then report controlled latency and memory comparisons. C.1 FINITE-ENSEMBLE APPROXIMATION A finite ensemble approximates a model’s predictive distribution through sampled paths. Forecast summaries and scores can vary with the returned ensemble due to Monte Carlo approximation. We first separate approximation error from model error, then describe ensemble construction; Section D.1.1 defines the scores of the empirical forecast. C.1.1 FORECAST QUANTITIES AND MODEL ERROR Condition on the available forecasting information I and on the fitted model. For m ≥1 iid paths from Pθ(· | I) and a fixed functional g of finite variance, write µθ = EPθ[g(X) | I]. The sample average is unbiased for µθ, and independence gives bµg = 1 m m X i=1 g(X(i)), EZ[(bµg −µθ)2 | I] = VarPθ(g(X) | I) m . (8) Thus ordinary iid Monte Carlo standard error scales as m−1/2. This error remains for nondegenerate queries even when Pθ is the true conditional law. Direct quantile outputs avoid estimating their reported quantiles from finitely many paths, but retain model error. Efficient ensemble generation therefore matters for both inference cost and the accuracy of downstream estimates. Let the finite value µ⋆be the corresponding

text: conditional law. Direct quantile outputs avoid estimating their reported quantiles from finitely many paths, but retain model error. Efficient ensemble generation therefore matters for both inference cost and the accuracy of downstream estimates. Let the finite value µ⋆be the corresponding expectation under the true conditional law. The sample average’s squared error relative to this target decomposes as EZ[(bµg −µ⋆)2 | I] = (µθ −µ⋆)2 + VarPθ(g(X) | I) m . (9) The cross term vanishes because EZ[bµg −µθ | I] = 0. The first term is error in the model’s conditional functional expectation; the second is Monte Carlo approximation error. This expression concerns estimation of a conditional expectation, not prediction error against one random future outcome, which also contains outcome variability. For an event A with model probability pθ = Pθ(A | I), taking g(X) = 1{X ∈A} gives sampling variance pθ(1 −pθ)/m. For 0 < pθ < 1, the relative standard error is p (1 −pθ)/(mpθ), making rare-event probability estimates demanding at small ensemble sizes. Increasing m reduces this sampling term but does not remove model error. Using conditional marginals or analytical integration, when available for a particular query, need not incur the same sampling error. Dependent or stratified draws require a different variance analysis. The m−1/2 rate describes the approximation error of the iid sample average at a

The m−1/2 rate describes the approximation error of the iid sample average at a finite sample budget. C.1.2 ENSEMBLE CONSTRUCTION AND STRATIFICATION At inference, we approximate the forecast distribution with an ensemble of m complete future trajectories, from which we estimate quantiles and other forecast summaries. Ensemble size controls the number of paths, independently of the one- or two-evaluation budget per path. With few draws, these summaries can be sensitive to sampling variability. Section C.2 measures the effect of sample count on marginal interval coverage across all 100 fev-bench test tasks. For more even source coverage at fixed m, each coordinate uses the midpoints of m equiprobable Gaussian bins, independently permuted across paths: ur = r −1 2 m , Zj ℓc = σΦ−1(uπℓc(j)), r, j ∈{1, . . . , m}, (10) Here Φ is the standard-normal CDF and each πℓc is an independent permutation. This assigns every rank once per coordinate without tying a path’s ranks across times or channels. 19

Building on the independent and comonotonic completions in Section E.1, we estimate temporal dependence from target-task history while retaining each baseline’s marginal quantile forecasts. Gaussian copula fitting. For each baseline and item, four forecast windows ending before the first test origin supply standardized residuals, which we rank-transform to normal scores. We estimate a lag-one coefficient within these windows, share it across target channels, clip it to [−0.95, 0.95], and fix it before testing. Items with insufficient information use a task-pooled estimate. All eligible items are retained; 27 tasks use shorter calibration horizons without changing their test windows. The fitted coefficient defines a stationary latent AR(1) process used to generate temporally dependent ranks for the baseline’s interpolated marginal quantiles, with constant tails outside probabilities 0.1–0.9. This parameterization restricts the fitted temporal dependence to AR(1). 24

text: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content Shuanglin Li1,2 Jiaying Lin3 Shuquan Ye2 1Southeast University 2Shenzhen Loop Area Institute 3The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
title: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content

text: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have significantly expanded AI capabilities in understanding and synthesizing 3D content. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. In this work, we make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven
title: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content

text: Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback. text: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have extended visual understanding toward increasingly complex spatial reasoning, while progress in 3D generation enables the synthesis and editing of assets with detailed geometry and appearance (Xu et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). Together, these developments bring models closer to understanding, creating, and manipulating 3D content through natural language. However, generated assets can still contain geometric artifacts, missing components, and inconsistencies with the requested attributes or structure (Wu et al., 2024; Duggal et al., 2025). Such errors limit their usefulness: An object may look convincing while failing the geometric or functional requirement for which it was created. To improve these systems, existing research has pursued broader pretraining, targeted post-training, and test-time scaling. These approaches strengthen perceptual representations, align outputs with instructions or preferences, and allocate additional computation to candidate search (Xu et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). For 3D content, this requires identifying which requirements are unmet and explaining why. We study this step through 3D verification, which checks a candidate against explicit requirements and explains contradictions. Despite progress in general visual verification (Zhang et al., 2026b), the reliability of such feedback across diverse 3D tasks remains underexplored. Realizing this goal in 3D, however, involves challenges beyond those of image-based verification. Native 3D perception requires specialized representations and language alignment, as illustrated by point-cloud language models (Xu et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025); these capabilities cannot simply be assumed in an image-based MLLM. Although multi-view rendering makes 3D assets accessible to such models, it provides partial, projection-dependent observations rather than the complete geometry. A verifier must consequently associate parts across views, resolve occlusion, and distinguish geometric differences from changes in viewpoint or appearance. For grasping, identity, and motion, it must further establish whether the specific constraint holds, rather than merely recognize the object or action. The two cases in Figure 1 illustrate this distinction: GPT-6 Astra

For grasping, identity, and motion, it must further establish whether the specific constraint holds, rather than merely recognize the object or action. The two cases in Figure 1 illustrate this distinction: GPT-6 Astra recognizes a rightward collapse but misses its unnatural motion, and accepts identity preservation despite a changed chin and face outline. These failures motivate both a systematic assessment of current verification ability and supervision that connects judgments to the relevant 3D evidence. Motivated by these challenges, our work addresses three connected questions, from measuring the capability gap to supporting its development and examining its downstream value. How far are current MLLMs from human-level 3D verification? We introduce 3DVeri- fierBench, a human-reviewed benchmark with 2,581 examples across ten complementary tasks. A common answer-and-explanation interface covers object properties, parts, relations, affordance regions, grasps, identity, reference geometry, and motion. In addition to individual judgments, linked counterfactuals test whether predictions respond consistently to changes in requirements or 2

text: candidates. Our experiments show that humans achieve 87.8% task overall accuracy, exceeding the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, by 21.6 percentage points (Figure 1, bottom). The benchmark thus establishes both the breadth and the remaining limitations of current 3D verification. What capabilities and supervision are needed to strengthen 3D verification? Our analysis shows that recognizing an object or action does not ensure verification of the decisive attribute, target, or geometric condition. Identity preservation, grasp validity, and motion compliance are particularly weak, while explanation checks reveal that even correct rejections can miss the reference contradiction. These findings motivate supervision that links a decision to a specific fact and its evidence. Motivated also by prior work on training multimodal verifiers (Zhang et al., 2026b), we develop an automated pipeline for large-scale verification data curation, combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled requirement and candidate changes, and native task annotations. With this pipeline, we produce a large-scale dataset with 14,126 samples across diverse tasks, which provides a data foundation for scaling domain-specific verification supervision. How can a 3D generation model reflect by verifying reliably? We examine both selection among existing candidates and recursive refinement of unsatisfied requirements. text: Recent 3D-language models connect native 3D representations to language and evaluate object, part, spatial, and embodied understanding (Xu et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026a). In parallel, 3D generation benchmarks and evaluators measure semantic alignment, human preference, geometric quality, and generation defects (Wu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a;b; Jia et al., 2026; Duggal et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Together, these works substantially improve our ability to describe and assess 3D content. However, predicting a property or scoring an asset does not directly measure whether a model can verify a specific requirement, reject a plausible but incorrect candidate, and identify heterogeneous 3D evidence that makes it wrong. We focus on this verifier-side evaluation against human judgments, with scope comparisons to prior work in Figure 2. 3 3DVerifierBench To benchmark AI against human verification, 3DVerifierBench unifies 10 tasks under a common interface, evaluating reliability across decisions, explanations, and consistency. Appendix H further provides details of category-wise quantitative analysis of these verification failures. 5.4 How Does Evidence Representation Affect Verification? Multi-view provides a practical protocol for 3D verification. Multi-view representation generally performs better than raw 3D input, indicating that rendering 3D evidence into views is currently a more effective way to elicit reliable judgments from existing MLLMs. We compare multi- view RGB and raw OBJ input on matched Object, Part, and Material subsets in Table 3(a). The multi-view results are also broadly consistent with the corresponding results in Table 1. This choice preserves the core difficulty of 3D verification, requiring models to aggregate partial observations, resolve occlusions, associate parts across views, and disentangle underlying geometry from viewpoint or appearance changes. As an early benchmark for 3D verifiers, 3DVerifierBench therefore adopts multi-view rendering as a practical and extensible protocol for grounding verification in 3D content. We examine how reliable verification feedback can help 3D systems reflect on their outputs. Parallel selection measures the value of recognizing successful candidates, while human-guided recursive refinement examines how explicit failure feedback can guide subsequent revisions. Parallel selection. For 40 source images, we fix seven factual requirements before generation and obtain eight candidates each from Pixal3D and Hunyuan3D-2.1 (Team Hunyuan3D et al., 2025), forming a sixteen-candidate pool per input. All candidates are reviewed by multiple humans with adjudication. Table 4 shows that human-oracle selection raises full factual success from 26.7% under uniform random selection to 90.0%, while Strict Full rises from 16.6% to 85.0%. Selection by GPT-6 Astra also improves over random, approaches human-level performance in factual success rate, but stays below the human oracle. Thus, the oracle results quantify the selection headroom available from reliable verification rather than the performance of an existing automatic verifier. Answer, explanation, and counterfactual-consistency evaluations reveal failures to identify decisive facts, their targets, and relevant contradictions. Our construction pipeline provides structured data to support training on these distinctions. In particular, generative AI tools were used in parts of our model-assisted data construction pipeline, including multi-view fact extraction, verification-claim construction and review, and the generation and editing of counterfactual candidates. text: A Tasks and Data Composition A.1 Task Definitions Object checks identity, global shape, and object-level properties. Part checks component presence, count, type, shape, and arrangement. Material checks color, texture, patterns, and visible surface appearance. Part Grounding presents a highlighted region and a named-part claim. Part Relation presents marked subject and object parts and a relation claim; the markings define its direction. Affordance Region checks whether a marked region supports a stated action. Grasp Validity displays a parallel-jaw pose relative to an object and uses source simulation labels. Identity Preservation asks whether two multi-view assets retain the same identity despite changes in expression or texture. Fine-grained Geometry asks whether a generated 3D candidate matches the reference object’s shape and structure, while explicitly ignoring differences in color, texture, and material. Motion Understanding evaluates the complete caption set and checks action correctness, naturalness, and geometric stability. Its three negative issue classes are internal diagnostics, not additional tasks. A counterfactual triplet contains a positive anchor, a specification-side negative, and a candidate-side negative. An anchor with only one available negative forms a pair rather than a complete triplet. A counterexample is not automatically a measured counterfactual pair. The latter requires the original and changed records, their shared specification or candidate, and the sibling link. An A/B identity comparison is likewise one verification input, not two

A.2 Model-Visible Inputs Object, Part, and Material receive the claim and eight frozen original views, without an additional task-specific instruction. Part Grounding, Part Relation, Affordance Region, and Grasp Validity receive their task-specific instructions and evidence sheets. Identity uses one 2-by-8 asset-pair sheet. Fine-grained Geometry uses one 2-by-7 reference/render sheet. Motion Understanding uses native MP4 or a frozen 4-by-4 sheet of sixteen uniformly sampled frames. A video and all its captions form one example. Reference answers, reference explanations, construction labels, and analysis labels are excluded from subject-model inputs. text: Fine-grained Geometry Text Prompt You are evaluating a generated 3D asset. Given reference images and rendered views of the generated asset, decide whether the candidate matches the reference object’s shape and structure. Differences in color, texture, material should not affect your judgment. Answer Y/N. Motion Understanding. The source collection contains 134 animation examples constructed using reference motions from AnimalML3D (Yang et al., 2024), with candidate sequences generated by AnimateAnyMesh and Animate3D. Each generated MP4 and its associated set of three to five captions are retained as one example. The videos use 24 fps and contain 13 to 151 frames. Native-video inputs retain the MP4. Image inputs use sixteen frames at indices round(k(F −1)/15) for k = 0, . . . , 15, arranged chronologically in a 4-by-4 sheet; short videos may repeat frames. The input contains neither source failure-folder names nor reference labels. The full text prompt for evaluating MLLMs’ verification in this task is: Motion Understanding Text Prompt Determine whether the 3D motion matches the intended motion described by the following captions. The captions describe different aspects or stages of the same intended motion. The candidate explanation is valid exactly when it identifies the same violated fact and contradiction as the reference explanation. Accept concise paraphrases and equivalent descriptions. It is invalid if it changes the count, value, relation, material, region, or direction; discusses the wrong fact; adds a conflicting hallucination; or merely says the claim is false without identifying the contradiction. The selected conditioning view exposes the intended change. The planner records the target, non- target preservation constraints, mask mode, and generation route. text: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Tianjiao Yu1 Zhilin Ou2 Yifan Shen1 Xinzhuo Li1 Yuanzhe Liu1 Onkar Kishor Susladkar1 Fan Wang3 Ismini Lourentzou1 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 2The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen 3Amazon ty41@illinois.edu lourent2@illinois.edu Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy’s failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task’s optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of- distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76%

text: Simulation has become a primary source of robot manip- ulation data, but building simulated environments has long been the bottleneck: each one requires a task de- sign, semantically appropriate assets, a plausible layout, and a training signal, often all specified by hand [38]. Generative simulation removes much of that cost. Cod- ing agents now synthesize scenes, articulations, and task specifications directly [25, 37–39, 43], and language models author the reward functions that accompany them [42, 48]. Environments are no longer scarce. A central challenge remaining is deciding which en- vironments to build next and what supervision will help the policy to learn from them. Existing engines sample variation from hand-specified ranges [29], refine a scene until it is physically valid [39, 43], or allocate budget by per-task success rate [10]. These signals indicate whether an environment is valid and how well the current policy performs, but do not by themselves measure how much the policy improves through training. Without such feedback, a generator risks spending its budget on environments the policy has already mastered or cannot yet learn to solve. 1 arXiv:2610.22362v1 [cs.RO] 15 Oct 2026
title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

text: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies CoDA closes this loop with a heterogeneous memory shared by the data generator and the action policy. It records repairs needed to make scenes valid, together with policy failure diagnoses grounded in rollout evi- dence and localized to one generative factor and one trajectory phase. The memory tracks learning progress for recurring difficulty modes to guide subsequent gener- ation. This evidence is compiled into separate programs for scene generation and policy training, with the latter specifying subgoals and learning tools [38, 42]. As tasks involve longer sequences of dependent subtasks, sparse success signals can slow value learning, while de- signing effective dense rewards can require manual effort. We therefore introduce Text2potential, which compiles a failure diagnosis into a potential over the simulator state and uses it to densify value targets for action chunks [7, 15]. The resulting value estimates guide policy updates through weighted regression on the policy’s own rollouts, favoring action chunks with higher estimated value. Across four manipulation tasks, CoDA achieves 27.6% out-of-distribution success, compared with 5.3% for the supervised fine-tuning baseline. With the same budget for generating environments, a loop guided by per-task success rates achieves 18.1%, while open-loop variants yield 8.5%. Extending our loop to more rounds in- creases out-of-distribution success to 42.1%. Moreover, on LIBERO-Pro, training on

text: fine-tuning baseline. With the same budget for generating environments, a loop guided by per-task success rates achieves 18.1%, while open-loop variants yield 8.5%. Extending our loop to more rounds in- creases out-of-distribution success to 42.1%. Moreover, on LIBERO-Pro, training on source-task variants gener- ated by CoDA increases success from 25% to 84% on po- sition generalization and from 1% to 76% on task gener- alization. Finally, we observe that reusing memory across policy backbones transfers accumulated experience, en- abling a second backbone to increase out-of-distribution success from 3.8% to 21.1%. In summary, the contributions of our work are: • Closed-loop co-evolution. We introduce CoDA, a framework that co-evolves a simulation data engine with a trainable action policy. Failure diagnoses grounded in policy rollouts guide environment gener- ation and training, while measured learning progress determines which difficulties to revisit. • Shared heterogeneous memory. We introduce a memory shared by the generator and policy that combines episodic evidence, reusable difficulty modes, and procedural programs. The same diagnosis com- piles into a generation program that recreates the difficulty and a training program that helps the policy overcome it. Both programs are indexed by difficulty mode, making them reusable across tasks. • Dense supervision through Text2potential. Text2potential compiles failure diagnoses into po- tentials over simulator states that provide dense targets for learning the value

Text2potential compiles failure diagnoses into po- tentials over simulator states that provide dense targets for learning the value of action chunks [15]. Reward shaping requires potential evaluations only at chunk endpoints and preserves the policies that maximize the original task return. • Improved out-of-distribution generalization. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA achieves 27.6% out-of-distribution success, compared with 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning and 18.1% for success- rate-guided generation using the same accepted- environment budget. On LIBERO-Pro, fifteen rounds of CoDA training increase π0.5’s success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations. text: Agentic asset and scene synthesis. Recent methods im- prove visual asset quality [40, 50] and model part struc- ture, articulation, or physical properties [2, 3, 13, 17, 36, 46, 47, 51]. For robot learning, RoboGen [38] generates tasks, scenes, and training supervision, while RoboTwin 2.0 [4] scales bimanual manipulation data through ex- pert data synthesis and domain randomization. Sim- Foundry [29] generates variations across objects, scenes and tasks, and agentic systems automate scene construc- tion and refinement for simulation [25, 37, 39, 43, 44]. Our work focuses on adapting environment generation to the policy’s learning progress, using feedback from training to guide what is generated next. Curriculum learning and policy improvement. Cur- riculum methods prioritize environments using regret, learning potential, or parameter changes [6, 9, 23, 27, 49]. POET [35] coevolves agents and parameterized environments, while language models synthesize re- wards [19, 41, 42] and generate adaptive environment programs [10, 16]. For policy improvement, VLA poli- cies learn from their rollouts using sparse success re- wards [14, 32]. Q-Planning [7] improves action selection while keeping the base policy frozen. We adopt a critic over action chunks [15] with advantage-weighted regres- sion to update the policy [24]. Lifelong methods retain reusable prompts or skill libraries [18, 45]. CoDA links scene generation and policy learning through failure di- agnoses localized to scene

CoDA links scene generation and policy learning through failure di- agnoses localized to scene factors and trajectory phases. 3. Method CoDA couples scene generation and policy learning through a shared memory that guides both. A data engine G, implemented as a tool-augmented coding agent, writes executable scene programs against a simu- lator SDK. Each program defines an environment and a machine-checkable success predicate ν. An action policy πθ collects rollouts in these environments, and a vision– language critic C diagnoses failures by identifying the responsible factor, a trajectory phase, and supporting rollout evidence. Failures intrinsic to motor execution are recorded separately from those attributed to scene factors. The memory M consolidates this evidence into reusable difficulty modes. Validated modes are compiled into two complementary outputs: generation programs 2

text: The CoDA framework. The data engine G generates executable scenes with independently editable task, spatial, and object-attribute factors (τ, σ, α) and a sparse success verifier ν. Construction traces and rollout-grounded failure diagnoses enter a shared memory, which organizes them into reusable difficulty modes. Validated modes are compiled into generation programs that reproduce the diagnosed conditions and training programs that specify subgoals, potentials, and learning tools. Text2potential supplies dense feedback through chunk-level value targets that guide policy updates, and measured learning progress guides the next generation round. that recreate the diagnosed conditions and training pro- grams that help the policy πθ overcome them. We first construct seed environments (§3.1) and de- fine the shared memory (§3.2). Each round then uses the memory to guide scene generation (§3.3), com- piles validated diagnoses into training programs through Text2potential (§3.4), and updates the policy using shaped value estimates (§3.5). The resulting learn- ing progress informs subsequent generation. Figure 2 provides an overview of the overall framework. 3.1. Seeding and Scene Representation Seeding begins with an object pool [5, 33, 51]. We use a task family’s assets when available and otherwise sample from a predefined pool. Given the sampled objects, the engine proposes a task [38] and specifies its instruction, participating objects, initial and terminal object states, and executable success predicate ν. text: task family’s assets when available and otherwise sample from a predefined pool. Given the sampled objects, the engine proposes a task [38] and specifies its instruction, participating objects, initial and terminal object states, and executable success predicate ν. Proposals without a verifier are discarded. Instead of committing to a specific data generation scheme, the engine writes factored scene programs. Task, layout, and object attributes can then be perturbed inde- pendently, letting the loop test a diagnosis by changing one factor while keeping the others fixed. Failure di- agnosis and scene generation need to share a common representation. The critic should identify factors that the engine can directly modify. We parameterize each environment as s = (τ, σ, α), generated by executing a scene program s=Exec(g) with g ∼G(·). The task fac- tor τ specifies the goal predicate, instruction, and initial and terminal object states. The object-spatial factor σ specifies poses, support and containment relations, clear- ances, and occlusion. The object self-attribute factor α specifies geometry, metric scale, mass, friction, articu- lation, and appearance. The SDK exposes these factors through set_task, set_layout, and set_attributes, so the engine can resample any one factor while keep- ing the other two fixed. This factorization provides a common representation for the critic’s diagnoses, the engine’s interventions, and the applicability conditions of compiled generation programs. Verification.

Each program emits a sparse, machine- checkable success predicate ν over its scene objects. This predicate determines task success independently of the critic’s judgments and provides the common success criterion across the methods we compare. Dense training feedback is introduced separately through potential-based shaping, rather than replacing the task predicate with a synthesized reward [42, 48]. Before policy deployment, each scene must pass verification checks for collision-free placement, static stability during a short passive simulation, and plausible metric scale. Programs that fail these checks are excluded from policy rollouts but retained in memory to inform subsequent scene generation. 3.2. Shared Heterogeneous Memory Memory combines two sources of experience: the engine’s construction and repair traces, and the pol- icy’s rollout outcomes and failure diagnoses. Follow- ing the episodic–semantic–procedural organization of language-agent memory [30], we retain individual records (episodic tier), abstract recurring failure patterns (semantic tier), and compile reusable programs for gen- eration and training (procedural tier). 3

text: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies Episodic tier: construction and rollout evidence. The append-only trace store B records each scene pro- gram g, its verifier ν, and summaries of the genera- tion trace, including violated constraints and verification outcomes. For deployed environments, it also records the success rate bp(s) over N rollouts and the learn- ing progress LV(s) obtained from training [49]. The vision–language critic C uses scene and rollout evidence to produce a failure diagnosis ψ = (δ, p, c, e), where δ∈{TASK, SPATIAL, ATTRIBUTE, EXECUTION} identifies the attributed factor, p the trajectory phase, c a natural- language description of the cause, and e the supporting evidence. These diagnoses are stored alongside the corre- sponding traces. The additional label EXECUTION covers motor-execution failures. Semantic tier: reusable difficulty modes. Episodic records are clustered online into difficulty modes Kj using the factor–phase pair (δ, p) and similarity between diagnosed causes. Each mode captures a recurring failure condition that can arise across tasks and policy backbones, such as “an occluder adjacent to the target on the approach side”. We characterize each mode by two quantities, hardness and importance. Hardness is measured by the policy’s success rate bpj, with lower rates indicating greater difficulty. Importance wj is a running score updated from mode-level learning progress, mea- sured as the change in
title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

text: each mode by two quantities, hardness and importance. Hardness is measured by the policy’s success rate bpj, with lower rates indicating greater difficulty. Importance wj is a running score updated from mode-level learning progress, mea- sured as the change in policy success rate on that mode before and after training [49]. These two quantities reflect different properties of a mode. A mode can re- main hard even when training on it yields little learning progress, or become easy after substantial improvement. Each mode also carries a validation status determined by control batches (§3.3), and only validated modes are compiled into procedural memory. Procedural tier: generation and training programs. The two consumers of memory improve differently. The data engine G adapts in context by retrieving and exe- cuting programs between rounds, while the action policy πθ learns through gradient updates and acts from obser- vations. We therefore compile the same validated mode into two complementary programs: • Generation programs, stored in Ω, encode how to reproduce and vary the diagnosed scene conditions. They retain the parent scene program, validated vari- ants along one factor, compilation-check outcomes, and the required relational structure expressed over symbolic object roles. • Training programs, stored in Φ, specify how to address the policy failure through subgoal decompositions, po- tentials, and learning tools. They retain the diagnosed

text: along one factor, compilation-check outcomes, and the required relational structure expressed over symbolic object roles. • Training programs, stored in Φ, specify how to address the policy failure through subgoal decompositions, po- tentials, and learning tools. They retain the diagnosed phase and evidence of which training programs im- proved policy performance. The generation compiler Rgrind produces the former, while Text2potential implements the training compiler Rhone (§3.4). During training, these programs evaluate subgoal completion and compute potentials that shape value targets. At deployment, the trained policy pre- dicts actions from observations and the task instruction without executing these programs. 3.3. Memory-Guided Scene Generation At each round, memory guides which difficulty modes to revisit and how to instantiate them in new environments. We allocate the generation budget across difficulty modes using an upper-confidence rule based on their hardness and observed learning progress. An ε-fraction of the budget is reserved for novel environments, while a separate replay fraction revisits previously encountered modes to detect performance regressions. A validated generation program is added to the pool Ωwhen the policy’s success rate on its variants falls within the designated success band and is removed when success rate is outside that band. For each selected mode, the engine retrieves a generation program specifying the scene conditions to reproduce and the factor to vary. Generation programs express

For each selected mode, the engine retrieves a generation program specifying the scene conditions to reproduce and the factor to vary. Generation programs express scene conditions in terms of symbolic object roles, allowing the engine to reuse them across task families by assigning those roles to objects in a new scene (Appendix A). For each selected candidate difficulty mode linked to a scene factor, the engine generates a targeted batch that varies the identified factor and a control batch that varies a different factor. After verification checks, we evaluate the current policy on both batches. If the targeted variants yield a lower policy success rate than the control variants, the proposed difficulty mode is com- piled into reusable generation and training programs. The policy learns from its rollouts using the success predicate ν and the potential-based feedback supplied by Text2potential (§3.4). A scripted planner also attempts each valid variant, and trajectories that satisfy ν are retained as demonstrations Dt, providing additional imitation supervision when available. 3.4. Text2potential The success predicate ν determines whether a gener- ated task is complete, but provides little feedback on intermediate progress. This makes value learning diffi- cult when success requires a long sequence of actions. Text2potential converts a validated

text: available. 3.4. Text2potential The success predicate ν determines whether a gener- ated task is complete, but provides little feedback on intermediate progress. This makes value learning diffi- cult when success requires a long sequence of actions. Text2potential converts a validated failure diagnosis into subgoals and potentials over simulator states. These po- tentials provide dense feedback for value learning (§3.5). Prior language-based reward synthesis provides dense training feedback, but its iterative refinement relies on humans to describe policy failures observed in rollouts, and can produce rewards that favor behavior other than task completion [42]. Text2potential instead uses a critic to diagnose failures from the policy’s own rollouts and compiles these diagnoses into a potential function that shapes the value critic’s training targets, providing dense feedback without replacing the original task reward. Experiments Experimental Setup. We evaluate CoDA on four manipulation task families and LIBERO-Pro [52] using π0.5 [8] as the primary policy backbone. text: We introduce CoDA, coupling environment generation and policy learning through shared heterogeneous memory. Failure diagnoses become reusable programs for generating environments and training the pol- icy. Text2potential provides dense supervision, while learning progress guides generation and refinement. text: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies A. Transferring Generation Programs Across Task Families A generation program can be reused in a new task family when its object requirements and relational constraints are satisfied in the new scene. We call this transfer lifting. Each program refers to objects by symbolic role, such as target, obstacle, or support, rather than by a specific object instance. Each role specifies a required object category, such as container, or an affordance, such as graspable. The program also specifies the rela- tions required between these roles, such as an obstacle occupying the approach path to the target. To apply a program to a new scene, Rgrind matches these requirements against the scene program’s symbol table, which records object identifiers, categories, affordances, poses, and relations. This information is available di- rectly because the data engine constructs the scene pro- gram. A valid binding assigns each role to a distinct scene object and satisfies all role requirements and relational constraints. If no valid binding exists, the program is not transferred to that scene. Matching is exhaustive: our programs contain at most five roles and our scenes contain a few dozen objects, with matching taking mil- liseconds in this setting. When several bindings are valid, they are ranked first by how closely their object categories match those
title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

text: our programs contain at most five roles and our scenes contain a few dozen objects, with matching taking mil- liseconds in this setting. When several bindings are valid, they are ranked first by how closely their object categories match those in the dif- ficulty mode’s previously validated variants. Ties are bro- ken using the margins by which the relational constraints are satisfied. We retain at most three bindings and exe- cute the generation program separately for each, produc- ing a scene variant and its own matched control batch. Transferred programs undergo the same validation as programs learned within the new task family. Their gen- erated variants must pass the scene-validity checks, and policy rollouts evaluate both the targeted variants and their controls. A transferred program enters Ωfor the new family only when the control comparison supports the attributed difficulty and the measured success rates of its variants fall within the success band. Thus, match- ing establishes whether a program is applicable to the new scene; evaluation establishes whether it reproduces a useful training difficulty. B. Implementation Details Environments and evaluation. We construct MuJoCo environments for four task families: pick-and-place, articulated open/close, put-inside, and stack/insert. Each family includes an in-distribution evaluation suite and four held-out suites of 100 environments each, testing generalization to unseen object instances, layouts, tasks, and categories, respectively.

text: We construct MuJoCo environments for four task families: pick-and-place, articulated open/close, put-inside, and stack/insert. Each family includes an in-distribution evaluation suite and four held-out suites of 100 environments each, testing generalization to unseen object instances, layouts, tasks, and categories, respectively. Held-out environments never enter M. In a second setting, we initialize the loop with the 30 LIBERO source tasks and evaluate on LIBERO-Pro [52] (Table 2). All results are reported as mean ± standard error over three random seeds. Assets, observations, and actions. The asset collection comprises 1,200 rigid objects from Objaverse across 60 categories, 300 articulated objects from ArtiCraft-10K, and 500 seed layouts from TableVerse [5, 33, 51]. The robot is a 7-DoF Franka Panda with front and wrist cam- eras, each providing 224 × 224 RGB observations. Con- trol runs at 10 Hz using seven-dimensional actions: six dimensions for the change in end-effector pose and one for the gripper command. Each action chunk contains h = 8 control steps. Policy backbones. Our primary policy is π0.5, a 3B- parameter model with a flow-matching action head [8]. We initialize it from the released openpi base checkpoint, or from its LIBERO-fine-tuned checkpoint for the LIBERO experiments [26]. We also evaluate the 7B-parameter OpenVLA-OFT [12] in table 7. Both policies are fine- tuned using LoRA with rank 32 and a learning
title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

text: it from the released openpi base checkpoint, or from its LIBERO-fine-tuned checkpoint for the LIBERO experiments [26]. We also evaluate the 7B-parameter OpenVLA-OFT [12] in table 7. Both policies are fine- tuned using LoRA with rank 32 and a learning rate of 10−5. At each rollout decision, the policy samples j = 8 candidate action chunks. These are combined using soft- max weights computed from Qϕ, with temperature 0.5. Scene generation, diagnosis, and potential compi- lation. The data engine, rollout-diagnosis model, and potential compiler all use GPT-5.5 [21]. Planner-certified demonstrations are obtained using cuRobo [31]. The diagnosis model receives rollout video, contact informa- tion, joint states, and the task success verifier’s output at each timestep. It assigns each diagnosed failure to one of four factors (TASK, SPATIAL, ATTRIBUTE, or EXECUTION) and one of five trajectory phases (approach, grasp, transport, place or insert, and release). For potential compilation, Text2potential retrieves three exemplar programs from Φj and uses a library of 12 helper functions. Generated programs undergo at most two rounds of repair for syntax or runtime errors. Value learning and policy optimization. The value critic Qϕ uses frozen DINOv2-B [22] and T5-base [28] encoders followed by a four-layer transformer decoder. It is trained by categorical value regression with 101 bins spanning [−βmmax, 1], where β = 0.5 is the shaping coefficient
title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies

text: optimization. The value critic Qϕ uses frozen DINOv2-B [22] and T5-base [28] encoders followed by a four-layer transformer decoder. It is trained by categorical value regression with 101 bins spanning [−βmmax, 1], where β = 0.5 is the shaping coefficient and mmax = 4 is the maximum number of subgoals. We use a discount factor of γ = 0.99 and an exponential moving average target network with update coefficient τ = 0.005. Each round includes KQ =20,000 critic-update steps with batch size 256 and Kπ = 5,000 policy-update steps with batch size 64. The advantage-weighted policy update uses λ=1. Generation budgets and rollout protocol. Experiments use n = 5 rounds, with per-family budgets of 320 ac- cepted environments, 1,280 planner-certified demonstra- tions, and 2.5M LLM tokens. Token counts include scene generation, diagnosis, and potential compilation. Ex- tended runs use n = 15 rounds. Each round generates B = 64 targeted environments and 64 control environ- ments per task family. The policy is evaluated on each environment using N =16 rollouts from the same initial simulator state. The diagnosis model processes at most C = 32 failed rollouts per difficulty mode. Broader Impact The ability to generate environments and training sig- nals automatically has far-reaching implications for robot learning, simulation, and embodied AI. CoDA contributes to this space by turning environment generation into a closed loop that responds to what a policy has learned, which lowers the cost of producing diverse, verifiable training data. This can accelerate the development of capable manipulation policies, improve the fidelity and coverage of simulated benchmarks, and support scal- able data generation for research groups without large teleoperation budgets. While lowering the barrier to training capable robot policies raises potential concerns about misuse and about biases inherited from the un- derlying foundation models, our framework is designed for research use, judges success only through machine- checkable verifiers, and audits every automated diagnosis with control experiments. text: We introduce P3-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal- directed planning through three complementary modes: PERCEIVE, which recon- structs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; PREDICT, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and PLAN, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual–action atten- tion. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision–language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. 1 arXiv:2610.22363v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

text: Dexterous manipulation requires more than mapping pixels directly to actions. An embodied model must answer three complementary questions: What happened in an observed interaction? What will happen under a specified action? What should be done to accomplish a desired goal? These questions correspond to three fundamental capabilities: perceiving the 3D motion underlying observed interactions, predicting action-conditioned world dynamics, and planning actions together with their anticipated consequences. Infants can use what they learn from observing adults’ actions to guide their own behavior (Hauf & Aschersleben, 2008). Through their own interactions, they learn to predict action outcomes and use those expected outcomes to select actions (Verschoor et al., 2013) and organize movements toward a goal (Claxton et al., 2003). Together, these findings suggest that perception, prediction, and planning are linked by knowledge of actions and their consequences. Despite these connections, prior work on egocentric manipulation has developed along three closely related but largely separate lines. Egocentric reconstruction methods recover structured 3D interaction information, such as hand motion and camera trajectories, from observed videos (Pavlakos et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2025). Action-conditioned world models predict future observations under prescribed motion trajectories (Hao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026). World action models jointly generate actions and future observations for goal-directed control (Ye et al., 2026). These capabilities, however,
title: Preprint

text: world models predict future observations under prescribed motion trajectories (Hao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026). World action models jointly generate actions and future observations for goal-directed control (Ye et al., 2026). These capabilities, however, are still largely learned in isolation or coupled only in subsets. To close this loop, we introduce P3-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that integrates three complementary modes: 3D interaction reconstruction (PERCEIVE), action-conditioned world prediction (PREDICT), and joint action–future planning (PLAN). Recon- struction develops the model’s capacity for 3D perception by recovering 3D motion from observed interactions. Prediction teaches the model to anticipate the visual consequences of prescribed actions. Together, these capabilities provide the foundation for world–action planning, in which the model learns to jointly generate goal-directed hand action trajectories and their anticipated visual futures. We learn all three modes through unified training. Figure 1 illustrates these three modes. We build P3-WAM on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (Wan et al., 2025) to draw on its rich visual and motion priors. We represent each action by the articulated poses of both hands and the camera pose, and encode these states as compact tokens alongside the video tokens. We integrate this representation into the video backbone through a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with a dedicated action expert, which

We integrate this representation into the video backbone through a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with a dedicated action expert, which shares the backbone’s base weights while incorporating modality- specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022). To train this architecture across all three modes, we randomly vary the visibility of visual observations and actions: providing video while withholding actions supports perception, providing actions while withholding future video supports prediction, and withholding actions and video supports joint action–future planning, exposing the model to complete modes and partially observed interactions. Over long sequences, successive visual subgoals specify the target arrangement for each planning window. Unified training improves all three modes over single-mode training. Our model outperforms the evaluated baselines in PERCEIVE and PREDICT. Its PLAN videos receive higher VLM scores for action process and instruction adherence. Robot demonstrations illustrate how generated human-hand motion can be transferred to a dexterous robot. text: We introduced P3-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that integrates perception, prediction, and planning. A coupled video–action transformer connects visual generation with explicit hand and camera trajectories and supports all three modes within the same model. Through extensive experiments, we show that unified training benefits hand reconstruction, action-conditioned video prediction, and planning. Limitations. Estimating the global 3D hand position from monocular video is inherently ambiguous. Incorporating tactile or depth sensing could provide stronger geometric constraints. Our robot experiments currently rely on open-loop execution. Introducing closed-loop feedback would allow the robot to correct its motion online, potentially improving robustness over longer-horizon interactions. 9

text: Preprint A ADDITIONAL METHOD DETAILS A.1 SHARED WEIGHTS AND MODALITY-SPECIFIC ADAPTATION Within each diffusion expert, RGB and action use the same base self-attention Q/K/V and output projections and the same two FFN projections. Each update has the form ∆Wa = (α/r)BaAa, with rank r = 128 and α = 128. Aa uses Kaiming initialization and Ba starts at zero. The pretrained base weights remain trainable. text: Preprint D.2 PREDICT RGB AND HAND-REGION METRICS For full-frame and hand-region CLIP-I (Radford et al., 2021), we compute paired image-feature cosine similarity using OpenAI ViT-B/32 with its standard bicubic short-edge resize to 224, center crop, and normalization. FVD (Unterthiner et al., 2018) uses the StyleGAN-V (Skorokhodov et al., 2022) Kinetics-400 I3D TorchScript model’s 400-dimensional pre-softmax features, bilinear resizing to 224 × 224, pixel scaling to [−1, 1], and one feature vector per video. We use unbiased empirical covariances and an exact low-rank Fréchet-distance calculation. Hand-region metrics use WiLoR detections with confidence threshold 0.3 and NMS IoU threshold 0.7. We expand ground-truth boxes by 1.5×, clip them to the image boundary, and apply the same crop to the reference and prediction. Crop PSNR, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004), and VGG-LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) are measured at the native crop resolution, with small boundary crops padded for LPIPS. For IoU, we match unexpanded boxes by maximum total IoU within handedness classes. We divide the matched IoU sum by the larger detection count, so unmatched detections contribute zero. Frames with no detections on either side are omitted; one-sided detections receive zero. Crop metrics average hands within a frame, valid frames within a window, and then windows within a dataset/method. Crop metrics use frames with a valid GT hand detection. FVD is computed

D.3 PERCEIVE TARGETS AND METRICS Following ViDiHand (Wang et al., 2026a), we report presence-aware MPJPE-p in camera-space, root- relative, and Procrustes-aligned coordinates. A reference hand is eligible when at least one annotated joint lies inside the image at camera depth greater than 0.01 m. This is also the positive GT definition for hand visibility. Joint errors use the valid annotated joints of each eligible hand; RR requires a valid wrist, and PA additionally requires at least three joints and a nondegenerate prediction. Association and missing-hand penalties. Our model emits a hand prediction when its maximum joint-visibility probability is at least 0.5; HaMeR and Dyn-HaMR use their released hand detections. All methods are matched to reference hands of the same side by descending mesh-box IoU, using a 1.1× enlarged reference box and an IoU threshold of 0.1. An eligible hand without a match receives a canonical MANO hand in the penalized metrics. Its

This evaluation tests whether 20
title: Preprint

text: Preprint the generated behavior captures sufficiently accurate object interactions and action ordering to support downstream robot execution. Starting from a generated manipulation video, we reconstruct the relevant objects and scene and recover their motion over time. The reconstructed hand motion is then retargeted to the robot hand to obtain an initial robot trajectory. The resulting action sequence is then deployed on the physical robot without further modification. Thus, the complete evaluation pipeline is generated video →scene and object reconstruction → robot retargeting →real-world execution. This follows do-as-I-do Paliwal et al. (2026) evaluation paradigm, in which a visual demonstration is converted into an executable robot behavior. For both experiments, we report whether execution reproduces the intended manipulation process and reaches the specified task outcome. These real-world trials complement the human and VLM evaluations above: whereas the perceptual metrics measure whether an action appears correct and physically plausible in the generated video, real-world execution provides a direct test of whether the predicted interaction can be grounded into a physically executable manipulation trajectory. text: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly ob- servable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time op- timization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact la- tent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what en- vironmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alter- nates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the la- 1 arXiv:2610.22364v1 [cs.RO] 15 Oct 2026
title: Preprint

text: Preprint tents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emer- gent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded fac- tors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory. 1

text: What a robot observes is insufficient to determine how the world will respond. Beneath visually similar scene configurations reside hidden environmental factors, such as friction, mass distribution, and unobserved human-defined interaction rules, that can fundamentally alter the consequences of the same action (fig. 1 (a)). Such factors are often revealed only through interaction with the target environments, as their influence becomes observable through the outcomes they induce. Explicitly representing these factors (Kumar et al., 2021), however, requires specifying in advance what factors may vary, their exact values, and how they should be parameterized, which is difficult to scale to unknown or compounded environmental variation. On the contrary, humans reason through “analy- sis by synthesis” (Yuille & Kersten, 2006), using internal generative models not only to anticipate future outcomes, but also in reverse to infer latent structure that best accounts for what they observe. This raises a natural question: can hidden environmental factors be similarly captured in a latent representation that is directly optimized from test-time interactions? We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environmental latents, which augments an action- conditioned robotic world model with a learnable environment latent ze. ze is a randomly-initialized compact representation that is expected to encode the unobserved factors governing how an envi- ronment responds to interaction, with no supervision about what environmental factors it should

text: robotic world model with a learnable environment latent ze. ze is a randomly-initialized compact representation that is expected to encode the unobserved factors governing how an envi- ronment responds to interaction, with no supervision about what environmental factors it should represent. The world model predicts future visual observations conditioned jointly on the action and ze. We iteratively optimize the world model and ze in an alternating two-stage procedure: 1) world-model optimization: with ze fixed, we train the world model across all trajectories to learn shared action-conditioned dynamics across environments; 2) environment-latent optimization: with the world model frozen, we optimize the conditioned latent ze through prediction error, so that it captures underlying environment-specific variation not explained by the general world model alone. Both stages are optimized with the same flow-matching loss and alternated for multiple rounds until convergence, allowing the environment representation to emerge directly through prediction without predefined physical-factor supervision or a separate environment encoder. At test time, the world model is frozen and T2-Z turns environment inference into a direct opti- mization problem. For a previously unseen environmental configuration, we initialize a new ze and optimize ze to explain the outcomes of one or more observed test-time interactions. Specifically, we update ze for multiple optimization steps through the same flow-matching objective used dur- ing stage-two training, minimizing prediction error

Specifically, we update ze for multiple optimization steps through the same flow-matching objective used dur- ing stage-two training, minimizing prediction error on the observed interactions. Because inference is optimization-based rather than amortized through a learned history encoder, T2-Z is not tied to the trajectory count used for training and can flexibly incorporate any number of test-time trajecto- ries. Once optimized, the latent turns the frozen world model into an environment-adapted test-time simulator, enabling prediction and comparison of candidate action outcomes before execution. We evaluate T2-Z across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks. Robotic world models have made rapid progress in predicting action-conditioned futures (Zhou et al., 2025; 2024; Zhu et al., 2024; Zhen et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). More recent work explores test-time adaptation to improve long-horizon memory or incorporate new behavioral supervision (Wan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026; Yoo et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2026). These approaches predict future outcomes from visual observations alone, without accounting for underlying environmental variation that is not directly observable. (fig. 2 (a)). In contrast, T2-Z disentangles unobserved environmental variation from the world model’s observable scene representation, through environment latent conditioning. Environment representations and system identification have demonstrated the value of environment-specific representations for system identification and rapid behavioral adaptation (Yu et al., 2017; Nagabandi et al., 2019; Rakelly et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2021; Miki et al., 2022; Nahrendra et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024). The Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) family and related methods typically rely on predefined privileged param- eters (Kumar et al., 2021; Miki et al., 2022; Nahrendra et al., 2023;
title: Preprint

text: Wang et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024). The Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) family and related methods typically rely on predefined privileged param- eters (Kumar et al., 2021; Miki et al., 2022; Nahrendra et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024). For example, RMA restricts adaptation to 5 factors and uses their ground-truth values to learn an em- bedding that an adaptation encoder later recovers from interaction history (Kumar et al., 2021). This prespecifies the environment representation and ties inference to a learned history-to-embedding mapping, limiting flexibility under unknown, compounded, or out-of-distribution variation (fig. 2 (b)). These methods also generally rely on a learned history encoder (Chen et al., 2024; Xing et al., 2026), limiting generalization when the amount of test-time interaction differs from that seen during training. In contrast, T2-Z learns representations of environmental factors implicitly through world prediction error, without predefined ground-truth physical parameters or a learned history encoder. Our method is also related to the literature on Test-Time Adaptation (TTA), which has enabled robots to improve after deployment by adapting policy, prompts, or memory rather than optimizing a dedicated environment representation. Existing approaches include test-time adaptation of diffusion and flow policies (Li et al., 2025; 2026), online policy adaptation (Liu et al., 2026; Jin & Zhang, 2026; Zhu et al.,
