We introduce T2-Z (fig. 2 & algorithm 1), a framework for adapting robotic world models to hidden environmental variation through direct optimization of an environment latent. Our key idea is to sep- arate the general visual predictive capability of a world model from unobserved environment-specific information. During training, we learn these two components through alternating optimization un- der a shared flow-matching objective. At test time, we freeze the world model and optimize only a newly initialized environment latent from observed test-time interaction trajectories. The optimized latent subsequently conditions the frozen world model to predict the outcomes of diverse actions. 3.1 PROBLEM SETUP We consider a robotic world model that predicts future visual observations y from the observation x and action a. We augment the world model with an environment latent ze and formulate prediction as: pθ (y | x, a, ze) , (1) where θ denotes the shared world-model parameters and ze is a latent representation of the environ- ment. Importantly, ze receives no supervision of which environmental factors it should represent. As the world model improves, latents are optimized against an increasingly capable predictive model; conversely, the refined latents provide more informative conditioning for subsequent world-model optimization. 3.1.2 TEST-TIME OPTIMIZATION At test time, we adapt to a previously unseen environment by optimizing only its environment latent while keeping the trained world model fixed. Because the world model is fixed, prediction errors over the observed interactions can only be reduced by updating ztest. The latent is therefore optimized toward a representation under which the frozen world model reproduces the interaction outcomes observed in the current environment. Once optimized, z∗ test is reused to condition the world model for actions that were not observed during latent optimization. Given a different action a′, we predict its outcome as ˆy′ ∼pθ∗(y | x, a′, z∗ test) . (8) The resulting conditioned world model serves as an environment-adapted test-time simulator, allow- ing it to predict the consequences of different actions under the inferred environment. Unlike amortized history-encoder approaches, T2-Z uses direct optimization. This avoids commit- ting to a fixed history mapping and searches for the representation that best explains the current envi- ronment. The formulation can naturally incorporate any number of test-time trajectories that differs from training, by optimizing a latent against all available evidence. Moreover, T2-Z is not restricted to the range of factor values during training, providing greater flexibility under out-of-distribution configurations. In simulation, Friction requires predicting how far an object moves after a push under different surface friction; Gravity varies gravitational strength and requires predicting the object motion; Mass Collision varies colliding object mass and predicts the resulting collision motion. Light Switch assigns dif- ferent human-defined hidden interaction rules that determine whether a robot action turns the light on or off; Mass Balance predicts the tilt of a dumbbell under different mass distribution; Mass × Friction jointly varies object mass and surface friction at the same time; Diverse Visual Back- grounds evaluates the same friction variations across 30 diverse scene setups, testing whether the learned environment representation remains consistent across visual changes.. In the real world, Door Close varies the spring-lock stiffness, which changes how the door responds to closing ac- tions; Ball Friction requires predicting the motion of a pushed ball of unknown mass; Stick Bal- ance requires predicting the motion

text: In the real world, Door Close varies the spring-lock stiffness, which changes how the door responds to closing ac- tions; Ball Friction requires predicting the motion of a pushed ball of unknown mass; Stick Bal- ance requires predicting the motion of a stick with objects of different masses attached to its ends; and Soft Pull requires predicting the deformation a soft object under different rotating actions. Implementation Details. We adapt BWM Team (2026), an action-conditioned world model built on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. The environment latent has a dimension of 32. Training starts with 300 world-model updates, followed by 200 latent updates and alternating 200-200 updates. Stage I/II use LR 10−5 / 0.03 respectively. At test time, we freeze the world model and use a coarse-to-fine LR schedule of 3.0/1.5/0.5/0.15, 10 steps each, for 40 steps. T2-Z uses only one test-time trajectory on randomly-sampled action for Friction, Gravity, Mass Collision, Mass × Friction, Ball Friction, and Soft Pull, and two for Light Switch, Mass Balance, Door Close, and Stick Balance. Evaluation Metrics. (1) Physical Error measures task-relevant state prediction: object-location error in pixels for Friction, Gravity, Mass Collision, and Diverse Backgrounds; lamp activation error for Light Switch; and bar-tilt angle error in degrees for Mass Balance. For real-world tasks, we measure tracked-state error in pixels. We report Physical Error (Mean), averaged over predicted
title: Preprint

text: for Friction, Gravity, Mass Collision, and Diverse Backgrounds; lamp activation error for Light Switch; and bar-tilt angle error in degrees for Mass Balance. For real-world tasks, we measure tracked-state error in pixels. We report Physical Error (Mean), averaged over predicted frames, and Physical Error (Final), measured at the final predicted frame. (2) Video Generation Quality is measured by LPIPS and PSNR between predicted and ground-truth videos. LPIPS mea- sures perceptual discrepancy in a learned feature space, capturing differences in visual structure and appearance, and serves as our primary measure of generation quality. In contrast, PSNR primarily reflects pixel-level reconstruction fidelity and is less informative about semantically meaningful dif- ferences or whether object motion is physically correct. (3) Action Success treats the world model as a simulator: given candidate actions, we predict their outcomes and select the action most likely to achieve the task goal, such as pushing a ball to a target, balancing a stick, or closing a door. We execute the chose action in real world and observe if meets the success criterions in Supp section C. 6

Stan- dard World Model uses no environment latent or test-time adaptation; LoRA TTA adapts attention LoRA parameters from test-time interactions; DINOv2 Context amortizes a 32-D environment con- text from interaction trajectories; and TTT-KQV adapts fast weights within the world model. Please refer to the Supplementary for more details about architecture (section A), task definitions (section C), baseline implementation (section D), and compute efficiency comparison (section E.4). 4.2 SIMULATION EXPERIMENTS Single-Factor Environmental Variation. We first evaluate T2-Z under individual unobserved environmental factors, spanning continuous physical properties, mass-dependent interactions, and discrete human-defined rules. As shown in table 1, T2-Z achieves the highest action success on all five tasks, increasing the five-task average from 36.9% for the Standard World Model to 76.6%, while reducing average LPIPS from 0.0469 to 0.0325. It also substantially improves task-relevant prediction, reducing mean error from 11.06 to 3.85 pixels on Friction, 21.93 to 6.45 pixels on Mass Collision, and 1.18◦to 0.64◦on Mass Balance. These gains arise because T2-Z directly optimizes an environment latent from observed interactions, capturing environment-specific variation more flexibly than non-adaptive or amortized baselines. 7

text: We introduce T2-Z which augments robotic world models with enviornment latent conditioning. T2-Z alternates between world-model optimization that learns action-conditioned dyanmics, and environment-latent optimization that captures hidden environment factors. For a new environment, the world model is frozen and only the latent is optimized. Across 7 simulation and 4 real-world tasks, T2-Z outperforms baselines a lot in both video prediction and action selection. text: Preprint A MODEL ARCHITECTURE AND OPTIMIZATION A.1 ARCHITECTURE AND LATENT CONDITIONING Inputs and inherited backbone. For an episode in environment e, the model receives one ini- tial RGB frame I0 and an aligned sequence a = (at)t of 14-D robot actions, and predicts the subsequent video frames. We initialize the video diffusion transformer (DiT) and action encoder from BWM (BWM Team, 2026), retaining its Wan2.2(Wan et al., 2025)-based action-conditioning pathway. The frozen video VAE encodes the initial frame into the video-latent stream and de- codes predicted latents back to RGB. Text conditioning is disabled; the initial frame is not an extra cross-attention token. In short, I0 enters the video-latent stream, a follows BWM’s two action- conditioning paths, and the environment latent augments both paths. Environment-indexed latent conditioning. We associate each environment e with a freely opti- mized vector ze ∈R32. Episodes assigned to an environment share its latent; their initial frames and actions vary, so predicting their different outcomes constrains the environment representation. There is no observation-to-latent encoder and no supervision from the numerical physical parameter. Let D = 3072 be the DiT width. Two separate projectors turn ze into model-width vectors: qb(ze) = Wb,2 GELU(Wb,1 LN(ze)) , b ∈{token, mod}, Wb,1 : 32 →128, Wb,2 : 128 →D. (9) The two linear layers in each projector have no bias;

(9) The two linear layers in each projector have no bias; the projectors do not share weights. The 128-D width is internal to these MLPs: both outputs are D-dimensional. Cross-attention branch. BWM’s action encoder maps each action to a D-dimensional condition- ing token. Let Atok(a) denote this token sequence and ue = qtoken(ze) the single environment token. With text disabled, each DiT block receives the conditioning sequence Ce = [ue; Atok(a)]. For video patch tokens Xℓ∈RN×D entering block ℓ, the attention operation can be written schemat- ically as CA(Xℓ, Ce) = softmax (XℓWQ)(CeWK)⊤ √dh  (CeWV )WO. (10) Here N is the number of video patches, dh is one attention head’s width, and WQ, WK, WV , WO are the block’s learned attention matrices. The actual operation is multi-head; the equation shows where the new token enters. Every video patch can attend to the environment token as well as the action tokens through keys and values. Modulation branch. BWM also groups four aligned 14-D actions at a time and maps each group to a D-dimensional action-modulation vector amod g . text: tokens through keys and values. Modulation branch. BWM also groups four aligned 14-D actions at a time and maps each group to a D-dimensional action-modulation vector amod g . Index g identifies the corresponding latent- video temporal group, and s identifies a spatial patch within it. Let τ be the current flow-matching timestep and bg,s(τ) ∈RD be Wan’s base timestep embedding at that video patch, before action or environment conditioning. The initial-frame latent uses the unnoised timestep, while predicted- frame latents use τ. The environment-modulation vector is ve = qmod(ze) ∈RD. The implementa- tion adds these three vectors and applies the existing time projection: ˜bg,s(τ) = bg,s(τ) + amod g + ve, Mg,s = TimeProj(˜bg,s(τ)) ∈R6×D. (11) The action and environment vectors are broadcast to every spatial patch in group g. The six D- dimensional outputs of Mg,s supply the DiT blocks’ adaptive-normalization shifts, scales, and resid- ual gates; the modified timestep embedding also conditions the output head. Thus ze influences both attention and per-patch modulation, while leaving BWM’s original action pathways in place. A.2 TRAINING AND TEST-TIME ADAPTATION Training schedule. Training uses the inherited flow-matching video-prediction loss, excluding the initial conditioning frame. A latent block freezes the shared model and updates the environment table; a model block freezes the table and updates the DiT, action encoder, and two projectors.

text: Preprint B.2 SIMULATOR AND REAL-WORLD SETUP Simulator. We construct the custom tasks in a LIBERO-based simulator (Liu et al., 2023) with a Franka Panda arm. Simulated RGB videos are recorded at 20 fps and 224 × 224 resolution. The action representation has 14 channels. Real world. The physical tasks use a Franka robot arm and a fixed Intel RealSense D435i camera. We use only its main RGB view, captured at 640 × 480 and 20 fps; the task-specific saved video crops and model-input sizes appear in Table 6. Model inputs are letterboxed to the listed sizes. All tasks use 14-channel action vectors; the target-action representation is task dependent. C EVALUATION PROTOCOLS C.1 SHARED PROTOCOL AND METRICS Shared comparison. For action-selection tasks, we sample candidate actions and use each model’s predicted videos to make an action decision. The selected action is then executed in the en- vironment, and success is determined from its actual outcome using the task-specific criteria below. Each evaluated candidate-action set contains at least one action that satisfies the target condition. All methods receive the same query inputs and candidate actions, and all methods that adapt at test time receive the same test-time interaction trajectories. The Standard World Model does not adapt at test time, and no method sees a query outcome before making its prediction. For tracked

D.4 TTT-KQV We adapt a video test-time-training fast-weight module (Dalal et al., 2025) to the BWM backbone. text: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models Andi Gu,1, 2, 3, ∗Alek H. Kemeny,4 Susanne F. Yelin,1, 2 and Mikhail D. Lukin1, 2, 5 1Harvard Quantum Initiative for Science and Engineering, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA 2Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA 3Anthropic STEM Fellows Program 4Anthropic 5QuEra Computing, 1380 Soldiers Field Road, Boston, MA 02135, USA Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps—a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic—viable and substantially improves the Toffoli–qubit
title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

text: the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps—a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic—viable and substantially improves the Toffoli–qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation. Computational primitives based on classical function evaluation play a central role in a wide range of quantum algorithms. Such primitives include decoding routines for optimization [1], numerical functions for quantum simula- tion [2], arithmetic routines for number theory [3], and quantum read-only memory (QROM), which coherently loads classically specified data into quantum registers [4]. To operate on quantum data, these functions must be compiled into circuits that can be executed coherently on quantum hardware. This imposes two constraints absent from ordinary classical programs. First, because the in- put may be in superposition, the circuit cannot inspect an intermediate value and select an ordinary classical control-flow path. Data-dependent behavior is instead expressed through controlled operations within a fixed gate sequence, so every branch contributes to the circuit’s cost even if it applies only to some inputs. Second, the computation must be reversible: intermediate information cannot simply be overwritten or discarded. Temporary values must eventually be uncomputed, returning their qubits to their
title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

text: every branch contributes to the circuit’s cost even if it applies only to some inputs. Second, the computation must be reversible: intermediate information cannot simply be overwritten or discarded. Temporary values must eventually be uncomputed, returning their qubits to their initial state and preventing residual infor- mation from remaining entangled with the output. Until they are uncomputed, these values occupy additional qubits. At the same time, when bounded error is permit- ted, machinery needed only for rare or atypical inputs can sometimes be omitted, reducing resource requirements while keeping the failure probability controlled. Efficient coherent compilation is of major practical importance, and recent reductions in resource requirements have come from coordinated changes to arithmetic algorithms, data representations, and their reversible implementation [5, 6]. Such redesigns are difficult for general quantum circuits ∗andigu@g.harvard.edu because directly testing correctness can require exponen- tially expensive classical simulation or fully operational large-scale quantum processors. Automated circuit op- timizers therefore typically preserve correctness by re- stricting the search to predefined equivalence-preserving rewrites [7], limiting them to variations of a fixed design. Here we introduce a framework that pairs large lan- guage model (LLM) proposals with an independent eval- uator that verifies and scores each candidate. We focus on a class of quantum circuits that compute a classical function f: for an arbitrary input |ψ⟩= P x,y

text: that pairs large lan- guage model (LLM) proposals with an independent eval- uator that verifies and scores each candidate. We focus on a class of quantum circuits that compute a classical function f: for an arbitrary input |ψ⟩= P x,y αx,y |x⟩|y⟩, the circuit must act as |ψ⟩7−→P x,y αx,y |x⟩|y ⊕f(x)⟩, where |x⟩and |y⟩are computational-basis states of the input and output registers, respectively. By linear- ity, this coherent action is correct if the circuit per- forms the required map on every computational-basis input: |x⟩|y⟩7−→|x⟩|y ⊕f(x)⟩. This basis-state re- duction makes candidate circuits amenable to program- matic evaluation, since every allowed operation maps a computational-basis state to another computational-basis state, possibly changing its phase, but never creating a superposition [8]. The action of a candidate on any chosen input can therefore be simulated by tracking a bit string and its phase, rather than 2n amplitudes. Resource ac- counting is also simple: we use the Toffoli count T and the peak qubit count Q, and rank circuits by their product, the TQ-cost. Together, these properties let us build an efficient, programmatic evaluator that checks the correct- ness and resource cost of any candidate circuit design. (a) A hand-written task specification defines the circuit design task (for example, Reed–Solomon decoding) and is given to an LLM. The LLM proposes architecturally different approaches (algorithm families; here extended Euclidean, Berlekamp–Massey, and Peterson–Gorenstein–Zierler (PGZ) decoders), which are then developed and optimized in parallel. Strong candidates are periodically shared between families to allow for cross-pollination of useful ideas. This allows a single conceptual change to reorga- nize operations throughout the circuit, while the evaluator tests its consequences for correctness and resource cost. However, purely iterative refinement of a single candi- date can remain tied to the architecture from which it began, resulting in convergence to local (but not necessar- ily global) optima. We therefore start with an ideation stage in which the LLM is prompted to propose several distinct algorithm families, each representing a different approach to the problem. Circuits within each family are optimized independently in parallel, allowing the search to explore different strategies rather than only variations of one design. Well-performing candidates are periodically shared between families so that an idea discovered in one approach can inform another. Across eight diverse compilation tasks, the discovered circuits repeatedly exhibit three common principles of algorithm–circuit co-design. These principles address the features of coherent compilation described above: express- ing data-dependent control flow, making intermediate computations reversible without retaining their entire his- tory, and using a failure budget to remove circuit resources devoted to atypical cases (see Figure 1).

text: 3 DESIGN PRINCIPLES One recurring principle in the circuits discovered by the search is to replace conditional arithmetic with condi- tional routing. A naïve coherent translation of a casewise classical algorithm includes a separately controlled arith- metic block for every branch. The discovered circuits instead use a representation in which the branches differ primarily in which values occupy particular computational roles. Relatively cheap controlled swaps then route the appropriate values into those roles, one unconditional arithmetic path performs the expensive work, and further routing places the results in their required registers. In this sense, where a classical program routes execution to the selected operation, the coherent circuit routes the selected data through a shared operation. The idea re- sembles bucket-brigade quantum random-access memory (QRAM) [11]. For example, consider four n-qubit fixed-point registers c, x, y, and z, together with a control qubit b. Suppose that we wish to perform x 7−→ ( x + cy for b = 0, x + cz for b = 1, (1) while returning c, y, and z unchanged. A naïve imple- mentation uses two controlled multiply-adds. Conditional routing instead swaps y and z according to b, applies one uncontrolled multiply-add, and undoes the swap. For the standard schoolbook construction [12], this re- duces the Toffoli count from Tnaive(n) = 3n2 + 17n −2 to

For the standard schoolbook construction [12], this re- duces the Toffoli count from Tnaive(n) = 3n2 + 17n −2 to Trouted(n) = (3n2 + 17n −2)/2, as shown in Figure 1(b). More generally, conditional routing requires canonical- izing branch-dependent states into a representation on which the same expensive computation applies. Schemati- cally, when the branch can be expressed as Ub = R−1 b KRb, the circuit need only control the inexpensive routing trans- formation Rb; the expensive kernel K appears once and need not be controlled. Finding such a decomposition typically takes more than recognizing identical arithmetic in two branches: it exploits an equivalence in the required output so that apparently different updates become in- stances of the same computation. The difficulty lies less in the routing circuit than in determining which branch- dependent differences matter and which can be absorbed into a shared representation. Reversibility creates a second challenge: reversing a conditional update requires knowing which branch was taken during the forward computation. A naïve imple- mentation records each decision in a history stack whose size grows with the number of updates. But the branch decisions need not always be stored explicitly: different branches may leave distinguishable patterns in

The ambiguity can disappear once the circuit is restricted to states reachable from the prescribed initialization, where a relation across the registers can distinguish histories that no single register can. The third principle exploits the small but finite fail- ure probability permitted by most quantum algorithms. Turning this failure budget into resource savings, how- ever, is not automatic. One must first identify the rare inputs that determine worst-case resource requirements. Unlike a classical program, a quantum circuit must con- tain the gates and ancillas required by every supported path. A rare input can therefore determine the circuit’s Toffoli count or peak qubit count. Yet identifying such inputs is not enough: the circuitry supporting them may not be separable from the computation on typical inputs. The co-design task is to reorganize the computation so that the additional resources required by rare inputs are localized—for example, to extra iterations, stack entries, or arithmetic lanes. Those components can then be omit- ted while confining failure to the low-probability inputs that require them (Figure 1(d)). In what

REVERSIBLE SYNDROME DECODING FOR DQI Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a quantum algorithm that turns certain optimization problems into decoding problems for classical error-correcting codes, using quantum interference to favor better solutions. A central application is optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a form of polynomial fitting over finite fields for which DQI offers a superpolynomial speedup over known classical algorithms. DQI achieves this by using a Reed– Solomon decoder as a subroutine within the quantum computation [1]. The decoder identifies the positions and values of errors from a collection of algebraic checks called syndromes. DQI requires this decoding to run coherently on a superposition of inputs, making the reversible decoder a dominant resource cost. Khattar et al. [13] compiled

REVERSIBLE MODULAR INVERSION Modular inversion is the task of finding x such that wx ≡1 (mod p), given a nonzero input w and a prime p. It is a central arithmetic subroutine in a range of quantum algorithms [3, 14]. A standard way to compute the inverse is through the extended Euclidean algorithm. Euclidean algorithms repeatedly simplify a

text: a nonzero input w and a prime p. It is a central arithmetic subroutine in a range of quantum algorithms [3, 14]. A standard way to compute the inverse is through the extended Euclidean algorithm. Euclidean algorithms repeatedly simplify a pair of integers while preserving their greatest common divisor. By tracking how this divisor is expressed in terms of the original inputs, they also recover coefficients α, β satisfying αp + βw = 1, so β is the inverse of w modulo p. Divsteps is a variant of the Euclidean algorithm that replaces division with conditional additions, subtractions, and halving [15]. Starting from f = p and g = w, the goal is to reduce the pair to f = ±1 and g = 0 while preserving their greatest common divisor. The basic strategy is to hold the odd integer f fixed while reducing g: if g is even, it can be halved directly; if g is odd, adding or subtracting f first makes it even. These operations preserve the great- est common divisor because f is odd. Holding f fixed indefinitely, however, would leave only one integer being reduced, so the algorithm must periodically swap their roles. These results suggest that some apparent costs of quan- tum arithmetic reflect limitations of existing reversible constructions rather than of the algorithms themselves. Finding such constructions requires reasoning about choices whose benefits depend on one another. An arith- metic saving may become useful only after the associated control and uncomputation costs have also been reduced. A candidate design must therefore be carried through sev- eral unresolved mathematical and implementation prob- lems before its resource advantage becomes apparent. The framework is bounded by the choices that define each task. One is the objective that ranks circuits: we use the TQ-cost for a uniform comparison, but other ob- jectives are equally reasonable. In practice, the relative importance of qubit count, depth, routing, and measure- ments depends on details such as hardware constraints, decoder performance, and error-correction architecture. The scoring function can be replaced with a hardware- appropriate combination of these resources, but deter- mining that objective remains a matter of application and hardware judgment. For example, coset representations can make modular addition cheaper by encoding each residue as a superposition of congruent integers, which avoids conventional comparisons and corrections at the cost of an exponentially small error [17, 18], but such encodings lie outside the present framework. More generally, the task boundary, input distribution, data representations, and accuracy target make a search well posed while also encoding assumptions about how the circuit is embed- ded in a larger algorithm (in particular, which states it receives and how its outputs are consumed). The same choices that bound the search also make re- liable programmatic feedback possible: they specify what each candidate must preserve and which resource trade- offs the evaluator should reward. Within these boundaries, our results show that evaluator-guided LLM search can go beyond refining a fixed circuit to uncover new reversible algorithms and representations. Related approaches have produced new algorithms in combinatorics and linear alge- bra [19, 20]. These observations suggest a practical crite- rion for extending the approach: wherever a problem ad- mits a sufficiently expressive task interface and its correct- ness and resource costs can be evaluated cheaply enough to sustain many rounds of search, the same evaluator- guided search may provide a

These results, together with related progress in rein- forcement learning and LLM-guided discovery of quan- tum error-correcting codes and encoding circuits [21–23], create an opportunity for end-to-end co-design of fault- tolerant computation. Choices that are usually made separately—the algorithm and its logical circuit, the error-correcting code and its method for universal logic, the supply of magic states, and the physical execution architecture—strongly determine one another’s costs. A programmatic evaluator that propagates logical errors, resource demand, and hardware requirements across these layers could allow an LLM search to redesign them to- gether, potentially discovering fault-tolerant algorithms and architectures that cannot be found by optimizing each layer in isolation. text: 9 METHODS A classical function cannot generally be applied directly within a quantum algorithm, because quantum evolution must be reversible. Instead, a function f is embedded in a reversible map |x⟩|y⟩7−→|x⟩|y ⊕f(x)⟩. A natural model for these subroutines is the kickmix circuit model of Babbush et al. [8], which augments reversible classical computation with measurement-based uncomputation (MBU) and diagonal sign gates. Despite these additional operations, kickmix circuits remain efficiently classically simulable. This allows candidate circuits to be tested for their action on coherent quantum superpositions, providing the reliable correctness signal needed for evolutionary search. Circuits that implement the same specification can have very different time and space requirements. We use Toffoli count and peak qubit count as proxies for these costs. Toffoli gates require expensive non-Clifford resources, so their count tracks a large part of the logical work and often the runtime [24, 25]. The peak qubit count measures the data and ancillas that must coexist during execution and therefore approximates the required logical processor footprint [26]. The two resources also typically trade against each other: additional ancillas can avoid recomputation, while recycling ancillas can reduce space at the cost of additional gates. We multiply these quantities to obtain the TQ-cost, which provides a single objective for comparing such designs. Together, the correctness tests and TQ-cost define a constrained optimization

We multiply these quantities to obtain the TQ-cost, which provides a single objective for comparing such designs. Together, the correctness tests and TQ-cost define a constrained optimization problem over circuit-generating programs. Motivated by recent advances in coding and reasoning agents and LLM-guided algorithmic discovery, we use an LLM to propose coordinated, task-specific redesigns within an evolutionary search [20, 27, 28]. Circuit model and validity A compilation task specifies a reversible action on computational-basis states: a permutation π and, when needed, a Boolean phase g. A circuit may use a ancilla qubits, but must return them to zero: V |x⟩|0a⟩= (−1)g(x) |π(x)⟩|0a⟩. (10) Every ancilla must return to |0⟩because quantum operations must be unitary, and thus reversible. For a numerical approximation, the required output relation may instead specify an error bound; interface preservation, phase correctness, and ancilla uncomputation remain exact. We separately allow some circuits to fail on a bounded fraction of inputs drawn from a stated distribution; this fraction is the failure budget. Following Babbush et al. [8], the kickmix model permits three classes of operation: 1. classical reversible gates: X, CNOT, Toffoli, and swap; 2. diagonal sign gates: Z, CZ, CCZ, and global sign flips; and 3. destructive X-basis measurements. Before any measurement, the evolution of a computational-basis input is simple. Reversible gates update its stored bit string, while diagonal gates update only its sign, so the state remains of the form (−1)ϕ |x⟩. A classical simulator therefore need only track the current bits x and the sign ϕ, rather than a full state vector. The operations apply phase kickback while mixing basis states, giving kickmix its name. To illustrate why uncomputation is costly, consider a temporary AND. A Toffoli computes t = uv into an ancilla. After t has been used, applying the same Toffoli again returns that qubit to zero: |u, v⟩|0⟩ Toffoli −−−−→|u, v⟩|uv⟩ use uv −−−−→|u, v⟩|uv⟩ Toffoli −−−−→|u, v⟩|0⟩. For a fixed computational-basis input and a particular sequence of measurement outcomes m, we call the resulting evolution a computational-basis trajectory. A kickmix circuit may perform several such measurements. Their outcomes may be combined by classical XOR and may control diagonal corrections, but cannot control gates that change the stored basis string. Every measurement record therefore induces the same basis permutation: Vm |x⟩= (−1)ϕ(x,m) |π(x)⟩. (15) Exact coherent correctness additionally requires ϕ(x, m) = g(x) (16) for every allowed input and every record of nonzero probability. The measurement register then factors from the logical output. Allowing an outcome to control a basis-changing gate would instead make the permutation depend on the record and could leave the logical output correlated with the measurement environment. text: 11 Cost model and scoring We define the TQ-cost of a circuit by TQ = Toffoli count × peak qubit count, (22) where T counts Toffoli and CCZ gates equally and Q is the largest number of logical qubits allocated at once. We weight space and time equally in this cost function for simplicity. In practice, their relative importance depends on the hardware and application. When qubits are scarce, for example, a cost of the form (qubit count)κ ×Toffoli count with κ > 1 may be more appropriate; resource estimates for factoring have used κ between 1 and 3 [6, 30]. Either T or Q can also be replaced with other measures of time or space. In particular, when there is limited magic-state-factory throughput (as is typically the case), runtime is bottlenecked by the Toffoli count, motivating its widespread use as a time proxy [24, 25]. However, with enough factories to supply magic states in parallel, Toffoli depth rather than Toffoli count limits runtime. Similarly, for architectures with cheap cold storage for inactive qubits [31], Q can be replaced by active volume [32], which counts only the qubits participating in logical operations. The search is not tied to the specific form of the TQ-cost: it can run with any computable objective. A later case study illustrates the available trade-offs: the

Evolutionary search We encode each candidate as Python code that constructs a circuit. Functions, loops, and named registers preserve the organization of the computation, allowing the LLM to reason about arithmetic subroutines and their composition without reconstructing that structure from a flattened gate sequence. For example, changing a shared arithmetic routine changes every place where it is used, while reorganizing calls to that routine can change when intermediate values are computed, retained, and uncomputed. The representation thus makes coordinated changes expressible as revisions to the underlying algorithm. We search over these circuit-generating programs with OpenEvolve [33], using Claude Mythos 5 [28] to propose architectures and program rewrites. Each of the eight searches uses a fixed, hand-written task specification, and all share the same generic circuit-building interface. text: the eight searches uses a fixed, hand-written task specification, and all share the same generic circuit-building interface. During ideation, the LLM receives only the specification, circuit model, and correctness criteria, and proposes several distinct circuit architectures. The LLM has no access to the evaluator beyond the feedback returned after each submission. Starting from a blank program, it chooses the algorithm, representation, and circuit structure and produces the discovered circuits without substantive human intervention. Each architecture proposed during ideation founds a separate family of candidate programs. Later iterations improve descendants of the first working implementation. Keeping the families separate at first gives each approach time to mature, even if its earliest circuits are less efficient than those based on another approach. Periodically, leading programs are shared across families, allowing successful ideas from different approaches to combine. The search retains candidate programs and their evaluation results, tracking which family each belongs to and which earlier program it was derived from. It also saves feedback on failures and short notes in which the LLM records useful insights. These programs, results, and notes carry information between iterations; the sessions do not share a continuously growing conversation. Each iteration starts a new LLM agent session with the task specification, a parent program to improve, and its evaluation feedback. The agent also receives alternative programs from

text: information between iterations; the sessions do not share a continuously growing conversation. Each iteration starts a new LLM agent session with the task specification, a parent program to improve, and its evaluation feedback. The agent also receives alternative programs from the archive and their resource costs, brief summaries of earlier attempts, and recorded insights where available. This context is limited; the agent never sees the complete search history. Within the session, it may rewrite the program, run drafts on test inputs, query a classical oracle for the required function on chosen inputs, and use the results to revise its design. It may also delegate focused subtasks to subagents. The iteration ends with submission of a revised program. The evaluator rejects a circuit that does not meet the task specification; a valid one is scored by its TQ-cost and considered for retention in its family. Thus the LLM is free to propose broad changes without having to judge their correctness: the evaluator supplies an independent test of every completed design. Extended Data Figure 1 shows the ideation and rewrite calls and a concrete feedback-and-repair cycle for a small finite-field inversion task. text: a concrete feedback-and-repair cycle for a small finite-field inversion task. To decide which valid candidates remain available within each family, the search retains circuits with different trade-offs between Toffoli count and qubit count. We implement this selection with MAP-Elites [34], which divides the (T, Q) resource plane into cells and keeps the circuit with the lowest TQ-cost in each cell. A space-efficient circuit can therefore remain available for later development even when its higher Toffoli count gives it a worse TQ-cost. Because the families preserve alternatives, progress need not be monotonic in either resource. The Gaussian lineage in Extended Data Figure 2, for example, contains descendants that temporarily worsen Toffoli count or qubit count before reaching a region of lower TQ-cost. We report the lowest TQ-cost reached across all families at the end of the search.

SYNDROME DECODING FOR DQI Consider an optimization problem over a finite field Fq. An assignment x ∈Fn q produces m linear values Bx. Given a set Fi ⊂Fq of acceptable values for each constraint, let f(x) = |{i : (Bx)i ∈Fi}| count the constraints satisfied by x; the goal is to maximize f(x). This family, known as max-LINSAT, includes linear constraint-satisfaction problems such as Max-Cut and max-XORSAT, as well as nearest-codeword problems and polynomial fitting over finite fields. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a quantum algorithm that aims to solve these optimization problems by arranging for constructive interference on assignments satisfying many constraints and destructive interference on assignments satisfying fewer [1]. DQI prepares a superposition over sparse vectors e ∈Fm q , each supported on at most ℓconstraints. Here H = BT can be viewed as a parity-check matrix, making e a low-weight error and He its syndrome. If the associated code has minimum distance dmin ≥2ℓ+ 1, a decoder can recover e uniquely from that syndrome. DQI uses the decoder in the following state-preparation sequence: X wt(e)≤ℓ ae |e⟩|0⟩ s=He −−−−−→ X wt(e)≤ℓ ae |e⟩|He⟩ uncompute e −−−−−−−−→|0⟩ X wt(e)≤ℓ ae |He⟩ QFT−1 −−−−−→ X x Ax |x⟩. (23)

(23) The middle step must erase e while retaining its syndrome s = He; otherwise the different contributions remain distinguishable and cannot interfere. The inverse quantum Fourier transform (QFT) then produces amplitudes Ax that favor assignments satisfying more constraints. The dominant cost in Equation (23) is uncomputing e, which requires solving a classical decoding problem; DQI thus reduces optimization to decoding. The space-efficient construction of Khattar et al. [13] replaces the middle decoding-and-uncomputation step with a phase correction. It generates one field symbol ei at a time, adds its contribution to s, and then removes it with an X-basis measurement. Decoding proceeds in two stages: first find the positions of the errors, then recover their values in F212. The first stage packages the unknown set of error positions into a single polynomial. That remainder is ω, and the coefficient that accompanies it is σ, up to normalization. The promise of at most 35 errors ensures deg σ ≤35 and determines this pair uniquely. The baseline next locates the errors by evaluating σ at every possible position. Associate position j with the field point βj = γ−j (since γ is primitive, these points enumerate all 4,095 nonzero field elements). The scan visits them one by one and tests whether σ(βj) = 0. It need not evaluate σ independently each time: advancing to βj+1 = γ−1βj multiplies its degree-r term by the fixed constant γ−r. This efficient scan is known as a Chien search [43]. Finding a root reveals an error’s position but not its value. At βj, the evaluator ω(βj) contains the error value multiplied by the contributions of the other locator factors, while the formal derivative σ′(βj)—the usual coefficientwise polynomial derivative over the field—contains those same factors without the error value. Their ratio therefore isolates ej, up to a fixed factor κj that depends only on the position: ej = κj ω(βj) σ′(βj). (30) This recovery step is Forney’s formula [44]. The circuit immediately uses that value and the matching twelve-bit block cj to apply the phase (24). It then reverses the computation to restore the syndrome and clear its ancillas. The EEA is the dominant cost of this baseline because its classical control flow depends on the syndromes: different inputs require different shifts, swaps, and numbers of iterations. A quantum circuit must instead apply one fixed sequence of gates across the syndrome superposition. The baseline therefore spreads the Euclidean solve over 222 synchronized cycles, controlling each operation so that it acts only when needed. Our implementation of this baseline, based on the authors’ released code [35], uses 5.1 million Toffoli gates and 1,938 qubits at peak, with the forward Euclidean solve and its reversal accounting for 3.8 million of the Toffolis [45]. The discovered circuit changes both stages of this baseline. First, it replaces the Euclidean solve with the arithmetically cheaper Berlekamp–Massey (BM) recurrence and arranges the recurrence so that reversibility does not require retaining much history state. (32) Thus the locator coefficients give a rule for predicting each syndrome from the preceding L syndromes. We call L the order of this recurrence. BM finds this recurrence by maintaining a candidate locator σ and refining it as the syndromes are incorporated [46]. At the start of round r, the candidate defines a lowest-order recurrence for the already processed syndromes S1, . . . , Sr−1. The round tests whether that recurrence also fits Sr. The discrepancy ∆= PL k=0 σkSr−k is the sum in Equation (31) for round r, computed with the current candidate. It measures the amount by which the recurrence fails: ∆= 0 means that the current candidate already fits Sr, while ∆̸ = 0 requires the candidate to be refined. When ∆̸ = 0, BM needs a correction that fixes the equation for Sr without invalidating any of the earlier equations. For this purpose, it retains an earlier candidate τ as a correction template, together with the nonzero discrepancy δ that candidate produced. At the start of each subsequent round, BM multiplies τ by z, shifting every coefficient one degree higher as the recurrence

text: it retains an earlier candidate τ as a correction template, together with the nonzero discrepancy δ that candidate produced. At the start of each subsequent round, BM multiplies τ by z, shifting every coefficient one degree higher as the recurrence advances to the next syndrome. Thus, if the template was saved k rounds earlier, it has acquired a factor zk and is aligned with the current syndrome equation while leaving the earlier equations unchanged. BM then scales this aligned template by α = ∆/δ and applies σ ←σ −ατ: at Sr, the correction contributes exactly αδ = ∆and so cancels the discrepancy. On a round with a nonzero discrepancy, BM must also decide whether the current candidate takes over as the template. A candidate of order L that fits n syndromes has predicted n −L of them. text: 4 lowest order, and a correction raises the order less when its template had predicted more syndromes at the time it was saved. BM therefore replaces the template when the current candidate has predicted more syndromes than the stored template had when it was saved, and retains it when the current candidate has predicted fewer. When the two counts are equal, either choice gives a correct decoder [46, p. 125]. Textbook BM retains in that case. text: 7 I.2. Hermitian-code decoding for HOPI HOPI requires the same phase (24) as the Reed–Solomon instance above, but its error word belongs to a 512-symbol Hermitian code over F64. A Reed–Solomon code with 512 positions would require symbols of about nine bits, since each position needs a distinct field element. A Hermitian code instead obtains 512 positions while retaining six-bit symbols by using the points (x, y) ∈F2 64 on y8 = x9 + y. (41) Polynomials in x and y are ordered by a weighted degree, the analogue of polynomial degree for Reed–Solomon codes. Here x has weight 8 and y has weight 9, so the monomial xayb has weighted degree 8a + 9b. These weights give the leading terms y8 and x9 of Equation (41) the same weighted degree, 72. Each finite point Pj = (xj, yj) is one code position. The syndrome construction is the two-variable analogue of the Reed–Solomon map above. A function ψ(x, y) assigns a field value to every position and therefore defines one parity check S(ψ) = 512 X j=1 ejψ(Pj). (42) The value S(ψ) is one syndrome symbol. This instance uses the 123 monomials ψa,b(x, y) = xayb of weighted degree 8a + 9b ≤150 [41]. We enumerate them as ψ0, . . . , ψ122 in increasing weighted degree [47]. The

Beyond error weight 33, some of the syndromes that the recurrence needs have weighted degree above 150, which the input does not supply. The circuit freezes the walk there and records the round, as the divstep circuit does (SI II.1). After the last round, it tests which of three cases holds and routes the corresponding vector into the locator register. If w = 0, the Krylov vectors have become dependent, and the accumulated vector is the null vector. If w̸ = 0 and Aw = 0, then w itself is a null vector. Each point on this curve is a pair of integers (x, y) satisfying the curve equation y2 ≡x3 + 7 (mod p), (51) where p = 2256 −232 −977 is a 256-bit prime number. The curve defines point addition, an operation that combines two points P and Q into a third point R = P +Q on the same curve (note that this addition is not the usual coordinate-wise addition). Geometrically, one draws the line through P and Q, finds its third intersection with the curve, and reflects that point across the horizontal axis. Algebraically, for the inputs considered here, with Qx̸ = Px, one first computes the slope λ ≡(Qy −Py)(Qx −Px)−1 (mod p), (52) where (Qx −Px)−1 denotes the inverse modulo p. The coordinates of the sum are then Rx = λ2 −Px −Qx, Ry = λ(Px −Rx) −Py. (53) We study the reversible point adder [52]: given an input point P and another, classically supplied point Q, it performs |P⟩7−→|P + Q⟩. (54) The modular inverse required by Equation (52) is the dominant cost of point addition: once the slope λ is known, the remaining coordinate updates require only a fixed sequence of relatively cheap modular additions and multiplications. In contrast, modular inversion follows a long input-dependent sequence of arithmetic transitions, which the circuit must later recover to reverse the computation and clear its ancillas. Prior point-addition constructions [8, 38] use the binary greatest common divisor (gcd) algorithm for modular inversion. The connection between gcd and inversion comes from expressing the gcd in terms of the original inputs. Because p is prime and w = Qx −Px̸ = 0, there are integers α and β such that gcd(p, w) = 1 = αp + βw. Reducing this identity modulo p gives βw ≡1, so β ≡w−1 (mod p). The extended binary-gcd algorithm finds these coefficients by tracking expressions for the two current values u and v as integer combinations of p and w. Binary gcd rests on two elementary identities. If u is even and v is odd, then gcd(u, v) = gcd(u/2, v); if u and v are both odd, then, for u > v, gcd(u, v) = gcd((u −v)/2, v). Making this reduction reversible is difficult because its control flow is input-dependent: which line of Equation (55) applies changes from one step to the next, and the reduced pair does not in general reveal which line produced it. A quantum circuit therefore cannot simply run the reduction backward to restore its input and clear its workspace; it must preserve enough information to identify each step. The prior constructions do so using the dialog introduced by Khattar et al. [13]. The direct approach would update the coefficients that become α and β alongside the two values throughout the reduction. The dialog avoids holding these growing coefficients in memory. Its first pass updates only the pair being reduced and records a compact symbol identifying each subtraction, swap, and halving choice. A second pass replays the same transformations to construct the required coefficient. Initializing this replay from the numerator a = Qy −Py produces aβ = aw−1 mod p directly, without ever storing w−1 in a separate register. The simple binary updates and the replay trick reduce the gate count, but the complete dialog record requires hundreds of additional qubits. Divsteps Rather than reorganize the binary-gcd constructions above, the search finds a new reversible prime-field inversion architecture built on divsteps [15, 53]. In the divstep recurrence of Equation (6), a small signed counter z, called the half delta, replaces the repeated magnitude comparisons in Equation (55): the sign of z and the parity of one value alone determine the next update. We call the choice of update at a step its decision. Appendix A proves that every decision can be computed exactly from the registers as they stand after the step. When a decision is cheap to decode, the circuit decodes it from the updated state. Otherwise, the circuit stores

text: its decision. Appendix A proves that every decision can be computed exactly from the registers as they stand after the step. When a decision is cheap to decode, the circuit decodes it from the updated state. Otherwise, the circuit stores the decision as a single bit on a fixed-size history stack. We call the sequence of divsteps for one input a walk. The point adder uses this inversion twice, once to form the slope λ and once to erase it after the coordinate update. Each use runs a forward walk and a reverse walk, for four walks in total. Unlike the quotient-based extended Euclidean algorithm (EEA) of SI II.2, which divides one remainder by the other at every iteration, a divstep never computes a multi-bit quotient or adds a multiple of one full register to another. A divstep walk needs more steps than the quotient-based EEA needs divisions, but each step is much cheaper. Reversible divsteps were previously developed over binary fields and polynomial rings [13, 54]. There, each step shrinks the polynomial pair by one coefficient, and the freed space can hold that step’s record. Integer divsteps free no such fixed space, so a stored history costs additional qubits. To our knowledge, this is the first reversible divstep inversion circuit over a prime field. The walk state is (z, f, g, fv, gv), and each step applies one of the three updates in Equation (6). Two bits label the update: s records whether the step swaps the roles of f and g, and b records whether the incoming g is odd. To run a step backward, the circuit must know s and b, and the updated state does not hold them explicitly. text: 12 Branch decoders. A forward step computes b from the parity of g and uses it to control the update. After the update, g no longer holds that parity, so the step is left with b in a qubit of its own. Uncomputing b there would require the decoder on the forward walk as well. The forward step instead disposes of b in one of two ways. If the decision is ambiguous at depth j ≥jstore, the step pushes b onto the history stack. Otherwise, the step removes b by MBU: it measures b in the X basis. The measurement frees the qubit but leaves a phase that depends on b and on the measurement outcome. The reverse walk is the uncomputation of the forward walk. Once the circuit has used the inverse, it undoes the forward steps in the opposite order, which restores w and returns the walk registers to zero. The matching reverse step obtains b again, either by popping the stack or by applying the tests and decoders to the updated state. It applies the phase correction for the measurement outcome and uses b to choose which update to undo. The restored g then holds b as its parity, so a CNOT from the low bit of g clears it. Decoders therefore appear only in reverse steps.

Beyond depth four, each further depth roughly triples the number of terms and removes half as much history as the depth before it. Early stopping. A walk terminates when g reaches zero: at that point f = ±1 and the inverse can be read from fv. Different inputs terminate at different steps, typically between steps 505 and 530 (Figure 3(b)), but the circuit runs a fixed schedule of 533 steps. The steps after termination must leave the state unchanged. Left alone, the recurrence would treat g = 0 as an even value, so it would keep doubling fv and incrementing z until both outgrow their registers. The circuit therefore freezes a terminated walk. On the first step where the test succeeds, the circuit sets a one-qubit frozen flag, and from then on the flag disables every update. The reverse walk must clear the flag at that same step. A frozen state looks identical at every later step, so the state alone cannot reveal when the walk froze. The circuit writes the step index into a small register when it sets the flag. Each reverse step compares the register with its own index, and a match clears both the flag and the register. This machinery costs Toffolis at every step: a test that every bit of g is zero, and one more control on every update. The test is most expensive in the early steps, where g is widest and termination is least likely. The first 498 steps omit the test, the flag, and the flag’s controls. NUMERICAL FUNCTION EVALUATION Elementary-function evaluation has been a central problem in numerical computing since the earliest mathematical software libraries. The routines conventionally collected in libm, the mathematical-function library supplied by C and Unix systems, evaluate roots, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions by combining range reduction, table lookup, polynomial approximation, and iterative refinement [57]. These functions also appear throughout quantum algorithms. They determine controlled rotation angles in quantum linear-systems algorithms [12, 58], set interaction phases in real-space Hamiltonian simulation [59, 60], and enter the amplitudes prepared for Hamiltonian simulation [4]. These classical techniques cannot simply be ported into coherent quantum circuits. Data-dependent choices must be compiled into a fixed gate sequence, and all temporary

text: phases in real-space Hamiltonian simulation [59, 60], and enter the amplitudes prepared for Hamiltonian simulation [4]. These classical techniques cannot simply be ported into coherent quantum circuits. Data-dependent choices must be compiled into a fixed gate sequence, and all temporary state must ultimately be returned to |0⟩. The latter reversibility constraint is particularly costly for numerical routines because many classical methods proceed through a long sequence of large, high-precision intermediate values. An ordinary implementation can overwrite each value and reuse the same storage as soon as the next value is formed. A reversible implementation must instead retain enough information to reconstruct the overwritten value, or recompute it when clearing the circuit. Consequently, composing individually efficient routines can accumulate many large live registers and may require running the complete computation backward after its result has been consumed. Iterative Newton-style methods repeatedly replace one full-precision estimate with another, so their reversible implementations carry large intermediate registers through every step [61]. Floating-point representations add exponent bits to every such register to track a wide range of magnitudes [62]. The approximation, fixed-point representation, and uncomputation schedule therefore become inseparable parts of circuit design [12]. We consider three numerical subroutines: Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) rotation-angle evaluation (arcsin), Coulomb-potential evaluation (1/ p ∥x∥2), and Gaussian evaluation (e−x2) [2, 58, 59]. Each implements an ad- ditive fixed-point map |x⟩|k⟩7→|x⟩|k + ef(x)⟩, with a uniform error bound over its promised domain [63]. The additive form serves both common uses of the result. An ordinary accumulator k holds the value for later bitwise-controlled operations, while a phase-gradient accumulator converts the addition directly into a phase. Our baselines use the piecewise-polynomial construction of Häner, Roetteler, and Svore (HRS) [12]. HRS partitions the domain, fits a low-degree polynomial on each interval, and coherently loads the selected polynomial’s coefficients. It evaluates the polynomial in general fixed-point arithmetic by Horner’s rule, which uses one multiplication per degree. It adds the result to the output and reverses the computation to clear its temporary registers. Its cost has four sources: locating an interval with arbitrary boundaries; the wide multiplications of the Horner polynomial-evaluation stage; the registers that hold intermediate products and the polynomial value; and the reverse pass that erases the loaded coefficients. For each task we tune the polynomial degree, fixed-point format, and published recomputation trade-offs, and widen each interval until it reaches the error bound. text: 23 V. NONABELIAN LATTICE-GAUGE SIMULATION In Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory, space is replaced by a grid. A gauge-field configuration assigns a group element Ui(x) to each directed edge, or link, from site x in direction i. This element describes how the gauge field transports a state between neighboring sites; traversing the link backward contributes its inverse Ui(x)−1. Multiplying the links around a closed path therefore describes the net transport along that loop. Although this product depends on an arbitrary convention at each site (the gauge), the real part of its matrix trace does not, and these loop traces form the magnetic energy [73]. Because the gauge group is nonabelian, its elements need not commute, so the links must be multiplied in the order in which the path traverses them. We consider the group-register formulation of Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory [73], in which a register holds the group element of each link. The Hamiltonian separates into an electric (kinetic) term HE and a magnetic (potential) term HB. A Trotter step evolves these terms separately. Here we implement the magnetic evolution e−i∆tHB for the improved Hamiltonian of Carena et al. [74]. The smallest loop contributing to HB goes around one square face of the lattice and is called a plaquette; the standard magnetic term sums a trace over these four-link loops. The
title: NONABELIAN LATTICE-GAUGE SIMULATION

text: for the improved Hamiltonian of Carena et al. [74]. The smallest loop contributing to HB goes around one square face of the lattice and is called a plaquette; the standard magnetic term sums a trace over these four-link loops. The improved Hamiltonian adds weighted 2 × 1 rectangles, which cancel the leading discretization error. Thus the magnetic evolution requires the same basic operation at many locations: follow a short closed path, multiply its links in order, extract a trace, and add the weighted result to the phase. text: Preprint SOFTCACHE: ADAPTIVE STEP SIZE CACHING FOR DIFFUSION TRANSFORMERS Shimon Malnick1, Nadav Orenstein1, Ohad Fried2, Shai Avidan1 1Tel Aviv University 2Reichman University Project page: malnick.net/softcache

text: Diffusion and flow models generate a sample over iterative steps, each a full pass through a large network, and that pass dominates generation cost. Training-free caching accelerates them by reusing activations from recent evaluations instead of recomputing them. Dynamic caching methods decide when to refresh by ac- cumulating a cheap probe of the network input into a staleness signal and spend- ing a fresh evaluation once it crosses a threshold. They perform hard caching: the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step, fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size. We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse. We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching: instead of a binary switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes. Where the headroom is large, the sampler jumps past several scheduled nodes, and as a refresh nears, its steps shrink back toward the original step. These adaptive jumps may land between the scheduled nodes, taking the sampler off its fixed grid. SoftCache requires no training and adds no per-backbone settings: on FLUX for images and on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video, at speedups from 3.5× to 6.9×, it is ahead of every baseline on all four fidelity

text: Diffusion and flow models set the state of the art in image and video synthesis (Black Forest Labs, 2024; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Esser et al., 2024). These models are slow at inference: producing a single output requires tens of full network evaluations, each a pass through the same large transformer. Yet the latent changes only slightly between steps, so successive passes largely recompute what the previous one already produced. This redundancy is the resource that accelera- tion methods draw on, and they differ in what they are willing to give up to reach it. In practice, this is done using distillation (Song et al., 2023; Salimans & Ho, 2022), fewer-step solvers (Song et al., 2021a; Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023), or cheaper attention (Yuan et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b;a), each with its own cost in training, calibration, or fidelity. A different lever is to reuse the model’s own output, i.e., caching, instead of solving faster or at- tending more cheaply. Successive steps can then share computation directly rather than recompute it. Every cache must still decide when to refresh, and many settle this before sampling begins, with a refresh pattern that is fixed in advance and shared by every prompt (Ma et al., 2024; Selvaraju et

text: directly rather than recompute it. Every cache must still decide when to refresh, and many settle this before sampling begins, with a refresh pattern that is fixed in advance and shared by every prompt (Ma et al., 2024; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b; Cui et al., 2026; Aliev et al., 2026). Dynamic caches instead make refresh timing their central question and decide it during sampling: a cheap probe of the network predicts how much its output is about to change, and this signal decides, per prompt, when the cached computation has gone stale (Liu et al., 2025a; Chung et al., 2026). Yet these dynamic caches spend the signal on a single binary decision, a form of hard caching: at every node of the sampler’s fixed grid, the signal is compared with a threshold, and the sampler either reuses the cached computation or refreshes it. How far below the threshold the signal sits plays no role. A node where the cache has barely aged and one on the verge of refresh are treated identically, and both advance by exactly the step the schedule prescribed. 1 arXiv:2610.22369v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

Hard caching walks the fixed grid of scheduled nodes one node at a time, deciding only whether to refresh or reuse. SoftCache also sets the step size: a reused step the cache still supports skips several nodes and lands between them (inset). We observe that this ignored distance is infor- mative. Below the threshold, the signal closely tracks the reuse error, the gap between the cached computation and a fresh one at the cur- rent node. The distance from the threshold, which we call the headroom, measures how safely the cache can be trusted, and we use it to set the step size instead of only the refresh deci- sion: this is soft caching. When the headroom is large, the cache is still reliable, so the sam- pler takes a long step that skips several sched- uled nodes and can land between them (Fig. 1). When the headroom is small, refresh is near, so the step shrinks back toward the scheduled one. We call this method SoftCache: the headroom sets the step continuously rather than picking how many nodes to skip, and every node a step passes over is one the sampler no longer visits.

We call this method SoftCache: the headroom sets the step continuously rather than picking how many nodes to skip, and every node a step passes over is one the sampler no longer visits. Set against both kinds of cache, this is a different form of adaptivity. A fixed schedule refreshes at the same nodes for every prompt. A dynamic cache refreshes at nodes that vary with the prompt, but at scheduled nodes all the same. Here the steps vary with the prompt too, and they also land where no node was scheduled. This freedom translates into fidelity: on FLUX, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, against caches of both kinds at comparable speed, SoftCache reproduces the uncached model most faithfully on every metric at every operating point we test. Adaptivity, then, does not stop at deciding when to refresh. It also decides where the sampler goes next. text: 2.1 DIFFUSION SAMPLING ACCELERATION Methods that cut sampling cost differ in what they modify. Some change the network or a single evaluation of it: distillation trains a student that needs fewer steps (Song et al., 2023; Salimans & Ho, 2022; Luo et al., 2023), while sparse attention (Yuan et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b;a) and token reduction (Bolya et al., 2023) make each step cheaper. Others change the grid: higher-order solvers reach a given quality in fewer steps (Song et al., 2021a; Lu et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023), and schedule design places the steps where they matter most (Karras et al., 2022; Esser et al., 2024; Sabour et al., 2024). We work in a third family, caching, which changes neither the network nor an evaluation of it: it exploits the redundancy between neighboring states along the trajectory and reuses computation from earlier steps, without training. 2.2 FEATURE CACHING Caching methods differ in what they store and when they refresh it. The stored quantity ranges from intermediate activations of U-Net or transformer blocks (Ma et al., 2024; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b) to the residual of a span of blocks or of the entire stack (Chen et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Chung et al., 2026), and it may be

text: et al., 2024; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b) to the residual of a span of blocks or of the entire stack (Chen et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Chung et al., 2026), and it may be refreshed for only a subset of tokens (Zou et al., 2025; 2024; Zheng et al., 2025b). Fixed schedules refresh periodically (Ma et al., 2024; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b) or at steps chosen offline, by thresholding a reuse error calibrated on a few samples (Ma et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026) or by optimizing for a fixed budget of full evaluations (Cui et al., 2026; Aliev et al., 2026). Online rules refresh once an accumulated cheap 2

text: Preprint proxy of the output change crosses a threshold (Liu et al., 2025a; Chung et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026; Bu et al., 2025). Such rules therefore refreshe at different nodes for different prompts, whereas a fixed schedule applies one refresh pattern to all of them. Either way, each node, or token, makes one binary choice between a full evaluation and reuse. SoftCache refreshes on the same spectral signal (Chung et al., 2026), but also reads its headroom below the threshold to make reuse soft rather than binary. 2.3 PREDICTIVE CACHING Between refreshes, most caches hold the stored quantity fixed (Ma et al., 2024; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a; Chung et al., 2026), so the reuse error grows with the time since the last refresh. Predictive caches extrapolate from recent history instead. Some forecast what the network returns, the output of the block stack (Cui et al., 2026), its increment over the input (Bu et al., 2025), or the velocity itself (Wang et al., 2026). Others forecast the increment each attention and MLP branch adds to its input, which the current node applies to its own activations, with Taylor (Liu et al., 2025b) or Hermite (Feng et al., 2026) coefficients built from several stored past values. Multistep formulas (Yu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025a)

Multistep formulas (Yu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025a) and a check on the prediction (Liu et al., 2025c) extend how far it can be carried. All of them predict only at the nodes of the sampler’s schedule, so the schedule itself is untouched. We extrapolate an increment as well, a single one for the entire stack, along the straight line through the two most recent fresh evaluations. Written in the flow time, that line is defined between nodes, which is what lets the sampler leave the schedule rather than only skip evaluations along it. 2.4 ADAPTIVE STEP SIZE CONTROL Adaptive ODE solvers set each step at runtime from an estimate of the local error, obtained by comparing two solutions of different order (Dormand & Prince, 1980), and the same control has been applied to diffusion sampling in both its SDE (Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2021) and ODE (Lu et al., 2022) forms. The estimate costs several network evaluations per step, which is the computation a cache exists to avoid. SoftCache takes its step size from the refresh signal the cache already computes, so the schedule adapts at no evaluations

Evaluating B accounts for nearly all of the cost of a model evaluation, whereas E and O are comparatively cheap, so it is B that a cache skips. text: Preprint 4 METHOD 4.1 HEADROOM AS A STEP SIZE Hard caching spends Ai on one decision: compare it with τ and either refresh or reuse (Liu et al., 2025a; Chung et al., 2026). We ask whether there is more to this signal, not whether the cached residual can still be used, but for how long. Instead of reading Ai against τ as a hard threshold, we read how far below it the accumulator sits, which says how much of the reuse budget is left, and we let that quantity set the length of the next step. We define the headroom Hi = 1 −Ai τ , (8) which lies in [0, 1] at a cached node. Reusing the anchor’s residual costs a relative reuse error Ei = ∥ri −ra∥/∥ra∥, between the residual the stack would produce at node i and the one Eq. (5) substitutes for it. Like every cached node it reuses ra, and the further a node sits from the anchor the worse that reuse gets. A jump puts it further than any scheduled step does. PSNR averages pixel error, so it rewards an output that blurs fine detail over one that keeps the detail but places it slightly off, which the perceptual metrics prefer. Sec. D.1 shows such a case. The scale β in Eq. (10) sets how far a cached node follows the linear extrapolation. The extrapolation grows with distance from the last fresh evaluation, through λi, so at high speed it reaches beyond the two evaluations it was fitted to and becomes less reliable. Damping it to β=0.5 loses to β=1 at 3× but beats it by 1.65 dB PSNR and 0.080 LPIPS at 7× (Tab. C.4.2). We therefore use β=1 below 4× and β=0.5 above it, the same rule on all three backbones. Raising the cap instead gains less: at 7× even J=20 gains 1.12 dB and 0.050 LPIPS, and it loses fine texture that β=0.5 keeps (Sec. C.4). Removing residual motion scores a higher PSNR than β=0.5 at 7× but a worse LPIPS (Tab. C.4.1). Comparing the images ourselves at that band, blind to the variant, we prefer β=0.5 to J=20 and to removing residual motion (Sec. C.3). 6

text: We presented SoftCache, a training-free method that turns hard caching into soft caching. A dynamic cache already measures how stale its cached computation has become, but spends the measurement on a binary choice between refresh and reuse. SoftCache reads the headroom below the threshold as how far the cache can still be trusted and lets it set the step size: cached steps jump past scheduled nodes while the cache is reliable and shrink back to the scheduled step as a refresh nears, the tail is re-spaced so that every node passed is dropped from the trajectory, and the cached residual is ex- trapolated to each off-grid landing at no extra network cost. On FLUX, HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, at wall-clock speedups from 3.5× to 6.9×, SoftCache stays closest to the uncached sample on all four fidelity metrics, with no per-model calibration. Adaptivity in caching, then, does not stop at deciding when to refresh. 9

C.3 CAP SWEEP AND THE BLIND-PICK PROTOCOL The cap ladder of Tab. C.4.2 fixes J=8 on DPG-50. Smaller caps (J=3, J=5) are perceptually worse from 5× on. Larger caps are a wash through 5×, gaining PSNR and giving it back on LPIPS and DreamSim, and win only at 7×, where they lose high-frequency texture (Sec. C.4). J=8 is therefore the smallest cap that gives up nothing through 5×. The 7× band is handled by β instead (Sec. 5.4), which costs no texture. Two blind checks below back this, both on DPG-50 only. In each, one author saw, per prompt, the uncached reference and several unlabeled variants in a random order, with only the speedup shown. 21

text: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation SeungJu Cha Ye-Chan Kim HyunGee Kim Sungho Koh Dong-Jin Kim† Hanyang University, South Korea {sju9020, dpcksdl78, khjiiii2002, ksh000906, djdkim}@hanyang.ac.kr † Corresponding author
title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics

text: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-α and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an

Experiments on PixArt-α and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation.
