text: Diffusion models [1, 2] have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality image [3–5] and video synthesis [6–8], owing to their strong fidelity and scalability. However, their iterative denoising process incurs substantial computational cost, as a large number of tokens are repeatedly processed at every inference step [9]. To address this, token merging [10] has emerged as an effective training-free acceleration strategy that groups similar tokens, merges them into representative tokens, and uses the merged representations in subsequent layers [9–13]. For example, early token merging methods such as ToMeSD [10] first construct local merge candidate groups in a content-agnostic manner, and then form merge pairs simply based on feature similarity within each group. Consequently, content-relevant tokens can be selected as merge sources, causing local details to be absorbed and leading to visual distortion [9]. This raises a central challenge: which tokens should be absorbed through merging, and which must be retained as anchors for subsequent computation. Prior work [9] leverages classifier-free guidance (CFG) [14] as a token importance signal, identifying tokens strongly steered by the text condition through the discrepancy between conditional and Preprint. arXiv:2610.22370v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

text: and structural coherence. We attribute this to CFG’s prompt-centric bias: by focusing exclusively on text-conditioned influence, CFG overlooks two key aspects of how diffusion models generate images. First, CFG fails to capture time-varying token importance. Diffusion generation follows a coarse-to- fine progression [15, 16], where tokens undergoing large inter-step changes represent regions in which the model is actively injecting details [17]. In this context, prematurely merging such still-evolving tokens directly attenuates their ongoing refinement by averaging their features with neighboring tokens. Crucially, the spatial distribution of these actively evolving tokens is time-varying: while it remains concentrated on foreground objects in early steps, it progressively expands toward broader spatial regions, including non-prompt areas, at later timesteps (Fig. 1(b)). High-ranked tokens in CFG importance signal, however, remain anchored to foreground objects throughout the entire timestep, confining its search for important tokens only to prompt-aligned regions. As a result, CFG fails to identify the very tokens that should be protected: actively evolving tokens outside the foreground are prematurely merged into nearby or similar tokens, suppressing their distinct updates. Second, CFG is insensitive to prompt-independent structural importance. To produce natural and coherent images, diffusion models actively generate scene elements that are not directly mentioned in the prompt such as background objects and supporting structures [1, 2]. Although these prompt- independent structures contribute little to

text: prompt-independent structural importance. To produce natural and coherent images, diffusion models actively generate scene elements that are not directly mentioned in the prompt such as background objects and supporting structures [1, 2]. Although these prompt- independent structures contribute little to text guidance, they carry essential structural information such as boundaries between homogeneous regions, edges of background objects, and fine textures that anchor visual coherence. However, because CFG only measures text-conditioned discrepancy, structural boundaries in such non-prompt regions tend to receive low scores across all timesteps (Fig. 1(c)), making them vulnerable to merging into neighboring homogeneous areas. Taken together, these observations indicate that token importance should not be defined solely by text relevance, but by diffusion dynamics: how unresolved a token remains and how much structural information it carries at the current denoising step [18]. To faithfully capture diffusion dynamics, we define two complementary signals that quantify the spatiotemporal dynamics of each token during denoising. For temporal dynamics, we start from the score function [19], which quantifies how each token is updated at the current denoising step. In particular, we project this score into clean-image space via the Tweedie denoised estimate [20, 21], and use its inter-step difference as the temporal signal, assigning high values to tokens that are unresolved. text: structures that CFG often underestimates. By jointly modeling temporal evolution and structural saliency, we obtain a dynamics-aware token importance signal that guides merging decisions. Building on this dynamics-aware importance, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free token merging framework for diffusion transformers [2, 5, 22]. At each denoising step, DaTMe assigns token roles at the intersection of the temporal and structural signals. High-scoring tokens are assigned as constraint tokens and excluded from merging as dynamically or structurally important regions, while low-scoring tokens are assigned as source tokens from relatively stable and homogeneous regions that can be safely merged. To meet the target compression budget, DaTMe supplements the source set with grid-based spatial sampling, preventing local collapse. The resulting source tokens are then merged only within nearby regions via locality-constrained matching, built upon [9]. We primarily evaluate DaTMe on PixArt-α and FLUX, where it outperforms prior methods while maintaining visual fidelity across the entire image. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce a dynamics-aware importance map derived from the Tweedie estimate, jointly capturing the temporal evolution and structural saliency of each token. • We propose DaTMe, a training-free token merging framework that leverages the proposed temporal and spatial importance signals to identify safely mergeable tokens while preserving structurally critical regions. • We validate DaTMe on DiT (PixArt-α) and MM-DiT

Token reduction is a widely used strategy for improving Transformer efficiency, mainly through token pruning or token merging [10, 23–26]. Representative methods such as ToMe [27] use training-free bipartite matching, while later approaches refine token selection using attention or frequency-domain cues [25, 26]. However, most of these methods target single-forward-pass architectures with relatively static token importance. Diffusion models, by contrast, update token representations over many steps, motivating diffusion-specific approaches such as ToMeSD [10]. Token Merging in Diffusion Models. A wide range of methods have been proposed to accelerate diffusion models, including improved samplers [28–32] and weight quantization [33, 34]. However, such approaches often require additional training or optimization, introducing non-trivial overhead. Training-free methods instead reduce the number of tokens processed during inference through prun- ing [18, 35], caching [36–38], or merging [9–13]. Among them, ToMeSD [10] extends token merging in ViTs [27] to diffusion models by grouping tokens based on feature similarity. Several subsequent methods [12, 13] leverage cross-attention

Among them, ToMeSD [10] extends token merging in ViTs [27] to diffusion models by grouping tokens based on feature similarity. Several subsequent methods [12, 13] leverage cross-attention maps to identify important tokens from semantically or structurally salient regions, aiming not merely to reduce computation but also to preserve informative representations during token reduction [39]. More recently, [9] uses classifier-free guidance (CFG) as a saliency signal without additional attention computation, but because CFG primarily reflects alignment with the conditioning signal, it fails to capture the spatially heterogeneous and temporally evolving dynamics of the full image. In contrast, our method leverages the Tweedie denoised estimate to construct a dynamics-aware importance map that captures both temporal evolution and spatial structure across the image. 3 Method Our goal is to design a token merging strategy for efficient image generation by accounting for diffusion dynamics. To this end, we first define a dynamics-aware importance signal that character- izes token importance from two complementary perspectives: temporal dynamics and structural saliency. Based on this importance map, we assign tokens into functional roles for merging, dis- tinguishing safe merge sources and structurally important constraint tokens. We then perform locality-constrained token merging, together with grid-based source completion to satisfy the target compression ratio. In the following,

In diffusion models [1–3], the forward process gradually corrupts a clean image x0 by adding Gaussian noise over t ∈[0, T] timesteps: xt = αtx0 + σtϵ, ϵ ∼N(0, I), (1) where αt and σt denote the signal and noise scales at timestep t, respectively, satisfying α2 t + σ2 t = 1. The reverse process aims to recover x0 from xT by iteratively denoising, guided by the score function ∇xt log pt(xt), which represents the gradient of the log-density of the noisy distribution pt(xt) with respect to xt [19]. Intuitively, the score function defines a vector field that

Intuitively, the score function defines a vector field that points toward regions of higher data likelihood, guiding the noisy sample toward the clean data manifold throughout the denoising process. In practice, the score function is estimated via a neural network ϵθ trained to predict the noise ϵ added at each timestep. The score is then obtained from the predicted noise as: s(t) = ∇xt log pt(xt) ≈−1 σt ϵθ(xt, t, c), (2) where c denotes the conditioning signal (e.g., text prompt). Tweedie’s Estimation. Tweedie’s formula [21] provides a closed-form expression for the posterior mean of the clean sample x0 given the noisy observation xt: ˆx0(t) = E[x0 | xt] = xt + σ2 t ∇xt log pt(xt) αt . (3) Substituting the learned score estimator from Eq. 2, this becomes: ˆx0(t) ≈xt −σt ϵθ(xt, t, c) αt , (4) which gives a denoised estimate of x0 at timestep t, termed the Tweedie denoised estimate. Unlike the noisy sample xt, which is directly modulated by the noise level σt, ˆx0(t) provides an estimate in the predicted clean image space [40], offering a noise-normalized view of the current generation state. 3.2

text: The first term reflects changes in the model prediction across timesteps and is therefore associated with actual token-level evolution. In contrast, the second term arises purely from the predefined global noise schedule σt rather than changes in the model prediction itself. As denoising approaches the late steps (σt →0), the inverse difference 1 σt−1 −1 σt grows rapidly. This suggests that the scale term can increasingly dominate the score slope in later stages, making the resulting signal less reliable. To obtain a cleaner temporal measure, we instead project the score into predicted clean-image space via the Tweedie estimate ˆx0(t) [41] and consider its inter-step residual, ˆx0(t) −ˆx0(t −1). Furthermore, the update is scaled by σt−1 αt−1 , and this factor decreases as denoising concludes, naturally attenuating the signal in late steps. These properties make the Tweedie difference a more stable temporal signal for measuring token evolution. Empirical Validation of Temporal Signals. In contrast, both score-based signals, namely the raw score slope and the Tweedie difference, initially show noticeably lower autocorrelation, indicating greater sensitivity to image-wide refinement than CFG. However, temporal autocorrelation alone does not naturally imply that a signal reflects token-level convergence. To evaluate whether a signal faithfully reflects token-level convergence, we measure its correla- tion with a reference signal constructed from the per-timestep Tweedie estimate ˆx0(t), which we treat as a proxy for the clean image following [41]. Building on this analysis, we define the temporal importance map as the inter-step residual in predicted clean-image space: M(t) temp = |ˆx0(t) −ˆx0(t −1)| , (7) which quantifies how much the predicted clean structure is still evolving at each spatial location. This temporal map captures when each token is actively changing during denoising. However, as previously observed in Fig. 1(c), CFG also fails to protect structurally salient tokens in non-prompt regions—those carrying essential boundary and texture information. Under CFG-based importance, such tokens consistently receive low scores throughout denoising, leading them to be mistakenly treated as safe merge candidates and causing object boundaries to be diluted (Fig. 8). To capture this structural property, we introduce a spatial axis derived from the same Tweedie estimate. Specifically, we use the spatial axis to distinguish structurally salient but temporally stable tokens from genuinely mergeable homogeneous regions. To this end, we define the spatial axis as the residual between ˆx0(t) and its coarse-scale approximation obtained via interpolation-based transformation [42]: M(t) spat = ˆx0(t) −UpSample×s  DownSample×s �ˆx0(t)  , (8) where s denotes the spatial scale used to construct the coarse approximation. A detailed step-by-step algorithm of DaTMe is provided in the Appendix B. Dynamics-Aware Role Assignment. Rather than imposing a hand-crafted cutoff for what should be considered important, DaTMe adaptively assigns token roles at each denoising step based on their temporal and spatial responses under the given compression ratio r. To prevent quality degrada- tion caused by merging temporally evolving or structurally salient tokens, we first define a conser- vative source set Ssrc ⊂Stot as the intersection of the lowest-r fractions of tokens ranked by Mtemp and Mspat. Conversely, we define a constraint set, Scon ⊂Stot, as the intersection of the top-(1 −r) fractions of tokens on both axes, preserving tokens that are both temporally unstable and structurally salient. By preserving Scon throughout merging, we use them as structural anchors that keep critical boundaries from dissolving into surrounding regions. Spatially Distributed Source Completion. We primarily conduct experiments on PixArt- α [5] using 10k image-prompt pairs sampled from the COCO 2014 validation set [44]. We set the interpolation scale to s = 4, and for grid-based source completion, we use P = 4 grid cells. We evaluate three compression ratios: 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. Following [9], we apply DaTMe to the middle- range self-attention layers of the DiT [2] backbone. To further evaluate scalability on a larger DiT model, we apply DaTMe to FLUX [22]. We use FLUX.1-dev and additionally apply DaTMe from the middle block to the final block within the joint-attention blocks using the same hyperparameters. In Fig. 5 and Fig. 6, we compare qualitative results at a compression ratio of 0.5. On PixArt-α, directly merging tokens based on feature similarity (ToMeSD) severely disrupts spatial structure, often leading to obvious structural distortion. Although the CFG-based method preserves foreground structures that are explicitly described in the prompt, it shows noticeably weaker preservation in background and other weakly conditioned regions, as highlighted by the red boxes. This qualitatively supports our analysis that CFG-based importance is strongly biased toward prompt-conditioned content and is therefore less effective at preserving the full image context. On FLUX, existing methods generally preserve the coarse prompt semantics, but still introduce noticeable deviations from the original generation. ToMeSD tends to alter the original composition, object geometry, or viewpoint, as seen in the relative arrangement of the cats, the fire hydrant structure, and the airplane viewpoint. ToMA shows similar structural drift while additionally introducing noisy visual degradation that weakens overall image quality. In contrast, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the original spatial configuration and object structure while maintaining the intended prompt semantics. These results demonstrate that DaTMe reduces both structural deviation and visual degradation across different architectures. Additional results under various compression ratios are in Appendix C. text: We presented DaTMe, a diffusion-dynamics-aware token merging framework for efficient image generation. By leveraging the Tweedie denoised estimate, DaTMe defines token importance along two complementary axes—temporal evolution and structural saliency—that reflect the image generation process. This allows DaTMe to identify safely mergeable tokens while preserving structurally critical regions, achieving strong image fidelity and favorable quality-efficiency trade-offs across DiT-based diffusion models. Our work shows that grounding token merging in the underlying generation dynamics is a key step toward faithful and efficient diffusion inference. text: A Formal Decomposition of Score Slope Instability We provide a formal analysis of why the score slope fails to reliably capture per-token convergence in late denoising steps. Decomposition of score slope. Recall that the score function is estimated as: st ≈−1 σt ϵθ(xt, t, c). (9) To understand the temporal variation of the score, we analyze the score slope between consecutive timesteps. For brevity, let ϵθ(t) denote ϵθ(xt, t, c). The score slope is: st −st−1 = ϵθ(t −1) σt−1 −ϵθ(t) σt . (10) By adding and subtracting the term ϵθ(t) σt−1 , st −st−1 = ϵθ(t −1) σt−1 −ϵθ(t) σt−1 + ϵθ(t) σt−1 −ϵθ(t) σt , (11) we can decouple this slope into two distinct components: st −st−1 = ϵθ(t −1) −ϵθ(t) σt−1 | {z } difference term + ϵθ(t)  1 σt−1 −1 σt  | {z } scale term . (12) This decomposition reveals a limitation. The first term captures the actual change in the model’s noise prediction, reflecting semantic token-level evolution. However, the second term is entirely dictated by the predefined noise schedule σt, scaled by the current noise prediction ϵθ(t). Behavior in late denoising steps. As generation progresses toward the final steps, the noise scale σt becomes extremely small. Because σt decays rapidly, the inverse difference 1 σt−1 −1 σt grows disproportionately large. Because σt decays rapidly, the inverse difference 1 σt−1 −1 σt grows disproportionately large. Meanwhile, since ϵθ is trained to match samples from N(0, I) [46], its norm is concentrated near √ D in expectation, where D is the dimensionality [47]. Consequently, the scale term in Eq. (12) significantly amplifies the raw noise prediction ϵθ(t), eventually overshadowing the difference term. Therefore, in later denoising stages, the score slope st −st−1 is heavily dominated by the noise schedule scaling rather than actual changes in each token, which is consistent with the high autocorrelation and loss of discriminative power observed in Fig. 2. (18) Comparing Eq. (18) with Eq. (12) reveals a difference in how the noise schedule enters each formu- lation. First, the problematic scale term—the 1/σt scaling that overshadowed the genuine signal— no longer dominates the slope. The Tweedie difference cleanly isolates the difference term change, ϵθ(t−1)−ϵθ(t). Second, instead of amplifying this change with a rapidly growing 1/σt−1 multiplier, the Tweedie difference scales it by σt−1 αt−1 (closely related to the inverse signal-to-noise ratio [48]). As t →0, we have σt−1 →0 and αt−1 →1, so σt−1 αt−1 →0. This decays the variation as the network’s prediction stabilizes, ensuring that the Tweedie difference provides a stable metric for convergence without scale-induced amplification. We further evaluate DaTMe on U-Net-based architectures, specifically Stable Diffusion 1.5 and SDXL. For these models, we set the interpolation scale to s = 2 and the number of grid cells to P = 4. Images are generated using 50 inference steps, with a guidance scale of 7.5 for Stable Diffusion 1.5 and 5.0 for SDXL. Following [9, 10], we apply token merging at the 64 × 64 latent resolution in both architectures. Unlike in DiT-based models, we do not explicitly construct the constraint set Scon for U-Net backbones. Because U-Net architectures already possess a strong spatial inductive bias through convolutions, tokens with similar features are naturally organized in nearby spatial regions [43]. Consequently, spatial locality is implicitly preserved. We therefore only identify the source set Ssrc and sample the remaining merge candidates without enforcing an additional constraint set. Finally, token merging begins at the same denoising step as in the DiT experiments. C Additional Experiments Additional Comparison Results. text: Preprint GEN4P: VIDEO GENERATORS ARE 4D PERCEIVERS Yitong Xia1 Zeren Jiang2 Chuanxia Zheng1 1PVG, Nanyang Technological University 2VGG, University of Oxford Figure 1: Gen4P repurposes a multi-step Video Generator into a single-step 4D Perceiver, enabling unified feed-forward prediction of dense 3D tracks, point maps, depth maps, and camera poses from a video input. Gen4P is able to track complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure of in-the-wild content, like the thin legs of the flamingo and long-range skiing motion.
title: Preprint

text: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained multi-step video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross- attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p. github.io/ for more visual results. 1

text: We consider the problem of feed-forward full 4D reconstruction from monocular video. A unified 4D representation of scene geometry, depth, camera poses, and 3D point trajectories provides a foundation for simulating and interacting with the physical environment. However, recovering such a representation remains challenging: it requires accurately capturing both the static geometry and the dynamic motion of the scene across viewpoints and over time. Recent advances in feed-forward reconstruction demonstrate the value of pretrained foundational vision models. Geometry Foundation Models (GFMs), including VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a), VGGT- Ω(Wang et al., 2026a), and DA3 (Lin et al., 2025), build on pretrained vision models (Oquab et al., 2023; Sim´eoni et al., 2025), adapting them through large-scale geometric supervision. These GFMs 1 arXiv:2610.22371v1 [cs.CV] 15 Oct 2026

text: Preprint then provide strong geometry priors for subsequent 4D reconstruction: V-DPM (Sucar et al., 2026) and 4RC (Luo et al., 2026), for instance, extend VGGT and DA3 to jointly recover geometry and motion. However, geometry priors alone do not explicitly model how points should evolve over time in dynamic scenes. Meanwhile, foundational generative models offer a complementary source of priors over appearance, geometry, and motion, by learning to synthesize images and videos (Wan et al., 2025; ByteDance Seed Team, 2026). Recent studies have exploited generative priors for 2D correspondence (Hedlin et al., 2023), depth estimation (Ke et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025), 3D geometry recovery (Zhang et al., 2025b; Lu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025), motion tracking (Zhu et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026a), and general perception (Wang et al., 2026b). However, they still address 4D perception through task-specific approaches. Besides, they often require dense, frame-aligned supervision, limiting their flexibility in handling arbitrary spatiotemporal video inputs. In this work, we introduce Gen4P, a 4D perceiver that leverages rich priors from large-scale pretrained video generators for full 4D reconstruction. Specifically, Gen4P tames a multi-step video generator into a single-step feed-forward 4D perceiver. text: 4D reconstruction. Specifically, Gen4P tames a multi-step video generator into a single-step feed-forward 4D perceiver. To this end, the objective is formulated as learning a direct regression network, instead of the iterative denoising for geometric reconstruction in prior works (Ke et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). Such a formulation requires only one encoder forward pass per input clip. The resulting scene tokens are then shared across queries, reducing the encoding cost over repeated 4D predictions. We obtain the full 4D attributes by querying the scene tokens using a lightweight cross-attention decoder. It decouples the output sampling from pre-extracted feature grids, allowing spatial flexibility in the output resolution. Additionally, we introduce a continuous-time query mechanism to handle variable-length video sequences effectively. Furthermore, we discover that a pretrained video-depth LoRA can further be incorporated as a frozen plug-in geometric prior, strengthening geometry without introducing additional trainable parameters. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: (i) we repurpose a video generator into a feed- forward 4D perceiver under sparse query supervision, offering an alternative to GFM-based methods; (ii) we introduce a continuous-time query mechanism together with on-demand decoding to provide temporal and spatial flexibility; (iii) we incorporate a frozen depth LoRA as a plug-in geometry prior, improving overall 4D reconstruction without adding trainable parameters; and (iv) we provide

text: Feed-forward GFMs directly regress pixel-aligned geometry, from pairwise point maps (Wang et al., 2024) to sequence models that use spatial memory (Wang & Agapito, 2025), recurrent scene states (Wang et al., 2025b), or joint multi-view attention with multiple prediction heads (Wang et al., 2025a). Later models remove the reference view (Wang et al., 2026c), accept optional geometric inputs (Keetha et al., 2026), or learn unified depth–ray targets (Lin et al., 2025). Point Tracking in 2D and 3D. 2D point tracking has been extensively studied in both sparse and dense settings (Doersch et al., 2022; Karaev et al., 2024; 2025; Lai et al., 2026). 3D point tracking methods lift pixels with monocular depth and iterative refinement (Xiao et al., 2024), improve dense long-range estimation through optimized surrogate queries (Ngo et al., 2025b;a), or jointly estimate geometry, camera, and object motion (Xiao et al., 2025). GFM-based 4D perceivers represent dynamic 3D scenes through per-frame point maps (Zhang et al., 2025a), dynamic point maps (Sucar et al., 2026), conditional frame-wise decoding (Luo et al., 2026), or motion bases (Lin et al., 2026). Other approaches include common-time point-map pairs (Feng et al., 2025), parametric trajectories (Liu et al., 2026), and scene flow (Zhu et al., 2026; Karhade et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2026). Most rely on frame-aligned grid decoding, coupling output sampling and

Instead of training a large-scale 4D geometric network from scratch, in Gen4P we repurpose a pretrained video generator ppre as a feed-forward 4D perceiver. As illustrated in Fig. 2, Gen4P adopts an on-demand query-based formulation inspired by D4RT (Sec. 3.1). A lightweight decoder queries spatiotemporal features from the pretrained video generator (Sec. 3.2.1) to predict 4D attributes at specified locations and times. Since real-world videos vary in duration, a practical 4D reconstruction method should accommodate different sequence lengths. Unlike D4RT, we introduce a continuous time query (Sec. 3.2.2) to enhance flexibility. We further introduce a plug-in geometry prior (Sec. 3.3) to enhance geometric performance. The training objective is described in Sec. 3.4. We detail each component below. 3.1 PRELIMINARIES: D4RT D4RT (Zhang et al., 2026a) formulates full 4D reconstruction as on-demand point querying. Given a fixed-length input video V ∈R48×H×W ×3, a VideoMAE-initialized (Wang et al., 2023) encoder E first encodes it into a global scene representation F that is shared by all subsequent point queries: F = E(V )

(1) Then F is decoded to produce 3D points and auxiliary 2D attributes, including positions, normals, visibility, and confidence, through parallelized independent point queries. Each input query token is parameterized as q(u, v, tsrc, ttgt, tcam) = MLPq �ϕuv(u, v) + ϕpatch(pu,v) + esrc(tsrc) + etgt(ttgt) + ecam(tcam)  ∈RC, (2) where ϕuv is the encoded query coordinate, ϕpatch(pu,v) denotes the MLP-encoded local 9 × 9 RGB patch centered at (u, v), and esrc, etgt, and ecam represent the temporal embeddings. The query q(u, v, tsrc, ttgt, tcam) asks “what are the 3D position and the other attributes of the 3D point corresponding to the pixel at (u, v) in source frame tsrc, at time ttgt, expressed in the camera coordinate system of tcam”. Taking source time tsrc as an example, we define: α(tsrc) = tsrc T −1, tsrc ∈{0, . . . , T −1}, esrc(tsrc) := (1 −α(tsrc)) esrc,0 + α(tsrc) esrc,1, (6) where esrc,0 and esrc,1 are two learnable temporal embeddings representing the start and end of the video clip, respectively. This parameterization represents each timestamp by its normalized position within the clip, making the time query independent of the absolute sequence length T and thereby enhancing the model’s temporal flexibility. Cross-Attention Decoder. The decoder consists of multiple cross-attention blocks, where the query attends to the scene tokens F at each layer. We construct the query embedding q from the continuous time query embeddings esrc, etgt, and ecam, the 2D position embedding ϕuv(u, v) and the RGB patch embedding ϕpatch(pu,v). Then we feed q and F into a cross-attention decoder D to obtain the query feature zq, which is further mapped by an MLP head H to the complete set of 4D attributes, as defined in Eqs. text: PRIOR Recent GFM-finetuned 4D perceivers (Sucar et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026) benefit from geometry priors, which are learned through large-scale dense 3D pretraining. In contrast, Gen4P adapts a pretrained video generator to exploit its motion prior, while its sparse query-based supervision alone provides a weaker signal for learning geometry than the GFM-finetuned methods. To narrow this gap, we propose a natural solution within our framework: by plugging in a pretrained video-depth adapter as a frozen geometry prior, we are able to reuse knowledge learned from dense depth estimation without a separate dense 3D pretraining stage. Double-LoRA Architecture. To incorporate pretrained dense geometric knowledge, we adopt a plug-in geometry prior from a pretrained video depth estimation model, DVD (Zhang et al., 2026b), which is also built upon Wan2.1. We combine the pretrained Depth-LoRA (∆WDepth) with our 4D-LoRA (∆W4D) (Sec. 3.2.1), forming a double-LoRA architecture. For each adapted layer, the effective weight is W = WDiT + ∆W 512 Depth + ∆W 512 4D , (7) where WDiT denotes the DiT weight of the pretrained video generator, and ∆W 512 Depth and ∆W 512 4D are the depth and 4D weight updates with a rank of 512, respectively. Lightweight Training. Following prior work on retaining pretrained adapters during task adapta- tion (Yu et al., 2025), we

text: generator, and ∆W 512 Depth and ∆W 512 4D are the depth and 4D weight updates with a rank of 512, respectively. Lightweight Training. Following prior work on retaining pretrained adapters during task adapta- tion (Yu et al., 2025), we freeze the VAE encoder, WDiT and ∆WDepth, and jointly optimize ∆W4D, the query embeddings, the query decoder, and the prediction head. Thus, the pretrained depth update is retained while a separate update is learned for 4D perception under the task objective. We point out that the double-LoRA variant requires no additional dense prediction head and has the same number of trainable parameters as the variant using 4D-LoRA alone. In Sec. 4.5, we compare several adaptation strategies, providing empirical support for our design. 3.4 TRAINING OBJECTIVE Our method predicts a full set of 4D attributes and is trained with a composite loss: L = λ3DL3D + λconfLconf + λ2DL2D + λvisLvis + λdispLdisp + λnormalLnormal, (8) where L3D, Lconf, L2D, Lvis, Ldisp, and Lnormal denote the 3D position, confidence, 2D position, visibility, 3D displacement, and surface-normal losses, respectively. text: We present Gen4P, a feed-forward 4D perceiver that processes monocular video input for full 4D reconstruction. The key to its success is to leverage prior knowledge from pretrained video generators in a single-step manner, which differs from traditional multi-step denoising-based 4D perceivers. Our on-demand decoder enables flexible spatial and temporal querying, while a frozen video-depth LoRA provides a plug-in geometry prior without additional trainable parameters. Crucially, we demonstrate 9
title: Preprint

text: Preprint that Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art and flexible 4D reconstruction, with future improvement expected as video generative pretraining continues to advance. We also demonstrate its capability to accurately capture dynamic motion and intricate details in real-world videos. Together, these findings support video generators as a promising foundation for unified 4D reconstruction. text: Preprint A ADDITIONAL RESULTS A.1 ADDITIONAL QUALITATIVE RESULTS In Fig. 7, we show additional qualitative results, including merged point clouds, tracking and camera pose estimation, and additional 3D tracking showcases. A.2 CONFIDENCE FILTERING We use the expp1 confidence activation, i.e., c = 1 + exp(ˆc) with ˆc denoting the raw confidence output, following VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a). This allows us to apply percentile-based confidence filtering to remove points that the model predicts with low confidence, typically distributed at the far-away background or foreground boundaries. In Fig. 8, we demonstrate an application of confidence filtering. As shown in the Raw column, the direct tracking outputs are already visually clean, but may contain a small number of flying points. By applying confidence filtering, with a percentile as low as 2%, these flying points can be effectively suppressed, resulting in cleaner foreground and background content. We hereby clarify that for fair comparisons, the visualization results for any method in Fig. 4 and Fig. 6 are NOT applied with confidence-based suppression. B TRAINING PREPARATION B.1 DATASETS We distinguish two types of input frames: encoder frames, which are fed to the encoder to extract scene tokens, and query frames, from which local RGB patches are extracted to construct decoder queries. The two share the same aspect ratio but may differ in spatial resolution. For

text: encoder frames, which are fed to the encoder to extract scene tokens, and query frames, from which local RGB patches are extracted to construct decoder queries. The two share the same aspect ratio but may differ in spatial resolution. For encoder frames, each raw video is maximally center-cropped to one of five predefined aspect ratios. The cropped frames are then uniformly resized to the largest resolution within a 480 × 832 bound, resulting in five encoder frame sizes: 480 × 480, 480 × 640, 480 × 832, 352 × 832, and 256 × 832. The corresponding query frames use the same cropped content before resizing, and their resolutions therefore depend on the native resolution of each dataset. The resulting encoder frame and query frame resolutions are reported in Tab. A1. We preprocess each dataset under these spatial configurations and report the approximate number of resulting subclips for each configuration in the “Est. Subclip Count Per Size” column. During training, datasets are sampled according to the probabilities reported in the final column. In practice, we tolerate a slight distortion between them. To vary the effective field of view of query patches, we apply downsizing-only augmentation to the query frames. For each training clip, we first resize them within a 960 × 1664 bound, then sample a side length scale factor from

text: To vary the effective field of view of query patches, we apply downsizing-only augmentation to the query frames. For each training clip, we first resize them within a 960 × 1664 bound, then sample a side length scale factor from [0.5, 1.0], and resize all query frames by the same factor. This augmentation is applied only to the query frames for the decoder, while the pre-encoded latents remain unchanged. We don’t apply random content cropping, color jittering or Gaussian blurring. B.2 PREPROCESSING AND SAMPLING Preprocessing. Each raw video is subsampled into 49-frame clips with frame intervals ranging from 1 to 4. We then pre-encode each clip with the Wan-VAE (Wan et al., 2025) and store the normalized latents. For each clip, camera poses are defined in the first-frame relative world coordinate. The 3D po- sition GT is expressed in the tcam camera coordinate. We adopt mean normalization as in Mo- tionCrafter (Zhu et al., 2026): valid visible 3D GT points are centered and normalized by their mean distance to the origin. Then they are transformed to tcam’s camera coordinate system. The displacement and normal GTs are represented in the same camera coordinate system. 17

text: physical definitions consistent, and we empirically find that they work well as auxiliary losses, consistent with the design in Li & Team (2026). Frame and Query Sampling. Since the Wan-VAE uses causal temporal convolutions, the latent at each timestamp doesn’t encode future RGB frames and thus can be safely head-truncated. Its encoding is first-frame anchored: the first latent corresponds to the first RGB frame, while each subsequent latent encodes four additional RGB frames. Thus, for T = 4N + 1, we slice the first T query frames and the first N + 1 latent frames. In practice, we randomly sample the query clip length from {21, 25, . . . , 49}. A too-short clip will fail to provide adequate context for motion learning and lead to a performance drop. During training, we sample at most 2048 queries per training clip, with tsrc independently sampled for each query. Temporally, we enforce ttgt = tcam for 40% of the queries, while the rest are randomly sampled. Spatially, 40% is sampled from the foreground and 10% is sampled from the foreground boundaries marked by Sobel-filtered depth maps. ADT, DR and PO contain both static and dynamic tracks, whereas PS contains only dynamic tracks. To reliably distinguish dynamic points from static ones for evaluation, we need to select an appropriate motion threshold that suppresses numerical noise in static GT tracks while preserving dynamic tracks with small motions. We measure the motion of each GT track by accumulating adjacent-frame 3D displacements over 64 frames in meters. As shown in Tab. A4, increasing the threshold from 5 × 10−3 →1 × 10−2 changes the average static ratio only marginally from 56.82% →57.29%, indicating that 5 × 10−3 is adequate for removing the majority of the numerical noise. In contrast, increasing the threshold from 5×10−3 →5×10−2 may lead to noticeably more wrongly classified static tracks. The static ratio on ADT shows 67.23% →74.30%, a non-negligible 7.07%, while on PStudio, despite being fully dynamic, increases to 2.00%. title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized

text: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user- profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. text: Household manipulation has been a long-standing goal in robotics and embodied AI, with the promise of improving daily life by enabling robots to perform chores from natural language instructions (e.g., “put an apple, bread, and milk on my plate”). Recent progress in generalist robotic manipulation has been driven in large part by Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3, 4], which show strong generalization across diverse multimodal inputs [5, 6] and heterogeneous embodiments [7, 8]. However, real-world deployment demands more than completing the nominal task: embodied agents must also execute tasks in ways that align with the preferences, habits, and constraints of individual users, a requirement we refer to as personalization. Preferences introduce diverse execution requirements for identical goals. For instance, placing a mug might require a specific handle orientation or a designated landing spot. Consequently, personalized manipulation must satisfy user-specific constraints on both what strategies are selected and how actions are performed. In this framework, preferences are treated as a learning dimension parallel to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Nevertheless, progress on personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) remains impeded by two major gaps. First, PeRM lacks a shared formulation and standardized evaluation protocol across prior work. Existing studies define personalization through diverse problem settings, including implicit preference alignment [9, 10], multi-user style adaptation [11], user-specific object-receptacle pairing [12], and helpful action prediction [13]; they also specify preferences through natural language [13, 14], few user examples [9], explicit preference functions [15], human speech [5],

Evaluation is similarly fragmented, spanning task success, user studies [9, 11, 13, 14], and preference-based scoring functions [16, 17], making methods difficult to compare and failure modes hard to diagnose. Second, existing benchmarks typically emphasize high-level navigation or semantic selection over fine-grained manipulation preferences and multi-preference conflicts. The closest preference-based RL benchmark [18] lacks robotic preference-learning datasets and multi- preference evaluation. Other personalization benchmarks focus on object navigation or high-level receptacle selection [19, 20], while recent memory-based manipulation benchmarks [21, 22] do not distinguish task-instance memorization from genuine user-preference-driven personalization. To address these gaps, we introduce a novel Personalized Robotic Manipulation Benchmark (LIBERO-PeRM), built using the popular LIBERO [23] framework. We elevate user preferences to a fundamental building block alongside tasks and layouts. Following the taxonomy of human preferences [24], we define a controlled taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering Motion Preference (trajectory constraints), Skill Preference (task strategies), and User Profile (seman- tic biases). Personalized robotic manipula- tion, therefore, requires a policy to select, among feasible trajectories that complete a requested task, one that also satisfies the user’s preference. Preference Selection and Layout Modification. The user first selects a preference instance and an initial LIBERO layout [23]. Given these inputs, the pipeline uses a VLM [72] to minimally modify the layout so the selected preference can be operationalized while limiting changes to the original scene. For Motion Preference and Skill Preference preferences, the layout and task language remain unchanged;

text: subtask plan, the pipeline makes minimal edits, such as adding a red object of the same category for a red-object preference, so preference-conditioned and no-preference trajectories can be generated in the same setting. The task language is also abstracted to cover both settings, ensuring that behavioral differences are driven by the preference rather than unrelated scene changes. Preference-Conditioned Subtask and Trajectory Generation. After the layout and task language are fixed, the pipeline uses a VLM with the task language and preference language to generate both a no-preference subtask plan and a preference-conditioned subtask plan. It then calls a library of pre-recorded heuristic skills to generate trajectory data. To construct each heuristic skill, we first collect one human demonstration for the skill, extract key waypoints, and use an OMPL planner [73] with randomized initial states to generate many successful trajectories. The generated trajectories are then smoothed; heuristic-skill parameters are manually offset-adjusted when needed. Empirically, we find more than 72% of skills require no offset adjustment across any task, suggesting the VLM-based edit is already very effective. Preferences are applied at different stages according to their type: User Profile affects subtask-plan generation via a prompt; Skill Preference affects skill selection, such as using pick_handle instead of a regular pick skill; and Motion Preference affects skill-level trajectory generation, such as reducing OMPL-sampled waypoints

Satisfaction Metric Generation. After preference-conditioned trajectories are generated, the pipeline constructs explicit preference satisfaction metrics for each selected preference. The form of each metric depends on the preference type. For Motion Preference, we directly compute satisfaction functions from trajectory quantities, such as the distance between the robot trajectory and the target object for the preference “avoid certain object”. For Skill Preference, we evaluate key waypoints and use VLM-based image checks to verify skill-specific execution, such as whether the object is grasped by its handle. For User Profile, we monitor the executed subtask plan, including which objects are manipulated, to verify that the plan adheres to the profile. Specifically, each episode is mapped to a fixed four-level Discrete Satisfaction Label d ∈{0, 1/4, 3/4, 1}, independent of the number of pipeline-generated subtasks. A continuous Satisfaction Score, such as speed, is binned by trajectory statistics and then incorporated into this label. Raw Satisfaction Scores provide denser feedback for training, while Discrete Satisfaction Labels provide a more interpretable evaluation signal at inference time. Initial Human Validation. To assess the real-world plausibility of the selected preferences and the human-likeness of the generated demonstrations, we conducted a survey with 15 participants using a 10-point scale. Across all preference categories, the demonstrations received an average human-likeness score of 9.11, and the preferences received an average real-world plausibility score of 8.35. These results provide initial human validation of the benchmark design; Appendix D reports the protocol and category-level results. 3.3 Task Suites Using the pipeline above, we generate five task suites: LIBERO-SinglePref, LIBERO-PrefScale, LIBERO-PrefConflict, LIBERO-PrefCompose, and LIBERO-ComprePref. We follow LIBERO terminology and call the inseparable combination of a task instruction, scene layout, and task-goal condition a mission. text: LIBERO-SinglePref. This suite evaluates single-preference learning and execution. It contains 100 tasks and serves as the foundation for evaluating personalization. LIBERO-PrefScale. This suite evaluates how preference learning scales across demonstrations, tasks, and layouts. It supports controlled analysis of preference acquisition and generalization across tasks and layouts. It contains 100 tasks. LIBERO-PrefConflict. This suite evaluates policy behavior when preferences conflict with other preferences or with the task goal. Preference-preference conflicts pair the same layout and task with mutually conflicting single preferences, while task-preference conflicts pair no-preference task data with task-incompatible preference data. It contains 48 tasks. LIBERO-PrefCompose. This suite evaluates multi-preference learning and preference composition in a controlled two-preference setting. For each aligned layout-task pair, it provides four conditions: no preference, PA, PB, and PA +PB, enabling controlled comparisons for composition and multi-preference learning. It contains 64 tasks. LIBERO-ComprePref. This suite rewrites prompts over tasks from the other suites so the preference must be inferred from contextual language rather than read from a separate explicit field. It includes explicit task-preference mixtures, where key preference words are preserved, and implicit preference reasoning, where contextual cues imply the preference without naming it. text: Task and Preference Metrics. We report two types of metrics: task success rate (SR), which measures task completion, and preference satisfaction (SA), which measures how well a preference is satisfied using the Discrete Satisfaction Label from Section 3.2. The Discrete Satisfaction Label for episode n is dn ∈{0, 1/4, 3/4, 1}, and I[G(τn)] is its task-success indicator. We compute SA = 1 N PN n=1 I[G(τn)]dn, so preference satisfaction contributes only when the task succeeds. Conflict Policy. For a task-preference conflict, completing the original task takes priority. For preference-preference conflicts, SA is computed using the higher of the two preference satisfaction scores for each episode, with task-failure episodes contributing zero satisfaction. These scoring conventions probe execution under inconsistent instructions; they do not evaluate conflict detection, preference weighting, or when a policy should ask the user for guidance. Generalization. We evaluate in-domain, task-or-layout, and preference-level generalization using SR and SA. In-domain evaluation keeps the training tasks, preferences, and layouts with small object-position perturbations. Task-or-layout generalization changes either the task or layout, while preference-level generalization changes tasks under unseen layouts while keeping the preference unchanged. 4 Experiments We conduct experiments on the five task suites introduced in Section 3.3 to evaluate zero-shot personalization, preference learning ability, preference learning efficiency, preference generalization, composition, and behavior under conflicts. text: In this work, we introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a comprehensive benchmark for personalized robotic manipulation. By treating preferences as a first-class building block alongside tasks and layouts, LIBERO-PeRM provides five task suites that isolate and evaluate preference learning under single- preference, scaling, conflict, composition, and comprehensive preference reasoning settings. Exper- iments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Compared with sequential adaptation, mixed training better preserves no- preference behavior and improves contextual-prompt robustness, but it weakens motion-preference performance relative to preference-only LoRA. Preference learning benefits more from layout diver- sity and same-layout no-preference data than denser demonstrations, but generalization to unseen layouts and different tasks remains difficult. Composition is only partially observed, decomposition fails, and conflicts often degrade execution instead of producing resolution. Limitations and Future Work. LIBERO-PeRM instantiates predefined, language-expressible, auto- matically measurable preferences in simulation. It therefore excludes implicit preference inference, interaction history, non-linguistic signals, and open-ended or evolving preferences. Its generated demonstrations may contain pipeline- and skill-library-specific biases despite randomized initial states, multiple missions per preference, and human review. The current composition suite combines only two preferences, and the conflict suite does not test conflict detection or clarification. Finally, the human survey provides only initial validation; no real-robot or longitudinal user study is included. Future work could extend LIBERO-PeRM in directions ranging

text: A Additional Information This appendix includes additional experimental details and results that support the main findings in Section 4.2. A.1 Ethics Statement LIBERO-PeRM is built from procedurally generated preference-conditioned tasks, layouts, trajec- tories, and evaluation signals in simulation. Human feedback is used to review generated data and validate preference plausibility, but no personal data or real-world user logs are released or used as policy-training data. Its intended use is research on personalized robotic manipulation, including preference learning, generalization, composition, and conflict handling. Our dataset construction process is designed to reduce ethical and legal risk. We build on LIBERO [23] scenes and simula- tor assets, then generate preference-conditioned variants through minimal layout edits, procedural trajectory generation, and automatic preference metrics. Preference descriptions, satisfaction rules, and benchmark annotations are created for research use rather than copied from external products or commercial systems. Any public release should preserve attribution to upstream assets and follow the licenses and terms of use of LIBERO and other dependencies. The benchmark also has important limitations. Our preference metrics only capture observable execution outcomes in simulation and cannot represent open-ended, private, or highly subjective human preferences. As a result, LIBERO- PeRM should not be treated as a substitute for human evaluation in safety-critical or real-world personalized deployment. We intend this benchmark to support controlled scientific evaluation, not direct

As a result, LIBERO- PeRM should not be treated as a substitute for human evaluation in safety-critical or real-world personalized deployment. We intend this benchmark to support controlled scientific evaluation, not direct real-world decision making. We take responsibility for the released benchmark artifacts. The LIBERO-PeRM dataset and open- source code are released under the MIT license. A.2 Training Details For non-zero-shot experiments, we further tune π0.5 with LoRA [75]. We scale the training budget with the number of rollouts: for every 4,000 rollout episodes, we use roughly 45,000 optimization steps on eight A6000 Ada GPUs with a learning rate of 5×10−5. For the main fine-tuning comparison, All-Pref denotes one checkpoint jointly trained on Motion, Skill, and User-Profile preference tasks; it is not an ensemble or an average of category-specific checkpoints. We evaluate each fixed checkpoint in 10 independent runs and report mean ± standard deviation in Table 3. The variation therefore reflects randomized evaluation rollouts, not training seeds. B Preference Selection Criteria We select a preference only if it satisfies five criteria: 1) expressible in natural language; 2) can be grounded in existing LIBERO [23] scenes; 3) satisfiable without changing the task goal; 4) measurable by an automatic preference metric; and 5) reusable across multiple tasks or layouts. text: C Model-Assisted Generation and Validation We use Claude Code with an Opus-family model and Gemini as backends for three model-assisted stages. In layout editing, the model receives a BDDL scene specification, preference language, object geometry, and spatial constraints, and proposes a modified BDDL layout. In personalized planning, it receives the original task and preference instructions, baseline plan, available objects and skills, and a scene image, and returns a sequence of (skill, object) pairs plus required, prohibited, and ordering constraints. In image inspection, independent VLM judgments assess task completion and visually observable preference compliance from rollout frames. Inspired by single- and multi-agent evaluations [76, 77, 78], the layout and plan candidates follow a generate-and-trial loop: each proposal is instantiated and tested in simulation, and any candidate violating the output format, physical constraints, task-success condition, or preference constraints is rejected. The observed failure is included when generating a revised candidate. The reported VLM failure rate in each stage was below 23%. For image inspection, inconsistent independent judgments are flagged for re-evaluation rather than accepted directly. Image judgments are restricted to visible properties such as contact location, approach direction, gripper orientation, and final placement. Motion speed, acceleration, trajectory smoothness, and clearance height are instead measured with trajectory-based geometric or kinematic metrics. D Human Review and Initial User Validation Construction and cross-review. Human contributors participated in three stages: 1) providing one reference demonstration for each newly introduced skill; 2) inspecting sampled generated demonstrations together with their satisfaction labels and metrics; and 3) rating preference plausibility and demonstration human-likeness. Before beginning, contributors received common instructions and task-specific training. Contributors were assigned to different portions of the generated data, after which a second group cross-reviewed the demonstrations and labels. Disputed cases were jointly re-examined before inclusion; the initial reviewer disagreement rate was 11.8%. All participants provided informed consent, and contributors were credited according to their level of involvement. Survey protocol and results. For initial user validation, 15 participants rated the selected preferences and their demonstrations on a 10-point scale along two dimensions: real-world preference plausibility, whether each preference was plausible and applicable in a household setting; and human-likeness of demonstrations, how closely the corresponding demonstration resembled

text: E A Worked Example of ComprePref Underlying task: Put the white mug on the left plate. Explicit preference: Pick by the handle. Input prompt: Put the white mug on the left plate. The mug just came out of the microwave—the body is too hot to touch. Implied behavior: Grasp the handle while completing the same placement task. What stays fixed: The task goal, scene, and preference evaluator. SR evaluates the original placement goal; SA uses the original handle-grasp preference label with task-success gating. What changes: The language supplied to the policy conveys the preference through context instead of a separate explicit preference field. A second example replaces the explicit preference “speed up” with “Guests will use them immediately” for the task of putting alphabet soup and a cream cheese box in a basket. The motion preference is still evaluated from the trajectory, not from a still image. These contextual prompts assess grounding of a specified benchmark preference; they do not establish recovery of an individual user’s unobserved preference history. F Adding a New Preference Adding a standard preference requires one human reference demonstration and a natural-language description of its satisfaction metric for the preference-conditioned generation pipeline, followed by approximately three to five validation trials for each applicable task. For a preference applied to roughly five tasks, the observed manual effort
title: A Worked Example of ComprePref

text: human reference demonstration and a natural-language description of its satisfaction metric for the preference-conditioned generation pipeline, followed by approximately three to five validation trials for each applicable task. For a preference applied to roughly five tasks, the observed manual effort is about 20 minutes on average; demonstration generation then proceeds automatically. This estimate covers preferences expressible through the current scene representation, skill library, and automatic programmable metrics. Preferences requiring a new skill or non-observable feedback incur additional work. For example, to add a preference for grasping a mug by its handle, a user provides one reference demonstration and a natural-language description of the satisfaction metric: the robot should grasp the handle rather than the mug body. The original mug-placement goal remains unchanged. The user then runs approximately three to five validation trials for each applicable task to check whether the generated trajectories follow the preference and whether the metric correctly evaluates grasp location. After validation, the pipeline automatically generates additional demonstrations. G Benchmark Release and Maintenance The benchmark has five evaluation suites. The 312 tasks include both preference-conditioned and no-preference tasks across SinglePref (100), PrefScale (100), PrefConflict (48), and PrefCompose (64); ComprePref reuses tasks with contextual prompts and does not add new mission-preference combinations to this count. Demonstrations are generated trajectories used as training/reference data; evaluation rollouts are executions of
